name: 7 Pot Barrackpore Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors under lights 8-10 weeks before the last frost, as this Trinidad strain is slow to establish and needs a long warm season.
directions: 7 Pot Barrackpore takes its name from the Barrackpore district of Trinidad and is prized among superhot growers for pods that are less bumpy and wrinkled than most other 7 Pot strains, ripening from green to a glossy orange-red. Its heat arrives with a noticeably smoky, savory edge that Trinidad cooks favor for pepper sauces rather than fresh eating. Provide rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture, since irregular watering causes blossom drop and stunted pod set on this variety. Because plants are tall and heavily branched once mature, stake or cage them early to keep the fruit-laden limbs from snapping in wind.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: 7 Pot Brain Strain Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, as this superhot needs a long warm season to size up and ripen.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, keeping the medium warm to encourage the slow-to-sprout chinense seed, then transplant once the soil has warmed well past frost danger. Stake heavily loaded plants and keep watering even to prevent blossom end rot on the convoluted pods. Brain Strain is a 7 Pot type selected for its intensely wrinkled, brain-like fruit surface and sits among the hottest strains within the already fierce 7 Pot family. It is grown in both yellow and red-fruited forms, both intensely pungent.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: 7 Pot Bubblegum Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; chinense superhots germinate slowly and need sustained warmth to break dormancy.
directions: 7 Pot Bubblegum is a Trinidad-origin selection prized for smooth, slightly bumpy orange pods that ripen from pale green through a distinctive salmon-pink stage before finishing deep orange. Growers favor it for a fruitier, less acrid heat than many 7 Pot strains, with fragrance reminiscent of tropical fruit alongside the scorching capsaicin load. Give plants a long warm season and consistent moisture, since irregular watering causes blossom drop and misshapen pods on this variety. Cage or stake mature plants, as heavy fruit clusters can snap brittle branches in wind.

name: 7 Pot Chaguanas Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil and nights are reliably warm.
directions: Named for the Trinidadian town of Chaguanas, this superhot pod is more elongated and pimpled than a typical 7 Pot, ripening from green to bright red. Heat runs 800,000 to 1,000,000 Scoville units with a notably fruity flavor alongside the characteristic 7 Pot heat. Give plants a long warm season, full sun, and even moisture to avoid blossom drop. Handle ripe pods with gloves and harvest once fully colored for peak flavor.

name: 7 Pot Cinder Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since this superhot strain is slow to germinate in cool soil.
directions: 7 Pot Cinder produces bumpy, classically wrinkled pods that shift from fluorescent green through caramel tones to a smoky, rust-red finish resembling a cooling cinder. Beneath its floral, fruity aroma lies an exceptionally intense, slow-building heat even by superhot standards. Plants grow vigorously and set fruit heavily given a long warm season, full sun, and even soil moisture. Stake plants to support heavy pod clusters and use gloves when harvesting, as the capsaicin oils are very persistent on skin.

name: 7 Pot Douglah Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, giving this slow-maturing superhot a long head start.
directions: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, since chinense seed can take several weeks to germinate, and pot up seedlings before moving them to the garden once nights are reliably warm. Support the branching stems as fruit accumulates, and reduce watering slightly as pods mature to concentrate flavor. Douglah is a Trinidad 7 Pot strain that ripens to a distinctive dull brown 'chocolate' color rather than red, and it is regarded as one of the hottest of the 7 Pot varieties with a smoky, earthy flavor. Always wear gloves when handling ripe fruit.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: 7 Pot Giant Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this rare Trinidad strain needs a full hot season to size up and ripen.
directions: 7 Pot Giant is an uncommon Trinidad superhot grown for unusually large, bumpy pods that ripen from green to a deep glossy red, bulkier than most other named 7 Pot strains. Collectors value it for crossbreeding and for its exceptionally heavy capsaicin load relative to its pod size. Grow in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture, since blossom drop is common under water stress in chinense superhots. Wear gloves and eye protection when handling and processing ripe fruit.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: 7 Pot Infinity Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost on a heat mat, as germination is slow; transplant only after nights stay reliably above 60F.
directions: A UK-bred superhot related to the Trinidad 7 Pot family, briefly holding a Guinness World Record for hottest chile in early 2011 before being displaced by other Trinidad Scorpion strains. Pods are wrinkled and habanero-shaped, ripening from green to deep red, with heat exceeding one million Scoville units. Give plants a long, warm season and full sun, and wear gloves when handling ripe fruit. Best grown in large containers or greenhouses outside tropical climates to accommodate its extended maturity time.

name: 7 Pot Jonah Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, since this is a slow-germinating, slow-maturing superhot that needs a long warm season to fully ripen its fruit.
directions: 7 Pot Jonah is a Trinidad-origin strain of the 7 Pot family, producing bumpy, elongated pods that ripen from green to a distinctive pale, almost bone-white to light-yellow or pinkish color rather than the deep red typical of most 7 Pot types. Heat runs from roughly 800,000 to over 1,000,000 Scoville units, placing it firmly among the world's hottest cultivated peppers alongside Douglah and Primo, but it is prized among chileheads for a sweet, fruity flavor that comes through despite the intensity. Plants grow tall and vigorous for a Capsicum chinense, often exceeding three feet, and benefit from staking once heavily laden with fruit. Always wear gloves when harvesting or processing ripe pods, and keep hands away from eyes and face.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: 7 Pot Lava Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this Trinidad strain is slow to establish in cool conditions.
directions: 7 Pot Lava is a Trinidad heirloom superhot bearing rounder, less deeply wrinkled pods than classic 7 Pot strains, ripening through a mottled green-to-orange stage before finishing a glowing red-orange reminiscent of molten lava. The flavor carries a fruity sweetness alongside ferocious, lingering heat prized by hot sauce and extract makers. Provide a long hot season, consistent watering, and staking once fruit clusters weigh down the brittle branches. Handle ripe pods with gloves, since the oils cling stubbornly to skin.

name: 7 Pot Mustard Pepper
plantingNote: Start extra early indoors, 10-12 weeks before last frost, given notoriously slow germination; needs the longest warm season of the Capsicum chinense types.
directions: A Trinidadian 7 Pot strain that ripens an unusual mustard-green color rather than red, orange, or chocolate, with wrinkled habanero-shaped pods carrying 400,000 to 1,000,000 Scoville units and a fruity, earthy, smoky flavor similar to Yellow 7 Pot. It needs a long, consistently warm season to reach full pod maturity in Gulf Coast gardens. Handle fresh and dried pods with gloves given the extreme heat level.
sources: Tyler Farms - Mustard 7 Pot Pepper Seeds

name: 7 Pot Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before the last frost with steady bottom heat near 85°F, since superhot Capsicum chinense types germinate slowly and unevenly; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 60°F.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; handle ripe fruit with gloves and avoid touching eyes or skin, since the extreme capsaicin content can cause burns even from brief contact. 7 Pot Pepper is a legendary superhot pepper from Trinidad, named for the traditional claim that a single pod is potent enough to season seven pots of stew — a nod to its extreme heat, which commonly measures in the range of 800,000 to over 1,000,000 Scoville heat units, placing it among the hottest peppers ever recorded alongside its close relatives Trinidad Scorpion and Trinidad Moruga Scorpion. The gnarled, bumpy, lantern-shaped pods ripen from green to a deep, glossy red and carry a fruity, floral Capsicum chinense aroma beneath the ferocious heat, making it prized by hot sauce makers who want maximum intensity along with genuine habanero-family flavor complexity. A serious specialty pepper for heat enthusiasts only, best grown where its extended season can be accommodated, zone 8–11.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University
Trinidad and Tobago Ministry of Agriculture

name: 7 Pot Primo Pepper
plantingNote: Start on a heat mat 10–12 weeks before last frost; 7 Pot Primo is a Louisiana-developed superhot cross between a Naga Morich and a Trinidad 7 Pot pepper, measuring 1.0–1.5 million Scoville units, with a distinctive elongated tail; handle with gloves and treat as an extreme culinary novelty — a single pod flavors a large batch of hot sauce.
directions: Germinate at 85°F on a heat mat for 2–4 weeks; grow under strong lights before transplanting outdoors after all frost risk has passed. 7 Pot Primo was developed by Louisiana hot pepper grower Troy Primeaux (the 'Primo' in the name) as a cross between a Naga Morich and a Trinidad 7 Pot variety; the name '7 Pot' refers to the traditional Trinidadian claim that one pod is hot enough to season 7 pots of food. At 1.0–1.5 million SHU it is among the most intensely hot peppers available to home growers, with a distinctive gnarled, elongated 'tail' that distinguishes it from the rounder Trinidad 7 Pot types. The flavor beneath the heat is described as fruity, earthy, and robust; used in extremely small quantities in hot sauces, fermented hot pepper mash, and as a smoking or drying chile for superhot spice blends.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University
Superhot Pepper Forum — The Hottest Pepper community records

name: 7 Pot Red Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this variety is slow and erratic to germinate even by chinense standards.
directions: 7 Pot Red is the original Trinidadian 7 Pot pepper from which the many modern 7 Pot strains (Douglah, Primo, Barrackpore, Bubblegum, and others) were later selected, named for the Trinidad claim that a single pod could flavor seven pots of stew. Pods are wrinkled, roughly bell-shaped with a small tail, ripening from green to a deep glossy red, with heat commonly falling in the 800,000-1,000,000 Scoville range alongside a sweet, fruity flavor. Give plants a long, warm growing season and full sun, since pods can take well over 100 days from transplant to fully ripen and develop their characteristic wrinkled skin. Handle ripe fruit with gloves and avoid touching eyes or skin, as oils linger on hands long after harvest.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: 7 Pot White Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil once nights are reliably above 60F.
directions: A rare Trinidadian 7 Pot strain that ripens to a pale ivory-white rather than the usual red or brown, with wrinkled habanero-shaped pods and a sweet, fruity flavor with hints of celery. Heat is in the superhot range, commonly reported above one million Scoville units. Plants are tall and vigorous with creamy yellow flowers and benefit from staking in windy sites. Harvest once pods fully whiten for the mildest flavor-to-heat balance this strain offers.

name: 7 Pot Yellow Pepper
plantingNote: Start on a heat mat 10-12 weeks before the last frost; superhot chinense types need a long head start and steady warmth to germinate.
directions: 7 Pot Yellow is a Trinidadian superhot that ripens from green to a bright yellow, wrinkled, habanero-shaped pod and is rated near 950,000 Scoville heat units, placing it alongside the Bhut Jolokia and Trinidad Scorpion among the world's hottest peppers and well above its red 7 Pot and Trinidad Scorpion cousins already common in backyard pepper collections. The name reflects the Trinidadian claim that a single pod can season seven pots of stew. Start seed indoors on a heat mat, since germination is slow even by superhot standards, and transplant into full sun only once nights are reliably warm. Fruity, floral flavor underlies the intense heat, making it popular for small-batch hot sauces and powders; always handle ripe pods with gloves.
sources: Trade Winds Fruit - 7 Pot Pepper, Yellow Seeds
Reimer Seeds - 7 Pot Yellow Pepper Seeds

name: A and C Pickling Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pick frequently to keep vigorous vines productive through the season.
directions: A and C Pickling is a 1928 open-pollinated heirloom pickling cucumber bred by the Abbott and Cobb seed house of Philadelphia, producing heavy yields of dark green, blocky fruit 8-10 inches long at full size. The dark color holds well after harvest, an important trait for market growers and picklers alike. Pick at 4-6 inches for classic dill or gherkin-style pickles, or let a few size up for fresh eating. Vigorous, productive vines continue setting fruit over a long summer harvest with regular picking.

name: A.L. Teff
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil reaches about 65°F after last frost; A.L. Teff is an Ethiopian grain selection, distinct from the American forage-grass teff cultivars already grown for hay.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil in full sun once the soil reaches roughly 65°F; A.L. Teff is an Ethiopian grain selection of teff, distinct from the American forage-grass breeding lines already in cultivation, grown specifically for its tiny, gluten-free grain used to mill injera flour. It is a fast-growing warm-season annual with no frost tolerance, reaching full maturity and seed set in 90-120 days. Harvest when seed heads turn golden-brown and thresh by hand or with a fine screen, since the grain is extremely small.

name: Abashi Bitter Melon
plantingNote: Direct-sow after soil has warmed above 70°F, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early where summers are short; this is a long-season type needing 90-110 warm days.
directions: An Okinawan heirloom prized for unusually mild bitterness, Abashi produces cylindrical, deep green fruit 8-10 inches long that is popular sliced into stir-fries and Okinawan goya chanpuru. Give it a sturdy trellis and full sun, since this long-season type also performs well in a large container with a stake, provided the container gives roots room to run. Pick fruit while still firm and green for the mildest flavor and best texture; overripe fruit turns orange and splits.

name: Abenaki Calais Flint Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed, feeding heavily with nitrogen; this strain was bred for short, unreliable Northeast seasons.
directions: Developed and selected for generations by the northern Vermont Abenaki, this flint corn was bred specifically to survive brutal Northeast growing seasons, including, by tradition, the catastrophic 1816 'Year Without a Summer.' Ears are long, thin, and cylindrical, carrying even rows of kernels that run in golden yellow, dark maroon, and orange tones, sometimes mixed on the same ear. Grind each color separately if you want to taste how flavor varies between them, or mix for a multicolor cornmeal. As a dry grinding corn it wants a full, warm season and heavy feeding to fill out ears before the first fall frost.

name: Abraham Lincoln Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant after all frost risk has passed; this vigorous indeterminate vine benefits from sturdy staking or caging.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply prepared, fertile soil in full sun. Abraham Lincoln is an American heirloom tomato dating to 1923, prized for large, deep-red, meaty beefsteak fruit with rich, well-balanced flavor and good disease tolerance for a variety of its age, which helped it remain popular with home gardeners for decades after its introduction. The vigorous indeterminate vines are strong producers over a long season and benefit from sturdy staking or caging to support the heavy fruit. Water evenly to reduce cracking and blossom end rot, and harvest once fruit is fully colored and yields slightly to gentle pressure for the best flavor.

name: Acadia Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall for cool-season production, or in late winter for an early spring crop; Acadia carries resistance to an unusually wide range of downy mildew races, a valuable trait for the damp, disease-prone conditions of a Gulf South winter spinach planting.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; thin to 2-4 inch spacing and use thinnings in salads. Acadia is a semi-savoy spinach hybrid, with leaves that carry moderate crinkle for good texture while staying easier to wash clean than fully savoy types, bred with resistance to an unusually wide range of downy mildew races that helps it stay healthy through the damp, humid conditions common in a Gulf South fall or winter garden. It is well suited to both field and high-tunnel production for a spring or fall crop. Harvest by cutting outer leaves for continued production or cutting the whole plant at the base once it has filled out, and use promptly since fresh spinach quality declines quickly after harvest.

name: Ace Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil and air have warmed; Ace, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, is an early-maturing bell pepper on a compact, productive plant.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55°F. Ace, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, is prized for reaching harvestable size unusually early compared with other bell peppers, producing blocky, thick-walled, mild green fruit that ripens to red if left on the plant longer, all on a compact, sturdy plant that sets fruit reliably even in less-than-ideal conditions. Its early maturity makes it a good choice for gardeners wanting a head start on the pepper harvest or a reliable crop in shorter growing seasons. Harvest at green stage for classic bell pepper use or let fruit ripen to sweeter red for a different flavor, and pick regularly to encourage continued production.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pepper Production

name: Ace Savoy Cabbage
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplant date; in zone 9 start in September and transplant October for fall through winter harvest. Savoy cabbage is more cold-hardy than smooth green cabbage types and can withstand harder freezes without head damage. In zone 9 the distinctive crinkled leaves provide more air circulation than smooth-headed types, which may help with the humidity-related disease issues common in Gulf South winters. Harvest when heads are firm; savoy holds in the garden longer than smooth cabbage after reaching maturity.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ace Savoy is a compact, early-maturing savoy cabbage producing small to medium (3–4 pound), round heads with the distinctively crinkled, blistered, dark blue-green leaves that define the savoy type — quite different from the smooth, pale heads of standard green cabbage. Savoy cabbage (Brassica oleracea var. sabauda) has a more complex, refined flavor than standard smooth cabbage: milder, sweeter, more tender, and less pungent, making it the preferred cabbage for fresh preparations where the subtle flavor can be appreciated rather than cooked down to blandness. The crinkled texture and tender leaves hold sauces and dressings differently than smooth cabbage — savoy is the cabbage preferred for upscale coleslaws, stuffed cabbage leaves (the larger, more pliable leaves wrap easily), and any preparation where delicate texture matters. Ace's compact size and rapid maturity (72–82 days) make it practical for fall planting in zone 9 where the cool growing window is relatively short.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Ace Savoy Cabbage Description
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Savoy Cabbage Varieties
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Cool-Season Cabbage for Gulf South

name: Aci Sivri Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant March–April. In zone 9 Aci Sivri will persist as a perennial through mild winters — cut back hard in late winter and the plant will regrow from the woody base, producing earlier and more heavily than first-year plants. Individual plants can grow to 3–4 feet tall over multiple seasons.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Aci Sivri (pronounced ah-juh SIV-ree, meaning 'hot sharp' in Turkish) is a Turkish heirloom cayenne-type pepper producing long (4–6 inch), thin, slightly wrinkled, pointed fruits that turn from pale green to deep red when ripe. The heat level ranges from mild when young and green to genuinely hot (15,000–30,000+ Scoville) when fully red-ripe, with the heat increasing significantly as the fruit matures and dries. The thin-walled, aromatic fruits dry quickly and are widely used in Turkish cuisine as a dried spice pepper, ground into flakes or paprika-style powder. Fresh green Aci Sivri is used in Turkish salads and grilled vegetable dishes where its mild-to-medium heat adds flavor without overwhelming. The prolific, heavily-bearing plants are extremely popular in Turkish home gardens and have been grown continuously for centuries. In zone 9 the long warm season allows multiple harvests and the plants often overwinter as perennials, returning larger each year.
sources: Turkish Ministry of Agriculture — Traditional Pepper Cultivars of Turkey
Seed Savers Exchange — Aci Sivri Heirloom Pepper
University of California Cooperative Extension — Turkish Pepper Varieties

name: Aconcagua Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Aconcagua is a large, late-season frying pepper requiring 75–90 days from transplant to reach full development — the largest fruits take the most time. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer production; the variety's heat tolerance allows continued production through Gulf Coast summers, and the late season ripening means peak harvests often come in July–August. Provide large containers (5-gallon minimum) if growing in pots — the tall (3–4 foot) plants and large fruit weight require good stability. Stake or cage plants to support the fruit load. Aconcagua is named for the highest peak in the Andes Mountains in Argentina, referencing the variety's South American origin. Harvest green for mild use or fully ripened to salmon-red for sweetest flavor and full carotenoid development.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Stake plants; harvest green or fully ripe to salmon-red. Aconcagua is an Argentine heirloom sweet frying pepper that produces some of the largest sweet pepper fruits of any variety in home garden cultivation — individual fruits typically measuring 8–12 inches in length and 2–3 inches wide, with a conical to slightly flattened form that tapers to a point. The variety takes its name from Aconcagua, Argentina's (and the Americas') highest mountain, a reference to the pepper's origin in the Andean region of South America where diverse pepper varieties have been cultivated for millennia. The fruit size is genuinely dramatic: Aconcagua peppers dwarf most other sweet peppers in the garden and attract immediate attention at farmers markets and in garden displays where their unusual scale distinguishes them from any standard frying or bell pepper. Despite the imposing size, the walls are moderately thin (thinner than bell peppers, in the frying pepper tradition) and the flavor is mild, sweet, and fruity — the flesh has the pleasant, slightly aromatic quality characteristic of good heirloom frying peppers. The ripening progression of Aconcagua goes from green through light yellow-green to a distinctive salmon-pink to pale red-orange, a color not typical of most peppers and part of the variety's visual distinction. The large individual fruit size makes Aconcagua exceptionally practical for stuffing (the hollow interior accommodates substantial filling) and for roasting whole, where the large peppers yield significant amounts of sweet roasted flesh per fruit. The variety is open-pollinated and seed-saving is straightforward from fully ripe fruits.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Aconcagua giant sweet pepper Argentine variety documentation
Seed Savers Exchange — Aconcagua heirloom pepper variety notes
Seeds of Change — Aconcagua sweet frying pepper variety description

name: Adirondack Blue Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; Adirondack Blue was released in 2003 by Cornell University's potato breeding program, specifically developed as a distinct improvement over older All Blue-type varieties with higher anthocyanin content, better yield, improved disease resistance, and more consistent blue-purple flesh coloration throughout the tuber without white streaking.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10–12 inches apart in rows 30–36 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost in cool weather; hill soil over emerging plants twice as they grow to increase yield and prevent tubers from greening. Adirondack Blue was developed by Dr. Walter De Jong and colleagues at Cornell University's potato breeding program and released in 2003, representing a significant improvement over older blue-flesh potato varieties; it was specifically bred for the uniformly intense blue-purple flesh coloration (without the white marbling or streaking common in older blue varieties), higher anthocyanin content (the pigment responsible for blue and purple coloration and associated health benefits), and better agronomic performance than heirloom blue types. The tubers have blue-purple skin and uniformly vibrant blue-purple flesh that holds its color remarkably well when boiled or steamed; the texture is waxy and the flavor is rich and earthy — similar to high-quality waxy potatoes with an additional visual dimension. The blue color is striking in potato salads, mashed potatoes (turns lavender-blue), and roasted presentations. Mid-season maturity of 70–90 days from planting; produces reliably in most US climates.

name: Adirondack Red Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; Adirondack Red was released in 2004 by Cornell University's potato breeding program as a companion to Adirondack Blue, producing uniformly red-pink flesh from peel to center with high anthocyanin content and excellent flavor — the color holds well through cooking and provides nutritional and visual value comparable to the blue version.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10–12 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost; hill twice as plants grow. Adirondack Red was released in 2004 by Dr. Walter De Jong's Cornell University potato breeding program, one year after Adirondack Blue, specifically developed to provide a red-fleshed complement to the blue-fleshed Adirondack Blue; both share the goal of combining high anthocyanin content, superior visual appeal, and reliable agronomic performance in a named, certified-disease-free variety. The medium-sized, round to oblong tubers have rose-red skin and uniformly pink to red flesh throughout — significantly more uniformly red than older red-flesh varieties like 'Red Gold' which tend to develop red only near the skin. The flavor is excellent — rich, waxy, earthy, and slightly nutty — with flesh that holds its color when boiled or steamed, making it excellent for colorful potato salads, roasted potato platters, and any presentation where the red color adds visual value. Disease resistance, yield, and overall agronomic performance are significantly improved compared to heirloom red-flesh types.

name: Adjuma Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant only after nights stay reliably above 60°F.
directions: Adjuma is a traditional pepper of Guadeloupe and Martinique, prized in Antillean kitchens for a strikingly fruity, floral aroma alongside solid habanero-level heat. Its squat, deeply wrinkled orange-yellow pods form in clusters and are typically used fresh, muddled into vinegar-based hot sauces rather than dried, so plan for repeated light harvests through the season instead of one large drying batch. Like other chinense types it thrives in consistent warmth and humidity, so mulch heavily and water deeply but infrequently to avoid the stress that triggers blossom drop. Choose Adjuma over a standard habanero when the goal is a more perfumed, less sharply citrusy aroma to complement Caribbean-style marinades and condiments.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Adriana Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Adriana is a Little Gem-type miniature romaine bred for fast maturity and heat tolerance, producing dense, sweet, crunchy heads well suited to close spacing and succession planting.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Adriana is a miniature romaine lettuce in the Little Gem tradition, producing small, dense, upright heads with crisp outer leaves and a sweet, tender heart, but bred for notably faster maturity and better heat tolerance than older Little Gem strains, letting gardeners push both the early spring and late fall ends of the lettuce season a bit further. Its compact size makes it well suited to intensive spacing and container growing, and the whole small heads work perfectly as individual salad or Caesar-salad portions without needing to be cut down for a mixed bowl. Harvest the whole head once it feels firm and dense at the base, or begin picking outer leaves earlier for a cut-and-come-again approach. Provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture for late-spring or early-fall plantings in zone 9 to delay bolting as temperatures rise.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Adriana Lettuce variety notes
High Mowing Organic Seeds — Little Gem-Type Romaine Comparison
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Lettuce Variety Trials

name: Affirmed Watermelon
plantingNote: Seedless triploid; start indoors or transplant after soil is thoroughly warm, and plant alongside a seeded pollenizer watermelon for fruit set. Affirmed is part of a modern seedless watermelon series bred for reliable yields in warm Southern production regions.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Affirmed is a seedless triploid watermelon hybrid bred as part of a modern commercial series developed for consistent, high-count yields under Southern growing conditions. Because triploid seedless varieties produce little viable pollen, plant a seeded pollenizer variety nearby to ensure good fruit set on the vines. It produces medium to large, crisp, sweet, deep red-fleshed fruit with the classic dark green striping. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned, and handle seedless melons gently since their rinds tend to be slightly thinner than seeded types.
sources: trade press reference (Growing Produce — Sakata watermelon variety coverage)

name: African Birdseye Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; African Birdseye is the tiny, extremely hot pepper traditionally used to make piri-piri sauce in southern and East Africa.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, since germination is slower and less even than most peppers; transplant only after nights stay warm. African Birdseye produces tiny, upright, intensely hot red pods on a compact, heavily branching bush, the traditional source pepper for piri-piri (peri-peri) sauce across southern and East Africa, later carried by Portuguese traders to become a staple flavoring in Mozambican and Angolan cuisine as well. In frost-free gardens the plant persists as a short-lived shrubby perennial; elsewhere grow it as a warm-season annual and pick continuously to keep new flowers setting.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

name: African Runner Peanut
plantingNote: Direct sow shelled, unroasted seed after the soil has warmed following the last frost, into loose, sandy, calcium-rich soil that lets the pegs push down easily to form pods.
directions: Direct sow shelled, unroasted seed after the soil has warmed following the last frost, into loose, sandy, calcium-rich soil that lets the pegs push down easily to form pods. This small-seeded heirloom peanut traces to peanuts brought to the American South through the transatlantic slave trade and was documented growing at Monticello in Jefferson's own garden notes, making it one of the oldest peanut lines still in American cultivation. Its bushy, low-spreading habit and heavy yield of small, sweet, easy-shelling pods make it well suited to home-scale roasting and boiling, and the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season matches its full maturity window better than most northern gardens can offer.
sources: Thomas Jefferson's Monticello Center for Historic Plants

name: African White Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; transplant only once nights stay reliably above 55F. African White is a tropical African heirloom that thrives in the sustained heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer and can be kept over as a short-lived perennial in zone 9-10.
directions: Start seed indoors with bottom heat and transplant into warm soil once nights are reliably above 55F; harvest fruit while still glossy white and firm, since pods age to yellow and then red as they overripen and lose their mild flavor. African White is a tropical African heirloom eggplant that produces abundant clusters of small, round, ivory fruits on a vigorous, glossy-leaved plant that doubles as an attractive ornamental in a mixed vegetable bed. The 2-3 inch fruits have a mild, faintly nutty flavor and few seeds when picked young, making them good for quick sautes, curries, and pickling. Because it hails from hot equatorial growing conditions, African White tolerates the extended heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer better than many standard purple-fruited types, continuing to set fruit through the stretch of the season when cooler-adapted eggplants slow down.

name: Agate Soybean
plantingNote: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; Agate is a compact heirloom bush type with unusually high yield for its small seed size.
directions: Direct sow in full sun into warm soil after frost danger has passed; Agate is a 1920s Japan-origin heirloom edamame with small olive-green seeds marked by a distinctive brown 'saddle' patch. The compact bush habit belies a very high yield for its small seed size, maturing in roughly 65-85 days depending on climate. Pods carry a buttery, rich flavor prized by edamame enthusiasts; blanch briefly in salted water and pop the beans free of the pod to eat warm or chilled.

name: Ailsa Craig Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Ailsa Craig is a compact-vined indeterminate variety long favored in Scottish and English glasshouses and outdoor gardens alike, so it appreciates staking and consistent moisture through fruit set.
directions: Sow seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 50 degrees F, staking or caging the vines as they grow. Ailsa Craig was bred in Girvan, Scotland in the early 1900s and quickly became one of the most widely grown tomatoes in British gardens and allotments, prized for producing heavy clusters of medium, smooth, bright red fruit with a well-balanced, classic tomato flavor. It remains a benchmark variety in the UK for home growers wanting a dependable, flavorful, mid-sized slicer.

name: Aji Amarillo Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Aji Amarillo has a long season to maturity (90–120 days from transplant) — in zone 9, the long warm season supports full production from spring transplants.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Aji Amarillo is the foundational hot pepper of Peruvian cuisine — considered one of the essential 'holy trinity' ingredients of Peruvian cooking (with garlic and onion) and the basis for Peru's iconic yellow sauces. The 3–5 inch, elongated-conical, thin-walled fruits ripen from green through orange-yellow to bright yellow-orange, with a distinctive fruity, tropical flavor and significant heat (30,000–50,000 Scoville units) that is entirely different from the neutral burn of jalapeños. The fruity, complex flavor — often described as combining apricot, mango, and passion fruit with a persistent, building heat — makes Aji Amarillo irreplaceable in Peruvian cooking and increasingly prized by chefs worldwide for its unique flavor profile. As a Capsicum baccatum species (the Andean species group distinct from C. annuum and C. chinense), Aji Amarillo requires somewhat warmer germination temperatures and a longer season than standard bell peppers. In zone 9, the long growing season is ideal for the 90–120 day maturity period, and the plants may become quite large (3–4 feet) and productive by mid-summer. Fresh fruits, paste, and dried/powdered form all have distinct culinary applications. The dried, rehydrated paste is the standard form used in traditional Peruvian cooking.

name: Aji Charapita Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Capsicum chinense requires warm soil (80–90°F) and is slow to germinate — use a heat mat. In zone 9 start in December–January and transplant in March–April. Aji Charapita is a short-day plant from equatorial Peru and may produce more freely with supplemental lighting in northern areas. In zone 9 the plant can be maintained as a perennial, returning to larger size each year from a woody base.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Aji Charapita is a wild-type Capsicum chinense pepper from the Peruvian Amazon, producing an extraordinary abundance of tiny pea-sized (3–5 mm) round yellow fruits on a prolific, heavily branching plant. The fruits are one of the most expensive peppers by weight in the world — sold as a specialty ingredient in high-end Peruvian and international cuisine for their unique combination of intense heat (30,000–50,000 Scoville), exceptional fruity citrus-tropical fragrance, and concentrated flavor. Because each fruit is pea-sized, a single productive plant can bear hundreds of fruits simultaneously, covering the plant in an impressive display of tiny yellow peppers. The flavor is described as intensely fruity with citrus, mango, and passion fruit notes beneath the heat — the signature Capsicum chinense fruity aromatic character concentrated into a miniature fruit. In Peru, Aji Charapita is used in ceviche, sauces, and as a table condiment in vinegar brine.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — Wild Capsicum chinense Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Specialty Pepper Production
Peruvian Ministry of Agriculture — Native Pepper Diversity

name: Aji Chombo Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since chinense types germinate slowly and need sustained warmth.
directions: Aji Chombo is Panama's everyday Scotch Bonnet-type chile, the signature heat behind the country's bottled hot sauces and pickled vegetable condiments. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with warm soil, since germination is slow and uneven at cool temperatures, then transplant into a sunny bed only once nights stay reliably above 60F. The compact, bushy plants bear small, lantern-shaped pods that ripen from green through yellow to orange-red, carrying classic fruity, citrusy chinense aroma alongside intense heat. Harvest continually with gloved hands to keep plants setting new flowers through the long warm season.
sources: general horticultural reference on Panamanian aji chombo

name: Aji Colorado Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since this Bolivian-Peruvian baccatum type needs a long warm season to fully ripen its pendant pods.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since this Bolivian-Peruvian baccatum type needs a long warm season to fully ripen its pendant, 3-5 inch pods. Fruit matures from green through orange to a deep brick-red, carrying a fast-hitting heat (roughly 20,000-30,000 Scoville units) that fades quickly and leaves a sweet, fruity aftertaste. Thin walls make it well suited to drying or blending into fresh aji sauces once red-ripe; harvest continuously to extend production into fall.

name: Aji Crystal Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Aji Crystal is a Capsicum baccatum species pepper, which requires slightly higher germination temperatures than C. annuum types and benefits from longer indoor growing time before transplanting. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer harvest. The pale, translucent-looking fruits develop their characteristic crystal-clear quality when harvested at the green-yellow stage; harvesting when pale yellow-cream rather than waiting for orange-red gives the mildest, most crisp results.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Harvest pale yellow to cream-white fruits for mildest flavor; allow to ripen orange-red for sweeter, more developed flavor. Aji Crystal is a Chilean baccatum pepper from the Capsicum baccatum species — a pepper species distinct from the common C. annuum and characterized by the spotted calyx markings at the base of the flower, a more complex flavor profile, and a heat level that can range from mild to medium-hot. Aji Crystal is at the mild end of the baccatum spectrum, with very low heat (typically under 500 SHU) that makes it essentially a sweet pepper with baccatum's distinctive flavor complexity. The fruits are elongated (4–5 inches), thin-walled, and pale yellow to near-white at the harvest stage — almost translucent in appearance, suggesting the crystal-clear quality for which the variety is named. The flavor is crisp, bright, slightly sweet and tangy with a fruity, aromatic quality distinctive of baccatum peppers — difficult to describe but clearly different from C. annuum sweet peppers and very pleasant raw in salads, stuffed, or used fresh in Peruvian-style preparations where baccatum peppers are traditional. Aji Crystal is popular among pepper enthusiasts and chefs interested in flavors beyond the standard C. annuum palette.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Aji Crystal pepper variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Specialty pepper variety descriptions

name: Aji Dulce Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes. Aji dulce is heat-loving and thrives in the Gulf Coast and tropical gardens — in zone 9 it often returns as a perennial from the base after mild winters. The flavor is essential in Caribbean cooking, particularly in Puerto Rican sofrito and Cuban recao sauce.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger; aji dulce is the sweet-fruited strain of the habanero pepper species (Capsicum chinense) — it looks exactly like a miniature habanero with thin, wrinkled skin in green ripening to yellow-orange or red, and has all the distinctive floral, fruity, intensely aromatic habanero fragrance without any heat whatsoever (Scoville 0–500, vs 100,000–350,000 for regular habanero). The aroma and flavor are extraordinary — simultaneously citrusy, floral, fruity, and deeply savory — making aji dulce irreplaceable in Puerto Rican, Dominican, Venezuelan, and Cuban cooking, where it is the backbone of sofrito, the aromatic base paste for countless dishes. In zone 9–12 gardens it often becomes a short-lived perennial shrub. An outstanding unique pepper for gardeners who love the habanero aroma but want zero capsaicin heat.

name: Aji Fantasy Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks ahead of the last frost; this compact, high-yielding baccatum variety matures faster than most aji types.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks ahead of the last frost; this compact, high-yielding baccatum variety was developed in Finland and matures faster than most aji types, making it a good option for shorter growing seasons. The roughly 2 inch, bonnet-shaped pods ripen to a translucent yellow and deliver a mild-to-medium heat (about 5,000-10,000 Scoville units) with pronounced tropical sweetness. Stake plants as they load up with fruit, and pick continuously to keep the heavily branching bushes producing.

name: Aji Mango Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost with bottom heat, since Capsicum baccatum germinates slowly; transplant only after nights stay reliably warm.
directions: Aji Mango is a newer selection within the aji (Capsicum baccatum) group, prized for tapered two- to three-inch pods that ripen from green through orange to red and deliver a distinctly sweet, tropical, mango-like fruitiness ahead of a moderate, lingering heat. Grow it exactly as you would other baccatum types: rich, well-drained soil, full sun, and even moisture, since the plants can turn woody and less productive if allowed to dry out repeatedly between waterings. The sprawling, heavily-branched bushes benefit from staking or a tomato cage once loaded with fruit, and picking ripe pods regularly keeps new flowers setting through a long warm season. In frost-free zones the plant can be overwintered and will return as a short-lived perennial, producing an even heavier crop in its second year.
sources: Trade Winds Fruit — Capsicum baccatum Variety Collection
New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — Aji Pepper Varieties

name: Aji Panca Pepper
plantingNote: Start on a heat mat 8–10 weeks before last frost; Aji Panca is one of Peru's most important culinary peppers, a large, deep red to dark chocolate-red chile with mild heat (1,500–2,500 SHU) and an exceptional smoky, fruity, berry-like flavor used as the base of many traditional Peruvian sauces, marinades, and stews including aji de gallina.
directions: Start seeds on a heat mat at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost when soil is warm. Aji Panca is one of the most important and distinctive chiles in Peruvian cuisine, a large (3–4 inch), elongated, deep brownish-red pepper belonging to Capsicum chinense but with very mild heat (1,500–2,500 SHU) and an extraordinary flavor profile: smoky, deeply fruity, berry-like, and slightly sweet with almost no raw pungency — it is more like a richly flavored dried fruit than a typical hot pepper. In Peru it is primarily used dried and pureed as a chile paste (pasta de aji panca) that forms the flavor base of marinades, braises, anticuchos (grilled beef hearts), and the classic preparation aji de gallina. Rarely found outside Latin American grocery stores in the US; growing your own from seed is the only way to access this unique pepper fresh in most American gardens.
sources: Dave DeWitt's The Chile Pepper Encyclopedia

name: Ajo Rojo Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves in fall; Creole types need less cold vernalization than northern hardnecks, making them reliable in mild-winter climates.
directions: Brought to the United States from Spain by way of Nevada growers in the early 1990s, Ajo Rojo is a Creole-type softneck prized for its brilliant purple-streaked clove wrappers and adaptability to hot, arid regions where hardneck garlics struggle. Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up in fall in well-drained soil, mulching lightly over winter in colder zones. The flavor is mild and creamy when roasted but builds into a slow, powerful heat when eaten raw, making it popular with cooks who want garlic with real punch. Harvest when the lower third of leaves has browned, then cure in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks; Creole types store notably longer than most hardnecks.

name: Akasanjaku Yard Long Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past last frost danger; Akasanjaku thrives in sustained summer heat and is slower to establish in cool soil than common snap beans.
directions: Sow directly at the base of a tall trellis or pole support, since vines regularly climb 8-12 feet in warm weather. Akasanjaku takes its name from its distinctive brick-red dried seeds, though the harvested pods themselves are a pencil-thin, stringless light green that reach 12-16 inches long and stay tender well past the size where Western pole beans would toughen. This heat-loving heirloom is a traditional favorite for Sichuan-style dry-fried beans, where the pods are cooked hot and fast until blistered. Pick pods every two to three days once vines start bearing to encourage continuous production through the hottest part of summer, since any mature, seed-filled pods left on the vine slow new flowering.

name: Aker's West Virginia Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Aker's West Virginia is a potato-leaf Appalachian family heirloom preserved through Seed Savers Exchange, grown for its huge pink beefsteak fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into deeply worked, fertile ground once nights stay reliably above 50F. Aker's West Virginia is a potato-leaf Appalachian family heirloom that produces very large, rosy-pink beefsteak fruit with meaty, low-acid flesh in the style of other West Virginia pink tomatoes, but on a distinct, separately preserved family line. Cage or stake plants early since the heavy fruit clusters can bend unsupported stems, and water evenly through fruit set to reduce cracking. Best suited to gardeners who already have room for one or two vigorous, long-season indeterminate vines.

name: Akers West Virginia Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March for spring production. Support the large, indeterminate vines with cages or stakes. In zone 9 the fall planting in August–September often produces the highest-quality fruits as temperatures moderate; spring crops should be harvested before peak summer heat reduces fruit quality.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with sturdy stake or cage support; Akers West Virginia is an heirloom tomato preserved in the Appalachian tradition of West Virginia seed saving, producing large, meaty, deep red beefsteak-type fruits with a classic, complex, sweet-acidic flavor typical of the best Old World tomato varieties maintained by Appalachian farm families for generations. The large (often 12–24 ounce) fruits have thick, meaty walls with small seed cavities and outstanding fresh-eating flavor — the balanced combination of sweetness and bright acidity makes Akers West Virginia one of the most satisfying large heirloom varieties for fresh slicing. The fruit shows good resistance to cracking despite its size. Like most Appalachian heirlooms, Akers West Virginia developed in a region with variable, challenging weather and has proven adaptability to different growing conditions. In zone 9 the fall crop (planted in August, harvested October–November) often produces exceptionally flavored fruits as cooler temperatures concentrate sugars and acid.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Akers West Virginia Tomato
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Appalachian Heirloom Tomatoes
West Virginia University Extension — Heirloom Tomato Varieties

name: Alabama Blackeye Butterbean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm, above 65°F; Alabama Blackeye is a vigorous, long-vining pole type that needs a tall, sturdy trellis or fence, often reaching 10 feet or more.
directions: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun after soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F, training the long twining vines up a tall, sturdy trellis, fence, or row of poles. Alabama Blackeye is a family-passed-down Alabama heirloom baby lima, also known regionally as a butterbean, bearing small, creamy white seeds marked with a distinctive small black eye at the hilum. It is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant and keeps setting pods heavily through the hottest, muggiest stretches of Gulf Coast summer that slow many other lima varieties, making it a reliable choice for zone 9a gardens. Pick pods at the green shell stage for fresh eating in classic Southern butterbean dishes and succotash, or let pods dry fully on the vine for storage; shell beans regularly to keep the vigorous vine productive into fall.

name: Alabama Blackeyed Butterbean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably above 60°F, ideally 70-90°F; this vigorous pole lima needs a sturdy trellis and thrives through Gulf Coast summer heat and drought.
directions: Direct sow seed 1-1.5 inches deep and space about 6 inches apart along a tall trellis in full sun; this Alabama family heirloom butterbean is a true lima bean prized for creamy white seeds marked with a distinctive black eye and for outstanding heat and drought tolerance once established. Avoid soaking seed before planting, as it can cause rot in warm, moist soil. Keep moisture consistent through flowering and pod set, and harvest pods once plump for fresh shelling or let them dry fully on the vine for storage beans.

name: Alabama Blue Collard
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring for a spring crop; Alabama Blue is a cold-hardy heirloom collard whose flavor sweetens noticeably after frost.
directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; thin or transplant to final spacing once seedlings have several true leaves. Alabama Blue is a Deep South heirloom collard grown for generations for its striking blue-green, slightly savoyed leaves and excellent cold hardiness, surviving hard freezes that damage less hardy greens and developing sweeter, milder flavor after exposure to frost. The tall, upright plants produce abundant leaves over a long harvest window when picked cut-and-come-again style, taking outer leaves as needed while the center continues producing. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season for the best leaf production, and watch for cabbage worms and aphids, which can be managed with row cover or a targeted organic insecticide.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange heirloom collard archive
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Collard Production

name: Alabama Blue Collards
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12-14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August-September for fall and winter production. Alabama Blue is a traditional open-pollinated Deep South collard passed down through generations of home gardeners.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Alabama Blue is a traditional open-pollinated Deep South collard with broad, slightly savoyed, distinctly blue-green leaves, maintained and passed down through generations of Southern home gardeners rather than developed by a commercial breeding program. The flavor is rich and full-bodied even before frost, and like other collards sweetens further after the first light freezes of fall. Plants are tall and vigorous, tolerating both Gulf South summer heat and winter cold well, and the open-pollinated nature means seed can be saved from the best plants each year to maintain the strain in a home garden. Harvest the lower and outer leaves as needed, leaving the growing tip intact so the plant keeps producing fresh leaves from the top over a long cool-season harvest window.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Collard Production in the Southeast

name: Alabama Red Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Alabama Red is a tall, productive Deep South heirloom okra with dark red pods developed and maintained in Alabama home gardens, one of several distinct regional red okra heirloom strains and generally taller and more vigorous than shorter red okra types.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 18–24 inches in rows 3 feet apart; soak seeds overnight before planting. Alabama Red is a regional heirloom okra from Alabama home gardens, one of the distinct Deep South red-podded okra strains that differs from Red Velvet in being taller, more vigorous, and producing somewhat more slender pods with an intensely dark red to mahogany coloring; the flavor is excellent, with a slightly richer taste than some green varieties, and the pods are harvested at 3–4 inches for peak tenderness. Like other red okras, the pigment is water-soluble and leaches from the pods during cooking unless they are quickly roasted or fried. The tall plants (5–8 feet) with deeply lobed leaves and large yellow-centered flowers make Alabama Red an outstanding ornamental-edible for the Southern food garden. Maintained by seed savers in Alabama and nearby states and representative of the regional diversity in Southern okra cultivation.

name: Alabaster Celeriac
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, since germination is slow and seedling growth is sluggish at first; transplant out once nights stay reliably above freezing.
directions: Alabaster is a light-skinned celeriac whose pale flesh discolors noticeably less than many other varieties once peeled or cooked, an advantage for cooks who want a bright white puree or gratin. The globes are typically smaller and more rounded than some maincrop celeriac, with a strong, clean celery flavor and good storage life in a root cellar. Grow exactly as other celeriac: start early indoors given the slow germination, transplant into deep, fertile, constantly moist soil, and remove developing side roots through the season to channel growth into a single dense globe. Harvest in fall after light frost, which improves the flavor.

name: Alamo Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall or late winter in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Alamo is a hybrid turnip greens variety bred for moderate bolt resistance and tolerance of aphids and mosaic virus, with vigorous regrowth for repeated cut-and-come-again harvest starting as early as 33 days.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Alamo is a modern hybrid turnip grown for its greens rather than its roots, producing up to 50% higher yield than standard turnip greens varieties along with excellent regrowth after cutting, letting a single planting support several harvests through the cool season. It shows moderate resistance to bolting and tolerates aphids and mosaic virus better than many older turnip greens varieties, useful for stretching a spring planting later into warming weather. Harvest young leaves at 6-10 inches for the most tender greens, cutting to about 4 inches above the crown and allowing regrowth for the next cutting. Because it establishes and regrows quickly, Alamo suits both a fall planting for winter greens and a spring planting for an early crop.
sources: seed catalog reference (Stokes Seeds, Park Seed, Gurney's)

name: Albina Vereduna Beet
plantingNote: Sow as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9; because Albina Vereduna's roots are pure white, they never stain cutting boards or bleed color into other foods the way red beets do.
directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to 3–4 inches once true leaves appear. Albina Vereduna is an old Dutch heirloom beet that produces round, creamy-white roots with a sweet, mild flavor generally regarded as less earthy than red beets, and because it contains no betalain pigment it can be roasted, pickled, or grated into salads without staining hands, cutting boards, or other ingredients pink. The glossy green tops are also excellent cooked as greens and, lacking red pigment, cook up a cleaner green than the tops of red beet varieties. Keep soil consistently moist for smooth, tender roots and harvest at 2–3 inches across for the best texture, since oversized roots can turn woody.

name: Albino White Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 the prime window is October–February for a fall/winter/spring crop. White beet seed is a cluster like all beets — one 'seed' germinates multiple seedlings that must be thinned to 4 inches apart for full-sized roots.
directions: Sow seed clusters 1/2 inch deep in loose, deep, well-amended soil; thin to 4 inches after seedlings reach 2 inches tall. Albino White Beet is a German heirloom producing smooth, round, pure white-fleshed roots that completely lack the red pigment (betalain) of standard beets. The absence of betalains means Albino White beets do not bleed red — they do not stain cutting boards, hands, clothing, or dishes, solving the primary practical complaint about cooking with beets. Flavor is milder, sweeter, and less earthy than red beets — some tasters describe the flavor as more like a very sweet parsnip than a classic beet. Excellent raw in salads where they won't discolor other ingredients, roasted until caramelized and sweet, or pickled in the traditional manner (they turn slightly golden-pink when pickled in wine vinegar). The greens are pale green and mild, also excellent cooked. White beets are often grown alongside red and golden beets for a colorful root vegetable display. In zone 9, fall-planted white beets mature beautifully through mild winters.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Albino White Beet variety notes
Territorial Seed Company — White Beet documentation

name: Alcosa Savoy Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 5-6 weeks before the last frost and set transplants out as soon as soil is workable, or start a second round in midsummer for a fall crop.
directions: Alcosa forms dense, medium-sized heads wrapped in deeply blistered, blue-green savoyed leaves that hold their crinkled texture well into cold weather. Its compact frame allows tighter in-row spacing than standard round cabbages, making it a good fit for smaller beds or intensive succession planting. The heavily textured leaves are notably tender for a savoy type and hold up in the garden without splitting for an extended harvest window. Choose Alcosa when you want the classic savoy crinkle and cold tolerance in a shorter-season, space-efficient package.

name: Alderman Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter to early spring; in zone 9 sow January–February for a March–April harvest before heat ends the season. Alderman is a tall vine (4–5 feet) requiring a sturdy trellis or fence. In zone 9 the spring pea season is brief — 6–10 weeks from planting to heat shutdown. A fall sowing in October can extend the season, but fall peas in zone 9 often produce a lighter crop than spring.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; provide a trellis or fence for the tall vines; Alderman (also known as Tall Telephone) is a large-vine heirloom shelling pea producing very large, dark green pods of 4–5 inches, each containing 7–9 fat, sweet, dark green peas — the largest peas of any standard shelling type. It has been grown in American gardens since the 1880s and remains a benchmark for flavor and production among home garden peas. The large, starchy-sweet peas are particularly good for freezing because their size and firm texture hold up better than smaller-seeded varieties. The tall vines (4–5 feet) require stout support but reward with heavy production when trellised properly. Alderman is specifically adapted to the heavy production that makes the short cool-season window economically worthwhile for home gardeners and market growers — the high pod count and large pod size maximize yield from the brief growing window in zone 9. Do not fertilize heavily with nitrogen; peas fix their own and excess nitrogen promotes foliage over fruit.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Alderman Pea Heritage Variety
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Tall Telephone Pea History
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Shelling Peas

name: Aleppo Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Aleppo pepper is grown primarily as a drying pepper — the fruits are harvested when fully red and ripe, then halved and dried before being crushed into the characteristic coarse flakes with their distinctive oily texture and dark red color. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer production. The variety is adapted to hot, dry Mediterranean conditions and performs well in zone 9's summer heat with moderate irrigation. A single productive plant can yield enough peppers for a year's supply of home-ground Aleppo pepper flakes. The drying process is critical to developing the characteristic flavor: Aleppo peppers are traditionally partially dried, then crushed while retaining some moisture and oil content — producing the characteristic slightly moist, aromatic flakes rather than the bone-dry texture of paprika or cayenne.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest when fully red; dry and crush for spice. Aleppo Pepper (also known as Halaby pepper, from Halab, the Arabic name for Aleppo) is a Capsicum annuum variety from Aleppo, Syria — a historic spice and trading city in northern Syria that gave its name to the region's most important spice pepper. Aleppo pepper occupies a unique position in global spice use: with a Scoville rating of approximately 10,000 units, it provides mild to moderate heat (significantly less than cayenne at 30,000–50,000 SHU) combined with a complex, distinctive flavor profile — fruity and slightly sweet, with undertones of cumin and salt, and a characteristic oiliness and depth unlike any other commonly used dried pepper spice. The pepper's distinctive quality comes from the drying and processing method: fruits are split, seeds are removed (seeds are slightly bitter), and the halved peppers are dried partially before being crushed into coarse, slightly moist flakes with a characteristic dark red color and shiny surface from the natural oils retained through partial drying. This traditional processing is quite different from completely desiccated paprika or cayenne, producing a spice with a unique fresh-dried quality. The Syrian civil war that began in 2011 severely disrupted Aleppo pepper production, causing supply shortages and price spikes in global markets; production has since been supplemented by Turkish-grown peppers of similar varieties and by growers in North America who have adopted the variety.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Aleppo pepper variety notes
Kalustyan's Spice Merchants — Aleppo pepper sourcing and historical notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Halaby/Aleppo pepper heirloom preservation documentation

name: Ali Baba Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is at least 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–April. Ali Baba is an Iraqi/Middle Eastern landrace watermelon specifically adapted to intense heat and dry conditions — an excellent choice for zone 9 where summer heat can stress ordinary watermelons.
directions: Plant in hills spaced 6–8 feet apart in full sun, well-drained, fertile soil; Ali Baba is an heirloom watermelon landrace from Iraq, where it has been cultivated for centuries in the intense heat and aridity of the Tigris-Euphrates region. The large (20–30 pound), pale green, blocky-oval fruits have vibrant red, exceptionally sweet and flavorful flesh with small seeds. What sets Ali Baba apart for Gulf Coast and zone 9 gardeners is its remarkable adaptation to heat: it continues setting fruit and maintains its characteristic sweetness through temperatures that stress modern commercial varieties, making it one of the best heirlooms for hot, dry or hot-humid summer conditions. It is also notably drought-tolerant compared to most watermelons once established. Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds introduced it to American growers and it has gained a devoted following among gardeners who prize heat tolerance and excellent flavor. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit dries and the skin lightens; the yellow ground spot also intensifies as fruit ripens.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Ali Baba watermelon variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Middle Eastern watermelon landrace documentation
USDA National Plant Germplasm System — Citrullus lanatus accessions

name: Alicante Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Alicante sets fruit reliably in cooler summers and short seasons, making it a mainstay of British allotments and greenhouses.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once temperatures are reliably warm, providing a stake or cage for the indeterminate vines. Alicante is a long-established open-pollinated British variety known for consistent early cropping and smooth, medium-sized, deep red fruit with a well-rounded, sweet-tart flavor that holds up in cooler, shorter growing seasons. It has been a staple recommendation of UK seed catalogs and gardening programs for decades as a reliable outdoor and unheated-greenhouse tomato.

name: Aljezur Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant rooted slips two to four weeks after the last frost into loose, sandy soil ridged for drainage in full sun; this landrace is grown along Portugal's southwest Atlantic coast around Aljezur and carries Protected Geographical Indication status.
directions: Grow in the loose, mineral-rich sandy soils that give this variety its name recognition, since Aljezur's coastal Costa Vicentina microclimate and sand-dune soils are credited with producing an unusually sweet, fragrant tuber compared to sweet potatoes grown on heavier inland soils. Vines sprawl vigorously across the sandy beds and should be hilled lightly as tubers swell, with minimal irrigation needed once established thanks to the region's mild, humid Atlantic air. Local smallholders have grown this landrace for generations, and the town celebrates it each November with a dedicated sweet potato festival. Dig before the first autumn frost, then cure the tubers at warm temperatures and high humidity for one to two weeks to concentrate their sweetness before storing.
sources: European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register — Batata Doce de Aljezur
Associação de Produtores da Batata Doce de Aljezur

name: All Blue Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces January–February in zone 9; All Blue is a mid-season variety (75–90 days) that maintains its striking blue-purple flesh color throughout cooking. Plan for May harvest before summer heat arrives in zone 9.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in rich, loose, well-drained soil; All Blue (also called All Purple) is a heritage variety with Andean ancestry, producing medium-sized, oblong tubers with deep blue-purple skin and intensely blue-purple flesh throughout — the color does not fade with cooking, making brilliant blue-purple mashed potatoes, blue potato salad, and striking roasted wedges. The color is produced by anthocyanins — the same pigments in blueberries — that are potent antioxidants. Flavor is earthy and slightly nutty, pleasant but not as rich as Yukon Gold or fingerlings. All Blue has relatively firm, waxy flesh that holds its shape when boiled or roasted. The plants are vigorous and productive. In zone 9, the unusual color makes them a conversation-starting crop at the farmers' market or dinner table; they are consistently one of the most visually dramatic vegetables in the garden when cut open. Plant alongside Red LaSoda for a striking red, white, and blue potato planting.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — All Blue potato heritage documentation
Wood Prairie Family Farm — Blue/Purple Potato varieties
Johnny's Selected Seeds — All Blue variety notes

name: All Purple Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F, in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; All Purple is a distinct named purple sweet potato sold alongside (but separate from) Stokes Purple and Okinawan types.
directions: Set slips 12-18 inches apart in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping fertility moderate since overly rich soil favors vine growth over root formation. All Purple is a heirloom sweet potato selection distributed by small specialty growers as its own distinct cultivar alongside other named purple types like Molokai Purple and Purple Passion, producing roots with purple skin over dense, uniformly deep-purple flesh from center to edge. The texture is drier and firmer than orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, with an earthy, mildly sweet flavor that holds its color well when roasted or steamed, though it fades somewhat when boiled in acidic water. Sprawling vines with purple-tinged, deeply lobed leaves make it a dual-purpose plant, since the young leaves and shoot tips are also edible and commonly cooked as greens. Harvest after vines begin to yellow and before frost, then cure in warm, humid conditions for a week or two to develop full sweetness and improve storage life.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Sweet Potato Production

name: All Seasons Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors ahead of the last frost and transplant hardened-off seedlings out as soon as the soil can be worked, or sow a second time in midsummer for an autumn crop.
directions: All Seasons is an old American heirloom cabbage valued for its unusual flexibility, producing good round to slightly flattened heads whether sown as an early spring crop or held back for a summer sowing destined for fall harvest. The heads are solid and medium-sized with a tender crisp texture that holds up reasonably well in storage, and the plants show decent tolerance of both the heat of a late planting and the cool snaps of an early one. Because it performs across a wider planting window than many single-purpose cabbages, it has long been a practical choice for home gardeners wanting one variety to cover more than one slot in the rotation. Harvest heads promptly once firm, since like most round cabbages they can split if left too long in wet conditions.

name: All Top Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer to early fall for a fall and winter greens crop, or in very early spring for a quick spring planting; in zone 9 Gulf South gardens, August-through-October sowings keep a steady cut-and-come-again harvest going well into winter.
directions: Direct sow thickly into fertile, loose soil in full sun and thin lightly, since All Top is grown purely for its leaves and forms little to no usable root. It is a classic Southern greens turnip, bred for a dense stand of large, smooth, deep green leaves rather than a marketable globe, and it regrows quickly after cutting, supporting repeated harvests from a single sowing rather than a one-time whole-plant pull. All Top matures fast — often ready to begin cutting in as little as 35 days — making it a dependable fast fall crop for gardeners who sowed other greens too late, and some seed catalogs note good tolerance to turnip mosaic virus. Harvest outer leaves regularly with scissors or a knife, leaving the center growing point intact, and expect sweeter flavor once leaves are touched by light frost.

name: Allgold Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips into warm, loose, well-drained soil after the last frost; Allgold's long vigorous vines need generous room to sprawl across the bed or into a pathway.
directions: Give Allgold's vigorous, far-ranging vines plenty of room, since this older variety was selected for heavy yield rather than a compact habit. Introduced in 1952 by Oklahoma State from a cross of the Creole and Triumph varieties, Allgold produces tan skin over orange flesh and was valued in its day for consistently heavy production across a range of Southern growing conditions. It is a straightforward, old-fashioned baking type without the modern disease-resistance packages bred into newer releases, so rotate planting beds to avoid a buildup of soil-borne sweet potato pests. Cure harvested roots in a warm, humid spot for roughly a week to firm the skin and bring out the full sweetness before storing.
sources: Gardener's Path and Mother Earth News heirloom sweet potato variety histories
List of sweet potato cultivars (horticultural variety records)
Oklahoma Agricultural Experiment Station historical variety release records

name: Alliance Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Alliance combines resistance to several races of bacterial leaf spot with tolerance to multiple viruses (potato virus Y, potato yellow mosaic virus, tobacco mosaic virus, and cucumber mosaic virus), an especially broad virus-resistance package for aphid-prone Gulf South gardens.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Alliance is a bell pepper hybrid bred for resistance to several races of bacterial leaf spot along with tolerance to an unusually wide range of viruses, giving it strong protection against both the bacterial and viral diseases that spread readily through humid Gulf South gardens via rain splash and aphid activity. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good flavor if left on the plant.
