Because viral diseases have no cure once a plant is infected, Alliance's broad tolerance package helps prevent the stunting, mottled foliage, and reduced yield that viruses cause in more susceptible varieties. Harvest at the green stage for milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red, and keep picking regularly to encourage continued fruit set.
sources: seed catalog reference (Totally Tomato, Tomato Growers Supply Company)
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pepper Production

name: Allsweet Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is 70°F or warmer; Allsweet is a large-fruited heirloom watermelon producing classic oblong fruits with dark green skin and bold pale green stripes weighing 25–35 pounds — one of the traditional 'picnic watermelons' prized for its high sugar content, bright red flesh, and excellent keeping quality after harvest; one of the defining watermelon varieties of Southern U.S. home gardens.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3–4 seeds (thin to 2 plants) or individual transplants after soil warms; provide ample space (6–10 feet in all directions) for vigorous vines; stop irrigation when fruits are nearly ripe to concentrate sugars; test ripeness by thumping (dull thud), checking the ground spot (turning yellow), or pressing on the vine end of the fruit. Allsweet is a large, oblong, open-pollinated watermelon developed and marketed by Dessert Seed Company that became one of the most widely grown home garden and commercial watermelons in the Southern states during the latter decades of the 20th century. The classic appearance — elongated oval fruits averaging 25–35 pounds with dark green skin boldly marked by lighter green stripes, bright red flesh, and black seeds in the traditional style — made Allsweet the archetypical 'picnic watermelon' of the American South. The flavor lives up to the name: exceptionally sweet (Brix 12–14), with the characteristic deep red color and firm, crisp texture that distinguished traditional open-pollinated watermelons from modern seedless varieties. Allsweet produces fruits with good keeping quality after harvest — they hold well in cool storage for 2–3 weeks — and the vines are productive and disease-tolerant under Gulf Coast and Deep South summer conditions. A standard comparison point against which other traditional watermelons are measured in Southern gardens, and an important landmark in the history of American watermelon breeding.

name: Alltop Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow thickly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Alltop was bred purely for greens production and does not bulb, so plant closer than a root-crop turnip and cut leaves repeatedly rather than thinning for roots.
directions: Direct sow thickly in fertile, well-drained soil, in full sun for the fastest growth or partial shade in warmer weather; Alltop is a Southern-bred turnip selected purely for its tops and produces no usable bulb at all, channeling its energy instead into a heavy, upright flush of smooth, dark, mild-flavored leaves. It is markedly more heat- and bolt-tolerant than dual-purpose turnip varieties, which lets it be sown earlier in late summer and later into spring than most turnip greens, and it regrows vigorously after cutting for repeated cut-and-come-again harvests through fall and winter. Because there is no root to size up, plants can be spaced tightly and simply mowed or sheared back by a third to a half whenever leaves reach eating size, making it an efficient, high-yield choice for gardeners who grow turnips strictly for potlikker and greens rather than roots.

name: Alma Paprika Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Alma Paprika is a Hungarian heirloom producing small round fruits (1.5–2 inches diameter) that ripen from creamy white through yellow to vivid red. The round shape and thick but not waxy flesh make it ideal for drying and grinding into genuine sweet Hungarian paprika. In zone 9, transplant March–April; the compact plant habit (18–24 inches) makes it suitable for containers. Fruits are very mild (500–1,500 SHU) with a rich, sweet paprika flavor that develops fully when dried. Unlike many commercially produced paprika peppers that are harvested by machine and dried at high temperatures, home-dried Alma Paprika can be slow-dried at low heat to preserve volatile aromatics.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost and harvest when fully red for drying. Alma Paprika Pepper is a Hungarian heirloom variety prized by home paprika makers for its compact, round fruits that dry easily and produce an aromatic, sweet paprika powder with far more complexity than commercially available dried paprika. The variety belongs to the traditional Hungarian paprika pepper classifications — distinguished from the longer 'szegedi' or 'kalocsal' types by its apple-like round shape — and is named 'Alma' (Hungarian for 'apple') in direct reference to this distinctive fruit form. The flavor progression through ripening stages is one of this variety's most interesting characteristics: at the creamy-white stage the fruit is mildly sweet and slightly starchy, similar to a mild Italian frying pepper; at yellow it develops a fruitier, slightly citrusy edge; at full red ripeness the paprika sweetness is fully expressed with a rich, slightly smoky underlying note. Gardeners can use Alma Paprika at any ripe stage for fresh eating — it performs well in salads, stuffed preparations, and light sautés — but its primary use is drying. Halved and laid cut-side-down on screens in warm sun or placed in a food dehydrator at 120–130°F, the fruits dry thoroughly within 3–5 days and grind to a vivid orange-red powder. Compact plant size makes Alma Paprika one of the most productive paprika types per square foot of garden space.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Alma Paprika Hungarian heirloom pepper variety documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Alma Paprika variety notes and drying instructions
University of New Mexico Chile Pepper Institute — Hungarian Paprika Classification and Home Production

name: Alpatieva 905 A Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 5-6 weeks before the last frost and set out promptly, since this dwarf variety is bred to ripen quickly in short, cool seasons.
directions: Alpatieva 905 A is a mid-20th-century Russian heirloom bred for fast, reliable production from a notably compact, almost dwarf-sized determinate plant only about two feet tall. Despite its small stature it carries a heavy set of two- to three-ounce, globe-shaped red fruit with a good, old-fashioned tomato flavor, making a single stake or small cage sufficient support. Its short stature and early ripening suit container growing, raised beds, and cold-climate gardens where a long season isn't available. Water evenly and harvest promptly as fruit colors up, since the small plant can only carry a limited load of ripening tomatoes at once.

name: Altrincham Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow into deeply dug, loose soil so the long tapering root can develop straight; a long season crop best started once soil has warmed slightly.
directions: Altrincham is an old English carrot named for the Cheshire market town where it was traditionally grown, producing a long, tapering orange root with a distinctive green-tinged shoulder above ground. Work the bed deeply before sowing so the root can push straight down without forking, and thin seedlings to several inches apart once established. It is a long-season type best suited to a full spring-to-fall growing window, rewarding patience with dense, sweet flesh that stores well after a fall harvest. Lift roots before hard freezes and trim the tops for winter storage in a cool, humid root cellar.

name: Alubia de Tolosa Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; a bush type that needs no staking and performs well in the cool, humid summers typical of northern Spain's Basque Country.
directions: Alubia de Tolosa is a small, matte-black dry bean grown under a protected designation of origin around Tolosa in Spain's Basque Country, where it is the star of the traditional autumn alubiada bean feast served with cabbage, chorizo, and pork. The beans cook to an intensely creamy, almost velvety texture with an earthy, faintly smoky flavor that Basque cooks prize above other black bean types. Bush plants stay compact and productive without support; allow pods to dry fully and rattle before harvesting, then shell and cure before storage. It performs best where summers are mild to moderately warm rather than scorching, echoing its native Atlantic-coast climate.

name: Alvaro Charentais Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow or set transplants after soil has warmed well into the 70s; Alvaro is one of the earliest-ripening Charentais types, a useful trait where summers are short.
directions: Alvaro is a French-type Charentais hybrid noted for ripening earlier than most other Charentais melons, producing compact, deeply sutured round fruit without netting on a smooth, yellowish-tan rind lightly striped in green. The thick orange flesh is dense and aromatic, filling the air with the intense perfume typical of Charentais types when fully ripe. Because Charentais melons slip from the vine only at peak ripeness, check daily as fruit nears maturity and watch for a slight crack or softening at the stem end. Give it full sun and warm, fertile, well-drained soil, keeping moisture steady through fruit set and tapering off as the small melons ripen to concentrate sugars.
sources: Territorial Seed Company — Alvaro Melon Seed

name: Amager Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes; the long maturity period is intended to bring heads to harvest just before hard fall frost for winter storage.
directions: Amager is a Danish heirloom bred for the cold, damp climate of its namesake island, producing extremely dense, round heads that keep in a root cellar longer than most cabbage varieties. The tight internal packing that makes it a slow, late-season grower is the same trait that gives it exceptional storage life, often into late winter under proper conditions. Its heavy cold tolerance lets it stay in the field later into fall than earlier-maturing cabbages, concentrating sugars and improving flavor after frost. Plant Amager specifically for long-haul winter storage rather than fresh summer eating.

name: Amana Orange Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Amana Orange originated in the Amana Colonies of Iowa, an historic German communal settlement that maintained distinctive traditional varieties; the tomato was preserved by colony members for generations before entering the American heirloom seed trade.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Amana Orange is one of the finest very-large orange beefsteak heirloom tomatoes — producing massive (1–2 lb), irregularly shaped, deeply orange-colored fruits with exceptionally sweet, very low-acid flesh that creates the most mild, sweet, non-acidic fresh tomato experience available from any heirloom type. The very large fruit size and characteristic sweet, almost candy-like low-acid flavor make Amana Orange one of the most distinctive eating experiences among heirloom tomatoes. The brilliant, uniform deep-orange color — consistent across the exterior and interior flesh without the bicolor patterns of Pineapple or Big Rainbow — provides a vivid single-color presentation that is striking in its own right. The meaty, dense orange flesh has relatively few seeds and an exceptionally high flesh-to-gel ratio that maximizes the edible portion. As an open-pollinated heirloom from the Amana Colonies of Iowa, the variety carries cultural significance alongside its outstanding eating quality. Amana Orange plants are large, vigorous indeterminate vines requiring sturdy 6-foot support. The long growing season (80–95 days) means zone 9 gardeners should start seeds as early as possible to ensure fruit development before summer heat. An outstanding choice for anyone who finds standard tomatoes too acid.

name: Amara Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before the last frost, or later in summer for a fall crop; leaves can be cut young or left to mature.
directions: Direct sow shallowly into fertile soil and thin seedlings as they grow, cutting outer leaves for continuous harvest or letting plants reach full size. This traditional Ethiopian selection produces large, smooth, paddle-shaped blue-green leaves with a sharper, more pungent bite than common mustard greens, and it is a staple ingredient in Ethiopian gomen dishes. It tolerates both heat and cool weather better than many mustards, giving it a longer harvest window through the season.

name: Amazing Cauliflower
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting; in zone 8-9 gardens transplant in August-September, adding roughly two extra weeks beyond the stated maturity to account for slower fall growth as light and temperatures decline.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart with 24-36 inches between rows, and feed generously since Amazing needs vigorous leaf growth to protect its curd. This variety is valued for its self-blanching habit: large, upright wrapper leaves naturally curl in over the developing curd, shielding it from sun and weather so it stays creamy white without the hand-tying required by older cauliflower varieties. Amazing's extended, somewhat uneven maturity window is actually an asset for home gardeners, since plants in the same bed don't all come ready at once, spreading a single planting's harvest out over several weeks instead of demanding it all be used or preserved immediately. It is widely regarded as one of the more forgiving fall cauliflowers for gardeners still learning to time brassica plantings against the first frost.

name: Amber Cup Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is warm; Amber Cup is a small, red-orange buttercup-type squash popular in Japanese and Korean cooking for its dense, sweet, dry flesh.
directions: Direct sow seed in hills after the soil has warmed, spacing plants to allow the moderately vigorous vines room to run. Amber Cup produces small, 2 to 4 pound, deep red-orange fruit with the flattened, ridged shape typical of buttercup-type squash, and the flesh is exceptionally dry, dense, and sweet, making it well suited to steaming, roasting, and inclusion in Japanese and Korean dishes where kabocha-type squash is traditional. Its compact fruit size makes it convenient for a single household meal without leftovers, unlike larger winter squash. Harvest when the rind has hardened fully and the vine begins to decline, and cure for a week or two in a warm spot before moving to cool storage.

name: Amber Globe Turnip
plantingNote: A classic fall storage turnip for the Gulf South; sow in late summer for harvest through winter, sweetens after light frost.
directions: A yellow-fleshed heirloom turnip documented since before 1840, grown for smooth globe roots with fine-grained, sweet flesh unlike the sharper white-fleshed types. Best picked around 3 inches across for peak sweetness and tenderness, though roots can size up to 6 inches for winter storage. Sturdy tops also cook well as greens, giving two harvests from one planting.

name: Ambercup Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Ambercup is a kabocha-type winter squash with golden-amber to deep orange skin and intensely rich, sweet, dry flesh — one of the best-flavored compact winter squashes for home gardens, producing 5–7 lb fruits with firm, dense flesh that stores well through winter; similar to Red Kuri in texture and sweetness but with a distinctive golden-orange skin.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in well-drained, fertile soil; vines are moderate in length (6–8 feet), more manageable than butternut or hubbard types; harvest when the skin is a uniform deep golden-amber and resists fingernail denting; cure for 2–3 weeks after harvest to maximize sweetness and storage life. Ambercup is an heirloom-type open-pollinated winter squash of the Cucurbita maxima species — the same species as kabocha, Red Kuri, Blue Hubbard, and Buttercup — that produces compact, round to slightly flattened fruits with smooth, glossy, deep golden-orange skin and a very small indented cavity at the blossom end. The flesh is the dry, dense, intensely orange, and very sweet type characteristic of the best maxima squashes, making Ambercup one of the most flavorful winter squashes for baking, roasting, and soup-making. The golden-amber skin is distinctive and attractive — warmer in color than the grey-green of standard kabocha, lighter than Buttercup's dark green, and different from Red Kuri's red-orange — making it visually distinctive in the garden and at market. Ambercup performs reliably across a wide range of climates from zone 3 to zone 9 and stores exceptionally well under cool, dry conditions — quality often improves with 1–2 months of storage as the starches convert to sugars. In zone 9a and the Gulf South, Ambercup should be direct-sown in late March or early April to allow the full season before summer heat arrives.

name: Ambition Shallot
plantingNote: Plant shallot sets 4–8 weeks before last frost in spring, or in fall in zones 7–10 for a June harvest; Ambition is a widely grown European F1 shallot producing uniform, oval, red-violet to copper-skinned bulbs in clusters of 5–10 per set with the classic shallot flavor — mild, sweet, and slightly garlicky — in a reliable, high-yielding variety preferred in professional kitchens throughout Europe.
directions: Plant shallot sets 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart, with the tip just at soil level; each set multiplies into a cluster of 5–10 bulbs; keep consistently moist during establishment and in spring; reduce watering as leaves begin to yellow and fall over; harvest when tops fall and bulb skins are dry and papery, then cure for 2–3 weeks before storage. Ambition is a European F1 hybrid shallot produced by commercial seed companies primarily in the Netherlands, where the commercial shallot industry has been refined over centuries into highly productive, uniform varieties for both professional kitchen use and home garden production. The Ambition variety produces medium-sized, uniformly shaped, oval to pear-shaped bulbs with red-violet to copper-mahogany skin and purplish-pink inner flesh; each planted set multiplies into a cluster of 5–10 distinct bulbs, the characteristic growth habit that distinguishes shallots from onions (which produce a single bulb from a set). The flavor is the classic shallot character — more subtle, sweet, and complex than onions, with a slightly garlicky undertone that distinguishes shallots as the preferred allium in French haute cuisine for vinaigrettes, pan sauces, and dishes where onion flavor would be too harsh. Storage life is excellent — 6–9 months under proper conditions (cool, dry, dark). The F1 hybrid nature of Ambition means it does not come true from saved seed, but sets (bulbs) from the previous year's crop can be replanted successfully.

name: Ambrosia Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (70°F+); in zone 9 plant March–May. Ambrosia is an open-pollinated variety requiring the full 84–90 days; succession is not practical but a single well-timed planting in zone 9 produces abundantly through summer. Ripe Ambrosia melons slip easily from the vine with a gentle tug — full-slip is the traditional ripeness indicator for cantaloupe. Reduce watering in the final 2 weeks before harvest to intensify sweetness and flavor. The powdery mildew resistance makes Ambrosia particularly reliable in zone 9's humid summer conditions.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil — melons require warm soil, abundant sun, and good air circulation; Ambrosia is an All-America Selections award-winning cantaloupe (muskmelon) that earned recognition for its exceptionally sweet, deeply aromatic, thick-fleshed, orange interior — with sugar content and fragrance significantly exceeding most commercial cantaloupe varieties bred for shipping durability. The medium-sized, rounded fruits with heavily netted tan rind and the unmistakable, intensely musky-sweet fragrance that announces ripeness from several feet away represent the classic cantaloupe eating experience at its best. Most commercial cantaloupes are harvested before full-slip (when they still cling to the vine) to withstand shipping without bruising — the result is fruit that is often underripe, bland, and lacking the musky sweetness that a vine-ripened cantaloupe develops. A homegrown Ambrosia harvested at true full-slip ripeness is fundamentally different from any commercial cantaloupe — genuinely aromatic, extremely sweet, and with a perfumed complexity that makes tasting it for the first time a revelation about what cantaloupe actually tastes like. Powdery mildew resistance makes Ambrosia reliable in the humid conditions of zone 9 summer.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Cantaloupe Production for Gulf South
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Muskmelon/Cantaloupe Growing Guide

name: Ambrosia Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September for a fall harvest. Plant in solid blocks of at least 4 rows for adequate wind pollination. Ambrosia is a sugary-enhanced (SE) bicolor variety — isolate from field corn and popcorn by at least 250 feet or 2 weeks of tasseling time to prevent starch dilution by cross-pollination. The sugary-enhanced trait gives better flavor retention after harvest than standard sweet corn.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ambrosia is an All-America Selections award-winning bicolor sweet corn recognized in 1982 for its outstanding combination of sweetness, tenderness, and one of the best flavor profiles of any bicolor sweet corn variety. The sugary-enhanced (SE) genetics give Ambrosia a higher sugar content and better post-harvest sugar retention than traditional open-pollinated sweet corn — the ears remain sweet and tender for several days after harvest rather than converting sugars to starch rapidly as standard sweet corn does. The bicolor ears with alternating white and yellow kernels have been the classic American sweet corn appearance for backyard gardens since the 1980s, and Ambrosia set the standard for bicolor flavor that later varieties aimed to match. The slender, well-filled ears (7–8 inches) have a fine kernel texture, tender pericarp (no toughness in the kernel skin), and outstanding raw flavor for eating directly off the cob without cooking. Ambrosia remains one of the most widely grown and recommended bicolor sweet corn varieties for home gardens.
sources: All-America Selections — Ambrosia Sweet Corn 1982 Award
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Sweet Corn Variety Evaluation
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sweet Corn for Florida Gardens

name: Amelia Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Amelia is a vigorous indeterminate slicing tomato with a comprehensive VFFNTAs disease resistance package: Verticillium wilt (V), two races of Fusarium wilt (F, FF), nematodes (N), tobacco mosaic virus (T), and Alternaria stem canker (As). The Alternaria stem canker resistance in Amelia is a notable differentiator — Alternaria is a fungal pathogen (Alternaria alternata f. sp. lycopersici) that causes stem canker and early fruit death in susceptible varieties and is particularly prevalent in warm, humid conditions. Amelia was developed to address the full suite of southeastern disease pressures in a single variety, making it particularly appropriate for zone 9's warm, humid climate where multiple diseases commonly limit tomato production. Transplant March–April in zone 9. Fruits are medium-large (8–12 oz), round to slightly flat, and ripen to a deep, uniform red.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and cage or stake to 6 feet. Harvest when uniformly deep red. Amelia Tomato is a commercially developed F1 hybrid slicing tomato specifically designed for production in the humid southeastern United States, where the combination of warm temperatures, high humidity, and disease inoculum in garden soils creates challenging conditions for standard tomato varieties. The variety's VFFNTAs resistance code represents one of the most comprehensive disease resistance packages available in a single tomato variety: resistance to Verticillium wilt (a soilborne fungal disease that colonizes the xylem and causes progressive wilting), two races of Fusarium wilt (a related soilborne pathogen with multiple strains that can overcome single-race resistance), root-knot nematodes (a serious pest in the warm, sandy soils of the Gulf Coast), tobacco mosaic virus (a seed- and contact-transmitted virus), and Alternaria stem canker (a foliar and stem fungal pathogen that can cause significant early-season damage in humid conditions). This combination of resistances directly addresses the primary disease challenges in zone 9 tomato production: nematode pressure is extremely common in the sandy soils of the Gulf Coast plain; Fusarium and Verticillium are endemic in soils with previous tomato production history; Alternaria stem canker increases in severity during warm, wet weather. For gardeners who have experienced repeated tomato crop failures in zone 9 from disease without knowing the specific cause, Amelia's broad resistance package provides protection across the most likely disease scenarios.
sources: Syngenta Vegetable Seeds — Amelia tomato F1 hybrid disease resistance documentation
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Disease-Resistant Tomato Variety Trials for Gulf South
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Disease Management and Variety Selection

name: American Early White Spine Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow an inch deep after soil has warmed following the last frost. This American type has been grown since the 18th century; Alexander Watson's 'The American Home Garden' (1859) cited the white-spined Long Green form among the best kitchen-garden cucumbers of its day.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil in full sun and grow on a trellis to keep fruit straight and clean. American Early White Spine produces dark green, white-spined cucumbers around 6-8 inches long with a somewhat warty skin surface and pale green lines running from blossom to stem end; the mild, crisp flesh suits both slicing and pickling. It was once a dominant market and home-garden slicer before modern burpless and disease-resistant hybrids replaced it, and in the late 19th century growers selected from it the shorter, blockier 'Improved White Spine.' Pick regularly to keep vines productive through the season.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Heirloom Cucumber Variety Histories
Mother Earth News — Heirloom Cucumber Varieties

name: Amethyst Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in spring or 4-6 weeks before first fall frost; Amethyst is a spring radish with smooth, bright purple skin and crisp white flesh, bred for uniform round shape and reliable color.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. Amethyst is a modern spring radish bred for uniform, smooth, round roots with bright, consistent purple skin and crisp white interior, offering reliable color and shape for gardeners and market growers who want a purple radish that performs predictably. Flavor is mild and clean, similar to other fast-maturing spring radish types, without the excess pepperiness that develops in some varieties left too long in the ground. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows. Harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch in diameter, and succession-sow every two to three weeks for a continuous supply.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Amethyst Radish variety notes
Territorial Seed Company — Colorful Radish Varieties
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Radish Variety Trials

name: Amish Butter Popcorn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks well after last frost and isolate from other corn types by distance or timing to keep popping quality true.
directions: Maintained for generations among Pennsylvania Dutch growers, Amish Butter is a pre-1885 heirloom popcorn that produces tall, dark-green stalks topped with two conical ears carrying a mix of rice- and pearl-shaped ivory-white kernels. Let ears dry fully on the stalk, or finish drying them indoors on their husks, until kernels rattle loosely in the cob before shelling and storing in a breathable container. Because the kernels are soft enough to also grind for flour, hominy, or polenta, gardeners get a genuinely dual-purpose corn from a single planting rather than a popcorn-only crop. The fluffy white pop and rich, naturally buttery flavor are the main reasons collectors keep this variety in circulation.

name: Amish Deer Tongue Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow or start indoors in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; more heat-tolerant and slower to bolt than many loose-leaf lettuces.
directions: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. Amish Deer Tongue is a longtime Pennsylvania Dutch heirloom named for its distinctive triangular, pointed leaves that resemble a deer's tongue, forming loose, upright rosettes of thick, crisp, richly flavored green leaves. It is notably more heat-tolerant and slower to bolt than many other loose-leaf lettuces, making it a dependable choice for extending the lettuce harvest into warmer weather in Gulf South spring gardens. Harvest outer leaves individually as a cut-and-come-again crop, or cut the whole rosette at the base once it fills out.

name: Amish Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger passes and soil has warmed thoroughly; give vines full sun and room to sprawl or a sturdy trellis with fruit slings.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to the strongest seedlings once established. Amish Melon is an open-pollinated heirloom muskmelon preserved and passed down through generations of Amish farming families, producing medium to large, netted, orange-fleshed cantaloupe-type fruit with a rich, sweet, aromatic flavor typical of well-grown heirloom melons. The vigorous, productive vines are known for reliable fruit set and good flavor even in less-than-ideal seasons, a hallmark of many Amish-preserved garden varieties bred for dependable performance in working farm gardens rather than showy uniformity. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with a gentle tug and the netted rind color has turned from green to tan, and reduce watering in the final week before harvest to concentrate sweetness.

name: Amish Paste Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; the large fruit size requires staking even as a paste tomato; prolific producer that benefits from a long growing season.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes; Amish Paste is an heirloom paste tomato from Wisconsin Amish communities, producing large (6–8 ounce) ox-heart to plum-shaped fruits with very few seeds, thick meaty flesh, low water content, and rich concentrated flavor that makes it outstanding for sauces, pastes, and canning. It far outperforms Roma for sauce production due to its greater size while retaining the low acidity and meatiness needed for good paste. Also excellent sliced fresh. An indeterminate vine with a long season; in short-summer climates, start early and use season-extension techniques.

name: Amish Pie Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow into warm soil after frost danger has passed; Amish Pie is a Plain-community heirloom pumpkin grown for its dense, sweet, fine-grained flesh, prized above the watery flesh of jack-o'-lantern types for baking.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in hills of warm, fertile soil and give the sprawling vines plenty of room to run, or trellis smaller fruit for a large vertical crop. Amish Pie is a heritage pumpkin passed down through Plain communities for its large, ribbed, deep-orange fruit and thick, dense, notably sweet flesh, considered by many bakers superior to jack-o'-lantern pumpkins, which tend to be stringy and watery by comparison. Fruits commonly run 10-20 pounds and store well into winter in a cool, dry spot, making it practical to bake from a single pumpkin over several months. Keep vines well watered as fruit sizes up and reduce watering as the rind hardens and colors fully in fall, then cure harvested pumpkins for a week or two before storage to concentrate sweetness and toughen the skin.

name: Amish Rocambole Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves pointed end up in fall, about 4-6 weeks ahead of hard frost, so root systems form before winter.
directions: Plant cloves 2 inches deep in well-drained, compost-enriched soil and mulch for winter insulation in cold regions. Snap off the coiling scape as it appears to send more energy into the developing bulb, and cure bulbs in a shaded, breezy spot before trimming roots and tops for storage. Amish Rocambole is a long-grown American heirloom hardneck strain passed down through Pennsylvania Dutch farming communities, admired for its rich, robust garlic flavor, easy-peeling cloves, and classic rocambole scapes once used fresh in early-summer cooking.

name: Amish Snap Pea
plantingNote: Sow directly in cool soil as early as it can be worked, and give vines a tall trellis or fence to climb, since this heirloom grows considerably taller than most modern snap peas.
directions: Amish Snap is a tall heirloom snap pea passed down through Amish and Mennonite farm families in Pennsylvania and the Midwest and preserved by seed savers rather than commercial breeding programs. Vigorous vines climb readily on a trellis and set heavy quantities of sweet, plump, stringless pods that hold their quality well in variable spring weather. Because the vines are unusually tall, plan on netting or a fence at least five to six feet high and harvest every couple of days once pods fill out to keep the plants productive. The pods are good eaten fresh off the vine, lightly steamed, or stir-fried.

name: Amsoi Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall through winter in zone 8-10; leaves can be harvested as baby greens in as little as three weeks or allowed to mature further for the fuller-flavored leaves traditionally used in pancit and other stir-fried dishes.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to partial shade; Amsoi is a broadleaf mustard type long grown in Filipino home gardens and widely used in Filipino cooking, particularly in noodle dishes and sauteed vegetable sides. The smooth, glossy, dark green leaves are broader and less deeply lobed than curled mustard types, with a flavor that is noticeably milder and less sharply pungent than Southern mustard greens, making it approachable for cooks who find typical mustard heat too strong. Because it prefers steady moisture and moderate temperatures, it performs best as a cool-season crop and tends to turn bitter and bolt quickly once hot weather sets in. Harvest by cutting outer leaves or the whole young plant, since regrowth from the cut stem is reliable during the cool months.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources Extension

name: Amsterdam Forcing Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow in loose, stone-free soil as soon as the ground can be worked; Amsterdam Forcing is bred for very fast, uniform early growth and is a classic choice for the first carrot sowing of spring or for tight succession plantings.
directions: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in loose, well-worked soil in full sun, keeping the surface evenly damp until the slow-to-emerge seedlings appear, then thin to about 2 inches apart. Amsterdam Forcing is a classic Dutch heirloom bred specifically for speed, producing slender, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots with a fine, sweet flavor and almost no core, ready to pull well before slower main-crop carrots. Its small size and rapid growth make it an excellent choice for containers, cold frames, and tight succession sowings every few weeks through the cool season. Harvest young, at finger to baby-carrot size, for the best texture and sweetness, since roots left in the ground too long lose the tenderness that defines the type.

name: Ananas Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, deeply amended soil; Ananas (French for 'pineapple') melon is a Middle Eastern and Mediterranean heirloom producing large (3–5 lb), netted, oval fruits with intensely aromatic, spicy-sweet orange or white flesh that many consider among the finest-flavored of all melons — widely grown from Israel to France.
directions: Sow in hills or rows after last frost in deeply enriched, well-drained soil; Ananas is a large-fruited type needing 6–8 feet of row space or a very strong trellis with hammock-style fruit supports. Ananas melon (ananas is French and many Mediterranean languages for pineapple) is a widely grown Middle Eastern, Israeli, and Mediterranean heirloom producing large, oval to round, netted fruits (3–7 lb) with a sweet, spicy, intensely aromatic fragrance when ripe that has been compared to pineapple, vanilla, and spiced honey. The flesh can be white (in the traditional Israeli 'Ananas Yokneam' type) or orange, always with a distinctive rich, complex fragrance that perfumes a room when a ripe fruit is present. Several regional strains exist: French Ananas (yellow netted, orange flesh), Israeli Yokneam (white smooth skin, white flesh), and American strains. Generally large-fruited and somewhat heat-sensitive; best grown in dry conditions as wet weather can dilute flavor. Considered by some the finest-flavored muskmelon type in existence.

name: Ananas Yokneam Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, deeply enriched soil; Ananas Yokneam is the traditional Israeli strain of Ananas melon, distinguished by its smooth white skin and white flesh rather than the netted, orange-fleshed French type.
directions: Ananas Yokneam is the traditional Israeli regional strain of Ananas ('pineapple') melon, distinguished from the netted, orange-fleshed French Ananas type by its smooth white skin and white flesh. Like other Ananas melons it is prized for an intensely aromatic, spicy-sweet fragrance that has been compared to pineapple, vanilla, and spiced honey, perfuming a room when a ripe fruit is present. Sow in hills or rows after last frost in deeply enriched, well-drained soil and provide 6-8 feet of row space or a strong trellis with hammock-style fruit support. Favor dry growing conditions where possible, since wet weather can dilute the fragrance and flavor that distinguish this strain.

name: Andover Parsnip
plantingNote: Direct sow fresh seed as soon as the soil is workable in spring, in deep, loose, stone-free ground; parsnip seed viability drops quickly, so use current-year seed.
directions: Andover is a British-bred parsnip widely recognized for combining strong field resistance to canker with the smooth, well-shaped, medium-length roots gardeners expect from older heirlooms. It has become a standard recommendation in cool, damp growing regions where canker-prone varieties like Hollow Crown often develop the disfiguring rust-brown shoulder rot that ruins a crop. Sow shallowly and keep the seedbed evenly moist through the slow, uneven germination typical of parsnip, marking rows carefully since seedlings emerge slowly and are easy to lose to weeding. As with all parsnips, flavor sweetens dramatically after the roots experience several weeks of near-freezing temperatures, so delay harvest until after hard frost for the best eating quality.

name: Andovy Hamburg Root Parsley
plantingNote: Direct sow into loose, deeply worked soil once it is workable in spring, since roots fork in heavy or rocky ground.
directions: Andovy is a Hamburg-type root parsley grown for its smooth, parsnip-like white taproot rather than its foliage, with a mild, earthy, parsley-scented flavor that works well roasted, mashed, or added to stocks. It produces uniform, straight, slow-to-fork roots when grown in loose soil, along with edible flat leaves that can be harvested lightly through the season without harming root development. As a hardy biennial root, it can be left in the ground and harvested through fall and into early winter after light frosts, which sweetens the flavor. Gardeners grow Andovy as a dual-purpose crop, choosing it over standard leaf parsley when a storable root vegetable is the goal.

name: Angela Rutabaga
plantingNote: Direct sow in mid to late summer so roots mature with cooling fall weather; thin to final spacing once seedlings are established.
directions: Angela is a refined English selection of the classic purple-top rutabaga, bred originally for the UK market and valued for its attractive purple-and-cream roots, light golden flesh, and winter hardiness. Sow directly in fertile, well-drained soil in mid to late summer, thinning to a final spacing of 6-8 inches. Keep the bed consistently moist to avoid woody or cracked roots. Harvest after a light frost sweetens the flesh, and store roots in a cool, humid root cellar or leave them in the ground under mulch through winter in milder climates.

name: Anna Russian Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; one of the earliest-maturing large heirloom tomatoes, making it excellent for short-season gardens and for getting a jump on the harvest before summer heat sets in at southern latitudes.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to well-prepared, deeply amended soil after all frost risk has passed and stake or cage firmly to support the heart-shaped fruits. Anna Russian is a Ukrainian/Russian oxheart-type heirloom with distinctive heart-shaped, pink-red fruits up to 12 ounces that are extremely fleshy, nearly seedless, and have a rich, sweet, mild flavor making them outstanding for eating fresh; it is one of the earlier-maturing large heirloom types at 68–80 days, which makes it especially valuable for growers who want to harvest ahead of the worst summer heat. The indeterminate vines set fruit in loose clusters of 2–3 and continue producing through the season if heat stress does not prevent fruit set; in the South, plant early for spring harvest.

name: Anna's Charentais Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into warm soil; Anna's Charentais was bred specifically for longer post-harvest storage than most French Charentais types.
directions: Anna's Charentais is a French-type melon hybrid bred for longer shelf life than typical Charentais varieties while keeping the classic small size and mild aromatic sweetness of the type. The compact 2-3 pound fruit has the traditional smooth, lightly ribbed Charentais look and stores six days or more at room temperature, considerably longer than most Charentais melons, which makes it well suited to fresh-market sales as well as the home garden. Harvest at forced slip or cut from the vine as the skin begins turning yellow. Resistance to Fusarium wilt and intermediate tolerance of powdery mildew help keep vines productive through harvest.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Anna's Charentais (F1) Melon Seed
Osborne Seed Company — Anna's Charentais F1 Melon Seeds

name: Annabel Organic Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring and succession-sow every couple weeks; also suitable for a late-summer sowing for fall harvest.
directions: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep as soon as the soil can be worked, thinning seedlings to about an inch apart so roots have room to size up without crowding. Keep the bed evenly moist, since inconsistent watering is the main cause of cracked or pithy roots in fast-growing radishes. This organic F1 hybrid matures quickly and uniformly, making it a good candidate for repeated succession sowings through spring and again in early fall.

name: Anne Arundel Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills once soil has thoroughly warmed past last frost; Anne Arundel is a colonial-era Maryland heirloom muskmelon needing a full warm season to size and sweeten its fruit.
directions: Anne Arundel is a colonial Maryland heirloom traced to Anne Arundel County, where it was grown by a small circle of local farmers for well over a century. Its nutmeg-shaped fruit ripens to a golden-yellow rind over sweet, pale green flesh with a flavor often compared to honeydew. The strain nearly vanished before being preserved through much of the twentieth century by a Maryland family, and it now circulates through Seed Savers Exchange membership. Give vines full sun and steady moisture through fruit set, then ease off watering as melons approach ripeness to concentrate their sweetness.

name: Annie Oakley II Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant April–June for main crop, or March under row cover. Annie Oakley II is among the earliest okra varieties to produce, making it valuable for gardeners in northern zones. In zone 9 the earlier production means pods are setting before peak summer heat reduces pod quality; plant a fall crop in August for continued production into November.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Annie Oakley II is a hybrid, spineless, compact okra developed as an improved successor to the original Annie Oakley hybrid — the 1988 AAS Award-winning variety that introduced the compact, spineless, early-maturing concept that transformed home garden okra production. Annie Oakley II improves on the original with earlier maturity (48 versus 56 days), heavier production, improved disease resistance, and better heat tolerance for extended season production. The compact, 3–5 foot plant produces straight, uniform, deep green, 5-ribbed pods with excellent tenderness when harvested at 3–4 inches. The thornless, compact habit makes Annie Oakley II the best choice for gardeners with limited space, raised beds, and those who find full-size okra plants too large to manage easily. In zone 9 the compact habit is advantageous because plants fit more naturally into intensive garden beds without overwhelming neighboring crops.
sources: All-America Selections — Annie Oakley Okra Award Record
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Compact Okra Varieties
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Annie Oakley II Okra

name: Annie Oakley Okra
plantingNote: Soak seeds overnight before planting to speed germination; direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F. In zone 9 plant March–July; Annie Oakley is earlier than most okra varieties and begins producing within 52 days of sowing, valuable for a longer harvest window.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms to 65°F in full sun; Annie Oakley is a spineless, compact hybrid okra that produces early (52 days) and prolifically on plants 3–4 feet tall — smaller than most standard okra and suitable for smaller gardens or containers. The smooth, straight, dark-green pods are 5-ridged and should be harvested at 3–4 inches for maximum tenderness; pods become fibrous and woody if left beyond 5–6 inches. The spineless habit makes harvest comfortable without gloves; hand-pick every 2–3 days in summer heat. An AAS Award winner, Annie Oakley has proven reliable across the South and performs especially well in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers.
sources: All-America Selections — Annie Oakley Okra Award Record
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Okra Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Okra Varieties

name: Antigua Eggplant
subcategory: Italian-type hybrid eggplant bred for productivity
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed.
directions: Start seed indoors under warm conditions and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights stay above 55F, since this hybrid performs best with steady heat. Provide even moisture and support for the upright plants as fruit clusters develop. Antigua is a modern Italian-type hybrid bred for a compact plant habit and heavy early set of glossy, dark purple, oval fruit, making it a reliable choice for market growers and small gardens alike. Its relatively quick maturity suits gardeners in cooler regions who want classic eggplant flavor without a long growing season.

name: Antohi Romanian Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Antohi Romanian is a distinctly early, mild, sweet frying pepper introduced to North American gardeners by Romanian dissident Silviu Antohi, who brought seeds from Romania to Canada in the 1980s — producing pale yellow to orange, blocky to elongated, thin-walled fruits with exceptional sweetness and very early production for a sweet pepper.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Antohi Romanian is notably earlier than most sweet peppers and can be productive even in short-season gardens. Antohi Romanian pepper arrived in North American heirloom seed circles through Romanian dissident Silviu Antohi, who escaped Romania during the Communist period and brought pepper seeds with him that he shared with gardeners and seed savers in Canada; the variety entered the Seed Savers Exchange network in the 1990s and has since become widely appreciated for its exceptional earliness and high quality. The medium-sized (3–4 inch), blocky to elongated-oval, pale yellow to orange fruits have thin walls and an exceptionally sweet, fruity flavor with virtually no bitterness; they are among the earliest sweet peppers to begin producing, with plants in production 60–72 days from transplant — significantly earlier than most sweet bell types. Outstanding fresh, roasted, or pickled; the thin walls cook down quickly and the fruits need no peeling when roasted. A highly productive plant for short-season gardens and an outstanding choice for Gulf Coast early-season plantings.

name: Anuenue Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow from early spring into late spring, or again in late summer for a fall crop; unlike most lettuce, Anuenue seed germinates readily even at soil temperatures above 80°F, which lets Gulf Coast gardeners sow it later into warming weather than typical lettuce varieties.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil, thinning to 8-12 inches, and harvest as a full head once the center fills in. Anuenue was released by the University of Hawaii in 1987 specifically for tropical and subtropical climates, forming a small, crisp, iceberg-type head with bright green outer leaves and a well-packed pale heart, but with seed and heat tolerance far beyond typical crisphead lettuce. It is one of the few lettuce varieties whose seed will germinate reliably in hot soil rather than going dormant, and the plant resists developing the bitterness that ruins most lettuce as summer heat builds. For Gulf Coast gardeners this makes Anuenue a valuable bridge variety, extending fresh salad lettuce production later into late spring and earlier into late summer than standard cool-season types allow.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources (CTAHR) — Lettuce for the Home Garden
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database

name: Aokubi Daikon
plantingNote: Direct sow in deeply worked soil in late summer for a fall harvest, or early spring once soil is workable; Aokubi is the standard F1 daikon grown across most of Japan and tolerates a range of conditions better than many heirloom strains.
directions: Direct sow a half inch deep in loose, stone-free soil and thin early to prevent forked roots. Aokubi gets its name, meaning 'green neck,' from the shoulder of the root that pushes up out of the soil and turns light green where sunlight hits it, while the buried lower two-thirds stays pure white; this exposed shoulder also makes the root easy to grip and pull. Roots size up quickly and hold well in the ground without turning pithy, with a sweet flavor and crisp texture suited to grating, simmering, and fresh salads. Mulch around the shoulders if you want a fully white root for a more traditional presentation.

name: Apache Bunching Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow every few weeks from early spring through late summer for a continuous supply; the purple-pink shank color intensifies with cool weather and full sun exposure.
directions: Apache is a fast-growing open-pollinated scallion selected for shanks that flush from rosy purple to a deeper wine color as the plant matures, set off nicely against slender blue-green tops. Sow thickly in shallow drills and thin as needed, since it is typically pulled young for salads, garnishes, and quick pickles rather than grown to full onion size. Flavor is mild and sweet compared with many bunching types, making it popular raw. Because it germinates and bulks up quickly in cool conditions, succession sowing every two to three weeks keeps a steady harvest through spring and fall.
sources: Specialty seed catalog variety descriptions (e.g. Southern Exposure Seed Exchange, Kitazawa Seed Company)

name: Aphrodite Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed into the 70s; its strong disease package suits growers who have had trouble with fusarium wilt or vine decline in previous melon plantings.
directions: Aphrodite is a widely grown commercial Eastern shipper-type cantaloupe bred with resistance to fusarium wilt and tolerance to several common vine and foliar diseases, traits that also make it a dependable performer in home gardens with a history of melon problems. It produces uniform, heavily netted, oval fruit averaging 5-6 pounds with firm, deep orange flesh and a small seed cavity, and vines hold up well and keep setting fruit through extended harvest periods. Ripe fruit develops a full slip, separating cleanly from the vine with light pressure, along with a shift to a more golden background color under the netting and a sweet aroma at the blossom end. Its vigorous, disease-tolerant vines and consistent fruit size make it a good choice for gardeners who want reliable yields without babying a finicky heirloom melon.

name: Apocalypse Scorpion Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; as an unstabilized hybrid, plants and fruit can vary somewhat from seed to seed.
directions: Apocalypse Scorpion was developed by members of AIASP, an Italian association of chile growers known for hybridizing extreme-heat peppers, and carries heat of 1,400,000 Scoville units or more, rivaling Carolina Reaper. Pods run 2-3 inches long with warped, pock-marked skin and the classic scorpion stinger tail, ripening from green to red. Despite the ferocity of the burn, which builds gradually and lingers for ten minutes or longer, tasters report sweet, fruity, and unusually floral notes up front. Because it remains an unstandardized hobbyist cross, grow it from specialty superhot seed and use only slivers of the ripe fruit in sauces, chilis, or stews.

name: Apollo Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant dormant one-year crowns in a deep furrow in early spring, filling in soil in stages as new spears push through.
directions: Apollo is one of the original Rutgers all-male hybrid asparagus releases, developed alongside Atlas and Eros before the breeding program's later Jersey-series introductions. Its all-male genetics mean plants never set the small red berries typical of female asparagus, so beds stay cleaner and free of the crowded volunteer seedlings that reduce spear size over time. Apollo produces a heavy early flush of medium-thick spears and shows good resistance to rust in humid regions. Wait until the third spring after crown planting to begin a full harvest season, cutting spears at soil level every one to two days during the peak flush.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

name: Apollo Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 10-12 weeks before the last frost, since this chinense superhot is slow to germinate and needs a long, warm season to fruit before cool weather sets in.
directions: Apollo is a Smokin' Ed Currie (PuckerButt Pepper Company) creation that pairs two of his own extreme chilies, Carolina Reaper and Pepper X, into a single superhot line said by the breeder and pepper enthusiasts to push past 3 million Scoville units, among the hottest named peppers ever reported. It is grown and sold mostly in small quantities for collectors rather than as a mainstream garden variety, and its wrinkled, rounded pods resemble a Carolina Reaper, sometimes with a short tail. Expect a fruity, earthy flavor buried deep beneath an intense, lingering burn, and always wear gloves when handling or harvesting ripe fruit. Give plants a long warm season, full sun, and stake them once pods set, since fruit load can be heavy for the plant's size.

name: Appaloosa Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Appaloosa bean is a distinctive bush dry bean with dramatic black and white spotted coloring reminiscent of an Appaloosa horse — a visually striking heirloom that produces excellent-flavored, creamy-textured beans for baking, soups, and slow-cooking.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; direct seeding is preferred as beans do not transplant well. Appaloosa bean is an heirloom dry bean named for its dramatic black and white spotted coloring that closely resembles the distinctive coat pattern of the Appaloosa horse breed; the irregular black speckles and splashes on creamy white background make each bean unique and the dried beans are among the most visually striking of all heirloom bean varieties, remaining attractive even after cooking. The flavor is rich and earthy with a creamy texture similar to pinto beans but with more character; they are excellent for baked beans, bean soups, and slow-cooked dishes. Can be eaten as a snap bean when pods are young and tender; most commonly grown for dry use at 85–100 days to full maturity. Drought-tolerant once established; performs well in Gulf Coast spring planting with harvest before summer heat peaks.

name: Applegreen Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Applegreen is a compact, high-yielding plant that performs well in containers as well as garden beds.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Applegreen is an All-America Selections winner grown for its smooth, round, apple-sized fruit with pale to medium green skin, mild flavor, and tender, virtually seedless flesh that resists browning better than many purple eggplants once cut. Plants are compact and heavily productive, setting fruit steadily over a long season and performing well in raised beds or large containers where space is limited. Harvest fruit while still glossy and firm, roughly the size of a baseball, since overripe fruit dulls in color and develops tougher skin and more seeds. Its mild flavor and quick cooking time make it a versatile choice for grilling, roasting, and stir-fries.

name: April Cross Daikon
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep into deeply worked, stone-free soil, thinning to a wide final spacing so the roots can size up without forking; also sowable in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep into deeply worked, stone-free soil, thinning to a wide final spacing so the smooth white Minowase-type roots can size up without forking. April Cross is prized among daikon growers for its unusually strong resistance to bolting, which lets it be sown earlier in spring than most daikon types without running to seed. Roots stay tender, mild, and non-pithy even when left in the ground to reach full size, making them well suited to fresh eating, pickling, and simmered dishes.

name: Aquadulce Claudia Fava Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter or very early spring, or in fall in mild-winter regions for an overwintered crop.
directions: Sow seeds 1.5 to 2 inches deep directly in the garden while soil is still cool, spacing plants closely in blocks so they can support each other or provide staking for tall stems. This classic English heirloom is prized for its exceptional cold hardiness, tolerating hard frosts that would kill other legumes, making it a favorite for autumn sowing in mild climates or the earliest possible spring planting elsewhere. Pods grow long and fleshy, typically holding six to eight large, buttery-flavored beans that are excellent shelled fresh, dried for storage, or used in traditional Mediterranean and British dishes. Pinch out the growing tips once the first pods set to discourage aphids and encourage the plant to channel energy into pod development.

name: Arava Galia Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into warm soil; Arava is noted for good powdery mildew tolerance and reliable performance across a range of climates, including cooler-than-ideal summers.
directions: Arava is a widely grown Galia-type melon hybrid originating from Israeli breeding programs, valued for uniform, round fruit up to about four pounds with a thin but tough, raised corky netting over the rind. The flesh is pale green, thick, smooth, and fine-grained, with the intensely perfumed sweetness characteristic of Galia melons rather than the heavier musk of American cantaloupe. Harvest at full slip, when the fruit separates cleanly from the vine with light pressure and the characteristic Galia fragrance is strong at the blossom end. Good resistance to powdery mildew helps vines stay productive over a long harvest season in full sun and warm, well-drained soil.
sources: Fedco Seeds — Arava Organic Galia-Type Melon
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Organic Arava (F1) Melon Seed

name: Arcadia Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Arcadia is specifically valued for its exceptional cold tolerance — the variety holds its heads in quality through heavy frosts and cool temperatures that would damage most broccoli. In zone 9, transplant August–September for November–January harvest. Arcadia's ability to hold heads without yellowing or loosening during cold weather provides a wider harvest window than cold-sensitive varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 65–75°F; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil with pH 6.0–7.0. Arcadia is an F1 hybrid broccoli that has become a benchmark variety for fall and overwintering broccoli production in zones 6–8 — valued specifically for the combination of excellent cold tolerance, uniformly dark blue-green head color, and disease resistance. Most broccoli varieties produce their best heads in the narrow temperature range of 60–65°F and deteriorate rapidly when exposed to hard frosts — heads yellow, open up, or develop loose, poor-quality florets. Arcadia was selected specifically for the ability to hold tight, well-formed heads through significantly colder temperatures, allowing gardeners and growers in the mid-Atlantic and Pacific Northwest to harvest marketable broccoli after hard frosts in October and November that would compromise most other varieties. The deep blue-green color of Arcadia heads is exceptionally attractive — darker and more uniform than many broccoli varieties — and holds through the cold exposure. Disease resistance includes downy mildew, black rot, and clubroot, which are important fall disease concerns in humid climates. Arcadia is a top recommendation from Johnny's Selected Seeds for fall production and has a loyal following among market gardeners who rely on fall broccoli as a key late-season crop.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Arcadia broccoli variety notes and trial results
Osborne Seed Company — Arcadia broccoli description
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Fall Broccoli Variety Evaluation

name: Arctic King Lettuce
plantingNote: Sow in late summer or early fall for overwintering under light cover; this old hardy type is bred to survive cold rather than for quick spring growth.
directions: Arctic King is an old hardy cabbage-type lettuce bred specifically to survive winter in the open garden or under minimal frame protection, standing through hard frosts that would collapse most other lettuces. Sow in late summer or early fall so plants reach a small, firm rosette before the coldest weather sets in, then let growth resume slowly as days lengthen for an early spring harvest. The compact, pale green heads fold into a dense, blanched heart that stays sweet rather than bitter through cold spells. Where winters are too harsh for open-ground survival, a cold frame or row cover substantially improves the odds of carrying plants through to spring.

name: Argentata Swiss Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow around the last frost date, or a bit earlier under cover, spacing seed clusters several inches apart.
directions: Sow seed clusters directly into fertile soil, thinning to one seedling per cluster once plants have a couple of true leaves, and keep beds evenly watered through summer heat. This old Italian type produces broad, dull green savoyed leaves atop wide, flat, silvery-white ribs that many cooks prize for braising separately from the greens. It is notably heat tolerant and slow to bolt, allowing continuous cut-and-come-again harvest well into the warm months.

name: Arikara Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after the soil has warmed, since this Northern Plains heirloom was bred for a shorter continental growing season than many maxima types.
directions: Cultivated for generations by the Arikara people along the Missouri River in present-day North Dakota, this heirloom bears oblong fruit in mottled orange and green with a distinctive pale star marking the blossom end. Plants are relatively compact for a maxima squash and set two to three fruits per vine, making efficient use of a shorter northern season. The moist, sweet flesh is reminiscent of a Hubbard and works well in soups and purees. Cure harvested fruit briefly in a warm location before moving to cool storage, where it keeps remarkably well into late winter.

name: Arikara Yellow Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; Arikara Yellow is an heirloom bush bean from the Arikara people of the Missouri River basin in present-day North Dakota, adapted to the short growing season and continental extremes of the northern Great Plains — exceptionally quick to mature for a dry bean (80–95 days) and tolerant of cool temperatures at both ends of the season.
directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in full sun; Arikara Yellow is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in poor to moderately fertile soils without supplemental irrigation in all but the driest conditions; harvest dry pods before fall rains can induce mold on the dried pods. Arikara Yellow Bean is a traditional heirloom dry bean of the Arikara people (also called the Ree), a Caddoan-speaking people who lived in permanent earth-lodge villages along the Missouri River in present-day North Dakota and South Dakota, where they practiced intensive agriculture including cultivation of corn, squash, sunflowers, and beans for centuries before European contact. The Arikara were important traders in the Missouri River trade network, and their agricultural products — including seeds — were traded widely, distributing their bean varieties to neighboring peoples and eventually to European and American settlers and traders. Arikara Yellow is characterized by small to medium-sized, oval, pale yellow to light tan seeds with a mild, earthy, somewhat buttery flavor that is excellent in soups, stews, and as a baked bean. The variety's most distinctive horticultural characteristic is its extremely short maturity for a dry bean — 80–95 days — which allows it to be grown and harvested in the short frost-free season of zones 3–4 where most dry beans cannot ripen before fall frost. This same short-season adaptation makes Arikara Yellow valuable for gardeners in any region who want a reliable dry bean with insurance against early fall frosts or a compressed summer schedule.

name: Aristocrat Hybrid Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil; compact size suits raised beds and small plots.
directions: Aristocrat won an AAS award in 1973 for combining a compact, space-saving bush habit with the kind of dark green fruit color and shape consistency that open-pollinated zucchini of the era could not match. Plants stay under two feet tall, making this a practical choice for raised beds and smaller Gulf Coast garden plots where vining winter squash would take over. Water deeply every few days rather than a light daily sprinkle to keep production steady through hot spells, and harvest fruit at 6-7 inches before the skin toughens. Decades after its release it remains available from mainstream seed catalogs, a testament to its enduring garden performance.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

name: Aristotle Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Aristotle carries resistance to three races of bacterial leaf spot (X3R), a disease that spreads rapidly in the humid, rain-splashed conditions typical of Gulf South summers and can defoliate less resistant bell pepper varieties.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Aristotle is a widely grown commercial and home-garden bell pepper hybrid bred specifically for resistance to three races of bacterial leaf spot, a disease that thrives in the warm, humid, rain-prone conditions common across the Gulf South and can otherwise strip a pepper plant of foliage and ruin fruit quality. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red if left on the plant, on a compact, well-branched plant that holds up well to heat. Because it keeps its leaf canopy healthier than more disease-susceptible varieties, Aristotle tends to shade and protect its own developing fruit from sunscald better through the peak of summer. Harvest at the green stage for a milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red for maximum sweetness.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pepper Variety Trials
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pepper Production

name: Arka Keshav Brinjal
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, well-drained soil once nights stay reliably above 55F; Arka Keshav is one of the bacterial-wilt-resistant brinjal releases bred by IIHR Bangalore from a cross of 'Dingras Multiple Purple' and 'Arka Sheel', alongside sibling release 'Arka Nidhi'.
directions: Arka Keshav is a long-season brinjal developed by the Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR) in Bangalore from the same 'Dingras Multiple Purple' x 'Arka Sheel' cross that produced sibling release 'Arka Nidhi', bred specifically to resist bacterial wilt, a disease that devastates many eggplant plantings in warm, humid regions. Give it the fullest possible warm window, consistent moisture through fruit set, and full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, same as other long-season warm-climate Asian eggplants in this breeding line.
sources: dataset cross-reference: citation-mining-vegetable-fruit-gaps-cass-overnight1.json ('Dingras Multiple Purple Eggplant' and 'Arka Sheel Brinjal' entries)

name: Arka Neelkanth Brinjal
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, well-drained soil once nights stay reliably above 55F; Arka Neelkanth is one of the bacterial-wilt-resistant brinjal releases bred by IIHR Bangalore from a cross of 'Dingras Multiple Purple' and 'Arka Sheel', alongside sibling release 'Arka Nidhi'.
directions: Arka Neelkanth is a long-season brinjal developed by the Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR) in Bangalore from the same 'Dingras Multiple Purple' x 'Arka Sheel' cross that produced sibling release 'Arka Nidhi', bred specifically to resist bacterial wilt, a disease that devastates many eggplant plantings in warm, humid regions. Give it the fullest possible warm window, consistent moisture through fruit set, and full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, same as other long-season warm-climate Asian eggplants in this breeding line.
sources: dataset cross-reference: citation-mining-vegetable-fruit-gaps-cass-overnight1.json ('Dingras Multiple Purple Eggplant' and 'Arka Sheel Brinjal' entries)

name: Arka Nidhi Brinjal
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, well-drained soil once nights stay reliably above 55°F; this is a long-season variety best suited to climates with an extended warm growing period.
directions: Developed by the Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR) in Bangalore from a cross of Dingras Multiple Purple and Arka Sheel, Arka Nidhi is a tall, well-branched brinjal bred for resistance to bacterial wilt, a disease that devastates many eggplant plantings in warm, humid regions. Its medium-long fruits have glossy blue-black-purple skin and a green-purple calyx, borne in clusters across two main flushes of production, with tender flesh whose seeds mature slowly, keeping bitterness low even in larger fruit. The dark purple young stems and purple-veined foliage make the plants easy to distinguish in a mixed vegetable bed. Because it is a longer-season type, give it the fullest possible warm window and consistent moisture to reach its full, heavy-bearing potential.

name: Arka Sheel Brinjal
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil once nights stay above 55F. Arka Sheel is a long-season, open-pollinated IIHR Bangalore release needing the fullest possible warm window to reach its 150-160 day picking stage.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Arka Sheel is a tall, open-pollinated brinjal from the Indian Institute of Horticultural Research (IIHR), Bangalore, with green leaves showing a purple tinge at the base when young and solitary purple flowers. Its medium-long fruit has deep, shining purple skin, reaching picking stage in 150-160 days with trial yields around 38 t/ha. Beyond its own cultivation, Arka Sheel is notable as a key parent — crossed with 'Dingras Multiple Purple' — behind IIHR's bacterial-wilt-resistant brinjal lineup, including Arka Nidhi, Arka Neelkanth, and Arka Keshav.
sources: IIHR (Indian Institute of Horticultural Research) — Arka Sheel variety profile
IIHR — Brinjal Arka Nidhi / Arka Neelkanth / Arka Keshav pedigree records

name: Arkansas Blackeye #1 Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed; this medium bush with no basal runners suits conventional row spacing.
directions: Arkansas Blackeye #1 was the first blackeye-type southern pea released specifically for commercial production in Arkansas, developed through the University of Arkansas cowpea breeding program. It forms a medium-sized bush, 20-26 inches tall with no basal runners, suited to conventional or narrow-row planting. Seeds carry a distinct, medium-sized black eye similar to California Blackeye No. 5, and the variety matures a few days earlier than Coronet or Pinkeye Purple Hull-BVR, typically 60-70 days from sowing.
sources: University of Arkansas cowpea breeding program

name: Arkansas Traveler Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes. In zone 9 this is an outstanding choice for both spring and fall seasons; plant a second crop in late July or August for fall harvest. Arkansas Traveler is notably heat-tolerant and continues setting fruit at temperatures where most tomatoes drop blossoms.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in warm (70–85°F) starting mix; transplant to full sun after frost risk passes; Arkansas Traveler is the quintessential heat-tolerant Southern heirloom, developed at the University of Arkansas and introduced around 1939 as a reliable producer through the oppressive midsummer heat of the South and Gulf Coast that causes most other tomatoes to drop blossoms and go dormant. The indeterminate vines produce medium to large (6–8 oz) pink, globe-shaped fruits with mild, low-acid flavor, thin skin, and very good crack resistance — exactly the qualities that make it a top recommendation for zone 8–10 gardeners frustrated by summer tomato failure. The meaty, juicy flesh has classic sweet tomato flavor without sharp acidity. A dependable heirloom for hot climates: one of the best-adapted tomatoes for gardens where summer heat is the limiting factor.
sources: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service

name: Arledge Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: A rare, pre-industrial Louisiana heirloom also sold as 'Louisiana Hots,' bearing 2-3 inch conical pods that ripen green to orange to red on compact 12-18 inch plants. Thick flesh gives it good drying and powder character with a Tabasco-like flavor and heat a notch above jalapeno. It thrives in Gulf humidity and sets fruit reliably through long hot summers; harvest red for maximum flavor or dry whole pods on the stem for a Cajun-style pepper flake.

name: Armageddon Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed.
directions: A commercially bred superhot introduced to the UK market in 2019 and selected for faster, more reliable production than most Capsicum chinense superhots. Compact, upright plants bear small, roughly 2-inch pods that ripen quickly and pack around 1.3 million Scoville units of heat. The shorter 75-to-95-day maturity window makes it more practical for cooler or shorter-season gardens than many superhot types. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture and stake lightly if plants become top-heavy with fruit.

name: Artichoke Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves 2 inches deep in October–November in zone 9; Artichoke types are adaptable softneck garlics that perform in a wide range of climates from cold zone 4 to warm zone 9. They are the garlic most commonly sold in grocery stores and braided in kitchens. Named varieties include California Early, California Late, Inchelium Red, and Red Toch.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Artichoke garlic (named for its overlapping layers of cloves resembling an artichoke) is the most widely grown garlic group in the world and the standard garlic of commercial production.
