The large, white to purple-streaked bulbs contain multiple layers of cloves (10–20 per head) with a mild to moderately pungent flavor that is the familiar 'standard' garlic taste of commerce. Artichoke types are softneck garlics (no central flower stalk), making them the type used for braiding and one of the longer-storing types. In zone 9, Artichoke types perform better than most Hardneck varieties (Rocambole, Porcelain, Purple Stripe) because they require somewhat less cold vernalization. Named Artichoke varieties recommended for the South include 'Inchelium Red' (already in the dataset), 'California Early,' 'Red Toch,' and 'Lorz Italian.' Plant in fall, fertilize in late winter with high-nitrogen fertilizer, and harvest in April–May when lower leaves are dry but 4–5 green leaves remain. Cure in a shaded, well-ventilated area for 3–4 weeks.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Artichoke Garlic for the Southeast
Filaree Garlic Farm — Artichoke garlic type overview
Ron Engeland: Growing Great Garlic, Filaree Farm Press 1991
University of California Cooperative Extension — Commercial Garlic Production

name: Artwork Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in mid- to late summer for a fall crop; Artwork is a stem-type (broccolini-style) broccoli that yields a small central head followed by a long, extended harvest of tender side shoots rather than one large main head.
directions: Start transplants and set out in early spring or midsummer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Artwork is an AAS-winning stem broccoli, closer in style to broccolini than a traditional single-head broccoli, forming a modest central head that is quickly followed by a long, heavy, extended flush of slender, tender side shoots that can be harvested continuously for weeks — total yield per plant far exceeds a standard main-head variety. It is notably more heat tolerant than most broccoli, holding quality and continuing to produce shoots even as warm weather sets in, which makes it a good choice for stretching the harvest later into a Gulf South spring than most broccoli allows. Harvest shoots with 4-6 inches of stem while the small flower buds are still tight; regular picking encourages more side shoots to form. Keep soil consistently moist and side-dress with compost partway through the harvest period to sustain the long production window.
sources: All-America Selections — Artwork Broccoli winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Ashley Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed past 65°F; a second sowing in mid-to-late summer keeps slicers coming once spring vines decline in Gulf Coast heat.
directions: Ashley was released in 1956 by the Clemson Agricultural Experiment Station's Truck Experiment Station in Charleston, bred to hold up under the humidity and downy mildew pressure typical of Lowcountry and Gulf Coast summers. Vines are vigorous and medium-length, producing dark green, slightly tapered slicers 7-9 inches long with a mild, sweet flavor. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from year to year, making it a practical choice for gardeners wanting a self-sufficient summer slicer rather than a hybrid. Provide a trellis or let vines sprawl, and pick regularly to keep production going through peak heat.

name: Asian Tempest Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes so roots establish before winter dormancy; mulch heavily in colder zones.
directions: Asian Tempest is an Asiatic-type hardneck garlic that came to American growers through an Oregon gardener who obtained it from South Korea, and it has since become known for its vigorous growth and heavy bulbil production on the scape. Cloves are fewer but plump, and the flavor starts mellow when cooked but turns notably sharp and intense when eaten raw. Grow it like other hardnecks, removing the curling scape in late spring to redirect energy into bulb size, and harvest once the lower leaves begin to brown. It stores only moderately well compared to Porcelain types, so plan to use it earlier in the season.

name: Asparagus Yard-Long Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed when soil is thoroughly warm (70°F+); in zone 9 plant April–July. Yard-long beans are a twining vine requiring a trellis, fence, or support of at least 6 feet tall — they are not self-supporting and will sprawl without structure. Harvest pods when 14–18 inches long and still tender and pliable; longer pods become tough and stringy. Harvest every 2–3 days during peak production — pods develop very rapidly in hot weather. In zone 9 these beans thrive in the summer heat that stresses or stops production of common snap beans.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with sturdy trellis support; Asparagus Yard-Long Bean is a traditional variety of the Chinese long bean (Vigna unguiculata subsp. sesquipedalis), producing impressively long (18–24 inch), slender, pale green to light-colored pods that hang in pairs from the vines, resembling bundles of very long, thin asparagus spears in their pendant arrangement. The flavor of Asparagus yard-long beans is distinctly different from common snap beans — denser, less watery, slightly nutty, with a pleasant asparagus-like quality that explains the variety name. The texture holds up well to stir-frying and high-heat cooking that would make common snap beans too soft, making yard-long beans the preferred bean for stir-fries, curries, and Asian vegetable preparations where snap beans would become unpleasantly mushy. As a heat-adapted legume related to black-eyed peas rather than to common beans (Phaseolus), yard-long beans genuinely thrive in zone 9's summer conditions — producing abundantly in temperatures that stop snap bean production — making them one of the most practical fresh-bean crops for the Gulf South summer garden.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Yard-Long Beans for Florida Gardens
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Asian Vegetables for Gulf South
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Warm-Season Vegetables for Texas

name: Aspen Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is warm; a thick, sturdy stem and solid flesh give this pumpkin good field-storage life through a hot, humid harvest season.
directions: Direct sow in hills after frost danger has passed, spacing hills three to four feet apart to suit the semi-bush growth habit, which takes up markedly less room than sprawling field-pumpkin types. Aspen finishes quickly at around 95 days, producing large, solidly fleshed fruit with a rich orange rind, a thick stem, and handles that hold up well through harvest handling and shipping. Its dense flesh and sturdy rind translate into good post-harvest storage and shipping quality, useful for growers who need fruit to hold up in warm regional markets. Cut fruit with several inches of stem once fully colored and firm, cure in a warm, airy spot, then move to cool, dry storage.
sources: Cornell University Long Island Horticultural Research and Extension Center

name: Astia Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost; well suited to large containers as well as garden beds.
directions: Astia is a French-bred bush zucchini selected specifically for container growing and tight garden spaces, with silvery, deeply lobed foliage that makes the compact plant almost as ornamental as it is productive. Fruit sets close to the base of the plant, which keeps harvest easy even in a large pot on a patio, and the smooth, glossy green zucchini are best cut at about 5 inches for peak tenderness. Because it stays under 30 inches across, Astia suits Gulf Coast gardeners who want fresh zucchini without dedicating a full bed to a sprawling vine, and frequent picking keeps the early, prolific plants setting new fruit.

name: Aswad Eggplant
subcategory: small round black-purple Middle Eastern heirloom eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date, providing consistent bottom heat, then transplant into hot, sunny beds after frost danger has passed.
directions: Start seed indoors with steady warmth and transplant into full sun after the soil has warmed, since this heirloom thrives in hot climates and resents cool, wet soil. Keep watering consistent to avoid stress that can toughen the skin. Aswad, whose name means "black" in Arabic, is an Iraqi heirloom prized for its small, round, near-black fruit and dense, creamy flesh that holds up well in stews and grilling. It is a favorite among growers seeking heat-tolerant regional varieties adapted to arid conditions.

name: Athena Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Athena is widely adapted and performs well across the eastern US including the Gulf South's humid, warm conditions. In zone 9, plant April–May for June–July harvest. Athena has powdery mildew resistance — an important advantage in zone 9's humid late-spring and summer conditions where mildew often terminates melon plantings prematurely. The fruit is large (5–8 lbs), round, with heavy netting and excellent shelf life after harvest — the flesh remains firm and sweet for several days post-harvest, making it practical for gardeners who harvest and store melons rather than eating immediately. Athena requires two plants or more for cross-pollination by insects; plant in groups and maintain good pollinator habitat nearby.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil; thin to 2 plants per hill, 3–4 feet between hills. Harvest when skin shows cream-yellow color under netting and fruit is fragrant. Athena Cantaloupe is an F1 hybrid melon developed by Seminis Vegetable Seeds for commercial production in the humid, warm conditions of the eastern United States — particularly the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast commercial melon-producing regions. Athena received All-America Selections recognition for its outstanding disease resistance, productivity, and flavor in eastern growing conditions, and became one of the dominant commercial cantaloupe varieties in the eastern US melon industry after its release. The eastern US commercial melon market has distinct requirements from California production: the combination of high summer humidity, heavy disease pressure (particularly powdery mildew, downy mildew, and Alternaria leaf blight), and earlier harvest requirements create conditions where California-bred varieties with limited disease resistance often underperform. Athena's development specifically addressed the eastern market's disease challenges, with strong powdery mildew resistance and tolerance to the other major eastern melon pathogens. The fruit quality is excellent for a hybrid: large, round melons with thick, deeply netted tan skin, firm orange flesh with good Brix (10–12 typical) and genuine cantaloupe flavor, and a shelf life after harvest of 10–14 days — significantly better than most heirloom types. For zone 9 Gulf Coast gardeners, Athena's disease resistance is particularly valuable: the Gulf South's combination of warm temperatures and high humidity creates ideal conditions for foliar diseases that terminate melon plantings before maximum fruit production.
sources: All-America Selections — Athena cantaloupe AAS winner recognition
Seminis Vegetable Seeds — Athena cantaloupe F1 hybrid commercial variety notes
North Carolina State University Extension — Cantaloupe Variety Selection for Southeastern Production

name: Athens Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Athens cantaloupe was selected specifically for the hot, humid Southeast and performs reliably under conditions that reduce quality in Western cantaloupe varieties. In zone 9, plant March–April for June harvest. Reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity to concentrate sugar content. Athens cantaloupe benefits from black plastic mulch to maintain soil warmth and reduce soil moisture contact with developing fruits.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost; maintain consistent moisture during vine development and fruit set, then reduce irrigation as fruits approach full size to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip (fruit pulls free from vine with light pressure). Athens is a cantaloupe variety developed by the University of Georgia (named for the city of Athens, Georgia, home of the university) specifically for performance in the hot, humid Southeast — a regional adaptation that addresses the specific challenges of cantaloupe production in the Gulf South and mid-Atlantic coastal plain where high humidity, heat, and disease pressure reduce quality and yield in the Western-adapted muskmelon types that dominate commercial production in California and Arizona. Athens produces medium-sized (4–5 lb), round, well-netted fruits with the orange flesh, small seed cavity, and aromatic sweetness that define quality cantaloupe; it has good disease resistance to Fusarium wilt and Alternaria leaf blight. The flavor is consistently excellent even under the humid, warm conditions that cause quality to drop in less-adapted varieties. Athens is the most commonly recommended cantaloupe for home gardens in the southeastern states, where the combination of heat tolerance, disease resistance, and consistent eating quality under Gulf South growing conditions makes it the appropriate regional choice over the Western-adapted varieties that dominate seed catalogs.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Athens cantaloupe development and variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cantaloupe Production Guide
North Carolina State University Extension — Cantaloupe Variety Recommendations for the Southeast

name: Atlas Asparagus
plantingNote: Set one-year-old crowns 6-8 inches deep in a trench in early spring once soil is workable, covering gradually as spears emerge over the season.
directions: Atlas was among the earlier Rutgers all-male supermale hybrids released before the later Jersey series, bred by crossing selected male parents to eliminate female seed-bearing plants and the volunteer seedling weediness they cause in a bed. Because no energy is spent on berry and seed production, Atlas channels more resources into spear number and thickness than open-pollinated heirlooms, and it carries improved tolerance to Fusarium crown rot compared to older strains. Skip harvest entirely the first year and take only a light cutting the second spring, letting the ferny top growth run all summer to recharge the crown. Established beds can remain productive for well over a decade with an annual fall topdressing of compost.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

name: Atlas Butternut Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after the last frost once soil has warmed thoroughly; Atlas is a vigorous long-vined butternut bred to size up beyond standard Waltham-type fruit, so give hills extra room and a full season to finish.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in enriched hills after the danger of frost has passed, thinning to the strongest two plants per hill. Atlas is a large-fruited butternut hybrid that regularly produces tan-skinned squash well above the size of standard butternut types, with dense, deep orange flesh and a small seed cavity that gives a high usable-flesh ratio for roasting, soup, and processing. The long vines need a full, warm season and ample spacing to support the bigger fruit load, and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit sizing. Harvest once the rind has hardened to a uniform tan and resists a fingernail, then cure in a warm spot for a week or two before moving to cool, dry storage to concentrate sweetness.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Atomic Red Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall-through-spring harvest. Atomic Red's red color deepens significantly after cooking — the lycopene pigment that makes the carrot red is more bioavailable from cooked carrots, and the color is more vivid in roasted or steamed preparations than in raw. For maximum color development, grow Atomic Red in cool weather — heat reduces the intensity of the red pigmentation. Thin to 2–3 inches apart after germination.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil free of rocks and compaction; Atomic Red is a red-exterior, red-interior carrot variety producing the color from lycopene — the same antioxidant carotenoid that makes tomatoes and watermelon red — rather than the beta-carotene that makes standard orange carrots orange. This makes Atomic Red carrots a rare lycopene-containing vegetable that is not a tomato, with research suggesting that lycopene from carrots has similar bioavailability to tomato lycopene. The flavor of Atomic Red is less sweet than orange carrots and has a slightly more complex, herbal quality — different from, not inferior to, standard orange. The intense red color makes Atomic Red striking in mixed-carrot salads and vegetable platters alongside yellow, white, purple, and orange carrots. Like all colored carrots, the unique color is the primary appeal for market gardeners and home cooks interested in visual diversity in vegetable cooking.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Colored Carrot Research
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Rainbow Carrot Varieties
University of Wisconsin Extension — Specialty Carrot Production

name: Aunt Ada's Italian Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow at the base of a trellis or pole after last frost; pick at about 3 inches, when the outline of the beans just bulges the pod, for the best snap-bean stage.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep and provide a tall pole or trellis, since this vigorous climber produces over a long season. Aunt Ada's Italian is a family heirloom pole bean brought from Italy to Colorado around the turn of the twentieth century, prized for its dual usefulness: the flat, tender pods make excellent snap beans when picked young, while pods left to mature and dry yield a flavorful soup bean. Its productivity and reliability across a long harvest window made it a treasured keeper variety passed down within one family for generations before wider seed-saver distribution. Pick regularly for fresh eating to keep vines producing, or let the last flush dry fully on the vine for winter storage beans.

name: Aunt Gertie's Gold Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Aunt Gertie's Gold is a large, golden-orange heirloom of Southern Appalachian origin with exceptionally sweet, low-acid, deeply flavored fruits that are among the finest of any golden tomato and particularly well-suited to hot, humid Southern summer conditions.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost has passed and provide staking or caging for the tall, indeterminate vines. Aunt Gertie's Gold is a Virginia heirloom reportedly traced to a Virginia woman named Aunt Gertie; it produces very large, golden-orange, oblate to slightly irregular fruits that can weigh 1–2 pounds, with sweet, rich, complex flavor that is noticeably lower in acid than red tomatoes — making it a preferred choice for people who find red tomatoes too acidic. The color is beautiful ranging from deep gold to orange-gold, and the fruits are meaty with dense flesh and few seeds. An outstanding fresh-eating tomato; the low-acid flesh is also excellent for sauces and drying. Grow as a standard indeterminate in full sun with consistent moisture and fertility.

name: Aunt Hettie's Red Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably warm; Aunt Hettie's Red is a Tennessee heirloom preserved for decades in one family's garden before wider seed-saver distribution, and it stays more compact than many other red-podded okra strains.
directions: Soak seeds overnight before direct sowing 1 inch deep after the last frost, thinning plants to 12-18 inches apart. Aunt Hettie's Red traces back to a Tennessee home garden, where it was kept true for generations before seed-saving groups began sharing it more widely, and it is now grown as far south as the Gulf Coast. Compared with taller red heirlooms, its plants stay a manageable 4-5 feet with deep red stems and leaf veins, setting plump, meaty burgundy pods that should be cut before they exceed 4 inches to keep them tender. In blind tasting panels among dozens of okra varieties it has repeatedly placed among the most flavorful reds, making it worth growing for the table as much as for its ornamental color.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Okra Varieties
Sow True Seed — Aunt Hettie's Red Okra
The Utopian Seed Project — Okra Variety Trials
Slow Food Asheville — Heritage Food Project

name: Aunt Mary's Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after frost danger has passed, in blocks of short rows for reliable wind pollination on these tall stalks.
directions: Stewarded by an Ohio farm family since before 1850, this open-pollinated white corn was once marketed as one of the finest white sweet corns available. Stalks reach 6-8 feet and typically carry one to two ears with eight to twelve rows of large, deep kernels that turn rich and creamy when cooked, with sweetness varying somewhat ear to ear. Because it needs a full season to fill out, give it consistent moisture and nitrogen through tasseling, and plant in blocks rather than single rows for full ears. Its Midwestern farmhouse pedigree makes it a good choice for gardeners wanting to grow and save a genuinely old regional corn.

name: Aunt Ruby's German Green Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Aunt Ruby's German Green stays green when ripe — tell ripeness by slight softening to pressure, subtle yellowing of the shoulder, and an internal color check revealing amber-green flesh rather than pure green.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Aunt Ruby's German Green is one of the most famous and beloved green-when-ripe heirloom tomatoes — a large (10–16 oz), irregularly shaped beefsteak type that retains a bright, chartreuse-green to apple-green exterior color even at full ripeness, producing green flesh with amber-yellow internal marbling that makes it unique among ripe tomatoes. The flavor is exceptional: sweet, rich, spicy, and complex with a distinctive quality often described as 'herbal' or 'spicy-sweet' — quite different from the fruity sweetness of yellow types or the savory depth of purple/dark varieties. This variety is named for Ruby Arnold of Greeneville, Tennessee, who saved the seed from German origins and preserved it for decades. The green color at full ripeness challenges harvest timing: rather than using color change as a ripeness indicator, judge by gentle pressure (ripe fruits yield slightly, like a ripe peach), by the subtle yellowing of the blossom-end shoulder, and by cutting a sample fruit to check for amber-green flesh and developed seeds. Aunt Ruby's German Green is outstanding in fresh preparations where the unusual green color and spicy-sweet flavor create memorable flavor combinations with standard red and yellow tomatoes.

name: Aurelia's Verde Amaranth
plantingNote: Direct sow at a shallow depth in warm, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seed about an eighth of an inch deep in warm soil after the last frost, keeping the bed evenly moist until seedlings are established. Aurelia's Verde produces thick, sturdy stalks topped with large, pale green seed heads that yield a generous grain harvest, and it holds up well in heat with only occasional weeding and watering. Let seed heads dry fully on the plant, turning papery and lightweight, before cutting and threshing for grain. Like most grain amaranths it tolerates drought and average soil once established, making it a low-input choice for a dedicated grain bed.

name: Auroch Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost for spring harvest, and again in late summer for a fall and winter crop; resow every 7-10 days for continuous baby-leaf harvest.
directions: Direct sow into cool, fertile soil and keep consistently moist; Auroch produces large, oval, smooth, dark green leaves on an upright plant with long, sturdy stems, a habit that resists leaf damage and soil-splash from heavy rain better than more sprawling spinach types. It can be picked at any stage from baby leaf through full bunching size, giving flexibility for both quick salad greens and larger cooking leaves, and it shows strong resistance to multiple downy mildew races. It performs best as a fall, winter, or early spring crop and tolerates moderate winter cold with light protection. Cut whole plants at the base or harvest outer leaves individually to extend the picking window.

name: Australian Brown Onion
plantingNote: Start seed indoors in late winter and set out transplants about 4-6 weeks before the last expected frost date.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant hardened-off seedlings into loose, well-drained soil after frost danger passes, spacing plants to give bulbs room to expand. Water consistently during bulb development, then withhold water once tops begin to yellow and fall, curing bulbs in a warm, airy spot before storage. Australian Brown is an old open-pollinated storage onion prized for its exceptionally firm, small-to-medium copper-brown bulbs and pungent flavor that mellows in cooking, and it has a long-standing reputation among heirloom growers for keeping longer in storage than many modern hybrids.

name: Australian Butter Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills of compost-enriched soil after all danger of frost, spacing hills widely for the vigorous vines.
directions: Australian Butter is an uncommon heirloom maxima squash producing large, pale peach-orange fruit with a hard rind and dry, deep-orange flesh that bakes up dense and sweet. It needs a long, warm season and generous spacing since a single vine can cover significant ground while setting several 15-pound fruits. Harvest once the rind hardens fully and the vine begins to die back, then cure in a warm, airy location for one to two weeks before storing. It appeals to gardeners hunting for lesser-known maxima types with outstanding dessert-quality flesh and long winter storage life.

name: Australian Yellowleaf Lettuce
plantingNote: Sow directly in early spring, and again in late summer where summers are mild, harvesting outer leaves as they size up.
directions: Sow directly in early spring, and again in late summer where summers are mild, harvesting outer leaves as they size up for extended cut-and-come-again production. An Australian heirloom loose-leaf lettuce with tall, crinkled, chartreuse-yellow leaves and notable heat tolerance, it is a reliable performer where many lettuces bolt or turn bitter in warm weather. It has been preserved largely through heirloom seed exchanges as a distinct warm-climate alternative to common green and red leaf types.

name: Austrian Crescent Potato
plantingNote: Plant seed potato pieces with 2-3 eyes per piece in cool soil; Austrian Crescent is a late-season heirloom fingerling. In zone 9, plant January-February for a spring harvest before summer heat arrives.
directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil, hilling as vines grow; harvest when vines begin to die back. Austrian Crescent is a classic heirloom fingerling potato with tan-gold skin and yellow, waxy flesh, prized for its rich, buttery, nutty flavor that many consider among the best-tasting of the fingerling types. Tubers grow in a distinctive curved, crescent shape, and the plant is a reliable, moderately high-yielding producer. As with other fingerlings, the low-starch, waxy texture holds its shape well through boiling, roasting, and potato salad preparations rather than becoming mealy or falling apart. Because it is a later-maturing variety, allow it a longer season than early potatoes; harvest for new potatoes once flowering finishes, or wait for full maturity and vine dieback for larger tubers with better storage life.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Austrian Crescent variety notes
Wood Prairie Family Farm — Fingerling Potato Descriptions
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Fingerling Potato Comparison

name: Autumn Crown Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost, or start indoors 3 weeks early in short-season climates and transplant out once soil has warmed.
directions: Autumn Crown is a modern interspecific F1 hybrid bred by crossing a Crown Prince-type maxima with a butternut moschata to combine butternut's sweet, dense flesh with earlier ripening and better cool-weather set. Its more compact vines and shorter days to maturity make it a good option for gardeners in cooler or shorter-season regions where standard butternuts often fail to fully ripen. Fruit develops a classic buff-tan skin and a small seed cavity, giving high usable flesh yield per squash. Grow it as you would any butternut, but expect a slightly earlier harvest window and more reliable ripening under marginal heat conditions.

name: Autumn Frost Squash
plantingNote: Direct-sow in warm soil; long vines need room to ramble.
directions: This hybrid butternut-type squash forms blocky, deeply ridged fruit that ripen from green to a distinctive tan rind dusted with a frosty white bloom. The deep orange flesh is dense and sweet with nutty, earthy undertones similar to standard butternut but richer. Vines are heavy producers, often setting 8-10 fruit averaging around 4 pounds each. Fruit store exceptionally well, holding good quality for up to four months after curing.

name: Autumn Giant Leek
plantingNote: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; Autumn Giant is a traditional European leek bred for very large shaft size — producing enormous, thick, long white shanks weighing up to 1–1.5 lbs per plant — and timed for autumn harvest from October through December before the hardest winter weather arrives.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; sow 1/4 inch deep in trays at 65–70°F; transplant when seedlings are pencil-thick, 6–8 inches tall, in late spring. Autumn Giant (sometimes listed as 'Autumn Giant Carentan' in older European catalogs) is a traditional European heirloom leek developed specifically for the production of very large, thick-shafted leeks harvested in autumn — it consistently produces some of the most substantial, heavy-yielding individual leek plants of any variety, with shanks that can exceed 2–3 inches in diameter and 8–10 inches of usable white shank. The name refers to both the size (genuinely giant compared to most leek varieties) and the harvest timing: Autumn Giant is best harvested from September through December, before the coldest winter weather arrives, as it does not have the extreme winter hardiness of specifically bred winter leeks like Bleu de Solaise or Musselburgh. Plant deeply in a trench or use a dibble to create 6-inch planting holes to encourage long, blanched shanks; the rich, mild, sweet flavor is excellent for any leek preparation.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Vegetable Trial Reports

name: Autumn Gold Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost; Autumn Gold's most important attribute is that it turns orange on the vine before most other pumpkins, allowing harvest of fully colored orange pumpkins 2–3 weeks earlier in the fall season — critical for growers who want to offer orange pumpkins at farm stands in early-to-mid September before standard varieties are ready. In zone 9, plant May–June for a September harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills after last frost in full sun, well-drained, fertile soil; fertilize generously and maintain consistent moisture. Autumn Gold is a 1987 All-America Selections-winning pumpkin that earned recognition for addressing one of the most practically important challenges in pumpkin production: the timing gap between Halloween (when orange pumpkins are in peak demand) and most pumpkin varieties' natural maturity schedule. Standard pumpkin varieties like Connecticut Field and Jack-O-Lantern reach their mature orange color in late September to October — sometimes too close to Halloween to allow adequate display time and recovery from any early-season shortfalls. Autumn Gold was bred to turn orange earlier than standard varieties while still maintaining an acceptable carving-type form, giving growers 2–3 extra weeks of salable orange pumpkins in the critical mid-September to early October market window. The fruits are medium-large (10–15 lbs), round to slightly flat, with bright orange skin and a good handle-stem; the flesh is moderately thick and adequate for cooking in addition to decorative use. Autumn Gold's earlier orange color development is driven by genetics that accelerate chlorophyll breakdown in the skin — the fruits reach full orange color when they are still in the immature stage compared to standard varieties. A consistently valuable variety for pumpkin patch operators and farm stand growers who want to extend the salable orange pumpkin window into early fall.
sources: All-America Selections — Autumn Gold pumpkin AAS winner 1987
Burpee Seeds — Autumn Gold pumpkin variety notes
Purdue University Extension — Pumpkin Production Guide

name: Autumn King Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow in deeply tilled, loose soil in late summer for fall and winter harvest; Autumn King is a large-rooted type that needs deep, unobstructed soil to develop its full potential (roots commonly reach 10–12 inches). In zone 9, sow August–October for harvest November–February; roots left in the ground over winter become sweeter after light frosts. Requires more soil depth than other carrot types and more growing time but produces substantially larger, longer-storing roots.
directions: Direct sow 0.25 inch deep in very deep, loose, stone-free soil enriched with compost; thin to 3–4 inches when seedlings reach 2 inches. Autumn King (also sold as 'Autumn King 2') is a Berlikum/Flakkee-type heirloom carrot that represents the large-rooted tradition of European storage carrot breeding — producing very large, long (10–12 inch), broad-shouldered, tapered roots with dark orange skin and rich orange flesh that are built for cold storage and extended winter use. The Berlikum/Flakkee type was developed in the Netherlands for large-scale commercial storage carrot production and is characterized by the widest shoulders and largest root volume of any carrot type, with correspondingly excellent storage characteristics: properly cured Autumn King roots keep 4–6 months in cold storage (32–38°F, high humidity) without significant quality loss. The flavor is rich, sweet, and distinctly carrot-forward — more concentrated and traditional in character than some modern sweet hybrids, with a satisfying density and substance that makes these carrots outstanding for soups, stews, roasting, and winter cooking generally. Autumn King is the standard large storage carrot in British gardens (where it has been grown since the 1950s) and is valued throughout northern Europe for its combination of large yield per plant, excellent storage, and authentic robust carrot flavor. An excellent choice for home gardeners who want to store carrots through winter.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Carrot variety guide (Autumn King 2)
Thompson & Morgan — Autumn King variety notes
Suttons Seeds — Storage carrot variety comparison

name: Autumn Mammoth Leek
plantingNote: Long-season autumn leek; start early indoors for shanks to reach full mammoth size before fall harvest.
directions: Also known historically as the Giant of Elbeuf, this Normandy heirloom is grown for its exceptionally thick, short shanks rather than height, with broad light-green fans of foliage instead of the blue-tinted leaves typical of winter types. Start seed early indoors since this is one of the longest-season leeks available, then transplant into deep holes or trenches and hill soil progressively around the stems as they thicken to maximize blanched length. It tolerates hard frost and can remain in the ground into early winter without losing quality. The mild, completely fiber-free white flesh is especially prized for braising and gratins.

name: Autumn Wings Gourd
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed well past 70F, since cool soil causes poor germination; provide a sturdy fence or trellis so the long-necked fruit hangs and forms straight.
directions: This heirloom ornamental gourd produces small to medium fruit ringed by five or six pronounced double fins or 'wings' running from a bulbous base to a slender curved or straight neck, in cream, yellow, and green tones with occasional warting. Grow on a trellis or arbor to let the necks hang straight and the wings develop evenly, watering consistently until the vines set fruit and then tapering off as the shells begin to harden. Leave fruit on the vine until the stem browns and dries, then cure gourds in a warm, airy space for several weeks until the shell is rock-hard and lightweight. Handle cured gourds gently, since the delicate wing ridges can chip or break if bumped.

name: Avalanche Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for a fall crop; Avalanche is an AAS-winning pure-white beet that does not bleed or stain, with sweet flavor and none of the earthy, bitter aftertaste some gardeners dislike in red beets.
directions: Direct sow seed clusters 1/2 inch deep into fertile, well-drained, loose soil in full sun, thinning to one seedling per cluster once plants have their first true leaves. Avalanche is an AAS-winning beet with pure-white roots and a sweet, clean flavor without the earthy or bitter aftertaste that some gardeners and children dislike in standard red beets. Because it produces no red pigment, it does not stain hands, cutting boards, or other ingredients when cooked or pickled — a genuine kitchen convenience, particularly useful for gardeners who want to combine beets with other vegetables without turning everything pink. The greens are tender and edible as well, cooked the same way as other beet tops. Keep soil consistently moist for smooth, evenly sized roots, and harvest at golf-ball to tennis-ball size for the best texture; oversized roots can become woody.
sources: All-America Selections — Avalanche Beet winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Averre Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost when soil is reliably warm above 65°F; Averre's root-knot nematode resistance makes it well suited to sandy, nematode-prone Gulf Coast soils where sweet potatoes are grown repeatedly.
directions: Averre was released by North Carolina State University's sweetpotato breeding program and named for plant nematologist Kenneth R. Averre, reflecting its strong resistance to root-knot nematode, a major limiting pest in sandy Southern soils. It produces moist, orange flesh and rose-copper skin similar in eating quality to Jewel and Beauregard, with smooth, uniform, fusiform roots well suited to fresh-market and home use. Averre performs reliably in the hot, humid conditions of the Gulf Coast growing season and is a good rotation option for gardeners working nematode-infested ground. Cure roots at warm temperatures and high humidity for about a week after harvest to develop full sweetness and improve storage life.

name: Avonresister Parsnip
plantingNote: Long season root; in mild Gulf Coast winters can also be sown in fall for a spring harvest.
directions: Bred at England's National Vegetable Research Station specifically for strong resistance to parsnip canker, a fungal disease that disfigures roots of many older varieties in humid climates. Roots are shorter and more bulbous than exhibition types, trading some length for reliability and more uniform shape. Its disease tolerance makes it a practical choice in warm, humid growing regions where canker pressure is high.
sources: UK seed trade catalogs (Thompson and Morgan, Marshalls)

name: Avoyelles Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; released by the LSU AgCenter in June 2024, named for the Avoyelles Parish sweet potato industry, and matures in as little as 90 days, notably earlier than the 110-120 days typical of many commercial varieties.
directions: Avoyelles has light rose-to-copper, mostly smooth skin over uniformly deep orange flesh that bakes to a bright color, and was bred for southern root-knot nematode resistance. It was the top-ranked variety for total and U.S. No. 1 yield across LSU AgCenter multi-state trials leading up to its release. Its early 90-day maturity makes it a good fit for Gulf Coast gardeners who want to free up bed space sooner than Beauregard or Covington allow. As the first new LSU sweet potato variety released in over a decade, it represents the current state of the breeding program's disease-resistance work.
sources: LSU AgCenter Sweet Potato Research Station

name: Ayocote Blanco Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed, and provide tall poles or a trellis; performs best where summer nights stay relatively cool, as with other runner beans.
directions: Ayocote Blanco is the white-seeded member of Mexico's ayocote runner bean group, grown alongside its better-known black (ayocote negro) and purple (ayocote morado) siblings in highland milpa plots from central to southern Mexico. The large, plump white seeds cook to a dense, mealy texture with a mild, earthy flavor, traditionally simmered slowly with epazote and used in regional bean stews and moles. Like other ayocote beans, plants are vigorous climbers that benefit from tall, sturdy support and consistent moisture during flowering and pod fill. Allow pods to dry completely on the vine before harvesting, then shell and cure the beans before sealing for storage.
sources: CIMMYT/INIFAP Mexican bean landrace germplasm documentation

name: Ayocote Morado Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow around last frost at the base of a tall trellis or pole tepee, as this Mesoamerican runner bean climbs vigorously and rewards a sturdy support.
directions: Direct sow around last frost at the base of a tall trellis or pole tepee, as this Mesoamerican runner bean climbs vigorously and rewards a sturdy support with a long season of striking scarlet-purple flowers that draw hummingbirds. Ayocote beans have been cultivated in the highlands of central and southern Mexico since long before European contact, and the deep purple-black seeds of this particular landrace are prized in Oaxacan and other regional cuisines for their dense, meaty texture and earthy flavor once cooked. Like other runner beans, it sets pods best when nights stay cool, so growers in hot-summer regions may see reduced yields in high summer. Allow pods to dry completely on the vine before shelling for the best storage-quality dry bean.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste

name: Ayocote Negro Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with a sturdy trellis; Ayocote Negro is a large-seeded black Mexican runner bean, a staple of central Mexican cooking.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, providing a sturdy trellis or pole for the vigorous vines to climb. Ayocote Negro bears large, glossy black seeds inside long runner bean pods, a traditional Mexican dry bean valued for its meaty texture and rich, earthy flavor in stews and slow-cooked dishes, distinct from the smaller common bean species most Americans grow. As a runner bean it produces attractive clusters of flowers that also draw hummingbirds before setting pods, making it ornamental as well as productive. Allow pods to dry fully on the vine before shelling for storage.

name: Ayote Green Flesh Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost and give each hill 8-10 feet of room to sprawl; as a moschata type it tolerates humid Southern heat markedly better than most maxima or pepo winter squash.
directions: A long-vining Guatemalan heirloom, traditionally grown in highland Mayan communities, bearing modest pear-shaped fruit of around 2.5 to 4 pounds with an unusual olive-green interior rather than the orange flesh typical of most squash. The flesh has a rich, dense sweetness often compared to a well-flavored butternut, with tropical, almost fruity undertones that come through most clearly when the squash is eaten raw or very lightly cooked. Because it is a Cucurbita moschata type, it carries the same strong resistance to vine borers and heat-related disease that makes moschata squash generally more dependable than maxima or pepo types through a long, humid Gulf Coast summer. Give the sprawling vines 8 to 10 feet of space and allow the long 115-125 day season to run its full course for the best flavor development.

name: Azoychka Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Azoychka is a rare Russian heirloom yellow-orange tomato of uncertain origin brought to the Seed Savers Exchange from Moscow in the early 1990s, producing medium-sized, flattened, lemon-yellow to pale orange fruits with an exceptionally bright, tangy, citrus-touched flavor unlike most yellow heirloom tomatoes, which tend toward the sweet and bland.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained, deeply prepared soil; provide staking or caging as plants grow 4–6 feet tall. Azoychka is a Russian heirloom yellow tomato brought to American seed preservation networks from Moscow in the early 1990s and distributed through the Seed Savers Exchange; its exact origins are unclear, but it is believed to be a traditional Russian variety grown in home gardens for generations before reaching Western gardeners. The medium-sized (4–8 oz), flattened to slightly oblate, lemon-yellow to pale golden-orange fruits are distinguished from other yellow heirloom tomatoes by their flavor profile — Azoychka has a bright, tangy, citrusy complexity rarely found in yellow tomatoes, which typically run sweet and mild; the flavor has been compared to a lemon-spiked yellow tomato with good acid balance for a yellow-fruited type. The combination of mild sweetness and tanginess makes Azoychka outstanding for fresh slicing, tomato salads where both color and flavor stand out, and gazpacho. An indeterminate variety of moderate size and good productivity; excellent for any region with a long warm season.

name: Aztec Half Runner Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; half-runner habit benefits from a short trellis or light staking, though plants can also sprawl along the ground with somewhat lower yields.
directions: Aztec is a Southern heirloom half-runner dry bean, producing seeds boldly patterned in black and white that stand out in storage jars and seed-saving collections alike. Plants split the difference between bush and pole habit, sending out short runners that benefit from a low trellis or a few stakes but do not require the tall support of true pole beans. The dense, meaty beans hold their shape through long simmering, making them well suited to soups and slow-cooked bean pots in the Appalachian and Southern dry-bean tradition. Let pods dry fully on the vine, harvesting once they rattle, then shell and cure before storage.

name: Aztec Red Flour Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow 1-2 inches deep after last frost in blocks of at least 4 rows for reliable wind pollination; Aztec Red descends from Mesoamerican landrace corn grown by indigenous farmers of central Mexico for its deep brick-red kernels and fine, soft-starch flour.
directions: Aztec Red is a Mexican heirloom flour corn grown for medium-sized ears densely packed with glossy, deep-red kernels that grind into a soft, faintly rose-tinted flour used for cornbread, atole, and tortillas. Like other flour corns, its soft, starchy kernels lack the hard glassy layer of flint or dent types, so ears should be harvested promptly once husks dry and finished drying indoors before storage to avoid weather damage and storage mold. It can be eaten fresh in the milk stage as a novelty sweet-adjacent corn, but its real value is as a dry grinding corn once fully mature and cured. Isolate plantings from other corn types by distance or timing if saving pure seed, since open-pollinated corn readily cross-pollinates with neighboring varieties.
sources: The Seed Collection (Australia) — Aztec Red corn variety notes
Seed to Seed: Seed Saving and Growing Techniques (Suzanne Ashworth)

name: Azufrado Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed; common beans germinate poorly in cold ground.
directions: Azufrado, Spanish for sulphur-colored, is a pale yellow Mexican dry bean market class especially associated with Sinaloa and other northwestern growing regions, prized for its thin skin, quick cooking time, and mild flavor that made it a major commercial bean class alongside Peruano and Flor de Mayo types. Direct sow seed into warm, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed and the soil has warmed, since common beans germinate poorly in cold ground. The upright bush plants require no staking and set a concentrated crop of small, oval, pale sulphur-yellow seeds that dry down uniformly for storage. Cooked azufrado beans turn a soft cream color and are valued in Mexican cooking for refried beans and soups where a smooth, quick-cooking texture is desired.
sources: INIFAP (Instituto Nacional de Investigaciones Forestales, Agrícolas y Pecuarias, Mexico) dry bean variety releases

name: Azur Star Kohlrabi
plantingNote: Start indoors ahead of the last frost for a spring harvest, or direct sow in late summer; purple skin color develops best with cool nights.
directions: Azur Star is a commercial F1 purple kohlrabi valued for its deep violet skin, uniform round shape, and white flesh that stays crisp and mild rather than fibrous at harvest size. The uniform habit and consistent bulb shape make it well suited to both home gardens and market growers wanting an attractive bunching crop. Harvest at 2-3 inches in diameter for the sweetest, most tender eating, slicing raw for salads and vegetable trays or cooking briefly to retain its crunch. Provide steady moisture and full sun, and succession sow every few weeks for a continuous supply through the cool season.

name: Baby Bear Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, rich soil, giving vines room to run; Baby Bear is an AAS-winning small pie pumpkin prized both for sweet baking flesh and for its hull-less, easy-to-roast seeds.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vines room to spread. Baby Bear is an AAS-winning small pie pumpkin, producing round, deep-orange fruit around 1.5 pounds each with sweet, fine-grained, good-baking flesh well suited to pies, soups, and purees, and small enough to make an attractive miniature carving or decorative pumpkin as well. Its standout feature is hull-less (naked) seeds — unlike most pumpkins, the seeds lack the tough outer hull, so they can be roasted and eaten whole with no shelling required, making Baby Bear a favorite for gardeners who want a dual-purpose crop of both good-eating flesh and easy snacking seeds from the same fruit. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and color deepens, cutting the stem with a few inches attached, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before use or storage.
sources: All-America Selections — Baby Bear Pumpkin winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Baby Blue Hubbard Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Baby Blue Hubbard is a compact, appropriately sized version of the giant Blue Hubbard squash, producing 4–8 lb teardrop-shaped, slate-blue fruits with the same exceptional sweet, dry, richly flavored flesh of the full-sized type — but in a manageable size that a typical household can consume in 2–3 sittings and a vine that requires much less space.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost; Baby Blue Hubbard produces compact vines of 4–6 feet, more manageable in home gardens than full-sized Hubbard; harvest when the teardrop-shaped fruits are fully blue-gray and the skin resists fingernail penetration; cure for 2–3 weeks and store up to 6 months in a cool, dry location. Baby Blue Hubbard is a compact selection from the classic Blue Hubbard squash (Cucurbita maxima 'Hubbard') — one of the premier American heirloom winter squash varieties, famous for its distinctive blue-gray, bumpy, teardrop-shaped fruits and its extraordinarily sweet, dry, richly flavored flesh. The standard Blue Hubbard can produce fruits of 15–25 lbs or more — too large for most modern households to use in one or even several meals, requiring the awkward step of cutting up a huge squash and storing the remainder. Baby Blue Hubbard addresses this practical limitation by producing fruits of 4–8 lbs with the same culinary qualities as the full-sized type: the thick, deeply orange, dry, intensely sweet flesh that has made Hubbard squash the gold standard of American winter squash for over a century. The skin is the same distinctive blue-gray, somewhat bumpy, teardrop-shaped form of the parent variety, recognizable at a glance, and equally hard to cut open (a mallet or drop from a height is the traditional method). The flavor after curing is superb — often described as the richest, most complex flavor of any winter squash, combining sweetness with an earthy, slightly nutty character. Stores exceptionally well for 4–6 months.

name: Baby Boo Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. Baby Boo pumpkins pair well with Jack Be Little (orange mini pumpkin) for two-color autumn arrangements from a single planting space. Allow fruits to cure on the vine until stem shrivels and skin is hard. The pure white skin of Baby Boo makes it a striking element in mixed ornamental displays — it retains its white color for months after harvest when kept in a cool, dry location.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Baby Boo is a white-skinned miniature pumpkin producing small (2–3 inch), perfectly round, deeply ribbed fruits of pure creamy white — the white color makes it the natural complement to the orange Jack Be Little in autumn decorating, where the two varieties together provide the classic orange-and-white color combination of fall décor. The white skin remains crisp and ornamental for 3–4 months after harvest, making Baby Boo extremely long-lasting in decorative arrangements compared to fresh-cut flowers. Like all miniature pumpkins, Baby Boo is edible — the small amounts of sweet, dense flesh inside the tiny fruits can be scooped out after roasting in the oven. The pure white skin is unusual among Cucurbita pepo varieties and results from absence of the carotenoid pigments that give most pumpkins their orange color. Baby Boo plants are productive, often generating 8–15 fruits per plant from compact vines.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Miniature Pumpkin Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Ornamental Pumpkins
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Small Pumpkin Production

name: Baby Bubba Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow an inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65 degrees F; soak seeds overnight in warm water before planting to improve germination.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Baby Bubba is a compact, dwarf okra cultivar bred specifically for smaller gardens and container growing, staying considerably shorter than standard okra varieties while still producing a good crop of tender, dark green, ribbed pods over a long summer season. Its shorter stature also makes harvesting easier, without needing a ladder or long reach for pods higher up on a tall plant. As with all okra, pick pods young, at two to four inches, and harvest every day or two during peak production to keep the compact plant setting new pods rather than diverting energy into maturing tough, oversized ones.

name: Baby Milk Bok Choy
plantingNote: Direct sow around the last frost and again in late summer for fall harvest, sowing in succession every couple of weeks; Baby Milk matures quickly to single-serving size and is best harvested promptly before hot weather or a hard freeze sets in.
directions: Direct sow thickly and thin gradually, using early thinnings as baby greens while remaining plants size up into small, palm-sized heads. Baby Milk forms neat, compact rosettes of ivory-white stems and dark green leaves that mature quickly enough to fit into tight rotations between other crops, and its small footprint and tolerance of a partly shaded spot make it well suited to container culture on a porch or balcony. Because heads reach usable size in about a month, it is an efficient way to work fresh bok choy into partially shaded beds that would leave slower crops undersized. Harvest whole heads at the base as soon as they feel firm, since older plants lose their tender, single-serving texture.

name: Baby Pam Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; give the vines room to run, and expect several small, uniform fruits per plant.
directions: Direct sow seed in warm, rich soil in full sun after the last frost, planting in hills with ample space for the vines to spread. Baby Pam is a widely grown pie pumpkin hybrid producing small, uniformly round, deep-orange fruit around 4 to 6 pounds, prized for dense, sweet, fine-grained flesh with less watery fiber than large carving pumpkins, making it excellent for pies, purees, and soups. It sets fruit reliably and uniformly across the vine, giving a more consistent harvest than many open-pollinated pie pumpkin varieties, and its handsome, deeply ribbed miniature form also works well for small-scale fall decorating. Harvest once the rind hardens and the stem begins to dry, then cure in a warm, airy spot for a week or two before moving to cool, dry storage.

name: Backlim Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant one-year crowns into a deep trench in early spring, covering gradually as spears develop through the growing season.
directions: Backlim comes from the same Dutch breeding program that produced Gijnlim, part of a family of hybrids bred in the Netherlands for uniform, high-yielding green asparagus grown both for fresh market and for forced early production under tunnels. It sends up thick, straight, deep-green spears with dense, tightly closed tips that hold their quality well during the flush of a heavy spring harvest. Like other modern Dutch hybrids, Backlim shows good vigor and reasonably even emergence, which simplifies daily cutting on a productive bed. Give the crowns at least two seasons to establish before harvesting, and maintain full fern growth after cutting ends each year to recharge the root system for the following spring.

name: BadaBing! Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; BadaBing! is indeterminate but stays fairly compact at around 40 inches tall, so it still benefits from a stake or cage.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun after the last frost, staking or caging the vine to support fruit clusters. BadaBing! is an AAS-winning large cherry, nearly cocktail-sized tomato, bearing juicy, bright red, roughly 1.5 to 2 inch fruit with excellent flavor and strong resistance to cracking even after rain. It carries notable resistance to septoria leaf spot, early blight, and late blight, which helps keep foliage healthier through a humid season. Despite an indeterminate growth habit, the plant stays relatively compact, making it a good fit for large containers as well as garden beds; pick fruit as it fully colors for the best flavor and to keep the vigorous plant setting more.
sources: All-America Selections — Tomato BadaBing! F1 winner announcement

name: Badger Flame Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop; Badger Flame was bred by Row 7 Seed Company and the University of Wisconsin specifically to minimize the earthy geosmin flavor many people dislike in beets.
directions: Direct sow seed clusters a half-inch deep in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to a few inches apart once they emerge, since each beet seed cluster produces several sprouts. Badger Flame was bred through a collaboration between Row 7 Seed Company and University of Wisconsin plant breeders specifically to reduce the earthy geosmin compound responsible for the polarizing 'dirt' flavor many people associate with beets, resulting in roots with a notably sweet, mild flavor and a distinctive flame-like pattern of yellow and red rings when sliced. Its mild sweetness holds up well eaten raw, shaved thin, or roasted, appealing to cooks and diners who normally avoid beets. Keep soil consistently moist for even root development, and harvest at golf-ball to tennis-ball size for the best texture and flavor.
sources: University of Wisconsin-Madison vegetable breeding program

name: Bahamian Goat Pepper
plantingNote: Start on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before last frost; Bahamian Goat is the traditional small, very hot pepper used to make Bahamian goat pepper sauce.
directions: Germinate seeds at 80-85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Bahamian Goat bears small, elongated, tapering pods that ripen from green to yellow-orange, carrying intense habanero-relative heat and a bright, fruity aroma, and is the traditional pepper behind Bahamian goat pepper sauce, a fiery condiment served throughout the islands with seafood and conch dishes. The compact, productive plants bear heavily over a long warm-season harvest. Handle ripe pods with gloves and harvest regularly to keep new flowers setting.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University
Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

name: Bailey Peanut
plantingNote: Direct sow shelled seed into loose, sandy soil once the ground is reliably warm after the last frost; the long Gulf Coast summer suits this Virginia-type peanut, which needs a full season to finish its large, two-kernel pods.
directions: Sow shelled, unroasted seed 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil, hilling soil gently at the base once flowering starts so the pegs can push into the ground easily. Bailey was released in 2008 by the North Carolina State University peanut breeding program and carries partial resistance to several diseases that thrive in warm, humid Southern growing seasons, including early leaf spot, Cylindrocladium black rot, Sclerotinia blight, and tomato spotted wilt virus. As a Virginia-type peanut it produces the large, two-seeded pods favored for in-shell roasting and the classic Southern tradition of boiled peanuts, rather than the smaller kernels typical of Spanish or Valencia types. Keep soil consistently moist through flowering and pod fill, then dig the plant once the foliage yellows and cure the pulled pods in a warm, airy spot before shelling or boiling.

name: Balena Celeriac
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant out once nights stay reliably above freezing.
directions: Balena is a Bejo-bred F1 celeriac known for its relatively early maturity and large, round, smooth-skinned roots with few surface rootlets, making it a favorite for growers who want less trimming at harvest. Sow indoors and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil after frost danger passes, then keep the bed evenly watered all season, since fluctuating moisture leads to cracked or hollow globes. Strip off lower leaves and side shoots periodically to channel energy into the swelling root. Harvest once roots reach full size in fall; Balena stores well in cold, humid conditions for winter use.

name: Baltic Rose Potato
plantingNote: Warm seed tubers before cutting and let cut surfaces heal over for a day or two before planting this late-season German heirloom.
directions: A German-bred late-season variety producing oblong, medium-large tubers with red skin over deep golden, silky flesh that fries and roasts especially well. Medium-large plants are heavy yielders and show useful resistance to potato leafhopper feeding damage in addition to moderate scab resistance. Space seed pieces about 9 inches apart in-row and allow the medium dormancy period before storage sprouting begins.

name: Bamberger Hörnla Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost in light, sandy soil, which this variety's home region of Bamberg is traditionally noted for.
directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep and 10-12 inches apart in light, friable soil to let the small, knobby tubers form cleanly. Bamberger Hörnla takes its name from the Franconian dialect word for 'little horn,' describing the short, curved, finger-like shape of its tubers, and traces back to the historic market-garden plots around Bamberg, Germany, a city whose old gardeners' quarter is recognized by UNESCO for its centuries of intensive vegetable cultivation. Thin-skinned with firm, waxy yellow flesh, it holds together well when boiled and is traditionally dressed simply with butter and herbs or used in regional Franconian potato salads.

name: Bambi Romaine Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, and again in late summer for a fall crop; can be grown at tight spacing in containers because of its small mature size.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or late summer, thinning or transplanting to close spacing since mature heads stay compact. Bambi is an All-America Selections winner bred as a true miniature romaine, forming dense, upright 6-inch heads with sweet, crisp leaves in about half the space and time of standard romaine, and it holds quality and resists bolting notably longer as temperatures rise. Its small size also makes it well suited to container growing and to serving as an individual single-portion salad head.

name: Bambino Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Bambino's dwarf stature makes it one of the few eggplant types suited to large patio pots as well as garden beds.
directions: Bambino is a true dwarf eggplant, growing only 12-20 inches tall on plants with dark stems and lavender flowers, yet it sets heavy clusters of one to three small purple-black fruits at nearly every node. Its small stature and shallow root system make it a strong performer in containers, where its compact form fits tight patios and balconies as easily as a garden row. It begins fruiting earlier than most standard-sized eggplants and keeps producing steadily once established. Pick the egg-sized fruit while still glossy and firm, before the skin dulls and seeds inside begin to harden.

name: Bamboo Leaf Water Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow into warm, moist soil or a shallow water tray well after last frost; Bamboo Leaf is more heat-tolerant and needs less standing water than the broad-leaf Chinese type.
directions: Direct sow into warm, consistently moist soil or a shallow water tray in full sun; Bamboo Leaf is a narrow-leaf type of water spinach with small, slender arrowhead-shaped leaves on long hollow stems, more heat-tolerant and less dependent on standing water than the broad-leaf Chinese type grown in wet paddies. It is a tropical perennial grown as a warm-season annual outside zones 9-11, ready to begin cutting within 30-45 days and resprouting readily for repeated harvests through summer. Stir-fry quickly with garlic and chile, the classic Thai preparation phak bung fai daeng, to preserve its crisp texture.

name: Banana Boom Sweet Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out once nights stay above 55F. A heavy-yielding sweet banana type, it tends to set long tapering fruit in flushes, so steady feeding and even moisture keep plants producing through summer.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, keeping soil warm for even germination, then harden off and transplant after nights stay reliably above 55F. Space plants 18-24 inches apart in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and stake or cage to support the heavy fruit load. Pick the elongated yellow banana-type pods once they reach full size for the mildest, sweetest flavor; frequent picking encourages continued flowering and extends the harvest.

name: Banana Legs Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March. Banana Legs is indeterminate and benefits from staking or caging. The golden-yellow paste tomatoes are sweet enough for fresh eating — useful as a dual-purpose paste/fresh tomato. In zone 9 fall planting in August extends the productive season well into December.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with stake or cage support; Banana Legs is a yellow paste tomato producing clusters of elongated, banana-shaped fruits (4–5 inches long, 1–1.5 inches across) with pale golden-yellow skin that deepens to a richer yellow at full ripeness. The low-acid, sweet, mild flavor of yellow paste tomatoes like Banana Legs fills a different culinary niche than standard red paste tomatoes — the mildness and sweetness make Banana Legs outstanding for golden tomato sauces, sun-dried yellow tomatoes, and fresh eating as a snack tomato, where the sweet, non-acidic character appeals to people who find standard red tomatoes too sharp. The thick walls and small seed cavities are characteristic of paste tomatoes, making Banana Legs efficient to process for sauce and giving it a meaty, dense texture when eaten fresh. Unlike many paste tomatoes that are primarily functional, Banana Legs produces well-flavored fruits suitable for both cooking and fresh eating.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Banana Legs Yellow Paste Tomato
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Yellow Paste Tomato Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Specialty Tomatoes for Florida

name: Banana Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil in hills or rows; needs a long, hot growing season to fully sweeten.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in hills 4 feet apart, or in rows 6 feet apart, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Banana Melon is a 19th-century American heirloom named for its distinctive shape — long, cylindrical fruit up to 20 inches that closely resembles an oversized banana — with smooth yellow skin and pale salmon-pink flesh that is sweet and aromatic when fully ripe. As a winter (inodorus) melon type, the fruit has little external fragrance even when ripe, so gardeners should judge readiness by the skin turning fully yellow and the blossom end softening slightly to the touch. Its long, heat-loving growing season makes it well suited to Gulf South summers with a long, warm stretch to fully mature and sweeten.

name: Banana Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost in rich, well-drained soil; Banana squash is one of the largest commonly grown winter squash varieties, producing enormously long (18–36+ inches), cylindrical, banana-shaped fruits in pale pink-orange-salmon skin with dense, sweet, golden-orange flesh — a Western US market and home-garden staple sold in cut wedges because the fruits are too large for whole-fruit sale.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in hills or rows; Banana squash requires a long season (105–120 days) and is best suited to zones 5–11 with warm summers; in short-season areas, start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting. Banana squash is a Cucurbita maxima type producing some of the longest and heaviest fruits of any winter squash, with cylindrical, slightly curved, banana-shaped fruits typically 18–36 inches long and weighing 10–35 lbs; the distinctive pale pink-salmon to peachy-orange skin makes it instantly recognizable and it is commonly sold in cut wedges at Western US grocery stores and farmers' markets where the whole fruit would be too large for most households. The flesh is dense, smooth-textured, golden-orange with excellent sweetness and a rich, slightly nutty flavor excellent for roasting, soups, and pies. A vigorous, sprawling vine requiring considerable space (at least 8 feet in each direction); store harvested fruits in a cool, dry location where they keep for 3–6 months.

name: Bandit Leek
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost and transplant pencil-thick seedlings out for a late-season crop that will stand through winter.
directions: Bandit is an open-pollinated late-season leek bred for standing through hard freezes without splitting or losing quality, making it a favorite for gardeners who want fresh leeks well into winter rather than a single fall harvest. Trench or hill soil around the dark blue-green shanks as they grow to lengthen and blanch the edible white portion, since this variety produces very little natural bulbing and stays uniformly thick and straight. Keep plants weeded and evenly watered through summer so the stalks bulk up before cold weather triggers the hardiness that lets Bandit sit in the garden, unharvested, through repeated freezes. Choose Bandit over early-season leeks when the goal is a reliable, cold-tolerant crop to pull as needed from November through late winter.

name: Barattiere Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after the soil has warmed; Barattiere is a southern Italian heirloom melon grown for its pale green, smooth-skinned fruit, picked young and used like a cucumber rather than eaten as sweet dessert melon.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in warm, fertile soil after frost danger has passed, thinning seedlings and giving vines room to sprawl. Barattiere is a traditional southern Italian carosello-type melon, harvested immature at just a few inches long when the pale green flesh is crisp, mild, and cucumber-like rather than sweet. Pick fruit frequently while still young and tender, since the texture coarsens and bitterness can develop if left to mature on the vine. Use fresh in salads or lightly pickled, as is traditional in Puglia and other southern Italian regions.

name: Barese Swiss Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost in spring, or in late summer for a fall/winter crop in mild climates; thin to final spacing once seedlings have true leaves.
directions: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep in rows a foot apart in rich, well-drained soil; Barese is a traditional Italian chard valued for exceptionally tender, delicate leaves and ribs that stay sweet rather than turning tough or bitter even as plants size up. It can be cut young as baby greens or left to grow into full heads, and tolerates both heat and a bit of shade better than many lettuce substitutes. Harvest outer leaves from the base while leaving the center intact so the plant keeps resprouting through the season; frost actually sweetens the flavor of late-season leaves.

name: Barker's Hot New Mexico Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights remain above 55°F. In zone 9 transplant February–March for a productive spring through fall season. Barker's Hot is one of the hottest New Mexico type varieties, producing 10,000–15,000 SHU, and thrives in the heat and low humidity of zone 8–9.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Barker's Hot is a New Mexico State University-developed hot New Mexico-type chile with significantly higher heat (10,000–15,000 SHU) than standard Hatch and New Mexico No. 9 varieties, making it the choice for gardeners who want traditional New Mexico flavor with serious heat. The long, 7–8 inch fruits are produced in abundance on large, productive plants and are harvested green for roasting or left to ripen and dry red for red chile powder and ristras. Roasting mellows the heat while concentrating the flavor; roasted Barker's Hot chiles freeze well for year-round use. This variety is particularly well-suited to hot, dry climates but also performs in the humidity of zone 9 Gulf Coast with good air circulation.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — Barker's Hot Variety
New Mexico State University Extension — Chile Pepper Variety Guide
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Hot Chile Pepper Production

name: Barletta Onion
plantingNote: Direct-sow thickly around the last frost; Barletta matures very quickly into pearl-sized bulbs and can be succession-sown for a continuous supply of small pickling onions.
directions: Barletta is a short-day Italian heirloom grown for its small, smooth, round-to-flattened white bulbs, typically harvested at only three-quarters of an inch to one inch across for use as pickled cocktail onions. Because the variety matures so quickly, it is usually direct-sown and grown at tight spacing so the crowded bulbs stay small rather than sizing up into full storage onions. The thin white skin and crisp, mild flesh make it a classic choice for traditional pickled pearl onions as well as kabobs and quick-cooked dishes. Lift the whole crop while bulbs are still young and tender, since Barletta's flavor and texture are best before the papery skins toughen.

name: Barossa Fest Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Barossa Fest is an Australian-bred Dwarf Tomato Project release with bicolor red-and-black fruit, named for the Barossa Valley wine region.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Barossa Fest bears medium fruit blending red and dusky purple-black tones in a distinctive bicolor pattern, combining the rich, complex flavor typical of dark-fleshed 'black' tomatoes with the compact habit of a Dwarf Tomato Project plant, developed through the program's Australian breeding collaboration and named for the country's famous Barossa Valley wine region. Its manageable size suits raised beds and containers. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

name: Basket of Fire Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Basket of Fire is a Texas Superstar pepper bred specifically for hanging baskets and containers, with a naturally cascading habit and strong heat tolerance for Texas summers.
directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into a hanging basket, large container, or garden bed in full sun. Basket of Fire is a Texas Superstar-designated ornamental-edible pepper bred for a compact, naturally trailing habit that shows off its abundant small, upright-then-cascading fruit especially well in a hanging basket, unlike most hot peppers, which grow upright. The fruit carries substantial heat, around 80,000 Scoville units, well into cayenne-and-above territory, ripening from green through yellow and orange to red, so a single plant often displays several fruit colors at once.
