It thrives in the heat and lower humidity of a Texas summer and continues producing heavily through the hottest months when many other peppers slow down. Harvest continuously to keep new fruit setting, and water container plantings regularly, since pots dry out faster than garden soil.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

name: Bassano Beet
plantingNote: Sow direct in fertile, stone-free soil; harvest young for the sweetest, most tender roots and tops.
directions: An Italian heirloom documented in 19th-century European seed catalogs, grown for its flattened roots with distinctive pink-and-white concentric rings when sliced, milder and less earthy than solid red beets. It matures quickly, making it well suited to early spring sowings ahead of summer heat or a late-summer succession crop. Sow direct in fertile, stone-free soil and harvest young for the sweetest, most tender roots and tops, which can also be cooked as greens.

name: Bates Cereal Rye
plantingNote: Direct sow 1-1.5 inches deep in fall (September-November in zone 9) in well-drained soil in full sun; Bates is an early-maturing, winter-hardy cereal rye selection bred with good grazing tolerance and vigorous fall establishment.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed in fall into well-drained, average soil in full sun; cereal rye tolerates poor, sandy, or compacted ground better than almost any other cover crop grain. Bates is an early-maturing cereal rye selection noted for rapid, vigorous fall establishment and good tolerance to grazing or repeated mowing, making it a practical dual-purpose choice for gardeners or small farms wanting both winter forage and spring soil-building biomass. Its dense, fibrous root system scavenges leftover soil nitrogen, prevents winter erosion, and suppresses weeds, while the extensive root mass and above-ground residue break up compacted soil and add substantial organic matter when terminated by mowing, rolling, or tillage in spring, generally two to three weeks before the following crop is planted to allow allelopathic residues to break down. Cereal rye is among the most cold-hardy of all cover crop grains and will continue growing through cold snaps that stop other winter cover crops.
sources: Kansas State University Research and Extension

name: Bath's Cos Lettuce
plantingNote: Small stature suits close spacing and cold-frame culture.
directions: Sow directly in cool soil; one of the oldest documented cos lettuces, dating to eighteenth-century England and named for the city of Bath, it produces compact, upright, small-to-medium heads with sweet, buttery, self-blanching hearts. Its small stature suits close spacing and cold-frame culture, and it was historically valued for delivering a fine cos lettuce in a smaller garden footprint than larger romaines. Heirloom seed savers maintain it as a variety predating most commercial romaine breeding.

name: Bauer Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before last frost for a spring crop; Bauer is a green oakleaf-type lettuce bred for slow bolting and good performance as days warm, extending the spring harvest window further than older oakleaf strains.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently, or start transplants indoors for an earlier crop; germinate at 50-70F. Bauer is an AAS-winning oakleaf lettuce recognized for outstanding heat tolerance and slow bolting compared to older oakleaf varieties, producing a loose, deeply lobed rosette of tender, mild green leaves that hold their quality and texture well into warmer weather. It is well suited to both cut-and-come-again harvesting of outer leaves and a single whole-head cut. In zone 9, use it as an early-spring or fall crop and provide afternoon shade during any unseasonably warm stretch to delay bitterness. Keep soil consistently moist for the sweetest, most tender leaves.
sources: All-America Selections — Bauer Lettuce winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Bayhorse Gold Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Bayhorse Gold was selected in a short, high-elevation Idaho growing season and reaches maturity earlier than most buttercup-type maxima squash.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing hills to give the vines moderate room to spread. Bayhorse Gold is a golden-orange buttercup-type squash selected by a home gardener at high elevation in Idaho, prized for setting a reliable crop of 3 to 5 pound fruit even where summers are cool and the frost-free window is short. The dense, dry, sweet flesh is well suited to baking and pureeing, matching the quality of better-known buttercup strains while maturing faster. Harvest once the rind has hardened and the vine begins to die back, then cure for a week or two before moving to cool, dry storage.

name: Bayo Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow once the soil has warmed well after last frost; like most common beans it resents cold or waterlogged ground at germination.
directions: Bayo, meaning tan or bay-colored in Spanish, is one of the principal traditional dry bean market classes of Mexico, especially common in the northern and central highland states, where its small, oval, tan seeds are a household staple distinct from the pinto, flor de mayo, and peruano classes often grown alongside it. Direct sow seed into warm soil after all frost danger has passed, since like other common beans it germinates poorly in cold, wet ground. The compact bush plants need no staking and produce a concentrated harvest well suited to home drying. Cooked bayo beans have a mild, earthy flavor and a slightly mealy, tender texture that holds together well in soups, stews, and refried preparations.

name: Bayou Belle Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65F in well-drained, loamy soil in full sun; Bayou Belle is an LSU AgCenter release selected for improved resistance to soil rot compared to older Louisiana sweet potato varieties.
directions: Plant certified sweet potato slips after the last frost in well-drained, loamy to sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Bayou Belle is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release bred to combine the deep-orange, sweet flesh Gulf South consumers expect with improved resistance to soil rot and other soil-borne diseases that build up in continuously cropped sweet potato ground. Roots are smooth-skinned, uniform, and size up reliably in Louisiana's long warm season. As with all sweet potatoes, cure freshly dug roots at 85-90F and high humidity for about a week to heal skin wounds and convert starches to sugars before storing or eating; uncured roots taste starchy rather than sweet. Start with certified, virus-indexed slips rather than sprouting grocery-store roots, since accumulated viral disease is the main long-term yield killer in home sweet potato patches. Rotate planting beds year to year to keep soil-borne disease pressure low.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Potato Variety Releases
Mississippi State University Extension — Sweet Potato Variety Guide
North Carolina State Extension — Sweet Potato Production

name: Beam's Yellow Pear Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun at or just after the last frost date. Beam's is a distinct, seed-saver-maintained strain of Yellow Pear kept true-to-type through generations of hand selection.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Beam's Yellow Pear is a named heirloom strain of the classic yellow pear cherry tomato, kept distinct from the generic commercial Yellow Pear seed line by seed savers who selected it over many generations for productivity and reliable pear-shaped fruit. The small, teardrop-shaped fruits ripen to a bright, glossy yellow and carry the same mild, low-acid, sweet flavor the type is known for, making them a favorite for salads and snacking as well as for gardeners sensitive to more acidic tomatoes. The indeterminate vine is vigorous and needs sturdy staking or caging, setting fruit in long, heavy clusters over a long season. Because it is an open-pollinated heirloom strain, seed can be saved true-to-type from the healthiest, most productive plants for future seasons.

name: Bear Island Flint Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks once soil has warmed; this variety was adapted for a short northern growing season, so it suits regions with cool summers despite its tall stature.
directions: Bear Island Flint originates with the Ojibwe (Chippewa) of the upper Midwest, traditionally grown on islands in lakes such as Leech Lake where the surrounding water moderated temperatures and reduced losses to animals. Despite its tall, vigorous stalks, it was selected over generations for a growing season short enough for the northern Great Lakes region. Ears carry a striking mix of yellow, red, white, pink, and blue kernels on the same cob. Grow in blocks for pollination and let ears dry fully in the husk before shelling; the multicolor kernels are traditionally processed into hominy or ground into cornmeal.

name: Beatrice Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and set out transplants once the soil is warm and nights are frost-free.
directions: Sow indoors with warm soil temperatures and transplant into full sun after frost danger has passed, keeping plants evenly watered so the tender skin does not toughen. Mulching helps retain the consistent moisture this heirloom prefers. Beatrice is an Italian heirloom similar in type to Rosa Bianca, producing rounded to oval fruit blushed rose-pink over creamy white, with dense, mild, and notably low-bitterness flesh. It is often grown for its striking market appearance as well as its tender texture when roasted or grilled.

name: Beauregard Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, sandy loam to loamy, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Beauregard produces best in loose, deep soil — heavy clay limits tuber expansion and produces misshapen roots; raised beds with amended soil are ideal in clay-heavy Gulf South soils.
directions: Plant certified sweet potato slips (rooted cuttings) after the last frost in well-drained, loamy to sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Beauregard is the dominant commercial sweet potato variety in the United States — developed by Louisiana State University AgCenter and released in 1987 to address both production efficiency and consumer preference for the deep-orange-fleshed sweet potato that now defines the American market standard. The deep orange-copper skin over vivid orange flesh, consistently uniform tuber shape, and high sugar content that develops fully after curing represent the qualities LSU breeders targeted: a variety that performs reliably in the humid Gulf South climate while producing the attractive, sweet, deeply colored roots that American consumers prefer. Beauregard matures in 90–110 days from slip transplanting, making it one of the faster-maturing sweet potato varieties and allowing good production within the Gulf South warm season. Sweet potatoes require curing to develop their characteristic sweetness — newly harvested tubers are starchy and less sweet than properly cured ones. Cure at 85–90°F with high humidity (85–90%) for 5–7 days to heal skin wounds and convert starches to sugars. Plant certified virus-indexed slips rather than home-grown slips from grocery store sweet potatoes to avoid introducing sweet potato virus diseases that reduce yield. As a Gulf South native crop commercially centered in Louisiana, Beauregard performs with particular reliability in zone 8-10 humid conditions.

name: Beauregarde Snow Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil reaches 45F, succession planting every two weeks until temperatures exceed 70F, or sow 8-10 weeks before the first fall frost for a second crop.
directions: Named for Violet Beauregarde and bred by Michael Mazourek, these snow peas carry high anthocyanin levels that give the pods a deep purple color that holds even after cooking. Sow thickly without thinning in well-drained soil between pH 6.0-7.0, and set up a trellis since the vines need about 4 feet of row spacing to climb properly. For the best flavor, let pods swell past the usual flat snow-pea stage until small peas are visible inside before harvesting, and watch for powdery mildew as the season warms.

name: Beaver Dam Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant after soil warms; a Hungarian family heirloom brought to Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, in 1912 and listed in the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste.
directions: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant outdoors once nighttime temperatures stay above 55F, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil. Beaver Dam is a Hungarian-American heirloom brought to Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, by immigrant Joe Hussli in 1912 and is still celebrated there with an annual pepper festival; it is also listed in the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste. Fruits are large, horn-shaped, and mildly hot, roughly comparable to a pimento in heat, ripening from lime green to a deep reddish-orange and reaching 6-9 inches long on tall, vigorous plants. Harvest green for milder flavor or let fruits ripen fully red for sweeter, more intense flavor; plants are heavy yielding and adapt well to a range of climates.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

name: Beck's Big Buck Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed once soil has warmed to at least 65°F; Beck's Big Buck is a Texas heirloom bred to hold size without turning woody, so it forgives gardeners who cannot harvest every single day.
directions: Soak seed overnight and direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun; Beck's Big Buck is a Texas heirloom prized for pods that stay tender and stringless even when allowed to grow well past the 4-inch mark where most okra varieties turn fibrous, making it far more forgiving for gardeners who cannot check the patch daily during peak summer production. Plants are tall and vigorous, often topping 6 feet by late summer, and keep setting pods heavily through the worst of the Gulf South's heat once regular blackeyed-pea-type production varieties have slowed. Harvest pods at 4–8 inches for the best balance of size and tenderness, and keep picking to encourage continued flowering; a single well-fed row easily supplies a household through the summer for gumbo, frying, and pickling.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Okra Production

name: Bedfordshire Champion Onion
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or set out onion sets as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring; as a long-day type Bedfordshire Champion needs the longer summer daylight of temperate northern latitudes to bulb well.
directions: Bedfordshire Champion is a Victorian-era English heirloom maincrop onion, introduced in the 1860s-70s and still valued for its large, well-shaped, straw-yellow globes and reliable heavy cropping. Sow indoors in late winter or set out sets after the ground has warmed, spacing plants to let bulbs size up fully, and keep weeds down since onions compete poorly with neighboring growth. It is prized among long-day storage onions for holding firm for many months when cured properly, making it a staple for root-cellar keeping. Lift once the foliage has fallen over and dried, then cure the bulbs in a warm, airy, shaded location before trimming and storing.

name: Beedy's Camden Kale
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring, or sow in late summer for a fall crop and overwintering in mild climates; Beedy's Camden is unusually tender for such a cold-hardy kale and tends to self-sow readily where left to flower.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; thin or space plants 12-18 inches apart and harvest outer leaves as needed. Beedy's Camden traces to a single kale plant that gardener Beedy Parker noticed overwintering in her Camden, Maine garden in the 1980s; she saved and shared its seed for years before Fedco Seeds arranged commercial production, introducing it more widely in 2009. The semi-savoyed, ruffled, medium-green leaves are notably more tender than the true Siberian types it resembles, staying pleasant through summer heat while also surviving hard New England winters, and the flavor turns markedly sweeter after several fall frosts. Its ready self-seeding habit and strong regional pedigree have made it a favorite among Northeast market growers and seed savers looking for a genuinely open-pollinated, locally adapted alternative to hybrid curly kales.

name: Beefmaster Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Beefmaster requires a very sturdy support system — heavy cages or strong staking — due to the extreme weight of mature fruit clusters.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Beefmaster is one of the most popular extra-large slicing tomato hybrids in American home gardens — an indeterminate hybrid producing truly giant fruits averaging 16–32 ounces (1–2 pounds) or more per fruit, with the classic beefsteak form: large, meaty, low-seed, deep-red flesh with rich, balanced tomato flavor that makes it the premier choice for thick-sliced tomatoes for sandwiches and BLTs. The extremely heavy fruit size requires robust support — the vines need strong cages or stakes and should have the heaviest fruit clusters supported or tied as they develop to prevent stem breakage. Beefmaster was developed to combine maximum fruit size with disease resistance (V, F, N, T, A resistance package) that most older beefsteak heirlooms lack, making it significantly more reliable in warm, humid Gulf South climates. In zone 9, Beefmaster performs best in the spring window (February–May transplanting) when temperatures allow the large fruits to develop without excessive heat during fruit set — temperatures above 95°F can cause blossom drop and inhibit fruit development on large-fruited varieties. Consistent, deep watering reduces blossom-end rot, which can affect the large-fruited types more than small-fruited varieties.

name: Beer Friend Edamame
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed well after last frost; soybeans are sensitive to cold, wet soil and germinate poorly if sown too early.
directions: A popular Japanese edamame cultivar named for its traditional role as a beer-hall snack, Beer Friend produces sturdy, upright plants that concentrate their pod set for an unusually uniform, once-over harvest. Pods are plump, hold 3 to 4 large light-green beans each, and mature earlier than many edamame types, making this a good choice for shorter-season gardens. Harvest whole plants or individual clusters when pods are fully filled but still bright green, then blanch briefly and serve pods lightly salted for snacking straight from the pod. Because the crop ripens together rather than trickling in over weeks, it is well suited to a single big harvest for freezing or serving fresh.

name: Beit Alpha Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and August–September for fall. Beit Alpha is heat-tolerant and parthenocarpic (sets fruit without pollination), making it excellent for hot, enclosed or pest-challenged gardens.
directions: Trellis for best results; sow 3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep, thinning to the strongest when 3 inches tall. Beit Alpha is the classic Middle Eastern cucumber type — short (4–6 inches), thin-skinned, virtually seedless, and extremely crisp and sweet, with no bitterness even at room temperature. It is parthenocarpic, meaning it sets fruit without pollinator visits, and gynoecious (predominantly female flowers), resulting in extremely heavy production from compact vines. The thin skin requires no peeling and wilts less in high summer heat than standard American slicing cucumbers. Harvest frequently — the fruits reach ideal eating size within 24–48 hours in zone 9's summer heat and become puffy if left too long.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Specialty Cucumbers
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Beit Alpha
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Middle Eastern Cucumber Guide

name: Belgian Endive
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring for summer root production, then force roots in fall or winter indoors; in mild climates, sow in late summer for fall root harvest followed by winter forcing. Do not direct sow too early — chicory bolts in the long days of late spring if sown too early.
directions: Sow seeds thinly in rows 12–18 in apart in late spring; thin to 8–10 in spacing when seedlings reach 2–3 in tall. Grow the plants through summer, then in fall dig the roots (which resemble fat parsnips), trim tops to 1 in, and store in a cool, dark, humid place. To force the distinctive tight pale chicons (the white-leaved heads sold in stores), pack roots vertically in a box of moist sand, cover to exclude all light, and keep at 50–60°F for 3–4 weeks — the blanched white chicons emerge from the root tops. The bitter, tender chicons are excellent braised, roasted, or eaten raw. Never allow light to reach the forcing roots or the chicons will turn green and bitter.

name: Belgian White Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; keep the seedbed consistently moist since carrot seed germinates slowly.
directions: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in loose, stone-free soil, thinning seedlings to a few inches apart once true leaves appear so roots have room to size up. Belgian White is a long, tapered, white-skinned and white-fleshed heirloom carrot historically grown across Europe as a large, productive dual-purpose root for both the table and livestock feed. The roots often push up out of the soil as they mature, developing a green shoulder where exposed to light, and can grow considerably larger than typical orange table carrots while staying reasonably tender. Its mild, less sweet flavor compared to orange carrots and unusual coloring make it a distinctive choice for gardeners wanting to diversify beyond the standard Nantes and Danvers types already common in home gardens.

name: Bell Boy Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes.
directions: A 1967 All-America Selections winner still sold decades later because it keeps setting four-lobed, thick-walled fruit through summer heat that stalls many other bell peppers. Its large leaf canopy shades fruit from sunscald, a real asset in zone 9a's intense midday sun. Tobacco-mosaic tolerant and reliably productive in containers or raised beds along the Gulf Coast.
sources: MyGardenLife plant library - Bell Pepper Bell Boy

name: Bella Rosa Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January for March transplanting to harvest in May–June. Bella Rosa is a determinate hybrid recommended specifically for Southern gardens where diseases and heat are primary challenges.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Bella Rosa is a determinate hybrid tomato developed for disease resistance and heat adaptation in humid Southern gardens, an AAS (All-America Selections) winner that earned recognition for reliable production in difficult growing conditions. The medium-large (8–12 oz), round, firm, bright red fruits have excellent flavor — more complex and acidic than purely mild hybrids but not harsh — with thick walls and small seed cavity that make them suitable for slicing, sandwiches, and fresh preparations. The broad disease resistance package (Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, root-knot nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus, and gray leaf spot) addresses the main failure modes of standard tomatoes in humid Gulf South gardens where disease pressure is severe. The determinate compact plants (3–4 feet) produce a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks, ideal for gardeners who want a concentrated harvest for preserving, sauce-making, or sharing with neighbors. An excellent choice for zone 9 spring and fall tomato seasons where disease resistance is more important than variety novelty.
sources: All-America Selections — Bella Rosa AAS winner
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Production Guide
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomato Variety Selection

name: Bellevue Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after the last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, loamy soil in full sun; Bellevue's strong resistance to root-knot nematode and common soil-borne fungal diseases makes it a dependable choice for gardens with a history of sweet potato problems.
directions: Plant certified virus-indexed slips in well-drained, loose loamy soil in full sun after the last frost; Bellevue is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release (trial line LA06-52) prized for its smooth copper skin with few surface indentations, bright orange flesh, and moist, sweet texture that holds a consistent shape and quality from field to plate. It carries good resistance to southern root-knot nematode along with the major fungal diseases Fusarium wilt and Streptomyces soil rot, all common problems in warm, sandy Gulf Coast garden soil that can cripple less resistant varieties. Bellevue also stores exceptionally well after curing, keeping its eating quality for months longer than many other varieties, which suits Gulf South gardeners who dig a large fall crop and want it to last through winter. Cure freshly dug roots at 85-90°F and high humidity for about a week before moving them to cool, dry storage.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Potato Research Station variety descriptions
LSU AgCenter — 'Hot' Intellectual Properties sweet potato variety notes

name: Bender's Surprise Melon
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 3-4 weeks before last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 50F. Market grower Charles Bender of New Scotland, NY began breeding this melon from the 1876 variety 'Surprise' starting in 1884, eventually commanding prices many times the market rate and shipping melons to thirty-three states.
directions: Start indoors in peat pots and transplant into warm, fertile soil once frost danger has passed, giving vines generous room to sprawl. Bender's Surprise produces oblong-to-round, distinctly ribbed, coarsely netted fruit averaging 6-7 lb, with thick salmon-colored flesh and a rich, sweet, old-fashioned muskmelon flavor; rinds turn grayish-yellow at full maturity. It was later used as a parent (crossed with 'Minnesota 99-36') by Cornell breeder Henry Munger to create the Fusarium-resistant 1944 release 'Iroquois.' The historic Bender farm itself is now preserved as the Bender Melon Farm Preserve in New Scotland, NY.
sources: Mohawk Hudson Land Conservancy — Bender Melon Farm Preserve history
Victory Seed Company — Bender's Surprise Muskmelon
Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (cucurbit.info)

name: Beniazuma Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; a classic Japanese satsumaimo cultivar first developed in Ibaraki Prefecture in the 1980s and needs the full warm season to size up.
directions: Beniazuma is a Japanese satsumaimo (sweet potato) cultivar first produced in Ibaraki Prefecture in the 1980s, with purplish-red skin, firm yellow flesh, and a drier, flakier texture than typical American orange-fleshed types. Its mild sweetness and dense texture make it well suited to Japanese preparations such as yaki-imo (stone- or oven-roasted sweet potato), tempura, and sweet potato desserts. It remains widely grown in Japan's Kanto region, though acreage there has been overtaken in recent years by the sweeter Beniharuka. Curing after harvest improves both sweetness and storage life.

name: Benicarló Artichoke
plantingNote: Plant rooted offshoots in autumn in the sandy coastal soils around Benicarló in Castellón, where mild Mediterranean winters allow buds to mature from late autumn through spring.
directions: This PGI-protected artichoke from the Castellón coast produces compact, tightly closed, nearly thornless heads prized fresh across Valencia for dishes like alcachofas a la plancha. Coastal sandy-loam soils with good drainage but regular irrigation suit it best, and plants benefit from a dry summer dormancy followed by a strong autumn watering to trigger the main bud flush. Harvest the primary terminal bud first, then continue cutting smaller lateral buds as they form through winter and into spring, discarding any that have begun to open and toughen.
sources: Generalitat Valenciana Conselleria d'Agricultura landrace documentation

name: Beniharuka Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; registered in March 2010 by Japan's Kyushu Okinawa Agricultural Research Center and became the most widely grown sweet potato variety in Japan by 2022.
directions: Beniharuka was bred from a cross of Beniazuma and Kyushu No. 30 in the early 1990s and registered as a cultivar in March 2010 by Japan's Kyushu Okinawa Agricultural Research Center. It has reddish-purple skin and pale yellow flesh that turns almost melt-in-the-mouth soft and intensely sweet when baked, and by 2022 it had become the top-acreage sweet potato variety in Japan, prized by growers for high yield and by consumers for its rich sweetness and moist, sticky texture after curing and long storage. It is popular for yaki-imo roasted sweet potatoes and other dessert-style preparations. Curing and extended storage continue to raise its sugar content, so it benefits from patience after harvest.

name: Benning's Green Tint Scallop Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed in spring; pick the scalloped fruit young and small for the finest-grained, most tender texture.
directions: Direct sow after soil has warmed in spring, spacing plants about 3 feet apart in full sun; this early-20th-century heirloom produces flattened, scalloped fruit in a pale, silvery-green that sets it apart from the more common yellow and white pattypan types. It was popular in home gardens well before many modern hybrid scallop squash were developed, valued for its fine-grained, nutty flavor when picked young. Harvest the scallop-shaped fruit at 3-4 inches across for the best texture, since older fruit becomes seedy and less tender.

name: Berkeley Tie Dye Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes; the vigorous indeterminate vine benefits from strong staking and even watering to support its heavy clusters of colorful fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Berkeley Tie Dye is a modern specialty tomato bred for its vividly striped fruit, splashed with purple, green, red, and orange in a swirled, painterly pattern that makes it one of the most visually striking tomatoes a gardener can grow, with rich, complex, sweet-tart flesh to match its looks. It is a strong, productive indeterminate vine that sets clusters of medium-to-large fruit over a long season. Stake or cage plants securely for the heavy fruit load, water evenly to reduce cracking, and pick once the stripes have fully developed and fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure.

name: Berlicum Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow from early spring through midsummer in deep, loose, stone-free soil in full sun; Berlicum can be sown successively for a summer-through-winter harvest.
directions: Direct sow into deep, loose, stone-free soil in full sun; Berlicum is a classic Dutch maincrop carrot producing smooth, blunt-tipped orange roots 7-9 inches long with a small core, maturing in about 80 days. It can be sown from February through August for a continuous summer-to-winter supply and stores well once pulled, making it a dependable workhorse for both fresh eating and juicing. Thin seedlings early to 2-3 inches apart for straight, well-formed roots.

name: Berrettina Piacentina Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow into warm soil once frost has passed, giving sprawling vines ample room, and water deeply during fruit development to build dense flesh.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil once frost has passed, giving sprawling vines ample room, and water deeply during fruit development to build the dense flesh this variety is known for. Named for its distinctive tan, beret-like elongated turban shape, this traditional squash from the Piacenza province of Emilia-Romagna has long been grown for the region's celebrated tortelli di zucca, a pumpkin-filled pasta requiring dry, intensely sweet flesh. Its knobby, ridged rind and rich orange interior set it apart from rounder turban types, and it stores well through winter when cured properly. Regional seed houses in northern Italy have kept the variety in circulation for home and market gardeners alike.

name: BeSweet 292 Edamame Soybean
directions: Sow directly in warm soil after frost danger passes, giving this vigorous bush soybean full sun and consistent moisture through pod fill. Developed as a food-grade variety for the edamame trade, BeSweet 292 was one of the cultivars studied in University of Illinois machine-harvest density trials and reliably fills pods with two to three large, flavorful beans prized for steaming and salting straight from the pod.

name: Better Boy Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring crop, or start in late July for transplant mid-August for fall. Better Boy is an indeterminate that benefits from sturdy staking or caging to support 4–5 foot plants.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–75°F and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after last frost; Better Boy is a Petoseed Company introduction from the 1960s that became one of the best-selling tomato varieties in US history, consistently appearing in Guinness World Records lists for the heaviest yields from a single plant — a Better Boy at the Chattanooga Times Free Press Demo Garden reportedly produced 342 pounds of fruit from a single plant. The large (8–16 oz), smooth, deep-red fruits are meaty with thick walls, excellent rich-sweet tomato flavor, and few seeds — the archetype of what many American gardeners consider an ideal home garden tomato. Indeterminate vines continue growing and producing until frost, requiring substantial staking or a heavy-duty cage. Disease resistance covers Fusarium wilt (race 1) and Verticillium wilt. Better Boy's long production season, large fruit size, and excellent flavor have kept it among the top five best-selling tomato varieties in the US for over 50 years. In zone 9, it thrives as a spring crop and can resume production in fall after summer heat subsides.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomato Varieties
Gurney's Seed and Nursery — Better Boy variety notes

name: Better Bush Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Better Bush is outstanding in containers (at least 15-gallon) — its compact habit and sturdy self-supporting stems are ideally suited to patio, deck, and balcony growing.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Better Bush is one of the finest compact tomatoes for container gardening and small-space production — a semi-determinate hybrid that naturally stays 3–4 feet tall with sturdy, stocky stems that are largely self-supporting (minimal or no staking required), compact enough for large containers, and productive enough to provide a meaningful harvest without the sprawling, aggressive growth of indeterminate types. The medium-sized (8–10 oz), round, globe-shaped, bright-red fruits have good flavor and firm texture appropriate for fresh eating and all standard culinary uses. Better Bush carries disease resistance to V, F, and N — a standard Gulf South disease package. The compact size, self-supporting habit, and container suitability make Better Bush the first recommendation for zone 9 gardeners growing tomatoes on patios, balconies, or in raised beds where space is limited. For best container production, use containers of at least 15 gallons with premium potting mix and consistent watering and fertilization — container-grown tomatoes require more frequent irrigation and feeding than in-ground plants. Two plants per patio can provide significant summer tomato production with only 30–40 square feet of container space.

name: Bettergreen Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is warm; let a portion of the crop dry fully on the vine to see the green-cotyledon trait that keeps the dried peas looking freshly shelled.
directions: Bettergreen was developed by the USDA Vegetable Laboratory in Charleston, South Carolina from a single mutant plant found in a Carolina Cream planting, and became the first pinkeye-type southern pea with the green-cotyledon trait. That trait lets the peas be harvested at full dry maturity without fading from green to the usual tan or brown, a quality that frozen-food processors and home gardeners both prize for appearance. The plant also carries useful tolerance or resistance to cowpea curculio, cercospora leaf spot, southern blight, rust, and powdery mildew, giving it a sturdier disease profile than many older pinkeye varieties. It is a good option for Gulf Coast gardeners who want the classic pinkeye flavor along with broader pest and disease tolerance.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

name: Betternut 401 Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; the semi-bush habit tolerates somewhat closer row spacing than sprawling vine-type butternut.
directions: Betternut 401 is a commercial hybrid butternut bred by Rupp Seeds for growers who want the uniform tan fruit and deep-orange flesh of classic butternut squash without the full sprawl of open-pollinated vining types. Its semi-bush growth habit keeps vines shorter and more manageable, allowing tighter spacing and easier harvest while still producing well-shaped, roughly two to three pound fruit with a small seed cavity. The variety carries tolerance to powdery mildew and better resistance to fruit cracking than many older butternut lines, both of which support cleaner, more uniform fresh-market packouts. Cure fruit in a warm location for one to two weeks after harvest to firm the skin and concentrate sugars before storing.

name: Betternut 900 Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Betternut 900 is a later, higher-yielding hybrid update to the older Betternut 401 butternut, producing uniform 1.5-2 pound fruit.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in hills after the last frost, once soil has warmed thoroughly. Betternut 900 is a hybrid butternut bred as a successor to the older Betternut 401, holding the same compact, personal-sized 1.5-to-2-pound fruit but with improved yield, a smaller seed cavity, and tan skin over deep orange, dense flesh. Vines are semi-vigorous and set fruit uniformly, making this a reliable choice for gardeners who want small butternuts sized for single meals without the sprawl of full-size vines. Harvest once the rind has hardened and resists a fingernail, cure for one to two weeks, then move to cool, dry storage.
sources: NC State University Extension vegetable variety trials

name: BHN 444 Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before transplanting; bred in Florida for heavy paste-tomato yields under Gulf South heat and disease pressure.
directions: BHN 444 is a determinate Roma-type hybrid tomato bred by BHN Seed Company of Immokalee, Florida specifically for commercial and garden production in Florida and the broader Gulf South. It carries resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1, 2, and 3, Verticillium wilt, and Gray Leaf Spot, diseases that are common in the region's hot, humid soils, and sets heavy clusters of firm, thick-walled paste fruit well suited to sauce and canning. Stake or support the compact plants to keep fruit off the soil, and harvest regularly through the season for the best continuous yield.

name: BHN 589 Tomato
plantingNote: Transplant after all danger of frost once soil has warmed, spacing plants generously for good airflow around the semi-determinate vines.
directions: BHN 589 is a widely grown Southeastern hybrid valued by market growers and home gardeners for combining excellent flavor with a strong resistance package to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, Verticillium wilt, and tobacco mosaic virus. Semi-determinate vines set heavy clusters of crack-resistant 8-10 ounce fruit that hold shelf life well after picking. Stake or cage for support and maintain even soil moisture to minimize splitting during the humid summer fruit set. Choose this variety where disease pressure is high but you still want dependable, large-fruited flavor rather than a purely commercial round tomato.

name: BHN 602 Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and set out transplants once soil has warmed; BHN 602 was bred in Florida specifically to keep setting fruit through the high heat and humidity that stall many other slicing tomatoes.
directions: Set out transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, staking or caging to support the compact determinate vines. BHN 602 is a Florida-bred hybrid slicing tomato carrying a strong disease package — resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1, 2, and 3, Verticillium wilt, and tomato spotted wilt virus — that holds up well against the soilborne and thrips-vectored diseases common in humid Gulf South gardens. The plants produce large, firm, deep-red, globe-shaped fruit averaging 10-12 ounces with good flavor for a hybrid of its size. It is widely recommended by Gulf South extension services as a reliable heat-set variety for both spring and fall planting windows, continuing to set fruit at temperatures that cause pollen sterility and blossom drop in less heat-adapted tomatoes.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Tomato Variety Recommendations
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Vegetable Variety Selector

name: BHN 968 Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed; BHN 968 is rated among the most heat-tolerant cherry tomatoes in university trials, continuing to set fruit through the hottest stretch of a Gulf South summer.
directions: Set out transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking the compact determinate plants to keep the heavy fruit clusters off the ground. BHN 968 produces abundant clusters of small, shiny, deep-red cherry tomatoes prized for being notably sweeter and better textured than most determinate cherry types, backed by broad resistance to Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt, tobacco mosaic virus, tomato spotted wilt virus, and root-knot nematodes. Its combination of compact habit, disease resistance, and standout heat tolerance makes it a dependable producer through the peak of Gulf Coast summer, when many indeterminate cherry varieties slow down or drop blossoms. Harvest continuously as fruit ripens to encourage ongoing production through the warm season.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Tomato Variety Recommendations
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database

name: Bianca di Maggio Onion
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Bianca di Maggio is a long-day Italian cipollini type that can also be pulled young as a sweet spring onion.
directions: Bianca di Maggio is an Italian heirloom cipollini onion forming petite, saucer-shaped bulbs with papery white skin and translucent white flesh, distinguished from the more familiar golden Borettana cipollini by its pale coloring. The flavor is firm, semi-sweet, and mildly pungent when raw, and the flattened shape makes bulbs especially convenient for grilling whole on skewers or kabobs. Harvested young, it serves as a tender spring onion; left to mature, the bulbs develop good storage life for a cipollini type. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil with even moisture, since the shallow, wide bulbs are more prone to drying out than deep-rooted globe onions.

name: Bianca Riccia Endive
plantingNote: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for fall harvest. Bianca Riccia is the standard Italian fine-cut white endive for winter production, producing a naturally pale center without tying. In zone 9 the cooler temperatures from October through December provide ideal growing conditions.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Bianca Riccia (White Curly) is an Italian fine-cut curly endive producing a loose, open rosette of very finely divided, heavily frizzy white-to-cream leaves — naturally self-blanching at the center without the tying required by some other frisee types. The fine cutting and natural pale color of the interior make Bianca Riccia one of the most elegant frisee types for Italian insalata recipes and for the French frisee au lardons preparation where the delicate pale center is the centerpiece. The outer leaves, being more exposed, are darker green and more bitter; the pale interior heart is the culinary prize with its mild, slightly bitter, elegant flavor. Unlike darker-centered frisee varieties, Bianca Riccia requires little or no artificial blanching because the dense, overlapping outer leaves naturally shade the center as the head matures. In zone 9 fall planting produces heads of excellent quality through November and December.
sources: Seeds of Italy — Bianca Riccia Endive Growing Notes
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Curly Endive Types
Territorial Seed Company — Italian Endive and Frisee

name: Bianco Avorio Cardoon
plantingNote: Start indoors six to eight weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger has passed into deep, fertile soil; Bianco Avorio's leaves are spineless and easy to handle compared with traditional spiny cardoons.
directions: Bianco Avorio, also sold as Ivory White cardoon, is an Italian heirloom selected for thick, meaty, ivory-pale leaf ribs and finely cut, nearly spineless silvery foliage that makes it almost as easy to handle as a thistle-free vegetable. The tall, architectural clump is ornamental in its own right even where it is not harvested, with deeply lobed gray-green leaves on stout stalks. About two weeks before harvest, blanch the bundled stalks by wrapping them in cardboard, newspaper, or straw to exclude light and mellow their flavor and texture, then cut the stalks at the base once pale and tender. In hot, humid, mild-winter climates like the Gulf Coast, cardoon is best grown as a cool-season annual started in fall or very early spring, since summer heat makes stalks tough and bitter and plants rarely overwinter as true perennials outside Mediterranean-type climates.

name: Bibb Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring; Bibb lettuce is a Kentucky heirloom developed by Jack Bibb of Frankfort around 1865, a butterhead type producing small, loose, cupped heads of buttery, sweet, tender leaves — the definitive American butterhead lettuce and considered by many the most flavorful lettuce for salads.
directions: Sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring in fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil; thin to 9–12 inches and harvest the whole head when the center begins to feel firm. Bibb lettuce was developed by amateur horticulturist Jack Bibb of Frankfort, Kentucky around 1865 and was distributed to neighbors and friends for decades before entering commercial seed trade; it is a butterhead-type lettuce producing small, loose, semi-cupped heads of exceptionally tender, silky, buttery leaves with a mild, sweet, distinctive flavor that many consider the finest of any lettuce for raw salads. The original Limestone Bibb (named for the limestone water of Kentucky) is more delicate and refined than commercial butterhead varieties but slightly slower and less uniform; it is the 'real' Bibb for flavor purists. Modern hybrid butterhead varieties ('Boston,' 'Summer Bibb,' etc.) are improvements in yield and bolt-resistance but lack some of the exceptional flavor of the true heritage Bibb.
sources: Weaver, William Woys. Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

name: Bicolor Pear Gourd
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is warm and frost risk has passed; train the vigorous vines up a trellis to keep the small fruit clean and well shaped.
directions: This classic heirloom gourd bears abundant small pear-shaped fruit, typically 2-3 inches long, with a green lower half and yellow upper half divided by cream streaking. Vines are vigorous and productive, so plan on a trellis or fence for cleaner fruit and easier harvest. Water regularly through bloom and fruit set, then reduce moisture as fruit approach full size to encourage the rind to toughen. Harvest once the shell resists denting, and cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location for two to three weeks until lightweight and hard, ready for autumn display or craft use.

name: Bienville Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips after last frost into warm, sandy-loam, well-drained ridges; Bienville was bred for exactly this kind of lighter-textured soil common across the Gulf Coast's sandier parishes and counties.
directions: Grow Bienville much as you would its close relative Beauregard, since the two orange-fleshed varieties are nearly identical at the table; Bienville's main advantage is its stronger resistance to southern root-knot nematode, the soil pest that plagues light, sandy ground. Released by the LSU AgCenter in 2002 and awarded a U.S. plant patent, Bienville was developed by breeder Don La Bonte specifically to give growers in nematode-prone sandy-loam parishes a lower-input alternative to standard commercial types. Vines are vigorous and sprawling, so allow generous row spacing or let them run into surrounding open ground. Harvest before the first fall cold snap and cure roots in a warm, humid location for about a week to improve storage life and sweetness.
sources: LSU AgCenter sweet potato variety patent and release records
LSU AgCenter publications on sweet potato patents (first US sweet potato patents awarded)
LSU AgCenter Sweet Potato Research Station profile

name: Bierzo Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since fruit needs a long warm season to fully ripen red before the traditional wood-smoke drying that gives this León variety its character.
directions: Grown in the Bierzo district of León, this mild, thick-walled red pepper is the raw material for pimentón de Bierzo, a smoked paprika cured over oak and chestnut wood fires rather than sun-dried as in Murcia. Let fruit ripen fully to deep red on the plant before harvest, since underripe pods lack the sugar needed to develop the variety's characteristic sweet, smoky depth once dried and ground. After picking, fruit is traditionally slow-smoked over several days, then ground to a fine powder; home growers without smoking facilities can still dry pods whole for a milder, sweet paprika substitute.
sources: European Commission PDO/PGI Register — Pimentón de Bierzo
Consejo Regulador de la Denominación de Origen Protegida Pimentón de Bierzo

name: Big Beef Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Big Beef is an All-America Selections winner hybrid that combines the large, meaty fruit of a beefsteak with broad disease resistance and consistent productivity — one of the most widely grown large-fruited tomatoes in American home gardens.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost and provide sturdy caging or staking for the vigorous indeterminate vines, which can reach 6 feet or more. Big Beef was introduced by Seminis Vegetable Seeds and won the All-America Selections award in 1994 — it has since become one of the best-selling tomato varieties in the United States, valued for combining the large size and exceptional flavor of old-fashioned beefsteak types with outstanding disease resistance (Verticillium and Fusarium wilt, nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus) that makes it more reliable across a wide range of climates and conditions. Fruits are large (8–12 oz or more), round to slightly oblate, meaty with few seeds and small blossom scars, and richly flavored — among the best-tasting large hybrid tomatoes available. Widely adaptable from cool northern gardens to Gulf Coast conditions.

name: Big Bertha Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Big Bertha's exceptional fruit size benefits from consistent fertility — apply balanced fertilizer at transplanting and again when fruits begin to size up for maximum development.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Big Bertha is one of the largest bell pepper varieties in general cultivation — producing extra-large, four-lobed fruits 7 inches long and 3.5–4 inches wide with very thick, crunchy walls and excellent sweet flavor. The enormous fruit size makes Big Bertha outstanding for stuffed pepper preparations where the cavity size determines how much filling can be used, and for slicing use where individual slices are large, substantial, and visually impressive. Big Bertha is a hybrid variety with disease resistance that includes tolerance to tobacco mosaic virus — an important practical quality in zone 9 gardens where virus pressure is a consistent challenge for sweet peppers. Fruits ripen from green to red, with the sweet flavor deepening and vitamin C content increasing significantly as the pepper fully ripens red. However, the thick-walled green stage is also excellent for fresh use. Big Bertha plants are vigorous and produce prolifically through the long Gulf South pepper growing season. The combination of extra-large fruit, good disease tolerance, and excellent fresh-eating quality makes Big Bertha one of the most popular large-fruited bell pepper varieties in American home gardening. Support plants with a stake or cage as the heavy fruits can cause branches to break.

name: Big Boston Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, and again in late summer for a fall crop; Big Boston is an improved, larger-headed selection of the older Boston Market butterhead type introduced in the late 19th century.
directions: Big Boston is a large-headed American butterhead heirloom from the late 19th century, bred as a bigger-growing improvement on the older Boston Market lettuce. Direct sow seed shallowly in cool, fertile soil in early spring, thinning plants to give heads 10 to 12 inches of room to fully round out. Outer leaves often blush bronze-red at the margins in cool weather, wrapping a pale, buttery, well-blanched heart that holds its quality longer than many smaller butterheads. Harvest whole heads once firm, or pull outer leaves individually for an extended cut-and-come-again harvest.

name: Big Boy Purple Hull Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past last frost; Big Boy is a long-podded purple hull southern pea valued for heavy yields of large, light tan peas packed into extra-long pods.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun once all frost danger has passed; Big Boy, also sold as Texas Big Boy, is a widely grown Southern purple hull pea prized for its unusually long pods, commonly eight inches or more, each packed with thirteen to sixteen large, light tan peas that give the variety its name and make shelling notably efficient for the yield. The semi-bush vines are heat- and drought-tolerant once established and, like other cowpeas, fix nitrogen in the soil, benefiting whatever crop follows. Harvest pods at the green shelling stage for fresh purple hull peas with excellent flavor, or let pods dry fully on the vine for a stored dry pea; pick regularly to keep plants setting new pods through the heat of summer.
sources: University of Florida/UF Seeds variety notes

name: Big Boy Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun after the last frost date; in zone 9 (Houston/New Orleans area), transplant in mid-February for spring production before summer heat ends fruit set.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after last frost; Big Boy is one of the most historically important and widely grown large-fruited tomato cultivars in American home gardens — introduced by Burpee in 1949 and still one of the most recognizable tomato names in American horticulture. The large beefsteak-type fruits typically weigh 1–1.5 pounds with deep red, meaty, flavorful flesh and the classic balanced tomato flavor — rich, full, and aromatic without the extreme acidity of some heirloom beefsteaks. Big Boy is an indeterminate, vining cultivar that continues to grow, flower, and fruit until killed by frost — it requires a strong cage or staking support to manage its vigorous 4–7 foot growth. The large fruit production and classic flavor made Big Boy the standard large-fruited tomato in American garden catalogs for decades. In zone 9, tomatoes should be transplanted in mid-February for the spring window, with the goal of harvesting as much as possible before temperatures consistently exceed 95°F (at which point pollen viability fails and fruit set stops). A second planting in late August captures the fall window. Prevent blossom end rot with consistent irrigation and calcium-balanced fertilization. Better Boy is the improved hybrid successor with added disease resistance — both are widely grown.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee Company — Historical Cultivar Records

name: Big Girl Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once frost danger has passed; Big Girl is a classic large-fruited hybrid slicing tomato, a companion release to Big Boy, on a vigorous indeterminate vine.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking or caging the vigorous indeterminate vine for support. Big Girl produces large, smooth, deep red slicing tomatoes with classic rich tomato flavor on a productive plant bred with improved disease resistance over older open-pollinated slicers, making it a dependable choice for home gardeners wanting big, reliable beefsteak-style fruit for sandwiches and slicing. It sets fruit over a long season from early summer through fall in the Gulf South's extended growing window. Water consistently to prevent blossom-end rot and cracking, and feed regularly through the season to sustain the heavy fruit load on the vigorous vine.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Production

name: Big Mama Lima Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm, above 65°F, providing a sturdy trellis for the vigorous climbing vine.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F, providing a sturdy trellis for the climbing vine. Big Mama is a pole lima bean bred for large, broad, flat pods carrying big, creamy-textured seeds, giving a substantial harvest per pod compared to smaller-seeded lima types and making shelling more efficient for a given volume of beans. The rich, buttery flavor and dense, satisfying texture have made it a popular choice for Southern home gardeners who want generously sized lima beans for classic Southern succotash, butter bean dishes, and freezing for winter use. Harvest pods at the green shell stage once well filled for the best flavor and texture, and pick regularly to keep the productive vine setting new pods through the season.

name: Big Mama Tomato
plantingNote: Transplant into full sun after frost danger passes and stake early since the indeterminate vines carry unusually heavy paste fruit.
directions: Big Mama produces oversized plum-shaped fruit up to five inches long, far larger than a typical Roma or San Marzano, while keeping the dense, low-seed flesh needed for thick sauce and paste. The indeterminate vines need sturdy staking and steady watering to support the heavy fruit load without splitting. Its meaty walls and easy-peel skin make it a favorite for home canners who want fewer tomatoes to process a given volume of sauce. Pick this cultivar when you want paste-tomato texture in a fruit large enough to slice and eat fresh as well.

name: Big Max Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–April for fall harvest in August–September. Big Max requires 120–130 days and substantial space — vines spread 8–15 feet. For maximum size, remove all but one or two developing fruits per plant, allowing the plant to concentrate energy into a single massive fruit. Provide a piece of cardboard or wood under developing fruits to prevent rot where they rest on soil. In zone 9 the extreme summer heat can cause pollination failure during the hottest weeks — hand-pollination in early morning may be needed.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, very fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with ample room for the extensive vines; Big Max is the standard large pumpkin variety for home gardeners seeking impressively large fruits — a Cucurbita maxima (not the common Cucurbita pepo pie/carving pumpkin) that can reach 100 pounds or more under ideal growing conditions, though typical well-grown specimens are 50–80 pounds. The large, round, ribbed, salmon-pink to orange fruits with thick orange flesh are primarily grown for fall display and competition rather than culinary use — the flesh is edible and has a sweeter, less stringy character than standard carving pumpkins, but the enormous size and thick shell make kitchen preparation challenging. The fascination with growing large pumpkins — a pursuit that becomes genuinely competitive at county fairs and pumpkin festivals across North America — has made Big Max and its descendants the gateway variety for the hobby of giant pumpkin growing, which extends through increasingly specialized varieties into fruits exceeding 2,000 pounds. For zone 9 gardeners, Big Max must be started in time to mature before the most intense summer heat — a March planting targets a July–August harvest that avoids both late spring cold and late summer heat extremes.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Large Pumpkin Production
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pumpkin and Gourd Growing
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Pumpkin Production for Gulf South

name: Big Moon Pumpkin
subcategory: open-pollinated giant pumpkin for exhibition and carving
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 3 to 4 weeks before the last frost, then transplant once soil is warm, leaving ample space for sprawling vines.
directions: Get a jump on the season by starting seeds indoors, then transplant into rich, well-drained soil with generous spacing once frost danger has passed, watering deeply and consistently as fruit develops. Big Moon is an open-pollinated giant pumpkin variety, registered in the USDA germplasm collection, capable of producing single fruits weighing up to around 200 pounds under good growing conditions. Its smooth orange rind and classic rounded form have made it a long-standing choice for both giant pumpkin hobbyists and fall carving displays.

name: Big Orange Candy Roaster
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills 5-6 feet apart after last frost, allowing generous room for very long, vigorous vines; Big Orange Candy Roaster was selected within the Appalachian candy roaster group specifically for larger fruit and a fully orange rind rather than the salmon-pink to tan skin of related strains.
directions: Big Orange Candy Roaster is an Appalachian candy roaster strain selected for larger fruit size and a solid, bright orange rind, setting it apart at a glance from the salmon-pink North Georgia type and the tan-bronze Tennessee type within the same regionally diverse candy roaster group. Fruits are elongated to slightly bulbous with a curved neck, commonly reaching 15-25 pounds or more under good growing conditions, and the thick, dense, deep-orange flesh shares the group's signature high sugar content that intensifies dramatically when roasted low and slow. Give the exceptionally long, vigorous vines plenty of room to sprawl in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, with steady moisture through flowering and fruit development to size the large fruit fully. Harvest once the rind has hardened and the stem has dried and corked, then cure two to three weeks in a warm, dry location before moving to cool storage, where the flesh continues to sweeten for months.
sources: Sow True Seed — Candy Roaster squash varieties
Seed Savers Exchange — Candy Roaster squash heritage documentation
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Appalachian heirloom squash notes

name: Big Rainbow Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Big Rainbow is a very large-fruited heirloom requiring a long growing season — start seeds 8 weeks before last frost in zone 9 to ensure adequate development time before summer heat arrives.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Big Rainbow is one of the most spectacular large bicolor heirloom tomatoes — a giant beefsteak type producing very large (1–2 lb), irregularly shaped, heavily ribbed fruits with a stunning golden-yellow to orange base skin suffused, streaked, and marbled with bold crimson-red blushing, creating a vivid yellow-and-red bicolor display on the exterior that is dramatically beautiful when the massive fruits are displayed sliced. The cut interior reveals the full character of the variety: a yellow-gold to orange flesh with red sectors and mottling arranged in irregular patterns — each fruit slightly different in its specific bicolor expression but consistently vivid and visually remarkable. The flavor is excellent: very sweet, fruity, and low-acid with a tropical, complex quality comparable to the Pineapple tomato in style but with a distinctly different appearance — Big Rainbow's background color tends toward deeper gold-orange while Pineapple's is more lemon-yellow. Big Rainbow is a Minnesota heirloom variety believed to have been maintained by northern seed savers. The very large fruit size requires the full spring growing season in zone 9 (February–June) to develop properly before summer heat diminishes fruit quality. As with all large bicolor heirlooms, Big Rainbow plants require sturdy cage or stake support and benefit from consistent moisture and fertility for maximum fruit development.

name: Big Red Ripper Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained soil in full sun; Big Red Ripper is a vigorous, sprawling vine that benefits from a trellis or ample row spacing, and can be sown successively through midsummer in zone 8–9.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has warmed; Big Red Ripper is a heirloom Southern cowpea grown for its large, dark brownish-red seeds and rangy, vigorous vines that produce heavily even in poor, dry soil where other legumes struggle. It serves double duty as both a dry-shell eating pea, with a rich, earthy flavor good in soups and stews, and as a soil-building summer cover crop or wildlife food plot planting, since the sprawling vines fix nitrogen and suppress weeds while the abundant seed feeds deer, quail, and dove. Let pods dry fully on the vine for shell-bean storage, or harvest young green pods for fresh shelling if a more tender pea is preferred. Because vines ramble extensively, either trellis plants for easier picking or allow them to sprawl as a living mulch between wider-spaced garden rows. Extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, it needs little irrigation through a Gulf Coast summer.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — heirloom cowpea variety notes
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Southern Pea Production
USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Cowpea Plant Guide

name: Big Stem Gai Lan
plantingNote: Direct-sow 1/4 inch deep in fertile soil in late summer for a fall crop, or in early spring after the soil has warmed.
directions: An open-pollinated heirloom Chinese broccoli selected for unusually thick, crisp main stalks alongside large, deep-green leaves, giving more edible stem per plant than standard gai lan types. Harvest the main stalk when it reaches 12-18 inches tall and 2-3 flower buds are just about to open, then peel any tough outer fiber before slicing for stir-fries, where its dense, succulent texture holds up well to high heat. Side shoots regrow readily after the main stalk is cut, extending the harvest window. Its heavier stems make it a favorite for gardeners who prize the stalk over the leaf in classic garlic and oyster-sauce preparations.

name: Big Top Bitter Melon
plantingNote: Direct-sow after soil has warmed above 70°F, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early for a head start; provide a sturdy trellis for the climbing vines.
directions: Big Top produces unusually large, softball-sized bitter melon with a rounded, heart-shaped profile and thick, bumpy dark green skin that ships and stores better than slender types. Grow it on a sturdy trellis in full sun and warm, fertile soil, harvesting fruit while it is still firm and bright green, since fruit left to yellow becomes markedly more bitter and eventually splits to release red-coated seeds. Regular picking every few days keeps the vine setting new fruit through the summer.

name: Big Zac Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Big Zac is a large, sprawling indeterminate that needs heavy-duty staking and fruit slings to support its oversized tomatoes.
directions: Big Zac is a hybrid beefsteak bred specifically for producing enormous fruit, regularly topping 2-3 pounds and capable of exceeding 5 pounds under heavy feeding and aggressive pruning to a few fruit per plant, making it a favorite at state fair giant-tomato competitions. The pinkish-red, ribbed, meaty fruit has a mild flavor and relatively low seed count typical of very large-fruited types, and is best used fresh since the huge slices don't fit standard sandwiches. Feed heavily and consistently through the season, remove most side shoots and excess flowers to concentrate the plant's energy into fewer, larger fruit, and support developing tomatoes with fabric slings tied to a heavy-duty stake or cage.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

name: Biker Billy Jalapeño Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Biker Billy is an All-America Selections winning jalapeño bred for unusually long, slender fruit and earlier, more prolific production than standard jalapeños, with milder, more consistent heat.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Biker Billy, named for a television chili-pepper personality, was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for producing notably long, slender jalapeño fruits, up to 5-6 inches, considerably longer than standard jalapeño varieties, along with earlier maturity and heavier overall yield. Heat is milder and more consistent than many jalapeño varieties, which can vary widely in spiciness depending on growing conditions, making Biker Billy a more predictable choice for recipes needing reliable, moderate jalapeño heat. Fruits ripen from dark green to red and can be harvested at either stage, with red fruit slightly sweeter. Its high productivity and vigorous, disease-resistant plants make it a dependable choice for home gardens and market growers alike. Harvest regularly to encourage continued fruit set through the season.
sources: All-America Selections — Biker Billy Jalapeño Award Notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Biker Billy Pepper variety notes
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Jalapeño Variety Comparison

name: Biker Leek
plantingNote: Sow indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost and transplant once seedlings are pencil-thick; direct seeding is possible in early spring but adds 20-30 days to maturity.
directions: Biker is an F1 hybrid leek with upright, tidy foliage and shanks that bulk up quickly through the mid-early season, resisting bulbing and staying easy to clean at harvest. Set pencil-thick transplants 4-6 inches apart in fertile soil with a pH of 6.2-6.8, and hill or trench soil around the stems two or three times as they grow to lengthen the blanched white shank. It holds good eating quality even at a large size and shows intermediate resistance to common rust, purple blotch, and white tip. Harvest through summer and fall and store several weeks near freezing in a humid cooler.

name: Bilko Napa Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant in late summer for a fall crop; Bilko carries high resistance to clubroot and Fusarium yellows, two soil-borne diseases that can persist in garden soil for years, along with excellent long storage life once heads are cut.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in late summer for a fall harvest, or in late winter for an early spring crop; Bilko is a napa (Chinese) cabbage hybrid bred with high resistance to clubroot and Fusarium yellows, two persistent soil-borne diseases that can build up in garden soil where brassicas are grown repeatedly and have no cure once established. It forms tall, dense, barrel-shaped heads with crisp, sweet, pale green and white leaves well suited to stir-fries, kimchi, and salads. Beyond its disease resistance, Bilko is noted for holding well in cold storage after harvest, letting a fall crop stretch well into winter use. Cut heads when firm and full-sized, and keep soil consistently moist through head formation for the best texture.

name: Billington Groundnut
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in spring into moist, slightly acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, and set up a trellis, fence, or shrub for the twining vine to climb; named selections like Billington are propagated from tubers or cuttings to keep their improved traits true.
directions: Billington is a named selection of American groundnut maintained and distributed by small perennial-vegetable seed companies for producing larger, more uniform strings of tubers than typical wild-collected stock. Like the straight species it is a nitrogen-fixing, twining legume vine native to moist woodland edges, streambanks, and hedgerows of eastern North America, and it carries the same long food history as a staple tuber crop for many Indigenous nations and early colonial settlers. It thrives in the dappled light of a woodland margin or at the partly shaded edge of a food-forest planting, climbing eagerly over a trellis or companion shrub once established. Tubers take a full growing season or more to bulk up and are best left undisturbed until harvested in fall after the vine dies back, at which point they can be dug, boiled, or roasted like a sweeter, nuttier potato.

name: Bintje Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost in cool soil; Bintje is a late-season, high-yielding Dutch heirloom potato dating to the early 20th century. In zone 9, plant January-February for a spring harvest before summer heat arrives.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10-12 inches apart, 3-4 inches deep, in fertile, well-drained soil, hilling twice as plants grow. Bintje is a classic Dutch potato bred in 1904 and, for much of the 20th century, one of the most widely grown potato varieties in Europe, prized for its pale yellow, moderately starchy flesh, excellent all-purpose cooking qualities, and reliable, heavy yields. It is especially well regarded for frying — Bintje is a traditional choice for Belgian and French fries — while also performing well boiled, mashed, or roasted, making it one of the more versatile heirloom varieties available. Tubers have smooth, light tan skin and store reasonably well after curing. Harvest for new potatoes once flowering finishes, or let vines die back fully for mature tubers with the best storage life and frying quality.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange heirloom potato notes
Wood Prairie Family Farm — Potato Variety Descriptions

name: Bishop Crown Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil warms and frost risk has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant March–April. Bishop Crown behaves as a perennial in zone 9 and 10 — cut back to 6–12 inches in late winter and the woody base will regrow vigorously, producing earlier and more heavily than first-year plants. Mature perennial plants can reach 4–5 feet tall.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Bishop Crown is a South American aji pepper (Capsicum baccatum) with an extraordinary, immediately recognizable shape — a round, slightly flattened main body like a small bell pepper, with 3 or 4 small, prominent, finger-like lobes hanging from the bottom equator like a bishop's miter or crown. This unusual shape (also sold as 'Chapeau de Frade' or 'Balloon Pepper') is unique among peppers and makes it instantly identifiable at markets and in the garden. The flavor is fruity, slightly sweet, and aromatic — mild to medium-hot (5,000–10,000 Scoville) with the distinctive citrusy, tropical fruitiness characteristic of Capsicum baccatum. The thick, crisp walls make it excellent for fresh eating and stuffing — the hollow interior and large body are well-suited to filling with cheese, meat, or grains. The bright red color at full ripeness is vivid and attractive. In zone 9 the perennial habit allows Bishop Crown plants to develop into productive multi-year specimens.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — Capsicum baccatum Cultivars
University of California Cooperative Extension — Specialty Pepper Production
Pepper Research Review — Bishop Crown Morphology and Heat Levels

name: Bishop Crown Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Bishop Crown is a Capsicum baccatum species requiring the same germination conditions as other hot peppers, but Capsicum baccatum species can be slower to germinate than Capsicum annuum — use a heat mat and be patient. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer production.
