The distinctive three-winged crown shape is fully visible from early in the fruit's development and becomes more pronounced as the pepper ripens through yellow to orange to deep red. Harvest at green for mild heat; red ripe for full flavor and slightly higher heat. The thin walls and hollow interior make Bishop Crown unsuitable for thick-walled fresh preparations but excellent for pickling, roasting, and as a garnish where the unusual shape is displayed.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost. Harvest green for mild use or red for maximum flavor. Bishop Crown (also called Balloon Pepper, Christmas Bell, or Joker's Hat) is a Capsicum baccatum variety named for the distinctive three-pointed crown shape of the fruit — which resembles a bishop's mitre hat from above, or a three-winged balloon when viewed from the side. The fruit has three prominent shoulder lobes that extend outward with a small pendant point below, creating a completely unique silhouette among commonly grown peppers. This shape is genetically characteristic of the Capsicum baccatum species (the Andean peppers, including the ají varieties of South America), where several related varieties share the winged crown form under different names. Bishop Crown fruits measure 2–3 inches in diameter and 1–2 inches in length — small but with a visually complex three-dimensional shape. The walls are thin and crisp, the interior is hollow with minimal placental tissue, and the heat level is mild to moderate (5,000–15,000 Scoville units) — substantially less hot than habanero types but with a fruity, slightly acidic flavor characteristic of the baccatum species. The visual novelty of Bishop Crown makes it one of the most attention-getting peppers in garden displays and at farmers markets, and its mild heat makes it accessible to gardeners who want interesting pepper shapes and flavors without extreme heat levels.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Bishop Crown pepper variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Capsicum baccatum variety collection documentation
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University — Capsicum baccatum species characteristics

name: Bishop's Crown Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Capsicum baccatum varieties are slower to establish than C. annuum types and benefit from an extra 2 weeks of indoor growing time. In zone 9, Bishop's Crown often functions as a short-lived perennial, developing into a woody shrub that overwinters in protected sites and produces more heavily in its second year. Harvest at any color stage — green, yellow, orange, or red — each offers slightly different flavor intensity.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant after last frost to full sun, well-drained soil, spacing plants 18–24 inches apart. Bishop's Crown is one of the most visually distinctive peppers available to home gardeners — a South American Capsicum baccatum variety that produces fruits with an unmistakable three-lobed shape resembling a bishop's crown or mitre when viewed from above, or an upside-down hat when viewed from the side. The fruits are typically 2–3 inches wide and 1.5–2 inches tall — flat, wide, and three-winged with a central pointed lobe — and they ripen from green through yellow and orange to deep red. The three-winged shape is unique among commercially available peppers and makes each fruit instantly recognizable. Beyond the striking visual character, Bishop's Crown delivers the distinctive fruity, citrusy flavor characteristic of Capsicum baccatum varieties — sweeter and more tropical-fruity than C. annuum types with a pleasant heat in the mild-to-medium range (approximately 5,000–20,000 SHU, varying with growing conditions) that builds gradually rather than hitting all at once. The thin walls make the fruits excellent for fresh eating, stuffing with soft cheeses, or quick-pickled as a garnish. The unusual shape makes every bite a conversation starter and the fruits are genuinely beautiful sliced or whole in salads. Very productive and beautiful in the garden as an ornamental-edible plant.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Bishop's Crown pepper variety notes
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Capsicum baccatum collection
New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — Baccatum species profiles

name: Black Aztec Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least four short rows once soil has warmed, since wind pollination in isolated single rows gives poor ear fill.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least four short rows once soil has warmed, since wind pollination in isolated single rows gives poor ear fill. Black Aztec dates to at least the 1860s in Mexico and the American Southwest and was long grown as a dual-purpose corn: pick the ears for fresh eating while the kernels are still pale cream and milky-sweet, or leave them on the stalk to dry, when the kernels darken dramatically to a glossy blue-black prized for cornmeal and corn flour. Its old-fashioned, richly sweet flavor at the milk stage made it a garden favorite before modern sugary hybrids replaced open-pollinated sweet corns, and the jet-black dried ears remain popular for autumn decoration as well as grinding.

name: Black Beauty Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds (thin to 2 plants per hill) after soil warms to 70°F; in zone 9, zucchini can be planted in February–March for spring harvest and again in late August for fall harvest — summer heat reduces pollination and triggers powdery mildew.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Black Beauty is the classic standard-setting zucchini cultivar — the benchmark dark-green zucchini against which other varieties are measured, widely grown since the mid-twentieth century and still the most recognizable and most-planted zucchini in American home gardens. The compact, bush-habit plant (non-vining, unlike winter squash) produces very dark green, slightly speckled, tender-skinned fruits with mild, slightly sweet flavor and excellent firm texture. Harvest at 6–8 inches for the best eating quality — zucchini left on the plant more than a day or two at peak size rapidly grows into oversized clubs with tough skin and poor flavor. Check plants daily during peak production. Black Beauty is remarkably productive for its compact habit, typically producing more fruit per plant than the garden can reasonably consume during the peak summer weeks. In zone 9, plant in late February to March for the spring window before summer heat triggers powdery mildew and reduces production; a fall planting in late August extends the season. Squash vine borers can devastate plants — check the base of stems for entry holes and use row covers to exclude the moth. Powdery mildew appears in summer heat; newer disease-resistant cultivars extend the productive season where mildew is persistent.

name: Black Bell Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting, setting out 2-3 weeks after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.
directions: A Petoseed-bred hybrid producing round-oval, glossy black-purple fruit, named in LSU AgCenter's Louisiana variety recommendations alongside Dusky and Night Shadow as an early, heavy-setting, adaptable eggplant. It holds fruit well above ground on a compact plant, which helps reduce soil-splash disease in humid Gulf gardens. Harvest at full glossy color before seeds enlarge for best texture.
sources: LSU AgCenter / Seeds to Success - Recommended Eggplant Varieties for Louisiana

name: Black Beluga Lentil
plantingNote: Sow directly in cool spring soil a few weeks before last frost, taking advantage of this lentil's tolerance for light frost and cool growing conditions.
directions: Sow directly in cool spring soil a few weeks before last frost, taking advantage of this lentil's tolerance for light frost and cool growing conditions. Black Beluga produces small, glossy, jet-black lentils that resemble caviar once cooked, a resemblance that has made it a favorite of chefs and market growers looking to diversify beyond the common brown lentil. The low, wiry plants need minimal input and thrive in lean soil, since excess fertility encourages foliage over pod set. Harvest the whole plant once the majority of pods have dried and rattle, then thresh and clean before storing the seed in a cool, dry place.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Crop Development Centre

name: Black Brandywine Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; like other Brandywine strains, the potato-leaf foliage looks different from typical tomato leaves and the heavy fruit needs sturdy staking.
directions: Transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun after frost risk passes, and stake or cage the vine early to support the heavy fruit clusters. Black Brandywine belongs to the celebrated Brandywine family of potato-leaf heirloom beefsteaks, distinguished from the classic pink Brandywine by fruit that ripens to a deep purplish-brown to brick-red color with dark green shoulders, carrying the smoky, rich, complex, almost wine-like flavor that 'black' tomatoes are prized for. The large, somewhat irregular fruit can run smaller and less uniform than standard pink Brandywine, a common trait of this style of dark heirloom tomato, but the depth of flavor more than compensates for growers seeking something beyond a standard slicer. Water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking, and pick as soon as color and give indicate ripeness, since the dark skin can make judging ripeness by color alone trickier than with red tomatoes.

name: Black Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Black Cherry is a true open-pollinated heirloom with seed that can be saved true-to-type.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Black Cherry is one of the most unusual and striking cherry tomato varieties — an heirloom producing small (1-inch), round fruits in a deep mahogany-purple to almost black color with brick-red flesh, offering a distinctly rich, complex, wine-like flavor with chocolate-tomato undertones that is remarkably different from standard red or yellow cherry tomatoes. The dark color comes from high anthocyanin content in the skin — the same antioxidant pigments responsible for the dark color of blueberries and black raspberries — giving Black Cherry a distinctive nutritional profile alongside its unusual flavor. The complex, slightly smoky, wine-tomato flavor makes Black Cherry outstanding in raw preparations where the flavor stands alone: fresh from the vine, in caprese-style salads with mozzarella and basil, or in mixed cherry tomato platters where its dark color contrasts dramatically with red Sun Gold and yellow pear tomatoes. The indeterminate vine produces prolific clusters from transplanting through the end of the warm season. As an open-pollinated heirloom, true seed can be saved from season to season. Resistance to cracking (a weakness of many dark-colored tomatoes) is better than many purple/black tomato varieties.

name: Black Chia
plantingNote: Sow after last frost; chia is a short-day plant that flowers in fall, so it is best suited to climates with a long frost-free autumn. Black Chia is the standard dark-seeded form most commonly grown and sold commercially.
directions: Surface-sow seed on a firm, moist seedbed and barely press in, as chia seed is mucilaginous and will stick to the surface when wet; thin plants to 18-24 inches once seedlings emerge. Black Chia is the standard, most widely grown dark-seeded chia strain, producing the small, deep-brown-to-black seeds most familiar from commercial chia products, on whorled flower spikes of small purple blooms that appear in autumn as day length shortens. Chia does not respond well to transplanting and should be direct-sown where it will grow. Harvest stalks when the calyces begin to dry and before birds consume the seed, placing harvested stalks head-first into paper bags to finish drying, then shake out seed and screen away debris.

name: Black Coat Runner Bean
plantingNote: Sow at the base of a tall, sturdy trellis around last frost; grown as much for its flowers and dry seed as for snap use.
directions: Black Coat is among the oldest documented runner beans still in cultivation, with references to it in European botanical writing dating back to the 1600s, long before most modern runner bean cultivars existed. Its flowers range from deep orange to cherry-red and are heavily visited by hummingbirds, while young pods can be picked for snap use in the same way as other runner beans. Left to mature, the pods yield glossy black seeds that dry well for winter storage and cooking, giving the variety a genuine dual purpose. Because of its age and rarity, it is grown today mostly by heirloom seed savers and gardeners interested in historic bean varieties.

name: Black Coco Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost into warm soil; a compact French heirloom bean that can be picked young as a snap bean or left to mature into a black dry bean.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed following the last frost, spacing dwarf bush plants 4-6 inches apart; no trellising is needed. Black Coco is a French heirloom valued for its versatility, with dark lilac flowers giving way to slender pods that are tender and crisp if picked young, meaty and flavorful as fresh shell beans about ten days later, and rich and nutty once fully dried. Harvest pods for shelling when seeds have filled but pods are still green, or leave plants standing until pods dry and rattle for storage as dry beans. This variety tolerates both drought and cooler conditions better than many bush beans, making it a dependable choice across a range of climates.

name: Black Crowder Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has thoroughly warmed and frost danger has passed; this bush-type crowder holds its long pods up at foliage level, making it faster to hand-harvest than sprawling vining types.
directions: Black Crowder is a bush-type Southern cowpea that produces an abundance of long (6-7 inch), slender green pods tightly packed with peas in the classic crowder arrangement. Freshly shelled peas show a deep purple cast and dry to a near-black color, offering the hearty, earthy flavor Southern cooks associate with crowder-type field peas. Like other cowpeas it is notably drought tolerant and fixes nitrogen in the soil through root nodules, making it a useful warm-season cover and food crop in lean garden soil. Pods can be picked at the green-shell stage for fresh eating, canning, or freezing, or left to dry fully on the vine for long-term dry storage.

name: Black Diamond Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 70°F; Black Diamond was the dominant commercial and roadside-stand watermelon of the American South in the 1950s and 1960s, producing very large, nearly spherical fruits with dramatically dark blue-green skin and exceptionally sweet red flesh — a classic variety now prized by home gardeners and heirloom melon enthusiasts.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile, warm soil after last frost; Black Diamond needs full sun and warm nights — it performs best in zones 7–11 and Gulf Coast gardens where the long, hot summers allow the large fruits to fully develop. Black Diamond was one of the most important commercial watermelon varieties of mid-20th century America, grown throughout the South for roadside stands, truck farming, and local markets; the very large (30–50+ lbs), round to oblong fruits have an unusually dark, blue-green skin that approaches black in color and firm, bright red flesh with excellent, classic sweet watermelon flavor. The tough skin and firm flesh gave Black Diamond reasonable shipping quality in an era before refrigerated transport was universal. Now prized as an heirloom variety for gardeners wanting the authentic large-fruited Southern watermelon experience. Days to maturity of 85–90 make it best for long-season Southern and Gulf Coast gardens.

name: Black Forest Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is warm; Black Forest grows on a more restrained, semi-bush vine than full-sized kabocha types, making it a reasonable choice where garden space is limited.
directions: Direct sow seed in warm, fertile soil after frost danger has passed, spacing plants to allow the semi-compact vines to spread without crowding. Black Forest bears small, deeply ribbed, near-black fruit with dense, dry, deep orange flesh and a sweet, nutty flavor reminiscent of kabocha, and its more restrained vine habit lets it fit into gardens too small for sprawling maxima types. Each plant sets several two- to three-pound fruits that store well once cured. Harvest when the rind has hardened and the stem has begun to dry and cork, then cure in a warm location for one to two weeks to deepen the sweetness before moving squash to cool, dry storage.

name: Black From Tula Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; a Russian black tomato from the city of Tula, south of Moscow; this and similar Russian black heirlooms have become staples of the dark tomato connoisseur community for their striking color and complex flavor.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, planting deeply and staking firmly. Black From Tula is a Russian heirloom beefsteak tomato from the Tula region south of Moscow, producing large 8–16 ounce fruits with very dark brownish-purple skin and deep reddish-brown flesh similar to Black Krim but with slightly more robust structure and a complex, smoky, earthy-sweet flavor; it is among the finest of the Russian black-type heirlooms and is particularly well adapted to conditions where hot days are followed by cool nights, which intensifies the dark pigmentation. Harvest when the blossom end yields to gentle pressure and the dark color has fully developed around the equator of the fruit.

name: Black Futsu Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Black Futsu is a Japanese heirloom squash known for deeply ribbed, warty, near-black skin that fades to a warm tan-orange as it cures in storage, with dense, sweet, chestnut-flavored flesh prized by chefs.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, allowing plenty of room for the vigorous, sprawling vines. Black Futsu is a Japanese heirloom squash valued for its striking appearance — small, flattened, deeply ribbed fruit covered in a warty, near-black rind when first harvested, which fades over several weeks of storage to a warm tan-orange with a slight bloom, a color transformation that also signals improving flavor and sweetness. The dense, dry, deep orange flesh has a rich, sweet, chestnut-like flavor considered among the best of any winter squash by many chefs, excellent roasted, pureed into soup, or used anywhere a rich kabocha-type squash is called for. Vines are vigorous and productive, typically setting several fruit per plant, each running 2-3 pounds, a manageable size for a single meal without excess storage bulk. Harvest when the rind resists a fingernail and the stem has dried and corked, then cure in a warm, dry spot for two to three weeks before eating — Black Futsu's flavor and sweetness improve markedly with curing and continue to develop in storage over the following months.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Black Futsu Squash variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Japanese Heirloom Squash Varieties
Row 7 Seed Company — Black Futsu Culinary Notes

name: Black Grape Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Black Grape is a compact to medium-sized indeterminate cherry tomato that produces clusters of elongated grape-shaped fruits. In zone 9, transplant March–April. Black Grape is one of the most distinctive cherry tomatoes visually — the fruits are uniformly dark purple-black when ripe, with no streaking or green shoulders, and in good growing conditions may have a slight sheen to the skin. The dark color comes from high anthocyanin content in the skin (the same pigments that make black tomatoes distinctive), which combines with lycopene in the flesh to produce the characteristic complex, sweet-rich flavor. The anthocyanin content of Black Grape and similar dark tomatoes is higher in plants grown in high-light conditions, so zone 9's full sun intensifies both the color and the antioxidant content compared to lower-light growing environments.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and stake. Harvest when fruits are uniformly deep purple-black throughout the cluster. Black Grape Tomato is a compact indeterminate variety producing clusters of small, oval to elongated-grape-shaped fruits that ripen to a very dark purple-black color — one of the darkest small-fruited tomato varieties commercially available. The dark coloration results from high anthocyanin content in the skin (the same class of pigments responsible for the color of blueberries, eggplant, and purple cabbage) combined with the lycopene that gives tomatoes their characteristic red color. When anthocyanins are expressed strongly in tomato skin and lycopene is present in the flesh, the result is a dark fruit that appears almost black in good light. This anthocyanin content has nutritional significance — anthocyanins are potent antioxidants, and dark-fruited tomatoes contain higher concentrations than red or yellow types. The flavor of Black Grape combines the sweetness of a cherry tomato with additional complexity and depth — a rich, almost wine-like quality that distinguishes dark tomatoes from standard red types. The texture is firm and the grape shape (elongated, 1–1.5 inch) makes Black Grape practical for packing and transporting without the splitting that affects rounder cherry types. This firmness combined with the dramatically dark color makes Black Grape particularly popular at farmers markets and in restaurant settings where visual distinction is valued. The variety's compact growth habit relative to Sweet 100 and similar indeterminate cherry types makes it easier to manage in average-sized garden spaces.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Black Grape tomato dark cherry variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Dark-fruited cherry tomato variety comparison
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Cherry and Grape Tomato Variety Evaluation

name: Black Jack Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; in zone 9, spring-sow February–March and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Black Jack is a classic open-pollinated dark green zucchini grown for its vigorous, upright bush habit and dependable, heavy yields of glossy, cylindrical, deep green fruit with tender, mild-flavored flesh. It has long served as a dependable garden standard for gardeners wanting a straightforward, reliable zucchini without the complexity of some newer hybrid disease-resistance packages, performing well across a wide range of soils and conditions. Pick fruit at six to eight inches long for the best flavor and texture, and harvest every day or two once the plant starts producing, since zucchini left on the vine even briefly can balloon rapidly into oversized, seedy, less flavorful fruit.

name: Black Kabuli Chickpea
plantingNote: Direct sow around the last frost date; Black Kabuli is an heirloom chickpea combining the larger seed size of Kabuli types with a dark, near-black seed coat, valued by gardeners for its rich, nutty flavor and striking appearance in salads and stews.
directions: Direct sow seed 1-1.5 inches deep in well-drained soil once the danger of hard frost has passed, giving plants full sun and lean-to-average fertility, since overly rich soil favors foliage over pod set. Black Kabuli produces the same bushy, drought-tolerant growth habit as other chickpeas, but each pod holds one or two dark brown to near-black seeds that keep their striking color when dried, making them a favorite for gardeners who like to grow and cook heirloom bean and legume varieties not found in stores. Flavor is often described as earthier and nuttier than standard tan Kabuli chickpeas, and the dried seeds hold their shape well in long-simmered stews. Handle mature plants carefully, since the foliage and pods carry the same sticky, irritating hairs typical of the species; harvest once most pods have dried and turned brittle, then thresh and store the seed somewhere cool and dry.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Cicer arietinum germplasm resources

name: Black Krim Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; darker-colored tomatoes absorb more heat and can sometimes ripen faster in cool seasons; stake firmly — indeterminate and vigorous.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost risk passes into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Black Krim is a heirloom beefsteak tomato originating from Crimea (the Black Sea region of Ukraine), producing medium-to-large fruits with a distinctive deep brownish-red to almost black skin with green shoulders, and dark red marbled flesh with a rich, complex flavor that is earthy, smoky, and slightly sweet. One of the most striking and flavorful of the dark or 'black' tomato types. Fruits show their best color in warm weather with cool nights; in hot climates the colors may be less dramatic but flavor remains outstanding. Harvest when the skin darkens significantly and gives slightly to pressure.

name: Black Nebula Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow in loose, stone-free soil once it can be worked; deep purple color is most intense on roots grown in cool spring or fall conditions.
directions: Black Nebula is a specialty carrot bred for pigment that runs all the way through the root rather than surrounding an orange core, giving nearly black-purple skin and a deep purple interior with only a faint lighter center. Sow seed 1/4 inch deep and keep the row consistently moist until germination, which is slower and less even than with standard orange carrots. The intense anthocyanin coloring holds up well in raw preparations, quick pickles, and shaved salads, though like other purple carrots it fades toward gray-brown if simmered without an acid. Thin seedlings to 2-3 inches apart for well-formed roots and harvest at 70-80 days for full flavor and color development.

name: Black Oca
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep after last frost; Black Oca is a prolific, high-yielding selection with distinctively dark tuber skin.
directions: Plant tubers in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Black Oca is a prolific, high-yielding oca selection with dark red-to-nearly-black tuber skin, standing out visually from the more common cream, yellow, and pink oca lines. It follows the same day-length-driven tuberization pattern as other oca cultivars, with tubers bulking through fall and harvest following the first light frosts, which also helps mellow the characteristic tangy flavor. It is hardy to about zone 7a with heavy mulch protecting the tubers over winter.

name: Black Olive Ornamental Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost under high light at 60-70 degrees F and transplant once frost danger has passed; Black Olive, a 2012 All-America Selections winner, is grown chiefly for its dark ornamental fruit and foliage rather than for eating.
directions: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into full sun in well-drained soil after frost danger has passed. Black Olive maintains an upright habit with dark purple-black foliage and small clustered fruit that emerges deep purple-black before maturing to red, set off by bright purple flowers for season-long ornamental contrast. It tolerates heat well, needs no deadheading or staking, and performs equally well as a border specimen, container plant, or cut-flower element. The fruit is technically edible and very hot but is grown primarily for its dramatic color display rather than culinary use.

name: Black Opal Tomato
plantingNote: Transplant after frost danger and stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines early for support.
directions: Black Opal is a modern English open-pollinated selection bred from Black Cherry for a firmer texture and sweeter flavor than its parent, ripening to a deep chocolate-black skin over dusky red flesh. Indeterminate vines are early and heavy-yielding, producing clusters of half-to-one-ounce fruit through the season on a slightly more compact growth habit than many dark cherry types. Regular even watering and full sun bring out the complex, well-balanced sweetness the variety is known for. Select this cultivar for gardeners who want the dark cherry-tomato flavor profile with improved earliness and cracking resistance.

name: Black Pearl Ornamental Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55°F; Black Pearl is grown primarily as an ornamental for its striking near-black foliage and fruit rather than for culinary heat, though the small round peppers are technically edible and quite hot.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, harden off, and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Black Pearl won the All-America Selections award in 2006 for its dramatic, glossy, near-black foliage and abundant small, round, pearl-like fruit that emerges black and ripens through deep red, creating a striking, ever-changing color display on a single compact plant that works as well in a decorative container or mixed bed as it does in a vegetable garden. The fruit carries substantial heat, comparable to a cayenne pepper, and while edible it is grown mainly for ornamental impact rather than as a culinary crop. Its dark foliage provides dramatic color contrast against silver or chartreuse companion plants, and the compact, well-branched habit needs no staking or special care beyond routine watering and feeding.
sources: All-America Selections — Black Pearl pepper 2006 winner notes
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database

name: Black Pearl Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant March–April. Black Pearl is compact (18–24 inches) and extremely ornamental — it is widely grown as a container plant where the black foliage and shiny black fruits transitioning to red create continuous seasonal interest. In zone 9 the plant can overwinter as a perennial woody shrub, regrowth from the base producing even heavier crops in subsequent seasons.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Black Pearl is an All-America Selections award-winning ornamental pepper notable for its intensely dark, shiny, almost black foliage throughout the growing season — one of the darkest-leaved edible plants available for ornamental garden use. The small, round, pea-sized fruits emerge shiny black, gradually transitioning through red-black to a final vivid red as they mature, so that at any moment the plant displays all three colors simultaneously against the near-black foliage — creating a dramatically ornamental display that performs equally well as a container specimen and in ornamental borders. The fruits are genuinely hot (approximately 10,000–30,000 Scoville) and fully edible — suitable for hot sauces, dried chiles, and as a garnish for dishes where both heat and visual drama are desired. The compact size and outstanding ornamental value make Black Pearl one of the most popular choices for edible ornamental garden design.
sources: All-America Selections — Black Pearl Pepper 2006 Award
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Ornamental Pepper Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Edible Ornamental Peppers

name: Black Plum Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Black Plum is an indeterminate heirloom that requires staking or caging and produces prolifically throughout the season. In zone 9, transplant February–March for May–July harvest. The distinctive dark, mahogany-red to near-black skin color intensifies with warm temperatures and full sun exposure; the rich flavor is best appreciated at room temperature rather than refrigerated.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun with strong cage or stake support and consistent, even moisture. Black Plum is a Russian or Eastern European heirloom paste-type cherry tomato that has become one of the most appreciated 'dark' tomato varieties in American heirloom tomato culture — producing small (1.5–2 inch), plum-shaped fruits with an extraordinarily dark skin color ranging from deep mahogany-red to near-black-purple on the sun-exposed surface and shoulders. The dark color comes from high levels of chlorophyll that breaks down to brownish-red tones in the skin, combined with the fruit's deep red flesh, creating an intensely rich, almost chocolatey appearance that makes Black Plum one of the most visually distinctive cherry/paste types. The flavor is equally distinctive: rich, complex, and deeply sweet with more winey, umami-forward notes than typical sweet red cherry types — a sophisticated flavor more commonly associated with large beefsteak types than small tomatoes. Black Plum produces in abundant clusters throughout the season and is excellent fresh in salads, halved on cheese plates, dried whole, or roasted — the meaty, paste-type interior with relatively few seeds makes it particularly good for drying and roasting. One of the most beautiful and flavorful of all dark tomato varieties.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Black Plum tomato variety notes
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Russian and Eastern European heirloom tomatoes

name: Black Prince Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Black Prince is a Siberian heirloom dark tomato producing medium-sized, round to slightly oblate fruits with dark red-purple to almost-black coloring at the shoulders that transitions to deep burgundy-red — an early, flavorful representative of the 'black tomato' category with a rich, earthy, complex taste profile associated with the high anthocyanin content of dark-skinned varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Black Prince performs exceptionally well in cool climates due to its Siberian origin and can be transplanted earlier than most heat-requiring varieties. Black Prince is a Russian heirloom tomato from Siberia, where it was developed to produce ripe fruits under cool growing conditions with a shorter summer season than most tomato-growing regions — a characteristic that makes it one of the earliest-maturing of the 'dark tomato' class, which typically run late. The medium (3–6 oz), round to slightly flattened fruits develop dark red-purple to near-black pigmentation in sun-exposed areas of the skin (from anthocyanin development under UV exposure), while shaded areas remain deep burgundy-red; the interior flesh is dark red to mahogany with dense, meaty texture and a distinctively complex flavor profile — sweet and rich with earthy, slightly smoky undertones and good acid balance. Black Prince is an excellent introduction to the 'dark tomato' flavor category for gardeners unfamiliar with the type; it is earlier, more compact, and more productive than larger dark varieties like Cherokee Purple or Paul Robeson, making it particularly suitable for containers, short seasons, and cooler gardens.

name: Black Quinoa
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring into well-drained soil in full sun; Black quinoa runs several weeks later to maturity than lighter-seeded quinoa strains, so give it the longest cool season available.
directions: Black quinoa produces tall seed spikes densely packed with small, glossy jet-black seed, a distinct type from the more familiar tan, red, or bicolor quinoa strains and one that takes noticeably longer to fully ripen. Its dark, tightly closed seed coat sheds moisture well, which can help it stand up to a wetter harvest window better than paler quinoa types. Grow it exactly as other quinoa: direct sow into cool spring soil, keep watering light once established since quinoa dislikes soggy roots, and stake or support plantings in windy sites given their height. Harvest whole seed heads once thoroughly dry and shattering starts, then thresh and rinse well before cooking, as the seed coat still carries the typical bitter saponin layer.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

name: Black Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow 6–10 weeks before first fall frost in well-drained, deeply cultivated, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; black radish is a large, winter-storage radish with a dramatically pungent, horseradish-like flavor that mellows considerably when cooked — plant in fall for harvest before hard freezes.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in deeply cultivated, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 4–6 inches for large root development. Raphanus sativus 'Black Spanish' (black radish or Spanish black radish) is a large, ancient European winter radish producing round to turnip-shaped roots with jet-black, rough, firm skin and strikingly white, dense, extremely pungent flesh — the flavor is intensely sharp, mustard-hot, and horseradish-like when raw, making it far more assertive than common spring radishes. Black radish is one of the oldest cultivated radish types — documented in ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome — and remains popular in Eastern Europe, Germany, and France as a traditional winter vegetable. Raw, it is grated and dressed with salt, sour cream, or vinegar as a condiment (German Schwarzer Rettich); cooked, the pungency mellows considerably and the radish becomes milder and sweet. The roots store exceptionally well in cool conditions for weeks to months — a genuine winter storage vegetable unlike spring radishes, which must be used immediately. Black radish is also highly valued in naturopathic medicine for liver-supportive and digestive-stimulating properties attributed to high glucosinolate content.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Cool-Season Vegetables

name: Black Scorpion Tongue Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; this compact variety does double duty as a bedding or container plant as well as a culinary chile.
directions: Black Scorpion Tongue is an American-bred ornamental annuum valued for pods that emerge nearly black-purple and ripen through red, sometimes developing dark striping or blotches where sun exposure is most intense, so a single plant can show several pod colors at once. Fruit is small, 1-2 inches long and about three-quarters of an inch wide, with a crisp, crunchy texture and a sweet, fruity, floral flavor with hints of apple that mellows as pods redden. Heat is moderate for a specialty pepper, in the 50,000-100,000 Scoville range, well short of true superhot territory but still a solid step above a jalapeño. The tall, heavily fruiting plants make a dramatic landscaping accent while still supplying usable pods for hot sauces, infused oils, and fresh salsas.

name: Black Sea Man Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this compact, potato-leaved variety needs only modest staking and suits containers or small gardens.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil after frost danger passes. Black Sea Man is a Russian heirloom with distinctive potato-leaf foliage and a naturally compact habit that makes it a good choice for smaller gardens or large containers where full-sized indeterminate vines would be unwieldy. The mahogany-brown fruit has olive-green shoulders and deep, marbled flesh with a rich, smoky-sweet flavor. Modest staking is usually enough to support the shorter, sturdier plants through their production window.

name: Black Sesame
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant April–June for a summer harvest. Black sesame requires the full warmth of the Gulf Coast summer to set and ripen seed pods. The plants are drought-tolerant once established and require no fertilization beyond initial soil preparation. Harvest when the lower pods begin to turn yellow-brown and before they split open and shatter — losing the seed. Cut the entire plant and hang upside down over a tarp to capture falling seeds.
directions: Direct sow thinly in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; black sesame is a color variant of common sesame producing jet-black seeds with a distinctly richer, nuttier, and more complex flavor than the pale white sesame seeds familiar from Western cooking — the higher pigment content is associated with higher concentrations of antioxidant sesamin, sesamolin, and lignans. Black sesame is the standard seed for traditional East and Southeast Asian preparations including black sesame paste (used in tang yuan rice balls and Asian pastries), black sesame ice cream, Japanese gomashio (sesame salt), Korean jook (sesame rice porridge), and black sesame halva. Toasted black sesame seeds have an almost smoky, deep nutty profile that white sesame cannot replicate. The slender, upright, ornamental plants with white-to-pink tubular flowers are attractive in the garden. Harvest by cutting and hanging entire plants over a cloth when pods begin to ripen — mature pods open at the top and shed seeds readily.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Sesame Production in the Southeast
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sesame Crop Profile

name: Black Shine Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights stay reliably above 55F.
directions: A Japanese-type F1 hybrid eggplant bearing long, slender, glossy black fruit with a purple calyx on an upright, medium-tall plant. It is notably early to mature compared to other Asian eggplant types, suiting both open-field and greenhouse production. Flesh is tender with a mild flavor typical of slender Asian types, good for stir-fries, grilling, or tempura. Harvest while the skin retains its deep sheen, since dulling skin signals overripe fruit.

name: Black Spanish Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–November for a December–February harvest. Black Spanish radish is a large winter storage type that requires the full 55–70 days of cool weather to develop properly — it is not a quick spring radish. In zone 9 fall planting is the primary season; spring planting usually bolts before the roots size up. Harvest roots before heavy spring rains cause them to split or become pithy.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep and thin to 4–6 inches in loose, deep, well-prepared soil in full sun; Black Spanish Radish is an ancient winter storage radish documented in cultivation since at least the 1500s and widely grown in France, Germany, and Eastern Europe as a cold-season storage crop. The round to slightly elongated roots are 3–4 inches across with striking jet-black skin and brilliant white, very firm, pungent flesh inside — the flavor is substantially stronger and more peppery than spring radishes, with a dry, dense texture and a sharp spicy bite that is characteristic of all large winter radish types. The traditional preparation is sliced paper-thin and eaten with butter and salt as a crudité, or grated raw into salads where the pungency is diluted by other ingredients. Black Spanish radish stores for 2–3 months in cold storage with the greens removed, making it a genuine cold-pantry root crop unlike the quick-to-deteriorate spring radish types. The distinctive black skin and white interior create dramatic visual contrast in raw preparations.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Black Spanish Radish Heritage Variety
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Winter Radishes
Seeds of Change — European Heirloom Root Vegetables

name: Black Summer Bok Choy
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile, evenly moist soil; also excellent for fall sowing about six to eight weeks before first frost.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile, evenly moist soil, spacing plants to allow the glossy dark-green leaves and tender white stems to fill out into a compact, slow-bolting head. Black Summer was bred as a heat-tolerant companion to white-stemmed types like Joi Choi, so it can be planted through the warmer parts of the growing season with far less risk of premature flowering. Harvest at 8-10 inches tall for a sweet, crisp bok choy suited to stir-fries, soups, and fresh use.

name: Black Valentine Bush Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Black Valentine shows better tolerance for cool soil germination than many snap beans, germinating as low as 55°F, allowing earlier planting. In zone 9, plant March–May and again August–September for fall harvest. Black Valentine is also grown as a dry shell bean — allow pods to dry completely on the vine for black-seeded dry beans excellent in soups.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost in rows 18–24 inches apart; harvest pods when 5–6 inches long and still tender before seeds swell. Black Valentine is one of the oldest continuously maintained snap bean varieties in American cultivation, introduced around 1897 — a bush snap bean with more than 125 years of documented garden history, making it one of the few surviving American snap bean varieties from the pre-hybrid, pre-modern-breeding era. The black seed (from which the name derives) is the seed coat color at the dry stage: the seeds are jet black when fully dried, producing a useful dry black bean with excellent flavor for soups and stews. As a snap bean, Black Valentine produces dark green, round to slightly flat pods of good length (5.5–6.5 inches) on compact, bushy 18–22 inch plants. The flavor is richer and more complex than most modern bush snap bean hybrids — characteristic of traditional open-pollinated varieties that were selected for eating quality over the decades of their use. Black Valentine shows good tolerance for cool soil germination (as low as 55°F, versus the 60–65°F requirement of most snap beans), which allowed earlier planting in the pre-modern gardening era when it was a primary garden staple.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Black Valentine bean variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Heirloom bean collection
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Traditional Appalachian bean varieties

name: Black Zebra Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Black Zebra is an indeterminate striped tomato related to Green Zebra and benefits from similar staking and spacing.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into well-drained soil after frost danger has passed, staking or caging to support the vines. Black Zebra produces small, round fruit striped in dark purple-brown over a deep green-gold background, a striking relative of Green Zebra with a richer, more complex sweet-tart flavor than its green counterpart. The compact, productive vines set fruit in good quantity over the season and make an attractive mixed-color addition to a salad or market display. Pick when the stripes have fully darkened and the fruit gives slightly to pressure, and use fresh for the best flavor and color impact.

name: Black-Seeded Simpson Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; sow succession plantings every 2–3 weeks for continuous harvest; widely available and one of the most heat-tolerant loose-leaf lettuces for warm-climate spring gardens.
directions: Broadcast or direct sow seed on the soil surface (light aids germination — do not cover) in early spring, thinning to 8–12 inches when seedlings are 2 inches tall; Black-Seeded Simpson is the most widely grown American heirloom loose-leaf lettuce, documented since at least 1850 and still one of the best choices for the home garden due to its excellent heat tolerance (bolts much more slowly than most head lettuces), fast maturity (45–50 days), light green crinkled leaves with a pleasant, mild flavor, and the heavy yields of a cut-and-come-again plant. Harvest outer leaves when plants are 6–8 inches tall, leaving the center growing point to continue producing. Self-shades the soil and benefits from afternoon shade in warm climates.

name: Blacktail Mountain Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-prepared soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for early summer harvest and June–July for a fall crop. Despite being bred for short northern seasons, Blacktail Mountain performs well in zone 9's heat — the early maturity allows harvest before the most intense late-summer heat, and the dark rind absorbs heat efficiently in cooler spring soil. Check for ripeness by thumping (hollow sound) and examining the tendril nearest the fruit, which should be dried and brown.
directions: Direct sow in hills or rows in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Blacktail Mountain is an early-maturing open-pollinated watermelon developed by Glenn Drowns of Seed Savers Exchange to produce reliably sweet, ripe melons in the short summers of northern Idaho and the northern Plains. The small to medium round fruits (8–12 pounds) have a strikingly dark — almost black-green — rind that distinguishes them instantly from most other watermelon varieties. The bright red, sweet, juicy flesh is comparable to the best commercial watermelons in flavor, with a thin rind and few seeds. In zone 9 the early maturity (70–80 days from direct sow) means it finishes before the most brutal August heat and is particularly useful for succession-planted summer crops that bridge the gap between spring and fall production. The dark rind warms faster in cool spring soil, giving Blacktail Mountain an advantage early in the season when soil temperatures are marginal.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Blacktail Mountain Watermelon
University of Idaho Extension — Watermelon Variety Trial
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Short-Season Watermelons

name: Blanco Lechoso Chickpea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost into well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding heavy or limy ground; Blanco Lechoso is a large-seeded Andalusian chickpea prized for its buttery texture.
directions: Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding heavy or limy ground, after frost danger has passed; Blanco Lechoso is a large, milky-white Andalusian chickpea with a very thin skin and buttery texture, considered excellent for hummus, purees, and stews where a smooth finished texture matters. It needs the same warm-season, drought-tolerant culture as other chickpeas, maturing in 100-120 days. Harvest when pods dry and rattle on the plant, then thresh and store the dried seeds for year-round use.

name: Blanco Yacon
plantingNote: Set out rhizome crown divisions around last frost in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Blanco flowers at an intermediate date and finishes somewhat earlier than later-flowering yacon strains.
directions: Blanco, previously sold as 'Early White,' is one of the two most common yacon strains grown in North America and has been in cultivation here since the mid-1990s. Propagate from rhizome crown divisions rather than storage roots, and set out after last frost in deep, fertile soil in full sun; plants reach a medium height of about six feet with reddish stems. Tubers are tan-skinned, developing light red blushing with extended light exposure, and the white flesh is moderately sweet with the characteristic crisp, juicy texture of yacon. Dormant rhizomes store for two to three months under cool, dry conditions if the growing season ends before replanting.

name: Blauhilde Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed to at least 60F; provide a tall trellis or pole tepee, since vines climb to about 9 feet and crop continuously through the season.
directions: Blauhilde is a German heirloom pole bean prized for its striking deep purple pods, which grow long and wide yet stay tender and stringless, set off nicely against rose-purple blossoms. The pods turn green when cooked but hold their purple color when lightly steamed, making raw and blanched harvests fun to tell apart in the kitchen. Vigorous, disease-tolerant vines bear over a long window when picked at 6-8 inches, and the plant's dramatic coloring makes it a popular choice for growers who want both a productive snap bean and an ornamental accent on the trellis.

name: Blauwschokker Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool soil as early as it can be worked; provide a trellis for the four to five foot vines and decide at planting whether you plan to pick pods green for fresh shelling or leave them to dry for soup peas.
directions: Blauwschokker is a centuries-old Dutch heirloom prized for its bicolor purple-and-white flowers and deep violet pods, making it as ornamental as it is useful in the vegetable garden. Pods can be picked young and shelled fresh like a standard garden pea, or left on the vine until they dry to a papery tan for storage as a marbled grey-green soup pea, traditionally used in Dutch pea soup. The vigorous climbing vines benefit from a trellis and produce over a long picking window in cool weather. This variety is a good choice for gardeners who want a dual-purpose pea that also adds color to a spring garden.

name: Bleu de Solaise Leek
plantingNote: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors in spring; harvest runs from autumn through winter, with flavor and hardiness improving after frost. Bleu de Solaise is a renowned French winter leek from the commune of Solaise in the Rhône valley near Lyon — prized for its extraordinary cold hardiness and the dramatic blue-green to steel-blue coloration the foliage develops in response to frost, one of the most visually striking of all leek varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost date; sow 1/4 inch deep in flats or cell trays at 60–70°F. Bleu de Solaise is a traditional French winter leek from the Rhône valley region near Lyon, classified as a winter-type leek because it is sown in late winter or early spring, transplanted in late spring, and harvested from autumn through the following spring — the main harvesting season runs from November through February in most climates. The most distinctive characteristic of Bleu de Solaise is its dramatic foliage color: the leaves develop an intense steel-blue to blue-violet pigmentation in response to cold temperatures through the anthocyanin response, making each plant increasingly vibrant and beautiful as winter progresses; in hard frosts the blue becomes almost purple-blue. Transplant seedlings in late spring when 6–8 inches tall, planting deeply in a trench or dibbling holes 6 inches deep to blanch the shanks and develop long, tender white stems; the thick shanks (6–8 inches long) have a sweet, mild, sophisticated flavor that intensifies rather than diminishes in cold weather. One of the most cold-tolerant of all leeks, surviving temperatures well below 0°F when established.
sources: French Ministry of Agriculture CTPS Variety Registry

name: Blondkopfchen Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Blondkopfchen is an indeterminate heirloom that requires strong staking or caging (6 feet minimum) and produces prolifically throughout the warm season. In zone 9, transplant late February–March for a May–July harvest. The extremely long clusters (30–50 small tomatoes per cluster) are one of the most visually remarkable features of this variety — a single plant in full production is spectacular.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun with a sturdy cage or tall stake. Blondkopfchen (German for 'little blonde girl' or 'little blondie') is a German heirloom cherry tomato that produces one of the most spectacular fruiting displays of any tomato variety — extremely long, drooping clusters of 30–50 or more tiny (0.5–0.75 inch), round, clear golden-yellow to light lemon-yellow fruits that cascade like bunches of golden grapes from indeterminate vines growing 6+ feet. The fruits are uniformly pale golden-yellow, translucent-skinned, and have an exceptionally sweet, mild, almost honey-sweet flavor with very low acidity — a delicate sweetness that is quite different from the richer red cherry types and makes Blondkopfchen appealing to those who find red cherry tomatoes too tart. The combination of the fruit's pale golden color, the translucent skin through which the interior is visible, and the long hanging clusters makes Blondkopfchen one of the most beautiful tomato plants in the garden — genuinely ornamental as well as productive and delicious. Very popular in European heirloom gardens and increasingly appreciated in the US by tomato collectors who value both visual character and eating quality. Seed Savers Exchange and specialty seed companies carry this variety as an example of German heirloom tomato excellence.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Blondkopfchen tomato variety notes
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — German heirloom tomato collection
Tomatoville (online heirloom tomato community) — Blondkopfchen discussions

name: Blondy Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; soak seeds overnight in warm water before planting to improve germination. Blondy's compact size (3–4 feet vs. the 5–6 feet of standard okra) makes it appropriate for smaller gardens. In zone 9, plant April–June for summer and fall harvest. Harvest pods every 2–3 days when 2–4 inches long — Blondy pods stay tender longer than dark green types, remaining usable up to 5–6 inches without becoming tough and fibrous.
directions: Soak seeds overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest cream-colored pods every 2–3 days at 2–5 inches. Blondy is a 1986 All-America Selections-winning okra that earned recognition for two distinguishing traits: compact plant size and distinctive cream-white to pale chartreuse pod color. Standard okra varieties like Clemson Spineless and Emerald are tall plants (5–7 feet) that require staking and become difficult to harvest at the top as the season progresses; Blondy stays compact at 3–4 feet, keeping all pods within easy reach throughout the harvest season. The pale cream-colored pods are the most visually distinctive feature — where standard okra is dark forest green, Blondy's pods are almost white-green to cream-yellow, giving a noticeably different appearance both in the garden and on the table. Beyond the visual novelty, the pale pods have a slight cooking advantage: they do not contribute the dark green color that sometimes bleeds into dishes, making them preferable for light-colored preparations like cream soups, gumbo with light roux, or pickled okra where visual clarity is desired. The pods remain tender at larger sizes than dark-green types, providing a more forgiving harvest window. Blondy produces heavily on its compact plants, making it particularly well-suited to small gardens and raised beds.
sources: All-America Selections — Blondy okra AAS winner 1986
Burpee Seeds — Blondy okra variety notes
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Okra Variety Recommendations

name: Bloody Butcher Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 55°F; Bloody Butcher is a 150+-year-old Appalachian and Virginia heirloom dent corn with dramatic deep blood-red and red-flecked kernels, used for meal, hominy, roasting ears, and heritage bourbon production — and one of the most visually striking of all heirloom corns.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least 4 rows to ensure cross-pollination; plant in fertile, well-amended soil with consistent moisture during pollination and kernel fill. Bloody Butcher is a tall, vigorous Appalachian heirloom dent corn documented in Virginia and the Appalachian region since at least the 1840s; the plants are impressive, reaching 10–12 feet, and produce 2–4 ears per stalk of medium-length (10–14 inch) ears with kernels that are dramatic deep blood-red to red-brick with darker red cob — the most vividly colored of the traditional red dent corns. Dried, the kernels are ground into deeply flavored, reddish-tinged cornmeal with a rich, earthy, sweet corn taste that is distinct from modern yellow dent meal. Also used for hominy, grits, masa, and heritage whiskey distilling. At the milk stage (80–90 days) the ears can be eaten as roasting ears; for grain and meal, allow to dry on the stalk or cure indoors.

name: Bloomer Potato
plantingNote: A rare Irish landrace rather than a modern breeding-program release; grow it as a maincrop and expect smaller yields than commercial cultivars.
directions: Bloomer is an old Irish Midlands landrace first documented in County Clare in 1936 and prized by seed-saving growers for its round tubers with a distinctive purplish-blue skin, deep eyes, and cream-colored flesh. By the mid-1980s it had been identified as a variety found nowhere outside Ireland, which is why heritage seed custodians still keep it in circulation today. Grow it as you would any maincrop potato, hilling the stems as the white-flowered plants grow and leaving the tubers in the ground until the foliage dies back naturally. Because it was never bred for commercial yield, treat Bloomer as a conservation and curiosity crop for the table rather than a high-volume staple, best boiled or roasted in small batches to show off its cream flesh.

name: Bloomsdale Long Standing Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, 4-6 weeks before the last frost, in rows about a foot apart.
directions: Direct sow seed a half inch deep into cool, moist soil as soon as the ground can be worked, thinning seedlings to a few inches apart once true leaves appear. This selection is one of the oldest named spinach types still grown today, prized for its heavily crinkled, dark green savoy leaves and slower tendency to bolt compared with smooth-leaf types. It tolerates light frost and often tastes sweetest after a cold snap, making it a dependable choice for both early spring and fall sowings.

name: Blue Ballet Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-amended soil; a compact, single-serving size blue-grey squash in the Hubbard family — ideal for gardeners who want the exceptional Hubbard flavor in a size manageable for a single meal.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, composted soil; Blue Ballet is a compact vine type needing 4–6 feet of space, much more manageable than giant Hubbard types while retaining the same outstanding eating quality. Blue Ballet is a small, 2–4 pound, blue-grey teardrop-shaped winter squash in the Cucurbita maxima (Hubbard) family, with dense, smooth, bright orange flesh that is extraordinarily dry, sweet, and nutty — essentially the same outstanding Hubbard flavor in a size perfect for a single serving or small family portion that eliminates the wrestling match of cutting a 15-pound Blue Hubbard. Excellent for roasting halved in the oven with butter and maple syrup; the small size also makes it practical for stuffing. Cure for 10 days and store for 3–4 months.

name: Blue Coco Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow at the base of a sturdy pole or trellis once soil has warmed after last frost; pick young for snap use, or leave pods to mature for fresh shelling or dry storage beans.
directions: Blue Coco is a dual- to triple-purpose French heirloom pole bean bearing slender, bluish-purple pods on vines with purple-tinged leaves and lavender flowers, an attractive plant as much at home on an ornamental trellis as in the vegetable rows. Young pods snap tender with a mild, sweet flavor, while pods left to fill out yield plump beans with rich chocolate-brown seed coats that shell fresh or dry down for winter soup beans. Its origins are debated, with some tracing the name to Central America rather than France, but it has circulated in French seed trade and heirloom collections for generations. Provide a tall, sturdy support, since the vigorous vines climb readily and produce over a long season when picked regularly.

name: Blue Curled Scotch Kale
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. sabellica 'Blue Curled Scotch'
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Blue Curled Scotch is a dwarf type (12–16 inch plants) appropriate for small gardens and container growing. In zone 9, transplant August–September for fall and winter harvest. The tightly curled leaves trap water in their crinkles, so watering and harvest timing after heavy rains requires slightly more care than with flat-leaf kale types. Multiple light frosts improve the sweetness significantly — the flavor peak is November–January in zone 9.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun or partial shade. Blue Curled Scotch (also called Dwarf Blue Curled Scotch or Blue Curled Dwarf) is one of the oldest and most recognized curly kale varieties in American cultivation — a compact, very tightly-curled kale with deeply blue-green, intensely frilled and crinkled leaves on a low, spreading, dwarf plant. The very dense curling of Blue Curled Scotch is the most extreme in the curly kale category — each leaf is curled and recurled into a compact, almost cabbage-like head of texture that is visually striking and creates distinctive culinary behavior when cooked (the very curly leaves trap oils and seasonings in their folds). The tightly frilled leaves also create the most decorative appearance among common kale varieties, making Blue Curled Scotch useful in ornamental kitchen gardens and edible landscape plantings where visual appeal is important. The dwarf habit (12–18 inches) is practical in raised beds and containers. Like all curly kales, flavor improves dramatically after frost — the sweetness increases and the bitterness decreases as cold temperatures convert starches to sugars, making fall and winter the optimal harvest window.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Blue Curled Scotch kale variety history
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Curly kale variety comparison
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Kale Variety Evaluation

name: Blue Goose Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1-2 inches deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F; this pre-1860 Southern heirloom thrives through the hottest weeks of a Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Direct sow into average garden soil and keep watered through flowering and pod set for the best yields, though established plants tolerate real dry spells. Blue Goose is a rare, richly flavored Southern heirloom cowpea dating from before 1860, named for its distinctive purple-gray seed packed roughly fifteen to a pod. Young pods can be snapped and cooked like green beans, and the tender leaves are edible as a cooked potherb similar to spinach. Let pods dry on the vine for a hearty, nitrogen-fixing dry pea crop.

name: Blue Hubbard Squash
plantingNote: Direct-sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep in hills of 3 seeds (thin to 2 plants per hill) after soil warms to 70°F and all frost danger passes; Blue Hubbard requires a long, warm growing season and is best planted in late July in zone 9 for fall harvest, allowing 100–110 days before the first expected fall frost.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost in full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Blue Hubbard is a classic, large-fruited heirloom winter squash producing enormous, blue-gray, warty, thick-skinned fruits typically weighing 15–35 pounds — the quintessential large storage squash that has fed families through winter for generations in American kitchen gardens. The flesh is deep orange, very dry and dense, richly flavored, and exceptional for pies, soups, and roasting — the flavor is often described as richer and more complex than the more commonly grown butternut squash. The thick, warty, blue-gray skin provides outstanding storage capacity — well-cured Blue Hubbard fruits store at room temperature for 6 months or longer. The vine is vigorous and space-demanding, spreading 8–15 feet — provide ample space and consider training the vine to maximize space efficiency. In zone 9, plant in late July for fall harvest (counting back 100–110 days from the average first frost date). Harvest after the skin hardens and turns fully blue-gray; cure in a warm location for 10–14 days before storage to harden the skin and improve sweetness. The large fruits are sometimes sold cut into sections at farm stands — cut pieces must be refrigerated and used within a week.

name: Blue Jade Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; Blue Jade is unique among sweet corns for its genuinely dwarf plant size (3–4 feet tall) that makes it the most practical sweet corn for container growing, small raised beds, and gardens where standard 6–8 foot corn stalks are not practical; the vivid blue to near-black kernels turn steel-blue when cooked and have a sweet, tender flavor despite their striking color.
directions: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for pollination — even dwarf corn requires block planting; thin to 6–9 inches; Blue Jade can be grown in large containers (15+ gallons) for patio gardens; harvest when kernels exude milky liquid when punctured; Blue Jade silk is blue and the husk has blue streaks; eat immediately for best sweetness as the sugars convert rapidly. Blue Jade is the most practical sweet corn for small gardens and containers — a genuinely dwarf sweet corn variety (plants only 3–4 feet tall) that was selected specifically for its compact habit, making it the rare sweet corn that can be grown in large containers, small raised beds, or urban gardens where standard corn's height and space requirements are prohibitive. The kernels are a vivid blue-purple when raw, turning a distinctive slate-blue when cooked — a color unlike any other common sweet corn, derived from the same anthocyanin pigments found in blue tortilla corn, blueberries, and purple cabbage. Despite the striking color, the flavor at the perfect milky stage is sweet and tender, comparable to standard sweet corn, though with a slightly more complex, starchy background flavor reflecting the corn's partial flint heritage. Blue Jade is classified as a sugary-enhanced (se) type sweet corn — not as sugary as supersweet (sh2) types but sweeter than old su types, with a longer window between milk and dough stages than original open-pollinated sweet corns. The entire plant is attractive: blue silk, blue-streaked husks, and blue-purple stalk coloring make Blue Jade an ornamental as well as productive corn. Excellent for children's gardens for its manageable size and dramatic appearance.

name: Blue Lake Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Blue Lake Pole requires a 6–8 foot trellis, fence, teepee poles, or other support structure — the vines will climb any vertical support readily using their tendrils. In zone 9, plant March–May for spring production and August–September for fall; pole beans are more heat-tolerant than bush types in high summer because the vine continues producing new flowers above the canopy where slightly cooler air circulates. Harvest when pods are 5–6 inches long and still tender and snappy; over-matured pods become fibrous and tough. Pick regularly to extend production — unpicked pods signal the plant to stop flowering.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost near trellis support; harvest pods at 5–6 inches length for best eating quality. Pick every 2–3 days to encourage continued production. Blue Lake Pole is the climbing, vining form of the Blue Lake bean family — the standard against which all green snap beans are measured in American vegetable gardening. The Blue Lake name comes from Blue Lake, California, where commercial snap bean growers in the Humboldt County area developed and refined the variety for the canning industry in the early 20th century. The Blue Lake type (both bush and pole forms) became the dominant American snap bean because it set the standard for straight, dark green, round pods with excellent tenderness, stringlessness, and flavor — characteristics that made it both the go-to home garden bean and the standard for the commercial canning and frozen bean industry. Blue Lake Pole's climbing habit (6–8 feet) gives it significant advantages over the bush form: the vine continues producing over a longer season (12–16 weeks vs. 6–8 weeks for bush), the elevated flowers and pods are slightly cooler and better-ventilated in humid conditions, and the vertical growth makes efficient use of small garden space with a supporting trellis. The beans are indistinguishable in flavor from the bush form — round, meaty, stringless, medium-dark green, with excellent eating quality fresh, frozen, or canned.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Blue Lake pole bean variety comparison
Seed Savers Exchange — Blue Lake bean heritage notes
University of California Cooperative Extension — Snap Bean Varieties for Home Gardens

name: Blue Lake Superior Bush Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed following the last frost; an improved take on the classic Blue Lake bean bred for heavier pod set and better disease tolerance.
directions: Direct sow once soil has warmed to at least 65F after the last frost, planting seeds an inch deep and spacing plants 3-4 inches apart in rows. Keep soil evenly moist during flowering and pod set to maximize yield, and pick pods while still slender and snappy for the best texture. This improved Blue Lake type is bred for rust, curly top, and mosaic virus resistance and holds its quality through a heavier flush of pods than the traditional Blue Lake 274 strain.

name: Blue Max Collards
plantingNote: Direct sow 10–12 weeks before the first frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Blue Max is a hybrid collard — it will not come true from saved seed but produces more uniform plants and potentially higher yields than open-pollinated varieties when purchased as fresh hybrid seed each season.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Blue Max is a hybrid collard variety valued for its large, smooth, blue-green, broadly rounded leaves and high-yield production — producing some of the largest, most productive collard plants available for home garden and small-farm production. The large leaf size (leaves reaching 18–24 inches across on well-fed plants) and tall, upright habit produce an impressive harvest volume from each plant. As a hybrid variety, Blue Max produces uniform, vigorous plants with excellent disease tolerance and the high-yield characteristics that result from hybrid vigor. The smooth, thick, waxy leaf surface holds up well in cooking and has good culinary quality in traditional preparations — braised with smoked meats, in Southern-style stewed greens, and in other long-cooked preparations where the thick leaves benefit from extended cooking time. Blue Max is cold-hardy and continues producing through Gulf South winters, sweetening after frost exposure as starches convert to sugars — the post-frost harvest typically produces the finest-flavored greens. In zone 9, plant in August–September for fall/winter production and harvest outer leaves progressively through November–February. The very large leaves and tall plants provide ample harvest from relatively few plants in a garden bed.

name: Blue Prince Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct-sow after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed; vines need ample room to trail.
directions: This AAS-winning pumpkin produces flattened, 9-10 pound fruit with pale blue-gray skin and deep orange, non-stringy flesh prized for baking and roasting. It matures earlier than many comparable blue pumpkins and shows good tolerance to powdery mildew. Vigorous trailing vines need a full season and plenty of garden space to size up fruit properly. Harvest when the rind hardens and the stem begins to dry and corky.

name: Blue Rose Rice
plantingNote: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; Blue Rose was selected in 1907 near Jennings, Louisiana, by breeder S.L. (Sol) Wright specifically to grow clean of red rice contamination in Gulf Coast paddy fields.
directions: Sow seed 0.5–1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated or flooded through the growing season. Blue Rose is one of the most historically important American rice varieties: Louisiana breeder S.L. (Sol) Wright selected it in 1907 from Japanese rice grown near Jennings, Louisiana, specifically to resist the red rice contamination that was devastating the milled quality of the era's crop, and released it commercially in 1911. Blue Rose went on to dominate American rice production for more than 25 years — by 1934, roughly three-quarters of all rice grown in the United States traced to Wright's Blue Rose breeding work, and Louisiana State Rice Milling sold it as its flagship short-grain product under the Water Maid brand. The short-to-medium grain mills cleanly and cooks up tender, making it well suited to jambalaya, dirty rice, and other Cajun and Creole one-pot dishes that favor a softer grain. The historic site of Wright's original selection in Crowley is preserved today at Crystal Rice Heritage Farm. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain hardens, then thresh and dry thoroughly before hulling.
sources: Crystal Rice Heritage Farm — Crowley, Louisiana (site of Sol Wright's original Blue Rose selection)
LSU AgCenter — History of the H. Rouse Caffey Rice Research Station
The Wright Group — Company History Archives

name: Blue Vantage Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Blue Vantage carries resistance to Fusarium yellows race 1 and tolerates excess soil moisture and tip burn better than many cabbage varieties, an advantage during the heavy rains common in Gulf South spring gardens.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; harden off before transplanting to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Blue Vantage is a cabbage hybrid bred for resistance to Fusarium yellows race 1, a persistent soil-borne disease, combined with unusually good tolerance for excess soil moisture and tip burn compared to most cabbage varieties. It forms dense, round, blue-green heads that hold well in the field without splitting even after reaching full maturity, giving gardeners flexibility in harvest timing. Because it handles wet soil better than many cabbage types, it is a strong choice for the heavy spring rains common across the Gulf South. Cut heads once firm and full-sized, and use promptly or store in a cool spot for best quality.

name: Blushing Beauty Pepper
