plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after all frost danger has passed.
directions: Blushing Beauty was named an All-America Selections winner for a fruit that skips green entirely, opening ivory and then blushing through light pink, orange-red, and finally deep scarlet as it ripens, often showing several colors on the plant at once. The thick-walled, blocky fruit is sweet and usable at any color stage, giving gardeners flexibility in when to harvest. Its compact, disease-resistant plants perform well in containers on a patio as well as in a garden bed, and the multicolored fruit display makes it as ornamental as it is productive. Pick some fruit at the pale stage to encourage continued setting through the season.

name: Bobcat Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this compact, container-friendly habit still produces full-sized beefsteak fruit, making it a good choice for patios and small-space gardens.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into a large container or garden bed once danger of frost has passed. Despite its compact, patio-friendly size, this determinate variety sets large beefsteak-style fruit, so provide a sturdy stake or small cage and consistent watering to prevent blossom end rot. Feed regularly through the season since container-grown plants exhaust soil nutrients faster than in-ground plantings.

name: Bodacious Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; plant in blocks of at least four rows and isolate from other corn types, since Bodacious carries the supersweet (sh2) gene and cross-pollination with standard corn produces starchy, tough kernels.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil in blocks for good pollination, keeping it isolated from other corn types to protect its supersweet genetics. Bodacious is a widely planted early yellow supersweet hybrid known for large, well-filled ears, dependable vigorous performance across a range of conditions, and excellent sweetness that holds up well for several days after harvest thanks to its sh2 supersweet trait. Its relatively early maturity makes it a good choice for a first planting of the season or for shorter growing windows, and it has long been a standard variety in home garden and market trials. Harvest once silks brown and kernels are plump and milky when tested, and refrigerate promptly to preserve peak sweetness.

name: Bogatyr Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves in fall, about 4-6 weeks before hard freeze, pointed end up, to allow roots to establish before winter dormancy.
directions: Plant large cloves pointed end up about 2 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil, mulching after planting for winter protection in colder zones. Remove the woody scape once it forms a loop to concentrate the plant's energy into bulb sizing, and cure bulbs in a warm, shaded, ventilated space before storage. Bogatyr, whose name means "hero" or "warrior" in Russian, is a vigorous porcelain-type hardneck valued for its very large bulbs, few but hefty cloves, and pronounced hot, pungent flavor that mellows somewhat with cooking.

name: Boldog Hungarian Spice Paprika Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Boldog Hungarian Spice takes its name from the Hungarian town of Boldog, a historic paprika-growing center, and produces compact plants loaded with small, thin-walled, sweet fruits bred specifically for drying and grinding into paprika.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and set plants out once the soil has warmed thoroughly. Boldog Hungarian Spice takes its name from the Hungarian town of Boldog, a historic center of paprika production, and produces compact plants loaded with small, tapering, thin-walled fruits that ripen to a deep brick red. Bred specifically for drying and grinding, the pods carry sweet, richly aromatic flesh with no heat, and their thin walls dry quickly once strung into ristras or dehydrated. The heavy, early fruit set makes it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting to produce their own homemade sweet paprika powder in a single season.

name: Boldor Golden Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall (zone 9: August–October) for winter harvest; each beet 'seed' is actually a corky seed cluster that may produce 2–3 seedlings — thin to the strongest plant at 3–4 inches. Boldor is a Bejo Seeds F1 hybrid selected specifically for the most vivid, deep golden-yellow root color of any golden beet variety, with the additional quality of very low bleeding — golden beets in general bleed far less than red types, and Boldor bleeds less than most golden varieties. The yellow color holds surprisingly well in cooking compared to red beets (which turn everything they touch crimson) — roasted Boldor can be served alongside lighter-colored ingredients without color contamination.
directions: Direct sow seed clusters 0.5 inch deep; thin to 3–4 inches. Harvest roots at 2–3 inches diameter for best texture; harvest greens at any size. Boldor is a Bejo Seeds F1 hybrid golden beet developed specifically to maximize the golden-yellow pigmentation of the root while maintaining the culinary qualities — tender, sweet, earthy — of the best red beet types. Golden beets (yellow beet varieties) differ from standard red beets in their pigmentation: instead of betacyanin (the red-purple betacyanin of standard beets), golden beets produce betaxanthin — a yellow-orange pigment in the same betacyanin family but in the yellow portion of the spectrum. This difference creates the visually striking golden color and the important culinary advantage of significantly reduced bleeding: while red beets stain everything they contact an intense crimson, golden beets' yellow betaxanthin pigment migrates far less during cutting and cooking, making golden beets practical for preparations where color bleeding would be problematic (roasted vegetable mixes, salads with white cheese, light-colored sauces). Boldor consistently achieves the most saturated, vivid golden color of any commonly available golden beet variety — the deep gold interior is visually striking when roasted and served as golden rounds, and the Bejo breeding produces more uniform root sizing than many open-pollinated golden beet types.
sources: Bejo Seeds — Boldor golden beet F1 hybrid variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Golden beet variety comparison
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Beet Variety Evaluation Guide

name: Bolero Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; a widely adaptable Nantes-type hybrid carrot with outstanding disease resistance to leaf blight, powdery mildew, and cavity spot — one of the most reliable carrots for home gardens in hot and humid zones 8–11.
directions: Sow seed thinly, 1/4 inch deep, in well-loosened, stone-free soil 2–4 weeks before last frost; thin to 2–3 inches between plants when seedlings are 2 inches tall to allow roots to develop fully. Bolero is an outstanding Nantes-type hybrid carrot developed for exceptional disease resistance, particularly to alternaria leaf blight and carrot fly, with excellent tolerance to heat and humidity that makes it one of the most reliable carrots for gardens in zone 7–11 where summer heat normally makes carrot culture difficult. The 6–8 inch, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots are uniformly deep orange, smooth-skinned, and have a sweet, mild flavor with good core-to-cortex ratio and excellent storage quality — they can be left in the ground for weeks without going woody. In zone 8–9, sow in late winter for spring harvest and again in late summer for fall harvest.

name: Bolita Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Bolita is a dry bean requiring the full growing season to dry. In zone 9, plant April–May for fall dry bean harvest. Bolita plants are semi-vining and may benefit from light support (a fence or string trellis) though they often sprawl adequately without staking. The beans are round (bolita = little ball in Spanish), cream to tan-pink at full dry maturity, and are harvested when pods are completely dry and papery. Bolita is adapted to the hot, dry, high-altitude conditions of the Southwest but grows well across a wide range of zones when given adequate heat during the growing season.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 4–6 inches. Harvest when pods are completely dry and papery; beans are round, cream to pinkish-tan. Shell and store in airtight containers. Bolita Bean is the traditional dry bean of New Mexico and the Pueblo cultures of the American Southwest — a variety with documented cultivation in New Mexico and Pueblo Indian communities for centuries, predating European contact and representing one of the most important food plants of southwestern Indigenous agriculture. The name 'bolita' (little ball in Spanish) describes the characteristic round, rotund shape of the dried seed, distinctly rounder than most common beans and immediately recognizable in any collection of dried bean varieties. The dried seeds are cream to pinkish-tan with a slightly glossy surface — a modest appearance that belies the exceptional culinary quality Bolita is known for among Southwest cooks and food historians. The flavor is earthy, slightly sweet, and deeply savory when slow-cooked — Bolita makes extraordinary refried beans (frijoles refritos): the beans cook to a very creamy, smooth texture when mashed and fried, with a richness that commercial pinto beans rarely achieve. Bolita is the traditional bean of New Mexican red and green chile preparations, cooked simply with onion, garlic, and salt or with rendered lard in the traditional method. Seed Savers Exchange and Native Seeds/SEARCH maintain diverse traditional Bolita strains.
sources: Native Seeds/SEARCH — Bolita bean New Mexico traditional cultivation documentation
Seed Savers Exchange — Bolita bean Southwest heirloom variety notes
University of New Mexico — Traditional Pueblo food plant documentation

name: Bolivian Giant Achocha
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 2-3 weeks early; provide sturdy trellising immediately as vines grow quickly and can reach 10-12 feet.
directions: Bolivian Giant is a large-fruited achocha selection popularized by UK seed savers, bearing smooth to lightly spined, hollow fruit noticeably bigger than the standard species type and well suited to stuffing whole. The vigorous, tendril-climbing vine easily covers 10 to 12 feet of trellis or fence in a single season and produces heavily even in cooler summers where cucumbers struggle. Harvest fruit while still young and tender, before the interior seeds harden and blacken, for the best crisp, mild, cucumber-like flavor. Because the plant self-seeds readily and can naturalize in mild climates, remove spent vines at season's end if volunteer seedlings are unwanted.

name: Bolivian Rainbow Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Bolivian Rainbow is particularly effective as a container plant, where the compact habit and upward-pointing multicolor fruits create an outstanding ornamental display. In zone 9, it often survives as a perennial in sheltered positions, developing into a woody shrub with increasing productivity in subsequent years.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; Bolivian Rainbow is one of the most visually spectacular ornamental-edible peppers available — a compact plant that simultaneously displays fruits at multiple stages of ripening, cycling through purple, yellow, orange, and red all at once on the same plant, creating a stunning multicolored display that earns it a place in ornamental borders and container arrangements as much as in vegetable gardens. The plants are dense, attractive, and heavily loaded with small (1–1.5 inch), upward-pointing conical fruits; the visual effect of dozens of multicolored fruits pointing upward from the dark green foliage is genuinely striking and unlike any other common garden plant. The fruits are very hot (50,000–100,000 Scoville units), with a clean, direct heat appropriate for hot sauce, spicy condiments, or any preparation where decorative whole dried peppers provide both heat and visual interest. The purple stage is particularly ornamental (purple pigmentation rarely seen in fruiting stage of other varieties) and fades to yellow, then orange, then the final red as the fruit matures. In zone 9+, established plants often behave as perennials, developing increasingly thick, woody stems and producing heavier crops each successive season.
sources: Kitazawa Seed Company — Ornamental pepper guide
University of New Mexico Chile Pepper Institute

name: Boltardy Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow earlier than most beets, several weeks before the last frost under cover or cloches; Boltardy's outstanding resistance to premature bolting is what allows the early start.
directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep in loose, fertile soil, thinning seedlings to three or four inches apart once true leaves appear. Boltardy is a Dutch-bred Detroit-type beet that has become one of the most widely grown home garden beets in Britain because it resists bolting to seed when exposed to the cold snaps and temperature swings of an early spring sowing, letting gardeners start the crop weeks ahead of standard varieties. It produces smooth-skinned, deep burgundy, globe-shaped roots with minimal internal ringing and a sweet, tender flavor well suited to boiling, roasting, or pickling. Keep the soil consistently moist for even root development and pull roots at two to three inches across for the best texture.

name: Bonanza Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outside once soil is warm and frost danger has passed.
directions: Bonanza is a new-for-2026 F1 hybrid eggplant from Burpee bred for large plants and season-long yields of extra-large fruit, averaging about 6 inches, on plants reaching roughly 5 feet tall and 4 feet wide. Burpee describes the fruit's flavor as rich with a firm yet velvety texture suited to roasting, grilling, or sauteing as a main dish or side. It needs a full growing season of warmth and full sun, so start it indoors and transplant after the soil has warmed.

name: Bonbon Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Bonbon is an AAS-winning buttercup-type winter squash bred for earlier ripening and more compact vines than standard buttercup squash, with exceptionally sweet, dense orange flesh.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Bonbon is an AAS-winning improvement on the classic buttercup winter squash, ripening earlier and growing on a more compact vine than standard buttercup types while producing the same dark-green, turban-shaped fruit with a distinctive gray-blue button on the blossom end. The dense, deep-orange flesh is notably sweet and dry-textured, excellent baked, mashed, or used in place of pumpkin in pies and soups. Its earlier maturity is a real advantage in areas with a shorter warm season or where gardeners want to fit squash into a tighter succession-planting schedule. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens and the stem begins to dry and corky; cure harvested squash in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks before storing to improve flavor and shelf life.
sources: All-America Selections — Bonbon Squash winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Bonda Ma Jacques Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; chinense types need sustained warmth to germinate reliably.
directions: Bonda Ma Jacques is a traditional habanero-type chile from the French Caribbean islands of Guadeloupe and Martinique, producing elongated, slightly wrinkled pods that ripen from green to yellow-orange with the characteristic fruity, floral chinense aroma. Heat is milder than most scotch bonnets or habaneros, generally in the low-to-mid habanero range, making it useful where chinense flavor is wanted without extreme heat. Give plants full sun, a long warm season, and consistent moisture, since pods develop slowly and ripen over an extended harvest window. It is used throughout the French Antilles in sauces, marinades, and the spicy condiment known locally as sauce chien.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Boniato
plantingNote: Plant slips (rooted cuttings) after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm above 65°F; boniato slips root readily; plant in well-mounded ridges for best tuber development and drainage.
directions: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, sandy-loam, enriched ridges in full sun after last frost when soil is warm; boniato is the traditional sweet potato of Cuban, Caribbean, and Latin American cuisine, prized for its dry, fluffy, white to pale cream flesh that is less sweet, less moist, and more starchy than orange sweet potatoes — more similar in texture to a russet potato and much preferred in savory preparations. The skin is irregularly shaped, pinkish to light brown, and the plants are slightly more drought-tolerant than standard sweet potatoes. Excellent roasted, mashed, or fried; does not have the cloying sweetness that makes American orange sweet potatoes unsuitable for some savory applications. Stores well in a cool, dry location.

name: Bonica Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay above 60 F; Bonica is an early, heavy-cropping hybrid well suited to tunnels or protected culture in cooler climates as well as open-field growing.
directions: Bonica is a widely grown French-bred F1 hybrid valued across Europe for its tall, vigorous plants and exceptionally heavy, early cropping. It produces long, oval fruit around 6 inches long with deep purple, glossy skin and tender, mild-flavored flesh that holds its quality well. The vigorous habit benefits from staking or caging and steady feeding, since plants continue setting fruit heavily through a long season once established. Grow it in full sun with consistent moisture, and harvest fruit while still glossy for the best texture and flavor.
sources: Thompson & Morgan — Aubergine Bonica F1 Hybrid Seeds

name: Bonita Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips (rooted stem cuttings) after soil has warmed to 65°F and all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant April–June. Bonita is adapted to the Gulf Coast's hot, humid summer conditions and produces reliably even in the high-heat periods of July–August when some varieties reduce tuber set. Harvest when vines begin to yellow and die back, or after 100 days. In zone 9 a second planting in late July can produce a fall harvest.
directions: Plant in full sun in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic, sandy to sandy-loam soil — sweet potatoes do not tolerate waterlogged or compacted soil; Bonita is a white-fleshed sweet potato released by the Louisiana State University AgCenter specifically for Gulf Coast production conditions, selected for its firm, dry, mildly sweet flesh that is used as a staple starchy vegetable rather than as a dessert-sweet orange-fleshed type. The large, oblong, tan-skinned tubers have creamy white flesh with a dry, starchy texture more similar to a dry-type white potato than to the moist, orange Beauregard type — making Bonita suitable for soups, stews, fried preparations, and the Latin American-style cooking (boniato) where a dry, non-sweet white sweet potato is traditional. The vine shows good heat and humidity tolerance and is specifically tested for performance in the Gulf South's challenging summer conditions. Bonita is popular in Louisiana and Gulf Coast markets catering to Caribbean and Latin American culinary traditions.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Bonita Sweet Potato Release
University of Florida IFAS Extension — White-Fleshed Sweet Potato Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Gulf Coast Sweet Potato Production

name: Bonnie Best Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–80°F and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; stake or cage as an indeterminate variety that continues producing over a long season.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed. Introduced around 1908 and long a staple of American home and market gardens, Bonnie Best produces smooth, deep red, medium-sized fruit with excellent classic tomato flavor and good production over a long season, having served for decades as a standard against which other tomato varieties were measured before modern hybrids became dominant. Its old-fashioned, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor and reliable performance make it a satisfying choice for gardeners seeking a historically significant slicing tomato with genuine heirloom character rather than a specialty color or shape. Harvest when fruit is fully red and yields to gentle pressure, and pick regularly to keep the vigorous vines producing.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — heirloom tomato variety notes
Victory Seed Company — historic tomato variety archive

name: Bonnotte Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces after soil has warmed slightly; Bonnotte is a prized early French new potato traditionally hand-harvested on the island of Noirmoutier.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in light, well-drained, sandy soil; Bonnotte is an early-maturing variety best harvested young as a thin-skinned new potato rather than left to mature fully. Bonnotte is celebrated in France as one of the earliest and most prized new potatoes, traditionally hand-harvested on the sandy, salt-influenced soils of the Île de Noirmoutier off the Atlantic coast, prized for delicate, thin skin and sweet, buttery flesh that needs little more than a quick steam and butter to shine. Harvest young, while the skin still rubs off easily, for the best texture and flavor, and use promptly since new potatoes do not store as long as mature ones.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

name: Bonny Best Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Bonny Best is a classic 1908 American heirloom slicing tomato — one of the most widely grown varieties in early 20th century American home gardens and commercial fields — valued for its reliable production, attractive round-globe shape, good acid-sweet balance, and relatively early maturity for a full-sized slicer.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Bonny Best performs well with or without staking — it is an indeterminate but moderately compact type compared to most indeterminate heirlooms. Bonny Best was introduced in 1908 (previously distributed as 'John Baer') and rapidly became one of the most widely grown tomatoes in early 20th century America, prized for reliable, heavy production of attractive, round to slightly oblate, medium to large (6–10 oz), uniformly red fruits with a classic balanced sweet-acid flavor that home gardeners and canners found superior to the watery commercial varieties of the era. Bonny Best's particular virtues are its productivity, disease resilience, and flavor — a reliable old-fashioned tomato that consistently produces good crops without fuss. By midcentury it was eclipsed in commerce by hybrid varieties but remained in home garden cultivation; it is now maintained by seed savers and available from heritage seed companies as one of the historically important American tomato varieties. Good canning and fresh-eating tomato.

name: Boone County White Corn
plantingNote: Sow in fertile, well-drained soil in blocks of at least four rows; give this long-season dent corn consistent moisture through pollination.
directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained soil in blocks of at least four rows, and give this long-season dent corn a full growing season with consistent moisture through pollination for best ear fill. Boone County White originated in Indiana and Illinois in the late 1800s and became one of the most widely grown white dent corns of the pre-hybrid Corn Belt, valued for tall, productive stalks and large, well-filled ears of smooth white dent kernels. It was historically important both as a table and livestock feed corn and as breeding stock, and it still produces excellent white cornmeal and hominy for gardeners wanting to grow a piece of Midwestern agricultural history.

name: Boothby Blonde Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and August–September for fall. Boothby Blonde is best harvested young at 3–4 inches for fresh eating; at full maturity the fruits are 5–6 inches and still mild but beginning to yellow. Remove overripe fruits promptly to keep the vine producing. Bush habit is compact; no trellis required but vines benefit from light support.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; Boothby Blonde is a Maine heirloom cucumber preserved by the Boothby family of Livermore Falls and introduced to the broader seed-saving community through Seed Savers Exchange. The small, oval fruits are ivory-to-pale-yellow with black or white spines — the pale color is the key distinguishing feature that makes identification by color a reliable harvest guide. Harvest when the fruits are still ivory-white at 3–5 inches; yellowing indicates over-maturity. The flesh is exceptionally crisp, mild, and sweet with thin skin that does not require peeling — the flavor is more delicate than standard green cucumbers, with less bitterness and a refreshing, clean taste ideal for fresh eating, simple salads, and sliced into yogurt or dressings. The unusual pale exterior makes it a novelty in the garden and at farmers' markets. Heat tolerance is adequate for zone 9 spring crops, but fall production is best.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Boothby Blonde Cucumber Heritage Variety
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Boothby Blonde
University of Maine Cooperative Extension — Cucumber Production

name: Boothby's Blonde Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Boothby's Blonde is a semi-vining variety (grows 3–4 feet before trailing) that can be trained up a trellis for cleaner fruit or allowed to sprawl. In zone 9, plant March–May and again August–September for fall production. Harvest fruits when cream-yellow in color (3–4 inches long) — do not allow to become large and yellow-orange, which indicates overripeness, bitterness, and seed hardening. The pale skin of Boothby's Blonde makes it easy to spot overripe fruits before they develop bitterness, unlike dark-green varieties where overripeness is harder to detect. The black spines (as opposed to the white spines of burpless/European types) indicate this is a traditional pickling-style heirloom, though it is most often eaten fresh.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches when cream-yellow and firm. Boothby's Blonde is a Maine family heirloom cucumber preserved by the Boothby family from Livermore Falls, Maine, and shared through the Seed Savers Exchange — the network through which most American home-saved heirloom vegetable varieties have been maintained and distributed since the organization's founding in 1975. The cucumber is immediately distinguishable from every other commonly grown variety by its fruit color: the skin is creamy white to pale yellow at harvest maturity, oval to oblong in shape (3–4 inches long), with black spines on the surface ribs rather than the white spines of European or Asian cucumber types. This combination of cream-yellow skin and black spines produces a visual character unlike any other cucumber commonly available — the pale fruit with dark spines stands out dramatically in the garden and on the plate. The eating quality is excellent: thin skin (no peeling needed), crisp and juicy flesh, mild sweet flavor with no bitterness, and a good seed cavity for a traditional cucumber type. Boothby's Blonde exemplifies the category of heirloom vegetables that persist not because of exceptional yield or disease resistance but because of unique visual and flavor qualities unavailable in commercial varieties — preserved specifically because gardeners valued those qualities enough to maintain the seed across generations.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Boothby's Blonde cucumber Maine heirloom documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Boothby's Blonde cucumber variety notes
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Heritage cucumber variety descriptions

name: Borettana Cipollini Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant in early spring; Borettana is an Italian heirloom cipollini type prized for its flat, disc-like shape that makes it ideal for whole-onion roasting and pickling.
directions: Direct sow or set transplants in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. This Italian heirloom produces distinctively flat, disc-shaped bulbs with coppery-gold skin and sweet, mild flesh, and is the classic cipollini used in Italian agrodolce (sweet-and-sour) roasted onion dishes as well as pickling, since the flat shape cooks evenly and looks attractive whole on the plate. It matures relatively quickly for an onion and the small-to-medium bulbs cure and store reasonably well for a sweet type. Space plants a bit closer than standard globe onions, since the flattened bulbs take up less lateral room, and reduce watering as the foliage begins to yellow and fall over near harvest.

name: Boro Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool soil; Boro's foliage resists common foliar blights and the roots are very resistant to bolting with good shelf life after harvest, useful traits for an extended Gulf South beet harvest window.
directions: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Boro is a hybrid beet whose tops resist common foliar blights that can weaken plants in humid, wet weather, while the roots show strong resistance to bolting and hold good quality in storage after harvest longer than many varieties. It produces smooth, round, deep red roots with sweet, tender flesh and healthy dark green tops good for cooking greens. Thin seedlings to 3-4 inches apart for well-sized roots, keep soil consistently moist, and harvest once roots reach 1.5-2.5 inches across; Boro's good storage quality makes it a solid choice for gardeners who want to hold part of the crop rather than using it all immediately.

name: Bossa Nova Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70°F; Bossa Nova is a 2015 All-America Selections winner with intermediate resistance to zucchini yellow mosaic virus and watermelon mosaic virus, along with an unusually long harvest window for a summer squash.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Bossa Nova is a distinctive Caserta-type zucchini with striking dark and light green mottled skin, bred with intermediate resistance to zucchini yellow mosaic virus and watermelon mosaic virus, two viruses spread by aphids that commonly shorten a summer squash season in humid Gulf Coast gardens. It is also noted for an unusually extended harvest window compared to most zucchini, continuing to produce good-quality fruit later into the season. Pick fruit at 6-8 inches for the best texture and flavor, checking plants daily during peak production since squash left on the vine quickly grows oversized and seedy.
sources: All-America Selections — Bossa Nova squash AAS winner 2015

name: Boston Marrow Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-amended soil; one of the oldest American heirloom squashes, documented in New England gardens since the 1830s, with vibrant orange-red skin and superb flavor.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, enriched soil, spacing hills 4–6 feet apart and thinning to 2 plants per hill; Boston Marrow requires 90–100 days of warm weather, so plant promptly after last frost. Boston Marrow is one of the oldest American heirloom winter squashes, offered by commercial seedsmen in New England since the 1830s; it produces round to pear-shaped fruits 6–10 pounds in weight with spectacular, deep orange-red skin and extremely sweet, fine-grained, nearly stringless flesh of exceptional quality — it was reportedly the standard squash for pies before Hubbard types became popular. Harvest when the rind is hard and the skin is fully colored; cure for 10 days and store in a cool, dry place for 2–3 months.

name: Boston Pickling Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; one of the oldest American pickling cucumbers, documented since the 1870s, producing short, blocky, thin-skinned fruits ideal for dill pickles and fermented pickles.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; Boston Pickling is a fast-maturing (55–65 days) pickling type that produces very early and keeps producing well if harvested at 2–3 inch length for small dill pickles or 3–4 inch length for whole dill pickles. Boston Pickling is an American heirloom documented since the 1870s, producing short, blocky, light-to-medium green fruits with slightly ridged skin, crisp white flesh, and a small seed cavity that gives pickles an excellent bite; the skin absorbs brine beautifully, producing crunchy pickles that store for months. Harvest at least every two days when production peaks to keep the vine producing; fruits left to yellow dramatically slow new production. Both vine-type and bush selections exist.

name: Boston Red Sunchoke
plantingNote: Plant tuber pieces 4-6 inches deep around last frost in any well-drained soil in full sun; Boston Red is an old New England heirloom grown for its deep red-skinned, moderately knobby tubers and should be sited in a permanent, contained bed since it spreads readily from any tuber left behind.
directions: Boston Red is a long-grown New England heirloom sunchoke selected for its striking maroon-red tuber skin, which contrasts sharply with the white flesh beneath and makes it a favorite of seed savers maintaining regionally distinct strains. Like other Jerusalem artichokes it grows into a coarse, sunflower-like stand 6-10 feet tall, topped with small yellow flowers in late summer, and tolerates poor soil and neglect once established. Dig tubers after the tops are killed by frost and continue harvesting through winter and into early spring as needed, leaving some tubers in the ground each year to regenerate the patch. Its flavor is the same nutty, sweet-earthy inulin-rich profile typical of the species, and it sweetens further after tubers experience a hard freeze.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension -- Jerusalem Artichoke

name: Boule d'Or Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills once soil has warmed past 65°F after last frost, or transplant peat-pot-started seedlings to avoid root disturbance; give Boule d'Or full sun and consistent moisture through the long ripening season typical of Gulf Coast summers. In zone 9, plant March–April for late-summer harvest.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills after frost danger has passed, thinning to 2 strong plants per hill; mulch to conserve moisture and suppress weeds around the sprawling vines. Harvest when the golden-yellow rind fully colors and the fruit releases a musky-sweet fragrance at the stem end, usually with a slight give when pressed. Boule d'Or ('Golden Ball') is a French heirloom cantaloupe-type melon dating to the late 1800s, bearing round, 2–3 lb fruit with a distinctive smooth, deep-gold rind faintly ribbed rather than netted, enclosing firm, pale orange flesh with a rich, honeyed sweetness that intensifies in storage. Unlike most cantaloupes, Boule d'Or keeps for several weeks after picking without losing flavor, making it valued by market gardeners for extending the melon season. Vines are moderately vigorous and benefit from trellising in smaller gardens if fruit weight is supported in slings.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Boule d'Or melon variety notes
Kitazawa Seed Co. and heirloom seed catalog descriptions
University of California Cooperative Extension — Specialty Melon Production Guide

name: Bowling Red Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow 1-3 weeks after the last frost once soil temperatures are consistently warm, soaking seed beforehand to improve germination.
directions: Sow directly into warm garden soil after frost danger has passed, since okra grows poorly if started indoors and transplanted. Pick the deep red pods small and often to keep plants productive through the heat of summer. Bowling Red is a Kentucky heirloom valued for its striking burgundy-red pods and reddish stems, which add ornamental interest to the vegetable garden as well as color to the harvest basket. The pods darken to a rich maroon-green when cooked but retain their tender texture if picked young.

name: Box Car Willie Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; a reliably productive red beefsteak heirloom with excellent disease resistance that performs consistently in both humid and dry climates — a good choice for beginners seeking a dependable large heirloom tomato.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed into deeply prepared, fertile, well-drained soil. Box Car Willie is an American heirloom red beefsteak tomato named with Old West flair and popular for its reliable productivity, large 8–14 ounce fruits with smooth, meaty red flesh and excellent balanced sweet-acid flavor, and its relative disease resistance compared to many other heirlooms — it typically outproduces more famous heirlooms like Brandywine under variable conditions. The vigorous, indeterminate vines need staking or caging; fruits are round to slightly flattened with smooth, crack-resistant skin. A solid everyday heirloom choice for gardeners who want large, flavorful tomatoes without the fussiness of some heritage types.

name: Boxcar Willie Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vine as it grows.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes and stake early to support the productive vine. Boxcar Willie is a widely grown red beefsteak heirloom, said to be named after country singer Boxcar Willie, prized among home gardeners for combining classic large, meaty, smooth, round-oblate red fruit with a more reliable, heavier yield and better disease tolerance than many older large-fruited heirlooms. The mild, well-balanced, classic tomato flavor and consistent fruit set make it a good gateway heirloom for gardeners moving beyond hybrid slicers, and the regular-leaf indeterminate vines keep producing steadily over a long season. Water evenly and feed regularly through fruit set, and stake generously, since the productive vine sets a heavy load of good-sized fruit.

name: Bradford Family Okra
plantingNote: Scarify seed and direct sow an inch deep after last frost once soil is reliably warm; Bradford Family has been grown by the Bradford family of Sumter, South Carolina since the 1920s and was reintroduced to chefs by Nat Bradford starting in 2017.
directions: Nick or scarify the hard seed coat before direct sowing an inch deep in full sun; Bradford Family is unusual among okra for staying tender even at 6 to 8 inches long, with pod tips that snap cleanly rather than turning fibrous at that size. The pods are notably sweet and large enough to stuff, and the plump seeds inside have drawn comparisons to caviar from chefs who have cooked with this once nearly-forgotten Lowcountry heirloom. Harvest every two to three days during peak summer production to keep plants setting new flowers, and expect strong continuous yields in Gulf South heat once plants are established.
sources: Sow True Seed — Bradford Family Okra
Anson Mills / Nat Bradford seed history accounts

name: Bradford Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, in deeply worked, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give vines 6–10 feet of room to sprawl and handle ripe fruit gently, since the thin, tender rind that gives Bradford its sweetness also makes it far more bruise-prone than commercial shipping melons.
directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained, deeply worked soil in full sun once soil has warmed; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off watering as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Bradford Watermelon is a South Carolina heirloom dating to the 1840s, developed by the Bradford family of Sumter County and grown continuously within the family for over 170 years before nurseryman Nat Bradford reintroduced it commercially in the 2010s. Large oblong fruits (often 25–40 pounds) have a distinctive soft, thin rind and exceptionally sweet, deep red flesh — historically prized enough that the whole melon, rind included, was cooked down into watermelon rind preserves and syrup. That same soft rind made it too fragile for the rail-shipping trade of the early 20th century, which nearly drove the variety extinct as tougher-rinded shipping melons took over the commercial market; it survived only because the Bradford family kept saving and replanting seed on their own land. A true living-history heirloom for the home garden, where a thin, easily bruised rind is no obstacle, in zone 4–11.

name: Bradley Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed well above 65°F; okra seedlings sulk and can rot in cool spring soil, so Gulf Coast gardeners generally wait until early-to-mid May.
directions: Bradley is a widely grown Deep South home-garden hybrid prized for smooth, spineless, dark green pods that stay tender well past the 3-4 inch stage, forgiving gardeners who miss a picking day or two in peak summer heat. Plants stay a manageable, well-branched height compared to rangy heirloom types, which makes hand-harvesting easier and keeps pods within easy reach all season. It sets pods heavily and continuously through the hottest, most humid stretch of summer, when many other vegetables shut down, and responds well to a side-dressing of nitrogen once plants begin flowering. Pick every day or two once pods start forming, since Bradley pods can pass tenderness quickly in hot weather.

name: Bradley Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January for March transplanting. Bradley is a University of Arkansas release long popular across the Mid-South and Gulf South for its smooth, meaty pink fruit.
directions: Start seeds 6-8 weeks before transplanting at 70-80F; Bradley is a pink-fruited slicing tomato released by the University of Arkansas and grown widely across the Mid-South and Gulf South for decades as a reliable home-garden standard. The large, smooth, globe-shaped fruits have the mild, sweet, low-acid flavor typical of pink tomatoes, with meaty flesh and few seeds that make them excellent for fresh slicing and sandwiches. Plants are vigorous and produce well through the first flush of Southern summer heat, though yields taper once nighttime temperatures climb into the mid-70s like most standard hybrids. Stake or cage plants early and keep watering even to prevent cracking and blossom end rot through the swings between Gulf South downpours and dry spells. A good companion to a heat-set variety like Neptune or Phoenix for a longer harvest window into peak summer.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture — Tomato Variety Notes
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomato Variety Selection
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Tomato Variety Descriptions

name: Brandy Boy Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Brandy Boy is a vigorous indeterminate vine that needs a tall, sturdy cage or stake from the start.
directions: Brandy Boy was bred by Burpee to reproduce the rich, complex flavor of the beloved heirloom Brandywine on a modern F1 hybrid frame that sets fruit far more reliably. The rosy-pink, deeply flattened beefsteak fruit runs 10-16 ounces with the dense, low-acid, old-fashioned flavor Brandywine fans expect, but the hybrid vigor and improved disease tolerance mean noticeably higher yields per plant than the open-pollinated original. Give the tall indeterminate vine a sturdy 6-foot cage or stake, prune lower suckers for airflow, and pick fruit at full color for the best flavor.

name: Brandywine OTV Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; OTV is a potato-leaf Brandywine type that sets fruit somewhat more reliably than the classic pink strain in variable weather.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply prepared soil once nights have warmed, staking firmly to support the heavy crop. Brandywine OTV is an orange-fruited sport of the classic pink Brandywine, keeping the same potato-leaf foliage and rich, old-fashioned tomato flavor but in a warm terra-cotta orange color with slightly earlier, more dependable fruit set. Fruit commonly runs a pound or more, with a meaty interior and relatively few seeds. Harvest at full color and handle gently, since the soft-fleshed fruit bruises easily and is best enjoyed fresh rather than stored.

name: Brandywine Platfoot's Strain Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this is a sprawling, potato-leaf, long-season vine that needs sturdy staking and ample room to spread.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into rich, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed, staking or caging the vine early since it grows tall and sprawling with heavy fruit. Platfoot's Strain is one of two documented true-breeding lineages of the classic pink Brandywine (the other being Sudduth's Strain), both preserved and distributed by seed-saving organizations as representing the original, authenticated form of this legendary heirloom. Like other Brandywine strains it carries the distinctive potato-leaf foliage and produces large, oblate, irregularly shaped fruit with deep pink skin and rich, complex, low-acid flavor prized by heirloom tomato growers. Expect a slow, demanding grow that rewards patience with a long, warm season — the plant matures later than most tomatoes but produces some of the most sought-after fruit in the heirloom world.
sources: Weaver, William Woys. Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

name: Brandywine Sudduth's Strain Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give the sprawling, potato-leaf, long-season vine sturdy staking and plenty of room.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes and provide strong staking, since this vigorous, long-season Brandywine strain produces very heavy fruit over an extended harvest. This is the specific pink Brandywine strain traced to the Sudduth family of Tennessee and distributed to the wider heirloom seed-saving community by collector Ben Quisenberry in the 1980s, and it is widely regarded among heirloom tomato growers as the strain most faithful to the original 19th-century Brandywine. The large, rosy-pink, potato-leaf beefsteak fruit carries the rich, sweet, well-balanced, classically 'old-fashioned' tomato flavor that made Brandywine famous, though yields can run lower and the season longer than modern hybrids. Water consistently and feed moderately through the season, since Brandywine strains are notably more sensitive to inconsistent care than modern disease-resistant hybrids.

name: Brandywine Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost risk passes; a potato-leaved variety that benefits from deep planting and very sturdy staking as the large fruits make vines top-heavy.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–80°F and transplant after frost risk passes, burying the stem deeply to encourage rooting; Brandywine is arguably the most celebrated American heirloom tomato, a large pink-red beefsteak type with potato-leaved foliage and 1–2 pound fruits that ripen slowly but reward the patient gardener with extraordinarily rich, complex, sweet-acidic flavor widely considered the gold standard of tomato taste. Stake or cage firmly — the vigorous indeterminate vines grow to 6 feet and heavy fruits weigh branches down without support. Days to maturity are long, making it best suited to long-season gardens; in the south, plant early for spring harvest before summer heat sets in.

name: Bravo Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting; sow in early summer for transplanting in July-August so heads mature during the cooler, drier stretch of a zone 8-9 fall and winter.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun, using tighter 12-inch spacing for smaller fresh-market heads or 18-24 inches for larger heads and kraut production. Bravo is a Bejo-bred hybrid valued for uniform, solid, blue-green round heads with good resistance to head cracking and to black rot and fusarium yellows, two disease pressures that build up quickly in warm, humid fall gardens. It has a reputation among market growers for performing well across a wide range of climates, from Deep South winter production to northern summer crops, which makes it a dependable second cabbage choice alongside more region-specific varieties. Feed consistently through head formation, since Bravo's large frame needs steady fertility to fill out its heads before a hard freeze.

name: Brazilian Crookneck Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is warm; Brazilian Crookneck is a giant, long-vined heirloom crookneck type that needs generous room and a full warm season to size up its 10-20 pound fruit.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in enriched hills once the soil has warmed well after the last frost, allowing the sprawling vines plenty of room to run. Brazilian Crookneck is a South American heirloom crookneck squash producing some of the largest fruit in the moschata group, with pale tan to gray-tan skin, a long curving neck, and dense, deep orange flesh with a nutty, sweet flavor well suited to roasting or soup. Like other moschata squashes it carries better resistance to squash vine borer and bacterial wilt than most pepo types, making it a dependable choice where those pests are a problem. Let fruit mature fully on the vine until the rind resists a fingernail, then cure in a warm spot for a couple of weeks before moving to cool, dry storage.

name: Brazilian Starfish Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost with bottom heat; the weeping, vining growth habit benefits from a cage or trellis once fruit weighs the branches down.
directions: Brazilian Starfish is a Peruvian aji type domesticated in Brazil and grown chiefly for its unusual flattened, deeply-lobed pods that flare out into a five- or six-pointed star shape as they mature from green to red. The flavor is floral and fruity with a medium heat in the 15,000-20,000 Scoville range, similar in punch to a serrano but with the tropical fruitiness typical of Capsicum baccatum. Plants have a lax, weeping, almost vine-like habit rather than the upright form of most peppers, so light staking or a small cage keeps the fruit-laden branches off the ground. Sliced starfish-shaped pods are a striking addition to pickle jars, salsas, and salads; consistent moisture and rich soil produce the heaviest pod set over a long warm season.
sources: Pepper Geek — Brazilian Starfish Pepper Growing Guide
Trade Winds Fruit — Capsicum baccatum Variety Collection

name: Bride Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into warm, fertile soil once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Bride is a compact, well-branching Asian type that sets clusters of two to three fruits per node rather than single large fruits.
directions: Bride is a Chinese-derived hybrid eggplant with slender, cylindrical fruit that emerges ivory-white and develops soft purple-lavender streaking as it fills out, topped by a distinctive green calyx. Fruit is best picked around 6-8 inches long and 1.5 inches thick, while the streaking is still light and the flesh is at its most tender and mild. The compact, branching plants set fruit in small clusters rather than singly, giving a steady succession of harvests through the hot part of the season. Because the thin skin bruises easily, handle fruit gently and cook it soon after picking in stir-fries or on the grill.

name: Bright Lights Swiss Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow or start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Bright Lights is a cool-season biennial treated as an annual. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall and winter production, or February–March for spring. Swiss chard tolerates light frost but is damaged by hard freezes — in zone 9, plants grown through the mild winter provide harvest from fall through spring. Bright Lights produces a mix of stem colors (yellow, orange, red, pink, white, purple, and intermediate shades) within each packet, creating a visually striking garden planting and a colorful harvest of mixed-stem bunches.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep; each chard 'seed' is actually a seed cluster that may produce 2–3 seedlings — thin to the strongest. Harvest outer leaves at any size; plants continue producing from the center. Bright Lights is a 1998 All-America Selections-winning Swiss chard — a variety selection that produces the same flavor and productivity as standard chard while dramatically expanding the visual appeal of the garden. Each individual plant in a Bright Lights planting develops stems of a single color, but a planting from any seed packet includes plants with yellow, orange, red, pink, white, lavender, and purple stems, with the blade of each leaf complementarily colored against the bright stem. Photographed in morning light, a mature Bright Lights planting is among the most colorful edible garden plantings available in any vegetable category. The flavor is identical to standard Swiss chard — the young leaves are mild and spinach-like for raw salads; the mature leaves are substantial and slightly earthy-sweet when cooked. The colored stems and midribs hold their color reasonably well through cooking (yellow and white stems hold best; red and pink stems bleed somewhat). Bright Lights is valued in both edible gardens and ornamental-edible plantings where it provides extended color through the cooler months.
sources: All-America Selections — Bright Lights Swiss chard AAS winner 1998
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Chard variety comparison
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Swiss Chard Production Guide

name: Bright Lights Swiss Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 the ideal sowing windows are September–November for fall/winter crop and February–March for spring. Bright Lights tolerates light frost and light heat but bolts in sustained high temperatures. In zone 9, fall-sown chard is often the finest and can continue through winter.
directions: Sow 1/2 inch deep and thin to 6–9 inches; chard seed is a cluster (multigerm) so thinning is essential. Bright Lights is an All-America Selections winner rainbow chard that transformed chard's reputation from a workmanlike spinach substitute to a showstopping ornamental-edible. The plants produce stems in a vivid spectrum of yellow, orange, red, pink, purple, and white — a single bed creates extraordinary visual impact in the garden. Leaves are tender, mild, and slightly earthy, superior to red chard for flavor; stems are crisp and colorful even when cooked, with a mildly sweet, earthy flavor that stands up to sautéing, braising, and pasta dishes. For zone 9 fall gardens, Bright Lights is one of the most reliable cool-season crops: it germinates quickly in September warmth, grows through October–November, survives light freezes, and can continue producing into January–February. Harvest outer leaves regularly for continuous production; plants can produce for months. Tolerates partial shade in hot weather, which extends the harvest season significantly.
sources: All-America Selections — Bright Lights Swiss Chard AAS winner 1998
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Bright Lights variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Swiss Chard for Florida Gardens
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Swiss Chard Production

name: Bright Yellow Swiss Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow around the last frost date, thinning to final spacing as seedlings develop true leaves.
directions: Sow directly and thin plants to stand several inches apart, keeping soil evenly moist to encourage broad, tender leaves. Unlike multicolor chard blends, this selection breeds true for solid golden-yellow stalks and veins beneath crumpled dark green leaves, giving a uniform look for market bunching. Its flavor is mild and slightly sweeter than red-stemmed types, and it holds up well as both a baby green and a mature cooking chard.

name: Brilliant Celeriac
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, since germination is slow, and transplant out once nights stay reliably above freezing.
directions: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost and transplant into deep, fertile, evenly moist soil, since celeriac's long development window punishes any lapse in watering with cracked or hollow roots. Brilliant is grown for its notably smooth-skinned, low-knobbed globes, which peel far more cleanly than older, rougher celeriac types while keeping the same concentrated celery flavor. Remove side shoots and surface roots from the developing globe through the season to channel growth into the main root, and harvest in fall for a dense, long-storing crop that holds well in a root cellar.

name: Brimmer Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Brimmer is a vigorous indeterminate variety that requires sturdy staking or caging to support its very heavy, often one- to two-pound fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil, staking firmly to bear the weight of the fruit. Developed in the early 1900s by a Richmond, Virginia seed company, Brimmer, marketed historically as Wood's Famous Brimmer, won a Grand Prize in 1907 for its large, round, pink-to-purple fruit that is thick-skinned, meaty, and low-acid, often exceeding a pound at full size. The variety fell out of commercial favor by the mid-1960s but has since been preserved and revived by regional seed savers, including Southern Exposure Seed Exchange.

name: Brindisino Artichoke
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant, or set out rooted offshoots in spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Mild Adriatic winters around Brindisi allow harvest from autumn through spring on established stools.
directions: Brindisino is the IGP-recognized artichoke grown around Brindisi in coastal Puglia, where mild Adriatic winters allow an extended harvest from autumn through spring. Heads are medium-sized, rounded, and tightly closed around a mild, tender heart that local cooks favor for stewing with potatoes and peas or braising whole in olive oil and garlic. Like other southern Italian landraces it is grown as a long-lived perennial and increased by dividing offshoots from established stools rather than annual reseeding. Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and water through dry summer stretches to keep crowns productive.
sources: Regione Puglia — Carciofo Brindisino IGP Disciplinare
European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register
Slow Food Presidia — Italian Heritage Artichoke Varieties

name: Broad-Leaf Batavian Endive
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 transplant August–September for harvest November–January. Batavian endive takes longer to mature than frisee; allow the full 80–95 days from transplant. Blanch the center by tying outer leaves together for 10–14 days before harvest to reduce bitterness and lighten the interior. The large, robust heads store well for 2–3 weeks under refrigeration.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Broad-Leaf Batavian Endive is the flat-leafed, large-headed escarole-type endive — distinct from frizzy curly endive in having broad, wavy, slightly ruffled leaves rather than finely cut, frilly ones. The large, open heads weigh 1–2 pounds with pale green to cream-white interior leaves (if blanched) and a mild, slightly bitter flavor that is more approachable than radicchio or frisee. Broad-Leaf Batavian endive is extensively used in Italian cooking — sautéed with garlic and olive oil, incorporated into soups and braised bean dishes, and used as a pizza or pasta topping where its mild bitterness counterbalances richer ingredients. It is also used raw in salads when blanched to a creamy interior. The large, substantial leaves hold up better to cooking than frisee or standard lettuces. In zone 9 it is a reliable fall crop that matures through November and December for harvest into January.
sources: Seeds of Italy — Batavian Endive Growing Notes
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Endive Types
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Endive and Escarole Production

name: Broadleaf Czech Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves pointed end up in fall, roughly 4-6 weeks before the soil freezes, so they root well ahead of winter.
directions: Set cloves 2 inches deep and 4 to 6 inches apart in fertile, well-worked soil, then mulch heavily for winter insulation in cold climates. Trim the tough central scape once it curls to push more energy into bulb development, and cure harvested bulbs in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks. Broadleaf Czech is a robust porcelain-type hardneck grown widely across the Czech Republic and imported to North America by garlic collectors, valued for its large, easy-to-peel cloves, strong hot flavor, and reliable cold hardiness in northern gardens.

name: Brock's Imperial Asparagus
plantingNote: Enrich the bed with well-rotted manure before planting one-year crowns, since this old heirloom rewards deep, rich soil.
directions: Brock's Imperial is an old open-pollinated English heirloom asparagus valued for producing exceptionally thick, well-flavored spears on vigorous, long-lived crowns. Because it is not an all-male hybrid, plants include both sexes, so expect some volunteer seedlings from the red berries that female plants set in late summer. Gardeners who favor traditional, seed-saveable strains over modern hybrids often choose it to keep an older lineage of asparagus in circulation. Allow a full two seasons of foliage growth before the first light harvest to build a strong root system.

name: Bronco Bush Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; Bronco carries excellent resistance to bean common mosaic virus (BCMV), a widespread aphid-transmitted disease, and holds up well to shipping and summer heat, making it a dependable choice for a long Gulf South bean season.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after all frost risk has passed; Bronco is a widely grown commercial bush snap bean valued for excellent resistance to bean common mosaic virus, an aphid-spread disease that can stunt and discolor susceptible bean plantings, along with good heat tolerance and strong pod quality under summer growing conditions. It produces glossy, dark green, straight pods on an upright, high-yielding bush that needs no staking. Harvest pods young and tender, before seeds bulge visibly through the pod wall, and pick every couple of days to keep plants setting new flowers. Succession sow every 2-3 weeks through the warm season for a continuous harvest.
sources: seed catalog reference (Stokes Seeds, Rupp Seeds, Fruition Seeds)

name: Bronze Arrow Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer for fall; can be harvested young as baby leaf or allowed to form full loose heads.
directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed shallowly in fertile, well-drained soil, thinning to a foot apart for full heads or leaving plants closer together for repeated baby-leaf cuts. Bronze Arrow forms an upright, loose, romaine-like rosette of narrow, pointed leaves that emerge green at the base and deepen to a rich bronze-red at the tips and edges, especially in cool weather and strong sun. It is notably slow to bolt and holds good quality longer into warm weather than many heirloom lettuces, making it a dependable choice for extending the spring lettuce season. The arrow-shaped leaves and striking two-tone coloring also make it a popular addition to mixed salad plantings for looks as well as flavor.

name: Bronze Mignonette Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow October–February for fall through spring harvest. Bronze Mignonette is a miniature butterhead that forms small, tight heads 3–5 inches across — perfect spacing is 6–8 inches in a grid pattern for maximum production in a small space. The tight, compact heading habit makes it one of the best lettuces for containers and small patio gardens. In zone 9 it performs excellently from fall through early spring; thin sowing in partial afternoon shade extends the season. Harvest the entire small head at once or harvest as baby leaves from the outside.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, consistently moist soil — lettuce requires steady moisture and cool temperatures; Bronze Mignonette is a miniature French heirloom butterhead lettuce forming small, compact, dense heads with deeply bronze-tinged outer leaves grading to butter-yellow in the blanched interior — the same color pattern as a large butterhead but scaled down to a single-serving head of 3–5 inches across. The Mignonette name (French for 'small and delicate') describes both the size and the tender, buttery character of these compact heads, which provide the soft, sweet, melt-in-the-mouth texture of butterhead lettuce in a size perfectly proportioned for a single-person salad. Unlike large butterhead varieties where a single head may be too much for one meal, Bronze Mignonette heads can be harvested and eaten in one serving — a practical advantage for small households and container growers who want variety without waste. The bronze outer leaves and buttery-sweet interior flavor make Bronze Mignonette one of the most attractive and best-tasting small lettuces for kitchen garden edging, window boxes, and mixed salad plantings.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Bronze Mignonette French Heirloom Lettuce
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Butterhead Lettuce Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lettuce Production for Florida

name: Brown Crowder Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; Brown Crowder is a vigorous, heat-loving heirloom that thrives through the hottest, most humid stretch of the Gulf South growing season.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in warm, well-drained soil, allowing extra room for the semi-vining growth habit to sprawl. Brown Crowder is a traditional Southern heirloom named for the way its brown-hulled peas pack tightly, or 'crowd,' against one another inside the pod, developing the rich, earthy flavor and quick-cooking texture prized in old-fashioned Southern pea dishes. Vigorous vines produce heavily even in the poor, sandy soils and intense heat that stall many other legumes, and the plants show good general tolerance to common cowpea pests and diseases. Like other cowpeas, Brown Crowder fixes nitrogen through its root nodules, leaving the soil enriched for a following crop. Pick pods green for fresh shelling once well filled, or let them dry fully on the vine for classic dried crowder peas.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension — Southern Pea Production Guide

name: Brown Dutch Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow shallowly in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; lettuce seed needs light to germinate well.
directions: One of the oldest documented lettuce names in cultivation, Brown Dutch appears in print as early as the 1740s in English gardening manuals and was carried by American colonial and nineteenth-century gardeners as a reliable cool-season green. It forms a loose, nonheading rosette of large, floppy, deep lime-green leaves with ruffled edges that take on a bronzy pink-brown tinge in cool weather or bright sun, making it as ornamental as it is edible. The old-fashioned, tender leaves have a mild flavor and hold up reasonably well to light frost and summer heat compared with tighter heading types. Because it is open-pollinated and easy to save, it remains a good choice for gardeners wanting to grow a genuinely centuries-old lettuce.
sources: William Woys Weaver - Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

name: Brown Flax
plantingNote: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, up to the last frost date; brown flax is the traditional oilseed color type and shares the same cool-season culture as other flax.
directions: Broadcast seed onto a firm, fine seedbed and rake in lightly to about 1/4 inch deep, sowing thickly so plants support each other against wind and rain. Brown flax is the older, more widely grown oilseed color type worldwide, with a stronger, earthier flavor than golden flax and a long history of use for both pressed oil and fiber where stands are allowed to grow taller and thinner. Harvest by pulling or cutting whole plants once the lower third of the stem has yellowed and most seed capsules have turned brown and dry, then shock the bundles upright to finish curing for about two weeks. Thresh over a tarp or inside a barrel and screen the seed carefully, since brown flaxseed is oily and can clump if stored before it is fully dry.

name: Brown Resilient
plantingNote: Sow after soil warms to 60F; the short-vined plants tolerate cool nights better than most dry beans.
directions: Plant breeder Carol Deppe developed this bean from Gaucho and her Beefy Resilient Grex specifically to produce well where spring is cold and summer nights dip into the 50s. Expect a mix of growth habits, from true bush to short vines, and a mottled crop of mostly brown seed with some gold or black mixed in, which actually correlates with better yields than a pure color line. Let pods dry hard on the plant until a fingernail can no longer dent the seed, then thresh for a rich, meaty dry bean comparable in yield to Jacob's Cattle or Soldier. Good air circulation and wider row spacing help prevent mold in the humid late season.

name: Brown Saxon Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves in fall in free-draining soil; Brown Saxon matures earlier than many hardnecks and tolerates milder, wetter winters than the coldest-climate types.
directions: Brown Saxon is an English heirloom hardneck with tan to light-brown bulb wrappers and a reliably mild, rounded flavor compared to sharper continental types, making it popular for growers in cooler, damper maritime climates where many hardnecks struggle. It bulks up a bit faster than late-season porcelain types, so watch for scapes to form and remove them promptly to concentrate growth in the bulb. Harvest once the lower leaves begin to brown, lift carefully to avoid bruising the relatively thin skins, and cure in a dry, shaded, airy location for a few weeks before storing. Because it is less cold-tolerant than extreme-climate hardnecks, gardeners in very harsh winter regions should mulch the planting bed well.
sources: The Garlic Farm (Isle of Wight, UK) variety guide

name: Brown Teff
plantingNote: Sow after last frost once soil is warm; brown teff is the traditional reddish-brown seed class most widely grown in Ethiopia and prized for its deeper, more robust flavor.
directions: Blend the minuscule seed with dry sand or fine compost before broadcasting onto a firm, well-prepared bed, then roll or tamp lightly instead of covering with soil. Brown teff carries the deeper reddish-brown seed coat and stronger, tangier flavor traditionally used for classic sour injera, and is generally the hardier, more widely adapted seed class for home growers experimenting with teff outside its native highlands. Its fine tillers form an airy stand that should be cut at the base once the majority of seed heads have dried to a rusty brown, well before a hard rain can shatter the crop. Dry the cut bundles under cover for a week or more, then thresh by gentle flailing and winnow in a light, steady breeze to separate the small heavy seed from the chaff.

name: Brune d'Hiver Lettuce
plantingNote: Sow in late summer or early fall for a winter and early-spring harvest, or in early spring for a standard-season crop.
directions: Sow in late summer or early fall for a winter and early-spring harvest, or in early spring for a standard-season crop, since it is also reasonably slow to bolt. This French heirloom butterhead, whose name translates to brown of winter, forms compact rosettes of bronze-tinged green leaves and ranks among the most cold-hardy lettuces in cultivation, often overwintering under row cover or in a cold frame. Its history traces to at least the nineteenth century in France, where it kept kitchen gardens supplied with greens through the cold months.

name: Bubba Blue Ginger
plantingNote: Pre-sprout rhizome pieces indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, then transplant outdoors once soil is consistently warm and frost danger has passed. 'Bubba Blue' is distinguished from common culinary ginger by the blue-tinged coloring at the base of its young shoots and pseudostems.
directions: Plant pre-sprouted rhizome pieces 2 inches deep in rich, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in dappled shade to part sun; keep evenly moist through the growing season. 'Bubba Blue' is a named culinary ginger cultivar grown in university variety trials alongside other named strains for rhizome yield and quality comparison, notable for the distinctive blue-purple blush at the base of its stems and buds, which distinguishes it visually from plain commercial ginger while producing rhizomes of comparable culinary quality. Harvest young 'baby' ginger in 4-5 months for a milder, less fibrous root, or allow foliage to yellow and die back for a fully mature, more pungent harvest. In zone 8-9, mulch heavily or lift and store rhizomes over winter.

name: Budai Torpe Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the short, rugose-leafed dwarf habit needs little to no staking.
directions: Budai Torpe, whose Hungarian name translates roughly to 'Buda dwarf,' is a compact, potato-leaf heirloom tomato from Hungary grown for generations before it entered wider international seed exchange. Its thick, rugose foliage and short, self-supporting stems are typical of old-world dwarf tomato lines, and it bears medium-sized red fruit with a brisk, well-balanced flavor. Along with other historic dwarf varieties, it was folded into the founding gene pool of the modern Dwarf Tomato Project, most notably crossed with Black From Tula to produce the early-maturing Dwarf Arctic Rose. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine.

name: Buena Mulata Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; an African-American heirloom pepper from Philadelphia with striking color changes through the ripening cycle — highly ornamental as well as edible.
directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed. Buena Mulata is a treasured African-American heirloom pepper with roots in Philadelphia's Black community, saved for generations and brought to wider attention through Seed Savers Exchange; it produces thin, cayenne-shaped pods 4–5 inches long that pass through a remarkable spectrum of colors as they ripen — pale cream to lavender-purple to orange to red — making the plant highly ornamental at every stage. The flavor is moderately hot (about 30,000 SHU) with a distinctive spicy, slightly fruity complexity; use fresh at any stage or dry to a rich red powder. This is a historically significant cultivar that deserves preservation and wider growing.

name: Buffon d'Glaces Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant in cool weather; the tight, juicy heads need consistent moisture to stay crisp rather than bolt under heat stress.
directions: Buffon d'Glaces is the first commercial release from a long-running Wild Garden Seed breeding project that crossed the heirloom crisphead 'Reine d'Glaces' with the colorful 'Jester' lettuce. It forms tight, juicy 8-inch heads wrapped in ruffled, toothed leaves marked with high-contrast red stripes and splashes over green. Inside, the color carries through as white with pink patterning that can deepen to solid pink in some heads. Grow it like other crispheads: cool soil, even moisture, and harvest promptly once heads firm up, since crisphead types bolt or lose crunch faster than looser lettuce types in sustained heat.

name: Buffy Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Buffy's upright, heavily fruited plants also work well in containers brought indoors over winter.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost. Buffy is a compact, upright AAS-winning pepper that sets an exceptionally heavy load of slender, two-inch fruit along its branches, ripening from dark green to glossy lipstick-red with real ornamental impact in beds or edible landscaping. It carries noticeable heat and cures quickly on the plant, making it well suited to drying or pickling as well as fresh use. The sturdy, deer- and disease-resistant plants hold up to heat stress better than many cayenne-type peppers.

name: Bugle Butternut Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; Bugle is a Cornell-bred butternut selected for strong powdery mildew resistance on a more compact vine than older butternut varieties, letting the foliage stay productive later into a humid Gulf South summer.
directions: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, allowing the vines room to spread; Bugle is a butternut squash bred at Cornell University with strong resistance to powdery mildew, the fungal disease that typically coats squash foliage in a white film and shuts down photosynthesis well before fruit has finished sizing and curing in humid Southern gardens. Because the leaf canopy stays healthier longer, Bugle tends to fill out a fuller crop of the classic tan, elongated-neck fruit with dense, sweet orange flesh than mildew-susceptible butternut varieties planted in the same conditions. Let the squash mature fully to a hard rind before harvest, then cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks; properly cured fruit stores for several months and is excellent roasted, baked, or pureed into soup.
sources: seed catalog reference (Rupp Seeds, True Leaf Market)

name: Bulgarian Carrot Pepper
