plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk passes and soil has warmed; this Bulgarian heirloom produces carrot-shaped, brilliant orange fruits that are thin-walled but very prolific.
directions: Start seed at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost in a moist starting mix and pot up once the first true leaves appear; transplant after frost danger passes and begin fertilizing with a low-nitrogen, high-phosphorus fertilizer to encourage fruit set. Bulgarian Carrot is an eastern European heirloom producing vivid orange, carrot-shaped fruits 3–4 inches long with thin, crispy walls and a surprising fruity, almost apricot-like sweetness that precedes a sharp, clean, medium heat (5,000 SHU). It is exceptionally productive, with dozens of fruits per plant, and is highly ornamental as fruits turn from yellow to brilliant orange at maturity. Use fresh in salsas and relishes where the fruity flavor is showcased, or pickle whole for a pantry staple.

name: Bulgarian Giant Leek
plantingNote: Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost, then transplant into a trench once seedlings are pencil-thick, backfilling gradually to blanch the shafts as the plants grow.
directions: Bulgarian Giant is a traditional Eastern European leek grown for its thick, blue-green-topped shafts and outstanding cold hardiness, making it well suited to autumn and winter harvest after flavor has been sweetened by frost. The shanks can reach several inches in diameter under good growing conditions, with a milder, less pungent character than many summer leek types. Transplant into a deep trench or dibbled holes to maximize the length of blanched white shaft, hilling soil around the base as the plants size up. Harvest from fall through winter as needed, since mature plants hold well in the ground in cold weather rather than requiring immediate pulling.

name: Bulgarian Triumph Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Bulgarian Triumph is a traditional Bulgarian heirloom bred for meaty, low-seed paste fruit.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Bulgarian Triumph is a traditional heirloom from Bulgaria, bearing medium-sized red fruit with dense, meaty, low-seed flesh well suited to sauce and paste, a style of tomato long favored in Eastern European home gardens for preserving. Its productive, reliable vines yield a heavy crop over the growing season in gardens with a long, warm summer. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor and texture in cooked preparations.

name: Bull Nose Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil and air have warmed; Bull Nose is one of the oldest documented American sweet peppers, grown by Thomas Jefferson at Monticello in the early 1800s.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55°F. Bull Nose is one of the oldest documented sweet pepper varieties in American gardens, grown by Thomas Jefferson at Monticello and preserved by seed savers as a living link to early American kitchen gardens, producing blocky, mild, thick-walled fruit that matures from green to red. It performs reliably through the long, hot Gulf South growing season on compact, productive plants well suited to garden beds or large containers. Harvest fruit green for a milder flavor or let it ripen fully to red for peak sweetness, and pick regularly to encourage continued fruit set through summer.
sources: Monticello / Thomas Jefferson Center for Historic Plants

name: Bull's Blood Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring, or in late summer for fall harvest; Bull's Blood is a Victorian-era heirloom beet grown as much for its strikingly deep burgundy-red, ornamental foliage as for the edible roots, making it one of the most beautiful of all vegetable garden plants and an outstanding edging or salad green.
directions: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep directly in the garden 2–4 weeks before last frost in fertile, deeply worked, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soil; soak seeds overnight to improve germination and thin to 3–4 inches when plants are 3 inches tall. Bull's Blood is a Victorian-era heirloom beet first listed in Burpee's catalog in the 1840s, grown for 175+ years for its spectacular deep burgundy-red to near-purple foliage that is among the most vivid of any vegetable; the young leaves and stems are intensely colored and are prized as a microgreen, baby salad leaf, and ornamental edging plant. The roots are also deep red, sweet, and excellent at any size from marble (35–40 days) to mature golf ball (55–60 days). The dramatic foliage remains strongly colored through the season and is highly heat-tolerant for a beet. An outstanding dual-purpose ornamental-vegetable for edible landscaping, container growing, and intensive salad gardens.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee Company catalog archives

name: Bun Long Taro
plantingNote: Plant corms or divisions in spring when soil has warmed to 65°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. Bun Long taro is a wetland-adapted variety that thrives in consistently moist or periodically flooded conditions — ideal for poorly drained garden spots, pond margins, and bog gardens. It can also be grown in well-watered containers. The corms are harvested 7–12 months after planting when the large leaves begin to yellow.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in rich, moist to wet soil — Bun Long thrives at pond margins and in consistently waterlogged conditions that would kill most vegetables; Bun Long is a Hawaiian-adapted wetland taro cultivar used as the primary taro for poi production in Hawaii, producing large starchy corms with a distinctive pale lavender-purple flesh that turns light gray-purple when cooked and pounded. The large corms (often 2–5 pounds each) are a primary poi taro precisely because of their excellent starch content and texture when cooked and pounded or processed. The leaves and stems are also edible when thoroughly cooked — the tender young leaves (luau leaves in Hawaiian cuisine) are used in laulau, stew, and other dishes. In zone 9 Bun Long taro is an outstanding productive crop for the long, hot, humid growing season and thrives in the wet spots and poorly drained areas of Gulf Coast gardens where other vegetables struggle. The handsome large leaves with their distinctive pale purple veins provide ornamental value as well.
sources: University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension — Poi Taro Cultivars
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Taro Production
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Taro Cultivation in Florida

name: Bunch Porto Rico Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant rooted slips 2–4 weeks after last frost in well-drained soil built into ridges in full sun; the compact, semi-bush vine habit takes noticeably less room to sprawl than most heirloom sweet potatoes, making it a better fit for smaller garden beds.
directions: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose soil formed into ridges in full sun; Bunch Porto Rico is an early-20th-century American selection from the old Porto Rico sweet potato line, valued for a more compact, semi-bush vining habit that spreads far less aggressively than standard long-vine heirlooms, making it practical for gardeners short on space. It produces copper-skinned tubers with moist, deep-orange, sweet flesh similar in eating quality to its Porto Rico parent, and its shorter vines are easier to manage, hill, and keep out of walkways through the growing season. Dig tubers once the vines begin to yellow and before frost threatens, then cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for a week or two to heal cuts and concentrate sweetness before storage.

name: Bunch Purple Hull Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep into warm, lean to moderately fertile soil once the soil has thoroughly warmed after last frost.
directions: Bunch Purple Hull is a compact, upright, bush-habit selection within the purple hull class of Southern peas, bred to concentrate pods near the top of self-supporting plants rather than the sprawling growth habit of older purple hull field types. Direct sow into warm, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun once the soil has thoroughly warmed, spacing plants a few inches apart in rows. The cream-colored peas marked with a purple-pink eye retain the classic mild, slightly sweet purple hull flavor prized in Southern cooking, and pods can be picked at the green-shell stage for fresh shelling or left to dry fully for storage. Bunch Purple Hull has served as parent breeding stock for later disease-resistant purple hull and blackeye releases, including Mississippi State University's Magnolia Blackeye.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension Service — Southern Pea Variety Recommendations
USDA National Genetic Resources Program — cowpea germplasm records

name: Bunyard's Exhibition Fava Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow February through May, or in fall (October-November) in mild-winter climates for overwintering; Bunyard's Exhibition is a heavy-cropping 1884 English heirloom.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Bunyard's Exhibition is a heavy-cropping English heirloom broad bean dating to 1884, producing long pods holding 8-9 white seeds on vigorous 54-inch plants. It can be sown in late winter through spring for a summer crop, or in fall in mild-winter climates to overwinter and crop earlier the following year. Its classic, robust fava flavor holds up well whether eaten fresh or frozen, and the heavy pod set makes it a dependable choice for a dedicated fava-bean bed.

name: Buran Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Buran is a Ukrainian heirloom valued for setting fruit early and heavily even where seasons are short.
directions: Sow seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after danger of frost has passed. Buran is a compact, early Ukrainian heirloom that sets clusters of tapered, bull's-horn-shaped fruit ripening from pale green to deep red, with thick walls and a sweet flavor well suited to fresh eating or roasting. Its early maturity and heavy fruit set make it a dependable choice for short-season gardens. Pick pods at either the green or fully red stage, harvesting regularly to keep plants producing.

name: Burbank Potato
plantingNote: Plant seed potato pieces (each with 2-3 eyes) in cool soil; Burbank is a late-season variety best suited to a long, cool growing season. In zone 9, plant January-February for a spring harvest before summer heat sets in; cooler zones 3-7 give the most reliable yields.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces in trenches 4 inches deep, hilling soil around the stems as they grow, and harvest once the vine tops die back. Burbank is the original white-skinned, smooth potato that plant breeder Luther Burbank developed and introduced from his farm in Massachusetts in the 1870s, prized in its day for its prolific yields and good cooking quality. A natural bud sport of Burbank with netted, russeted skin emerged in the late nineteenth century and was selected for superior baking and frying quality, eventually eclipsing the parent entirely under the name Russet Burbank, now the dominant commercial potato in the United States. The original smooth-skinned Burbank is rarely grown today outside of historic seed collections and potato breeding programs, having been almost entirely supplanted by its russet-skinned offspring. Cure tubers in a cool, dark location for 10-14 days before storage.

name: Burbank Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; this compact determinate variety does not need staking.
directions: Developed around 1915 by plant breeder Luther Burbank in Santa Rosa, California, this determinate heirloom yields heavy crops of medium-sized, round, deep-red fruit well suited to canning as well as fresh eating. The fruit resists cracking, and the compact plants tolerate drier conditions without staking, making this an easy-care choice for shorter growing seasons. Even watering and full sun give the most reliable yields.

name: Burgess Buttercup Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Burgess Buttercup requires a full season (100–110 days) and benefits from the long, warm summers of zone 7–10. In zone 9, plant March–April for September–October harvest. Harvest before hard frost when the gray-green button (the distinctive flattened cap on the blossom end) is visible and the stem is dry and corky; cure for 10 days at 80°F. Burgess Buttercup stores 3–4 months in cool, dry conditions.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after last frost; thin to 2 plants. Cure harvested fruits at warm temperature for 10 days to harden skin. Burgess Buttercup is an heirloom winter squash introduced by the Burgess Seed and Plant Company in 1932 — the original 'buttercup' type squash from which the entire buttercup squash class takes its name. The distinctive physical characteristic of Burgess Buttercup is the prominent gray-green button or cup on the blossom end — a flat, circular, gray-green protrusion that sits like a cap on the bottom of the round, turbaned, dark green-and-striped fruit. The fruits are medium-sized (3–5 lbs), round and flattened, with dark forest green skin and narrow lighter stripes. The flesh is very deep orange-yellow, extremely dry and dense with a fine, smooth grain — a floury, potato-like texture (similar to kabocha, to which it is related) rather than the moist, stringy texture of acorn or some other winter squash types. The flavor is intensely sweet and rich, widely considered among the finest-flavored of all winter squashes — sweeter than butternut, drier and more concentrated than acorn. Burgess Buttercup improved on by the sweet, slightly dry, concentrated squash flavor that has made the buttercup/kabocha class the most highly-rated squash type in culinary comparison.
sources: Burgess Seed and Plant Company — Original 1932 introduction documentation
Seed Savers Exchange — Burgess Buttercup variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Heirloom winter squash collection

name: Burgundy Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep, in October-November in zone 9; Burgundy is a Creole type that needs little winter chill to bulb reliably.
directions: Burgundy is a Creole-type softneck garlic named for the deep purple-red streaking on its clove wrappers, one of a small group of regional Creole selections — alongside Ajo Rojo, Creole Red, and Pescadero Red — bred for the mild, low-chill winters of the Gulf South and similar hot, humid climates. Like other Creole garlics it forms a tight, symmetrical bulb of roughly 8 to 12 plump cloves with a rich, moderately hot flavor and notably better storage life than most northern hardneck types. Because it needs little cold exposure to trigger bulbing, it performs reliably in zone 9 gardens where Rocambole and Porcelain garlics often fail without pre-chilling. Harvest once the lower leaves have browned and 4 to 5 green leaves remain, then cure in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks before storage.
sources: Gourmet Garlic Gardens — Creole garlic variety descriptions

name: Burgundy Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after the last frost when soil is warm (70°F+) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; soak seeds overnight before planting to improve germination; harvest Burgundy pods at 2–3 inches for best tenderness — they toughen rapidly after 3–4 inches.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Burgundy is an All-America Selections award-winning okra cultivar with outstanding dual ornamental and culinary value — producing deep burgundy-red to crimson-red pods, stems, leaf veins, and flowers that make it one of the most visually spectacular edible garden plants available. The crimson coloration extends through virtually every part of the plant: the pods are deep red-burgundy rather than the standard green, the main stems carry the same red coloring, leaf veins are crimson, and the large (3–4 inch), yellow hibiscus-like flowers have a red center. The dramatic color creates an outstanding ornamental display in the summer garden that standard okra varieties cannot approach. The pods are edible and flavorful when harvested young (2–3 inches) — tender and mild, with the typical okra character. A critical practical note: the dramatic burgundy pod color disappears when cooked — the pods turn green when heated, which surprises first-time Burgundy okra growers. For the best ornamental and culinary effect, harvest pods at 2–3 inches (they toughen very quickly after 3–4 inches on this variety). In zone 9, Burgundy okra thrives through the brutal Gulf South summer when most other vegetables struggle, and produces prolifically from May through October with regular harvest.

name: Burgundy Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; breeding line LA 04-175, matures equal to or slightly earlier than Beauregard and was released by the LSU AgCenter with strong multi-disease resistance.
directions: Burgundy is a red-skinned, orange-fleshed, high-yielding sweet potato developed by the LSU AgCenter, valued for resistance to Streptomyces soil rot, Fusarium wilt (stem rot), and southern root-knot nematode. It matures on roughly the same schedule as Beauregard, making it a straightforward substitute for growers wanting improved disease tolerance without a longer season. Flesh color and eating quality are similar to other standard orange-fleshed Louisiana releases, cooking moist and sweet after curing. Its multi-pathogen resistance package is particularly useful in Gulf Coast gardens with a history of nematode or soil rot pressure.
sources: LSU AgCenter Sweet Potato Research Station

name: Burmese Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow an inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65 degrees F; soak seeds overnight in warm water before planting to improve germination.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Burmese is a vigorous heirloom okra producing long, tender, ribbed green pods on tall, productive plants that continue bearing heavily through the hottest part of summer, a season when many other vegetables slow down. It has a reputation among heirloom seed savers for strong yields and reliable performance across a range of Southern growing conditions. Harvest pods every day or two once production begins, picking at three to four inches for the most tender texture, since pods left too long on the plant quickly become tough and fibrous.

name: Burpee Butterbush Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Burpee Butterbush is a compact, non-vining bush-type butternut squash bred to produce full-sized butternut fruit on a plant small enough for raised beds and container culture, unlike standard sprawling butternut vines that need 50-100 square feet.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills spaced 2-3 feet apart, or start indoors and transplant after the danger of frost has passed. Burpee Butterbush was bred to solve the space problem that keeps many gardeners from growing butternut squash — standard butternut vines sprawl 10-15 feet and can overrun a small garden — by combining a compact, bush-type growth habit that stays within a 3-4 foot footprint with fruit that is essentially identical in size, shape, and sweet, nutty flavor to full-sized vining butternut varieties. This makes it one of the few butternut options practical for raised beds, small gardens, and even large containers. Vines still produce a running habit to a modest degree as the season progresses, but nowhere near the sprawl of standard butternut, and yield per plant is comparable to vining types when given full sun and consistent water. Harvest when the tan rind is hard enough to resist a fingernail and the stem has begun to dry and corky, then cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks before storage to concentrate sugars and toughen the skin for long keeping.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Winter Squash Variety Trials

name: Burpee Garden Sown Flying Saucer Tomato
plantingNote: Part of Burpee's Garden Sown line bred with cold-tolerant seed for direct sowing around the last frost date.
directions: Flying Saucer is a paste tomato bred so its seed can be sown directly in garden soil around the last frost date instead of started indoors. The indeterminate vines need staking and produce roughly eight-ounce fruit in waves rather than a single flush, giving a long sauce-making harvest into fall. Thin seedlings after germination and keep soil evenly moist to avoid blossom-end rot on the meaty fruit.

name: Burpee Garden Sown Little Big Boy Tomato
plantingNote: Part of Burpee's Garden Sown line bred with cold-tolerant seed for direct sowing right around the last frost date rather than indoor starting.
directions: Little Big Boy is bred with cold-tolerant seed that germinates reliably when sown straight into garden soil instead of started indoors. Sow directly around the last frost date, thin seedlings as they establish, and stake or cage the indeterminate vines as they grow. The plant yields a steady supply of three-ounce slicers through late summer, a lower-effort option for gardeners who want to skip seed-starting trays.

name: Burpee Hybrid Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm and all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Burpee Hybrid is a long-standing American cantaloupe standard, producing medium-large, heavily netted, orange-fleshed melons with sweet, aromatic flavor and reliable, heavy production that made it a home garden mainstay for decades. The vigorous vines set fruit dependably under a wide range of growing conditions, and the variety's decades-long track record reflects genuinely good, consistent performance rather than novelty. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with a gentle tug and the netted rind has turned from green to golden-tan, and reduce watering in the final week before harvest to concentrate sweetness.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Burpless Beauty Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Burpless Beauty is a classic slicing cucumber selected for thin, dark-green skin and a mild flavor with little of the bitterness or gas-causing compounds found in older slicing types.
directions: Direct sow seeds an inch deep into warm, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a trellis to keep fruit straight and reduce disease pressure. Burpless Beauty produces long, slender, dark-green fruit with thin, tender skin that can be eaten unpeeled, and it was bred specifically to be milder and easier to digest than standard slicing cucumbers, a trait long marketed as burpless. Vines are vigorous and productive over a long summer harvest window when picked regularly. Harvest fruit at 8-10 inches while still glossy and firm; letting cucumbers oversize on the vine slows further production and can make the skin tougher and more bitter.
sources: Burpee — Burpless Beauty Cucumber variety description
Park Seed — Burpless Beauty Cucumber growing guide

name: Bush Delicata Squash
plantingNote: Sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Bush Delicata forms a compact, short-vined plant that fits raised beds and small gardens where a standard sprawling delicata vine would take up far too much room.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 2 to 3 feet apart since the compact bush habit needs far less room than a standard vining delicata. Bush Delicata produces the same sweet, creamy, striped-skinned fruit prized in classic delicata squash, but on a tidy, short-vined plant that stays contained rather than rambling 6 to 10 feet like the traditional vining type, making it a good fit for raised beds, small gardens, or anywhere space is at a premium. Provide steady, even moisture through flowering and fruit set, and mulch around the base to conserve water and suppress weeds. Harvest once the rind hardens and the cream-and-green stripes deepen in color, then cure fruits in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before storing to concentrate their sweetness and extend keeping quality.

name: Bush Early Girl Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into full sun after danger of frost has passed; this compact determinate selection needs no staking beyond a small cage.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights stay reliably above 50F, or grow directly in an 18-24 inch container. Bush Early Girl is an All-America Selections winner bred as a true determinate, space-saving counterpart to the classic indeterminate Early Girl, staying under 30 inches tall while still producing full-flavored, 6-8 ounce red slicing tomatoes only a few days later than its parent. Its short, sturdy frame makes it a favorite for patios, raised beds, and small gardens where staking a full-size vine is impractical, and it carries verticillium and fusarium wilt resistance for reliable production.

name: Bush Pickle Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Bush Pickle is a compact, determinate pickling cucumber that grows as a bush (18–24 inch spread) rather than a long vine, making it ideal for raised beds, containers, and small gardens where standard pickling cucumber vines (4–6 feet) would be unmanageable; it produces a concentrated set of uniform pickling cucumbers and then declines — plant a second succession for extended harvest.
directions: Sow directly 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; no trellis required for the compact bush plants; harvest pickling cucumbers at 3–4 inches for small gherkin-style pickles or 4–5 inches for standard dill pickle size; pick every 2–3 days to maintain production. Bush Pickle is a compact, determinate (bush-habit) pickling cucumber developed specifically for small-space gardening — raised beds, containers, urban gardens, and patios where growing the standard trailing pickling cucumber vines (Boston Pickling, National Pickling, Calypso) is impractical due to their 4–6 foot spread. The compact plants (18–24 inches wide) produce a dense cluster of uniform, blocky, 3–5 inch pickling cucumbers with the classic pickling cucumber characteristics: firm, crisp flesh; thin skin; minimal hollow seeds; and a blocky, multi-bumped exterior that is traditional for dill pickles. Production is somewhat concentrated in a shorter harvest window compared to vining types — Bush Pickle tends to set most of its fruit within 2–3 weeks of first harvest, then declines, making succession planting (a second sowing 3–4 weeks after the first) useful for extended pickle production. Still holds well under warm summer conditions for Gulf Coast gardeners growing in small raised beds.

name: Butch T Trinidad Scorpion Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Capsicum chinense requires warm temperatures (80–90°F) for germination and is slow to germinate. In zone 9 start in January and transplant in March–April. Butch T thrives as a perennial in zone 9 and 10 — the woody plants return from the roots after light winter die-back and produce extremely heavily in their second and subsequent years. Wear gloves when handling fruits; the extremely high capsaicin content can cause skin burns and eye damage.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and handle fruits with protective gloves; Butch T Trinidad Scorpion was recognized as the world's hottest pepper by the Guinness World Records in 2011 (since surpassed by the Carolina Reaper), measuring over 1.4 million Scoville Heat Units in official testing — placing it among the most intensely hot peppers ever documented. The variety was developed by Troy Primeaux ('Butch T') in Louisiana from Trinidad Moruga Scorpion genetics. The small to medium, wrinkled, deeply colored red-orange fruits have the distinctive scorpion tail-like protrusion at the tip that gives the Trinidad Scorpion type its name. The extreme heat is accompanied by a pronounced fruity, tropical Capsicum chinense flavor beneath the intense burn. Used in tiny quantities in hot sauce production, powders, and as a daring culinary challenge. In zone 9 the long warm season and perennial habit allow Butch T plants to develop into large, extremely productive multi-year shrubs.
sources: Guinness World Records — Butch T Scorpion Pepper 2011 Record
New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — Super-Hot Varieties
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Specialty Pepper Production

name: Butch T Trinidad Scorpion Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Butch T Trinidad Scorpion once held the Guinness World Record for the hottest pepper in the world, with extreme heat well over one million Scoville Heat Units, requiring careful handling with gloves.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Butch T Trinidad Scorpion, a selection developed by grower Butch Taylor, held the Guinness World Record for the world's hottest pepper in 2011, testing over 1.4 million Scoville Heat Units, among the most extreme heat levels achievable in a pepper. The small, wrinkled, scorpion-tail-shaped fruits ripen from green to a deep red and carry the fruity, slightly sweet undertone typical of superhot Capsicum chinense peppers beneath the overwhelming heat. Always wear gloves when handling fresh or dried fruit and avoid touching the face, since the capsaicin can cause serious skin and eye irritation; use in tiny quantities, typically a single pepper diluted into a large batch of hot sauce or infused oil. Plants are moderately productive and benefit from a long, warm growing season and consistent moisture. This is a specialty pepper for heat enthusiasts and hot sauce makers, not general culinary use.
sources: Guinness World Records — World's Hottest Pepper 2011
Chile Pepper Institute — Superhot Pepper Cultivars
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Trinidad Scorpion Variety Notes

name: Butte Russet Potato
plantingNote: Give this large, late-maturing russet extra elbow room at planting since it is a vigorous, heavy-setting plant.
directions: A long, brown-russeted baking potato with white mealy flesh, grown by Wood Prairie as a favorite russet that is rarely offered by other seed suppliers. Large plants with white flowers set tubers heavily, giving high yields along with very high scab resistance and strong late blight tolerance, making it a low-input choice for a long growing season. Space seed pieces 14-18 inches apart to accommodate the big plants and expect good keeping quality thanks to the long post-harvest dormancy.

name: Butter and Sugar Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed, in blocks of at least four short rows for reliable pollination.
directions: This long-popular bicolor normal-sugary (SU) hybrid produces two ears per stalk with kernels randomly mixed between golden yellow and creamy white, giving each cob a distinctive speckled look on the plate. Because it is a standard SU type rather than a supersweet, it does not need to be isolated from other sugary corns and holds its eating quality on the stalk for several days past peak, giving gardeners a wider harvest window. Keep plants well watered from tasseling through ear fill, since drought stress at that stage is the most common cause of poorly filled tips. It remains a favorite roadside-stand and home-garden choice for gardeners who want classic old-fashioned corn flavor rather than the extra crunch of newer sh2 hybrids.
sources: Iowa State University Extension and Outreach

name: Butter Lamp Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Butter Lamp grows on shorter vines than standard butternut, needing less garden space, and can also be trained up a trellis.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has warmed. Butter Lamp is an AAS-winning butternut-type squash bred for a mini, pumpkin-shaped fruit weighing about 1 to 2 pounds, with rich yellow, smooth, sweet and nutty flesh and strong resistance to powdery mildew, heat, and insect pressure. The short-vined plant needs notably less garden space than traditional butternut squash and can be grown as a trellised hanging fruit or left to sprawl on the ground. Harvest once the rind hardens fully and resists a fingernail scratch; fruit stores exceptionally well into winter when cured in a warm, dry spot for a week or two first.
sources: All-America Selections — Squash winter Butter Lamp F1 winner announcement

name: Butterbaby Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; a semi-restricted vine that can be grown in-ground or trellised, producing single-serving butternuts ideal for small households and space-limited gardens.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after the last frost in fertile, well-drained soil; Butterbaby's semi-compact vines can be left to sprawl or trained up a trellis to save garden space. Butterbaby is a hybrid mini butternut bred for uniform, single-portion fruits weighing about a half to one and a half pounds, with the same tan skin and rich, nutty-sweet, deep orange flesh as full-size butternuts but scaled down for one or two servings. Plants set fruit heavily and consistently, making them well suited to succession harvests through the fall. Harvest when the rind has hardened and turned fully tan, cure for a week or two, and store in a cool, dry spot for several months.

name: Butterbeans Edamame
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, since seedlings are sensitive to cold, wet ground.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in rows or wide bands, inoculating with rhizobia bacteria if soybeans have not been grown in that bed before to boost nitrogen fixation and yields. Harvest whole pods while still bright green and plump but before the beans inside turn hard and yellow, usually indicated by pods filling out fully along the stem. This variety produces unusually large, sweet-flavored beans on tall, productive plants, making it a favorite among home gardeners who want bigger portions per pod than typical edamame types. Blanch or steam the harvested pods briefly and pop the beans free of the fuzzy pod before eating as a snack or adding to salads and stir-fries.

name: Buttercup Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, enriched soil; Buttercup is a classic Cucurbita maxima winter squash with a distinctive button-like cap on the blossom end, dark green to grey-green skin, and dense, dry, sweet orange flesh — for decades the standard of flavor comparison for all winter squash and still considered one of the finest for table use.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in hills or rows after last frost when soil is above 65°F; thin to 2 plants per hill and allow 5–8 feet between hills. Buttercup squash was introduced by Harris Seeds of Rochester, New York in 1932 and became the gold standard for winter squash flavor for much of the twentieth century; a Cucurbita maxima type with a distinctive flattened-round shape, dark green skin with grayish-green stripes, a small, warty 'button' (the remnant of the blossom end), and dense, dry, sweet, deep-orange flesh that is exceptionally dry and rich — much less watery than kabocha or acorn types. The sweet, nutty, slightly dry flesh is outstanding for mashing, baking, and pies; it stores for 2–3 months. The modern 'kabocha' squash type is very similar in form and is often confused with Buttercup; true Buttercup is larger and has the distinctive button. Cure for 10 days at room temperature before storage.

name: Butterscotch Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Butterscotch is an AAS-winning personal-size butternut squash on compact semi-bush vines, bred for notably sweet flavor and a manageable single-serving fruit size.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Butterscotch is an AAS-winning butternut-type squash bred for a compact, semi-bush vine and small, personal-size fruit — about a pound each, roughly half the size of standard butternut squash — making it easy to fit multiple plants into a smaller garden and giving perfectly portioned single-serving squash for roasting or stuffing without leftovers. The tan-skinned, elongated fruit has dense, sweet, deep-orange flesh with the classic butternut flavor, and its smaller size means faster cooking too. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens fully and turns a deep tan color; cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two after harvest to improve flavor and storage life. Watch for squash vine borer and squash bugs, common problems on all winter squash in the Gulf South.
sources: All-America Selections — Butterscotch Squash winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Butterstick Hybrid Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost into warm, fertile soil; single-stem habit needs less room than sprawling squash types.
directions: Butterstick is a straightneck-type hybrid that carries the zucchini plant's productive, single-stem habit but sets bright golden-yellow, straight-necked fruit instead of green cylinders. Its smooth skin and creamy flesh stay tender at a generous 7-8 inches, giving a bit more forgiveness than crookneck types if a fruit is missed during a hot Gulf Coast picking cycle. Plants bear over a long season with a steady, single-stem habit rather than sprawling widely, so regular spacing in a sunny bed keeps air moving through the foliage. Consistent moisture and twice-weekly harvest keep the plant setting new fruit rather than bottlenecking on a few oversized squash.

name: Byadgi Chilli
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant once soil is warm and nights stay above 55°F. Byadgi needs a long warm season to fully develop its deep red color and thin, wrinkled skin.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Byadgi Chilli takes its name from the town of Byadagi in Karnataka, India, and carries Geographical Indication protection for its distinctive deep red, wrinkled pods. Unlike most chiles grown for pungency, Byadgi is prized above all for color: the slender 2–3 inch pods have a thin, oily skin packed with red pigment but comparatively mild-to-moderate heat, generally cited around 5,000–15,000 Scoville units with a faintly sweet, smoky flavor. Pods are harvested fully red, sun-dried, and used whole or ground to give curries, rasam, and chili powder blends a vivid red color without overwhelming heat. A reliable, productive plant for gardeners who want a true chili flavor and color without intense fire.
sources: Geographical Indications Registry of India — Byadagi Chilli GI documentation
ICAR–Indian Institute of Horticultural Research — Byadgi Chilli variety notes

name: Cabernet Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil and air have warmed well past frost danger; Cabernet is a 2006 All-America Selections winner hybrid eggplant bred for vigor, high yield, and classic glossy purple-black fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 60°F. Cabernet, a 2006 All-America Selections winner, produces glossy, deep purple-black, oval fruit on a vigorous, high-yielding hybrid plant that holds up well to the heat and disease pressure of a long Gulf South growing season. Its strong vigor and heavy fruit set make it a reliable choice compared with some older open-pollinated eggplant varieties that struggle in extended summer heat. Harvest fruit while the skin is still glossy and taut, before seeds inside begin to harden, and pick regularly to keep the plant setting new fruit through the season.

name: Cabernet Onion
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost; Cabernet is a long-day (14+ hour) hybrid red onion best suited to northern gardens with long summer daylight, zones 3-7.
directions: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after hardening off, and space 4-6 inches apart. Cabernet is a long-day hybrid red onion producing large, globe-shaped bulbs with deep wine-red skin and firm, moderately pungent flesh with good color that holds up well through cooking, giving dishes an attractive red tint. It stores notably well for a red onion, holding firm in a cool, dry, well-ventilated location for several months after curing. As a long-day type, it needs the 14 or more hours of summer daylight found north of about the 35th parallel to bulb properly, making it best suited to northern and mid-latitude gardens rather than the Gulf South. Harvest when the tops fall over and begin to yellow, then cure for two to three weeks before trimming and storing.

name: Cajun Belle Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Cajun Belle is a compact, productive sweet pepper variety developed specifically for garden performance in hot, humid conditions — the type of climate where standard large bell peppers often struggle to set fruit. In zone 9, transplant March–April. The plant stays compact (18–24 inches tall) and produces small blocky bell-shaped fruits that ripen from green through red. The Cajun Belle name emphasizes its adaptation to Gulf Coast conditions where Creole and Cajun culinary traditions use sweet peppers heavily in the Holy Trinity (onions, celery, bell pepper) base of most dishes. This is an appropriate name for a variety that performs well where those culinary traditions are strongest: Louisiana, Mississippi, and the Gulf Coast region.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest green or fully red. Cajun Belle is an All-America Selections (AAS) winning pepper variety recognized for its consistent performance across diverse North American growing conditions, including the hot-humid southeastern United States where standard large bell pepper varieties often underperform due to blossom drop during heat peaks. The variety produces compact plants (18–24 inches) bearing abundantly on the small, blocky 3-inch bell-shaped fruits — smaller than the standard 4-lobed market bell but produced in much greater abundance per plant, especially in conditions that cause larger-fruited varieties to set poorly. The fruit profile of Cajun Belle differs from standard market bell peppers not only in size but in flavor: the smaller, thinner-walled fruits ripen fully and develop sweetness more quickly in the garden than large bells, which can take additional weeks to reach full red-ripe stage in the garden. Cajun Belle can be harvested green (mild, slightly sweet, similar to grocery-store green bell peppers) or allowed to ripen to red (sweeter, more complex, with the characteristic sweetness of fully ripe sweet peppers). The flavor is genuinely sweet — comparable to the best large red bell peppers — with none of the bitterness associated with unripe green bell peppers. The variety's most important attribute for zone 9 gardeners is heat tolerance: Cajun Belle continues setting fruit during warm periods that cause standard bells to drop their blossoms, providing reliable production through more of the Gulf Coast growing season.
sources: All-America Selections — Cajun Belle pepper AAS recognition and performance data
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Cajun Belle pepper compact sweet pepper variety notes
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Pepper Variety Recommendations for the Gulf South

name: Cajun Delight Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Cajun Delight is an early hybrid that begins production 55–60 days from seed — about 2 weeks earlier than standard okra types. In zone 9, sow March–May for summer production; the compact habit (4–5 feet) is manageable without staking and fits smaller garden spaces better than tall heirloom types.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; nick or soak seeds overnight to improve germination. Cajun Delight is a 1997 All-America Selections-winning compact hybrid okra developed for Southern garden production — selected specifically for early production (55–60 days, versus the 65–80+ days typical of older varieties), compact plant habit (4–5 feet vs. the 6–8 feet of full-size types), and exceptional pod quality. The dark green, straight, smooth-ridged, spineless pods are harvested at 2–4 inches for best tenderness and flavor; at this size they are non-fibrous, mild-flavored, and have the classic okra texture that makes them outstanding for gumbo, fried okra, and all Southern okra preparations. The compact habit makes Cajun Delight ideal for smaller plots, raised beds, and gardens where the full-height traditional types would be difficult to manage, and the early production date extends the productive season at both ends. Recognized as one of the best commercial and home-garden okra varieties for the Gulf South, where early establishment before peak summer heat is advantageous.
sources: All-America Selections — Cajun Delight okra AAS winner 1997
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Okra Production Guide
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Okra Production

name: Cajun Jewel Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost when soil is warm above 65°F; soak seeds 12–24 hours before planting to improve germination. Cajun Jewel was developed at the Louisiana State University AgCenter specifically for the humid, disease-pressure conditions of the Gulf Coast.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; Cajun Jewel was developed by LSU AgCenter plant breeders as a compact, dwarf-type okra specifically adapted to Gulf Coast conditions, producing spineless, dark-green, tender pods on 4–5 foot plants that are more manageable in home garden beds than the 6–8 foot giants of traditional varieties. The pods are ready to harvest at 2–4 inches long and have excellent flavor and tenderness; harvest every 2–3 days to keep plants producing — pods left too long become fibrous and woody in days in Gulf Coast heat. The compact size makes it easier to pick, the spineless pods reduce irritation from the fine hairs on standard varieties, and the improved disease package helps the plants maintain production through the summer. Outstanding for zone 7–10 gulf coast gardens.

name: Cajun King Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil; semi-dwarf, few-branched habit allows closer in-row spacing than tall heirloom cowhorn types.
directions: Cajun King is a Louisiana market-garden okra prized for its straight, dark-green, ribbed pods that stay tender well past typical harvest size, reportedly up to 15 inches, without becoming tough or fibrous. The semi-dwarf plants branch less than many heirloom types, maturing roughly 10 days earlier than Clemson Spineless and producing heavily over a long Gulf Coast season. Pick regularly at 4-8 inches for the best texture in gumbo, frying, and pickling.
sources: Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (NC State University)

name: Cal Sweet Bush Watermelon
plantingNote: Start indoors or transplant after soil is thoroughly warm; Cal Sweet Bush is a 2019 All-America Selections winner with a true short-internode bush habit, growing on vines only 14-18 inches long rather than sprawling 8-10 feet like standard watermelon, making it ideal for small Gulf Coast raised beds and containers.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Cal Sweet Bush is a genuine dwarf-vine watermelon, growing on compact 14-18 inch vines instead of the sprawling 8-10 foot vines of standard varieties, so it fits in a small raised bed or even a large container without taking over the garden. It still produces good-sized, 8-10 pound, round melons with sweet red flesh and the classic striped rind. Because the compact vines carry fewer leaves to shade developing fruit, keep an eye on ripening melons in intense heat to prevent sunscald. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned.
sources: All-America Selections — Cal Sweet Bush watermelon AAS winner 2019

name: Calabaza de Castilla Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost in warm soil; Calabaza de Castilla is a Mexican and Central American calabaza-type heirloom with mottled green-and-cream rind, traditionally cooked into candied calabaza en tacha.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in enriched hills once soil has warmed thoroughly after the last frost. Calabaza de Castilla is a traditional Mexican and Central American calabaza heirloom, flattened and ribbed in form with a mottled green-and-cream rind that often turns more tan as it cures, enclosing sweet, fine-grained orange flesh. It is the type most associated with calabaza en tacha, the whole or sliced squash slow-candied in piloncillo syrup for Day of the Dead celebrations, though it is equally good roasted or added to soups. Harvest once the rind has hardened and resists a fingernail, cure for a week or two in a warm spot, and store in a cool, dry location for long keeping.

name: Calabrian Peperoncino
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Calabrian peperoncino is the foundational hot chile of southern Italian cuisine, particularly from Calabria (the 'toe' of Italy's boot) — small, round to slightly elongated, intensely red, moderately hot (25,000–40,000 SHU) fruits used dried, in olive oil, as chili flakes, and as the spicy heat element in Calabrian cuisine.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Calabrian peperoncino benefits from a long, hot growing season and thrives in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens where it often behaves as a perennial in zone 9–11. Calabrian peperoncino (piccante calabrese, diavolicchio) is the defining hot chile of Calabria in southern Italy, where it has been grown for centuries as the primary heat element of the local cuisine; the small (1–2 inch), round to conical, bright red fruits (at 25,000–40,000 Scoville) are moderately hot with a fruity, complex flavor that distinguishes them from the clean heat of cayenne or the fruity intensity of habanero. Calabrian peperoncino is most commonly used dried — strung in traditional pepper braids (sporte di peperoncini) to air-dry in the Mediterranean sun — and is used throughout Italian cuisine as 'nduja filling (the spreadable Calabrian salumi), peperoncino in olio (chiles preserved in olive oil), as crushed dried flakes on pizza, pasta, and grilled meats, and as chili paste. The plants are highly productive and the small fruits dry readily on the vine or indoors.
sources: Italian Ministry of Agricultural Heirloom Variety Registry

name: Calçot de Valls
plantingNote: Sow bulb-type seedlings in spring, then let them bulb fully through summer before cutting back; the same plants resprout new white shanks that are repeatedly mounded with soil through autumn and winter.
directions: Calçots are grown in a distinctive two-stage method unique to the Valls area of Tarragona: a regular sweet onion bulb is grown to maturity, cut back hard, and then regrown from the same root, with soil mounded progressively up the regrowing shoots to blanch them into long, thick, sweet white shanks. Keep soil consistently moist through both the bulbing and regrowth stages, since dry spells toughen the blanched shanks that are the entire point of the crop. Harvest by pulling the whole plant once shanks reach finger thickness, then traditionally char them whole over an open flame and peel back the blackened outer layer before eating with romesco sauce.
sources: European Commission PDO/PGI Register — Calçot de Valls

name: Calhoun Crowder Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65F and all frost danger has passed; Calhoun Crowder was developed at the Calhoun Research Station in Louisiana in 1949 and bred for resistance to fusarium wilt and nematodes.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Calhoun Crowder, developed in 1949 at the Calhoun Research Station in Louisiana, bears speckled crowder-type peas packed tightly in the pod, bred specifically for resistance to fusarium wilt and root-knot nematodes, two pressures that limit cowpea production in the heavy, humid soils of the Deep South. Its disease resistance makes it a dependable choice for gardens where cowpeas have struggled in the past, without sacrificing the rich, hearty crowder-pea flavor Southern cooks favor. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil for whatever crop follows. Harvest continuously at the green-shell stage for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully for long-term storage.

name: Calhoun Gray Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after soil has warmed past 70°F; space hills generously since vines are vigorous and disease-tolerant enough to be grown in humid climates without heavy spray programs.
directions: Released in 1965 from the LSU AgCenter's Calhoun Research Station as a cross involving Calhoun Sweet and Charleston Gray, this variety was bred specifically to bring stronger disease resistance to the classic gray-rind Southern watermelon type. It produces 25-30 pound oblong fruits with light gray-green rind and sweet red flesh, and it holds up better against fungal wilts than its Charleston Gray parent, letting it succeed as far north as Massachusetts with proper season length. Give it full sun, warm fertile soil, and steady moisture through fruit development, then withhold water as fruits near maturity. It's a solid choice for gardeners who want old-style picnic-watermelon size and flavor with fewer disease headaches than older heirlooms.

name: Calhoun Sweet Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after soil has warmed past 70°F; give vines ample room since Calhoun Sweet is a full-sized vining type.
directions: Calhoun Sweet is a Louisiana watermelon strain grown and selected at the LSU AgCenter's Calhoun Research Station for exceptionally high sugar content, producing oblong, light green-rinded fruit with sweet, crisp red flesh. On its own the strain carries limited resistance to the fungal wilts that plague Southern watermelon patches, which is why breeders crossed it with the disease-tolerant Charleston Gray to create the widely grown Calhoun Gray in 1965. Grown today mainly by heirloom seed savers and regional variety trial programs rather than commercial growers, it remains of interest as the sweetness parent behind one of the Deep South's standard disease-resistant watermelons. Give it full sun, warm fertile soil, and steady moisture through fruit development, then withhold water as fruit nears maturity to concentrate sugars.

name: Calico Crowder Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Calico Crowder is a vining type — provide a trellis or fence for support, or allow plants to sprawl on the ground in traditional field-pea planting style.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Calico Crowder is an heirloom Southern pea producing the characteristic multi-colored seeds that give it its calico name — tan, brown, black, and cream mottled seeds with a distinctive pattern that creates a beautiful, rustic visual when dried and stored, distinguishing this traditional variety from the uniform-colored modern selections. Crowder peas are named for their growing habit: the seeds are so tightly packed in the pod that they are 'crowded' and develop flattened sides where they press against each other — this crowding is a defining type characteristic that distinguishes them from black-eyed peas and cream peas. The crowder texture — denser, starchier, and more potato-like than cream peas — produces a hearty, substantial broth when slow-cooked, which is the traditional cooking method for old-field varieties like Calico. As a vining-type crowder, Calico produces well on a trellis or fence and can be managed in a smaller space than sprawling bush types. The heirloom seeds can be saved year after year from the dried pods. In zone 9, Calico Crowder can be planted from April through August for multiple successive crops through the long warm season — Southern peas are uniquely suited to Gulf South heat that stops most other legumes.

name: Calico Lima Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; in zone 9 plant March–May for spring and July–August for fall. Lima beans require warm, settled weather to germinate and thrive — cold or wet soil at planting causes rot. Calico is a pole type requiring support; provide a trellis or bean poles at least 6 feet tall. In zone 9 the vines may overwinter as short-lived perennials in mild winters.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Calico lima bean is a large, pole-type heirloom producing spectacular seeds splashed with deep red-purple and cream in an irregular speckled pattern — each seed is uniquely marked, no two alike, and the visual drama makes them among the most beautiful beans in the garden and at harvest. The large seeds are best used as fresh-shell or dry beans; the meaty, starchy texture and rich, buttery lima flavor are excellent. Fresh-shell calico limas cook faster than dried and have a creamier texture. Despite the striking appearance of the dried seeds, the calico pattern largely disappears when cooked as the pigments are water-soluble. The vigorous pole vines need substantial support and are highly productive through the long Gulf Coast growing season. Heat tolerance is excellent, and the plants continue to set pods when green beans have long since quit in summer heat.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Calico Lima Bean Heritage Variety
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lima Bean Production
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Heirloom Lima Bean Types

name: Calico Ornamental Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; transplant after frost danger passes or grow in a decorative container. Calico is grown chiefly for its variegated cream, green, and purple foliage rather than for culinary fruit production.
directions: Transplant into well-drained potting mix or garden soil in full sun, where bright light keeps the foliage variegation most vivid. Calico's cream, green, and purple-splashed leaves provide season-long color even before fruiting begins, and the small, conical fruits continue the theme as they ripen through purple, cream, orange, and red in the same cluster. The dense, mounding habit suits mixed containers, hanging baskets, and bedding borders as much as any flowering annual. Fruit is pungently hot and edible but is typically treated as a colorful accent rather than a kitchen crop; pinch growing tips early to encourage fuller branching.
sources: university extension bedding plant trial notes

name: Calico Popcorn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks after danger of frost has passed, and isolate from other corn types by distance or timing to keep ears true to the popcorn type.
directions: Calico popcorn produces 5-8 inch ears patterned in red, yellow, brown, purple, and white kernels, making it as popular for fall decorating as for popping. Grow it in blocks of at least four rows for reliable wind pollination, and keep it isolated from sweet corn or field corn plantings since cross-pollination can affect kernel quality on both. Let ears dry fully on the stalk, then finish curing indoors for several weeks until kernels rattle loosely in the husk before shelling and storing. The same decorative ears used for autumn displays can be popped afterward, giving this variety a genuine dual purpose.

name: California 500 Asparagus
plantingNote: In mild-winter regions, plant crowns in late winter to early spring in a deep, well-drained trench; in colder zones wait until the soil has warmed and danger of hard freeze has passed.
directions: California 500 is a widely grown open-pollinated selection developed for the mild-winter, low-chill growing conditions of California's commercial asparagus districts, where it has long served as a dependable field standard. It produces vigorous, uniform, medium-green spears with good tip retention over an extended cutting season in regions too warm for northern selections to go fully dormant. Because plants are not all-male, expect a mix of male and female asparagus and remove any weak or overly seedy female plants over the years to keep the stand productive. It performs best where winters are too mild for deep dormancy but summers still bring enough heat to fuel strong fern growth after the harvest window closes.
sources: California Department of Food and Agriculture

name: California Blackeye 46 Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed past 65°F; CB46's two main flushes of pods come fairly close together, so plan harvest help for a concentrated picking window rather than a long trickle.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in warm, lean to moderately fertile soil, since this upright bush type is bred for compact, easy-to-harvest growth rather than sprawling vines. Developed and released in 1987 by the University of California, Davis, and the California Agricultural Experiment Station, California Blackeye 46 was bred for resistance to fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 as well as root-knot nematode, making it a dependable standard in fields and gardens with a history of those soil problems. Plants produce two concentrated flushes of well-filled 6 to 8 inch pods borne above the foliage, with classic cream-colored, black-eyed peas inside. Pick at the green-shell stage for fresh eating, or allow pods to dry fully for the traditional dried black-eyed pea used in Southern New Year's dishes.
sources: Registration of 'California Blackeye 46' Cowpea (Crop Science Society of America)
University of California, Davis cowpea breeding program records
Browning Seed / University of Florida IFAS cowpea variety descriptions

name: California Blackeye 5 Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after soil is thoroughly warm; California Blackeye 5 was bred at UC Davis from a California Blackeye x Iron cross and carries resistance to root-knot nematode and cowpea (Fusarium) wilt, valuable traits for the sandy, nematode-prone soils common along the Gulf Coast.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil is thoroughly warm; California Blackeye 5 is an improved release from the University of California, Davis, bred from a cross of California Blackeye and the nematode-resistant Iron cowpea to combine the classic black-eyed pea's mild, earthy flavor with real genetic resistance to root-knot nematode and cowpea (Fusarium) wilt, two soil-borne problems that persist for years in garden soil and are especially common in sandy Gulf Coast ground. The semi-bush plants are more compact and manageable than old-fashioned vining types and need no staking. Harvest the fresh green pods as snap beans, pick the shelled green peas for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully on the vine for the classic dried black-eyed peas of Southern cooking. Like other Southern peas, it fixes nitrogen and improves soil fertility as it grows.
sources: University of California, Davis — Foundation Seed Program

name: California Blackeye Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; in zone 9, plant from late spring through midsummer for successive harvests, since California Blackeye thrives in peak summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after the soil has warmed, and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which promotes foliage at the expense of pod set. California Blackeye is an upright, semi-bush cowpea developed by University of California breeding programs and grown extensively as the standard commercial black-eyed pea, valued for its concentrated pod set that ripens fairly uniformly for efficient once-over harvest, along with good disease resistance and dependable yields. The classic cream-colored pea with its signature black eye has excellent flavor whether cooked fresh, dried for storage, or prepared in the traditional Southern black-eyed pea dishes served for New Year's luck. Like all cowpeas it fixes nitrogen in the soil and thrives in hot summer weather that stalls cooler-season legumes, making it a reliable, low-input crop for Gulf South vegetable gardens.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — cowpea variety records
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database

name: California Blackeye Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after soil is thoroughly warm (minimum 65°F); in zone 9, sow April through July for summer production — the long warm season allows 2–3 successive plantings for continuous harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the soil is thoroughly warm; California Blackeye is the most commercially significant blackeye pea cultivar — the variety responsible for most of the blackeye peas sold in American grocery stores. The distinctive black-eyed, cream-colored dry beans cook quickly, have a mild, earthy, slightly sweet flavor, and a mealy texture that makes them a staple of Southern cooking — particularly the iconic Southern New Year's Day dish of hoppin' john (black-eyed peas and rice), eaten for good luck. California Blackeye is a semi-bush type that is more compact and less sprawling than old-fashioned vine types, making it manageable in typical garden beds without staking. The fresh green pods are eaten as snap beans or the fresh shelled green peas are eaten before the seeds dry; the dried seeds are the standard black-eyed peas of commerce. In zone 9, California Blackeye thrives in the long hot season, producing crops from June through September with successive plantings. Southern peas fix nitrogen in the soil through symbiotic bacteria and actually improve soil fertility — one of the few warm-season vegetables that enriches rather than depletes garden soil.

name: California Early Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 1-2 inches deep in fall; California Early has one of the lowest chilling requirements of any garlic type and is the softneck silverskin grown commercially through California's mild-winter Central Valley, making it one of the more dependable garlics for zone 8-10 gardens where hardneck types divide poorly.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 1-2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in loose, well-drained soil; in mild-winter zones like the Gulf Coast, planting in October-November gives roots time to establish before the brief winter chill. California Early is the classic commercial silverskin softneck grown across California's Central Valley and is prized for its adaptability to warm-winter regions, low chilling requirement, and tight, easy-to-braid skins. Bulbs are medium-sized with 12-16 cloves in white to faintly purple-blushed wrappers and a flavor that is strong raw but mellows well when cooked. As the name suggests, it matures earlier than most other varieties, often ready for harvest by late spring, which helps it dodge the fungal pressure that builds in humid Gulf Coast soil as summer heat arrives. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have yellowed, cure in a warm, dry, shaded, well-ventilated spot for 3-4 weeks, then trim and store; well-cured bulbs keep 6-8 months.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Garlic Production in California
Filaree Garlic Farm — Silverskin variety descriptions
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Garlic Variety Selection for Texas

name: California Late Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 1-2 inches deep in fall; like its sister strain California Early, California Late has a very low chilling requirement and grows reliably in mild-winter zone 8-10 gardens, but needs several extra weeks in the ground to size up its larger bulbs.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 1-2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in loose, well-drained soil enriched with compost. California Late is the other pillar of California's commercial silverskin garlic industry alongside California Early, grown for its higher yield, larger bulb size, and notably long storage life of up to 10-12 months when well cured — among the best of any garlic type. Bulbs typically hold 16-20 cloves in tight white wrappers arranged in the overlapping layers characteristic of true silverskins, with a flavor that is sharp raw and mellow when roasted. Its low chilling requirement makes it as well suited to warm-winter Gulf Coast gardens as California Early, though it needs several additional weeks in the ground to fully size before harvest. Harvest once the lower third to half of the leaves have yellowed and browned, cure in a warm, dry, shaded, airy location for 3-4 weeks, then trim and store somewhere cool and dry.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Garlic Production in California
Filaree Garlic Farm — Silverskin variety descriptions
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Garlic Variety Selection for Texas

name: California Striped Sugarcane
plantingNote: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. California Striped is grown as an ornamental sugarcane for its boldly striped stalks rather than for sugar or syrup production.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. California Striped is grown as an ornamental grass for its distinctly striped stalks, which add strong vertical color and pattern to large borders, tropical-style plantings, and big containers. As with other sugarcanes the stalks can be chewed fresh or pressed for juice, but this type is chosen in Gulf South gardens mainly for its ornamental stalk pattern rather than for sweetness or yield. The tall, clumping perennial grass typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze in zone 8-9 and regrows from the root each spring.

name: California Wonder Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost date; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun at or just after the last frost date; in zone 9, transplant in mid-February for spring production — peppers require consistent warmth and will stall in cool spring weather below 55°F.
directions: Set out transplants in warm, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; California Wonder is the standard classic bell pepper — introduced in 1928 and for most of the twentieth century THE bell pepper grown in American home gardens and produced commercially. The large, blocky, thick-walled, four-lobed fruits are harvested green when mature (70–80 days after transplant) or allowed to ripen to deep red for sweeter, fully ripe peppers. The thick, crisp walls and mild, sweet, distinctly 'bell pepper' flavor are the benchmarks against which other bell peppers are measured. California Wonder is a vigorous, productive plant well-suited to Gulf Coast growing conditions — tolerant of heat and humidity better than some northern-bred bell peppers. In zone 9, bell peppers can produce from February transplants through June and then resume production in September–October after the worst summer heat passes — temperatures above 90°F during flowering cause blossom drop. Apply calcium-containing fertilizer (or side-dress with gypsum) to prevent blossom end rot, which is common in bell peppers during irregular watering. The plants are technically short-lived perennials in frost-free zone 9 and can be carried over winter for a second year of production in protected locations.

name: Calliope Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Calliope is a compact F1 hybrid eggplant producing small globe-shaped fruits with distinctive magenta-purple and white striping. In zone 9, transplant March–April; the plant's compact size (18–24 inches) and heavy production habit make it excellent for containers, raised beds, and small gardens where a standard large eggplant would be impractically large. Harvest fruits when 2–3 inches in diameter while still firm and glossy — at this stage the flesh is tender, the seed cavity is minimal, and the flavor is sweet without bitterness. Like all eggplants, Calliope thrives in the heat of zone 9 summers and can produce through the entire warm season with irrigation and occasional fertilization.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at 2–3 inches diameter when firm and glossy. Calliope is a compact F1 hybrid eggplant bred for small-fruit production with an Italian-type rounded form and striking bicolor fruit appearance. The fruits are globe to slightly pear-shaped, 2–3 inches in diameter, with a distinctive pattern of deep magenta-purple on the upper half and creamy white on the lower half — a color distribution that differs from the vertical striping of varieties like Fairy Tale or Listada de Gandia. The bicolor magenta-white pattern makes Calliope one of the most visually distinctive eggplants in garden displays and farmers market presentations. As a culinary variety, Calliope's small globe form is practical for preparations requiring the whole fruit: the 2–3 inch fruits are ideal for stuffing (halved or hollowed), for roasting whole, for grilling cut in half, or for slicing into rounds for layered preparations. The flesh is tender and sweet at harvest size, with minimal seed development and no bitterness — a consistent characteristic of modern F1 hybrid eggplant varieties. The compact plant habit and prolific fruiting make Calliope one of the best eggplant choices for container gardens where standard varieties would be impractically large and less productive per square foot.
sources: Ball Horticultural Company — Calliope eggplant F1 hybrid introduction notes
Harris Seeds — Calliope eggplant commercial greenhouse and field trial data
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Small-fruited eggplant variety comparison

name: Caloro Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Caloro is a yellow wax hot pepper in the Hungarian Wax style developed in California, with conical yellow fruits that ripen to red and carry moderate heat of 5,000–10,000 Scoville units — excellent for pickling, roasting, and fresh use in California-Mexican cuisine.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost when nighttime temperatures are consistently above 55°F into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Caloro is a yellow wax-type hot pepper developed in California in the mid-twentieth century and widely grown in commercial agriculture as the standard pickled yellow hot pepper of California; the conical, medium-sized fruits (3–4 inches long) emerge green, ripen to bright yellow (the commercial harvest stage for pickling), and eventually turn orange-red at full maturity. Heat level is moderate at 5,000–10,000 SHU — noticeably hot but not extreme — with a waxy, crisp texture ideal for pickled pepper rings, banana pepper-style pickles, roasting, and fresh eating. Highly productive and disease-resistant; particularly well-suited to warm California, Gulf Coast, and Southwestern climates.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension Vegetable Research

name: Calypso Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; a bush bean requiring no support — excellent for market gardeners and home canners.
directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Calypso is a bush dry bean with a striking black and white two-toned pattern — each seed is precisely half black, half white — that has earned it nicknames such as 'yin yang bean' and 'oreo bean' for the dramatic visual contrast. The pattern fades somewhat on cooking but the bean retains excellent earthy, full-bodied flavor with a smooth creamy texture when fully cooked. Among the fastest dry beans to reach maturity, making it suitable for short-season gardens; the compact bush habit produces a concentrated flush excellent for preserving. Color fades on drying — store in a dark, cool location to preserve seed appearance.

name: Calypso Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Calypso is a gynoecious (all-female) pickling cucumber that produces an extremely concentrated set of fruits — a male pollenizer (typically a small percentage of open-pollinated seed included in the packet) is required for fruit set. Harvest frequently, every 1–2 days, to maximize production; fruits left on the vine signal the plant to stop producing.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; train vines to a trellis for straighter fruits and improved air circulation. Calypso is a 2009 All-America Selections-winning pickling cucumber that earned recognition for its exceptional disease resistance package and concentrated production — bred to perform reliably in a wide range of climates and conditions where fungal and viral diseases limit cucumber yields. Calypso carries resistance to angular leaf spot, cucumber scab, cucumber mosaic virus, papaya ringspot virus, watermelon mosaic virus, and zucchini yellow mosaic virus, plus tolerance to powdery mildew — one of the most comprehensive disease resistance packages available in a pickling cucumber. The dark green, warted, blocky fruits (3–4 inches for fresh pickle use, 1.5–2 inches for whole baby pickles) have thick, crisp walls and excellent pickle texture that holds up to both quick-process and long-fermented pickle methods. The gynoecious (all-female) breeding concentrates fruit set into a shorter, more predictable harvest window — convenient for processing large pickle batches. An outstanding choice for home pickle-makers, zone 9 summer gardens where disease pressure is high, and any gardener wanting maximum yields with minimum disease management input.
sources: All-America Selections — Calypso cucumber AAS winner 2009
