Johnny's Selected Seeds — Calypso variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cucumber Production Guide

name: Camaro PMR Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after the last frost; built-in powdery mildew resistance is especially valuable in the humid Gulf Coast growing season, when foliar disease usually cuts vines down before fruit finishes sizing.
directions: Direct sow in hills after danger of frost has passed, giving the reduced-vine plants a bit less room than sprawling heirloom types but still allowing air circulation between hills. Camaro PMR carries genetic resistance to powdery mildew, keeping foliage photosynthesizing later into the season so that fruit reaches its full 20-22 pound, near-round, lightly ribbed potential even under heavy disease pressure. The strong handles and deep orange rind make it a reliable choice for growers selling carving pumpkins, and the shorter vine habit suits smaller Gulf Coast garden plots better than old-line field pumpkin types. Watch soil moisture during fruit set, since consistent watering paired with the plant's disease tolerance produces the most uniform, market-ready fruit.
sources: Cornell University Long Island Horticultural Research and Extension Center

name: Cambodian Green Giant Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; transplant once nights stay warm. Cambodian Green Giant is a Southeast Asian heirloom bred for hot, humid tropical conditions and ramps up production in the second half of a long Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Start seed indoors with bottom heat and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights stay warm; harvest fruit while pale green with dark green stripes and firm, before the skin dulls and seeds enlarge. Cambodian Green Giant is a Southeast Asian heirloom producing large, round, slightly flattened fruit striped in pale and dark green on compact 2-3 foot plants, giving strong yields relative to the space the plant occupies. The dense, full-bodied flesh holds its texture well on the grill or in a wok, a quality suited to the quick high-heat cooking common in Southeast Asian cuisine. Because it is bred for tropical growing conditions, it handles the sustained heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer with ease and produces most heavily from midsummer into fall, right as many spring-planted eggplants begin to decline.

name: Camelot Shallot
plantingNote: Plant bulbs about an inch deep and four to six inches apart in early spring as soon as the soil is workable; Camelot is a British-trade shallot selected for round, coppery-brown bulbs and heavy cropping.
directions: Camelot is a round-bulbed shallot cultivar grown for its coppery-brown skin, dense clove-free flesh, and consistently heavy yields from each planted set. Set bulbs shallowly in loose, fertile, well-drained soil and keep the row weeded, since shallots have a shallow, easily shaded root system. Each bulb divides into a cluster of several new bulbs over the growing season, ready to lift once the foliage yellows and falls over in midsummer. Cure the whole cluster in a warm, dry, airy location for two to three weeks before separating the bulbs for storage or replanting a portion for next year's crop.

name: Camouflage Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–June. Camouflage produces attractive vines with lobed leaves and is vigorous enough to suppress weeds when given room to ramble. Harvest carefully with a digging fork to avoid puncturing the skin; purple-white streaked flesh appearance is best when roots are not damaged.
directions: Plant slips 4–6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil amended with sand or compost in full sun; Camouflage is an ornamental-edible sweet potato selected for striking purple-and-cream streaked or mottled flesh that creates a dramatic presentation when sliced — the irregular pattern of cream and purple pigmentation resembles military camouflage when cut crosswise. The flavor is mild and moderately sweet, suitable for roasting, baking, and mashing where the color pattern is partially preserved; water-boiling dulls the visual effect. The exterior skin has a similar mottled purple-green or purple-tan coloring that makes the roots attractive at harvest and at market. Flavor quality is secondary to the ornamental value of the flesh pattern — for pure eating quality, standard colored varieties outperform Camouflage, but for presentations and table drama it is unmatched among commonly grown sweet potatoes. Cure harvested roots at 85°F and high humidity for 7–10 days to develop sweetness.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Specialty Sweet Potato Varieties
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Potato Variety Trials
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sweet Potato Production

name: Campbell's Long Green Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil; semi-dwarf habit suits closer spacing than tall cowhorn-type okras.
directions: Campbell's Long Green is a mid-20th-century processing okra bred for uniform, slender, deep-green pods with strong color retention, and it later served as breeding stock for other canning-type okra selections. The semi-dwarf plants are compact relative to older heirloom cowhorn types, making them easier to manage in a home garden row. Pick pods at 3-5 inches for best tenderness and continue harvesting every couple of days to keep plants setting new pods through the heat of summer.
sources: Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (NC State University)

name: Camus de Bretagne Artichoke
scientificName: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Camus de Bretagne'
plantingNote: Transplant after last frost into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Camus de Bretagne is the classic large, rounded artichoke of Brittany, France, holding Protected Geographical Indication status there.
directions: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, working in plenty of compost before planting. Camus de Bretagne produces very large, rounded, tightly closed globe artichokes with a pale green color and tender, meaty heart, the classic variety grown in Brittany, France, where it holds Protected Geographical Indication status and accounts for the majority of French artichoke production. Like other globe artichokes it is a true perennial in mild-winter climates, though it can be grown as an annual from an early start in colder zones. Harvest buds while still tightly closed, before the scales begin to loosen, for the best eating quality.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

name: Camus de Bretagne Leek
scientificName: Allium ampeloprasum var. porrum 'Camus de Bretagne'
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting, or start in summer for a fall and winter main crop; Camus de Bretagne is a classic French heirloom leek noted for exceptionally thick, short stalks and good cold tolerance.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting, or sow in summer for a main fall and winter crop, then set pencil-thick seedlings 4-6 inches apart into fertile, well-drained soil. Camus de Bretagne, a classic French heirloom leek from Brittany, is prized for exceptionally thick, short, sturdy stalks with a mild, sweet flavor and good cold tolerance that allows it to stand in the garden through cool weather without becoming tough. Hill or trench soil around the stems as they grow to blanch and lengthen the tender white portion. In the Gulf South's mild winters, it can often be left in the ground and harvested as needed through the cool season rather than lifted all at once, giving a long, flexible harvest window.

name: Canada Crookneck Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost; vigorous moschata vines need room to spread.
directions: Canada Crookneck traces to the Iroquois Nations and was first offered commercially in the 1830s, making it one of the oldest named squash varieties still in cultivation in North America. The bottle-shaped, curved-neck fruits are relatively small, typically 2-4 lbs, with a warty tan rind and sweet, fine-grained orange flesh. It is listed on the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste as a variety worth preserving for its history and flavor. As a Cucurbita moschata, it has notably better resistance to squash vine borer than C. pepo or C. maxima types.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

name: Canada Red Rhubarb
plantingNote: Plant crowns or divisions in early spring while dormant; Canada Red performs best in zones with reliable cold winters that provide the extended chilling rhubarb needs for vigorous dormancy break and growth, and it is milder and sweeter than many green-stalked rhubarb varieties.
directions: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Canada Red is a cold-hardy rhubarb cultivar prized for its uniformly deep red stalks that stay red all the way through the flesh, not just the skin, along with a sweeter, milder flavor than many tart green-stalked rhubarb varieties, meaning less sugar is needed when cooking. It performs best in climates with cold winters that satisfy its chilling requirement for strong spring growth, making it less reliable in the mild winters of the Deep South. Harvest by pulling individual stalks from the outside of the crown rather than cutting, and always discard the leaves, which are toxic and should never be eaten.

name: Canadian Wonder Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; a reliable dwarf bush bean that performs well in cool, damp conditions.
directions: Canadian Wonder is a dwarf bush bean dating to at least 1873, long grown in Canada and popular as a heritage variety in British gardens. The flat, oval green pods can be picked young and eaten as snap beans around 60 days, or left on the plant roughly 90-100 days to mature into red kidney-shaped dry beans. The compact bush habit needs no staking, and the variety is noted for cropping reliably even in cool or wet seasons. Harvest pods regularly for fresh use, or let the final flush dry fully on the plant for storage beans.
sources: Kings Seeds (UK) — Canadian Wonder Dwarf French Bean
Mother Earth News — Heirloom Bean Varieties

name: Canary Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm (70°F+); in zone 9 plant March–May. Canary melons require warm to hot weather for full sugar development and are at their best in the extended heat of zone 9 summers. Unlike cantaloupe, canary melons do not slip from the vine when ripe — gauge ripeness by skin color turning from lime-green to brilliant chrome-yellow, slight softening at the blossom end, and the characteristic mild sweet fragrance. Cut from the vine when fully yellow and allow to rest at room temperature for 1–2 days for best flavor. The long shelf life (10–14 days at room temperature) compared to cantaloupes makes canary melons practical for home garden production.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-amended soil with consistent moisture during fruit development; Canary Melon (also called Spanish Melon or Yellow Melon) is an Inodorus-group muskmelon producing large (5–7 pound), oval to oblong fruits with a distinctive, intense, brilliant chrome-yellow skin at full ripeness — one of the most visually striking melons available, with the vivid yellow color making ripe fruits immediately identifiable in the garden and market. The flesh is white to pale ivory, very sweet, very juicy, with a mild, clean, faintly musky flavor that differs from cantaloupe's complex aromatic sweetness — canary melon's flavor is cleaner, lighter, and more delicate, making it the preferred melon for many people who find cantaloupe flavor too intense. The Inodorus (winter melon) classification means canary melons have firmer flesh and longer shelf life than cantaloupes — they don't 'slip' from the vine at ripeness, can be kept at room temperature for up to two weeks, and ship better than soft-fleshed types. Zone 9's extended warm season and summer heat are ideal for canary melon production, providing the long, hot growing period these melons need for full sugar development.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Specialty Melon Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Spanish and Canary Melons for Texas
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Winter Melon Types for Florida Gardens

name: Canary Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. Canary Melon is ripe when the skin turns from yellow-green to vivid canary yellow and the fruit gives slightly under thumb pressure at the blossom end. Unlike netted muskmelons, Canary does not separate from the vine easily when ripe — check for color, firmness, and fragrance rather than slip. The thick rind allows extended storage (several weeks at room temperature) compared to most melons.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Canary Melon (also called Juan Canary or amarillo melon) is an oblong to football-shaped melon with dramatically vivid, glossy, bright canary-yellow skin that makes it one of the most visually striking melons in the market or garden — the name describes the intense yellow of a canary bird's plumage. The creamy white to very pale green flesh is smooth, firm-crisp rather than soft, mildly sweet, and extremely mild-flavored with a delicate freshness completely different from the musky richness of cantaloupe — the flavor is subtle and refreshing, with a light sweetness and almost no aroma. This delicate flavor profile is characteristic of Spanish-type melons (inodorus group), which are also notable for their thick rind and long post-harvest shelf life. Canary Melon is widely grown in Spain and is a standard melon type in Spanish and Latin American markets. In zone 9 the long, warm summer produces the full sweetness that Canary Melon develops best in extended heat.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Specialty Melon Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Watermelon and Melon Production
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Specialty Melons for Gulf South

name: Canary Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil in hills or rows; Canary melon (Juan Canario, Yellow Canary) is a popular commercial and home-garden melon throughout the Mediterranean and Latin America, known for its brilliant canary-yellow skin and very sweet, pale white-to-green flesh with a mild, honey-like sweetness distinct from other melon types.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in hills 4 feet apart or in rows 6 feet apart; Canary melon is an inodorus type that stores well on the vine and post-harvest — harvest when skin turns deep canary yellow and the blossom end yields to gentle pressure. Cucumis melo var. inodorus 'Canary' (Juan Canario, Yellow Canary melon) is a winter melon type grown extensively in Spain, Latin America, and the Middle East and sold widely in American Hispanic grocery markets; the medium to large (5–10 lb), elongated oval fruits have a striking, smooth, bright canary-yellow skin and white to pale green flesh with a delicate, honey-sweet flavor that is milder and less aromatic than muskmelon or cantaloupe types but refreshingly sweet and very appealing. The inodorus type means the ripe fruit has little fragrance from the exterior — you must taste to judge ripeness; the flesh is crisp at the center and creamy near the rind. An excellent heat-tolerant melon for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens that maintains flavor even in high temperatures; stores well at room temperature for 2–4 weeks after harvest.

name: Candle Fire Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; soak seed overnight to speed germination. Candle Fire is a red, round-podded okra bred to stay tender even at a larger pod size, giving a wider harvest window than most okra before pods turn woody.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost into warm soil in full sun; thin to 18-24 inches apart. Candle Fire is an AAS-winning okra selected for round (not sharply ribbed), deep-red pods that resist the rapid fiber buildup common in older red okra varieties, so pods stay tender for harvest over a longer size range and a more forgiving picking schedule — useful in the Gulf South's fast summer growth, when okra can go from tender to woody within a day or two. The tall, upright plants are heavy producers with attractive maroon-tinted foliage and pale yellow, red-throated flowers that make the whole plant a good-looking addition to the summer vegetable garden. Like other red okra, the color is water-soluble and fades during cooking unless pods are quickly grilled, roasted, or fried rather than boiled. Harvest every day or two once pods start forming to keep the plant productive.
sources: All-America Selections — Candle Fire Okra winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Candy Corn Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Candy Corn is an ornamental-edible pepper bred to produce upright, tapered, yellow-to-orange-to-red fruit that resembles the classic autumn candy, providing striking multicolor display alongside genuine culinary use.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Candy Corn is compact enough for containers and makes an eye-catching patio or border plant. Bred for its ornamental-edible dual purpose, Candy Corn produces upright clusters of small, tapered fruit that ripen through a sequence from pale yellow at the base through orange to a bright red tip while still on the plant, closely mimicking the look of the classic Halloween candy for which it is named. Fruits carry moderate heat, milder than a typical cayenne but with real chile flavor, and are fully usable fresh, dried, or in hot sauce at any color stage, though flavor and heat both increase slightly as fruit ripens toward red. The compact, well-branched plant holds its colorful fruit upright above the foliage for maximum visual display, making it as valuable in a mixed ornamental border or container planting as in a dedicated vegetable bed. Harvest fruit continuously through the season to encourage more flowering and fruit set.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Candy Corn Pepper variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Ornamental Pepper Varieties

name: Candy Onion
plantingNote: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; Candy is an All-America Selections award-winning intermediate-day (12–13 hour) hybrid onion that fills the gap between long-day northern onions and short-day southern onions — it performs across a wider geographic range than most onion types and produces large, round, flat-topped bulbs with white skin and exceptionally sweet, mild flesh that can be eaten like an apple.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost (onion transplants tolerate light frost); set 4–6 inches apart with the bulb base at soil level; keep consistently moist through bulb formation; reduce watering as tops begin to yellow and fall over; harvest and cure 2–3 weeks before storage. Candy is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning hybrid onion developed specifically for its exceptional sweetness and adaptability as an intermediate-day variety capable of producing high-quality bulbs across a wider latitudinal range than either long-day or short-day types. Intermediate-day onions (requiring 12–13 hours of daylight to trigger bulbing) are particularly valuable in zones 5–8 — the mid-latitude transition zone where long-day varieties (14+ hours required) often form small bulbs in the shorter days of the mid-latitudes and short-day varieties (10–12 hours) often bolt prematurely in the longer summer days further north. The result is that Candy succeeds in climates from Maine to Georgia where the 'wrong type' onion is a common gardening mistake. The large, round to slightly flattened, white-skinned bulbs have extraordinarily sweet, mild flesh with low pyruvate content — the same characteristic that makes Vidalia and other famous sweet onions nearly non-pungent; Candy onions can be eaten raw like a mild apple, used in salads without overwhelming other flavors, or caramelized into an intensely sweet onion jam. Yields are excellent for a sweet onion type.

name: Candy Roaster Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; this Southern Appalachian heirloom has been grown in the mountains of North Carolina and Tennessee for generations and is one of the best-flavored large winter squashes for warm-climate gardeners.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in a prepared hill of well-composted soil after last frost, planting 3 seeds and thinning to the strongest; Candy Roaster needs a long season of 90–110 days, so in zone 9–11 plant in late winter for a spring harvest or late summer for fall. Candy Roaster is a Southern Appalachian heirloom producing large, elongated, banana-shaped fruits 12–20 inches long with pinkish-tan to salmon-orange skin often tipped with blue-green at the stem end, and sweet, orange, dry-textured flesh that roasts to a concentrated, candy-like sweetness the name describes perfectly. Fruits can reach 15–30 pounds; cure for 2 weeks in warm, dry conditions and store for 3–5 months. An essential heirloom for gardeners who want an authentic piece of Appalachian foodway heritage.

name: Candyland Red Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once frost danger has passed; Candyland Red is a 2020 All-America Selections winner currant tomato bred for a prolific, intensely sweet harvest of tiny fruit on a tall indeterminate vine.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine for support. Candyland Red, a 2020 All-America Selections winner, is a currant-type tomato producing an enormous quantity of tiny, intensely sweet, deep red fruit in loose clusters continuously from midsummer until frost, offering some of the highest sugar content of any tomato type for snacking straight off the vine. The vigorous vine benefits from regular watering and feeding to sustain its heavy, continuous fruit set through the Gulf South growing season. Harvest clusters as fruit ripens to full red color, and expect the plant to keep producing right up until cold weather ends the season.

name: Candystick Dessert Delicata Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed; give vines room to run.
directions: Candystick Dessert is a modern open-pollinated delicata bred by independent plant breeders Carol Deppe and Nate France in Corvallis, Oregon, and released through the Open Source Seed Initiative to keep it permanently free of patent restriction. Fruits are tan with green stripes and notably larger than standard delicata, averaging 2-3 lbs, with thick flesh and a smaller seed cavity. The dense flesh has an intensely sweet, dessert-like flavor that many compare to Medjool dates, and it holds its sweetness in storage longer than most delicata types. It is widely adapted, grown successfully from the Pacific Northwest to the Southeast and Northeast.

name: Canesi Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost, giving the long, vigorous vines ample room to run; a sturdy trellis can support the developing fruit off the ground if garden space is tight.
directions: Canesi is an Italian heirloom in the butternut group, grown historically for producing unusually large, pale tan fruit that can dwarf standard butternut in size while keeping the same sweet, dense, deep-orange flesh. Vines are exceptionally vigorous and productive, so plants benefit from generous spacing or a strong support structure to keep the heavy fruit from resting directly on wet soil. Harvest once the rind has turned mostly tan with only faint traces of green remaining, since fruit picked too early lacks the full sweetness the variety is known for. Like other moschata squash, cured Canesi fruit stores well through winter in a cool, dry location.

name: Cannellini Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile soil 2–3 inches deep; cannellini is a cool-to-warm season crop — in zone 9 plant in early spring (February–March) for a late spring harvest, or again in fall (September–October) for a winter harvest when temperatures are cooler. Avoid planting in summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; cannellini is the classic Italian white kidney bean — an heirloom variety of the white kidney bean with large, plump, white seeds and a distinctly creamy, mild, earthy flavor that absorbs olive oil, garlic, rosemary, and sage beautifully. It is the essential bean of Tuscany: the foundation of ribollita and pasta e fagioli, the bean that defines Florentine cuisine, and arguably the finest-flavored dry bean for Italian cooking. The seeds are harvested dry for storage or 'semi-dried' (fresh-shelled and briefly cured) for a fresh-eating texture that is superior to fully dried beans. Bush-type plants produce pods that are allowed to dry on the vine before harvest; the dry seeds store indefinitely in cool, dry conditions.
sources: Slow Food International Ark of Taste
University of Gastronomic Sciences — Italian Heritage Vegetables

name: Cannellino di Atina Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; provide poles or a trellis, since the variety is a vigorous climbing type traditionally grown along the Melfa and Mollarino river valleys near Atina.
directions: Cannellino di Atina holds Protected Designation of Origin (DOP) status for the river valleys around Atina in southern Lazio, where mineral-rich alluvial soil and clean valley water are credited with the bean's thin skin and especially smooth, buttery texture once cooked. The slender white seeds are larger and more elongated than ordinary cannellini beans. Give vines a tall pole or trellis and even moisture through pod fill, then allow pods to dry completely before shelling. Cure the harvested beans indoors for a week or two before sealing them away for winter storage.
sources: Region of Lazio agricultural heritage crop records

name: Cara Potato
plantingNote: Give this late maincrop variety the longest possible season; its strong blight tolerance makes it forgiving of damp, disease-prone summers.
directions: Cara was released in Ireland in 1973 and remains valued above all for its notably strong resistance to late blight in both foliage and tubers, a trait that let generations of Irish growers skip extra fungicide passes in wet years. The large, round white tubers with faint pink-flushed eyes keep growing late into the season, so leave Cara in the ground longer than early varieties before lifting. Its white flesh is dense and holds together well, making it a favorite for roasting and baking rather than a fluffy mash. Because the thick skin stores exceptionally well, Cara is a dependable choice for a root cellar that needs to carry potatoes deep into winter.

name: Cardinale Radicchio
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for a November–February harvest. Cardinale is a mid-season radicchio that heads reliably in zone 9 fall conditions without requiring excessively cold temperatures to form tight heads. The color deepens and bitterness mellows after exposure to several light frosts.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cardinale is an Italian radicchio variety producing medium-sized, round to slightly elongated heads with deep garnet-red to cardinal-red leaves and white midribs — the color is consistently deeper and more saturated than many other radicchio varieties, which gives it its name. The bitter-sweet, complex radicchio flavor is characteristic of the Cichorium intybus species, with the bitterness mellowing appropriately after cold exposure. Cardinale is valued by market growers for its reliable head formation in variable fall weather and its consistent deep color that holds through the harvest and storage period. In Italian cooking, Cardinale works in all standard radicchio preparations — grilled, braised, in risotto, in pasta, or raw in salads where its deep color provides dramatic visual contrast. In zone 9 the fall-winter-early spring season produces the most deeply colored and best-flavored heads, with improvement after the first frosts.
sources: Seeds of Italy — Cardinale Radicchio Growing Notes
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Radicchio Varieties
University of California Cooperative Extension — Radicchio Production Guide

name: Cardy Cardoon
plantingNote: Start indoors six to eight weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger has passed into deep, fertile soil; Cardy was bred to self-blanch as it grows, so it needs little or no wrapping or earthing-up before harvest.
directions: Sow indoors and transplant into deep, well-drained soil enriched with compost, in full sun with steady moisture through the growing season. Cardy is a modern cardoon selection bred to naturally pale and mellow its leaf ribs as the plant matures, largely eliminating the traditional multi-week job of bundling and wrapping stalks in cardboard or straw to exclude light. The tall, silvery, deeply cut foliage still makes an imposing ornamental clump even where it is not harvested, and a light earthing-up of the base in the final weeks before cutting can further improve rib color and tenderness. Harvest the thick leaf stalks in autumn once they have filled out, trimming away the spiny leaf blades before cooking.

name: Cargamanto Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F, and set poles or a trellis in place at planting time since vines climb quickly to 8 feet or more.
directions: Cargamanto is the iconic cranberry-mottled dry bean of the Antioquia region of Colombia, grown up cornstalks or poles in Andean smallholder plots and central to dishes such as frijoles antioqueños and bandeja paisa. The mottled cream-and-maroon seeds resemble North American cranberry beans but tend to be larger and starchier, softening to a dense, creamy texture that holds together well in slow-simmered pots. Let pods dry fully and rattle on the vine before picking, then shell and cure the beans another week or two indoors before sealing them for storage. Because it is a true pole type, give plants sturdy 8-foot supports and consistent moisture while pods are filling out.

name: Caribbean Red Habanero
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Capsicum chinense species require warmer germination temperatures (80–90°F) and longer germination times than C. annuum — use a heat mat for reliable, fast germination.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Caribbean Red is a habanero-type pepper (Capsicum chinense) producing wrinkled, lantern-shaped fruits that ripen from green to bright scarlet-red — one of the hottest commercially available habanero types, typically measuring 400,000–500,000 Scoville heat units compared to the 100,000–350,000 SHU of standard orange habaneros, making it roughly 2–4 times hotter than standard habanero by Scoville measurement. The heat is the intense, building, lingering habanero burn style — not the immediate sharp heat of cayenne — accompanied by the same characteristic fruity, tropical, citrus-floral aroma that makes habanero-type peppers uniquely valuable in hot sauces, salsas, Caribbean jerk seasonings, and mango-habanero condiments. The red color produces a visually different (and often considered more attractive) hot sauce than the orange of standard habanero, making Caribbean Red popular with home hot sauce makers. The large, productive plants grow well in zone 9's long warm season, often continuing to fruit into November after a spring transplant. In zone 9b and warmer, the plants may overwinter and become large perennial pepper shrubs producing for multiple seasons.

name: Caribe Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces as soon as the soil can be worked in late winter; Caribe tolerates warmer soil better than most potatoes, making it a favorite early variety for Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Caribe is an early-season potato notable for its striking purple-pink skin over pure white flesh, and for tolerating warmer soil temperatures better than many other potato varieties, which has made it a long-time favorite among Southern gardeners. The moist, waxy flesh holds its shape well after cooking, making Caribe well suited to potato salad and roasting. Its quick maturity and heat tolerance are especially useful in zone 9, where potatoes must be planted early and harvested before the ground becomes too warm for good tuber set. Plant seed pieces as early as the soil can be worked in late winter and hill regularly as the vigorous vines grow.

name: Carlin Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as early as the ground can be worked in late winter, several weeks ahead of the last frost, since this small brown-seeded field pea shrugs off cold snaps.
directions: Direct sow as early as the ground can be worked in late winter, several weeks ahead of the last frost, since this small brown-seeded field pea shrugs off cold snaps. Carlin Pea is a survivor of a once-widespread English tradition of eating dried, soaked, and pan-fried peas on Carlin Sunday in the weeks before Easter, and it remained a staple crop in northern England long after most gardeners moved on to modern shelling peas. Give the vining plants light twiggy brush or netting for support, and either pick pods young for shelling green or let them dry fully on the vine for the traditional parched preparation. The plants tolerate poor soil and are notably resilient compared with modern pea cultivars.

name: Carmagnola Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant after danger of frost has passed, in well-drained, sandy loam soil.
directions: Carmagnola pepper is a Piedmontese landrace grown for over a century around the town of Carmagnola near Turin, where it carries Italian IGP protected status and is cultivated in several traditional fruit shapes including blocky square, elongated horn, and flattened tomato-like forms. Fruit matures from green through yellow to red with notably thick, sweet, easily peeled flesh once roasted. It is traditionally eaten raw with bagna cauda, roasted and peeled, or preserved in oil or vinegar. Grow in full sun on sandy, well-drained soil and harvest by hand as fruit colors fully for best sweetness.
sources: Consorzio di Tutela del Peperone di Carmagnola IGP

name: Carmen Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Carmen is an F1 hybrid Italian frying pepper developed for superior earliness and productivity compared to heirloom Italian frying pepper types like Corno di Toro. In zone 9, transplant March–April; Carmen performs well through the Gulf Coast summer and fall. As an Italian frying pepper type, Carmen produces elongated (4–6 inches), slightly blocky-to-tapered fruits that ripen from green to bright red. The fruits are meaty, sweet, and thin-walled — more uniform in shape and earlier to ripen than heirloom Italian types. Carmen received All-America Selections (AAS) recognition in 2006, confirmed as performing well across diverse North American growing conditions. The early maturity of Carmen compared to heirloom frying types makes it practical for zone 9's spring production window before summer heat limits continued fruit set.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest green or fully red for best flavor. Carmen pepper is an F1 hybrid Italian frying pepper that received the All-America Selections recognition in 2006 for its consistent performance across varied North American growing conditions — specifically for its combination of earliness (reaching harvest stage significantly sooner than traditional Corno di Toro types), productivity (high fruit set per plant), and fruit quality. The All-America Selections program evaluates new vegetable and flower varieties across multiple trial locations nationwide, and a 2006 AAS designation reflects verified performance advantages over competing varieties at the time of release. Carmen's fruits are medium-large (4–6 inches long, 2 inches wide), with a form intermediate between a large Cubanelle and a Corno di Toro: longer and more pointed than a Cubanelle, but somewhat less dramatically curved and elongated than a classic Corno di Toro. The flesh is thick enough to provide substance for roasting and stuffing but still thinner-walled and more flavorful at full ripeness than standard bell peppers. The ripening process in Carmen goes through green to light orange to fully red — a complete color change that signals maximum sweetness and vitamin C content. Carmen's Italian frying pepper lineage gives it the characteristic sweetness and frying quality that makes this pepper type so valued in Mediterranean cooking: roasted Carmen peppers develop a silky, caramelized richness that is genuinely different from roasted bell peppers. For zone 9 gardeners, the early-producing quality of Carmen means productive harvests before midsummer heat stress limits continued flower and fruit production.
sources: All-America Selections — Carmen pepper 2006 AAS winner recognition
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Carmen Italian frying pepper F1 hybrid notes
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Italian Frying Pepper Variety Comparison

name: Carmen Sweet Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes; Carmen is one of the fastest-maturing sweet peppers available, particularly valued in short-season northern gardens and in hot Southern gardens where the season window for maturing peppers before fall temperatures drop can be compressed; an All-America Selections 2006 winner recognized for early maturity, high yield, and exceptional sweet flavor.
directions: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to rich, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Carmen peppers ripen from green to vivid red about 2 weeks earlier than most bell peppers, making them excellent for northern gardens; harvest at any stage from green (mild, slightly tangy) to full red (sweet, rich, complex flavor). Carmen is a top-performing Italian-style sweet frying pepper that won the All-America Selections award in 2006 — one of the most widely grown sweet pepper varieties to emerge from recent AAS trials, valued for combining the Italian frying pepper form (long, tapered, thin-walled, easy to peel) with exceptional earliness and garden productivity. The peppers are long (5–7 inches), tapered, and horn-shaped in the classic Italian style, maturing from pale green through deep red in about 70–80 days from transplant — significantly earlier than standard bell peppers (85–95 days) and most sweet Italian types. The flavor at full red maturity is distinctively sweet, rich, and complex in a way that sets Italian frying peppers apart from bell peppers: the thin walls cook faster and more evenly, caramelize beautifully in a hot pan, and develop a sweeter, more concentrated flavor than the thick-walled bell. Carmen is the go-to recommendation from most seed companies and extension services for gardeners who want a reliable sweet Italian frying pepper that performs consistently across a wide range of climates from zones 3 to 11. Excellent raw in salads, roasted, sautéed, or used for Italian-American pepper-and-egg preparations.

name: Carmine Splendor Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably above 65°F; Carmine Splendor is an early F1 hybrid that begins producing in as little as 51 days, among the fastest red-podded okra varieties available.
directions: Sow seed 1/2 to 1 inch deep in full sun after soil has warmed; stalky, upright plants stay manageable while producing heavily. Carmine Splendor is a modern F1 hybrid bred for uniform, stout, five-pointed pods that emerge deep red and soften to a lighter red-pink as they enlarge, giving a longer tender-harvest window than many older red okra types. The pale yellow, red-throated flowers are edible and often used fresh as a garnish or lightly battered and fried, in addition to the pods themselves. Harvest pods at 3-4 inches every day or two during peak summer heat, since red okra fibers up quickly once pods exceed that size.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Carmine Splendor F1 okra variety notes
Seedway — Carmine Splendor okra key characteristics
Known-You Seed America — Carmine Splendor okra product information

name: Carnival Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. Carnival is a compact acorn-type squash on a semi-bush vine well suited to smaller gardens. No two fruits look identical — the cream, orange, and green patterning varies on every squash, making Carnival ornamentally striking for fall displays as well as edible. Cure harvested fruits for 2 weeks at room temperature before eating to improve sweetness; storage improves flavor.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Carnival is an All-America Selections award-winning acorn-type winter squash that produces medium-sized (1–2 lb), acorn-shaped fruits in an extraordinarily variable pattern of cream, orange, yellow, and green — no two Carnival squash are identical in coloration, with each fruit displaying a unique combination of the variety's characteristic colors in an irregular patterned display. The diversity of color on each individual squash and across the harvest makes Carnival as ornamental as it is edible, used for autumn fall displays, Thanksgiving centerpieces, and decorative arrangements alongside pumpkins. The flesh is orange, mildly sweet, and nutty — essentially the same eating quality as high-quality acorn squash, with a dry, dense texture that accepts butter, brown sugar, or maple syrup preparations well. Carnival is extremely productive and compact for an acorn-type, making it practical for backyard gardens with limited space.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Winter Squash Variety Trial
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Winter Squash Production

name: Carola Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January-February for harvest before summer heat sets in. Cut seed pieces to egg size with 1-2 eyes each and let cut surfaces cure a day or two before planting.
directions: Plant seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun. Carola is a German-bred potato valued for its smooth, thin, light tan skin and dense, waxy, deep yellow flesh with rich, buttery flavor, performing well boiled, roasted, and in potato salads where a firm texture that holds together is wanted. It is a reliable, heavy-yielding variety with good resistance to common potato diseases and stores reasonably well after curing. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge, and harvest for storage after the vines have died back naturally.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Potato Production for Texas Home Gardens
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Potato Production in Florida

name: Carolina Black Peanut
plantingNote: Direct sow shelled seed once soil has warmed well past the last frost date; this small-seeded heirloom needs a long, hot growing season to fill its pods before fall's first frost.
directions: Sow raw, unroasted seed about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil, since the pegs that carry developing pods underground need soft ground to penetrate easily. Carolina Black is a rare African-heritage heirloom, distinguished from ordinary tan-skinned peanuts by its jet-black seed coat and a sweet, rich flavor that is prized by preservationist growers and heirloom seed keepers in the Carolinas and across the Deep South. Pods typically hold two kernels and are slightly larger than a Spanish peanut, so plants respond well to light hilling of loose soil around the base once yellow blooms appear. Because the variety is scarce commercially, growers often treat a first planting as seed increase, saving pods for replanting the following season.
sources: Peanut Grower magazine — heirloom peanut coverage

name: Carolina Broadleaf Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or, better in zone 9, from late summer through fall for a winter harvest; the large, wrinkled leaves develop best flavor after cool weather and light frost.
directions: Direct sow a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade during the cool season. USDA Agricultural Research Service breeders released Carolina Broadleaf in the mid-2010s as a deliberate improvement on the beloved old Florida Broadleaf mustard, developed specifically to resist a strain of bacterial leaf blight that had begun devastating Florida Broadleaf plantings across the South. It keeps the same large, crinkled, deep-green leaves and classic peppery mustard-green flavor gardeners expect, so it substitutes directly into traditional Southern cooking, but its added disease resistance makes it a more dependable choice where blight has become a recurring problem. Harvest young leaves for salads or let plants mature for the bolder-flavored cooking greens central to Southern braises.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service variety release notes

name: Carolina Bunch Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil is reliably warm; the short, compact vines make this a good candidate for raised beds or large containers.
directions: Carolina Bunch was developed at North Carolina State University specifically for small-space growers, with a tight, semi-bush habit that stays under 3 feet of spread instead of sprawling 6-8 feet like standard vining sweet potatoes. Despite the compact vines, it is a solid producer of light copper-skinned, dark orange-fleshed roots that store and bake well. Because the plants don't sprawl and cover ground the way most sweet potatoes do, keep the bed mulched to suppress weeds and maintain even soil moisture. This is a practical choice for raised beds or anywhere a gardener wants sweet potatoes without letting vines take over the whole plot.
sources: NC State University Plant Breeding Consortium

name: Carolina Cayenne Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Carolina Cayenne is an All-America Selections winning cayenne bred for earlier maturity and a more compact, uniform plant than traditional cayenne varieties, with classic thin, curved, hot red fruit.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Carolina Cayenne was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining classic cayenne heat and flavor with notably earlier maturity and a more compact, well-branched plant habit than older cayenne varieties, making it a reliable choice for gardeners with a shorter growing season or limited space. Fruits are thin, curved, and about 5-6 inches long, ripening from green to bright red with the sharp, straightforward heat cayenne is known for, well suited to drying, grinding into cayenne powder, or using fresh in cooking. The compact plants are heavily productive relative to their size, and the early maturity allows for a longer overall harvest window within the growing season. Harvest regularly, or let a portion of the crop ripen fully red and dry on or off the plant for storage as dried cayenne.
sources: All-America Selections — Carolina Cayenne Award Notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Carolina Cayenne variety notes
North Carolina State Extension — Pepper Variety Trials

name: Carolina Cream Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed past 65°F and frost danger has fully passed; this cream-type pea benefits from a slightly later start than blackeye types since it prefers consistently warm ground.
directions: Sow in full sun in warm, well-drained soil of moderate fertility, since cream peas like this one are prone to excess vine growth at the expense of pods in overly rich beds. Carolina Cream is a smaller-statured, light-seeded cream southern pea associated with Clemson University's long-running southern pea breeding program, which also produced well-known releases such as Zipper Cream and Colossus. The pale, cream-colored peas cook up with a notably light-colored pot liquor and mild, delicate flavor compared to the darker broth of crowder and field pea types. Harvest at the green-shell stage for the best fresh eating quality, picking every couple of days during peak summer production to keep plants setting new pods.
sources: Clemson University Home & Garden Information Center southern pea factsheet
Seed World / Growing Produce coverage of Clemson southern pea breeding program
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange cowpea variety records

name: Carolina Cross #183 Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed, giving each vine a generous hill with heavily amended soil since this hybrid is bred purely for enormous fruit size, routinely exceeding 100 lbs and holding several giant-watermelon world records.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in a heavily amended hill after last frost, allowing at least 8-10 feet in every direction per vine since this variety produces exceptionally long, vigorous runners. Carolina Cross #183 is an oblong striped hybrid bred specifically for maximum fruit size rather than eating quality, and it has been the variety of choice for generations of giant-watermelon growers at county fairs and record competitions, with individual fruits commonly reaching 100-200 lbs and record specimens well over 200 lbs. To grow oversized fruit, limit each vine to one or two developing melons, feed heavily throughout the season, and water deeply and consistently since the huge fruit places large demands on the root system. Flesh is red and reasonably sweet, but the plant's primary appeal is spectacle and competition rather than refined flavor.

name: Carolina Crowder Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed; forms large, bushy plants and is easy to shell by hand.
directions: Carolina Crowder is a classic Southern crowder pea selected and maintained by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange, updated over time for broader Fusarium wilt resistance while keeping its old-fashioned flavor. Pods are straw colored with a purple tint, 7-9 inches long, and packed tightly with light-brown crowder-type seeds that shell out easily. Large, prolific, bushy plants make it a reliable choice for a big drying-pea harvest, ready in about 61 days to first picking.

name: Carolina Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65F; its very short days-to-maturity suit an early spring planting plus a second fall sowing once temperatures ease.
directions: Developed at the North Carolina Agricultural Experiment Station as a high-yielding commercial pickler, this fast, gynoecious hybrid produces blocky, dark green fruit with broad disease resistance covering angular leaf spot, anthracnose, cucumber mosaic virus, downy and powdery mildew, and scab. Its very short days-to-maturity make it ideal for an early spring planting that beats the worst of Gulf Coast midsummer disease pressure, with a second fall sowing possible.
sources: LSU AgCenter / Seeds to Success - Recommended Cucumber Varieties for Louisiana

name: Carolina Gold Rice
plantingNote: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant April–May for an August–October harvest. Carolina Gold can be grown in standard garden beds kept consistently moist rather than flooded, though paddy conditions give the highest yields. Expect 2–4 pounds of rough rice per 100 square feet in garden conditions.
directions: Sow seed 0.5–1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Carolina Gold is America's most historically significant rice variety, the first variety commercially grown in colonial South Carolina and Georgia during the 18th century, and the foundation of lowcountry cuisine including pilau, perloo, and hoppin' john. It is a long-grained, gold-hulled, aromatic variety with exceptional flavor — nutty, fragrant, and creamy when cooked — that is the standard against which all Southern rice is measured. The variety nearly disappeared after the Civil War but was revived by dedicated seed savers and is now grown by specialty mills in the Carolinas. Home gardeners can grow it in consistently moist beds without true paddies; simply keep soil saturated throughout the growing season. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain has turned golden, then thresh and process as whole-grain brown rice or hull fully.
sources: Anson Mills — Carolina Gold Rice Heritage Grain
Clemson University Cooperative Extension — Carolina Gold Rice
University of South Carolina — Lowcountry Digital History Initiative: Rice Culture

name: Carolina Reaper Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost at 85°F with bottom heat; Carolina Reaper is slow to germinate and slow to reach transplant size. In zone 9, start in November–December for February transplant. Plants are perennial in zone 9b–11 and can be kept as multi-year producers with frost protection.
directions: Start seeds at 85–90°F soil temperature with bottom heat — germination is erratic and may take 3–4 weeks; transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay above 60°F. Carolina Reaper was certified by Guinness World Records as the world's hottest pepper in 2013, averaging 1.57 million Scoville Heat Units (SHU) with peak measurements above 2.2 million SHU — roughly 200 times hotter than a jalapeño and significantly more potent than habaneros. It was bred by Ed Curlin (PuckerButt Pepper Company) in Rock Hill, South Carolina, by crossing a Pakistani Naga with a Red Habanero. The distinctive wrinkled, red-orange fruits are small (1–2 inches) with a characteristic scorpion-tail sting at the tip and a fruity, complex flavor underneath the extreme heat. Handle with nitrile gloves and eye protection — touching eyes or face after handling can cause serious irritation. Used in hot sauces, salsas, and challenge eating. The plants are attractive and productive in warm climates. In zone 9, treat as a long-season annual or overwinter as a perennial in zone 9b.
sources: Guinness World Records 2013 — Carolina Reaper hottest pepper certification
PuckerButt Pepper Company — Carolina Reaper breeding notes
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University
Journal of Experimental Botany — Capsaicinoid analysis

name: Carolina Ruby Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F; ridge rows to keep the developing roots loose and well-drained.
directions: Carolina Ruby was bred at North Carolina State University and released in the late 1990s as an earlier-maturing companion to Beauregard, with striking deep red-purple skin and moist orange flesh. It bulks up quickly and can be dug a couple of weeks ahead of most other orange sweet potatoes, which is a real advantage for beating fall's first frost in a home garden. Vines are thin and trailing rather than bushy, so give them room to ramble or trellis them along a fence. Roots can develop pronounced lenticels if soil stays wet close to harvest, so time digging for a dry stretch and avoid heavy irrigation in the final weeks.
sources: NC State University Plant Breeding Consortium

name: Carolina White Rice
plantingNote: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant April–May for an August–October harvest. Carolina White can be grown in standard garden beds kept consistently saturated rather than true flooded paddies, though paddy conditions give the highest yields.
directions: Sow seed 0.5–1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated or flooded through the growing season. Carolina White was the pale-hulled sister landrace grown alongside gold-hulled Carolina Gold throughout the antebellum South Carolina and Georgia Lowcountry, part of the same rice culture built on enslaved West African agricultural expertise that made Charleston one of the wealthiest colonial ports. Like Carolina Gold, Carolina White nearly vanished after the Civil War and through the collapse of Lowcountry rice culture in the early 20th century; the two landraces are close kin, and rice geneticists working with the Carolina Gold Rice Foundation and Anson Mills have noted that recovered Carolina Gold populations can express Carolina White characteristics. Grow it exactly as Carolina Gold — in a saturated bed or shallow paddy — and expect a tall, long-grained rice with a milder, less golden husk color but similar exceptional cooking quality. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain hardens, then thresh and dry thoroughly before hulling.
sources: Anson Mills — Artisan Mill Goods from Heirloom Grains
Rice Today (International Rice Research Institute) — Carolina Gold and Carolina White Rice: A Genetic Odyssey

name: Carolina Wonder Sweet Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Carolina Wonder was developed by North Carolina State University as a disease-resistant sweet bell pepper with resistance to Phytophthora blight, bacterial leaf spot, and tobacco etch virus — disease complex that significantly limits sweet bell pepper production in humid Southeastern climates — making it one of the most reliable sweet bells for home gardeners across the Atlantic and Gulf Coast states.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil after last frost; Carolina Wonder's disease resistance package makes it superior to susceptible commercial bell varieties in humid climates where Phytophthora blight and bacterial leaf spot cause mid-season collapse of unprotected plants. Carolina Wonder was developed at North Carolina State University's pepper breeding program to address the specific disease challenges of Southeastern sweet bell pepper production — the combination of summer heat, humidity, rainfall, and the disease complex it creates (Phytophthora capsici root and crown rot, bacterial leaf spot caused by Xanthomonas, tobacco etch virus) creates extremely difficult conditions for standard sweet bell varieties that lack specific resistance genes. Carolina Wonder combines resistance to multiple diseases with excellent sweet bell quality: the large (4-lobed, blocky, 3.5–4 inch), thick-walled fruits are green-to-red with crisp, sweet flesh typical of the best sweet bells. The disease resistance package — particularly the Phytophthora crown and root rot resistance — gives Carolina Wonder dramatically better survival in wet years and poorly drained soils compared to susceptible varieties. Carolina Wonder is sometimes paired with Charleston Belle (which adds nematode resistance not included in Carolina Wonder) in gardens where both nematodes and Phytophthora are concerns; together they address the full disease complex of Gulf South pepper production.

name: Carouby de Maussane Snow Pea
scientificName: Pisum sativum var. saccharatum 'Carouby de Maussane'
plantingNote: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked; Carouby de Maussane is a tall (4–5 foot) snow pea requiring trellis support. In zone 9, direct sow November–February for spring harvest (March–April); fall planting is preferred in zone 9 where the mild winter allows establishment and early spring production before summer heat arrives. The distinctive large flat pods (3–5 inches) are harvested when still flat and before seeds develop — the snow pea stage. The purple flowers and bicolor pods make this one of the most ornamental of edible pod pea varieties.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep along a trellis or fence; thin to 3–4 inches. Provide 4–5 foot support. Harvest pods flat before seeds bulge. Carouby de Maussane is a French Provençal heirloom snow pea — a mangetout (French for 'eat all,' referring to the edible pod) variety from the village of Maussane-les-Alpilles in the Alpilles region of Provence that has been grown continuously in the gardens and small farms of that region for generations. The variety is distinguished by unusually large flat pods (3–5 inches long) that are visually unlike standard snow peas: broader, larger, and often tinged with purple at the shoulders when young — and by the ornamental beauty of the plant itself, which produces the bi-colored purple-and-white flowers of the original pea species (most modern pea varieties have been selected for white-only flowers) against dark green foliage on 4–5 foot vines. The pods have the flat, wide, meaty snow pea character at optimal harvest — tender, crisp, and sweetly flavored without the starchy density of fully-podded shelling peas. Carouby de Maussane is a cold-hardy, vigorous variety well-suited to fall planting in zone 8–9 where it can grow through the mild winter and produce the spring snap-pod harvest before summer heat arrives. The variety is maintained by seed savers and heirloom seed companies as an example of the genetic and culinary diversity that existed in traditional European peasant food gardens.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Carouby de Maussane snow pea variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — French heirloom pea collection
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Edible pod pea variety notes

name: Carpathian Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves pointed end up in fall, roughly 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes solid, allowing roots to establish before dormancy.
directions: Set cloves 2 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil and mulch heavily through winter, especially in northern climates, removing mulch gradually in spring. Cut the scape once it curls to direct the plant's energy into bulb formation, then cure bulbs for several weeks in a dry, shaded, well-ventilated space. Carpathian is a cold-hardy porcelain-type hardneck originating in the Carpathian Mountains of Eastern Europe, grown for its large white bulbs, thick papery wrappers, and strong, long-lasting garlic flavor well suited to harsh winter climates.

name: Carver Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost into ridged, loose soil in full sun; Carver is a mid-20th-century Southern release named in honor of George Washington Carver, grown for dependable yields of deep orange, blocky roots.
directions: Set slips into ridged, well-drained soil two to four weeks after the last frost, spacing plants a foot to eighteen inches apart along the row. Carver was developed and released in the mid-1900s as a disease-tolerant Southern market type with deep rose-copper skin and deep orange, moderately moist flesh, and carries the name of George Washington Carver in recognition of his sweet potato research and promotion work at Tuskegee Institute. Vines are vigorous and roots size up fairly uniformly, making the variety a steady producer for home gardeners who want a classic baking sweet potato without heavy disease pressure. Dig before the first hard frost, cure for a week to ten days at warm, humid conditions, and store cool and dry to sweeten the flesh.
sources: NC State University Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America
USDA National Agricultural Library — George Washington Carver Historical Publications

name: Casaba Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Casaba is the longest-season common American melon (105–120 days), requiring the extended heat of Gulf Coast and Western summers for reliable ripening, but rewarding patient gardeners with large, golden-yellow, wrinkled-skinned fruits that store for months and have a distinctive mild, sweet, creamy-white flesh.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Casaba needs dry conditions at harvest to prevent splitting and rind cracking — reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity. Casaba melon takes its name from Kasaba (now called Turgutlu), a city in western Turkey from which seeds were brought to the United States in the late 19th century; it is an inodorus winter-type melon with no surface netting and little external fragrance when ripe, unusual among American melons. The large (8–14 lb), round to slightly pointed-at-one-end fruits have deeply furrowed, wrinkled, golden-yellow skin and creamy-white to pale yellow flesh with mild, sweet, cucumber-like flavor that is less intensely aromatic than cantaloupe but refreshing and distinct. Casaba's extraordinary keeping quality (3–5 months at cool room temperature without refrigeration) made it historically important as a late-season melon available well after other varieties were finished; harvested in October it could remain in good condition through December. Excellent for dry summer climates (California, Arizona, Gulf Coast with good drainage); susceptible to powdery mildew in humid conditions.

name: Cascabel Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; a traditional Mexican dried chile harvested red and used primarily dried — do not harvest green. Zone 8–11 gardeners can grow this easily as a spring crop in the ground.
directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to the garden in warm soil after all frost risk has passed. Cascabel — named for the rattle the seeds make inside the dried pod — is a round, 1.5-inch, deep red-brown dried Mexican chile with mild to moderate heat (1,500–2,500 Scoville), a uniquely nutty, slightly smoky, woody flavor with an earthy depth that is used in traditional Mexican moles, salsas, and braised meats; it is harvested fully red on the plant and dried for 2–3 weeks in a warm, airy location. Plants are compact and bushy, producing round pods in clusters; the fully dried pods have a distinctive rattling sound from the loose seeds inside, making them easy to identify in a pantry. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture to maximize fruit set.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Cascade Glaze Collard
plantingNote: Direct sow or set transplants 10-12 weeks before the first fall frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Cascade Glaze is a modern re-selection of the 1820s Southern heirloom Green Glaze, sharing its glossy, waxy, insect-resistant leaves.
directions: Set transplants or thin direct-sown seedlings to 24-30 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Cascade Glaze was bred as a careful re-selection of the classic 1820s Southern heirloom Green Glaze collard, retaining the same smooth, glossy, waxy leaf surface that sheds cabbage worm eggs and deters other leaf-eating pests better than fuzzier-leaved collard varieties, while offering improved uniformity from the breeding work. The open, non-heading rosette produces tender, mild-flavored leaves that hold up well to both heat and light frost, making it productive across a long Gulf South growing season. Harvest outer leaves continuously as the plant grows, and expect sweeter flavor after the first light frosts convert starches to sugars.

name: Cascadia Snap Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Cascadia is an Oregon State University-bred snap pea noted for disease resistance and reliable production on compact vines.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked, providing light support such as netting or twiggy brush for the vines. Cascadia was bred at Oregon State University and is valued for good resistance to powdery mildew and other common pea diseases, along with sweet, crisp, edible pods on compact, easy-to-support vines that produce reliably even in less-than-ideal spring weather. Its snap-pea type pods are eaten whole, pod and all, once they fill out but before the peas inside become starchy. Harvest regularly once pods reach full size to encourage continued production through the relatively short Gulf South pea season.

name: Case Knife Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 65°F, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; provide an 8-foot pole or trellis, since this vigorous semi-runner climbs readily and produces best when given full support.
directions: Sow at the base of poles or a trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pick young for snap beans, at the shelly stage for a creamy fresh bean, or let pods dry fully on the vine for storage beans. Case Knife is an old Southern heirloom pole bean named for its long, flat, slightly curved pods, which resemble the folding blade of a case knife (a traditional pocketknife). The vigorous vines climb readily to 6–8 feet and bear heavily over a long summer season, producing broad, tender pods best picked young for snap use before the beans inside swell; left to mature, the pods yield plump, cream-white beans that shell out easily and cook to a smooth, buttery texture, or can be dried fully for winter storage. Valued in old Southern gardens for its dependable heat tolerance and heavy yield from a small footprint of trellis space, making it a practical choice for Gulf South vegetable gardens where many bush beans falter in midsummer heat.

name: Caserta Italian Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and August–September for fall. Caserta is one of the most heat-tolerant open-pollinated zucchini varieties, typically yielding well into summer heat that causes hybrid types to stall. The AAS-winning bush habit is compact and manageable in small gardens.
directions: Direct sow 2–3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and thin to the strongest plant; Caserta is an All-America Selections award-winning heirloom Italian zucchini with distinctive gray-green striped skin and creamy interior, different in appearance and texture from the solid dark-green standard zucchini. The cylindrical, 6–8 inch fruits have firmer, denser, less watery flesh than most hybrid zucchini — excellent for grilling, sautéing, and stuffing where a firmer texture is preferred. The compact, AAS-winning bush plant produces abundantly in both spring and fall crops in zone 9; summer production may slow during peak heat. Harvest at 6–8 inches for best flavor and texture — oversized fruits become seedy and pithy. The attractive, striped fruits are ornamental as well as useful.
sources: All-America Selections — Caserta Squash Award Record
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Italian Zucchini
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Zucchini Production

name: Cash Flow Hybrid Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed after last frost, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early for a jump on the season.
directions: Cash Flow was bred as a market-grower's zucchini, prized for setting an unusually high number of straight, uniform dark-green fruit in quick succession from an open, easy-to-harvest plant. Pick fruit small, at 6-8 inches, for the best texture and to keep the vigorous plant cranking out more; a single well-fed plant can produce for weeks with regular harvest. The open habit makes fruit easy to spot under the leaves, cutting down on the oversized zucchini that hide until harvest day. A dependable choice for gardeners who want a steady, heavy zucchini harvest without much fuss.

name: Casper Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Harvest fruit when glossy and firm, before the skin dulls and yellows, which signals overripeness and increasing bitterness.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pick fruit young and glossy for the mildest, sweetest flavor and fewest seeds. Casper is a classic heirloom eggplant producing smooth, pure ivory-white, oblong fruit with tender skin that needs no peeling, and notably mild, sweet, non-bitter flesh that browns less than purple varieties once cut — a practical advantage for dishes where appearance matters, like gratins or stuffed preparations. The productive, well-branched plants set fruit reliably over a long summer season and are less prone to the bitterness that can develop in some eggplant varieties under stress. Its striking white color and mild flavor make it a favorite for gardeners wanting a visually distinctive eggplant with excellent kitchen versatility, zone 4–12.

name: Casper White Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Casper white eggplant shows good heat tolerance and performs well in zone 9. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer and fall production. Harvest when fruits are 5–7 inches long and creamy white — white eggplants turn slightly yellowish as they over-ripen, which is the signal to harvest before quality declines. Do not allow to over-ripen on the plant; harvest slightly early compared to purple types.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun. Harvest when fruits are 5–7 inches and solid creamy white before yellowing. Casper is an Italian-style white eggplant — a medium-sized, oval-to-elongated variety producing distinctive ivory-white to cream-white fruits in the 4–7 inch range. White eggplant varieties have a long tradition in Italian cooking, where they are considered particularly well-suited to oven-roasted preparations and eggplant parmesan, as the white skin and flesh remain visually lighter during cooking compared to the purple-flesh types that can discolor. The flavor of Casper white eggplant is noticeably different from standard purple varieties: consistently milder, creamier, with significantly less bitterness — white-skinned eggplants in general tend toward less bitterness than dark-skinned types, though the reason may be as much cultural (bred and selected for mild flavor in the white-eggplant tradition) as biological. The flesh is very creamy and smooth-textured, making Casper an excellent choice for dips, spreads, baba ganoush-style preparations, and dishes where a mild, creamy eggplant flavor is desired without the assertiveness of purple types. The ivory-white skin also makes Casper a visually interesting garden plant and conversation piece at farmers markets.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Casper eggplant variety notes
High Mowing Organic Seeds — White eggplant variety descriptions
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Eggplant Variety Evaluation

name: Caspian Pink Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Caspian Pink is an indeterminate beefsteak that produces large, heavy fruits (8–14 oz) and benefits from strong stake or sturdy cage support. In zone 9, transplant March–April for July–August harvest. Like many large beefsteak types, Caspian Pink requires warm nights to set fruit well — the Gulf South's warm summer nights are typically favorable for fruit set in this variety.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun in fertile, deeply prepared soil. Stake securely — the large, heavy fruits can pull down unsupported vines. Caspian Pink is a Ukrainian-Russian heirloom beefsteak tomato introduced to the United States by Marianna Kezenberger, an immigrant from the Caspian Sea region of the former Soviet Union — the name references both the geographic origin and the distinctive color. The variety is a large-fruited, low-acid pink-skinned beefsteak type: fruits weigh 8–14 oz or more, with the flattened, slightly irregular, shouldered shape characteristic of traditional beefsteaks. The skin is thin, smooth, and a clear rose-pink rather than true red, indicating the absence of the yellow skin gene — a characteristic associated with lower perceived acidity and sweeter flavor in tomatoes. The flavor profile is rich, complex, and less sharp than red-skinned beefsteaks — noticeably sweeter at the same sugar content because lower acid allows sweetness to predominate. Caspian Pink is consistently rated among the best-tasting pink heirloom beefsteaks in comparative tastings, often mentioned in the same conversation as Brandywine and Cherokee Purple as a top-tier beefsteak for eating quality.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Caspian Pink tomato variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Russian heirloom tomato collection
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Heirloom tomato tasting trial notes

name: Castelfranco Radicchio
plantingNote: Sow in midsummer (late July to August in most climates) for fall and winter harvest; this Italian heirloom requires cool temperatures to develop its distinctive markings and mild flavor, so timing is critical — too-early sowing leads to bolting, too-late means insufficient size before hard freezes.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in summer, thinning to 12–14 inches apart; Castelfranco is sometimes called the 'Flower of the Veneto' for its extraordinarily beautiful, loosely ruffled heads that open like a rose, with creamy white or pale yellow leaves splashed and spotted with deep wine-red markings — no two heads are alike. The flavor is distinctly milder and more buttery than the sharply bitter Chioggia or Treviso types, making it accessible to diners who find radicchio too harsh. Cool autumn temperatures intensify the color development — heads grown in warm weather are primarily green. Use individual leaves as edible cups for salads or hors d'oeuvres; the visual presentation is stunning. In the South, this is an ideal late-fall and winter salad green for gardens in zones 8–9.

name: Castellano Chickpea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost into well-drained soil in full sun; Castellano is the classic chickpea of Castile and León, traditionally used in Spanish cocido stew.
directions: Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Castellano is a medium-to-large, light cream chickpea with a semi-wrinkled skin and a distinctive curved beak, originating in the Castile and León region of Spain. It is the traditional chickpea used in the classic cocido stew, prized for holding its shape and texture through long simmering. Grow it with the same warm-season, drought-tolerant culture as other chickpeas, harvesting dried pods once they rattle on the plant.

name: Catalina Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer or early fall for fall and winter harvest; Catalina is particularly valued for fall sowing in zone 8–10 where it establishes quickly in warm soil and then grows through winter. In zone 9, sow September–November for November–February harvest. Spring planting is possible (sow February–March) but Catalina shows its best performance in the cooler temperatures of fall and winter production.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; thin to 2–4 inch spacing for full-sized leaves or leave more densely sown for baby spinach harvest.
