Chile Puya produces slender pods closely resembling guajillo but shorter, narrower, and notably hotter, typically left on the plant to ripen fully to deep red before drying. Dried pods are toasted and rehydrated for robust red salsas, adobos, and marinades across central and western Mexico, often blended alongside guajillo and ancho for layered heat and flavor.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Chilean Red Mashua
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Chilean Red is a vigorous, very productive mashua selection.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Chilean Red is a fast-growing, very productive mashua selection with tubers colored yellow to deep red. Like other mashua it is a short-day plant, with tuberization triggered by shortening autumn daylength and harvest beginning in mid-November onward. It tolerates light freezes to about zone 7a with heavy mulch protection over winter, and the tubers mellow from a sharp, peppery raw flavor to a sweet, starchy taste similar to parsnip once cooked or frost-touched.

name: Chilhuacle Amarillo Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost in a warm location (75-85F); transplant after all frost danger passes. Amarillo is the slowest and least productive of the three chilhuacle types, so give it the longest warm season available and do not expect the heavy yields of standard garden peppers.
directions: Chilhuacle amarillo is the rarest and mildest of the Cañada region's three chilhuacle types, grown today by only a small number of families around Cuicatlan in Oaxaca's Cañada district. The shoulder-shaped fruit ripens from green through gold to a dusty ochre-tan rather than the dramatic black or red of its negro and rojo siblings, and it carries a gentler, more delicate heat alongside a fruity, faintly tangy flavor. Harvest at full color and dry thoroughly on screens in a single layer; the dried pod is the defining ingredient of mole amarillo, the palest and lightest of Oaxaca's classic mole sauces. Because cultivation has dwindled to a handful of growers, treat seed from any specialty source as precious and save it carefully from your best plants.
sources: Diana Kennedy -- The Cuisines of Mexico
Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity -- Ark of Taste chilhuacle documentation
Rick Bayless -- Mexico One Plate at a Time

name: Chilhuacle Negro Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost in a warm location (80–85°F); transplant after all frost danger passes; chilhuacle negro is a large-fruited Mexican landrace chile that takes 110–130 days from transplant to reach its distinctive dark reddish-black mature color — the key stage for authentic Oaxacan mole negro and mole coloradito sauces.
directions: Start indoors in a warm seedling tray 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to a sunny, fertile bed after all frost danger passes; chilhuacle plants are large and productive but slow-maturing — plan the long growing season carefully; harvest when fruits turn fully dark reddish-black to black and the skin begins to feel slightly leathery; dry thoroughly on screens in a single layer. Chilhuacle Negro is one of the most important and irreplaceable chiles in Oaxacan cuisine — the primary chile in mole negro, one of the canonical seven moles of Oaxaca and arguably the most complex mole sauce in Mexican gastronomy. The fresh chile is a medium-large (2–3 inch wide, 3–5 inch long), slightly squat, triangular to shoulder-shaped fruit with thick, dark green walls that transitions through red to a very deep reddish-black at full maturity — the darkened color indicating the presence of additional flavor compounds that develop in the fully mature and dried state. The dried chilhuacle negro is unique among Mexican dried chiles for its distinctive flavor: deeply complex, somewhat fruity, mildly earthy with a chocolate-like depth, moderately hot (2,500–5,000 Scoville units), and with a characteristic thick skin that retains more texture when rehydrated than thinner-skinned chiles. Only three types of chilhuacle exist: negro (black), rojo (red), and amarillo (yellow) — all grown in the Cañada region of the northern Sierra Norte of Oaxaca, particularly around the town of Huajuapan de León and the Mixteca Alta, where the specific combination of altitude, temperature, and local soil conditions produces chiles with flavor characteristics impossible to replicate elsewhere. A critical ingredient for cooks interested in authentic Oaxacan cuisine.
sources: Diana Kennedy — The Cuisines of Mexico
Rick Bayless — Mexico One Plate at a Time

name: Chilhuacle Rojo Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger passes; chilhuacle rojo matures slightly earlier than negro, turning vivid bright red at full maturity; it is the key ingredient in Oaxacan mole coloradito and enchiladas coloradas — a brighter, somewhat fruitier dried chile than the negro with moderate heat.
directions: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes in fertile, well-drained soil; harvest at full red maturity for drying; dry on screens in a single layer in a warm, airy location until leathery-crisp; store dried chiles in airtight containers away from light. Chilhuacle Rojo is the red form of the chilhuacle chile, one of the three varieties grown specifically in the Cañada district of Oaxaca state in Mexico. While the chilhuacle negro (black) is the defining ingredient of mole negro, the chilhuacle rojo plays the lead role in Oaxacan mole coloradito — a complex red mole that, while less dark and mysterious than mole negro, is equally complex and represents one of the pillars of Oaxacan cooking. The dried rojo chile is a vivid brick-red to deep red color with moderately thick walls that rehydrate to a smooth, velvety texture. The flavor is distinctively fruity and somewhat tart-sweet, with moderate heat (3,000–6,000 Scoville units), and a characteristic sweetness that distinguishes it from the guajillo and other red dried chiles with which it is sometimes confused. The shoulder-shaped, somewhat flattened form (wider near the stem, tapering to the tip) is characteristic of all three chilhuacle varieties and distinguishes them from other Oaxacan chiles like the negro or costeño. In Mexican markets, chilhuacle rojo is sometimes substituted with a blend of ancho and guajillo chiles, but genuine chilhuacle rojo has a unique flavor profile that the blend does not replicate. Increasingly available from specialty seed companies as interest in authentic regional Mexican cuisine grows among American gardeners and home cooks.
sources: Diana Kennedy — The Cuisines of Mexico
Rick Bayless — Mexico One Plate at a Time

name: Chilly Chili Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55°F; Chilly Chili is bred specifically to lack capsaicin, the compound responsible for pepper heat, making it safe to grow around children who may be tempted to pick and taste the colorful fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, harden off, and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Chilly Chili won an All-America Selections award as the first heatless ornamental pepper, bred to eliminate capsaicin entirely so its abundant small, slender, upright fruit — which ripens through a colorful progression of purple, yellow, orange, and red, often several colors present on the plant at once — can be safely tasted by curious children without any burning heat. Its compact, tidy habit and long-lasting, weather-resistant fruit display make it an excellent choice for children's gardens, containers, and edging where the bright, changing fruit color provides months of interest from summer through fall. Because the fruit holds its color and shape well after ripening, plants often remain colorful and attractive right up until frost.
sources: All-America Selections — Chilly Chili pepper winner notes
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database

name: Chimayó Chile
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant once soil has warmed and frost danger has passed. Chimayó is a high-desert landrace adapted to hot days, cool nights, and low humidity, and it performs best where summer nights cool down rather than staying hot and muggy.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Chimayó Chile is a true landrace pepper grown for at least three centuries by Pueblo and Hispanic farming families in the village of Chimayó, in the foothills of New Mexico's Sangre de Cristo Mountains. The thin-walled, 4–6 inch tapered pods ripen from green to deep red and carry a moderate, warming heat (roughly 4,000–6,000 Scoville units) alongside a complex, sweet, smoky flavor that distinguishes it from other New Mexico-type chiles. Pods are traditionally strung into ristras and air-dried, then ground into the red chile powder used for New Mexican posole, carne adovada, and red chile sauce. Because it developed in an isolated, arid high-desert valley, seed-grown plants stay relatively compact and thrive with less humidity and lower water than Gulf Coast or Southeastern pepper varieties.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — Chimayó Chile Variety Notes
Native Seeds/SEARCH — Chimayó Chile Landrace Collection

name: China Express Napa Cabbage
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in rich, well-drained soil timed for a fall harvest; thin plants to their full spacing early so uniform heads can develop.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in rich, well-drained soil timed for a fall harvest, since this fast-growing hybrid is bred for slow bolting and reliably forms dense, barrel-shaped heads even under variable weather. Thin plants to their full spacing early so uniform, well-wrapped heads can develop without stress cracking. The crisp, mildly sweet leaves are well suited to fresh salads, quick stir-fries, and kimchi, and mature heads store well in a cold, humid location for several weeks.

name: China Rose Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, since this radish is slower to mature and stores better than quick spring types.
directions: Sow seeds directly a half-inch deep and thin seedlings to a few inches apart, since crowded roots stay thin and pithy. Unlike fast-maturing spring radishes, this nineteenth-century heirloom is grown as a fall crop and left in the ground longer, forming a smooth, tapered root five to six inches long with rose-pink skin and crisp white flesh. Its flavor is notably more pungent than spring salad radishes, and its roots hold their quality in the ground or in cold storage well into winter, making it a traditional keeper variety for root cellars. Cool fall temperatures improve both texture and flavor, so avoid sowing it for a hot-weather harvest.

name: China Yellow Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; this short, early-maturing bush bean suits short-season gardens and can also be fall-sown in mild climates.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil after the danger of frost; the low, compact bushes need no support and mature quickly compared with most dry beans. China Yellow, also called the Sulphur Bean, is a New England heirloom documented before 1870, valued for its small, plump, pale sulphur-yellow seeds that cook down quickly to a soft, creamy consistency ideal for stewing and baking. Despite the name, it has no connection to China; the name simply describes its distinctive pale yellow color. Let pods dry fully on the plant, then thresh and store the beans in an airtight container.

name: Chinese Five-Color Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun once nights stay above 55°F.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun, well-drained soil after frost danger passes. Chinese Five-Color is a compact ornamental hot pepper prized for producing small, upward-facing fruit in purple, cream, yellow, orange, and red all at once on the same plant, since individual peppers ripen through this color sequence at slightly different rates, creating a constantly shifting, jewel-like display against the plant's purple-tinged green foliage and purple flowers. The small, tapered fruit carries real heat in the cayenne range and is fully edible, useful in hot sauces or pickling, though most growers treat the plant primarily as a container or bedding ornamental. The compact, well-branched habit needs no staking and performs equally well in the ground or in a decorative pot on a sunny patio; harvest fruit at any color stage once past the initial pale coloring.

name: Chinese Giant Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before the last frost; Chinese Giant, introduced in the early 1900s, was noted at the time for producing bell fruit roughly twice the size of other bells then available, and it remains one of the largest-fruited open-pollinated sweet peppers grown today.
directions: Chinese Giant is a pre-1900s heirloom sweet pepper prized for its nearly square, extra-large, thick-walled fruit that can reach 4-6 inches long and wide, ripening from dark green to a bright cherry red with mild, sweet, fruity flavor. The compact, 2 to 2.5 foot plants stay relatively short despite the outsized fruit, so working compost into the planting hole and providing steady, even moisture helps size the peppers to their full potential without stressing the plant. Its thick flesh and generous cavity make it an outstanding stuffing pepper, and the large flat surfaces also suit it well to slicing for salads or grilling. Support heavily loaded branches with light staking in windy sites, since the fruit's weight can snap stems on an otherwise sturdy plant.

name: Chinese Pink Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; this is one of the earliest hardnecks to mature, so watch for yellowing lower leaves ahead of other varieties.
directions: Chinese Pink is a Porcelain-type hardneck known for finishing about two weeks ahead of most other hardneck garlics, making it useful for gardeners wanting an early harvest or a hedge against unpredictable weather. Bulbs are smaller, typically holding just 4 to 6 plump cloves wrapped in blush pink-tinged wrappers, with a flavor many describe as gentler and easier on the stomach than sharper varieties. Grow and cure it like other hardnecks: plant in fall, remove the scape once it curls, and harvest when the lower leaves begin to brown. Its mild character makes it a good entry point for cooks who find stronger hardneck garlics overpowering raw.

name: Chinese Red Ripper Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed; heat tolerant enough to succession-sow through the hottest part of a Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Chinese Red Ripper, also sold as Chinese Red, is a smaller-seeded, bushier selection of the classic Red Ripper cowpea. It is highly heat tolerant, blooms and sets pods early, and produces long 12-14 inch pods holding 18-21 seeds each, making it a heavy producer for a bush-type pea. It works equally well as a fresh green-shelled pea, a dried storage pea, or a summer cover crop and wildlife forage planting.

name: Chinese String Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil after frost danger has passed.
directions: An East China heirloom named for its remarkably thin, string-like pods, which grow 10 to 15 inches long with lavender-violet skin over white, buttery flesh. The thin skin needs no peeling and the fruit is tender enough to eat raw in salads when picked young. Plants are high-yielding and quick to mature, performing well in both greenhouse and outdoor culture in warm climates. Pick young and often, as older fruit can toughen and develop seeds.

name: Ching Chiang Bok Choy
plantingNote: Sow in early spring or late summer for fall harvest; this semi-dwarf type is unusually tolerant of heat, cold, and rain swings, making it forgiving for shoulder-season plantings.
directions: Ching Chiang is a semi-dwarf Taiwanese bok choy with smooth, medium-green leaves and pale green petioles, bred to reach usable baby-bok-choy size quickly while still holding quality if left to mature further. It shrugs off the weather swings of shoulder-season planting better than many bok choy types, tolerating both a late cold snap and an early warm spell without much bolting or damage. Harvest whole plants at about five inches tall for the most tender baby heads, or let them grow another week or two for a larger stir-fry-sized crop.

name: Ching-Chiang Pak Choi
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to a close final spacing; also sown in early spring after last frost.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to a close final spacing, since Ching-Chiang forms a compact, vase-shaped baby Shanghai-type plant with pale-green, spoon-shaped petioles and medium-green leaves. This variety is notably tolerant of heat, rain, cold, and dampness, which makes it more forgiving than many pak choi types for both early spring and late summer sowings. Harvest whole plants at about 6 inches tall for tender stir-fry and soup greens with a mild, sweet flavor.

name: Chinook Leek
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or sow several seeds per pot and separate seedlings for transplanting into a shallow trench.
directions: Chinook is a fast-growing, adaptable F1 leek bred for reliable summer production, reaching harvest size faster than most fall and winter types. Grow in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil at pH 6.0-7.0, spacing plants 4-5 inches apart in rows 12-18 inches apart. Despite its quick summer maturity it is frost-hardy, and in mild climates can be left in the ground and harvested through winter or stored in the ground until the soil freezes.

name: Chioggia Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost as soon as soil can be worked; in zone 9 sow September–February for winter-spring harvest. Chioggia beet is best harvested at 2–3 inches diameter — the candy-stripe pattern is most vivid and the texture most tender at medium size. Large over-mature Chioggia beets lose the distinct stripe clarity as the rings merge. Thin seedlings to 3–4 inches apart; the thinnings are edible as beet greens. In zone 9 the cool season from fall through early spring is the primary growing window.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, loose, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of stones and compaction; Chioggia is an 1840s Italian heirloom beet from the town of Chioggia near Venice, producing medium-sized, round roots with distinctive alternating concentric rings of deep rose-red and white when sliced — resembling a bulls-eye or candy cane pattern that makes the cross-section one of the most visually striking of any vegetable. The candy-stripe pattern is most vivid in raw beets; cooking softens the color contrast. Chioggia has a notably milder, sweeter, less earthy flavor than standard red beet varieties — the 'dirt' or 'earthiness' commonly associated with beets is less pronounced in Chioggia, making it preferred by people who enjoy the sweetness of beets but find the strong earthy undertone of red beets off-putting. Raw Chioggia slices are excellent in salads and cheese boards where the color pattern can be appreciated, and they don't stain hands and cutting boards with the deep red juice of standard beets.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Chioggia Heirloom Beet
Slow Food USA — Chioggia Traditional Beet Cultivar
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Heirloom Root Vegetables

name: Chirimen Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; provide plenty of room, since vines are unusually prolific and can set eight or more fruit each.
directions: Chirimen is an old Japanese squash of the Yokohama group, named for its deeply ribbed, warty rind reminiscent of crinkled chirimen crepe fabric. Fruit starts dark green and ripens to a mottled bronze-orange, enclosing thick, moist, deep-yellow flesh with a sweetness similar to kabocha or butternut. The vines are extremely productive, often setting eight to twelve flattened, globe-shaped fruit weighing five to eleven pounds apiece over a season. Popular in Japan since the Edo period, it is well suited to simmering in broth, roasting, or tempura once fully cured, and stores for months when kept cool and dry after harvest.

name: Chocolate Bhut Jolokia Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat; pods need a long, hot season to fully darken to chocolate-brown.
directions: Chocolate Bhut Jolokia is a dark-podded strain of the classic ghost pepper, ripening through green and reddish-brown before settling into a deep, glossy chocolate color. It carries the same wrinkled pod texture and formidable heat as red bhut jolokia, with a slightly earthier, roasted undertone favored by hot sauce makers. Because the fruit colors up slowly, gardeners in shorter-season climates should start seed as early as feasible and consider container culture to extend the ripening window. Keep soil evenly moist and handle harvested pods with gloves.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Chocolate Bhutlah Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; Bhutlah is among the slowest superhots to mature and needs the longest season possible.
directions: Bhutlah, sometimes sold as Chocolate Bhutlah, is a deliberate cross of bhut jolokia (ghost pepper) and Trinidad Scorpion lines, producing small, extremely gnarled dark-brown pods that rank among the most searing chiles grown by home superhot enthusiasts. Because the fruit is slow to size up and slower still to fully color from green to chocolate-brown, gardeners in short-season climates should start seed as early as feasible and consider container culture so plants can be moved to protect them from early frost. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since chinense superhots are prone to root stress that shows up as blossom drop weeks later. Handle harvested pods with gloves, as oleoresin transfer from Bhutlah is unusually persistent even after washing.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Chocolate Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–80°F and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; stake or cage firmly, since Chocolate Cherry is a vigorous, sprawling indeterminate producer.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, staking or caging plants firmly to support their vigorous, indeterminate vines. Chocolate Cherry is an heirloom cherry tomato bearing clusters of round, one-inch fruit in an unusual dusky brownish-red color reminiscent of the larger Cherokee Purple, carrying the same rich, complex, sweet-and-smoky flavor in a bite-sized package rather than a full beefsteak-size fruit. Its productive, long-season vines yield heavily from midsummer through frost, making it a favorite for snacking, salads, and roasting where its deep color and complex flavor stand out from ordinary red cherry tomatoes. Harvest when fruits soften slightly and the color deepens fully, as the dusky skin tone makes visual ripeness cues subtler than on standard red tomatoes.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — heirloom tomato variety notes

name: Chocolate Fatalii Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then harden off only after nights stay reliably warm.
directions: Chocolate Fatalii ripens to a glossy chocolate-brown pod and carries roughly 125,000-325,000+ Scoville heat units, in the same intense range as a habanero but with a smokier, earthier, more floral background flavor than the sharply citrusy yellow Fatalii. Start seed indoors on a heat mat well ahead of the last frost, since germination is slow and uneven in cool soil, then transplant into full sun only after nights stay warm. Pods ripen from green through brown over a long season, so give it the longest warm window your climate allows. Dark pods can be harder to judge for ripeness than red or yellow superhots, so squeeze gently for firmness rather than relying on color alone before harvesting for sauces or drying.
sources: Pepper Joe's - Chocolate Fatalii Pepper Seeds
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Chocolate Habanero Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; chocolate habanero requires warm germination temps (80–90°F) — use a heat mat for reliable sprouting; transplant outdoors only after soil is consistently warm.
directions: Start seeds on a heat mat at 85°F for reliable germination 10–21 days; transplant after last frost when nighttime temperatures stay above 60°F. Chocolate Habanero (also called Congo Black or Dark Habanero) is a Capsicum chinense variety that ripens to a deep chocolate brown color rather than the typical orange, with heat levels of 300,000–400,000 Scoville units — significantly hotter than standard orange habaneros and with a distinctive earthy, smoky-sweet flavor that many hot pepper enthusiasts consider more complex and interesting. Originally from Jamaica and Trinidad, it is prized by hot sauce makers for its unique color and flavor profile; the pods are slightly larger than standard habaneros, with thick walls and a rich, fruity aroma. Grow in full sun with warm nights for the best fruit set; perennial in zone 9–12, often producing for multiple years as a shrubby plant.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Chocolate Scotch Bonnet Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors on a heat mat; transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 60°F.
directions: The chocolate-brown form of Scotch Bonnet carries the classic lantern-shaped, crinkled pod and is generally considered a bit hotter and more earthy-tasting than the standard yellow type, landing in a similar 100,000-350,000 Scoville range but with a deeper, smokier edge. It is widely used in Caribbean jerk marinades, hot sauces, and seasoning blends where its darker color and richer flavor are prized. Sow indoors on a heat mat well before the last frost, as germination is slow, and move plants to full sun only once nights stay warm. Compact, bushy plants bear heavily over a long season, so plan on steady harvest through summer and fall.
sources: Reimer Seeds - Chocolate Scotch Bonnet Pepper Seeds
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Chocolate Stripes Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into deeply prepared, fertile soil after frost danger passes; give the large-fruited indeterminate vine strong support and even watering for the best-formed fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Chocolate Stripes is a dark-fruited heirloom beefsteak tomato with dusky mahogany-brown skin overlaid with darker green-brown stripes radiating from the stem, and rich, complex, slightly smoky-sweet flesh characteristic of the best dark-colored heirloom tomatoes. Fruit runs large for slicing and sandwiches, and the deep coloring makes it a striking addition to a mixed heirloom tomato platter. Stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vine well, water evenly to reduce cracking and blossom end rot, and harvest once fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure and the shoulders have darkened fully.

name: Chocolate Trinidad Scorpion Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this strain is distinct from the red Butch T scorpion and needs a full hot season to ripen.
directions: Chocolate Trinidad Scorpion produces the same tailed, stinger-tipped pods as the classic red scorpion strains, but ripens to a rich mahogany brown with a deeper, more smoky flavor beneath the intense heat. It is a separate color strain from Butch T and Moruga lines, grown by superhot collectors for hot sauce and extract use. Provide a long warm season, steady moisture, and staking once fruit clusters get heavy, since chinense superhots are prone to blossom drop under water stress. Handle ripe pods with gloves and avoid touching eyes or face.

name: Choctaw Sweet Potato Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after all frost danger has passed; this is a long-season, heat-loving moschata type that needs the full length of a Southern summer to size up and cure properly.
directions: A large oblong winter squash, known traditionally as isito, preserved within Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma seed-keeping programs and bearing tan-skinned fruit commonly 10-30 pounds, with deep orange flesh prized for a dense, sweet, sweet-potato-like eating quality. Like other moschata-type squash it tends toward strong tolerance of humid summer heat and the pest pressure that plagues maxima and pepo squash in the Deep South, and cured fruit reportedly stores for up to nine months indoors. Vines are vigorous and need substantial room to sprawl; let fruit mature fully on the vine until the skin hardens and dulls before harvest for the best storage life and flavor.
sources: Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma Historic Preservation Department

name: Chonggak Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow in fertile, loose soil in late summer for the classic fall kimchi harvest, thinning so finger-sized roots and their leafy tops both have room to develop.
directions: Named for its leafy top said to resemble the braided ponytail worn by unmarried young men in old Korea, this small white radish is harvested whole, leaves and all, while the root is still finger-sized and tender. Both the crisp root and its slightly peppery greens are used together, most famously fermented whole into chonggak kimchi, so plants are grown at closer spacing than daikon-type radishes and pulled young rather than left to bulk up. It prefers the same cool fall conditions as other Asian radishes and resists pithiness well if kept consistently watered. Because the greens are eaten along with the root, avoid any mulch or soil splash that would leave grit between the leaf ribs.

name: Choppee Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably warm; Choppee is a South Carolina Lowcountry heirloom named for the community along the Black River, prized for its early, heavy-yielding, nearly spineless pods.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep after the soil has warmed, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart in full sun. Choppee is an heirloom okra passed down among South Carolina Lowcountry gardening families near the Choppee community in Georgetown County, valued for producing tender, nearly spineless, slightly ridged green pods with a reddish tinge at the base earlier in the season than many other Southern heirlooms. The plants are productive and well adapted to the humid, hot conditions of the coastal Southeast, and pods should be picked at 3-5 inches for the best table quality. Like most heirloom okras it is open-pollinated and easily saved from year to year, helping preserve a piece of Lowcountry foodways history.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

name: Chou Moellier
plantingNote: Direct sow after the soil has warmed in spring and thin to final spacing, allowing a long season of growth before the thick stems and leaves are harvested for winter feed.
directions: Chou Moellier is an old French heirloom fodder kale grown for its massive, pith-filled stem and abundant leaf growth, traditionally chopped and fed to livestock through the winter months. The thick, succulent stalk stores more moisture and nutrients than slimmer kale types, which historically made it valuable in regions where winter forage was scarce, and both the stem and the large leaves are palatable to animals once cut. Plants grow tall and sturdy over a long season, tolerating cold well and standing in the field for a late harvest after other crops are finished. While bred for the farmyard rather than the table, the young leaves are also edible for people and taste similar to other non-heading kales, making it a crop of interest to gardeners curious about historic dual-purpose brassicas.

name: Christmas Lima Bean
plantingNote: Sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Christmas Lima is a large-seeded pole type needing 5–6 feet of trellis support; plant along fences or provide sturdy poles.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil (above 65°F) after last frost at the base of a sturdy trellis, fence, or poles in full sun, in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Christmas Lima is a striking heirloom pole lima with large seeds dramatically streaked and mottled in red-maroon and cream — the colors fade somewhat on cooking but the flavor more than compensates, often described as chestnut-like with a rich, buttery texture superior to common limas. A long-season variety that rewards gardeners in warm climates; in zone 9–10, the extended growing season produces heavy yields late into fall. Dry the seeds for storage as beautiful speckled beans that are prized for soups, stews, and succotash. Requires cross-pollination and benefits from hand removal of diseased pods.

name: Christmas Pole Lima Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 3-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed past 60°F; this tall pole lima needs a sturdy trellis and a long, hot season to mature its large seeds.
directions: Direct sow seed 1-1.5 inches deep along a trellis tall enough for 10-foot vines, in well-drained soil enriched with compost; Christmas Pole, also known regionally as Christmas Lima or Chestnut Lima, traces back to Lima, Peru and produces large, flat seeds nearly 3/4 inch across packed into 4-6 inch pods. Cooked seeds have a rich, chestnut-like flavor and texture that historically made the variety a holiday substitute for chestnuts. Grow in consistently warm, moist soil through the full length of summer, and harvest pods once plump for fresh shelling or allow them to dry on the vine for long-term storage beans.

name: Chullpi Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; isolate from other corn varieties if saving seed, since this landrace is prized specifically for its naturally sweet, translucent kernel.
directions: Sow directly in warm soil in full sun and keep evenly watered through tasseling and ear fill. Chullpi is an Andean landrace valued for kernels that stay naturally sweet and glassy-translucent, unlike the starchy field-corn types grown alongside it in the highlands, and it is traditionally eaten fresh off the cob or fermented into chicha de jora. Note that this maize landrace shares its name with an unrelated quinoa landrace of the same name grown in the same region — the two are different crops distinguished by scientific name. Harvest at the milk-to-early-dough stage for fresh eating, or let a portion dry fully on the stalk for seed saving or chicha brewing.
sources: National Research Council — Races of Maize in Peru (Grobman et al.)

name: Chullpi Quinoa
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Chullpi quinoa prefers cool growing conditions and can bolt or perform poorly in extended hot, humid weather.
directions: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Chullpi quinoa prefers cool growing conditions and can bolt or perform poorly in extended hot, humid weather. A traditional Andean landrace distinct from the more familiar white, red, and black quinoa sold commercially, this variety is prized in its native Peru and Bolivia for translucent, pale golden seed with a naturally sweet flavor reminiscent of corn, traditionally toasted and eaten as a snack rather than cooked as a grain like standard quinoa. It grows on tall, colorful seed-head spikes typical of quinoa and is naturally low in the bitter seed coating (saponin) found on many quinoa varieties, requiring less rinsing before cooking or toasting. Harvest seed heads once they dry and the seeds rattle loosely, then thresh and winnow before storing or toasting.
sources: Slow Food International Ark of Taste
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

name: Chun Yeon Gold Napa Cabbage
scientificName: Brassica rapa subsp. pekinensis 'Chun Yeon Gold'
plantingNote: Sow in early spring or, better, in mid to late summer for a fall crop, since this slow-bolting Korean type tolerates spring planting better than most napa cabbage but still sizes up best in cool autumn weather.
directions: Chun Yeon Gold is a modern Korean napa cabbage bred for the tight, cylindrical, uniform heads and bright golden-yellow interior leaves that Korean cooks favor for kimchi, wrapped around deep green outer leaves. It is notably slow to bolt, which makes it more forgiving of an early spring sowing than older napa types, and it carries resistance to downy mildew and soft rot that helps it hold up in humid conditions. Keep the soil consistently moist as heads fill out, since drought stress toughens the ribs and encourages tip burn. Harvest when heads feel firm and dense, then use fresh in kimchi, soups, or braises, or store whole heads in a cold, humid space for several weeks.

name: Church Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this late-season variety benefits from an early start.
directions: This Virginia family heirloom produces massive pink beefsteak fruits, often 1-2 pounds, with a well-balanced, old-fashioned tomato flavor and subtle sweet undertones. It is a late-season, indeterminate variety, so gardeners in shorter-season climates should start seed early and provide sturdy staking to support the heavy fruit. Preserved through seed-saving networks, it has been noted for its resemblance to Radiator Charlie's Mortgage Lifter.

name: Churchill Brussels Sprout
plantingNote: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost for a fall harvest; Churchill is a vigorous, reliable mid-season hybrid favored by market growers for its heavy, even sprout set.
directions: Start seeds indoors 12-16 weeks before the first fall frost and transplant into firm, fertile, well-drained soil; stake tall plants to keep them upright as sprouts fill in. Churchill is a dependable mid-season Brussels sprout hybrid known for setting a heavy, closely spaced column of smooth, dark green sprouts along a sturdy stalk, and for standing well in the garden without the stems toppling or the sprouts loosening. Its moderate cold tolerance lets it carry a harvest through the first hard frosts, which sweetens the sprouts. Pick from the bottom of the stalk upward once sprouts firm to about an inch across, and remove yellowing lower leaves as you go to improve air circulation.

name: Cimarron Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow thinly with 0.125 inch soil coverage; thin to 8–12 inches for full-sized heads or 4–6 inches for small heads. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall and winter harvest, February–March for spring. Cimarron shows notably better heat tolerance than standard romaine varieties, making it suitable for late spring production in the Gulf South when other lettuces have bolted — a practical advantage for extending the spring lettuce season by 2–3 weeks.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.125 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; thin to 8–12 inches for full-sized heads. Cimarron is a heat-tolerant romaine-type (cos) lettuce with beautiful bronze-red outer leaves that fade to green-red at the interior — a coloring that is visually distinctive from standard green romaine types while maintaining the characteristic romaine form: tall, upright, with a slightly folded, elongated head and the crisp, crunchy mid-rib texture that makes romaine the preferred lettuce for Caesar salad. The red pigmentation in Cimarron is not as deep or uniform as fully red romaines, but the attractive mottled bronze-red appearance combined with the green interior gives a bicolor effect that is especially attractive when heads are cut crosswise to reveal the color contrast. Cimarron's standout characteristic is its heat tolerance — while standard romaine types bolt (send up a seed stalk and become bitter) at sustained temperatures above 75–80°F, Cimarron holds its quality better at higher temperatures, extending the productive window by 2–3 weeks in warm spring conditions. This heat tolerance makes Cimarron particularly valuable in zone 8–10 gardens where spring temperatures rise quickly and the window for lettuce production is narrow. Named for the Cimarron Territory of the historic Southwest.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Cimarron lettuce variety notes
High Mowing Organic Seeds — Romaine lettuce variety comparison
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Lettuce Production Guide

name: Cimmaron Romaine
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–February for spring. Cimmaron is a full-sized red romaine that heads up well in zone 9 cool-season conditions. The tall, upright habit makes it efficient in raised beds. Successive sowings every 3 weeks through fall provide a continuous supply through winter.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Cimmaron is a large, full-headed red romaine lettuce from the American Southwest — its name evokes the Cimarron River of the Oklahoma-Kansas plains country. It produces tall, upright, well-formed romaine heads with bronze-red to mahogany-red outer leaves and a pale green-to-cream interior heart, combining the classic romaine flavor and crunch with deep red coloration. The large, mature heads at 58–68 days are suitable for Caesar salad in the traditional whole-leaf format, where the combination of romaine structure and visual color impact makes Cimmaron stands out among red romaine options. Cimmaron is slower-bolting than most red looseleaf types and holds quality in the garden longer as a planted head. The flavor is mild, crisp, and slightly sweet — traditional romaine quality with no bitterness. In zone 9 fall planting produces the most satisfying heads; spring-planted Cimmaron benefits from light shade cloth in late spring to delay bolting.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Cimmaron Romaine Heritage Variety
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Red Romaine Lettuce Types
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Cos and Romaine Lettuce

name: Cincinnati Market Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or again in late summer for a fall crop; Cincinnati Market is a nineteenth-century heirloom producing long, slender, bright red roots with crisp, mild white flesh.
directions: Sow seed a half-inch deep directly in loose, well-worked soil, and thin seedlings early to a couple of inches apart so roots have room to elongate without forking. Cincinnati Market is an old market-garden heirloom prized for its long, cylindrical, bright scarlet-red roots with crisp, mild-flavored white flesh that stays tender without turning pithy or overly hot if harvested promptly at full size. It matures quickly, making it a reliable choice for succession sowing every couple of weeks through the cool season for a steady radish supply, and its uniform, attractive shape made it a historic favorite for market bunching. Keep the soil consistently moist as roots size up, since inconsistent watering causes cracking and harsh flavor, and harvest promptly once roots reach full size, since radishes left too long in warm soil quickly turn woody and overly pungent.

name: Cinderella's Carriage Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, rich soil, giving vines room to run; Cinderella's Carriage is an AAS-winning hybrid version of the classic flattened, deep-orange Cinderella-type pumpkin, bred for powdery mildew resistance and higher, more reliable yields than the older open-pollinated heirloom.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vigorous vines ample room to spread. Cinderella's Carriage is an AAS-winning hybrid take on the classic Cinderella-type pumpkin — the flattened, deeply ribbed, deep-orange-red fruit famously associated with the Rouge Vif d'Etampes heirloom — bred to add meaningful powdery mildew resistance and more consistent, higher yields than the older open-pollinated version, while keeping the same striking flattened silhouette prized for fall display. Fruit reaches 15-25 pounds with dense, good-flavored flesh usable for cooking as well as decoration. Because it is naturally more disease-resistant than the heirloom, the vines tend to stay productive and healthy later into the season in humid climates. Harvest when the rind hardens and color deepens fully, cutting the stem rather than pulling to avoid damaging the fruit, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before storing.
sources: All-America Selections — Cinderella's Carriage Pumpkin winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Cinnamon Girl Squash
plantingNote: Sow directly outdoors once soil has warmed thoroughly, allowing semi-compact vines room to spread, and water consistently until fruit sets to support even sizing.
directions: Sow directly outdoors once soil has warmed thoroughly, allowing semi-compact vines room to spread, and water consistently until fruit sets to support even sizing. Named an All-America Selections winner in 2018, this hybrid butternut produces uniform, single-serving fruit around a pound each with deep tan skin and dense, sweet, richly colored flesh well suited to roasting whole. Bred for strong disease tolerance and heavy yields of personal-portion squash, it fits neatly into small households and market growers wanting consistent, easy-to-handle fruit. Cure harvested squash in a warm spot for a week or two to improve storage life and sweetness.

name: Citrus F1 Chinese Cabbage
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for a fall crop into fertile, moisture-retentive soil; Citrus is a cool-season biennial grown as an annual and bolts quickly in hot weather.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Citrus is a Johnny's Selected Seeds hybrid napa cabbage forming a tall, barrel-shaped head around 11 inches tall and 5.5-6 pounds, distinguished by a striking deep-orange interior and orange-ringed cut stems rather than the usual pale yellow-green. It performs best as a fall crop sown in late summer, since the cool-season biennial bolts quickly if grown through summer heat. Use it fresh in slaws and salads or fermented into a colorfully different kimchi.

name: Clara Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Clara is a vigorous, disease-tolerant Italian hybrid that yields heavily over a long harvest window.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Clara is an Italian hybrid eggplant grown for its striking, brilliantly white, oval fruit set off by a bright green calyx, giving it strong visual appeal at market and in the garden alike. The dense white flesh is mild and free of the bitterness that can affect some white-skinned types, holding its color well when cut and cooking down smoothly for baked and roasted preparations. Clara shows good tolerance to common eggplant diseases and sets fruit heavily and early relative to many other Italian-type hybrids, extending the productive harvest window in a single season. Harvest fruit at 6 to 7 inches long while the skin is still glossy and firm, since white eggplant dulls and toughens quickly once past its prime.

name: Classic Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant only once nights stay reliably above 55F. Classic is an upright, vigorous plant that benefits from staking as fruit load builds, and it holds fruit quality well through summer heat.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has warmed, spacing plants far enough apart for good air circulation. Classic is a widely grown commercial hybrid bred for a heavy, uniform set of large, glossy black-purple, oval fruit on a productive, disease-tolerant plant, and it has become something of a benchmark against which other standard American-type eggplants are compared. Harvest fruit while the skin is still glossy and firm; dull, matte skin signals over-mature fruit with more seeds and a bitter edge. Consistent watering during fruit set is important, since moisture swings can trigger blossom drop and misshapen fruit.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — eggplant production

name: Clay Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1-2 inches deep once soil has warmed well past last frost; this sprawling heirloom rewards a long, hot season, so Gulf Coast gardeners can sow successively from late spring into midsummer.
directions: Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil and allow the sprawling vines room to run, since this variety spreads farther than bush-type cowpeas. Clay is a historic Southern cowpea type, named for the earthy, clay-brown color of its dry seed, stewarded by African American seed-keeping families since at least 1867 and valued for producing a hearty, protein-rich dry pea as well as tender snap-stage pods. It tolerates poor, droughty soils and fixes nitrogen for whatever crop follows. Harvest young for fresh shelling or let pods dry fully on the vine for long-term storage.

name: Clearwater Jerusalem Artichoke
plantingNote: Plant tuber sections 3-4 inches deep around the last frost date in well-drained soil in full sun; Clearwater was discovered in Maine and is prized for tubers that stay smooth and round rather than knobby, making them far quicker to clean than most sunchoke stock.
directions: Plant tuber sections 3-4 inches deep in well-drained soil around the last frost date. Clearwater is a Maine-origin Jerusalem artichoke selection valued among sunchoke growers for two traits that set it apart from most named varieties: tubers that form smooth, rounded, potato-like shapes rather than the knobby, eye-covered lumps typical of the species, and a notably mild, sweet, nutty flavor that lacks the faint piney or resinous aftertaste some people notice in standard sunchoke stock. Plants are tall even by Jerusalem artichoke standards, often topping 11-12 feet by late summer, and are crowned with the same small yellow sunflower blooms typical of the species, which are also edible. Clearwater spreads by underground tubers less aggressively than many sunchoke varieties, producing fewer long runners, though it should still be given a dedicated bed since any missed tuber will resprout. Dig tubers after fall frost kills the foliage and continue harvesting through winter into early spring; cold exposure sweetens the flavor further by converting stored inulin to sugar.
sources: Prairie Gardens Nursery — Clearwater Jerusalem Artichoke variety notes
University of Minnesota Extension — Jerusalem Artichoke

name: Clemson Spineless Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (65°F+); in zone 9 plant March–June. Okra thrives in zone 9's hot, humid summers and is one of the most productive and reliable summer vegetables for the Gulf South — plants can produce continuously for months in summer heat. Soak seeds overnight before planting to improve germination; okra seeds have a hard seed coat that benefits from scarification. Harvest pods every 2–3 days when 2–4 inches long — larger pods become fibrous and tough and should be removed to keep the plant producing. Mature plants (3–6 feet) may need support in wind-prone locations.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — okra thrives in the same hot, humid conditions that challenge most other vegetables; Clemson Spineless is the most widely grown okra variety in the United States, a 1980 All-America Selections winner and the standard against which all other okras are measured — smooth, bright green, spineless pods in the classic okra shape eliminate the spine irritation that makes harvesting traditional okra varieties uncomfortable. The spineless pods (technically very few small, soft spines compared to original okra types) can be harvested without gloves, a significant practical improvement over older varieties. Clemson Spineless produces straight, uniform 5-ribbed pods with the mild, slightly mucilaginous flavor that defines okra — the mucilage (a natural thickener) is the basis for gumbo's characteristic body-giving quality that makes real gumbo unmistakably different from any other soup. In zone 9 okra is among the most productive and reliable summer vegetables available — it is native to Africa and genuinely thrives in the same conditions (intense heat, humidity, heat soil) that defeat cool-season crops and stress many warm-season vegetables.
sources: All-America Selections — Clemson Spineless Okra 1939 and 1980 Awards
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Okra Production for Gulf South
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Okra Varieties for Texas

name: Cloud Nine Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting; mulch heavily and keep moisture consistent, since white skin shows sunscald more readily than purple types in intense summer sun.
directions: A pure-white, teardrop-shaped specialty eggplant with mild, non-bitter flesh and tobacco mosaic virus resistance, one of the miniature specialty varieties LSU AgCenter and UF/IFAS both list for Gulf South gardens. Mulch heavily and keep moisture consistent to prevent bitter, seedy fruit under heat stress, since white-skinned types scorch more readily than purple ones.
sources: LSU AgCenter / Seeds to Success - Recommended Eggplant Varieties for Louisiana

name: Cloud Nine Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant in February–March. The white tomatoes can be difficult to judge for ripeness by color — ripe fruits develop a creamy, slightly yellowish blush and become slightly soft to the touch. Cloud Nine is indeterminate and produces most productively with cage or stake support. In zone 9 the fall planting in August produces exceptional quality fruit.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with cage or stake support; Cloud Nine is a large, beefsteak-type heirloom tomato producing very large (often 1–2 pound) fruits with ivory-white to pale cream skin and nearly white flesh — one of the few tomato varieties that is genuinely white rather than pale yellow or cream-colored at full ripeness. Like other white tomatoes, Cloud Nine lacks the red lycopene pigment that colors standard tomatoes, instead producing a nearly colorless fruit with very low acid content. The flavor is exceptionally mild, honey-sweet, and rich without the sharpness of red varieties — often described as having a complex sweetness that is difficult to describe as 'tomato-like' in the traditional sense, more like eating a sweet, meaty fruit with subtle complexity. Cloud Nine is preferred for fresh eating and mild preparations where the low-acid, ultra-sweet character can be fully appreciated — it is less well-suited to cooking where the delicate pale color and mild flavor are lost.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Cloud Nine White Tomato
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — White Tomato Varieties
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Heirloom Tomato Trials

name: Cluster Ridge Luffa
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; this long-season type needs 110-130 warm days and benefits from the head start in all but the longest summers.
directions: This ridged luffa sets several fruits together at each node rather than singly, giving a concentrated flush of harvest when the small orb-shaped young gourds are ready to pick for stir-fries, curries, and soups. Left on the vine through its long 110-130 day season, the fruit dries into the familiar fibrous sponge once the skin turns brown and papery. Train the vigorous vines up a tall trellis in full sun to keep the ridged fruit straight and improve airflow, and keep soil consistently moist and mulched through the hot months it needs to finish.

name: Coastal Star Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or fall; Coastal Star is a heat-tolerant romaine bred to hold full-size, heavy hearts and resist bolting longer than standard romaine types, extending the spring harvest window before summer heat sets in.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Coastal Star is a dark green romaine bred for heat tolerance and slow bolting, producing full-size, dense, heavy hearts even as temperatures climb toward the point where most romaine varieties turn bitter and send up a seed stalk. The upright heads have crisp, sweet leaves with excellent texture through to the crunchy heart. Provide afternoon shade during the hottest stretches of a Gulf Coast spring to further extend the harvest window, and keep soil consistently moist, since drought stress accelerates bolting even in heat-tolerant varieties. Harvest whole heads once hearts have filled out, or pick outer leaves as a cut-and-come-again crop.

name: Cobham Improved Marrow Parsnip
plantingNote: Direct sow thinly in deeply worked ground, thin seedlings to a few inches apart, and harvest after frost for the sweetest flavor.
directions: A classic English heirloom developed from the older Marrow parsnip type and long favored by British allotment gardeners for its short neck and broad shoulders that taper to a blunt, well-filled root. It shows better resistance to canker than many older parsnip lines, an important trait in the damp, heavy soils common in British gardens. Direct sow thinly in deeply worked ground, thin seedlings to a few inches apart, and harvest after frost for the sweetest flavor; it has long held a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for reliable garden performance.

name: Cocke's Prolific Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60F; Cocke's Prolific is one of the oldest documented Virginia dent corns, grown since the colonial era for its habit of setting two to four ears per stalk rather than the single large ear typical of most modern corn.
directions: Direct sow in blocks for good wind pollination and give plants extra room, since Cocke's Prolific grows tall and leafy and puts its energy into multiple smaller ears rather than one big one. This Virginia heirloom dent corn has been passed down since the 1700s and was long valued by small farmers precisely because a prolific, multi-eared plant hedges against a poor pollination year better than a single-ear hybrid does. Ears are white to pale yellow dent kernels good for cornmeal and grits once fully dried on the stalk, and the tall, leafy plants also produce useful fodder. Because it is open-pollinated, isolate it by distance or timing from other corn varieties to keep the seed line true for saving.
sources: Monticello Thomas Jefferson Center for Historic Plants

name: Coco de Paimpol Bean
plantingNote: Sow directly once the soil has warmed after last frost, providing light support such as brush or netting for its semi-climbing habit.
directions: Sow directly once the soil has warmed after last frost, providing light support such as brush or netting for its semi-climbing habit near the cool, damp Brittany coast where it was traditionally grown. Coco de Paimpol earned its own French protected designation for a distinctive fresh-shelling bean — plump, cream-colored seeds lightly speckled with rose, picked while the pods are still green rather than left to fully dry. Harvest pods when the seeds inside have filled out but the pods remain supple, then shell immediately for the tender, buttery texture the variety is prized for. It can also be left to dry fully on the vine for storage as a soup bean, though the fresh-shell stage is when its flavor is best known.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste
Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualité (INAO)

name: Cocodrie Rice
plantingNote: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65F; in zone 9 plant April-May for harvest August-September. Cocodrie is an LSU AgCenter long-grain release once grown on more Gulf South acreage than any other rice variety.
directions: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Cocodrie is a semi-dwarf, long-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter in 1998 and named for Louisiana's Bayou Cocodrie, quickly becoming the dominant commercial rice variety across the Gulf South rice belt because of its early maturity, high milling yield, and reliable performance under both flooded and continuously moist conditions. Home gardeners can grow it in beds kept saturated through the season rather than in true paddies, though yields are highest with standing water for at least part of the cycle. The semi-dwarf, sturdy stalks resist lodging (falling over) better than older tall varieties, which matters most in wet, windy Gulf Coast summers. Harvest when the seed heads droop and turn golden-tan, then dry and hull. As a widely proven Louisiana-bred variety, Cocodrie is an accessible entry point for gardeners curious about growing their own rice in zone 8-10 conditions.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Rice Variety Releases
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Rice Production Guide
University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture — Rice Cultivar Notes

name: Cole's Early Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed following last frost; Cole's Early was bred by A.B. Cole of Iowa in 1908 specifically to ripen watermelon reliably in a short northern growing season.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following the last frost, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Bred by A.B. Cole in Iowa in 1908, this heirloom was developed specifically to bring reliable, sweet watermelon to gardeners in short-season Northern climates where later-maturing Southern varieties often failed to ripen before fall frost. It bears medium-sized, oval, dark green striped melons with crisp, sweet red flesh on vigorous, productive vines. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit has dried and browned and the underside spot has turned from white to cream-yellow, reliable signs of ripeness in a short-season melon bred for gardens with a narrow window to work with.

name: Collective Farm Woman Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil in hills; Collective Farm Woman (Kolkhoznitsa) is the most widely grown open-pollinated melon in Russia and Eastern Europe, developed in the Soviet era and still the standard home-garden melon across the former Soviet republics — extraordinarily flavorful despite the unglamorous name.
directions: Sow 3–4 seeds per hill after last frost in well-amended, well-drained soil; thin to 2 strongest plants per hill; direct vines along rows or up a strong trellis. Collective Farm Woman (Russian: Kolkhoznitsa) is a Ukrainian/Russian heirloom muskmelon introduced in 1930 that became the standard garden melon across the Soviet Union and is still the most widely grown open-pollinated melon in Russia and Ukraine; the small (1–2 lb) round to oval fruits ripen to creamy-white to yellow with thin, smooth skin and extremely aromatic, sweet, creamy-white flesh that has an exceptional honey-floral fragrance when perfectly ripe. Despite its short ripening window once mature, the flavor is outstanding — rich, sweet, and intensely perfumed. One of the earliest-maturing muskmelons (75–85 days from transplant), making it excellent for short-season northern gardens and for early production in the South and Gulf Coast. Harvest when skin turns creamy-yellow and the blossom end softens slightly.

name: Colorado Red Rhubarb
plantingNote: Plant crowns or root divisions in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked, setting the bud just below the soil surface.
directions: Colorado Red is a widely sold American heirloom selection prized for thick, deeply pigmented red stalks and the vigorous, cold-hardy habit that made it a staple in high-plains and mountain-region kitchen gardens. It tends to produce especially large, robust plants once established, with broad crinkled leaves shading a productive clump of stalks each spring. As with all rhubarb, only the stalks are eaten — the leaves contain concentrated oxalic acid and should always be removed and composted rather than consumed. Harvest by pulling stalks with a twisting motion rather than cutting, and stop picking by midsummer to let the plant rebuild energy reserves for next year.

name: Colorado Star Artichoke
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost; Colorado Star sets buds reliably in its first year with only modest cold exposure, making it one of the easier annual artichokes to bring to harvest in a single season without precise vernalization timing.
directions: Start seed indoors and set transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes; Colorado Star is a compact, early-maturing F1 hybrid bred for reliable first-year flowering across a wide range of climates, including regions with cooler or shorter growing seasons than traditional artichoke territory. Buds are medium-sized with an attractive purple-tinged blush over green, tender at a smaller size than many varieties, and produced in good quantity on a plant more compact than older perennial types, making it a reasonable choice for smaller gardens. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for its ease of first-year production from seed. Water regularly and mulch to keep roots cool through summer heat, and harvest buds promptly while tightly closed for the best texture and flavor.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Artichoke Production Guide

name: Colossus 80 Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; Colossus 80 is a widely grown commercial purple hull pea selected for a concentrated, mechanically harvestable pod set.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and harvest pods once they color up to a deep purple. Colossus 80 is a widely grown purple hull cowpea developed for commercial production, bred for a concentrated fruit set that ripens in a narrow window well suited to a single mechanical or hand harvest, along with high yield and vigorous, productive vines. Its purple-hulled pods contrast clearly against the foliage, making ripe peas easy to spot for hand-picking home gardeners as well. Like other cowpeas, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility for whatever crop follows. Harvest continuously at the fresh shelling stage for the best flavor, or allow pods to dry fully on the vine for long-term dry storage.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension — cowpea variety notes

name: Colossus Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant March–May for spring and July–August for fall. Colossus is named for its exceptionally large seeds and long pods — it is one of the largest-seeded blackeye-type cowpeas available, making shelling more efficient than small-seeded varieties.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any well-drained soil in full sun; Colossus is a vigorous, bush-type Southern pea selected for exceptionally large seeds and long, productive pods — the big, cream-colored seeds with the characteristic black eye shell out more quickly than the smaller-seeded varieties, making it a practical choice for preserving and cooking in large quantities. Like all cowpeas, it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and thrives in the heat and humidity of Gulf Coast summers when most other legumes fail. The high yield per plant and large seed size make Colossus a commercial and home-garden standard in the Gulf Coast South, particularly for fresh-shell operations. Harvest when pods are fully plump and light green, before the hull begins to dry and yellow.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Southern Pea Variety Trials
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Cowpea Production
Alabama Cooperative Extension System — Southern Peas for Alabama

name: Comanche Leek
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, planting into a 5-inch-deep trench and filling in gradually as plants grow to blanch the shanks.
directions: Comanche is a high-yielding, adaptable F1 leek especially favored in Pacific Northwest gardens for its clean, upright habit and long, thick white shanks under dark blue-green flags. It performs well as both a summer and fall crop, and gradually filling the planting trench with soil as the plants grow lengthens the blanched shank for a milder, more tender base. Harvest young at finger size for a mild flavor or let stems reach a half-inch or more in diameter for fuller texture. It tolerates frost well and holds in the garden into the fall harvest window.

name: Concerto Artichoke
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and give young seedlings a period of cool temperatures once they have several true leaves to encourage first-year bud formation. Transplant outdoors after frost danger has passed into full sun and fertile, well-drained soil.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and give young seedlings a period of cool temperatures once they have several true leaves to encourage first-year bud formation. Transplant outdoors after frost danger has passed into full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and harvest buds while the scales are still tightly closed. Concerto is a compact F1 hybrid bred to reliably flower and produce full-sized rounded green buds in its very first season, making globe artichoke growing practical in shorter-season gardens that could not otherwise ripen a traditional perennial variety in time. Where winters are mild it can also be left in the ground to behave as a genuine short-lived perennial, cropping again in subsequent years.

name: Confection Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after frost danger has passed, spacing plants for their semi-bush habit, and maintain even moisture as small acorn-shaped fruit begin to form.
directions: Direct sow after frost danger has passed, spacing plants for their semi-bush habit, and maintain even moisture as small acorn-shaped fruit begin to form and ripen to deep orange. Recognized as an All-America Selections winner in 2017, this hybrid was bred for markedly sweeter, less fibrous flesh than typical acorn squash along with strong resistance to powdery mildew that keeps foliage productive later into the season. Its semi-compact vines produce a heavy, uniform set of small fruit ideal for roasting or stuffing whole. Harvest once rinds are fully colored and hardened, then cure briefly before storing in a cool, dry space.

name: Confite Morocho Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; this highland landrace is grown through to full dry maturity rather than harvested green.
directions: Grow exactly like other dry field corn, direct sown after soil warms and left on the stalk until husks and kernels are fully dry and hard. Confite Morocho is the traditional small, flinty-kerneled Andean race toasted in a hot skillet or oven to make 'cancha' (also called cancha serrana or corn nuts), a crunchy snack and common garnish for Peruvian ceviche and soups. Shell and store dried kernels in a sealed container; to prepare cancha, toast kernels in a dry pan or with a touch of oil until they pop open and turn golden and crisp. Its hard, low-moisture kernel is what allows it to toast rather than scorch the way softer sweet corn kernels do.
sources: National Research Council — Races of Maize in Peru (Grobman et al.)

name: Congo Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost, since Capsicum chinense types are slow to germinate and mature; transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun once nights stay above 60°F.
directions: Start seed indoors well ahead of the season, since Capsicum chinense types germinate slowly and need a long, hot growing season to fully ripen; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the weather is reliably warm. Congo Pepper is a traditional Trinidad and Tobago chile closely related to the island's famous Trinidad Scorpion and Moruga Scorpion lines, producing wrinkled, lantern-shaped pods that ripen from green through yellow, orange, and finally deep red, carrying extreme superhot heat well beyond a habanero. Beneath the heat is a distinctly fruity, almost tropical flavor that makes it prized in Trinidadian pepper sauces and hot sauce blends despite its intensity. Handle ripe fruit with gloves, since the capsaicin level is high enough to cause skin irritation, and harvest as pods fully color for the best flavor and heat development.

name: Congo Trinidad Pepper
plantingNote: Start on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before last frost; Congo Trinidad is a traditional Trinidadian habanero-type pepper with wrinkled orange-red pods and intense heat.
directions: Germinate seeds at 80-85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Congo Trinidad bears wrinkled, lantern-shaped pods that ripen from green through orange to red, carrying intense heat well into superhot territory along with the characteristic fruity habanero aroma, a traditional variety long grown in home gardens across Trinidad. It is prized for hot sauce and pepper sauce making, where its heat and fruity depth of flavor come through strongly. The vigorous plants are productive in warm climates over a long season; handle ripe pods with gloves.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Congo Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-prepared, well-drained soil; Congo is a classic Southern 'picnic' watermelon producing enormous oblong fruits (35–50+ lbs) with dark green skin and excellent deep red flesh — one of the largest-fruited traditional Southern watermelon varieties and a staple of Gulf Coast summer gardens and roadside stands.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Congo requires plenty of space (hills or rows 6–8 feet apart) for its vigorous, spreading vines and very large fruits. Congo is a classic Southern summer watermelon of the 'picnic' or 'family' type, producing very large, elongated-oblong fruits (35–50+ lbs) with dark green skin patterned with lighter green stripes and solid deep red flesh with excellent sweetness and rich melon flavor; Congo-type watermelons were an important part of Gulf Coast and Deep South truck farming and summer culture in the first half of the 20th century, when enormous watermelons were hauled to market and sold by the slice from wagons and stands. The very large size makes Congo impractical for modern small households (a single fruit can feed 30 people) but it remains grown by enthusiasts of traditional Southern garden culture and heirloom melon growers. Best suited to long-season Southern gardens (zones 7–11) where 85–95 day maturity can be fully achieved.

name: Conlon Barley
plantingNote: Sow in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked; Conlon is a two-row malting barley released by North Dakota State University for the Upper Midwest.
directions: Conlon is a two-row spring malting barley from North Dakota State University that gave growers in the Upper Midwest a shorter-strawed, lodging-resistant alternative to older six-row malting types. Drill into a firm, well-drained seedbed in early spring, since barley tillers and establishes best while the weather is still cool. The compact plant holds its head upright through wind and rain better than taller barleys, which helps keep grain quality high going into harvest. Combine once fully dry and store the kernels in a cool, well-ventilated space to protect their malting potential.

name: Connecticut Field Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills (3–4 seeds per hill, thinned to 2 plants) after last frost in rich, well-drained soil; Connecticut Field requires a long growing season (100–120 days) and ample space for the sprawling vines (8–12 feet). For fall pumpkin harvest, count back 110–120 days from desired harvest date in October. In zone 9, plant in late May for a September–October harvest, or plant in February–March for a summer harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills or rows after last frost in full sun; provide ample space for vigorous vines and fertilize generously with balanced fertilizer or compost. Connecticut Field Pumpkin is the traditional American carving and field pumpkin — an open-pollinated heirloom that has been the archetypal 'pumpkin' in American agriculture and home gardens for well over a century, serving as the standard from which Halloween carving pumpkins, field decoration pumpkins, and processing pumpkins have all descended. The deeply ribbed, round to slightly flattened fruits typically weigh 15–25 pounds, develop a deep, saturated orange color at maturity, and have thick, firm walls that support carving without collapsing — the defining characteristics for jack-o-lantern use. Connecticut Field has a very long cultivation history in New England and the mid-Atlantic states where it was grown both for decorative autumn use and as a livestock feed crop; the tough, fibrous flesh is not considered prime for pie (Long Island Cheese, Small Sugar, and Winter Luxury pie pumpkins have been favored for baking), but it is edible and was historically used for pumpkin butter and pie. One of the most iconic American vegetables with strong cultural associations to autumn, harvest season, and Americana — a variety that connects any garden to a centuries-long tradition of pumpkin growing in the Eastern United States.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Connecticut Field pumpkin variety history
University of Vermont Extension — Pumpkin Production Guide
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Pumpkin Variety Evaluation

name: Connover's Colossal Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring into a trench 6-8 inches deep with a ridge of loosened, compost-enriched soil, spreading the roots over the ridge before backfilling. Let all spears grow into fern the first year and delay harvest until the third spring to build strong root reserves.
directions: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring into a trench 6-8 inches deep with a ridge of loosened, compost-enriched soil, spreading the roots over the ridge before backfilling. Let all spears grow into fern the first year and delay harvest until the third spring to build strong root reserves. Connover's Colossal is a nineteenth-century English heirloom, one of the oldest named asparagus varieties still commercially available, originally selected for its unusually thick, early spears at a time when most asparagus was thin and slow to establish.
