The rind has sparse netting, and the thick green flesh has a small seed cavity and an exceptionally sweet, aromatic eating quality typical of Galia types. Harvest at full slip, when the skin turns yellow and the fruit releases cleanly from the vine with light pressure. Grow in full sun with warm, fertile, well-drained soil and even moisture through fruit set, tapering off as the melons approach ripeness to concentrate their sugars.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Diplomat (F1) Galia Melon Seed
William Dam Seeds — Diplomat Hybrid Melon

name: Diva Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 70°F, or start transplants indoors 3 weeks early; provide a trellis for vertical growing to maximize air circulation and ease of harvest; in zone 9, sow March–April for spring and again August for fall.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; Diva is an All-America Selections Award winner (2002) and one of the most acclaimed cucumbers introduced in the past quarter century — a parthenocarpic (self-fruitful, seedless) cucumber that produces extremely uniform, smooth-skinned, 6–8 inch fruits with thin, tender, never-bitter skin that requires no peeling and no bitterness removal. Unlike most cucumbers that require cross-pollination by insects for reliable fruit set, Diva is parthenocarpic — each flower sets fruit without pollination, ensuring consistent production regardless of pollinator activity. The fruit is reliably seedless or nearly so, with crisp, mild, sweet flesh and completely absent the bitterness that affects some cucumbers. Diva's thin skin, which requires no peeling, and its mild, sweet, never-bitter flavor make it outstanding for fresh eating, salads, and children's snacking. The vigorous, prolific vines produce heavily over a long season — harvest fruits at 6–8 inches before seeds begin to develop for the best eating quality. In zone 9, Diva performs well in the spring and fall growing windows and is among the most heat-tolerant, productive cucumbers for the Gulf South.

name: Divergent Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Divergent is a galia-cantaloupe cross bred for high resistance to Fusarium wilt races 0-2 and intermediate powdery mildew resistance, a strong disease package for humid Gulf South melon growing.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil, thinning to 2 plants per hill spaced 3-4 feet apart; Divergent is a galia-type melon crossed with cantaloupe genetics, bred for high resistance to Fusarium wilt (a soil-borne fungal disease that can persist in garden soil for years) along with intermediate resistance to powdery mildew, making it a resilient choice for gardens where melons have struggled with disease in the past. The smaller, aromatic fruit has the sweet, floral flavor typical of galia melons with the familiar netted rind of a cantaloupe, ripening earlier than many standard cantaloupe varieties. Harvest when the skin turns from green to golden-tan under the netting and the fruit slips easily from the vine with a fragrant aroma at the stem end. Because it is an organic-bred hybrid popular with market growers, it performs well under lower-input, disease-conscious growing conditions.
sources: seed catalog reference (High Mowing Organic Seeds, Territorial Seed)

name: Dixie Butterpea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm, above 65°F; the compact bush habit needs no trellis, unlike pole-type limas.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F. Dixie Butterpea is a compact bush-type lima bean, sparing gardeners the trellising that pole lima varieties require while still delivering the classic small, mild-flavored, buttery-textured seeds Southern cooks know as butterpeas or butter beans. The bush habit concentrates its harvest into a shorter window than pole types, making it convenient for a single large batch of shelling and canning or freezing, and the plant's heat tolerance suits it well to Southern growing conditions. Harvest pods at the green shell stage once well filled for classic butterpea flavor, and succession sow every few weeks through summer for a more continuous supply if desired.

name: Dixie Crimson Clover
plantingNote: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in fall (October–November in zone 9) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; inoculate seeds with Rhizobium trifolii inoculant before planting to ensure effective nitrogen fixation in new planting areas.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed in fall in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Dixie is the preferred crimson clover variety for Gulf South cover crop use — selected specifically for the warmer winter conditions of the Deep South where it outperforms northern varieties by remaining vegetative longer before bolting to flower, providing a longer window of ground cover, weed suppression, and nitrogen fixation. Crimson clover is the most widely used winter annual legume cover crop in the Gulf South, seeded after the main crop harvest in October–November, establishing through the cool months, fixing atmospheric nitrogen through Rhizobium symbiosis, then terminated by mowing, rolling, or light tillage in spring before planting warm-season vegetables. A well-established stand of crimson clover can fix 50–100 pounds of nitrogen per acre — equivalent to a significant fertilizer application — while also improving soil organic matter, preventing winter erosion, and suppressing winter weeds. The 'Dixie' variety's later bolting (compared to 'Autauga' and other early varieties) is its primary advantage in zone 9: it maintains active vegetative growth through February and into March in most years, providing several extra weeks of weed suppression and soil coverage before initiating the red, conical flower heads that signal the end of the vegetative growth period. The showy crimson flower heads that precede termination are also excellent for early-spring pollinators. Inoculate seed with legume inoculant when planting in fields with no history of crimson clover.

name: Dixie Golden Giant Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Dixie Golden Giant has been maintained and distributed through southern seed saving networks as a locally-adapted golden variety that performs reliably in Gulf South heat.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Dixie Golden Giant is a southern heirloom beefsteak tomato producing very large (1–2+ lb), round to slightly flattened fruits in a golden-yellow to deep-yellow color with exceptionally sweet, very low-acid, meaty flesh that is characteristic of the finest golden beefsteak types. The very large size and golden-yellow color combine to make Dixie Golden Giant one of the most visually impressive golden tomatoes — the large yellow fruits sliced on a plate have a beautiful, rich golden color and the thick, dense flesh produces substantial slices without excess seeding or gel. The flavor is typical of the best large yellow heirlooms: very sweet, very mild, fruity, and low in acid — appealing to those who find standard red tomatoes too sharp or acidic. As a southern-adapted heirloom that has been selected and maintained in Gulf South gardens, Dixie Golden Giant may show somewhat better adaptation to zone 9 conditions than northern golden beefsteak types — though all very large beefsteak tomatoes are challenging to grow through Gulf South summer heat and produce best in the spring growing season (February–June). An open-pollinated variety with saveable seed that grows true-to-type from season to season.

name: Dixie Queen Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give vines 6-8 feet of room to sprawl.
directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once soil has warmed; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off watering as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Dixie Queen is a classic Southern heirloom watermelon dating to the early 20th century, producing round-to-oval fruit with light and dark green striping and sweet, bright red flesh with good old-fashioned watermelon flavor. It was once a popular commercial variety before being largely displaced by modern hybrids bred for tougher rinds and shipping durability, but it remains a favorite among heirloom growers for its reliable production and classic taste in the home garden. Vines are vigorous and productive over a moderate-length season, and fruits typically run in the 15-25 pound range, a manageable size for home use. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saves true when isolated from other watermelon varieties.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Dixie Queen variety notes

name: Dixie Speckled Butterpea
plantingNote: Direct sow an inch deep once soil is reliably warm past 65F, since this bush-type sieva lima rots quickly in cool, damp spring ground.
directions: Direct sow into warm, light, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants close in rows about two feet apart since this variety stays compact and needs no support. This old Southern bush butterpea produces heavily branched plants that keep flowering and setting pods through the hottest, driest stretches of summer when many bean types shut down. Pods run about four inches long and typically hold three or four small, rounded seeds boldly mottled maroon-on-pink, a color pattern that sets it apart from plain cream-seeded butterpea types. Pick at the green-shell stage for classic buttery flavor, or let pods dry fully for long-term storage and seed saving.
sources: Southern heirloom seed retailers (Thresh Seed Co., Mary's Heirloom Seeds, Harvesting History)

name: Dixielee Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil after all frost danger has passed; Dixielee carries strong resistance to root-knot nematode and fusarium wilt, making it a dependable choice for southern gardens where those soilborne problems have limited other southern pea varieties.
directions: Direct sow in full sun into warm, well-drained soil, choosing this variety over other cream peas if root-knot nematode or fusarium wilt has been a problem in the bed. Dixielee was released by the University of Georgia specifically for its combined resistance to root-knot nematode, fusarium wilt, and southern pea mosaic virus, packaged into a productive, semi-vining plant that yields extra-large cream-colored peas with excellent fresh and canning quality. Pods are borne well above the foliage for easy picking and hold their quality over a longer harvest window than many older cream-type varieties. As with other cowpeas it fixes nitrogen in the soil, benefiting whatever crop follows. Harvest pods once they fill out and begin to yellow for fresh shelling, or leave to dry fully for storage.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Southern Pea Variety Recommendations
Mississippi State University Extension — Southern Pea Production Guide

name: Djena Lee's Golden Girl Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes; this productive indeterminate vine benefits from staking and consistent watering through fruit set.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Djena Lee's Golden Girl is an American heirloom yellow beefsteak tomato producing large, smooth, deep-golden fruit with sweet, mild, notably low-acid flesh that is easy on sensitive stomachs and a favorite for gardeners who find red tomatoes too sharp. It is a heavy, dependable producer for an heirloom, setting good yields of large fruit over a long season on a vigorous indeterminate vine. Stake or cage plants for support, water evenly to prevent cracking and blossom end rot, and pick fruit once the skin turns fully golden-yellow and gives slightly to gentle pressure.

name: Doe Hill Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55F; a pre-1900 family heirloom sweet pepper from Doe Hill in Highland County, Virginia.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost at warm soil temperatures, then transplant into the garden once nights stay reliably above 55F and space plants 18-24 inches apart. Doe Hill is a pre-1900 Appalachian family heirloom named for the small town in Highland County, Virginia, prized for its small, flattened, deeply lobed bells that mature quickly from green to bright orange. The thick flesh and sweet, multidimensional flavor are notably good for such a small fruit, and its early, dependable production makes it an excellent choice for short-season gardens. Plants are compact and disease tolerant; harvest at the green stage for a milder flavor or wait for full orange color and maximum sweetness.

name: Dolloff Pole Bean
plantingNote: Wait until soil has warmed past 60F and frost risk has passed, then sow at the base of 6-8 ft fencing for vines to climb.
directions: This pole bean was kept alive for generations by Roy Dolloff of Burke Hollow, Vermont, specifically because it reliably finishes a dry-bean crop even in short, cool Northeast seasons. Give it legume inoculant at planting and sturdy 6-8 ft support, since it is a vigorous climber. Pick some pods young at the salmon-pink shell stage for fresh shelling, or leave the rest to dry down into flat, chestnut-brown beans. Frequent harvesting of the earliest pods keeps the vines producing right up to frost.

name: Doon Major Rutabaga
plantingNote: Long-season root best started in mid to late summer for a Gulf Coast fall-through-winter harvest; flavor improves after frost.
directions: Also sold under the name Major Dunne, this Scottish-origin swede was once a commercial variety in the British Isles before falling out of the seed trade and being preserved by seed-saving networks. Roots are more elongated than a typical rutabaga, with smooth golden-tan skin and purple shoulders, standing tall above the soil with vigorous leafy tops. It retains good texture and mild, sweet flavor even when roots are allowed to grow quite large.

name: Doric Brussels Sprout
plantingNote: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; Doric is a sturdy, shorter-statured early variety well suited to exposed or windy gardens, cropping from November into February.
directions: Start seeds indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant firmly into rich, well-drained soil and firm the base of each plant well since Doric's strength is its short, sturdy stem rather than height; harvest sprouts from the bottom upward as they firm and tighten. Doric is a widely grown F1 hybrid Brussels sprout that carries the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, prized for its strong, compact, wind-resistant stems and heavy yields of smooth, bright, tightly rounded sprouts with good resistance to fusarium and useful tolerance of white blister and mildew. Because the plants stay shorter and stockier than many hybrids, staking needs are minimal even in exposed sites, and the whole stalk can be cut and stood in a cool spot to extend the usable harvest well past when the sprouts would otherwise be picked. Doric's long cropping window, from late autumn through midwinter, and its dependable disease tolerance make it a practical workhorse choice for a sustained home sprout harvest.

name: Dorset Naga Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since chinense superhots germinate slowly and need consistent warmth.
directions: Give Dorset Naga a long, warm season indoors before transplanting, since it needs more heat units than a standard habanero to fully ripen its fruit to deep red. This English-developed selection was bred from Bangladeshi naga stock and yields smoother, more elongated pods than typical wrinkled bhut jolokia types, with fruity aroma alongside intense heat. Stake plants once fruit load builds, and pick some pods slightly early if frost threatens since later flushes often fail to color up in short seasons. It is best suited to collectors in long, hot-summer regions or to greenhouse culture where a longer ripening window can be guaranteed.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Double Standard Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; Double Standard is a sugary-enhanced (SE) bicolor hybrid bred for tender, evenly sweet kernels and reliable germination in cooler soil than supersweet types allow.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in blocks of at least four short rows rather than one long row, since corn is wind-pollinated and needs neighbors on all sides for full ears. Double Standard is a sugary-enhanced bicolor hybrid that carries the classic tender-creamy texture of older SE types rather than the crisper, sometimes tough texture of supersweet (sh2) hybrids, and it germinates dependably in soil a bit cooler than most supersweets tolerate, which suits an early planting. Ears fill out with a mix of white and yellow kernels and hold good eating quality in the garden for several days past peak without turning starchy as fast as older open-pollinated types. Succession-sow every two to three weeks through early summer for a extended harvest, and pick when silks have browned and a punctured kernel weeps milky juice.

name: Doux d'Espagne Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55°F; this old French heirloom sets fruit reliably in warm weather but benefits from afternoon shade cloth during the hottest stretch of Gulf Coast summers. In zone 9, transplant in March and again in midsummer for a fall crop.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost, harden off seedlings, and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed. Harvest elongated fruit green for a mild, grassy flavor or let them ripen fully to red for a sweeter, richer taste well suited to roasting and frying. Doux d'Espagne ('Sweet of Spain') is a 19th-century French heirloom frying pepper producing long, tapered, blocky-shouldered fruit up to 6–8 inches that are thin-walled and entirely sweet with no heat, similar in use to Italian frying types but with a distinctively rich, old-world flavor. Plants are productive and tolerate a range of soils, making this a dependable choice for gardeners wanting a classic European sweet pepper for skillet cooking rather than fresh salad use. Fruit is best picked while walls are still tender, since older peppers can develop a slightly tougher skin.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — heirloom pepper variety notes
Kokopelli Seed Foundation — European heirloom pepper archive
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — pepper variety descriptions

name: Doux Long des Landes Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Doux Long des Landes is a traditional French heirloom sweet pepper from the Landes region of southwestern France, producing long, tapering, thin-walled fruits that ripen from pale green to red with a mild, sweet flavor.
directions: Sow indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55°F. Doux Long des Landes is a traditional French sweet pepper named for the Landes region of southwestern France, producing long, tapering, thin-walled fruits that ripen from pale green to red with a mild, sweet flavor and virtually no heat. Its thin flesh makes it well suited to quick pan-frying in oil in the French country style, or to roasting whole until the skin blisters and slips off easily. The plants are productive over a long season and tolerate the warm, humid summers common in the Gulf South.

name: Dr. Martin Lima Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is thoroughly warm, since Dr. Martin is a rampant pole lima that needs the full length of a hot summer to fill its outsized pods; set a sturdy 8-foot or taller trellis at planting time.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, well-worked soil once all frost danger has passed, training vines up a tall, sturdy trellis or pole from the start since this variety climbs far higher than most garden limas. Dr. Martin is a pre-1900 heirloom pole lima known for its enormous vigor and outsized flat pods, each holding three to four quarter-sized beans, borne on vines that can top ten feet in a long, hot season. Pick pods at the plump green-shell stage for the best flavor and tenderness, or leave them to dry fully on the vine for storage beans; consistent picking keeps the vines setting new flowers through summer heat. Because the vines invest heavily in height before bearing, give plants a long, warm season and avoid crowding so pods lower on the trellis still get good airflow and light.

name: Dr. Wyche's Orange Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into deeply prepared soil after all frost risk passes; this is an indeterminate variety that needs staking or caging to support the heavy orange beefsteak fruits.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost, transplant into fertile, well-draining soil in full sun, and bury the stem deeply for a stronger root system. Dr. Wyche's Orange honors Dr. John Wyche, a Cherokee chief and circus impresario from Hugo, Oklahoma, who grew tomatoes fertilized with circus animal manure and shared his seeds with Seed Savers Exchange; the variety produces large, up to 2-pound, brilliant orange beefsteak fruits with very meaty, nearly seedless flesh and a mild, sweet, low-acid flavor that appeals especially to those who find red tomatoes too acidic. Stake or cage plants solidly as the vines are vigorous and the fruits are heavy; consistent watering prevents cracking. Harvest when fully orange and slightly soft at the blossom end.

name: Dr. Wyche's Yellow Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Dr. Wyche's Yellow is an indeterminate beefsteak type requiring staking or caging. In zone 9, transplant February–March for spring production; the tomato's excellent flavor quality at full orange-yellow ripeness makes timely harvest important — overripe fruits crack and lose flavor. The color at full ripeness is a warm orange-gold to orange-yellow, not pale yellow or greenish — harvest when the fruit has achieved a uniform orange-gold color and has slight give to gentle pressure.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Stake or cage. Harvest when uniformly orange-gold and slightly soft. Dr. Wyche's Yellow is a large-fruited heirloom tomato from an extraordinary source: Dr. John Wyche, a circus man from Hugo, Oklahoma, who operated King Brothers Circus and simultaneously maintained an extensive collection of heirloom seeds that he distributed to seed savers and gardeners over many years. Dr. Wyche reportedly used manure from the circus animals (elephants, big cats, and other exotic animals) to fertilize his prodigious garden at his Hugo farm, giving his tomatoes — which he claimed grew unusually large and vigorous — the colorful story of being 'circus-fertilized.' The tomatoes that bear his name are large beefsteak-type fruits ripening to a warm orange-gold to orange-yellow, with a complex, rich flavor that many tasters describe as fruity, sweet, and low-acid with more depth than typical yellow tomatoes. The fruits are large (often 12–16 oz or more under ideal conditions) and meaty — the solid orange-yellow flesh is dense and flavorful with relatively few seed cavities for a beefsteak type. Dr. Wyche's Yellow has been distributed by Seed Savers Exchange and other heirloom seed sources and has gained a devoted following among heirloom tomato enthusiasts who value the combination of large size, distinctive warm orange-gold color, and excellent flavor.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Dr. Wyche's Yellow tomato heirloom documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Dr. Wyche's Yellow variety notes
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Large-fruited yellow tomato variety comparison

name: Dragon Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall (August–September in zone 9) in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Dragon's intense skin color develops most vividly in full sun and cool temperatures — the purple-red pigmentation is an anthocyanin response to sunlight and cold that peaks in fall conditions.
directions: Direct sow in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Dragon is a distinctive heirloom carrot producing long, tapered roots with deep red-purple to maroon skin — an unusually vivid exterior color caused by high anthocyanin content — and orange interior flesh with a reddish core that bleeds red-orange color when cut. The flavor is excellent: sweet, slightly spicy, and more complex than standard orange carrots, with the characteristic flavor depth often associated with high-anthocyanin vegetables. Raw Dragon carrots turn a stunning deep red-orange when sliced, making them visually dramatic in fresh salads, crudité platters, and fresh presentations — the color contrast of the purple-red exterior against the orange-red interior is striking and unique. When cooked, the anthocyanin pigments partially convert to blue-gray tones (as with all purple vegetables cooked without acid), so Dragon carrots are best appreciated raw, lightly pickled in vinegar, or roasted at high heat for caramelized flavor development. The excellent flavor and extraordinary color make Dragon an outstanding choice for market gardeners and home gardeners who value both flavor and visual interest. In zone 9, sow in August through September for a fall/winter crop — the cool temperatures intensify both the purple skin color and the sweetness of the flesh.

name: Dragon Egg Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Dragon Egg is a Croatian heirloom cucumber with egg-shaped, creamy-white to pale yellow fruits harvested before they turn orange, with a mild, sweet flavor, thin skin, and exceptional heat tolerance — one of the most productive and beautiful novelty cucumbers for warm summer gardens.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; train vines on a trellis or fence to make harvesting easier and keep fruits off the ground. Dragon Egg is a Croatian heirloom cucumber with a charming and unusual appearance — the fruits are oval to distinctly egg-shaped, smooth-skinned, and creamy-white to pale yellow when ripe, with a delicate internal structure of mild, sweet flesh and small seeds. They are harvested when fully white-to-cream colored (before they turn orange, which indicates over-maturity and seedy, bitter flesh); at the right stage the flavor is mild, refreshing, and virtually non-bitter even in hot conditions. The plants are extremely productive in warm weather and the fruits hang in clusters, making them easy to spot and harvest. Outstanding for hot summer gardens where standard cucumbers become bitter; one of the most reliably productive white-fruited novelty cucumbers.

name: Dragon Radish
plantingNote: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop; longer maturity than spring radishes means an earlier start.
directions: Dragon is a Chinese-type radish whose brilliant red skin wraps a pure white, crisp interior, splitting the difference in size between a quick spring radish and a full daikon. Direct-sow seed about a half inch deep and thin to 4 to 6 inches for roots to size up properly without forking. The flavor stays mild and juicy rather than sharp, which makes it good for both raw snacking and quick pickling, and the color holds up strikingly well when sliced into rounds or julienned. Because it takes longer to mature than a standard breakfast radish, give it the full six weeks before expecting harvestable roots.

name: Dragon Tongue Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is at least 65°F; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September. Dragon Tongue is a bush bean requiring no support. The distinctive yellow and purple streaked pods should be harvested at 6–7 inches when pods are still flat — the purple markings disappear entirely when cooked, leaving a uniform golden-yellow wax bean. For use as a shelled bean, allow pods to fill and seeds to plump. In zone 9 summer heat can cause plants to drop flowers; fall plantings often produce higher quality pods.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Dragon Tongue is a Dutch heirloom wax bean producing flat, wide, golden-yellow pods dramatically streaked and splashed with deep purple markings — one of the most visually striking beans in the garden and the most eye-catching bean at farmers markets and in kitchen displays. The pods are harvested as a wax bean (snap bean without strings) in the flat stage before seeds swell, when the crisp, flat pods have a buttery, mild wax bean flavor noticeably different from standard round snap beans. The purple streaking serves no flavor function but makes the pods immediately recognizable and appealing; the color vanishes completely during cooking. Dragon Tongue also works as a shellout bean if pods are allowed to mature fully, with cream-colored seeds streaked with black-purple markings. The bush habit and early maturity (55–60 days) make Dragon Tongue productive in relatively short growing seasons, and the ornamental pods add visual interest to the vegetable garden beyond what most productive bush beans offer.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Dragon Tongue Dutch Heirloom Bean
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Dragon Tongue Bean History
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Wax Bean Varieties

name: Dragon Tongue Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall for best production in zone 9; Dragon Tongue Mustard is a cool-season green that performs best when temperatures are below 75°F. In zone 9, sow August–November for fall and winter harvest, or February–March for spring. Harvest young leaves at 30–40 days for mildest flavor, or allow plants to reach full size (45+ days) for more pungent, mature leaves. The distinctive red-purple veining on bright green leaves intensifies in cool weather.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.25 inch deep in rows 12 inches apart; thin to 4–6 inches. Harvest outer leaves from 30 days or cut the whole plant at 40–45 days. Dragon Tongue Mustard is a visually striking Asian mustard green with broad, frilly, bright green leaves overlaid with vivid red-purple veining and midribs — the colorful contrasting veination giving the leaves a dramatic appearance unlike any other mustard type and making Dragon Tongue one of the most ornamental edible greens in the winter garden. The name describes the leaf form: long, broad, and pointed like a tongue, with the red-purple coloring suggesting the fieriness appropriate to a dragon. The flavor is spicy, sharp, and pungent in the characteristic Asian mustard style — more aggressive than mild Asian greens like tatsoi or pak choi, but that pungency mellows significantly with cooking. Raw leaves are assertive and best used in small quantities as a spicy accent in salad mixes; cooked leaves (sautéed, steamed, or braised) are excellent alongside other winter vegetables and complement pork, sausage, and beans. Dragon Tongue grows rapidly in cool weather and is one of the most productive and visually interesting additions to a fall and winter garden in the Gulf South.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Mustard green variety comparison
Kitazawa Seed Company — Asian mustard green varieties
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Asian Greens for Southern Gardens

name: Dragon's Breath Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, since Capsicum chinense germinates slowly; transplant only after nights stay reliably above 55F, since this is one of the slowest-fruiting chiles to mature.
directions: Dragon's Breath was bred in Wales through a collaborative trial investigating the essential oil's potential as a topical anesthetic, and it produces small, wrinkled, roughly one-inch fruits on a compact, well-branched plant that suits container growing as easily as garden beds. Independent lab testing reported an extraordinary capsaicin concentration around 2.48 million Scoville units, though this figure has not been formally certified, so treat it as a claimed rather than official record. Because of its almost unmanageable heat, growers treat the fruit as a novelty or oil-extraction crop rather than a table pepper, and any handling should be done with gloves, eye protection, and excellent ventilation. Give plants the same warm, sunny, well-drained conditions used for habaneros, and expect a long season since fruit set and full ripening take considerably longer than most annuum peppers.
sources: Nottingham Trent University research announcements on Dragon's Breath essential oil
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Dragon's Tongue Cucumber
plantingNote: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost or direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; harvest while fruits are cream with purple stripes — they become fully yellow and bitter if left on the vine too long.
directions: Direct sow or transplant to well-amended, warm soil in full sun after last frost; Dragon's Tongue is a strikingly beautiful Dutch heirloom cucumber producing medium-sized (5–6 inch) cucumbers with creamy-white skin dramatically streaked and splashed with purple-violet, resulting in an ornamental appearance unlike any standard green cucumber. Harvest when fruits are creamy-white with purple markings and firm to the touch — as they continue to mature they turn yellow then bitter. The flavor when harvested at prime ripeness is mild, crisp, and slightly sweet, excellent for fresh eating and pickling. A productive and prolific vining type that does not require trellis but benefits from it.

name: Drunken Woman Frizzy-Headed Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–February for spring. The slow-bolting tendency of this Italian heirloom variety makes it an excellent choice for late-spring extension in zone 9, where it holds quality 1–2 weeks longer than standard looseleaf varieties before bolting. Successive sowings extend the harvest window through the cool season.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Drunken Woman Frizzy-Headed is an Italian heirloom looseleaf lettuce with one of the most whimsical names in the vegetable kingdom — a literal translation of the Italian 'Ubriaca della Testa Frizzy' — producing large, loosely-headed plants with heavily frilled, ruffled, wavy leaves in a mix of red-bronze tones on green, giving the plant an exuberant, disheveled appearance that the name aptly describes. The large, floppy, curly leaves have a mild, tender, slightly buttery flavor with the red-bronze pigmentation adding a slight edge of complexity over standard green looseleaf. The decorative appearance makes it a standout in the garden and at market, where the dramatic frilly form catches the eye among more uniform types. Drunken Woman Frizzy-Headed is notably slow to bolt and holds in the garden longer than many other looseleaf types, a quality valued in warm climates. The large leaf size makes it easy to harvest by stripping outer leaves for a continuous cut-and-come-again operation.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Italian Heirloom Lettuce
Seed Savers Exchange — Frizzy-Headed Looseleaf Lettuces
Seeds of Italy — Lattuga Ubriaca della Testa Frizzy

name: Druzba Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost risk passes; stake or cage firmly as an indeterminate variety known for good crack resistance.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant into warm, fertile soil once frost danger has passed. Druzba is a Bulgarian heirloom whose name means 'friendship,' prized for combining an unusually early harvest window with the deep, balanced flavor more typical of longer-season tomatoes. The smooth, red, slightly flattened globes resist cracking better than many heirlooms and the vigorous indeterminate vines stay productive over a long season. Stake or cage securely and pinch suckers lightly to keep the sprawling growth manageable.

name: Duborskian Rice
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into rich, heavy soil kept flooded with 1-2 inches of water through the growing season in full sun; Duborskian rice is a short-season, cold-adapted paddy variety that can mature even in cool-summer northern climates.
directions: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into rich, heavy soil kept flooded with 1-2 inches of water through the growing season in full sun; Duborskian rice is a short-season, cold-adapted paddy variety that can mature even in cool-summer northern climates. Bred in Russia for a much shorter and more cold-tolerant growing season than typical rice, it is one of the few rice varieties that home gardeners in temperate, non-tropical climates can realistically bring to harvest, maturing in around 100 days compared to 150 or more for most tropical rice. Grow it in a lined kiddie pool, stock tank, or purpose-built paddy bed that can hold standing water, keeping the bed flooded through most of the growing season and draining it as the grain heads mature and dry down in late summer. Hand-harvest by cutting whole seed heads once grains have hardened and the plant has yellowed, then dry, thresh, and hull before cooking.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

name: Duganski Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Duganski is a purple stripe hardneck that needs a real winter chill for good bulb formation and performs best in zone 3-7.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Duganski is a purple stripe hardneck garlic originally from Russia, valued for its notably strong, hot, spicy raw flavor that mellows into a rich, robust taste when roasted or cooked, making it a favorite among gardeners who want an assertive, full-flavored garlic. Bulbs have deep reddish-purple streaked skin over 8-10 tightly packed cloves. As a hardneck, it sends up a curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to focus the plant's energy on bulb development; scapes are tender and flavorful when harvested young. Duganski also stores somewhat better than many other purple stripe types, often holding for 6-8 months in a cool, dry location. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, then cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot before trimming.
sources: Chester Aaron: The Great Garlic Book, Ten Speed Press 1997

name: Duke of Albany Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool soil well before the last frost; this tall Victorian exhibition pea needs a sturdy trellis or fence from the start to support its long vines.
directions: Direct sow in cool, well-drained soil and provide tall support immediately, since this nineteenth-century English heirloom climbs four to five feet and produces exceptionally long, well-filled pods. Duke of Albany belongs to the same Victorian lineage of large-podded exhibition peas as Telegraph and Stratagem, grown both for the table and for competitive showing in its day. It has been preserved in cultivation by heritage seed organizations after disappearing from mainstream commercial catalogs. Harvest pods while still glossy and full for the sweetest flavor, as older, drier pods lose tenderness quickly.

name: Dunja Zucchini
plantingNote: Sow directly in warm soil about 1-2 weeks after the last spring frost, or start indoors slightly earlier for a head start in short-season regions.
directions: Sow seeds directly in warm soil 1-2 weeks after the last spring frost, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early for short-season climates. Dunja was bred specifically for organic growers and shows strong resistance to zucchini yellow mosaic virus, watermelon mosaic virus, and papaya ringspot virus, making it dependable where aphid-transmitted viruses commonly cut a squash planting short. The medium-green, cylindrical fruit forms on an open, easy-to-harvest plant; picking regularly at 6-8 inches keeps vigorous plants producing all season.

name: Duplex Scorzonera
plantingNote: Direct sow in loose, deeply worked, stone-free soil; scorzonera is a long-season root that benefits from a full cool season and can be left in the ground through winter and dug as needed.
directions: Duplex is a long-cultivated Continental European scorzonera selected for heavy, uniform yields of long, black-skinned, white-fleshed roots and for notable resistance to bolting compared with older strains. Direct sow into deeply loosened soil, since the taproot resents disturbance and will fork in compacted or stony ground, and thin seedlings early to give roots room to size up straight. The cooked root has a sweet, mild, faintly oyster-like flavor similar to salsify, and is traditionally peeled, cut into pieces, and steamed or simmered before finishing with a sauce. Roots can be left in the ground over winter in most climates and lifted through the cold months, with flavor improving after frost.

name: Dusky Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Dusky is one of the earliest classic dark-skinned hybrid eggplants to reach harvest size.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Dusky is a compact hybrid eggplant that became a home-garden standard for its combination of early maturity, good disease resistance, and heavy sets of deep purple, glossy, oval-to-teardrop fruit. Fruits reach a full 8 to 9 inches while still maturing notably faster than many older large-fruited eggplants, which lets gardeners in shorter-season regions get a reliable harvest before fall cooling slows production. The dense, disease-tolerant bush habit performs well in raised beds and large containers as well as open garden rows. Pick fruit while the skin is still glossy and firm and the flesh gives slightly to gentle pressure, since fruit left to overripen turns dull, seedy, and bitter.

name: Dwarf Arctic Rose Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the compact 2-3 ft dwarf habit and unusually early maturity suit raised beds, containers, and short-season gardens.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the thick, rugose-leafed stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Dwarf Arctic Rose bears round to oblate pink fruit with smooth shoulders and clear skin over red flesh, offering well-balanced flavor on one of the earliest-maturing plants in the Dwarf Tomato Project lineup, sometimes ready weeks ahead of other dwarf releases. It was bred from a 2005 cross of Budai Torpe and Black from Tula made by Patrina Nuske Small, with selection work carried out largely by Alaska-based growers well-suited to short seasons. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

name: Dwarf Blue Scotch Kale
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. sabellica 'Dwarf Blue Scotch'
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer 8–12 weeks before first fall frost, or in early spring 4–6 weeks before last frost; Dwarf Blue Scotch is one of the most cold-hardy and compact kale varieties available — the low-growing (12–18 inch), intensely blue-green, finely curled plants survive temperatures well below 0°F in established gardens and produce some of their finest quality after repeated frost exposure through winter.
directions: Sow directly 1/2 inch deep in cool weather and thin to 12–18 inches apart; Dwarf Blue Scotch is very compact and can be planted more closely than full-size curly kales; harvest outer leaves continuously as cut-and-come-again; the plants tolerate temperatures well below 0°F and produce through winter in zones 5–7 without protection. Dwarf Blue Scotch is an old heirloom curly kale variety that combines three notable characteristics: exceptional cold hardiness, compact plant habit, and an attractive, intensely blue-gray-green leaf color that gives it its name. The plants grow only 12–18 inches tall with tightly packed, finely curled and ruffled leaves of a distinctive blue-green color — sometimes described as 'glaucous' or 'sea blue' — that deepens and intensifies after cold exposure, making Dwarf Blue Scotch one of the most visually attractive kales in the winter garden. The flavor is traditional curly kale — somewhat peppery and earthy raw, becoming sweet and mellow after frost exposure, with the classic kale character that mellows beautifully with cooking in soups, stews, sautés, and traditional Scottish 'kail' preparations. The 'Scotch' name reflects the deep Scottish culinary tradition of kale (kail in Scots dialect), where kale was so central to the diet that the kitchen garden was historically called the 'kailyard' and kale broth (kail brose) was a daily staple. The dwarf habit makes it ideal for raised beds, intensive planting, and smaller gardens where space is limited.

name: Dwarf Champion Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the short, rugose-leafed dwarf habit is self-supporting and needs only light staking in exposed sites.
directions: Dwarf Champion is a 19th-century American heirloom notable as one of the earliest true dwarf, potato-leaf tomato varieties grown in home gardens, predating both the modern Dwarf Tomato Project and its own later yellow-fruited sport, Golden Dwarf Champion, by roughly a century. Plants stay short and stocky with thick, rugose foliage and need little to no staking, setting round to slightly oblate, medium-sized pink-red fruit with mild, old-fashioned tomato flavor. Its compact, self-supporting genetics made it valuable breeding stock for later short-statured tomato lines long before dwarf habit became a deliberate modern breeding goal. Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, harvesting as fruit fully colors and softens slightly at the blossom end.

name: Dwarf Emerald Giant Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; the sturdy, dwarf-indeterminate plant grows only 2-4 feet tall, making it well suited to large containers and raised beds.
directions: Dwarf Emerald Giant produces large beefsteak-type fruit that ripens from deep green to a green-gold color with an amber blush at the blossom end, revealing translucent lime-green flesh with a rich, spicy-sweet flavor reminiscent of full-size green heirloom beefsteaks. The compact, dwarf-indeterminate plant packs that big-fruit heirloom character onto a manageable 2-4 foot frame suited to raised beds and large containers. It is a release of the Dwarf Tomato Project, the volunteer breeding collaboration begun in 2005 by Craig LeHoullier and Patrina Nuske Small to combine heirloom flavor and color diversity with compact plant habit.

name: Dwarf Golden Gypsy Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the compact, tree-like 2-4 ft dwarf-indeterminate habit with potato-leaf foliage suits raised beds and large containers.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking the sturdy, potato-leaf stems lightly for support. Dwarf Golden Gypsy bears medium to large oblate yellow fruit with pale yellow flesh and an intense, sprightly, refreshingly tangy flavor rated among the best of the newer dwarf releases. It began as a Golden Dwarf Champion x Elbe cross made by Patrina Nuske Small, was selected and renamed by Wendy Montanez, and stabilized over multiple generations by Dwarf Tomato Project volunteers before its 2015 release as an OSSI-pledged variety. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for best flavor.

name: Dwarf Green Long Pod Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow 1-3 weeks after the last frost once the soil is warm, spacing seed to allow the compact bushy plants room to branch.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil after the last frost, soaking seed overnight to promote even germination, then thin to give plants adequate spacing for good air circulation. Harvest the ribbed, tapering pods young and often to keep the compact plants producing steadily. Dwarf Green Long Pod is a long-standing heirloom selected for its shorter, bushier habit compared to older tall okra types, making it easier to harvest while still delivering abundant, tender green pods. Its manageable size has kept it a staple in home gardens with limited space.

name: Dwarf Grey Sugar Pea
plantingNote: One of the earliest snow peas to mature; sow very early in spring (8 weeks before last frost) for a quick cool-season harvest before summer heat arrives; compact habit needs only minimal support (24–30 in twiggy branches or short netting).
directions: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep in early spring (up to 8 weeks before last frost) in cool, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Dwarf Grey Sugar is an old heirloom snow pea, documented since at least the 1800s, distinguished by its unusually attractive purple-tinged vines and flowers against blue-grey foliage — the purplish cast coming from anthocyanins that also make the young tendrils and pods slightly reddish before the pods mature to green. Compact habit (24–30 inches) makes it ideal for small gardens and containers. An early and productive snow pea; harvest pods frequently when flat and young before seeds swell.

name: Dwarf Hannah's Prize Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; the compact, dwarf-indeterminate habit of 2-4 feet suits container growing and small raised beds.
directions: Dwarf Hannah's Prize bears medium-to-large orange-gold beefsteak fruit with the mild, fruity sweetness and creamy texture typical of gold-fruited heirloom tomatoes. Named for a member of the LeHoullier family, it grows as a sturdy, dwarf-indeterminate plant reaching just 2-4 feet, concentrating heirloom-quality fruit onto a footprint well suited to containers and small gardens. It is one of the many named releases from the Dwarf Tomato Project, the volunteer-driven breeding collaboration coordinated by Craig LeHoullier and Patrina Nuske Small since 2005.

name: Dwarf Jade Beauty Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; the dense, dwarf-indeterminate 2-4 foot habit makes it a good candidate for large pots and small raised beds.
directions: Dwarf Jade Beauty produces medium round fruit that ripens to a translucent jade-green with an amber blush at the blossom end, offering the sweet-tart, slightly spicy complexity typical of green-when-ripe tomatoes. The plant keeps a compact, dwarf-indeterminate habit of 2-4 feet, making it a practical choice for gardeners with limited space who still want an unusual green-fleshed heirloom. It emerged from the Dwarf Tomato Project, the international volunteer breeding effort founded by Craig LeHoullier and Patrina Nuske Small in 2005 to pair dwarf growth habit with heirloom flavor and color diversity.

name: Dwarf Kelly Green Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the compact 2-4 ft dwarf-indeterminate habit with thick stems suits raised beds and large containers.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the thick, rugose-leafed stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Dwarf Kelly Green bears medium, round fruit that stays green with a translucent amber-tinged skin even at full ripeness, offering the tangy, well-rounded flavor typical of green-fleshed tomatoes. It came from the same 2005 Golden Dwarf Champion x Green Giant cross that produced Dwarf Sweet Sue, stabilized through the Dwarf Tomato Project and named for Australian bushranger Ned Kelly. Harvest when fruit softens slightly, since color alone will not signal ripeness.

name: Dwarf Liz Birt Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; the compact, dwarf-indeterminate habit of 2-4 feet suits raised beds and large containers.
directions: Dwarf Liz Birt produces medium-to-large pink beefsteak fruit with the balanced sweet-tart flavor and meaty texture prized in pink heirloom tomatoes. Named in honor of a longtime Dwarf Tomato Project volunteer, the plant keeps a compact, dwarf-indeterminate habit of 2-4 feet that suits raised beds and large containers. It is one of dozens of named cultivars to come out of the Dwarf Tomato Project since its founding in 2005 by Craig LeHoullier and Patrina Nuske Small.

name: Dwarf Moonglow Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; the compact, dwarf-indeterminate plant stays 2-4 feet tall, a good choice for patio containers and small-space gardens.
directions: Dwarf Moonglow bears medium round fruit in a glowing golden-orange color with a mild, sweet flavor and low acidity typical of orange-fruited tomatoes. It grows as a compact, dwarf-indeterminate plant reaching 2-4 feet, making it a good choice for patio containers and small-space vegetable gardens. The variety is a release of the Dwarf Tomato Project, the collaborative volunteer breeding effort that has produced well over 100 named dwarf-growth-habit tomato varieties since 2005.

name: Dwarf Orange Cream Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the compact, tree-like 2-4 ft dwarf-indeterminate habit with thick, rugose stems suits raised beds and large containers.
directions: Dwarf Orange Cream traces to the same Elbe x Golden Dwarf Champion 'Tipsy' lineage within the international Dwarf Tomato Project that also produced Dwarf Golden Gypsy, carrying the same thick, rugose potato-leaf stems and tidy, tree-like habit that suits raised beds and large containers. The round to slightly oblate fruit ripens to a warm orange with a soft, creamy-textured interior and a mild, well-rounded sweetness rather than sharp acidity. Like its Dwarf Tomato Project siblings, it was stabilized over several generations by volunteer growers before release as an open-pollinated, seed-saveable variety. Stake lightly for support and harvest once fruit colors fully and softens slightly for the best flavor.

name: Dwarf Sarah's Delight Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; the sturdy, dwarf-indeterminate bush stays 2-4 feet tall, well suited to containers and small gardens.
directions: Dwarf Sarah's Delight bears small-to-medium round fruit in a warm apricot-orange hue with a sweet, mild flavor good for fresh eating and salads. The plant grows as a sturdy, dwarf-indeterminate bush 2-4 feet tall, concentrating heirloom-quality fruit onto a footprint well suited to containers and small raised beds. It was released through the Dwarf Tomato Project, the breeding collaboration founded by Craig LeHoullier and Patrina Nuske Small to pair dwarf growth habit with heirloom flavor and color diversity.

name: Dwarf Sunray Jerusalem Artichoke
plantingNote: Plant tuber pieces 3-4 inches deep around the last frost date; this compact selection stays manageable in size compared to standard sunchokes and can be grown in smaller beds or large containers.
directions: Dwarf Sunray was selected long ago as a shorter, tidier alternative to towering standard sunchoke varieties, topping out around 4-5 feet instead of the 8-10 feet common to most Helianthus tuberosus strains, which makes it far less prone to toppling in wind or shading neighboring crops. It concentrates its white-skinned tubers in a tight cluster close to the base of the stem rather than scattering them widely underground, so harvest is quicker and the planting is easier to contain within a bed. Foliage dies back with the first hard frosts, at which point tubers can be dug as needed through fall and winter, with flavor sweetening after cold exposure converts stored inulin to sugar. As with all sunchokes, leave a few tubers in the ground each season to regenerate next year's crop, and dig thoroughly at bed's end if you want to remove the planting entirely.

name: Dwarf Sweet Sue Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the compact 2-4 ft dwarf-indeterminate habit with thick, sturdy stems suits raised beds and large containers.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy, potato-leaf stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Dwarf Sweet Sue bears round to oblate golden-yellow fruit, often blushed pink at the blossom end when fully ripe, with a rich, well-balanced, notably sweet flavor for a yellow tomato. It was bred from a 2005 cross of Golden Dwarf Champion and Green Giant by Patrina Nuske Small and named by Craig LeHoullier for his wife, one of the earlier stabilized releases of the international Dwarf Tomato Project. Harvest as fruit colors fully and softens slightly for peak sweetness.

name: Dwarf Wild Fred Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Dwarf Wild Fred is one of the original releases from the international, all-volunteer Dwarf Tomato Project, bred to combine full-size tomato flavor on compact, container-friendly plants.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy, stout stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Dwarf Wild Fred bears clusters of medium red fruit with good, rich flavor on a compact, potato-leaf plant that stays under 4 feet, one of the early releases from the Dwarf Tomato Project, an international collaboration of home breeders working to create full-flavored heirloom-quality tomatoes on space-saving dwarf plants. Its manageable size suits raised beds and large containers where sprawling indeterminate tomatoes would be impractical. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine.

name: Eagle Pass Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed thoroughly; Eagle Pass is a Texas borderland heirloom valued for exceptional heat and drought tolerance, well suited to South Texas and other hot, dry summer gardens.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep once soil is thoroughly warm, since this variety germinates poorly in cool soil; space plants 12-18 inches apart in full sun. Eagle Pass is a Texas heirloom okra originating from the border region around Eagle Pass, Texas, selected over generations for tolerance of extreme heat and limited water, making it a strong performer in South Texas and other arid warm-climate gardens where many other okra varieties struggle. Plants grow tall and produce ribbed green pods that should be harvested young, at around 3-4 inches, for best tenderness. It remains a favorite among regional seed savers for its resilience and reliable yields under harsh summer conditions.

name: Earl of Edgecombe Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; this New Zealand heirloom is a tall indeterminate that needs sturdy staking to carry its large orange fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, well-drained soil once the weather has warmed, staking vines firmly as fruit loads increase. Earl of Edgecombe is a New Zealand heirloom beefsteak prized for its large, smooth, deep orange fruit and mild, sweet, low-acid flavor, traits that have made it a favorite among gardeners who find red heirlooms too tart. The indeterminate vines are productive over a long season given consistent moisture and feeding. Harvest at full orange color and handle carefully, since large-fruited heirlooms are prone to cracking after uneven watering.

name: Earliana Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this is one of the earliest tomatoes available, bred specifically for short northern growing seasons.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant to the garden after frost danger passes, spacing plants about two feet apart since this is a compact determinate variety. Earliana, developed in the late 1800s and popularized by seedsmen including George Sparks of Ohio, became one of the first reliably early red tomatoes available to American gardeners and remained a market standard for decades before being supplanted by modern hybrids. The smooth, medium-sized red fruits ripen in a tight window, making this variety useful for gardeners who want an early flush of slicing tomatoes before the main-season crop comes in. Stake lightly for support and pick promptly as fruits color to extend the harvest window.
sources: William Woys Weaver: Heirloom Vegetable Gardening, Henry Holt 1997

name: Earlidew Honeydew Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after soil has warmed well past 70°F, since honeydew is slower to establish than cantaloupe.
directions: Earlidew was developed to bring honeydew melon within reach of gardeners in shorter, cooler growing seasons where standard honeydew varieties often fail to ripen before fall. It produces smooth, pale green-white rinds around sweet, light green flesh on vines noticeably more compact than typical honeydew types. Because honeydew does not slip from the vine at maturity the way cantaloupe does, watch for the blossom end to soften slightly and the rind to take on a faint yellow cast as ripeness cues. Its earlier maturity window makes it one of the more practical honeydew choices for northern vegetable gardens.

name: Early Acre Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and again July–August for a fall crop. Early Acre is one of the quickest-maturing field peas available, making it valuable for both short-season production and getting a crop into the ground before summer heat peaks.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in well-drained soil in full sun; Early Acre is a compact, early-maturing bush cowpea that completes its fresh-shell harvest in just 55–65 days, among the earliest of any southern pea type. The small, cream-colored seeds with a small eye have a mild, slightly sweet flavor preferred by many over the stronger-flavored crowder and black-eye types. This variety is well-adapted to the Gulf Coast's brief spring and fall shoulder seasons, fitting in a productive crop before summer extremes take hold or closing out the season after summer heat breaks. The drought tolerance of cowpeas generally extends to Early Acre, which needs minimal irrigation once established. Harvest pods while the hulls are firm and the seeds have fully plumped but before the hull begins to dry.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Southern Pea Variety Trials
Alabama Cooperative Extension System — Southern Pea Production
Mississippi State University Extension — Field Pea Varieties

name: Early Alaska Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 6–10 weeks before last frost — one of the earliest peas available, germinating in soils as cold as 38°F; Early Alaska is the traditional extra-early pea for late winter and earliest spring planting, maturing before all other commonly grown varieties and finishing before summer heat arrives — ideal for short-season northern gardens and earliest-possible spring pea harvests in the South.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep as soon as soil can be worked in early spring; in zone 6+ this means January–February; in zone 3–5, as soon as soil thaws. Early Alaska is one of the oldest and most cold-tolerant pea varieties, germinating in soils as cold as 38–40°F and maturing in 55–60 days from seed — making it one of the fastest peas available. The smooth-seeded peas are not as sweet as wrinkled-seed types but have traditional pea flavor and historically represent the 'early pea' of American kitchen gardens. Short (24–30 inch), self-supporting plants produce cylindrical pods with 5–7 peas; smooth seeds tolerate cold, wet soil better than wrinkled types that can rot. In Gulf Coast and Southern gardens (zones 8–10), Early Alaska planted in January finishes before March heat ends the pea season.

name: Early Bird Tomato
plantingNote: Bred for direct outdoor seeding rather than indoor transplants; sow once soil has warmed slightly past frost date for an early slicing crop.
directions: Sow seed directly in the garden bed once the soil is workable, skipping the usual indoor seed-starting step this variety was bred to avoid. Thin seedlings to their final spacing and stake or cage plants as they grow, since vigorous early vines benefit from support. Expect a quicker-than-average harvest window for a slicing tomato grown entirely outdoors from seed.

name: Early Blood Turnip Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as the soil is workable in spring; can be resown for a fall crop.
directions: One of the earliest American beet varieties on record, grown widely since the early 1800s and named for its flattened, turnip-like shape rather than any relation to actual turnips. It was the dominant garden beet in the United States for much of the 19th century before newer selections like Detroit Dark Red largely replaced it commercially. Direct sow as soon as the soil is workable in spring; the deep red roots have dense, sweet flesh good for both fresh eating and pickling, and the plant can be resown for a fall crop as well.
sources: William Woys Weaver, Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

name: Early Butternut PMR Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is warm; Early Butternut PMR reaches harvest 15 to 20 days sooner than standard Waltham-type butternut and carries improved resistance to powdery mildew.
directions: Direct sow seed in hills after the last frost in rich, well-drained soil, spacing hills to give vines moderate room to spread. Early Butternut PMR was bred to bring the classic tan-skinned, orange-fleshed butternut squash to gardeners in shorter growing seasons, reaching harvest well before standard Waltham-type strains while carrying built-in resistance to powdery mildew, a common late-season problem on butternut vines. Fruit averages 2 to 3 pounds, a convenient size for single-meal use, with the same dense, sweet, nutty flesh gardeners expect from butternut squash. Harvest once the rind has turned uniformly tan and hardened, then cure for one to two weeks in a warm spot to improve storage life and sweetness.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Early Curled Simpson Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow shallowly as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in fall for overwintering under a cold frame or light mulch in mild climates.
directions: Descended from the French heirloom Silesia and known by several names over the years, including Curled Silesia and White-Seeded Simpson, this loose-leaf lettuce came into wider American use in the 1850s as a quicker-maturing alternative to older sorts. It forms a tight, quick-growing bunch of light green, crumpled leaves about a foot across, without ever forming a true head. Exceptionally cold-hardy, it was traditionally the lettuce of choice for overwintering in cold frames or under straw mulch, shrugging off hard freezes that would kill tenderer types. Its speed and hardiness make it a good pick for the earliest spring salads or a late fall planting pushed into winter.
sources: William Woys Weaver - Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

name: Early Fortune Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed after last frost; its early maturity makes it a good choice for a spring crop ahead of Gulf Coast summer heat and disease pressure, plus a possible fall sowing.
directions: Early Fortune was selected by a Michigan grower from the older Davis Perfect cucumber and introduced commercially around 1910 as an early, dependable white-spine slicer, quickly becoming one of the most widely planted cucumbers in the country. Fruits reach 7-8 inches with smooth, deep green skin and crisp, mild white flesh, and the vines begin bearing notably faster than many other open-pollinated slicers of similar type. It is a traditional monoecious variety needing insect pollination between separate male and female blossoms, so plant in blocks rather than single rows for reliable fruit set. Its short time to harvest and long production history make it a forgiving choice for gardeners wanting a classic slicing cucumber without relying on modern hybrid seed.

name: Early Girl Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Early Girl is named for its ability to produce ripe tomatoes weeks earlier than standard-season varieties.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Early Girl is one of the most popular home garden tomato varieties in American history — a determinate-to-indeterminate hybrid introduced by Petoseed in 1975 that produces medium-sized (4–6 oz), globe-shaped, deep-red slicing tomatoes 50–60 days from transplant, weeks before most main-season varieties ripen. The combination of early maturity, classic tomato flavor, reliable production, and adaptability to a wide range of climates made Early Girl the best-selling tomato variety in many US markets for decades. In zone 9, Early Girl performs best in the spring window (February–June transplanting), producing the first ripe tomatoes well ahead of main-season varieties while temperatures are still moderate. The plant is a compact to medium-sized indeterminate that requires staking but is less vigorous than large-vined cherry tomatoes — a cage of 48–60 inches is usually sufficient. The classic red, round, full-flavored fruits are excellent for fresh slicing, sandwiches, and summer salads where a moderately sized, well-flavored tomato is preferred over giant beefsteak types. Good disease resistance package makes it dependable in humid Gulf South conditions.

name: Early Golden Summer Crookneck Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; Early Golden Summer Crookneck is a colonial-era heirloom squash, first listed commercially in 1828, with warty, curved-neck golden-yellow fruit.
directions: Direct sow in hills in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the danger of frost has passed. Early Golden Summer Crookneck is one of the oldest documented American squash varieties, first offered commercially by Thorburn's seed catalog in 1828 and grown in Thomas Jefferson's Monticello garden, producing bright golden-yellow, warty-skinned fruit with the classic curved neck of crookneck squash. Its early, prolific bearing and compact bush habit make it a reliable, fast-producing choice for a home vegetable garden. Harvest young, four to six inches long, for the best tenderness and flavor, picking every day or two during peak production to keep the plant setting new fruit.
sources: Monticello Thomas Jefferson Center for Historic Plants

name: Early Hakucho Edamame
plantingNote: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; Early Hakucho ripens with unusually uniform timing, suited to a single-pass harvest.
directions: Direct sow in full sun into warm soil after frost danger has passed; Early Hakucho is an extra-early, compact bush edamame maturing in just 75 days, among the earliest soybean cultivars grown for fresh eating. Its pods ripen with unusually uniform timing, making it well suited to a single efficient harvest pass rather than picking over several weeks, which is also convenient for home freezing. The beans carry a sweet, creamy flavor typical of the best edamame types; blanch pods briefly in salted water and pop the beans free to eat.

name: Early Hegari Grain Sorghum
plantingNote: Direct sow after the soil has warmed well past last frost; Early Hegari's short season also allows a second, later planting in long-summer regions.
directions: Early Hegari is an open-pollinated grain sorghum released in 1940 and valued for combining a short growing season with a compact, broad-leafed plant only 3 to 4 feet tall, making it easy to manage in a home garden bed rather than a field. Its open heads carry white grain with a pink blush, and the plant is notably drought-tolerant and tolerant of poor soils, producing sweet, juicy stalks along the way. Because it matures faster than most grain sorghums, it is a good option for gardeners with shorter summers or those wanting to fit a grain crop into a succession planting. Harvest heads once grain has reached hard dough stage and dried down, then thresh and store the seed for flour, cereal, or poultry feed.

name: Early Jade Gai Lan
plantingNote: Direct-sow 1/4 inch deep in spring for an early crop or in late summer for a fall crop; this fast, slow-bolting hybrid tolerates a wider sowing window than older gai lan strains.
directions: A fast, uniform hybrid Chinese broccoli bred for reliable slow-bolting performance across spring, summer, and fall plantings. Dark green, tender leaves and thick, juicy stalks top out with small clusters of edible white buds that taste milder and sweeter than standard broccoli. Cut the main stalk once it reaches pencil thickness and buds are just starting to open, then keep harvesting side shoots for several more weeks of production. Its speed and dependable bolt resistance make it a good choice for gardeners who want repeated gai lan harvests through an entire growing season rather than a single spring or fall flush.

name: Early Jersey Wakefield Cabbage
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Early Jersey Wakefield'
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost and transplant out 2–3 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop; in zone 8–9, also sow in fall (August–September) for a mild-winter crop, since the small, quick-maturing heads beat both spring heat and hard freezes.
directions: Set transplants 12–15 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the tight spacing and quick maturity make this variety well suited to succession planting and small-space gardens. Early Jersey Wakefield is one of the oldest cabbage varieties still in cultivation, introduced to American gardens from England in the 1840s and named for Wakefield, England, where it was developed. It forms small, dense, distinctively cone-shaped (pointed) heads of 2–3 pounds that mature earlier than nearly any other cabbage, historically prized for beating both the spring heat and cabbage-worm buildup that plague later varieties. The compact plants and short row-space needs make it a classic choice for small kitchen gardens, and its speed makes it valuable for a quick spring crop ahead of summer vegetables, or a fast fall crop in mild-winter climates. A true living heirloom with over 180 years of continuous garden use, in zone 3–9.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Early Long Purple Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant once the soil is consistently warm and nights are frost-free.
directions: Sow indoors under warm conditions and transplant into rich, well-drained soil once temperatures are reliably warm, since this heirloom is sensitive to cold snaps. Space plants generously and water evenly to keep the slender fruit from developing a bitter edge. Early Long Purple is a traditional Italian variety valued for producing its slim, curved, deep-purple fruit earlier than many other eggplant types, making it a useful choice for gardeners in shorter-season regions. Its thin skin and few seeds make it popular for frying and grilling whole.

name: Early Mizuna
plantingNote: Direct sow 3-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, and again 6-8 weeks before first fall frost; this traditional strain germinates and establishes reliably in cold soil.
directions: Scatter seed thinly over fertile, well-drained soil and cover lightly, keeping the bed evenly moist for fast, even germination. Early Mizuna is a traditional strain originating in the mountainous Kyoto region of Japan, prized for its particularly fast growth and strong cold tolerance even during germination, which allows sowing earlier in spring than most other mizuna types. It forms a loose rosette of deeply cut, feathery, mild-flavored leaves that can be cut young for salad mixes or allowed to grow larger for stir-fries and hot pot. Harvest by cutting the whole rosette an inch above the soil for quick regrowth, or pick outer leaves continuously; flavor stays mild and peppery without the bitterness that heat-stressed plants can develop.

name: Early Prolific Straightneck Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; in zone 9, plant spring crops in February–March and fall crops in August–September; summer squash is susceptible to squash vine borers in zone 9 — the fall crop planted in August often misses peak vine borer pressure and may produce more reliably than the spring planting.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Early Prolific Straightneck is the classic American yellow summer squash — the standard straightneck type that has defined the yellow summer squash category in American home gardens and commercial production for decades. The smooth, straight, medium-yellow to golden-yellow squash (6–8 inches at ideal harvest) has the classic straight-neck shape (no bulge or curve at the blossom end) that distinguishes straightneck from crookneck types. The tender, mild-flavored flesh is excellent sautéed, grilled, steamed, stuffed, and in casseroles — the standard all-purpose yellow summer squash for every culinary application. An All-America Selections winner recognized for its exceptional productive performance and consistent quality. Harvest squash when small to medium (6–8 inches) for best flavor and tenderness — oversized squash develop tough skin, large hard seeds, and coarse, watery flesh. In zone 9, summer squash is best grown in spring (February–April) and fall (August–October) — the summer heat accelerates production to the point of difficulty managing harvests. The squash vine borer is the primary pest challenge in zone 9; fall planting (August) often escapes the peak infestation period. Extremely productive — a few plants provide more squash than most families can use during peak season; succession planting at 2–3 week intervals provides more manageable quantities.

name: Early Scarlet Globe Radish
