plantingNote: Direct sow as early as soil is workable in spring; Early Scarlet Globe is one of the oldest and most widely grown spring radish varieties in American gardens — a very fast-maturing (22–28 days), perfectly round, bright scarlet-red radish with crisp white flesh, mild peppery flavor, and a slow tendency to become pithy after maturity, making it one of the most reliable and forgiving of the traditional spring radish varieties.
directions: Sow in thin rows 1/4 inch deep; no need to thin closely if sown sparsely; harvest when roots are 3/4 to 1 inch across; Early Scarlet Globe holds slightly better in the ground than some varieties without becoming immediately pithy — useful for succession plantings where exact harvest timing is impractical. Early Scarlet Globe is a foundational heirloom spring radish that has appeared continuously in American seed catalogs since the 19th century and remains one of the most widely recognized and consistently reliable spring radish varieties for home garden use. The name describes it precisely: the variety matures early, produces globe-shaped (round, not oval or elongated) roots, and has the classic bright scarlet skin color of traditional spring radishes. The roots are smooth and round, typically reaching 3/4 to 1 inch in diameter at the ideal harvest stage, with bright white, crisp, mildly peppery flesh that is refreshing and clean-flavored. Early Scarlet Globe is somewhat more forgiving than some spring radish varieties — it maintains quality for a few extra days in the ground after reaching harvest size before becoming pithy or hollow — a useful characteristic when garden timing is imprecise. Its very fast maturity (22–28 days) makes it one of the quickest-maturing vegetables a gardener can grow and ideal for teaching children about gardening: almost immediate gratification. In zone 9a and the Gulf South, Early Scarlet Globe thrives in the short cool season windows of January–March and October–November before heat forces bolting.

name: Early Scarlet Horn Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow early in cool soil; this short-rooted, fast-maturing type suits shallow or heavy soils where longer carrots struggle to form straight roots.
directions: Early Scarlet Horn is one of the oldest named carrot varieties still in circulation, a short, blunt, horn-shaped root tracing back to early French market gardens long before the longer Nantes and Imperator types were developed. Direct sow seed shallowly in cool soil in early spring, thinning seedlings to about 2 inches apart; the stubby 4 to 5 inch roots mature quickly and tolerate the shallow or stony soils that defeat longer-rooted carrots. Its small size and rapid maturity made it historically valuable for early spring crops and for forcing under frames before the ground fully warmed. Pull roots as soon as they reach usable size, since quality declines and roots can become woody if left too long in warm soil.

name: Early Snowball Cauliflower
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or sow in mid-summer for fall harvest; Early Snowball has been a mainstay of American seed catalogs since the late 1800s and remains one of the fastest, most reliable open-pollinated cauliflowers for gardeners in short-season climates.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant sturdy seedlings into rich, evenly moist soil once frost danger has passed, spacing plants 15-20 inches apart; Early Snowball is a compact, open-pollinated heirloom that has stayed popular for well over a century because it forms tight, pure-white 5-6 inch heads faster and more dependably than many modern hybrids. Tie the outer leaves loosely over the developing curd once it reaches golf-ball size to shield it from sun and keep the head bright white, checking every few days since this variety heads up quickly once it starts. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from healthy plants that are isolated from other Brassica oleracea varieties in bloom. Harvest as soon as heads reach full size and are still tight and smooth, since Early Snowball's curds loosen and turn ricey faster than slower-maturing types if left too long in the field.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee Company historical seed catalogs

name: Early Spanish Peanut
plantingNote: Direct sow shelled, raw seed once soil has warmed well past 65 degrees F; Early Spanish is the fastest-maturing common peanut type, making it a good fit for gardeners with a shorter warm season than Virginia types need.
directions: Sow shelled seed about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil, since the flower stalks (pegs) must push down into the soil after pollination to form pods underground. Early Spanish is a small-seeded, upright bunch-type peanut with a single kernel per pod more often than the two-seeded Virginia types, and it reaches maturity noticeably faster, which suits it to gardens outside the Deep South's longest growing seasons as well as within them. Mound soil gently around the base of the plants once flowering begins so pegs have an easy path into loose earth, and keep the bed evenly moist through flowering and pegging since drought at that stage sharply cuts yield. Dig the whole plant once the foliage begins to yellow, then cure the pods in a warm, airy spot for one to two weeks before shelling, boiling, or roasting.

name: Early Sunglow Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows wide for wind pollination; Early Sunglow germinates in cooler soils than most hybrid sweet corn (as low as 55°F), allowing it to be planted 1–2 weeks before standard hybrids in spring. The short (4–4.5 foot) stalks and compact habit make Early Sunglow suitable for smaller garden spaces. In zone 9, plant February–March for a May harvest as one of the first corn varieties of the season.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows; fertilize at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Early Sunglow is the gold standard of early-maturing sweet corn for home gardeners who want corn on the table as soon as possible in the season — a yellow su (standard sugary) hybrid that ripens in just 62–68 days from planting, providing corn approximately 3–4 weeks before mid-season varieties like Silver Queen. The compact (4–4.5 foot) stalks are one of Early Sunglow's most practical attributes for home gardens: shorter plants are less susceptible to lodging in wind or storms and fit better in smaller garden plots where standard 6–7 foot corn would be too tall. Early Sunglow's germination in cooler soils (down to about 55°F) also allows planting 1–2 weeks earlier in spring before soils warm fully, extending the effective growing season at the front end. The ears are smaller than mid-season varieties (6–7 inches, 12–14 rows) but are well-filled with tender, sweet, yellow kernels with the classic su corn flavor — pleasantly sweet without the overwhelming intensity of sh2 supersweet types. For gardeners in zones 4–6 with short seasons, Early Sunglow may be the only way to reliably produce sweet corn before fall frosts; in zones 7–10, it provides the season's earliest fresh corn while later varieties are still maturing.
sources: Stokes Seeds — Early Sunglow sweet corn variety description
University of Minnesota Extension — Early Sweet Corn Variety Recommendations
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Sweet Corn Maturity Comparison Chart

name: Early White Bush Scallop Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, spacing hills to give the bushy plants room to spread.
directions: This is one of the oldest American summer squash types, grown by colonial gardeners well before it was formally selected and named in the 19th century, producing the classic ivory-white, scallop-edged flying-saucer fruit. Harvest at 2-3 inches across while the rind is still soft enough to pierce with a fingernail; older fruit turns starchy and tough quickly. The compact bush habit suits small beds and containers better than vining winter squash, and steady picking every couple of days keeps the plant setting new fruit through the season. Its pale color and mild, delicate flavor make it a good choice for gardeners wanting a change from the more common yellow and green scallop types.

name: Early White Vienna Kohlrabi
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. gongylodes 'Early White Vienna'
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall through spring harvest. Kohlrabi is one of the fastest-maturing Brassica crops — ready in 45–60 days from seed. Harvest when the swollen stem reaches 2–3 inches diameter; larger sizes can become woody and fibrous. In zone 9 fall planting produces excellent quality; plants handle light frost with no damage. The rapid maturity makes kohlrabi valuable for succession planting between other slower crops. Peel the tough outer skin before eating.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Early White Vienna is the standard open-pollinated kohlrabi variety — the pale green, globe-shaped swollen stem that has defined kohlrabi's appearance in seed catalogs and markets for more than a century. Kohlrabi is among the most distinctive of all vegetables because the edible part is neither a root nor a leaf but a dramatically swollen, above-ground stem that balloons into a globe shape at the base of the plant with the leaves attached at the sides — a growth habit that surprises gardeners encountering kohlrabi for the first time. The crisp, juicy white flesh beneath the thin pale-green skin has a flavor often described as a mild, sweet, slightly broccoli-stem-flavored apple — kohlrabi is excellent eaten raw like an apple, cut into sticks for snacking and dipping, shredded into slaws, or cooked in stir-fries and soups where it retains some crunch even when heated. The flavor is far milder and sweeter than most brassicas, making kohlrabi one of the most approachable and snackable vegetables directly from the garden, particularly attractive to children who enjoy the mild sweetness and the theatrical process of peeling and eating the unusual globe.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Kohlrabi Production Guide
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Kohlrabi for Florida Gardens
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Early White Vienna Kohlrabi Description

name: Early Yellow Globe Onion
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant as soon as soil is workable; Early Yellow Globe is a long-day type suited to the Mid-Atlantic and northern growing regions.
directions: Early Yellow Globe is an American long-day heirloom introduced around 1930 and long maintained by commercial growers in New York's Orange County before entering heirloom seed networks. It forms a medium-sized, flattened-globe bulb of about two and a half to three inches with light yellow skin and firm, mildly pungent flesh suited to both cooking and winter storage. The variety is noted for resisting pink root, a common soil-borne onion disease, which has helped it remain in cultivation in the regions where that pressure is high. Start early, since its earlier maturity compared to full-season storage onions makes it a reliable choice where the growing season runs short.

name: Easter Egg Radish Blend
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall/winter/spring crops. Easter Egg radishes mature in 25–35 days and should be harvested promptly before roots become pithy in warm weather. Succession sow every 10 days for continuous harvest.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep and 1 inch apart, thinning to 2–3 inches after germination; Easter Egg is a blend of radish varieties producing a cheerful mix of purple, red, white, and pink round radishes (all similar in size to a chicken egg) in the same row — the variety gets its name from the surprise of digging mixed-color 'eggs' from the soil. Individual plants in the blend mature at slightly different rates over 2–3 weeks, naturally extending the harvest window. The crisp, mild, slightly spicy roots are excellent raw in salads, on veggie platters, or sliced and eaten with butter and salt in the classic French crudités style. This mixed-color planting is particularly popular in children's gardens for its surprise-reveal at harvest. In zone 9, fall and winter plantings (October–January) produce the crispest, mildest roots — spring radishes bolt quickly as temperatures rise. Harvest promptly when roots reach egg size; leaving them too long makes them hollow and pithy. One of the fastest and most satisfying crops for impatient gardeners.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Easter Egg Radish Blend variety notes
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Easter Egg variety
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Radish Production

name: Ebenezer Onion
plantingNote: Can also be grown from sets planted as soon as the soil is workable in spring; Ebenezer is an old long-day storage onion best suited to northern gardens with long summer daylength.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 4–6 inches apart, and keep the bed evenly moist and weed-free through bulb development. Ebenezer is a classic Dutch-derived heirloom onion, long grown in American gardens both from seed and from sets, producing firm, globe-to-slightly-flattened yellow-brown bulbs with pungent flesh and outstanding storage life compared to sweeter modern hybrids. It is one of the parent lines behind several later commercial yellow storage onions and remains popular with gardeners who want an old-fashioned, strong-flavored keeper for cooking rather than fresh eating. Stop watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall, then pull, cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot for a few weeks, and store in a cool, dry place where it will keep considerably longer than sweet onion types.

name: Ebisu Kabocha Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is consistently warm; can also be started indoors 2-3 weeks early in short-season regions and transplanted carefully to avoid root disturbance.
directions: A traditional Japanese kabocha type especially popular around Tokyo, prized for its dry, deep-yellow, chestnut-flavored flesh. Sow directly after frost danger passes, or start indoors for an earlier crop in cool climates. Vines set three to four uniform, squat globe-shaped fruits with dark green skin and faint white speckling. Harvest once the skin dulls and resists puncture, then cure in a warm location for a week or two; curing converts starches to sugars and noticeably improves flavor. Stores well for several months in a cool, dry spot.

name: Ebony Acorn Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed; the compact bush habit suits smaller gardens and needs no trellising.
directions: Ebony Acorn is an All-America Selections winner from the 1960s bred for its deep, glossy black-green rind and compact bush vines that need far less garden space than sprawling acorn types. Fruit develops the classic deeply ribbed acorn shape and matures to a dense, dry, sweet orange flesh well suited to baking or stuffing. Because the bush habit concentrates fruit near the crown, side-dress with compost partway through the season to sustain the shorter root run, and harvest once the rind hardens and resists a fingernail scratch. Cure harvested fruit in a warm, airy spot for one to two weeks before long-term storage to improve flavor and shelf life.

name: Ed's Red Shallot
plantingNote: Start true seed indoors 6-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out after hardening off; unlike most shallot varieties Ed's Red is open-pollinated and bulks up to full size from seed in a single season rather than from replanted clonal sets.
directions: Ed's Red is an open-pollinated, true-seed shallot improved by farmer-breeder Beth Rasgorshek of Nampa, Idaho, grown fresh from seed each year rather than propagated as replanted clonal sets. It produces larger-than-typical, dark crimson-skinned bulbs with mild, pink-ringed flesh, and is notably productive for a seed-grown shallot. Reduce watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall over, then lift, cure in a warm airy spot, and store; Ed's Red is prized for exceptionally long keeping, often reported to hold firm for the better part of a year. Because it is grown fresh from seed each season, it sidesteps much of the virus buildup that can shorten the vigor of old clonally propagated shallot strains.

name: Eddo Taro
plantingNote: Plant cormels or divisions after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Eddo taro is root-hardy in zone 9 and may overwinter in the ground with mulch protection, resuming growth in spring from the persistent corm. Plants grown in zone 9 can be left in the ground for multiple seasons, harvesting corms and cormels as needed without replanting.
directions: Plant cormels in moist, organically rich soil in partial shade to full sun with consistent moisture; Eddo (eddoe, eddo taro) is the small-corm type of Colocasia esculenta widely grown in the Caribbean, West Africa, and Southeast Asia for its edible corms and cormels — small, round to ovoid corms 1–2 inches across with hairy brown skin and white-to-purple-tinged starchy flesh. Unlike the large dasheen-type taro that produces a single massive central corm, eddo produces numerous small cormels clustered around a small central corm, making harvest easy — simply pull the plant and break apart the cormel cluster. The flesh is starchy and mild, with a slightly mucilaginous, creamier texture than dasheen, and is used in soups, stews, boiled as a side dish, and fried into chips throughout the African and Caribbean diaspora. The oxalic acid in raw taro requires thorough cooking; always boil or roast before eating. Eddo tolerates partial shade and moist soils and thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Edible Aroids for Florida
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Taro and Related Aroids
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Colocasia esculenta for Food Production

name: Eden's Gem Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed and all danger of frost has passed, in hills spaced to give vines room to spread.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil after frost danger has passed, spacing hills to let the compact vines spread, and water evenly while fruit is sizing. Developed at Rocky Ford, Colorado and introduced in 1905 as a descendant of the older Green Nutmeg melon, Eden's Gem produces softball-sized, heavily netted fruit with green flesh and a distinctive spicy-sweet flavor. Its early maturity made it a popular shipping melon in the early twentieth century, and it remains prized by heirloom growers for its complex flavor in a compact package.

name: Eder Kohlrabi
plantingNote: Start indoors early for the first harvest of the season; Eder's speed to maturity makes it a good choice for gardeners wanting kohlrabi before the main spring crop comes in.
directions: Eder is a fast-maturing green kohlrabi hybrid bred for an especially short time to harvest, reaching usable bulb size well ahead of standard varieties. Its compact habit and quick turnaround suit tight succession plantings or gardeners looking to slot a crop into a short cool-weather window. Pick bulbs promptly once they reach 2-3 inches across, since early types can turn woody faster than slower-maturing kohlrabi if left in the ground too long. Flesh is crisp and mild, equally good sliced raw or added to stir-fries and soups.

name: Edisto 47 Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow in sandy, well-drained soil in hills after last frost; Edisto 47 was specifically developed at the Edisto Research and Education Center in Blackville, South Carolina, for the hot, humid Southeast and has outstanding resistance to powdery mildew and other diseases that devastate most cantaloupe varieties in the Deep South.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun, well-drained sandy soil, 1–2 weeks after last frost; Edisto 47 is a Clemson University (South Carolina) heirloom cantaloupe developed in 1953 specifically for the humid, disease-pressure conditions of the Deep South where most cantaloupe varieties fail to powdery mildew, downy mildew, and Alternaria blight. It produces medium-sized (3–5 lb), oval, heavily netted fruits with thick, salmon-orange flesh of very good, rich cantaloupe flavor. The 'Edisto' name honors the Edisto Research and Education Center in Blackville, SC, and '47' the year development began. For over 50 years it was the cantaloupe of choice for Deep South gardeners because no other variety could reliably produce through summer humidity — even as newer hybrids have been developed, Edisto 47 remains a benchmark for disease resistance and regional adaptation.

name: Edmonson Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Edmonson is a vigorous, productive Southern heirloom grown for its reliable yield of blocky pickling-type fruit.
directions: Sow seed directly in warm soil after frost risk has passed, giving the vigorous vines a trellis or open ground to spread. Edmonson is a Southern heirloom pickling cucumber kept alive for generations by home gardeners who valued its heavy, dependable fruit set through hot, humid summers. Pick fruit at 3-5 inches, firm and blocky with pale green skin, checking plants daily during peak season since pickling types quickly overgrow and turn seedy if left unharvested. Its long history as a dooryard garden variety means it has had little formal breeding, so some variation in fruit shape between plants is normal and part of its heirloom character.

name: Egyptian Wheat
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil has warmed above 65°F; Egyptian Wheat is an exceptionally tall, sturdy forage sorghum type grown for biomass, screening, and wildlife habitat rather than as a food grain.
directions: Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, and thin or drill to a moderate stand since plants grow extremely tall and can shade neighboring rows. Egyptian Wheat is a tall, robust forage sorghum, despite the common name it is not a true wheat, prized for reaching 8 to 12 feet with thick, sturdy stalks and broad leaves that produce heavy summer biomass, build organic matter, and outcompete summer weeds. Its height and density make it a popular seasonal screen, windbreak, or living privacy hedge in addition to its cover-crop role, and the seed heads that follow provide valuable food for doves, quail, and songbirds through fall and winter. Mow, roll, or cut and drop the stalks at the end of the season to return biomass to the soil, or leave standing for winter wildlife cover; it is killed outright by the first hard freeze.

name: Eight Ball Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Eight Ball is a round zucchini type producing perfectly round, dark green fruits on a compact, upright bush plant. In zone 9, plant March–May and again August–September for fall production. The round form is Eight Ball's defining characteristic — rather than the elongated cylinder of standard zucchini, Eight Ball fruits are globose (round), producing a shape ideal for hollowing and stuffing. Harvest at 3–4 inches diameter (roughly golf ball to baseball size) for best flavor and tenderness; the skin toughens and the flesh becomes starchy if allowed to grow to tennis ball or softball size. Eight Ball's compact plant (18–24 inches tall) makes it excellent for raised beds and containers. The round shape also means the squash sits stably when stuffed and baked, without rolling — a practical advantage over elongated zucchini in stuffed preparations.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 18–24 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches diameter when skin is dark green and glossy. Eight Ball is a compact, round-fruited zucchini variety that produces unusually shaped globose fruits — perfectly spherical when harvested at optimal size — on upright, compact bush plants significantly smaller than standard elongated zucchini types. The name 'Eight Ball' references the eight-ball billiards ball — a solid black sphere — which the dark green, round squash resembles at small harvest size. The round form is the primary distinctive quality: while standard zucchini is selected for elongated cylindrical shape that makes it easy to slice into uniform rounds, Eight Ball's round form creates a naturally shaped container ideal for hollowing and stuffing. For stuffed squash preparations, Eight Ball provides several practical advantages: the round form creates a stable base for baking without additional support, the natural cavity when the top is removed is more generous relative to fruit size than elongated squash, and individual fruits at optimal 3–4 inch harvest size provide a single-serving portion that is visually appealing when presented whole. The flavor is typical mild zucchini with slightly denser flesh than elongated types at comparable harvest sizes — the round form concentrates more flesh relative to surface area than a cylinder of comparable diameter. Eight Ball was developed and released by Park Seed, with the AAS award confirming performance across diverse North American trial conditions.
sources: Park Seed — Eight Ball round zucchini variety development and AAS recognition
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Round and compact summer squash variety comparison
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Summer Squash Production and Variety Selection

name: Eight Ball Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, enriched soil; Eight Ball is an AAS winner round zucchini producing billiard-ball-shaped, dark green, glossy fruits ideal for stuffing whole — an outstanding novelty-and-culinary squash for the summer garden that produces prolifically on compact bush plants.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained, enriched soil; Eight Ball is a compact bush type that needs 2–3 feet of space but no support. Eight Ball is an All-America Selections award-winning round zucchini producing compact, perfectly spherical, dark green fruits 2–4 inches in diameter — essentially billiard ball-shaped summer squash with the same mild, tender, slightly sweet flavor as regular zucchini but in a form perfect for stuffing whole. Hollow them out (a melon baller works perfectly), fill with cheese, rice, meat, and herbs, and bake for a complete stuffed vegetable presentation; they hold their round shape beautifully when baked. Harvest at 2–3 inches for perfect stuffing size; larger fruits become seedy and tougher. Highly productive on compact, bushy plants; good for small-space and container gardens.

name: Eight-Row Flint Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in blocks; Eight-Row Flint is the original New England corn of the Narragansett, Wampanoag, and other Indigenous peoples of the Northeast — the corn that the Pilgrims learned to grow and which sustained early colonial New England, and the genetic ancestor of nearly all modern flour and sweet corn varieties.
directions: Sow in blocks of 4+ rows after last frost; Eight-Row Flint is earlier-maturing than most heritage corns and well-suited to shorter northern seasons. Eight-Row Flint (also called New England Flint, Rhode Island Flint, and Narragansett Flint) is the traditional corn of the Algonquian peoples of the northeastern United States — the corn that sustained the Wampanoag, Narragansett, Mohegan, and neighboring peoples for centuries before European contact, and the corn that taught early colonists of Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay how to survive in New England. It bears exactly eight rows of hard, flinty, small kernels in orange-red, white, or multi-colored patterns on slender 7–9 inch ears; the flint kernel type (hard, glass-like outer layer rather than dented) grinds into a fine, sweet, dense cornmeal. This is the corn of traditional New England johnnycakes, the grain type tested by Narragansett Flint Corn restoration projects. A critical piece of American agricultural heritage.

name: El Dorado Tropical Pumpkin Hybrid
plantingNote: Direct-sow or transplant after frost danger passes; its compact habit fits smaller garden beds better than sprawling calabaza landraces.
directions: Bred at the University of Florida as a compact-plant tropical pumpkin hybrid, this cultivar was developed to give home and market gardeners calabaza-type fruit without the space demands of traditional long-vine landraces like Seminole or La Primera. The restrained vine habit makes it a practical option for raised beds and smaller Gulf Coast plots while still tolerating the region's heat and humidity well. Harvest when the rind hardens and dulls for the best storage life.
sources: HortScience (American Society for Horticultural Science journal)

name: Elba Potato
plantingNote: A workhorse late-season variety good for containers as well as rows; plant 3-5 weeks before last frost.
directions: Bred as an improvement on Kennebec, Elba is a late-season white-skinned, white-fleshed potato producing large round tubers on medium-large plants with white flowers. It combines high late blight tolerance with high scab resistance, making it one of the more disease-resistant all-purpose potatoes available, and it sets a moderate-to-heavy crop that yields heavily overall. Its waxy mid-dry texture and good all-purpose cooking performance, plus its tolerance of container culture, make it a dependable workhorse choice for home gardens.

name: Elbe Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost risk passes; the large, leafy potato-leaf vine and heavy fruit need sturdy staking from an early age.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun once frost danger passes, staking the vigorous potato-leaf vine early to carry its heavy fruit load. Elbe takes its name from Germany's Elbe River region and was introduced to American seed savers through Seed Savers Exchange in 1997, though its original source before that is undocumented; it produces 8-12 ounce yellow-orange beefsteak fruit on a big, leafy indeterminate plant that performs especially well in cooler summer climates. The flesh is juicy and meaty with a balanced sweet-tart flavor that is milder and less acidic than a typical red beefsteak, making it a popular salad slicer. It served as a breeding parent in the Dwarf Tomato Project, crossed with Golden Dwarf Champion to found the 'Tipsy' line that produced the dwarf releases Dwarf Golden Gypsy and Dwarf Orange Cream.
sources: Dwarf Tomato Project / Patrina Nuske Small

name: Electric Onion
plantingNote: Plant sets in early autumn so plants establish before winter; Electric is a red-skinned overwintering onion bred for cold survival, giving an earlier red-onion harvest than spring planting allows.
directions: Electric is a popular overwintering red onion prized for combining the deep reddish-purple skin of a standard red onion with the earlier harvest timing of autumn-planted sets. Push sets into firmed, well-drained soil in early fall, leaving the tip exposed, and provide light winter protection only in the coldest parts of its range. Growth resumes quickly as spring days lengthen, and bulbs color up well even under the shorter, cooler growing period overwintering onions experience. Because overwintered red onions tend to be milder and slightly less firm than maincrop reds, plan to use the harvest within a few months of the early-summer lift.

name: Elinitsa Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after frost danger has passed; this early, compact Greek heirloom begins setting pods sooner than most Southern okra varieties.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep into warm soil in full sun. Elinitsa is a century-old heirloom from a small village in Greece, grown there for generations before being preserved and distributed through seed-saving networks. The spineless, slender green pods carry a mild, delicate flavor, and the plants are noticeably more compact and far less bristly or itchy to handle than many Southern okra varieties, making harvest more pleasant in the heat. It begins producing earlier than most okra, giving a head start on the summer harvest before the big Southern heirlooms hit their stride.

name: Elite Cream Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed past 65°F and all frost danger has passed; Elite's early maturity allows a Gulf Coast gardener to fit in two or more successive sowings across a long summer.
directions: Direct sow in warm, lean to moderately fertile soil, avoiding heavy nitrogen fertilizer, which pushes foliage growth at the expense of pods. Elite is a compact, bush-type open-pollinated cream southern pea prized among market growers and home gardeners for being among the heaviest-yielding of all the cream-type cowpeas, producing abundant 7-inch pods that shell easily. The small, pale cream peas cook up light in color and mild in flavor, making a classic side dish alongside cornbread. Like all cowpeas, Elite fixes nitrogen in the soil as it grows and thrives in the peak summer heat that stalls cooler-season legumes, making it a reliable, low-input crop for Gulf South vegetable gardens.
sources: Willhite Seed Company southern pea variety records
Thresh Seed Co. cowpea variety descriptions
Victory Seed Company southern pea catalog records

name: Ellen Felton Dark Collard
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. acephala 'Ellen Felton Dark'
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant for a fall crop, or sow in early spring; this variety tolerates cold down to about 20F, and light frost sweetens the leaves further.
directions: This slightly-heading collard traces to at least 1935 in Beaufort County, North Carolina, where a family seed saver grew and passed it down before it was shared with a USDA heirloom-collecting effort and later added to the Seed Savers Exchange catalog. The elliptic, wavy-to-toothed green leaves form a loosely gathered rather than open habit, distinguishing it from fully open Southern collards like Georgia Southern. Cooked leaves carry a notably sweet, faintly fruity flavor compared to more assertive collard types, and the plant handles hard cold well into the low 20s Fahrenheit.

name: Emerald Artichoke
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and hold seedlings near 50-55F for 10-14 days once several true leaves have formed to encourage reliable first-year bud set; transplant after frost danger has passed into deeply worked, fertile soil.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, richly amended soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Emerald is a spineless, dark green annual hybrid bred as a seed-grown alternative to older perennial artichoke types, forming a slightly more compact plant than some annual comparisons while still setting a good number of medium, tightly furled buds in its first season. It shares the same need for a brief cool spell after transplanting to trigger uniform first-year flowering, and it holds up well to the heat of long, dry summers once established. Keep the soil evenly moist and fertile through the growing season and harvest buds while the scales are still closed tight for the best texture.
sources: Harris Seeds -- Emerald artichoke variety description
University of California Cooperative Extension -- Artichoke Production Guide

name: Emerald Bush Buttercup Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; this compact, non-vining strain of Buttercup fits raised beds and small plots where a sprawling squash vine would not.
directions: Emerald Bush Buttercup is a compact, short-vined strain selected from classic Buttercup squash, holding the same turban shape and small blossom-end button but on a plant that stays within a few feet rather than running eight feet or more. Give it consistent moisture and full sun; because the foliage is dense and close together, watch for powdery mildew in humid climates and space plants for airflow. Fruit averages about four to five pounds with nearly black-green skin and dry, sweet, deep orange-yellow flesh well suited to baking and mashing. Cure harvested fruit at room temperature for a week or two before moving it to cool, dry storage.

name: Emerald Fire Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this disease-resistant hybrid sets fruit heavily on compact, 3-foot plants.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost. Emerald Fire sets heavy yields of extra-large, glossy, thick-walled jalapenos that resist cracking even as they mature from green to red, an AAS-winning improvement over older jalapeno types prone to splitting. The thick flesh holds up especially well to stuffing and grilling, while the compact, disease-resistant plants stay productive over a long harvest window. Pick at the deep green stage for classic jalapeno heat and crunch, or let fruit ripen to red for a sweeter, slightly milder flavor.

name: Emerald Gem Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; Emerald Gem arose as a chance seedling in a Michigan garden, was purchased and introduced by W. Atlee Burpee in 1886, and quickly became one of the most popular American muskmelons of the late 19th century for its rich, spicy-sweet flavor.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after last frost, thinning to the strongest two or three plants per hill. Emerald Gem produces small, globe-shaped, deeply ribbed fruits with smooth, dark emerald-green skin that conceals thick, richly flavored, pale orange flesh often described as having a distinctive spicy sweetness beyond typical cantaloupe. Discovered as a chance seedling in the Michigan garden of William G. Voorhees, it was purchased and introduced commercially by W. Atlee Burpee in 1886 and quickly became a benchmark variety praised for combining fine flavor with dependable, uniform type. Because the fruit is compact and matures relatively quickly for a melon, it suits shorter-season gardens; keep soil evenly moist through fruit set and harvest at full slip, when the stem releases cleanly from the vine.

name: Emerald Giant Sweet Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost; Emerald Giant is a commercial-type pepper that responds well to consistent fertility — apply a balanced fertilizer at transplanting and a calcium-containing fertilizer mid-season to prevent blossom-end rot.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after the last frost date; Emerald Giant is one of the standard large-fruited bell pepper varieties for American home and commercial gardens — producing very large (4–5 inch long, 3–4 inch wide), blocky, 4-lobed, thick-walled green bell peppers with the classic sweet bell pepper flavor and firm, crunchy flesh that defines the standard bell pepper for American cooking. The name reflects both the large fruit size ('Giant') and the deep green color at the typical fresh-market harvest stage — the brilliant, deep-green, shiny-skinned fruits are the archetypal green bell pepper form. Left to ripen fully, Emerald Giant turns red, producing a sweeter, more complex flavor than the green stage. The thick walls (3/8–1/2 inch) provide more usable pepper flesh per fruit than thin-walled types, better heat retention in cooking preparations, and superior durability at harvest. In zone 9, bell peppers produce best in the spring season (March–June) and a brief fall window (September–October) — the extended summer heat reduces fruit set and causes sunscald on exposed fruits. The large, heavy fruits on 'Emerald Giant' require staking or caging to prevent branch breakage when the plant is heavily loaded.

name: Emerald Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is reliably above 65F; plants run tall, so site where they won't shade shorter crops.
directions: Bred by Campbell Soup Company in 1950 from a cross of several classic okra lines specifically to hold color and texture through canning, still a good choice for anyone processing okra rather than just eating it fresh. Pods stay tender even at 4-5 inches, which forgives missed picking days in a hot Gulf Coast August. It is drought-tolerant once established despite its warm-season water needs during fruit set.

name: Emerite Filet Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to 60°F; Emerite is a French pole-type filet bean (haricot vert) producing slender round pods (under 0.25 inch diameter) at pencil-thin harvest stage of 4–6 inches. The pole habit (to 5–6 feet) requires trellis support but produces far more heavily and over a much longer period than bush filet types. Harvest daily or every other day at pencil-thin stage for the finest texture; pods become starchy and coarse within 2–3 days of reaching optimal harvest size. Emerite is one of the most productive filet pole beans available, making it a practical choice for gardeners who want restaurant-quality haricots verts without the heavy labor input of bush varieties that must be replanted every 2–3 weeks.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart; provide trellis or pole support to 6 feet and harvest every 1–2 days when pods reach 4–5 inches and are no thicker than a pencil. Emerite Filet Bean is a French-bred pole-type haricot vert that delivers the classic thin-podded, tender filet bean quality of French cuisine on a vigorous climbing plant that produces heavily over months rather than the 2–3-week harvest window of bush filet types. The haricot vert category — defined by pod diameter under 6mm and harvest at pencil-thin stage before any internal seed development is visible — requires frequent harvesting to maintain pod quality; pods left on the plant for even an extra day begin to develop seeds and shift from the tender, fine-textured filet bean to a coarser snap bean. This harvesting discipline rewards with pods of extraordinary tenderness: lightly steamed for 3–4 minutes, Emerite haricots verts have a delicate, slightly squeaky texture and refined mild flavor that is categorically different from mature-harvested snap beans. Pole-type filet beans like Emerite provide a practical advantage over bush types for home production: a single planting in spring can continue producing through fall in zone 9 (with a brief mid-summer slowdown during peak heat), whereas bush filet varieties exhaust themselves within 2–3 weeks and require successive plantings every 3 weeks to maintain a continuous harvest. The climbing habit also improves air circulation around pods in the humid Gulf Coast environment, reducing the fungal disease pressure that can limit bush bean production in midsummer heat and humidity. Blanch harvested pods in salted boiling water for 2–3 minutes, shock in ice water to set the bright green color, then serve simply with butter, lemon, and salt to showcase the delicate flavor.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Emerite Filet Pole Bean variety notes and harvest timing for haricot vert production
Fedco Seeds — French pole filet bean varieties for extended season production
Vilmorin-Andrieux, 'The Vegetable Garden' (English translation) — French haricot vert bean culture and variety selection

name: Endurance Lablab
plantingNote: Direct sow 1-1.5 inches deep after soil has warmed well past last frost and inoculate seed with a cowpea-type Rhizobium; Endurance's weakly perennial habit means an established stand in mild Gulf Coast winters can resprout from the crown the following spring instead of needing full replanting.
directions: Endurance was bred by crossing the widely grown forage cultivar Rongai with a vigorous wild perennial accession from Zimbabwe (CPI 24973), then released as a weakly perennial lablab selection for tropical and subtropical forage systems. Unlike standard annual lablab cultivars, established Endurance stands can regrow from the crown into a second and even third growing season after grazing, mowing, or cutting, provided winters stay mild, making it a candidate for reduced-replanting cover cropping in zone 9 and warmer. It climbs and sprawls vigorously, fixes nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis, and produces heavy biomass valued for grazing, green manure, or trellised summer cover in the Gulf South. Because true commercial seed supply is limited compared to Rongai or Highworth, gardeners wanting Endurance may need to source it through tropical forage seed banks or university research collections.

name: Enorma Runner Bean
plantingNote: Sow at the base of a tall, sturdy trellis or obelisk around last frost; runner beans prefer cool summer nights and drop flowers in intense heat.
directions: Enorma is a long-established British exhibition runner bean, holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit, prized by show growers for its extremely long, smooth, slender pods that can reach 20 inches under good conditions. Bright scarlet flowers cover the vigorous vines early and heavily, drawing hummingbirds and bumblebees and setting an abundant crop over a long season. Pods are best picked well before they reach exhibition length for eating quality, since very long pods used for showing tend to be tougher and more fibrous. Give it a tall, sturdy support, since well-fed plants can climb well over 8 feet.

name: Enorma Scorzonera
plantingNote: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep as early as 2-4 weeks before last frost into deeply worked, loose soil free of stones so roots can grow long and straight.
directions: Enorma is a market-grower favorite scorzonera variety producing long, straight, black-skinned roots averaging 9-11 inches long with a rich, savory, mildly sweet flavor often compared to oysters or artichoke hearts. Direct sow thinly in deeply cultivated soil, since the long taproots need unobstructed depth to size up properly, and thin to final spacing once seedlings have their first true leaves. Water consistently through summer and fall. Harvest roots in autumn or leave them in the ground through winter for an even sweeter spring harvest; the tender young shoots and flower buds that emerge in spring are also edible.

name: Ensoro Ewia Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; this Ashanti heirloom scarlet eggplant from Ghana tolerates drought and heat better than most Solanum melongena types, so it rewards a long, hot warm season.
directions: Ensoro Ewia is a drought- and heat-tolerant scarlet eggplant grown for generations by Ashanti farmers in Ghana, where seed keepers describe a history stretching back more than a century and a half. Start seed indoors and transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 60F, since this African eggplant relative shrugs off prolonged heat that stresses standard garden eggplant. Plants build a sturdy, bushy frame and respond well to frequent picking; harvest fruit once it turns firm and reaches its full mature color, since lingering too long on the plant lets the flesh turn bitter and seedy. The line has grown scarce in its home region, so growing it out and saving seed helps keep this old Ghanaian strain in circulation.

name: Enterprise Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70°F; Enterprise is a hybrid zucchini bred for resistance to a broad package of common cucurbit mosaic viruses, an important advantage in aphid-prone Gulf South gardens where virus pressure often shortens the summer squash season.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Enterprise is a hybrid zucchini bred for resistance to a broad spectrum of the mosaic viruses that commonly spread through squash plantings via aphids, keeping foliage healthier and fruit better colored later into a humid Gulf South summer than more virus-susceptible varieties. The compact, open bush habit produces uniform, dark green cylindrical fruit that is easy to spot and harvest as the plant fills in. Pick fruit at 6-8 inches for the best texture and flavor, checking plants daily during peak production since summer squash quickly grows oversized and tough if missed for even a couple of days.

name: Envy Edamame
plantingNote: Sow after last frost when soil has reached at least 60°F; Envy is one of the earliest-maturing edamame cultivars available and tolerates cooler soil at planting better than many other edamame varieties, allowing an earlier sowing date in spring.
directions: Sow seed 1 to 1.5 inches deep in rows 18–24 inches apart in full sun; inoculate with soybean-specific rhizobium inoculant for best nitrogen fixation. Envy is a widely grown edamame cultivar valued for its notably early maturity — among the fastest edamame varieties to reach harvest — and for better cold-soil tolerance at planting than many other edamame types, making it a good choice for gardeners wanting the earliest possible edamame crop or a second planting for fall harvest. Plants are compact and productive, with pods clustering densely on relatively short, sturdy bushes. Harvest when pods are bright green, plump, and fully filled but before the shell begins to yellow — sample a pod for tenderness and flavor to judge exact timing. For the classic preparation, boil or steam whole pods briefly in well-salted water, then squeeze the beans directly from the pod to eat; pods themselves are fibrous and not eaten.

name: Epic Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Epic carries resistance to tobacco mosaic virus and is specifically recommended for Florida and Texas growing conditions, making it a solid choice for Gulf Coast eggplant growers.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date, once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Epic is a vigorous, high-yielding hybrid eggplant carrying resistance to tobacco mosaic virus and is specifically recommended by Southern extension programs for Florida and Texas growing conditions. It produces large, classic glossy black-purple, oval fruit on a sturdy, well-branched plant that holds up well to summer heat. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and the fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure — dull skin and hard flesh signal overripe fruit with more seeds and a bitter edge. Keep picking regularly through the season to encourage continued flowering and fruit set, and provide consistent moisture, since eggplant grown under drought stress tends to develop tougher skin and more bitterness.
sources: seed catalog reference (Osborne Seed Company, Jung Seed)
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Eggplant Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Eggplant Variety Selection

name: Erbette Chard
plantingNote: In mild-winter regions sow in early fall for a winter-into-spring harvest; elsewhere direct sow around the last frost date.
directions: Broadcast or row sow seed clusters thickly and shallowly, since this type is grown for its abundant tender leaves rather than for large stalks. This unusual Italian chard lacks the thick, wide ribs of standard Swiss chard, instead producing slender stems and smooth, spinach-like leaves that regrow quickly after cutting. Favored by cooks for its mild flavor and quick-cooking texture, it tolerates both cool weather and mild heat better than many leafy greens, making it useful for extended cutting through a Gulf Coast winter.

name: Erfurter Mairübchen
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring; Mairübchen ('May turnip') is bred for fast growth to a small, tender root rather than a large storage turnip.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep directly in the garden as soon as the soil can be worked, thinning seedlings to 2-4 inches apart. Erfurter Mairübchen is a fast-maturing German heirloom turnip from Erfurt, long one of Germany's principal centers of vegetable seed growing, bred to produce small, round, white-skinned roots suited to a quick early-spring harvest rather than long storage. Pull roots while still small and young, since the mild, sweet flavor and tender texture this variety is prized for both coarsen quickly once roots size up in warming weather. Young roots are good raw, briefly braised, or added whole to spring vegetable soups along with their tender greens.

name: Erlene's Green Cotton
plantingNote: Direct sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep once soil has thoroughly warmed well past last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Erlene's Green is a naturally green-lint heirloom selection of upland cotton and needs the same long, hot, frost-free season as any cotton.
directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the growing season is reliably warm, following standard upland cotton culture. Erlene's Green is a Southern heirloom naturally colored cotton, maintained and passed down by home seed savers, that produces sage-green lint instead of the usual white -- part of the same tradition of naturally pigmented cottons that inspired the modern Foxfibre breeding work reviving colored cotton for eco-conscious textile spinning. Pale yellow, hibiscus-like flowers fade to pink before dropping, and bolls split open at maturity to reveal soft green fiber that is prized by hand-spinners and fiber artists for producing yarn and cloth that needs no dye. Pick bolls promptly once open, since color and fiber quality can both fade with prolonged weather exposure, and rotate the planting site yearly to limit soil-borne disease buildup as with any cotton.

name: Eros Asparagus
plantingNote: Set crowns into a 6-8 inch deep trench as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, backfilling progressively through the season.
directions: Eros rounds out the trio of early Rutgers all-male supermale hybrids bred from crosses with the 'Rutgers Beacon' and related male lines, predating the better-known Jersey series. Like its siblings Atlas and Apollo, it directs all of its energy into spear production rather than seed set, giving heavier early yields than older open-pollinated Mary Washington-type strains. Give the crowns two full seasons to build a root system before any harvest, then cut spears daily during the flush to keep the plant signaling new growth. A well-maintained Eros bed rewards gardeners with a productive asparagus patch for fifteen years or more.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

name: Escamillo Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Escamillo is an early-maturing Corno di Toro-type Italian frying pepper that colors up to gold well before most sweet peppers finish ripening.
directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Escamillo is an AAS-winning Italian frying-type sweet pepper producing long, tapered, elegantly curved fruits that ripen unusually early from green to a rich golden yellow, giving a full harvest of fully ripe, sweetest-stage peppers well before many other sweet pepper varieties finish coloring. Fruits are thin-walled and sweet, excellent sautéed or grilled as well as eaten fresh, and the plant is productive and reasonably compact for a frying-pepper type. Stake plants loosely if fruit load bends the branches, and harvest continuously once fruits reach full gold color to keep new peppers setting.
sources: All-America Selections — Escamillo Pepper winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Esmee Arugula
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost; sow every 2 weeks for a continuous supply, and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed thinly in fertile, well-drained soil and keep evenly moist to slow bolting; Esmee is a fast, cold-tolerant arugula with deeply lobed, rounded oakleaf-shaped foliage that is fluffier and more ruffled than standard salad arugula, giving noticeably more visual loft in a mixed salad bowl. Its flavor leans nutty and mild rather than sharply peppery, making it approachable for gardeners and eaters who find standard rocket too pungent. Harvest baby leaves as early as three weeks for salad mixes, or let plants grow on for a fuller-size cutting at about six weeks. Like all arugula it bolts quickly in heat, so it performs best as an early spring or fall crop.

name: Espanola Improved Chile
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Espanola Improved was specifically bred for the short, cool growing season of north-central New Mexico's high-altitude valleys, so it reaches usable green-chile size faster than most New Mexico types and suits gardeners in shorter-season northern or high-elevation regions.
directions: Espanola Improved was released by New Mexico State University in 1984 as an early-maturing red chile bred for the shorter growing season and higher elevation of the Espanola Valley north of Santa Fe, where standard New Mexico chiles often fail to reach full red maturity before fall frost. The medium-length, tapered pods carry mild-to-medium heat and are traditionally harvested green for roasting or left on the plant to ripen fully red for the dried red chile ristras the region is known for. Compared to longer-season New Mexico cultivars, Espanola Improved sets fruit earlier and matures its red crop reliably even where the frost-free window is tight, making it a good choice for gardeners at altitude or in northern climates who still want authentic New Mexico chile flavor. Provide full sun, even moisture, and a warm start, since fruit set benefits from getting plants established as early as safely possible after the last frost.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute
New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension

name: Espelette Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Espelette is the Basque Country's PDO (Protected Designation of Origin) chile pepper, grown in the Espelette region of southwest France since Basque explorers brought capsicums from the Americas in the 16th century and now the defining spice of Basque cuisine.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed. Piment d'Espelette is the unique chile pepper of the Espelette commune and neighboring villages in the Pays Basque region of southwest France and northern Spain, where it holds PDO (Appellation d'Origine Protégée) status — meaning the authentic product can only come from that specific area. The elongated, 3–5 inch, initially green peppers ripen to brilliant red and are traditionally strung in long chains and dried in the mountain air; the resulting dried, ground powder has a distinctive mild-to-medium heat (1,500–4,000 SHU), sweet pepper aroma, and earthy-fruity flavor that is unlike any other pepper spice. Used to season virtually all savory foods in Basque cooking in place of black pepper — on eggs, fish, piperade, axoa (veal stew), chicken basquaise, and fromage de brebis (Basque sheep cheese). Grow in any warm garden; the fresh peppers have excellent flavor even without the Basque drying climate.
sources: Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualité (INAO) France
Dave DeWitt's The Chile Pepper Encyclopedia

name: Essex Hybrid Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after soil has warmed; this rare 1880s New England heirloom is a natural turban-Hubbard cross and needs a full warm season to fully harden its thick rind.
directions: Essex Hybrid dates to an 1880s New England seed catalog description as a natural cross between a turban squash and a Hubbard, combining the turban's rounded shape with the Hubbard's tough, heavily warted rind in a bright orange-red skin. Once a popular fall display squash in the Northeast, it faded from commerce and now survives mainly through small heirloom seed savers, so seed can be harder to source than mainstream Hubbard types. Grow it exactly as you would any vining Cucurbita maxima, giving the sprawling plant six to eight feet of room and steady moisture through fruit set. The dense, sweet flesh cooks well for pies and mashing, and the thick, warty rind makes it an excellent long-term keeper once cured.
sources: historical J.J.H. Gregory & Son seed catalog references

name: Estamino Rootstock Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors early alongside a favorite scion variety; graft the two together once stems are pencil-thick, heal in a humid shaded chamber, then transplant after frost into full sun.
directions: This vigorous interspecific hybrid rootstock is grown to be grafted onto a favorite tomato scion variety rather than eaten itself, valued for a somewhat more moderate, better-balanced vigor than the extremely aggressive Maxifort rootstock, making it a popular choice where growers want the disease resistance and yield benefits of grafting without excessive vegetative growth crowding out fruit production. It carries strong resistance to fusarium and verticillium wilts, corky root rot, and nematodes, and its more restrained root vigor compared to Maxifort suits closer plant spacing or shorter growing seasons where overly rampant rootstock growth would be a liability. Start rootstock and scion seed together indoors, graft when stems are pencil-thick, heal grafted plants in a humid, shaded chamber for about a week, then harden off and transplant after frost into full sun with sturdy support.

name: Estate Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant after danger of frost; plan for a tall 6-7 foot vine needing sturdy staking or caging.
directions: Estate is a Wild Garden Seed farm original built from three generations of on-farm crossing: Stupice x Homestead was later crossed with the disease-tolerant Peron Sprayless, combining cool-climate reliability with good flavor. The result is a smooth, round, 3 to 3.5 inch fruit with large juice-filled locules and a meaty interior that holds up well for slicing. Vines grow tall, to 6-7 feet, so plan for sturdy staking or a cage system from the start. Give it full sun and even watering through fruit set to avoid cracking on the smooth skin.

name: Eston Green Lentil
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring a few weeks ahead of the last frost, since young lentil plants tolerate light frost and grow best through a long cool stretch before summer heat sets in.
directions: Released by the University of Saskatchewan's Crop Development Centre and long grown across the Canadian and northern U.S. prairies, Eston is the classic small, green-seeded lentil behind most grocery-store green lentils sold in North America. The low, wiry, bushy plants need lean soil and minimal fertility, since excess nitrogen pushes foliage at the expense of pods, and they hold up well to the light frosts common during early spring establishment. The small round seeds keep a firm bite and hold their shape better than red lentils when simmered, making them well suited to soups, pilafs, and salads. Harvest the whole plant once most pods have dried and rattle, then thresh and clean before storing the seed in a cool, dry place.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Crop Development Centre

name: Etna Runner Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed, and set poles or a trellis at planting time; can be picked young as a snap bean or left to mature for dry shelling beans.
directions: Etna is an Italian heirloom runner bean grown for its solid, glossy black-seeded pods, a striking departure from the mottled reds and pinks typical of most runner bean varieties. Grown as a dual-purpose bean, young pods can be picked and cooked like a broad snap bean while the surface is still tender, or left on the vine to mature into fully dried black shelling beans with a rich, dense flavor suited to long-simmered pots. As with other runner beans, give the vigorous climbing vines tall support and steady moisture, since pod set falters in hot, dry conditions. Allow pods intended for drying to turn brown and papery on the vine before harvest.

name: Eureka Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65F; harvest young for pickling or let size up for fresh eating.
directions: An early, very productive dual-purpose hybrid, good fresh-eating at full size or pickled younger, carrying an unusually broad disease-resistance package covering angular leaf spot, anthracnose, downy and powdery mildew, scab, and several mosaic viruses. That breadth of resistance is a real asset in Gulf Coast summers, where several of these diseases overlap and often end a cucumber planting by midsummer.
sources: LSU AgCenter / Seeds to Success - Recommended Cucumber Varieties for Louisiana

name: Eva Purple Ball Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Eva Purple Ball is noted for holding up well in hot, humid conditions and shows useful foliar disease tolerance in the garden.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil, staking the indeterminate vines as they grow. Eva Purple Ball traces to Germany's Black Forest region in the late 1800s and was carried to New Jersey by the Bratka family, producing smooth, round, rosy-pink fruit of five to seven ounces with a sweet, well-balanced flavor. Gardeners in hot, humid regions especially value it for staying productive and relatively blemish-free when many other heirlooms struggle with disease pressure.

name: Evangeline Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips in warm soil after last frost when soil reaches 65F; Evangeline was bred at the LSU AgCenter as an earlier-maturing, crack-resistant alternative to Beauregard and performs especially well in Louisiana's heavy, sometimes wet clay soils where standard varieties are prone to splitting.
directions: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, sandy-loam soil in full sun after last frost; Evangeline is an LSU AgCenter release named for the Cajun heroine of Longfellow's poem and bred to match Beauregard's rich orange flesh and copper skin while ripening slightly earlier and resisting the growth cracking that Beauregard develops in wet Louisiana clay. Vines are moderately compact, and roots are uniform, smooth-skinned, and store well. Flavor is sweet and moist, excellent baked, mashed, or roasted. Because it matures a week or two earlier than Beauregard, Evangeline is a good choice for gardeners wanting an earlier harvest window or extra insurance against fall frost. Cure roots at 80-85F and high humidity for about a week after digging to heal skins and concentrate sugars, then store in a cool, dark, well-ventilated spot.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Evangeline sweet potato release notes
Mississippi State University Extension — Sweet Potato Variety Trials

name: Even' Star Ice-Bred Collards
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. viridis 'Even' Star Ice-Bred'
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting and set out in late summer to fall so the crop is maturing as hard freezes arrive; this landrace was developed by repeatedly selecting survivors of severe Mid-Atlantic winter freezes, so it performs best when allowed to stand through cold rather than being harvested young.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously to allow air movement through the dense winter canopy. This is a farmer-bred landrace rather than a fixed variety, so individual plants show some variation in leaf shape and color, a trait intentionally preserved because it broadens genetic resistance to hard freezes. Repeated exposure to temperatures well below freezing triggers a marked increase in sweetness as the plant converts stored starches to sugars for cold protection, so flavor peaks after the first several freeze events rather than at first harvest. Because the strain was selected under working-farm winter conditions rather than in a breeding trial, gardeners should expect a rougher, more variable-looking plant than commercial hybrids in exchange for exceptional cold survival.
sources: Even' Star Organic Farm variety notes

name: Evergreen Hardy White Bunching Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for a fall crop; this bunching onion does not form a bulb and is exceptionally cold-hardy, often overwintering in the ground to provide scallions the following spring even in fairly cold climates.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; unlike bulbing onions, this classic bunching onion (Welsh onion type) never forms a true bulb, instead producing clusters of straight, white-shanked scallions with mild, tender green tops. Its exceptional cold hardiness lets it overwinter in the ground in many climates, providing an extra-early harvest the following spring, and it can be cut back repeatedly through the growing season for a continuous supply. Because it multiplies by division at the base, an established clump can be divided every year or two to keep plantings vigorous and productive.

name: Evertender Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed well after last frost; Evertender's spineless pods make repeat picking easier through a long harvest season.
directions: Evertender is a spineless hybrid okra bred for pods that stay tender and stringless days longer than most varieties, reducing the pressure to pick every single day to avoid tough, fibrous pods. The smooth, spineless pods and foliage also make harvest far more comfortable, since typical okra plants are covered in fine irritating spines. Direct sow after the soil has warmed, since okra germinates poorly in cool, wet ground, and pick pods at 3-4 inches for the most tender eating. Its extended tenderness window makes Evertender a practical choice for gardeners who can only harvest okra every few days rather than daily.

name: Excel Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; a North Carolina State University release bred for high yield and broad disease resistance, useful where nematodes, stem rot, or internal cork have been problems for other varieties.
directions: Excel has light copper skin over orange flesh and is noted for out-yielding Jewel by roughly 15% in North Carolina State University trials. It carries strong resistance to southern root-knot nematode, stem rot (Fusarium wilt), and internal cork, making it a dependable choice for gardens with a history of these problems. Baking and canning quality are considered excellent, and roots store well after curing. Flavor and texture are comparable to other classic moist, orange-fleshed dessert-type sweet potatoes.

name: Exclamation Watermelon
plantingNote: Seedless triploid; start indoors or transplant after soil is thoroughly warm, and plant alongside a seeded pollenizer watermelon for fruit set. Exclamation carries intermediate resistance to Fusarium wilt race 1 and anthracnose race 1, and was bred to reduce hollow heart, a common quality defect in large seedless melons grown in Southern heat.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Exclamation is a full-season seedless watermelon hybrid bred with intermediate resistance to Fusarium wilt race 1 and anthracnose race 1, along with reduced tendency toward hollow heart, a cracking defect that can hollow out the center of large seedless melons grown under Southern heat stress. Because triploid seedless varieties need a seeded pollenizer nearby for fruit set, plant a compatible pollenizer variety in the same bed. It produces large, blocky, crimson-fleshed fruit with excellent sweetness and firm texture. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned.
sources: seed catalog reference (Rupp Seeds, Stokes Seeds)

name: Explosive Ember Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55F; Explosive Ember is bred for compact hanging baskets and containers as much as garden beds.
directions: Explosive Ember is an ornamental pepper bred as a companion to the popular Black Pearl variety, distinguished by bright purple young foliage and white-and-purple flowers rather than Black Pearl's near-black leaves. Its slender, upright, conical fruit emerges a vivid neon purple and ripens through orange to red, often showing all three colors in the same cluster for a long-lasting, ever-changing display. The fruit carries genuine heat in the tabasco-to-cayenne range, roughly 30,000 Scoville units, and while technically edible it is grown almost entirely for ornamental impact in beds, containers, and hanging baskets. Plants stay compact and well-branched without pinching, tolerate summer heat well, and continue setting new fruit clusters over a long season with routine watering and light monthly feeding.
sources: Proven Winners — Capsicum ornamental pepper series descriptions

name: Extra Dwarf Pak Choi
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed thinly and shallowly, about 1/4 inch deep, in fertile soil; also excellent for fall sowing six weeks before first frost.
directions: Direct-sow seed thinly and shallowly, about 1/4 inch deep, in fertile soil, since this miniature pak choi matures in as little as 30 days and can be grown at very tight spacing for dense baby-green production. Its curled, glossy dark-green leaves sit atop short, thick white petioles, giving each plant a compact, rounded form even smaller than standard baby bok choy. Because it thrives across a wide range of temperatures, it can be succession-sown nearly year-round in mild climates for continuous harvests of whole tender plants used raw, steamed, or stir-fried.

name: Extra Early Blackeye Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep once soil has thoroughly warmed after last frost; cowpeas germinate poorly in cold ground.
directions: Extra Early Blackeye is a fast-maturing selection within the classic blackeye cowpea group, historically valued for reaching harvest noticeably sooner than standard blackeye types, an advantage for gardeners working within a short frost-free window or wanting an early flush of black-eyed peas. Direct sow seed into warm, well-drained soil after all danger of frost has passed, since cowpeas germinate poorly in cold ground. Plants carry the familiar cream-white, black-eyed seed in slender pods on compact, semi-bush vines that need little to no staking. Extra Early Blackeye has been used as breeding stock in university cowpea improvement programs, including as one of the parent lines of the disease-resistant Magnolia Blackeye released by Mississippi State University.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension Service — Southern Pea Variety Recommendations
USDA National Genetic Resources Program — cowpea germplasm records

name: Extra Long Handled Dipper Gourd
plantingNote: Nick or file the hard seed coat and soak overnight before sowing to speed germination; this selection is bred for necks reaching two to three feet, so a tall overhead trellis is essential for straight handles rather than the curled shapes that form when fruit trails on the ground.
directions: This selection of Lagenaria siceraria is bred specifically for exceptionally long, slender necks that can stretch two to three feet, far exceeding the handle length of a typical dipper gourd. Provide an overhead arbor or fence at least eight feet tall so the developing handle hangs straight down under its own weight instead of curling on the ground. The large white flowers open in early evening and are pollinated mainly by moths, so hand-pollinating with a soft brush at dusk improves fruit set where night pollinators are scarce. Let fruit remain on the vine until the stem shrivels and the shell turns hard, then cure the gourds in a warm, airy space for one to several months until they feel light and the seeds rattle before cleaning and finishing them as dippers or ladles.

name: Extra Precoce a Grano Violetto Fava Bean
scientificName: Vicia faba 'Extra Precoce a Grano Violetto'
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter or earliest spring, or in autumn in mild-winter regions for an overwintered crop; this Italian strain is bred to mature notably faster than standard favas.
directions: Long grown in home gardens across Liguria and Tuscany, this heirloom takes its name from its dark violet-to-near-black seed coat and its notably early maturity compared to standard English broad beans. Sow directly into cool, fertile soil in blocks so the sturdy stems support one another, and pinch the growing tips once the lowest pods have set to slow aphid buildup. Pods can be picked young for fresh shelling, but many Italian cooks let a portion dry fully on the plant, since the violet seed coat holds its color and the beans store and cook well for soups and purees. Because it matures earlier than most fava strains, it suits gardeners with a short cool season or those looking to free the bed for a following summer crop.

name: Eye of the Goat Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-drained soil; Eye of the Goat (Ojo de Cabra) is a traditional Mexican and Southwestern heirloom bean with striking beige seeds marked by a tan-ringed dark eye — one of the most beautiful and flavor-rich heirloom beans in the Southwestern tradition.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost in warm, well-drained to dry soil; Eye of the Goat is adapted to dry conditions and does well with minimal supplemental irrigation in zones 7–11 once established. Eye of the Goat (Ojo de Cabra) is a traditional Mexican heirloom dry bean with large, oval, cream-to-beige seeds marked with a distinct tan 'eye' or ring surrounding a dark hilum — resembling, as the name suggests, the eye of a goat. This bean has been grown in Mexico and the American Southwest for generations and is particularly heat- and drought-tolerant, making it valuable in hot, dry climates. When cooked, the seeds have a rich, earthy, slightly sweet flavor with a creamy texture that holds its shape well; excellent in soups, stews, and as refried beans in traditional Mexican cooking. An outstanding heirloom for Gulf Coast and Southwest gardeners who need a reliable dry bean in hot, occasionally dry summers.

name: Faba Asturiana Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed after last frost; this tall climbing type benefits from a sturdy trellis or pole support.
directions: Faba Asturiana is a large, flat, creamy-white kidney-shaped dry bean grown in Asturias, Spain, where it is protected as the regional PGI 'Faba Asturiana' and forms the base of the traditional stew fabada asturiana. Plants are tall, indeterminate climbers that need a strong trellis or tall poles to support vigorous vines through the season. Leave pods on the plant until fully dry and papery before shelling, then store the smooth white seeds in a cool, dry place. The thin skin and creamy texture make it prized for slow-simmered bean stews with pork and sausage.
sources: EU eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register — Faba Asturiana PGI
Fabada asturiana / Fabes de la Granja (regional food heritage documentation)

name: Facing Heaven Pepper
