plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 Facing Heaven can be grown as a perennial, producing prolifically for multiple seasons from the same plant when protected from hard frost. Harvest fruits at the red stage for fresh use or drying; dried Facing Heaven peppers are essential in many Sichuan and Hunan dishes.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 78–85°F; Facing Heaven pepper (朝天椒, Cháo Tiān Jiāo, meaning 'facing heaven pepper') is one of the foundational chili pepper varieties of Chinese cuisine — a small to medium-sized (1.5–2.5 inch), bright red, upward-pointing hot pepper produced in prolific clusters where each plant can carry 50–100 fruits simultaneously, the upward orientation giving the variety its evocative name as the fruits point skyward like tiny flaming torches. The peppers are hot (30,000–70,000 Scoville units), with a clean, direct heat and a characteristic bright, slightly fruity flavor that is distinct from Mexican or Caribbean chiles — a flavor that has made this pepper type essential in the cooking of Sichuan, Hunan, Yunnan, and Guizhou provinces, where it appears in red oil (hóng yóu), chili pastes, dried whole peppers for stir-fries, and fermented condiments like dòubànjiàng. The dried bright red fruits maintain excellent color and retain their heat well; they are often dry-roasted in oil with Sichuan peppercorns as the starting point for the characteristic ma-la (numbing-hot) flavor profile of Sichuan cooking. Very productive in the Gulf South's warm climate, producing abundantly from midsummer through fall.
sources: Kitazawa Seed Company — Asian pepper guide
Sichuan Agricultural University publications on regional chile varieties
USDA National Plant Germplasm System — Capsicum annuum accessions

name: Faerie Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed; Faerie was bred by Known-You Seed Company and named a 2012 All-America Selections winner for its creamy yellow, thin-striped rind, sweet pink-red flesh, and unusually compact vines that suit smaller gardens.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after last frost, or start indoors 2-3 weeks earlier for a head start in cooler climates; vines are notably more restrained than most watermelons, spreading to roughly 10-11 feet rather than sprawling widely. Faerie was bred by Taiwan's Known-You Seed Company and named a 2012 All-America Selections winner for its distinctive creamy yellow rind marked with thin light stripes, enclosing crisp, high-sugar pink-red flesh, and for producing a heavy set of personal-size, 4-6 lb oval fruit on a comparatively space-efficient plant. Keep soil consistently moist through flowering and fruit set, then ease back as melons near maturity. Harvest by watching the ground spot shift from white to creamy yellow and the nearby tendril dry and brown, since the pale rind makes color-based ripeness cues less obvious than on dark-skinned watermelons.

name: Fagiola di Venanzio Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after frost danger has passed; grown traditionally as a bush dry bean in Tuscan kitchen gardens.
directions: Fagiola di Venanzio is a small, flattened, mostly white heirloom dry bean cultivated since the mid-19th century near Murlo in the Siena province of Tuscany, Italy. Its very thin seed coat makes it notably quick-cooking and easily digestible once shelled and dried. Harvest pods after they have fully dried and yellowed on the plant, then thresh and store the seeds in a sealed container. The variety has drawn scientific interest for the antioxidant and polyphenol content of its seed extracts.
sources: Finetti et al., 'Phaseolus vulgaris L. var. Venanzio Grown in Tuscany,' Antioxidants journal

name: Fagiolo del Purgatorio Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; this is a compact bush type, so no poles or trellis are needed.
directions: Fagiolo del Purgatorio is a small, thin-skinned white heirloom bean traditionally grown around Gradoli on the shores of Lake Bolsena in Lazio, where it takes its name from the Lenten custom of eating the beans, plain and unadorned, as a form of penance in the weeks before Easter. The tiny, nearly translucent-skinned seeds cook quickly to a smooth, creamy texture without an overnight soak. Grow as a compact bush bean with no staking required, and harvest pods once they have dried and rattle on the plant. Thresh and cure the beans a further week indoors before sealing them away for storage.
sources: Region of Lazio agricultural heritage crop records

name: Fagiolo della Regina di Gorga Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed; a vigorous climbing type traditionally hand-sown in early summer and trained on tall poles.
directions: Fagiolo della Regina di Gorga is a pearlescent white, rounded-to-oval heirloom bean grown in the Cilento area of Campania, Italy, around the hamlet of Gorga, and recognized as a Slow Food Presidio in 2018. Vines are vigorous climbers that can exceed several meters in height and need tall, sturdy support. Pods can be harvested green for fresh eating or left to dry fully on the plant before threshing and storing the thin-skinned, quick-cooking seeds. The bean is valued locally for its tenderness, rapid cooking time, and high digestibility.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Fagiolo della Regina di Gorga Presidio
Italian Wikipedia — Fagiolo della Regina di Gorga

name: Fagiolo di Controne Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; grown traditionally on the terraced slopes of the Alburni mountains in Campania, so a sunny, well-drained hillside bed or raised bed suits it well.
directions: Controne bean is a small, ivory-white heirloom grown for centuries on the terraced slopes around Controne in Campania and recognized as a Slow Food Presidium variety. Its defining trait is an exceptionally thin, delicate skin that lets the beans cook through in well under an hour without an overnight soak, softening to a smooth, buttery interior. Provide poles or a trellis for the climbing vines and consistent moisture while pods fill, then let pods dry fully before shelling. Because the thin skin bruises and splits more easily than thicker-skinned beans, handle dried pods gently during threshing and winnowing.
sources: Region of Campania agricultural heritage crop records

name: Fagiolo di Lamon Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably warm; provide poles or a trellis, as this is a true climbing type traditionally grown alongside corn in the foothills of the Dolomites.
directions: Fagiolo di Lamon carries Protected Geographical Indication status for the mountain valleys around Lamon in Italy's Belluno province, where cool nights and mineral-rich alluvial soils are credited with the bean's thin skin and rich, nutty flavor. The plump borlotto-type seeds are cream colored with deep maroon streaking, nearly indistinguishable in appearance from cranberry beans but noted by Italian cooks for cooking down into an especially creamy, unified texture rather than staying distinctly bean-shaped. Harvest pods once fully dry and papery, then shell and finish curing indoors for a week before storing airtight. Give vines full sun and a tall support, since plants can reach 8 feet in a long warm season.

name: Fagiolo di Sarconi Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably warm; provide poles or a trellis, as plants climb vigorously in the irrigated valley fields of the Val d'Agri where the variety is traditionally grown.
directions: Fagiolo di Sarconi carries Protected Geographical Indication (IGP) status for the Val d'Agri valley around Sarconi in Basilicata, where several traditional bean types — including cannellino, borlotto, and fagiolino forms — are grown together under the single collective name. The variety is known for thin skins and a creamy, evenly cooking interior prized in regional soups and stews. Provide a tall pole or trellis for the vigorous climbing vines and consistent irrigation through pod fill, mirroring the valley's irrigated fields. Let pods dry fully on the vine before shelling, then cure the beans indoors for a week before storing airtight.
sources: Region of Basilicata agricultural heritage crop records

name: Fagiolo di Sorana Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in loose, sandy loam if possible; traditionally trained up reed or cane tepees along the Pescia river valley, so provide similar tall support.
directions: Sorana bean is a Slow Food Presidium variety grown in the sandy river-bottom soils near Pescia in Tuscany, prized for a seed coat so thin it seems to dissolve into the cooking liquid, leaving a velvety, almost skinless texture. The flattened, kidney-shaped white seeds are smaller and more delicate than typical cannellini types, and growers traditionally avoid heavy clay soils that thicken the skin. Allow pods to dry fully on the vine, since the thin-skinned seeds are more prone to splitting if picked while still damp, then cure indoors before storage. A well-drained, sandy raised bed is a reasonable substitute for the variety's native river-valley soil.

name: Fairy Tale Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Fairy Tale is an F1 hybrid from Sakata Seed that won All-America Selections in 2005 and has become one of the most popular eggplant varieties for home gardens and farmers markets. In zone 9, transplant March–April for spring and summer production; eggplants thrive in Gulf Coast heat and can produce from May through October or beyond with proper care. The compact plant size (18–24 inches) makes Fairy Tale excellent for containers and small spaces. Harvest when fruits are 3–4 inches long and still have their distinctive lavender-white striping — do not let fruits mature to full purple, which indicates overripeness and seed development.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 80–85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost when nights are consistently above 55°F. Harvest fruits at 3–4 inches before they fully mature. Fairy Tale is a Sakata Seed F1 hybrid eggplant that earned All-America Selections recognition in 2005 for its exceptional productivity, compact plant habit, and near-elimination of the bitterness and seedy texture that can make standard large eggplants unpalatable to some cooks. The fruits are distinctively beautiful: elongated-oval, 3–4 inches long, with an eye-catching pattern of alternating lavender-purple and creamy white vertical stripes — a color combination different from any other commonly grown eggplant type. The white striping on mature fruits is genetically stable and does not fade with cooking, making Fairy Tale attractive in stir-fries, roasted vegetable mixes, and fresh preparations where the color contrast remains visible. The key culinary advantage of Fairy Tale over standard large eggplant varieties (Black Beauty, Diamond) is the dramatically lower seed count and virtually absent bitterness: Fairy Tale fruits have fewer, smaller seeds than large types, and the flesh requires no salting or pressing to remove bitterness before cooking. A single established plant can produce 30–50 fruits over a long season in zone 9's warm climate — significantly more than a comparable large-fruited variety — making Fairy Tale an exceptionally productive choice for gardeners who want consistent eggplant supply through summer.
sources: All-America Selections — Fairy Tale eggplant AAS 2005 Edible Vegetable winner
Sakata Seed Corporation — Fairy Tale eggplant F1 hybrid variety development
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Fairy Tale eggplant commercial variety notes

name: Falstaff Brussels Sprout
plantingNote: Start indoors 14–18 weeks before first fall frost; Falstaff is a striking purple-red Brussels sprout F1 hybrid whose intense color comes from very high anthocyanin concentrations — the same antioxidant pigments in red cabbage and blueberries — that intensify with cold exposure; it is the classic 'purple Brussels sprout' for gardeners who want visual drama alongside the vegetable's traditional nutty, sweet flavor.
directions: Start seeds indoors 14–18 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into rich, firm, well-drained soil; Falstaff needs consistently cool fall temperatures to develop its deepest purple color — color intensifies dramatically after frost; harvest when sprouts are 1–1.5 inches across. Falstaff is the premier purple Brussels sprout for home gardeners and is named for the colorful, exuberant Shakespearean character Sir John Falstaff — the name suggests something robust, larger-than-life, and visually dramatic, which the deep red-purple sprouts certainly are. The intense color comes from very high concentrations of anthocyanin pigments distributed throughout the outer leaves and (to a lesser degree) the interior of each sprout; the color deepens dramatically with cold temperatures, making late-season fall-harvested Falstaff significantly more deeply purple than sprouts harvested in early fall before hard frost. The purple color fades to an unappetizing grayish-green if overcooked in water, but holds better with roasting, steaming, or quick stir-frying — and the raw purple sprouts are spectacularly visual in slaws and salads where the color impact is undiminished. The flavor is equivalent to standard green Brussels sprout varieties: nutty, slightly bitter, sweet — some gardeners find the flavor of purple types slightly milder than green types, possibly because the anthocyanin pigmentation is linked to somewhat lower glucosinolate levels.

name: Famosa Savoy Cabbage
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil for a late summer or fall harvest.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Famosa is a Bejo-bred hybrid savoy cabbage with dark-green, heavily savoyed leaves wrapping bright green, compact round heads of 2-4 pounds. It matures in about 70 days from transplant and shows good disease tolerance along with the mild, tender flavor savoy types are known for. Spring-sow for a late summer or fall harvest, and expect it to hold well in the garden without splitting for a reasonable harvest window.

name: Fanfare Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, spacing plants about 24 inches apart; the compact, semi-dwarf vines need less room than standard slicing cucumbers but still benefit from a short trellis or support.
directions: Fanfare is a 1994 All-America Selections winner valued for its unusually compact, semi-dwarf vine habit combined with full-sized, high-quality slicing cucumbers. Fruits are straight, cylindrical, and slightly tapered at the blossom end, reaching about 8-9 inches with crisp, flavorful, less-bitter flesh. The monoecious flowering habit (producing both male and female flowers) supports strong, extended fruit set and good disease tolerance. Its small plant footprint makes it a good option for gardeners with limited space who still want a classic full-size slicer.

name: Far North Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil warms; bred for extremely short seasons, Far North can also be started indoors a couple weeks early in very cool climates to guarantee a harvest.
directions: Far North is a compact, extra-early heirloom muskmelon bred specifically for gardeners in short-season and far-northern climates, ripening its small, lightly netted fruit in as little as two months from direct seeding. It trades the larger fruit size and richer sugars of long-season eastern cantaloupes for the reliability of actually finishing before fall frost arrives, making it a practical fallback where standard cantaloupe varieties routinely fail to ripen. Vines stay relatively compact compared with vigorous heirloom types, so they fit reasonably well in smaller garden beds. Today the variety is kept in circulation mainly through small regional seed-preservation growers rather than mainstream catalogs.

name: Farao Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting for an early spring crop; Farao is one of the earliest-maturing fresh-market cabbage hybrids available, bred for resistance to tip burn and to hold in the field without splitting, letting Gulf Coast gardeners bring in a cabbage crop before summer heat arrives.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; harden off before transplanting to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Farao is one of the earliest-maturing fresh-market cabbage hybrids available, forming compact, round, 2-3 lb heads that size up quickly, an advantage for Gulf Coast gardeners racing to finish a spring cabbage crop before summer heat sets in. It is bred for resistance to tip burn, a physiological disorder that browns and damages inner leaves under fluctuating moisture and heat, and holds well in the field for a week or more past maturity without splitting. The mild, tender heads work well fresh in slaw or lightly cooked. Because of its early maturity, Farao is also a good choice for a second, fall planting timed to mature before the first hard freeze.

name: Faro Quinoa
plantingNote: Direct sow from a couple of weeks before to a couple of weeks after the last frost; Faro was bred at a Danish university for day-length neutrality and early maturity in short, cool growing seasons.
directions: Faro came out of the same Danish university quinoa breeding effort that produced other day-neutral, short-season lines, aimed at letting growers in northern Europe and similarly short-summer regions ripen a quinoa crop reliably before fall frost. It grows into a relatively compact, early-maturing plant, which helps it dodge lodging and late-season disease pressure compared to taller heirloom Andean types. Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun around the last frost date and thin plants to give their seed heads room to bulk up. Harvest whole plants once the seed heads dry and rattle, then thresh and rinse thoroughly to remove the bitter saponin coating before cooking or storing the grain.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

name: Fascination Watermelon
plantingNote: Seedless triploid; start indoors or transplant after soil is thoroughly warm, and plant alongside a seeded pollenizer watermelon for fruit set. Fascination carries intermediate resistance to Fusarium wilt race 1 and anthracnose race 1, and holds and ships well, an advantage for gardeners who store melons rather than eating them immediately.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Fascination is a seedless triploid watermelon hybrid bred with intermediate resistance to Fusarium wilt race 1 and anthracnose race 1, two diseases that can build up quickly in warm, humid Gulf Coast soil. Because triploid seedless varieties produce little viable pollen of their own, plant a seeded pollenizer variety nearby to ensure good fruit set. It produces large, crisp, sweet red-fleshed fruit with excellent post-harvest holding quality, staying in good eating condition longer after picking than many other seedless types. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned.
sources: seed catalog reference (Stokes Seeds, Rupp Seeds, Osborne Seed Company)

name: Fast Lady Northern Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil reaches 65F; the short-season breeding makes it useful as a quick spring or late-summer catch crop between longer-season southern peas.
directions: Bred by Carol Deppe in Oregon specifically to mature fast in cool Pacific Northwest summers, this compact, bushy southern pea handles Gulf South heat well despite its cool-climate breeding origin, making it a good fast-maturing choice for a spring or late-summer planting window. Plants are semi-erect and bear 7-8 inch yellow pods that are easy to pick and shell by hand. The small white 'lady pea' type seed cooks quickly without soaking, a real advantage for a fast weeknight side dish in zone 9 summer heat.

name: Fat Baby Achocha
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors on their sides 4-6 weeks before last frost at a warm 73-80F for reliable germination; transplant out after all frost danger has passed and nights stay warm.
directions: Fat Baby is a compact, early-fruiting achocha selection with softer spines and smaller, rounder fruit than the typical Cyclanthera brachystachya type, reaching harvestable size in as little as two months from transplanting. Its quicker maturity and gentler spines make it one of the easier achocha types for short-season or cool-summer gardens. Train the twining vine onto netting or a trellis, where it climbs vigorously by tendrils and sets fruit continuously if picked young and often. Slice or stuff the immature, hollow fruit as a mild, crunchy cucumber substitute; older fruit toughens and its black seeds become bitter.

name: Fatalii Pepper
plantingNote: Start on a heat mat 8–10 weeks before last frost; Fatalii originates from central and southern Africa, where it has been grown for generations as a culinary pepper; it ripens to bright yellow (sometimes orange or red) with a distinctive citrus-like fruity aroma combined with extreme heat of 125,000–400,000 Scoville units.
directions: Germinate seeds at 85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Fatalii is a Capsicum chinense variety originating in central Africa — most likely from the Central African Republic or surrounding region — that has been grown by chileheads and pepper enthusiasts for decades as an outstanding 'extreme fruity heat' pepper; at 125,000–400,000 SHU it surpasses most habaneros in heat while delivering a distinctive, intensely citrusy, almost lemon-lime fruity aroma that makes it popular in hot sauces and fruity salsas where both extreme heat and complex flavor are desired. The fruits are elongated, pointed, and wrinkled at maturity, ripening to a brilliant golden yellow. Highly productive in warm climates; the plants are vigorous and tall for a Capsicum chinense, often reaching 3–3.5 feet.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University
Dave DeWitt's The Chile Pepper Encyclopedia

name: Fatalii Red Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; Capsicum chinense superhots are slow and erratic to germinate without steady warmth.
directions: Fatalii Red is the red-ripening sibling of the classic Central African yellow Fatalii, sharing its sharp, citrusy flavor but ripening to a glossy red instead of pale yellow. Expect roughly 125,000-325,000 Scoville heat units, noticeably hotter and more acidic-tasting than a standard habanero, so handle ripe pods with gloves. Start seed indoors on a heat mat, since this variety germinates slowly even by chinense standards, and give it a long, warm season outdoors in full sun. The thin-walled, elongated pods dry and powder well, making this a favorite for hot sauce makers who want bright citrus heat rather than the sweeter, fruitier notes of a habanero.
sources: Trade Winds Fruit - Fatalii Red Pepper Seeds
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Fava Larga di Leonforte
plantingNote: Direct sow in autumn in mild Mediterranean climates for an overwintered crop, or as early as soil can be worked in colder zones; this Sicilian heirloom carries a long tradition of fall sowing around Leonforte in the Enna province.
directions: Named for the inland Sicilian town of Leonforte, this heirloom broad bean is prized for unusually large, flat pods that can hold six or more oversized, pale green seeds, a trait local growers have selected for over generations through careful seed saving. Direct sow an inch deep in cool, workable soil in fall or very early spring, spacing plants close so they lean on one another without staking in open ground. Harvest some pods young and tender to eat raw with young pecorino and a glass of wine in the classic Sicilian spring pairing, and let later pods mature and dry fully for storage as a dried pulse through the rest of the year. Pinch growing tips once the lowest pods have set to discourage aphids and push energy into filling the beans already underway.

name: Feaster Family Heirloom Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or late summer through fall; a fast, mild mustard suited to the classic Southern greens rotation alongside turnip and collard greens.
directions: This family heirloom was grown and saved by generations of a family in rural Marion County, Florida, with stewardship reportedly reaching back to the Civil War era, before being shared with Seed Savers Exchange. The plant produces smooth green leaves that cook up milder and slightly sweeter than many Southern mustards, making it a gentler entry point for gardeners who find sharper types like Southern Giant Curled too pungent. Its fast maturity and mild flavor place it well alongside collard and turnip greens in a traditional fall Gulf Coast greens patch.

name: Federle Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and stake the tall indeterminate vines well at transplant.
directions: Federle, also called Federle's Italian Paste, is an heirloom preserved through Seed Savers Exchange that produces unusually long, slender paste fruit up to seven inches, distinct from the more common blocky Roma shape. Indeterminate vines are highly productive and keep setting fruit steadily through the season, so gardeners canning or making salsa get an extended harvest window rather than one heavy flush. The dense, nearly seedless flesh cooks down quickly with little waste, and the deep red color holds well in finished sauce. Grow this variety when you want an open-pollinated, seed-saveable paste tomato with a distinctive elongated shape for home preserving.

name: Fedora 17 Hemp
plantingNote: Direct sow at or just after last frost into a dense, well-prepared seedbed; 'Fedora 17' is a French-bred, monoecious, day-neutral cultivar developed for combined fiber and grain harvest and requires state or federal licensing to grow in the United States.
directions: Drill seed about 3/4 inch deep at a dense rate to encourage tall, straight stalks with reduced branching, since crowding improves both fiber quality and lodging resistance; 'Fedora 17' is one of the most widely certified industrial hemp cultivars in Europe and appears on many US state-approved variety lists because its THC content reliably stays under the 0.3% compliance threshold. Being monoecious, every plant in the stand can be left to mature and set seed, simplifying dual-purpose harvest compared with dioecious cultivars that separate male and female plants. Cut stalks for fiber once flowering finishes and the lower leaves begin to yellow, or wait longer for the grain harvest if seed is the primary goal, though delaying reduces fiber quality as stems coarsen. A license from the appropriate state hemp program or the USDA is required before planting, and growers must submit to pre-harvest THC testing in most jurisdictions.
sources: European Union Common Catalogue of Varieties of Agricultural Plant Species
Kentucky Department of Agriculture Industrial Hemp Research Program

name: Feher Ozon Paprika Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Feher Ozon is a Hungarian heirloom paprika pepper grown for drying and grinding into homemade sweet paprika.
directions: Feher Ozon is a Hungarian heirloom whose name translates roughly to 'white torrent,' referring to the ivory-white color of its immature pods before they ripen through orange to red. Compact, upright plants stay productive under garden conditions and set heavy clusters of thick-walled, tapering pods around five inches long, with a mild, fruity sweetness and essentially no heat. It belongs to the classic family of Hungarian paprika peppers grown specifically to be dried and ground into homemade sweet paprika, though the fresh pods are equally good sliced raw, roasted, or stuffed. Its dwarf, self-supporting habit makes it easier to manage in small gardens than taller Hungarian paprika types.

name: Ferris Wheel Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; a tall, regular-leaf indeterminate vine that needs sturdy staking to carry its large flattened fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply prepared soil once all frost risk has passed. Ferris Wheel is an 1894 commercial release from the John A. Salzer Seed Company of Wisconsin that nearly vanished before being rediscovered and reintroduced by heirloom tomato researchers in the 1990s. It produces large, slightly flattened pink beefsteak fruit with colorful shoulders that blush attractively as they ripen, and the flesh is juicy, mild, and slightly sweet. Provide sturdy staking for the tall, regular-leaf indeterminate vines, which can exceed six feet over a 90-day season.

name: Fesols de Santa Pau Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; this determinate bush type matures quickly and needs no staking.
directions: Setsetmanera is a small, round, white dry bean grown on the volcanic soils around Santa Pau in the Garrotxa region of Catalonia, Spain, and is one of the traditional varieties covered by the Fesols de Santa Pau DOP. Plants have an upright, determinate growth habit and a notably short cycle, making the crop easy to manage without staking. Harvest pods once fully dry, then shell and store the small navy-type beans, which are prized for their fine flavor and short cooking time. The name references its traditionally fast maturation compared to older local varieties.
sources: EU eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register — Fesols de Santa Pau DOP
Generalitat de Catalunya DOP product documentation

name: Fiaschetto di Manduria Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; this compact bush type tolerates drier soil once established.
directions: A traditional tomato of Manduria in Puglia and a Slow Food Ark of Taste variety, this small, plum-shaped fruit has a slight pointed tip and hangs in grape-like clusters on compact, bushy determinate plants only 1-1.5 feet tall. Historically grown without irrigation in the dry soils of southeastern Italy, it tolerates heat and drought well once established and is used fresh, for passata, or dried. Its small stature also makes it a good candidate for containers and hanging baskets.

name: Fiero Radicchio
plantingNote: Direct sow from just before the last frost through early summer for a warm-season crop, or in late summer for a fall crop. 'Fiero' colors up reliably without the cutback-and-regrow forcing technique that traditional Tardivo-type Treviso radicchio requires.
directions: This elongated, torpedo-shaped F1 hybrid resembles the classic heirloom Treviso radicchios but matures in a much shorter 50 to 60 days and colors reliably without the traditional post-cutback forcing that old-style Tardivo types need. Leaves are deep wine-red with prominent white midribs, held in slim, upright, self-blanching heads that stay tender as they size up. 'Fiero' tolerates a wider sowing window than most chicories, performing well from both an early sowing and a late-summer sowing for fall harvest. Its quicker cycle and forgiving nature make it a practical way to get Treviso's elegant shape without the long season or hands-on forcing older varieties require.

name: Fife Creek Cowhorn Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow 1-3 weeks after the last frost once the soil has warmed, since okra seedlings resent cold, wet soil and transplant poorly.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed, soaking seed overnight to speed germination, then thin seedlings to allow room for these towering plants to spread. Harvest curved pods every day or two while young and tender, since they toughen quickly once mature. Fife Creek Cowhorn is a Southern heirloom known for its exceptionally tall growth, often reaching well over six feet, and its long, curved, rib-free pods reminiscent of a cow's horn. Gardeners who grow it out for seed appreciate its reliable productivity in hot, humid summers.

name: Figueres Onion
plantingNote: Start seed in a cold frame or indoors in late winter and transplant young onion sets out while soil is still cool, giving this long-day type a full spring to bulb before heat sets in.
directions: This flattened, golden-skinned sweet onion from the Figueres district of Girona in Catalonia is prized for mild, low-pungency flesh that is traditionally eaten raw, thinly sliced, with just bread and olive oil. Grow it in loose, fertile ground with steady moisture through bulb swell, then cut back watering once the tops begin to yellow and fall over to concentrate sugars and cure the skins. Harvest when roughly half the foliage has flopped, then field-cure for several days before braiding or storing in a dry, airy spot, since the thin skins and high sugar content make this variety a poor long-term keeper compared with pungent storage onions.
sources: Institut Català de la Vinya i el Vi / Generalitat de Catalunya agricultural registers
Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Catalan onion varieties

name: Filderkraut Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant after the last frost, spacing generously since mature heads and outer leaves grow quite large.
directions: Filderkraut is a traditional German conical cabbage from the Filder plain near Stuttgart, prized for tall, dense, pointed heads that can weigh several pounds each. The tapered shape and tightly wrapped leaves pack unusually well for shredding, making this heirloom the historic variety of choice for large-batch sauerkraut production. It tends to tolerate warm spells better than round-headed cabbages while still standing up to fall frost, giving it a wide harvest window. Grow Filderkraut where a heavy-yielding, storage-friendly cabbage with genuine heirloom pedigree is wanted for preserving.

name: Filius Blue Ornamental Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into containers or beds once frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings into pots or beds once nights are warm, since this compact annuum is often grown as a patio or container ornamental. Keep it evenly watered and in full sun for the heaviest, most colorful fruit display. Filius Blue is bred for its dense, upright habit and small purple-flushed leaves, with round fruits that ripen through purple and cream shades before finishing bright red, making the plant look multicolored all at once. The pods carry real heat and are edible, though the plant is grown mainly for its ornamental fruit color.

name: Fino Fennel
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring once soil is workable, or sow again in midsummer for a fall-maturing crop, since Fino tends to bolt if grown through long, hot summer days.
directions: Fino is a traditional open-pollinated Florence fennel grown for its rounded, tightly layered white bulbs and sweet anise flavor. Direct sow into rich, evenly moist soil, since the taproot does not tolerate transplanting well, and thin seedlings to give bulbs room to expand. Being open-pollinated rather than a hybrid, Fino shows a bit more variability in bulb size and bolting tendency than modern F1 types, so timing sowings for cool conditions in spring or fall gives the most reliable results. Harvest once bulbs reach the size of a tennis ball to a fist, before any sign of a flowering stalk.

name: Fire N Ice Radish
plantingNote: Also excellent as a fall Gulf Coast crop sown 6-8 weeks before first frost; roots size up fast in cool soil.
directions: An improved French Breakfast-type radish bred for a striking two-tone root: bright scarlet shoulders fading cleanly to white at the tip. The elongated roots stay crisp and mild-flavored even as they size up, resisting the pithiness that hits many spring radishes in warm soil. Direct-sow in cool weather and harvest young for the best color contrast and snap; excellent sliced raw for its visual appeal on a relish tray.

name: First Lady Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; First Lady is an indeterminate slicing tomato with a broad disease resistance package: resistance to Verticillium wilt (V), two races of Fusarium wilt (F, F2), nematodes (N), tobacco mosaic virus (T), and Alternaria (A). In zone 9, transplant March–April. The comprehensive disease resistance makes First Lady particularly practical for zone 9's warm, humid conditions where soilborne pathogens (Verticillium, Fusarium) and nematodes significantly limit yields in susceptible varieties. First Lady was developed specifically for home garden production and has remained one of the most widely sold tomato transplants at garden centers throughout the southeastern United States for decades. Fruits are medium (8–10 oz), round, smooth-shouldered, uniformly red, and produced abundantly through the season. The flavor is balanced — typical of the reliable but moderate flavor of disease-resistant F1 hybrids rather than the complex intensity of heirloom types.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost. Stake or cage. Harvest when uniformly red and gives to slight pressure. First Lady Tomato is an F1 hybrid indeterminate slicing tomato developed by Seminis Vegetable Seeds (now Bayer Vegetable Seeds) with a comprehensive disease resistance package that has made it one of the most reliably productive backyard tomato varieties in the humid southeastern United States. The 'VFFNTAs' resistance package (Verticillium wilt, two races of Fusarium wilt, Nematodes, Tobacco Mosaic Virus, Alternaria) addresses virtually every major soil-borne and airborne pathogen that limits tomato production in the Gulf South — in humid zone 9 conditions where tomato plants commonly succumb to one or more of these diseases before the season ends, First Lady's resistance allows plants to remain productive through the summer. The variety's profile — medium-sized (8–10 oz) red tomatoes on vigorous indeterminate plants with the comprehensive disease package — represents a classic template for southeastern home garden tomato production that prioritizes plant health and extended production over extreme fruit size or complex flavor. First Lady was marketed and sold through retail garden center channels for decades and became one of the most recognized tomato variety names in southeastern garden retail, appearing consistently on transplant packs in spring garden center displays across the Gulf South. For zone 9 gardeners dealing with nematode pressure (very common in sandy Gulf Coast soils) or Fusarium wilt (endemic in soils with tomato production history), First Lady's 'N' and 'F' resistances provide practical protection that keeps plants alive and producing when susceptible varieties decline.
sources: Seminis Vegetable Seeds — First Lady tomato F1 hybrid disease resistance package documentation
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Tomato Variety Recommendations for Gulf South Home Gardens
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Disease-Resistant Tomato Variety Selection for Florida

name: First Prize Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in deeply enriched soil; a hybrid giant-pumpkin selection bred for competitive weigh-off growers wanting reliably massive fruit without decades of seed-line selection.
directions: Start indoors 2-3 weeks before last frost or direct sow into hills of heavily composted soil, allowing at least 15-20 feet of space per plant since a single vine can spread over several hundred square feet. First Prize is a hybrid giant pumpkin bred for competitive growers, capable of producing fruit up to 300 pounds under intensive management, though most home-garden fruit lands well under that with less aggressive pruning and feeding. For maximum size, growers typically remove all but one or two developing fruits per vine and pinch side shoots to direct the plant's energy into the remaining pumpkins. Heavy, consistent watering and monthly feeding through the growing season are essential; harvest before hard frost once the rind hardens and the stem begins to dry.
sources: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension

name: Fish Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; the spectacular variegated foliage and striped fruit coloring of Fish Pepper make it equally valuable as an ornamental in herb and pepper gardens.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Fish Pepper is an African American heirloom pepper with a unique history — the variety was maintained in the Black community of Baltimore and the Chesapeake Bay region through the 19th and early 20th centuries, where the unripe green-striped fruits were used to season fish and shellfish dishes without the red coloring that would be visible in pale-sauced seafood preparations. Rediscovered by artist and food historian William Woys Weaver through Seed Savers Exchange, Fish Pepper is now recognized as one of the most historically significant African American food heritage vegetables. The ornamental impact is extraordinary: the plant produces dramatically variegated, cream-and-dark-green streaked foliage unlike any other pepper variety, and the immature fruits are striped in cream and pale green, ripening through orange-and-cream striped stages to solid deep red at full maturity. The range of stripe patterns and color stages at different ripeness levels creates a constantly changing visual display. The heat level is medium-hot (comparable to cayenne, 30,000–50,000 SHU) — appropriate for seasoning fish sauces, seafood dishes, and hot sauces. The ornamental quality of both foliage and fruit at all stages makes Fish Pepper an outstanding choice for kitchen garden beds and container growing on patios.

name: Fiskeby V Soybean
directions: Direct sow once soil has warmed in late spring, since this short, bushy soybean was bred in Fiskeby, Norrkoping, Sweden, by Dr. Sven Holmberg specifically to set and finish pods reliably in cool, short-growing-season climates where most edamame struggle. Harvest at the green-shell stage when pods are plump but still bright green for sweet, crunchy edamame, or leave them to dry fully for a high-protein dry soybean.

name: Flageolet Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; flageolet is a French semi-dry bean harvested at the shell bean stage (before pods are fully dry) when the seeds are pale green — the beans retain this delicate green color when cooked, making them the classic French accompaniment to roast leg of lamb and the basis of cassoulet in some regional traditions.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost, 4–6 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart; flageolet is harvested at the shell bean stage — when pods are plump and seeds are well-developed but still pale green, before the pods begin to yellow and dry. Flageolet (from the Latin 'flagellum' referring to the flute or pipe shape) is a uniquely French bean variety that occupies the role of the 'shell bean' par excellence in French cuisine — it is neither a fresh snap bean nor a fully dried bean, but is harvested at the intermediate shell-bean stage when the kidney-shaped, pale green to white seeds have developed fully in size and shape but retain their characteristic pale green color and fresh, delicate flavor. The distinctive color persists through cooking when properly prepared (not overcooked), making the finished beans a beautiful pale sage green on the plate — dramatically different from the drab gray-white of common dried beans. Flageolet is most famously the traditional accompaniment to gigot d'agneau (roast leg of lamb) in classic French cuisine, where the delicate flavor of the beans perfectly complements the rich lamb; it is also an important ingredient in traditional cassoulet and flageolets au gratin. Seeds can also be allowed to dry fully for storage and reconstituted, though the characteristic green color is then lost.
sources: French Ministry of Agriculture Heirloom Variety List

name: Flakkee Carrot
plantingNote: Best sown from mid-spring through early summer for a fall harvest; a true maincrop storage carrot that keeps exceptionally well.
directions: Named for the Flakkee polder region of Zeeland in the Netherlands, this sturdy Dutch heirloom produces broad-shouldered, blunt-tapered roots up to 8-9 inches long with strong tops that hold up well for bunching. It is a true maincrop storage carrot, best sown from mid-spring through early summer for a fall harvest that keeps exceptionally well in a root cellar or clamp. Flakkee's productivity and keeping ability made it foundational breeding stock behind many of today's Imperator and Autumn King-type carrots.

name: Flame Star Cauliflower
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in mid- to late summer for a fall crop; Flame Star is an orange-curded cauliflower that holds its color and forms well-domed heads under warmer conditions than most cauliflower tolerates.
directions: Start transplants and set out in early spring or midsummer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Flame Star produces smooth, well-domed heads in a vivid, natural, sunny orange, colored throughout the curd (not just the surface) by a higher-than-normal beta-carotene content, so the color holds through cooking rather than fading like some orange cauliflower selections. It is notably more heat tolerant during head formation than white cauliflower varieties, making it a more forgiving choice for a Gulf South spring crop that runs into early-summer warmth before harvest. Blanching is unnecessary since sun exposure does not bleach or damage the orange curd the way it can discolor white types. Harvest heads while curds are still tight and firm, before the individual florets begin to separate and loosen.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Flame Star Cauliflower variety notes

name: Flaming Flare Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once soil has warmed, after all danger of frost has passed.
directions: Transplant into full sun once the soil has warmed, growing it as either a landscape edging plant or a container specimen. Flaming Flare is an All-America Selections winner grown as much for its upright, torch-like clusters of small fruit that shift from purple to yellow to orange to red as it matures as for its edible use, giving a single compact plant several color stages at once. The fruit carries mild-to-moderate heat and can be harvested for cooking at any color stage, making the plant genuinely dual-purpose in the garden.

name: Flamingo Chinese Toon
plantingNote: Plant a young grafted or rooted-cutting specimen of 'Flamingo' in spring into fertile, well-drained soil, siting it where dappled or partial shade protects the brilliant rose-pink new growth from being bleached out by intense midday sun.
directions: Plant a young grafted or rooted-cutting specimen of 'Flamingo' in spring into fertile, well-drained soil, siting it where dappled or partial shade protects the brilliant rose-pink new growth from being bleached out by intense midday sun. Keep the root zone evenly moist while the tree establishes, and prune hard each late winter to keep the plant at a manageable shrubby size that resprouts with an even heavier flush of the prized pink shoots. The blush-colored young leaves and shoot tips share the same onion-garlic, slightly resinous flavor as the green-leaved species and are harvested the same way, stir-fried or folded into egg dishes while still tender. Because the pink coloring is most vivid in filtered light, 'Flamingo' doubles as a striking foliage accent for a partly shaded edible garden bed.

name: Flamingo Water Celery
plantingNote: Plant rooted divisions in spring into consistently wet soil or very shallow water (up to 2 inches deep) at a pond margin, rain garden, or bog bed in partial shade; this variegated sport does not come reliably true from seed and is propagated exclusively by division.
directions: 'Flamingo' is a compact, boldly variegated sport of water celery, its narrow leaves splashed in pink, cream, and green rather than the plain green of the wild species, making it a dual-purpose plant for the edge of a shaded pond or rain garden bed. The tender young stems and leaves carry the same crisp, mild parsley-celery flavor used fresh in Korean and Japanese cooking and can be snipped regularly for salads, garnishes, and cold noodle dishes. Because the color is brightest in cooler weather and with some direct morning sun, site it where it gets a few hours of light before afternoon shade takes over in a hot Gulf Coast summer. Divide congested clumps every year or two in spring to maintain vigorous color and prevent the planting from reverting toward plain green foliage.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Plant Toolbox

name: Flash Collards
plantingNote: Direct sow 10–12 weeks before the first frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Flash is the fastest-maturing collard option, useful for late-season planting when the window for establishing standard 75–80 day varieties has closed.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Flash is a fast-maturing collard hybrid reaching harvest in only 55–65 days from sowing — significantly faster than traditional open-pollinated collard varieties (70–90 days), making Flash particularly valuable for late-season zone 9 plantings where the window for establishing slow-maturing varieties has closed. The smooth, dark-green leaves are more tender and less coarse than the thick leaves of older collard varieties — the faster maturity corresponds with a younger, more tender leaf stage at harvest, making Flash better suited to raw preparations and quick sautés where tenderness is important. Flash has the same excellent cold-hardiness as other collards — exposure to light frost sweetens the leaves by converting starches to sugars, improving flavor quality through the Gulf South winter. As a hybrid variety, Flash cannot be saved for seed but produces reliable, vigorous, uniform plants each season from purchased seed. The faster maturity also allows two consecutive collard plantings within a Gulf South fall season — a first planting in mid-August for October–November harvest and a second planting in late September for December–January harvest. Excellent disease tolerance reduces the need for preventive fungicide applications in the humid Gulf South fall garden.

name: Flashy Trout Back Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November or January–February. Flashy Trout Back is cold-hardy and slow to bolt, making it suitable for the full cool season in zone 9. The red spotting pattern is more pronounced in cool weather and may fade in warm spring conditions. Harvest outer leaves continuously or pull entire heads at 55–65 days.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Flashy Trout Back (Forellen or Forellenschluss variant) is an Austrian heirloom romaine-type lettuce producing upright, semi-cos heads with large, spoon-shaped, bright green leaves heavily spotted with wine-red to maroon splashes and streaks — the pattern resembles the speckled back of a brown trout, giving the lettuce its evocative name. The combination of romaine structure (crisp, upright leaves with a prominent midrib) with the unique spotted coloring makes Flashy Trout Back one of the most visually distinctive lettuces for mixed plantings and specialty salad mixes. The flavor is mild, slightly sweet, and crisp — typical romaine quality without bitterness. The Austrian origin indicates good cold hardiness and a slow-to-bolt character that extends the harvest window in zone 9's warm springs. The dramatic spotted pattern on each leaf makes every head unique and immediately recognizable in market displays; it is one of the most frequently photographed heirloom lettuce varieties.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Flashy Trout Back Lettuce Heritage Variety
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Austrian Heirloom Lettuce
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Romaine and Cos Lettuce

name: Flat White Boer Pumpkin
plantingNote: Wait until soil has warmed past 65F, since this South African heirloom is notably frost-sensitive even by pumpkin standards.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills spaced widely apart once soil is reliably warm, as this variety resents any lingering chill. Vines are vigorous and sprawling, so give them ample room or train them along a fence. The flattened, pale ivory fruit develops slight ribbing and deep orange flesh as it matures, and it is ready to harvest once the rind resists a thumbnail. Cure fruit in a warm spot for one to two weeks before moving to cool storage, where the flat shape makes stacking easy through winter.
sources: Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste

name: Flavorburst Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Flavorburst is a blocky bell-type sweet pepper bred for its unusual ripening sequence, passing from green through deep purple to yellow before finishing at bright orange, an AAS-recognized cultivar prized for both color and sweet flavor.
directions: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after frost danger has passed. Flavorburst is a blocky bell-type sweet pepper bred for its unusual ripening sequence, with fruit passing from green through deep purple to yellow before finishing at bright orange, giving multiple colorful harvest stages from a single planting. The thick, crisp walls carry a sweet, mild flavor at every color stage, though sweetness increases as the fruit reaches its final orange color. Because the color changes track ripeness, gardeners can pick fruit at whichever stage suits their taste rather than waiting solely for full color change.

name: Flor de Durazno Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; a compact bush type that needs no staking.
directions: Flor de Durazno takes its name, 'peach blossom,' from the soft pink-and-cream mottling on its seed coat, a color pattern reminiscent of peach flowers rather than the bolder maroon speckling of many other Mexican dry beans. This bush-type heirloom produces a heavy set of pods on compact plants, yielding beans with a smooth, buttery texture and mild flavor once cooked, well suited to simple pot beans, soups, and refried preparations. Allow pods to dry completely and turn tan on the vine before harvest, then shell and cure the beans for another week or two indoors before sealing for storage. Its moderate days-to-maturity make it a good option for gardeners without a long, hot growing season.
sources: CIMMYT/INIFAP Mexican bean landrace germplasm documentation

name: Flor de Mayo Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Flor de Mayo is one of the most important dry bean varieties in Mexican cuisine — known for its distinctive speckled appearance (magenta, pink, and cream-colored fresh seeds), quick cooking, and mild, sweet flavor that makes it the preferred bean in many regions of central Mexico for everyday frijoles, refried beans, and rice-and-bean dishes.
directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in full sun; Flor de Mayo is well-adapted to semi-dry, warm conditions and performs particularly well in the hot, dry growing season of zone 7–10 areas with low humidity; harvest when pods are fully dry and papery. Flor de Mayo (Spanish for 'May Flower') is one of the oldest and most culturally significant dry bean varieties in Mexico, where it has been grown for centuries as a primary food staple — ranking among the most commercially important beans in the Mexican market alongside Bayo, Peruano/Canario, and Azufrado varieties. The fresh seeds are distinctively beautiful: oval, slightly plump, and marked with magenta, rose-pink, and cream-white in a speckled and streaked pattern reminiscent of the flowers it was named for; the pattern and color intensify at the fresh-shell stage and fade to a more subdued cream-and-tan speckled pattern when fully dried. When cooked, the beans become uniformly pale tan-brown, but the texture and flavor are the key appeal: Flor de Mayo cooks to a mild, slightly sweet, creamy texture with thin skins that are almost imperceptible — making them one of the quickest-cooking dry beans and one of the smoothest for refried beans where texture matters. In Mexican home cooking, Flor de Mayo is the bean that many home cooks from Jalisco, Nayarit, and Michoacán states grew up eating; it is available in Mexican markets under this name and under regional names including 'Flor de Mayo Brillante' and 'Crema'.
sources: CIMMYT (International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center)

name: Floradade Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Floradade is an open-pollinated variety — seeds can be saved from the best fruits to maintain a self-sufficient seed supply across seasons.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Floradade is a University of Florida open-pollinated tomato variety developed specifically for Florida and Gulf South production — one of the older heat-tolerant open-pollinated varieties that has served as a reliable standard for Gulf South home garden production since its introduction. As an open-pollinated variety with good heat tolerance, Floradade produces medium-large (6–8 oz), round, firm, deep-red fruits with excellent fresh-eating and processing quality on a determinate plant that requires minimal staking. The disease resistance package includes Fusarium wilt race 1 — the most common race affecting Gulf South gardens. The primary practical advantage of Floradade over hybrid varieties is the ability to save seeds: since Floradade is open-pollinated, seeds saved from the best fruits grow true to type, allowing Gulf South gardeners to maintain a self-sufficient seed supply without annual seed purchases. This seed-saving advantage is significant for Gulf South gardeners who find locally-adapted, open-pollinated varieties often outperform northern hybrids in their specific climate. In zone 9, Floradade performs well in both spring and fall planting windows. The combination of local adaptation, open-pollination, heat tolerance, and reliable production has kept Floradade in production and recommendation by Gulf South cooperative extensions for decades.

name: Floradel Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; one of the foundational University of Florida heat- and disease-tolerant slicing tomatoes for Gulf South gardens.
directions: Floradel is a large-fruited slicing tomato released by the University of Florida in the late 1950s, bred with Verticillium and Fusarium wilt resistance for growers facing the heat, humidity, and soilborne disease pressure of Florida and the broader Gulf South. It was an early link in a long chain of Florida tomato breeding that went on to produce related heat-adapted varieties such as Manalucie and Manapal, and it remained a dependable market and dooryard tomato for Southern gardeners for years after its release. Stake or cage the vigorous plants and keep moisture consistent to limit cracking and blossom end rot.

name: Floralina Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost into cages or stakes; expect strong performance against Gray Leaf Spot, a foliar disease that thrives in Gulf Coast humidity.
directions: A 1997 joint release from NC State's Mountain Horticultural Crops station and the University of Florida's Bradenton research center, bred collaboratively for fresh-market performance across the hot, humid Southeast. LSU AgCenter lists it heat-tolerant with resistance to Fusarium races 1-3 and Gray Leaf Spot. Fruits run medium at 8-10 ounces, round, and red on a determinate plant, filling the same summer heat-set niche as other recommended determinate slicers and worth trialing side by side if disease pressure in a given yard differs from the standard package.

name: Floramerica Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before transplanting; an AAS Gold Medal winner bred by the University of Florida for disease resistance and fruit set under Southern heat and humidity.
directions: Floramerica is a globe-shaped slicing tomato bred by the University of Florida and named an All-America Selections Gold Medal winner in 1978, a distinction awarded only rarely to tomatoes. It carries resistance to Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt, and nematodes (VFN), a disease package assembled specifically to help it perform reliably in the hot, humid, nematode-prone soils of Florida and the Gulf South. The semi-determinate plants produce heavy clusters of smooth, deep-red, well-flavored fruit over a long summer season. Stake plants and water evenly to minimize blossom end rot during the region's alternating heavy rain and dry spells.

name: Floriani Red Flint Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows after last frost when soil has warmed; Floriani Red Flint is a long-season Italian heirloom (100–120 days) requiring a full summer to mature — in short-season climates (zones 3–5) start a week or two early under plastic mulch; this is the finest polenta corn available, producing deeply colored red-orange kernels that grind into a rich, nutty, complex polenta unequaled by commercial varieties.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks; allow ears to dry fully on the stalks until the husks are completely papery before harvest; dry further at low heat (under 100°F) to bring moisture content below 12% before milling; stone-grind for the finest polenta texture; the distinctive deep red-orange color of the meal is unique among American corns. Floriani Red Flint is widely considered one of the finest polenta corns in the world — an Italian heirloom from the Fiemme Valley (Val di Fiemme) of Trentino, in the northeastern Italian Alps, where this particular strain of red flint corn has been grown by mountain farmers for centuries and is deeply embedded in the local food culture. The name 'Floriani' commemorates the Floriani family who maintained and preserved this specific strain. The corn produces large, deeply pigmented red-orange to brick-red flint kernels with a very hard, glassy endosperm characteristic of flint corn — the same endosperm structure that gives flint corns their superior milling quality and longer shelf life compared to dent corns. When stone-ground, the flour from Floriani Red Flint is a rich deep gold-orange color with a complex, nutty, slightly sweet fragrance quite unlike the pale, bland commercial cornmeal most American cooks know. Cooked polenta from this corn has a dense, complex flavor with depth that fully justifies the artisan price of stone-ground Italian polenta. Chefs at farm-to-table restaurants have sought out this variety specifically for its polenta quality. American growers in zones with a full summer can produce the authentic Italian-quality polenta grain that was formerly available only through import.

name: Floribibb Lettuce
plantingNote: Best sown in fall through early spring along the Gulf Coast, where Floribibb's heat tolerance stretches the harvest window well past when ordinary bibb types would bolt and turn bitter.
directions: Bred at the University of Florida's lettuce program at the Everglades Research and Education Center specifically for the state's warm, humid growing seasons, Floribibb is a gourmet butterhead with soft, buttery rosettes and bred-in resistance to two common lettuce viruses that otherwise thrive in hot, muggy weather. Direct sow or transplant small starts 8-10 inches apart in loose, moisture-retentive soil, and keep it out of the most intense afternoon sun once temperatures climb, since it tolerates heat far better than it tolerates drought or deep shade. Along the Gulf Coast this is a cool-season crop best grown fall through early spring rather than through summer; harvest whole heads or outer leaves once rosettes fill out, generally 55-65 days from seed.

name: Floricream Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed; Floricream's determinate, top-bearing habit concentrates pods for an efficient once-over hand or machine harvest.
directions: Floricream was developed at the University of Florida as an all-purpose cream-seeded southern pea, bred from Mississippi 32, Korean Crowder, Running Acre, and Tavares lines. It grows as a determinate, top-bearing semi-crowder type with long pods around eight inches, and the creamy-white peas carry a light brown eye and classic smooth, buttery flavor. The plant shows useful field resistance to scab and fusarium wilt, both persistent problems for southern peas in hot, humid gardens, and its concentrated fruit set makes it well suited to mechanical harvesting as well as home garden picking. It remains a solid choice for Gulf Coast growers wanting a dependable cream pea with some built-in disease tolerance.
sources: Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (cucurbit.info)

name: Florida 47 Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 Florida 47 can be grown as a spring crop (transplant February–March for May harvest) or fall crop (transplant August for October–November harvest). Florida 47 is a determinate type well-adapted to the Florida and Gulf Coast growing windows.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Florida 47 is a University of Florida-developed determinate hybrid tomato bred specifically for commercial and home production in the hot, humid Florida and Gulf Coast environment — part of a long series of Florida-bred tomatoes (including Florida 91, Floradade, and Solar Set) developed by UF's tomato breeding program to address the unique challenges of Southern tomato production. The large (8–12 oz), globe to slightly flattened, firm, bright red fruits have the thick walls, uniform shape, and long shelf life that commercial producers require, but perform equally well for home gardens; the flavor is balanced and pleasant without the blandness of many commercial types. Excellent disease resistance including Fusarium wilt races 1, 2, and 3, Verticillium wilt, gray leaf spot, and tobacco mosaic virus — the full-package resistance crucial for reliable performance in disease-prone Southern soils. Florida 47 is widely planted commercially in the Immokalee, Florida production region during the fall and spring seasons and performs similarly well for home gardeners across zone 8b–11.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gulf Coast Research and Education Center — Tomato Breeding Program
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Commercial Tomato Production Guide
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Vegetable Variety Evaluations

name: Florida 91 Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Florida 91 carries one of the most comprehensive disease resistance packages of any Gulf South tomato — V, F1, F2, N, A, L — minimizing pesticide inputs in the disease-intensive Gulf South environment.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Florida 91 is a University of Florida hybrid tomato developed specifically for Gulf South production, representing one of the most disease-resistant commercially available tomato varieties — carrying resistance to Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, root-knot nematodes, Alternaria stem canker, and leaf mold (V, F1, F2, N, A, L), providing broad-spectrum protection against the primary soilborne and foliar diseases that devastate less protected varieties in the humid Gulf South climate. The large (6–8 oz), round, deep-red, firm-fleshed fruits have excellent fresh-eating and processing quality with good shelf life compared to softer varieties. Florida 91 is determinate (bush-type), maturing its crop in a compressed 4–6 week window and requiring minimal staking — a practical advantage for gardeners who prefer a defined harvest period over the continuous production of indeterminate types. In zone 9, Florida 91 is outstanding for both spring (February–June) and fall (August–November) planting windows. The comprehensive disease resistance package makes Florida 91 particularly valuable for gardeners who have experienced soilborne disease problems in their garden soil — the resistance package allows production in locations where unprotected varieties fail repeatedly. A primary recommendation from University of Florida and Louisiana State University extension services for Gulf South home garden tomato production.

name: Florida Basket Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into a hanging basket or large container once frost risk has passed; Florida Basket was released in 1981 by the University of Florida's Bradenton research station specifically for basket and container growing.
directions: Florida Basket is a compact, determinate dwarf tomato bred at the University of Florida for hanging baskets and patio containers, needing no staking or caging as its short, self-supporting stems spill gently over the container rim. It sets clusters of small, red, plum-shaped saladette fruit around 2 inches long with good flavor for a container type, ripening over a relatively short, concentrated window typical of determinate dwarf tomatoes. Because container soil dries out quickly, water consistently and feed every couple of weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer to keep the shallow root system productive through the season. Florida Basket later became scientifically significant as one of the two parent cultivars, alongside Ohio 4013-3, used to breed Micro-Tom, the ultra-dwarf tomato now used worldwide as a model organism in plant genetics research.
sources: University of Florida IFAS — Florida Basket tomato release notes
Journal of Experimental Botany — Genetic and physiological characterization of tomato cv. Micro-Tom

name: Florida Broadleaf Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 9, sow September through February for fall and winter production — the primary growing season runs October through April, with spring plants bolting in May when temperatures rise.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during the cool season; Florida Broadleaf is the classic Southern mustard green — the most widely grown mustard green cultivar in the Gulf South for generations, with large, flat, broad, smooth, dark-green leaves with a pungent, spicy mustard flavor that is a cornerstone of traditional Southern cooking. Unlike curled mustard varieties (Southern Giant Curled, Green Wave) that have ruffled, frilly leaves, Florida Broadleaf has smooth, flat leaves that are easier to wash and which have a slightly more robust, bold flavor. Florida Broadleaf is grown in zone 9 gardens from September through April — the cool-season growing window when mustard greens develop the best flavor and avoid the extreme bitterness and quick bolting that heat causes. Young leaves are mild enough for salads; mature leaves are best cooked, typically braised with smoked meat (ham hock, smoked turkey) and seasoned vinegar in the traditional Southern style. Frost improves mustard green flavor — the conversion of starches to sugars after cold nights produces a richer, more complex, slightly sweeter flavor. Harvest outer leaves continuously or cut the entire plant at 4–6 inches above the crown for a cut-and-come-again harvest.

name: Florida Conch Pea, Bush
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed in full sun; this is the bush-type strain, selected later from the originally vining conch pea.
directions: Florida Conch is a now-rare southern pea that arrived in north Florida in the late 1800s, likely from the West Indies, and became prized for its tiny white seeds, delicate texture, and short cooking time. The original conch pea was a vining plant, and a vining strain still exists, but this bush-type selection was developed later as vining peas fell out of favor for home gardens. Green-shell shellies are ready in about 63 days, with fully dry peas following around 70 days, and the mild, delicate flavor sets it apart from heartier crowder and blackeye types.

name: Florida Cranberry Roselle
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant April–June. Florida Cranberry roselle is a short-day flowering plant — it begins setting calyces as days shorten in September–October regardless of when it was planted, so earlier planting results in a larger, more productive plant at calyx-setting time. The large calyces ripen October–November in zone 9.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Florida Cranberry is a named roselle cultivar selected specifically for very large, fleshy, deeply colored calyces — the thick, star-shaped, burgundy-red sepals that encircle each seed pod after the flower drops and are the edible product of roselle cultivation. The deep cranberry-red calyces have an intensely tart, cranberry-like flavor with hibiscus floral notes, used to make a vivid crimson tea (agua de Jamaica), jam, syrup, sauce, and desserts. The exceptional calyx size and deep color of Florida Cranberry make it the standard named cultivar for calyx production in the Gulf South. In zone 9 the short-day flowering response means calyces set abundantly in October–November when temperatures are cooling — a natural alignment with the Thanksgiving and holiday season when cranberry-flavored products are in demand. Harvest calyces before the seed pod matures for best flavor; the calyces are easily separated from the seed capsule by hand.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Roselle Florida Cranberry Cultivar
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Roselle Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Roselle and Hibiscus Tea Production

name: Florida Giant Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May for June–August harvest. Florida Giant requires a long warm season (85–100 days) and ample space for the vigorous, sprawling vines — allow 6–10 feet diameter per plant. Very heat-tolerant and well-adapted to Gulf Coast summer conditions.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F, planting 4–5 seeds per hill and thinning to 2 plants; harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit has dried and the ground spot has turned from white to cream-yellow. Florida Giant is a classic large-fruited Southern heirloom watermelon producing enormous fruits (30–60 pounds or more) with light green to dark green striped skin and deep red, sweet flesh — the quintessential 'picnic' or 'table' watermelon of the Gulf South where the long, hot summer provides adequate heat units for the 85–100 day maturation period. The very large fruits are challenging to transport single-handed but are impressive in the garden and at the table, providing abundant fresh fruit for summer gatherings. Florida Giant performs excellently under Gulf Coast hot humid summer conditions, showing reasonable tolerance of the fungal diseases (Fusarium wilt, anthracnose) common in humid climates, and is well-adapted to the sandy, fertile, moderately acid soils of Florida and the Gulf Coast region. The traditional size and flavor make it a regional staple and a nostalgic choice for gardeners who remember the giant watermelons of summer cookouts.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Watermelon Production Guide

name: Florida Green Chayote
plantingNote: Plant a whole, slightly sprouted fruit on its side at a 45-degree angle with the narrow (stem) end up and just barely covered, once soil is reliably warm; this University of Florida-favored smooth green selection needs the full length of the Gulf Coast growing season to size up before first frost.
directions: Florida Green is the standard smooth, light-green, pear-shaped chayote cultivar recommended by University of Florida IFAS Extension for home gardens across the state, prized for consistent fruit set even through the region's oppressive summer humidity. Fruits run six ounces to a pound and are lightly grooved but essentially spineless, making them easier to handle and peel than heirloom spiny types. Give the sprawling vine a very sturdy arbor or fence, since a single well-sited plant can cover several hundred square feet and yield dozens of fruit from late summer into the first hard freeze. Along the Gulf Coast the rootstock often survives mild winters and resprouts, so mulching the crown heavily after dieback can save a year of establishment.

name: Florida High Bush Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost at 80–85°F for germination; transplant into full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Florida High Bush grows into a tall, vigorous plant and benefits from staking once fruit load is heavy.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun once the soil and nights are warm; Florida High Bush is an old Southern heirloom eggplant bred for reliable production through the intense heat and humidity of a Deep South summer, when many standard eggplant varieties stall or drop blossoms. Plants grow tall and vigorous — notably taller than most eggplant cultivars, as the name suggests — and bear a heavy, extended crop of glossy, deep purple-black, oval to pear-shaped fruit with classic mild, creamy flesh. Because the bushes get large and top-heavy once loaded with fruit, stake or cage plants at transplanting to prevent wind and fruit-weight damage. Harvest fruit at about two-thirds of full size, while the skin is still glossy and taut — dull skin signals over-mature, seedier flesh. Regular harvesting encourages continued flowering and keeps plants productive from early summer through the first fall frost in zone 8–9.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — heirloom eggplant variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Eggplant Production
Seed Savers Exchange — heirloom eggplant collection

name: Florida Market Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start December–January and transplant February–March. Florida Market is specifically developed for Gulf Coast and Florida conditions, with superior heat tolerance and disease resistance compared to northern eggplant varieties. In zone 9 it will produce through the hot summer months when other eggplants pause; a second planting in July–August extends production into fall. Provide full sun and consistently warm soil for best production.
