directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture and warm soil temperatures; Florida Market is an open-pollinated eggplant variety developed specifically for production in hot, humid, disease-prone Gulf Coast and Florida conditions — it shows markedly better performance in zone 8b–11 than northern varieties selected for cool, short-season growing conditions. The large, oval to cylindrical fruits are 6–8 inches long with smooth, glossy deep purple skin and dense, firm white flesh with relatively few seeds — the classic eggplant form ideal for slicing, grilling, roasting, baba ghanoush, moussaka, and Parmesan preparations. The superior heat tolerance allows Florida Market to continue flowering and setting fruit through Gulf Coast summers when temperatures regularly exceed 95°F — a period when many northern varieties drop their flowers. Consistent irrigation is more critical than for most vegetables, as uneven moisture causes fruit development problems and bitter flesh.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Eggplant Production in Florida
University of Georgia Extension — Eggplant Varieties for Georgia
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Eggplant Production for Texas

name: Florida Speckled Lima Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm, above 65°F; this Southern heirloom pole lima tolerates the heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer better than many Northern-bred lima varieties.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F, providing a trellis or pole for the climbing vine. Florida Speckled is a Southern heirloom pole lima bean grown for its handsome maroon-and-white speckled seeds and, more importantly, for genuine heat tolerance that lets it set pods reliably through the hot, humid conditions of a Deep South summer that cause many lima varieties to drop blossoms and stop producing. The vigorous vine climbs readily and produces well over an extended season once established. Harvest pods at the green shell stage for the classic buttery lima flavor, or allow pods to dry fully on the vine for a dry bean harvest that stores well through winter.

name: Florina Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay warm; Florina peppers need a long, warm season for the elongated fruit to ripen fully to red.
directions: Florina pepper is a long, tapering, thin-walled sweet pepper grown around the Macedonian town of Florina in northern Greece, where it carries European PDO status and is the pepper of choice for the roasted, oil-and-vinegar pepper salads served across the region. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil with a stake or cage to support heavily laden branches, and harvest once fruit has turned from green to a deep glossy red for the sweetest flavor and easiest peeling after roasting. Char the thin-fleshed pods whole over flame or under a broiler, then peel and marinate in olive oil, garlic, and vinegar in the traditional Macedonian style. Pick successively through the season to keep plants setting new fruit.
sources: Greek Ministry of Rural Development and Food

name: Florunner Peanut
plantingNote: Direct sow shelled, unroasted seed once soil has warmed well past the last frost date, into loose, sandy ground; Florunner needs the full length of a Gulf Coast summer to fill out its heavy pod load.
directions: Plant shelled seed about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, since the flowering pegs must push easily into the ground to form pods. Florunner was released in 1969 by the Florida Agricultural Experiment Station as a Spanish x Virginia-derived runner-type, and its spreading, decumbent habit and exceptionally heavy pod set drove a major jump in peanut yields across the Southeast when it was introduced. The sprawling vines cover more ground than bunch-type peanuts, so give plants extra room, and keep soil evenly moist through flowering and pegging to maximize pod set. Dig the whole plant once leaves begin to yellow in fall and cure pods in a warm, airy spot before shelling, boiling, or roasting.
sources: Crop Science Society of America registration records

name: Fordhook 242 Lima Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (65°F+); in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September for fall production. Lima beans require warm soil and warm nights to develop properly — cool temperatures cause poor pod set and seed development. Fordhook 242 is a bush type that requires no support; harvest pods when seeds are plump and green but before the pods yellow. Shelling fresh lima beans immediately after harvest produces the sweetest, most tender flavor — the sugars begin converting to starch within hours of harvest.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — lima beans fix atmospheric nitrogen and improve soil quality for subsequent crops; Fordhook 242 is the standard large-seeded bush lima bean — an All-America Selections award-winning variety from the Burpee Fordhook line that has defined the Fordhook (large, flat, meaty-seeded) type of lima bean in American horticulture for nearly a century. The large, flat, creamy-green seeds are the classic 'butter bean' of Southern cooking — much larger and meatier than baby lima beans, with a rich, starchy, almost buttery flavor and firm-yet-creamy texture that makes them one of the most satisfying of all shelling beans. Lima beans are often unfairly associated with canned or frozen product quality that gives no sense of their fresh garden character — freshly shelled and immediately cooked Fordhook lima beans have a completely different, far superior flavor to processed versions, with genuine sweetness and a rich, filling character. The large seeds also dry well for winter use, expanding culinary possibilities beyond the fresh-shelled season.
sources: All-America Selections — Fordhook Lima Bean Award
W. Atlee Burpee Company — Fordhook 242 Lima Bean
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Lima Beans for Gulf South Gardens

name: Fordhook Fancy Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before the last frost, or in late summer for a fall crop; harvest outer leaves young for the mildest flavor.
directions: Direct sow shallowly and thin seedlings to stand several inches apart, harvesting outer leaves regularly to keep the plant productive. This old American selection, once distributed under the Fordhook name, forms dense rosettes of tightly curled, ruffled bright green leaves with a peppery mustard bite that mellows when cooked. Its frilly texture makes it a distinctive addition to mixed braising greens, and it tends to hold in the garden a bit longer than plain-leaf mustards before bolting.

name: Fordhook Giant Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–March for fall through spring harvest. Fordhook Giant is a large, vigorous variety that reaches impressive size in cool conditions — individual leaves can exceed 2 feet long in optimal growing. Harvest outer leaves continuously from the bottom of the plant, leaving the central growing tip intact to keep plants producing; plants can produce for many months with this cut-and-come-again approach. In zone 9 plants are productive from fall through early spring and may bolt in warming spring weather.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Fordhook Giant is the classic white-stalked Swiss chard — one of the oldest and most productive chard varieties in American seed catalogs, developed by the Burpee seed company and named for Burpee's Fordhook Farm in Pennsylvania where it was trialed and selected. The very large, heavily blistered, dark green leaves with thick, pure white, celery-like stalks represent the classic Swiss chard appearance and deliver maximum productivity per square foot — the substantial white stalks are among the meatiest and most impressive of any chard variety, making Fordhook Giant the preferred choice in preparations where stalks are eaten separately from the leaves. The thick stalks can be prepared raw like celery, steamed and buttered like asparagus, or braised for their mild, slightly sweet, beet-adjacent flavor; the large leaves cook down like spinach with a mild, earthy, slightly mineral character. Individual plants in good conditions can produce leaves exceeding 2 feet long, making the garden presence of Fordhook Giant among the most dramatically large of any leafy vegetable. The partial shade tolerance makes it one of the best vegetables for kitchen gardens with limited full-sun exposure.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee Company — Fordhook Giant Chard History
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Swiss Chard Production Guide
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Swiss Chard Varieties for Florida

name: Fordhook Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills or rows after soil has warmed following last frost; in Gulf Coast gardens a second sowing in midsummer keeps production going once early plants decline from squash vine borer or powdery mildew.
directions: Fordhook Zucchini was bred at Burpee's historic Fordhook Farm trial grounds in Pennsylvania and became an early All-America Selections winner, predating most of the modern hybrid zucchini lines still sold today. It forms a compact, upright bush rather than a sprawling vine, producing straight to slightly curved, smooth dark-green fruit best picked young at 6-8 inches for the most tender, seedless texture. Because it sets fruit heavily and quickly, plants benefit from daily harvesting during peak summer heat to prevent oversized, seedy squash and to keep new blossoms coming. Its open-pollinated seed can be saved true from year to year, unlike the many F1 hybrids that have largely replaced it in seed catalogs.

name: Forellenschluss Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 6–8 weeks before last frost; most beautiful when harvested as a whole head; also excellent as cut-and-come-again greens at baby stage.
directions: Sow seed on the soil surface in early spring in fertile, moist, well-drained soil; Forellenschluss is a legendary Austrian heirloom butterhead lettuce — the name means 'trout's back' in German for its distinctive pattern of bright red-bronze speckles scattered across brilliantly green leaves, giving each leaf the dappled appearance of a brook trout. Considered one of the most beautiful and best-flavored lettuces in the world, with butter-soft, sweet, melt-in-the-mouth leaves. Also sold as 'Flashy Trout's Back' in the United States. Suitable for both spring and fall, it is less tolerant of summer heat than loose-leaf types; harvest heads when full but before bolting.

name: Forono Beet
plantingNote: Sow as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9; succession sow through the cool season for a continuous harvest.
directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3-4 inches once true leaves appear; keep soil consistently moist for smooth, tender roots. Forono is an Italian heirloom beet distinguished by its long, cylindrical, carrot-like shape rather than the typical round beet form, an advantage in the kitchen because its uniform diameter yields evenly sized slices from end to end with almost no waste, and a single root often provides several servings. The deep red flesh is sweet, tender, and free of the pale internal rings some other beets show, and because the roots grow mostly upward out of the soil rather than swelling wide, more roots can be grown in the same row space. Harvest at 4-6 inches long for the best texture, and the tops are also good cooked as greens.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Forono variety notes

name: Fort Umpqua Turnip
plantingNote: Sow in early spring for a summer crop or in late summer for a sweeter fall crop; roots hold their quality in the ground after light frost.
directions: Fort Umpqua produces a classic purple-shouldered, white-bottomed turnip root that stays firm and dense rather than becoming pithy as it sizes up, which gives growers more flexibility on harvest timing than many fast-bolting salad turnips. Direct-sow seed shallowly in loosened soil and thin to 3 to 4 inches, since crowding leads to misshapen roots. Both the root and the tender young greens are good eating, with the root holding a mild, slightly peppery bite that mellows when cooked. A fall sowing timed so roots mature after a light frost generally produces the sweetest flavor.

name: Fortex Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Fortex is a vigorous climbing pole bean reaching 7–9 feet — provide a sturdy trellis, pole tepee, or strong fence for support. Harvest pods frequently and while still young (10–11 inches long) before seeds begin to bulge, which keeps the plants productive and maintains pod tenderness.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 60°F; provide a sturdy trellis or support structure before planting and harvest regularly while pods are still slender and young. Fortex is considered by many gardeners and chefs to be the finest French filet (haricot vert) style pole bean available — a European heirloom that produces extraordinarily long (10–12 inch), very slender, round-podded, deep green beans with exceptional tenderness and refined flavor that places it far above standard snap beans for fresh eating and French-style preparations. Unlike flat, wide snap beans, Fortex pods are round, very slender (filet-style), and remain tender and flavorful well beyond the size at which most beans become tough — they can be harvested at any point from finger-thin to full pencil thickness and maintain excellent quality. The flavor is genuinely superior, with a rich green bean taste and very fine texture that makes Fortex the preferred bean for blanching, sautéing with garlic and butter, and all preparations where bean quality is the focus. Very productive vines climb 7–9 feet and bear continuously when picked frequently. An outstanding bean for serious vegetable gardeners and those who want restaurant-quality produce from their home garden.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Fortex pole bean variety notes
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Snap Bean Variety Evaluation

name: Fourth of July Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Fourth of July produces ripe tomatoes 49–55 days after transplanting — approximately 2–3 weeks earlier than mid-season varieties. In zone 9, transplant in late February or early March for a first harvest in late April to early May. The very early maturation is particularly valuable in zone 9 where the summer window closes before many standard varieties finish producing.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Fourth of July is an indeterminate hybrid tomato that holds the distinction of being one of the earliest-producing standard-sized tomatoes available to home gardeners — producing its first ripe fruits approximately 49–55 days after transplanting, roughly the same time that slower varieties are just beginning to set fruit. The name references the plant's ability to provide ripe tomatoes by or before the Fourth of July holiday in northern gardens when planted on schedule. The medium-small (4–6 oz), round, bright red fruits have good sweet-tart tomato flavor for an early variety — notably better than most extremely early types, which often sacrifice flavor for speed. The indeterminate vines continue producing throughout the summer and fall after early harvests, unlike determinates that produce one concentrated crop. Fourth of July is outstanding for gardeners in any climate who want fresh home-grown tomatoes as early as possible, and particularly valuable in Gulf South gardens where early production before summer heat peak extends the harvest season significantly. A practical, reliable early variety that should be in every serious tomato garden alongside a mid-season variety.
sources: Burpee Seeds — Fourth of July tomato variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Early tomato variety comparison
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Variety Evaluation

name: Foxfibre Cotton
plantingNote: Direct sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep once soil has thoroughly warmed well past last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; needs the same long, hot, frost-free season as any cotton.
directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the growing season is reliably warm, following standard upland cotton culture. Foxfibre is the trademarked line of naturally colored, organically grown upland cotton developed by California breeder Sally Fox beginning in the 1980s from a chance discovery of brown, pest-resistant cotton seed; through years of selection and crossing with long-staple and Pima lines, Fox produced the first naturally colored cotton fiber strong and long enough to be spun on modern commercial machinery. Foxfibre bolls open in shades of camel, tan, rust-brown, and soft sage green that need no dye, and the plants show useful natural pest resistance. Pick bolls promptly once open, since color and fiber quality fade with prolonged weather exposure, and rotate the planting site yearly to limit soil-borne disease buildup as with any cotton.

name: Franklim Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant one-year crowns in trenches enriched with well-rotted manure as soon as soil can be worked; this early all-male Dutch hybrid was one of the pioneering supermale-derived lines bred for uniform, seedling-free beds.
directions: Franklim was bred in the Netherlands from a supermale line derived from self-pollinated 'Ruhm von Braunschweig,' making it one of the earliest all-male asparagus hybrids widely grown in Europe. Because every plant is male, beds put no energy into seed production and never develop the volunteer seedling problem common to older open-pollinated strains, so spear production stays concentrated and beds keep a tidy, even stand for years. Spears emerge thick, straight, and closely spaced along the crown, tolerating both traditional green cropping and mounded cultivation for blanched white spears. Give it deep, fertile, well-drained soil and avoid cutting for the first two years so crowns can build the reserves needed for a long productive life.

name: Freckles Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool weather with seeds barely covered; Freckles / Flashy Trout's Back is a loose-head romaine type that performs best in cool temperatures and is an excellent fall-through-spring crop in zone 9 (September–March).
directions: Sow seeds shallowly in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in cool weather; Freckles lettuce (Austrian name: 'Forellenschluss', meaning 'Trout's Back', also sold as 'Flashy Trout's Back') is a traditional Austrian/Central European heirloom romaine-type lettuce with one of the most distinctive and beautiful appearances in the lettuce world — pale green, slightly upright loose-romaine leaves dramatically spotted and splashed with burgundy-red markings in irregular patterns that genuinely resemble the markings of a brook trout's back. Despite its ornamental appearance, Freckles is an excellent eating lettuce with the substantial, crisp, slightly crunchy texture of romaine and mild, sweet, pleasant flavor without bitterness. The visual impact makes it outstanding for decorative vegetable gardens and for using fresh as a centerpiece lettuce. Freckles is moderately heat-tolerant for a lettuce and somewhat slow to bolt, extending the spring harvest window. An outstanding conversation-piece heirloom lettuce that combines genuine beauty with excellent eating quality.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Forellenschluss/Freckles lettuce variety notes

name: Fremont Cauliflower
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for spring, or in midsummer for a fall crop; Fremont's leaves naturally wrap over the developing curd, so it needs little to no manual blanching.
directions: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before setting out transplants into rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil. Fremont is a self-blanching hybrid whose upright inner leaves curl naturally over the forming curd, shielding it from sunlight and keeping the head bright white without the usual step of tying leaves up by hand. It performs reliably through the warmer, less predictable conditions of a summer planting, forming smooth, dense, well-domed heads. Harvest as soon as the curd is tight and fully formed, since cauliflower heads can quickly become ricey or loose if left too long once mature.

name: French Breakfast Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in well-drained, loose, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 9, sow September–November for the main fall crop and January–February for a spring crop; succession sow every 2 weeks for a continuous harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in well-drained, loose, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during cool seasons; French Breakfast is a classic European heirloom radish with a history dating to the early nineteenth century — producing oblong-to-cylindrical, 3–4 inch roots with a distinctive two-tone color pattern: brilliant scarlet-red over the upper two-thirds grading to crisp white at the tip. The elongated, elegant shape is distinctly different from the standard round red radish and makes French Breakfast instantly recognizable in the garden and at market. The flavor is mild and crisp — somewhat milder than globe radishes when harvested young, with a light, clean pepper-radish flavor that becomes stronger and more pungent if roots are left in the ground too long or grown during warm weather. Traditional French usage was to eat them dipped in butter with a pinch of salt at breakfast — hence the name. In zone 9, French Breakfast radishes are a cool-season crop performing best September through April; they bolt and become pungent in the summer heat. Succession sow every 2 weeks for continuous harvest. Thin to 2–3 inches for the best root development. Harvest when roots reach 3/4–1 inch diameter for the mildest flavor.

name: French Charlotte Potato
plantingNote: Well suited to large containers and raised beds in addition to open garden rows; plant 4-6 weeks before last frost.
directions: A mid-season French variety popularized among organic growers, producing long-oval, medium-small golden tubers with golden, waxy-moist flesh prized for its flavor and good storage life. Medium-sized plants with violet flowers set tubers heavily, though overall yield stays moderate, and the variety shows medium-high blight tolerance with moderate scab resistance. It performs notably well in containers, making it a good pick for gardeners with limited in-ground space.

name: French Fingerling Potato
plantingNote: Plant seed potato pieces in cool soil with 2–3 eyes per piece; French Fingerling is a mid-season fingerling type that produces elongated, finger-shaped tubers 2–4 inches long with distinctive pink skin and cream to pale yellow flesh marbled with pink veins. In zone 9, plant January–February for a March–May harvest before summer heat arrives. The compact vines (18–24 inches) produce tubers in clusters that remain relatively close to the surface and are easily harvested by digging carefully around the plant. French Fingerling is not a traditional French heirloom in the way Rattes or other older varieties are, but the name reflects the variety's French-inspired culinary aesthetic and elegant appearance. Like most fingerling varieties, French Fingerling is waxy-fleshed and holds its shape well through roasting, sautéing, and boiling.
directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3–4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil; harvest when vines begin to die back. French Fingerling is valued primarily for its visual distinction and culinary versatility: the combination of rose-pink skin and cream-yellow flesh with distinctive pink marbling through the interior makes French Fingerling one of the most visually striking fingerling varieties when halved or sliced — the pink marbling pattern within the creamy flesh is unique and makes the roasted or halved potato distinctly attractive in presentations. The texture is waxy and firm — a characteristic of fingerling potato varieties that have lower starch content than baking types (Russet Burbank) and retain their shape well through cooking. This waxy texture makes fingerlings the preferred choice for roasting whole (they develop a crispy exterior while staying firm inside), for potato salads (they don't become mushy when dressed), and for sautéed preparations where pieces need to hold their shape. French Fingerling's flavor is described as nutty, sweet, and complex — more interesting than the relatively neutral flavor of standard Russet types, with a richness that farmers market customers and restaurant chefs find particularly valuable. The variety performs well for small-scale and home garden production, producing enough tubers per plant for household use without requiring the large-scale inputs (cool storage, extensive land) of commercial Russet production.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — French Fingerling potato variety notes
Wood Prairie Farm — French Fingerling fingerling potato certified seed potato information
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Fingerling potato variety comparison for Southern gardens

name: French Green Lentil
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring a few weeks ahead of the last frost, since young lentil plants tolerate light frost and grow best through a long, cool stretch before summer heat sets in.
directions: Direct sow in early spring a few weeks ahead of the last frost, since young lentil plants tolerate light frost and grow best through a long, cool stretch before summer heat sets in. This variety takes its name from the volcanic plateau around Le Puy-en-Velay in France's Auvergne region, where a legally protected growing area produces small, marbled slate-green lentils famous for holding their shape and delivering a peppery, mineral flavor after cooking. Skip heavy nitrogen fertilizer, which pushes leafy growth at the expense of pods, and let the sparse, wiry plants lean on light twiggy brush if needed. Harvest the whole plant once most pods have turned tan and papery, then dry and thresh before storing the seed.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste
Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualité (INAO)

name: French Red Shallot
plantingNote: Plant individual bulbs or sets in early spring (or fall in mild-winter zones) in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; French Red is a true shallot with coppery-red skin and rich, mild-pungent flavor.
directions: Plant individual bulbs pointed-end-up, just below the soil surface, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 6-8 inches apart to allow each bulb to multiply into a cluster. French Red produces clusters of small, round-to-oval bulbs with distinctive coppery-red skin and pale purple-tinged flesh, carrying the rich, complex, mild-pungent flavor that distinguishes true shallots from ordinary onions and makes them prized in French cooking. Grow much like garlic, keeping soil evenly moist through bulb development and reducing water as the tops begin to yellow and fall over. Harvest when most of the foliage has died back, cure in a warm, dry, airy spot for two to three weeks, then store in a cool, dry location; shallots typically store longer than onions of similar size.

name: Frenzy Frisee Endive
plantingNote: Direct sow around the last frost for a spring-to-summer crop, or in late summer for the traditional fall crop. Improved bolt resistance lets 'Frenzy' be sown earlier in spring than older frisee-type endives, which tend to bolt if planted before day length starts to shorten.
directions: 'Frenzy' is a fast, uniform frisee-type endive with finely dissected, frizzy leaves and improved bolt resistance that lets it be direct sown in spring as well as in the late-summer window most curly endives need. Heads self-blanch as the deeply cut outer leaves arch over the pale, feathery heart, though tying the outer leaves closed for the last week or two before harvest produces a larger blanched center. Its quicker 45 to 55 day cycle and heat tolerance make it more forgiving of an early sowing than older frisee varieties. Harvest whole heads at the base once the centers are tight, or pick individual outer leaves as a cut-and-come-again crop while the heart keeps developing.

name: Friariello Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Friariello grows tall and heavy with fruit, so stake or cage plants to prevent breakage.
directions: Friariello is a traditional Neapolitan frying pepper whose name derives from the Italian verb for frying, reflecting centuries of use in southern Italian home kitchens. Tall, vigorous plants bear small, tri-lobed, thin-walled pods only a few inches long that mature from green to bright red, with a sweet flavor and no measurable heat. The classic preparation fries the whole pepper, seeds and skin included, in olive oil with garlic until blistered, then finishes it with tomato and fresh basil. Because the plants grow taller and set a heavier fruit load than many bell-type sweet peppers, staking or caging helps keep the brittle branches from snapping under the weight.

name: Frisee Endive
plantingNote: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for fall harvest. Direct sowing is also possible. Frisee blanches naturally at the center as the outer leaves close over the interior; for the maximum pale center and milder flavor, tie the outer leaves loosely with twine 2 weeks before harvest. In zone 9 fall planting gives the most reliable head development; spring planting bolts too quickly in warming conditions.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Frisee is the fine-leaved, deeply curled, frizzy form of curly endive — a classic French bistro salad ingredient produced by its pale, blanched interior heart surrounded by a halo of fine, frizzy dark-green outer leaves. The pale interior (the blanched portion) has a mild, gently bitter, nutty flavor that is the defining taste of the classic frisee salad with lardons and a warm poached egg — one of the most recognizable French bistro dishes. The dark green outer leaves are more bitter and are usually removed or used for cooking. Frisee blanches naturally when the outer leaves overlap and shade the center, but deliberate blanching (tying the outer leaves for 1–2 weeks before harvest) produces a larger, more uniform pale center. In zone 9 frisee is a fall-through-winter crop that produces its characteristic delicate, pale center in the cool, short-day conditions from November through February.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Frisee Endive Variety Notes
Territorial Seed Company — Curly Endive and Frisee
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Endive and Chicory

name: Frizzy Lizzy Mustard
plantingNote: Sow in early spring or late summer; fast enough to harvest as a baby-leaf cut in as little as three weeks.
directions: Frizzy Lizzy produces deeply toothed, intensely ruffled mustard leaves that add texture as well as a sharp, peppery bite to a baby-leaf salad mix. Broadcast or sow in close rows and begin cutting at about three weeks for the tenderest baby leaves, or let it grow longer for a spicier, more mature green. It regrows readily after a light cut-and-come-again harvest, giving several pickings from a single sowing in cool weather. The frilled leaf edge also makes it a visually interesting addition to the garden bed, not just the salad bowl.

name: Fuentes de Ebro Onion
plantingNote: Sow in protected beds in winter and transplant in early spring; this PGI-protected onion needs the Ebro valley's long, steadily warming season to reach its full globe size.
directions: Grown under European PGI protection around Fuentes de Ebro in Aragón, this large, pale-skinned onion is famous for an exceptionally sweet, almost fruity flesh with very low pungency, making it the base of the region's cold ensalada de cebolla. It needs deep, well-worked alluvial-type soil and consistent irrigation through bulb development, since the thin cell walls that give it sweetness also make it prone to stress cracking in uneven moisture. Harvest as soon as tops fall and skins set, then use promptly or refrigerate, as the same delicate structure that makes it sweet also makes it one of the shortest-storing onions grown commercially.
sources: Diputación General de Aragón agricultural extension

name: Fuentesaúco Chickpea
plantingNote: Direct-sow in early spring on the dry plains around Fuentesaúco in Zamora as soon as the ground can be worked, relying on winter soil moisture to carry the crop through its mostly unirrigated growing season.
directions: This large, thin-skinned, pale chickpea from the Zamora plateau is prized for cooking down to a notably creamy, buttery texture without needing the long pre-soak many chickpeas require. It thrives in the region's deep clay-loam soils under dry-farmed conditions, tolerating drought well once established, though a wet spring during flowering can both help yields and risk fungal disease, so good air movement between rows matters. Harvest whole plants once pods have dried and rattle, then thresh, and favor minimal irrigation throughout to avoid diluting the dense, starchy texture this variety is known for.
sources: European Commission PDO/PGI Register — Garbanzo de Fuentesaúco
Junta de Castilla y León agricultural extension

name: Ful Medames Fava Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter regions for an overwintered crop.
directions: Sow seed early, spacing plants more closely than large-seeded fava types since this is a compact, small-seeded selection bred for dense pod set rather than individual bean size. Ful Medames is the small, brown-skinned fava named for the classic Egyptian breakfast dish of the same name, in which the whole beans — skins left on — are simmered for hours until completely soft, then mashed with garlic, lemon, cumin, and olive oil. The smaller seed size shortens the long stovetop cooking time somewhat compared with large fava varieties, though the dish is still traditionally cooked low and slow. Pinch growing tips after the first flush of pods sets to curb aphids and push more energy into pod fill, and harvest once pods have dried on the plant if saving beans for the signature stewed preparation.
sources: Agricultural Research Center (ARC), Egypt — Field Crops Research Institute

name: Full Heart Escarole
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 transplant August–September for harvest November–January. Full Heart Batavian self-blanches at the center more reliably than other escarole types as the outer leaves naturally close over the heart. In zone 9 the mild fall allows slow, steady head development from September transplants through November harvest.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Full Heart Batavian is the classic escarole for Italian home cooking — a broad-leaved chicory endive forming a large, dense head with a characteristic self-blanching, creamy-yellow interior heart surrounded by darker outer leaves. The center heart has the mildest, most tender flavor of any escarole or endive type; the outer leaves are more bitter and are often removed or reserved for long-cooked soups and braises. Full Heart Batavian is the standard escarole used in Italian-American cooking — the primary green in Italian wedding soup (minestra maritata), in braised escarole with white beans and garlic, and as a pizza topping. The dense, substantial head stores well for 2–3 weeks in the refrigerator after harvest, making escarole one of the most practical winter greens for home cooks. In zone 9 the fall growing season from August transplants produces excellent heads by November; the plants are cold-hardy and withstand light frosts that improve flavor.
sources: Seeds of Italy — Full Heart Batavian Escarole Growing Notes
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Escarole
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Escarole and Endive Production

name: Full Moon Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in deeply enriched soil; a giant white pumpkin that needs a long, warm season and heavy feeding to reach its full 60-90 pound potential.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in heavily composted soil, spacing hills at least 8-10 feet apart to accommodate the large-fruited vines. Full Moon is a giant white pumpkin producing smooth, lightly sutured fruit that commonly reaches 60-90 pounds and stands roughly 3 feet tall by 2 feet wide under good growing conditions, with a long 120-day-plus season needed to size up fully. The pale rind is retained best when fruit is left to mature fully on the vine rather than harvested early, and consistent deep watering through fruit set is important to avoid rind cracking on such large specimens. Harvest before hard frost once the rind has hardened completely, and handle carefully since the size and weight make the fruit prone to bruising and stem breakage.

name: Full Pint Barley
plantingNote: Sow in early spring once soil is workable; Full Pint is a hull-less two-row barley from the Oregon State University barley breeding program, popular with small-scale craft maltsters.
directions: Full Pint is a hull-less two-row spring barley from the Oregon State University barley breeding program that has become a favorite of small-scale craft maltsters in the Pacific Northwest for the distinct, grainy flavor it brings to malt. Because the hull threshes almost completely free, the harvested kernels require little further processing before malting, which appeals to growers supplying local breweries and distilleries directly. Drill into a firm seedbed in early spring like other spring barleys, and manage moisture carefully since naked barley kernels are more exposed to weathering and pre-harvest sprouting than hulled types. Harvest promptly once mature and dry the grain well before storage to protect quality.
sources: Oregon State University Barley Breeding Program

name: Fuseau Jerusalem Artichoke
plantingNote: Plant whole or cut seed tubers, each with at least one or two eyes, about 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil once the soil can be worked in spring. Because sunchokes spread aggressively from any tuber left in the ground, choose a bed where the planting can be permanently contained or is not a problem to leave in place.
directions: Plant whole or cut seed tubers, each with at least one or two eyes, about 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil once the soil can be worked in spring. Because sunchokes spread aggressively from any tuber left in the ground, choose a bed where the planting can be permanently contained or is not a problem to leave in place. Fuseau is a long-established French heirloom named for its elongated, relatively smooth, club-shaped tubers, which are far easier to scrub and peel than the knobby, eye-covered tubers typical of unnamed Jerusalem artichoke stock. Its tall late-summer sunflower-like blooms are followed by a fall and winter tuber harvest that continues after light frosts, and the tubers themselves have the same nutty, sweet flavor common to the species, sweetening further after cold exposure.

name: Fushimi Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile soil after frost danger passes. Fushimi is one of the traditional Kyo-yasai vegetables of Kyoto.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; Fushimi is one of the Kyo-yasai, the traditional heirloom vegetables of Kyoto, producing thin-walled, glossy, slender tapered pods up to 6 inches long with a mild heat (1,000-2,500 SHU). The productive plants bear continuously through the season; harvest pods green for the best texture, especially for tempura, where Fushimi's thin walls fry up light and crisp. It performs well in both garden rows and containers.

name: Futo Spindle Bitter Melon
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep after soil is thoroughly warm and all frost danger has passed, training vines up a sturdy trellis.
directions: A traditional Japanese heirloom bitter melon prized for exceptional heat tolerance and vigorous, dense vining growth. The long, spindle-shaped fruit has deeply ridged, heavily warted dark-green skin and can reach 7-12 inches, ripening to orange-yellow if left unpicked. Harvest while still firm and green for the classic assertively bitter flavor used in goya champuru and other Okinawan stir-fries, or let a few fruit fully color for milder, sweeter eating. Its climbing habit and heat tolerance make it a good choice for a hot, humid summer trellis planting where other bitter melon types struggle.

name: Futura 75 Hemp
plantingNote: Direct sow at or just after last frost into a dense stand; 'Futura 75' is a tall, late-maturing, monoecious French fiber cultivar and, like all hemp, requires state or federal licensing to grow legally in the United States.
directions: Drill seed at a high density of roughly 25-30 lb per acre to force tall, slender, largely unbranched stalks, since crowded stands are essential to good fiber quality in this cultivar. 'Futura 75' was bred in France for bast fiber production and has been used in several US university trials, including early Kentucky industrial hemp research plots, as a benchmark fiber-type cultivar because of its reliable low-THC compliance and strong stalk yield. Plants can reach 10 to 13 feet in a full season under good conditions, considerably taller than dual-purpose or grain cultivars, and stems become increasingly coarse and woody as flowering finishes. Harvest for fiber at the onset of flowering, when bast fiber content and quality peak, then ret and process the stalks as with any bast fiber crop; a hemp growing license and pre-harvest THC testing are required in nearly all US jurisdictions.
sources: European Union Common Catalogue of Varieties of Agricultural Plant Species

name: Gala Mâche
plantingNote: In cold-winter regions sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop or as early as soil can be worked in spring; in mild-winter regions sow in late summer or early fall to overwinter for a spring harvest.
directions: Sow seed about 1/4 inch deep and keep the bed consistently moist and weeded, since Gala develops slowly and germinates over a long, uneven window even in ideal cool conditions. This heirloom French selection is valued for good mildew resistance and a rich, buttery texture, forming neat, fist-sized rosettes of oval leaves with a mild, nutty flavor. It tolerates light frost well and holds in the garden through cold snaps better than many quick-maturing salad greens. Harvest whole rosettes by cutting them at the base once they reach full size.

name: Galahad Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Galahad's compact, well-branched growth habit still benefits from a cage even though it sets fruit earlier and on a smaller frame than a typical indeterminate beefsteak.
directions: Galahad was named an AAS Edible-Vegetable Winner for combining large, meaty beefsteak-type fruit with a shorter, more compact, well-branched plant that needs less space than a typical vining slicer. It carries resistance to Fusarium wilt, Verticillium wilt, and tobacco mosaic virus, and sets its 8-12 ounce fruit earlier in the season than most large-fruited hybrids. Cage or stake the plant even though it stays relatively compact, since the heavy fruit load can still bend unsupported stems, and keep up regular watering to reduce blossom end rot on the big first fruits.

name: Galia Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Galia requires warm conditions throughout its development and performs well in the Gulf South's warm summer climate. In zone 9, plant March–April for June–August harvest. Reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the skin transitions from green to golden-yellow and a sweet, tropical fragrance is detectable at the stem end — the skin color change from green to yellow-gold is the primary harvest indicator for Galia.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after last frost; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when skin turns yellow-gold and a sweet tropical aroma is detectable at the stem end. Galia is an Israeli hybrid muskmelon type developed in the 1970s at the Newe Ya'ar Research Center by Dr. Zvi Karchi, named for his daughter — an F1 hybrid that combines the netted, aromatic skin characteristics of cantaloupe/muskmelon with the pale green, spicy-sweet flesh of honeydew, creating a novel flavor profile found in no other commonly available melon type. The round to slightly oval fruits (3–5 lb) have heavily netted, yellow-green to yellow-gold skin at maturity (the skin begins green and transitions to yellow-gold as the melon ripens — a useful visual harvest cue not present in cantaloupe types that stay tan). The flesh is pale green to cream-green, aromatic, and extremely sweet with a distinctive tropical character — floral, spicy, and complex, distinctly different from both orange-fleshed cantaloupe and the blander honeydew. Galia melons are widely grown and marketed throughout Europe, Israel, and Central America and have become increasingly available in American specialty markets, where they are often sold under the name 'Israeli melon.' The flavor is among the most complex and interesting of any melon type, making Galia a top choice for gardeners who want to explore beyond standard cantaloupe.
sources: Newe Ya'ar Research Center, Israel — Galia melon development documentation
Seed Savers Exchange — Galia melon variety notes
University of California Cooperative Extension — Specialty Melon Production Guide

name: Galina's Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost; this fast-maturing Siberian heirloom tolerates cooler soil and air temperatures at transplant time better than most cherry tomatoes, making it a good choice for an early spring or extended fall crop.
directions: A Siberian heirloom with soft, blue-green potato-leaf foliage that sets abundant clusters of translucent, pale-yellow, one-inch cherry tomatoes with a rich, sweet flavor. Bred for a short, cool growing season, Galina's sets fruit reliably in cooler spring and fall conditions that cause many other cherry tomatoes to drop blossoms, making it a strong choice for a Gulf South fall tomato planting timed to ripen as temperatures moderate. The prolific, early-bearing vines need only routine staking and produce continuously from first ripe fruit until frost.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds Variety Catalog

name: Galine Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay above 55F. Galine's early maturity makes it a good option for gardeners in cooler, shorter-season climates who still want a classic elongated slicing eggplant.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after danger of frost has passed. Galine is a French-bred hybrid eggplant valued for its notably early maturity and reliable fruit set even in cooler summers, producing slender, cylindrical, glossy near-black fruit on a compact, manageable plant. The thin skin and few seeds make it well suited to quick-cooking preparations like grilling and stir-frying without the bitterness that can develop in larger, later-maturing types. Harvest at about two-thirds full size while the skin is taut and glossy for the mildest flavor and tenderest texture.

name: Ganjyu Bitter Melon
plantingNote: Direct-sow after soil has warmed above 70°F, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early; set plants slightly closer than most bitter melon and trellis from planting.
directions: Known in Okinawa as a 'longevity' vegetable, Ganjyu is an extra-large, light green type with deeply ridged skin and notably milder bitterness than typical dark green bitter melons. Set plants slightly closer than most bitter melon at 12-18 inches and provide a sturdy trellis at planting time, since the fast-growing vines need vertical support from early on. Keep soil consistently moist through flowering and fruiting, and encourage bee activity or hand-pollinate to ensure good fruit set on the long ridged fruit.

name: Garden of Eden Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil has warmed above 60°F, next to a sturdy trellis, pole, or fence at least 6 feet tall for this vigorous climbing heirloom.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep at the base of poles or a trellis after the soil has warmed, thinning to one strong seedling per pole or every 6 to 9 inches along a fence. Garden of Eden is a dual-purpose heirloom pole bean, grown from seed stock originating in Iberia, that produces broad, flat, deep-green pods up to 7 inches long that stay tender and sweet even as they size up. Pick young for a mild snap bean, or let pods mature and dry fully on the vine to harvest light brown, darkly striped seeds for a rich shell or dry bean. Keep vines picked regularly through the 6 to 8 week harvest window to encourage continued pod set.

name: Garden Peach Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Garden Peach is a unique and charming heirloom tomato that genuinely resembles a peach — producing small, round, blush-yellow to pale cream fruits covered in a delicate fuzz of dense trichomes that gives them the texture and appearance of a ripe peach skin — one of the most visually distinctive and surprising novelty tomatoes available.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Garden Peach is an indeterminate, moderately sized variety requiring staking or caging; it is quite productive and continues bearing through the season. Garden Peach tomato is a remarkable heirloom curiosity that mimics a real peach in appearance with unusual fidelity — the small (2–3 oz), round fruits have pale cream to blush-yellow skin covered in tiny dense hairs (trichomes) that create a distinctly fuzzy, velvet-textured surface virtually identical to peach fuzz; when held in the hand, a ripe Garden Peach tomato is nearly indistinguishable from a small peach by touch alone. The flavor is sweet and mild with a hint of fruity peach character, very low acidity, and soft, juicy texture — appealing to those who find standard tomatoes too acidic. The novelty factor is considerable: Garden Peach tomatoes generate immediate curiosity and conversation, and children in particular are captivated by the peach resemblance; they are excellent for farm stands and markets as well as home garden curiosity. The fuzzy skin, unlike most tomatoes, does not split in rain or overhead irrigation. A productive and reliable variety for any garden where the growing season exceeds 70 days.

name: Gargoyle Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Gargoyle is an All-America Selections winner grown strictly for its heavily warted, bicolor orange-and-green ornamental fruit rather than eating quality.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in full sun and well-drained soil, giving vines room to sprawl and set their oddly textured fruit. Gargoyle earned its All-America Selections award for an unmistakable look: dense, bumpy warts cover the entire orange-and-dark-green rind, giving each pumpkin a rugged, almost reptilian surface unlike smooth carving types. The tough, thick rind holds up well through a full season of fall display without softening, making it a durable choice for porch and entryway arrangements. Harvest before hard frost once color and warting have fully developed, and expect several fruits per vine across the season.

name: Garnet Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant sweet potato slips (rooted cuttings) after the last frost when soil has warmed to 60°F or above; Garnet sweet potato produces slips from mature tubers grown in a warm, moist environment (place in a jar of water or bury in moist sand at 80°F for 2–4 weeks until sprouts are 4–6 inches long). In zone 9, plant April–June for fall harvest; sweet potato vines grow vigorously in Gulf Coast heat and humidity. Dig roots before the first frost (or in zone 9 before sustained temperatures below 55°F, which can cause chilling injury to stored roots). Cure at 85°F and 90% humidity for 4–7 days after harvest to sweeten and harden the skin before storage.
directions: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, loose soil; do not overwater or over-fertilize with nitrogen (promotes vine over root). Cure harvested roots before storage. Garnet Sweet Potato (also sold as 'Red Garnet') is one of the most widely grown and commercially important sweet potato varieties in the United States, recognizable to millions of shoppers as the 'yam' with reddish-purple to copper-red skin and brilliant orange flesh sold in most American supermarkets. The confusion between true yams (Dioscorea species, tropical tubers with starchy white flesh) and sweet potatoes is a historical American marketing accident: in the mid-20th century, Louisiana farmers and marketers began calling their orange-fleshed sweet potatoes 'yams' to distinguish them from the paler-fleshed Northern sweet potato types, and the term 'yam' became permanently associated with moist, orange-fleshed sweet potatoes in American grocery retail. Garnet's moist orange flesh has the classic American sweet potato eating character: very sweet, soft when baked, and vibrantly orange — characteristics that come from a high beta-carotene content (beta-carotene is the pigment in carrots, orange squash, and other orange vegetables that converts to Vitamin A in the body). The roasted Garnet sweet potato is one of the most nutritionally dense foods in regular American cooking: high in complex carbohydrates, very high in beta-carotene (Vitamin A precursor), and a good source of potassium, fiber, and Vitamin C.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Sweet Potato Variety Descriptions and Production
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Potato Production for the Gulf South
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Sweet potato variety database

name: Garrofón Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed following last frost; Garrofón is a vining lima bean type and needs a trellis or other support to climb.
directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile soil in full sun alongside a trellis or other support for the vigorous climbing vines; Garrofón is the Valencian lima bean essential to authentic paella valenciana, producing flattened wide pods with large speckled or white seeds depending on the strain. Pick fresh at 3-4 months for the classic paella ingredient, or leave pods to dry fully on the vine past that point for storage beans. It is frost-tender like other lima beans and needs a full warm season to mature a complete crop.

name: Gaspe Flint Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks after soil has warmed, since this variety's main value is its extremely short season rather than yield, so there is little benefit to pushing the planting date earlier than usual.
directions: This is one of the fastest-maturing corns grown in North America, tasseling in about a month and finishing its small 3-4 inch ears well before most other corn has silked, which makes it useful for short, cool growing seasons or for breeding projects needing an early parent. Plant it in blocks of at least four short rows for reliable wind pollination rather than a single long row. Because the plants are compact and finish so quickly, a gardener can often fit in a second planting of another crop afterward, or stagger plantings to extend a short corn harvest window. Dry the small ears fully before shelling; the flint kernels store well and are traditionally soaked and simmered into stews or ground for meal.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

name: Gbogname Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Gbogname is grown mainly for its leaves rather than fruit.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Gbogname is an ancient Togolese landrace of gboma eggplant, grown primarily as a leafy green for its densely nutritious, regularly harvestable leaves, with its bitter yellow fruit of secondary culinary interest. It is treated as a tropical perennial in frost-free climates or a warm-season annual elsewhere, reaching 2-4 feet. Harvest leaves continually through the growing season for the best yield, much like harvesting a cut-and-come-again green.

name: Gem Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Gem squash is a South African heirloom summer squash producing compact, round, dark green fruits the size of a tennis ball to softball (3–4 inches diameter) that are harvested at a small, tender stage unlike other summer squashes — the immature Gem squash is cooked whole or halved rather than sliced, and is the most widely grown squash in home gardens throughout South Africa.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; Gem squash grows as a compact bush (unlike most squash vines) and is excellent for small gardens and containers; harvest when fruits reach 3–4 inches (tennis-ball to softball size) with dark green skin — do not allow to mature to yellow or tan as flavor and texture degrade; cook whole (boiled, steamed, or baked) until just tender. Gem squash is a South African heirloom variety with deep roots in the home gardens of South Africa, where it is so culturally central that it appears in traditional Afrikaner recipes, South African school cookbooks, and family food traditions going back to the early colonial period. The small, round, dark green fruits are harvested at a much smaller stage than American summer squash — when they are about the size of a tennis ball to softball, with soft seeds and tender flesh — and are traditionally cooked whole rather than sliced. The most common preparation in South Africa involves boiling or steaming the whole small squash in salted water until tender, then halving and scooping out the seeded core, filling the cavity with butter, cream cheese, or condensed milk (a classic dessert preparation), and serving the squash halves on the plate. The flavor of properly young Gem squash is milder and sweeter than zucchini, with a delicate texture that makes it very versatile. The bush-type plant (not a vine) is exceptionally productive, producing many small fruits from a compact plant, making it practical for small raised-bed gardens. Increasingly available in American specialty and heirloom seed catalogs as gardeners discover this productive, compact, and culturally interesting vegetable.

name: General Lee Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65F; trellis to keep fruit straight and improve airflow, reducing disease pressure in Gulf Coast humidity.
directions: Bred specifically for Southern growing conditions, this gynoecious hybrid produces uniform, dark green, white-spined fruit with high resistance to scab and intermediate resistance to cucumber mosaic virus and powdery mildew. LSU AgCenter lists it as adaptable and bred for the South. Trellising keeps fruit straight and reduces disease pressure in Gulf Coast humidity.
sources: LSU AgCenter / Seeds to Success - Recommended Cucumber Varieties for Louisiana

name: Gentry Crookneck Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Gentry is a modern hybrid yellow crookneck bred for disease tolerance and heavy, uniform fruit set, commonly recommended alongside 'Supersett' as a mildew-tolerant alternative to older open-pollinated crookneck varieties.
directions: Gentry is a hybrid yellow crookneck squash selected for improved disease tolerance and heavy, uniform production of smooth, warty-skinned, classically curved fruit, giving Southern gardeners a more resilient alternative to older open-pollinated crookneck lines that decline quickly once powdery mildew takes hold. The compact, open bush habit keeps fruit visible and easy to pick, and plants continue setting well through the heart of summer heat if harvested regularly. Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed; pick fruit young, at 5-6 inches, for the most tender texture and mildest flavor, checking plants daily during peak season since oversized fruit quickly turns tough, seedy, and signals the plant to slow production. As with all summer squash, consistent moisture and a thick mulch layer help maintain steady yields through hot, humid Gulf South summers.
sources: Willhite Seed Co. — Gentry Hybrid Crookneck

name: Genuine Cornfield Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm (65°F+); traditionally interplanted at the base of standing corn stalks, which the vigorous climbing vines use as a living pole in the old 'three sisters' style of companion planting.
directions: Sow at the base of standing corn or a sturdy pole in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; a true climbing type, it needs tall support to perform well. Genuine Cornfield Bean is an old-time American heirloom pole bean, so named because it was traditionally grown climbing up living corn stalks in the cornfield rather than on a dedicated trellis — a direct descendant of the indigenous 'three sisters' companion-planting tradition of interplanting corn, beans, and squash, in which the bean's nitrogen-fixing roots benefit the heavy-feeding corn while the cornstalk provides the bean a ready-made climbing pole. The vigorous vines produce a heavy crop of medium green pods good for snap use when young, or left to mature and dry for a flavorful winter soup bean. A practical, space-efficient heirloom for gardeners who want to grow beans and corn together in the traditional way, zone 4–10.

name: Genuwine Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun; the heavy fruit clusters need sturdy staking or caging from transplant onward.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, and stake or cage early to support the heavy fruit load. Genuwine is a modern open-pollinated selection bred by crossing Brandywine and German Johnson to combine the rich, complex flavor of Brandywine with German Johnson's smoother skin, more regular fruit shape, and improved productivity. The large, pink-red beefsteak fruit, often exceeding a pound, has a meaty, low-seed interior and a sweet, deep flavor that heirloom-tomato fans compare favorably to Brandywine itself while avoiding some of its notoriously erratic, lower-yielding habit. Feed and water consistently through fruit set, and pick as soon as fruit colors fully to avoid splitting during Gulf Coast summer rain.

name: Georgia Blue Stem Collard
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. acephala 'Georgia Blue Stem'
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting, or direct sow in late summer for a fall-through-winter Gulf South crop; large plants need room to spread.
directions: Documented under the names Blue Stem and Georgia Blue Stem in American seed literature predating 1900, this large heirloom was preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange member network before returning to wider circulation. Its obovate leaves are blue-green with prominent white midribs and a rounded, toothed margin, carried on a big, open plant with narrow petioles. It is prized among older Southern collard types for a notably sweet, juicy eating quality once cooked, distinct from the coarser bite of some other heirloom strains.

name: Georgia Cabbage Collards
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall/winter crop, or 4-6 weeks before last spring frost; sweetens after a touch of frost.
directions: Sow seed 1/4-1/2 inch deep and thin or transplant to final spacing in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; this semi-prostrate North Carolina heirloom, preserved by the Prevatte and Britt families near Lumberton and later shared through the Heirloom Collard Project, has a moderate tendency to form a loose cabbage-like head. Its sweet, tender yellow-green leaves carry a nutty, cabbage-like flavor that is less pungent than many collard types, and the plants are vigorous and hardy to around 20°F. Harvest outer leaves continuously through fall and winter, or cut the loosely headed center once it firms up; flavor improves noticeably after frost.

name: Georgia Flame Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant once nights stay above 55°F. Give plants full sun and steady moisture through fruit set for the heaviest yields.
directions: Georgia Flame is an old heirloom pepper from the country of Georgia in the Caucasus, not the American state, passed down as a dual-purpose sweet-to-mild roasting pepper for generations there. Plants set an abundance of long, tapered, conical pods that ripen from green to a deep, glossy red, with thick walls and a fruity flavor that sits right at the sweet-hot border, roughly on par with a mild jalapeno. Because the pods hold their shape and thick flesh under high heat, they are especially well suited to open-flame roasting, grilling, and salsa, and the plants are vigorous, heavy producers once established in warm soil.

name: Georgia Green Peanut
plantingNote: Direct sow shelled peanuts (seed) after last frost when soil temperature is reliably above 65°F; in zone 9 sow March–May. Plant shell-on or shelled peanuts (not roasted) 1.5–2 inches deep; do not remove the seed coat. Georgia Green is the leading commercial Virginia-type peanut variety in the US, widely grown across the South for its disease resistance, high yield, and excellent flavor. Peanuts form their pods underground — after the yellow flower petals fall, the fertilized ovary elongates into a 'peg' that grows downward and pushes into the soil where the pod develops. In zone 9 dig peanuts when the inner pod shell shows the characteristic veining pattern and the pods have formed mature kernels (110–130 days from planting). Sandy, well-drained, calcium-rich soil is ideal — peanuts require calcium around the developing pods.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic to neutral, calcium-rich soil — peanuts require loose, deep, well-drained soil for the pegs to penetrate easily and the pods to develop properly; Georgia Green is the leading commercial and home garden Virginia-type peanut variety in the United States, released by the North Carolina State University breeding program and immediately adopted across the peanut belt for its superior resistance to late leaf spot (Cercosporidium personatum) and Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV) — the two most economically important peanut diseases in the Southeast. The Virginia type produces larger kernels than Spanish or Valencia peanuts, with the characteristic elongated, two-kernel pods and excellent roasted flavor that make Virginia peanuts the preferred type for in-shell roasting, boiling, and gourmet peanut products. Georgia Green has maintained commercial adoption for over 25 years — an unusual longevity for a field crop variety — because the disease resistance package continues to provide practical advantages over older and newer alternatives under Gulf South conditions. In zone 9 the long, hot growing season (110–130 days) and sandy coastal plain soils are ideal for peanut production, making Georgia Green one of the most naturally adapted and rewarding warm-season food crops available for Gulf South gardens.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Georgia Green Peanut Variety Profile
University of Georgia Extension — Peanut Production for Georgia Home Gardens
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Peanut Production in Texas

name: Georgia Jet Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips after last frost when soil is warm above 65°F; Georgia Jet is one of the most early-maturing and productive sweet potato varieties for northern and transition-zone growers, reaching harvest in 90 days — useful in zone 9 as a reliable second crop that fits in a shortened growing window. Excellent for home slips from purchased roots.
directions: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose, sandy-loam soil in full sun; Georgia Jet is a productive open-pollinated sweet potato variety that reaches harvest in 90 days — one of the earliest-maturing sweet potatoes available, making it a reliable choice for shorter growing seasons and for gardeners in zones 5–7 who need a variety that matures before fall frost. In zone 9 it is equally useful as an early-maturing variety that can be planted as a second crop after spring vegetables finish. The deep reddish-purple skin and vivid orange flesh are very attractive; the flavor is sweet, moist, and rich — considered excellent for baking, steaming, and as a dessert sweet potato. An outstanding heirloom variety that produces well without synthetic fertilizers and stores reliably.

name: Georgia Red Sugarcane
plantingNote: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Georgia Red is a traditional all-red dooryard chewing cane named by University of Florida IFAS Extension alongside Yellow Gal among the region's heirloom chewing-type canes.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Georgia Red is an heirloom chewing cane with deep red to maroon, slender stalks, softer-rinded and juicier than syrup types, whose fibers stick together in a wad rather than shredding apart when chewed — the trait that defines a true chewing cane. It was traditionally bundled and sold fresh at farm stands, country stores, and gas stations across Georgia and the Gulf South each fall as a hand-peeled snack, gnawed in short sections for the sweet juice, though the stalks can also be pressed or cooked into syrup like any other cane. Propagate from stalk sets saved over winter: cut healthy stalks before hard frost, bed them in a shaded, well-drained trench under a heavy mulch of soil or pine straw to keep them dormant without freezing, and replant the sets in spring once the soil has warmed. Harvest for fresh eating can begin once stalks reach full size in September, but flavor and sweetness improve markedly after the first cool nights of fall concentrate the sugars in the stalk.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Backyard Sugarcane (SS-AGR-253/SC052)
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sugarcane Production and Heirloom Varieties
Southern Foodways Alliance — Cane Syrup Traditions

name: Georgia Red Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost into loose, ridged soil; Georgia Red is an old Southern heirloom valued for its coppery-red skin and strong keeping quality.
directions: Plant slips into raised, loosened ridges two to four weeks after the last frost date, in full sun. Georgia Red is a traditional Southern dooryard heirloom, distinct from the red-skinned 'Georgia Jet' hybrid, grown for its coppery-red skin and reputation among older growers for holding up in storage longer than many softer-fleshed heirloom types. Vines are rangy and roots form somewhat irregularly, so hill soil generously through the season to keep developing roots covered. Dig before frost, cure about a week at warm, humid conditions to firm the skin and sweeten the flesh, then store in a cool, dry spot.
sources: NC State University Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America

name: Georgia Southern Collard Greens
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall through spring harvest. In zone 9 collards are best grown as a fall-through-spring crop when temperatures are cooler — frost actually improves the flavor by converting starches to sugars in the leaves. Summer heat causes bitterness and reduced quality. Georgia Southern is especially heat-tolerant compared to most collards and can be harvested in zone 9 from October through April. Harvest outer leaves as needed.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Georgia Southern is the original Southern heirloom collard variety — one of the oldest and most historically significant vegetables in American Southern cooking, with documented continuous cultivation in the southeastern United States for well over a century. The large, smooth, blue-green leaves with a prominent pale midrib are the defining collard green appearance in traditional Southern cuisine — different from the crinkled leaves of kale and the heading structure of cabbage, collards are a non-heading form of Brassica oleracea that produces large individual leaves harvest continuously from the outer portions of the plant. The slow-cooked Southern preparation — simmering collards with smoked pork (ham hock, fatback, or smoked turkey) for hours with salt and vinegar until tender — transforms the tough, slightly bitter raw leaves into silky, rich, deeply flavorful cooked greens that are a cornerstone of Southern food culture. Georgia Southern is particularly valued for its mild flavor, large leaf size, and exceptional heat tolerance that allows spring and fall production in zone 9.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Georgia Southern Heirloom Collard
Seed Savers Exchange — Georgia Southern Collard History
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Collard Greens for Gulf South

name: Georgia Southern Collards
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12–14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August–September for fall and winter production or February–March for spring. Georgia Southern is the traditional large, open, heat-tolerant collard of the Deep South — it grows larger and more productively in zone 8–9 than most other collard varieties and is particularly adapted to the Gulf Coast's mild winters. Light frost improves the flavor; hard freezes below 20°F can damage large plants.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun in fertile, well-drained soil. Georgia Southern (also simply 'Georgia Collards' or 'Old Georgia') is the foundational heirloom collard variety of the American South — an open-pollinated type with a continuous documented growing history in Southern gardens spanning well over a century, representing the traditional collard before the development of modern compact hybrids. Plants grow 3–4 feet tall and 2–3 feet wide, producing large, broad, blue-green, relatively smooth leaves with a somewhat open, non-heading habit. The flavor is the classic Southern collard character: substantial, slightly bitter when raw, sweet and savory when cooked slowly with salt pork, ham hocks, or smoked turkey — the traditional pot-likker preparation where the cooking liquid becomes as important as the greens themselves. Georgia Southern is notably heat-tolerant for a brassica, surviving Gulf South summers better than most collard varieties, and produces some of the most vigorous growth in the warm, humid conditions of zone 8–10 fall and winter gardens. Its open-pollinated nature allows seed saving from the most productive plants year after year.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Georgia Southern collard variety history
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Traditional Southern collard varieties
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Collard Production in the Southeast

name: Georgia Streak Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Georgia Streak is a Southern heirloom bicolor beefsteak with a yellow background marbled in red, grown for its sweet, low-acid flavor and striking sliced appearance.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date and stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines early. Georgia Streak is a Southern heirloom beefsteak in the same bicolor family as Pineapple and Hillbilly, producing large, golden-yellow fruit marbled and streaked with red through the flesh as well as the skin, so each slice shows the same vivid marbling as the exterior. The flavor is sweet and mild with low acidity, characteristic of yellow-red bicolor heirlooms, and the fruit's soft shoulders and juicy flesh make it a fresh-eating and slicing tomato rather than one suited to canning or long storage. In the Deep South it performs best in the spring crop before peak summer heat interferes with fruit set, so get transplants in as early as the weather allows and mulch well to keep roots cool. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saves true from year to year with basic isolation from other tomato varieties.

name: Georgia Sweet Onion
plantingNote: In the Deep South, start seed in fall for overwintered transplants or set out sets in late winter, since a short-day type that needs the shorter daylight of southern winters to trigger bulbing.
directions: Set transplants or sets 4 to 6 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping weeds down early since onions compete poorly with weeds while bulbs are sizing up. Georgia Sweet is a Yellow Granex-type short-day onion grown throughout the Vidalia region of southeast Georgia, where the area's naturally low-sulfur soils contribute to the same mild, sweet flavor that makes true Vidalia onions famous, even though only onions grown within the legally defined Vidalia district may carry that trademarked name. The flattened globe bulbs have thin, pale yellow skin and mild, juicy flesh best eaten fresh, since the low pungency that makes sweet onions so pleasant raw also shortens their storage life compared to pungent keeping onions. Reduce watering as tops begin to yellow and fall over, then cure bulbs in a warm, airy, shaded spot for one to two weeks before moving them to storage.

name: Georgia-06G Peanut
plantingNote: Direct sow shelled seed in loose, sandy soil once the ground has warmed well past the last frost; this variety wants a full warm season of 135 days or more to finish its pods, which the extended Gulf Coast summer readily provides.
directions: Sow shelled, unroasted seed 1.5 inches deep in loose, well-drained, sandy soil, hilling lightly around the base once yellow blooms open so the pegs that carry developing pods have an easy path into the ground. Georgia-06G was released in 2006 by the University of Georgia's Coastal Plain Experiment Station in Tifton and quickly became the dominant runner-type peanut grown across the Southeast, prized for strong resistance to tomato spotted wilt virus along with consistently high yield and grade quality. The dark green, decumbent runner vines spread widely, so space plants generously, and keep soil evenly moist during flowering and pegging since drought at that stage sharply reduces pod set. Dig when foliage starts to yellow and the inner pod veining has darkened, then cure the pulled plants in a warm, airy spot for a couple of weeks before shelling.
