name: Georgia-2 Pigeon Pea
subcategory: perennial legume / dry pea (also used as warm-season cover crop)
plantingNote: Direct-sow once soil has fully warmed, since this day-neutral selection flowers on its own schedule rather than waiting for shortening fall daylength.
directions: Developed at the University of Georgia's Tifton research station, this short-duration, day-neutral pigeon pea flowers and sets pods well before fall frost, unlike many tropical pigeon peas that need a long season to trigger bloom. It is a nitrogen-fixing shrub-like legume that tolerates Gulf Coast heat and drought once established, yielding edible green or dry peas as well as a vigorous cover crop. Its semi-determinate, more compact growth habit makes it easier to manage in a vegetable bed than taller tropical pigeon pea types.
sources: ECHO Community (Educational Concerns for Hunger Organization)

name: Georgian Crystal Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Georgian Crystal is a porcelain hardneck that needs a real winter chill for good bulb formation and performs best in zone 3-7.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Georgian Crystal is a porcelain-type hardneck garlic originating in the country of Georgia, valued for its large, glossy white bulbs with just 4-6 very large cloves that are quick and easy to peel, along with a mild-to-medium, clean garlic flavor that works well both raw and cooked. It is a vigorous, reliable producer that adapts well across a range of cold-winter climates. Like other hardnecks, it sends up a curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to direct energy into bulb growth; scapes are excellent sautéed or made into pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot, then trim and store; storage life is moderate, typically 5-7 months in a cool, dry location.
sources: Chester Aaron: The Great Garlic Book, Ten Speed Press 1997

name: Georgian Fire Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Georgian Fire is a porcelain hardneck from the Republic of Georgia known for notably hot, spicy raw flavor.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Georgian Fire, originating from the Republic of Georgia, is a porcelain hardneck garlic valued for notably hot, spicy raw flavor that mellows into a rich, savory sweetness when roasted, along with large bulbs of four to six big, easy-to-peel cloves under smooth white skin typical of porcelain types. As a hardneck, it produces a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to channel the plant's energy into bulb development; the scapes are edible and excellent in stir-fries or pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot, then trim and store; porcelain types like Georgian Fire generally offer good storage life of six months or more under proper conditions.

name: Georgian Fire Hardneck Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, a few weeks before the ground freezes, in loose, well-drained, fertile soil; Georgian Fire is a vigorous porcelain type that tolerates cold winters well and stores longer than most Rocambole garlics.
directions: Plant cloves pointed end up, 2 inches deep, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Georgian Fire is a porcelain-type hardneck heirloom, also brought out of the Republic of Georgia, producing large bulbs with just four to six plump, easy-to-peel cloves under bright white wrappers, and it is prized among heirloom garlic growers for a noticeably hotter, more pungent bite than milder porcelain varieties like Georgian Crystal or Music. Cut the curling scapes in early summer once they appear to push more energy into bulb development, and cure harvested bulbs in a warm, dry, airy spot for several weeks before trimming and storing. Porcelain types store considerably longer than Rocamboles, generally holding good quality for six months or more under cool, dry conditions.

name: German Butterball Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; German Butterball is a German heirloom potato renowned as one of the most richly flavored and richly colored yellow-flesh potatoes available — the name accurately describes the extraordinary buttery, creamy flavor and golden-yellow flesh that makes it the benchmark yellow potato for flavor among heirloom enthusiasts.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10–12 inches apart in rows 30 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost; German Butterball is a late-mid-season variety (70–90 days) that produces medium-large, round to slightly oval, netted-skin, golden-fleshed tubers. German Butterball is a traditional German heirloom potato that entered American heirloom potato circles through the Rodale Institute and seed saver networks in the 1980s; it is consistently rated among the finest-flavored potato varieties by tasting panels — the rich, buttery, dense golden-yellow flesh has a flavor intensity that significantly exceeds Yukon Gold (the most popular yellow potato commercially) and makes German Butterball a benchmark for those seeking the very best potato flavor. The tubers have thin, netted tan-gold skin and deep golden-yellow flesh with a texture that is semi-waxy when young and becomes more floury when mature, making it excellent for all cooking purposes: baked, roasted, mashed, boiled, or fried. The exceptional flavor when simply roasted or baked with olive oil is what defines German Butterball's reputation — no other potato consistently delivers this depth of rich, buttery potato flavor without any embellishment. One of the most sought-after varieties in the specialty potato market.

name: German Extra Hardy Garlic
scientificName: Allium sativum var. ophioscorodon 'German Extra Hardy'
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, so roots establish before dormancy; German Extra Hardy is a porcelain hardneck bred for exceptional winter survival and needs a real cold period to form well-divided bulbs, making it best suited to zone 3-7.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. German Extra Hardy is one of the most popular and reliable porcelain hardneck garlics for cold-climate gardeners, prized for its outstanding winter hardiness and consistent production of large bulbs with 4-5 big, easy-to-peel cloves under bright white skin, sometimes with faint purple streaking. Flavor is strong and full-bodied raw, mellowing to a rich, savory sweetness when roasted. As a hardneck, it produces a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to channel energy into bulb development; the scapes are edible and excellent in stir-fries or pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded location, then trim and store; German Extra Hardy has only moderate storage life, typically 4-6 months, so use it earlier in the year relative to longer-storing softneck types.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing Garlic

name: German Head Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun; the heavy fruit clusters need sturdy staking or caging from an early age.
directions: Transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking or caging early to support the heavy fruit. German Head is a German heirloom beefsteak grown for enormous, smooth, pink-red fruit with dense, meaty, low-seed flesh and a rich, sweet, well-balanced flavor typical of the great German pink beefsteak tradition that also produced varieties like German Johnson and German Pink. Individual fruit regularly tops a pound, making it an excellent slicing tomato for sandwiches and fresh eating, and the indeterminate vine remains productive over a long season when given consistent water and feeding. Provide sturdy support for the heavy fruit clusters, and water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking on the large, smooth-skinned fruit.

name: German Johnson Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; German Johnson is a large, pink-fleshed Southern heirloom widely grown across the Mid-Atlantic and Gulf Coast states for its outstanding flavor and generous yields of meaty, 1–2 pound fruits with a classic old-fashioned tomato taste.
directions: Start seeds indoors under grow lights 6–8 weeks before the last frost date; transplant outdoors after frost danger has fully passed with a wire cage or stout stake, setting the plant deep to encourage root formation along the buried stem. German Johnson is a large-fruited, indeterminate, pink-fleshed heirloom long popular throughout the American South and Mid-Atlantic states — it is considered a parent variety of the famous Mortgage Lifter, crossed by M.C. Byles of Logan, West Virginia to produce that legendary tomato; the fruits themselves are large, slightly irregular, meaty, and deeply flavored with a rich, slightly acidic, classic old-fashioned tomato taste and minimal gel content. The plants are vigorous and highly productive, with good resistance to common foliar diseases in hot, humid Southern conditions. Excellent for slicing, sandwiches, and home canning.

name: German Pink Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; German Pink is a vigorous potato-leaved indeterminate that benefits from sturdy staking to support its large fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant deeply into warm soil, staking or caging the sprawling vines. German Pink descends from seed brought from Bavaria to Iowa in 1883 by the family of Seed Savers Exchange co-founder Diane Ott Whealy, and it produces huge, meaty, nearly seedless pink-skinned fruit with a mild, sweet flavor well suited to slicing and canning alike. It remains one of the founding heirloom varieties associated with the Seed Savers Exchange movement.

name: German Red Hardneck Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 4–6 weeks before first frost in fall; German Red is a Rocambole-type hardneck garlic originally from Germany and popularized in the Pacific Northwest — it produces 8–12 cloves per bulb with a rich, complex, full-bodied flavor considered among the finest of all Rocambole garlics; harvest in early to midsummer when scapes have curled and straightened and 5–6 lower leaves remain green.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end up, 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart, in fall 4–6 weeks before hard freeze; mulch with 4–6 inches of straw after ground cools; keep consistently moist in spring and remove scapes when they curl to redirect energy to bulbs; stop watering as lower leaves yellow and harvest in early to midsummer. German Red is a Rocambole-type hardneck garlic with origins in Germany, gaining wide recognition in North America through garlic enthusiast and seed-saver networks in the Pacific Northwest and through specialist growers like Filaree Garlic Farm — Rocambole types are considered by many garlic connoisseurs to produce the finest flavor of all garlic types, and German Red is consistently ranked among the best Rocamboles for its deep, rich, complex, slightly spicy flavor and the full-bodied pungency that distinguishes well-grown Rocambole from milder softneck types. The bulbs produce 8–12 large, easy-to-peel cloves arranged in a single layer, with brownish-purple outer skin typical of Rocamboles; the cloves are rounded-edged and notably easy to peel (another Rocambole characteristic). The flavor is excellent when raw but truly reveals its complexity when roasted, sautéed, or used in slow-cooked dishes. The main limitation of Rocambole types including German Red is storage life — typically only 3–5 months under good conditions, compared to 10–12 months for softneck types; grow what you will use by midwinter and source next season's seed before that.

name: German Red Strawberry Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; German Red Strawberry is a vigorous indeterminate variety reaching 5-7 feet that needs sturdy staking or caging to support its large heart-shaped fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, staking well as vines can reach 5-7 feet. German Red Strawberry is a German oxheart heirloom prized for its large, strawberry- or heart-shaped fruit, typically 3-4 inches long and 10-16 ounces, that ripens to a deep red with smooth shoulders and thick, meaty, relatively low-seed flesh. The flavor is rich and well-balanced with classic old-fashioned sweetness, making it popular for slicing as well as sauce, though fruit shape can be somewhat variable from plant to plant.

name: German Stripe Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; German Stripe is a large Mennonite heirloom beefsteak tomato with stunning bicolor red and gold-yellow striped and marbled flesh — the visual effect when the fruit is sliced is extraordinary, with crimson and golden streaks radiating through the flesh in an irregular pattern, accompanied by an outstandingly rich, honey-sweet flavor.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes into fertile, deeply prepared, well-drained soil; provide substantial staking or caging as plants reach 5–8 feet. German Stripe (also sometimes called 'Old German' or 'Old German Stripe') is a large Mennonite heirloom beefsteak tomato of the bicolor class — producing very large (12–28 oz), flattened to slightly lobed fruits that are visually unremarkable from the outside (reddish-gold exterior) but stunning when sliced: the interior flesh is dramatically streaked and marbled with alternating crimson red and golden yellow in bold, irregular patterns radiating from the blossom scar, making each cross-section unique and visually captivating. The flavor matches the dramatic appearance — exceptionally sweet and rich with a honey-complexity that is one of the hallmarks of the best bicolor heirlooms; the sweetness from the golden areas contrasts with the more acid-forward richness of the red portions to create a layered, complex taste. One of the finest beefsteak heirlooms for fresh eating, tomato salads, and caprese where the bicolor slices can be displayed to advantage.

name: German Wine Rhubarb
plantingNote: Set out crown divisions in early spring in full sun and deeply worked, fertile soil, positioning the crown bud just below the surface. Keep the planting bed weed-free and consistently moist through the first growing season while the perennial root system develops.
directions: Set out crown divisions in early spring in full sun and deeply worked, fertile soil, positioning the crown bud just below the surface. Keep the planting bed weed-free and consistently moist through the first growing season while the perennial root system develops. German Wine is an old European heirloom prized for stalks that are colored a deep wine-red from skin to core, a trait that produces especially rich, richly colored sauces, pies, and the traditional home-brewed rhubarb wine that gave the cultivar its name. It is a moderately vigorous grower with good cold hardiness, making it a dependable choice for northern kitchen gardens.

name: Gernika Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Gernika peppers are harvested young and green, well before full ripening, so successive picking every few days over a long season keeps plants productive.
directions: Gernika (Gernikako Piperra) is a slender, thin-walled sweet frying pepper protected under Spain's Denominacion de Origen Protegida in the Basque Country, where it is a signature tapas ingredient traditionally flash-fried whole in olive oil and finished with coarse salt. Pods are harvested small and immature, typically 2.5 to 3.5 inches long, while still green, since the variety is never grown to full ripeness for market; frequent harvesting at this young stage also keeps the compact plants setting new fruit continuously through summer. The thin flesh cooks in under a minute in hot oil, blistering the skin while the interior stays tender, with a flavor that is mild and sweet with only an occasional peppery bite from scattered hotter individual fruits, similar to Spain's Padron pepper but generally milder and more consistent. Grow in full sun with steady moisture and a support stake or cage for the heavily branched, fruit-laden plants.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Basque pepper variety documentation

name: Gete Okosomin Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost, giving vines ample room to sprawl; Gete Okosomin, meaning roughly 'big old squash' in Anishinaabemowin, is an ancient variety grown by the Miami and other Great Lakes Native nations, propagated from seed found in a centuries-old archaeological cache and reintroduced to cultivation by tribal seed-saving efforts.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, giving the vigorous, sprawling vines generous room. Gete Okosomin — an Anishinaabemowin name often translated as 'big old squash' or 'cool old squash' — is an heirloom traced to seed recovered from a centuries-old clay pot in an archaeological context associated with Native peoples of the Great Lakes region, and subsequently grown out, verified, and shared by Miami Nation seed keepers and Native seed-saving networks, making it one of the oldest documented squash varieties still in cultivation in North America. Fruits are large, often 10-15 pounds, striped in shades of green, orange, and cream on a somewhat elongated, ribbed form, with dense, deep orange, sweet flesh well suited to baking, soups, and pies. As a Cucurbita maxima type, it needs a long, warm growing season and ample space for its long vines, along with consistent moisture during flowering and fruit set to size the large fruit properly. Beyond its culinary value, growing Gete Okosomin is a way for gardeners to participate directly in the ongoing revival of an Indigenous foodway; seed saved from open-pollinated fruit can be replanted, continuing a lineage that stretches back many generations. Harvest when the rind is fully hardened and the stem has dried, then cure for two to three weeks before storing in a cool, dry location.
sources: Michigan State University Extension — Gete Okosomin Squash history and revival
Seed Savers Exchange — Indigenous Heirloom Squash Varieties
Sierra Seeds — Gete Okosomin cultivation notes

name: Ghostbuster Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant once soil is warm and nights stay above 55°F.
directions: Ghostbuster is a compact, early hybrid eggplant that produces smooth, glossy, pure-white oval fruit with creamy flesh and notably fewer seeds than many heirloom white varieties. Its hybrid vigor and disease resistance make it more forgiving for beginners than older open-pollinated white eggplants, which can be slower and less productive. Harvest fruit at 4-5 inches while the skin is still glossy and firm, since white types can develop a yellow tinge and bitter flavor if left too long on the plant. Choose Ghostbuster when you want the striking look of a white eggplant on a plant with the reliability and earliness of a modern hybrid.

name: Giant Belgium Pink Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Giant Belgium Pink is a large-fruited heirloom beefsteak tomato producing flattened, deeply lobed pink-red fruits frequently exceeding 1–2 lbs, with sweet, rich, low-acid flesh similar in character to Brandywine but from a distinct European heirloom lineage — one of the great large pink beefsteak tomatoes for home garden growing.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes into deeply prepared, fertile, well-drained soil. Giant Belgium Pink (also called Belgian Giant) is an indeterminate heirloom tomato with large, flattened, sometimes deeply lobed, pink to pinkish-red beefsteak fruits that frequently weigh 1–2+ lbs, rivaling Brandywine in size and beauty; the flesh is dense, meaty, sweet, and low-acid with a rich complexity suited for fresh slicing and sandwich use. The fruits share the large-pink-beefsteak class with Brandywine and Mortgage Lifter, providing an additional option with slightly different flavor character for gardeners who prize this class of tomato. Indeterminate; stake or cage as plants reach 5–8 feet; productivity is good for a giant beefsteak but individual fruits require time to develop fully. Outstanding for Gulf Coast spring tomato production planted February through March for May–June harvest.

name: Giant Carentan Leek
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors early since leeks are slow to size up, then transplant seedlings into deep holes or trenches once they are pencil-thick and outdoor soil has warmed.
directions: Sow seeds indoors in flats or trays well ahead of the last frost, then transplant seedlings into holes or shallow trenches several inches deep so soil can be gradually mounded up around the stems to blanch them white as they grow. This classic French heirloom is known for its thick, broad blue-green leaves and unusually wide, well-blanched shaft, making it one of the largest and most substantial leeks commonly grown in home gardens. It has good cold tolerance and can often stay in the ground for a late fall or early winter harvest in milder climates, developing a mild, sweet flavor after light frost. Hill soil around the stems every few weeks through the growing season for the longest, whitest shafts.

name: Giant Exhibition Longpod Fava Bean
directions: Give this vigorous English show-bench heirloom sturdy staking since its thick, fleshy pods can reach 12 inches and weigh the plant down as they fill with up to 10 light greenish-white beans each. It remains a favorite on the British show bench for sheer pod length, but home cooks value it just as much for the buttery, nutty flavor of beans harvested young and steamed whole in the pod.

name: Giant Japanese Butterbur
plantingNote: Divide rhizome sections in early spring or fall and plant them into consistently moist to wet, rich soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants generously since 'Giganteus' is the larger-leaved, more dramatic form of Japanese butterbur commonly offered by nurseries.
directions: Divide rhizome sections in early spring or fall and plant them into consistently moist to wet, rich soil in partial to full shade, spacing plants generously since 'Giganteus' is the larger-leaved, more dramatic form of Japanese butterbur commonly offered by nurseries. Its rounded leaves can exceed three feet across on stout petioles, creating a bold, almost tropical look in a shaded, damp corner of the garden where few other food plants would thrive. The thick petioles are harvested in early spring before the leaves fully unfurl and prepared the traditional Japanese way, peeled, blanched, and simmered in dashi or miso as fuki. Because the rhizomes spread aggressively in wet shade, confine 'Giganteus' with a buried barrier or dedicate it to a naturally moist, shaded low spot where its size and vigor become an asset rather than a nuisance.

name: Giant Marconi Sweet Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Giant Marconi is an Italian frying/roasting pepper type that produces best with consistent moisture and good fertility. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer and fall harvest. Harvest green for frying and grilling, or allow to ripen red for sweeter roasting and antipasto use. The very large, thick-walled fruits hold up exceptionally well to heat for frying, stuffing, and grilling.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil. Giant Marconi is a 1997 All-America Selections-winning Italian sweet frying/roasting pepper that produces some of the largest and most productive sweet non-bell peppers available to home gardeners — long (7–10 inch), slightly tapered, blocky-shouldered fruits with very thick flesh and virtually no heat. The distinctive form is characteristic of Italian frying peppers: longer and more tapered than bell peppers, with a ridged, slightly irregular exterior and a meaty, thick-walled interior with surprisingly few seeds relative to total volume. The large, thick-walled fruits are extraordinary for roasting and grilling — the thick flesh holds its structure as the skin blisters and chars, and after peeling, the roasted flesh is silky, sweet, and rich with concentrated pepper flavor. Giant Marconi is the ideal choice for Italian peperonata (braised peppers with olive oil and garlic), stuffed peppers, antipasto, and any application calling for large quantities of roasted sweet pepper. The plants are tall and productive, often requiring staking when heavily loaded; they produce heavily from midsummer through fall in zone 9. The very sweet, mild flavor at the red-ripe stage is excellent raw in salads and on cheese boards where the visual impact of the large, vivid red fruits is attractive.
sources: All-America Selections — Giant Marconi pepper AAS winner 1997
Burpee Seeds — Giant Marconi variety notes
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Pepper Production

name: Giant of Barman Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; give this giant-fruited heirloom from Barman village in Madhya Pradesh extra room and sturdy support, since the elongated fruit can swell to several pounds.
directions: Giant of Barman is a heritage eggplant from the village of Barman along Madhya Pradesh's Narmada River, prized by local growers for fruit that can reach several pounds on a single plant. Transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun once the soil has warmed, and set sturdy stakes or a cage early, since the elongated green fruit with fine white pinstripes grows heavy enough to snap unsupported branches. The dense, sweet, comparatively seedless flesh holds up well to roasting and baking, so harvest while the skin is still glossy and keep watering consistent to prevent fruit from turning fibrous. Check plants every few days during peak season, since fruit size balloons quickly once pollinated and is best picked before it grows oversized.

name: Giant of Naples Celery
scientificName: Apium graveolens var. dulce 'Giant of Naples'
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, since the seed germinates slowly and seedlings need a long head start before it is warm enough to transplant; Giant of Naples is a traditional southern Italian heirloom grown for its thick, tender, mild ribs prized for braising and slow-cooked dishes.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil that stays consistently moist, since celery's shallow roots suffer quickly in dry spells and stress produces tough, stringy, bitter stalks. Giant of Naples is a classic heirloom from the Campania region of Italy, grown less often as a raw salad celery and more as a cooking celery, since its thick, pale-green ribs soften into a rich, mellow flavor that anchors soffritto, braises, and long-simmered sauces. The stalks are notably broad and fleshy compared to standard American celery, and the plant tends to be more heat-tolerant and less prone to bolting than delicate salad types. Harvest by cutting individual outer stalks as needed through the season, or dig the whole plant once it reaches full size; a light frost sweetens the flavor rather than damaging the crop.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Celery Production

name: Giant Pascal Celery
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-12 weeks before last frost, since celery seed is slow to germinate and seedlings grow slowly at first; transplant into rich, consistently moist soil after frost danger passes, or start in mid-summer for a fall and winter storage crop.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into very fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Giant Pascal, also sold as Giant Golden Pascal, is a French-derived heirloom celery documented in American seed catalogs since the late nineteenth century and long regarded as the standard for winter keeping. Its stalks grow notably thick and full-bodied, with a rich, nutty flavor that many gardeners find fuller than modern hybrid celery, and the ribs stay crisp and remarkably tolerant of cool fall and winter conditions. Blanch by tying the outer stalks together and mounding soil or wrapping paper around the base of the plant for two to three weeks before harvest, which lightens the green color to gold and softens any bitterness. Because it stores and holds in the garden well into winter, Giant Pascal has traditionally been the go-to celery for late-season harvest and root-cellar storage.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee Company historical seed catalogs
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Giant Prague Celeriac
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost transplant date; in zones 5–7 start in January–February and transplant in March–April. Celeriac requires a very long cool growing season of 110–120 days from transplant and cannot tolerate summer heat — zones 3–7 are ideal growing regions. Consistent moisture throughout development is critical; uneven watering produces cracked, malformed roots. Remove side shoots and small roots from the base of the developing globe to concentrate growth. In zone 9 celeriac is very challenging due to limited cool season length.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, consistently moist, very fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil — celeriac demands high fertility and absolutely consistent moisture throughout its long development; Giant Prague is the standard open-pollinated celeriac variety — celery root — one of the most important and widely grown vegetables in European cuisine that remains dramatically underutilized in American cooking despite its extraordinary culinary versatility. The edible part of celeriac is not a root but a swollen hypocotyl (the base of the stem) that develops into a large, round, rough-surfaced globe of dense, white flesh with an intense, concentrated celery flavor — pure celery essence without the stringy fiber or water content of celery stalks. Celeriac's culinary applications are among the most diverse of any European vegetable: raw in the classic French preparation celeriac rémoulade (grated raw celeriac in mustardy mayonnaise), pureed into silky soups and mashes as a potato alternative, roasted, braised, or added to stocks for their distinctive aromatic depth. The dense, concentrated flavor means a small amount of celeriac adds substantial impact — a quarter of a root can flavor an entire pot of soup that whole bunches of celery stalks would struggle to match.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Celeriac Production Guide
University of Vermont Extension — Celeriac for Northern Gardeners
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Celeriac Growing Guide

name: Giant Red Celery
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, moisture-retentive soil after danger of frost passes.
directions: Giant Red is a 19th-century English heirloom celery valued for its tough, deep pink-to-red stalks and pronounced, old-fashioned celery flavor that is stronger and more concentrated than modern green types. Traditionally grown in trenches and earthed up to blanch and sweeten the ribs, it can also be left unblanched for a more intense, almost peppery flavor better suited to cooked dishes than raw eating. It tolerates cool fall weather better than many stalk celeries, holding quality after light frost. Gardeners grow it for its striking color in soups and braises and as a genetic link to celery grown before uniform green hybrids became standard.

name: Giant Ristra Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Giant Ristra, a 2014 All-America Selections winner, carries cayenne-level heat on a Marconi-shaped fruit and is bred specifically for stringing into traditional drying ristras.
directions: Transplant into full sun in well-drained soil after the last frost, spacing plants closely since the bushy habit needs little room and rarely requires staking. Giant Ristra bears heavy yields of bright red, 6-7 inch elongated horn-shaped chiles carrying cayenne-level heat, with a flavor suited to fresh use, roasting, or drying. The thin-walled pods dry quickly once strung into ristras, making this variety a strong choice for gardeners who want a traditional dried red chile harvest. Reduce watering as fruit matures to concentrate flavor and speed drying.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute

name: Giant Syrian Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil after danger of frost has passed.
directions: This West Virginia heirloom beefsteak produces huge pink, often heart-shaped fruits that can weigh a pound or more, with dense, juicy flesh and comparatively few seeds. The sweet, well-balanced flavor makes it a favorite for slicing, and the vigorous indeterminate vines perform especially well in hot, humid summers. Stake or cage plants and provide consistent moisture to limit cracking on the large fruits.

name: Giant Szegedi Paprika Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Giant Szegedi is a long-fruited Hungarian paprika type named for the city of Szeged, historically the center of Hungarian paprika production.
directions: Sow seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after frost danger passes. Giant Szegedi produces long, tapered, mild sweet fruit that ripens from pale yellow-green to deep red, grown primarily for drying and grinding into traditional sweet Hungarian paprika powder. Plants benefit from a long hot season to bring the full crop to red ripeness for harvest. String ripe pods to air-dry in a warm, airy spot, or use a dehydrator before grinding into powder.

name: Giant Winter Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer to early fall for a hardy overwintering crop, or as soon as soil can be worked in earliest spring; Giant Winter is bred to shrug off hard freezes and hold in the garden through winter cold better than most spring-sown spinach.
directions: Direct sow a half inch deep into cool, moist, fertile soil, thinning seedlings to four to six inches apart once true leaves appear. Giant Winter is an old European heirloom selected for exceptional cold hardiness and large, heavily crinkled, dark green savoy leaves that hold quality through hard freezes and short winter days far better than most spinach varieties, making it a strong choice for a Gulf Coast fall-through-winter planting. The extra-large, thick leaves are slower to bolt in cool weather and develop a sweeter, richer flavor after exposure to frost. Harvest outer leaves as needed for a cut-and-come-again crop, or cut the whole rosette once plants reach full size.

name: Gigante di Romagna Cardoon
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes into deep, richly amended soil; Gigante di Romagna is one of the largest cardoon strains grown, so give it ample room and generous feeding to reach full size.
directions: Start seed indoors and set transplants into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, allowing generous space for its large mature footprint; Gigante di Romagna is a heirloom Italian cardoon from the Romagna region prized for producing unusually thick, wide, nearly spineless leaf ribs that are easier and less prickly to handle at harvest than most other cardoon strains. As with other cardoons, the coarse, bitter raw ribs are transformed by blanching, achieved by wrapping the mature plant in cardboard, burlap, or straw for three to four weeks before harvest to exclude light and mellow the flavor. The blanched ribs are classically braised, breaded and fried, or baked into a gratin, and the plant's tall, silvery, deeply cut foliage and thistle-like purple flower heads make it a dramatic architectural presence in the garden even where it is not harvested.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Mediterranean Vegetable Crops

name: Gigante Tomatillo
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March. Tomatillos require two plants for cross-pollination and fruit set; always plant at least two plants regardless of variety. Gigante produces the largest fruits of commonly available tomatillo varieties, making it the choice for recipes requiring large quantities of salsa verde with minimal prep work.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Gigante (also called Grande) tomatillo is a large-fruited Mexican selection producing fruits 2–3 inches in diameter, substantially larger than the standard tomatillo — each fruit can weigh 3–4 ounces, compared to 1–2 ounces for standard types. The large fruit size dramatically reduces the number of fruits needed per batch of salsa verde and makes individual-fruit processing (husking, cleaning) more efficient. The flavor is bright, mildly tart, and herbal — characteristic of the tomatillo — without the papery, husked fruit becoming bitter at full size. Harvest when husks begin to split and feel papery but before they yellow significantly. Plant at least two individuals for cross-pollination, which is essential for good fruit set. Plants sprawl widely and may benefit from staking or support.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Tomatillo Varieties
New Mexico State University Extension — Tomatillo Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomatillo for Texas

name: Gigantes Kastorias Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow at the base of a tall, sturdy trellis after the last frost; this vigorous runner bean needs the full season and cool nights common at its native highland elevation to size up its outsized seed.
directions: Gigantes Kastorias is a runner bean landrace grown in the cool highland basin around Kastoria and the Prespa Lakes in northwestern Greece, prized for producing some of the largest dry bean seeds in cultivation and holding European PDO status. Provide a tall trellis for the vigorous climbing vines, which, like other runner beans, set pods most reliably where summer nights stay cool rather than scorching hot. Leave pods on the vine until fully dry and papery before shelling the broad, flat, cream-colored seeds, then slow-bake them with tomato, olive oil, and herbs in the classic Greek gigantes plaki. Store dried seed in a sealed container out of light to preserve its creamy texture.
sources: Greek Ministry of Rural Development and Food

name: Gijnlim Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant crowns in raised ridges or mounded soil so spears can be earthed up for blanching if white asparagus is desired.
directions: Gijnlim is a Dutch all-male hybrid developed for the European white and green asparagus trade, prized for spearing very early in spring and producing an unusually concentrated first flush of thick, straight spears. Growers who mound soil over the crowns get pale, tender spears for traditional white asparagus, while unmounded beds yield classic green spears just as reliably. Its early emergence means it can beat frost-sensitive varieties to market by a week or more in cool climates. Established beds reward deep, fertile, well-drained soil and a thick mulch layer to suppress weeds between rows.

name: Gila River A'al Hu:n Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost; A'al Hu:n is a low-desert flour-flint corn of the Gila River Indian Community (Akimel O'odham) in central Arizona, traditionally dry-farmed or grown with minimal irrigation through the hot low-desert season.
directions: A'al Hu:n is a traditional flour-and-flint corn of the Gila River Indian Community (Akimel O'odham) in the low desert of central Arizona, historically grown with minimal irrigation under dry-farmed or lightly irrigated conditions. Ears are relatively small but combine cream-colored flour kernels with harder, clear flint kernels on the same cob, and occasional red chinmark ears can appear from natural cross-pollination in a seed-saver's stand. It is valued for reaching maturity quickly on little water, a trait suited to the long, hot low-desert growing season. Give it full sun and warm soil, and water during establishment even though mature plants handle significant drought stress.

name: Gilfeather Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer for fall and winter harvest; Gilfeather turnip develops best in cool weather and improves significantly in flavor after light frosts. In zone 9, direct sow late August through September for harvest November through January. The very large roots (up to 5 pounds) require adequate space and a full growing season of cool weather for best development.
directions: Direct sow seeds thinly in well-tilled, moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil, thinning to 8–12 inches when plants are 3 inches tall; harvest in late fall after light frosts have sweetened the roots. Gilfeather turnip is one of the most historically significant and culinarily distinctive heirloom vegetables in New England — the Vermont state vegetable, named for John Gilfeather of Wardsboro, Vermont, who reportedly kept this variety secret by cutting off the tops and bottoms of roots before selling or trading them to prevent others from saving seed, maintaining a monopoly on his exceptional variety for decades in the early 20th century. The Gilfeather is not a standard turnip but appears to be a cross between turnip (Brassica rapa) and rutabaga (Brassica napobrassica), inheriting characteristics of both — the roots are large (up to 5 lbs), elongated to round with a distinctive greenish-white skin, and the white flesh is significantly sweeter, milder, and less peppery than standard turnips, with a creamy texture when cooked that many tasters prefer to either parent species. The flavor is sweet, rich, and substantial — excellent mashed, roasted, or in soups and stews — without the sharpness that can make standard turnips polarizing. A unique and genuinely outstanding heirloom vegetable with an authentic piece of New England agricultural heritage behind it; a excellent fall/winter root vegetable for zone 9 production.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Gilfeather turnip variety history
University of Vermont Extension — Gilfeather turnip

name: Gill's Golden Pippin Acorn Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the soil has warmed; Gill's Golden Pippin is a semi-bush heirloom acorn squash with golden-yellow rind rather than the dark green skin of standard acorn types.
directions: Sow seed directly in warm, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing hills to give the semi-vining plants room without the sprawl of a full-size squash vine. This heirloom stands apart from the ubiquitous dark green acorn squash by ripening to a bright golden-orange rind, and its dry, fine-grained flesh has a milder, sweeter flavor that many gardeners prefer for baking and stuffing. Harvest once fruit reaches full color and the stem has begun to dry and cork over, since acorn types do not continue to ripen off the vine. It stores for two to three months in a cool, dry spot, making it a good keeper for a squash that matures relatively early in the season.

name: Ginseng Orange Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant rooted slips 2-5 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Ginseng Orange is a naturally occurring orange-skinned, orange-fleshed sport discovered within Ginseng Red plantings, sharing the same early, semi-bush, cut-leaf habit as its parent.
directions: Ginseng Orange is a color-sport selection derived from the Virginia heirloom Ginseng Red, retaining the same early maturity, semi-bush vine habit, and cut, lobed leaf, but with orange skin and orange flesh in place of Ginseng Red's pinkish-red skin and light orange flesh. Its compact, semi-bush growth is well suited to smaller garden beds where a fully sprawling vine variety would be unwelcome. Set slips in full sun in loose, fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost, keeping the row lightly hilled as vines fill in to protect developing roots from sun exposure and cracking. Growers note this variety produces reliably above-average yields for an heirloom type; cure roots for about a week in warm, humid conditions after digging to firm the skin and improve storage life before moving them to cooler, drier long-term storage.
sources: Sand Hill Preservation Center sweet potato variety descriptions
Dave's Garden PlantFiles — Ipomoea batatas 'Ginseng Orange'

name: Ginseng Red Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant rooted slips 2-5 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Ginseng Red is a semi-bush heirloom with a cut-leaf habit, kept in circulation by a Virginia family for over four decades before wider seed-saver distribution.
directions: Ginseng Red is a semi-bush heirloom sweet potato with a distinctive cut, lobed leaf and pinkish-red skin over light orange flesh, an early-maturing variety long grown by a Virginia farm family before it entered wider seed-saver circulation. Its more restrained, semi-bush vine habit takes up less garden space than sprawling standard sweet potato varieties, making it a reasonable choice for smaller plots. Plant slips in full sun in loose, well-drained soil after the danger of frost has passed, and hill soil lightly around the base as vines establish to encourage even root development. After harvest, cure roots for about a week at warm temperatures and high humidity, then continue storing them for several additional weeks, since growers report the flavor and sweetness of Ginseng Red noticeably improve the longer it is kept in storage.
sources: Sand Hill Preservation Center sweet potato variety descriptions
Dave's Garden PlantFiles — Ipomoea batatas 'Ginseng Red'

name: Glacier Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Glacier is a notably early-maturing, cold-tolerant slicing tomato capable of setting fruit when nighttime temperatures fall to 45–50°F — ideal for short-season northern gardeners, high-altitude gardens, or Pacific Northwest coastal conditions where most tomatoes fail to set fruit in cool summers.
directions: Transplant into warm, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after last frost; Glacier is a determinate to semi-determinate variety that does not require extensive staking; it produces most of its fruit in a compressed season (excellent for northern and coastal climates) and can be grown without pruning. Glacier is an open-pollinated early-season slicing tomato specifically suited to cool-summer and short-season climates: it sets fruit at nighttime temperatures as low as 45–50°F, a capability that distinguishes it from most standard tomato varieties (which require consistent nighttime temperatures above 55°F for pollen viability and fruit set). This cold-setting ability makes Glacier valuable for Pacific Northwest coastal gardens where summer temperatures rarely exceed 75°F, high-altitude Rocky Mountain gardens with cool nights, and short-season northern gardens (zones 3–5) where the growing season is compressed. The medium-small (3–4 oz), round to slightly oblate, red fruits ripen early (55–65 days from transplant) and have good flavor for an early variety — pleasantly sweet-acidic balance with classic fresh tomato character; the flavor intensifies if warm conditions prevail at harvest time. The determinate to semi-determinate plants (36–48 inches) do not require the extensive staking that indeterminate varieties need, making them convenient for short-season production in smaller garden spaces.

name: Gladalan Brown Onion
plantingNote: In mild-winter regions sow directly in autumn so bulbs can begin forming as day length increases in spring; in colder climates sow as early as soil can be worked.
directions: Gladalan Brown is an early-to-midseason Australian heirloom storage onion developed in Western Australia in the early twentieth century and grown as a short-day type for mild-winter climates. It produces medium to large, firm, brown-skinned globes with a mild flavor that mellows further in cooking, and it has a reputation for keeping unusually well in storage. Because it is day-length sensitive, bulbing is triggered earliest in regions with shorter winter days, so gardeners outside its traditional short-day range should expect smaller bulbs. Thin direct-sown seedlings to their final spacing early to allow bulbs room to size up evenly.

name: Gladiator Parsnip
plantingNote: Long season root; in mild Gulf Coast winters can also be sown in fall for a spring harvest.
directions: The first F1 hybrid parsnip bred in Britain, combining vigor with smooth, blemish-free skin and strong canker resistance. Roots are wide-shouldered and taper to a short body, staying tender and free of a woody core even at large sizes. It has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit and is popular with both home gardeners and show growers for its consistency.
sources: UK seed trade catalogs (Thompson and Morgan, Mr Fothergill's)

name: Gladiator Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained soil; intermediate powdery mildew tolerance and firmly rooted handles suit the long, hot, humid pumpkin-growing season along the Gulf Coast.
directions: Sow seeds directly in hills after frost danger has passed, spacing hills widely since Gladiator carries a full, sprawling vine that needs room to support its large fruit load. Fruit grows round to slightly ribbed, deep orange, and sizeable at 20-25 pounds, with a thick, well-anchored handle that stands up to hauling and display without snapping off. Its intermediate resistance to powdery mildew keeps the canopy productive later into the season than older open-pollinated field types, which matters most where warm, humid nights push disease pressure hard in late summer. Cut fruit from the vine with several inches of stem once the rind has hardened and colored fully, then cure before storing in a cool, dry, well-ventilated space.

name: Glaskin's Perpetual Rhubarb
plantingNote: Sow seed directly or start indoors in early spring; unlike most rhubarb it can be lightly cropped in its first year.
directions: Glaskin's Perpetual is a seed-grown heirloom rhubarb bred to bolt (flower) far less readily than most seed strains, so stalk production stays steady all season instead of stalling after the plant runs to seed. Its notably low oxalic acid content lets gardeners take a light first-year harvest, a rarity among rhubarbs that normally need a full year or two to establish before cropping. Stalks are medium-thick and pink-green rather than deep red, with a mild, less astringent flavor suited to lighter sweetening. It remains popular with gardeners who want a reliable, true-breeding rhubarb they can start cheaply from seed rather than buying divisions.

name: Glass Gem Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of 4+ rows for adequate wind pollination; isolate from other corn by 300 feet to preserve jewel-color purity, though crossing with other corn simply diversifies the colors in interesting ways. In zone 9, plant March–May. Glass Gem requires a long season (100–120 days) and must be harvested as a dried corn — leave ears on the plant until husks are completely dry and papery. The translucent jewel colors are most vibrant after drying.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in blocks of 4 rows after last frost; harvest ears 3–4 weeks after the husks become fully dry and papery. Peel back husks and hang in a dry, well-ventilated place for additional drying before storage or decorative use. Glass Gem is a visually extraordinary ornamental flour corn that became an internet sensation in 2012 when photographs of its polychrome, jewel-toned ears went viral — sparking massive interest in heirloom and decorative corn that had not previously existed in the gardening public. The corn was developed by Carl Barnes, a half-Cherokee seed saver from Oklahoma, who spent decades crossing and back-crossing different traditional Cherokee corn varieties to create a flour corn capable of producing kernels in any color of the rainbow — deep red, crimson, burgundy, purple, violet, blue, aqua, green, gold, orange, pink, cream, and white, often on the same ear in translucent, jewel-like forms. Barnes shared seed with fellow seed saver Greg Schoen, who further developed and distributed the variety through Native Seeds/SEARCH. Each ear is unique — no two are identical — and the translucency of the kernels in bright light has no equivalent in any other corn or vegetable. While Glass Gem can be ground into flour (it is a genuine flour corn with functional starch composition), its primary use is ornamental — for corn arrangements, wreaths, and displays where the extraordinary color variation is the attraction.
sources: Native Seeds/SEARCH — Glass Gem corn origin and documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Glass Gem corn introduction and notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Carl Barnes and Glass Gem corn history

name: Glory of Enkhuizen Cabbage
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Glory of Enkhuizen'
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer for a fall crop in mild-winter climates; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once seedlings have 4–5 true leaves.
directions: Set transplants 18–24 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the round, dense heads benefit from consistent moisture to avoid splitting as they finish sizing up. Glory of Enkhuizen is a classic Dutch heirloom cabbage introduced in the late 19th century from the seed-growing town of Enkhuizen in the Netherlands, long one of Europe's most important vegetable-seed production centers. It forms medium-large, round to slightly flattened, blue-green heads with a tender, sweet, finely grained interior that holds its quality well both fresh and cooked, and it has a good reputation for splitting resistance and reasonable storage life for a mid-season type. Widely grown across Europe and North America through the 20th century as a dependable, high-yielding main-crop cabbage, it remains a favorite heirloom for gardeners wanting classic round-head cabbage with proven, old-world reliability, in zone 3–9.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Go Big Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow once danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Go Big's large mature size calls for wide rows and sturdy support in windy spots.
directions: Go Big is a modern hybrid bred to produce noticeably thick, dark green pods that hold their tenderness at a larger size than most standard okra. Plants grow tall and wide over the season, so give them room to branch and check pods every day or two once production ramps up in midsummer heat. Because the pods stay fry- and stew-worthy even when picked slightly larger, Go Big forgives a missed harvest day better than finer-podded heirlooms. Consistent moisture and full sun keep this vigorous hybrid setting new pods until temperatures cool in fall.

name: Goat Horn Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; harvest at the red stage for drying and grinding into chili flakes or powder, the pepper's primary use in Chinese and Southeast Asian kitchens.
directions: Goat Horn is a long, tapered cayenne-type Capsicum annuum whose curved, horn-shaped four- to six-inch pods ripen from green to a deep orange-red and carry a robust 20,000-50,000 Scoville heat with a bright, fruity edge. Despite its popularity in Sichuan and other Southeast Asian cooking, the variety traces to the Caribbean and grows vigorously in any warm-season garden with full sun and well-drained, fertile soil. Plants are heavy bearers of thin-walled pods that dry quickly on or off the plant, making Goat Horn a good choice for home-ground chili flakes, infused oils, and the toasted whole dried chiles used in stir-fries. Space plants to allow good airflow and stake tall specimens, since a fully loaded plant can carry dozens of pods at once.
sources: Sandia Seed Company — Goat Horn Pepper
Trade Winds Fruit — Goat Horn Pepper Seeds
USDA National Plant Germplasm System — Capsicum annuum PI 321003

name: Gobbo di Nizza Cardoon
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant into deep, rich soil once frost danger has passed; Gobbo di Nizza takes its name from the traditional Piedmontese practice of tipping plants over and burying the stalks in trenches in fall, which curves and blanches them into their signature hunchbacked shape.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Gobbo di Nizza Monferrato is a heritage Piedmontese cardoon, listed by Slow Food's Ark of Taste, grown for its broad, fleshy, greeny-gray leaf ribs that carry relatively few strings and spines compared with wild cardoon. In late fall growers traditionally dig a shallow trench, lay the whole plant over into it, and bury the stalks in soil for several weeks, which both blanches the ribs pale and forces them into the curved, hunchbacked form that gives the variety its name. Blanched stalks are braised, fried, added to gratins, or eaten raw dipped in olive oil, and the fleshy root is edible as well, prepared much like a parsnip.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste

name: Gogosari Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 55F.
directions: Gogosari is a Romanian heirloom 'cheese pepper' prized for its flattened, tomato-shaped fruit with thick, crisp walls that ripen from green to deep burgundy-red. It has been grown commercially in central and eastern Romania for roughly a century and remains a key ingredient in zacusca, the traditional Romanian roasted vegetable spread. The blocky, ribbed fruit is well suited to roasting and pickling whole, since its flattened shape and thick flesh make for easy peeling after charring. Give plants full sun and even moisture, and stake heavily fruiting plants since the dense, fleshy peppers can weigh down branches.
sources: Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste

name: Gold Coast Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Gold Coast is a compact, well-branched heirloom developed at LSU that tolerates drought and root-knot nematode pressure better than most okra, making it a dependable choice for lean or sandy Gulf South soils.
directions: Direct sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep after soil has warmed, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart; Gold Coast was developed at the LSU AgCenter and selected for a compact, heavily branched habit with long petioles that make hand-harvesting easier than on tall heirloom types. The spineless, light green pods stay tender to about 6 inches and hold up well to canning and freezing. Its strong root system gives Gold Coast above-average tolerance of both drought and root-knot nematodes, two of the most common stresses on okra grown in the sandy soils of the Deep South. Because pods are slower to fiber up than many varieties, Gold Coast forgives an occasional missed picking day better than fast-maturing hybrids.
sources: LSU AgCenter — Seed Preservation Program, Recovered LSU Varieties: Gold Coast Okra
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Gold Coast okra variety notes
university extension okra variety trial records

name: Gold Medal Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March. Provide sturdy cage or stake support for the large, indeterminate vines. The bicolor flesh — yellow-gold base with red internal streaking — makes Gold Medal one of the most beautiful tomatoes when sliced. In zone 9 fall planting in August produces exceptional flavor.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with sturdy stake or cage support; Gold Medal (also known as B&L's Gold Medal) is a large, beefsteak-type heirloom tomato producing spectacular bicolor fruits with bright golden-yellow skin blushed with red and dramatically marbled interior flesh — when sliced, the cross-section reveals a swirled pattern of deep red-orange and golden-yellow that makes Gold Medal arguably the most beautiful heirloom tomato variety for fresh-cut presentations and tomato salads. The flavor combines the mild, low-acid sweetness characteristic of yellow tomatoes with the rich, complex notes of a large beefsteak type, producing a fruit that is simultaneously sweet and substantial in flavor without the sharp acidity of most large red heirlooms. The low-acid, sweet character makes Gold Medal appealing for people who enjoy the fresh sweetness of yellow tomatoes but want a larger, meatier fruit. Large fruits commonly reach 1–2 pounds and have meaty walls with small seed cavities, making them outstanding for fresh slicing.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Gold Medal Heirloom Tomato
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Gold Medal Bicolor Tomato
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Bicolor Tomato Varieties

name: Gold Medallion Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is warm; Gold Medallion is a commercial hybrid buttercup-type squash bred for uniform fruit size and reliable yields for market growers.
directions: Direct sow seed in hills spaced widely apart in rich, well-drained soil, since vines run vigorously across the season. Gold Medallion is a hybrid buttercup-type squash that sets a heavy crop of uniform, 3 to 4 pound, deep-orange fruit with the characteristic small button at the blossom end, and its dense, dry, sweet flesh cooks up well for baking and pureeing. Growers value it for setting fruit reliably even under variable weather, giving a more consistent harvest than many open-pollinated buttercup strains. Harvest when the rind has hardened and the vine begins to decline, then cure for one to two weeks in a warm space before moving to cool storage to concentrate the sugars.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Gold Nugget Squash
plantingNote: Sow directly in warm soil after the last frost, spacing plants closely since this variety's bush habit needs far less room than sprawling buttercup types.
directions: Sow directly in warm soil after the last frost, spacing plants closely since this variety's bush habit needs far less room than sprawling buttercup types. Bred at North Dakota State University for the region's short, cool growing season and named an All-America Selections winner in 1966, it produces small, round, deep-orange fruit with sweet, fine-grained flesh similar to buttercup squash but ready weeks earlier. Its compact, non-vining plants make it a practical choice for northern gardens and small plots where space and season length are limited. Harvest once the rind resists thumbnail pressure, then cure briefly to concentrate sugars before storage.

name: Gold Rush Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.8–6.5) soil in full sun; Gold Rush is a longer-season potato (90–100 days) — in zone 9, plant as early as January to ensure tubers mature before summer heat arrives; protect young shoots from late frost with row cover.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Gold Rush is a North Dakota State University russet-type potato introduction combining the classic russet potato appearance (oblong, netted-brown skin) with the bright golden-yellow flesh of yellow-flesh varieties — providing a visually distinctive combination of the familiar russet form with surprisingly vivid yellow-gold interior color. The golden-yellow flesh — darker than standard Russet Burbank white flesh and more intense than the pale yellow of Yukon Gold — creates an attractive visual quality in baked, mashed, and roasted preparations where the golden color adds visual appeal to the finished dish. Gold Rush has the high-starch, dry, fluffy interior texture of classic russet-type potatoes — ideal for baking (fluffy, dry-textured baked potato), French fries (crispy exterior, dry interior), and mashed potatoes where a light, dry texture is desired. The russet skin type and long oblong shape produce the classic large baked potato form. In zone 9, Gold Rush's longer season (90–100 days) requires early planting (January) to ensure harvest before summer heat ends the cool potato growing season. Plant deeper than most varieties (6–8 inches) and hill aggressively to promote maximum tuber development in the long cool season before heat forces harvest.

name: Gold Rush Wax Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 60°F; Gold Rush is a compact stringless yellow wax bush bean producing uniform straight pods (5–6 inches) in a concentrated set over 2–3 weeks. The bright golden-yellow color of the pods makes harvesting easy — the pods stand out clearly against green foliage, reducing the chance of overlooking mature pods that would become tough and seedy if missed. Successive sowings every 3 weeks through midsummer extend the harvest; in zone 9, sow February–April for spring and again September–October for fall production. Gold Rush is one of the highest-yielding yellow wax bush beans, with pods borne in dense clusters just above the soil surface on a compact upright plant.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart; harvest when pods reach 5–6 inches before seeds swell noticeably inside. Gold Rush Wax Bean is a high-yielding yellow wax bush bean developed by Burpee for home garden production, distinguished by the uniformity and straightness of its bright golden pods and its concentrated harvest set that makes it one of the most productive yellow wax types per planting. The wax bean category — yellow-podded varieties that lack the green chlorophyll of standard snap beans — developed historically as a distinct preference in European-American cooking traditions where the pale color was associated with tenderness and delicacy; wax beans are botanically identical to green snap beans, with the yellow coloration resulting from the absence of chlorophyll development in the pod walls, allowing carotenoid pigments (which would normally be masked by green) to express visibly. Gold Rush's pods are straight and uniform (an advantage for commercial packing but also convenient for home preparation), stringless from the earliest edible stage through full harvest size, and have a mild flavor with a slightly more buttery taste than equivalent green snap varieties — a characteristic that many cooks attribute to the different pigment chemistry of wax pods, though the underlying flavor compounds are essentially the same. The compact bush plant reaches 18–24 inches with an erect, self-supporting habit that keeps pods above soil contact and makes one-pass harvesting efficient. For highest yield and quality, harvest every 2–3 days throughout the peak bearing period and do not allow pods to yellow beyond the characteristic bright gold; overripe pods become pale, stringy, and starchy.
sources: Burpee Seeds — Gold Rush Wax Bean variety development notes and productivity data
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Yellow Wax Bush Bean Variety Comparison for Home Garden Production
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Snap Bean and Wax Bean Variety Performance in Florida

name: Gold Rush Yellow Wax Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; succession plant every 2–3 weeks for continuous yellow wax bean harvest. Gold Rush produces a well-concentrated pod set ideal for once-over harvest or a 1–2 week intensive harvest window. In zone 9, plant March–May and again August–September for fall production.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep in rows 18–24 inches apart; harvest pods when 4–6 inches long and still tender. Gold Rush is a 1980 All-America Selections-winning yellow wax bush bean that earned recognition for producing exceptionally straight, slim, uniformly golden-yellow pods in a well-concentrated set ideal for both fresh market and home canning. Yellow wax beans are a distinct culinary category from green snap beans — the pale golden-yellow color (which remains after cooking), slightly creamier texture, and subtle flavor difference (milder, slightly less grassy than green beans) make wax beans a favorite in German and Eastern European cooking and preferred by many home gardeners for pickled beans and canned beans. Gold Rush produces pods of exceptional straightness and uniformity — the 5–6 inch pods are nearly pencil-straight, a quality attribute for both visual appeal at the table and ease of packing for canning. The plants are compact, upright, and productive, concentrating the pod set over a 7–10 day harvest window suitable for once-over mechanical harvest or home garden batch picking.
sources: All-America Selections — Gold Rush bean AAS winner 1980
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Yellow wax bean variety comparison
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Snap and Wax Bean Production

name: Gold Rush Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; in zone 9, sow spring crops in February–March and fall crops in August–September for the best production before summer heat or fall cold limits the season.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Gold Rush is an All-America Selections-winning yellow zucchini hybrid — producing the classic straight, cylindrical zucchini form (6–8 inches at optimal harvest) in brilliant golden-yellow skin rather than the standard dark-green of typical zucchini. The golden-yellow skin is visually striking and creates attractive contrast with standard green zucchini in market displays, mixed vegetable dishes, and grilled presentations — the same tender, mild, slightly sweet flesh as green zucchini in a color that makes it immediately distinguishable. Gold Rush is a compact bush-type plant reaching 18–24 inches with a moderate 3–4 foot spread — appropriate for typical garden spacing without the sprawling habit of some summer squash. The AAS recognition reflects exceptional performance across multiple growing regions and conditions. In zone 9, Gold Rush is best grown as a spring crop (February–March planting for April–May harvest) or fall crop (August planting for September–October harvest) — summer heat causes powdery mildew and reduced production. Harvest at 6–8 inches for best flavor and tenderness; oversized fruits become seedy and tough. Squash vine borers are the primary pest challenge in zone 9; monitoring and early action against eggs is essential for spring production.

name: Goldberg Golden Purslane
plantingNote: Direct sow thickly in warm soil (70F+) in well-drained soil in full sun; Goldberg is a named golden purslane cultivar distinguished by unusually large, golden-yellow leaves.
directions: Goldberg is a named cultivar of golden purslane distinguished by unusually large, golden-yellow leaves, grown alongside the more upright, green-leaved 'Gruner' as one of the two most commonly named selections of culinary purslane. Scatter seed on warm, bare soil and press in lightly, since seed needs some light to germinate; thin to 4-6 inches or harvest as a cut-and-come-again crop. Like other golden purslane selections it thrives in the summer heat and drought that cause most other salad greens to bolt, and its succulent, mildly tart leaves are notably rich in omega-3 fatty acids, vitamin C, and beta-carotene.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Summer Vegetables

name: Golden Ball Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall for the best turnip production in zone 9; turnips grown in cool fall weather are sweeter and less pungent than summer-grown turnips. In zone 9, sow August–October for harvest October–January. Spring planting is possible (February–March) but quality is often reduced by warming temperatures. Golden Ball's yellow flesh is notably sweeter than standard purple-top white-fleshed types and makes it excellent roasted.
directions: Direct sow 0.25 inch deep in rows 12 inches apart; thin to 4–6 inches as plants establish. Golden Ball (also known as Robertson's Golden Ball and Amber Globe) is a Victorian-era heirloom turnip with a strikingly different appearance from the standard purple-top white-fleshed types that dominate American turnip culture: the round, smooth roots are golden-yellow skinned with deep golden-yellow flesh, rather than the white flesh of standard types. The yellow flesh color indicates a different carotenoid profile and, notably, a distinct flavor: Golden Ball is considered one of the sweetest, mildest turnips available — the yellow-fleshed types tend toward greater sweetness and less sulfur-pungency than white-fleshed types when grown in the same conditions. This mild, sweet quality makes Golden Ball excellent for eating raw (rare for turnips), roasted whole (the golden color makes an attractive presentation), and in preparations where the sulfur bite of standard turnips would be unwelcome. Golden Ball has been grown in British kitchen gardens since at least the 1850s and represents the traditional European approach to turnip cultivation that emphasized flavor diversity across multiple colors and flesh types rather than the American focus on the single purple-top type.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Golden Ball turnip variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Heirloom turnip collection
Royal Horticultural Society — Traditional British vegetable variety documentation

name: Golden Bantam Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 week after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 60°F; in zone 9 plant March–April for spring crop and August for fall. Plant in blocks of at least 3–4 rows for adequate wind pollination of ears.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; plant in blocks rather than single rows to ensure adequate pollen distribution to every silk. Golden Bantam is perhaps the most historically important sweet corn variety in American garden history. Introduced in 1902 by W. Atlee Burpee Company from a selection by E.L. Coy of New York, it was the first widely successful yellow sweet corn at a time when white corn was considered superior — Golden Bantam changed American tastes permanently and proved that yellow sweet corn could surpass white in flavor. The short (6–7 foot), early-season plants produce 6–7 inch ears with 8 rows of deep golden-yellow kernels with a distinctive rich, full sweet corn flavor different from modern supersweeet hybrids — a milk-and-sugar intensity that is the archetype of 'real corn flavor.' Still one of the best open-pollinated sweet corns and superior to any hybrid for seed saving. Harvest at milk stage (silk brown, kernel milky when pierced) and cook or freeze immediately — sugar converts to starch within hours of picking.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee Company historical catalogue 1902
Seed Savers Exchange — Golden Bantam sweet corn documentation
William Woys Weaver: Heirloom Vegetable Gardening, Henry Holt 1997

name: Golden Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for winter-spring harvest. Golden beet germinates more slowly than red types and requires consistently moist soil until seedlings emerge. Thin to 3–4 inches for best root size. The golden color is most vibrant in young to medium-sized beets (2–3 inches diameter); very large golden beets may develop an orangey-brown skin. The tops are edible — harvest baby leaves for salads or cook mature greens like chard.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of rocks and hard pan; Golden Beet produces roots with bright golden-yellow skin and deep orange-gold flesh that stands out dramatically from red beet varieties — the color results from betaxanthin pigments rather than the betacyanin (red-purple) pigments of standard beets. The most important practical difference from red beets is that Golden Beet does not bleed or stain hands, cutting boards, or other foods with the intense crimson juice of red beets — a major advantage in salads and prepared dishes where red beet juice can dominate the visual presentation. The flavor of Golden Beet is also distinctly sweeter and milder than most red beet varieties, with less of the earthy 'dirty' undertone that some people find off-putting in red beets. The combination of non-staining, mild sweetness, and attractive golden color makes Golden Beet the preferred choice for beet salads, roasted vegetable medleys, and restaurant presentations.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Beet Variety Trial
University of Wisconsin Extension — Root Vegetable Production
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Golden Beet History and Production

name: Golden Bush Scallop Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 65°F, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the compact bush habit needs less room than vining squash but still benefits from generous spacing for airflow and easy harvest.
directions: Sow directly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest fruit young, at 2–3 inches across, for the sweetest, most tender flesh and thinnest skin, and pick every couple of days to keep the compact bush producing all summer. Golden Bush Scallop is a classic American heirloom summer squash producing the traditional flying-saucer-shaped 'patty pan' fruit in a bright, buttery golden-yellow, with a scalloped edge and creamy, mild, slightly nutty flesh when harvested young. The compact, non-vining bush habit keeps the plant tidy and productive in a relatively small footprint compared to sprawling vine squash, making it a good choice for smaller vegetable gardens and raised beds. Like all summer squash, frequent harvest at a small size is the key to extended production — fruit left to grow large quickly turns tough and seedy and signals the plant to slow down. A cheerful, productive, old-fashioned squash for zone 3–11 gardens.

name: Golden California Wonder Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Golden California Wonder is the gold counterpart to the standard red-ripening California Wonder — same fruit form and size, different final color.
