directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Golden California Wonder is the gold-maturing selection from the California Wonder bell pepper family — producing the same blocky, four-lobed, large, thick-walled bell pepper fruit as standard California Wonder but ripening to a golden-yellow color rather than red. The fruits begin green and ripen to a warm, rich golden-yellow at full maturity — a color stage with sweeter, more mellow flavor than the green stage and a different flavor profile from fully red bell peppers. Golden bell peppers are noticeably sweeter and lower in Scoville units than green bell peppers — the color change from green to gold/yellow reflects the conversion of chlorophyll to carotenoids and the simultaneous conversion of starches to sugars. As an open-pollinated variety, Golden California Wonder seeds can be saved reliably from season to season. The golden fruits create visual contrast in mixed salads, stir-fries, and grilled vegetable platters where the gold color pairs beautifully with red and orange companions. The same thick walls and blocky form as California Wonder make Golden California Wonder outstanding for stuffed peppers. In zone 9, plant in spring (February–March) for a spring crop and in August for a fall crop.

name: Golden Crispy Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early in short-season gardens, in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; space plants 18-24 inches apart in rows 4-6 feet apart.
directions: Golden Crispy is a small Japanese melon that built a following as a commercial gourmet variety before disappearing from catalogs in the early 1980s; seed was later tracked down and reintroduced by specialty heirloom growers. The smooth, golden-skinned fruit are oblong to pear-shaped and notably small, averaging about half a pound each, which lets a single vine set an unusually high number of melons for its size. The white flesh is crisp rather than soft-textured, with a sweet, distinctively aromatic flavor that sets it apart from typical musky cantaloupe types. Grow it like other melons in warm, fertile soil with consistent deep watering through fruit development, switching to drip or soil-level irrigation to limit the foliar disease that overhead watering invites.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Golden Crispy Melon
Smart Gardener — Melon: Golden Crispy Growing Guide

name: Golden Cross Bantam Sweet Corn
scientificName: Zea mays var. saccharata 'Golden Cross Bantam'
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least four short rows after soil has warmed well past the last frost, since corn relies on wind pollination and needs neighboring plants to fill ears properly.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in blocks rather than single long rows to ensure reliable pollination, and side-dress with nitrogen once plants reach knee height. Introduced in the 1930s as one of the first widely grown hybrid sweet corns, this variety became a benchmark standard for decades thanks to its resistance to Stewart's wilt and its dependable yields of seven-inch ears filled with tender, golden-yellow kernels. Its classic old-fashioned sweet corn flavor, rather than the ultra-sugary taste of modern supersweet hybrids, still appeals to gardeners who remember it from earlier generations of home gardens. Harvest when kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pierced.

name: Golden Crown Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70F and all frost danger passes; Golden Crown is an AAS-winning early, compact icebox watermelon whose rind ripens to solid golden-yellow instead of green, giving an easy visual ripeness cue unlike most watermelons.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms. Golden Crown is an AAS-winning early, compact icebox-type watermelon with an unusual and genuinely useful feature — the rind ripens from green to a distinctive solid golden-yellow at full maturity, giving gardeners a clear, unmistakable visual cue for ripeness instead of relying only on the ground-spot color, tendril drying, and thump-sound methods needed for green-rind watermelons. Inside, the flesh is sweet and red, with a compact plant habit and fast maturity that suit smaller gardens and shorter growing seasons well. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil and consistent irrigation through fruit development for the best size and flavor; ease off watering slightly as fruit nears full color to help concentrate sugars.
sources: All-America Selections — Golden Crown Watermelon winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Golden Delicious Squash
plantingNote: Sow directly into warm, fertile hills once soil temperatures are reliably above 65°F, well after last frost.
directions: Golden Delicious is a 1920s Oregon-bred heirloom, a cross of Delicious and Boston Marrow, grown for its top-shaped, red-orange fruit and thick, fine-grained flesh originally favored for commercial baby food production. Give the long vines plenty of room and consistent moisture through fruit development, then let fruit finish on the vine until the rind resists a thumbnail. It stores exceptionally well for a maxima squash, often holding good eating quality into winter without special curing conditions. Gardeners choose it today for its old-fashioned sweetness in pies and its reliability as a dependable keeper compared to showier modern hybrids.

name: Golden Detroit Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; Golden Detroit's yellow-orange roots never bleed color the way red beets do.
directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters about half an inch deep in loose, fertile soil in full sun, and thin seedlings to three or four inches apart once true leaves appear. Golden Detroit is a yellow-fleshed sport of the classic Detroit type, producing round, orange-skinned roots that cook down to a warm mustard-gold color instead of bleeding red, so it can be roasted, pickled, or shaved raw into salads without staining hands or other ingredients. The flavor is sweet and mild, generally considered gentler and less earthy than red beet varieties, and the tender tops are excellent cooked as greens. Harvest at two to three inches across for the best texture, and keep the soil evenly moist throughout to prevent tough, fibrous roots.

name: Golden Dwarf Champion Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the compact, rugose-leafed dwarf habit needs only light staking.
directions: Golden Dwarf Champion is a yellow-fruited sport of the 19th-century heirloom Dwarf Champion tomato, one of the earliest true dwarf, potato-leaf tomato lines grown in American gardens. Plants stay short and self-supporting while producing round to oblate golden-yellow fruit with a mild, sweet flavor typical of yellow heirloom tomatoes. Along with other old dwarf lines, it was preserved by seed savers into the era of the modern Dwarf Tomato Project, where its compact genetics have been bred into newer releases such as Dwarf Sweet Sue, crossed with Green Giant. Harvest as fruit turns fully golden and softens slightly for peak sweetness.

name: Golden Flax
plantingNote: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, up to the last frost date; golden flax needs cool weather to establish and struggles once summer heat arrives.
directions: Broadcast seed thickly over a firm, weed-free bed and rake in to about 1/4 inch, since golden flax relies on dense stands to keep its slender stems from lodging. This yellow-seeded type is grown specifically for the table — the mild, nutty flaxseed is favored for grinding into meal for baking and smoothies over the more assertive brown-seeded types. Watch the sky-blue flowers give way to round seed capsules, and cut whole plants at the base once most capsules have dried to a tan color and rattle when shaken. Dry the cut bundles under cover for one to two weeks before threshing by flailing or treading, then winnow thoroughly, as golden seed shows any chaff more readily than brown flax.

name: Golden Frill Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer or fall (zones 7–11) or early spring (zones 3–7); Golden Frill is a yellow-green counterpart to Ruby Streaks mustard — both have deeply serrated, feathery leaves, but Golden Frill's chartreuse to light yellow-green color provides a dramatic visual contrast when planted alongside purple or red mustard varieties; flavor is milder than red mustard types at the same leaf age, making it versatile for fresh salads.
directions: Broadcast or sow in rows 1/4 inch deep; for baby leaf harvest sow thickly and cut at 3–4 inches; for mature plants thin to 6–8 inches; harvest outer leaves continuously or cut the whole plant 4–6 inches above the crown for cut-and-come-again; milder than red frills types at the same growth stage. Golden Frill is a deeply serrated, feathery-leaved mustard green with the same fine, lacey, frilly leaf form as Ruby Streaks but with chartreuse to bright yellow-green coloring — a deliberate complement to red frills types in mesclun mixes and specialty salad production. The deeply incised, pinnately cut leaves (resembling an extremely large, pungent parsley) are the characteristic form of the 'frills' mustard group, but Golden Frill's bright color is distinctive and valuable in ornamental kitchen garden plantings where the yellow-green foliage contrasts dramatically with red-leaved varieties, dark green kales, and purple cabbages. The flavor is mustard-sharp but somewhat milder than red-leaved mustard varieties at the same stage of maturity — mild enough to use raw in quantity in salads at the baby leaf stage, with more heat developing in mature leaves. Golden Frill is a standard component of mesclun and Asian salad mixes alongside Ruby Streaks, mizuna, and tatsoi; the combination of all four creates dramatic visual contrast (red, chartreuse, dark green, and pale green) with complementary flavors. Extremely fast-growing in cool weather — baby leaves in 21 days, full plants in 35–40 days.

name: Golden Frills Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop; spring sowings are more prone to flea beetle damage than late-summer ones.
directions: Direct sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop, since Golden Frills grows best in the cool temperatures of spring and autumn and can suffer flea beetle damage in warm weather. Golden Frills is a strikingly ornamental mustard green with finely dissected, deeply lobed, chartreuse-gold leaves that add texture and bright color to salad mixes and cut-and-come-again plantings. Its flavor is sweet and aromatic with a mustard bite that is milder than many mustard greens, and mature plants sometimes develop a crisp, edible root reflecting a mustard-turnip heritage in its lineage. Harvest young for baby leaf salads at around three weeks, or allow plants to grow to full size for a spicier, more robust cooking green.

name: Golden Giant Amaranth
plantingNote: Sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Golden Giant bears tall, upright, golden-yellow seed plumes on a vigorous grain amaranth suited to both harvest and cut-flower use.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly, barely covered, in warm soil after the last frost, or start indoors a few weeks early. Golden Giant produces tall, dense, upright golden-yellow flower plumes on vigorous, sturdy stems, grown both for its abundant edible grain and as a dramatic fresh or dried cut flower for fall arrangements. Heat-tolerant and low-maintenance, it thrives in full sun and average soil, producing heavy yields of small, protein-rich seed by the time the plumes fully color and dry. Harvest seed heads once they rattle and the seed sheds easily when rubbed, then thresh and winnow; cut plumes for drying just as they color for the best cut-flower use, and expect self-sowing if seed heads are left in place.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

name: Golden Globe Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep 6–10 weeks before the first fall frost for the sweetest roots, or as early as the soil can be worked in late winter; in zone 9, an October sowing usually outperforms a spring one since the roots size up in cool, mild weather without bolting.
directions: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep and thin to 3–4 inches apart once seedlings have their first true leaves, using the thinnings as tender salad greens. Golden Globe is a 19th-century English heirloom valued for its smooth, golden-skinned, yellow-fleshed roots, which are noticeably sweeter and milder than white-fleshed turnips and hold good texture even when they size up past baseball size. It bulks up quickly from a compact top, making it a good choice for close spacing and succession sowing, and the mild flavor suits it equally well to roasting, mashing, or eating raw and thinly sliced. Keep soil evenly moist for fast, uninterrupted growth, since checks from drought or heat toughen the roots and sharpen their flavor.

name: Golden Gopher Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills 2-3 weeks after last frost once soil is reliably warm; thin to two or three vigorous seedlings per hill and give plenty of room to ramble.
directions: Golden Gopher was released by the University of Minnesota in the 1930s from a cross thought to include honeydew parentage, giving it unusually high sugar content and useful resistance to fusarium wilt for a melon of its era, though it remains susceptible to powdery mildew. The lightly ribbed, sparsely netted, roughly two-and-a-half-pound fruits carry deep orange flesh of excellent eating quality and are known among growers as 'pop open' melons for how they sometimes split at the blossom end when fully ripe. Its compact vine and dependable production have kept it in circulation with small seed stewardship organizations long after most other university-bred melons of its generation disappeared from commerce. Watch fruit closely as it nears maturity and harvest promptly once it slips or begins to crack to avoid loss to splitting.

name: Golden Gourmet Shallot
plantingNote: Plant shallot sets 4–8 weeks before last frost in spring, or in fall in zones 7–10 for overwintering harvest; Golden Gourmet produces uniform, elongated oval bulbs with golden-amber to bronze outer skin and pale yellow to white flesh — a Dutch-type yellow shallot with classic mild, sweet shallot flavor and excellent productivity and storage life that make it a top-selling shallot variety in European commercial production.
directions: Plant shallot sets 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart, with the tip just at or slightly above soil level; each set multiplies into a cluster of 5–8 bulbs; maintain consistent moisture during spring growth; reduce watering when tops begin to yellow and fall over; harvest when bulb skins are dry and golden, then cure 2–3 weeks in a warm, dry location before storage. Golden Gourmet is a Dutch-type yellow shallot produced by seed companies primarily in the Netherlands, the global center of commercial shallot breeding and production; the variety represents the classic 'Dutch shallot' style — elongated-oval (sometimes banana-shaped), golden to copper-amber skinned bulbs with very pale yellow to white inner flesh, as opposed to the red-violet type represented by Ambition and Zebrune. The flavor profile is mild, sweet, and delicately onion-like with the characteristic shallot complexity — somewhat different from red-type shallots, with a cleaner, lighter character that particularly suits cream sauces, light vinaigrettes, and dishes where the golden color and mild flavor complement pale or delicate ingredients. Each planted set multiplies into a cluster of 5–8 uniform bulbs that cure to a beautiful, uniform golden-amber appearance — the classic appearance of the shallots found in upscale grocery stores and restaurant supply. Stores 8–10 months under good conditions, outlasting most red-type shallots. Can be replanted from the previous year's sets.

name: Golden Honeymoon Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early where the growing season is short; Golden Honeymoon ripens roughly two weeks ahead of standard green-fleshed honeydew types.
directions: Golden Honeymoon is a honeydew-type heirloom prized for combining a brilliant gold rind with the classic pale green flesh of honeydew melon, maturing roughly two weeks earlier than standard honeydew selections. Fruit reach three to five pounds, round and smooth-skinned, with juicy flesh that holds the mild, sweet flavor honeydew fans expect without the long, heat-hungry season many winter melons require. Because it finishes earlier than most inodorus-type melons, it is a practical choice for gardeners in cooler or shorter-summer regions who still want a true honeydew experience. Water deeply once or twice a week, keeping the soil evenly moist through fruit set, and harvest when the rind's gold color deepens and the blossom end yields slightly to thumb pressure.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Golden Honeymoon Melon
True Leaf Market — Golden Honeymoon Melon Seeds
Albert Lea Seed — Golden Honeymoon Melon

name: Golden Hubbard Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; an 1898 introduction and one of the most widely grown Hubbard types, with brilliant red-orange skin and an easier-to-cut size than the giant Blue Hubbard.
directions: Sow 2–3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 1–2 plants once true leaves appear and keep hills evenly moist through fruit set. Golden Hubbard was introduced around 1898 as a smaller, easier-to-handle alternative to the large blue Hubbard types, producing teardrop-shaped fruits 6–10 pounds in weight with vivid orange-red, bumpy skin and dense, sweet, yellow-orange flesh with excellent dry texture ideal for baking and puréeing. Harvest after the first light frost has killed the vines and the rind resists puncture with a fingernail; cure in a 70–85°F location for 10–14 days then store at 50–60°F for up to 4 months. The relatively manageable fruit size makes it more practical for home cooks than the 15–20 pound Blue Hubbard.

name: Golden Jenny Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; Golden Jenny was selected from the historic Jenny Lind muskmelon line and produces small, round, golden-skinned fruit with sweet orange flesh on a plant well suited to compact gardens and short growing seasons.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after last frost, thinning to the strongest two or three seedlings per hill; the compact vines and small fruit size make this a good candidate for raised beds or smaller vegetable plots. Golden Jenny produces round, one to two pound fruits with smooth golden-yellow skin and juicy, aromatic, orange-gold flesh, and was developed from the classic 19th-century Jenny Lind muskmelon, retaining that heirloom's sweetness and old-fashioned melon aroma in a smaller, quicker-maturing package. Keep soil evenly moist through vine growth and fruit set, then let it dry slightly as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip, when the stem separates cleanly from the vine with light pressure and the fruit releases a strong, sweet fragrance at the blossom end.

name: Golden Jubilee Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Golden Jubilee is a tall indeterminate that needs a sturdy stake or cage for the full season.
directions: Golden Jubilee is a classic open-pollinated slicing tomato introduced by Burpee in 1943, producing smooth, globe-shaped, deep golden-orange fruit with a mild, notably low-acid flavor that has made it a long-standing favorite for gardeners who find red tomatoes too tart or acidic. The 6-8 ounce fruit holds its shape well for slicing and has a pleasant, sweet flavor without the intensity of tangier heirlooms, giving it a reputation as an easygoing, family-friendly garden tomato. Stake the vigorous indeterminate vine well, and because the fruit ripens to a lighter color than red tomatoes, judge readiness by gentle give at the shoulders as much as by color alone.

name: Golden Midget Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of short rows or in large containers; compact stature makes it practical for small gardens and pots.
directions: Direct sow in blocks of short rows or in large containers, since its compact stature makes it one of the few sweet corns genuinely practical for small gardens, raised beds, and pots. Golden Midget was bred at a New Hampshire agricultural research station in the mid-1900s specifically to give home gardeners a fast, space-saving sweet corn, reaching only two to three feet tall while still producing petite four-inch ears of golden-yellow kernels. Its short season and small footprint have kept it a favorite heirloom for northern gardeners and anyone growing corn in limited space, and it remains a genuinely useful, if lesser-known, member of the open-pollinated sweet corn family.

name: Golden Midget Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Golden Midget is a compact, early-maturing watermelon (70–75 days) producing icebox-sized fruits (6–8 lbs, 6–8 inches diameter) on shorter vines (4–5 feet) than standard large watermelon varieties. In zone 9, plant April–June; the short maturity allows two plantings in the season. Golden Midget's most remarkable feature is its ripeness indicator: the skin is light green with darker green stripes when unripe, and it turns golden-yellow when fully ripe — a color change that is unmistakable and provides a clear visual cue to harvest timing without the need to thump, check tendril dried status, or use other indirect indicators. This visual ripeness indicator is unique among common watermelon varieties and is Golden Midget's primary practical advantage. The flesh is red, sweet, and of good quality for an early compact variety. The compact vine size makes Golden Midget more manageable in average-sized home gardens than standard watermelon types.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms; space 4–5 feet apart. Harvest when skin turns solid golden-yellow. Golden Midget Watermelon was developed and introduced by Elwyn Meader and Albert Yeager at the University of New Hampshire in the 1950s, specifically targeting short-season northern gardens where standard large watermelons require more summer heat than is available. The breeding goals — early maturity (70–75 days), compact vine, and small fruit — made Golden Midget one of the pioneering compact watermelon varieties for home garden production. The most distinctive characteristic is the skin color change at ripeness: unlike any other standard watermelon variety, Golden Midget's skin transitions from striped green to solid golden-yellow as the fruit reaches full maturity inside, providing the clearest possible visual harvest cue. Standard watermelon ripeness indicators (dried stem tendril, ground spot color change, sound when thumped) require interpretation and experience; Golden Midget's golden skin change is unambiguous and visible from across the garden. The fruit size (6–8 lbs, fits in a refrigerator shelf whole) suits modern households that cannot easily consume a 25-pound watermelon and want a seedless or small-fruited option. The flesh is pink to red with conventional watermelon sweetness — appropriate for fresh eating, salads, and summer use — without the extraordinary flavor intensity of the best large heirloom varieties, but reliable and consistent in flavor quality across the growing season.
sources: University of New Hampshire — Golden Midget watermelon variety development by Meader and Yeager
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Golden Midget watermelon early variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Compact and early watermelon variety comparison

name: Golden Orach
plantingNote: Sow directly in early spring and successively every few weeks for a steady supply of tender young leaves.
directions: Sow directly in early spring and successively every few weeks for a steady supply of tender young leaves, since older leaves and stems toughen as plants approach flowering. This golden-yellow-leaved form of mountain spinach has been grown as a spinach substitute since antiquity and tolerates heat and poor soil far better than true spinach, eventually bolting to tall, ornamental seed spikes in summer. Its bright color makes it a popular contrast alongside the more familiar red and green orach forms in mixed salad plantings.

name: Golden Promise Barley
plantingNote: Sow in early spring once soil is workable; Golden Promise is a short-strawed two-row barley originally bred in Scotland and long favored by distillers for single malt whisky.
directions: Golden Promise is a two-row spring barley developed in Scotland and best known for its long association with single malt Scotch whisky production, prized by distillers for the character it lends to new-make spirit even though it yields less than many modern varieties. Its notably short, stiff straw resists lodging well, which made it attractive to growers before semi-dwarf barleys became common. Drill into a firm seedbed in early spring and manage as a typical spring malting barley, giving it a cool start and avoiding excess nitrogen that can push protein content too high for malting specifications. Harvest once fully ripe and dry, and store the grain carefully to preserve germination for malting or distilling use.

name: Golden Purslane
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost; in zone 9 plant March–May or August–September. Golden Purslane requires warm soil and warm weather to germinate and grow — do not attempt in cool conditions. It self-sows readily in zone 9 and may naturalize in garden beds; pull unwanted seedlings before they set seed. Harvest tender stem tips continuously to keep the plant producing new growth.
directions: Direct sow in lean, well-drained soil in full sun — purslane thrives in the heat and poor soils that discourage other vegetables; Golden Purslane is a cultivated, golden-yellow-stemmed selection of the common wild purslane (Portulaca oleracea), developed for the edible vegetable trade and producing larger, more succulent stems and leaves than the weedy wild type. The thick, fleshy, yellow-green leaves and golden stems have a mild, slightly lemony, succulent flavor with a mucilaginous texture when raw and a spinach-like softness when cooked. Purslane is one of the highest plant sources of omega-3 fatty acids and contains significant amounts of vitamins A, C, and E — nutritionally rich in a plant that requires almost no inputs and grows vigorously in the heat that exhausts other summer vegetables. In zone 9 it is one of the most productive summer greens from May through October when the heat prevents all other leafy green production. The golden color distinguishes it from the wild weedy type and makes it more attractive in salads. Harvest young stem tips and leaves continuously; older stems become woody.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Purslane as an Edible Green
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Portulaca oleracea for Florida Gardens
Nichols Garden Nursery — Culinary Purslane Varieties

name: Golden Queen Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Golden Queen is an indeterminate regular-leaf variety that needs staking or caging to support its large smooth fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, staking the vigorous vines to support fruit. Released by Livingston Seed Company in 1882, Golden Queen was long marketed as the finest smooth yellow tomato available, producing large, 8-12 ounce, waxy golden-yellow fruit that is sometimes blushed with pink at the blossom end, with meaty, low-seed flesh and a mild, sweet flavor that made it a favorite among 19th- and early 20th-century home gardeners seeking a low-acid alternative to red slicers.

name: Golden Self-Blanching Celery
plantingNote: Start indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, since celery seed germinates slowly and can take up to three weeks; transplant into rich, moist soil in tight blocks or double rows so the crowded plants self-blanche without tying or hilling.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun, spacing plants closely in a block rather than a single row; Golden Self-Blanching Celery was introduced in the United States in the early 1880s and became one of the most widely grown home garden celeries of its era because it needs no earthing up or wrapping to pale its stalks. Grown tightly together, the inner stalks naturally shade one another and turn a soft golden-green by fall, staying crisp and largely stringless with a clean, mild celery flavor. It matures somewhat faster than many older celery types, making it a practical choice for gardeners without a long, reliably cool season to spare. Water evenly and consistently throughout the growing period, since irregular moisture is the most common cause of stringy, bitter stalks in any celery.

name: Golden Sweet Pea
plantingNote: Sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; a tall climber (4–5 ft) with attractive purple flowers requiring trellis support; pods change from bright yellow-green to full yellow at harvest — pick when flat and yellow-green.
directions: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep in cool, fertile soil in full sun 4–6 weeks before last frost with trellis support; Golden Sweet is a distinctive heirloom snow pea from India with vivid lemon-yellow pods against deep green foliage and attractive purple flowers — one of the most ornamental edible peas available. The flavor of the bright yellow flat pods is sweet and delicate with a slightly more tender texture than green snow peas; they make a visually striking addition to salads and stir-fries. Harvest pods when fully yellow and flat before seeds begin to swell for best quality. The yellow color provides an interesting contrast to green and purple-podded pea varieties grown together.

name: Golden Udo
plantingNote: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Golden Udo, a 2020 Perennial Plant of the Year, is a golden-leaved sport of edible udo bearing brilliant chartreuse-gold foliage best colored in part shade, while still producing edible blanched shoots.
directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; foliage color is most vivid in a few hours of morning sun with shade during the hottest part of the day, and the leaves turn lime-green rather than scorching in fuller shade. Golden Udo, named the 2020 Perennial Plant of the Year, is a dramatic ornamental sport of the Japanese vegetable udo, producing huge, bold, compound leaves in a luminous chartreuse-gold that light up a shaded border from spring through fall, while retaining the parent species' edible young shoots, which can be blanched and harvested in spring and prepared much like asparagus. It dies back to the ground each winter and re-emerges vigorously in spring, forming a large, architectural clump within a couple of seasons. Divide congested clumps in early spring, and provide consistent moisture, since the large leaves wilt readily in dry soil.

name: Goldie Ground Cherry
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to garden after frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start seeds in January–February and transplant in March–April. Ground cherries drop ripe fruits in their papery husks — harvest by collecting fallen fruits daily. In zone 9 ground cherries often self-sow and naturalize as short-lived perennials in mild winters.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Goldie is a named ground cherry cultivar specifically selected for larger-than-average fruit size and superior sweetness compared to standard ground cherry selections — the distinctive golden-yellow to pale orange fruits inside their papery lantern-like husks are significantly larger and sweeter than wild-type plants, with a complex tropical flavor combining vanilla, pineapple, and tomatillo notes with a sweet-tart finish unlike any other common garden fruit. Ground cherries (Physalis pruinosa) are closely related to tomatillos but used as a sweet fruit rather than a savory vegetable — excellent eaten fresh, baked into pies and cobblers, or made into jam with a natural pectin content that produces a firm set. The plant grows as a sprawling, somewhat sticky annual related to tomatoes, producing continuously from midsummer until frost. In zone 9 Goldie ground cherries produce abundantly and the plants often self-sow from fallen fruits.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Goldie Ground Cherry
Cornell University Extension — Ground Cherry Varieties
University of Vermont Center for Sustainable Agriculture — Physalis pruinosa

name: Goldilocks Acorn Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Goldilocks is a semi-bush acorn squash bred for a much more compact vine than traditional sprawling acorn types, so it fits well in smaller vegetable gardens and raised beds.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously even though the semi-bush habit takes noticeably less room than traditional sprawling acorn squash vines. Goldilocks is an AAS-winning acorn squash producing golden-orange, deeply ribbed fruit with sweet, fine-textured, deep-orange flesh, on a plant compact enough for smaller gardens while still yielding a full crop of 4-6 fruits per plant. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens and the color deepens to a solid gold-orange, typically as the vine begins to decline in late summer or fall; cure harvested squash in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before storing to improve flavor and shelf life. Watch for squash vine borer and squash bugs, which are common problems for all Cucurbita pepo squash in the Gulf South.
sources: All-America Selections — Goldilocks Acorn Squash winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Gonzales Baby Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Gonzales produces compact, 3–4 lb cabbage heads on plants spaced 12–14 inches apart — significantly closer spacing than standard full-sized cabbage types (18–24 inches) — making it practical for small raised beds, intensive planting, and gardens where standard cabbage would take too much space. In zone 9, start in July–August and transplant late August–September for November–December harvest. Gonzales is an F1 hybrid with excellent uniformity — plants in a block ripen within a narrow window, allowing single-harvest timing.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun, fertile soil. Harvest when heads feel firm and solid. Gonzales is a compact, early-maturing F1 hybrid green cabbage designed specifically for closer plant spacing, smaller garden plots, and the restaurant/market garden demand for mini or baby vegetable formats — a market segment that has grown substantially with the trend toward smaller household sizes and the restaurant emphasis on individual-portion vegetables. The heads average 3–4 pounds (compared to 5–8 lbs for full-sized standard green cabbage types) but form a properly tight, round, firm head with the same dense, crinkle-free outer leaves and pale, crisp interior of larger standard types — not a soft or immature head, but a fully developed compact head. Gonzales's early maturity (66–75 days from transplant vs. 80–110 days for full-sized storage types) combined with its compact size makes it particularly practical in zone 9's fall garden where planting time from mid-summer is limited. The flavor is classic mild, sweet, crisp green cabbage — excellent for coleslaw, stir-fries, braises, and fresh salads. The small size is practical for household use where a standard large cabbage requires several meals to consume before it deteriorates.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Gonzales cabbage F1 hybrid variety notes
Harris Seeds — Mini cabbage variety comparison
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Cabbage Production Guide and Variety Selection

name: Good Mother Stallard Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil has warmed above 60°F; a vigorous pole bean that needs a trellis or fence 5–6 feet tall and is harvested as a dry bean in fall after the pods have dried on the vine.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep after all frost danger has passed into fertile, well-drained soil against a tall trellis; do not soak beans before planting as it can cause the seed coat to split. Good Mother Stallard is an heirloom pole bean introduced through Seed Savers Exchange with beautiful, plum-purple and white mottled pods and seeds that develop into a creamy, meaty dry bean with a remarkably rich, complex, steak-like flavor when cooked — widely considered one of the best-flavored dry beans available to home gardeners. Allow pods to mature and dry completely on the vine before harvesting; if frost threatens, pull the entire vine and hang in a protected location to finish drying. Store shelled dry beans in a cool, airtight container for up to a year.

name: Goosebumps Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Goosebumps is a hybrid warty pumpkin producing dense, fine-textured bumps over a mid-size orange fruit, a finer texture than the larger warts on some competing varieties.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost in rich, well-drained soil, spacing hills widely to accommodate vigorous 15 to 20 pound fruit. Goosebumps produces an orange jack-o-lantern-shaped pumpkin covered in fine, dense bumps rather than the larger, sparser warts seen on some novelty pumpkins, giving it a distinctively pebbled texture that has made it popular with retail growers and fall-festival displays. The heavy warting develops progressively as the fruit matures, so color and texture continue to intensify right up to harvest. Pick before hard frost once the rind has hardened and the bumpy texture has fully developed, and expect the thick rind to hold up well through weeks of autumn display.

name: Gowrie Rutabaga
plantingNote: Direct sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest after frost sweetens the roots; thin seedlings to final spacing once established.
directions: Gowrie is a traditional Scottish rutabaga selection grown for its sweet, round, purple-topped roots with firm golden flesh, used historically as the base for Scottish 'neeps and tatties.' Sow seed 1/2 inch deep directly in the garden in mid to late summer, thinning seedlings to 6-8 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil. Roots mature in fall and develop their best flavor after exposure to light frost, which converts starches to sugars. Harvest and store in a cool root cellar, or leave roots in the ground under heavy mulch in milder climates for a winter-long harvest.

name: Gradus Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter or very early spring, since this first-early pea needs a long cool stretch to fill its large pods before summer heat arrives.
directions: Sow seed about an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil as early as the ground can be worked, since Gradus is a first-early wrinkled pea bred to mature quickly in cold weather. Provide brush, netting, or a low trellis for the three-to-four-foot vines, which otherwise sprawl and tangle. This English Victorian-era variety, associated with the nurseryman Thomas Laxton, was long valued for pods as large and well-filled as main-crop types despite ripening weeks earlier, making it a favorite for both the table and the show bench. Pick pods promptly once plump, since flavor and sweetness fade quickly as the peas mature past their prime.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange heirloom pea records

name: Graffiti Cauliflower
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring planting or in midsummer for fall crop; Graffiti is a vivid purple cauliflower whose dramatic color comes from anthocyanins — the same antioxidant pigments in red cabbage and blueberries — and while the color fades when cooked (unlike Cheddar's beta-carotene), the raw purple makes it spectacularly visual in crudités platters, salads, and vegetable displays.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; transplant into rich, moist, fertile soil with consistent watering; fall crops typically produce the most vivid purple color as cool temperatures intensify the anthocyanin pigmentation; harvest when heads are tight. Graffiti is a vivid purple cauliflower developed by Syngenta Seeds, with intensely purple heads caused by very high anthocyanin concentrations — the same pigments responsible for the colors of red cabbage, blueberries, blackberries, and purple sweet potatoes, and associated with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory health properties. Unlike the orange beta-carotene in Cheddar cauliflower, the purple anthocyanins in Graffiti are water-soluble and somewhat heat-sensitive: the vivid purple color turns gray-blue or fades when the vegetable is boiled or steamed, though the color remains more stable with roasting or stir-frying. For maximum visual impact, Graffiti is best used raw — in crudités platters, purple cauliflower hummus, raw salads, and grain bowls where the intense purple provides a visual anchor. The flavor is typically cauliflower — slightly nutty, mild, sweet — with no unusual taste despite the dramatic color. Cool temperatures intensify the purple color, making fall-grown Graffiti more vividly colored than spring crops. An excellent conversation piece and visual anchor for vegetable gardens.

name: Grand Duke Kohlrabi
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplant date; in zone 9 transplant September–October for fall and January–February for spring. Grand Duke is an All-America Selections winner that performs best in cool weather — fall crops in zone 9 from September transplants have the best flavor and texture. In zone 9 summer heat causes rapid bolting and fibrous, pithy stems; stick to the cool seasons. Harvest when stems are 2–3 inches across for best tenderness.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Grand Duke is the 1979 All-America Selections-winning kohlrabi cultivar and remains the standard cool-season kohlrabi for home gardens. The pale green, smooth-skinned swollen stem enlarges more uniformly and remains tender longer than older varieties — it can be harvested at 2–3 inches and still be mild and crisp, even as other varieties turn woody and pungent. The flavor is mild, sweet, and slightly turnip-like — excellent raw, sliced thin in salads, or stir-fried. In zone 9 kohlrabi is a fall-through-winter vegetable, transplanted in September–October for harvest from November through February. The plants are relatively frost-hardy and will survive most zone 9 winters without protection. Pull the entire plant at harvest; the leaves are also edible when young and cooked like kale.
sources: All-America Selections — Grand Duke Kohlrabi Award Record
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Kohlrabi
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Brassica Crop Production

name: Grand Rapids Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, and again in fall; fast-growing and reasonably heat tolerant for a leaf lettuce, making it a good choice for stretching the Gulf Coast lettuce season.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, thinning seedlings to six to eight inches apart. Grand Rapids is a historic American loose-leaf lettuce introduced in the late 1800s that became the standard commercial greenhouse lettuce variety across the United States for much of the early 20th century, prized for its light green, deeply frilled, crinkled leaves and fast, dependable growth. It does not form a true head, instead producing a loose rosette that can be harvested leaf by leaf for a cut-and-come-again crop or cut whole at the base once full size is reached. Grand Rapids is more heat- and cold-tolerant than many lettuce varieties, extending the usable harvest window on either end of the cool season, though very hot weather will still eventually push it to bolt and turn bitter.

name: Grandad's Favourite Rhubarb
plantingNote: Plant a dormant crown division in early spring in fertile, well-drained soil, setting the bud just below the surface and firming in well.
directions: Grandad's Favourite is a traditional English heirloom passed down through generations of allotment growers and prized for its reliably sweet flavor and tender texture even in stalks left to grow a bit larger than usual. It forces well for an early, pale pink forced crop when covered with a forcing pot in late winter, then produces a second flush of deep red, more strongly flavored stalks in open growth through spring. Established clumps are notably vigorous and long-lived, often remaining productive in the same spot for well over a decade with minimal care beyond an annual mulch. As with other rhubarb, discard the leaves and harvest only the stalks, pulling rather than cutting them from the crown.

name: Granddaddy's Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed once soil has warmed above 65F; Granddaddy's traces to four generations of the Eubanks family of Whitney, Texas, and was later found growing in the garden of a Texas Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association founder before Seed Savers Exchange and Sow True Seed helped preserve and distribute it.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun once the ground has heated up after the last frost. Granddaddy's produces long, slender pods with good flavor that stay tender past the size where many other okra turn fibrous, though picking under 6 inches still gives the best eating quality. Pick every two to three days through the heat of summer to keep the vigorous, heavily branched plants setting new pods, and expect production to hold up well even under typical late-season disease pressure. This is a true multigenerational family heirloom rather than a commercial release, so seed stock traces directly back to the Eubanks family line.
sources: Texas Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association

name: Grandma Nellie's Mushroom Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is reliably above 60F; provide tall support since vines climb 7-9 feet.
directions: The lineage of this bean traces to a Russian immigrant who gave the seed to Nellie Chernoff in Kamsack, Saskatchewan, who grew it for thirty years before passing it to her granddaughter. It is prized for a savory, almost meaty flavor when the creamy-yellow pods are cooked at about 5 inches long, well before the brown seeds inside mature. Train the long vines up a trellis or pole and pick every few days to keep plants setting new pods. Because it's an early, heavy producer, it's a good choice for gardeners who want fresh beans quickly in a short season.

name: Grandma Nellie's Yellow Mushroom Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and provide a tall trellis or pole for the vigorous climbing vines.
directions: This family heirloom pole bean traces to seed a Russian immigrant gave to Nellie Chernoff, who grew it for decades before it was passed down and eventually shared with seed preservationists. Pick pods at about 4 to 5 inches while still tender for fresh eating; cooked pods develop a distinctive savory, umami-like richness that sets this variety apart from typical green beans. Provide sturdy 6 to 8 foot poles or a trellis, as the vines are vigorous climbers that bear over a long harvest window. Keep pods picked regularly to keep the plant productive through the season.

name: Grandpa Admire's Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or again in late summer for a fall crop; thin seedlings as they grow to give each head room to fully form.
directions: Sow seed shallowly in cool, moist soil and thin plants as they grow to give each head room to fill out. Grandpa Admire's is an Ozark family heirloom lettuce preserved and distributed by Seed Savers Exchange, forming a loose, semi-heading rosette that bridges the gap between a butterhead and a romaine in both leaf shape and texture. The pale green leaves are tender and mild-flavored with a buttery crunch, and the variety is valued for holding in the garden without turning bitter longer than many spring lettuces. As a passed-down heirloom with a documented family origin, it is a good choice for gardeners interested in preserving lesser-known regional lettuce lines.

name: Granex Sweet Onion
plantingNote: Transplant onion sets or starts in November through January in zone 9 in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun; Granex is a short-day onion requiring 12 hours or fewer of daylight to form bulbs — it is the correct onion type for Gulf South gardens and bulbs where days are short during the winter growing season.
directions: Transplant onion sets or starts in November through January in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Granex is the foundational sweet onion cultivar behind the famous Vidalia onion — a short-day, mild, sweet onion variety grown in the Vidalia, Georgia, area since the 1940s that became the basis for the legally protected Vidalia Onion designation. The Granex onion (and closely related Granex 33 and similar cultivars) produces round to slightly flattened, large, sweet, mild bulbs with high sugar content and low pyruvic acid — a combination that creates the characteristic sweetness and lack of pungency that makes Vidalia-type onions so prized for fresh eating. Granex is a short-day onion (bulbs when day length reaches 12 hours or less), making it the correct onion type for Gulf South gardens where the short winter days trigger bulbing in March through May. Long-day onion varieties (grown in the northern US) will not bulb in the Gulf South — short-day varieties (Granex, Texas 1015, Red Creole) are essential for zone 9 production. In zone 9, transplant November through January and harvest when the tops begin to fall over (May–June), indicating full bulb development. The mild, sweet Granex onion is outstanding for fresh salads, burgers, and raw applications where a sweet onion is desired.

name: Granny Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow at the base of a pole or trellis after last frost; this comparatively quick-maturing pole bean rewards an early start in the warm-soil window.
directions: Collected from farm families in the Smoky Mountains of Cocke County, Tennessee, this old pole bean produces fat, slightly curved pods over round, brownish-gray seeds. It was traditionally grown both as a canning bean while pods were still fleshy and as a shelled dry bean later in the season. Vines are productive climbers and should be given a tall, sturdy support from planting onward. Its several folk names reflect how widely it was passed hand-to-hand among Appalachian gardeners before formal seed-saving networks preserved it.

name: Granny Franklin Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Granny Franklin is an Alabama family heirloom bred for heavy, reliable yields through the long, humid Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Soak seed overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep once the soil is warm; pick pods every 1-2 days at 3-4 inches for the most tender texture. Granny Franklin is an Alabama family heirloom, kept going for generations by home gardeners specifically for its heavy, consistent yield of classic green pods and its reputation as an outstanding frying okra. The tall, vigorous plants shrug off the intense heat and humidity that stress many other vegetables through a Deep South summer, continuing to set pods reliably as long as they are harvested regularly. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saved from healthy plants breeds true, letting Gulf Coast gardeners maintain their own line of this regional variety year after year.
sources: Alabama Cooperative Extension System — Growing Okra in the Garden

name: Greasy Back Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost at the base of a trellis, corn stalks, or other tall support; this vigorous climbing pole bean traditionally grown alongside corn needs sturdy support to reach its full length.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep at the base of a trellis or tall support in fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger passes. Greasy Back belongs to a distinctive family of Appalachian heirloom 'greasy bean' varieties named for pods that lack the fine fuzz found on most bean pods, giving them a smooth, shiny, almost oiled appearance that is unmistakable at a glance. Traditionally grown climbing up corn stalks in mountain garden plots, the vigorous vines produce tender, flavorful pods that can be picked young as snap beans, allowed to mature further for flavorful fresh shell beans, or left to dry fully for a rich, hearty dry bean prized in Appalachian cooking. Pick regularly to keep vines productive over a long season, and let the last flush of pods dry on the vine if a dry bean harvest is wanted.

name: Greasy Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm (65°F+), at the base of a sturdy pole or trellis, since Greasy Bean is a vigorous climber needing 6–8 feet of support.
directions: Sow at the base of poles or a trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest young for snap beans or let pods mature for a rich, flavorful shelly or dry bean. Greasy Bean is a distinctive category of heirloom Appalachian pole bean named for the unusual smooth, glossy, almost oil-slicked appearance of the pods, which lack the fuzzy surface texture of most common beans — a trait that has made these beans prized heirlooms passed down through generations of mountain families in Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, and West Virginia, with many distinct named strains maintained within individual families. The tender, stringless pods have excellent flavor as snap beans when young, and the plump, flavorful seeds shell out well for cooking as a traditional Appalachian soup bean. Vigorous, productive vines reward a sturdy support and reliable moisture through the growing season. A true regional heirloom treasure for gardeners interested in Appalachian foodways, zone 4–10.

name: Greasy Cutshort Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil warms above 60°F; cutshort beans get their name from seeds packed so tightly inside the pod that the pod tip appears squared off.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing 6-9 inches apart along a trellis or corn stalks. Greasy Cutshort combines two classic Appalachian heirloom bean traits in one variety: smooth, shiny, fuzz-free 'greasy' pods, and seeds packed so densely inside each pod that the tip is squared off rather than tapered, the 'cutshort' trait long selected for by mountain gardeners saving their own seed. The tender pods are good for snapping young, and the beans shell out well for a flavorful dry bean later in the season. Allow some pods to dry fully on the vine each year to save seed and maintain the strain.

name: Greasy Grits Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1-2 inches deep after last frost in well-drained soil; Greasy Grits is a pole-type Appalachian heirloom needing a trellis, teepee, or corn stalks to climb.
directions: Sow seeds 1-2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a sturdy trellis, pole, or teepee for the vigorous climbing vines; Greasy Grits is one of the many named strains of Appalachian greasy bean, so called for the smooth, shiny, almost oil-slick sheen on the pod surface caused by a lack of the fine fuzz found on most snap beans. Pods are stringless and tender when picked young for snapping, with a rich, savory flavor prized in traditional mountain cooking, and the plant can also be left to mature for shelling as a dry bean. Like other greasy beans it is a genuine landrace maintained by generations of Appalachian seed savers rather than a modern breeding-program release, so some variation between seed lots is normal and part of its heirloom character. Provide consistent moisture through pod set and pick regularly to keep the vigorous vine productive over a long summer harvest window.

name: Great Lakes Iceberg Lettuce
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; iceberg crisphead lettuce is challenging to grow in zone 9 because of the long time-to-maturity (82–90 days from transplant) and strict cool-temperature requirements. In zone 9, start seeds in August and transplant in October for a December–January harvest — the brief cool window in zone 9 is marginally adequate for iceberg if timing is precise. Iceberg lettuce heads only in cool temperatures: if warmth arrives before heading is complete, plants bolt to seed without forming the characteristic tight, firm head. Many zone 9 gardeners find that heat-tolerant romaine or butterhead types are more reliably productive than iceberg in zone 9 conditions.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to cool-season bed. Harvest when head is firm and compact. Great Lakes is the original American crisphead (iceberg) lettuce — developed by W.D. Blystone at the Michigan Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1941 (awarded All-America Selections in 1944), Great Lakes defined the iceberg lettuce type that became the dominant American commercial and restaurant lettuce through the mid-20th century. Before Great Lakes, commercial head lettuce was dominated by softer butterhead types; Great Lakes demonstrated that crisp, tight-heading lettuce could be grown reliably across a wider range of conditions and shipped the long distances needed for national distribution — characteristics that made it the foundation of the California iceberg lettuce industry that supplied American consumers coast-to-coast. The 'iceberg' name comes from the practice of shipping these firm-headed lettuces packed in ice during rail transport — an innovation in food distribution that made fresh lettuce available nationally for the first time. Great Lakes produces large (1.5–2 lb), very firm, round, pale-green to white-interior heads with the extreme crispness and mild flavor of the classic iceberg type. While largely replaced in commercial production by more uniform hybrid iceberg varieties, Great Lakes remains the reference open-pollinated iceberg for home garden and seed-saving use.
sources: All-America Selections — Great Lakes lettuce AAS winner 1944
University of California Davis — Crisphead Lettuce Variety History
Seed Savers Exchange — Great Lakes iceberg lettuce open-pollinated variety notes

name: Great Northern Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost when soil is warm; Great Northern is a bush-type dry bean that requires a warm growing season to dry properly. In zone 9 plant in spring for early summer harvest; the plants will decline in midsummer heat, so spring planting is preferable to early summer.
directions: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Great Northern is the most widely grown white dry bean in the United States, a medium-large, oval, white-seeded bush-type bean with mild, creamy flavor and a tender skin that cooks quickly — the standard white bean for baked beans, soups, and casseroles in American cooking. Developed in the northern Great Plains, it matures in 70–85 days and stores indefinitely as a dry bean. More delicate in flavor than navy beans and larger in size, making it the preferred choice for premium baked bean recipes and New England-style preparations where the bean is the star. Harvest by pulling entire plants when most pods are dry and golden; dry in a warm, airy location and thresh to remove seeds. Great Northern beans are nutritionally excellent, high in protein and fiber.

name: Great White Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March for a spring crop. Great White is indeterminate and requires staking or caging. The white-skinned fruits can be difficult to judge for ripeness by color change — look for a subtle cream to ivory-yellow blush and a slight softening of the fruit. In zone 9 the fall planting in August often produces the finest-flavored fruits as cooler temperatures reduce stress.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with sturdy cage or stake support; Great White is a large, beefsteak-type heirloom tomato producing fruits that ripen to an unusual cream-white to pale ivory-yellow color — one of the most distinctive-appearing heirloom tomatoes in any garden collection. The color difference from standard red tomatoes stems from the absence of normal red lycopene pigments: Great White produces primarily colorless carotenoids that result in the pale white-cream skin and flesh. The flavor is extraordinarily mild, sweet, and very low in acid — often described as honey-sweet with almost no tartness, making it popular for people who find acidic tomatoes hard to digest. The thick, very meaty flesh with small seed cavities makes Great White outstanding for fresh eating and mild salsas where a lower-acid tomato flavor is preferred. The pale color also makes it a striking visual contrast element in colorful heirloom tomato salads alongside red, purple, orange, and yellow varieties.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Great White Heirloom Tomato
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Great White Tomato Description
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Heirloom Tomato Varieties for Texas

name: Green Boy Komatsuna
plantingNote: Direct sow from early spring into fall; Green Boy holds up to cold better than most komatsuna, so it is a good choice for late-fall and even overwintered plantings in mild climates.
directions: Green Boy is a modern komatsuna hybrid selected for compact, glossy, deep green leaves on pale, tender petioles, with a flavor that sits between spinach and mild mustard. It stands out among komatsuna types for its cold tolerance, continuing to produce usable leaves well into cool weather when other Asian greens have stalled or bolted, which extends the harvest window in fall and early winter. Direct sow and harvest young for salad-size baby leaves or let plants develop further for bunching greens suited to stir-fries and quick braises. Succession sow every few weeks in the cooler shoulder seasons for a steady supply.

name: Green Comet Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a fast spring crop, or in midsummer for fall; Green Comet was one of the earliest hybrid broccolis widely sold and remains valued for reaching harvest well before slower open-pollinated types.
directions: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before setting transplants into fertile, evenly moist soil, spacing plants closer than later-maturing types since this hybrid stays compact. Green Comet earned an All-America Selections award for its speed, forming a tight, uniformly domed blue-green head only about eight weeks after transplanting, which makes it a reliable choice for short-season gardens or an early jump on the spring harvest before summer heat arrives. Side shoots follow the main head, though they are smaller and less numerous than in later hybrids. Cut the central head promptly once buds are tight, since this variety runs to flower quickly in warm weather.

name: Green Curled Ruffec Endive
plantingNote: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall and early-winter harvest, since it tolerates light frost and even improves in flavor after cool weather.
directions: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall and early-winter harvest, since it tolerates light frost and even improves in flavor after cool weather, or sow in early spring for a summer crop. A French heirloom frisée-type endive named for the town of Ruffec, it is prized for its finely dissected, deeply curled dark-green leaves and notable cold hardiness compared to other curly endives. Traditionally the outer leaves are gathered and tied to blanch the heart, producing the pale, tender center prized in French bistro salads.

name: Green Delicious Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil; allow vines ample room to run.
directions: Green Delicious was introduced in 1903 by James J.H. Gregory and Sons of Marblehead, Massachusetts, and was described in the historical reference The Vegetables of New York as among the finest-flavored of all squash. Its thick, hard green rind protects dense, orange, fine-grained flesh with an exceptionally sweet, dry texture prized for pies and baking. It later served as a parent, crossed with Boston Marrow, in the 1926 development of the now much more widely grown Golden Delicious squash by Gill Brothers Seed Company. Green Delicious survives today mainly through heirloom seed preservationists.
sources: U.P. Hedrick, The Vegetables of New York

name: Green German Sugarcane
plantingNote: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Green German is a traditional Gulf South dooryard syrup cane named by University of Florida IFAS Extension among the low-sucrose canes preferred for kettle syrup over crystal sugar.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Green German is an old dooryard heirloom, unstriped and solid deep green-stalked, that UF/IFAS Extension lists alongside Louisiana Ribbon as one of the traditional syrup-type canes: its juice carries a lower sucrose-to-total-sugars ratio than crystal (refining-grade) cane, which resists graining up in the kettle and cooks down into a smooth, pourable table syrup rather than crystallized sugar. Because sugarcane rarely sets viable seed true-to-type in Gulf South conditions, growers propagate it entirely from stalk sets: in fall, before the first hard freeze, the healthiest, disease-free stalks are cut, laid horizontally in a shaded trench or covered cane bed, and mulched heavily with soil, pine straw, or plastic sheeting to keep them dormant but unfrozen through winter. Harvest for syrup runs from the first light frosts in late October through December, when cool nights have converted starches to sugar; stalks are stripped of leaves, crushed, and the juice slow-cooked in an open kettle or pan evaporator into dark, mild-flavored cane syrup.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Backyard Sugarcane (SS-AGR-253/SC052)
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sugarcane Production and Heirloom Varieties
Southern Foodways Alliance — Cane Syrup Traditions

name: Green Giant Mustard
plantingNote: Sow in early spring or late summer into fall; the cross between tatsoi and pak choi gives it both cold hardiness and heat tolerance beyond either parent alone.
directions: Green Giant combines the glossy, rounded leaf of tatsoi with the thicker, more upright petiole of pak choi, producing a sturdy rosette that resists both bolting and bitterness better than either parent type alone. Direct-sow shallowly and thin plants to 6 to 10 inches for full heads, or grow crowded for cut-and-come-again baby greens. It holds up in both the cool damp of early spring and the heat of late summer, making it a reliable filler crop between main brassica plantings. Harvest whole rosettes or individual outer leaves for stir-fries, soups, and braises.

name: Green Giant Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake or cage, since the vigorous indeterminate vines need support through a long season.
directions: Green Giant is a large-fruited, green-when-ripe heirloom beefsteak tomato grown for its sweet, richly flavored amber-green flesh rather than the red color most gardeners expect at harvest. Because the skin stays green to yellow-green even at full ripeness, judge readiness by a slight give under gentle thumb pressure and a faint softening or blush at the blossom end rather than by color change alone. It is best known in tomato-breeding circles as one of the two parent varieties, alongside Golden Dwarf Champion, crossed in 2005 to create the compact, gold-fruited Dwarf Sweet Sue for the Dwarf Tomato Project. Grow the sprawling indeterminate vines on a sturdy cage or stake in full sun, and pick fruit promptly once it softens, since overripe green tomatoes are easy to mistake for underripe ones and can spoil on the vine if left too long.

name: Green Glaze Collard
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring for a spring crop; Green Glaze's thick, waxy cuticle deters cabbage worms and other leaf-chewing pests better than most collard varieties.
directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Green Glaze is a Southern heirloom collard, prized among organic growers for its thick, glossy, cabbage-like leaf surface that gives noticeably better natural resistance to cabbage worms, loopers, and flea beetles than standard collard varieties, reducing the need for pest control sprays. The tall, vigorous plants produce large, tender leaves with good flavor over a long cut-and-come-again harvest season, and cold exposure sweetens the flavor further, as with other collards. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season, and although the glossy leaves offer real pest resistance, monitor young transplants closely, since seedlings are more vulnerable before the waxy cuticle fully develops.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange heirloom collard archive

name: Green Glaze Collards
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12-14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August-September for fall and winter production. Green Glaze's waxy, glossy leaf coating gives it unusually strong resistance to cabbage worms and other leaf-feeding pests.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Green Glaze is a Southern heirloom collard distinguished by unusually smooth, thick, glossy, jade-green leaves with a waxy cuticle that makes it noticeably more resistant to cabbage worms, cabbage loopers, and other leaf-chewing pests than standard fuzzy-leaved collard varieties, an especially useful trait for organic growers. The flavor is mild and sweet for a collard, and the smooth leaf texture that deters pests also makes the leaves pleasant for fresh use in wraps as well as traditional slow-cooked greens. Like other collards it tolerates both summer heat and considerable cold, with flavor sweetening noticeably after the first light frosts of fall. Harvest outer leaves as needed and the plant continues producing new growth from the top through a long cool-season harvest window.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Collard Production in the Southeast

name: Green Globe Improved Artichoke
scientificName: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Green Globe Improved'
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant when 8–10 inches tall. In zone 9 plant transplants in February–March or divisions in fall. Vernalization (exposure to temperatures below 50°F for several weeks) stimulates the first-year flowering that produces edible buds — in zone 9, the mild winters naturally provide this, and the plants flower each spring from February through May. After harvest, cut plants back by half in late spring and they will resprout for a fall secondary harvest in zone 9.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Green Globe Improved is the primary commercial artichoke variety grown in California's Monterey County — the heart of American artichoke production — and the selection standard against which most other artichoke varieties are measured. The large, globe-shaped, tightly-closed heads of deep green overlapping bracts contain the edible fleshy bract bases and the prize, the meaty, tender artichoke heart at the center. The 'Improved' designation indicates a more consistent, uniform selection with better vigor than the original Green Globe. In zone 9, artichoke is particularly well-adapted — the mild winters provide the natural vernalization required to initiate bud production, and the plants can persist for 5–8 years as perennial specimens if given adequate space and annual fertilization. Zone 9's long growing season supports two harvesting periods: the main spring crop (February–May) and a secondary fall crop (September–October) after the summer regrowth period.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Artichoke Production Guide
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Artichoke Production in the Gulf South
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Globe Artichoke for Texas Gardens

name: Green Goliath Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Green Goliath produces a large central head followed by prolific side shoots that continue for weeks after the main head is harvested. In zone 9, transplant August–September for November–January harvest. For spring production, start indoors January–February and transplant when temperatures allow — spring-harvested broccoli is excellent in the Gulf South before temperatures rise.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 65–75°F; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil with good calcium availability. Harvest the central head while florets are still tight and before the head begins to open or yellow; side shoots will continue for 4–6 weeks. Green Goliath is an open-pollinated broccoli that produces large central heads — typically 8–10 inches across and 1–2 lbs — with the classic well-domed, dark green form that represents the traditional ideal of quality broccoli. The 'goliath' name refers to the head size: substantially larger central heads than many modern hybrid varieties that have been bred for smaller, more uniform heads suited to commercial harvest. After the central head is harvested, Green Goliath produces abundant and persistent side shoots — small 2–4 inch heads — that continue for 4–6 weeks, extending the productive season significantly beyond a single harvest. The side-shooting characteristic makes Green Goliath particularly valuable for home gardeners who want an extended harvest rather than a single concentrated yield. The open-pollinated status means seed can be saved from year to year, making it a popular choice for seed savers and those interested in maintaining productive self-sustaining vegetable gardens. Very good flavor at both the head and side-shoot stages.
sources: Burpee Seeds — Green Goliath broccoli variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Open-pollinated broccoli collection
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Broccoli Production Guide

name: Green Grape Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Green Grape is an indeterminate open-pollinated cherry tomato that retains green color at maturity, ripening to an amber-green with a slight golden blush when fully ripe. The key challenge for new growers is learning to identify ripe fruits by feel and slight color shift rather than waiting for red coloration that will never arrive. When fully ripe, Green Grape fruits yield slightly to gentle pressure and develop a translucent quality that distinguishes them from the opaque green of an immature tomato. In zone 9, transplant March–April; like all indeterminate types, Green Grape benefits from caging or staking to 5–6 feet and continues producing until heat stops fruit set in midsummer or until fall frost.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F; transplant after last frost and cage or stake to 6 feet. Harvest when fruits yield to gentle pressure and show a slight translucent amber-green glow rather than the opaque dark green of unripe fruit. Green Grape Tomato is an open-pollinated cherry tomato variety that remains green at full maturity — a characteristic that surprises first-time growers accustomed to using color change as the primary ripeness cue. The variety was developed by Tim Peters of Peters Seed and Research in Oregon and introduced in the 1990s as part of a wave of interest in non-standard-colored tomatoes that offered novel flavors and visual interest compared to standard red types. Green Grape fruits are approximately 1 inch in diameter with a round to slightly oval shape and thin green skin that ripens to a yellow-green or amber-green with characteristic translucency at peak ripeness; experienced growers learn to identify this translucency as the reliable ripeness indicator. The flavor is notably sweet with a complex, slightly tropical undertone — a combination that many tasters find more interesting than the straightforward sweetness of yellow or red cherry types. The green color is not from chlorophyll retained past ripening but from specific chloroplast development patterns that persist through the normal ripening process; the fruit is fully ripe when the color reaches amber-green, not when it turns red. Fruits cluster in medium-sized trusses of 8–12 and tend to hold well on the vine for several days after reaching peak ripeness without cracking, which is an advantage for gardeners who can't harvest daily.
sources: Peters Seed and Research — Green Grape Tomato original variety development documentation
Seed Savers Exchange — Green Grape cherry tomato heirloom listing and grower notes
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Green Grape tomato variety description and ripeness identification tips

name: Green Hubbard Squash
plantingNote: Direct-sow in hills after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; needs a long, warm season and plenty of room to vine.
directions: Green Hubbard, sometimes offered as True Green Improved Hubbard, is regarded by many seed historians as the original Hubbard type from which the more familiar blue- and orange-skinned Hubbard squashes were later selected. It bears large, teardrop-shaped fruit with a hard, dark green rind that is smoother and less warted than the later Chicago Warted strain, protecting dense, dry, golden-orange flesh with a rich, sweet flavor well suited to soups and purees. Like other Hubbard types, well-cured fruit stores for months in a cool, dry spot, making it a genuine long-season keeper squash. It needs generous vine space and a full warm season to size up and fully mature before harvest.

name: Green Ice Loose-Leaf Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow or start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting; Green Ice is a loose-leaf type harvested as individual outer leaves (cut-and-come-again) or as whole young plants (baby leaf at 25–30 days, full plant at 45–55 days). In zone 9, sow September–November and February–March. Green Ice's glossy leaf surface is unusual among loose-leaf lettuces — the glossy texture reduces water evaporation and may contribute to the variety's better-than-average heat tolerance.
