The deep crinkle of the leaves gives Green Ice a distinctive appearance in the garden and in harvested mixes, and provides good texture contrast when mixed with smoother lettuces. One of the most productive loose-leaf varieties for baby leaf and cut-and-come-again harvesting.
directions: Scatter seeds 0.25 inch deep; thin to 6–9 inches for full plants or leave dense for baby leaf cut-and-come-again. Harvest outer leaves, leaving 4–5 inner leaves to continue growing. Green Ice is a loose-leaf lettuce with a distinctive appearance that sets it apart from other common loose-leaf varieties: the leaves are deeply frilled and crinkled — more so than standard looseleaf types — and have an unusual, almost waxy glossiness on the upper leaf surface that gives the fresh leaves a bright, polished look unlike any other commonly grown lettuce. The deep green color is vibrant and consistent, making Green Ice one of the most visually striking lettuces in garden displays, cut flower and produce market presentations, and harvested salad mixes. The flavor is mild, clean, and slightly sweet — typical of loose-leaf types, without the bitterness of romaine or the grassiness of some outer head leaves. Green Ice's combination of heat tolerance (better than most loose-leaf types), productivity in cut-and-come-again harvest systems, glossy visual appeal, and excellent shelf life after harvest has made it a popular variety with market gardeners and home growers seeking a reliable, attractive loose-leaf for continuous harvest through the cool seasons of zone 8–10.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Green Ice loose-leaf lettuce variety notes
Harris Seeds — Green Ice lettuce heat tolerance description
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lettuce Variety Selection for Gulf South Gardens

name: Green in the Snow Mustard
plantingNote: Exceptionally cold-hardy; sow in late summer for a fall and winter harvest that survives frost and light snow, or in early spring for a quicker crop.
directions: This traditional Chinese mustard, known as xue li hong, meaning red amid the snow, is grown specifically for its ability to keep producing tender, deeply toothed serrated leaves through hard frosts and light snow cover. Direct sow into fertile soil in late summer for the best cold-season crop, harvesting leaves continually as a cut-and-come-again green. Leaves develop a purplish tinge and a distinctive sharp, mustardy tang in cold weather, and are traditionally salted or lightly fermented as a pickle as well as used fresh in soups and stir-fries. Its extreme hardiness makes it one of the last leafy greens standing in an unheated winter garden.

name: Green Lance Gai Lan
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile soil and thin to stand so the thick, tender flowering stalks can develop; also direct-sown in early spring after last frost.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile soil and thin to stand so the thick, tender flowering stalks can develop; Green Lance is a hybrid Chinese broccoli bred for better heat tolerance than older gai lan strains, letting it be sown over a longer window without bolting prematurely. Harvest the central stalk with its small cluster of unopened flower buds once it reaches pencil thickness, then continue cutting side shoots for several more weeks. The mildly bitter, broccoli-like stems and leaves are classically blanched and stir-fried with garlic and oyster sauce.

name: Green Light Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost in warm soil; Green Light is an All-America Selections winner bred as a compact, high-yielding, seedless snacking cucumber that produces thin-skinned, burpless mini cucumbers without needing a pollinator, making it well suited to small gardens and containers.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after the danger of frost has passed, or set out transplants, providing a small trellis or cage for the compact vines. Green Light was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining parthenocarpic (seedless, self-fruitful) fruit set with a compact plant habit and outstanding yield of crisp, thin-skinned, 4-5 inch mini cucumbers ideal for snacking whole or slicing. Because the plant sets fruit without pollination, it performs reliably even when bee activity is low and produces cucumbers with essentially no seed cavity or bitterness, with skin tender enough that peeling is unnecessary. The compact vines are well suited to small raised beds, large containers, and gardens with limited trellis space, and the plant's dense productivity means frequent picking — every one to two days once fruiting begins — keeps cucumbers at the ideal small size and encourages continued production through the season. Consistent watering during fruit development prevents bitterness and misshapen fruit.
sources: All-America Selections — Green Light Cucumber award notes
PanAmerican Seed — Green Light Cucumber variety description
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Cucumber Variety Trials

name: Green Lightning Pattypan Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Green Lightning is an early, compact bush pattypan suited to smaller gardens, with fruit ready to pick quickly after flowering.
directions: Direct sow seed after the danger of frost has passed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Green Lightning is an AAS-winning pattypan summer squash with a compact bush habit and glossy, scalloped fruit striped in dark green over a lighter green background, giving it a more vivid, eye-catching look than typical solid-colored pattypans. A small seed cavity keeps more of the fruit as tender, edible flesh compared to older scallop types. Harvest young, at about 3-5 inches across, for the best texture and flavor, and pick every day or two once plants start producing to keep the vigorous bush setting new fruit.
sources: All-America Selections — Squash Green Lightning F1 winner announcement

name: Green Machine Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70°F; Green Machine is a market-grower favorite bred for heavy, sustained yields and strong disease tolerance, holding up well to the mosaic virus and powdery mildew pressure that builds quickly in Gulf South summer humidity.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Green Machine is a vigorous hybrid zucchini widely grown by market farmers for its exceptionally heavy, sustained yield and improved tolerance to common summer squash viruses, which spread fast via aphids in humid conditions and can quickly stunt and discolor fruit on less tolerant varieties. It produces uniform, dark green, cylindrical fruit on an open, upright bush habit that makes harvesting easy even as the plant fills out. Because it keeps producing healthy, well-colored fruit later into the season than many older zucchini varieties, it is a strong choice for gardeners who have struggled with virus or mildew cutting squash harvests short. Pick fruit at 6–8 inches for the best eating quality, checking plants daily during peak production since zucchini left on the plant quickly grows oversized and tough.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Squash Production

name: Green Magic Broccoli
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplant date; in zone 9 start in August and transplant September–October for fall broccoli harvest November–January. Green Magic is an F1 hybrid with excellent downy mildew resistance — important in zone 9's humid fall conditions. After cutting the central head, side shoots continue producing small florets for weeks. In zone 9 fall-planted broccoli produces much higher quality heads than spring plantings that must mature in warming spring weather.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Green Magic is an F1 hybrid broccoli producing well-domed, tightly beaded, medium-green central heads with excellent side-shoot production after the main head is harvested — extending the productive harvest period significantly beyond varieties that produce only a central head. The hybrid vigor produces uniformly sized plants and large, dense heads that reach harvest size in 60–70 days from transplant. Broccoli flavor is at its absolute best when grown to maturity in cool weather — the combination of cool nights (below 50°F) and cool days in fall and winter concentrates the sulfur-containing compounds responsible for broccoli's characteristic flavor while reducing the bitterness that heat stress introduces. Green Magic's F1 hybrid status provides disease resistance and uniformity that open-pollinated varieties often lack, making it one of the most reliable fall broccoli varieties for humid Gulf South conditions.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Green Magic Broccoli F1
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Broccoli Production for Gulf South
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cool-Season Broccoli for Florida

name: Green Malabar Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed when soil is thoroughly warm; in zone 9 plant April–June. Green Malabar Spinach produces entirely green stems and foliage, lacking the ornamental purple-red stem color of the red form but otherwise identical in culture and culinary use. Provide a trellis, fence, or string support — the vines reach 6–10 feet in a full season. Harvest regularly by cutting stem tips 4–6 inches long to stimulate branching; regular harvesting keeps production high throughout the season. Soak seeds overnight before planting to improve germination, which can be slow and irregular.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil; Green Malabar Spinach is the all-green form of Basella alba, producing the same climbing vine, thick succulent leaves, and heat-tolerant growth habit as the red-stemmed form but with completely green stems, petioles, and developing berries. The green form is less ornamental than the red-stemmed type but produces the same culinary product — thick, glossy, succulent leaves with a mild, slightly mucilaginous flavor that makes an excellent heat-season substitute for true spinach (Spinacia oleracea) during zone 9's summers when cool-season spinach is impossible to grow. The green form's less distinctive appearance makes it blend more naturally into vegetable garden beds without the ornamental statement of the red-stemmed variety — a practical choice for gardeners who want the culinary benefit without the color drama. The slight mucilage in the leaves and stems — the same compound that gives okra its characteristic texture — naturally thickens soups, stews, and green smoothies and contributes a smooth, slightly viscous mouthfeel to cooked preparations. In zone 9's summer heat and humidity, Malabar spinach (both forms) is one of the most productive leafy green crops available.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Malabar Spinach for Florida Gardens
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Heat-Tolerant Greens for Gulf South
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Warm-Season Leafy Vegetables

name: Green Meat Radish
plantingNote: Sow in early spring or, for the best size and flavor, as a late-summer crop timed to mature in cool fall weather, similar to daikon.
directions: Direct sow about half an inch deep in loose, well-worked soil, thinning seedlings to 4-6 inches apart; because the roots grow larger than a typical spring radish, deep, stone-free soil helps them develop a smooth, well-formed shape. Green Meat is prized in Chinese cuisine for its bright green skin and vivid green-and-white interior flesh, a striking contrast to the familiar red-skinned, white-fleshed Western radishes. It has a milder, sweeter flavor than most spring radishes and holds its crisp texture well, making it good raw in salads or lightly cooked. For the best size and flavor it is often grown as a late-summer to fall crop like daikon, though early spring sowing also works.

name: Green Mountain Celtuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or sow in late summer about 50 days before first fall frost for a fall crop.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep directly in the garden or start in trays for later transplant; Green Mountain produces an especially large, jumbo central stalk that stays crisp and juicy, with a flavor many compare to cucumber crossed with sweet corn. Keep soil consistently moist and harvest once the stalk has swollen to an inch or more across but before the plant bolts, since heat and flowering quickly turn the stem pithy and bitter. Peel the tough outer skin before eating the stalk raw in salads, stir-fried, or shredded as a pasta substitute; young outer leaves are edible too.

name: Green Mountain Multiplier Onion
plantingNote: Plant small saved bulbs in fall for the largest harvest the following summer in mild-winter regions, or in very early spring as soon as soil is workable where winters are severe.
directions: Green Mountain Multiplier is a modern potato-onion selection developed around the year 2000 by Utah onion breeder Kelly Winterton from a chance flowering and seedling generation of the heirloom Yellow Potato Onion. It was selected and named for producing notably larger bulbs than most multiplier onions, approaching the size of a regular storage onion while keeping the multiplying, cluster-forming habit that defines potato onions. Set small bulbs about two inches deep with the tip near the soil surface; each one divides underground into a cluster of new bulbs by midsummer. Harvest once the tops die back, saving the largest bulbs to replant for next year's crop; true seed is also increasingly offered by specialty growers for gardeners who want to breed their own strains or refresh stock without carrying over soil-borne disease.

name: Green Noodle Yardlong Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is reliably above 70 degrees F, 1-3 weeks after last frost; provide a sturdy 6-8 foot trellis before vines take off, since Green Noodle climbs vigorously in summer heat.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep at the base of a tall trellis once the soil is warm, since yardlong beans germinate poorly and grow slowly in cool soil compared to bush snap beans. Green Noodle produces the classic slender, pale to medium-green pods of 18-24 inches typical of the yardlong bean group, and unlike red-podded forms it keeps its color through cooking, making it a versatile stand-in for standard green beans in stir-fries and braises. The vines thrive in the hottest, most humid part of summer when many Phaseolus beans stop setting pods, so plan for continuous harvest from midsummer through early fall in the Gulf South. Pick pods while still slender and before the seeds inside swell noticeably, since older pods turn fibrous quickly; frequent picking also keeps the vines producing new flowers.

name: Green Nutmeg Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil has warmed past 65°F; this heirloom needs a full warm season to ripen and benefits from black plastic mulch or row cover in cooler climates to speed early growth.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in enriched, well-drained hills spaced a yard apart, keeping soil evenly moist until vines establish and then easing off water as fruit ripens to concentrate sugars. Green Nutmeg is a 19th-century American heirloom muskmelon named for its ribbed, netted rind, which resembles the wrinkled shell of a nutmeg seed and sets it apart from smoother-skinned melon types of the same era. The pale green flesh is notably sweet and aromatic for an old variety, ripening to a musky perfume that signals harvest readiness alongside the classic full slip from the vine. It is a good choice for gardeners wanting an old American melon type distinct from the many French and Charentais heirlooms already common in seed catalogs.

name: Green Sausage Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Green Sausage is an indeterminate vine that needs staking, and fruit is picked ripe when it turns yellow-green rather than waiting for red color.
directions: Green Sausage is an open-pollinated paste tomato bred by Wild Boar Farms, producing elongated, sausage-shaped fruit striped in yellow-green over a base of deeper green that ripens to a translucent chartreuse-yellow rather than red. The firm, meaty flesh with a bright, tangy flavor holds up well when sliced fresh, fried green, or made into a distinctively colored salsa verde or sauce. Judge ripeness by softening and color shift toward gold-green rather than by looking for red, since this variety never turns the classic tomato red, and stake the indeterminate vine for season-long support.

name: Green Star Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to 70°F minimum; Green Star is a compact F1 hybrid okra variety with a shorter internode spacing (reduced distance between leaves and pod sets) than standard tall varieties, producing more pods per foot of plant height and remaining productive at 4–5 feet compared to standard varieties that can reach 8–10 feet. In zone 9, plant April through July for summer production. The compact plant habit of Green Star makes it easier to manage in home gardens and more efficient in raised-bed and small-garden situations where standard tall okra varieties would overgrow their space. Harvest pods at 3–4 inches — Green Star's pods stay tender at slightly larger sizes than some varieties due to its spineless, smooth pod texture. Regular harvesting (every 2–3 days at peak production) is essential to maintain pod quality and stimulate continued production.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches every 2–3 days. Green Star is an F1 hybrid okra variety selected for compact plant habit, high productivity per plant, and good pod quality — attributes that make it one of the more practical hybrid okra varieties for small-scale and home garden production in the Gulf South. The hybrid vigor of F1 varieties (first-generation crosses between distinct parental lines) typically produces improved uniformity, vigor, and productivity compared to open-pollinated varieties, and Green Star's compact growth habit — reaching 4–5 feet rather than the 6–10 feet of some tall heirloom types — makes it easier to harvest without a ladder and fits better in standard garden plots. The pods are dark green, slightly ridged in the standard okra style, spineless to low-spine (important for comfort in harvesting), and tender and good-flavored at the 3–4 inch harvest stage. Green Star's earliness — first harvest approximately 50–55 days from direct seeding — is competitive with the fastest-maturing okra varieties and allows harvest to begin before the peak of Gulf Coast summer heat. Okra is one of the most important and culturally significant vegetables in Gulf South cooking: a staple of gumbo (where it serves as a natural thickener via its mucilaginous properties), fried okra (a Southern culinary tradition), pickled okra, and fresh vegetable side dishes. Zone 9 is ideal for okra production — the combination of heat and humidity that limits most cool-season vegetables is precisely what okra requires to thrive.
sources: Harris Seeds — Green Star okra F1 hybrid commercial performance notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Compact okra variety comparison for home and market gardens
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Okra Variety Selection and Production for the Gulf South

name: Green Striped Cushaw
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm (70°F); Green Striped Cushaw is a Cucurbita argyrosperma type — the cushaw species — which has significantly better heat and humidity tolerance than the Cucurbita maxima and C. pepo species, making it one of the most reliable winter-type squash for hot-summer zone 9 and tropical climates. In zone 9, plant April–June for summer production; the heat tolerance allows Cushaw to thrive through Gulf Coast summers that stress or kill other squash species. Fruits develop over 90–110 days and can be harvested young (summer squash stage) or left to mature fully for storage. The large vines (15+ feet) require substantial space. Cushaw's heat tolerance is legendary in Gulf South gardening circles — this is the squash that produces reliably when standard varieties have died from the summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in hills 5–6 feet apart after soil is warm; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when skin pattern develops full color and stem begins to dry. Green Striped Cushaw is the classic variety of Cucurbita argyrosperma — the cushaw species native to Mexico and Central America — that has been grown in the American South for centuries as one of the most heat-tolerant large squash available. The 'cushaw' name is of Native American origin and has been applied to this distinctive squash type in the South since colonial times. The Green Striped Cushaw produces large fruits (10–20 lbs) with a distinctive form: a rounded to oblong base swelling to a thick, curved neck — quite different from the globular or flattened form of most Cucurbita maxima pumpkins. The skin is cream-white with longitudinal green stripes that fade to tan-green at full maturity. The flesh is cream-yellow to pale orange, mild and sweet, with less of the rich pumpkin flavor of darker-fleshed types but with an important practical advantage: it is the squash that can be grown in zone 9's summer heat when virtually all other squash species have died. Cucurbita argyrosperma's heat and humidity tolerance is substantially greater than C. maxima, C. pepo, or C. moschata, and in the historical Gulf South kitchen, cushaw was the standard large winter-storage squash precisely because it produced reliably in the climate where other species failed. Cushaw's mild flesh is used in pies (a Southern tradition), as a cooked vegetable, and in Mexican and Central American cuisines where the species originated.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Green Striped Cushaw Southern heirloom documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Cushaw squash Gulf South variety notes and heat tolerance
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Summer and Winter Squash Variety Selection for the Gulf South

name: Green Thai Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start December–January and transplant February–March. Green Thai Eggplant is exceptionally heat-tolerant and continues producing through zone 9 summer heat when other eggplant varieties slow. Multiple plantings (February and July) provide nearly year-round production in zone 9. Plants may survive mild winters in zone 9b as short-lived perennials and re-grow from the base.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with warm soil temperatures; Green Thai Eggplant produces small, round to oval, golf-ball-to-tennis-ball-sized fruits in bright green to greenish-white with striping or mottling, harvested young at marble to golf ball size for the best flavor and texture. The flesh is firmer, drier, and significantly more bitter than standard globe eggplant — the characteristic bitterness and firm texture are intentional qualities in Thai and Southeast Asian cooking, where the small green eggplants are sliced and added raw to green curry pastes or braised whole in red curry. They absorb coconut milk and spice sauces without becoming mushy, maintaining their distinctive firm bite even in extended cooking. Unlike the standard Italian or Japanese eggplants where bitterness is considered a defect, the natural bitterness of green Thai eggplant is a flavor feature that rounds and deepens the overall taste of Thai curries. In zone 9 the plants are extremely heat-tolerant and productive through the hottest months.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Asian Eggplant Varieties for Florida
Kitazawa Seed Company — Thai Eggplant Growing Notes
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Specialty Eggplant for Southeast Texas

name: Green Tomatillo
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; the standard green heirloom tomatillo produces medium to large (1.5–2 inch) green to yellow-green fruits in papery husks and is the backbone of Mexican salsa verde, enchiladas verdes, and countless other dishes — plant at least two plants for cross-pollination.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil; stake or cage plants as they sprawl. Green tomatillo is the standard culinary tomatillo of Mexican cuisine — not a green tomato but a distinct species (Physalis ixocarpa) with a characteristic papery husk that expands around the developing fruit; fruits are harvested when the husk splits and the fruit fills it completely, at a bright green to yellow-green stage with a tangy, tart, citrus-herbal flavor that is distinctly different from any tomato flavor. The tart flavor of the fresh tomatillo is the foundation of salsa verde, a primary sauce in Mexican cooking alongside salsa roja; tomatillos are also used in mole verde, enchiladas verdes, chile verde, and canned as salsa. Highly productive and heat-tolerant; does extremely well in Gulf Coast and Southwestern gardens. Two or more plants are needed for pollination — a single plant produces little to no fruit.

name: Green Velvet Okra
subcategory: classic smooth dark green heirloom okra
plantingNote: Direct sow 1-3 weeks after the last frost once the soil has warmed to at least 65F, since cold soil causes poor, uneven germination.
directions: Sow seed directly in the garden after all frost danger has passed, soaking it overnight to speed germination in warm soil. Pick pods every day or two once they begin forming, since Green Velvet quickly grows past its tender stage. This long-cultivated variety produces smooth, spineless, dark green pods on a vigorous, productive plant, and it has been a dependable garden staple for generations of Southern cooks who value its mild flavor in gumbo and frying. Its smooth pod surface also makes it easier to handle at harvest than spinier heirloom types.

name: Green Wave Mustard Green
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall crop. Green Wave is cold-tolerant to about 15°F when established, making it one of the most cold-hardy mustards for Gulf Coast winters.
directions: Sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 12–18 inches; Green Wave is an AAS winner mustard green producing large, beautifully ruffled, deep green leaves with a distinctive curled and frilled edge that gives it strong ornamental value as well as excellent eating quality. Flavor is pungent and spicy like Southern Giant Curled but with finer leaf texture and more cold-hardiness. Green Wave is the recommended mustard green for raw use in salads (young leaves) and sautés where texture is prized; the intricate ruffling and curling increases leaf surface area, creating both a decorative appearance in the garden and a textural interest on the plate. In zone 9, fall-planted Green Wave produces beautifully through winter, the cold sweetening and mellowing its characteristic spicy bite — the finest mustard green eating comes after temperatures drop below 40°F. Harvest outer leaves regularly; the plant regrows vigorously. An excellent substitute for kale or collards in anyone who wants a faster-maturing, more flavorful cooking green.
sources: All-America Selections — Green Wave Mustard AAS winner
LSU AgCenter — Mustard Green Production in Louisiana

name: Green Zebra Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; ripeness is tricky to judge by appearance — harvest when the skin softens slightly, shows yellow-green stripes against deeper green, and gives to gentle pressure.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to deeply prepared, fertile soil after all frost risk has passed; Green Zebra is a modern heirloom tomato developed by Tom Wagner in 1983, producing attractive 2–3 inch fruits with distinctive lime-green skin and dark green stripes that warm to yellow-green stripes against chartreuse skin when ripe, with a bright, tangy, acidic flesh that is a refreshing counterpoint to sweeter tomatoes. Excellent sliced fresh in salads, as a garnish, or for green salsa — one of the most visually striking tomatoes available. An indeterminate vine, it tends toward compact growth relative to larger beefsteak heirlooms. Yields prolifically over a long season.

name: Gregori's Altai Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; this early, cold-set variety can go into the ground as soon as night temperatures stay reliably above 50°F, giving a jump on the Gulf Coast spring crop before summer heat shuts down fruit set.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun once nights are reliably mild, staking the moderately vigorous indeterminate vine as it grows. Gregori's Altai is a Siberian heirloom from the Altai Mountains region prized for setting medium-large, four-inch, deep red fruit with a faint golden blush at the shoulders unusually early and even in the cool, fluctuating spring temperatures that stall most other beefsteaks. The rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor rivals much larger, later-maturing heirlooms, and the plant's tolerance for cool nights makes it an excellent first-wave spring tomato for Gulf Coast gardens that need to beat the arrival of intense summer heat. Keep watering even as fruit sizes up to avoid cracking on the thin, tender skin.

name: Gretel Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Gretel is the white-fruited companion variety to Hansel (purple), both from PanAmerican Seed and both AAS winners in consecutive years. Gretel produces clusters of 3–4 inch white eggplants on the same compact (20–24 inch) upright bush plant. In zone 9, start seeds January–February for March–April transplanting. Gretel's most important characteristic beyond its striking pure-white color is the complete absence of bitterness — white eggplants generally lack the anthocyanins and related phenolic compounds responsible for bitterness in purple eggplants, and Gretel has been bred for minimal astringency and very sweet, mild flavor. The flesh is tender and creamy-white with minimal seeds at proper harvest size (3–4 inches); left to overripen, the skin yellows and seeds increase. Unlike purple eggplants that can turn bitter when cut and exposed to air, Gretel's white flesh remains stable. Harvest before any yellowing appears on the skin.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at 3–4 inches while skin is pure white; yellowing indicates overripeness. Gretel Eggplant won the All-America Selections award in 2009, one year after its companion Hansel (purple mini eggplant), both from the same PanAmerican Seed breeding program and sharing the same compact plant habit, prolific cluster fruiting, early maturity, and exceptional eating quality. Gretel's white fruit color distinguishes it visually and culinarily from standard purple eggplants: the white coloration (caused by the absence of the anthocyanin and chlorogenic acid pigments present in purple eggplant skin) correlates with a fundamentally different flavor profile — white eggplants, including Gretel, are consistently sweeter, milder, and less bitter than purple varieties because they lack the phenolic compounds that contribute bitterness. This means white eggplant varieties like Gretel can be used raw in preparations where purple eggplant's bitterness would require salting to draw out (a traditional technique for reducing eggplant bitterness before cooking): Gretel's naturally sweet, mild flesh is pleasant raw in thin slices or cubed in salads. The AAS recognition of Gretel in consecutive years with Hansel highlighted the appeal of offering home gardeners a white-fruited alternative to the standard purple that combined the same outstanding productivity and compact habit with meaningfully different flavor characteristics. For zone 9 gardeners growing multiple eggplant varieties for culinary diversity, Gretel and Hansel planted together provide a visually striking paired harvest of white and purple mini eggplants from compact, easily managed plants.
sources: All-America Selections — Gretel eggplant 2009 AAS winner documentation
PanAmerican Seed — Gretel white mini eggplant variety development
Johnny's Selected Seeds — White eggplant variety comparison including Gretel

name: Grey Eyed Greasy Bean
plantingNote: This is a later-maturing greasy bean, so direct sow as soon as the soil is reliably warm to give the long vines a full season to produce.
directions: A rare Kentucky heirloom from the greasy bean tradition, this variety is named for the gray coloring that rings the eye of an otherwise white seed. Pods are smooth, shiny, and stringless, hanging from tall, heavy-yielding vines that need sturdy staking to support the crop. Being a later-maturing type, it rewards patience with rich, hearty flavor whether cooked fresh or dried for winter use. Because true greasy bean lines are uncommon outside Appalachian seed-saving networks, isolate plantings if you intend to save true seed.

name: Greyzini Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; thin to final spacing once seedlings have true leaves.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once danger of frost has passed. Greyzini produces straight, medium-green zucchini fruit lightly flecked and mottled with gray, a distinctive hybrid-vigor cross between green and golden zucchini types that earned it an All-America Selections award. The compact bush habit and early, heavy fruit set make it a dependable choice for small-space vegetable gardens, and fruit stays firm and non-seedy if picked at 6-8 inches. Harvest every day or two during peak season to keep plants productive.

name: Griselet Charentais Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost; Griselet is a modern hybrid bred to recreate the heirloom Petit Gris de Rennes with improved disease resistance.
directions: Griselet is a Charentais hybrid bred as a disease-resistant counterpart to the French heirloom Petit Gris de Rennes, reproducing its old-fashioned appearance and flavor on vigorous, healthier vines. The fruit has a distinctive greenish-yellow rind marked with green sutures and an intoxicating perfume as it ripens. Inside, the flesh is succulent, sweet, and creamy, with a flavor many describe as touched with exotic spice notes beyond typical Charentais sweetness. Harvest by cutting from the vine once the skin yellows and the rind gives slightly under gentle pressure, and grow in full sun with warm, fertile, well-drained soil for the best flavor concentration.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Griselet (F1) Charentais Melon Seed

name: Griselle Shallot
plantingNote: Plant small bulbs four to eight weeks before the last frost in spring; Griselle, the true French grey shallot, is grown from bulb divisions rather than seed and does not store as long as red or Dutch yellow shallot types.
directions: Plant individual bulbs about an inch deep and four to six inches apart in loose, well-drained soil, and each will multiply into a cluster of several new bulbs by midsummer. Griselle is regarded by French cooks as the only true shallot, a distinct species from common onion-derived shallots, forming small, teardrop-shaped bulbs under a papery grey-brown skin around pinkish flesh with fine purple veining and an intensely complex, refined flavor prized raw in vinaigrettes and salads. Reduce watering once the tops yellow and topple over, then lift the cluster and cure it in a warm, airy, shaded spot for one to two weeks. Because Griselle does not keep as long as red or Dutch yellow shallots, plan to use the harvest within a few months or replant a portion of the smaller bulbs the following season.

name: Groninger Blue Kale
plantingNote: Sow in mid to late summer, 10-14 weeks before the first fall frost, for a fall and winter harvest after cold sweetens the leaves.
directions: Direct sow in mid-summer and thin to wide final spacing so plants can develop their large, sprawling frames before winter sets in. This traditional Dutch farmhouse kale, long grown around the province of Groningen, produces finely divided, feathery blue-green leaves on tall stems and was historically a winter storage vegetable harvested straight from the frozen garden. Repeated frost exposure noticeably mellows its flavor, and the plant continues producing new leaves from the top through much of the winter.

name: Gros Vert de Laon Artichoke
scientificName: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Gros Vert de Laon'
plantingNote: Transplant after last frost into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this hardy old French cultivar, sometimes called 'cat head' for its rounded shape, produces very large heads on a vigorous, architectural plant.
directions: Gros Vert de Laon is a hardy French heirloom grown for its very large, rounded, tightly scaled green heads with fleshy, delicately flavored bracts, produced on a bold, silvery-leaved plant substantial enough to anchor a bed on its own. It is somewhat more cold-tolerant than many Mediterranean artichoke cultivars, a legacy of its long cultivation in the cooler climate of northern France. Cut the terminal bud while still firm and tightly closed for the best eating quality, which encourages the plant to push out smaller side buds afterward. Divide and replant offsets every three to four years to keep clumps vigorous and productive.

name: Grosse Blonde Paresseuse Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool, fertile soil in early spring; Grosse Blonde Paresseuse, French for 'big blonde lazy one,' is named for its unhurried, slow-bolting habit rather than any difficulty to grow.
directions: Grosse Blonde Paresseuse, literally 'big blonde lazy one,' is an old French butterhead heirloom named for its unhurried, slow-bolting habit rather than any trouble to grow. Direct sow in cool, fertile soil in early spring, thinning plants to 10 to 12 inches so the large, pale-green, loosely folded heads have room to form their soft, buttery hearts. It tends to stand in good garden condition longer than many butterheads before turning bitter or running to seed, making it a forgiving choice for gardeners who cannot harvest the moment a head matures. Cut whole heads once the center feels full, or harvest outer leaves through the season.

name: Grote Noordhollandse Mâche
plantingNote: Direct-sow in early fall for a hardy overwintering crop, or in very early spring as soon as soil is workable; this large-leaved Dutch heirloom tolerates light shade and short days better than most salad greens.
directions: This classic Dutch heirloom mâche produces notably larger, rounder rosettes of spoon-shaped leaves than standard corn salad, giving a bigger harvest per plant while keeping the same mild, nutty, slightly sweet flavor. Sow thickly in cool, moist, fertile soil in fall for overwintering under light mulch or a cold frame in colder zones, or in earliest spring; it grows well in the dappled shade of taller crops or deciduous trees, making it a useful filler for partially shaded beds during the short days of fall and early spring when little else will thrive. Keep soil consistently moist, since mâche bolts and turns bitter quickly in dry or hot conditions. Harvest whole rosettes or individual outer leaves once plants reach a usable size, and succession-sow every few weeks through the cool season for a continuous supply.

name: Grumolo Verde Chicory
plantingNote: Sow in midsummer (July in most climates) for a spring harvest; the plants survive winter and produce their distinctive rosette heads in early spring from the overwintered root. In zone 9, sow September–October for harvest in January–March.
directions: Sow seeds in late summer and allow plants to grow through autumn; after hard frosts, the tops die back and the plant enters semi-dormancy before the root drives up a tight, flat rosette of dark green leaves in late winter or early spring — a delicacy treasured in northern Italy as a salad green when little else is available. The name 'grumolo' means 'little cluster' in Italian, describing the compressed button-rosette form. Grumolo verde is exceptionally cold-hardy and virtually maintenance-free through winter. The bitter, nutty flavor is characteristic of chicory; young spring leaves are the most tender and least bitter. In warm-winter climates like zones 8–9, the plants may not go fully dormant but still produce acceptable rosettes in winter.
sources: Italian seed heritage sources (Sezione Ortiva Italiana)

name: Gruner Golden Purslane
plantingNote: Direct sow thickly in warm soil (70F+) in well-drained soil in full sun; Gruner is a named golden purslane cultivar with green leaves and a more upright habit than other golden purslane selections.
directions: Gruner is a named cultivar of golden purslane with green rather than golden-yellow leaves and a more upright habit than other golden purslane selections, grown alongside the large, golden-leaved 'Goldberg' as one of the two most commonly named culinary purslane cultivars. Scatter seed on warm, bare soil and press in lightly, since seed needs some light to germinate; thin to 4-6 inches or harvest as a cut-and-come-again crop. Its more upright growth habit makes it easier to harvest by hand than sprawling purslane types, while it retains the same heat tolerance, drought tolerance, and high omega-3 content that make golden purslane an outstanding summer salad green.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Summer Vegetables

name: Guajillo Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; a widely used dried Mexican chile that requires a long warm season — ideal for zone 8–11 where it can produce two harvests in warm years.
directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost, harden transplants thoroughly, and plant into warm, well-drained, moderately fertile soil after all frost risk has passed. Guajillo is one of the most commonly used dried chiles in traditional Mexican cooking, the dried form of the Mirasol pepper, producing long (3–5 inch), tapered, shiny red fruits with smooth, thin skin that dries to a deep red-brown; heat is mild to medium (2,500–5,000 SHU). The distinctive sweet, tangy, slightly fruity flavor with mild heat makes guajillo an indispensable base for authentic red enchilada sauce, pozole rojo, and adobo marinades. Harvest fully red and dry slowly on the plant or by hanging in a warm, ventilated space; dried guajillos store for 6–12 months.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Guardsman Bunching Onion
plantingNote: Sow in mid- to late summer for overwintering and an early spring harvest, or sow in early spring for a summer crop; mulch overwintered plantings in the coldest zones.
directions: Guardsman resulted from breeding between bunching and bulb onion types, combining a vigorous root system and thicker, milder shank with the non-bulbing habit of a scallion. It was bred specifically to survive cold winters when sown in late summer, resuming growth early the following spring ahead of most other bunching cultivars. The larger tops and root vigor also make it a strong performer for a standard spring or summer sowing. Because it is milder than many bunching onions, it suits fresh eating as well as light cooking, and clumps can be divided to extend a planting.
sources: J.W. Jung Seed Company catalog description

name: Guatemalan Blue Banana Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills once soil has warmed after last frost; give vines a lot of open ground or a sturdy trellis since fruits can run two feet or more.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep after the soil has thoroughly warmed, since this Guatemalan heirloom needs a long, hot growing season to fill out its elongated, club-shaped fruit. Vines are vigorous and sprawling, so allow generous room or train them up a strong trellis to keep the two-to-three-foot fruits off wet ground. The thin, slate-blue to gray-blue rind hides deep orange, dense, sweet flesh that is excellent baked, and well-cured fruit stores for months in a cool, dry spot. Cure harvested squash in a warm location for one to two weeks before moving to long-term storage to firm the rind and concentrate sweetness.

name: Guelph Millennium Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant 1-year-old crowns 6–8 inches deep in a prepared trench in early spring; Guelph Millennium breaks dormancy a bit later than older varieties, which helps it dodge late spring frosts, and it establishes an unusually dense, productive root system over its first two non-harvest years.
directions: Plant crowns 6–8 inches deep in a prepared, well-drained trench in full sun, and resist harvesting at all during the first year to let the fern grow and build root reserves. Guelph Millennium is an all-male hybrid developed at the University of Guelph in Ontario and has become the standard replacement for the older Jersey series across much of North America, valued for exceptionally high, concentrated spear yield, uniform smooth green spears with tight tips, and a root system that establishes unusually quickly for a full-sized harvest by year three. Its later spring emergence than most varieties is an advantage in regions with unpredictable late frosts, since fewer emerging spears are lost to cold snaps. Harvest lightly in year two, moderately in year three, and the full six-to-eight-week season from year four onward, snapping or cutting spears at soil level once they reach 6–8 inches.
sources: University of Guelph — Vineland Research and Innovation Centre asparagus breeding program

name: Guernsey Parsnip
plantingNote: Sow directly as early as the ground can be worked, using fresh seed since parsnip germination declines quickly with seed age.
directions: An old Channel Islands and northern French heirloom parsnip valued for its shorter, broad-shouldered roots, a useful trait in shallow or stony soils where long-rooted parsnip types tend to fork or stall. Sow directly as early as the ground can be worked, using fresh seed since parsnip germination declines quickly with seed age. The dense white flesh has the classic sweet, nutty parsnip character and improves further after exposure to autumn frost, making it best left in the ground and dug through fall and early winter.

name: Gulf Annual Ryegrass
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall into well-drained soil in full sun; Gulf is a Gulf Coast-bred annual ryegrass cultivar selected for rapid germination and vigorous establishment, commonly overseeded on dormant warm-season lawns and pastures across the Deep South.
directions: Broadcast seed onto well-drained, average soil in full sun in fall, raking lightly to ensure good seed-to-soil contact. Gulf is a fast-germinating, vigorous annual ryegrass cultivar developed for the humid, mild-winter conditions of the Deep South and Gulf Coast, where it is widely used to overseed dormant bermudagrass and bahiagrass lawns and pastures for winter green cover, as well as as a general-purpose erosion-control and biomass cover crop on bare fall ground. Its fibrous, shallow root system germinates and establishes faster than most other cool-season cover crops, quickly stabilizing loose or eroding soil and suppressing winter weeds, then dies back naturally with warming spring temperatures or can be mowed and turned under to add organic matter ahead of spring planting. It tolerates close, repeated mowing better than cereal grains, making it a good choice where winter foot traffic or turf appearance matters.

name: Guntur Chilli
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Guntur Chilli needs a long, hot summer to fully redden and dry its pungent pods for storage.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Guntur Chilli is a landrace grown for generations in the Guntur and Prakasam districts of Andhra Pradesh, India, where the Guntur Sannam (S4) type has earned Geographical Indication status and become one of the most heavily traded chili types in the world. Plants bear slender, crimson, thick-skinned pods 2–5 inches long with fierce, wine-red pungency, typically cited in the 35,000–75,000 Scoville range depending on strain and growing conditions. Grown almost exclusively as a drying chile, pods are left to fully redden on the plant, then sun-dried and ground into the vivid, pungent chili powder that underlies much of South Indian cooking. A heavy-yielding, heat-loving plant well suited to long, hot growing seasons.
sources: Geographical Indications Registry of India — Guntur Chilli GI documentation
ICAR–Indian Institute of Spices Research — Guntur Chilli variety notes

name: Gypsy Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for spring, or in midsummer for fall; Gypsy is bred to tolerate the heat and stress of summer plantings better than most broccoli, so it fills the gap between spring and fall crops.
directions: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before setting out transplants into rich, evenly moist soil. Gypsy is a widely grown hybrid selected for adaptability across a broad sowing window, holding quality through the heat and inconsistent weather of a summer planting better than many broccoli varieties, which makes it a dependable choice for closing the gap between an early spring crop and a fall one. It forms medium-large, tightly beaded blue-green heads and continues producing a generous flush of side shoots after the main head is harvested. Cut the central head while the buds are firm and tightly closed, then keep picking side shoots as they reach the same stage.

name: Gypsy Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Gypsy's earlier maturity (60–70 days) compared to bell peppers (70–80 days) gives zone 9 gardeners an earlier start on sweet pepper harvest.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Gypsy is an All-America Selections winner (1981) — a sweet, elongated, tapering pepper that produces medium-sized (4 inches long, 2.5 inches wide), semi-thick-walled fruits that ripen through a distinctive color progression from pale creamy-yellow, through orange, to bright red, with excellent flavor at every stage. The early maturity (60–70 days) gives Gypsy a head start on the sweet pepper season compared to larger bell types, and the disease resistance package includes tobacco mosaic virus tolerance — a significant advantage. Gypsy is a semi-sweet, elongated type rather than a classic blocky bell — closer to an Italian frying pepper shape but with thicker walls and a sweeter, less pungent flavor than traditional frying types. The elongated fruits are outstanding for fresh eating, stuffing (the tapering shape holds stuffings differently than blocks), grilling, and roasting. The color progression from pale yellow through orange to red creates an attractive multi-colored harvest display when fruits at different maturity stages are present on the plant simultaneously. Plants are productive, compact, and well-suited to both spring and fall production in zone 9. An outstanding early-maturing sweet pepper for home garden use.

name: Ha'Ogen Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is reliably above 65°F, or start indoors 3–4 weeks earlier in peat pots for a head start; Ha'Ogen thrives in the long, hot Gulf South summer but needs steady moisture through fruit set. In zone 9, plant March–April for a June–July harvest and consider a fall crop in late July for October picking.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after danger of frost has passed, thinning to the strongest 2 plants per hill once true leaves appear. Keep soil evenly moist during flowering and fruit set, then taper watering in the final week to concentrate sugars, and harvest when the melon slips easily from the vine with a full, sweet aroma at the blossom end. Ha'Ogen is a kibbutz-bred Israeli heirloom named for Kibbutz HaOgen, prized for its compact 2–3 lb round fruit with lightly netted, gold-green rind that streaks orange as it ripens, enclosing pale green flesh with an intensely sweet, spicy-floral flavor reminiscent of Charentais melons. Because it slips clean from the vine at peak ripeness rather than holding firm like shipping cantaloupes, it is best suited to home gardens and farmers markets rather than long-distance transport. Vigorous, disease-tolerant vines produce heavily over a relatively short window, so successive plantings extend the harvest.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Ha'Ogen melon variety notes
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — melon variety descriptions
University of California Cooperative Extension — Specialty Melon Production Guide

name: Habanada Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors under lights 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since habanero-type peppers are slow to germinate and establish; Habanada carries the full fruity, floral habanero aroma and flavor entirely without heat.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed. Habanada was bred at Cornell University and further developed by Row 7 Seed Company by selecting for the characteristic fruity, floral, tropical habanero flavor and aroma while breeding out the capsaicin that gives habaneros their intense heat, resulting in a pepper that tastes like a habanero but can be eaten fresh in quantity without any burn. Small, lantern-shaped fruits ripen from green to a bright golden-orange, and the plant is productive over a long season much like a standard habanero. It is excellent fresh in salsas, salads, and sauces where habanero flavor is wanted without the heat. Harvest at the fully ripe orange stage for the strongest flavor, and expect steady production through summer into fall.

name: Hackensack Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after the soil has thoroughly warmed past last frost; Hackensack is a large-vined 19th-century Northeastern heirloom muskmelon that needs a full warm season and generous room to sprawl to size up its heavily netted fruit.
directions: Sow several seeds per hill an inch deep in well-amended soil once the ground has warmed, thinning to the strongest two plants and giving the sprawling vines several feet of room in each direction. Hackensack is an old American heirloom muskmelon named for the New Jersey town where it was popularized in the late 1800s, prized in home gardens of the era for its large, round, deeply ribbed and heavily netted fruit and its thick, sweet green flesh. Keep soil evenly moist through vining and fruit set, then let it dry out slightly as melons near maturity to concentrate sugars. Judge ripeness by a shift to full slip, where the fruit separates cleanly from the vine with light pressure, along with a strong musky aroma at the blossom end.

name: Hainan Yellow Lantern Chili
plantingNote: Start indoors on a heat mat; this chinense type needs warm soil and a long season to size up its lantern-shaped pods.
directions: Native to Hainan Island in southern China, this habanero-type chinense ripens to a bright yellow, lantern-shaped pod carrying roughly 300,000 Scoville heat units, squarely in habanero-to-superhot territory, well beyond the typical jalapeno or Thai chile grown in most home gardens. Its sharp, fruity heat is traditionally fermented with salt and garlic into the distinctive yellow lantern chili sauce popular along the Hainan coast. Start seed indoors on a heat mat, since chinense types are slow to germinate, and give plants a long, warm growing season in full sun to fully ripen the thick-walled pods. Harvest continually through summer and fall for fresh use or fermenting, wearing gloves to handle the ripe fruit.
sources: Wikipedia - Hainan yellow lantern chili (horticultural and culinary background)
Patrick's Pepper Patch - Hainan Yellow Lantern seeds
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Hakurei Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring crop; in zone 9 the ideal window is January–February for spring and September–November for fall, when mild temperatures produce the sweetest roots. Fall crops are typically superior in taste and texture.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in well-prepared, loosened soil and thin to 3–4 inches apart; crowding produces forked or stunted roots. Hakurei is a Japanese F1 hybrid turnip bred to be eaten raw: the pure-white, smooth globe roots (2–3 inches in diameter at harvest) are remarkably sweet, mild, and almost fruity — nothing like the sharp, peppery flavor of conventional turnip varieties. Unlike storage turnips, Hakurei is best harvested small and young; roots toughen and lose their fresh crispness if left past 2 inches. The greens are also tender and mild and excellent raw or lightly sautéed. In zone 9, fall-sown Hakurei seeded in October is often the finest salad turnip in the cool-season garden, maturing just before the holidays. A favorite for farmers' market growers because of its eye-catching appearance and reliably sweet flavor.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Hakurei F1 variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cool Season Vegetables

name: Hale's Best Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm (70°F); in zone 9, plant April–May. Melons need full sun, warm soil, and consistent moisture from transplant through fruit development. Hale's Best develops fruits 5–7 inches in diameter on trailing vines 4–6 feet long. Detect harvest maturity by smell (strong sweet melon aroma from the blossom end), the fruit slipping slightly from the vine, and the underlying skin color shifting from white-green to creamy yellow. In the Gulf South, mildew can affect melon foliage by late summer; early planting for a June harvest before peak humidity helps maintain plant health. In zone 9's hot, dry springs (before the summer humidity builds), melons are ideally suited — the combination of heat and adequate moisture produces the sugar development that distinguishes a good cantaloupe from a bland one.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills 3–4 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when slip from vine and fragrant. Hale's Best is the quintessential American heirloom cantaloupe — a variety that defined the flavor standard of what a good cantaloupe should taste like for generations of American home gardeners and market growers. The variety was developed in the early 20th century by Paul Halladay of Turlock, California, from melon seed brought from Japan, and selected specifically for shipping quality, flavor, and thick, deeply netted skin. The resulting variety — medium to large, round to slightly oval, covered in a thick network of raised tan netting over a gray-green background, with a heavily perfumed blossom end and deeply orange, very sweet flesh — became so widely grown in California's San Joaquin Valley melon production region that 'Hale's Best' essentially defined the commercial cantaloupe market in mid-20th-century America. The flesh is thick, dense, and intensely orange — higher in beta-carotene than pale-fleshed cantaloupe varieties — with genuine sweetness and the rich, complex melon aroma that distinguishes a truly good cantaloupe from a bland one. The Brix (sugar content) of properly grown, vine-ripened Hale's Best in warm conditions can reach 14–16, producing sweetness comparable to the best modern hybrid melons. Several numbered strains of Hale's Best were selected for regional performance: Hale's Best #36 and Hale's Best Jumbo are among the subvarieties that have remained in commerce through heirloom seed preservation.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Hale's Best cantaloupe California heirloom documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Hale's Best cantaloupe variety history and notes
University of California Cooperative Extension — Historical California melon variety production

name: Hale's Best Jumbo Melon
scientificName: Cucumis melo var. reticulatus 'Hale's Best Jumbo'
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed past 70F, or start indoors in peat pots 2-3 weeks ahead in short-season climates; thin to 2 plants per hill.
directions: Hale's Best Jumbo is an early twentieth-century open-pollinated cantaloupe selected in California that became the historic benchmark 'full-slip' muskmelon other western shipping types and later hybrids were measured against. Vigorous, sprawling vines set oval, heavily netted fruit with firm, deep-orange flesh and the classic sweet, musky cantaloupe fragrance that peaks as the fruit ripens. It was long favored by home gardeners and small growers for dependable yields and rich flavor before more disease-resistant hybrids took over commercial production. Reduce watering in the week before harvest to concentrate sugars, and pick as soon as the stem separates cleanly from the vine under gentle pressure.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Melon Variety History

name: Halona Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; plant 4–5 seeds per hill 1 inch deep, thin to 2 strongest plants when 3 inches tall. In zone 9 plant March–April for summer harvest; Halona's short season (73–80 days) makes it one of the better choices for zone 9's limited spring melon window before extreme summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; Halona is a 2015 All-America Selections Gold Medal winner cantaloupe — one of the most highly awarded AAS winners in recent years — developed for exceptional eating quality combined with early maturation and disease resistance. Halona produces medium-sized (4–5 pound), deeply netted, tan-skinned fruits with dense, deep orange flesh and exceptional sweetness (Brix 14–17°, very high for an open-pollinated type) with complex, honey-like flavor that compares to the finest specialty melons. The fruit set is consistent and the plants show resistance to powdery mildew — a significant disease in humid climates. Halona's early maturation (73–80 days) and compact vine habit make it suitable for small gardens and shorter growing seasons; two plants produce more than enough for a family. The small seed cavity and thick, firm flesh give excellent eating quality with no watery texture. Halona is the recommended first melon for new growers due to its reliable production, disease resistance, and superior flavor — and one of the best choices for zone 9 spring production where a short fruiting window requires a reliable early variety.
sources: All-America Selections — Halona cantaloupe AAS Gold Medal winner 2015
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Halona variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cantaloupe Production Guide

name: Hami Melon
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 2-3 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil after all frost danger has passed. Hami needs a long, hot growing season to develop full sweetness.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Hami melon is a famous Chinese melon from the Xinjiang region, producing oval fruit with crisp, aromatic orange-white flesh that is prized more for its satisfying crunch and sweetness than for strong aroma. It needs a long, hot growing season, 85-100 days, to fully develop its characteristic sugar content, making it best suited to regions with reliably hot, dry summers. Harvest when the fruit develops a full aroma and the skin color deepens, then eat fresh chilled as is traditional.

name: Hannah Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F; Hannah is a white-fleshed sweet potato that produces in approximately 90–100 days and is harvested before the first fall frost. In zone 9, set slips in late March through April for a July–September harvest; mulch beds to conserve moisture and suppress weeds through the hot summer growing period.
directions: Plant rooted slips after last frost when soil is above 65°F, setting each slip 3–4 inches deep with the crown at or just above soil level; Hannah is a white-fleshed, cream-to-tan skinned sweet potato developed by North Carolina State University that has become one of the most popular white-fleshed varieties in US production — offering a substantially different culinary experience than the familiar orange-fleshed types. The flesh is cream to pale ivory, firm, and notably dry (less moist than orange varieties), with a mild, subtly sweet flavor that reads more like a russet potato than a typical sweet potato — making Hannah uniquely versatile for preparations like roasted potato dishes, gratins, soups, and anywhere a firm, dry-textured potato is preferred. The dry, non-gummy texture means it mashes cleanly, holds together in casseroles, and is excellent when baked whole with a crisp skin. Hannah produces smooth-skinned, uniform tubers in a standard 90–100 day window and yields reliably in Southern and Gulf Coast production areas. For gardeners familiar only with orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, Hannah represents a practical bridge variety that can replace russet potatoes in the garden while still being a true sweet potato culturally and agronomically.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Sweet Potato Variety Handbook
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Potato Varieties
National Sweet Potato Collaborators Group variety evaluations

name: Hannibal Leek
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings into holes about 6 inches deep, spaced roughly 6 inches apart; can also be sown thinly outdoors in early spring and transplanted later.
directions: Hannibal is a reliable, heavy-cropping leek that matures early and heavily, producing long, thick white shafts under dark green leaves from midsummer well into fall. It can be grown at closer spacing and pulled young as an excellent baby leek, or left to size up for a standard harvest. With soil mounded around the base and a layer of mulch, Hannibal tolerates cold well and can overwinter in the ground for a late harvest in mild climates.

name: Hanover Salad Green
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall as temperatures moderate, or in very early spring, and thin seedlings to stand a few inches apart for continuous cut-and-come-again harvest of the smooth, rounded, non-bolting leaves.
directions: Direct sow in fall as temperatures moderate, or in very early spring, and thin seedlings to stand a few inches apart for continuous cut-and-come-again harvest of the smooth, rounded, non-bolting leaves. Hanover Salad is a colonial-era Southern heirloom green in the same species as rutabaga, prized historically in Virginia and Gulf South gardens for its mild, cabbage-like flavor eaten raw as salad greens when young or cooked like collards once mature. It tolerates both cold snaps and the on-and-off warmth of a Gulf Coast fall and winter better than many mustards, holding quality in the garden for extended picking rather than bolting at the first warm spell.

name: Hansel Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Hansel is a compact eggplant variety producing prolific clusters of slender, 3–4 inch long deep purple eggplants on an upright, bushy plant reaching 20–24 inches. In zone 9, start seeds January–February for March–April transplanting. Hansel was an All-America Selections winner in 2008, recognized for its extraordinary productivity, early maturity (55–60 days from transplant — faster than most large eggplant varieties), compact habit suitable for container growing, and excellent eating quality: the slender fruits are tender-skinned with virtually no bitterness, very few seeds, and flesh that stays white and creamy without the sponginess or discoloration that can affect larger eggplant varieties. The cluster fruiting habit — multiple fruits set in groups at each branch node rather than singly — contributes to the spectacular production that made Hansel notable in AAS trials. Harvest at 3–4 inches for best texture; fruits become slightly seedy and tough-skinned if left much longer.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at 3–4 inches when skin is glossy deep purple. Hansel Eggplant was developed by PanAmerican Seed and won the All-America Selections award in 2008, one of a pair of complementary mini eggplant varieties (Hansel purple, Gretel white) from the same breeding program that were recognized in consecutive years for their outstanding performance in AAS trials. The Hansel and Gretel naming reflects the paired nature of the complementary varieties and their petite, fairy-tale proportions compared to standard full-sized eggplants. Hansel's outstanding AAS trial performance was attributed to several factors that distinguish it from both standard large eggplant varieties and other small-fruited eggplants: the combination of extremely early production (55–60 days from transplant, compared to 70–80+ days for large varieties), prolific cluster fruiting (multiple fruits per node vs. one to two for standard types), compact plant size (20–24 inches, easily managed in containers), and excellent eating quality (tender skin with no bitterness, minimal seed content, clean white flesh) created a variety with compelling advantages in every direction. For zone 9 gardeners, Hansel's short days-to-maturity is particularly valuable: zone 9 eggplant production spans March–October, but the most productive and high-quality harvest period is before the peak summer heat (June–July); Hansel's early maturity allows significant harvest before conditions become stressful.
sources: All-America Selections — Hansel eggplant 2008 AAS winner documentation
PanAmerican Seed — Hansel eggplant mini purple variety development
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Eggplant Variety Recommendations for Gulf South

name: Hanson Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow shallowly in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; this large old crisphead needs a bit more room than compact lettuces.
directions: According to family tradition, this lettuce was grown for generations by a Maryland farm family before a Philadelphia seed house introduced it commercially around 1870. It forms a large, light green head of curly, fringed leaves around a crisp white heart, giving it the crunch of a crisphead with more cold tolerance and less fuss than modern iceberg types. A classic nineteenth-century French gardening reference even illustrated and described the variety, evidence of how far its reputation traveled. Its large old-fashioned heads are well suited to slicing for sandwiches, and it holds in the garden respectably before bolting.
sources: William Woys Weaver - Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

name: Haogen Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Haogen is a celebrated Israeli melon developed at Kibbutz Ein HaMifratz, prized for its extraordinarily sweet, aromatic flesh of exceptional quality — considered by melon enthusiasts and chefs to be among the finest-flavored melons in the world, the Israeli equivalent of the French Charentais for concentrated sweetness and intense melon aroma.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in well-amended, well-drained soil in full sun; Haogen is ready to harvest when the skin transitions from green to orange-yellow in patches and the fruits slip from the vine with minimal pressure — like all aromatic melons, it deteriorates rapidly after peak ripeness. Haogen (also spelled Ogen) was developed at Kibbutz Ein HaMifratz in Israel and remains the most celebrated Israeli melon variety, known throughout the melon-growing world for its extraordinary flavor; the small to medium (1–3 lb), round fruits start with pale green skin that develops orange and gold patches and creeping yellow-green net as they ripen. The flesh is salmon-orange to greenish, with an intensely sweet, highly aromatic, complex melon fragrance and flavor with notes of honey and tropical fruit that many consider the finest melon eating experience available. Short shelf life after harvest (1–2 days at room temperature, 3–5 days refrigerated) means Haogen is fundamentally a garden and local market melon rather than a commercial shipping variety — its reputation rests on the incomparable quality of fruit eaten within hours of harvest. Widely grown in Israel, Netherlands, and by American melon enthusiasts.
sources: Israel Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development

name: Harrington Barley
plantingNote: Sow in early spring once soil is workable; Harrington is a two-row spring malting barley bred at the Crop Development Centre in Saskatchewan that became a dominant malting variety across the northern Great Plains and Canadian Prairies.
directions: Harrington is a two-row spring barley released by the Crop Development Centre at the University of Saskatchewan that, for a long stretch, was the most widely grown malting barley in Canada and much of the northern United States. It produces plump, uniform kernels prized by maltsters, along with short, sturdy straw that resists lodging better than many older two-row types. Drill into a firm seedbed early in spring, since it needs a cool start and a full season of moderate temperatures to fill its heads properly. Combine once the crop has dried down fully in the field, keeping harvested grain clean and well aerated in storage to preserve germination for malting.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Crop Development Centre

name: Harris Model Parsnip
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring — parsnip requires a long, cool growing season of 100–130 days and cannot tolerate summer heat. Germination is notoriously slow (14–28 days) and erratic; sow thickly and thin to 3–4 inches after germination. Parsnip performs best in zones 3–7 where hard fall frosts convert the roots' starches to sugars — the classic technique of leaving roots in the ground through fall frosts and harvesting in late fall/winter produces the sweetest, most intensely flavored roots. Zone 9 gardeners will find parsnip very challenging due to insufficient cold for sweetness development.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, stone-free soil — parsnip requires the same deep, uncompacted growing conditions as carrots but needs even more space due to the larger root; Harris Model is the standard American parsnip variety, selected in the 1880s by the Joseph Harris Seed Company as a smooth, uniform improvement over the traditional English Hollow Crown parsnip — fewer hollow crowns, smoother skin, and better root uniformity make Harris Model the most widely grown American parsnip. The long, tapering, ivory-white roots develop a rich, complex flavor that is unmistakably its own: sweet and aromatic with earthy, celery-like, and nuttily caramelized notes when roasted — a flavor that lacks any close comparison among other vegetables. The signature technique for maximizing parsnip flavor is 'frosting' — leaving harvested or in-ground roots exposed to repeated hard frosts that convert starches to sugars, creating a dramatically sweeter root than summer-harvested parsnips. Roasted parsnips (with butter, herbs, and honey) are one of the great classic British-American root vegetable preparations, where high heat caramelizes the natural sugars and transforms the texture from firm-and-dense to tender and lightly crisp at the edges.
sources: Joseph Harris Seed Company — Harris Model Parsnip Historical Introduction
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Parsnip Production Guide
University of Minnesota Extension — Root Vegetable Growing Guide

name: Hartman's Yellow Gooseberry Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 5-6 weeks before the last frost; this old currant-type heirloom sets heavy clusters of tiny yellow fruit and benefits from early staking on its sprawling vines.
directions: Sow indoors 5-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once the soil has warmed, giving vines a trellis or tall cage since they sprawl readily. Hartman's Yellow Gooseberry is a historic small-fruited heirloom that sets long, grape-like clusters of marble-sized, golden-yellow fruit with a tart-sweet, old-fashioned currant-tomato flavor. The prolific, viny plants keep producing over a long season and are well suited to pickling or preserves as well as fresh snacking. Pick clusters whole once fruit has fully colored, since individual berries continue to size up unevenly within a truss.

name: Harvest Moon Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70F and all frost danger passes; Harvest Moon is an AAS-winning seedless watermelon bred for extra sweetness and very uniform, round, icebox-size fruit. Plant alongside a seeded pollinizer variety, since seedless watermelons need pollen from a seeded type to set fruit.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms, and plant a seeded watermelon variety nearby to supply the pollen seedless watermelons need to set fruit. Harvest Moon is an AAS-winning seedless watermelon bred for very uniform, round, icebox-sized fruit — a manageable size for a refrigerator, unlike the largest field watermelons — with exceptionally sweet, crisp, deep-red flesh and only small, soft, edible white seed traces rather than the hard black seeds of standard watermelon. Its consistent size and shape make it a strong choice for home gardeners who want reliable, high-quality fruit without needing to manage a huge sprawling harvest. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil and consistent irrigation through fruit development; drought stress during fruit fill reduces size and quality. Judge ripeness by the ground spot turning from white to yellow and a dull, hollow thump when the fruit is tapped.
sources: All-America Selections — Harvest Moon Watermelon winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Hasta La Pasta Spaghetti Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Hasta La Pasta is an open-pollinated spaghetti squash bred for noticeably larger fruit than standard varieties, often 6 to 8 pounds each.
directions: Direct sow seed in hills spaced widely apart in rich, well-drained soil, since the vigorous vines need considerably more room than a compact bush spaghetti type. Hasta La Pasta produces oblong, pale cream fruit that dwarfs standard spaghetti squash, often reaching 6 to 8 pounds per fruit, so a single squash can provide strands enough for several meals. Once baked or boiled, the flesh separates into the same long, mild, pasta-like strands that make spaghetti squash a popular low-carbohydrate substitute, but the increased size makes it a better fit for larger households or preservation. Harvest when the rind has toughened to a deep cream color and resists a fingernail, then cure briefly before storing in a cool, dry location for two to three months.

name: Hatch Green Chile
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed; multiple varieties exist under the 'Hatch' name (Big Jim, Joe Parker, 6-4, Sandia) — all are New Mexico-bred long green chiles best harvested green and roasted.
