directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, well-drained soil rich in phosphorus after all frost risk has passed. Hatch green chile refers to New Mexico-style long green chiles — varieties such as NuMex Big Jim, Joe Parker, and the heritage 6-4 — bred at New Mexico State University and grown in the Hatch Valley of southern New Mexico; they produce 6–10 inch, elongated, thick-walled green pods with heat levels ranging from mild to hot depending on cultivar and growing conditions. The distinctive flavor comes from the dry, high-altitude climate, but home gardeners in zones 7–11 with hot, dry summers can produce excellent results in-ground. Harvest green when pods are fully sized and char-blister them on a grill or under a broiler; the roasted flavor is unmatched for green chile sauces, stews, and salsas.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University
New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension

name: Hatch Green Chile
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights remain above 55°F. In zone 9 transplant February–March for a productive spring through fall season; New Mexico type chiles produce heavily through summer heat and can be roasted and frozen in quantity for year-round use.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the New Mexico type chile, particularly Hatch and its relatives, is the defining pepper of Southwestern cuisine, eaten green (roasted), red (dried), or ground into chile powder. This long, mildly hot pepper (1,500–3,000 SHU) averages 6–8 inches and is the standard for roasting — the thick walls blister perfectly under a broiler or over an open flame, and the roasted, peeled chiles freeze beautifully for months. Harvest green through September, or leave some to ripen red for a fully different flavor profile. The Hatch designation technically refers to chiles grown in the Hatch Valley of New Mexico, but the variety performs excellently throughout zone 9.
sources: New Mexico State University Extension — New Mexico Chile Varieties
Chile Pepper Institute — New Mexico Type Chile Varieties
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Chile Pepper Production

name: Havasupai 60-Day Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is warm, ideally timed with the onset of a region's summer monsoon moisture if grown dryland-style; this variety was selected for a short, intense growing window and tolerates heat well.
directions: Havasupai 60-Day is a fast-maturing common bean maintained by the Havasupai people of the Grand Canyon's Havasu Canyon, bred over generations for the short frost-free window and monsoon-dependent moisture of a high-desert canyon growing season. The compact bush plants set pods quickly and dry down within about two months, yielding small, mottled tan-and-brown seeds with a mild, earthy flavor typical of Southwestern dry beans. Because it was selected for arid conditions, it tolerates heat and irregular watering better than many bush dry beans, though a deep soak at flowering improves pod set. Harvest once pods are fully dry and papery, and save seed from the earliest-maturing plants to maintain the variety's signature speed.
sources: University of Arizona Arid Lands Studies

name: Hawaiian Ipu Gourd
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after all frost danger passes and let the vine sprawl over open ground rather than climb, since trellising elongates the fruit away from the rounded shape traditionally wanted for hula implements.
directions: This Hawaiian strain of bottle gourd is traditionally grown along the ground rather than on a trellis, which lets the fruit develop the rounder, double-bulbed form prized for carving the ipu heke gourd drum and other hula implements, rather than the elongated shapes that result from vertical training. Give the sprawling vine a generous patch of warm, fertile soil in full sun and water regularly through fruit set. Both a sweeter-fleshed strain historically used for food and a more bitter strain grown strictly for vessels have been selected over centuries, so flavor of immature fruit can vary by seed source. Harvest for craft use only after the fruit fully matures and the stem dries, then cure for several weeks in a dry, ventilated space until the shell hardens completely before hollowing and finishing.

name: Hawaiian Yellow Ginger
plantingNote: Pre-sprout rhizome pieces indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, then transplant outdoors once soil is consistently warm. 'Hawaiian Yellow' produces golden-skinned rhizomes with canary-yellow flesh and can be grown as a warm-season annual in cooler parts of its range.
directions: Plant pre-sprouted rhizome pieces 2 inches deep in rich, well-drained, evenly moist soil in dappled shade to morning sun; hill soil up around the base as the plant grows, similar to potatoes, to encourage larger rhizome development. 'Hawaiian Yellow' is a distinct culinary ginger strain grown widely in Hawaii, prized for its thin brown skin covering bright golden-yellow flesh with a fuller, more pungent bite than typical grocery-store ginger. It can be harvested young in late summer for tender, mild 'stem ginger,' or left in the ground until foliage dies back in fall for fully mature, storable rhizomes. In zone 9, plants die back after frost but the rhizome survives if mulched; further north, treat as an annual or lift and store rhizomes indoors over winter.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources (CTAHR)

name: Hawke's Champagne Rhubarb
plantingNote: Divide and plant dormant crowns in autumn or very early spring into deeply enriched soil, leaving the growing bud just below the surface.
directions: Hawke's Champagne is a classic English forcing rhubarb known for pushing up exceptionally early, slender pink-red stalks when crowns are covered with a forcing pot or brought into a dark shed in late winter. Left unforced it still crops earlier than most maincrop varieties, making it a favorite for gardeners chasing the first rhubarb of the year. Its slender stalks are sweeter and less fibrous than the stalks of many later, thicker-stemmed cultivars, needing less added sugar in cooking. Rest forced crowns for a full season afterward so they can rebuild reserves before forcing again.

name: Hayman Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant rooted slips 3–4 weeks after the last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F; Hayman is a long-season Southern heirloom that rewards the full length of a Gulf South growing season with heavy yields of long-storing roots.
directions: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in loose, well-drained, sandy-loam soil in full sun, ridging the row to keep the developing roots from sitting in wet soil. Hayman is an old-time Southern heirloom sweet potato, once one of the most widely grown varieties across the Carolinas and Georgia before modern commercial types like Beauregard displaced it, valued for its pale tan skin, dry, mealy, cream-white to pale-yellow flesh, and a mild, chestnut-like sweetness quite different from the moist orange-fleshed types now common in supermarkets. Vines are vigorous and heat-tolerant, sprawling widely and shading out weeds once established, and the roots store exceptionally well through winter when cured properly. Cure freshly dug roots at warm temperature and high humidity for about a week before storing to heal skins and convert starches to sugar, improving both flavor and keeping quality.

name: He-Shi-Ko Bunching Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or late summer; He-Shi-Ko clumps and regrows from the base, so a single sowing can be harvested repeatedly.
directions: He-Shi-Ko is a traditional Japanese heirloom bunching onion that never forms a bulb, instead sending up tall, slender, silvery-white stalks that clump and multiply from the base as the plant matures. Sow thickly in rows and thin gradually, harvesting the largest stalks first and letting the remaining plants continue dividing for a repeated, cut-and-come-again supply through the season. Its mild, non-pungent flavor and tender texture make it a preferred variety for fresh eating raw or lightly cooked rather than for strong-flavored cooked onion dishes. He-Shi-Ko tolerates both cold and heat reasonably well, so gardeners often maintain a planting from early spring sowing through fall harvest without needing a second crop.

name: Health Kick Tomato
plantingNote: Transplant compact determinate plants after last frost; little to no staking is needed given the tidy, self-supporting habit.
directions: Health Kick is a determinate saladette-paste hybrid bred by Seminis to concentrate roughly 50 percent more lycopene than a standard tomato while keeping a broad disease-resistance package that includes Fusarium wilt, Verticillium wilt, tomato spotted wilt virus, and bacterial speck. Compact plants stay under three feet and need only minimal caging, making them well suited to smaller raised-bed plantings. The 3-5 ounce cylindrical fruits work equally well diced fresh, roasted, or cooked into sauce. Choose this variety when disease resistance and nutritional density matter as much as culinary versatility.

name: Heartogold Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; developed by LSU AgCenter breeder Julian C. Miller and released in 1947. Young transplants look spindly at first but grow vigorously once established.
directions: Heartogold is an early, heavy-yielding heirloom bred by Julian C. Miller at the LSU Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1947, producing tan-skinned roots with bright orange flesh on vigorous vining plants. It is one of the older Louisiana-bred varieties still maintained in germplasm collections, predating the Jewel-Beauregard-Covington succession of commercial standards. Sclerotial blight, a soil-borne fungal disease, tends to show up on Heartogold more readily than on many other varieties, so avoid planting in poorly drained or previously infected beds. Cure roots at warm temperature and high humidity after harvest to develop full sweetness before storage.
sources: LSU AgCenter Sweet Potato Research Station

name: Heat Wave II Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Heat Wave II's primary advantage is fruit set at temperatures above 95°F — when most standard tomato varieties drop flowers without setting fruit, Heat Wave II continues to produce.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Heat Wave II is one of the most important tomato introductions for Gulf South gardeners — a hybrid specifically developed for heat tolerance to maintain fruit set during the high-temperature periods (daytime highs above 90–95°F) that cause standard tomato varieties to drop flowers without setting fruit. In zone 9, most standard tomato varieties produce well in spring (March–May) then cease fruiting when summer heat arrives in June; Heat Wave II's genetic ability to set fruit at high temperatures extends the productive season into summer conditions that defeat other varieties. The medium-large (6–8 oz), round, globe-shaped fruits have bright-red color, firm flesh, and good fresh-eating flavor — not the finest gourmet tomato, but extremely reliable production in conditions that eliminate the competition. Heat Wave II is a determinate (bush-type) tomato growing 4–5 feet that can be grown with minimal staking. Disease resistance includes V, F, FF, N, T — a comprehensive disease package for Gulf South conditions where soilborne disease pressure is high. For zone 9 gardeners who want tomatoes through the summer rather than only spring and fall, Heat Wave II is the primary recommendation.

name: Heatmaster Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 transplant February–March for spring crop. Heatmaster is specifically bred to set fruit when nighttime temperatures remain above 75°F — the primary reason most tomatoes fail in Gulf Coast summer. It is the recommended choice for gardeners who want a spring crop that extends into early summer in zone 9.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant in full sun, fertile, well-drained soil; Heatmaster is a hybrid tomato developed specifically for gardeners in hot-summer climates (USDA zones 8–10) where standard tomato varieties drop their blossoms and fail to set fruit when nighttime temperatures exceed 70–75°F and daytime temperatures exceed 95°F. The proprietary Seminis breeding program tested hundreds of crosses before selecting a plant that maintains viable pollen and fruit set under extreme heat — making it one of the most important varieties for Gulf Coast, Southwest, and Deep South gardeners who struggle with the narrow spring window before heat arrives. Fruits are medium-large (8–10 oz), red, globe-shaped with good flavor and firm flesh. The indeterminate plant continues producing through periods of heat that stop Celebrity and Better Boy cold. Disease resistance includes Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, Verticillium, Tobacco mosaic virus, and nematodes. For zone 9 gardeners frustrated by tomatoes that stop producing in May, Heatmaster extends the harvest window by 3–5 weeks.
sources: Seminis Vegetable Seeds — Heatmaster tomato variety notes
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Heat-Tolerant Tomato Varieties for Texas
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Tomatoes in the Low Desert
Arizona Master Gardener Program — Tomato Variety Trials

name: Heavy Hitter Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep after last frost once soil reaches at least 65°F; Heavy Hitter branches heavily and sets multiple pods per node, so plants need the full recommended spacing to support the heavy pod load through a long summer harvest.
directions: Sow seed directly in the garden after danger of frost has passed, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart in rows 3 feet apart. Heavy Hitter was developed by grower Ron Cook of Dry Creek Farm in Oklahoma and selected specifically for extreme productivity, with well-branched plants reaching up to 7 feet tall that can set well over 100 pods per plant across a season. Because multiple pods form at each node rather than one at a time, plants need daily or near-daily picking once production ramps up to keep pods from fibering over and to keep the heavy-bearing plant setting new fruit. This branching habit makes Heavy Hitter a strong choice for gardeners who want maximum yield from a small number of plants.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Heavy Hitter okra variety notes
Dry Creek Farm — Heavy Hitter okra origin and growing notes

name: Hedou Tiny Bok Choy
plantingNote: Direct sow every 3-4 weeks from before the last frost into fall for a continuous supply; Hedou traces to a village near Hong Kong and forms mature heads no bigger than a large grape, so tight successive sowings keep the harvest coming.
directions: Direct sow shallowly and keep the soil surface consistently moist, since this micro bok choy's shallow roots dry out quickly compared to standard-sized types. Hedou produces miniature, whole heads barely larger than a bite, with pale stems and small tender leaves that need no chopping before cooking, and it thrives in the light shade of a container on a partly shaded porch or the dappled edge of a garden bed. Its small stature and fast pace make it forgiving of less-than-full sun, since a shorter daily light window still lets it reach harvest size before bolting becomes a concern. Pick whole heads at the base as soon as they firm up, and resow every few weeks for uninterrupted harvests through the cool season.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Heinz 1350 Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Heinz 1350 is a determinate canning tomato that ripens a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks, ideal for processing in large batches — time transplanting to allow harvest before peak summer heat in zone 9.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Heinz 1350 is the classic determinate processing tomato developed by the H.J. Heinz Company, once widely grown commercially for ketchup production, that became a home garden favorite for anyone serious about canning, sauce-making, or tomato processing — it produces a concentrated set of uniform, medium-sized (5–6 oz), globe to slightly blocky, bright-red fruits with thick, meaty walls, small seed cavities, and very firm texture that holds up exceptionally well to cooking and reduces beautifully to rich tomato sauce without excessive water. The determinate compact plants (3–4 feet) produce the entire crop within a 3–4 week window, which is exactly what canners need — a predictable large harvest all at once rather than a continuous trickle. VF resistance (Verticillium and Fusarium wilt) keeps plants healthy through the season. For zone 9, plant in late January to early February so the harvest window falls in late April through May before summer heat stresses the plants. An outstanding choice for serious home canning enthusiasts who want a reliable, high-yield processing crop.
sources: H.J. Heinz Company seed breeding historical records
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Production Guide
National Center for Home Food Preservation (USDA-NCHFP)

name: Helda Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed at the base of a sturdy 6 to 8 foot trellis or pole; this vigorous climbing Romano-type bean is a staple in Lebanese market gardens.
directions: Direct sow at the base of a tall, sturdy support once soil has warmed, since vines will climb vigorously to six feet or more and need the structure to stay productive and easy to pick. Helda produces broad, flat, pale-green pods eight to ten inches long that stay tender and nearly stringless even at a larger size, making it well suited to loubieh bi zeit, the braised green bean and olive oil dish common across Lebanese and wider eastern Mediterranean tables. Pick every two to three days once pods begin forming to keep plants setting new flowers rather than diverting energy into maturing seed. Provide consistent moisture during flowering and pod fill for the best yield and texture.

name: Helenor Rutabaga
plantingNote: Direct sow in early to midsummer so roots bulk up in cool fall weather; Helenor is a widely grown commercial standard prized for uniform shape and good storage.
directions: Direct sow into loose, fertile soil and thin seedlings to six to eight inches apart, giving the globes plenty of room to size up evenly. Helenor produces smooth, round roots with a purple-blushed shoulder above soil level fading to pale cream below, and dense, pale orange flesh with a fine texture and a mild, well-balanced flavor. Its coloring develops early and evenly, and mature roots hold their quality well in cool storage through winter. Leave roots in the ground into cooler fall weather before harvest, since a touch of cold noticeably sweetens the flavor.

name: Helios Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in spring or 4-6 weeks before first fall frost; Helios is a golden-yellow-skinned spring radish with crisp white flesh and mild flavor, an unusual color choice that stands out in mixed radish plantings and relish trays.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. Helios is a round spring radish with smooth, bright golden-yellow skin and crisp, mild white flesh, an eye-catching alternative to standard red radishes that adds warm color contrast to salads, relish trays, and mixed radish plantings. Flavor is clean and only mildly peppery, similar to other fast-maturing spring radish types. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows. Harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch in diameter, since radishes left too long in the ground become pithy and hollow; succession-sow every two to three weeks for a continuous supply.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Helios Radish variety notes
Kitazawa Seed Co. — Yellow Radish Varieties
Territorial Seed Company — Specialty Radish Collection

name: Henderson Bush Lima Bean
plantingNote: Sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Henderson is very sensitive to cold soil and seed will rot rather than germinate in cold wet ground — be patient and wait for warm conditions.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil (above 65°F) after last frost in full sun, in fertile, well-drained soil; Henderson Bush Lima is the standard small-seeded bush lima bean, an heirloom selection dating to the 1880s that remains the most widely grown small white lima because of its outstanding heat tolerance, compact growth requiring no staking, and prolific production of small, tender, buttery beans in a compressed time frame. The small seed size means faster cooking than large limas and a creamier texture; it is excellent fresh, frozen, or dried as a dry bean. Space rows 18–24 inches apart for good air circulation and reduce disease pressure. Mulch to keep soil moist as pods develop.

name: Henderson Lima Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil (65°F minimum); Henderson is a baby lima (smaller seed than Fordhook types) that excels in hot weather — it sets pods reliably in the Gulf South heat that causes many bean varieties to drop flowers. In zone 9, plant April through July for summer production; late plantings mature in September when temperatures moderate for the fall harvest. The bush habit (no staking needed) and compact plant size (18–24 inches) make Henderson practical for raised beds and small gardens. Plant at 4-inch spacing in rows 24 inches apart for the highest yield per square foot. Henderson is widely available as a named 'baby butter bean' in Gulf South seed racks and is one of the most heat-adapted dry and fresh lima bean types for the region.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in warm soil; thin to 4–6 inches. Harvest green for fresh use when pods are plump; leave to dry on the plant for dry beans. Henderson is a small-seeded bush lima bean — one of the most widely grown lima bean varieties in the American South and Gulf Coast region, where it is often marketed and sold as 'baby butter bean' or 'speckled butter bean' (referring to the speckled seed coloring of some strains). Henderson was introduced in the 1880s and has remained a staple in Southern gardening for over a century, valued for its small, tender seeds, heat tolerance, and reliable production in the warm, humid conditions of the Gulf South that challenge larger-seeded lima types (such as Fordhook). The primary distinction between Henderson and Fordhook-type limas is seed size: Henderson produces small seeds roughly half the size of Fordhook, with a more tender skin and a creamier texture when cooked fresh or dried. In the Gulf South culinary tradition, 'butter beans' (the Southern name for fresh lima beans) are a staple of summer cooking — simmered low and slow with fatback or ham hock until very tender, the small Henderson seeds achieve a creamy, buttery texture that the variety's Southern common name accurately describes. Henderson also performs well as a dry bean: the small seeds dry quickly on the vine and cook to a smooth, creamy texture in soups and stews without requiring the long soaking and cooking time of larger bean types. The heat tolerance of Henderson is a practical advantage in zone 9: while cool-season beans (snap beans, peas) cannot be grown in summer, Henderson sets pods reliably in July-August temperatures that stop production in more sensitive varieties.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Henderson lima bean heritage butter bean documentation
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lima Bean Production for the Gulf South
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Warm-Season Bean and Pea Variety Recommendations

name: Hercules Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed; a semi-erect, short-runnered bush with straight pods held above the foliage for easy shelling.
directions: Hercules was released in 1981 by the Clemson Agricultural Experiment Station, bred by longtime breeder Roy Ogle. It is a large-seeded crowder type with straight 8-9 inch pods held upright on a bushy, short-runnered plant, and coffee-colored crowder seed that shells easily. Matures around 75 days, later than most bush purple hull types, rewarding the wait with an especially large, meaty pea. Best suited to gardeners who want a heavier-seeded crowder flavor distinct from cream or blackeye types.

name: Heritage White Walking Onion
plantingNote: Plant topset bulbils in early fall so they root before winter; bulbils of this strain mature and ship later in the fall than many other walking onion strains.
directions: Heritage White is a pigment-free strain of Egyptian walking onion whose topset bulbils stay ivory-white to pale green with no red or purple blush anywhere on the plant, unlike most walking onion strains, which show at least some color. Growers favor it for a notably milder, sweeter flavor than the common strain, both in the underground bulbs and the aerial topsets. It is planted and managed the same way as other walking onions: set the topset bulbils an inch or two deep in fall, harvest hollow green tops through the season like scallions, and dig the small underground bulbs once the foliage dies back. Left undisturbed, the heavy topset clusters bend the flowering stalk to the ground and root themselves, letting the clump expand on its own year after year.

name: Hernandez Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set rooted slips after the last frost once soil has warmed well past 65°F, planting into loose, well-drained, mounded rows; sandy loam soils bring out Hernandez's best root shape.
directions: Plant slips into ridged, sandy-loam rows for the smoothest, most uniform roots, since Hernandez performs best where drainage is quick and soil is loose rather than heavy clay. Released by the LSU AgCenter sweet potato breeding program in 1992 under breeder Don La Bonte, Hernandez carries reddish-brown skin over deep orange, smooth, string-free flesh with a mild, sweet flavor that holds up well whether baked or boiled. The variety was bred for resistance to fusarium wilt, root-knot nematodes, soil rot, and internal cork, which makes it a dependable, low-input choice for a Gulf Coast garden bed that has grown sweet potatoes before. Cure roots in a warm, humid spot for one to two weeks after harvest to set the skin and sweeten the flesh before long-term storage.
sources: LSU AgCenter Sweet Potato Research Station variety descriptions
LSU AgCenter publications on Don LaBonte sweet potato breeding program
Gardener's Path sweet potato cultivar guide

name: Hestia Brussels Sprout
plantingNote: Start indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; Hestia is an All-America Selections Regional Winner for the Southeast, specifically validated for Gulf Coast-type climates, tolerating both warm weather during establishment and cool temperatures during sprout development, with sprouts resistant to bursting and rot.
directions: Start seeds indoors 12-16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into rich, firm, well-drained soil with consistent moisture; stake tall plants and top the growing tip once bottom sprouts reach marble size to concentrate the plant's energy into sprout development. Hestia was named an All-America Selections Regional Winner for the Southeast specifically for its ability to tolerate the warmer fall temperatures typical of a Gulf Coast growing season while still developing tight, high-quality sprouts as the weather cools, and its sprouts resist bursting and rot better than many older varieties in humid conditions. Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as they reach 1-1.5 inches across and are still tight and firm, and expect flavor to sweeten after a light frost.
sources: All-America Selections — Hestia Brussels sprout Regional Winner

name: Hi-Crop Collards
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting; this hybrid's faster maturity and heat tolerance allow an earlier late-summer planting date than open-pollinated Southern types, extending the harvest window on both ends of the season in zone 8-10 gardens.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this F1 hybrid was bred for commercial-style uniformity, producing tall, upright plants with smooth, dark blue-green leaves held tightly on a strong central stalk that resists lodging in wind. Hi-Crop tolerates late-summer heat noticeably better than heirloom Southern collards, allowing growers to set plants out a few weeks earlier in fall and still avoid the bitterness that heat stress causes in less tolerant types. Its uniform growth habit and heavy leaf set make it well suited to multiple-pass harvesting, where the lower leaves are stripped repeatedly over several months while the growing point continues producing new leaves at the top.

name: Hickory Cane Dent Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least four short rows after frost danger has passed, for reliable wind pollination of this very tall heirloom dent corn.
directions: Sow in blocks rather than single rows for good pollination, in fertile soil with steady moisture through tasseling and ear fill, since stalks of this variety can tower up to 15 feet. Hickory Cane predates 1875 and traces to corn grown in north Florida and south Georgia before spreading north through the Southern Appalachians as a staple grain corn. Plants typically carry one to two ears with large white kernels, and tightly wrapped husks help shield developing ears from weevils and earworms in the field. Left to dry fully on the stalk, the grain grinds into classic coarse white cornmeal and grits, and also makes excellent hominy.

name: Hidatsa Red Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil warms above 60°F; a Native American heirloom dry pole bean from the Hidatsa people of the northern Great Plains, traditionally grown in the Three Sisters system with corn and squash; plant at the base of corn stalks for traditional companion planting.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing 6 inches apart along a trellis or the stalks of sweet corn in the traditional Three Sisters companion planting arrangement. Hidatsa Red is a Native American heirloom dry pole bean from the Hidatsa people of the upper Missouri River region (present-day North Dakota), with deep maroon-red seeds that cook to a creamy, full-bodied texture with an earthy, robust flavor well-suited to soups and stews; the variety was collected and preserved through the work of Alfred Mandan and introduced more widely by Seed Savers Exchange. Allow pods to ripen and dry completely on the vine; pods are tan with dark mottling when ready. An important cultural heritage bean that rewards the grower with both excellent eating and connection to a long agricultural tradition.

name: Hidatsa Red Indian Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Hidatsa Red is a traditional bean of the Hidatsa people of the upper Missouri River valley in North Dakota, traditionally grown as one of the Three Sisters (corn, beans, and squash) in the fertile bottomlands of the Missouri and its tributaries, producing striking dark red, kidney-shaped seeds with excellent rich flavor that made it a staple of Hidatsa cuisine.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost; Hidatsa Red is a bush dry bean that does not require staking; harvest when pods are fully dry and papery, typically 85–100 days from planting. Hidatsa Red is a traditional bean variety of the Hidatsa people (also called Minitari or Gros Ventre), a Native American nation of the upper Missouri River valley in what is now North Dakota, where they cultivated beans, corn, and squash in the fertile bottomlands for centuries before European contact; the bean entered American heirloom preservation networks through ethnobotanical work documenting traditional Plains agriculture and was distributed by the Seed Savers Exchange. The medium-sized, kidney-shaped seeds are an unusual deep brick-red to maroon-red color — distinctive enough to recognize immediately among other dry beans — and cook to a tender, creamy texture with rich, earthy, complex flavor somewhat similar to kidney beans but with more character. In traditional Hidatsa cooking, the beans were dried and stored for winter use, then slow-cooked in stews with dried meat and corn; they are equally excellent in modern preparations — chili, soups, slow-cooked bean dishes, and baked beans where the robust flavor is showcased. Well-adapted to short seasons and the variable conditions of the Northern Plains; good drought tolerance.

name: Hidatsa Shield Figure Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after frost danger passes and soil has warmed to at least 65°F; grow to full dry-down for shell beans rather than picking green.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil, since beans resent transplanting and rot readily in cold ground. Hidatsa Shield Figure is a Native American heirloom dry bean maintained by the Hidatsa people of the upper Missouri River region, producing plump white beans strikingly marked with a dark maroon shield-shaped figure on one side, a traditional variety preserved and shared through indigenous seed-saving networks. Grown on sturdy bush plants, it is left on the vine until pods dry and rattle before harvest, then shelled for storage as a dry bean valued for its rich, creamy texture in soups and stews. Because it is open-pollinated and true-breeding, seed can be saved season to season, continuing a variety with deep cultural and agricultural history.

name: Hidatsa Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost, traditionally planted alongside corn and beans in a Three Sisters arrangement.
directions: A traditional squash of the Hidatsa people of the upper Missouri River valley in present-day North Dakota, grown for generations as part of the Three Sisters companion planting system with corn and beans. Sow seeds directly in hills after frost danger passes; the vigorous vines are notably drought tolerant, reflecting their origin on the Northern Plains. Fruit is teardrop-shaped with salmon-pink skin and thick, deep orange flesh, typically ten to twenty inches long. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists puncture, then store in a cool, dry place, where its excellent keeping quality made it a reliable winter food source.

name: Highland Burgundy Red Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces once soil is workable; this maincrop heirloom needs a full cool season to develop its solid red interior color.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; this British heirloom is one of the few potato cultivars with deep burgundy-red flesh that runs solidly through the tuber rather than just tinting the skin. The color, driven by anthocyanin pigments, fades only slightly with cooking, producing striking pink-tinged mash, roasted wedges, and chips. Flavor is earthy and slightly nutty with a moderately dry, floury texture suited to baking and roasting more than boiling. Grow it as a novelty maincrop alongside white- and yellow-fleshed varieties for a dramatic color contrast at harvest and on the plate.

name: Highlander Onion
plantingNote: Extra-early long-day hybrid; can be direct-seeded as soon as soil can be worked.
directions: This extra-early long-day hybrid delivers large, uniform globes with light brown skin well before most main-season yellow onions are ready, making it a favorite for growers who want an early fresh-market crop. Direct-seed into fertile, well-worked soil as early as the ground can be tilled, thinning to final spacing once seedlings are a few inches tall. Because it bulbs quickly rather than storing long-term, plan to use or sell the crop within a few months of harvest rather than holding it over winter. Keep beds weed-free and evenly moist through bulb formation for the largest, most uniform onions.

name: Hijinks Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost once soil is warm; notable powdery mildew resistance and a long, vining habit make this a dependable small pumpkin for humid southern gardens.
directions: Direct sow in hills after frost danger passes, giving the long vines, which can reach 15 feet, plenty of open ground or a sturdy trellis to climb. Hijinks was named an All-America Selections winner in 2011 for its unusually uniform 7-9 pound fruit, smooth deep-orange skin with distinctive grooves, and a strong, durable stem that makes an excellent handle. The variety shows notable resistance to powdery mildew and releases cleanly from the vine at harvest, both practical advantages in warm, humid growing regions. Pick once the rind has colored fully and hardened, leaving the handle intact, since Hijinks is prized as much for painting and porch display as for carving.

name: Hill Country Heirloom Red Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; in zone 9 plant March–July. Hill Country Heirloom Red is a Texas heirloom variety adapted to deep summer heat and limestone-influenced soils, producing earlier and more prolifically than most standard green okra varieties under Central Texas and Gulf Coast conditions.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in full sun in any well-drained soil; Hill Country Heirloom Red is a striking Texas heirloom okra with deep burgundy-red pods, stems, and leaf veins that make it as ornamental as it is productive. The pods are smooth with 5 ridges and should be harvested at 3–4 inches for peak tenderness; like all okra, the pods become fibrous if left to exceed 5–6 inches. The red pigmentation fades to green when cooked, similar to red-pod okra generally. Plants grow vigorously in the limestone soils and intense heat of Central Texas, where this variety has been grown by generations of families in the Hill Country region. Soaking seeds overnight in warm water before planting speeds germination. Harvest every 2–3 days in summer.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Hill Country Heirloom Red Okra
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Okra Varieties for Texas
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Heirloom Okra Collection

name: Hillbilly Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Hillbilly is an Appalachian heirloom from West Virginia that has been preserved and distributed through regional seed-saving networks for decades before entering the commercial heirloom seed trade.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Hillbilly (also called Hillbilly Potato Leaf) is a West Virginia heirloom beefsteak tomato of Appalachian origin — a large (12–24 oz), irregularly shaped, golden-yellow-orange fruit streaked and mottled with red to produce the characteristic bicolor pattern of this historic mountain heirloom. The Hillbilly's distinctive coloration differs from closely related varieties (Pineapple, Big Rainbow) in its specific yellow-orange background tone and the characteristic way the red streaking distributes across the fruit surface in bold, irregular patches. The flavor is outstanding: very sweet, fruity, and low-acid with a mild, rich character that has made Hillbilly one of the most enthusiastically recommended heirlooms by those who have grown it. 'Hillbilly Potato Leaf' plants display the characteristic potato-leaf (undivided, smooth-margined) foliage common among certain old Appalachian heirloom lineages. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds save true to type season after season. In zone 9, Hillbilly produces best in the spring window (February–June) before summer heat arrives — the very large fruits require the full spring season to reach their finest size and flavor quality. Sturdy support is required for the vigorous indeterminate vines.

name: Hinkelhatz Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil has warmed. Hinkelhatz is a Pennsylvania Dutch heirloom whose name translates roughly to 'chicken heart,' describing the small, pointed, heart-like shape of its fruit.
directions: Transplant into well-drained garden soil in full sun once nights stay warm, giving plants room to branch and set their heavy fruit load. Hinkelhatz produces abundant small, tapered, heart-shaped peppers about one to two inches long that ripen from yellow to orange to red, carrying noticeable heat in a tiny package. Long grown in Pennsylvania German communities, the fruits are traditionally strung and dried or steeped into hot pepper vinegar used to season greens and preserved foods. The bushy, productive plants continue setting new fruit clusters through the growing season with minimal maintenance.

name: HoCP 96-540 Sugarcane
plantingNote: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. HoCP 96-540 (the HoCP designation refers to the USDA-ARS sugarcane research station at Houma, Louisiana, working in cooperation with the LSU AgCenter) became one of the leading commercial varieties in the Louisiana sugar belt, succeeding earlier releases as growers shifted acreage to newer cultivars.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. HoCP 96-540 emerged from the Houma, Louisiana USDA-ARS/LSU AgCenter sugarcane breeding program and became a widely planted commercial variety across the Louisiana sugar belt, valued by growers for its yield and disease resistance relative to older releases. While bred for large-scale sugar production rather than dooryard use, home growers can treat it like any other cane: harvest in late fall after cool nights sweeten the stalks, strip the leaves, and press or chew the stalks fresh, or cook the juice into syrup. The tall, clumping perennial grass typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze in zone 8-9 and regrows from the root each spring.
sources: USDA-ARS Sugarcane Research Unit, Houma, Louisiana

name: Hollow Crown Parsnip
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall in zone 9 (September–October) for winter and spring harvest; parsnip takes 14–28 days to germinate and must be sown in loose, deep (12+ inch), stone-free soil for straight root development. In zone 9, parsnip is a fall-sown root vegetable harvested January–March; the roots require exposure to cold (below 40°F for several weeks) to convert starches to sugar — this 'sweetening by frost' is essential to the parsnip experience and in zone 9's mild winters the temperature drops are sufficient, especially at night. Use fresh seed each year — parsnip seed has notoriously short viability (1–2 years under good storage conditions, far less under poor conditions). Mark the row well as emergence is slow and the seedlings are easy to miss or accidentally weed out.
directions: Sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in loose, deep, well-prepared soil; thin to 3–4 inches when 2 inches tall. Keep soil consistently moist during germination. Hollow Crown Parsnip is the standard American garden parsnip — an open-pollinated variety that has been the dominant parsnip type in American kitchen gardens and seed catalogs since at least the 1820s. The name 'Hollow Crown' describes a shallow depression or crown at the top of the root where the leaves emerge — a characteristic of this variety's root shape rather than an internal hollowness. The roots are long (10–16 inches), creamy-white, tapered, and aromatic — a distinctive sweet, earthy, and spicy character that is unlike any other common vegetable. Parsnip's flavor transformation with cold exposure is the most dramatic of any commonly grown root vegetable: fresh-dug roots in warm weather have a starchy, slightly bitter character, but roots exposed to several weeks of near-freezing temperatures convert their starch to sugar and develop a rich, complex sweetness with spicy, aromatic notes that make parsnips one of the great vegetables of the cold-season kitchen. Roasting parsnips at high heat caramelizes the surface sugars and creates the classic preparation: crisp, brown-edged exterior with creamy, sweet interior. Hollow Crown has remained the standard parsnip in American catalogs because no modern breeding has significantly exceeded its combination of good flavor, long roots, and reliable production.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Hollow Crown parsnip heirloom variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Hollow Crown parsnip variety notes
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Root Vegetable Production and Storage Guide

name: Holstein Bloodred Rhubarb
plantingNote: Set crowns in early spring in deeply worked, humus-rich soil, positioning the bud at or just below the surface.
directions: Holstein Bloodred is a German heirloom originating in the Holstein region, grown for stalks that run a deep, almost uniform red from base to tip, among the darkest-colored of the traditional European rhubarb strains. It is a heavy-feeding, vigorous grower that rewards an annual topdressing of compost or well-rotted manure with larger, more numerous stalks each following spring. The intense color makes it a favorite for preserves and rhubarb wine, both traditional uses in its region of origin, in addition to the usual pies and sauces. Keep the crown well mulched over winter in colder zones and divide every four to five years to maintain vigor as the clump matures.

name: Holstein Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep near a trellis or fence after soil has warmed; this running, semi-climbing heirloom needs support to produce its best in a Gulf Coast garden.
directions: Direct sow near a trellis, fence, or other support, since this cowpea runs and climbs rather than staying in a tidy bush. Holstein takes its name from the striking black-and-white mottled pattern on its seed, reminiscent of the dairy cow's coat, and was recorded under the older name Polecat in an 1860s survey of Southern cowpea varieties. Vigorous vines bear pods of ten to twelve peas that are excellent picked green for fresh shelling or left to dry for storage. Like other cowpeas it fixes nitrogen and tolerates heat and humidity better than most legumes.

name: Home Green Sugarcane
plantingNote: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Home Green (also called Georgia Green or Homeowner Green) is a dual-purpose heirloom dooryard cane grown for both chewing and syrup.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Home Green is a long-grown Gulf South dooryard heirloom, green-stalked through summer and ripening to a golden yellow with red-blushed, sunset-like mottling as stalks mature in fall; the rind is soft and easy to peel, the juice notably greener than most other heirloom canes, and growers describe the flavor as a simple, syrupy sweetness reminiscent of old-fashioned cane syrup. It is valued as a dual-purpose variety, equally suited to fresh chewing and to pressing and cooking down into syrup, and was traditionally kept in home dooryard patches rather than grown commercially. As with other heirloom canes, propagation is entirely from saved stalk sets: healthy stalks are cut before the first hard freeze, bedded horizontally in a shaded, well-drained trench, and covered with soil, pine straw, or plastic to hold them dormant through winter without freezing, then replanted the following spring. Harvest runs from the first light frosts of late fall, after cool nights have sweetened the stalks, through early winter.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sugarcane Production and Heirloom Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Backyard Sugarcane (SS-AGR-253/SC052)
Southern Foodways Alliance — Cane Syrup Traditions

name: Home Stoop Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors and set out after frost; semi-determinate vines still reach 6-7 feet, so give them support similar to an indeterminate tomato.
directions: Home Stoop crosses the same cold-hardy 'Stupice' used in Estate with 'Homestead,' but is selected to push fruit size up rather than keep it small. Fruits are somewhat flattened and can reach up to 4 inches across, with a cross-section netted with small, juicy locules that makes for a great fresh slicer. Despite being described as semi-determinate, vines still grow 6-7 feet, so stake or cage them as you would an indeterminate variety. Full sun and steady, even watering help the larger fruit size develop without splitting.

name: Homestead 24 Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; a spring and fall tomato for zone 9–11. Homestead 24 is one of the most heat-tolerant open-pollinated tomatoes available, developed for the intense summer heat of South Florida where standard tomatoes fail.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set plants in full sun, fertile soil with good drainage; Homestead 24 is a University of Florida IFAS heirloom bred at the Homestead Experiment Station in Homestead, Florida, selected for heat tolerance and disease resistance under South Florida's extreme subtropical growing conditions. The '24' designation indicates a selection within the Homestead series, the result of many generations of selection for performance in tropical heat and humidity. Determinate plants produce medium (6–8 oz), red, globe-shaped fruits with good flavor, firm flesh, and resistance to fusarium wilt and gray leaf spot. An important open-pollinated variety for zone 9b–12 gardeners who want to produce tomatoes reliably in hot, humid summer conditions where most varieties fail to set fruit — one of the trio of UF heirlooms (with Tropic and Walter) that carried South Florida vegetable gardening through decades before modern disease-resistant hybrids became available.

name: Homestead 61 Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; this University of Florida release was bred specifically to keep setting fruit through Deep South heat and humidity.
directions: Homestead 61 is a determinate open-pollinated tomato released by the University of Florida in 1961 as an improved selection of the earlier Homestead 24, developed specifically for growers in Florida and the Gulf South who needed a tomato that would keep producing through intense heat and humidity without the blossom drop that plagues many standard varieties. Fruits are large, firm, and meaty with good disease tolerance for its era, and the variety became a long-standing dooryard and small-farm standard across the Deep South. Stake plants for cleaner fruit and better airflow in humid gardens, and maintain even watering to reduce cracking.

name: Homestead Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March. Homestead was bred at the University of Florida to set fruit in high heat and humidity, making it one of the classic Southern tomato varieties. Also plant in late July for fall production.
directions: Transplant into fertile, deeply amended, well-drained soil and stake or cage; Homestead 24 is a determinate variety developed by the University of Florida that bears a concentrated crop of medium-large, smooth, red fruits ideal for canning and fresh use in hot, humid climates. Its primary attribute is heat tolerance — the variety was specifically selected to set fruit when night temperatures remain above 75°F, a condition that causes blossom drop in most standard varieties. Fruit size averages 6–8 ounces with good wall thickness for slicing or canning. This heirloom-type determinate variety has been a Southern garden standard since the 1950s and remains popular throughout the Gulf Coast.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Florida Tomato Varieties
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Tomato Cultivars for Louisiana
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomato Varieties for Texas

name: Honey 'n Pearl Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed to at least 65F; Honey 'n Pearl is a supersweet (sh2) bicolor corn, an early landmark AAS winner bred to hold its sweetness in storage far longer than standard sweet corn.
directions: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows (rather than one or two long rows) for reliable wind pollination, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, after the soil has warmed to at least 65F. Honey 'n Pearl is an AAS-winning bicolor supersweet (sh2, shrunken-2 gene) corn, one of the landmark early supersweet varieties that changed home and commercial sweet corn breeding by holding its sugar content — and therefore its sweet flavor — for up to two weeks after harvest, far longer than older standard-sugary sweet corn varieties that begin converting sugar to starch within hours of picking. Ears are well-filled with a classic mix of yellow and white kernels. Because supersweet corn types can cross-pollinate badly with standard or sugary-enhanced corn and lose their sweetness, isolate plantings from other corn varieties by distance or timing. Keep soil consistently moist, especially during silking and ear fill, and side-dress with nitrogen when plants are about knee-high for the best ear development.
sources: All-America Selections — Honey 'n Pearl Sweet Corn winner announcement

name: Honey and Cream Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September. Plant in solid blocks of at least 4 rows for good wind pollination — single rows pollinate poorly. Isolate from field corn, popcorn, and other sweet corn varieties by at least 250 feet or stagger planting dates by 2 weeks to prevent off-type pollination. Honey and Cream is a standard su (normal sugary) type — harvest promptly at peak ripeness and use quickly, as sugar conversion to starch begins immediately after harvest.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Honey and Cream is a classic bicolor sweet corn producing attractive ears with alternating yellow and white kernels in the traditional American bicolor pattern — it was among the earliest widely available bicolor sweet corn varieties and remains popular for its straightforward, reliable, pleasant sweet corn flavor without the extreme sweetness of modern super-sweet types. Honey and Cream represents the standard sugary (su) bicolor corn flavor profile that defined American sweet corn for most of the 20th century — rich, substantial corn flavor with moderate sweetness and a tender, slightly milky kernel texture when eaten at peak ripeness. The reliable production, good ear appearance, and familiar flavor make it a trusted heirloom-style bicolor variety for home gardeners seeking a classic sweet corn experience. The ears are well-filled and typically 7–8 inches long — a proper size for fresh eating and corn-on-the-cob presentations.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Sweet Corn Variety Trials
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sweet Corn Production Guide
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Corn for Home Gardens

name: Honey Bear Acorn Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for a June harvest and August for fall. Honey Bear's compact vine habit makes it suitable for smaller garden spaces than standard sprawling acorn squash vines. The small, single-serving fruit size means home gardeners can harvest as needed without worrying about using a large squash before it spoils.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Honey Bear is a 2009 All-America Selections-winning acorn squash that produces a compact, semi-bush vine with small, single-serving fruits — typically 1 pound, the perfect size for splitting and roasting as one serving for two. The deep green, ribbed, acorn-shaped fruits have exceptionally sweet, dry, nutty flesh — rated significantly sweeter in taste trials than standard acorn squash types including Table King and Table Queen. The compact plant habit (3–4 feet spread versus 8–12 feet for standard acorn squash) makes Honey Bear one of the few winter squashes genuinely suitable for raised beds and smaller gardens. Each plant produces multiple fruits over the harvest season. Cure harvested fruits at room temperature for 10 days to convert starches to sugar and extend storage life to 3–4 months.
sources: All-America Selections — Honey Bear Acorn Squash Award Record
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Compact Acorn Squash
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Winter Squash Production

name: Honey Dew Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm (70°F+); in zone 9 plant March–May. Honeydew requires the longest growing season of any common melon (90–110 days) and the most heat to develop full sugar. Unlike cantaloupe, honeydew does not 'slip' from the vine when ripe — check for ripeness by skin color (cream to white-green), slight giving when pressed at the blossom end, and a characteristic sweet aroma. In zone 9 the heat of June through August is ideal for honeydew sugar development; consistent moisture during fruit development then reduced irrigation as fruits approach maturity produces the sweetest flesh.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, sandy or loamy soil — honeydew requires warm soil, abundant heat, and consistent moisture during fruit development; Honey Dew is the standard honeydew melon variety — a winter melon type (Cucumis melo, Inodorus group) producing large (5–8 pound), oval to round fruits with a distinctive smooth, creamy-white to pale green skin that develops a subtle gold or cream color at full ripeness. The flesh is pale green, firm but juicy, with a mild, clean, very sweet flavor that is quite different from the musty, complex, aromatic sweetness of cantaloupe — honeydew's sweetness is cleaner and more neutral, making it the preferred melon for many people who find cantaloupe flavor too strong. Honeydew's longer shelf life and later harvest timing compared to cantaloupe made it historically important as a late-summer melon that could be stored and shipped where cantaloupe could not. Zone 9 is ideal for honeydew production — the extended summer heat and long growing season align perfectly with honeydew's need for consistently warm conditions over a long development period.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Honeydew Melon Production
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Honeydew Melon for Florida Gardens
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Honeydew and Winter Melon for Gulf South

name: Honey Drip Sorghum
plantingNote: Direct sow into warm soil well after the last frost; Honey Drip is a regionally acclimated Southern heirloom syrup sorghum valued for its drought and heat tolerance, reliable yields, and comparatively early maturity for a syrup type.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in average, well-drained garden soil once the ground has warmed after frost, thinning seedlings to their final spacing. Honey Drip is a Southern heirloom syrup sorghum that has been grown and re-selected in the region for generations, giving it strong heat and drought tolerance and dependable yields on soils too lean or dry for some other syrup canes. Plants top out shorter than many syrup sorghums, with upright, honey-colored seed heads, and reach cutting stage somewhat earlier in the season than late-maturing types. Harvest canes at hard-dough stage and press promptly, since the sweet, mellow syrup Honey Drip is known for depends on getting the juice to the evaporator soon after cutting.

name: Honey Nut Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 2–3 weeks earlier for zone 5–6 shorter seasons; in zone 9, plant March–April for fall harvest. Honey Nut requires the same long season as standard butternut (100–110 days) but stores well through winter (3–4 months in a cool, dry location) and cures similarly — allow 2 weeks at warm temperatures (80–85°F) to harden the skin after harvest. The mini size (5–6 oz) means individual fruits serve 1–2 people perfectly.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after last frost; thin to 2 plants per hill. Cure harvested fruits at 80–85°F for 2 weeks to harden skin, then store in cool, dry conditions. Honey Nut is a miniature butternut-type winter squash developed at Cornell University by plant breeder Michael Mazourek, introduced commercially around 2011–2015 — a squash that has rapidly gained status as one of the most innovative new vegetable introductions of the decade. The standard butternut squash (Waltham Butternut and similar) is widely considered one of the best-flavored winter squashes but weighs 3–5 lbs — more than most households can comfortably consume in one meal. Honey Nut produces single-serving-sized fruits of only 4–6 oz, with the same classic butternut shape (pear-shaped with a long cylindrical neck and round base) compressed to a palm-sized scale. Beyond the practical size advantage, Honey Nut has exceptional flavor that often outperforms standard butternut in blind tastings — the small size means the fruits must mature fully before harvest, when starches have converted to sugar, resulting in a consistently sweeter, more intense squash flavor. The deep orange flesh is very sweet, smooth-textured, and rich — ideal for roasting (a single halved fruit roasts in 30–35 minutes, faster than the 45–60 minutes for full-size butternut), soups, and purees.
sources: Cornell University Plant Breeding — Honey Nut squash development by Michael Mazourek
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Honey Nut squash introduction and notes
Bon Appétit magazine — Honey Nut squash feature (2015)

name: Honey Select Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for wind pollination; Honey Select is a synergistic (sy) type combining sh2 and su kernels on the same ear — it does not need isolation from su/se types but should be isolated from other sh2 varieties by 250 feet or staggered planting dates. Soil should be 65°F minimum for reliable germination. In zone 9, plant March–April for June–July harvest or in August–September for a fall harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows; fertilize at planting and side-dress at knee height with nitrogen. Honey Select is a 1999 All-America Selections-winning bicolor sweet corn from Rogers Brothers/Syngenta that represents one of the most successful expressions of synergistic (sy or triplesweet) sweet corn genetics — a breeding system that places approximately 75% supersweet (sh2) kernels and 25% standard su kernels randomly across each ear, creating a flavor profile that integrates the long-lasting sweetness and slow starch conversion of sh2 types with the richer, more complex corn flavor that su kernels contribute. The resulting flavor is considered by many tasters to be more balanced, complete, and authentically corn-flavored than pure sh2 types (which can be very sweet but thin in traditional corn character) while retaining the extended harvest window advantage of sh2 genetics. The bicolor (yellow and white) ears are large (8–8.5 inches, 16 rows), well-filled, and visually attractive; the synergistic type's mixed kernel genetics produce slightly irregular but appealing ear fill. Honey Select has been a top-selling sweet corn variety since its release and remains one of the most consistent performers in home garden and market garden trials, with good disease resistance including tolerance to Stewart's wilt, NCLB, and SCLB. An outstanding all-around bicolor corn for any climate where premium flavor and extended postharvest quality are priorities.
sources: All-America Selections — Honey Select AAS winner 1999
Syngenta / Rogers Brothers — Honey Select variety development
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Sweet Corn Variety Trials

name: Honeynut Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer (July–August in zone 9) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for a fall harvest; Honeynut is a moschata type with better heat tolerance than pepo squash types, making it more reliable for late-season zone 9 production.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Honeynut is a landmark squash introduction from Cornell University and Row 7 Seed Company — a diminutive butternut-type squash (3–4 inches long, 6–8 oz) that is completely different from standard butternut squash in flavor intensity: the Honeynut's flesh has dramatically more concentrated sweetness, nuttiness, and butternut flavor than full-sized butternut because the ratio of flesh to seed cavity is much higher in the mini fruit. When roasted, the deep-orange flesh caramelizes beautifully and develops an intense, complex butterscotch-butternut flavor that has made Honeynut one of the most talked-about new vegetables of the 2010s since its public introduction in 2015. The small fruit size (one squash per serving) makes Honeynut practical for individual servings without the waste of a large standard butternut. As a Cucurbita moschata variety, Honeynut has better heat and disease tolerance (particularly vine borer resistance) than pepo-type winter squash — an important practical advantage in the Gulf South where squash vine borers and heat challenge pepo types in summer. In zone 9, direct sow in July–August for a fall harvest (September–November). Cure for 4–6 weeks after harvest to develop maximum sweetness.

name: Honeypatch Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost once soil tops 70F, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early and transplant out.
directions: Bred for personal-size portions rather than a whole family, Honeypatch produces compact 5-6 inch fruit weighing under a pound on short 4-5 foot vines, making it a good fit for smaller gardens. Thin to one plant every 24 inches in fertile, well-drained soil and water on a schedule that lets the foliage dry fully between waterings to discourage disease. Protect young plants with row cover for an early growth boost, removing covers once flowers open so pollinators can reach them, and let fruit fully ripen on the vine for peak sweetness.

name: Honeyshaw Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil has warmed past 70°F; Honeyshaw ripens roughly a week to ten days earlier than standard Crenshaw, which makes it a workable choice for gardeners outside the hottest, longest-summer regions where true Crenshaw struggles to finish.
directions: Honeyshaw was introduced by Petoseed Company around 1980 as an earlier-ripening, Crenshaw-type melon bred for growers in the sunbelt who wanted Crenshaw's rich flavor without the full 90-110 day commitment the classic heirloom demands. Fruits are medium-sized with ribbed skin that shifts from dark green toward yellow as they mature, and the pastel-pink-to-orange flesh carries a sweet, distinctive flavor reminiscent of its Crenshaw parentage. Plant in hills of three to four seeds in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil, and keep moisture even through flowering and early fruit set before easing back as fruit ripens to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the blossom end softens slightly and the rind's green cast has given way to yellow, since Honeyshaw loses its characteristic aroma quickly once overripe.
sources: NC State University Cucurbit Breeding Program — Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America
Harvest to Table — Growing Galia, Honeydew, and Crenshaw Melons

name: Hong Kong Green Bitter Melon
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep after soil has thoroughly warmed and all frost danger has passed, providing a sturdy trellis for the vigorous climbing vines.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep after soil has thoroughly warmed and all frost danger has passed, providing a sturdy trellis for the vigorous climbing vines. This classic Cantonese-type cultivar produces oblong, blunt-ended fruit with a pale-green, gently warty surface that is larger and milder than typical Indian bitter melon types. Harvest fruit while still firm and light green, before the surface begins to yellow, for use in stir-fries, stuffed dishes, and soups where its characteristic bitterness is balanced with garlic, black bean, or egg.

name: Hooker's Sweet Indian Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least four rows for good pollination. This variety was bred for cool Pacific Northwest summers, so in zone 9a it performs best sown as early as soil temperature allows to mature before peak summer heat.
directions: Hooker's Sweet Indian was developed more than seventy years ago by Ira Hooker near Olympia, Washington, who worked from Native American corn strains to produce a sweet corn that would reliably ripen in a short, cool growing season. The short four to four-and-a-half foot stalks are unusually compact for a corn variety and typically set two ears per plant, five to seven inches long with 10-12 rows of kernels, starting out white and darkening through purple to a deep blue-black as they dry. Because it holds sweetness at the fresh eating stage and also grinds into flavorful cornmeal once fully dried, it works as a genuine dual-purpose corn for gardeners who want both a fresh crop and a grain harvest from the same planting.

name: Hooligan Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Hooligan is an All-America Selections winner producing miniature two-tone orange-and-cream pumpkins on a compact, high-yielding vine.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun, spacing hills so the compact vines have room to set their heavy load of fruit. Hooligan won an All-America Selections award for a striking two-tone pattern that splits each miniature pumpkin between deep orange and creamy white, a novelty look that has made it a favorite for fall tablescapes and porch displays rather than cooking. A single vine can produce dozens of the palm-sized fruits over the season, giving far more usable pieces per plant than standard-size decorative pumpkins. Harvest once the rind fully hardens and the color pattern has set, and the small size means the whole crop keeps well for weeks without curing.

name: Hopi Black Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow an inch deep once the soil has warmed well past last frost, since this bush-type dry bean sulks in cold, wet ground.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep once the soil has warmed well past last frost, since this bush-type dry bean sulks in cold, wet ground. Hopi Black has been grown for generations by Hopi farmers in the arid mesas of northeastern Arizona, selected over centuries for its ability to set a reliable crop of small, glossy black beans on minimal rainfall. Let pods dry fully on the plant before shelling, and expect a compact, drought-tolerant bush that needs no staking. The dried beans cook to a rich, dense texture well suited to stews and traditional Southwestern dishes.

name: Hopi Blue Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for wind pollination; isolate from other corn by 300 feet or by 2-week timing difference to prevent color dilution from cross-pollination. In zone 9, plant March–May for summer harvest; Hopi Blue matures as a dried corn (allow ears to dry on the plant before harvesting). The blue color in the flour and tortillas is enhanced by the alkaline lime-processing (nixtamalization) used in traditional corn preparation.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in blocks of 4+ rows; harvest ears when husks are fully dry and brown (typically 3–4 weeks after the milk stage of sweet corn). Hopi Blue is a traditional open-pollinated flour corn grown by the Hopi people of the Colorado Plateau for centuries — one of the most culturally significant food plants in the Southwestern United States, where blue corn (technically any of several traditional pueblo corn varieties) is the foundation of traditional Hopi cuisine and ceremony. The deep blue-purple to near-black kernels are soft starch corn (flour type) ground into the fine blue cornmeal used for piki bread (the traditional thin, paper-like blue corn bread), blue corn tortillas, atole (blue corn porridge), and blue corn mush. The blue color comes from anthocyanin pigments in the aleurone layer, and the striking blue color is enhanced rather than destroyed by traditional lime processing (nixtamalization). Modern American markets for blue corn tortilla chips and blue corn products have dramatically increased interest in blue corn varieties. Hopi Blue requires isolation from other corn types to maintain kernel color purity; crossing with yellow or white sweet corn produces offspring with diluted color. The variety shows good drought tolerance adapted to its ancestral dry-mesa homeland.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Hopi Blue corn variety documentation
Native Seeds/SEARCH — Hopi Blue traditional corn
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Traditional Pueblo Corn Varieties

name: Hopi Orange Watermelon
plantingNote: Sow in warm soil after frost; Hopi Orange is a desert-adapted heirloom traditionally dry-farmed by the Hopi people of northern Arizona using deep planting and wide spacing to capture scarce moisture, and it tolerates heat and drought better than most modern watermelon varieties.
directions: Sow seeds 1-2 inches deep in warm hills spaced widely apart, thinning to the strongest one or two vines per hill; in dry-farmed desert tradition the seed is planted deeper still, up to 4-6 inches, to reach residual soil moisture, though garden beds with regular irrigation can plant at a normal depth. Hopi Orange is a Native American heirloom watermelon developed by the Hopi people of northern Arizona and preserved through seed banks such as Native Seeds/SEARCH, selected over generations for the ability to produce a crop with minimal supplemental water in arid, sandy soil. Fruit is medium-sized with light green rind and sweet, deep orange flesh that is less common among heirloom watermelons than the standard red. Vines are vigorous and sprawling and still benefit from consistent moisture during fruit set even though the variety tolerates drought once established. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the melon turns from white to pale yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned.
sources: Native Seeds/SEARCH — Hopi Orange Watermelon variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Native American Heirloom Watermelons
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Desert-Adapted Crop Varieties

name: Hopi Pale Grey Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil, giving the sprawling vines ample room; this drought-adapted Hopi heirloom tolerates arid conditions better than most winter squash once established.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in hills, giving the vigorous, far-ranging vines generous room to spread. Hopi Pale Grey is a traditional Hopi heirloom squash grown for centuries in the arid Southwest, producing large, round to slightly oval fruit with smooth, pale bluish-gray skin and dense, deep orange, sweet flesh well suited to baking, soups, and traditional Hopi cooking. It is notably drought tolerant once established, reflecting its origins in a low-rainfall growing region, and stores exceptionally well, often keeping through much of the winter in a cool, dry location. Harvest once the rind hardens fully and resists a fingernail scratch, then cure for a couple of weeks in a warm, airy spot before moving to long-term storage.

name: Hopi Red Dye Amaranth
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Hopi Red Dye amaranth grows very rapidly in warm weather — plants can reach 6 feet or more in zone 9's summer conditions. The tiny seeds can be broadcast over prepared soil and raked in lightly; thin to 18 inches when seedlings are 4–6 inches tall. Harvest seed heads when the seeds begin to turn from dark purple to brownish-red and shatter easily when rubbed between the fingers. Shake or rub seed heads over a container to collect seeds; winnow to remove chaff.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile to lean, neutral soil — amaranth grows in poor soils and does not need fertilization to thrive; Hopi Red Dye is an heirloom grain amaranth variety cultivated by the Hopi people of the American Southwest for centuries — the deep burgundy-red to maroon pigment extracted from the dried seeds and flowers was used as a traditional food dye for piki (paper-thin corn bread) and other ceremonial foods, creating a vivid magenta-red color central to Hopi cultural celebrations. The plant is simultaneously ornamental and productive: growing 5–7 feet tall with dramatic, deep burgundy-red seed heads and richly colored foliage that makes it one of the most striking large-scale garden plants for summer use. The small seeds (grain) are a nutritionally exceptional whole grain — very high in protein (13–17%), lysine (an amino acid deficient in most grains), and various minerals — usable as a cooked grain substitute for rice or quinoa, ground into flour, or popped like popcorn. Young leaves can be eaten as a cooked green similar to spinach. The drought-tolerance and heat-adaptability of amaranth make Hopi Red Dye one of the best grain crops for zone 9's challenging summer conditions.
sources: Native Seeds SEARCH — Hopi Red Dye Amaranth Heritage Preservation
Seed Savers Exchange — Hopi Red Dye Amaranth
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Amaranth as Alternative Crop

name: Hot Portugal Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil after frost danger has passed. Hot Portugal is a New England heirloom long maintained in Portuguese-American gardening communities of southern New England.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil has warmed, giving plants ample room for their tall, branching growth. Hot Portugal produces long, tapering fruit six to eight inches in length that ripens from green to red with substantial, lingering heat similar to a large cayenne. Fruits are traditionally steeped whole in vinegar to make the hot pepper vinegar splashed over fish, greens, and beans in New England Portuguese-American kitchens, though they are equally good fresh, roasted, or dried. The vigorous plants bear heavily over a long season and handle humid summer conditions well.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Hot Portugal Pepper

name: Hot Sunset Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Hot Sunset, a 2015 All-America Selections winner, is a hot wax-type pepper bred for an earlier, more prolific harvest than older wax pepper varieties.
directions: Transplant into full sun after the last frost in well-fertilized soil, feeding regularly to support heavy, early fruit set. Hot Sunset ripens elongated, tapered banana-shaped pods from green to red, carrying a moderate heat that works well fresh, grilled, roasted, or pickled. The variety also offers resistance to Xanthomonas bacterial spot and tomato spotted wilt virus, improving reliability where those diseases are common. No staking is required, though sturdy support helps under especially heavy fruit loads.

name: How Sweet It Is Corn
