plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F, planting in solid blocks of at least 4 rows for adequate wind pollination; How Sweet It Is, a 1986 All-America Selections winner, is a sugary-enhanced white sweet corn with excellent post-harvest sugar retention.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil in solid blocks rather than single rows to ensure thorough wind pollination of the ears. How Sweet It Is, a 1986 All-America Selections winner, produces pure white, sugary-enhanced kernels with outstanding sweetness and tenderness that hold their sugar content well after harvest rather than quickly converting to starch, giving a longer window of peak eating quality than standard sweet corn. Isolate from field corn, popcorn, or other corn types by at least 250 feet or two weeks of tasseling time to prevent cross-pollination from diluting sweetness. Harvest when ears are well filled and kernels exude a milky liquid when pressed, and cook or refrigerate promptly for the best flavor.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Sweet Corn Variety Evaluation
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sweet Corn for Florida Gardens

name: Huayleño Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; this central-highland Peruvian landrace needs a long frost-free season to fill its large kernels fully.
directions: Sow in deep, fertile soil in full sun and allow a long season for the large, starchy kernels to fully develop and dry on the stalk. Huayleño is a traditional landrace from the central Peruvian highlands grown for its big, soft kernels, which are soaked and boiled whole into mote, a staple cooked-corn side dish served throughout Andean Peru alongside stews, cheese, and roasted meats. Dry ears fully before shelling and store kernels in a cool, dry, sealed container; dried kernels are typically soaked overnight before the long simmer that softens them for mote. As an open-pollinated landrace it shows more natural variation in ear size than modern hybrid field corn.
sources: National Research Council — Races of Maize in Peru (Grobman et al.)

name: Hubbard Essex Red Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills or rows after soil has warmed; this vigorous vining heirloom needs ample room to sprawl through the season.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile soil in full sun once the danger of frost has passed, giving vines plenty of room to spread. Hubbard Essex Red, discovered in 1883 as a natural cross of Turban and Hubbard squash in Essex, Massachusetts, produces large, drum-shaped, deeply warty fruit with bright orange-red skin and sweet, dense orange flesh prized for pies and baking. Like other hubbard types it stores exceptionally well in a cool, dry spot through much of the winter once properly cured. Cure fruit in the sun for a week or two after harvest to toughen the rind before long-term storage.

name: Huckleberry Gold Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before the last frost in hilled, loose soil and re-hill as sprouts emerge to keep tubers covered.
directions: This mid-season variety sets oval, medium-large tubers with dark purple skin wrapped around dense golden flesh that cooks up creamy with a touch of dryness. The medium-large plants carry lavender flowers and show moderate scab resistance with only medium blight tolerance, so rotate beds and avoid overly wet soil. Space seed pieces 8-10 inches apart and hill generously, since tuber set is moderate but yields run medium-heavy under good conditions.

name: Humptulips Ulluco
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in cool, moist soil after last frost; Humptulips is notable as one of the first seed-grown (true-seed) ulluco varieties ever commercially offered, since ulluco seed production is historically very difficult.
directions: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in loose, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Humptulips is a Cultivariable breeding-program release, documented on the Open Source Seed Initiative registry, and notable for being grown from true seed rather than only vegetative propagation, a genuine breakthrough for this historically seed-shy crop. It produces large, lumpy yellow tubers lightly marked with red at the eyes and deep yellow flesh, on a vigorous, drought-tolerant plant. Like other ulluco it needs a long, cool-summer season with tuberization beginning after the fall equinox, hardy only to about zone 9a.

name: Hungarian Black Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Hungarian Black tolerates cooler temperatures than most peppers and can be set out slightly earlier than tender tropical types.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun, well-drained soil after the coldest weather has passed. Hungarian Black is a dual-purpose ornamental and culinary pepper with striking deep purple flowers and foliage that darkens to near-black, setting slender purple-black fruit that ripens through purple to bright red, giving the plant multicolor visual interest across a single growing season. Fruit carries mild to medium heat, roughly comparable to a jalapeño, and is entirely usable in the kitchen even though the plant is most often grown for its dramatic dark coloring in ornamental beds and containers. Among peppers it is notably more tolerant of cool temperatures than typical tropical types, allowing a slightly earlier transplant date and better performance into cool fall weather. Harvest at any color stage; purple fruit is milder and firmer, while fully red fruit is sweeter and slightly hotter.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Hungarian Heart Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; the pointed oxheart fruit is heavy and low-seeded, so stake this indeterminate vine firmly.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, well-drained soil once nights stay reliably warm. Hungarian Heart is an oxheart-type heirloom traced to a village near Budapest around 1900, valued for producing pointed, meaty pink fruit that often exceeds a pound with very few seeds and little core. The dense flesh and low moisture content make it especially good for sauces and canning as well as fresh slicing. Stake the vigorous indeterminate vines well, since the heavy fruit clusters can pull down unsupported branches.

name: Hungarian Hot Wax Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil warms above 60°F; a prolific variety that sets fruit well in warm, humid conditions, making it excellent for Gulf Coast and zone 8–10 gardens.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant to the garden once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55°F; Hungarian Hot Wax is a medium-heat open-pollinated pepper (5,000–10,000 Scoville units) that produces waxy, pale-yellow 5–7 inch fruits that ripen through orange to deep red, and it is among the most versatile peppers for pickling, stuffing, frying, and fresh eating. Fruits are ready to pick at the yellow stage for the mildest heat and thickest walls, or left to ripen red for maximum color and slightly more intensity. This variety is highly productive and disease-tolerant, thriving in both humid and dryer conditions; plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil and avoid overwatering once plants are established.

name: Hungarian Sweet Wax Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; harvest Hungarian Sweet Wax at the waxy-yellow stage (65–70 days) for pickling and fresh use, or allow to ripen to orange and red for a sweeter flavor. The sweet wax type is distinct from the hot wax type (Hungarian Hot Wax) — both look similar at the yellow stage but the sweet type has virtually no heat. Harvest frequently to encourage continued production.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 78–85°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Hungarian Sweet Wax (also commonly called banana pepper, though this term covers both sweet and hot wax types) is one of the most widely grown pickling peppers in North America — a long (5–7 inch), tapered, waxy-skinned, pale yellow to golden-yellow pepper with very mild to no heat that has become the standard home pickle pepper for generations of American gardeners. The waxy, smooth skin characteristic gives these peppers excellent structure for pickling — the thin walls absorb brine quickly, the skin maintains its integrity through the canning process, and the mild flavor showcases the pickling brine without competition from pepper heat. Hungarian Sweet Wax is the standard banana pepper of pizza restaurants and deli sandwiches across the United States, where it appears in countless jar formats — whole, sliced into rings, or pickled in brine. Beyond pickling, the fresh peppers are excellent eaten raw (sweeter and crisper than bell peppers), stuffed with cream cheese, and sliced in salads. Prolific plants produce heavily throughout the summer, yielding more peppers per plant than bell types. The sweet type should not be confused with Hungarian Hot Wax (which has 1,000–15,000 SHU); both look nearly identical at the yellow harvest stage.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Hungarian Sweet Wax pepper variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pepper Production Guide
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Pepper Variety Evaluation

name: Hungarian Wax Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to a warm, sunny location after all frost danger has passed. Hungarian wax peppers are productive and easy to grow in most climates.
directions: Start indoors and transplant to warm, fertile soil after last frost; Hungarian wax pepper produces elongated, 5–6 inch pale yellow (wax-colored) fruits that mature to red and have a medium heat level (2,500–10,000 SHU) — hotter than banana peppers but milder than jalapeños. The waxy, thick-walled fruits are outstanding for pickling (Hungarian pickled peppers are a traditional condiment), stuffing, grilling, and use in Hungarian goulash and paprikash. They are also excellent raw in salads and are often confused with banana peppers in grocery stores, though the two have different heat levels and slightly different flavors. The plants are extremely productive, producing dozens of fruits per plant through the growing season.

name: Hungry Gap Kale
plantingNote: Direct sow in mid to late summer so plants are well established before winter, since this kale is grown through the cold months for a harvest the following early spring rather than in the same season it is sown.
directions: Hungry Gap takes its name from its traditional role in English kitchen gardens, filling the lean stretch in late winter and early spring when stored roots and autumn crops have run out and new spring vegetables have not yet come in. Sown in summer, plants grow slowly through autumn and stand hardy through winter frosts and snow, resuming active growth as days lengthen to supply a flush of tender leaves and shoots exactly when little else is ready. It is typically grown as a cut-and-come-again crop, with young leaves and emerging flower shoots both harvested before the plant bolts fully to seed in spring. Because it is bred for cold survival rather than fast growth, it rewards patience over a long season rather than quick turnover.

name: Husky Cherry Red Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant after frost danger passes; a stout, dark-stemmed dwarf plant that produces heavily in containers or small beds with only light staking.
directions: Transplant into full sun after the last frost, giving the sturdy, thick-stemmed vine a small cage to support its heavy cherry tomato clusters. Husky Cherry Red is an All-America Selections winner in the Husky series bred for a compact, potato-leaf indeterminate habit that concentrates energy into abundant 1-1.5 inch, deep-red, sweet-tart fruit rather than excess vine growth, making it a dependable choice for smaller gardens that still want continuous cherry tomato production. It is distinct from the larger-fruited Husky Red slicer in the same series.

name: Husky Red Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Husky Red is a semi-determinate tomato with a compact growth habit that reaches 4–5 feet and produces a heavy concentrated set of medium-large red slicing tomatoes before tapering off, making it more manageable in containers and small raised beds than fully indeterminate varieties. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer production. Husky Red carries VFNt disease resistance (Verticillium, Fusarium, nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus) — a practical package for zone 9's disease pressures. The semi-determinate habit (more compact than indeterminate varieties, more productive than determinate types) allows the plant to be managed with minimal staking — a light cage or 4-foot stake is sufficient compared to the 6–7 foot support needed for indeterminate types. Fruits average 8–10 oz, round, and ripen to deep red with good flavor.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F; transplant after last frost and stake lightly. Harvest when uniformly deep red and gives slightly to pressure. Husky Red is a hybrid tomato variety bred for compact growing habit, good disease resistance, and productive fruit set in a semi-determinate plant that provides a midpoint between the sprawling unpredictability of indeterminate varieties and the one-time heavy crop of fully determinate types. The 'Husky' designation refers to the sturdy, self-supporting nature of the plant — Husky varieties were developed specifically to stand upright with minimal staking, making them practical for gardeners without room for large cage structures or tall stakes. The semi-determinate growth habit means Husky Red sets a substantial crop of fruits over a productive period and then slows significantly, unlike true indeterminate varieties that continue to grow and produce until frost. This concentrated production is an advantage for gardeners who want a substantial harvest over a defined period for preserving, canning, or fresh eating without managing continuous production throughout a long season. For container growing, Husky Red is one of the most practical full-sized slicing tomato varieties — its compact plant produces genuine slicing tomatoes (not just cherry or grape types) in a footprint manageable in a 15–20 gallon container. The VFNt resistance package provides meaningful protection against the soilborne diseases (Verticillium, Fusarium wilt, nematodes) and tobacco mosaic virus that limit tomato success in zone 9.
sources: Burpee Seeds — Husky Red tomato compact hybrid variety development and notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Semi-determinate tomato variety comparison for container and small-space growing
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Variety Selection for Gulf South Home Gardens

name: Hutterite Soup Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May. Hutterite Soup Bean is grown primarily as a dry bean — allow pods to dry fully on the vine before threshing. In zone 9 the summer heat accelerates pod drying; harvest entire plants when most pods are dry and thresh indoors out of weather. Beans dry best in the pod; shell after the pods are fully crisp to avoid shattering. Store dried beans in cool, dark, dry conditions for multi-year storage.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil; Hutterite Soup Bean is a pole bean heirloom preserved by the Hutterite communities of the northern Great Plains and Canada — religious agricultural communities known for maintaining exceptional heirloom seed collections. The small, round, pale yellow seeds are outstanding soup beans with a creamy, slightly buttery, mild flavor and a texture that breaks down smoothly in long-simmered soups without becoming mushy — they were specifically selected and maintained by Hutterite cooks for soup making over many generations. The small seed size (similar to a navy bean) and mild flavor make Hutterite Soup Bean versatile in white bean soups, bean salads, and cassoulet-style dishes. The climbing pole bean vines are productive and the pods dry down cleanly for harvest. The Hutterite selection demonstrates exceptional adaptation to cool, short-season climates of the northern plains, but grows successfully in a wide range of conditions.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Hutterite Soup Bean Heirloom
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Hutterite Soup Bean
Montana State University Extension — Heirloom Dry Bean Varieties

name: Hutterite Soup Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Hutterite is a bush dry bean with buff-yellow seeds from the Hutterite communities of the northern Great Plains — a cold-adapted heritage variety maintained for generations by Hutterite colonies in Montana, South Dakota, and Canada, renowned for its extremely creamy, thick texture when cooked into soups and stews — its primary traditional use as the 'Sunday soup bean' of Hutterite communal kitchens.
directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in full sun; Hutterite beans tolerate short cool growing seasons (80–95 days makes them practical for zones 3–4 short summers); harvest dry pods when fully papery and rattle when shaken. Hutterite Soup Bean is an heirloom dry bean variety maintained by the Hutterite communities of the northern Great Plains — communal Anabaptist communities of German and Austrian origin who settled the Montana, South Dakota, and Alberta regions in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, bringing their traditional agricultural varieties with them from Europe. The Hutterites maintain strict communal farming traditions including seed saving, and have preserved many heritage varieties of beans, grains, and vegetables that might otherwise have been lost. Hutterite beans have buff-yellow to light cream seeds with a mild, delicate flavor and an unusually thick, creamy texture when cooked — thicker than navy beans or great northern beans, with less tendency to break down or become mushy when simmered long. This creamy texture makes them particularly well-suited for thick soups and stews in the German-Russian culinary tradition of the Hutterite communities — served weekly in communal dining halls as 'bean soup Sunday.' The variety is adapted to the short, cool growing seasons of the northern plains, making it also excellent for short-season northern gardeners who struggle with longer-season dry beans. Good flavor for use in any white-bean recipe; outstanding in soups.

name: Hyak Oca
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep after last frost; Hyak is a Cultivariable-bred, OSSI open-source oca cultivar introduced in 2016, selected for fewer but notably larger tubers.
directions: Plant tubers in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Hyak is a Cultivariable-bred oca cultivar introduced in 2016 and released as an open-source variety through the Open Source Seed Initiative, selected for producing fewer but notably larger tubers (to 4.6 inches) for higher per-plant yield than typical oca lines. White skin with red eyes covers dense, firm white flesh that carries only slight tartness when cooked, giving it a texture closer to potato than the sharper tang of many other oca cultivars. Tuber initiation begins after the fall equinox, with foliage frost-tender but tubers surviving light freezes under mulch, reaching harvest in about 7-8 months from spring planting.

name: Hyskin Onion
plantingNote: Plant sets in early autumn, about a month before the first hard frost, so plants establish roots before winter; Hyskin is a traditional British autumn-planting onion selected for reliable overwintering.
directions: Hyskin is a hardy British heirloom onion grown from autumn-planted sets to give an earlier harvest the following summer than spring-planted types. Push the small bulbs into firmed, well-drained soil in early fall, leaving just the tip exposed, and mulch lightly in the coldest regions to protect against hard freezes. Growth resumes as days lengthen in spring, and the brown-skinned bulbs size up quickly ahead of standard maincrop onions. Because overwintered onions generally store less well than spring-planted maincrop types, plan to use Hyskin bulbs within a few months of the early-summer harvest.

name: I'itoi Onion
plantingNote: Plant small bulbs about 1 inch deep and 6-8 inches apart from late summer through fall; I'itoi goes summer-dormant in Gulf Coast heat and resprouts as temperatures cool, making fall the most reliable planting window.
directions: Plant individual bulbs about an inch deep in well-drained soil in full sun, spacing them 6-8 inches apart to give clumps room to multiply. I'itoi is a heirloom perennial multiplier onion long cultivated by the Tohono O'odham of the Sonoran Desert borderlands, and it is unusual among onions for tolerating both intense summer heat and winter cold, which lets it persist as a perennial clump in Gulf Coast gardens rather than needing yearly replanting. A single planted bulb divides into eight or more bulbs within a season, and gardeners typically harvest by pulling scallion-like greens continuously while leaving part of the clump to keep multiplying underground. Dig and divide the clump when the foliage dies back in summer dormancy, replanting a portion immediately to keep the planting going indefinitely.
sources: Native Seeds/SEARCH — I'itoi Onion Growing Guide
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Pima County Master Gardener Program
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Aggie Horticulture Onion Growing Guide

name: Ianto's Return Fava Bean
plantingNote: Bred for autumn sowing in mild-winter regions; can also be spring sown in colder zones.
directions: In mild-winter regions sow in fall for a fresh-eating spring crop; this fava shrugs off cold that collapses other varieties, making it a reliable overwintering cover and food crop in one. It is named for fava collector and natural-building pioneer Ianto Evans, and its pods carry seeds ranging from pale green to dark purple and mauve, all good at the green-shell or dry-bean stage, with the young shoot tips also edible as a salad green.

name: Ibis Celeriac
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost, since germination is slow, and transplant out once nights stay reliably above freezing; Ibis tolerates an early, cool start better than many celeriac types.
directions: Ibis is a fast-developing celeriac prized by market growers for its smooth, oval-round white globes that clean up with minimal peeling loss compared to older, knobbier types. Its strong field resistance to septoria leaf spot keeps the canopy healthy through the long season needed to size up a root, and its bolt-hardiness makes it a reasonable choice for an early start under cover. As with all celeriac, keep the bed evenly and continuously moist, since inconsistent watering cracks and hollows the developing globe, and strip away side shoots through summer to concentrate growth into the root. Harvest in fall for a dense, long-storing root with a clean, nutty celery flavor.

name: Ice Cream Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed well past last frost, since this early-maturing 19th-century type was prized for extending the watermelon season into cooler regions.
directions: Ice Cream is a 19th-century American heirloom watermelon, also sold historically as Peerless, grown round with pale greenish-white rind. The original white-fleshed, white-seeded strain dates to around 1860; a sweeter pink-fleshed, black-seeded form was being offered by Philadelphia seedsmen by the early 1870s and became the more widely grown version. Its notably early maturity and tolerance of cooler nights made it a favorite in northern growing regions that struggled to ripen larger southern watermelon types. Sow in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil after the soil has warmed, and reduce watering as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sweetness.

name: Ichiban Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.5) soil in full sun when night temperatures remain above 55°F; in zone 9, transplant in mid-February to early March and again in late July for a productive fall crop.
directions: Set out transplants in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun when night temperatures stay above 55°F; Ichiban is the classic Japanese-type slender eggplant — producing long (10–12 inch), slender (1.5–2 inch diameter), cylindrical, deep purple-black fruits that are harvested young and tender with exceptionally thin, delicate skin, very few seeds, and mild, sweet, non-bitter flesh. The thin skin and low seed content of Ichiban-type eggplants produce a fundamentally different culinary result from standard oval Italian-type eggplants — the flesh is tender-soft rather than dense, the flavor is milder and sweeter, and the skin is thin enough to be eaten without peeling. This makes Ichiban particularly well-suited to quick stir-frying, grilling, and Asian cooking methods. In zone 9, Ichiban is one of the most heat-tolerant vegetables available — eggplants love the hot, humid Gulf Coast summer that defeats many vegetables, and Ichiban's slender fruit type tends to size up and set fruit more reliably in extreme heat than standard round or oval types. Harvest when the fruit skin is deep, glossy purple-black and before any softening or browning of the calyx — once the skin loses its gloss, the fruit is overripe. The plants can be maintained year-round as perennial shrubs in frost-free zone 10–11, and in zone 9 they often survive mild winters and produce prolifically in their second year.

name: Icicle Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55F. Icicle is a spineless white eggplant bred for long, slender fruit with fewer seeds than most white eggplant varieties.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pick fruit young and glossy for the mildest flavor and fewest seeds. Icicle is an AAS-winning eggplant producing long, slender, pure-white fruit on spineless plants, a genuine convenience for hand-harvesting compared to the sharp spines that guard the calyx of many eggplant varieties. It carries noticeably fewer seeds than typical white eggplant, giving a creamier, less bitter texture, and its tender skin needs no peeling. The productive, well-branched plants set fruit reliably over a long summer season. Harvest regularly while fruit is still glossy and firm, since letting fruit overripen on the plant both reduces quality and slows further production; the plant responds to frequent picking with a steady stream of new fruit through the season.
sources: All-America Selections — Icicle Eggplant winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Idaho Silverskin Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves 2 inches deep in fall in well-drained soil; softneck Silverskins tolerate slightly later fall planting than hardneck types.
directions: Idaho Silverskin is a softneck garlic strain adapted to the high desert growing conditions of southern Idaho, producing tightly wrapped, bright white bulbs with 12-18 small, densely packed cloves ideal for braiding. It stores exceptionally well, often keeping firm for 9-12 months past harvest, longer than most hardneck types. Because it lacks a hard central stalk, the flexible leaves make traditional garlic braids easy to weave for kitchen storage or gifting. Choose this variety for its outstanding shelf life and adaptability to warmer, drier growing regions where hardneck types underperform.

name: Iditarod Red Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Iditarod Red is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bred to produce unusually large red fruit on a compact plant, named for the Alaskan sled dog race.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Iditarod Red bears notably large, deep red beefsteak-style fruit for a dwarf tomato, often rivaling full-size indeterminate slicers in fruit weight despite growing on a compact, manageable plant bred through the Dwarf Tomato Project. Its combination of big fruit and small plant footprint makes it a standout choice for gardeners short on space who still want a substantial slicing tomato. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine.

name: Igloo Cauliflower
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant two to four weeks before the last frost; its short maturity window also suits a late-summer sowing for a fall crop.
directions: Igloo is a fast, open-pollinated cauliflower that reaches harvest in under two months, notably quicker than most named cauliflower cultivars. Its compact upright leaves naturally curl inward over the curd, giving a degree of self-blanching protection from sun exposure without extra tying. The speed and reliability of Igloo make it especially well suited to succession sowing through a cool season or to squeezing in a crop where the growing window is short. Select Igloo when quick, dependable snow-white curds are the priority over large head size.

name: Illikomban Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; transplant once nights stay reliably above 55F. Illikomban is a Kerala backwater-region heirloom bred for tropical heat and humidity, well matched to a Gulf Coast summer, and benefits from a sturdy stake or cage to support its long fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors with bottom heat and transplant into warm, fertile soil once nights stay reliably above 55F; harvest fruit young and glossy for the sweetest flavor and most tender texture. Illikomban is a rare heirloom from the Onattukara backwater region of South Kerala, India, named for its resemblance to an elephant tusk and prized for producing glossy, light green fruit that can reach two feet or more in length. The silky, nearly seedless flesh has a sweet, nutty flavor that cooks down quickly, making it well suited to curries and stir-fries where the fruit is sliced and absorbs bold spices readily. As a variety selected for tropical growing conditions, it takes the sustained heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer in stride, continuing to set long fruit through the hottest stretch of the season when many Western eggplant types slow production.

name: Illimani Ulluco
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in cool, moist soil after last frost; Illimani is heat-intolerant above about 75-80°F, needing a genuinely cool-summer climate to thrive.
directions: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in loose, moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Illimani is an ulluco selection with bright yellow tubers lightly speckled with pink, requiring steady irrigation through the growing season. It is heat-intolerant above roughly 75-80°F, so a genuinely cool-summer climate is necessary for good tuber set, which begins only after days shorten past the fall equinox. Harvest continues through winter as tubers size up, with cold hardiness to roughly zone 7a-9a under heavy mulch.

name: Illini Xtra Sweet Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Wait until soil has warmed well past the last frost date, since shrunken-2 kernels have almost no seed reserves and rot readily in cold, wet ground. Isolate from standard (SU) sweet corn or field corn by distance or planting date to prevent cross-pollination, which produces starchy, tough kernels.
directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile soil in blocks of at least four rows for dependable wind pollination. Illini Xtra Sweet was developed at the University of Illinois around the discovery and early commercialization of the shrunken-2 (sh2) gene, which keeps sugars from converting to starch after picking, giving it a longer sweet eating window than older sugary (SU) corns like Golden Bantam. Unlike most modern sh2 hybrids, it is open-pollinated, so seed can be saved from year to year as long as isolation from other corn types is maintained. Keep soil consistently moist from tasseling through ear fill, since the plant is somewhat less vigorous in cool or wet spring conditions than newer hybrid supersweets.
sources: University of Illinois Department of Crop Sciences — corn breeding history
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange catalog notes

name: Illinois Squash
plantingNote: Wait until soil is thoroughly warm and nighttime temperatures stay mild, since this long-season cushaw type needs a full, uninterrupted stretch of heat to fill out its large fruit.
directions: A long-vining cushaw-type heirloom grown in the southern Corn Belt since the early nineteenth century, producing oblong, crook-necked fruit with pale cream rind faintly striped in green and firm, dry flesh suited to pies and baking. Give the sprawling vines generous room, often trained along cornfield rows in its traditional culture, and keep moisture even through flowering and fruit set. Harvest once the rind resists a fingernail and the stem has dried, then cure in a warm spot for a week before moving fruit to cool, dry storage. Well-cured fruit keeps for months, a trait that made it a staple winter keeper long before modern butternut and cheese types became common.

name: Imperator Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in very deep (14–16 inches), loose, stone-free soil; Imperator-type carrots require excellent soil preparation — any stones or compaction causes forking; raised beds filled with light, sandy loam are ideal.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in very deeply prepared, loose, stone-free soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Imperator is the long, slender carrot of the grocery store — 8–10 inches long with a tapered tip, thin skin, high sugar content, and the satisfying snap of commercial carrots eaten fresh from supermarkets. It requires deep, perfectly loose, stone-free soil to reach full size without forking; raised beds with sandy loam are ideal. The flavor of home-grown Imperators freshly harvested is dramatically better than commercial versions; the high sugar content makes them outstanding for juicing, fresh eating, and the carrot sticks in lunch boxes.

name: Imperial Green Longpod Fava Bean
plantingNote: Can also be sown in October-November in mild winter regions for an early spring crop.
directions: Sow directly into fertile, moisture-retentive soil and support the tall, square-stemmed plants with stakes and string along the row in exposed gardens. Another RHS Award of Garden Merit holder, this heavy-cropping English heirloom produces pods to about a foot long packed with up to nine green-skinned beans, and its scented black-and-white flowers make it one of the more ornamental vegetables in a spring kitchen garden.

name: Imperial Star Artichoke
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; Imperial Star requires vernalization — expose seedlings to temperatures of 50–55°F for 10 consecutive days when plants have 6–8 leaves (typically 4–6 weeks after germination) to trigger first-year flower bud production. Without this cold treatment, plants grow vegetatively but do not produce artichoke buds in their first year. In zone 9, start seeds January–February and transplant March–April after cold treatment for spring harvest (April–June); a second planting (October transplant) can produce a fall-winter harvest. The vernalization cold treatment is the critical step that distinguishes Imperial Star from older artichoke types that require a full second year to produce.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 65–70°F; expose seedlings to 50–55°F for 10 days (vernalization) before transplanting. Harvest buds when still tight and before the scales begin to open. Imperial Star is the pioneering annual artichoke variety bred by Keith Mayberry of the University of California Cooperative Extension in Imperial County — the variety that made artichoke production as an annual possible for the first time. Traditional artichoke varieties (such as Green Globe) are perennials that produce their first commercial harvest in the second or third year after planting from divisions; they require mild winters to survive (zone 8–9), making them impractical or impossible in colder climates. Imperial Star changed this by introducing the genetic characteristic of first-year flowering when exposed to a period of cool temperatures (vernalization) — the same cold-stimulus mechanism that triggers biennial flowering in brassicas, adapted to artichoke. When properly vernalized, Imperial Star plants produce their first artichoke buds in the same season they are planted, allowing artichoke cultivation as an annual across a much wider range of zones and eliminating the 2–3 year establishment period. The artichokes produced are full-sized, rounded, traditional artichoke form — not meaningfully different in size, flavor, or eating quality from perennial types. Imperial Star remains the dominant annual artichoke variety decades after its introduction, maintained by Johnny's Selected Seeds and other specialty vegetable suppliers as the standard annual artichoke reference.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Imperial Star artichoke annual variety development notes
University of California Cooperative Extension — Keith Mayberry artichoke annual variety research
University of California Davis — Artichoke Production Guide

name: Improved Golden Wax Bush Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; succession sow every two to three weeks for a continuous harvest of tender wax pods.
directions: Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun once the ground has warmed. Improved Golden Wax is an early-twentieth-century refinement of the old Golden Wax bean, bred to add resistance to common bean mosaic and improve pod straightness while keeping the same flat, buttery-yellow, stringless pods and compact bush habit. Pick pods young, while still slender and snapping cleanly, since wax beans quickly develop tough strings and a fibrous texture if left to mature on the plant. Because it is an open-pollinated heirloom, seed can be saved for the next season by letting a few pods dry fully on the vine.

name: Improved White Spine Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow an inch deep after soil has warmed following last frost, since this vigorous vining type sets fruit best once nights stay reliably above 55°F.
directions: Improved White Spine is a refinement of the old American Early White Spine type, selected in the late 19th century for a shorter, blockier fruit than its predecessor. Vines produce dark green, white-spined cucumbers 5-7 inches long with crisp, mild, pure-white flesh that stays sweet without turning bitter in warm weather. It was once a dominant market and home-garden slicer before modern burpless and disease-resistant hybrids largely replaced it, but open-pollinated seed has been kept alive by heirloom seed savers. Grow on a trellis to keep fruit straight and off the soil, and pick regularly at 5-7 inches to keep vines productive through the season.

name: Inca Red Drop Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Capsicum baccatum species benefit from a heat mat during germination — the higher soil temperature (80°F+) significantly improves germination speed and percentage compared to ambient room temperature germination.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Inca Red Drop is a Capsicum baccatum pepper from the Andean tradition of Peru — the species group that also includes Aji Amarillo and Aji Cristal, characterized by the distinctly fruity, citrusy, tropical flavor profile that distinguishes Andean peppers from the more neutral heat of C. annuum varieties. Inca Red Drop produces small to medium (2–3 inch), elongated, pendant, bright-red fruits with a pointed tip — the 'drop' shape giving the variety its name. The heat level is medium to medium-hot (30,000–60,000 SHU) — more heat than a jalapeño but less than a habanero — with the fruity, berry-like undertones characteristic of quality C. baccatum selections. The fruit flavor combines the fruity complexity of the aji family with a clean, bright heat that builds persistently. In Peruvian and Bolivian cooking, aji baccatum varieties are used fresh, dried, and as the base for sauces and marinades where the fruity complexity is as important as the heat level. The long season to maturity (90–120 days from transplant) is well-suited to zone 9's extended warm season. The ornamental value of the small red pendant fruits on attractive plants makes Inca Red Drop equally at home in ornamental pepper displays and in dedicated vegetable gardens.

name: Incredible Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows wide for adequate wind pollination; Incredible is an se (sugar-enhanced) type that holds quality on the plant and after harvest better than su types. In zone 9, plant March–April for a May–June harvest, or plant August–September for a fall crop. SE types can be isolated from sh2 (supersweet) varieties but can be planted adjacent to su types without significant quality reduction.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows; apply balanced fertilizer at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Incredible is one of the most respected and widely grown sugar-enhanced (se) yellow sweet corn hybrids in American home and market gardens — a Seminis-developed variety that consistently rates among the top performers for flavor, tenderness, and eating quality across multiple decades of university and commercial variety trials. The se (also called EH, everlasting heritage, or sugar-enhanced) gene doubles the sugar content at harvest compared to standard su varieties, and — critically — slows the conversion of sugar to starch after picking, giving se-type corn a 2–4 day postharvest quality window compared to the 24-hour window of su types. This extended holding quality made se types like Incredible a significant practical advance for home gardeners, allowing harvest and consumption at leisure rather than immediately. The 8–9 inch ears carry 16–18 rows of golden-yellow, tender, plump kernels with excellent flavor that is noticeably sweeter and more tender than older su types. Incredible consistently places first or second in tasting panels for yellow se corn and offers good disease resistance including northern corn leaf blight tolerance. An outstanding all-around sweet corn variety that has earned its perennial top-seller status.
sources: Seminis Vegetable Seeds — Incredible sweet corn variety development
University of Illinois Extension — Sweet Corn Variety Trial
North Carolina State University Extension — Sweet Corn Variety Evaluation

name: Indian Long Bitter Melon
plantingNote: Nick or soak the hard seed coat before sowing and plant after soil is thoroughly warm; this narrow, spiny-warted Indian-type bitter melon needs a long hot stretch and a sturdy trellis to produce well.
directions: Indian Long is the slender, pointed-ended bitter melon type covered in sharp, jagged, triangular ridges rather than the smooth warts typical of Chinese and Taiwanese cultivars, and it carries the sharper, more assertive bitterness favored in Indian and Vietnamese cooking. Fruits are best picked young and firm, 6-9 inches long, while still glossy green, for use in stuffed karela, stir-fries, and curries; the intense bitterness mellows somewhat with salting, parboiling, or frying. The vigorous climbing vine performs well in Gulf Coast heat and humidity but benefits from a strong trellis and consistent moisture during fruit set to avoid stress-induced flower drop. Seeds have a hard, slow-to-imbibe coat, so nicking or an overnight soak speeds germination noticeably.

name: Indian Pearl Millet
plantingNote: Direct sow after danger of frost once soil has warmed, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early and transplant out; this millet grows fast enough to still produce a crop after a late, cool spring ruins corn.
directions: Indian Pearl Millet is a grain-type strain of pearl millet grown for its distinctive blue-grey seed rather than for forage, producing corn-like stalks topped with dense, cattail-shaped seed heads. It is markedly drought-tolerant and grows quickly enough to take advantage of short windows of good weather, often outperforming corn or wheat in a poor season. The grain is naturally gluten-free and notably high in protein, potassium, and B vitamins, and can be ground into flour, cooked whole as a porridge grain, or left for backyard poultry to forage. Cut whole seed heads once the grain has hardened and dried, then thresh by rubbing the heads between gloved hands or over a screen.

name: Indian Stripe Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Indian Stripe shares the dark-shouldered coloring and potato-leaf foliage common to the Cherokee Purple family of heirlooms.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, well-drained soil after frost risk passes, bracing plants with a sturdy cage. Indian Stripe produces potato-leaf vines and dusky purple-pink beefsteak fruit with darker, almost black-green shoulders, part of the same dark-fruited heirloom lineage as Cherokee Purple, with a deep, smoky-sweet flavor favored by collectors of purple and black tomatoes. Because the unusual coloring makes ripeness hard to judge by color alone, check for a slight give at the blossom end before picking. Fruit is best used fresh, since the thinner skin and soft texture of dark-fruited heirlooms don't hold up as well to long storage.

name: Indigo Apple Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Indigo Apple is an indeterminate variety that requires staking or caging. The distinctive blue-black anthocyanin pigmentation develops on sun-exposed areas of the fruit and fades on shaded portions, creating a characteristic bicolor appearance (blue-black on top, red on the shaded side). In zone 9, transplant February–March; the deep blue color develops most intensely in bright sun and cool temperatures.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun for maximum anthocyanin expression — the blue-black pigmentation only develops in sun-exposed areas and fades entirely in shade. Indigo Apple is a product of the Oregon State University tomato breeding program led by Dr. Jim Myers, who developed the 'Indigo' series of tomatoes by crossing commercial tomatoes with a wild species (Solanum cheesmaniae from the Galapagos Islands) that carries genes for anthocyanin production in fruit tissue. The anthocyanins (the same pigments in blueberries and purple cabbage) accumulate in the skin of Indigo tomatoes when exposed to sunlight, creating a striking blue-black to deep purple coloration on the sun side while the shaded side remains red — a unique bicolor effect that changes as the fruit ripens and is genuinely unlike any other common tomato. Indigo Apple produces medium-sized (3–4 oz) round fruits that hang in clusters; the flesh inside is red and has good complex tomato flavor with moderate sweetness and acidity. Beyond the visual novelty, the anthocyanin compounds are genuine antioxidants of nutritional significance — the same compounds studied for potential health benefits in blueberries. Indigo Apple, Indigo Rose, Indigo Blue Berries, and other Indigo series varieties represent a fascinating example of targeted nutritional breeding combined with ornamental appeal.
sources: Oregon State University Department of Horticulture — Indigo tomato breeding program
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Indigo Apple tomato variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Indigo series tomato collection

name: Indigo Radicchio
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks after the last frost for a summer crop, or in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop. Unlike many heirloom Chioggia-type radicchios that need a hard freeze to redden and firm up, 'Indigo' reliably forms tight round heads without an extended cold period, making it one of the few radicchios suited to spring planting.
directions: This early-maturing F1 hybrid produces tight, softball-sized heads of glossy garnet-red leaves with crisp white ribs in as few as 55 to 65 days, making it one of the more dependable radicchios for gardeners outside the classic Italian growing regions. Unlike many open-pollinated Chioggia-type radicchios that need a hard freeze to redden and firm up, 'Indigo' forms well-blanched, uniformly colored heads even from a spring sowing, though a light fall frost still sweetens the flavor. Harvest as soon as heads feel firm to the touch, since they can split or bolt if left too long in warm weather. Its dependable heading habit and shorter cycle make it a good choice for succession planting through the growing season.

name: Innovator Shallot
plantingNote: Start true seed indoors 6-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out after hardening off, the same way as other seed-grown F1 shallots.
directions: Innovator is a Conservor-type F1 hybrid true-seed shallot producing elongated, mostly single bulbs with reddish-bronze papery skin, bred with improved field tolerance to downy mildew compared with older shallot lines. Start it indoors and transplant like other seed-grown shallots rather than planting it from sets, keeping the bed evenly moist during establishment and tapering off water as the tops begin to yellow and fall. It is suited to both fresh-market use and long-term storage, and its disease tolerance makes it a reliable choice in regions where downy mildew pressure on alliums runs high.

name: Iochief Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least four rows in fertile soil with consistent moisture during pollination.
directions: Direct sow in blocks of at least four rows in fertile soil with consistent moisture during pollination for full, well-filled ears. Iochief was released by Iowa State University in the early 1950s as a productive, open-pollinated main-season yellow sweet corn, at a time when hybrid sweet corns were rapidly displacing older varieties, and it has survived among heirloom growers for its vigorous stalks, large ears, and genuinely excellent old-fashioned sweet corn flavor. It remains a solid choice for gardeners who want to save their own seed year to year, something not possible with modern hybrid sweet corns.

name: Iran Winter Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed; tolerates heat and dry conditions better than many C. maxima types.
directions: Iran is a rare heirloom winter squash originally collected in northeastern Iran in the 1940s and preserved in the USDA seed bank before being reintroduced to home gardeners by Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds. Long, vigorous, heat- and drought-tolerant vines produce large round-oval fruits with silvery-green skin mottled in pale orange. The orange flesh is sweet and can be baked, roasted, or pureed like other Cucurbita maxima squash. Its notable heat and drought tolerance make it a useful choice for hot, dry-summer gardens.

name: Ireland Creek Annie Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; this English-origin bush bean was carried to British Columbia in the 1920s and has been maintained at Ireland Creek Farm ever since.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep directly in the garden once soil has warmed after the last frost, spacing plants 4-6 inches apart in rows 18-24 inches apart. Ireland Creek Annie is a compact, heavy-yielding bush dry bean prized for its unusually early maturity and cool-tolerance, making it a reliable choice for short-season gardens. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant before shelling; the buff-yellow to mustard-colored seeds cook down quickly to a rich, creamy texture well suited to soups and purees. Keep beds weeded and evenly moist through flowering and pod set, then withhold water as pods mature and dry for harvest.

name: Irish Cobbler Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost, or January-February in zone 9, 4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil; Irish Cobbler's quick maturity fits neatly into a Gulf Coast winter growing window before summer heat arrives.
directions: Irish Cobbler is one of the oldest potato varieties still grown in North America, dating to the late 19th century and long valued as one of the earliest potatoes to reach harvestable size. The round-to-irregular tubers have thin, buff-tan skin with shallow eyes and dense white flesh that is excellent for boiling, mashing, and creaming, though it does not store as long as later-maturing varieties. Because it matures quickly, Irish Cobbler is a good fit for a Gulf Coast winter-planted potato crop that needs to finish before summer heat arrives. Plant certified seed pieces in late winter and hill the developing plants as they grow to keep tubers covered and prevent greening.

name: Irish White Potato
plantingNote: A long-season heritage variety; give it the full maincrop window and expect tubers closely resembling the famous Irish Lumper in shape.
directions: Irish White was raised around 1882 by Robert Christie of Ballytaggart and became a traditional kitchen-garden potato in County Donegal and County Antrim. The tubers are long and irregularly shaped with white skin and notably deep eyes, closely resembling the famine-era Lumper in form though kept alive today mainly by heritage growers rather than commercial farms. Plant whole or cut seed pieces in deep, loose soil and hill the rows as the plants grow to shade the tubers from sunlight. Give it a full maincrop season before lifting, and expect a historic, old-fashioned potato better suited to boiling and mashing than to modern chip production.

name: Iron Clay Pea
scientificName: Vigna unguiculata subsp. unguiculata 'Iron and Clay'
plantingNote: Broadcast or drill after soil reaches 65°F; Iron Clay is typically seeded at 40–80 lbs per acre or 1–2 lbs per 1000 sq ft. In zone 9 the primary window is April–July; a late summer planting (July–August) provides excellent late-season biomass before frost.
directions: Broadcast at 40–80 lbs per acre (or 1 lb per 1000 sq ft) onto a loosened seedbed and rake in lightly; no inoculant is required in soil with prior cowpea history, but rhizobium inoculant greatly improves nitrogen fixation in new ground. Iron Clay is a hybrid between iron cowpea and clay cowpea types bred specifically as a summer cover crop and forage legume for the southeastern US. It is one of the most heat- and drought-tolerant summer cover crops available, providing dense weed suppression, substantial nitrogen fixation (80–150 lbs N/acre under ideal conditions), erosion control, and wildlife habitat simultaneously. The vining, semi-prostrate plants knit together to form a dense ground cover; deer and other wildlife browse the foliage heavily, making it popular as a food-plot crop. Terminate before seed set by mowing or incorporation. In a garden context, till under green at peak vegetative growth for maximum nitrogen credit.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Guide — Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata)
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Cover Crops for Texas
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Summer Cover Crops

name: Iron Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed; Iron was documented by USDA plant pathologist W. A. Orton in 1903 as one of the first cowpea varieties bred specifically for resistance to root-knot nematode and cowpea (Fusarium) wilt.
directions: Iron cowpea is a tall, half-bush heirloom Southern pea with a landmark place in American crop breeding history — one of the earliest cultivars developed with genuine, durable resistance to root-knot nematode and cowpea wilt, two soil-borne problems that devastated cowpea plantings across the South before its release in the early 1900s. Its resistance genetics went on to found much of the region's cowpea breeding, most visibly in the blended Iron and Clay mix still grown today as a cover crop and forage, and later in modern resistant releases such as California Blackeye 5. Grown as a food crop, Iron produces good yields of peas suited to fresh shelling or drying, performing reliably on sandy, nematode-prone soils where susceptible varieties decline mid-season. Like other Southern peas it fixes nitrogen as it grows, so it also serves well as a soil-building rotation crop between heavier feeding vegetables.
sources: USDA Bureau of Plant Industry — Iron Cowpea, a Variety Resistant to Wilt and Root-Knot (1903)
USDA National Agricultural Library — George Washington Carver Historical Publications on Crop Development: Cowpeas
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Iron and Clay Southern Pea notes

name: Iron Lady Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Iron Lady is indeterminate, requiring staking or caging. In zone 9, transplant February–March for spring production — the heat-resistance and disease package makes Iron Lady one of the better choices for the challenging Gulf South summer, though even Iron Lady will slow in peak summer heat. The disease resistance package (Early Blight, Late Blight, Septoria Leaf Spot, Fusarium and Verticillium wilts, plus tolerance to TSWV) is specifically valuable in the humid Gulf South where foliar fungal diseases devastate unprotected varieties within weeks of transplant. A fall planting (September transplant) often extends production into December.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–80°F; transplant after hardening off. Stake or cage immediately; Iron Lady is an indeterminate vine requiring vertical support. Iron Lady is a disease-resistant F1 hybrid tomato developed through the Cornell University Vegetable Program in collaboration with the Public Seed Initiative — a breeding program committed to developing open-access (non-patented) vegetable varieties for organic and conventional farmers. Iron Lady carries one of the most comprehensive disease-resistance packages available in a slicing tomato: confirmed resistance to Early Blight (Alternaria solani), Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans — the disease responsible for the Irish Potato Famine), Septoria Leaf Spot, and Fusarium and Verticillium wilt, plus tolerance to Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus. For Gulf South gardeners in zone 8–10, where the combination of high humidity, warm nights, and heavy summer rainfall creates near-ideal conditions for fungal tomato diseases, Iron Lady's disease package addresses the primary reason tomato plants fail prematurely in the region — not heat or drought, but the rapid defoliation by Early and Late Blight that kills plants before the crop is fully harvested. The tomatoes themselves are medium-sized (4–8 oz), round, deep red, with excellent flavor quality for a disease-resistant type — a notable achievement given that breeders historically faced trade-offs between disease resistance and eating quality.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Program — Iron Lady tomato development and disease resistance notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Iron Lady tomato variety description
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Tomato Variety Recommendations for the Gulf South

name: Iron Man Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun; the vigorous, powdery-mildew-tolerant vine and rot-resistant fruit hold up well through a long, muggy Gulf Coast season.
directions: Direct sow in hills once the soil has warmed, allowing the full, vigorous vines plenty of room to run through the second half of the growing season. Iron Man produces round, dark orange fruit only 6-7 inches across and 3-4 pounds, sized for painting projects, porch groupings, and small-space carving rather than large jack-o'-lanterns. The unusually hard rind resists Fusarium and Phytophthora fruit rot, an advantage in the wet, humid soils common along the Gulf Coast, and cured fruit stores for months without softening. Harvest once the shell has fully hardened and cannot be dented with a thumbnail, then cure in a warm, dry spot for a week before moving pumpkins into long-term storage.

name: Ironbark Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after all danger of frost; needs a long, warm season and ample vine room.
directions: Ironbark is an Australian heirloom dating to the Victorian gold-rush era of the 1850s, prized for its thick, hard, dark blue-green bumpy rind that is notoriously difficult to cut, which gives the variety its name. The round, flattened, deeply ribbed fruits weigh roughly 5-18 lbs and are packed with dense, dry, bright orange flesh that is sweet and excellent baked or roasted. The exceptionally hard rind gives Ironbark outstanding storage life, often keeping well past other winter squash. It remains a popular home-garden variety in Australia but is still uncommon in North America.

name: Iroquois Melon
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 3 to 4 weeks before the last expected frost date, then transplant out once nights stay reliably above 50°F.
directions: Start seeds indoors in peat pots 3 to 4 weeks before your last frost date, or direct sow once soil has warmed past 70°F, then thin or space plants generously to allow the sprawling vines room to run. Released by Cornell plant breeder Henry Munger in 1944 as a cross of 'Minnesota 99-36' and 'Bender's Surprise', Iroquois was the first muskmelon bred specifically for resistance to Fusarium wilt. Its thick, heavily netted rind covers deep salmon-orange flesh with a rich, musky-sweet flavor, and its disease tolerance made it a long-time favorite for northern and Midwestern home gardens.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

name: Ishikura Bunching Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow or start transplants in early spring; Ishikura can also be sown in late summer for a fall and winter harvest in zone 9. Successive sowings every 3-4 weeks keep a steady supply of scallions coming.
directions: Sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to about an inch apart; hilling soil up around the base as plants grow blanches the shanks white and tender. Ishikura is a classic Japanese bunching onion, or negi, that forms a long, straight, pure-white shank without ever swelling into a bulb, staying tender and mild even as it grows tall. It is slow to bolt, tolerates both summer heat and winter cold well, and can be harvested at scallion size or left to mature into thick, leek-like stalks. Because it does not form a storage bulb, Ishikura is best used fresh, sliced into stir-fries, soups, and as a raw garnish; cut-and-come-again harvesting of the outer leaves extends the picking season from a single planting.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Bunching Onion Growing Guide

name: Isis Candy Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Isis Candy is an indeterminate open-pollinated cherry tomato producing 1-inch round fruits that ripen to cherry-red with distinctive gold-yellow cat's-eye markings at the blossom end and subtle pink striping on the skin. In zone 9, transplant March–April and stake or cage; indeterminate types need support throughout the season. Isis Candy is an open-pollinated variety developed by tomato breeder Carolyn Male, one of the foremost American heirloom tomato breeders and authors of the landmark book '100 Heirloom Tomatoes for the American Garden.' The variety combines outstanding flavor — consistently rated among the sweetest and most complex of cherry tomatoes — with the striking visual appearance of the bicolor pattern. The gold-yellow markings develop clearly at full ripe (some cherry varieties show ambiguous color breaks; Isis Candy's blossom end marking is a clear, distinct gold circle on red). Production is prolific throughout zone 9's warm season.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and cage or stake. Harvest when fully red with gold markings showing clearly at blossom end. Isis Candy is an open-pollinated cherry tomato variety developed by Carolyn Male, a New York tomato enthusiast and breeder who spent decades collecting and evaluating heirloom tomato varieties and documented her work in the widely respected '100 Heirloom Tomatoes for the American Garden.' Among cherry tomato varieties, Isis Candy stands out for both flavor quality and visual appeal: the flavor combines genuine tomato sweetness with a candy-like fruitiness and enough natural acidity to provide complexity rather than simple sweetness — the kind of balanced flavor profile that makes cherry tomatoes irresistible eaten directly off the vine. The appearance is striking: when ripe, the 1-inch round fruits display a candy-apple red with distinctive gold 'cat's-eye' markings — a golden-yellow circle centered at the blossom end — and sometimes faint pink striping on the red skin, creating a two-tone effect visible even from a distance in the garden. This visual distinction makes Isis Candy particularly attractive for multi-variety cherry tomato plantings where color diversity adds visual interest, and for farmers market and fresh-eating contexts where the unusual patterning captures attention. The variety is open-pollinated and stable, meaning saved seed reliably reproduces the variety's characteristics — an advantage over F1 hybrid cherry types that cannot be seed-saved. For zone 9 gardeners, Isis Candy's heat tolerance and prolific production throughout the Gulf Coast's long warm season make it a consistently productive choice among open-pollinated cherry varieties.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Isis Candy cherry tomato breeder documentation (Carolyn Male)
Seed Savers Exchange — Isis Candy open-pollinated cherry tomato variety notes
Carolyn Male — '100 Heirloom Tomatoes for the American Garden' (Workman Publishing)

name: Isis Candy Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Isis Candy is a productive indeterminate vine that benefits from staking or caging and bears heavily over a long season.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost, staking or caging the vigorous indeterminate vines for support. Isis Candy is a beloved heirloom cherry tomato producing round, golden-yellow fruit marbled and streaked with red, with a rich, sweet, well-balanced flavor that consistently ranks among the best-tasting cherry tomatoes in home garden trials. Plants are heavy, reliable producers over a long season, and the striking bicolor fruit makes an attractive addition to a mixed cherry tomato harvest or salad. Pick fruit as it fully colors for the best flavor, and water consistently to reduce splitting, since the thin skin is prone to cracking after heavy rain.

name: Islander Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after danger of frost has passed; Islander's compact habit makes it well suited to containers and patio plantings as well as garden beds.
directions: Islander is an All-America Selections-winning bell-type pepper bred for a striking color progression, with fruits maturing from ivory through lavender-purple before finishing orange and finally red, so the plant often carries several colors simultaneously. Start seed indoors in warm conditions and transplant after the soil has warmed, since fruit color development is strongest in full sun and consistent warmth. The compact, well-branched plants were selected as much for garden and container ornamental value as for eating quality, though the blocky fruit is genuinely sweet and crisp at any ripeness stage. Pick continually through the color stages both to enjoy the visual display and to keep the plant setting new fruit.

name: Italia Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Italia is an early corno di toro-type Italian frying pepper, and its compact, upright habit makes it a good choice for smaller beds or containers.
directions: Italia is a corno di toro-type sweet pepper introduced to American gardeners by Johnny's Selected Seeds in 1987, with curved, tapering fruit that looks like a long hot pepper but carries no heat at all. Plants are upright and not very branching, reaching a modest 14-28 inches, and set long (5-8 inch) thin-walled pods that can be picked green as early as 55 days after transplant or left to ripen to red by 70-80 days for fuller sweetness. The sweet, thin flesh is well suited to frying in olive oil, roasting, and fresh eating, in keeping with traditional Italian frying-pepper use. Its early maturity and compact size make it a practical option for gardeners with limited space or shorter growing seasons.

name: Italian Heirloom Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the indeterminate vine as it grows.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Italian Heirloom was preserved and shared through the Seed Savers Exchange network from a family's own long-held Italian seed stock, producing large, distinctively ribbed and slightly flattened, deep pink-red fruit with sweet, well-balanced, richly flavored flesh reminiscent of classic Italian slicing tomatoes. The pronounced ribbing and irregular shoulders give the fruit an old-world, rustic appearance that sets it apart from the smoother modern hybrids most gardeners are used to, while the vigorous indeterminate vine produces reliably through a long season. Water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking around the ribbed shoulders, and harvest once fruit fully colors for the best flavor.

name: Ithaca Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in fall for a cool-season crop.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to ten to twelve inches apart. Ithaca was bred at Cornell University for good resistance to tipburn, a physiological disorder that causes browning at leaf edges in crisphead lettuce under heat or irregular watering stress, along with a degree of heat tolerance that lets it hold quality longer into warm weather than many older iceberg-type varieties. The dense, crisp, pale green heads deliver the familiar crunchy texture prized in classic iceberg lettuce, well suited to sandwiches and salads calling for texture over deep flavor. Keep soil consistently moist through head formation to further reduce tipburn risk, and harvest once heads feel firm and solid when gently squeezed.

name: Ivory Teff
plantingNote: Sow after last frost once soil is warm; ivory teff is the pale, mild-flavored seed class used for lighter-colored injera and other food-grade teff products.
directions: Mix the dust-fine seed with dry sand for even coverage and surface-broadcast onto a firm, rolled seedbed, pressing lightly rather than covering, since ivory teff germinates poorly if buried. This is the pale-seeded food-grade class prized for producing lighter-colored injera and for grinding into a mild flour, in contrast to the stronger flavor of brown teff. Cut whole plants near the base once most of the fine seed heads have turned from green to golden-tan but before shattering begins in wind, then finish drying under cover for a week or more. Thresh gently by beating bundles over a smooth tarp and winnow in the lightest possible breeze, as the tiny ivory seed is easily lost.

name: Jack Be Little Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–June. Jack Be Little is a compact vining plant that produces many fruits — allow all fruits to develop since the small size means production of 10–20 fruits per plant is achievable. The tiny fruits cure in place on the vine; harvest when stems are dry and skin is hard. Cured properly (2 weeks in warm, dry conditions) the fruits store for 3–4 months as decorative pieces and can still be eaten after the ornamental season.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Jack Be Little is an All-America Selections award-winning miniature pumpkin producing perfectly proportioned, deeply ribbed, orange fruits only 2–4 inches across and weighing 3–8 ounces — a precisely scaled-down replica of a full-size pumpkin that has become one of the most popular autumn decorating elements for tabletop arrangements, wreaths, and centerpieces since winning its AAS award in 1989. The tiny fruits are also fully edible: halved and roasted in the oven or microwave, they produce a small amount of dense, sweet, pumpkin-flavored flesh that can be eaten directly from the shell — the shell becoming the natural serving bowl. The vine produces abundantly (often 10–15 fruits per plant) from a relatively compact plant footprint, making it highly space-efficient for ornamental pumpkin production. Jack Be Little became the defining mini pumpkin that launched the specialty ornamental squash market and has remained the most recognized mini pumpkin variety.
sources: All-America Selections — Jack Be Little Pumpkin 1989 Award
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Miniature Pumpkin Production
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Ornamental Pumpkin Varieties

name: Jackson Wonder Lima Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Jackson Wonder is earlier and more heat-tolerant than most Lima beans, making it the best-adapted Lima for the Gulf Coast and Deep South. In zone 9 plant March–May for spring and again July–August for a fall crop.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jackson Wonder is a compact, bush-type speckled lima bean that has been the standard Lima for Southern kitchen gardens since the 1880s — it is heat-tolerant where other lima varieties fail to set pods and is the recommended lima bean variety for zone 8–9 gardens. The small-seeded beans are harvested green (fresh shelled) as baby limas at 50–60 days or left to dry on the vine for use as dried beans; the dried seeds are attractively speckled in purple and white. Inoculate seeds with lima bean rhizobia at planting for nitrogen fixation; no fertilization is needed beyond a light dose of phosphorus and potassium at planting.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Jackson Wonder Lima Bean
Alabama Cooperative Extension — Lima Beans for Alabama
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Lima Bean Production

name: Jacob's Cattle Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Jacob's Cattle is a dry bean grown to full maturity and dried on the plant. In zone 9, plant March–May; pods dry on the plant in August–September when the garden has dried after summer heat. Shell and store dried beans in airtight containers. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant until papery and rattling before harvest — or cut the whole plant at the soil line and hang to finish drying indoors in humid fall weather. Jacob's Cattle is a bush bean (18–24 inch plants) requiring no support.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 4–6 inches. Allow pods to dry completely on the plant before harvesting. Shell and store in airtight containers. Jacob's Cattle Bean (also called Trout Bean or Dalmatian Bean in some regions) is a New England heirloom dry bean with one of the most visually distinctive appearances in the bean world — white beans irregularly splashed and dotted with maroon-red spots in a pattern that resembles the speckled coat of Jacob's Cattle described in the Book of Genesis, from which the variety's evocative name derives. The spotted appearance is due to anthocyanin pigmentation in the seed coat that creates the irregular, non-repeating pattern on each individual bean — a genetic expression that varies slightly bean to bean within the variety but maintains the distinctive red-on-white motif overall. Jacob's Cattle has been grown in Maine and New England since at least the mid-19th century, where it became the traditional bean for authentic New England-style baked beans: the creamy, meaty texture and moderately earthy flavor of Jacob's Cattle holds up beautifully in long, slow cooking with salt pork and molasses, developing richness without falling apart or becoming mushy. The beans are also excellent in soups, stews, and chili, where the spotted appearance adds visual interest to the finished dish. Being open-pollinated, seed can be saved indefinitely from the best plants.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Jacob's Cattle bean variety history and New England documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Jacob's Cattle dry bean variety notes
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Heirloom Dry Bean Variety Evaluation

name: Jacob's Cattle Gold Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; no staking needed, as this is a compact bush-type dry bean.
directions: A stabilized cross between the classic maroon-and-white Jacob's Cattle bean and a paint-type bean, this variety produces oblong white seeds dotted with striking golden-tan spots instead of the traditional dark red. Sturdy bush plants stay compact and self-supporting, bearing 4 to 5 inch pods with 6 to 8 seeds each that should be left on the plant until pods rattle and dry down fully for storage beans. The golden speckled beans hold their shape well through long cooking and take on other flavors readily, making them a favorite for baked beans, chili, and soups. Because it is bush-habit and matures reliably within a single season, it suits gardeners who want a distinctive heirloom dry bean without trellising.

name: Jade Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; harvest Jade pods when they are 4–5 inches long and still slender — the smaller pods are more tender and flavorful. Unlike standard snap beans, Jade should not be allowed to develop visible seeds inside before harvest, or the pods become fibrous. Regular picking every 2–3 days maximizes quality and production.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Jade is a refined bush snap bean with slender, deep jade-green pods that occupies a quality niche between standard American snap beans and the more delicate French haricot vert types. The pods are round (not flat), uniformly dark green, stringless, and noticeably more tender and flavorful than standard bean varieties when harvested young at 4–5 inches — with a mild, sweet, delicate green bean taste and a fine texture that makes them excellent for light steaming, quick sautéing with butter and herbs, and all preparations where bean flavor is the centerpiece. Unlike the very slender haricot vert types (such as Maxibel or Espada), Jade has a slightly more substantial pod that is easier to harvest and handle in quantity, while still maintaining considerably more refinement than standard snap beans like Blue Lake or Provider. A popular choice for market gardeners, farm-stand vendors, and home gardeners who want a more elegant snap bean without committing to the exacting harvest schedule of true filet-type beans. Very productive and relatively heat-tolerant for a fine-podded bean.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Jade bean variety notes
