University of Massachusetts Cooperative Extension — Bean Variety Trials

name: Jade Cross Brussels Sprout
plantingNote: Start indoors 12–16 weeks before first fall frost for fall harvest; Jade Cross is an All-America Selections award-winning F1 hybrid Brussels sprout notably more tolerant of warm fall temperatures than heirloom types like Long Island Improved — it sets sprouts at higher temperatures, making it the recommended variety for zones 7–9 where fall temperatures remain warmer longer and standard Brussels sprouts may fail to develop tight, round sprouts.
directions: Start seeds indoors 12–16 weeks before first fall frost at 70–75°F; transplant into rich, firm, well-drained soil with consistent moisture; stake tall plants; when bottom sprouts reach marble size, remove the growing tip ('topping') to concentrate energy; harvest sprouts from the bottom upward when 1–1.5 inches across. Jade Cross is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning F1 hybrid Brussels sprout that has been a reliable performer in American gardens since its introduction; it was specifically developed for improved performance in warmer fall conditions compared to the standard heirloom types. Standard Brussels sprouts (Long Island Improved, Catskill, etc.) require consistently cool temperatures (40–60°F) to develop tight, round, high-quality sprouts; in zones 7–9 where fall remains warm well into October, these traditional varieties often produce loose, bitter, or poorly formed sprouts. Jade Cross was selected for earlier sprout initiation at warmer temperatures, allowing it to begin developing sprouts before cool weather arrives and then perfect them as temperatures fall. The sprouts are uniform, round, tightly wrapped, and excellent in flavor — milder and sweeter than heirloom types, with the classic Brussels sprout character that intensifies after frost exposure. Jade Cross is the standard recommendation from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and Louisiana State University AgCenter for Gulf South Brussels sprout production.

name: Jade Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant April–June for main crop, or as early as March under row cover. Jade okra is spineless and one of the most productive varieties per plant. Soak seeds 8–12 hours before planting to speed germination. In zone 9 fall plantings (August–September) often produce high-quality pods as temperatures cool.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Jade is a spineless, open-pollinated okra producing straight, medium-green, ribbed pods with a texture and appearance valued in Asian cuisine — the name reflects its appeal in Chinese and Vietnamese cooking where the mild-flavored, tender pods are stir-fried, braised, and used in soups. The medium-height plant produces generous yields of pods that hold their quality for harvest at 3–4 inches without becoming fibrous as quickly as some varieties. The spineless habit makes harvesting considerably more comfortable than thorny-spine varieties and allows the plants to be handled without protective clothing. In zone 9 Jade okra thrives in the long, hot growing season and can be planted in spring for an early summer crop and again in late summer for a fall harvest — two full production cycles are achievable in zone 9.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Okra Variety Trials
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Spineless Okra Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Okra Production Guide

name: Jade Pagoda Chinese Cabbage
plantingNote: Direct sow in well-tilled, fertile soil or start indoors and transplant; Jade Pagoda is best grown as a fall crop in zone 9 — direct sow August through September for harvest November through January. Spring crops can bolt in warming weather; direct sow March for early spring harvest. Thin to 12–15 inches for full-sized heads. Chinese cabbage is a heavy feeder and benefits from consistent moisture and regular nitrogen applications.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in well-tilled, fertile soil; thin to 12–15 inches for full-sized heads. Jade Pagoda is a tall, columnar Chinese cabbage (napa cabbage) that differs in form from the more squat, barrel-shaped types like Michihili and standard napa types — the heads are distinctly elongated (14–18 inches tall, 8–10 inches wide), with a compact, upright, tower-like form reminiscent of a pagoda spire, which gives the variety its name. The elongated form produces a higher proportion of the central, tightly blanched, pale yellow-green interior leaves relative to total head weight — the most tender and mildly flavored portion — compared to rounder, more compact types. Jade Pagoda has excellent storage quality: the tight, dense heads keep well in refrigeration (4–6 weeks) without significant quality loss. The flavor is mild, slightly sweet, and delicate — the characteristic Chinese cabbage flavor that is far milder than Western cabbage types — excellent raw in salads (particularly Korean kimchi-style preparations), cooked in stir-fries and soups, and in the braised Chinese preparations where the sweet, soft, cooked texture complements soy and ginger sauces. An excellent variety for gardeners who want to grow Chinese cabbage and experiment with Korean or Asian cooking traditions.
sources: Bejo Seeds — Jade Pagoda Chinese cabbage variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Chinese cabbage variety comparison
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Chinese Cabbage Production

name: Jalafuego Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 55°F; Jalafuego was named a national All-America Selections winner in 2011 for its heavy, uniform yields.
directions: Jalafuego produces glossy, blocky jalapenos that run noticeably hotter than standard types like Early Jalapeno, ripening on compact, well-branched plants that set fruit heavily over a long season. It earned an AAS award for combining that extra heat with high yield and good field tolerance to several strains of bacterial leaf spot, a disease that thrives in the Gulf South's humid summers. Harvest pods green for classic jalapeno heat and crunch, or let some ripen to red on the plant for a sweeter, even spicier finish. Consistent moisture and full sun keep plants productive and help prevent blossom drop during peak summer heat.

name: Jalapeño Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun 2–4 weeks after the last frost date when soil is reliably warm; in zone 9, jalapeños often overwinter as perennials and produce a second season's harvest.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the soil has warmed thoroughly; Jalapeño is the most widely grown and most universally recognized hot pepper in American gardens and cuisine — a medium-heat (2,500–8,000 Scoville units) pepper with thick-walled, cylindrical to conical, dark-green fruits that turn red when fully mature. The glossy green jalapeños are harvested at 2.5–3.5 inches long before turning red for the classic fresh, pickled, and canned jalapeño used in Mexican, Tex-Mex, and American cooking. Red-ripe jalapeños are sweeter and somewhat hotter than green-harvested fruit. In zone 9, jalapeños thrive through the warm season and often survive mild winters as perennials, re-sprouting from the base to produce a large, established second-year plant with significantly higher fruit production than first-year plants. The compact, bushy habit requires no staking and makes jalapeños appropriate for container culture as well as garden beds. Harvest green jalapeños when the fruit is firm and full-sized; allow some fruits to turn red for a sweeter product. Excellent for fresh salsa, pickling, stuffing (chile poppers/jalapeños stuffed with cream cheese), and smoking (chipotles are dried, smoked jalapeños).
sources: University of New Mexico Cooperative Extension

name: Jamaican Hot Chocolate Pepper
plantingNote: Start on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before last frost; Jamaican Hot Chocolate is a chocolate-brown habanero-type pepper from Jamaica with fruity, smoky heat.
directions: Germinate seeds at 80-85°F on a heat mat; transplant after last frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun with regular moisture. Jamaican Hot Chocolate bears wrinkled, lantern-shaped pods that ripen to a deep chocolate-brown, carrying the characteristic fruity, floral habanero aroma along with intense heat and a subtly smoky depth of flavor that distinguishes it from orange and red habanero types. It is a favorite among hot sauce makers for the complex flavor it lends alongside its heat. The vigorous plants are productive in warm climates over a long season; pick pods once fully colored for the best flavor.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Jamaican Yellow Scotch Bonnet Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; chinense types germinate slowly and erratically without steady warmth.
directions: Jamaican Yellow Scotch Bonnet produces the classic squat, bonnet-shaped pods of the type, ripening to bright yellow with the fruity, almost tropical aroma that distinguishes true scotch bonnets from habaneros of similar heat. Heat runs in roughly the same 100,000-350,000 Scoville range as habanero but with a sweeter, less sharply acidic flavor that is prized in Jamaican jerk seasoning and Caribbean hot sauces. Give plants a long, warm season, steady moisture, and full sun, and expect a heavy main flush of fruit in late summer. Handle ripe pods with gloves and harvest once fully colored for the best balance of heat and characteristic fruity flavor.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Jambalaya 2.0 Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow (or transplant for an earlier start) after frost danger has passed once soil is warm; Jambalaya 2.0 is a newer F1 hybrid update to the original compact Jambalaya okra, sold by Johnny's Selected Seeds for its earlier maturity and more uniform pod set.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun, or start indoors for an earlier harvest in cooler springs; Jambalaya 2.0 is a compact, early F1 hybrid producing highly uniform, dark green pods with five distinct ridges. Harvest at 3-4 inches for tenderness, checking plants every couple of days once production ramps up, since this hybrid's uniform pod set means a flush of pods can mature together. The large showy flowers are edible and, combined with the plant's compact size, make it a good option for containers and small raised beds where a shorter okra plant is wanted without giving up yield.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Jambalaya 2.0 F1 Okra

name: Jambalaya Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after the last frost when soil is warm (70°F+) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Jambalaya's compact size (36–42 inches vs 6–8 feet for standard okra) makes it practical for raised beds and container growing — even a 5-gallon container supports one plant.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Jambalaya is a compact, dwarf okra hybrid producing the full flavor and productivity of standard okra on a plant roughly half the height of traditional okra varieties — reaching only 3–4 feet versus the 6–8 feet of older varieties like Clemson Spineless. The compact size makes Jambalaya practical for raised beds, containers (5-gallon minimum), and gardens where standard-height okra would create shade problems or require staking. Despite the reduced height, fruit production per plant is excellent — the compact branching structure holds pods within easy reach without the ladder-or-bending situation that harvesting from full-height okra plants requires. The pods are standard green okra with the classic flavor, tender at 3–4 inches and maturing at the typical rapid okra pace (daily checking required at peak production). Jambalaya's compact habit also makes it attractive as a temporary summer ornamental — the large, lightly lobed leaves, yellow hibiscus-like flowers with red centers, and developing pods create a tropical visual effect that is ornamental as well as productive. In zone 9, Jambalaya thrives through the hottest Gulf South summer months when most other vegetables are stressed — okra is one of the few crops that genuinely performs at its best during July and August heat.

name: James Hopper Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed; this medium-height heirloom fits well in beds where taller okra would shade neighboring crops.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep into warm, well-drained soil in full sun. James Hopper is a preservation-collection heirloom valued for its moderate, manageable height compared to rangier Southern okra types, making it easier to harvest without a ladder in a home garden. Plants set standard green pods of 3-5 inches with reliable, steady production through the summer. Pick frequently once pods reach 3-4 inches for the most tender texture, since this variety can fiber up quickly if left too long between pickings.

name: James Scarlet Intermediate Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow into loosened, stone-free soil and thin early to avoid misshapen roots; roots hold well in the ground for late-season harvest.
directions: A Victorian-era English heirloom that became a staple of British kitchen gardens and allotments soon after its introduction in the 1880s, prized for combining a deep scarlet-orange color with reliably heavy yields. The roots are medium-long with a blunt tip, sitting between short stump-rooted carrots and the longest tapering types, which makes them adaptable to a range of soil depths. Direct sow into loosened, stone-free soil and thin early to avoid misshapen roots; roots hold well in the ground for late-season harvest.

name: January King Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors in late summer (26–20 weeks before first frost) for a fall and winter harvest; January King is a savoy-type heirloom with semi-crinkled leaves that develop its characteristic red-purple outer coloring only after cold exposure — the heads taste best after frost has touched them.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before the transplanting date (late summer, aiming for outdoor planting in August–September for a winter harvest) or direct sow in early summer for fall maturity. January King is a centuries-old French and British heirloom winter cabbage that produces medium-sized, semi-round, savoy-type heads with beautifully crinkled, reddish-purple-flushed outer leaves and green-white inner leaves; it is exceptionally cold-hardy, standing in the garden through temperatures well below freezing and becoming sweeter with each frost. Transplant into well-amended, deeply prepared, slightly alkaline to neutral soil and firm the seedling in well to prevent wind-rocking; collar or brassica cage against caterpillars and aphids which are the main pests. In zone 8–9, grow as an overwintering crop planted in September for harvest January through March.

name: Japanese Black Trifele Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Japanese Black Trifele was actually developed in Russia (despite the 'Japanese' name) and introduced to American seed savers through Russian seed trading networks.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Japanese Black Trifele (also called Japanese Truffle) is a Russian heirloom producing unusual pear-shaped to truffle-shaped (the 'trifele' name references the truffle mushroom shape) fruits in a striking deep mahogany-black to brownish-red color with complex, rich, wine-like flavor that has made it one of the most celebrated dark-fleshed heirloom tomatoes in American seed-saving circles. The pear shape and dark color are both distinctive — the elongated, slightly rounded-bottom pear form with its near-black exterior creates an unusual appearance that is immediately recognizable at the farmers market and in the garden. The red-brown flesh has a rich, dense, complex flavor with deep savory undertones that differ from the fruity brightness of standard red or the simple sweetness of yellow tomatoes — a flavor profile well-suited to cooking, sauces, and combinations with cheese and herbs. Despite the 'Japanese' in the name, this variety was developed and preserved in Russia. The medium-sized fruits (4–6 oz) are more practical for everyday use than giant beefsteaks while still providing exceptional flavor. The dark color comes from anthocyanin production in the skin triggered by sun exposure.

name: Japanese Long Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Japanese cucumber thrives on vertical trellising — the climbing vines produce straighter fruits and better air circulation when grown vertically, and trellising is standard practice for this cucumber in Japanese and Asian-style gardens.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; train vines to a trellis for straight fruits and good air circulation. Japanese long cucumber ('Kyuri' in Japanese) is the standard cucumber of Japanese cuisine and is distinct from both the thicker-skinned American slicing cucumber and the ribbed Chinese varieties — producing slender (1–1.5 inch diameter), uniformly dark green, smooth-skinned fruits 8–12 inches long with exceptionally thin, tender skin that needs no peeling, very small seed cavity, dense crisp flesh, and mild, sweet, refreshing flavor with virtually no bitterness. The thin skin and low cucurbitacin content make it 'burpless' and highly digestible, and the crisp, dense flesh holds its texture remarkably well in sliced preparations. Japanese cucumbers are the standard for pickled cucumber preparations (as in the Japanese salted tsukemono tradition) because of their superior texture, and they are equally outstanding for fresh eating, in salads, and in Korean oi sobagi kimchi. Multiple varieties are grown in Japanese commercial and home horticulture, all sharing the smooth skin, thin wall, dense flesh, and mild flavor characteristics. Production is very heavy when vines are trellised and harvested regularly, and the plants perform well in the hot, humid conditions of the Gulf South summer.
sources: Kitazawa Seed Company Asian Vegetable Guide
Tokyo University Faculty of Agriculture vegetable research publications

name: Japanese Oxheart Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Japanese Oxheart is a large, meaty, heart-shaped heirloom tomato of Japanese origin.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Japanese Oxheart bears large, heart-shaped fruit in pink to pink-red with dense, meaty flesh and few seeds, the classic oxheart form prized for slicing and sauce alike, on productive indeterminate vines. Its rich, well-balanced flavor and substantial fruit size have kept it popular among heirloom tomato collectors. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor and texture.

name: Jarrahdale Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Jarrahdale is a Cucurbita maxima type that requires at least 95 days and performs well in zone 9's long growing season. Plant March–April for October harvest. The distinctive flat, deeply-ribbed, blue-grey skin of Jarrahdale does not change color significantly at harvest maturity — look instead for dried stem, firm rind, and overall size (typically 7–10 lbs when ripe). The blue-grey skin of Jarrahdale is unique and is associated with a specific group of Australian heritage pumpkins that produce the grey-blue skin color from a specific combination of pigments and wax bloom; this color group includes Queensland Blue, Crown Prince, and other varieties sharing similar heritage and the distinctive blue-grey appearance. The flesh is deep orange, dense, dry, and very sweet — particularly well suited for pumpkin soups, curries, pies, and roasting where a dry, high-starch pumpkin flesh is preferred.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost; harvest when stem dries and skin is firm grey-blue. Jarrahdale Squash (also called Jarrahdale Pumpkin in its native Australia, where 'pumpkin' is the standard term for what North Americans call both pumpkin and winter squash) is an Australian heritage variety named after the town of Jarrahdale in the Darling Ranges southeast of Perth, Western Australia, where the variety was grown and maintained by local families before being recognized and distributed more widely. The Jarrahdale pumpkin belongs to a distinctive Australian heritage pumpkin group characterized by grey-blue skin — a color produced by a combination of pigmentation and a powdery wax bloom on the skin surface — that distinguishes these varieties from the orange and tan pumpkins dominating North American markets. This blue-grey color group, which includes Queensland Blue, Crown Prince (United Kingdom), and related European heritage varieties, represents a distinct aesthetic and culinary tradition in which the blue skin and dense, dry orange flesh are valued for specific culinary properties. The flesh of Jarrahdale is particularly dry and dense for a large pumpkin — significantly less watery than most carving pumpkins and many North American pie pumpkins — which makes it exceptional for preparations where moisture content affects texture: pumpkin soup (concentrated flavor without excessive water thinning), pumpkin curry, and baked preparations where excess moisture causes sogginess. The flavor is genuinely sweet and complex, with a depth that makes Jarrahdale one of the most culinarily respected heritage pumpkin varieties in Australian cooking and in North American heirloom vegetable circles.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Jarrahdale pumpkin Australian heritage variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Blue-grey pumpkin heritage variety documentation
Royal Horticultural Society — Cucurbita maxima heritage pumpkin variety comparison

name: Jarvis Golden Prolific Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows well after last frost; needs its full 110+ day season of Gulf South heat to dry down properly.
directions: Registered around 1930, Jarvis Golden Prolific was once a widely grown open-pollinated Southern field corn, known for its sizeable 10-inch yellow dent ears on comparatively shorter 6-to-8-foot stalks. Give it full sun, block plantings for wind pollination, and consistent moisture through tasseling and silking, which matter more in Gulf Coast humidity than drought stress does. Because it runs a longer season than modern hybrids, start it as soon as the soil is reliably warm in spring to give it time to mature before the latest, most brutal stretch of late-summer heat. Dry ears fully on the stalk and shell for cornmeal, grits, or chicken and livestock feed.
sources: The Historic Foodie (heirloom corn variety survey)

name: Jasper Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Jasper is a 2013 All-America Selections winner and one of the only cherry tomatoes resistant to both early and late blight along with Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and septoria leaf spot, a rare disease package that suits the humid, blight-prone Gulf South growing season.
directions: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, then stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines; Jasper was named an All-America Selections winner for being one of the very few cherry tomatoes with resistance to both early and late blight, alongside resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and septoria leaf spot, giving it an outstanding disease package for humid, disease-prone gardens. It produces heavy, extended clusters of small, deep red, exceptionally sweet cherry fruit with a crack-resistant skin that holds up on the vine. Because it keeps healthy foliage even under the fungal disease pressure that builds in a wet Gulf Coast summer, Jasper tends to remain productive well after less resistant cherry tomatoes have declined. Pick fruit as clusters ripen to full red color and harvest regularly to keep the vine setting new flowers.
sources: All-America Selections — Jasper tomato AAS winner 2013

name: Jaune Flamme Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost; transplant into warm soil after all frost danger passes and stake or cage the vines.
directions: A French heirloom prized for its abundant clusters of smooth, round, apricot-orange fruits about 2-3 ounces each, with thin skin and a balanced, fruity-sweet flavor often compared to a ripe apricot. Start seed indoors 6 weeks before the last frost, transplant into warm, fertile soil, and stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines, which crop heavily and hold up well through Gulf South heat. Pick fruit as soon as it colors fully to keep the thin skins from splitting after summer rain, and expect steady production from early summer until frost.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds Variety Catalog
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange Variety Catalog

name: Jaune Gros de Paris Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after the soil has warmed past 65°F; this historic French heirloom needs a long, warm season and heavily enriched soil to size up its huge fruit, making the Gulf Coast's extended frost-free window an advantage.
directions: Jaune Gros de Paris is a market-garden heirloom long grown around the French capital, prized for its enormous, flattened, lightly ribbed fruit in soft pastel yellow-pink that can weigh anywhere from 25 to well over 100 pounds. Sow into hills enriched with compost or aged manure and thin to two vigorous vines per hill, allowing plenty of room for the sprawling growth. The deep orange flesh is dense and moderately sweet, well suited to soups, gratins, and baked dishes rather than fresh eating. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists a fingernail, then cure in a warm spot for a couple of weeks before moving to cool, dry storage, where the fruit keeps for several months.

name: Jaune Paille des Vertus Shallot
scientificName: Allium cepa var. aggregatum 'Jaune Paille des Vertus'
plantingNote: Plant bulb sets 4-8 weeks before last frost in spring, or in fall in mild-winter zones 7-10; Jaune Paille des Vertus is a nineteenth-century French heirloom named for the village of Vertus in the Champagne region and prized above all for its exceptionally long storage life.
directions: Plant individual bulb sets pointed-end-up, about 1 inch deep and 6-8 inches apart, in fertile, well-drained soil, and keep the bed evenly moist through the growing season while easing off water as the foliage begins to yellow and fall over. Jaune Paille des Vertus, whose name translates roughly as "golden straw of Vertus," is one of the oldest documented French shallot varieties still in commerce, each set multiplying into a tight cluster of coppery-gold, papery-skinned bulbs with pale yellow flesh and the classic mild, sweet-sharp shallot flavor. It has long been regarded by French market gardeners as the standard keeping shallot, holding firm in storage for many months longer than most modern shallot varieties when properly cured. Harvest once the tops have fully collapsed and dried, cure the bulbs in a warm, airy, shaded spot for two to three weeks, and store the cleaned bulbs somewhere cool, dry, and dark.
sources: Kokopelli Seed Foundation (French heirloom vegetable archive)

name: Jazzman Rice
plantingNote: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65F; in zone 9 plant April-May for harvest late August-September. Jazzman is an aromatic, jasmine-type long-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter as a domestic alternative to imported jasmine rice.
directions: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Jazzman is an aromatic long-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter and bred to rival imported jasmine rice in fragrance and cooking quality, giving Gulf South growers a domestically adapted option for fragrant rice. The grain develops a distinctive popcorn-like aroma during cooking and a soft, slightly sticky texture similar to Thai jasmine rice, making it well suited to Southeast Asian and Cajun-Creole dishes alike. Keep the bed continuously saturated through the growing season, since consistent moisture through grain fill is especially important for developing the variety's signature aroma and flavor. Harvest when seed heads droop and turn golden-tan, then dry thoroughly before hulling and storing; aromatic rice varieties are somewhat more prone to losing fragrance in storage than standard long-grain types, so use home-hulled grain within the first several months for the best aroma.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Rice Variety Releases
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Rice Production Guide
University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture — Rice Cultivar Notes

name: Jefferson Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed and soil is reliably warm; Jefferson's early maturity means a Gulf Coast gardener can often squeeze in a second planting in early summer.
directions: Space plants a bit closer than tall heirloom types since Jefferson's semi-dwarf, sparsely branched habit takes up less garden footprint while still producing a full-season crop. Bred in the University of Arkansas horticulture program from a cross involving Clemson Spineless, Emerald, Perkins, Gold Coast, and other parent lines, Jefferson was selected to mature roughly ten days ahead of Clemson Spineless, giving an earlier start to the harvest window in a warm Gulf South spring. Pods are straight, dark green, and ribbed with few spines, making them easy to handle during the frequent picking okra demands. Because the plants stay relatively compact, Jefferson also works well in a raised bed or smaller garden plot where a 6-foot okra stand would crowd out neighboring crops.
sources: University of Arkansas Department of Horticulture variety release records
Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (NCSU)

name: Jellicorse White Dent Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 short rows for reliable wind pollination once soil has warmed well past last frost.
directions: Jellicorse is a white-cobbed, 12-to-14-row dent corn selected by farmer Reginald Jellicorse of Elmwood, Tennessee in the 1910s, descended from Tennessee Red Cob and Tuscarora White lines; the Tennessee Experiment Station trialed it from 1919-1923 and clocked it second only to Neal's Paymaster for yield while noting it consistently set two ears per stalk even on poor, under-fertilized ground. Its deep Southern pedigree translates to genuine tolerance for the brutal heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer, where many Midwestern dent corns stall out or fail to pollinate. Sow into warm soil in blocks rather than single rows, keep moisture steady through silking, and let the ears dry down fully on the stalk before shelling for cornmeal, grits, or hominy. Save the best double-eared stalks for next year's seed to keep the twin-ear trait strong.
sources: USDA National Plant Germplasm System (GRIN, PI Ames 3004)

name: Jenny Lind Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; Jenny Lind is a small (1–2 lb), very heavily ribbed, deeply lobed heirloom muskmelon with distinctive turban-like bumps at the blossom end and unusually light green to apple-green flesh — one of the oldest American named melon varieties (dating to the 1840s), named for the famous Swedish opera singer Jenny Lind who toured America in 1851 to enormous popular acclaim.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost; Jenny Lind melons are small and compact compared to modern varieties, making them suitable for small gardens; harvest when the melon slips easily from the vine with gentle pressure and the blossom-end softens slightly; the green flesh is unusual for American melons and has a delicate, sweet, slightly floral flavor. Jenny Lind is one of the oldest and most historically documented named melon varieties in American horticulture — it was listed in seed catalogs by the 1840s and became extremely popular in the northeastern states (particularly New Jersey, where it was widely grown for the Philadelphia and New York markets) during the latter half of the 19th century, remaining a garden standard well into the early 20th century before modern hybrids displaced it. The variety is named in honor of Jenny Lind (1820–1887), the Swedish opera singer known as the 'Swedish Nightingale,' whose American tour managed by P.T. Barnum in 1850–1851 created an extraordinary popular sensation — everything from hairstyles to trains to songs to garden plants were named for her in that era. Jenny Lind melon is distinctive in several ways: the small (typically 1–2 pound) round fruits are deeply ribbed with prominent ridges running from stem to blossom end, and the blossom end has a characteristic raised, button-like knob in the center of a depression — a 'turban' or 'navel' that is unique among common muskmelons. The flesh is a pale sea-green to apple-green color (not the familiar salmon-orange of modern cantaloupes) that is thin relative to the total fruit size but very sweet and floral in flavor. Jenny Lind ripens about 2 weeks earlier than standard cantaloupes, making it an excellent choice for short-season gardens.
sources: Fearing Burr Jr. Field and Garden Vegetables of America (1863)

name: Jericho Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring through early summer (Jericho tolerates warmer soil and air temperatures than most lettuces), or in fall; this variety was developed in Israel for the extreme heat of the Jordan Valley — the name references Jericho, one of the hottest inhabited cities on earth — and is the premier heat-tolerant Romaine for gardeners who want salad lettuce through warm spring and early summer when other Romaine varieties bolt rapidly.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep; Jericho tolerates warmer soil and air temperatures than most lettuces, extending the spring sowing season by 2–4 weeks beyond the window suitable for other varieties; provide afternoon shade in the hottest weather; thin to 8–12 inches; harvest full heads or use as cut-and-come-again. Jericho is an Israeli-developed Romaine (Cos) type lettuce bred specifically for the extreme heat of the Jordan Valley and the Mediterranean climate of Israel, where summer temperatures regularly exceed 100°F and conventional lettuce bolts immediately. The variety was developed to remain productive longer into warm weather than any other Romaine, and delivers this through exceptional heat tolerance — it is typically the last lettuce still producing usable heads when spring heat arrives in mid-latitude gardens, and one of the earliest candidates for late-summer planting when other varieties would bolt immediately. The large, upright heads have crisp, pale green Romaine-style leaves with excellent flavor — sweet, slightly nutty, and refreshing — and the heads are notably larger than many other heat-tolerant varieties. For Gulf Coast gardeners (zones 8b–10), Jericho is the most valuable Romaine for the challenging transition from cool-season winter lettuce into warming spring, providing 2–4 extra weeks of production compared to standard varieties. Highly recommended by Territorial Seed and Johnny's for hot-summer and transition-zone gardens.

name: Jericho Romaine Lettuce
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Jericho is exceptional for late spring and early fall planting in zone 9 where standard romaine varieties bolt quickly in warming temperatures. In zone 9, transplant February–March for spring, or September–October for fall. Jericho's heat tolerance means it continues producing for 2–4 weeks longer into spring warming than standard romaine types before bolting — a significant practical advantage in zone 9 where the spring growing window for lettuce is brief. The variety's Israeli breeding (developed near the city of Jericho in a very hot, arid climate) was specifically targeted at producing quality lettuce in conditions that challenge European and North American varieties.
directions: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting in early spring or fall; transplant to partial shade in warm seasons to extend the harvest. Harvest outer leaves or whole heads when compact and firm. Jericho Romaine is an Israeli-bred romaine (cos) lettuce developed by breeders working in the conditions of the Jordan Valley near the ancient city of Jericho — an arid, extremely hot agricultural region where the development of heat-tolerant lettuce was driven by practical necessity to extend the local growing season. The breeding produced a romaine variety with substantially better heat tolerance and bolt resistance than standard European and American romaine types, and Jericho has become one of the most recommended romaine varieties for warm-climate gardeners and for late-spring plantings in temperate zones where other romaine varieties rapidly bolt when temperatures rise. The heads are upright, tightly folded, medium-large, dark green, with the crisp, mildly bitter interior quality of classic romaine. For zone 9 gardeners, Jericho's heat-tolerance advantage translates to a 2–4 week extension of the spring romaine harvest window before heat triggers bolting — a meaningful extension in climates where the transition from cool to hot weather happens rapidly. Jericho is also appropriate for early fall planting when temperatures are still warm but declining.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Jericho romaine lettuce heat tolerance trial data
Territorial Seed Company — Jericho romaine variety description
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Heat-Tolerant Lettuce Varieties for Extended Production

name: Jermor Shallot
plantingNote: Plant sets four to eight weeks before the last frost in spring, or in fall in mild-winter regions; Jermor is a French-bred banana-type shallot noted for its elongated shape and refined flavor.
directions: Plant individual sets about an inch deep and six to eight inches apart, with the tip just at or slightly above the soil surface, and keep the bed weeded and evenly watered through spring growth. Jermor is a French 'banana' or échalion-type shallot bred in Brittany, producing clusters of medium to large, elegantly elongated bulbs with glossy rose-copper skin and pale pink-tinged flesh prized for its refined, mild-sweet flavor. Reduce watering once the foliage begins to yellow and fall over, then lift the bulbs and cure them in a warm, dry, airy spot for two to three weeks before trimming and storing. Well-cured bulbs keep for several months in cool, dry storage.

name: Jersey Devil Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Jersey Devil is an indeterminate vine that benefits from sturdy caging or trellising. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer production. The elongated banana-shaped fruits (6–8 inches, pointed at the blossom end) are meaty with very few seeds — excellent for sauce, roasting, and drying, where the low moisture and dense flesh concentrate flavor and reduce cooking time.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun in rich, well-drained soil after last frost. Stake or cage plants before or at transplanting. Jersey Devil is a New Jersey heirloom paste tomato with an immediately recognizable elongated, banana-shaped to horn-shaped fruit form: 5–8 inches long, tapered to a sharp point at the blossom end, with bright red skin and very dense, meaty flesh. The distinctive shape — sometimes described as resembling a long red chili pepper at a glance — makes Jersey Devil one of the most visually unusual paste tomatoes. The eating quality matches the visual appeal: the flesh is very dense and dry with minimal gel and seeds, a high solid content that makes it ideal for tomato sauce (concentrates quickly without extended cooking), sun-dried tomatoes, and oven-roasted preparations where the low moisture prevents the pan from becoming soupy. Jersey Devil is an indeterminate vine that produces heavily over a long season; the fruits ripen mid-season (78–88 days from transplant) and continue until frost. The variety is strongly connected to New Jersey, where it appears in the regional heirloom seed tradition alongside other East Coast paste types.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Jersey Devil tomato variety notes
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Paste tomato collection
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Heirloom Paste Tomato Variety Evaluation

name: Jersey Giant Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jersey Giant is an all-male hybrid that puts no energy into seed production, channeling more resources into thick, vigorous spear growth and higher yields than older open-pollinated varieties.
directions: Plant crowns 6-8 inches deep in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, backfilling gradually as shoots emerge over the growing season. Jersey Giant is one of the Rutgers University all-male hybrid asparagus cultivars, bred so that plants never set seed and instead direct all their energy into producing thick, vigorous, high-yielding spears over a long productive lifespan. It also carries good resistance to Fusarium crown and root rot, a serious disease problem in older asparagus plantings, making it one of the more reliable modern choices for a home asparagus bed. Do not harvest any spears the first year and only lightly the second year, allowing the fern-like foliage to grow through summer to build a strong root system for many years of future harvests.

name: Jersey King Asparagus
plantingNote: Set dormant one-year crowns into trenches 6-8 inches deep as soon as soil is workable in spring, then gradually backfill as spears emerge.
directions: Jersey King is one of the Rutgers all-male hybrid asparagus lines bred for resistance to Fusarium crown rot and asparagus rust while eliminating the volunteer seedlings that female plants produce. It sends up thick, uniform, deep-green spears with tightly closed tips over a long spring harvest window. Because energy is not diverted into seed production, established beds tend to build vigor faster than open-pollinated types like Mary Washington. Give plants a full season to establish before taking any harvest, and top-dress with compost each fall to sustain crown health for decades.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

name: Jersey Knight Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant 1-year-old crowns (rhizomes) in early spring 6–8 inches deep in a prepared trench with a mound of loose soil under each crown; spread the roots over the mound and cover. Asparagus is a long-lived perennial that may remain productive for 15–25 years if properly established — invest in thorough soil preparation (18 inches deep, well-amended with compost) before planting. Do not harvest in the establishment years: the first year after planting, allow all spears to grow into ferns (foliage) to build root reserves; in the second year, harvest for just 2 weeks; in the third year, harvest 4–6 weeks; from year four onward, harvest the full 6–8 week season. In zone 9, asparagus is challenging — it needs cold winters for adequate dormancy and in the warmest years may not set adequate root reserves for the following season.
directions: Plant crowns 6–8 inches deep in a prepared trench; allow all fern growth in the first year. Feed annually with balanced fertilizer after harvest. Jersey Knight is an all-male F1 hybrid asparagus from the New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station at Rutgers University — part of the 'Jersey' series of asparagus hybrids (including Jersey Giant and Jersey Supreme) that revolutionized asparagus production in the United States from the 1980s onward by introducing all-male genetics, disease resistance, and dramatically improved yield over the open-pollinated varieties that had been standard for a century. The key innovation of the Jersey series is their all-male genetics: asparagus is naturally dioecious (separate male and female plants), and female plants divert significant energy into berry and seed production that could otherwise go to spear production; all-male hybrids eliminate this energy diversion and direct all plant resources to the edible spears, resulting in 2–3× the yield of traditional open-pollinated varieties under the same conditions. Jersey Knight carries improved resistance to asparagus rust and Fusarium crown rot — two diseases that significantly reduce the productive lifespan of traditional varieties in warm, humid climates. In zone 9, Jersey Knight is among the better-adapted of the Jersey hybrids due to its moderate heat tolerance and disease package; while asparagus is genuinely challenging in zone 9's warm winters, Jersey Knight has performed better in southern trials than many other varieties.
sources: Rutgers University — Jersey Knight asparagus development and all-male hybrid technology
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Jersey Knight asparagus variety comparison
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Asparagus Production in Florida and the Gulf South

name: Jersey Orange Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost in loose, ridged soil; Jersey Orange is the orange-fleshed counterpart to the drier-fleshed White and Yellow Jersey sweet potato types once common along the Mid-Atlantic coast.
directions: Plant rooted slips into raised, loosened ridges two to four weeks after the last frost date, in full sun. Jersey Orange belongs to the old Jersey group of sweet potatoes grown historically along the New Jersey and Delmarva coastal plain, sharing the group's orange-brown skin but distinguished from its White Jersey and Yellow Jersey relatives by deep orange, sweeter flesh instead of the drier, starchier texture typical of Jersey types. The vines are moderately vigorous and the roots tend toward a tapered, uniform shape that stores well. Harvest before frost damages the vines, cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for about a week, then move to cool, dry storage.
sources: NC State University Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America

name: Jersey Supreme Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jersey Supreme is an improved Rutgers all-male hybrid selected for earlier spring emergence and higher total yield than older asparagus cultivars.
directions: Plant crowns 6-8 inches deep in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, backfilling gradually as shoots emerge. Jersey Supreme is a later-generation Rutgers all-male hybrid asparagus bred for earlier spring spear emergence and higher overall yield than older selections like Jersey Giant, while retaining the same good disease resistance and long-term productivity that made the Jersey series a standard choice for home and commercial asparagus plantings. As an all-male hybrid it never sets seed, so all of the plant's energy goes into vigorous spear production over what can be a fifteen-to-twenty-year productive bed lifespan. Avoid harvesting the first year and harvest only lightly the second year to let the root system establish fully before full production begins.

name: Jester Hybrid Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct-sow once soil is warm; semi-vining habit still benefits from generous spacing.
directions: Jester stands out for its bumpy, salmon-red rind and deeply flattened, ribbed shape, offset by surprisingly bright yellow flesh inside. Fruit average 7-10 pounds and work equally well as fall decoration or as a cooking pumpkin. The semi-vining plants set fruit early and reliably for a specialty pumpkin. Cure harvested fruit in a warm, dry spot for a week to toughen the skin before storing.

name: Jet Star Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start seeds in January for March transplanting. Jet Star is an indeterminate hybrid that bears over a long season and is well-suited to staking or caging in full sun.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Jet Star is a popular indeterminate hybrid tomato introduced by Harris Seeds in the late 1960s that earned a lasting following among home gardeners for its combination of large, smooth, red, globe-shaped fruits (8–12 oz) with distinctively mild, low-acid flavor that appeals to people who find standard tomatoes too tart — the low-acid character makes Jet Star the variety of choice for those who love the fresh tomato experience without acid sensitivity. The smooth, crack-resistant fruits have few seeds and thick walls, making them excellent slicing tomatoes for sandwiches and salads; they also hold up well in cooking but are really at their finest fresh off the vine at warm room temperature. VF disease resistance (Verticillium and Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2) keeps plants productive through the season. Jet Star is a mid-season tomato (70–75 days from transplant) and bears continuously as an indeterminate variety — plants will need staking or caging as they can reach 5–6 feet. An excellent choice for gardeners who prefer mild, low-acid tomatoes, and a reliable producer in zone 8–10 spring and fall tomato seasons.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Production Guide
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomato Variety Selection for Texas

name: Jetstar Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once frost danger has passed; Jetstar is a popular hybrid slicer bred for disease resistance and a mild, low-acid flavor on a productive indeterminate vine.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking or caging the indeterminate vine. Jetstar is a widely grown hybrid slicing tomato valued for its mild, low-acid flavor that appeals to gardeners sensitive to more acidic tomatoes, combined with good resistance to verticillium and fusarium wilts that helps it stay productive through a long growing season. It produces smooth, round, meaty red fruit with few seeds and good crack resistance. Water consistently to prevent blossom-end rot, and feed regularly through the season to keep the vigorous vine productive from early summer into fall.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Production

name: Jewel Marble Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting; the naturally compact, bushy habit makes Jewel Marble one of the better eggplants for large containers as well as small beds.
directions: Jewel Marble is a compact, dwarf eggplant bred for containers and small garden beds, producing an abundance of small fruit marbled in violet, mauve, and eggshell white with a glossy, almost lacquered finish. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights are reliably warm, since the naturally tidy, bushy habit needs little pruning to stay productive in a pot. Pick fruit at about 2-3 inches across while the skin is still taut and shiny; the mild, nutty-sweet flesh is tender enough to roast whole or simmer into ratatouille without peeling. Frequent harvesting keeps these compact plants loaded with new flowers and fruit through a long summer.

name: Jewel Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F; Jewel was released in 1970 by North Carolina State University and was the dominant American commercial sweet potato variety from the late 1970s through the 1990s, grown primarily in North Carolina, Louisiana, and Virginia — it remains a reliable home garden standard with excellent moist orange flesh and consistent yields.
directions: Plant slips 12–18 inches apart in loose, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms above 65°F; Jewel tolerates less-than-ideal soil conditions better than many newer varieties. Jewel was developed and released in 1970 by North Carolina State University as part of the USDA–state cooperative sweet potato breeding program and became the dominant American commercial sweet potato throughout the 1970s–1990s; it produced the standard against which American sweet potatoes were judged for two decades before Beauregard's introduction. The medium to large, elongated, smooth, coppery-orange to red-orange-skinned roots have intensely orange, moist, sweet flesh that softens to a creamy consistency when baked — an excellent texture for traditional sweet potato preparations. Flavor is sweet and complex with good caramel development during baking. Self-reliant and productive; excellent for Gulf Coast spring planting in late March through April and fall planting in June through July.

name: Jicarilla Apache White Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; this corn was selected over generations for the short, cool growing season of the Jicarilla Apache Reservation's high mountain country (roughly 6,000 feet) in northern New Mexico, so it tolerates cool nights better than lowland corn types.
directions: Jicarilla Apache White is a flour-flint corn maintained at roughly 6,000 feet elevation on the Jicarilla Apache Reservation in northern New Mexico, selected for the shorter, cooler growing season of high mountain country rather than the low desert. Ears run 6 to 8 inches long and are packed with flinty, pearl-white kernels, with an occasional pink-tinged kernel appearing in a stand. Stalks stay relatively short at 3 to 5 feet, an advantage in exposed mountain plantings, and the crop is traditionally processed into chicos, posole, and tortillas. Direct sow once the soil has warmed, since its cool-elevation origin makes it tolerant of cool nights once established but not frost-hardy as a seedling.

name: Jimmy Nardello Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Jimmy Nardello is a Slow Food Ark of Taste heirloom — an irreplaceable variety of historical and culinary significance that merits preservation in home garden seed collections.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Jimmy Nardello is one of the most beloved heirloom sweet peppers in American home gardening — an Italian variety brought to Connecticut from Basilicata, Italy, by Giuseppa and Jimmy Nardello's family in 1887 and preserved in that family for nearly a century before being donated to the Seed Savers Exchange. The long, thin, curved, brilliant red fruits (8–10 inches, very thin walls) are among the sweetest of all peppers when fully ripe red — intensely concentrated sweet pepper flavor without any heat whatsoever. Jimmy Nardello is the premier sweet frying pepper: the thin walls mean the fruits cook in seconds in hot oil (traditional Italian fritto method) or over high heat on a grill, caramelizing immediately to a concentrated, smoky-sweet, almost jammy flavor that is entirely different from the fresh fruit character. The dried fruits are also exceptional for crushing into sweet paprika with excellent color and flavor. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved indefinitely and the variety preserved — Jimmy Nardello is recognized on the Slow Food Ark of Taste as a culturally significant food variety worth preserving. In zone 9, the plants are very productive from late spring through fall. The abundant, long, curved red fruits hanging from productive plants are visually beautiful and practically abundant.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

name: Jimmy Red Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for reliable wind pollination, in fertile soil in full sun, after all frost danger has passed. Allow the full season to dry down on the stalk for grinding into meal or distilling.
directions: Sow in blocks at least 4 rows wide in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; let ears fully dry on the stalk for the deepest color and best grinding or distilling quality. Jimmy Red is a South Carolina heirloom dent corn with a dramatic history — the variety nearly vanished entirely, surviving through only a handful of ears kept by a single South Carolina farming family, before being rediscovered and reintroduced in the 2010s by chef and miller Glenn Roberts of Anson Mills and distiller Scott Blackwell, who used it to help revive heirloom Southern corn whiskey and grits production. The deep garnet-red, almost purple-black kernels grind into a rich, distinctively flavored meal and grits, and the variety has become especially prized by craft distillers for producing bourbon and moonshine with a uniquely deep, earthy character credited to the corn's high oil content and pigmentation. A striking, historically significant heirloom for gardeners interested in Southern foodways and heritage grain, zone 6–10.

name: Jing Orange Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (65°F+); Jing Orange is a Chinese heirloom okra grown for its striking orange-red pods and stems, doubling as an ornamental as well as edible plant.
directions: Soak seed overnight before direct sowing an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun. Jing Orange is a Chinese heirloom okra bearing vivid orange-red pods on stems and foliage tinged with the same warm color, making it as striking in the garden as it is productive, while retaining good tenderness a bit longer than typical green okra before pods toughen. Harvest at 2-4 inches for the best texture, picking every couple of days through the growing season to keep plants producing continuously in the Gulf South's long, hot summer. The colorful pods make an attractive addition to a mixed vegetable bed or ornamental edible border in addition to their culinary use in gumbo, frying, and pickling.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Okra Production

name: Joan Rutabaga
plantingNote: Direct sow in summer, allowing a longer season than most rutabagas, so roots size up before fall harvest; thin seedlings to final spacing.
directions: Joan produces uniform, round roots with purple tops and pale flesh that is sweet and mild even when harvested young, though it also sizes up well for longer fall storage. Direct sow in fertile, well-worked soil and thin to a final spacing of 6-8 inches, watering consistently through the growing season to prevent woody texture. Because Joan takes somewhat longer to mature than many rutabagas, sow it earlier in summer than quicker varieties to ensure roots finish sizing before hard freezes. Harvest after light frost for the best flavor and store in a cool, humid cellar through winter.

name: Joe's Long Cayenne Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Joe's Long Cayenne needs a long warm season to fully color and dry its extra-long pods, so an early indoor start pays off.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking plants if pod weight bends the stems. This Calabrian heirloom traveled from Italy to Italian-Canadian growers in Toronto and then to Joe Sestito of Troy, New York, whose name became attached to it when Dr. Carolyn Male introduced the variety to American gardeners through Seed Savers Exchange in 1996. Plants produce heavy clusters of slender, thin-walled cayenne-type pods that can reach up to a foot long, ripening from green to bright red with medium-high heat in the 30,000–50,000 Scoville range. The thin walls make whole pods easy to string into ristras for air-drying, and dried fruit grinds readily into pepper flakes or crushed cayenne.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Joe's Long Cayenne Pepper
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners Database — Cayenne-type Peppers

name: Joi Choi Pak Choi
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1/4 inch deep or transplant in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during cool seasons; Joi Choi bolt resistance is notably better than standard pak choi cultivars, extending the harvest window in warm spring conditions.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during cool seasons; Joi Choi is the most widely recommended pak choi (bok choy) cultivar for American home gardens — an All-America Selections award winner producing an upright, well-formed head with crisp, white, thick, succulent stems and dark-green, smooth leaf blades in a clean, classic pak choi form. Joi Choi's excellence comes from the combination of very clean, upright growth habit (the stems don't spread outward messily like some varieties), exceptional bolt resistance for an early-maturing type (30–50 days), and excellent flavor — the stems are tender and mildly sweet, the leaves are tender with mild cabbage flavor, and the whole plant can be used in stir-fries, soups, and raw preparations. In zone 9, Joi Choi is grown September through April as a cool-season crop; in the heat of summer it bolts quickly. The bolt resistance is Joi Choi's key advantage — allowing it to be planted in late February and early March (early spring zone 9) before the heat arrives, with harvest extending a week or two longer than standard varieties. Harvest the whole head at soil level when it reaches full size (10–12 inches tall) or harvest outer leaves continuously for a prolonged cut-and-come-again harvest.

name: Jolant Leek
plantingNote: Start indoors in modules and transplant out once seedlings are pencil-thick; can also be sown into an outdoor seedbed and transplanted later for a late-summer through early-winter harvest window.
directions: Jolant is a European mid-season leek bred to bridge the gap between quick summer types and the toughest overwintering varieties, giving a long stretch of harvest from late summer well into early winter. Plants form thick, well-blanched white shanks with a moderate flavor and hold in the ground without bolting or splitting for weeks once mature, which spreads out the harvest window instead of forcing a single cutting date. Moderate winter hardiness lets a fall-sown planting carry through the first hard frosts in milder climates, though it is not as cold-tolerant as dedicated winter leek strains. Hill soil around the base as the shanks thicken to maximize the tender white portion.

name: Juana's Orange Amaranth
plantingNote: Surface sow with minimal covering after the soil has warmed, since seed needs light and warmth to germinate reliably.
directions: Scatter seed over warm soil and press it in rather than burying it, thinning seedlings once they reach a few inches tall to give stalks room to thicken. This heirloom was revived by Maya communities in Baja Verapaz, Guatemala, and produces vivid orange-bronze seed heads atop vigorous plants grown for both nutritious grain and edible leaves. It tolerates poor soil and dry spells well once rooted, needing little more than full sun and occasional watering to thrive. Harvest seed heads as they dry and lighten in color, then thresh and winnow to collect the grain.

name: Jubilee Hysor Fava Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring, or fall in mild-winter climates; Jubilee Hysor is an early-maturing improved Windsor-type fava bean.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jubilee Hysor is an improved Windsor-type fava bean among the earliest to crop from a spring sowing, producing well-filled pods with 6-8 seeds on tall, vigorous plants. It can also be sown in fall where winters are mild enough for the seedlings to overwinter. Its robust, old-fashioned broad bean flavor holds up even as the beans size up, making it forgiving of a slightly later harvest than some modern fava cultivars bred for a narrow picking window.

name: Jubilee Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks after last frost; Jubilee is a midseason yellow sweet corn with excellent flavor, good disease resistance, and adaptability to both Northern and Southern climates — a reliable, high-quality variety that performs well throughout zones 4–11 and is particularly well-suited to Gulf Coast gardens where it can be planted for both spring and fall corn seasons.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in blocks; Jubilee is an SU type that benefits from block planting for good pollination and is best planted at least 400 feet from supersweet (SH2) types to prevent cross-pollination that reduces sweetness. Jubilee is a midseason (82–87 days) yellow sweet corn that has been widely grown in American gardens and markets since the 1950s and maintains a reputation for reliable production, excellent flavor, and adaptability to a wide range of climates from the Upper Midwest to the Gulf Coast; the large ears (8–9 inches) carry 14–16 rows of bright golden-yellow kernels with classic, rich sweet corn flavor — the balance of sweetness and traditional corn taste that makes fresh summer sweet corn a culinary experience distinct from the excessive sweetness of modern hybrid types. Jubilee has better disease resistance than many older varieties (including some tolerance to Stewart's wilt and common rust) and holds slightly longer in the field than older SU types. Outstanding in Gulf Coast gardens for both the spring crop (April–May planting) and fall crop (late July–August planting).

name: Jubilee Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant in well-amended sandy-loam soil 1–2 weeks after last frost; Jubilee is a large, long-season Florida-bred watermelon well-adapted to the Gulf Coast, requiring ample space (8–12 feet between plants) and 3 months of warm weather for best production.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3–4 seeds, thinning to 2 plants per hill; Jubilee is a Florida-developed heirloom watermelon introduced in 1963 by the Florida Agricultural Experiment Station, producing oblong, striped fruits weighing 25–40 pounds with bright red, crisp, sweet flesh and gray-green skin with dark stripes — one of the classic large Southern watermelons grown at commercial scale for roadside markets. The long, oblong shape distinguishes it from round varieties; the sweet, firm, seedless-type flesh holds up well for transport and has excellent flavor. Resistant to fusarium wilt, which historically decimated Southern watermelon crops. A traditional choice for gardeners in the Gulf South who want a truly large, impressive watermelon with Southern heritage adapted to regional heat and humidity.

name: Judión de La Granja Bean
plantingNote: Sow seed around or just after last frost at the foot of a tall, sturdy trellis, since this runner-type bean is a vigorous climber that needs a strong structure to support its weight.
directions: Sow seed around or just after last frost at the foot of a tall, sturdy trellis, since this runner-type bean is a vigorous climber that needs a strong structure to support its weight through the season. Grown for centuries in the volcanic soils around La Granja de San Ildefonso in Segovia, Spain, it produces some of the largest bean seeds in cultivation — broad, flat, and ivory-white — traditionally simmered slowly into the region's celebrated judión stew. Like other runner beans it flowers and sets pods best where summer nights stay relatively cool, dropping blossoms in prolonged heat. Leave pods on the vine until fully dry and papery before shelling the outsized beans for storage.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste
European Commission Protected Geographical Indication registry

name: Juliet Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 transplant February–March for spring. Juliet is an indeterminate grape type that grows vigorously to 6–8 feet and sets fruit abundantly even during heat, making it excellent for zone 9 spring and fall plantings.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Juliet is a 1999 All-America Selections winner widely regarded as the standard-setter for the grape tomato category. The oval, grape-sized (1.5–2 inch) fruits grow in large trusses of 30–40 tomatoes and have a particularly rich, complex flavor — a balance of sweetness and acidity often described as more 'adult' and interesting than the purely sweet cherry types. Juliet is notable for its outstanding crack resistance (thin-skinned cherry tomatoes frequently split in rain; Juliet resists this), its prolific production, and its reliable fruit set under warm conditions. The thick-walled, meaty fruits have an unusually long shelf life and hold on the vine for weeks without cracking, making them practical for casual harvesting. Disease resistance is strong. In zone 9, Juliet is especially valuable because it continues setting fruit at temperatures that shut down many indeterminate varieties; the heavy trusses of beautiful red grape tomatoes become a summer landmark in the garden.
sources: All-America Selections — Juliet tomato AAS winner 1999
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Juliet tomato variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Grape Tomato Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomato Variety Evaluation

name: Jumbo Romano Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Jumbo Romano requires 6-foot pole or trellis support. In zone 9, plant March–May for summer harvest and again late August–September for fall. Romano-type flat-pod beans have a longer harvest window than round-pod snap beans — the wide, flat pods remain tender and flavorful at a much larger size, so harvesting every 3–4 days rather than every 1–2 days as with round-pod types is acceptable without significant quality loss.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; install a 6-foot support structure before planting. Harvest flat pods when 5–8 inches long — the wide, flat pods stay tender longer than round-pod snap beans. Romano-type flat-pod beans are the classic Italian snap bean — the distinctive wide, flat pods (0.5 to 0.75 inch wide, versus the round cross-section of standard snap beans) with a meaty, thick-walled character that gives them a very different cooking quality from American round-pod types. Romano beans are the traditional choice for Italian green bean preparations: braised with olive oil, garlic, and tomato (fagiolini al pomodoro), slow-cooked until completely tender and silky, or simply boiled and dressed with good olive oil and salt. The thick walls mean romano beans absorb oil and flavors particularly well during cooking, and the flat shape increases surface area contact with the cooking medium. Jumbo Romano is a large-podded version of the classic Italian romano pole type — pods reach 7–9 inches at full size while remaining tender — and one of the most widely available and productive romano-type beans in North America. The flavor when cooked is richer and fuller than round-pod snap beans — a deeper, more substantial bean flavor that makes romano beans a favorite of Italian cooks and everyone who discovers them.
sources: Burpee Seeds — Jumbo Romano pole bean variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Romano flat-pod bean comparison
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Snap Bean Production and Variety Guide

name: Jupiter Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; in zone 9, plant in late February through March and again in August–September for a productive fall crop — peppers often produce best in the cooler temperatures of fall.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Jupiter is one of the largest and most productive open-pollinated bell pepper varieties — producing extra-large, four-lobed, thick-walled fruits that are larger and more blocky than standard California Wonder types. The fruits are harvested green for fresh use or allowed to ripen fully to a rich, sweet red (occasionally yellow to orange). Jupiter is prized for its combination of very large fruit size (often 4–5 inches long, 4 inches wide), thick walls that hold up well in cooking, and outstanding sweet flavor that improves markedly when allowed to ripen fully red. As an open-pollinated, non-hybrid variety, Jupiter seeds can be saved from the best fruits for replanting — an important advantage for seed-saving gardeners who want consistent results without purchasing new seed annually. Jupiter's disease tolerance (particularly to tobacco mosaic virus) represents an improvement over older open-pollinated varieties. In zone 9, bell peppers thrive in spring (late February through June) and even more productively in fall (August transplants through November) — the fall crop in zone 9 consistently produces the largest, most flavorful fruits as temperatures moderate from the summer peak. Zone 9 gardeners have two full productive seasons for bell peppers, providing fresh peppers for much of the year.

name: Jupiter Rice
plantingNote: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; Jupiter is an LSU AgCenter medium-grain release widely grown across Louisiana rice country.
directions: Sow seed 0.5-1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated through the growing season whether in a flooded paddy or a well-watered garden bed. Jupiter is a widely grown Louisiana medium-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter, valued by commercial growers and home gardeners alike for high, dependable yields and grain that cooks up moist, tender, and slightly clingy in the style favored for jambalaya, risotto-style dishes, and sushi rice rather than the fluffy separate grains of long-grain types. The sturdy, semi-dwarf plants stand up well to wind and rain compared to older tall varieties, making it a practical choice for a home rice patch. Harvest when seed heads droop and the grain has turned golden-brown, then thresh and dry thoroughly before hulling or storing.

name: Just Right Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Just Right was the first true F1 hybrid turnip and stays mild and non-pithy even at a large size, unlike most turnips which turn woody and strong-flavored once they size up.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loose soil in full sun; Just Right was the first true F1 hybrid turnip ever introduced and remains notable for staying mild, sweet, and non-pithy even when its pure-white, flattened roots are allowed to grow to a large 5-6 inches across — most turnip varieties turn woody, hollow, or sharply pungent well before reaching that size, forcing gardeners to harvest small. This gives more flexibility in harvest timing and a bigger yield per root without sacrificing quality. The tender greens are edible as well and hold up well in the kitchen. In zone 9, grow it strictly as a fall and winter crop, since heat above the mid-70s causes turnip roots to become pithy and bitter regardless of variety; sow from late summer through early fall for a harvest running into winter.
sources: All-America Selections — Just Right Turnip winner announcement

name: Just Sweet Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Just Sweet is a compact, heavily fruiting snacking pepper bred to hold up well in containers as well as garden beds.
directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Just Sweet is an AAS-winning snack-type sweet pepper bred for a compact, well-branched plant that produces heavy clusters of small, elongated, bell-flavored fruits that ripen quickly from green to bright red and are sweet and crunchy enough to eat straight off the plant. The small, tidy plant size makes it an excellent choice for large containers and patio growing, not just garden beds. Pick fruit continuously through the season, either green or fully ripe red, to keep the plant producing; the earlier and more often fruit is harvested, the more the plant sets. Feed lightly through the season, since heavy nitrogen encourages foliage over fruit.
sources: All-America Selections — Just Sweet Pepper winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Jwala Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant once soil has warmed and nights stay above 55°F. Jwala is a heavy, continuous producer that rewards frequent picking of young green pods.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Jwala ('flame' in Hindi) is one of the most widely grown chilies in India, prized as the classic Indian finger hot pepper for everyday cooking. Slender, curved, slightly wrinkled green pods grow 3–4 inches long in dense clusters and carry a fruity, sharp heat (roughly 25,000–50,000 Scoville units) well above a jalapeño. Pods are usually picked and used green — deep-fried whole for the popular mirchi bhaji snack, sliced into curries, or pickled — though left to ripen they turn red and can be dried. Prolific, compact plants perform well in containers as well as garden beds and keep producing through summer heat if picked regularly.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners Database — Jwala Pepper
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Jwala Pepper

name: Jyunpaku Okinawan Pure White Bitter Melon
plantingNote: Direct-sow (or start indoors 3-4 weeks before last frost in cooler areas) after soil is thoroughly warm, providing a sturdy trellis; in zone 9 this Japanese type thrives in the long, humid summer season.
directions: A Japanese Okinawan heirloom-type bitter melon grown for its smooth, creamy-white, blunt-ended fruit, typically 8-10 inches long, that carries noticeably milder bitterness than the common green Indian and Chinese types. As the fruit fully ripens it develops a sweet, bright-red seed coating that is considered the best-flavored of any bitter melon type when eaten out of hand. Okinawan bitter melon (goya) has long been associated with the traditional Okinawan diet and its reputation for longevity, and the pale, gently bitter fruit is well suited to raw preparations like thin-sliced salads as well as classic stir-fries such as goya champuru. Provide a tall, sturdy trellis and consistently moist, fertile soil for strong summer production in Gulf Coast heat.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Jyunpaku Okinawan Pure White Bitter Melon
University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension — Bitter Melon

name: Kabocha Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 3–4 weeks early; kabocha squash produces sprawling vines that need 6–8 feet in all directions. In zone 8‑9, plant in early spring for summer harvest or plant in late summer for a fall crop to avoid the most intense heat.
