directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; kabocha is a Japanese-style winter squash with a dumpling-shaped, dark green (or orange in some types) skin and incredibly dense, dry, sweet bright-orange flesh that has a texture more like sweet potato or chestnut than watery summer squash. The flavor is distinctive — nutty, sweet, and complex — and kabocha is prized in Japanese, Korean, and Thai cuisines for tempura, braised dishes, soups, and desserts. It stores 3–5 months in a cool, dry location. Harvest when the skin resists fingernail puncture and the stem has dried and corked over. The flavor actually improves after 2–3 weeks of curing at room temperature as starches convert to sugars.
sources: Asian Vegetable Research and Development Center

name: Kabuli Chickpea
plantingNote: Direct sow around the last frost date once the soil has warmed slightly; Kabuli is the large, cream-colored, thin-skinned chickpea market class familiar from grocery-store dried and canned garbanzo beans, distinct from the smaller, darker Desi types grown mainly in South Asia.
directions: Direct sow seed 1-1.5 inches deep into well-drained soil with a neutral to slightly alkaline pH, since chickpeas rot quickly in cold, wet ground and dislike heavy clay. Kabuli chickpeas produce the large, plump, beige-cream seeds most familiar to home cooks as garbanzo beans or hummus chickpeas, borne one or two per small, inflated pod on bushy, ferny-leaved plants that rarely need staking. The foliage and pods are covered in fine glandular hairs that exude a sticky, mildly acidic secretion, so wear long sleeves and gloves when working among mature plants to avoid skin irritation. Pick pods green and shell them for fresh eating like a shelling pea, or let the crop dry down fully in the field and harvest whole plants once most pods have turned tan and papery, then thresh, winnow, and store the dried seed in a sealed container.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Cicer arietinum germplasm resources
Washington State University Extension — Dry Pea and Chickpea Production

name: Kagraner Sommer Lettuce
plantingNote: Sow in successive batches from spring through summer, since it holds its tender texture and mild flavor in warm weather far longer than typical soft-head lettuces.
directions: Sow in successive batches from spring through summer, since it holds its tender texture and mild flavor in warm weather far longer than typical soft-head lettuces. Developed near Kagran outside Vienna, this Austrian heirloom butterhead is prized for exceptional heat tolerance and slow bolting, unusual traits among classic butterheads. It remains a benchmark variety for gardeners needing a butterhead that survives real summer heat.

name: Kaiware Daikon
plantingNote: Sow thickly on a damp sprouting tray or shallow soil indoors; Kaiware grows year-round indoors and is harvested as a sprout, not a mature root crop.
directions: Sow thickly on a damp sprouting tray or shallow soil indoors, out of direct hot sun; Kaiware is daikon radish grown specifically as a sprout rather than for its root, harvested in just 5-10 days once the cotyledons unfurl above the thin white stems. It carries a spicy, sharp, radish-forward flavor that makes it a classic garnish for sashimi and sushi and a crunchy addition to salads and sandwiches. Keep the growing medium consistently moist and harvest by cutting at the base once the sprouts reach 2-4 inches tall, well before any true leaves fully develop.

name: Kakai Pumpkin
plantingNote: Sow seeds directly into warm soil a week or two after the last frost, spacing hills widely to accommodate sprawling vines, and keep beds evenly moist through flowering and fruit set.
directions: Sow seeds directly into warm soil a week or two after the last frost, spacing hills widely to accommodate sprawling vines, and keep beds evenly moist through flowering and fruit set. This Austrian landrace from Styria produces medium orange pumpkins prized not for their stringy flesh but for their thin-hulled, dark-green naked seeds, which are roasted or pressed for the region's famous dark green pumpkinseed oil. Harvest when rinds harden and vines die back, then cure fruit briefly before scooping and drying seeds for eating or oil pressing. It has become a staple specialty crop among home seed-savers and oil producers in North America since the late 20th century.

name: Kaleidoscope Kale
plantingNote: Direct sow or start indoors a few weeks before last frost; also sow in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: This 2026 Burpee introduction is a compact kale bred for small-space growing, reaching maturity in about 45 days. Its densely packed, heavily ruffled leaves pack a lot of texture and nutrition into a small footprint, and hold up well whether eaten raw in salads, cooked into stews, blended into smoothies, or baked into chips. Burpee specifically markets it as a patio, deck, and balcony container variety for gardeners with limited space. Give it full sun and consistent moisture for the best leaf production.

name: Kalettes
plantingNote: Start indoors 14–18 weeks before the first fall frost so the tall stalks mature during cool autumn weather, the same schedule used for Brussels sprouts.
directions: Kalettes are an open-pollinated cross between Brussels sprouts and kale, first bred by Tozer Seeds in the UK and released commercially in the early 2010s; the result is a tall stalk lined with loose, frilly, purple-green rosettes instead of the tight round buttons of a standard Brussels sprout. Grow exactly as you would Brussels sprouts: stake the tall stalks against wind, keep soil evenly moist, and top the growing point once the lowest rosettes reach marble size to concentrate energy in the remaining buds. Harvest rosettes from the bottom of the stalk upward as they firm up; flavor becomes noticeably sweeter and less bitter after a hard frost. A single stalk can be harvested over several weeks as rosettes mature sequentially up its length.

name: Kalibos Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or sow in midsummer for a fall crop, since Kalibos develops its deepest color and best flavor with a longer, cooler growing season.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in midsummer for transplanting out in late summer, since Kalibos develops its best color and flavor with a longer, cooler fall growing season. Kalibos is a Central/Eastern European heirloom cabbage, likely developed from the older Vysoky (Vysocke) type, distinguished by small, dense, cone-shaped heads of deep purple-red leaves that form a striking pointed rosette rather than the round or flattened heads of typical cabbage. The tender, crisp, juicy leaves are deep red to violet clear through to the core, making Kalibos as prized for its color in raw slaws and pickles as for its mild, sweet flavor. It stores for a moderate period after harvest and remains something of a novelty in North American gardens despite long popularity in Eastern Europe.

name: Kamo Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; give plants extra room since Kamo grows larger and bushier than slender Asian eggplant types.
directions: Kamo Nasu is a traditional heirloom from the Kamo district of Kyoto, grown for its large, softball-sized round fruit with thick, dense flesh that stays creamy and never turns spongy even at full size. It is the classic eggplant used for dengaku, where thick slices are grilled or pan-fried and topped with sweet miso glaze, since the dense flesh holds together better than thinner-skinned slicing types. Give plants rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture, as the large fruit can stress the plant if it dries out between waterings. Choose Kamo when you want an eggplant suited to grilling and roasting whole slices rather than the elongated Asian types more common in home gardens.

name: Kandy Korn Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for adequate wind pollination; Kandy Korn is an EH (Everlasting Heritage) or se-type variety and can be planted adjacent to su types without significant flavor reduction. In zone 9, plant March–April for June–July harvest. The later maturity (85–92 days) means Kandy Korn is one of the last sweet corn varieties of the season for most gardens, providing continuity after mid-season types are finished.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least 4 rows; side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Kandy Korn EH is a yellow EH (Everlasting Heritage) or se-type sweet corn — a variety from the Illinois Foundation Seeds stable that occupies an important niche as a late-season yellow corn with a distinctive flavor profile that many traditional corn enthusiasts prefer to modern hybrid types. The 'EH' designation refers to 'Everlasting Heritage,' a genetic trait that increases sugar content and slows the sugar-to-starch conversion rate compared to standard su types but maintains more of the complex, traditional 'field corn' flavor notes that characterize classic American sweet corn — a richer, deeper, more complex corn flavor than the clean sweetness of modern se or sh2 types. Kandy Korn is particularly popular with older gardeners and those who grew up eating sweet corn from small farms and roadside stands, where the flavor of the corn itself (rather than just sweetness) was the primary quality attribute. The medium-large ears (7.5–8 inches, 14–16 rows) carry well-filled rows of golden-yellow, tender kernels with extended holding quality compared to standard su. At 85–92 days, Kandy Korn extends the sweet corn season to the later summer window when earlier varieties have finished.
sources: Illinois Foundation Seeds — Kandy Korn EH variety notes
Burpee Seeds — Sweet corn variety descriptions
University of Illinois Extension — Sweet Corn Production Guide

name: Kanota Oat
plantingNote: Broadcast or drill into cool, workable spring soil as early in the season as the ground allows; Kanota is a quick, early-maturing spring oat rather than a fall-sown type.
directions: Kanota is an open-pollinated red spring oat released in California in 1928 that has stayed in circulation among small grain growers and homesteaders ever since, valued for maturing only a few days behind the earliest oat varieties available. Broadcast or drill seed into firm, cool spring soil and rake it in shallowly for even emergence; the crop grows into a tall, leafy stand that heads out and ripens well before summer heat and humidity peak, which helps it dodge some of the rust and mildew pressure that hits later-maturing oats. Because Kanota is more susceptible than modern varieties to crown rust, stem rust, powdery mildew, and barley yellow dwarf virus, it is best suited to smaller-scale, closely watched plantings rather than large monoculture fields. Harvest when the panicles are fully dry and golden, then thresh and store the hulled grain for rolling, milling, or replanting.

name: Kanpyo Gourd
plantingNote: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, or start indoors 3-4 weeks early in short-season regions; give the vigorous vine a strong arbor or wide bed to sprawl since fruit is harvested well before the shell hardens.
directions: Kanpyo is the Japanese bottle gourd cultivar grown specifically to be peeled into long ribbons and sun-dried into the sweet-savory strips used in kanpyomaki sushi rolls and simmered dishes, distinct from gourds grown for eating fresh or for hard dried shells. Vines are vigorous and need a sturdy trellis or wide open ground, with large white flowers opening at dusk for moth pollination, so hand-pollinating with a small brush in the evening improves fruit set where night pollinators are scarce. Harvest the pale green fruit while still immature and tender, before the seeds and rind harden, then peel it in one continuous spiral ribbon with a vegetable peeler or specialized gourd slicer and hang the strips to dry in a warm, airy spot out of direct sun. Because the plant is a heavy, sprawling grower that benefits from consistent warmth and moisture through fruit development, it performs best where summers are long and hot.
sources: Purdue University — New Crop Resources — Lagenaria siceraria

name: Kansas Muskmelon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is warm; its tolerance of humidity and uneven rainfall makes it a solid pick for muggy Gulf Coast summers where many melons struggle with fruit splitting.
directions: Kansas Muskmelon is a Great Plains heirloom kept alive through regional seed savers and now offered by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange, valued for holding up to humid weather and inconsistent rainfall better than many other old melon varieties. The oval, sutured, moderately netted fruits average about four pounds and ripen almost all the way out to the rind for little waste, with fine-textured, richly flavored flesh that has kept the variety in demand among heirloom growers. It also shows good resistance to sap beetles, a common pest that ruins fruit of other melon varieties late in the season. As with other open-pollinated melons, isolate plantings from other Cucumis melo varieties if you intend to save true seed.

name: Kanthari Chili Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; productive and heat-tolerant, setting clusters of two to three fruits per node.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this compact, bushy frutescens landrace from Kerala, India, is prized in South Indian cooking for its small, marble-round, glossy red pods. Heat runs high (roughly 50,000-100,000 Scoville units) but dissipates faster than many other hot peppers, leaving a bright, citrusy flavor that's central to Kerala fish curries, chutneys, and pickles. Plants are productive and heat-tolerant, setting clusters of two to three fruits per node through a long harvest season.

name: Karikachi Edamame
plantingNote: Direct-sow after soil has warmed following last frost; this Hokkaido-bred cultivar tolerates cooler summer conditions better than many edamame types, suiting short-season gardens.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in rows in full sun, inoculating with rhizobia bacteria for improved nitrogen fixation. Karikachi No. 3 is a compact, determinate Japanese heirloom bred on the island of Hokkaido for cool, short growing seasons, setting three large, sweet-flavored beans per pod on reliably productive, disease-resistant plants. Harvest whole pods once they are plump and bright green but before the shells begin to toughen or yellow. Blanch briefly in salted water before shelling and serving as a snack or in salads and stir-fries.

name: Karma Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Karma is a blocky bell pepper hybrid bred with resistance to common mosaic viruses, which spread readily through aphid activity in warm Gulf South gardens.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Karma is a hybrid bell pepper bred with resistance to common mosaic viruses, letting it keep its foliage healthier through the aphid pressure that builds over a long, warm Gulf South growing season. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good sweetness if left on the plant longer. The compact, well-branched plant provides good leaf cover that helps shield developing fruit from sunscald during peak summer heat. Harvest at the green stage for a milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red for maximum sweetness, and keep picking to encourage continued fruit set.
sources: seed catalog reference (Tomato Growers Supply Company)
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pepper Production

name: Kashi Anmol Chilli
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; the compact, dwarf plants suit tight spacing and container growing and begin cropping about 55 days after transplanting.
directions: Developed by ICAR's Indian Institute of Vegetable Research through recurrent selection from a Sri Lankan introduction, Kashi Anmol is a determinate, dwarf chile with dark, pigmented nodes and slender green pods held upright in attractive pendant clusters. Its compact stature and short internodes make it productive in a small footprint, and it begins yielding earlier than many taller Indian chile types. Grow it in full sun with rich, well-drained soil, and pick pods green for the mild-to-moderate heat favored in everyday Indian cooking, or allow some to ripen red for drying. Because plants stay short and self-supporting, Kashi Anmol is a good choice for raised beds and container vegetable gardens.

name: Kashi Dhawal Ash Gourd
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after soil has fully warmed, giving the sprawling vines a large trellis or open ground space; this is a released Indian research-station cultivar bred specifically for high flesh yield rather than long storage.
directions: Kashi Dhawal is an ash gourd cultivar released by ICAR's Indian Institute of Vegetable Research in Varanasi, selected from a local landrace for its oblong fruit, thick white flesh, and unusually high flesh-to-rind ratio. Vines are long and vigorous, reaching well over 20 feet, and fruits mature in about 120 days into large, greenish-white, waxy-coated gourds commonly weighing 11-12 pounds. Its dense, high-recovery flesh makes it the preferred type for making petha, the popular Indian candied ash gourd sweet, though it cooks and stores like any other winter melon in curries and soups. Grow it exactly as you would standard winter melon, in full sun on deeply worked, fertile, moisture-retentive soil with a heavy-duty trellis or generous ground space to support the long vines and heavy fruit.
sources: ICAR-Indian Institute of Vegetable Research (IIVR), Varanasi - Ash Gourd Varieties

name: Katahdin Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; Katahdin was released in 1932 by the USDA Potato Breeding Program and named for Mount Katahdin in Maine — for much of the 20th century it was the most widely grown potato in the eastern United States, prized for good yields, excellent storage quality, and versatile white flesh suitable for all cooking purposes.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10–12 inches apart in rows 30–36 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost; Katahdin is a main-season variety producing large, round to oval, smooth, buff-white-skinned, white-fleshed tubers of excellent quality. Katahdin was developed by the USDA Potato Research Laboratory in Presque Isle, Maine and officially released in 1932, named for the highest peak in Maine; for the next several decades it was the most widely grown potato in the northeastern and mid-Atlantic United States, valued for its consistent productivity, reliable storage quality, and disease resistance (including moderate resistance to late blight). The large, smooth, nearly round tubers have thin, buff to light tan skin and white flesh with a slightly waxy texture when young — excellent for boiling and potato salad — that transitions toward semi-floury when fully mature, making them good for baking and mashing as well; a genuinely all-purpose variety in the tradition of the great white American storage potatoes. Flavor is clean, mild, and characteristic of the best white potato types; stores 4–6 months under proper conditions (35–40°F, high humidity). Still grown commercially in the Northeast and available from heritage potato suppliers.

name: Katarina Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer for a fall crop; Katarina is a very early, small-headed cabbage bred for close spacing in containers and small beds, forming a solid head faster than most cabbage varieties.
directions: Start transplants and set out in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container. Katarina is an AAS-winning cabbage bred for very early maturity and a small, tidy head about 4 inches across, forming a solid, sweet, light-green head faster than nearly any other garden cabbage — a useful trait for squeezing a crop into a short spring or fall window, or for a large container where a full-size storage cabbage would be impractical. Its small stature and rapid maturity also make it a good choice for succession planting through a cool season. Harvest as soon as heads feel firm and dense, since even fast-maturing types can split if left too long once mature. Watch for cabbage worms and aphids, common pests on all brassicas in the Gulf South.
sources: All-America Selections — Katarina Cabbage winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Katrina Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into warm soil in full sun; a trellis or support helps keep the smooth mini fruits clean and easy to harvest; well suited to high tunnels and hydroponic systems as well as open ground.
directions: Katrina is a hybrid Beit Alpha-type mini cucumber bred for snacking, bearing smooth, thin-skinned, nearly seedless fruit about 5.5-6.5 inches long with a sweet, crisp bite. It is heat-tolerant and highly productive, often setting multiple fruits per node for a heavy, early-to-midseason harvest. The seedless, parthenocarpic fruit set makes production reliable in both open gardens and protected culture. Harvest young and often at full size for the sweetest, crunchiest cucumbers with no need to peel.

name: Katsouni
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after the last frost once soil has warmed; give the sprawling or trellised vines room to run, and harvest young and often for the mildest flavor.
directions: Katsouni is a traditional Cretan landrace botanically classed with melons rather than true cucumbers, yet grown and eaten exactly like a cucumber, picked young and pale green before the fruit's latent melon sweetness develops. Train the rampant vines onto a trellis or fence to keep the long, slightly ribbed fruit straight and easy to harvest, and pick every few days once fruiting begins to prevent oversized, seedy specimens. The thin skin and crisp, mild flesh make it a favorite sliced raw in Cretan salads with olive oil, oregano, and feta. Leave a few fruit to mature fully on the vine each season if saving seed, since overripe specimens shift toward true melon flavor and texture.

name: Katydid Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Katydid is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bearing green-striped fruit on a compact plant.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Katydid bears medium fruit striped green over an amber-green background even when fully ripe, a striking novelty color pattern with tangy, well-balanced flavor typical of green-fleshed tomato types, on a compact plant bred through the Dwarf Tomato Project. Its manageable size and eye-catching fruit suit raised beds and containers. Harvest when fruit softens slightly, since color alone won't signal ripeness in green-fleshed types.

name: Kculli Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; Kculli is among the oldest documented Andean corn races and is grown for its deep purple-black kernels and cob tissue.
directions: Sow in full sun once soil has warmed, grouping blocks of plants rather than single rows since corn is wind pollinated and isolation from other corn preserves the deep anthocyanin pigmentation in the kernels. Kculli, better known commercially as maíz morado or Peruvian purple corn, is harvested fully dry and the kernels and cobs are boiled down to make the dark purple base for chicha morada and mazamorra morada, two of Peru's best-known purple corn preparations. Let ears dry completely in the husk before shelling, and store kernels (with some cob fragments, which carry much of the pigment) in a cool, dry place. This landrace is one of the pigments-richest corns used in Andean anthocyanin research.
sources: National Research Council — Races of Maize in Peru (Grobman et al.)

name: Kellogg's Breakfast Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; an indeterminate orange beefsteak with deep-meaty flesh and very small seed cavities; plant early in warm climates to get harvest before summer heat peaks.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to a rich, well-drained site in full sun after frost danger has passed, burying the stem to the lowest leaves. Kellogg's Breakfast is an American heirloom orange beefsteak tomato that originated with William Kellogg of Michigan, introduced to the larger seed-saving community through Seed Savers Exchange, and has since become one of the most celebrated orange heirlooms for its extraordinary flavor — sweet, mild, and low-acid with a rich, fruity depth that makes it ideal fresh. Fruits weigh 1–2 pounds and have very meaty, almost seedless flesh that is deep orange throughout; they ripen relatively slowly but the wait is well worth it. Stake or cage plants firmly and thin to two or three main leaders for the largest fruits.
sources: Heirloom Tomato Growers Guide, Eastern Michigan University Extension

name: Kelsae Onion
plantingNote: Sow seed indoors in mid-winter, 12-14 weeks before the last frost, to give this giant exhibition type the long growing season it needs; transplant out once hardened off and frost danger has passed.
directions: Kelsae is a British giant exhibition onion bred to produce enormous, mild-flavored globes that regularly place among the largest onions grown at horticultural shows. Start seed early under lights, prick out into individual pots, and transplant into deeply dug, heavily enriched soil with generous spacing so each bulb has room to reach show-winning size. Feed and water generously through the growing season, since exhibition size depends on sustained, uninterrupted growth rather than stress-hardening. Because the huge, thin-skinned bulbs are milder and less pungent than standard storage onions, they are best used soon after harvest rather than held for long-term storage.

name: Ken Aslet Mashua
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ken Aslet flowers and tuberizes somewhat earlier than typical mashua, holder of a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit.
directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Ken Aslet is an intermediate-daylength mashua selection that flowers and tuberizes earlier in the season than the typical species, having arisen as a volunteer seedling at RHS Wisley in the 1950s and since earned the RHS Award of Garden Merit. Foliage is killed by any hard frost, but established tubers survive short freezes down to roughly 20-25°F under mulch. It is best suited to zone 9a or cool-summer climates like the Pacific Northwest, with tubers reaching harvestable size about 10 weeks after tuber initiation begins following the fall equinox.

name: Kenearly
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil; space rows generously to reduce white mold risk in humid weather.
directions: Kenearly is a refinement of the old Maine Yellow Eye strain, selected at the Kentville research station in Nova Scotia for a larger, more uniform yellow eye and more even maturity than its parent. The plump, cream-colored beans can be picked at the shelling stage or left to dry fully on the vine. Avoid working around plants when foliage is wet, since the variety is susceptible to fungal disease in damp conditions, and give it wide spacing for airflow. It is a dependable keeper for winter baked-bean cookery once fully dried.

name: Kennebec Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January–February. Kennebec is a mid-season white potato (75–90 days) that adapts well to the Gulf Coast's winter growing window. Plant 4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil and hill regularly.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-drained, fertile soil; Kennebec is an All-America Selections winner introduced by the USDA in 1948 from a cross of B127 x USDA 96-56, named for the Kennebec River in Maine. For many decades it was the most widely grown potato in the eastern United States, dominating both fresh market and potato chip production because of its outstanding adaptability, disease resistance, and excellent culinary quality. The large, oval tubers have thin, buff-white skin and firm, white flesh that performs equally well baked, fried, mashed, or roasted — a true all-purpose potato. Kennebec shows good resistance to late blight and is tolerant of common scab, making it more reliable than many varieties in the variable conditions of Gulf Coast winter gardens. It remains a benchmark variety offered by heritage seed companies for its proven performance and consistent quality. In zone 9, plant January–February and harvest May–June before summer heat arrives.
sources: USDA Bureau of Plant Industry — Kennebec potato release notes 1948
Maine Potato Board — Kennebec variety documentation
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Kennebec potato notes

name: Kentucky Beefsteak Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Kentucky Beefsteak is an Appalachian heirloom prized for its golden-orange, notably low-acid flesh and large beefsteak-type fruit.
directions: Start seeds indoors under grow lights 6-8 weeks before the last frost date; transplant outdoors after frost danger has fully passed with a wire cage or stout stake, setting the plant deep to encourage root formation along the buried stem. Kentucky Beefsteak, an heirloom collected from the hills of eastern Kentucky, produces large, meaty, golden-orange fruit with notably low acidity and a mild, sweet flavor, distinguishing it from the more common red and pink Southern beefsteak heirlooms. The indeterminate vines are vigorous and productive through a long summer season in hot, humid Southern conditions. Its low-acid flavor makes it a favorite for slicing and eating fresh for gardeners sensitive to the tang of more acidic tomato varieties.

name: Kentucky Blue Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; provide a sturdy trellis, pole tepee, or wire fence at least 5–6 feet tall. Kentucky Blue vines climb to 6–7 feet and require strong support. Harvest pods frequently at 5–6 inches for maximum tenderness and continued production.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Kentucky Blue is a 1991 All-America Selections-winning pole bean that crossed two of the most beloved pole bean varieties — Kentucky Wonder and Blue Lake — to combine the best traits of both parents. Kentucky Wonder contributes vigor, heavy production, excellent traditional pole bean flavor, and the characteristic meaty pod texture; Blue Lake contributes its renowned stringless quality, mild sweetness, and the refined, crisp texture that made it the gold standard of snap bean flavor. The resulting Kentucky Blue produces long (6–8 inch), round, deep green, completely stringless pods with excellent flavor that tasters consistently rate among the best of all snap beans — more substantial than filet beans but more refined than older Kentucky Wonder strains. Very productive vines climbing 6–7 feet continue bearing throughout the summer and fall when harvested regularly. The combination of classic pole bean character, genuine stringlessness, superior flavor, and heavy production has made Kentucky Blue one of the most popular and recommended pole beans in American gardens since its introduction.
sources: All-America Selections — Kentucky Blue pole bean AAS winner 1991
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Pole bean variety comparison
University of Massachusetts Cooperative Extension — Bean Variety Trials

name: Kentucky Wonder Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after the last frost date when soil has warmed to at least 60°F; provide a trellis, pole, or fence 5–8 feet tall for the climbing vines; in zone 9, sow February–April for spring crop and again August–September for fall crop.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0) soil in full sun after last frost when soil is warm; Kentucky Wonder is the most famous and most enduring American heirloom pole bean — an heirloom variety in continuous cultivation since the 1860s that remains one of the most widely grown and best-regarded pole beans in American home gardens. The vigorous climbing vines reach 5–8 feet and require a sturdy support structure — traditional pole, trellis, or fence. Kentucky Wonder produces heavy yields of long (7–9 inch), round-to-flat, stringless-when-young green pods with exceptional flavor — a rich, full, classic green bean taste that is considerably more complex and satisfying than modern bush beans bred for commercial production. Seed can be saved true-to-type from open-pollinated Kentucky Wonder. The dry seeds (beans) can be used as shell beans or dried for winter storage, giving the plant dual utility as both green snap bean and dry bean. In zone 9, the spring season (February–May) and fall season (August–October) provide two productive growing windows. The combination of outstanding flavor, prolific production, historical significance, and heirloom status makes Kentucky Wonder the gold standard of American pole beans.

name: Kentucky Wonder Wax Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost at the base of a trellis or pole; a yellow-podded sport of standard Kentucky Wonder, it needs the same tall support and regular picking.
directions: Kentucky Wonder Wax is a yellow-podded selection of the classic brown-seeded Kentucky Wonder pole bean, offering the same vigorous climbing habit and heavy yields but with round, buttery-yellow pods instead of green. Pods run 7-8 inches, stringless and meaty, with a slightly sweeter, more delicate flavor than the green original, and they show up clearly against the foliage for easy picking. Like its parent variety, it climbs readily to 6-8 feet and needs a sturdy trellis, rewarding gardeners with continuous production when harvested every few days. It remains a favorite where gardeners want a wax bean with genuine pole-bean vigor rather than a compact bush habit.

name: Kermit Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Kermit thrives in Gulf South heat and humidity, continuing to produce heavily through the hottest part of summer.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest young at golf-ball to ping-pong-ball size for the crisp, mild, seed-free texture prized in Thai cooking. Kermit is a small, round Thai eggplant with pale green skin streaked and mottled with cream-white striping, borne in heavy clusters on compact, productive plants that thrive in hot, humid conditions. The firm, dense flesh has very few seeds when harvested young and holds its shape well in curries, stir-fries, and stews — traditional uses in Thai cuisine, where round green eggplants are added whole or halved directly into simmering curry. Its heat tolerance and continuous production over a long summer season make it an excellent, prolific choice for Gulf South vegetable gardens, zone 4–12.

name: Kerr's Pink Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces once soil is workable; this vigorous maincrop variety tolerates a wide range of soils better than many modern cultivars.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil and hill generously, as this old Scottish cultivar produces a heavy crop of round to oval tubers with distinctive rose-pink skin and creamy white, floury flesh. Bred in Scotland in 1917, Kerr's Pink became a staple maincrop potato across Ireland and Scotland thanks to its reliable yields, good disease tolerance, and adaptability to poorer, wetter soils than many refined modern varieties tolerate. The floury texture makes excellent mash and roast potatoes but causes it to break apart in soups and stews, so reserve it for dry-cooking preparations. Grow it where a rustic, high-yielding heirloom maincrop with real cold-region pedigree is wanted over a fussier modern hybrid.

name: Kestrel Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring; the monogerm seed produces a single seedling per node, so stands need little or no thinning even at close spacing.
directions: Kestrel is a widely grown market hybrid beet valued for its true monogerm seed, smooth dark-red globe roots, and dependable resistance to premature bolting when spring temperatures swing warm and cold. Sow thinly 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and keep the bed evenly moist through germination, since the single-seedling habit removes the usual thinning labor but still needs even moisture for uniform root size. Roots hold quality in the ground longer than older open-pollinated types, which makes Kestrel a dependable choice for succession plantings and for growers who bunch beets with their tops still attached. Harvest at 1.5-2.5 inches across for the sweetest, most tender roots.

name: Kettle River Giant Garlic
scientificName: Allium sativum var. ophioscorodon 'Kettle River Giant'
plantingNote: Plant large cloves 3 inches deep in October-November after several nights of cold weather so roots establish before hard freeze.
directions: Kettle River Giant is a Porcelain-type hardneck garlic originating from the Kettle River valley near the Washington-British Columbia border, prized for producing some of the largest bulbs of any hardneck strain, often exceeding 3 inches across with just 4-6 oversized cloves per head. Grow it in rich, well-drained soil with consistent moisture through bulb sizing, and mulch heavily over winter in colder zones since Porcelain types are somewhat less cold-hardy than Rocambole strains. The flavor is strong and full-bodied with a lingering heat, and the tall, sturdy scapes make excellent garlic scape pesto in early summer. Choose this variety when garden space is limited but you still want big, easy-to-peel cloves for the kitchen.

name: Keuka Gold Potato
plantingNote: A robust northern-climate variety bred at Cornell; plant 4-6 weeks before last frost in well-drained soil.
directions: Bred at Cornell University, this mid-to-late-season golden potato forms oval, medium-large tubers with golden skin and golden flesh and a reputation as an easy, dependable grower in cold-winter regions. Medium plants with white flowers set a moderate-to-heavy crop of tubers, and the variety carries high scab resistance along with medium late blight tolerance. Expect heavy overall yields and good storage keeping from this reliable Northeastern selection.

name: Keystone Resistant Giant Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Keystone Resistant Giant is an open-pollinated heirloom that tends to produce more large fruits when staked or caged. In zone 9, transplant March–April for a June–September harvest. The 'Resistant' in the name refers to Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV) resistance — important in an era before comprehensive disease resistance packages in peppers.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 75–85°F; transplant to full sun with consistent moisture and balanced fertility. Keystone Resistant Giant is a Pennsylvania-origin heirloom bell pepper that was one of the most important commercial bell pepper varieties in the eastern United States from the 1940s through the 1970s, valued as the largest-fruited TMV-resistant open-pollinated bell pepper available during a period when disease resistance was achieved only through strain selection rather than modern breeding techniques. The 'Keystone' name connects the variety to Pennsylvania (the Keystone State), where it was grown extensively by commercial growers, home gardeners, and the Pennsylvania Dutch communities who prize large, thick-walled peppers for stuffing with meat and rice. The fruits are distinctly large (4–5 inches tall, 3–4 inches wide), blocky, 3-4 lobed, dark green ripening to red, with moderately thick walls and an upright, pendant orientation on strong-stemmed plants. Keystone Resistant Giant represents the pre-F1-hybrid era of American pepper breeding and occupies an important place in American heirloom pepper history — it was the standard against which American bell peppers were measured for decades and remains a valued open-pollinated option for seed savers who want a true-breeding large stuffing pepper. The flavor at the red stage is rich, sweet, and classically bell-pepper, with none of the bitterness that characterizes some heirloom types.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Keystone Resistant Giant variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Pennsylvania heirloom pepper collection
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Historical Bell Pepper Variety Documentation

name: Kherson Oat
plantingNote: Broadcast or drill at the earliest workable spring date on the Northern Plains and Corn Belt; Kherson is an early, drought-tolerant spring oat rather than a fall-sown type.
directions: Kherson was brought into the United States in 1896 from the Kherson region of southern Russia by way of the Nebraska Agricultural Experiment Station, and within twenty years it had become one of the most widely sown oats across the Great Plains and Corn Belt thanks to its short season and unusual drought tolerance. Sow as early as the ground can be worked in spring; the crop germinates in cool soil and races to maturity ahead of the worst summer heat, which is what made it so valuable on dry, marginal prairie ground before irrigation was common. It tillers modestly and stands a bit shorter than many modern oats, so it tolerates lean soil without lodging heavily. Harvest when straw and hulls turn pale gold, then thresh promptly since the loose hull shatters somewhat more readily than modern oat varieties.
sources: USDA Bureau of Plant Industry historical bulletins
South Dakota State University Extension oat variety records

name: KickStart Sweet Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm soil after frost danger passes; fruit can be harvested green at 50-55 days or left to ripen fully red at 70-75 days.
directions: An early, high-yielding upright bell pepper producing medium-to-large, blocky fruit well suited to stuffing or chopping, with a sweet flavor at full ripeness. Transplant into full sun once the soil has warmed; the upright 20-30 inch plants hold fruit well off the ground. Expect green-stage harvest around 50-55 days from transplant or fully red fruit at 70-75 days, with individual peppers averaging 8-9 ounces. The variety carries resistance to multiple bacterial leaf spot strains, which helps reduce foliage loss in humid growing conditions.

name: Kikuza Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early in short-season climates; allow ample space for sprawling vines.
directions: Kikuza is a Japanese heirloom kabocha-type squash bearing flattened, deeply lobed fruit with a dark green rind roughened by prominent grayish-tan warts and scarring, a distinctive look among the smoother-skinned kabocha commonly sold in supermarkets. The dry, dense flesh is deep orange-yellow and intensely sweet with the chestnut-like flavor characteristic of the finest kabocha strains, and it stores well for months when cured properly. Grow it as you would other maxima kabocha types, keeping vines evenly watered until fruit sets and then letting soil dry somewhat as the rind hardens and corking develops around the stem. Cure harvested squash in a warm, dry location for one to two weeks to toughen the skin and sweeten the flesh before storage.

name: Killarney Red Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, about 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, so roots establish before winter dormancy.
directions: Separate cloves shortly before planting and set them pointed end up about 2 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Mulch after planting to buffer winter temperature swings and remove mulch gradually as green shoots emerge in spring; cut off curling scapes in early summer to redirect energy into bulb growth. Killarney Red is a cold-hardy rocambole strain originating from Irish and Canadian growers, prized for its rich, full-bodied garlic flavor and easy-to-peel purple-blushed skins, though like other rocamboles it does not store as long as porcelain or silverskin types.

name: Kincho Bunching Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring for summer harvest or in late summer for a cold-hardy overwintering crop; Kincho is bred to hold in the field through cold snaps without bolting.
directions: Kincho is a Japanese non-bulbing bunching onion bred for reliable cold hardiness and improved resistance to pink root and botrytis leaf blight compared to older heirloom types. It forms upright, uniform stalks well suited to late-season and overwintered plantings where other bunching onions struggle. Sow thickly and thin gradually, harvesting outer plants first while allowing remaining stalks room to thicken. Its disease tolerance and cold resilience make it a dependable choice for extending green onion harvests into fall and winter in temperate climates.

name: King Arthur Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably above 55°F; vigorous foliage on this hybrid helps shade developing fruit from sunscald.
directions: Start seed indoors under warm conditions and transplant seedlings out after all frost danger has passed, giving plants room to build the heavy foliage cover that protects fruit from sun scorch. Fruit sets as extra-large, thick-walled blocky bells that can be harvested green or left on the plant to sweeten and ripen fully to red. This disease-resistant hybrid holds up well against bacterial leaf spot and other common pepper pressures, making it a dependable choice for stuffing peppers or thick slicing. Pick regularly with pruners to avoid snapping brittle branches and to keep the plant setting new fruit through the season.

name: King Harry Potato
plantingNote: A good choice where Colorado potato beetle, leafhopper, or flea beetle pressure is high; plant 4-6 weeks before last frost.
directions: King Harry is a mid-season, roughly 90-day potato bred for unusually hairy foliage that makes it highly resistant to Colorado potato beetle, potato leafhopper, and flea beetle feeding, a major advantage for organic growers battling these pests. It forms round, white-skinned tubers with waxy, moist flesh and is a high-yielding variety under good care. Because its main strength is insect resistance rather than disease tolerance, still rotate plantings and monitor for blight in wet seasons.

name: King Naga Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since chinense superhots germinate slowly in cool soil.
directions: King Naga is a large-podded Naga-type superhot producing elongated, slightly wrinkled fruit that ripens from green to red and can grow longer than most of its Bhut Jolokia and Naga Morich relatives. Flavor and heat are similar to Naga Morich, with a fruity edge beneath the intense capsaicin load. Give plants a long, warm growing season, rich well-drained soil, and even moisture, since irregular watering causes blossom drop on chinense superhots. Stake or cage plants as pod clusters grow heavy, and wear gloves when harvesting ripe fruit.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: King of Hearts Watermelon
plantingNote: Start seed indoors and transplant after soil is thoroughly warm; as a seedless triploid, King of Hearts needs a nearby seeded watermelon variety planted for pollen to set fruit properly.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting a seeded watermelon variety nearby to supply the pollen this seedless triploid needs to set fruit. King of Hearts is an All-America Selections winning seedless hybrid producing large, oval, striped fruit with sweet, firm, deep red flesh and only soft, edible white seed traces rather than hard black seeds, a genuine convenience for fresh eating. The vigorous vine is a reliable, heavy producer when properly pollinated, and the flavor and texture rank among the better seedless hybrids available. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit stem browns and dries and the ground spot turns creamy yellow, since seedless watermelons give fewer reliable ripeness cues than seeded types and are easy to pick too early.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: King of the Early Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed; this is one of the fastest-maturing dry beans available, letting northern gardeners harvest a dry crop even in short seasons.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep directly in the garden once the soil has warmed, thinning plants to four to six inches apart in rows. King of the Early is a compact bush bean prized by Northeastern and Midwestern growers for reaching dry-bean maturity well ahead of most other shelling varieties, making it a reliable choice where the frost-free window is short. Let pods dry fully on the plant until they rattle, then shell and store the plump white beans in an airtight container. The beans cook up tender and mild, making a good all-purpose soup or baking bean.

name: King of the Garden Lima Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; King of the Garden is one of the oldest and most celebrated American pole lima beans, introduced by Burpee in 1883 and prized for its very large, flat, creamy-white seeds with exceptional buttery lima flavor — the archetype of the 'large lima' bean and ideal for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens where the long season allows full development.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost with soil above 65°F; provide poles or strong trellising 6–8 feet tall for support. King of the Garden is a classic American pole lima bean introduced by W. Atlee Burpee in 1883 and considered for much of its history the finest large-seeded lima bean available; the plants are vigorous, 6–8 foot climbers that produce long, broad, flat pods with 4–6 very large (up to 1 inch), flat, creamy-white bean seeds with an extraordinarily rich, buttery, full lima bean flavor superior to most modern bush varieties. The large seeds require a relatively long, warm season to develop fully (85–95 days from seed); in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens the long growing season makes King of the Garden ideal for both spring and fall plantings. Excellent for fresh green lima use (harvested at the flat-but-not-yet-wrinkled stage when seeds are fully developed), freezing, and drying. One of the foundational American heirloom vegetables.

name: King of the North Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; King of the North is an early-maturing sweet bell pepper (57–68 days from transplant) bred for cool, short-season climates where standard bell peppers ripen too slowly to produce before frost. In zone 9, where the problem is opposite (heat rather than cold), King of the North is best suited to fall planting (starts July, transplant August, harvest October–November) when cooling temperatures approach the 65–75°F range that bell peppers prefer for fruit set and maturation. The variety's short days-to-maturity allows it to complete ripening within the fall cool window. Harvest green or allow to fully ripen red for full sweetness. King of the North is an open-pollinated heirloom available from multiple seed sources and is notable for germinating and growing vigorously at lower temperatures than most other bell pepper varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost or in late summer for fall production. Harvest green or red. King of the North is an heirloom sweet bell pepper variety bred and popularized specifically for short-season, cool-climate gardens where standard bell pepper varieties (requiring 70–90+ days and substantial heat to develop fully) cannot be relied upon to ripen before fall frosts. The breeding goal of short-season bell peppers like King of the North is to compress the fruit development timeline while maintaining adequate size, wall thickness, and flavor — a challenging tradeoff since bell peppers that ripen quickly tend to be smaller and thinner-walled than late-maturing types. King of the North succeeds reasonably well at this balance: the fruits are large enough to be genuinely useful (3–4 inches, 3-lobed form), with walls adequate for stuffing and fresh use, and flavor that develops to full sweetness when ripened to red. The variety is open-pollinated and seed-saving is straightforward, making it a practical choice for seed-saving gardeners. In zone 9, the short days-to-maturity of King of the North are most valuable for the fall growing season rather than spring: a late-July start from seed produces plants that can be transplanted in late August and begin producing before October heat drops, allowing harvest through November in a climate where long-season varieties started at the same time might not mature before plants are compromised by cool weather. This fall-planting application in zone 9 mirrors King of the North's primary value in zone 3–5 gardens — speed of production in a constrained growing window.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — King of the North pepper heirloom open-pollinated variety documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — King of the North short-season bell pepper variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Short-season sweet bell pepper variety comparison

name: King Philip Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow once the soil has warmed, in blocks rather than single rows; its short season lets it succeed even in cool, short-summer regions.
directions: Direct sow once the soil has warmed, in blocks rather than single rows, and take advantage of its short season to succeed even in cool, short-summer regions of northern New England. King Philip is one of the oldest documented flint corns in cultivation, recorded in Massachusetts and Rhode Island since colonial times and traditionally said to honor the Wampanoag leader Metacomet, known to English colonists as King Philip. The eight-rowed ears bear hard, deep red-brown kernels that dry quickly on the stalk and grind into a flavorful, reddish cornmeal long used for johnnycake and other traditional New England cornbreads.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

name: King Sieg Leek
plantingNote: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start August–September and transplant October–November. King Sieg is selected for mild winters and performs exceptionally well in zone 9, where it can be harvested through the winter without bolting. Transplant seedlings at pencil thickness into deep, wide holes or a trench; blanch the lower shank by earthing up soil as the plant grows. Harvest from November through March in zone 9 before spring warming initiates bolting.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into deep, fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun; King Sieg is a Belgian-bred leek cultivar selected for the mild winter climates of the maritime Pacific Northwest and Gulf South — specifically bred to produce long, thick, white-blanche shanks without premature bolting in mild, frost-free or light-frost winters. Standard leek cultivars selected for cold northern climates often bolt prematurely when grown in mild zone 8–10 winters because the mild temperatures signal the plant that spring has arrived; King Sieg has delayed bolting response, allowing harvest through February and March in zone 9 without quality loss. The thick, tender white shanks with a mild, sweet leek flavor are excellent in potato-leek soup, braised whole, sautéed as a vegetable side, or used in place of onions where a milder allium is needed. Earth up soil around the shanks as the plants grow to extend the white, blanched portion and reduce the proportion of green.
sources: Territorial Seed Company — King Sieg Leek Variety Notes
Oregon State University Extension — Leek Production for the Pacific Northwest
University of California Cooperative Extension — Leek Varieties for Mild Climates

name: Kipfler Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; Kipfler is a late-maturing Austrian fingerling that needs the full season to form its characteristic curved tubers.
directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-worked soil, since the curved fingerling tubers form best where they can expand without obstruction. Kipfler, whose name references its slender, curved shape resembling a crescent roll, produces thin-skinned, yellow-fleshed tubers with a dense, buttery, nutty flavor that holds up well to roasting whole with the skin left on. Long popular as a specialty fingerling in Austria and widely grown in Australia and New Zealand, Kipfler stores reasonably well but is often prized most for fresh eating soon after harvest.

name: Kleckley Sweet Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm (70°F minimum); Kleckley Sweet requires ample space (vines 8–12 feet), full sun, and warm nights for maximum sugar development. In zone 9, plant April–May for a June–August harvest season. Kleckley Sweet is NOT a shipping watermelon — the extremely thin rind that makes it ideal for home eating shatters and bruises too easily for any commercial transport. This restricts Kleckley Sweet to home garden and very local market production, where the fruit can be carried by hand and consumed immediately after harvest. At full maturity in zone 9 heat, Kleckley Sweet produces fruit reaching 25–40 pounds with some individual specimens heavier, bright red flesh, and a sweetness level that has made it the benchmark by which Southern watermelon enthusiasts measure the flavor of other varieties. Detect ripeness by the dried tendril nearest the fruit, the ground spot color transition to creamy yellow, and a dull thud when thumped.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms; allow 6–8 feet between hills. Harvest when tendril nearest fruit dries and ground spot turns yellow. Kleckley Sweet (also called Monte Cristo in some seed catalogs) is one of the great heirloom watermelons of the American South — a variety with an extraordinary reputation for eating quality that has been maintained by home gardeners and seed savers for well over a century, despite being completely impractical for commercial production due to its extremely thin rind. The rind of a ripe Kleckley Sweet is so thin that the fruit can crack simply from being set down too hard — a catastrophic liability for commercial shipping but an indication of the rind's extreme thinness that is part of what makes it so desirable for eating, where rind thickness is inversely proportional to flesh proportion per fruit. The flesh is brilliant red, dense and fine-grained, with very small seeds relative to the flesh volume, and of the highest natural sweetness of any standard-sized watermelon variety — the flavor is intensely, purely sweet with the clean watermelon taste that distinguishes vine-ripened, heat-grown Southern watermelons from the bland, watery specimens produced from short-season varieties in cool climates. The variety was introduced by W. Atlee Burpee around the 1890s-1900s and became one of the most popular garden watermelons in the South through the mid-20th century, maintaining a devoted following among heirloom gardeners long after commercial production shifted to thick-rinded shipping varieties.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Kleckley Sweet watermelon heirloom Southern variety documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Kleckley Sweet watermelon variety history and notes
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Heritage watermelon variety descriptions for the South

name: Klondike Striped Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Klondike Striped is an early 20th century California heirloom watermelon that became the commercial standard for Western US watermelon production, producing medium-large, uniformly striped, oblong fruits with firm, excellent-quality red flesh.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Klondike Striped is drought-tolerant once established and performs well in hot, dry Western climates and Gulf Coast sandy soils. Klondike Striped was developed in early 20th century California, where it became the primary commercial watermelon for California's San Joaquin Valley and other Western growing regions; the medium-large (25–35 lbs), oblong fruits have attractive, uniform, alternating light and dark green stripes and firm, deep red to scarlet flesh with excellent, rich, sweet flavor and few seeds relative to its size. The variety became widely grown in the West and South for its reliable production, attractive appearance, and good quality; the firm flesh holds well after cutting, making it a practical variety for families and market growers. Days to maturity of 80–90 suit it well for both long-season Southern and moderately short Pacific Coast growing seasons.

name: Knuckle Head Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; part of the Superfreak series of warted novelty pumpkins bred by Siegers Seed Co. for exaggerated, gnarled rind texture.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, well-drained soil, spacing hills 6 feet apart for the sprawling vines. Knuckle Head is a hybrid novelty pumpkin from the Superfreak series, producing 12-16 pound, slightly tall, dark-orange fruit densely covered in gnarled warts that range from dark green through light green to orange; unlike some warty types, wart color is not a reliable ripeness indicator here. The variety carries useful powdery mildew resistance, which helps keep foliage productive through the fruit-finishing stage of the season. Grown almost exclusively for its shock-value texture at pumpkin patches and fall markets rather than for eating, it should be harvested once the rind is fully hard and stored in a cool, dry spot for display.

name: Knuckle Purple Hull Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Knuckle Purple Hull is a semi-determinate type that concentrates its pod set in a shorter period than indeterminate types — useful for gardeners who want a defined harvest window rather than continuous production.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Knuckle Purple Hull is a semi-determinate purple hull southern pea that matures faster and concentrates its pod set in a shorter window than standard indeterminate purple hull types — producing the characteristic purple-hulled pods on a compact, upright plant that reaches 18–24 inches without trailing vines, making it more manageable for raised-bed and intensive garden production. The name 'Knuckle' refers to the distinctive bunching habit of pod production — the pods tend to cluster near the stem joints ('knuckles') in groups rather than being spread along extended vining stems, which concentrates the harvest and makes picking more efficient. The peas themselves are the classic purple hull type: green hulls with purple coloring at maturity, and cream-colored seeds with the mild, sweet flavor characteristic of purple hull peas. At 55–65 days, Knuckle Purple Hull is also earlier than standard purple hull types (typically 65–75 days) — allowing earlier first harvests from spring plantings and more productive use of the warm season in zone 9 where succession planting through summer is common practice. The compact, determinate-tending growth habit requires no staking and makes Knuckle Purple Hull suitable for higher-density plantings than trailing types.

name: Knucklehead Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Knucklehead is an All-America Selections winner covered edge to edge in dense, knobby warts over an otherwise standard orange jack-o-lantern shape.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost in rich, well-drained soil, giving the vigorous vines ample room since fruit can reach 15 pounds or more. Knucklehead won an All-America Selections award for a texture unlike any standard carving pumpkin: dense, rounded warts cover the entire orange rind from stem to blossom end, creating a rugged, knuckled surface that stands out in any fall display. Despite the unusual texture the rind stays firm and workable, making the fruit suitable for both painting and light carving around the bumps. Harvest before hard frost once the color has fully developed and the warting has set, and expect a long-lasting fall display since the thick, tough rind resists rot better than smooth-skinned pumpkins.

name: KnuckleHull-VNR Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow into lean, well-drained soil once reliably warm, exactly as with standard crowder-type southern peas.
directions: Released by USDA-ARS in 2002 as a direct replacement for the classic Alabama 'Knuckle Purple Hull,' bred to add resistance to blackeye cowpea mosaic virus and root-knot nematode, both serious limiters of cowpea yield in sandy Gulf Coast soil. Pods are slightly curved, roughly 8 inches long, purple-hulled, holding about 14 smaller, smooth brown peas per pod, with seed running noticeably smaller than the old-line strain. Expect similar yield to the original Knuckle Purple Hull but with meaningfully better performance where nematodes have historically been a problem.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service variety release notice (Fery, Thies and Gillaspie, 2002)

name: Kodiak Brown Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow 1/4 to 1/2 inch deep in fall or early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Kodiak is a high-glucosinolate brown mustard bred at the University of Idaho specifically for biofumigation, suppressing soilborne pathogens and nematodes when incorporated at flowering.
directions: Broadcast or drill seed into well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, and mow or flail-chop the stand right at early flowering, then incorporate the shredded residue into the top few inches of soil immediately and irrigate to seal it in — the biofumigant effect depends on releasing volatile isothiocyanate compounds from the chopped tissue quickly, before they dissipate into the air. Kodiak was bred at the University of Idaho for an unusually high concentration of glucosinolates, the sulfur compounds that break down into natural soil fumigants capable of suppressing soilborne fungal pathogens, weed seed germination, and plant-parasitic nematodes, offering a lower-input alternative to chemical soil fumigation ahead of a susceptible vegetable crop. Beyond its biofumigant role, the fast, leafy growth smothers weeds and scavenges excess soil nitrogen, and the bright yellow flowers, if allowed to open, are attractive to early-season pollinators. Avoid planting into a bed just biofumigated with mustard for several weeks to allow residues to fully break down.

name: Koginut Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Koginut is a cross between kabocha and butternut squash bred by Row 7 Seed Company in collaboration with chef Dan Barber, selected for a rich, dense, exceptionally sweet flesh.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the vigorous vine room to sprawl. Koginut combines the deep, nutty sweetness and dry, dense texture of kabocha squash with the smoother shape and easier peeling of butternut, developed through a chef-driven breeding collaboration specifically to concentrate flavor rather than yield or shelf appearance. The tan, ribbed, acorn-shaped fruit has an intensely sweet, richly flavored orange flesh that roasts especially well. Harvest when the rind hardens and dulls to a matte tan color, usually as the vine declines in late summer or fall, and cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks before storing to further concentrate sweetness. Watch for squash vine borer and squash bugs, common problems for cucurbits in Gulf South gardens.

name: Kokuho Rose Rice
plantingNote: Direct sow into a warm, flooded paddy bed well after last frost; this semi-dwarf California variety needs a full, warm-summer season similar to other Central Valley rice types.
directions: Kokuho Rose was bred by a family rice farm in California, crossing Japanese short-grain lines with a Middle Eastern long-grain parent to produce a semi-dwarf medium-grain rice with better flavor than the era's standard Calrose. The family has continuously grown and sold it since the 1960s, making it one of the longest-lived named rice selections still in commercial production in the United States. Grow it flooded in a paddy bed or stock tank through the warm season, maintaining standing water while the plant tillers and fills, then draining as the panicles ripen and dry. Cooked grains turn creamy and slightly sticky with a mild sweetness, making this variety a longtime favorite for sushi rice and home rice cookery on the West Coast.

name: Kolb's Gem Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills spaced widely apart after soil has thoroughly warmed, giving the sprawling vines plenty of room to ramble.
directions: Plant in deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun, watering consistently through fruit set and tapering off as melons approach ripeness to build sugar. Reuben Kolb of Alabama developed this variety around 1885, and its unusually tough, bruise-resistant rind made it one of the first watermelons durable enough for long-distance rail shipping, briefly making it a dominant commercial melon of the late 19th century before later shipping varieties displaced it. Fruits are large and nearly round, often reaching 50 pounds or more under good growing conditions, with sweet, deep red flesh prized for home and market eating. Because the rind is tougher than modern melon-market types, it also stores and travels unusually well for a home garden heirloom.

name: Kolibri Kohlrabi
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, and again every few weeks through midsummer plus a late-summer fall sowing, since Kolibri matures quickly and mildest in cool weather.
directions: Direct sow seed ½ inch deep in early spring 2-4 weeks before the last frost, and again in mid- to late summer for a fall crop, since Kolibri grows fastest and mildest in cool weather. Kolibri is a widely grown F1 hybrid noted as one of the most uniform and reliably deep-purple kohlrabi varieties available, forming a smooth, round, above-ground bulb with crisp, nearly fiberless white flesh beneath the vivid purple skin. Its rapid 45- to 50-day maturity and compact, neat habit make it well suited to succession planting, small-space beds, and early-season cloche or row-cover production. Harvest bulbs at about the size of a tennis ball for the sweetest, most tender texture, since kohlrabi can turn woody if left too long in the ground.

name: Komodo Dragon Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, since chinense superhots are slow to germinate and mature.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, and transplant only once the soil is thoroughly warm, since seedlings stall in cool conditions. Stake plants as the fruit load builds and keep moisture consistent to avoid blossom drop during heat spikes. Komodo Dragon was bred in the United Kingdom by chile grower Salvatore Genovese and is known as one of the hottest peppers developed in Britain, with elongated, ridged red pods and a sharp, intense burn. It is popular among superhot collectors for its productivity in cooler UK-style greenhouse growing.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Konan Kohlrabi
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before last frost; Konan is a compact, fast-maturing globe kohlrabi bred to stay tender and crack-free even when bulbs size up, and it grows well in containers as well as open beds.
directions: Direct sow, or start transplants and set out 2-4 weeks before last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Konan is an AAS-winning kohlrabi bred for a compact plant habit and smooth, uniform, pale-green globes that stay crisp, sweet, and free of the woodiness or cracking that plagues older kohlrabi varieties even at a larger harvest size, giving gardeners a wider window to pick. The neat, upright plant fits well in small beds, raised beds, and large containers. Harvest bulbs when they reach 2-3 inches across for the best texture; peel the tough outer skin before eating raw in slaws or cooked. As a cool-season crop it can bolt and turn woody in summer heat, so grow it as an early spring or fall crop in zone 9.
sources: All-America Selections — Konan Kohlrabi winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Konstance Kohlrabi
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before last frost, and again in late summer for a fall crop; Konstance holds in the garden longer than older purple kohlrabi without becoming pithy or cracking.
directions: Direct sow, or start transplants and set out 2-4 weeks before last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Konstance is an AAS-winning purple kohlrabi bred from the same breeding line as Kolibri, improved with smoother skin, more upright foliage, and better resistance to fusarium, and it holds a vivid purple color that extends into the leaf stems. The crisp, sweet, peppery bulb stays crack-resistant and tender over a longer harvest window than older varieties, so a planting does not have to be picked all at once. Harvest bulbs at 2-3 inches for the most tender texture, and use young leaves as a cooked or raw green in addition to the bulb itself.
sources: All-America Selections — Kohlrabi Konstance F1 winner announcement

name: Kopec Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting; Kopec descends from a USDA seed collection made in South Africa in 1956 but its variegated fruit points to the Indonesian 'kopek' eggplant tradition.
directions: Kopec is a rare eggplant preserved from a USDA germplasm collection made in South Africa in 1956, though its lilac-and-deep-purple variegated fruit points to roots in the Indonesian kopek eggplant tradition. Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil in full sun, giving plants 18-24 inches of spacing to branch out fully. Fruit size falls between a typical Japanese type and a globe eggplant, so harvest at 4-6 inches long and quarter it lengthwise for roasting to show off the marbled skin. Because it readily cross-pollinates with other eggplants, isolate plantings if you intend to save true-to-type seed.

name: Korean Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Korean cucumber vines benefit from trellising and regular harvesting — pick fruits at 6–8 inches for best flavor and texture for pickle-making, or allow to reach full size for fresh eating.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Korean cucumber (Joseon Oi or 'Korean local cucumber') is the traditional cucumber of Korean agriculture — a light green to whitish-green cucumber with a bumpy, spiny-warted surface (similar to pickling cucumbers but larger and paler), crisp, dense, mildly flavored flesh, very thin skin, and a shape that ranges from short and stout (about 6 inches) to long and slender depending on the local strain. It is the essential ingredient in oi sobagi (cucumber kimchi) where the crisp texture and thin skin allow quick pickling and absorption of spicy, garlicky brine without becoming soft or mushy — texture properties that make Korean cucumber distinctly superior to standard American slicing or pickling cucumbers for Korean-style preparations. The pale color and slightly different flavor profile also distinguish it from Japanese kyuri types; Korean cucumber has a slightly more pronounced flavor with a mild earthiness. Very heat-tolerant and productive under summer conditions; an excellent Asian specialty cucumber for Southern gardens with access to Korean or Asian seed suppliers.
sources: Kitazawa Seed Company Asian Vegetable Guide
Korea Rural Development Administration agricultural publications
University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension — Asian Vegetables

name: Korean Long Hot Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; Korean Long Hot is a slender, pale green pepper widely used fresh in Korean cooking, from mild to moderately spicy depending on growing conditions.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Korean Long Hot produces long, slender, pale to medium green pods with thin walls and mild-to-medium heat that can vary with growing conditions, a staple pepper in Korean cooking eaten fresh, dipped in ssamjang, sautéed, or stuffed. The plants are productive over a long summer harvest season, and pods can be picked green or allowed to ripen to red for a sweeter, hotter flavor. Harvest regularly to encourage continued production.

name: Korean Melon
plantingNote: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil in zone 9 February–March. Korean melons are fast-maturing and can be succession-planted for multiple crops in zone 9 — spring, summer, and fall plantings are possible. The small fruit size and bush habit make them practical for raised beds and containers. Harvest when the skin turns fully golden-yellow and the stem begins to slip.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; Korean melon (chamoe, chamgwoe) is a small, oval to round melon of East Asian origin that ripens from green-striped to a brilliant golden-yellow with white stripes running longitudinally along the skin — visually distinct from any Western melon type. The small (4–8 ounce) fruits have crisp, white flesh with a delicate floral fragrance and exceptionally sweet flavor; the thin skin is edible and the seeds and surrounding gel are also consumed in Korean tradition. Unlike large Western muskmelons, Korean melons are picked at peak ripeness and eaten immediately — they do not store well, and the flavor deteriorates quickly after harvest. Grow on trellises for cleaner fruits or allow to sprawl on mulched ground. The fast maturity (60–75 days from transplant) makes Korean melon one of the quickest-maturing melons available, allowing multiple crops per season in zone 9.
sources: Rural Development Administration (Korea) — Cucumis melo var. makuwa
University of California Cooperative Extension — Asian Melon Production
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Specialty Melon Varieties for Florida

name: Korean Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–November for a December–February harvest.
