Korean radish can also be sown in early spring in zone 9 (January–February) for a spring crop before heat causes bolting. The large roots require loose, deep, well-tilled soil for straight development; rocky or compacted soil causes forking. Fall crops have the best flavor and texture.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep and thin to 4–6 inches apart in loose, well-tilled, deep, fertile soil in full sun; Korean radish (mu, 무) is the standard radish of Korean cuisine — a large, stout, mostly white root with a green shoulder, shorter and more rounded than Japanese daikon but crisper, denser, and somewhat spicier. The typical Korean Giant root weighs 1–3 pounds with a firm, juicy, slightly peppery crunch used extensively in kimchi (kkakdugi, cubed radish kimchi), pickled banchan side dishes, and stir-fried radish sides (musaengchae). The flavor is richer and more assertive than mild daikon while remaining far milder than small European radish types. Young tops are also edible and used in soups and kimchi. Harvest when roots reach 2–3 inches in diameter for the best texture — over-mature Korean radishes become pithy and hollow at the core.
sources: Rural Development Administration (Korea) — Raphanus sativus var. hortensis
University of Hawaii Extension — Radish Production in Hawaii
Rutgers University — Asian Vegetable Production: Radish Types

name: Korean Red Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Korean Red is an Asiatic-type hardneck that needs a real winter chill to form well-divided bulbs and performs best in zone 3-7.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Korean Red is a vigorous Asiatic-type hardneck garlic prized for its early maturity, reliable productivity, and strong, spicy-hot flavor with a pleasant lingering sweetness once cooked. Bulbs are medium-sized with glossy, deep reddish-purple-streaked skin and 6-10 cloves, and the plants tend to size up and mature earlier in the season than many other hardneck types, making it a good choice for gardeners who want an early garlic harvest. As a hardneck, it produces a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to redirect energy into the bulb; the scapes are tender and flavorful when harvested young. Harvest bulbs once the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, then cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot before trimming and storing; like most hardnecks, storage life is moderate, around 4-6 months.
sources: Chester Aaron: The Great Garlic Book, Ten Speed Press 1997

name: Korist Kohlrabi
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost for an early crop, or direct sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop that often sizes up sweeter in cool weather.
directions: Korist is a widely grown commercial F1 kohlrabi producing uniform, pale green globes with crisp, mild white flesh that resists getting woody as bulbs size up. Its even bolt resistance and uniform maturity make it a dependable choice for successive plantings through spring and fall. Harvest when bulbs reach tennis-ball size for the best balance of tenderness and flavor, peeling the outer skin before eating raw in slaws or cooked in soups and stir-fries. Keep soil evenly moist, since drought stress toughens the bulb and can trigger premature bolting.

name: Kosovo Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the indeterminate vine as it grows.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Kosovo is a Balkan heirloom valued for large, smooth, pink-red, slightly oxheart-shaped fruit with dense, meaty, low-seed flesh and a mild, sweet flavor, and it is notably productive for a tomato of its size, setting a heavier crop than many other large-fruited heirlooms of similar fruit weight. The low acidity and thick, low-moisture flesh make it especially good for slicing and sandwiches, since the fruit holds together well without excess juice. The vigorous indeterminate vine benefits from sturdy staking to support the heavy fruit load; water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking, and harvest once fruit fully colors for the best flavor.

name: Kossak Kohlrabi
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring production; in zone 9, plant October–November for winter-to-spring harvest (December–March). Kossak is a late-maturing giant kohlrabi variety (80–100 days) developed specifically for the ability to grow very large bulbs without becoming woody or pithy — a problem that plagues standard small-bulb kohlrabi varieties when they overstay their welcome in the garden. While standard varieties turn fibrous and tough above 3–4 inches, Kossak can be harvested at 6–10 inches diameter (tennis ball to softball size) and remain tender and sweet. In zone 9, fall planting allows a December–March harvest window before spring heat terminates cool-season growth. Kossak tolerates light frost well, making it a good choice for zone 9 winter gardens.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in cool soil; keep consistently moist for best growth. Harvest from 3 inches up to 10 inches diameter. Kossak is an F1 hybrid kohlrabi variety developed and introduced by Bejo Seeds (Dutch seed company) specifically for the giant kohlrabi market — a category of extra-large kohlrabi varieties that can reach 6–10 inches in diameter while remaining tender and palatable, unlike standard kohlrabi varieties that become woodily fibrous above 3–4 inches. The distinction between Kossak and standard kohlrabi varieties is fundamental: standard types (Purple Vienna, White Vienna, Early White Vienna) must be harvested promptly at small size or become inedible, while Kossak was specifically selected for an extended harvest window at large sizes. This makes Kossak practical for gardeners who cannot monitor their garden daily, for home gardeners who want a few large plants rather than many small ones, and for fall gardeners who want kohlrabi that overwinters in the ground without quality loss. The bulbs are pale green (white type), extremely smooth-skinned, and can reach weights of 1–2 pounds or more while retaining the characteristic kohlrabi flavor — mild, sweet, slightly peppery, somewhere between broccoli stem and turnip — without the harsh bitterness and woodiness of overmature standard types. The flesh is very juicy and crisp, excellent raw in slaws and salads (where the sweetness is most apparent), roasted (where it caramelizes beautifully), or braised. Kossak is also more cold-hardy than many kohlrabi varieties, holding quality in the garden through light freezes, which extends its usability in zone 9 winter gardens.
sources: Bejo Seeds — Kossak giant kohlrabi F1 hybrid variety development and commercial notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Kossak kohlrabi variety performance comparison
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Kohlrabi Variety Selection for Home Gardens

name: Kousa Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed and all frost danger has passed; this pale, round-to-cylindrical squash is grown throughout the Levant specifically for stuffing.
directions: Direct sow once soil has warmed, in hills spaced to give the sprawling plants room; harvest fruit young and small, around three to four inches long, when the thin pale-green skin is still tender and the seed cavity is small. Kousa is the light-colored, mild-flavored Levantine squash used for kousa mahshi, hollowed out with a corer and stuffed with rice and spiced ground lamb before braising in tomato sauce or yogurt. Pick every one to two days during peak season, since fruit left on the vine quickly swells, toughens, and develops larger seeds that make hollowing and stuffing harder. Keep plants evenly watered and pick off any overripe fruit promptly to keep the vine producing.

name: Kraken Scorpion Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost, and plan for a tall, sprawling plant that will need staking once pods load up.
directions: Mike Hess of Peoria, Illinois bred Kraken Scorpion in 2013 by crossing Bhut Jolokia India Carbon with Trinidad Scorpion Chocolate, producing a large, dark brown, elongated pod 3-4 inches long with rough, pimply skin and occasionally a short tail. Heat runs 1,000,000 to 1,200,000 Scoville units, and the flavor opens floral, earthy, and faintly smoky before a delayed, lingering burn takes over. Plants grow unusually tall for a chinense superhot, often topping four feet, and reward staking and a long warm season with a heavy harvest. Reserve the fruit for extreme hot sauces, barbecue sauce, or dried chile flakes where its smoky-floral character stands out.

name: Krobonko Luffa
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, or direct-sow once soil has warmed above 70°F; this Ghanaian heirloom needs a long, hot 90-100 day season to finish.
directions: This West African heirloom luffa is grown along the Gold Coast of Ghana for its dual harvest: young ridged fruit around 12 inches long can be sliced into soups and stews for a mild, slightly sweet flavor, while fruit left on the vine to fully mature and dry yields a fibrous sponge. Provide a sturdy trellis or arbor, since the vigorous vines can climb well over 15 feet in a single warm season. Give it full sun, evenly moist soil, and a long frost-free season of at least 90 days, switching to a phosphorus-heavy feed once flowering begins to support fruit set.

name: Krug Yellow Dent Corn
plantingNote: Sow in blocks in rich, deeply worked soil and keep watered through tasseling and silking; rewards a full-length warm season.
directions: Sow in blocks in rich, deeply worked soil and keep watered through tasseling and silking; this is a tall, vigorous dent corn that rewards a full-length warm season. Krug was developed by Iowa farm families in the second half of the 1800s through careful ear-to-row selection and became one of the most influential open-pollinated dent corns in American corn breeding, serving as parent stock for many of the early hybrid corn lines that transformed Corn Belt agriculture in the twentieth century. Its smooth yellow dent kernels grind into hearty cornmeal, and growing it today offers a direct link to the open-pollinated corns that underlie much of modern commercial corn genetics.

name: Krymka Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after the soil has warmed; Krymka is a Crimean heirloom melon valued for ripening in regions with a shorter or cooler summer than classic Western cantaloupes need.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in warm, fertile soil after frost danger has passed, thinning to the strongest seedlings and giving vines room to sprawl. Krymka is a Crimean heirloom melon bearing smooth to lightly netted, pale green-skinned fruit with aromatic, sweet, pale green to cream-colored flesh, grown across Eastern Europe in gardens with shorter or less reliably hot summers than classic American cantaloupe regions require. Keep soil evenly moist while vines establish and fruit develops, then reduce watering as melons approach ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the fruit develops a strong sweet fragrance at the blossom end and yields slightly to gentle pressure.

name: Kujo Negi Bunching Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring or late summer for a fall crop; hill soil around the base as stalks grow to blanch and lengthen the tender white shank.
directions: Kujo Negi is a traditional Kyoto brand vegetable recorded since the Edo period, prized for its exceptionally dark green, tender, glossy leaves and mild, slightly sweet flavor compared to Western scallions. Sow thickly in a nursery row and transplant into trenches, hilling soil up gradually as the plants grow to blanch a long white base similar to a leek, or grow it more thickly spaced for a scallion-style harvest. It tolerates cold well and is traditionally harvested through Kyoto winters, when cold exposure sweetens the leaves for use in nabe hot pots, yakitori, and miso soup. Because it does not form a bulb, cut-and-come-again harvesting of outer leaves from an established clump extends the picking season.

name: Kuroda Dawn Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow anytime from spring through about 10 weeks before a hard fall frost; this variety does not transplant well.
directions: This yellow-rooted carrot is distinguished by green shoulders that catch the light where the root pokes above the soil line, and it delivers a crisp, sweet bite without the earthiness typical of standard carrots. Sow thickly and thin to about 2 inches apart in deep, fertile, well-drained soil at pH 6.0-6.8 so roots can elongate to their full 6-8 inch length unobstructed. It stores well for months when kept cold, unwashed, and with tops removed, making it a good succession crop for continuous harvest.

name: Kuroshinju Black Edamame Soybean
plantingNote: Direct-sow once soil has warmed well past last frost, since this black-seeded heirloom needs a full season of steady summer warmth to fill its pods.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in full sun, inoculating with soybean rhizobium if soybeans are new to the bed. Kuroshinju, meaning 'black pearl' in Japanese, is a rare heirloom edamame prized for its striking black seed coat and rich, nutty, sweeter-than-average flavor, borne two to three beans per pod on upright, 2 to 2.5 foot plants. Harvest at the green-shell stage, while pods are fully plump and still green with just a cast of black showing through, rather than waiting for the beans to dry and darken completely. Steam or boil briefly in salted water and pop the beans free of the pod for eating fresh.

name: Kurtovska Kapia Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; a traditional field variety from the Plovdiv region of Bulgaria, grown for both fresh eating and preserving.
directions: Kurtovska Kapia is a traditional Bulgarian heirloom sweet pepper from the Plovdiv area of central southern Bulgaria, recognized on Slow Food's Ark of Taste as a distinctive regional food. Plants stay relatively low and bushy but produce heavy, hanging clusters of large, flattened, heart-shaped pods that ripen from dark green to deep red with tender, juicy, notably sweet flesh. Its broad, meaty shoulders and pointed tip typify the wider kapia class of Balkan and Turkish sweet peppers used fresh, roasted, or preserved into spreads such as lutenitsa and ajvar. Because fruit is often left to fully redden before harvest for maximum sweetness, this variety benefits from a long, warm growing season.

name: Kurume Long Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant once soil has warmed.
directions: An open-pollinated Japanese eggplant named for the city of Kurume in Fukuoka Prefecture, bearing shiny, deep purple-black fruit 9 to 10 inches long on black stems with a purple calyx. The flavor is mild and the flesh notably soft, making it a favorite for tempura and pickling as well as stir-frying and braising. It is vigorous and one of the earliest Japanese types to mature. Harvest while fruit is still glossy and firm for the best texture.

name: Kwintus Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost at the base of a trellis; Kwintus matures roughly two weeks earlier than standard pole beans like Kentucky Wonder, making it a good choice for shorter seasons.
directions: Kwintus, also sold as Early Riser, is a Dutch-bred flat-podded pole bean that combines the buttery texture of an Italian Romano type with unusually early maturity for a climbing bean. Pods grow 8-10 inches long, broad and stringless, and stay tender and flavorful even as they size up on the vine, which makes for a more forgiving harvest window than narrow round-podded snap beans. Vigorous 6-9 foot vines need sturdy support and reward regular picking with continuous production through the season. Its combination of early cropping and long harvest tolerance has made it a favorite among market gardeners and home growers alike.

name: Kyona Mizuna
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or again in late summer for a fall crop; Kyona regrows quickly after cut-and-come-again harvest.
directions: Sow seed thinly a quarter inch deep in rich, well-drained soil and thin seedlings to reduce crowding once established. This selected mizuna strain produces dense clumps of finely serrated, feathery dark-green leaves with slender white stalks and holds flavor well without becoming overly pungent. Harvest outer leaves continually for salads and stir-fries, or cut the whole plant an inch above the crown for regrowth. Bolts in sustained heat, so it performs best as a spring or autumn crop.

name: Kyoto Market Bunching Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow from early spring through midsummer for a succession of harvests into fall; Kyoto Market also overwinters well in milder climates.
directions: Kyoto Market is a vigorous, fast-growing Japanese bunching onion long associated with the traditional Kyo-yasai vegetables of the Kyoto region, prized for its long, straight white shanks and heavy, uniform yields. Sow seed directly and thin as stalks develop, harvesting young plants as slender scallions or letting them grow thicker without losing tenderness or flavor. Hilling soil around the base as the plants grow lengthens the blanched white portion for a more traditional Japanese-style leek-like scallion. Its disease resistance and tolerance of both heat and cold make Kyoto Market a reliable choice for extended-season plantings from spring through fall.

name: Kyoto Red Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow into deeply worked, loose soil in mid-to-late summer for a fall and winter harvest; Kyoto Red needs a long, cool growing season to develop its full length and deep color, so it is best sown as a fall crop in zone 9.
directions: Sow seed thinly in deep, loose, stone-free soil in full sun and thin seedlings to 3–4 inches apart, since this variety needs a long, undisturbed taproot run to reach its full 10- to 12-inch length. Kyoto Red, also known as Kintoki carrot, is a traditional Japanese heirloom prized for its striking, uniformly deep red-orange color that holds even after cooking, along with a sweet, dense flesh valued in Japanese New Year dishes and simmered preparations. It grows more slowly than Western carrot types and performs best with a long, cool finish, so a late-summer sowing timed to mature through fall and winter gives the best color and flavor. Harvest once roots reach full size and store dug roots cool and slightly moist for extended keeping.

name: Kyoto Three Feet Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; this traditional Kyoto-region Japanese heirloom is grown on a tall trellis to produce its characteristically long, slender fruit.
directions: Sow directly in warm soil after frost danger passes, then train vines up a tall trellis so the long, thin-skinned fruit hangs straight rather than curling on the ground. This traditional cucumber from the Kyoto region of Japan is grown for slender, dark green fruit that can reach well over a foot in length while staying tender and mild, in the same style as other long Asian slicing cucumbers. Harvest regularly while fruit is still slender and glossy, since letting any one cucumber oversize on the vine slows further production and coarsens the skin. Keep the shallow-rooted vines consistently watered, as uneven moisture is more likely to show up as misshapen or curled fruit in long types like this one.

name: Kyzyl Shala Upland Rice
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into moist, fertile soil; its extremely early maturity makes it one of the more forgiving upland rices for short-season northern gardens.
directions: Kyzyl Shala is a landrace upland rice from Uzbekistan prized for being one of the earliest-ripening rices available to home growers, often setting harvestable grain within about three months of transplanting. Its long, colorful awns are a landrace trait that helps deter birds from stripping the ripening panicles, a useful feature for gardeners without netting. Plants stay compact and stand well without lodging, and the purplish hulls with light brown bran make it easy to spot at harvest time. Because it does not require flooding, it can be grown as a dryland crop with attentive watering rather than a true paddy.

name: La Estrella Calabaza
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills once soil is warm; matures noticeably faster than old-style vining calabaza landraces, a real advantage in gardens with a shorter frost-free window.
directions: Developed by University of Florida breeders specifically for Gulf Coast and Caribbean growing conditions, La Estrella is a medium-vine calabaza selected to flower and fruit earlier than the extra-long-vine landrace types traditionally grown further south, making it a better fit for home gardens with limited trellis or ground space. Fruits run boxy to round, averaging 6-10 pounds, with a mottled green-and-tan waxy rind and dense, vividly orange, nutty-flavored flesh that is unusually heavy for its size. Direct sow into warm soil in full sun, keep moisture even through fruit set, and expect a noticeably shorter season to harvest than old heirloom calabaza vines. Let fruit fully harden on the vine, cure briefly in a warm spot, and store in a cool, dry location for use in soups, stews, and Caribbean and Creole-style savory dishes through winter.

name: La Primera Tropical Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct-sow into hills once soil is reliably warm, since this long-season landrace needs the full heat of a Gulf Coast summer to size up its fruit.
directions: This is an open-pollinated Florida calabaza released from the state's tropical pumpkin breeding program, grown as a sprawling long-vine type that performs reliably through subtropical heat and humidity. Give it generous room to run, since vines can cover 15 to 25 feet, and let fruit mature fully on the vine for the densest, sweetest orange flesh. It stores well after harvest and holds up better to Gulf Coast disease pressure than many northern pumpkin varieties.

name: La Ratte Fingerling Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January-February for harvest before summer heat sets in. Cut seed pieces to egg size with 1-2 eyes each and let cut surfaces cure a day or two before planting.
directions: Plant seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun. La Ratte is a classic French fingerling potato long prized by chefs for its exceptionally rich, nutty, almost chestnut-like flavor and dense, waxy, pale yellow flesh that holds its shape beautifully when boiled or roasted whole. The small, knobby, finger-shaped tubers mature over a somewhat longer season than standard round potatoes and yield less per plant, but the superior flavor has made it a long-standing favorite for specialty and high-end cooking. Harvest once vines begin to yellow and die back, and handle the thin-skinned tubers gently, since they bruise more easily than thicker-skinned storage potatoes.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Potato Production for Texas Home Gardens
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Potato Production in Florida

name: Lacinato Rainbow Kale
plantingNote: Sow direct in spring or late summer; the added vigor from its Redbor parentage lets it overwinter and even behave as a short-lived perennial in mild coastal climates.
directions: This farm-original population was created by crossing classic Lacinato with the purple hybrid kale Redbor, layering shades of red, purple, and blue-green over Lacinato's familiar savoyed leaf texture. The cross also added noticeable vigor and cold hardiness, and in milder Pacific Northwest winters some plants will survive to flower and resow themselves the following year. Grow it like any lacinato kale: full sun, steady moisture, and repeated harvest of the lower leaves as the central rosette lengthens upward.

name: Lady Cream Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in warm soil after last frost; Lady pea is one of the smallest of the Southern peas with very small seeds, so somewhat more of them are required per planting. It is heat tolerant and produces reliably in zone 8–10 Gulf Coast summers.
directions: Sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep in any well-drained, lean soil in full sun after last frost; Lady cream pea is a traditional Southern heirloom cowpea producing small, white, round peas with a notably sweet, mild, delicate flavor — milder and less earthy than crowder peas or black-eyed peas, and considered by many Southern pea aficionados to have the finest flavor of all the cream peas for fresh eating and freezing. The small size and mild sweetness make it the variety most often served to guests unfamiliar with Southern peas, as the flavor is more approachable and universally liked. A true bush-type plant that is drought-tolerant once established; performs reliably in the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast. Excellent boiled simply with butter and salt and served as a side dish, or incorporated into succotash, hoppin' John, and traditional Southern vegetable plates.

name: Lakota Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Lakota is a striking Native American heirloom winter squash with vivid deep orange skin dramatically marked with irregular dark green and black mottling — one of the most visually beautiful and historically significant native food squashes, producing teardrop-shaped fruits of 5–8 pounds with exceptionally sweet, rich, deeply colored orange flesh.
directions: Direct sow in hills of 3 seeds (thin to 2) after soil warms; provide 4–8 feet of vine space; harvest when the skin hardens completely and can no longer be dented with a fingernail, and the stem begins to dry and cork; cure at room temperature for 10–14 days after harvest to develop optimal flavor and maximize storage life. Lakota squash is an heirloom winter squash associated with the Lakota (Sioux) people of the Great Plains, one of the native peoples of North America who cultivated squash as a primary food staple long before European contact. The variety produces one of the most visually distinctive squashes in cultivation: teardrop or pear-shaped fruits with deep orange-red skin boldly marked with irregular splotches and streaks of dark green and near-black — a coloration so striking that Lakota is as ornamental as it is edible. The flesh is the intensely orange, dry, sweet, and finely textured type characteristic of the best Cucurbita maxima varieties: rich enough to need nothing added beyond butter and salt, sweet enough to serve as dessert, and dry enough to bake or purée without becoming watery. The flavor is often compared favorably to kabocha and red kuri squash — comparable sweetness and dryness but with a distinctive terroir-like richness that differentiates it from commercial varieties. Lakota stores exceptionally well — 4–6 months under cool, dry conditions — making it a true long-keeping winter provision. Average fruits weigh 5–8 lbs with moderate vine length suitable for home gardens.

name: Lambkin Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed; Lambkin's early maturity and compact habit make it well suited to shorter-season gardens and large containers.
directions: Lambkin is a Burpee-introduced, All-America Selections-winning melon bred to bring French Charentais-style eating quality to a compact vine and an early, personal-size fruit about the size of a small cantaloupe. The smooth, lightly ribbed gray-green rind encloses deep orange, richly perfumed flesh with the concentrated sweetness and floral aroma typical of Charentais types, but on a plant far more manageable than the long-vining French heirlooms it descends from. Grow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping moisture steady through fruit set and easing off as the small melons approach ripeness to intensify their sugars. Because Charentais-type melons slip cleanly from the vine only at full ripeness, check plants daily near the expected harvest window and watch for a softening and light cracking at the stem end as the surest sign of peak flavor.
sources: All-America Selections — Lambkin melon variety notes

name: Lancaster Surecrop Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks after soil has warmed; tolerates drier conditions and lighter soils better than many dent corns.
directions: Direct sow in blocks after soil has warmed; this variety tolerates drier conditions and lighter soils better than many dent corns, though it still performs best with even moisture during pollination. Lancaster Surecrop was developed by Pennsylvania Dutch farmers in Lancaster County and became, over generations of selection, the source of the Lancaster heterotic group that later proved foundational in commercial hybrid corn breeding across the eastern Corn Belt. Grown today, it produces sturdy stalks and well-filled ears of yellow dent kernels well suited to cornmeal and traditional livestock feed, preserving a genetic line with an outsized influence on modern corn.

name: Lancelot Leek
plantingNote: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; Lancelot is an early-season leek variety (70–85 days from transplant) with more slender, tender stalks than overwintering types — it is harvested in summer and early fall while still tender, rather than being held through winter; ideal for gardeners who want leeks available early in the season before winter storage types are ready.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost at 65–75°F; transplant outdoors after last frost, setting transplants 4–6 inches apart in a trench 4–6 inches deep to blanch the shafts; gradually backfill the trench as plants grow; harvest beginning at 1 inch shaft diameter for best tenderness. Lancelot is a European-bred early-season leek variety that fills an important niche in the leek production calendar: unlike the classic overwintering leek varieties (such as Bleu de Solaise or Giant Musselburgh) that require 130–150+ days from transplant and are intended to overwinter in the garden for winter and spring harvest, Lancelot matures in just 70–85 days from transplant and is harvested in late summer and early fall while stalks are still slender, tender, and at their best eating quality. The stalks are typically 1–1.5 inches in diameter at harvest — more refined in texture and milder in flavor than fully mature overwintering leeks — making Lancelot the superior choice for preparations where tenderness and delicate leek flavor are paramount: vichyssoise, leek gratin, braised leeks, and fresh leek salads where the young stalks are excellent raw. The blue-green foliage and cylindrical white shaft create an attractive plant in the garden from late spring through summer. Lancelot does not have the cold hardiness or overwintering capability of late types but excels as a summer-season leek in climates too hot for fall-planted overwintering types.

name: Lancer Parsnip
plantingNote: Direct sow fresh seed once soil is workable in spring; mark rows clearly since parsnip emergence is slow and easy to mistake for weeds.
directions: Direct sow shallowly into loose, deeply dug soil free of rocks and clods so the long roots can develop without forking, and thin seedlings early to prevent crowding. Lancer is valued by market gardeners for its smooth white skin, uniform wedge shape, and strong resistance to canker, a common fungal problem that disfigures many older parsnip varieties. Allow roots to remain in the ground after the first fall frosts to develop their full sweetness before digging for storage or immediate use.

name: Landreth Stringless Bush Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost danger has passed; no support needed for this compact bush variety, and successive sowings extend the harvest.
directions: Landreth Stringless is an American heirloom bush bean first offered by the D. Landreth Seed Company in the 1880s and notable historically as one of the earliest widely marketed stringless snap beans, a trait that was a genuine novelty in that era. It produces medium-green pods a little over 5 inches long with a meaty texture and good flavor, backed by seeds in a rich chocolate-brown color. The plant matures quickly and yields heavily over a relatively short window, making it a reliable choice for succession planting and home canning. Its long, continuous availability from Landreth makes it one of the oldest still-commercially-offered American bean varieties.

name: Langedijker (Bewaar) Storage Cabbage
plantingNote: Start seed indoors a few weeks before last frost; transplant for a long-season harvest meant for winter storage rather than fresh summer eating.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Langedijker is a centuries-old Dutch heirloom cabbage named for the Langedijk region, producing large, firm, round heads of about 4 pounds that hold their light color exceptionally well in long-term storage. It needs a long season, 120-150 days, to reach full size and density, making it best suited to an early spring start and a fall harvest timed just before hard freeze. This is the classic winter-keeper and sauerkraut cabbage of Dutch tradition, bred specifically for root-cellar storage rather than immediate fresh use.

name: Langston Longhorn Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed once soil is warm; this heirloom moved from DeQuincy, Louisiana to Lawrence Langston of Dripping Springs, Texas, who maintained and eventually shared it through Seed Savers Exchange.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Langston Longhorn is an old-fashioned heavily branched okra with green stems showing red blushing, capable of reaching well above standard okra height in a long warm season. The slender, pale yellow-green pods carry spines near the cap, so gloves are a good idea at harvest, and pods are best picked under 4 inches for tenderness since this variety fibers up quickly past that size. Pick frequently — ideally daily once plants hit stride — to sustain the heavy, continuous pod set this variety is known for.
sources: Sow True Seed — Langston Longhorn Okra

name: Lanro Kohlrabi
directions: An open-pollinated Swiss heirloom from the Roggli family of Hilterfingen rather than a modern hybrid, Lanro is worth growing for seed-saving gardeners who want a true-breeding kohlrabi alongside its F1 competitors. Compact plants form tender green bulbs weighing roughly half a pound, best picked while still young since open-pollinated kohlrabi tends to toughen faster than hybrids once past peak size.

name: Larac Asparagus
plantingNote: Set crowns in a deep, well-drained trench in early spring, filling in soil gradually as new spears emerge over the season.
directions: Larac is a French-bred green asparagus hybrid developed from INRA breeding lines and widely grown across French production regions for its reliable early emergence and consistent spear quality. Spears are medium to thick, cylindrical, and hold their tight tips well even during a fast spring flush, making the variety popular where harvest timing matters for fresh-market bunching. It shows solid tolerance to common rust and performs reliably across a range of soil types provided drainage is good. As with other named hybrids, resist harvesting until the crowns have had two full seasons to establish, then cut spears daily at ground level through the six-to-eight-week spring season.
sources: Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique (INRA)

name: Latah Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 5-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant promptly once danger of frost passes, since this variety's main advantage is a short, early season.
directions: Latah was bred at the University of Idaho to give gardeners in the state's short, cool-summer growing regions a dependable early harvest, and it has been passed along by seed savers since it first appeared in exchange listings in the early 1980s. The compact determinate bush stays tidy enough for a cage or short stake and sets its crop of small, bright red, sweet-flavored fruit earlier than most other open-pollinated tomatoes. Because the plant matures and ripens quickly, it suits northern gardens, high-elevation sites, and anywhere a reliable early tomato is wanted before the main crop comes in. Keep watering consistent through the compressed fruiting window to get the best flavor and size from the small fruits.

name: Late Flat Dutch Cabbage
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Late Flat Dutch'
plantingNote: Start seed 12–16 weeks before the first fall frost for a fall/winter-maturing crop, or start in very early spring for a summer harvest in cooler climates; in zone 8–9, Late Flat Dutch is best grown as a fall-planted crop that matures through winter, since it tolerates hard freezes and stores in the garden far better than it handles summer heat.
directions: Set transplants 24–30 inches apart in deeply worked, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the large, heavy heads need ample room and rich soil to size up properly over their long season. Late Flat Dutch is a 19th-century American heirloom prized for producing enormous, flattened, blue-green heads that commonly reach 10–15 pounds and can grow considerably larger under good conditions, with dense, crisp interior leaves that make it an outstanding keeper — heads store for months in a root cellar or cool garage, and the variety was historically favored for large-batch sauerkraut and winter storage before refrigeration was common. Its long season and excellent cold hardiness make it best suited to fall planting in mild-winter climates like the Gulf South, where the heads mature slowly through the cool months and can stand in the garden through hard freezes without splitting. A workhorse heirloom for gardeners who want maximum storage cabbage from a single planting, in zone 3–9.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Laurentian Rutabaga
plantingNote: Direct sow 12–16 weeks before first fall frost so roots mature in cool fall weather; in zones 3–7 sow June–July. Rutabaga requires a long, cool growing season — unlike turnips, which can be harvested young in 50–60 days, rutabagas need the full 85–95 days to develop their full size and flavor. Frost dramatically improves rutabaga flavor by converting starches to sugars — leave roots in the ground through hard frosts and harvest in late fall or winter. Thin to 6–8 inches apart. In zone 9 the late-fall/winter growing season is too short for full rutabaga development — zones 3–7 are the primary growing regions.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, stone-free soil; Laurentian is the standard North American rutabaga variety — a natural hybrid between turnip and cabbage producing large, round to slightly elongated roots with the characteristic purple shoulder above ground and yellow-tan below, with golden-yellow, dense, starchy flesh distinctly different from the white flesh of turnips. Rutabaga (called 'swede' in British English, reflecting its Swedish origin) has a richer, more complex flavor than turnip — the yellow flesh is denser, starchier, and more nutrionally robust with a sweeter, more earthy, complex flavor that becomes significantly more intense and sweet after hard frost exposure. The classic rutabaga preparations — mashed ('neeps' in Scotland, traditionally served with haggis), chunked in beef stew, roasted with butter and herbs, or pureed into soups — take full advantage of the dense, deeply flavored flesh that holds its shape better than potato while contributing its own distinctive sweetness and earthiness. Laurentian's large size (roots can reach softball size in good conditions), excellent storage quality (roots keep for months in cool storage), and consistent purple-top appearance make it the most reliable and widely grown rutabaga for home and market garden production.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Rutabaga Production Guide
University of Minnesota Extension — Root Vegetable Growing in Northern Climates
University of Wisconsin Extension — Rutabaga and Turnip Production

name: Laxton's Progress Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1-1.5 inches deep as soon as the ground can be worked in spring; the short, sturdy vines need only light twiggy support.
directions: Laxton's Progress is an early-maturing English heirloom shelling pea bred by the historic Laxton Brothers nursery, valued for its short, sturdy vines and heavy set of well-filled pods on plants that need only light support. It was one of the two parent lines, alongside 'Perfection', that USDA breeders crossed in 1943 to create the heat-tolerant modern classic 'Wando'. Direct-sow into cool, workable spring soil as early as the ground can be prepared, since like all garden peas it grows and yields best well ahead of summer heat. The dwarf, self-supporting habit suits raised beds and smaller gardens where taller vining peas would need substantial trellising.

name: Lazy Housewife Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Lazy Housewife is an 1810 German heirloom pole bean that is one of the oldest and most historically significant American heirloom beans, documented in German seed catalogs since the early 1800s and named for the ease of shelling — the pods are stringless and the beans pop out with minimal effort.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil at the base of a trellis, teepee poles, or corn stalks; provide 6 feet of vertical support for the vigorous vines. Lazy Housewife is one of America's most documented heirloom pole beans, appearing in American seed catalogs since at least 1810 and recorded by seed historian William Woys Weaver as a bean brought to America by German immigrants; the name refers to the ease of preparation — the pods are stringless when harvested young as snap beans, and the mature white seeds shell out of the dried pods with minimal effort, hence 'lazy housewife.' The pods are 5–7 inches long, round, and stringless, with plump white seeds marked with a distinctive black eye at maturity. Equally excellent as a snap bean (harvest young), shell bean (harvest green pods when seeds have filled), or dry bean; the cooked flavor of the mature seeds is rich, creamy, and outstanding.
sources: Weaver, William Woys. Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

name: Lazy Wife Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Lazy Wife requires a pole or trellis 6–8 feet tall and produces abundantly over a long season. In zone 9, plant April–May; the variety performs adequately but prefers somewhat cooler conditions than the peak Gulf South summer. A late-July or August planting for fall production is often more productive in zone 9 than a late spring planting that encounters July-August heat. The 'lazy' in the variety's name refers not to any person but to the ease of preparation: Lazy Wife is stringless and requires no tedious stringing of the pods before cooking — a significant advantage in the era when most snap beans had tough, fibrous strings running the length of each pod. This stringless quality was unusual and highly valued when the variety was widely grown in the 19th century.
directions: Direct sow 1.5 inches deep after last frost; provide tall support (6–8 feet). Harvest at 5–7 inches as snap bean or leave to dry for shell/dry use. Lazy Wife is a German immigrant heirloom pole bean that was introduced to American seed catalogs around 1810 and became one of the most popular snap beans in the 19th century — a status maintained until modern stringless hybrid varieties provided equivalent ease of preparation with higher yield. The name 'Lazy Wife' refers to the bean's stringless character: in the 19th-century farm kitchen where snap bean preparation required long sessions of stringing pods by hand before cooking, a truly stringless bean required no stringing at all — hence the tongue-in-cheek name suggesting the homemaker could be 'lazy' about bean preparation. The implied humor of the name was accepted in its era; the bean's quality was the real selling point. Lazy Wife produces broad, flat, pale green pods (5–7 inches long, 0.75 inches wide) with a somewhat different form than round-pod types — the flat pod shape and relatively thick walls give Lazy Wife a characteristic visual distinction from most modern snap beans. The pods are truly stringless through their snap-bean stage and have rich, full flavor that heirloom enthusiasts prize. The seeds are creamy-white and excellent as a shell bean (picked young) or dry bean (left to fully mature), giving Lazy Wife three-stage versatility as a snap, shell, or dry bean from a single planting.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Lazy Wife pole bean German heirloom documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Lazy Wife bean historical notes
William Woys Weaver, Heirloom Vegetable Gardening — Historical snap bean variety documentation

name: LCP 85-384 Sugarcane
plantingNote: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. LCP 85-384 was released from the joint LSU AgCenter/USDA-ARS sugarcane breeding program and for many years became the dominant commercial variety grown across the Louisiana sugar belt.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. LCP 85-384 (the LCP designation reflects its origin in the joint Louisiana-USDA sugarcane cooperative breeding program) rose to become the overwhelmingly dominant sugarcane variety in the Louisiana sugar industry for many years, prized for high early-season sugar yield, good cold tolerance for Louisiana's subtropical-to-temperate climate, and strong ratooning ability. It was later grown on well over half of the state's cane acreage before increasing disease pressure led growers to diversify into newer releases. Home growers can treat it like any heirloom cane: harvest in late fall after cool nights concentrate the sugars, strip the leaves, and press or chew the stalks fresh, or cook the juice into syrup. The tall, clumping perennial grass typically freezes back to the rhizome in hard winters and regrows from the root each spring.
sources: USDA-ARS Sugarcane Research Unit, Houma, Louisiana

name: Lee Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed; Lee's compact, mostly unbranched habit suits closer spacing and dense home-garden or trial rows.
directions: Lee was bred at the University of Arkansas from Gulfcoast, Emerald, and Clemson Spineless parentage to give a semi-dwarf plant that stays largely free of side branches, which simplifies picking. Straight, spineless, bright green pods form close along the main stem and should be cut every couple of days at three to four inches for the best texture. The compact, upright habit lets gardeners plant Lee more densely than sprawling heirloom types without sacrificing airflow. Regular harvest keeps the short growing season this variety was bred for producing right up until fall's first cool nights.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture

name: Legend Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Legend is an Oregon State University tomato released in 1996 with the highest level of late blight (Phytophthora infestans) resistance available in an open-pollinated tomato variety — developed specifically for the damp, foggy conditions of the Pacific Coast where late blight is a persistent annual challenge that can devastate unprotected tomato crops.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Legend is determinate and does not require staking, though a cage prevents fruit from resting on the soil; provides excellent production without fungicide sprays in conditions where late blight is present. Legend was released in 1996 by Dr. Jim Baggett at Oregon State University, culminating many years of breeding for late blight resistance in open-pollinated tomatoes; at the time of release it had the highest documented level of late blight resistance in any open-pollinated variety, making it a breakthrough for organic and low-spray gardeners in humid, blight-prone climates. The large (10–16 oz), round to slightly flattened, smooth, uniform deep red fruits have thick walls, good meaty texture, and classic sweet-balanced tomato flavor superior to most disease-resistant commercial varieties; the determinate plant ripens a heavy concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks rather than producing continuously. Legend performs exceptionally well in the Pacific Northwest and humid Eastern climates; it is also valuable in Gulf Coast gardens planted in fall (August–September) when late blight risk from summer thunderstorm humidity is highest. One of the most important contributions to open-pollinated tomato breeding in the late 20th century.

name: Lehua Maoli Taro
plantingNote: Set huli (corm tops) or whole corms once soil has warmed; can be grown in either boggy wetland beds or evenly moist upland rows.
directions: This is the traditional 'ordinary' Hawaiian poi taro, grown successfully in both flooded wetland patches and evenly moist upland beds beneath light tree cover. Its yellowish-green petioles and purplish-lilac corm flesh are the source of prized 'Lehua red poi,' a variety long favored across the islands for home and small-farm cultivation. Give it rich, consistently damp soil and some afternoon shade in hot Gulf Coast summers to keep leaves from scorching, and expect corms ready to dig 8 to 12 months after planting. Corms and the young leaves must be thoroughly cooked to break down calcium oxalate before eating.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR, Taro Varieties in Hawaii database (Lehua Maoli)

name: Lemon Boy Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; one of the most reliable large yellow tomatoes available, with good disease resistance and consistent fruit set even in warm, humid conditions — well-suited to zone 8–10 spring planting.
directions: Start seed indoors at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed, burying the stem deeply and providing a sturdy cage or stake from the outset. Lemon Boy is one of the most widely grown large yellow tomatoes, an F1 hybrid introduced in 1984 that remains a top performer for home gardeners seeking a reliable, large, lemon-yellow salad tomato; it produces 6–8 ounce round fruits with smooth, bright canary-yellow skin and mild, sweet, very low-acid flesh that is ideal for slicing fresh, for guests who find red tomatoes too acidic, and for adding visual contrast in salads and on plates. Disease resistance to verticillium, fusarium, and nematodes makes it particularly valuable in humid southern gardens. Water consistently and stake firmly as the indeterminate vines are tall and productive.

name: Lemon Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–April for a spring crop and again July–August for fall. Lemon Cucumber is best harvested when pale yellow to ivory colored — fully yellow fruits are overripe and develop a slightly bitter skin. The round shape and distinctive color make it easy to spot on the vine when it's time to harvest. Plants are productive and compact enough for small trellises and can be grown in containers.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with trellis support; Lemon Cucumber is an 1894 American heirloom producing distinctive round to oval, lemon-sized fruits with pale yellow-white skin when ripe — the resemblance to a lemon is strictly visual, as the flavor is mild, sweet, and refreshing with none of the tartness of actual lemon. The thin skin, small seeds, and crisp, sweet, very low-bitterness flesh make Lemon Cucumber one of the most palatable cucumbers for fresh eating without peeling — the skin remains tender and palatable throughout the eating-ripe stage (pale yellow to ivory) unlike the tough skins of slicing cucumbers. The round shape also makes Lemon Cucumber excellent for serving as a natural bowl — hollow out the round fruit and fill with dips, salads, or other fillings. The mild, sweet flavor and easy digestibility (lower cucurbitacin bitterness than many cucumbers) makes it popular for people who find regular cucumbers hard to digest.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Lemon Cucumber Heirloom History
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Cucumber Variety Trial
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Lemon Cucumber Production

name: Lemon Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moist, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Lemon cucumber (Crystal Apple) produces round to oval, tennis-ball-sized, pale-creamy-yellow fruits with exceptionally mild, sweet, non-bitter flavor — harvest when the skin is pale yellow to white; allowing it to turn deeper yellow indicates overripeness and seed development.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile, moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun after soil reaches 65°F; thin or transplant to 18–24 inches; harvest when pale yellow. Cucumis sativus 'Crystal Apple' (Lemon cucumber) is a heritage cucumber variety — one of the best-loved heirloom types — producing distinctive round to oval, tennis-ball-sized fruits with pale cream to pale yellow skin and white flesh that is exceptionally mild, sweet, and non-bitter compared to most standard cucumbers. Despite the name, the flavor is not lemony — it tastes like a very mild, sweet, refreshing cucumber. The thin skin makes peeling unnecessary, and the mild flavor means the seeds and seed cavity are also mild and not bitter, unlike some full-sized cucumbers. Lemon cucumbers are extremely popular with home gardeners for several reasons: the unusual round shape is attractive and different from grocery store varieties; the mild, non-bitter flavor appeals to people who find standard cucumbers too strong; and the fruits are easy to spot when harvesting (by size and color rather than hunting in dense vines). The variety produces prolifically over a long season. Best harvested young — large, deep-yellow specimens tend toward bitterness and seedness. An excellent choice for fresh eating, quick pickles, and cucumber water.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Heirloom Cucumber Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cucumber Production
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Lemon Cucumber

name: Lemon Drop Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Capsicum baccatum species takes longer to germinate and matures more slowly than C. annuum. In zone 9 start in January and transplant March–April. Lemon Drop thrives as a perennial in zone 9 and 10 — cut back hard in late winter and the plant will regrow from the roots, producing earlier and more heavily in its second year.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Lemon Drop is a Peruvian aji pepper (Capsicum baccatum) producing small, wrinkled, bright lemon-yellow fruits that ripen from pale green through various shades of yellow with a distinctive fruity, citrusy, bright heat very different from the harsher burn of jalapeños or the floral heat of habaneros. The heat level is medium-hot (15,000–30,000 Scoville units) with a pronounced fruity, lemony flavor note that makes Lemon Drop one of the most culinarily versatile hot peppers — used in salsas, ceviches, hot sauces, and Peruvian-style pepper pastes where the citrus-forward flavor complements seafood and poultry. Capsicum baccatum species peppers are widely grown in South America and increasingly popular in North American specialty gardening. In zone 9 the perennial habit is a major advantage — the plant can grow to a small shrub 4–5 feet tall over multiple seasons, producing far more fruit than annual plantings.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Aji Pepper Cultivars
New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — Capsicum baccatum Species
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Specialty Pepper Production

name: Lemon Drop Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before transplanting (C. chinense is slower to germinate and develop than C. annuum); transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost; Lemon Drop requires a long warm season — in zone 9, the long growing season supports full production.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Lemon Drop is a traditional Peruvian pepper (Ají Lemon in Peru) — a small (1–1.5 inch), thin-walled, conical fruit with a distinctive bright-lemon-yellow color at maturity and a unique combination of intense heat (15,000–30,000 Scoville units — comparable to a serrano but with more heat variability) and fruity, distinctly citrus-lemon flavor. The characteristic lemon flavor — a fruity, citrus-forward quality quite unlike the neutral heat of jalapeños or the fruity sweetness of habaneros — makes Lemon Drop one of the most flavorful hot peppers for cooking applications where heat AND flavor complexity are desired simultaneously. The dried and powdered fruit has an exceptional flavor that is widely used in traditional Peruvian cuisine for adding heat and bright citrus notes. As a Capsicum chinense species, Lemon Drop requires somewhat higher temperatures for germination (80–90°F) and a longer season than C. annuum peppers — start seeds 10–12 weeks before transplanting for adequate development time. The plant is productive in zone 9's long warm season, producing prolifically from late spring through frost. Fresh fruits, dried fruits, and powder form are all excellent culinary applications. The vivid yellow color and intense fruity aroma make Lemon Drop a distinctive addition to the pepper garden.

name: Lemon Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed past 65F, since this old American variety sulks in cold, wet ground the way most summer squash do.
directions: Lemon Squash has been grown in American gardens since the 1890s, prized for its round, pale yellow fruit that genuinely resembles a lemon in size and shape rather than a typical zucchini or crookneck. Pick fruit at 2-3 inches across for the sweetest, most tender eating, since the thin skin toughens and the flavor turns bland if left to balloon past baseball size. The sprawling bush produces steadily through summer heat, so check plants every day or two once fruiting begins to avoid a surprise crop of oversized squash. It can be used wherever a round summer squash is wanted — sliced, stuffed, or sauteed — and its unusual shape makes it a conversation piece at farmers markets.

name: Leningrad Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves 2-3 inches deep 4-6 weeks before hard freeze so roots establish before ground freezes solid.
directions: Leningrad is a Porcelain-type hardneck garlic sourced from the historic seed collections of St. Petersburg, Russia, valued by cold-climate growers for exceptional winter hardiness and vigorous growth even after harsh, deep-freeze winters. Bulbs form with 4-6 large, easy-to-peel white-wrapped cloves and a robust, sharp flavor that mellows nicely when roasted. Because Porcelain types need a strong cold vernalization period, Leningrad performs best in northern gardens with reliably cold winters and struggles in warm-winter regions. Select this cultivar for its proven reliability in USDA zones 3-5 where many other garlic strains falter.

name: Leutschauer Paprika Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March. Leutschauer Paprika is a slow-to-ripen variety — allow the full season for fruits to turn deep red; in zone 9 the long warm season suits this variety particularly well and allows full color development without rushing.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Leutschauer Paprika is a Slovak heirloom paprika pepper that produces elongated, pendant, 5–6 inch fruits with exceptionally thin walls and high sugar content — characteristics that make it one of the premier varieties for drying and grinding into fresh paprika. The bright red, fully ripe fruits are dried whole in strings (paprika ristras) or sliced and dehydrated before grinding. The flavor is sweet, slightly fruity, and aromatic — quite different from commercially ground paprika that has lost volatile compounds in processing. Plants are productive on fertile soil with consistent moisture; fruit set can stall during the hottest weeks in zone 9 but resumes in September. This is primarily a drying variety, though the fresh ripe fruits are also edible.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Paprika Types
University of New Mexico — Southwest Pepper Drying Traditions

name: Liana Yardlong Bean
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep once the soil is thoroughly warm, providing a tall, sturdy trellis for the vigorous 10- to 12-foot vines to climb.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep once the soil is thoroughly warm, providing a tall, sturdy trellis for the vigorous 10- to 12-foot vines to climb. Bred to be day-length neutral, Liana is one of the earliest-maturing yardlong bean types and performs reliably in both northern and southern gardens, tolerating heat and humidity better than many snap bean varieties. Harvest the slender green pods at 12-18 inches, well before they reach their full 23-inch potential, for the most tender texture in stir-fries and braised dishes.

name: Liberty Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips after soil has warmed above 65F into sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; a good nematode-resistant option for sandy Gulf Coast ground where standard boniato varieties struggle.
directions: Developed jointly by USDA-ARS and Clemson University as the first multiple-pest-resistant boniato release, highly resistant to nematodes and moderately resistant to soil insects and Fusarium wilt. Dry, light-yellow flesh with dark-red skin gives a notably bland, starchy character closer to a true potato-eating experience than a dessert-sweet type, and unlike most boniatos it doesn't darken after peeling, which makes it more forgiving for home cooks doing Caribbean or Latin-style preparations.
sources: ScienceDaily - Not-So-Sweet Potato Resists Pests, Disease

name: Light Red Kidney Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed; this widely adapted bush type sets a reliable crop even in cooler, wetter summers that can trouble other dry beans.
directions: Sow directly outdoors once frost has passed and soil temperatures are consistently warm, growing on a sturdy, medium-sized bush that adapts well across a wide range of climates. Allow pods to mature fully on the plant until they turn tan and papery and rattle with dry seed inside, which distinguishes this variety grown for drying rather than for fresh snap pods. Harvest by pulling or cutting whole plants once most pods are dry, then cure them further indoors before threshing. The thin-skinned, silky-textured beans hold their shape well in soups, salads, and baked bean dishes.

name: Lillian's Yellow Heirloom Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Lillian's Yellow is a tall, late-season potato-leaf indeterminate that needs a long, warm growing season and sturdy staking for its large fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil, staking to support the tall, vigorous potato-leaf vines. Lillian's Yellow was collected from a Tennessee grower and passed on for distribution through a Seed Savers Exchange yearbook; it requires a long season, typically 90-100 days from transplant, to produce its large, 12-20 ounce, pale yellow fruit that is sometimes blushed pink at the blossom end. The meaty, low-seed flesh is prized among heirloom growers as one of the finest-tasting yellow tomatoes, with a mild, citrusy sweetness distinct from more golden-orange yellow varieties.

name: Lily White Sea Kale
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring in deep, sandy, well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun; Lily White is a selected seed strain bred for uniform germination and unusually pale, tender forced shoots, and like the species it needs two full growing seasons before its first light harvest.
directions: Lily White is a named UK seed strain of sea kale selected over generations for producing especially pale, blanch-white forced shoots with minimal bitterness, along with more reliably true germination from seed than typical wild-collected sea kale seed. It forms the same billowing mounds of crinkled, blue-gray, cabbage-like leaves and honey-scented white summer flowers as the species, and is grown identically: choose a permanent bed for its long taproot, let plants establish for two to three years, then cover dormant crowns with a forcing pot in late winter to produce sweet, nutty, asparagus-textured shoots in early spring. Because plants are deep-rooted and drought-tolerant once established, they perform especially well in coastal gardens and sandy, low-fertility soils where few other vegetables thrive.

name: Lina Sisco's Bird Egg Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed above 60°F; a compact bush dry bean that needs no staking and is left on the plant until pods rattle and dry down in late summer.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm garden soil in rows spaced 24 to 30 inches apart, since this upright bush variety needs no trellising. Lina Sisco's Bird Egg is a Missouri family heirloom, carried west from the Ozarks in the 1880s and shared through Seed Savers Exchange, prized for its off-white seeds splashed with maroon streaks that resemble a speckled bird's egg. The dry beans cook up with a creamy, almost potato-like texture and mild flavor that holds up well in soups and baked bean dishes. Let pods dry fully on the plant before pulling the whole vine to finish curing indoors if fall rains threaten.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

name: Lincoln Leek
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant seedlings out once pencil-thick; Lincoln is a dual-purpose open-pollinated leek that can be pulled young as tender 'baby' finger leeks in about 50-60 days or left to size up to a full 16-20 inch stalk.
directions: Start Lincoln leeks indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant pencil-thick seedlings 4-6 inches apart into fertile, well-drained soil. Lincoln is a flexible, open-pollinated leek that rewards impatient gardeners as well as patient ones — pull it young at 50-60 days for slender, tender 'baby' or finger leeks with a mild, delicate flavor, or let it grow on to a full-sized 16-20 inch stalk for a heartier harvest later in the season. Hill or trench soil around the growing stems to blanch and lengthen the tender white portion as the plants mature. Keep the soil consistently moist and weed-free, and harvest through fall and into winter in mild climates, since leeks tolerate cold far better than onions.

name: Lincoln Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–8 weeks before last frost; Lincoln (also sold as Homesteader, the same variety under a different name) is one of the most highly regarded American shelling peas for flavor — a mid-season bush pea with wrinkled seeds and large, well-filled pods that many home gardeners consider the finest-flavored of all commonly available shelling peas.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep, 2–4 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart; direct seed as soon as soil can be worked in early spring. Lincoln (sold as Homesteader in Britain and by some American companies — both names refer to the same variety) is a mid-season American shelling pea considered by many gardeners and seed savers to produce the finest overall flavor and texture among commonly available bush peas; the compact plants produce blunt-tipped pods with 7–9 large, wrinkled (sweeter) peas each, ripening in 65–70 days from sowing. The wrinkled seed type indicates higher sugar content compared to smooth-seeded varieties; like all garden peas, Lincoln must be harvested at precise peak ripeness and eaten promptly before sugars convert to starch. An excellent variety for freezing as well as fresh eating; it remains the benchmark for shelling pea flavor among serious home gardeners.

name: Linda Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; Linda is a late maincrop German variety that benefits from a full season to size up smooth oval tubers.
directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep and 10-12 inches apart, hilling soil over the stems twice during the season to protect developing tubers from light and keep the crop evenly moist. Linda is a German heirloom known for smooth-skinned, deep yellow-fleshed tubers with a rich, dense texture well suited to roasting and mashing; it became widely known outside Germany around 2004 when lapsed EU variety registration briefly threatened its legal sale, prompting seed-saving groups to campaign for its continued availability as a garden heirloom. Allow vines to die back fully before harvesting for storage, since Linda keeps well through winter in a cool, dark location.

name: Lingot du Nord Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil typical of its native clay-loam growing region.
directions: Lingot du Nord is a white, elliptical dry bean with straight, often truncated ends, grown on about fifty communes straddling the Nord and Pas-de-Calais departments of France, where it holds both Label Rouge and PGI status. Pods are left on the plant until fully dry, historically finished on wooden drying racks called 'perroquets' in open air. The beans cook up with less skin separation than ordinary white beans and are noted for a more pronounced, chestnut-like flavor. Shelled dry beans should be stored in a cool, dry place for use in slow-cooked white bean dishes.
sources: INAO (Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualite) — Label Rouge LA 15/98 Lingot du Nord specification
Semence Mag — Le Lingot du Nord

name: Lipstick Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Lipstick is a compact sweet pepper producing small to medium pimento-shaped fruits (about 4 inches long, heart-shaped with a pointed tip). In zone 9, transplant March–April. Lipstick produces prolifically on compact plants (18–24 inches) suitable for containers and small gardens. Harvest green or allow to fully ripen to deep red for sweetest flavor — red-ripe Lipstick has exceptional sweetness and thick walls ideal for roasting, fresh eating, and stuffing. The compact plant habit means Lipstick can be grown in 5-gallon containers on patios, making it useful for zone 9 gardeners without significant ground space. Unlike the large, blocky bell pepper types that often struggle to set fruit in zone 9's summer heat, the pimento type peppers like Lipstick are generally more heat-tolerant and continue producing through the Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest green or red; red is sweeter. Lipstick Pepper is an All-America Selections (AAS) winner in the sweet pepper category, recognized for its combination of compact plant size, prolific productivity, and exceptional fruit quality in the pimento pepper class. The variety belongs to the pimento type — a group of sweet peppers distinct from bell peppers in fruit shape (heart-shaped, conical, or tapered rather than blocky), flesh thickness (very thick walls with small seed cavity), and flavor (sweeter, with less of the grassy quality of green bell peppers). Pimento peppers have a long history in American cooking: the red pimento paste used to stuff olives and fill pimento cheese sandwiches is made from this type, and the pimento's thick, sweet walls make it the preferred pepper for roasting, where the flesh caramelizes to an exceptional sweetness. Lipstick's AAS recognition was awarded specifically for its performance across diverse North American climates — including hot-summer regions where standard bell peppers underperform — making it a practical choice for gardeners in zone 9 who find that large bell peppers drop their blossoms or produce poorly during the Gulf South's summer heat peak. The fruit is medium-sized (3–4 inches long, 2.5 inches wide), heart-shaped to conical with a small pointed tip, and ripens from green to a deep, brilliant red. The skin is thinner than a bell pepper and the flesh is proportionally thicker, with a small, easily removed seed cavity. The flavor at red-ripe stage is very sweet, almost candy-like, with none of the bitterness that some tasters detect in green bell peppers.
sources: All-America Selections — Lipstick pepper AAS recognition and performance trials
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Lipstick pimento pepper variety notes
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Sweet Pepper Variety Selection for Home Gardens

name: Lipstick Sweet Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Lipstick is a compact plant (24 inches) bearing 3–4 inch pimiento-type fruits that ripen from green to deep, vivid red. Unlike most bell peppers, Lipstick ripens to red relatively quickly (70–80 days) without the extended 3-week+ green-to-red window of larger types. In zone 9, transplant March–April; plants often continue producing into fall. Lipstick does not require as much fertilizer as standard bell types — moderate fertility produces best flavor.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun after last frost with spacing of 15–20 inches. Lipstick is a Burpee-developed pimiento-type sweet pepper that produces small to medium (3 x 3.5 inch), heart-shaped, very thick-walled fruits of the pimiento class — a pepper type characterized by a rounder, more compact form than standard bell peppers, extraordinarily thick walls relative to total size, very few seeds, and exceptional sweetness. The pimiento type has been prized by Spanish and Mediterranean cooks for centuries for its superior eating quality (pimientos are what give pimento-stuffed olives their distinctive flavor and the Spanish name 'pimiento' itself means pepper in Spanish). Lipstick delivers the classic pimiento character in a compact, prolific plant suitable for small gardens and containers: the fruits have very thick walls that hold up to heat, an extremely sweet, mild flavor with no heat, and the characteristic heart-shaped cross-section when sliced that makes them visually distinctive from bell peppers. The vivid, saturated red color at full ripeness is striking and the thick walls make Lipstick excellent for roasting, stuffing with cheese, and eating raw where the thickness provides a satisfying crunch. Ripens more completely and uniformly than many larger bell types, making it practical for gardeners who want to harvest primarily red-ripe peppers.
sources: Burpee Seeds — Lipstick sweet pepper variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Pimiento-type pepper comparison
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Pepper Variety Evaluation

name: Lipstick Sweet Pimento Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; an early-maturing pimento-type pepper that performs well in shorter seasons; transplant after all frost has passed and soil warms to 60°F.
directions: Start seeds at 75–85°F 8–10 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, rich, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed. Lipstick is an early-maturing sweet pimento-type pepper that produces heart-shaped, 4-inch fruits with thick, candy-sweet walls, minimal seed cavity, and zero heat; they ripen from green to a brilliant lipstick red earlier than most pimentos, making it one of the better sweet pepper choices for northern gardens and short-season growers. The fruits are remarkably thick-walled and sweet when roasted, and they peel cleanly after charring, making them ideal for preserving as roasted red peppers. Compact plants are well-suited to containers.

name: Listada de Gandia Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun after the last frost date; in zone 9 also transplant in August for a fall crop — eggplants often produce their most abundant crop in the cooler fall weather.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Listada de Gandia is one of the most beautiful and visually distinctive eggplant varieties — a traditional Italian heirloom from the Valencia region of Spain producing oval to oblong, medium-large fruits with a stunning two-tone pattern of cream-white base with vivid purple-lavender stripes or splashes covering much of the surface. No two fruits have exactly the same pattern, making each harvest visually unique. Beyond its striking appearance, Listada de Gandia is prized for its exceptionally mild, tender, low-bitterness flesh — the thin skin and low seed content make it one of the finest eggplants for fresh preparations, grilling, and Italian dishes where eggplant bitterness would be unwelcome. The mild, creamy flesh has a slightly sweet, delicate flavor that is quite different from the stronger flavor of large black globe eggplants. Harvest at medium size (4–6 inches long) when the skin is shiny — the stripes fade and seeds become noticeable if left too long. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved true-to-type. The ornamental quality of the fruits and foliage makes Listada de Gandia attractive even as an edible ornamental in mixed garden beds and containers. In zone 9, eggplants are among the most heat-tolerant vegetables, thriving in the Gulf South summer.

name: Little Darling Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed; Little Darling is a compact hybrid bred to deliver classic dark-rind, red-fleshed watermelon flavor and high sugar content on vines that take up notably less garden space than standard icebox types.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart since vines run only about 4-5 feet, considerably shorter than traditional watermelon varieties. Little Darling produces oblong, dark-striped fruits around 5 by 8 inches and 5-7 lbs, with crisp, sweet red flesh rating around 12 on the Brix sugar scale, making it a good choice for gardeners who want full-flavored, classic watermelon character without the space demands of large-vine heirlooms. Water deeply and consistently through flowering and fruit set, then reduce watering as fruit nears maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip and by checking that the tendril nearest the fruit has dried and browned, since the compact plant can otherwise make ripeness easy to misjudge.

name: Little Finger Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Little Finger is a productive, compact eggplant that performs extremely well in zone 9 hot summers. In zone 9, transplant March–April for June–November production.
