Harvest fruits when 3–5 inches long and deep purple-black — do not allow to over-ripen, as the thin skin becomes tough and the few seeds develop rapidly. The plants produce prolifically in clusters, and frequent harvesting encourages continued production.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun in well-drained, fertile soil. Harvest slender purple-black fruits at 3–5 inches. Little Finger is a slender, finger-shaped Asian eggplant — a compact variety producing clusters of elongated, narrow fruits (2–5 inches long, 0.5–1 inch in diameter) of the finger eggplant type. The finger eggplant category is distinct from the large, globe-shaped Italian types and the longer Asian slicers: finger eggplants are the smallest category, producing bite-sized to small fruits in prolific clusters on bushy plants. Little Finger's small fruits are characterized by very thin, tender skin; virtually no seeds; and mildly sweet, creamy flesh without the bitterness sometimes found in large-fruited types. The thin skin means no peeling is required — fruits can be cooked whole (roasted, grilled, or sautéed) without preparation. The compact cluster-fruiting habit makes Little Finger one of the most productive eggplants per plant for its size, making it excellent for small gardens and containers. The fruits are harvested frequently (every 2–3 days at peak production), and the small size makes them ideal for stir-fries, kebabs, and preparations where bite-sized pieces are desired.
sources: Burpee Seeds — Little Finger eggplant variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Asian eggplant variety comparison
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Eggplant Production in Florida

name: Little Fingers Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil and air have warmed; Little Fingers, a 1985 All-America Selections winner, is a slender, finger-sized Asian-type eggplant well suited to container growing.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 60°F. Little Fingers, a 1985 All-America Selections winner, produces clusters of slender, finger-sized, deep purple Asian-type eggplant fruit that mature quickly and prolifically, giving a much faster and heavier harvest than large-fruited standard eggplant types. Its compact plant size and quick maturity make it a good fit for containers, small raised beds, or gardeners wanting an early eggplant harvest. Pick fruit young while still glossy and tender, several inches long, since Asian-type eggplant quickly becomes seedy and bitter if left to overmature, and harvest often to keep clusters coming through the season.

name: Little Gem Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Little Gem is a miniature romaine-butterhead cross that produces small, compact, dense heads of exceptional quality — the 'sucrine' of French cuisine, considered by many the most flavorful lettuce for whole-head salads and prized by restaurant chefs for its combination of crunch and buttery flavor.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50–70°F. Little Gem is a miniature romaine/butterhead cross producing small (4–5 inch), compact, upright heads with firm, crunchy outer leaves and a sweet, butter-cream interior heart — essentially a mini Caesar salad head in one plant. Also known as 'Sucrine' in France (from the French for 'sugar'), it has become extremely popular in restaurant and farmers market contexts as a whole-head salad lettuce grilled or served halved with dressings. The outer leaves have romaine's crunch while the hearts are as sweet and buttery as buttercrunch — the best of both types in a small, space-efficient package. 4-6 inch spacing allows intensive planting; harvest the whole head when firm and compact. More heat-tolerant than standard butterhead and holds well in the garden without bolting quickly.

name: Little Leaf Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; this Cornell-bred pickling cucumber has unusually small leaves that reduce cucumber beetle damage and improve airflow, making it a favorite for organic growers.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing plants to allow good air circulation. Little Leaf, formally H-19, was developed by Cornell University plant breeders specifically for its diminutive foliage, a trait that exposes fewer leaf surfaces to cucumber beetles and their associated bacterial wilt while still allowing plenty of sunlight to reach developing fruit and improving disease airflow around the vines. It is gynoecious, so interplanting with a small percentage of a standard pollenizer variety, or relying on nearby bees for cross-pollination from other varieties, improves fruit set. Fruits are small, blocky, and dark green, ideal for classic dill pickles, and should be harvested every one to two days at 2-4 inches for best quality.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

name: Little Lucy Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; nick or soak seeds overnight to improve germination. Little Lucy is a 1998 All-America Selections-winning dwarf hybrid okra, only about 2 feet tall with burgundy pods and maroon-veined foliage, doubling as an ornamental in a small Gulf Coast bed or container.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Little Lucy is a genuine dwarf okra, growing only about 2 feet tall with attractive maroon-veined foliage and burgundy-red pods, making it as much an ornamental accent for a small bed or large container as a food crop. Despite its small stature it produces a real, usable harvest of tender pods best picked young at 2-3 inches, since the compact plant sets pods close together on short internodes. Its diminutive size means it needs no staking and takes up a fraction of the space of full-size okra varieties, a practical advantage for small Gulf Coast gardens where summer heat makes okra one of the most reliable producers. Harvest every couple of days during peak summer heat to keep pods tender and encourage continued flowering.
sources: All-America Selections — Little Lucy okra AAS winner 1998

name: Little Marvel Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–8 weeks before last frost; Little Marvel is a 1934 All-America Selections winner — a remarkably compact dwarf bush pea (15 inches tall) that produces an outsized crop relative to its tiny size, making it ideal for small-space gardens, raised beds, containers, and intensive succession planting.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep; Little Marvel can be planted in raised beds at 15-inch row spacing due to its dwarf habit and needs only minimal support. Little Marvel pea won an All-America Selections award in 1934 and remains one of the most productive and most compact garden shelling peas available — the dwarf 15-inch plants are among the shortest of all shelling peas while producing an outsized crop of well-filled pods with 6–8 wrinkled, sweet peas each. The compact habit makes Little Marvel excellent for small raised beds, succession planting in containers, and tight-spaced intensive gardens where full-sized pea varieties would be impractical. Does not require staking even in wind, though a small 12–18 inch support fence improves harvestability. The 60–65 day maturity is relatively early for a sweet wrinkled-seeded pea.

name: Little Napoli Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; the dwarf, compact habit grows well in an 18-24 inch container and needs only a small stake or none at all.
directions: Little Napoli was named an AAS Winner for packing a full-size San Marzano-type paste tomato onto a true dwarf plant barely 18 inches tall, making it one of the few sauce tomatoes practical for a patio container or small raised bed. The compact, sturdy determinate plants stay tidy without staking and still produce a generous crop of elongated, meaty 2-3 ounce plum fruit with classic low-moisture paste texture suited to sauces and canning. Keep the container evenly watered since dwarf plants in small pots dry out faster than in-ground vines, and harvest as fruit turns fully red for the best sauce flavor.

name: Livingston's Beauty Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the indeterminate vine as it grows.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, staking the vine as it grows. Livingston's Beauty was introduced in 1886 by Alexander W. Livingston of Reynoldsburg, Ohio, one of the most important early tomato breeders in American history, whose systematic selection work through the late 1800s helped transform the tomato from a distrusted curiosity into a smooth, reliably productive garden staple. The medium to medium-large fruit is a rosy pink-red, smooth, and globe-shaped with good, well-balanced flavor for its era — a marked improvement over the ribbed, irregular tomatoes common before Livingston's breeding program, and a variety that directly influenced the smooth, round tomato shape gardeners now take for granted. Grow it as a piece of American horticultural history as much as a garden tomato; water and feed evenly through the season for the best fruit set and flavor.

name: Livingston's Paragon Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Paragon is a vigorous indeterminate regular-leaf variety that benefits from staking to keep the abundant medium-round fruit off the ground.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil once frost danger has passed, staking to support the heavy fruit set. Introduced by Ohio seedsman Alexander W. Livingston in 1870, Paragon is historically significant as the first tomato widely recognized for producing smooth, uniformly round, evenly red fruit without the deep ridges and cracking typical of tomatoes at the time, a breakthrough that helped popularize the tomato as a garden and market crop across 19th-century America. The plants are productive and disease-tolerant for an heirloom, yielding clusters of medium-sized red fruit with classic old-fashioned flavor suited to fresh eating and canning.

name: Lizzano Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into a hanging basket or rail planter after frost danger passes, letting the trailing stems cascade over the container edge.
directions: Transplant into a hanging basket or rail-mounted container after the last frost and let the trailing stems spill downward rather than staking them upright. Lizzano is an All-America Selections winner noted for combining a true cascading habit with strong early blight tolerance, an unusual pairing that keeps foliage healthier through the season than most basket-type tomatoes. It produces abundant clusters of sweet, 1-inch red cherry tomatoes continuously from mid-summer until frost.

name: Lobjoits Green Cos Lettuce
plantingNote: Sow directly; reliably slow to bolt for a romaine type, allowing extended spring and early-summer sowings.
directions: Sow directly in cool soil; this classic English cos lettuce from the early twentieth century forms tall, upright, dark-green heads that fold in on themselves to blanch a firm, sweet heart. It is reliably slow to bolt for a romaine type, allowing extended spring and early-summer sowings in cooler climates. Long a favorite of British kitchen gardeners, it is still maintained by seed-saving groups as one of the best-flavored traditional cos varieties.

name: Loche Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost in warm soil; Loche is a Peruvian landrace squash grown almost exclusively around Lambayeque, prized for its dense, starchy, nutty-flavored flesh used fresh rather than cured and stored.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in hills after danger of frost has passed, in warm, fertile soil. Loche is a distinctive elongated, dumbbell-shaped squash landrace long grown around Lambayeque in northern Peru, where it is a signature ingredient in regional dishes such as arroz con pato and causa rather than a storage squash; its dense, pale, nutty-flavored flesh is normally cooked fresh rather than cured for long keeping. The crop has a reputation for growing true to type only in its home region, with fruit grown elsewhere from the same seed often reverting toward more typical moschata shapes. Harvest once the skin has toughened and the characteristic curved, narrow-waisted shape has filled out, and use the flesh promptly for best flavor and texture.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste
International Potato Center (Peru) crop diversity records

name: Lodero Red Cabbage
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant in late spring for a fall harvest. Lodero carries clubroot resistance, a genuine advantage in soil with a history of that disease.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Lodero is a Bejo-bred red cabbage notable as the first clubroot-resistant red cabbage cultivar, a significant advantage in gardens with a history of that soilborne disease. Medium heads of 3-6 pounds are held high off the ground, maturing in roughly 105 days from a late-April-to-May sowing for a late September to November harvest. It stores exceptionally well into winter and makes excellent pickled red cabbage or braised dishes.

name: Lolla Rossa Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–February for spring. Lolla Rossa can be harvested as baby leaves (cut 2–3 inches tall) or allowed to develop to full rosettes. Successive sowings every 3 weeks provide a continuous supply. The red color is most intense in cool weather; warm temperatures reduce pigmentation.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Lolla Rossa is an Italian looseleaf lettuce producing rosettes of tightly frilled, deeply ruffled, deep burgundy-red to crimson leaves — the most intensely frilled and ruffled of all red lettuces, with a texture often compared to coral or ruffled fabric. The heavy frilling maximizes surface area and catches dressings exceptionally well, making Lolla Rossa a favorite in mixed salad bowls and mesclun mixes where its dramatic appearance creates visual impact. The flavor is mild and tender with a slight bitterness from the red pigments that is barely perceptible in young leaves and becomes slightly more pronounced in older, larger leaves. The deep red color makes Lolla Rossa one of the highest-anthocyanin lettuces, providing significant antioxidant content. It is the standard red frilly lettuce in European market and supermarket displays, where it has been in continuous commercial production since the 1970s, and is equally valuable in North American specialty salad production and home gardens.
sources: Seeds of Italy — Lolla Rossa Lettuce Growing Notes
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Red Looseleaf Lettuce
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Specialty Lettuce Production

name: Lollo Bionda Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow thinly with minimal soil coverage; grow as cut-and-come-again from 40 days or harvest whole heads at 55–65 days. Often grown alongside Lollo Rosso for visual contrast in mixed salad plantings. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall/winter production and February–March for spring. Performs best in cool weather and does not tolerate summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, fertile, well-drained soil or barely cover with 0.125 inch of fine soil; maintain consistent moisture through germination. Lollo Bionda (Italian for 'blonde curly') is the green counterpart to Lollo Rosso — sharing the identical intensely frilled, ruffled leaf margin and open loose-leaf habit but expressing uniformly bright chartreuse-green to golden-green coloring throughout rather than the Rosso type's red pigmentation. The two varieties are frequently grown together in alternating rows or blocks, where the intense green-and-crimson contrast creates a visually striking planting that is both ornamental and practical. Mixed bags of Lollo Bionda and Lollo Rosso leaves form the foundation of the Italian insalata mista tradition. Like Lollo Rosso, Lollo Bionda has a mildly bitter, distinctly Italian loose-leaf character — more complex and interesting than flat-leafed American loose-leaf types — and the same extremely frilled, ruffled texture that gives the leaves visual and textural interest in salads. Lollo Bionda is somewhat more heat-tolerant than Lollo Rosso in some trials, extending the spring salad season by 1–2 weeks before bolting. Both Lollo types are excellent for cut-and-come-again harvesting, where the plant continues producing from the center after outer leaves are removed, providing multiple harvests from a single planting.
sources: Fedco Seeds — Lollo Bionda variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Italian lettuce variety comparison
Organic Seed Alliance — Lettuce Diversity Collection

name: Lollo Rosso Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow thinly and barely cover with fine soil (lettuce needs light for germination); Lollo Rosso is best grown as a cut-and-come-again crop, harvesting outer leaves from 40 days onward or cutting the whole plant at 55–65 days when full size. In zone 9, sow September through November for fall and winter harvest, and again February through March for spring. Lollo Rosso performs best in cool weather (50–70°F) and tends to bolt quickly in summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds on the surface of moist, fertile, well-drained soil or cover with 0.125 inch of fine soil; keep moist until germination. Lollo Rosso is the defining Italian loose-leaf lettuce — a variety whose intensely frilled, ruffled, deeply cut leaf margins and vibrant crimson-red to dark wine-red coloring at the leaf tips (fading through red-purple to green at the base) have made it the visual centerpiece of European mixed salad culture and one of the most recognizable lettuce varieties in the world. The name means 'red curly' in Italian, describing both the color and the extraordinarily frilled leaf margin that distinguishes Lollo Rosso from all other common loose-leaf types. The frilling is dramatic and consistent — the leaf margins curl so tightly that they create a lace-like appearance when the lettuce is displayed whole, making Lollo Rosso not only a component of salads but a visual garnish in its own right. The flavor is mildly bitter in the Italian leaf lettuce tradition — more complex and interesting than bland American loose-leaf types but not unpleasantly so — and pairs well with vinaigrette-dressed salads where the slight bitterness provides welcome contrast. Lollo Rosso is the standard accompaniment to Italian prosciutto and melon, appears in mixed salad bags throughout Europe as the red accent component, and is excellent alone dressed simply with olive oil and sea salt.
sources: Fedco Seeds — Lollo Rosso variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Italian lettuce variety comparison
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Lettuce Variety Evaluation

name: Long Black Spanish Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer/early fall for fall and winter harvest; Long Black Spanish is a winter radish that requires a longer growing time than spring radishes (60–70 vs. 25–35 days). In zone 9, sow August–September for November–January harvest. Winter radishes should not be planted in spring — they bolt quickly in warming temperatures. Harvest when roots reach 6–8 inches; they keep in the ground for weeks and can be stored in damp sand in a cool location for months.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in fall in rows 12 inches apart; thin to 4–6 inches. Harvest when roots are 6–8 inches long; peel before eating as the black skin is tough and astringent. Long Black Spanish Radish is a winter storage radish with a very distinctive appearance: the long (6–10 inch), cylindrical root has deeply black skin — nearly jet black — contrasting with crisp, white flesh within. It is one of the oldest documented European radish varieties, with references dating to the 16th century; it was the standard large winter radish of European cuisine before the introduction of Asian types and remains common in Polish, German, and Ashkenazi Jewish food traditions where it appears in salads (grated with onion and oil) and as a medicinal digestive herb. The flavor is significantly sharper and more pungent than spring radishes — a biting, horseradish-adjacent pungency that mellows somewhat when the grated flesh is salted and rested. The winter storage capability distinguishes Long Black Spanish from spring radishes: properly harvested and stored in damp conditions near freezing, the roots keep for 3–4 months, providing a root vegetable throughout the winter.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Long Black Spanish radish variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Winter radish collection
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Root Cellar Storage Vegetable Guide

name: Long Green Improved Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; trellising keeps the long fruit straighter and reduces contact with humid, disease-prone soil in Southern gardens.
directions: Dating to at least 1842, Long Green Improved was for decades the standard American slicing and pickling cucumber before modern hybrids took over seed racks, and it remains one of the longest-cultivated open-pollinated cucumbers still commercially available. Vigorous vines produce dark green, often faintly ribbed fruit that can be picked small for pickles or left to grow 8-10 inches or more for fresh slicing, with crisp, mild flesh that holds up well in hot weather. Because it is an old-style monoecious variety rather than a modern gynoecious hybrid, it needs both male and female flowers present for pollination, so plant a full row rather than just one or two hills to ensure good fruit set. Save seed from fully ripened (yellowed) fruit for a true-breeding crop next season.

name: Long Green Trailing Marrow
plantingNote: Direct sow after frost danger passes and give the vigorous trailing vines a generous bed or sturdy support, since this is a true running type rather than a compact bush.
directions: Long Green Trailing is one of the traditional English vegetable marrows, grown on long rambling vines rather than the compact bush habit of most modern zucchini. Gardeners can pick it young, at 8-10 inches, for a tender zucchini-like squash, or let it grow on toward 18-24 inches for the classic British marrow, which is typically halved, stuffed, and baked rather than eaten raw. Because the vines run rather than stay in a tidy mound, train them along a fence or let them ramble through an open bed to keep the dark green, pale-striped fruit easy to find. This old allotment favorite is prone to the same squash vine borer and powdery mildew pressures as other pepo squash, so monitor the sprawling stems through the season.

name: Long Island Cheese Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow in rich, well-drained soil 1–2 weeks after last frost; Long Island Cheese is a Cucurbita moschata type (related to butternut squash) with exceptional disease resistance and heat tolerance compared to jack-o-lantern types — excellent for zone 8–10 gardens. Vines are vigorous, reaching 10–15 feet.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3–4 seeds, thinning to 2; Long Island Cheese Pumpkin is a large, flat, deeply ribbed, tan-buff heirloom that looks remarkably like a wheel of French cheese — hence its popular name. Developed by Long Island market gardeners in the 19th century, it was once the dominant commercial pumpkin variety in the northeastern United States because of its excellent eating quality, dense orange-yellow flesh with a smooth, rich, sweet flavor particularly prized for pumpkin pies (significantly better than jack-o-lantern types). Being a Cucurbita moschata variety, it is substantially more resistant to squash vine borers, powdery mildew, and heat than C. pepo types, making it one of the most practical large pumpkins for zone 8–10 Gulf Coast gardens where summer disease and pest pressure is high. Fruits weigh 8–15 pounds and store well for months.

name: Long Island Cheese Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; as a moschata-type squash it resists squash vine borer better than maxima or pepo types, a real advantage in Gulf South gardens.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vines plenty of room to run. Long Island Cheese is a 19th-century New York heirloom named for its flattened, ribbed, buff-tan fruit that closely resembles a wheel of cheese, with dense, sweet, deep-orange flesh well suited to pies, soups, and roasting. As a Cucurbita moschata type, it shares that species' strong resistance to squash vine borer, a serious pest of pepo- and maxima-type squash in warm, humid climates. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and resists a fingernail, then cure in a warm, dry spot for one to two weeks to concentrate sweetness and improve storage life, which can extend several months in a cool, dry space.

name: Long Island Improved Brussels Sprouts
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera 'Long Island Improved'
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before transplant date, transplanting 12–16 weeks before first expected frost; in zones 3–7 start in late spring for fall harvest. Brussels sprouts require a very long cool growing season (90+ days) and develop best flavor only after exposure to hard frost — zones 3–7 are ideal, with zones 8–9 being very challenging due to insufficient sustained cool weather for quality sprout development. In zone 9 Brussels sprouts may produce a partial crop in the coolest winters but results are often disappointing compared to more appropriate cool-climate growing.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, very fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil — Brussels sprouts are heavy feeders requiring substantial nitrogen throughout their long growing season; Long Island Improved is the standard open-pollinated Brussels sprouts variety — the classic 'compact' type (as opposed to taller, older varieties) that has dominated American horticulture since the early 20th century. The small, round, tightly packed miniature cabbage heads (sprouts) that form along the stem are harvested from bottom to top as they mature, with each stem producing dozens of 1–2 inch sprouts over several weeks of harvest. Brussels sprouts' reputation for strong, unpleasant flavor is entirely a product of poor growing conditions — specifically, heat stress — rather than the plant's inherent flavor. Brussels sprouts grown to maturity in cool weather with frost exposure are mild, nutty, sweet, and completely different from heat-stressed sprouts with the intense sulfurous off-flavors that give the vegetable its negative reputation. The conversion of starches to sugars after frost exposure transforms Brussels sprouts from a challenging, strong-flavored vegetable into a genuinely delicious one — a transformation that zone 9 gardeners rarely witness but that northern gardeners who harvest after repeated freezes experience routinely.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Brussels Sprouts Production Guide
University of Wisconsin Extension — Brussels Sprouts for Cool Climates
University of Minnesota Extension — Brussels Sprouts Variety Trials

name: Long Keeper Onion
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil can be worked; as a long-day type Long Keeper performs best in northern and mid-latitude gardens with a full summer to size up.
directions: Long Keeper lives up to its name as a pungent yellow storage onion selected specifically for exceptional shelf life, commonly holding firm for eight months to a year in a cool, dry pantry. Transplant seedlings into fertile, well-drained soil and give plants full sun and consistent moisture through bulb formation, then reduce watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall. Because the flavor is sharp and the flesh dense, it is best suited to cooked dishes rather than fresh raw use. Cure the bulbs thoroughly in a warm, airy spot for several weeks before storage, since a complete cure is what gives this variety its outstanding keeping quality.

name: Long Keeper Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; harvest fruit while still pale orange-yellow just before frost for the longest storage life, rather than waiting for vine-ripening.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil, caging or staking the semi-sprawling vines. Long Keeper is grown specifically for its ability to ripen slowly off the vine when picked mature-green to pale blush before the first fall frost, gradually coloring to an orange-red over weeks or months in cool, dark storage so gardeners can enjoy fresh tomatoes well into winter. The flavor is milder than a summer-ripened tomato but remains a valued novelty among gardeners who want to extend the tomato season past the growing year.

name: Long of Naples Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant March–April for spring and August for fall. Long of Naples produces very long vines (12–15 feet) requiring generous space or a large trellis. The moschata type is more heat-tolerant and powdery mildew-resistant than pepo squashes, making it a better choice for zone 9 summer production. Harvest immature fruits at 12–18 inches for summer squash use, or leave to mature fully for winter storage.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Long of Naples (Lunga di Napoli, Serpentina di Napoli) is a renowned Italian heirloom squash from the Campania region surrounding Naples, producing extraordinarily long cylindrical fruits of 24–36 inches or more — occasionally reaching 4–5 feet under optimal conditions. At maturity the tan-to-buff skin covers dense, deep-orange flesh with a sweet, rich flavor similar to butternut but with a creamier texture and less watery flesh. Immature fruits at 12–18 inches can be harvested and used as a superior summer squash — far more flavorful than standard zucchini, with firmer flesh and more concentrated sweetness. Fully mature fruits cure well and store for 6–12 months in a cool, dry location. As a Cucurbita moschata type, Long of Naples shows excellent heat and humidity tolerance, resistance to vine borers, and superior performance in zone 9 compared to pepo-type squashes. The vines are vigorous and spreading — allow 8–12 feet per plant.
sources: University of Naples Federico II — Campanian Heirloom Vegetable Varieties
Slow Food Foundation — Presidia Long of Naples Squash
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Moschata Squash Production

name: Long Orange Improved Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow into deeply worked beds and thin early for straight roots; a strong, old-fashioned keeper well suited to fall storage.
directions: A refined selection of the historic Dutch Long Orange carrot line that traces back to 17th-century Netherlands and was further developed by American seed houses in the 1800s, making it one of the direct ancestors of modern Danvers and Chantenay types. It produces long, tapered, deep-orange roots with a somewhat coarser core than modern Nantes hybrids but dependable yields in open garden soil. Direct sow into deeply worked beds and thin early for straight roots; it is a strong, old-fashioned keeper well suited to fall storage.
sources: William Woys Weaver, Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

name: Long Pie Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost, giving vines ample room to run; the elongated fruit needs a long, dry curing period after harvest for maximum storage life.
directions: Plant seeds in hills of two or three after frost danger passes, and let the long vines sprawl since the fruit is too heavy and elongated to trellis practically. Long Pie is an old New England heirloom, cylindrical rather than round, growing two to three feet long and resembling an overgrown zucchini more than a typical jack-o'-lantern pumpkin. Its smooth orange rind and dense, mild-flavored flesh make it a traditional substitute for butternut or sugar pumpkin in pies and baking, and its thick shell allows it to store for many months longer than most winter squash. Harvest before hard frost when the rind resists a fingernail scratch, then cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before moving to cool winter storage.

name: Long Red Cayenne Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Long Red Cayenne is the standard, classic cayenne pepper variety — a long-season heirloom producing pencil-thin, wrinkled, 6–8 inch red pods with 30,000–50,000 SHU heat, the benchmark from which all other cayenne peppers are measured and the source of commercial cayenne powder, hot sauce, and the classic Louisiana-style hot sauce heat.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, well-drained, fertile soil; Long Red Cayenne is a vigorous grower that benefits from staking when loaded with fruit; pick all red and drying fruits promptly to encourage continued production through the season. Long Red Cayenne is the classic cayenne pepper — an old heirloom open-pollinated variety that represents the original 'cayenne' type from which the broad category of cayenne peppers takes its name (likely from Cayenne, French Guiana, where related chiles were grown). The fruits are distinctive: pencil-thin (1/2 to 3/4 inch in diameter), 6–8 inches long, wrinkled and irregular in cross-section, tapering to a point, and ripening to a bright red — characteristics that make Long Red Cayenne immediately identifiable and distinct from the smooth-skinned, shorter 'Ring of Fire' type. The heat level of 30,000–50,000 SHU is moderate-hot — significantly hotter than jalapeños but substantially milder than habaneros — in the range that defines 'cayenne heat' in American cuisine. Long Red Cayenne is the source (via cultivated strains) of commercial cayenne powder, an essential spice in Cajun and Creole cooking, Indian cuisine, and most dry spice blends; of Louisiana-style hot sauce; of the dried cayenne pods used in Chinese and Sichuan cooking; and of the classic sriracha-style sauces. Prolific production on vigorous plants (24–36 inches) in warm climates; excellent for drying on the plant or on strings.

name: Long Red Florence Onion
plantingNote: In mild-winter regions start seed indoors in late summer and transplant in fall for a spring harvest; in cold-winter climates sow in early spring instead. Long Red Florence is an Italian heirloom that can also be pulled young as a sweet salad onion before bulbing fully.
directions: Long Red Florence is a traditional Tuscan heirloom onion grown for its elongated, torpedo-shaped bulbs of glossy deep-red skin and mild, sweet white-and-red flesh. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil and space plants closely enough to encourage the characteristic slender shape rather than a rounded bulb. It can be harvested at three distinct stages: pulled very young as a scallion-like salad onion, at mid-size for grilling whole, or left to mature into a full torpedo bulb for slicing raw over pizza and salads. Because its flesh is milder and higher in moisture than standard storage onions, plan to use the harvest within a couple of months rather than holding it in long-term storage.

name: Long Red Slim Cayenne Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Long Red Slim produces the classic thin, wrinkled, fiery red cayenne pods traditionally strung and dried for homemade cayenne pepper powder and pepper flakes.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Long Red Slim is a classic, widely grown cayenne cultivar producing narrow, tapering, thin-walled pods that ripen from green to bright red, packing substantial heat in a lightweight, easily dried pod. The thin walls make it ideal for stringing into traditional pepper ropes (ristras) or oven-drying and grinding into homemade cayenne powder or crushed red pepper flakes. Plants are productive over a long season and tolerate heat well, making cayenne one of the more reliable hot peppers for Gulf South summers; pick pods at full red color for maximum heat and flavor when drying.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute

name: Long Red Surrey Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow into deep, loose, light or sandy soil in full sun; Long Red Surrey needs stone-free soil for its long tapering roots to form straight.
directions: Direct sow into deep, loose, light or sandy soil in full sun; Long Red Surrey is an English heirloom carrot dating to the 1830s, producing long, tapering orange roots with a yellow core, best grown in light, well-drained ground where its length can develop without forking. It matures in 75-85 days with a strong, sweet flavor that has kept it in cultivation as an exhibition and storage carrot for nearly two centuries. Thin seedlings early to allow full root development and harvest before hard freeze for the best texture.

name: Long Scarlet Short Top Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring and succession sow every 2 weeks until temperatures climb; the compact foliage tolerates closer spacing than most spring radishes, allowing more roots per row-foot.
directions: Broadcast or row-sow 1/2 inch deep and thin to about 1 inch apart, since the short, upright tops leave little room for foliage to compete for light. Long Scarlet Short Top is a nineteenth-century market variety producing tapered, cylindrical scarlet roots 5-6 inches long, distinguished from other 'long scarlet' types by its notably reduced leaf growth, which was bred deliberately to permit tighter row spacing for commercial growers. Pull roots promptly once they reach usable size, as the slender shape can turn pithy and hollow faster than round varieties if left in warm soil. The tapered form and quick maturity made it a standard early-spring forcing radish before greenhouse culture became common.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee & Co. historical seed catalog archives

name: Long Slim Cayenne Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January and transplant in March. Long Slim Cayenne is highly productive in zone 9's long warm season and often overwinters as a perennial — cut back in late winter and the woody plant regrows to produce even more heavily the next year. For dried cayenne, harvest fully red fruits and dry on strings or in a dehydrator. The thin-walled fruits dry quickly and completely.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Long Slim Cayenne is the standard form of cayenne pepper — the elongated, thin-walled, moderately wrinkled red pepper that is one of the most important culinary chile peppers in the world and the source of commercial cayenne pepper powder and red pepper flakes. The fruits are 4–6 inches long, pencil-thin, and bright red when fully ripe, with heat levels typically measuring 30,000–50,000 Scoville Heat Units — a penetrating, clean, sharp heat that has made cayenne the dominant hot pepper in Louisiana Cajun and Creole cuisine, Indian cooking, and dozens of other culinary traditions. Long Slim Cayenne dries easily and completely due to the thin walls, and the dried pepper grinds to the characteristic bright red powder of commercial cayenne spice. Fresh red cayenne peppers are also used in hot sauce production — Tabasco-style sauces use fermented cayenne-type peppers as their primary ingredient. In zone 9 the plants bear enormous crops of drying-quality peppers over the full warm season.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Cayenne Pepper Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Long Slim Cayenne Variety Information
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cayenne Pepper for Florida Gardens

name: Long White Cow Horn Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow 8-10 weeks before the first fall frost into loose, deeply worked soil so the tapered root can push freely; a spring sowing is possible but the root tends toward more pungent flavor and faster bolting in warming soil.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep and thin to 4-6 inches apart; because much of the root pushes up out of the soil as it grows, mounding a little loose soil around the shoulders keeps the exposed portion from toughening or turning green. Long White Cow Horn is an early American heirloom named for its distinctive shape: a slender, curved, carrot-like white root that tapers to a point, growing half-exposed above ground rather than forming a globe. It matures faster than round white-fleshed turnips and was traditionally valued for both table use when young and livestock feed when left to size up. The exposed shoulders develop a slight green blush in sunlight, which does not affect the mild flavor of the flesh beneath.
sources: Sturtevant's Notes on Edible Plants (U.P. Hedrick, ed.)

name: Long White Reishi Bitter Melon
plantingNote: Direct-sow after soil reaches 70°F or start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; provide a tall arbor or trellis so the long, pale fruit can hang freely for straight, unblemished pods.
directions: A striking, elongated white bitter melon that dangles from the vine like pale stalactites, reaching about 16 inches long with slender, smoothly ridged, faintly mint-green-tinged white skin. Its bitterness is notably gentler than green-skinned types, making it a good choice for fresh stir-fries and soups where a milder flavor is wanted. Beyond its culinary use, the long, glossy, pale fruit hanging against dense green foliage makes the vine a genuine edible ornamental for an arbor or fence-line trellis, drawing attention in the summer garden even before harvest begins. Give it a tall, sturdy support and steady moisture through the long fruiting season to develop full-length, well-formed fruit.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Long White Reishi Bitter Melon
University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension — Bitter Melon

name: Longfellow Flint Corn
plantingNote: Plant in blocks after the soil has warmed; its short, reliable season suits northern New England gardens.
directions: Plant in blocks after the soil has warmed; its short, reliable season makes it well suited to northern New England gardens where longer-season dent corns struggle to dry down before frost. Longfellow is an old New England eight-row yellow flint corn, kept in circulation by regional seed savers and small farms in Maine and neighboring states for its dependable yields and cold-season resilience. Ears dry hard and quickly on the stalk, and the kernels grind into a sweet, full-flavored yellow cornmeal typical of the flint corns that sustained early New England farm households through winter.

name: Longor Shallot
plantingNote: Plant shallot sets 4-8 weeks before the last frost in spring, or in fall in zones 7-10 for a heavier early-summer crop.
directions: Longor is a traditional French shallot valued for producing unusually long, slender bulbs with coppery skin and pink-tinged flesh, distinguishing it from the rounder Dutch-type shallots grown for the fresh market. Plant sets shallow with the tip just showing above the soil surface and keep the bed weed-free, since each set divides into a cluster of several elongated bulbs by midsummer. Reduce watering once foliage begins to yellow and topple, then lift, dry, and cure the bulbs in a warm, airy spot before storing. Longor is prized in French cooking regions such as Brittany for its slightly sweet flavor and long storage life, and gardeners choose it over rounder shallot types specifically for its distinctive shape and keeping quality.

name: Lorz Italian Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March after nights stay above 55°F. Lorz Italian is productive through the Gulf Coast summer and performs best when harvested green; if left to ripen red, pick before fruits become overripe and mushy in summer humidity.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Lorz Italian is a Washington State heirloom sweet frying pepper, a classic Italian-style variety with thin-walled, pendent fruits that are 8–10 inches long — among the longest sweet peppers available. The mild, sweet flesh is nearly seedless and ideal for the classic Italian-American preparation of frying in olive oil with garlic and salt (peperonata), as well as roasting, stuffing, and fresh eating. The thin walls roast and collapse beautifully without the wateriness of thicker-walled sweet peppers. Plants produce prolifically once established, with multiple fruits per branch; the long, elegant fruits are also ornamental hanging from the plant. Harvest green for crispest texture or allow to ripen red for sweetest flavor.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Lorz Italian Pepper
Washington State University Extension — Heritage Vegetable Varieties
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Sweet Frying Pepper Types

name: Lorz Italian Softneck Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves in fall around the time of first frost; Lorz Italian is a softneck Artichoke-type garlic brought to the Walla Walla area of Washington State by Italian immigrant Lorenzo 'Lorz' Lorenzi in the late 1800s, where it was grown and preserved through generations of Italian-American farming families in the Columbia River valley before entering heirloom seed networks.
directions: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall; softneck types like Lorz Italian can be planted over a wider window than hardnecks — from 4 weeks before first frost to a week or two after; mulch after planting; keep weed-free in spring; harvest when 5–6 lower leaves have yellowed and cure thoroughly. Lorz Italian is an Artichoke-type softneck garlic with a remarkable Italian-American immigrant story: it was brought to the Walla Walla Valley of eastern Washington State by an Italian immigrant named Lorenzo 'Lorz' Lorenzi in the late 19th century, where it became a staple of the Italian immigrant farming community in the Columbia River valley region, passed down through family seed-saving for generations before being preserved by heirloom garlic collectors and specialist growers. The large, roundish bulbs typically contain 12–20 cloves arranged in multiple overlapping layers (characteristic of Artichoke types), with white to pale ivory outer skin; the cloves are plump, meaty, and moderately spicy — a full-flavored softneck with more character than commercial supermarket garlic but without the intensity of the finest Rocambole hardnecks. The great practical advantage of Lorz Italian and other Artichoke softnecks is excellent storage — bulbs typically keep 9–12 months in good conditions, far outlasting any hardneck type; the flexible stems also make it excellent for braiding. Adapted to a wide range of climates from cool Pacific Northwest conditions to warm Southern winters.

name: Loto Upland Rice
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after all danger of frost into warm, moist (not necessarily flooded) soil; unlike paddy rices, Loto can be grown as a dryland crop with regular irrigation rather than standing water.
directions: Loto is a short-grained, awnless upland rice from the Emilia-Romagna region of northern Italy, traditionally used for risotto rather than steamed rice. It tillers freely into compact clumps on lodging-resistant stalks and, unlike most rice grown in the United States, does not need to be flooded — consistent moisture and warm soil are enough to bring it to maturity in a single temperate growing season. Home growers in cooler climates have had success direct-seeding it alongside a nurse crop of fast-germinating radish to mark the slow-emerging rice rows. Its easy-to-thresh, easy-to-hull grain makes it a practical choice for small-scale growers without dedicated rice processing equipment.

name: Louisiana 16 Inch Long Pod Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed well beyond last frost; this Louisiana heirloom rewards patience with pods that can stretch far longer than typical okra while staying fry-and-gumbo tender.
directions: Louisiana 16 Inch Long Pod is a tall, vigorous Southern heirloom selected over generations for pods that stay tender even as they grow far beyond the length most okra turns woody. Give plants generous room since they build large leaves and reach considerable height, and consider staking in exposed sites prone to summer storms. Harvest ribbed green pods every day or two once they reach a usable size to keep the heavily branching plant setting new flowers all season. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from the driest, most mature pods for replanting the following year.

name: Louisiana Green Velvet Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–6 weeks after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; Louisiana Green Velvet is a smooth-podded, heavy-yielding heirloom okra variety that produces long (5–7 inch), straight, smooth dark green pods with minimal ribbing and particularly tender texture — one of the top-recommended varieties by LSU AgCenter for Gulf Coast okra production, prized for consistent tenderness and yield through humid Louisiana summers.
directions: Soak seeds overnight before planting; direct sow 1 inch deep 12–18 inches apart after soil warms; harvest pods at 4–5 inches for the finest texture; once production begins, harvest every 2 days during peak summer heat as pods elongate rapidly. Louisiana Green Velvet is an heirloom open-pollinated okra variety with a strong association with Louisiana and Gulf Coast traditional food culture — it is one of the most historically prominent varieties in the region and has been grown by Louisiana gardeners for generations as the standard for gumbo okra and fresh summer side dishes. The pods are smooth, deep green, and slightly ridged rather than heavily ribbed like Clemson Spineless, with a velvety (not bristly) surface texture that makes handling comfortable and gives the variety its name. 'Green Velvet' pods remain tender at 4–5 inches under high summer temperatures — a practical advantage in the Gulf South where summer heat causes many okra varieties to become tough and fibrous quickly if not harvested every day. The variety is adapted to the humid, hot climate of coastal Louisiana and the Gulf South and performs especially well in the clay soils and high humidity of the Louisiana bayou region where it originated as a preferred variety. Louisiana Green Velvet is the traditional okra of Cajun and Creole cooking — most commonly used in gumbo, where the natural mucilage (thickening quality) of properly cooked okra is considered essential to authentic texture and flavor.

name: Louisiana Long Green Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Louisiana Long Green is particularly productive in the Gulf South's long, hot growing season — transplant in spring and again in August for maximum productivity.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Louisiana Long Green is a traditional old-South eggplant variety producing elongated, cylindrical fruits 8–12 inches long in an unusual pale green to light green-white color that stands in stark contrast to the standard purple-black American eggplant. The pale green color indicates ripe fruit — unlike purple-black types where color darkens as they ripen, Louisiana Long Green turns a light, creamy green to yellow-green when mature. The flesh is white, mild, and very low in bitterness — outstanding for frying, grilling, and the classic Louisiana preparation of eggplant dressing (a traditional Gulf South casserole combining eggplant with shrimp, crabmeat, bread crumbs, and Cajun seasonings). Louisiana Long Green is a regional heirloom that has been grown continuously in Louisiana and lower Mississippi kitchen gardens for generations — selected by Southern gardeners for its outstanding heat tolerance, prolific production in the Gulf South summer, and excellent culinary qualities in traditional regional recipes. Harvest when fruits are 8–10 inches long with pale, slightly shiny skin — over-mature fruits become yellowish and develop more seeds and bitterness. Plants are vigorous and can reach 4 feet tall in the long Gulf South growing season, requiring staking when heavily loaded with fruit.

name: Louisiana Market Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed; this Gulf South-bred selection is well adapted to Louisiana's heat and humidity.
directions: Louisiana Market okra was developed at a Louisiana agricultural research station and entered All-America Selections trials in 1950, bred for Gulf South market growers wanting heavy, reliable yields. The plants carry their pods where foliage and flower stalks part readily, making harvest faster and more efficient for market picking. Pods are thick-walled, smooth, and green, best picked at 3-4 inches for tenderness; the variety performs well in the long, humid growing season typical of southern Louisiana.
sources: Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (NC State University)

name: Louisiana Purple Pod Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60F; Louisiana Purple Pod is a vigorous heirloom pole bean bred for Gulf South heat and humidity, and its deep purple pods stand out sharply against the green foliage for fast harvest. In zone 9, plant March-May for a summer crop and again in August for a fall harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep at the base of a sturdy 6-8 foot trellis or pole support after the danger of frost has passed. Louisiana Purple Pod is a Deep South heirloom pole bean selected over generations for reliable production through the heat and humidity that stall many snap bean varieties, and it shows good resistance to common bean mosaic virus and rust compared to older commercial types. Pods emerge deep purple, which makes them easy to spot among the leaves at harvest time, and the color cooks away to ordinary green so the beans can be prepared exactly like any other snap bean. Pick pods at 5-6 inches long while still tender for the best snap texture, and pick regularly to keep vines producing; left longer, pods can also be shelled fresh or dried for winter storage. Vines climb vigorously and benefit from consistent moisture during flowering and pod set to prevent blossom drop during extreme heat.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Louisiana Purple Pod Bean
Seed Savers Exchange — Heirloom Bean Collection
LSU AgCenter — Home Garden Vegetable Variety Recommendations

name: Louisiana Purple Sugarcane
plantingNote: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Louisiana Purple is a deep-purple-stalked heirloom cane traditionally grown for cane syrup and chewing cane.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Louisiana Purple is an heirloom sugarcane variety with deep purple-to-maroon stalks, long grown in Deep South dooryard patches both for chewing fresh (stripping and gnawing the sweet fibrous stalk) and for cooking down into dark cane syrup. Its rich color makes it a popular choice for ornamental use along fences and property lines in addition to its culinary role. Traditionally harvested in November and December after the first light frosts sweeten the stalks, it is then stripped of leaves, crushed to extract the juice, and slow-cooked into syrup, a staple of Southern country cooking. The tall, clumping perennial grass typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze in zone 8-9 and regrows vigorously from the root each spring, though a hard freeze can reduce syrup yield if it strikes before harvest.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sugarcane Production and Heirloom Varieties
Southern Foodways Alliance — Cane Syrup Traditions
Mississippi State University Extension — Sugarcane for the Home Garden

name: Louisiana Ribbon Cane
plantingNote: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Ribbon Cane is a traditional Gulf South heirloom variety grown chiefly for syrup rather than table sugar, prized for its distinctive green-and-purple striped stalks.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Louisiana Ribbon Cane is a historic heirloom sugarcane variety, distinguished from modern commercial hybrids by its slender, green-and-purple striped stalks, that has been maintained by Deep South farm families and seed savers for generations specifically for making cane syrup rather than refined sugar. It is traditionally harvested in November and December after the first light frosts sweeten the stalks, then stripped, crushed, and the juice slow-cooked down into dark, richly flavored cane syrup, a staple of Louisiana and Georgia country cooking. The tall, clumping perennial grass also makes a striking, fast-growing screen or accent planting; in zone 9 it typically dies back to the rhizome after a hard freeze and regrows vigorously each spring.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sugarcane Production and Heirloom Varieties
Southern Foodways Alliance — Cane Syrup Traditions
Slow Food USA Ark of Taste — Louisiana Ribbon Cane entry

name: Louisiana Short Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70F; Louisiana Short is a late, stocky heirloom that keeps branching and setting fruit through the season, so a longer sowing window into early summer still gives a strong fall crop in zone 9.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after the soil is thoroughly warm, since this late-season heirloom needs the full length of a Gulf Coast summer to hit its stride. Louisiana Short produces stocky, heavily branching plants bearing short, fat, dark green pods that stay tender at a larger diameter than slim-podded types, so pods can be picked at 3-5 inches without turning woody. The compact branching habit keeps fruit within easy reach and yields hold up right until a hard frost, making it one of the more forgiving okra choices for gardeners who cannot pick every single day during peak heat. Originally maintained by an Oklahoma seed saver and preserved through Midwest heirloom seed banks, it performs reliably in the humid, clay-heavy soils common along the Gulf Coast.

name: Low's Champion Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost into warm soil; pick young for a flat snap bean or leave pods to fully dry on the bush for a mahogany-red dry shell bean.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in well-drained garden soil after frost danger has passed; the compact bush habit needs no staking, making it an easy dry bean for smaller gardens. Low's Champion is a New England bush bean introduced in 1884 by the Aaron Low Seed Company of Boston and believed to derive from an older Abenaki variety, producing broad, flat pods that can be picked young as tender snap beans or left to mature into glossy mahogany-red oval dry beans. Its dual usefulness as both a green bean and a soup bean made it a dependable staple in old New England kitchen gardens. Harvest pods regularly if using fresh to keep plants productive, or let the whole crop dry down at season's end for winter storage beans.

name: Lower Salmon River Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; this drought-tolerant heirloom from Idaho river country adapts well to short, dry growing seasons.
directions: A rare Pacific Northwest heirloom preserved by home gardeners along the Lower Salmon River in Idaho and later distributed through Slow Food Ark of Taste seed-saving networks. Sow directly in hills after frost danger passes; the vines are relatively compact and early-maturing compared to many winter squash. Fruits are round with peach-to-orange skin, occasionally showing faint turban shaping, and average five to seven pounds. Harvest when the rind is hard and stem has begun to dry, then cure briefly before storing; the thick skin resists rot and rodent damage, allowing fruit to keep for many months.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

name: Loxton Lad Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the compact, tree-type 2-4 ft dwarf-indeterminate habit suits raised beds and containers.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking the thick, rugose-leafed stems lightly for support. Loxton Lad bears large, smooth, oblate orange beefsteak fruit with well-balanced, delicious flavor, notably bigger than its sibling release Loxton Lass. It originated from a 2009 Rosella Purple x orange heirloom cross made by Patrina Nuske Small, stabilized over several seasons by Dwarf Tomato Project volunteers, and released as an OSSI-pledged variety. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for peak sweetness.

name: Loxton Lass Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the compact, dwarf-indeterminate habit suits raised beds and large containers.
directions: Loxton Lass bears smooth, oblate orange beefsteak fruit with the same well-balanced, rich flavor as its sibling release Loxton Lad, but on a noticeably smaller-fruited plant. It shares the same origin as Loxton Lad: a 2009 cross of Rosella Purple and an unnamed orange heirloom made by Patrina Nuske Small, stabilized by Dwarf Tomato Project volunteers and released as an OSSI-pledged variety. Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, staking the sturdy, rugose-leafed stems lightly for support. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the sweetest flavor.

name: LSU Improved Groundnut
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in spring into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade to full sun; this line was selected to set a dense string of good-sized tubers in a single season even without a trellis, though yields and vigor still improve with one.
directions: This selection descends from the decades-long American groundnut domestication program run at Louisiana State University under researchers William Blackmon and Berthal Reynolds, who screened thousands of wild and cultivated groundnut plants for larger tuber size, denser tuber set, and the ability to produce a useful harvest in a single growing season rather than the two or more years wild stands typically need. Like all groundnut it is a twining, nitrogen-fixing woodland-edge legume that tolerates considerably more shade than most root vegetables, making it a good match for the dappled light along a fence line, hedgerow, or food-forest understory. Because improved lines like this were bred mainly for untrellised, more compact production, they can be grown as a sprawling ground-covering patch as well as trained up a support. Dig tubers in fall once top growth dies back, and save some uncooked to replant the following spring for next year's patch.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter historical breeding research (Blackmon & Reynolds)

name: Lucea Yam
plantingNote: Plant tuber head-sets (the crown end, 3-6 oz with intact skin) 4-6 inches deep once soil has warmed well past last frost; provide a sturdy 8-10 foot trellis immediately since vines climb fast and are heavy once laden with foliage.
directions: Grow this named Jamaican export-quality yam type on a tall, sturdy trellis in full sun and deep, well-drained, fertile soil mounded or ridged to ease harvest. Unlike the deep-purple-fleshed winged yam types already common in cultivation, the Lucea strain produces large, smooth-skinned tubers with firm, white to pale-yellow flesh prized for its dry, mealy texture when boiled or roasted. Water regularly during the long warm season but reduce irrigation as vines begin to yellow and die back near harvest, typically 9-12 months after planting in a zone 9a season extended with early spring planting and season-end curing. Store cured tubers in a cool, dry, well-ventilated spot out of direct sun.
sources: Caribbean Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI)
Jamaica Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries - Bodles Research Station

name: Lucky Boy Angled Luffa
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Lucky Boy is a named angled-luffa selection recommended by Florida extension resources for its productive, mild-flavored young fruit.
directions: Lucky Boy is a named cultivar of ridged (angled) luffa grown for its deeply ten-ribbed, dark-green fruit, harvested young at 6-8 inches when the flesh is still tender, mild, and free of the fibrous skeleton that develops later. It is favored in South and Southeast Asian home gardens and by Florida growers for heavier, more reliable fruit set through hot, humid summers than smooth luffa types, and it climbs vigorously on a trellis, fence, or arbor. Regular picking every few days keeps the vine productive continuously from early summer through fall in Gulf Coast conditions. Young shoots and leaves are also edible and used in some Southeast Asian cooking, though the fruit is the primary crop.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions

name: Lucky Cross Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; a large bicolor beefsteak with stunning golden-orange skin blushed red and equally beautiful red-and-gold marbled flesh — one of the most visually dramatic heirloom tomatoes available.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into deeply amended, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed and stake or cage firmly to support the large, heavy fruits. Lucky Cross is an exquisite heirloom bicolor tomato producing large, 1–2 pound beefsteak fruits with golden-yellow to orange skin blushed with a red blush at the blossom end and extraordinarily beautiful red-and-gold marbled flesh that is as ornamental sliced on a plate as it is delicious — the flavor is sweet, low-acid, and tropically fruity with exceptional richness. Its rarity and stunning appearance make it a prize at farmers' markets and seed saving circles. The indeterminate vines are vigorous and productive; harvest when fruit softens at the blossom end and the skin transitions fully from green.

name: Lucullus Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep; Lucullus produces very large plants and benefits from wider spacing (9–12 inches) than many chard varieties for full-sized leaves. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall and winter harvest, February–March for spring. Lucullus is one of the most productive and heat-tolerant chard varieties for warm climates, making it particularly well-suited to the Gulf South winter garden where it can be grown nearly year-round with mild management.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in fertile, well-amended soil; thin to 9–12 inches for full-sized production. Harvest outer leaves regularly from 40 days onward; the plant continues producing new leaves from the center for months with consistent harvesting. Lucullus is one of the oldest and most established Swiss chard varieties in American cultivation — named after Lucullus, the Roman general and gourmet famous for his extravagant feasts, a name that captures both the impressive size of the plant and the generous quality of its harvest. Lucullus produces very large (18–28 inch tall), broadly spreading plants with thick, heavily crinkled, dark green leaves and thick, ivory-white to pale green stems and ribs — a classic white-stemmed chard in the traditional style before the development of colored-stem varieties. The large, deeply savoyed leaves have substantial texture and rich, minerally chard flavor that is excellent cooked — wilted with olive oil and garlic, added to soups and pasta, or incorporated into quiches and casseroles. The very large leaf size makes Lucullus impractical for baby salad mixes (too coarse when young) but exceptionally productive for cooked greens — a single plant at peak production can provide a large bundle of cooking greens per week. Lucullus is often noted for better heat tolerance than some other chard varieties, making it one of the more productive summer leaf vegetables in hot climates.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Lucullus chard variety history
Burpee Seeds — Lucullus chard variety notes
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Swiss Chard Production

name: Lumina White Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; a white-skinned pumpkin that makes a striking alternative to orange jack-o'-lanterns for fall decoration and has sweet, edible flesh that works well in baking.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-amended soil, spacing hills 5–6 feet apart; Lumina is a vigorous vine type that needs plenty of room and full sun. Lumina is the most widely grown white pumpkin, producing round, 10–20 pound fruits with a smooth, creamy-white to ghostly-white exterior rind that makes it one of the most sought-after decorative pumpkins for Halloween and fall displays; the interior flesh is orange, sweet, and of good quality for cooking and pies — better than many orange carving pumpkins. The white skin provides an excellent canvas for painting, engraving, or decorative carving. Harvest when the rind is hard and the skin resists puncture with a thumbnail; cure for 1 week and store in a cool, dry location for 2–3 months.

name: Lunar White Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow into deeply worked, loose, stone-free soil in early spring or late summer; Lunar White is a pigment-free white carrot grown for its mild, sweet flavor and striking appearance in mixed rainbow carrot bunches.
directions: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in deeply worked, loose, sandy loam free of rocks and clumps, keeping the surface consistently moist until the slow-germinating seedlings emerge. Lunar White produces smooth, tapered, ivory-white roots with a crisp texture and mild, sweet flavor free of the slight bitterness some white carrots carry, making it a popular addition to mixed-color carrot bunches for market and home use. Because it lacks the orange and purple pigments of most carrots, it shows soil staining and surface blemishes more readily, so grow it in well-worked, debris-free soil for the cleanest roots. Thin seedlings early to prevent crowded, twisted roots, keep beds weeded while carrots are young and slow to establish, and harvest once roots reach full size, since white carrots left too long in the ground can develop a coarser texture.

name: Lunchbox Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Lunchbox is an AAS-winning series of compact plants producing abundant small, sweet, snack-sized peppers in red, orange, and yellow, perfect for eating whole straight from the garden.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Lunchbox is a popular sweet pepper series bred to produce large numbers of small, thin-walled, crunchy, sweet fruit about the size of a large grape or small egg, perfect for snacking whole, tossing into lunchboxes, or adding to salads without any need to slice. The compact, well-branched plants are productive over a long season and work well in both garden beds and containers. Harvest continuously as pods ripen to their full color (red, orange, or yellow depending on the specific variety) to keep the plant producing more fruit.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute

name: Luther Hill Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least 4 rows after last frost for reliable wind pollination; Luther Hill is a compact, heavily suckering plant that benefits from wide spacing to let side shoots also produce ears.
directions: Luther Hill was bred by New Jersey farmer Luther Hill in 1902 and became the most popular sweet corn in parts of New Jersey for half a century before serving as a direct parent of the later hybrid 'Silver Queen'. Plants stay relatively compact at around five and a half feet, typically producing two small, tender white-kerneled ears per stalk plus extra ears on the vigorous suckers if given room to spread. Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, planting in blocks for dependable pollination. The flavor is notably sweet and rich even by modern standards, which is why breeders have continued to draw on its genetics long after more productive hybrids replaced it commercially.
sources: Fedco Seeds — Luther Hill Organic White Sweet Corn

name: Lutz Green Leaf Beet
plantingNote: Sow as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9; Lutz is a late-maturing beet bred specifically for long storage rather than early eating, so allow it a full season to size up.
directions: Sow the multigerm seed clusters half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3-4 inches once true leaves appear; keep soil consistently moist to prevent woody roots. Lutz Green Leaf, also called Winter Keeper, is a classic American heirloom beet bred to grow to a large size (often 3-5 inches or more) without becoming woody, fibrous, or losing its sweet flavor the way most beets do when oversized — a trait that makes it uniquely suited for fall harvest and long winter root-cellar storage. The tender, mild, sweet flesh holds its quality even at full size, and the abundant deep green tops are excellent cooked as beet greens. Because it needs a longer season to develop its full storage-quality size, plant it in time to mature before hard frost, then harvest and store roots in damp sand or a root cellar for use well into winter.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Lutz Green Leaf variety notes

name: M81E Sorghum
plantingNote: Direct sow after the soil has warmed well past last frost; M81E is a late-maturing, full-season syrup sorghum bred at Mississippi State's agricultural experiment station, so it needs the Gulf South's long, hot growing season to reach its towering 10-12 foot height and load its stalks with sugar.
directions: Sow seed roughly an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil once the soil has thoroughly warmed, thinning to final spacing as seedlings establish. M81E is a tall, late-season Mississippi-bred syrup cultivar with brown seed heads that needs a longer stretch of hot weather than earlier varieties like Dale to fully mature, making it especially well suited to the long warm season along the Gulf Coast. Harvest when the canes reach hard-dough stage in the seed head and the lower leaves begin to dry, then press and boil the juice quickly into a mild, light amber syrup. Because of its late maturity, gardeners in shorter-season areas should get it in the ground as early as safely possible after frost to ensure the stalks finish sweetening before fall's first cold snap.
sources: MAFES Foundation Seed Stocks — 'M-81E: A New Variety of Sweet Sorghum'
National Sweet Sorghum Producers and Processors Association

name: MacDonald Rhubarb
plantingNote: Plant dormant crown divisions in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, setting the bud eyes 1-2 inches below the soil surface in a bed enriched with aged manure or compost. Space plants generously and avoid harvesting stalks the first year so the crown can establish a deep root system for winter survival.
directions: Plant dormant crown divisions in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked, setting the bud eyes 1-2 inches below the soil surface in a bed enriched with aged manure or compost. Space plants generously and avoid harvesting stalks the first year so the crown can establish a deep root system for winter survival. MacDonald was developed by a Canadian prairie breeding program specifically to withstand the extreme winter cold and short growing seasons of the Canadian plains, and it remains a favorite in Manitoba and Saskatchewan home gardens for its reliability where many other cultivars struggle. Its stalks are medium-thick and rosy-pink to red, with a balanced tart flavor well suited to pies, sauces, and preserves.

name: MacGregor's Favorite Beet
plantingNote: Grows well as a Gulf Coast fall crop; sow in late summer for harvest through the cool season.
directions: A Scottish heirloom bunching beet, grown for over a century, notable for its striking dark magenta-purple leaves as much as its slender, conical red roots. Bred for rapid early growth so it can be harvested young in bunches rather than left to bulk up like a storage beet. The dramatic foliage doubles as an attractive edible green, sauteed like chard, while the roots are sweet and tender when pulled small.

name: Machiaw Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Machiaw performed among the top Asian-type entries in a Midwest university eggplant trial and holds up well under hot, humid summer conditions.
directions: Machiaw is an Asian-type hybrid bearing slender fruit that ranges from pale purple to a striking deep pink, typically 10-12 inches long and about 1-1.5 inches thick. The skin stays thin and tender even as the fruit lengthens, giving mild, non-bitter flesh that needs no peeling or salting before cooking. Plants set fruit continuously through hot weather, making Machiaw a dependable choice for a long Gulf Coast harvest season. Pick fruit while the color is bright and the surface glossy, since the thin skin toughens and dulls quickly once fruit is left to over-mature.
sources: Purdue University Midwest Vegetable Variety Trial Report

name: Mad Hatter Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Mad Hatter produces distinctive flattened, lobed, flying-saucer-shaped pods with mild heat and a fruity, citrusy flavor, an AAS award-winning novelty pepper as much for its shape as its flavor.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Mad Hatter is an All-America Selections winner grown for its unusual, whimsical, flattened flying-saucer-shaped pods with distinctive lobed edges, a shape unlike almost any other common pepper, combined with a mild, sweet, subtly citrusy flavor reminiscent of its Capsicum baccatum relatives like aji peppers. It works well fresh in salads, pickled whole for a striking presentation, or lightly cooked, and the productive plants continue setting fruit over a long summer season. Harvest at any color stage from green to ripe yellow-orange, since the mild heat and flavor are enjoyable throughout ripening.

name: Madame Jeanette Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; Madame Jeanette, like all Capsicum chinense, requires very warm germination temperatures (80–95°F) on a heat mat and is slow to germinate compared to C. annuum — allow 14–21 days. In zone 9, transplant March–April into full sun.
