Capsicum chinense thrives in Gulf Coast heat and may overwinter as a perennial in zone 9b if protected from frost, sometimes producing for 2–3 seasons and yielding heavier crops in subsequent years. Harvest when fruits have fully transitioned from green to their ripe yellow color — do not harvest green. The heat level (150,000–300,000 SHU) makes Madame Jeanette one of the hotter commonly grown Capsicum chinense varieties; handle with gloves and avoid touching eyes or face.
directions: Start seeds on heat mat at 85–90°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Harvest when fully yellow. Madame Jeanette is a Surinamese Capsicum chinense variety that is one of the most important chiles in Dutch-Caribbean cuisine — particularly in the culinary traditions of the Surinamese and Antillean communities that immigrated to the Netherlands beginning in the mid-20th century. The pepper is named after a legendary entertainer from Paramaribo, Suriname's capital, and carries strong cultural significance in Surinamese cooking, where it is used to season traditional dishes such as pom (tayer root casserole) and various rice preparations. Morphologically, Madame Jeanette produces elongated, lantern-shaped to irregular pendant fruits — 2–3 inches long, tapering to a point — that ripen from green to yellow (occasionally to orange or red in some strains). The shape is somewhat different from the round, wrinkled habanero and the bell-shaped Scotch bonnet, falling between those types and the elongated fatalii in form. The heat level is substantial (estimated 150,000–300,000 Scoville units) with the characteristic fruity, floral habanero-type aroma of C. chinense — sweet, tropical, and intensely fragrant. The flavor that accompanies the heat is distinctly fruity and aromatic with apricot-like qualities that distinguish C. chinense from the more neutral heat of cayenne. In zone 9, Madame Jeanette performs exceptionally well — the heat and humidity that challenge cool-season crops are ideal conditions for this tropical species, which can produce abundant fruit through summer and fall.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Madame Jeanette pepper Surinamese variety documentation
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University — Capsicum chinense heat levels and Caribbean varieties
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Madame Jeanette pepper variety notes

name: Madeley Rounded Leaf Kale
plantingNote: Direct seed in May for summer harvest, or sow in July-August for overwintered plants that resume growth and throw spring shoots.
directions: This English heirloom reached American gardens through Adaptive Seeds via the Heritage Seed Library's Seeds Ambassadors Project, and it is closely related to the old Thousand Headed kale type. Its large, slightly savoyed, rounded leaves look more like a collard than a typical curly kale, but it keeps that distinctive tenderness even on big, mature leaves and through repeated freeze-thaw cycles. It has performed especially well as a winter crop in unheated high tunnels, pushing out productive spring greens once the days lengthen. Shield young plants from flea beetles with row cover, and expect abundant sprouting side shoots after the main leaves are harvested.

name: Madhu Ras Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-drained soil; this variety is adapted to the hot, dry growing conditions of Rajasthan and performs best where summers are long and intensely hot.
directions: Madhu Ras, meaning "honey nectar" in Hindi, is a small-fruited heirloom muskmelon still grown in home gardens and local markets across Rajasthan, India, and was brought into North American seed trade after being collected at a Delhi market by plant explorer Joseph Simcox. The compact fruit are yellow with green striping and weigh roughly one to one and a half pounds, with soft, silky, intensely sweet orange flesh carrying a classic muskmelon aroma. Because it evolved under the hot, arid conditions of western India, it tolerates heat and drier soil better than many Western cantaloupe types, though fruiting and sweetness both improve with regular watering once fruit begins to set. Harvest at full slip, when the stem releases cleanly from the fruit with light pressure, for the best sugar content and aroma.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Madhu Ras, Rajasthan Honey Melon
Experimental Farm Network — Joseph Simcox heirloom melon collections

name: Madiira 1 Leaf Amaranth
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost into warm, fertile soil in full sun; Madiira 1 was bred specifically as a leafy vegetable type, not for grain or ornamental use.
directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile soil in full sun; Madiira 1 was released in 2011 by Horti-Tengeru and the World Vegetable Center in Tanzania as a leafy vegetable amaranth, also known regionally as Ex-Zim or KK Mrambi, selected for leaves that stay green longer and for preferred taste and cooking quality compared to common landraces. It carries higher iron, calcium, and fiber content than typical amaranth greens, making it a nutritionally valuable warm-season crop. Harvest young leaves and shoot tips repeatedly through the season as a cut-and-come-again potherb.

name: Madiira 2 Leaf Amaranth
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost into warm, fertile soil in full sun; Madiira 2 is the companion release to Madiira 1, with a similarly improved nutritional profile.
directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile soil in full sun; Madiira 2 is a companion release to Madiira 1 from the same Tanzania-based World Vegetable Center breeding program, also known regionally as AM38 or KK Livokoyi, offering a similarly improved iron, calcium, and fiber content along with stable leaf yield through the growing season. It is grown the same way as Madiira 1, as a cut-and-come-again leafy green in East African home gardens and increasingly elsewhere. Harvest young leaves repeatedly for the best quality and continued production.

name: Maestro Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in spring, or in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in cool, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing light support such as pea netting or twiggy brush. Maestro is a modern shelling pea bred for reliable, heavy yields of dark green, well-filled pods carrying good resistance to powdery mildew and fusarium wilt, two of the most common diseases that shorten a pea harvest, particularly as the season warms toward summer. The sweet, tender peas inside are excellent fresh, frozen, or cooked, and the disease resistance helps the vine keep producing later into the season than many older, more disease-susceptible varieties manage. Pick pods promptly once well filled but before peas inside turn starchy, and keep the vine picked clean to prolong the harvest window as long as cool weather allows.

name: Magda Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Magda is a bush-type squash (no trailing vines) that produces compact, upright plants suitable for small gardens and raised beds. In zone 9, plant March–May for spring production and August for fall. Harvest Magda squash at 3–4 inches for best flavor — the nutty, sweet quality that distinguishes cousa-type squash from standard zucchini is most pronounced at this young harvest stage. Slightly larger fruits (4–6 inches) are good for stuffing; overripe fruits become bland and seedy. The pale, almost celery-green skin of Magda is a useful visual cue for harvest maturity — harvest when skin is pale and slightly waxy. In hot Gulf Coast summers, squash plants typically decline after 6–8 weeks; replanting in August extends the season through fall.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches for best flavor; up to 6 inches for stuffing. Magda is a cousa-type Lebanese summer squash — a form of summer squash with a fundamentally different eating character from the Italian zucchini types (such as Black Beauty, Costata Romanesco) that dominate American garden squash production. The cousa squash group, originating in the Middle East and Mediterranean, produces fruits that are pale sage-green to celery-green, cylindrical to club-shaped with a distinctively bulging blossom end, and with a pale, waxy skin surface that is noticeably different in appearance and texture from the darker, shinier skin of Italian zucchini types. The defining characteristic of cousa squash flavor — and the reason Magda has a devoted following among cooks — is a nutty, creamy sweetness distinctly different from the mild, slightly vegetal flavor of standard zucchini. Cousa squash flesh has a firmer, drier texture and more pronounced sweetness than Italian types, making it the preferred squash for Middle Eastern preparations: the primary culinary use of cousa squash in Lebanese, Syrian, and Egyptian cooking is kousa mahshi (literally 'stuffed squash') — the small fruits cored and filled with a spiced meat and rice mixture before being simmered in tomato sauce, a preparation where the firmer flesh and nutty flavor of the cousa type are essential to the dish's character. Magda is an F1 hybrid cousa-type that produces prolifically with good uniformity, adapts well to North American growing conditions, and provides the cousa flavor character more reliably than open-pollinated Middle Eastern varieties.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Magda cousa squash variety notes and culinary description
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Cousa squash variety background
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Summer Squash Variety Selection Guide

name: Magdalena Big Cheese Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is warm; this heat-tolerant moschata type suits long, hot growing seasons.
directions: Magdalena Big Cheese is a Sonoran Desert heirloom pumpkin with roots in Sonora, Mexico, grown by Southwestern gardeners and maintained by regional seed-saving organizations. It produces large, flattened, wheel-shaped fruits weighing 15-30 lbs with light orange, ribbed skin resembling a wheel of cheese. The dense, fine-grained flesh is richly sweet and well suited to soups, purees, and roasting. As a Cucurbita moschata, it carries useful resistance to squash vine borer and tolerates heat well, fitting arid Southwestern growing conditions.

name: Magenta Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in late winter for spring, or in early fall while still hot; in zone 9a, afternoon shade during the final weeks before harvest extends the usable window.
directions: A Batavian summer-crisp type bred specifically to hold quality through heat, rated tolerant of bolting, tipburn, and bottom rot, and carrying resistance to downy mildew and lettuce mosaic virus, which matters in Gulf South humidity. The red-tipped, thick, crisp leaves stay sweet rather than turning bitter as temperatures climb, and at a fast 48 days it can squeeze in before spring heat sets in or go in for an early-fall planting while still hot. It makes a strong companion or rotation choice alongside other heat-tolerant Batavian lettuces.

name: Magic Lantern Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; a reliable hybrid jack-o'-lantern type valued by growers for uniform, well-shaped fruit and strong handles suited to market sales.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, well-drained soil, spacing hills 6 feet apart for the vigorous vines. Magic Lantern is a hybrid carving pumpkin producing classically shaped, medium-ribbed fruit in the 16-24 pound range with bright orange skin and a sturdy, well-attached handle that holds up through harvest and transport to market. Its uniform round-to-slightly-tall shape and consistent sizing make it a dependable choice for growers selling by the piece at pumpkin patches and farm stands. Harvest when the rind has fully colored and hardened, before the first hard frost, and cure briefly in a warm, dry spot to toughen the skin for longer display life.

name: Magic Molly Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost in cool soil; Magic Molly is a late-season, high-anthocyanin purple potato. In zone 9, plant January-February for a spring harvest before summer heat arrives.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 10-12 inches apart, 3-4 inches deep, in fertile, well-drained soil, hilling twice as plants grow to boost yield and prevent tuber greening. Magic Molly is a striking purple potato with deep violet-black skin and vivid, uniform purple flesh throughout, prized for its exceptionally high anthocyanin content, dense, moist texture, and rich, earthy flavor that some describe as slightly nutty. Unlike some older blue and purple varieties, Magic Molly holds its intense color well through cooking, making mashed potatoes a striking lavender-purple and roasted wedges deep violet inside. The medium-sized, round-to-oval tubers form in good numbers per plant, and the variety performs reliably across a range of climates. Harvest for new potatoes once flowering finishes, or wait until vines die back for full-sized, better-storing tubers.
sources: Wood Prairie Family Farm — Specialty Potato Descriptions
Seed Savers Exchange heirloom and specialty potato archive
Oregon State University Extension — Potato Variety Trials

name: Magnolia Blackeye Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep once soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; Magnolia Blackeye was bred at Mississippi State University for resistance to fusarium wilt and root-knot nematode, both persistent problems in warm, sandy Gulf South garden soils.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, checking plants regularly since pods are not always held well above the foliage and can be easy to miss at harvest. Magnolia Blackeye is a Mississippi State University release bred from a cross involving Extra Early Blackeye, Bunch Purple Hull, and Dixielee, combining a compact, medium-sized bush habit with strong resistance to fusarium wilt and root-knot nematode along with tolerance to common cowpea viruses. Pods are light green-yellow at the green-shell stage, holding cream-to-light-green peas marked with the classic black eye, and the seed coat is notably smoother and less wrinkled than most other blackeye-type southern peas. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix nitrogen, and the plant's disease resistance package makes it a practical choice for Gulf South gardens where nematode or wilt pressure has limited other blackeye varieties.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension Service — Southern Pea Variety Recommendations
Cucurbit Genetics Cooperative — Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America: Southernpea (Cowpea)
USDA National Genetic Resources Program — cowpea germplasm records

name: Magnolia Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after frost danger has passed; block-plant for good pollination.
directions: New for 2026, Magnolia is an F1 supersweet (SH2) hybrid bred for Southern and hot-climate gardens, with Burpee noting improved disease resistance and heat tolerance to over 100 degrees F. It grows to roughly 80 inches tall and produces pearly-white ears that Burpee describes as exceptionally sweet with a melt-in-your-mouth texture. Direct sow in warm soil after the last frost in blocks of rows rather than a single line to ensure good wind pollination.
sources: Burpee (burpee.com) — Magnolia Sweet Corn product page

name: Malachite Box Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; like other green-when-ripe tomatoes, Malachite Box needs a gentle squeeze test rather than color alone to judge ripeness.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights have warmed, staking the indeterminate vines for support. Malachite Box is a Russian heirloom named for the deep jade-green color of its ripe skin and flesh, producing medium to large round fruit with a mild, sweet flavor and little of the acidity associated with unripe green tomatoes. Because the fruit never turns red, judge ripeness by a slight softening and a shift from bright to a duller, warmer green rather than by color change alone. Handle ripe fruit gently, since it softens readily, and use promptly once picked.

name: Malaga Violet Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in spring or 4-6 weeks before first fall frost; Malaga Violet is a French heirloom radish with striking violet-purple skin, white flesh, and a slightly milder flavor than many spring radishes.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. Malaga Violet is a classic French heirloom radish valued for its striking, uniform violet-purple skin over crisp white flesh, a distinctive color that stands out clearly from the more common all-red or bicolor spring radishes. The round to slightly oval roots have a clean, mild, only lightly peppery flavor, and the purple skin holds its color well even as the radish sizes up, unlike some varieties that fade. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows. Harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch in diameter, since radishes left too long in the ground become pithy and hollow; succession-sow every two to three weeks for a continuous supply.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Malaga Violet Radish variety notes
Kitazawa Seed Co. — French Heirloom Radish Varieties
Seed Savers Exchange — European Radish Collection

name: Malagueta Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out 1–3 weeks after the last frost once soil has warmed in full sun; Malagueta pepper is a heavy-yielding, upright frutescens type similar to tabasco pepper that continues producing through summer heat.
directions: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out 1–3 weeks after the last frost once soil has warmed in full sun; Malagueta pepper is a heavy-yielding, upright frutescens type similar to tabasco pepper that continues producing through summer heat. Capsicum frutescens 'Malagueta' is the iconic hot pepper of Brazilian cuisine, prized for the tangy, piri-piri-style hot sauce and pepper-infused vinegar (molho de pimenta) served at Brazilian steakhouses, producing prolific clusters of small, slender, upward-pointing fruit that ripen from green through yellow-orange to red with intense, sharp heat around 60,000–100,000 Scoville units. Plants form a bushy, productive shrub over the growing season and, like other frutescens peppers, tolerate heat and humidity well, making them reliable producers through the hottest part of a Gulf Coast summer. In frost-free zones plants can be overwintered as a short-lived perennial shrub; elsewhere grow as a warm-season annual and harvest continuously to encourage further fruit set.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute (New Mexico State University)

name: Malanga Blanca
plantingNote: Plant whole cormels 3-4 inches deep in rich, moisture-retentive soil once the ground has warmed; this is the pale-fleshed, mild-flavored malanga clone most commonly sold fresh in Caribbean and Latin markets, distinguished from other Xanthosoma color types by its white-to-cream corm flesh and relatively smooth skin.
directions: Plant cormels in deep, humus-rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade to full sun; this white-fleshed market type is a staple in Cuban, Dominican, and Puerto Rican cooking, prized for a milder, starchier result than purple or yellow malanga types when boiled, fried, or mashed. Keep soil evenly moist throughout the 8-11 month growing season and mulch heavily, since the shallow corm system dries out quickly in sandy Gulf Coast soils. Harvest once the lower leaves yellow and die back, usually after the first light frost knocks the foliage down in zone 9a. Always cook thoroughly before eating, as raw corms and leaves contain irritating calcium oxalate crystals.
sources: University of Puerto Rico Agricultural Experiment Station

name: Malaysian Dark Red Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; this rare Malaysian heirloom sets long, slender fruit best picked young and often through a long, hot growing season.
directions: Malaysian Dark Red is a rare heirloom eggplant from Malaysia, grown for long, slender fruit in a deep reddish-violet that darkens further as it matures. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the weather is reliably warm, allowing roughly 75 to 85 days from transplant to first harvest. The creamy, tender flesh carries a mild, faintly sweet flavor without the bitterness that affects many long Asian types, making it well suited to stir-fries, curries, and frying. Pick fruit while still glossy and firm at 6-8 inches long, and harvest frequently to keep plants setting new fruit through the season.

name: Mama Mia Giallo Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Mama Mia Giallo is a modern Italian frying pepper hybrid bred for earliness and heavy production, bearing slender, tapering fruits that mature from green to glossy golden yellow with thin, sweet, corno-type walls.
directions: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger passes. Mama Mia Giallo is a modern Italian frying pepper bred for earliness and productivity, bearing slender, tapering fruits that mature from green to a glossy golden yellow with the thin walls and sweet flavor typical of classic Italian corno-type peppers. Market growers favor it for its ability to set fruit heavily even under cooler, less-than-ideal conditions, giving a longer harvest window than many heirloom frying types. Harvest at the yellow stage for peak sweetness, or pick some pods green for a milder, more vegetal flavor.

name: Mambo Kabocha Squash
plantingNote: Direct-sow after soil warms; vigorous vines need standard squash spacing.
directions: Mambo bridges buttercup and kabocha squash types, forming a classic blocky, squat shape with little to no 'button' on the blossom end. The rind holds an exceptionally dark green color even after months in storage, distinguishing it from older kabocha varieties that fade. Fruit average 3-4 pounds and yield uniformly across the vine, making this a reliable producer for market growers and home gardeners alike. Flesh is dense and sweet, best enjoyed after a few weeks of curing to build sugars.

name: Mambo Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant once soil has warmed above 70°F, a week or two after the last frost; Mambo's compact 4–6 lb personal-sized melons and relatively short 75–85 day maturity make it a good fit for shorter or more compact garden spaces.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil after the last frost, in hills spaced to allow the vigorous vines to sprawl, or trellis to save space. Mambo is an AAS Edible-Vegetable Award winner bred as a personal-sized icebox watermelon, producing dark green, dark-striped 4–6 pound fruit with sweet, firm, deep red flesh and notably good disease tolerance for a home garden variety. Its compact fruit size and relatively fast maturity make it a practical choice for smaller gardens, raised beds, or trellised growing where full-sized watermelon varieties are impractical. Consistent watering through fruit development is important for good sugar content and to prevent hollow heart, and fruit is ready to pick when the tendril nearest the stem browns and dries and the ground spot beneath the melon turns from white to creamy yellow.
sources: Sakata Seed — Mambo watermelon variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Watermelon Variety Trials

name: Mammola Artichoke
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant, or set out rooted offshoots in spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Calabria's mild hill-country winters suit long-lived perennial stools maintained by division.
directions: Mammola is a traditional Calabrian artichoke landrace associated with the town of Mammola in the province of Reggio Calabria, listed as a regional traditional product for its spineless, violet-green, elongated heads. It is valued locally for a tender heart with less fibrous bract tissue to trim than spinier types, which makes the smaller side buds suitable for eating raw or lightly cooked. Grown as a long-lived perennial in Calabria's mild hill country, it is traditionally increased by dividing rooted offshoots from mature clumps rather than from seed. Give it full sun and deep, well-drained soil, and divide crowded clumps every few years to maintain vigor.
sources: Regione Calabria — Prodotti Agroalimentari Tradizionali (PAT) List
Slow Food Presidia — Italian Heritage Artichoke Varieties
University of California Cooperative Extension — Italian Artichoke Varieties

name: Mammoth French White Sunchoke
plantingNote: Plant whole or cut tuber sections, each with at least one or two eyes, 3-5 inches deep around the last frost date in loose, well-drained soil; Mammoth French White is an old heirloom strain selected for unusually large, pale tan-to-white tubers and needs a full season to bulk up fully before frost.
directions: Plant tuber sections 3-5 inches deep in a dedicated, well-drained bed, since sunchokes spread aggressively from any tuber left in the ground and this vigorous heirloom is difficult to fully eradicate once established. Mammoth French White is an old French-derived heirloom strain valued for producing notably large, pale tan-to-white tubers substantially bigger than wild-type or unnamed sunchoke stock, which means fewer tubers are needed to fill a basket and less scrubbing per pound at harvest, though the tubers still carry some of the knobbiness typical of the species rather than the smooth club shape of Fuseau-type strains. Plants grow tall and coarse, 6-9 feet, topped with small yellow sunflowers in late summer before dying back with frost; tubers are ready to dig once tops are killed and can be harvested through winter into early spring as needed. A light frost is said to sweeten the flavor by converting stored inulin into simple sugars. Leave a portion of tubers in the ground each year to regenerate next season's crop, and rotate or contain the bed to keep the planting from spreading into unwanted areas.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Jerusalem Artichoke

name: Mammoth Melting Sugar Pea
plantingNote: Sow in early spring 4–6 weeks before last frost; a tall climber to 4–5 feet requiring netting or trellis support; harvest young pods before seeds begin to swell for best eating quality.
directions: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep in cool, fertile soil in full sun 4–6 weeks before last frost, providing 4–5 feet of netting or trellis support; Mammoth Melting Sugar is the most widely grown heirloom snow pea, an heirloom variety documented since at least the early 1900s producing large (4–6 inch), flat, tender pods with a delicate, melt-in-the-mouth texture when harvested young and cooked lightly in stir-fries or eaten raw. The pods are stringless when young and the standard against which other snow peas are judged for tenderness and flavor. Harvest when pods are 3–4 inches long and absolutely flat with no seed bulge visible for the premium eating experience.

name: Mammoth Red Rock Cabbage
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Mammoth Red Rock'
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start August and transplant September–October for a December–March harvest. Mammoth Red Rock is a late-season storage type that needs the full fall-to-winter growing period to develop its characteristic large, dense heads — rushing it with too-late planting produces undersized heads. In zone 9 the purple-red color deepens and intensifies after frost, which converts some starches to sugars and improves flavor.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Mammoth Red Rock is a large, late-season red cabbage heirloom that forms very dense, dark red-purple heads of 8–10 pounds — among the largest and densest of red cabbage types. The firm, tightly-packed heads have a robust, slightly peppery flavor that mellows to rich sweetness after frost exposure and is perfect for braised red cabbage with apples and vinegar (the classic Scandinavian and German preparation), coleslaw, sauerkraut, and long-storage use. Red cabbage keeps far longer than green cabbage — 3–4 months in cold storage at near-freezing temperatures — making Mammoth Red Rock particularly valuable for homesteaders and home food preservation. The deeply saturated red-purple color comes from anthocyanin pigments that are natural pH indicators, turning more blue-purple in alkaline cooking water and more red in acidic conditions (add vinegar to fix the red color when braising). In zone 9 Mammoth Red Rock is a fall-planted crop that matures through the winter months.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Mammoth Red Rock Cabbage Heritage Variety
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Late-Season Red Cabbage
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Storage Cabbage Varieties

name: Mammoth Sandwich Island Salsify
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall (zone 9: August–September) in deep, loose soil; salsify has a long taproot that requires 12+ inches of loosened, stone-free soil. In zone 9, sow August–September for harvest December through March — the roots improve in flavor after cold temperatures sweeten them. Salsify is a long-season crop (120–150 days) requiring a full cool season to develop; the roots can be left in the ground through winter and dug as needed since they keep best in the ground. Fresh seed germination is much higher than old seed — use seed from the current year when possible.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in deeply loosened soil; thin to 3–4 inches. Do not transplant — the taproot is sensitive to disturbance. Harvest roots at 1 inch diameter or larger by carefully loosening the soil with a fork. Mammoth Sandwich Island Salsify is the standard American garden salsify — a biennial root vegetable in the daisy family grown as an annual for its long, tapering, white-skinned edible root. Salsify occupies an unusual position in the vegetable world: it is one of a handful of vegetables whose flavor genuinely resembles a different food — in this case, oysters. The cooked root has a subtle, oceanic, slightly mineral quality reminiscent of mild oysters, earning salsify its traditional common name 'Vegetable Oyster' and giving it appeal in preparations that highlight this unusual flavor character. Salsify was widely grown in American kitchen gardens in the 18th and 19th centuries when root vegetables formed a much larger portion of the winter diet than today, and Mammoth Sandwich Island was the primary named variety in this period. The roots are peeled (the skin oxidizes brown immediately, like artichokes — drop into acidulated water) and boiled, roasted, or prepared like other root vegetables. In zone 9, salsify provides a distinctive cool-season root that few gardeners grow, offering variety from the more standard parsnip, turnip, and carrot roots.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Mammoth Sandwich Island salsify variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Salsify variety notes
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Specialty Root Vegetable Production Guide

name: Manalucie Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 both a spring and a fall planting are productive — Manalucie's resistance to gray leaf spot makes it particularly reliable in the high-humidity conditions of Gulf Coast summers where this disease devastates susceptible varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set out in full sun, fertile, well-drained soil; Manalucie was developed by the University of Florida in the 1950s and named for the Manalucie experimental farm in Homestead, Florida — one of several important tomato varieties developed by UF plant breeders for subtropical Florida conditions. An indeterminate variety producing large, red, globe-shaped fruits (8–12 oz) with solid flesh, good flavor, and outstanding resistance to gray leaf spot (Stemphylium solani), a fungal disease that is especially destructive in Florida and humid Gulf Coast conditions but for which most tomato varieties have no resistance. Manalucie was for decades the standard large beefsteak-type tomato for Florida home gardens because of this specific disease resistance. It remains valuable today for any gardener in zone 8b–11 who has struggled with leaf spot diseases in tomatoes.

name: Manapal Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; a University of Florida release bred to perform through Gulf South heat and humidity.
directions: Manapal is an indeterminate slicing tomato released by the University of Florida in the early 1960s, carrying resistance to Verticillium and Fusarium wilt and bred specifically for the hot, humid growing conditions of Florida and the Gulf Coast. It became a widely grown dooryard and market tomato across the Deep South for decades thanks to its large, smooth, flavorful fruit and dependable fruit set during warm nights that stall many Northern-bred varieties. Stake or cage the vigorous vines and provide consistent moisture to reduce cracking and blossom end rot.

name: Manchester Market Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow for a fall crop in late summer; this variety tolerates a later sowing date than many turnips, so it is also useful as a follow-on crop after an early planting has been harvested.
directions: Manchester Market is a 19th-century English field and market turnip named for the city where it was widely grown for sale, producing a creamy white, globe-shaped root topped with light green, edible foliage. It carries a stronger, more peppery bite than modern salad turnips once roots size up past tennis-ball diameter, which suits it well to stews and long-cooked dishes rather than raw eating. It is notably forgiving of a later sowing date than many turnip varieties, making it a practical choice for filling a gap after an earlier crop is cleared. Harvest at a moderate size for the best balance of texture and flavor, since older roots turn fibrous.

name: Mandan Bride Bean
plantingNote: Sow seed directly after all frost danger has passed and provide poles, a tepee, or sturdy netting for this vigorous climbing habit.
directions: Sow seed directly after all frost danger has passed and provide poles, a tepee, or sturdy netting for this vigorous climbing habit. Mandan Bride descends from beans grown along the upper Missouri River by the Mandan people, prized as much for its dramatically streaked and mottled seed coat — ranging through maroon, tan, and cream in a single pod — as for its flavor. Keep the vines evenly watered through flowering and podset, then allow pods to dry completely before shelling for storage. It is best treated purely as a dry bean, since pods are fibrous and not suited to snap eating.

name: Mandan Bride Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks after the soil is thoroughly warm, allowing the full season needed for kernels to dry down on the stalk.
directions: Mandan Bride is an heirloom flour corn attributed to the Mandan people of the upper Missouri River, grown historically alongside beans and squash in traditional Three Sisters plantings. Each ear carries an unpredictable mix of red, orange, black, yellow, and white kernels, and because the whole kernel is soft and starchy rather than hard-hulled like flint corn, it grinds easily into flour once fully dried. Leave ears on the stalk until husks are papery and kernels are rock-hard before harvesting, then cure indoors for several weeks in a well-ventilated spot before grinding or storing. Beyond its culinary use, gardeners often grow it for its striking multicolored ears, which make excellent autumn braids and decorations.

name: Manganji Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably above 55°F, 0-2 weeks after the last frost date.
directions: Grow like a sweet pepper in warm, well-drained soil with steady moisture to keep pods tender and mild. Manganji is a traditional Kyoto vegetable cultivar producing large, glossy, thin-walled pods similar in shape to shishito but noticeably bigger and generally sweeter, though occasional fruits turn hot under heat or drought stress. Harvest young and green for pan-frying or grilling whole, a popular preparation in Kyoto cuisine.

name: Manoa Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before last spring frost, or 4-7 weeks before first fall frost; in mild Gulf Coast winters can be grown through the cool season for a late-fall to winter harvest.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil; Manoa was bred at the University of Hawaii for heat tolerance and forms full, uniform heads of tender, sweet-flavored leaves that resist the quick bolting typical of butterhead types in warm weather. Growing it with afternoon shade or shade cloth through the hottest months helps keep the heads from turning bitter. Harvest whole heads once firm, or pick outer leaves individually for a longer cut-and-come-again harvest.

name: Mantovano Fennel
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring once soil is workable, or sow in summer for a fall harvest; Mantovano was bred for spring sowing and shows strong resistance to bolting compared with older Italian fennel strains.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, evenly moist soil, since fennel resents root disturbance; Mantovano is a traditional Italian heirloom named for the Mantua region, valued for its large, flattened, very white bulbs and a sweeter, more assertively anise-forward flavor than many other Florence fennel strains. It matures earlier than most bulbing fennel and has an unusual habit of continuing to bulk up in the ground for weeks after reaching harvest size rather than splitting or turning woody, which gives growers real flexibility in harvest timing. Mound soil lightly around the base as the bulb swells to keep it pale, and use young bulbs raw in salads or slice and roast larger ones for a milder, caramelized flavor.
sources: Organic Seed Alliance / Northern Organic Vegetable Improvement Collaborative (NOVIC) variety trials

name: Mara Bitter Gourd
plantingNote: Start indoors 3-4 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay warm; Mara is a vigorous hybrid that wants consistent heat (80-90F) to germinate reliably and grow well.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and provide a sturdy trellis, since vines can climb 10-15 feet in a single warm season. Mara is a hybrid bitter gourd bred to be noticeably milder than typical Indian bitter melon types, producing large, cylindrical, shiny green fruit up to 11 inches long and about a pound each, with a flavor that stays lightly bitter raw but mellows further with cooking. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and firm, before fruit begins to yellow or soften, for the best balance of crunch and mild flavor. Pick promptly and often, since mature fruit left on the vine turns orange, splits open, and signals the plant to slow new fruit set.

name: Maraş Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. Maraş is grown as a drying pepper, so plan on a full season outdoors for pods to ripen fully red before harvest.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Maraş Pepper is a landrace long grown around Kahramanmaraş in southeastern Turkey, where sun-dried, coarsely crushed pods become the fragrant, oil-glossed red pepper flake known as pul biber. The 3–4 inch, moderately wrinkled pods ripen to a deep brick red and carry a mild-to-moderate heat, generally around 4,000–8,000 Scoville units, with a rich, slightly sweet, faintly smoky flavor distinct from the tangier Aleppo pepper it is often compared to. Traditionally pods are partially sun-dried, seeded, and crushed while still a little moist, which is what gives Maraş flakes their characteristic dark color and oily texture rather than the bone-dry look of standard chili flakes. A single productive plant can supply a household's pepper flakes for a year; harvest fully red pods and dry in a low oven or dehydrator if humid outdoor air prevents full sun-drying.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Kahramanmaraş Pepper
Two Seeds in a Pod — Pul Biberlik Maraş Pepper Seed Notes

name: Marathon Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop; Marathon is a Sakata-bred industry-standard hybrid noted for exceptional cold tolerance and reliable overwintering, including documented success as a winter crop in Florida — a strong fit for the Gulf Coast's mild winter growing window.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in late summer for a fall and winter crop, or in late winter for an early spring crop; Marathon is a broccoli hybrid recognized industry-wide for exceptional cold tolerance, holding up through hard frosts and cold snaps that would damage less hardy varieties while continuing to develop a large, dense, tightly beaded blue-green head. This cold hardiness makes it especially well suited to the Gulf South's mild winter growing window, where it can be grown as a true overwintering crop instead of racing to beat summer heat. After the main head is harvested, the plant produces a strong flush of side shoots for continued picking. Cut heads while the buds are still tight, before any yellow flower color shows.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Broccoli Production

name: Marblehead Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after soil has warmed past 65°F; give this rare 1896 Massachusetts heirloom a full long season, since its exceptionally hard rind takes the entire warm-season window to develop.
directions: Marblehead was introduced in 1896 out of Massachusetts as a selection valued for the stony hardness of its smooth grey-green rind, a trait that earned it the name and made it one of the longest-storing winter squashes of its era. Sow in enriched hills and let the vigorous vine sprawl over six to eight feet, watering steadily through the growing season to size up the large, rounded fruit. The deep orange flesh is fine-grained and flavorful, holding up well in soups and baked dishes even after months of storage. Because the shell is so hard, cure fruit for two to three weeks in a warm spot before moving it to a cool, dry root cellar or pantry, where it can keep considerably longer than thinner-skinned squash.

name: Marconi Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Marconi is a classic Italian heirloom sweet frying pepper with long, tapering, ridged fruit, similar to Corno di Toro but a distinct traditional strain.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75-80°F and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost. Marconi is a classic Italian heirloom sweet pepper producing long, tapering, thin-walled fruit that ripens from green to red, prized for a sweet, mild flavor and a thin flesh that chars and caramelizes quickly when roasted or fried, much like its well-known relative Corno di Toro. It is a traditional variety in Italian-American gardens, used roasted for antipasto, sautéed in olive oil, or stuffed. The vigorous, productive plants bear over a long season through summer heat; harvest fruit green for a milder flavor or let it ripen fully to red for maximum sweetness, and pick regularly to keep plants producing.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Italian frying pepper variety comparison

name: Marconi Red Sweet Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Marconi Red is a traditional Italian sweet frying pepper producing long (6–8 inch), slender, deeply ribbed, bright red fruits with thin walls and exceptional sweet, rich flavor — outstanding for frying in olive oil, roasting, and sautéing, used throughout Italian cuisine where its sweetness intensifies dramatically with heat.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Marconi is productive and begins bearing early for a long sweet pepper; the fruits can be harvested green or left to ripen fully red for the sweetest, richest flavor. Marconi Red is an Italian heirloom sweet frying pepper producing long, tapering, deeply lobed, 6–8 inch fruits that ripen from green to brilliant red; unlike blocky bell peppers, Marconi has thin, tender walls with very sweet, rich, slightly smoky pepper flavor that intensifies dramatically when fried in olive oil or roasted over a flame. Used throughout Italian and Mediterranean cooking as the classic 'frying pepper' for peperonata, antipasto, and pan-fried pepper dishes. The thin walls mean the fruits cook quickly and evenly without becoming tough; they also need minimal or no skin removal after roasting. Marconi is one of several related Italian frying pepper varieties (along with Corno di Toro and Jimmy Nardello) that together represent the tradition of Italian long sweet peppers, each with slightly different fruit shape, texture, and flavor profile. Very productive plants set fruit continuously through summer.

name: Marfax Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil has warmed; a compact bush type requiring no trellis; one of the earlier-maturing heirloom dry beans, well-suited to shorter seasons and successive plantings.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after last frost, spacing 4–6 inches apart in rows 18 inches apart; Marfax germinates quickly in warm soil and the compact bush plants require no staking or support. Marfax is a New England heirloom bush dry bean with attractive tan-and-brown mottled seeds that are smaller and rounder than kidney-type beans and have a creamy, buttery texture when cooked with a mild, nutty flavor excellent in baked beans, soups, and salads. Allow pods to fully mature and begin to yellow and rattle before harvesting; if a wet spell threatens, pull plants and hang them under cover to finish drying. Marfax stores well for a year or more when dried thoroughly and kept in an airtight container at room temperature.

name: Marglobe Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Marglobe was a landmark All-America Selections winner in 1925 when it became the first widely adopted disease-resistant tomato, and for decades it was the standard commercial and home garden tomato across the United States.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes and stake plants early. Marglobe, introduced by the USDA in 1925 and awarded the first All-America Selections Gold Medal, was the standard American home and market tomato for much of the twentieth century; bred at the Arlington, Virginia USDA experiment station to resist Fusarium wilt and nailhead rust, it was the first widely successful disease-resistant tomato and allowed commercial tomato production to expand dramatically into areas where disease pressure had previously made growing difficult. The fruits are medium-sized (6–8 oz), round to slightly globe-shaped, smooth, bright red, and of solid, crack-resistant construction with a firm skin and classic tomato flavor; Marglobe Supreme is a later improved selection. Grows as an indeterminate vine; productive over a long season and well-suited to home gardens, canning, and fresh market.

name: Mariachi Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Mariachi is a prolific, compact pepper plant that produces clusters of 3-inch elongated fruits in colors that transition through ivory, yellow, and orange to red as they mature — multiple colors appear simultaneously on the plant, creating a colorful and ornamental appearance. In zone 9, start seeds in January–February and transplant March–April. Mariachi won the All-America Selections award in 2006 for its outstanding productivity, compact plant habit, and unique combination of mild fruity flavor with very low heat (500–600 SHU, far below the heat level of jalapeño) that makes it versatile for both fresh eating and cooking without the heat restriction of spicier varieties. The individual fruits are tapered and elongated (3–4 inches) with a slightly irregular shape; the mild heat level means even heat-averse eaters can enjoy Mariachi fresh.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at ivory-yellow for mild flavor or let ripen to red for maximum sweetness. Mariachi Pepper is a 2006 All-America Selections winner in the vegetable category, developed for its extraordinary visual display of multicolored fruits at different ripeness stages and its mildly spiced fruity flavor that makes it accessible to a wide range of palates. The name 'Mariachi' evokes the colorful, festive nature of the plant at peak production, when ivory, yellow, orange, and red fruits appear simultaneously in clusters on the same compact plant — the visual effect is immediately striking. Unlike standard bell pepper development where fruit transitions from green to fully ripe (green→red, green→yellow, etc.), Mariachi's fruit transition from ivory cream through progressive warm tones to red creates a more complex visual palette on the plant. The heat level of Mariachi is technically mild rather than sweet — at 500–600 SHU (Scoville Heat Units), it is substantially less hot than a jalapeño (2,500–8,000 SHU) but not as completely heat-free as a standard bell pepper. This small amount of heat adds a fruity warmth that enhances the flavor without causing heat discomfort for most people, making Mariachi useful in both sweet pepper contexts (fresh eating, salads) and mild chili contexts (salsas, roasting, stuffed preparations). The compact plant habit (24–30 inches) and prolific production of Mariachi's clusters make it an excellent candidate for container growing on patios and decks where the ornamental and culinary value combine effectively.
sources: All-America Selections — Mariachi pepper 2006 AAS winner documentation
PanAmerican Seed — Mariachi pepper variety development and production notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pepper Variety Selection for Gulf South Home Gardens

name: Marian Rutabaga
plantingNote: Direct sow in summer for a fall harvest; this relatively quick-maturing rutabaga can be sown a bit later than slower varieties.
directions: Marian produces large, yellow-fleshed roots with purple tops that can size up to 8 inches across while remaining sweet and fine-grained. Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in summer and thin to a final spacing of 6-8 inches, keeping the bed evenly watered to avoid pithy or cracked roots. Marian matures somewhat faster than many storage rutabagas, making it useful where the fall growing window is shorter. Harvest after a light frost and store in a cool root cellar, where roots keep their flavor and texture for several months.

name: Marianna's Peace Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this potato-leaved, indeterminate variety needs sturdy staking to support its large fruit and long season.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil after frost risk has passed. Marianna's Peace is a Czechoslovakian family heirloom carried to the United States after World War II and later introduced commercially in honor of the woman whose story gave the variety its name. The potato-leaved, indeterminate vines produce large pink beefsteak fruit with a rich, well-balanced sweet flavor and relatively few seeds. Give it sturdy staking and a full growing season, as the heavy fruit and long maturity window reward patient care.

name: Marina di Chioggia Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow or start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplanting; sow after last frost in warm soil; a traditional Italian heirloom from the Chioggia coastal region near Venice that stores exceptionally well into winter.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after last frost, or start 3–4 weeks early indoors; plant in hills of 2–3 seeds per mound spaced 5–6 feet apart and thin to the strongest plant. Marina di Chioggia is a prized Italian heirloom winter squash from the Chioggia lagoon region, producing large 8–15 pound fruits with deeply ridged, blue-green skin covered in grey-green bumps and warts, and brilliant orange flesh that is dense, sweet, nutty, and nearly stringless — among the finest-flavored winter squashes. Cure fruits for 2 weeks in a warm, dry location after harvest to harden the skin and concentrate the sugars; properly cured fruits store for 4–6 months. The large vines need ample space; train them onto a trellis or let them sprawl in open ground.

name: Marion Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors roughly six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 50°F, staking or caging the compact determinate plants as fruit sets.
directions: Start seed indoors roughly six weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 50°F, staking or caging the compact determinate plants as fruit sets. Marion was bred at North Carolina State University and released for Southern gardens, combining Fusarium wilt and gray leaf spot resistance with reliable fruit set under the hot, humid conditions that cause many slicing tomatoes to falter. The medium-sized, deep-red fruit has firm flesh and balanced flavor well suited to fresh eating and canning. Because it sets a concentrated main crop, it remains a dependable choice for Gulf Coast gardeners who want an early, disease-resistant harvest before peak summer heat shuts down fruit set.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

name: Maris Piper Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before the last frost; this late-maincrop variety needs a long cool season to size up its oblong russet-skinned tubers.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in deep, loose, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing rows generously since this vigorous variety produces a heavy underground spread. Maris Piper was bred in Britain in the 1960s and became the standard chip-shop and baking potato across the UK, prized for its high dry-matter content, floury texture, and thin cream-colored skin that crisps well when fried. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge to prevent tuber greening, and expect a longer season than early varieties before the vines die back and tubers can be lifted for storage. Choose this cultivar over a general baking potato when a reliably fluffy, low-moisture interior for chips, roasting, and baking is the priority.

name: Market Express Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or succession-sow through late summer for a quick fall crop, since this variety is bred for speed.
directions: Thin seedlings early to two to three inches apart so the small, smooth globes develop evenly without competing for space. Market Express is among the fastest hybrid salad turnips available, reaching harvestable size in close to a month, which lets growers fit extra succession plantings into a short cool season. Roots stay mild and tender even if harvest is briefly delayed, resisting the woody, pithy texture that often develops in slower turnip varieties. Both the smooth white roots and the tender tops are good eaten raw or quickly cooked.
sources: University of Massachusetts Amherst Extension — Vegetable Program

name: Marketer Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; train vigorous vines up a trellis to save space and keep fruit clean and straight.
directions: Marketer is a 1943 All-America Selections winning slicing cucumber prized for its slender, smooth, dark green fruit with white spines, typically 8-9 inches long, and its sweet, mild flavor. The vigorous, heat-tolerant vines are highly productive over a long harvest season, performing well even in hot, humid conditions that stress newer hybrids. Though largely superseded in commercial production by disease-resistant modern hybrids, it remains a reliable, long-cropping choice for home gardeners wanting an old-fashioned slicer. Pick at 8-9 inches for the best fresh-eating quality.

name: Marketmore 70 Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed following last frost; train on a trellis for straighter fruit and better air circulation.
directions: Marketmore 70 was bred by Henry Munger at Cornell University as an early strain in the Marketmore breeding line, preceding the widely grown 1976 release Marketmore 76, which improved on it with a broader disease-resistance package. It set the vining, productive growth habit later carried forward by its successors: vigorous vines bearing straight, dark green, cylindrical slicing cucumbers with thin, non-bitter skin and crisp white flesh. Grow it on a trellis or fence where possible, since vertical training improves airflow and keeps fruit straighter and easier to pick. Harvest at 7-8 inches while still firm and uniformly dark green, checking vines daily during peak production since oversized fruit turns the plant's energy away from setting new cucumbers.
sources: Cornell University Department of Plant Breeding cucumber breeding history

name: Marketmore 76 Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and again August–September for fall. Cucumbers grow fastest with soil temperatures above 70°F and decline in extreme summer heat above 95°F; fall plantings often outperform spring in zone 9.
directions: Direct sow 3–4 seeds per hill 1 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil, then thin to the 2 strongest seedlings; trellis to maximize air circulation and fruit quality. Marketmore 76 is the Cornell University-developed standard slicing cucumber, bred for disease resistance to multiple fungal and viral pathogens including cucumber mosaic virus, scab, and powdery mildew — resistance that makes it especially valuable in humid Southern gardens. The smooth, dark-green fruits are 8–9 inches long with crisp, bitter-free flesh and very small seed cavity. Consistent, even watering is the most critical cultural practice — irregular moisture leads to bitter-tasting fruits. Harvest daily when fruits reach full size before they yellow.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Marketmore 76
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cucumber Production
North Carolina State Extension — Cucumber Varieties

name: Marketmore 80 Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; in zone 9, sow spring cucumbers in February–March and fall cucumbers in late July–August for the best production in the shoulder seasons before summer heat or fall cold limits the crop.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Marketmore 80 is a Cornell University slicing cucumber introduction that has become one of the most widely grown home garden cucumbers in America — producing straight, cylindrical, 8–9 inch, deep-green cucumbers with excellent fresh-eating flavor, thin skin, and small seed cavities. The significant disease resistance package — scab, cucumber mosaic virus (CMV), and angular leaf spot resistance — makes Marketmore 80 substantially more reliable in Gulf South gardens where summer humidity drives disease pressure. The 'Marketmore' series from Cornell represents a succession of improvements beginning with the original Marketmore in the 1960s; Marketmore 80 was selected for improved scab resistance and CMV tolerance critical for humid-climate production. The non-bitter fruits have classic cucumber flavor and good crispness. Plants are indeterminate vines that perform best on a trellis or fence where air circulation reduces disease and fruits hang straight. In zone 9, cucumbers are most productive in the spring season (March–May) and fall season (August–October) — summer heat causes reduced fruiting and increased disease. Succession sowing every 2–3 weeks through spring extends the harvest window. Harvest fruits at 6–9 inches for best flavor; over-mature cucumbers become bitter and seeds harden.

name: Marketmore Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; arguably the most widely grown slicing cucumber in American home gardens, selected at Cornell University for disease resistance and consistent productivity.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil after all frost risk has passed, in hills of 3–4 seeds thinned to 2, or in rows 12 inches apart against a trellis; cucumbers germinate quickly in warm soil and grow fast — do not plant in cold ground. Marketmore 76 was developed at Cornell University and released in 1976 as an improvement on the original Marketmore line, and for decades it has been the benchmark slicing cucumber for home gardeners: a vigorous, disease-resistant vine producing straight, dark green, 8–9 inch fruits with thin, non-bitter skin and crisp, mild white flesh that stays productive over a long harvest window. The variety carries resistance to cucumber mosaic virus, angular leaf spot, powdery mildew, and scab. Pick fruits when uniformly dark green and firm, before any yellowing begins, to encourage continued production; cucumbers left on the vine too long signal the plant to stop setting new fruit.

name: Marmango Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-7 weeks before transplanting; move outside after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Marmango is one of Johnny's new-for-2026 F1 tomato introductions, bred to pair heirloom-like flavor and appearance with modern productivity and disease tolerance. Small 5-8 ounce ribbed beefsteak fruits develop vivid orange color inside and out early in ripening, giving growers a wide harvest window across several maturity stages. The indeterminate vines stay vigorous through an extended production cycle and perform as a greenhouse or tunnel crop as well as in the open field. Trellis and prune to a single or double leader, allowing 4-6 square feet of growing area per leader.

name: Marquis Wheat
plantingNote: Drill or broadcast as soon as spring soil can be worked; young Marquis wheat shrugs off light frost and grows quickly through the cool spring weeks before summer heat sets in.
directions: Marquis was bred by a Canadian agronomist from a Red Fife and Hard Red Calcutta cross, and released around 1909-1910 as a spring wheat that matured one to two weeks earlier than Red Fife while keeping its outstanding bread-baking strength. That earlier ripening let wheat farming push much further north and west across the Canadian Prairies and the U.S. Northern Plains, and by 1920 Marquis accounted for the great majority of hard red spring wheat grown on the continent. Sow it in early spring into a firm, fertile seedbed; it performs best where summers are not too long or humid, ripening ahead of the worst rust and heat pressure. Because it was never patented, home millers and small grain growers can still source and replant true Marquis seed today as a living piece of agricultural history.

name: Marrowfat Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile soil; this bush type needs no staking but has a longer season than most dry beans, so give it the full growing window.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in well-drained soil after frost danger passes; the sturdy bush plants carry four-inch pods that need no support. Marrowfat, also known as the White Egg bean for the plump, egg-shaped form of its seed, is a mid-1800s New England baking bean recognized by Slow Food USA's Ark of Taste for its creamy texture and rich, almost bacon-like savoriness when cooked. It was once a mainstay of the region's baked-bean tradition before falling out of common cultivation, and is now kept alive mainly by small seed savers and heirloom specialists. Allow pods to dry completely on the plant before shelling, and store the beans in a cool, airtight container for baking and soups through winter.
sources: Slow Food USA - Ark of Taste

name: Mars Celeriac
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant to the garden after danger of hard frost has passed and soil has warmed somewhat.
directions: Mars is an organically bred celeriac selection grown for its large, uniform, bulbous roots and clean celery flavor. Sow seed indoors in flats or cell trays, barely covering it, since light aids germination, and keep consistently moist and warm until seedlings emerge. Transplant into rich, well-drained soil and water deeply and regularly through the season, since any moisture stress produces hollow or cracked roots. Harvest in fall once the knobby crown reaches full size, trimming the fibrous lower rootlets before cooking or storing in damp sand.

name: Martha Washington Asparagus
plantingNote: Set dormant one-year crowns into trenches 6-8 inches deep as soon as soil is workable in spring, then gradually backfill as spears emerge.
directions: Martha Washington is a companion strain to the better-known Mary Washington, both bred in the early 1900s through USDA-led work with Massachusetts growers to overcome asparagus rust that had devastated eastern plantings. Like other old open-pollinated Washington strains it is dioecious, so female plants set seed and can self-sow into a weedy stand if spent berries are not removed each fall. Spears are thick and well-flavored but yields lag well behind modern all-male hybrids such as Jersey Knight or Millennium, since female plants divert energy into seed rather than spear production. Top-dress beds with compost each fall and let plants establish for a full year before taking any harvest, as with any asparagus crown.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing Asparagus in the Home Garden
University of Illinois Extension — Watch Your Garden Grow: Asparagus
North Dakota State University Extension — Millennium Is the New Leader in Asparagus

name: Maruba Santoh
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–November for harvest October–February. Maruba Santoh can also be sown January–March for a spring crop before summer heat causes bolting. Successive sowings every 3 weeks provide continuous harvest. The round, smooth leaves are harvested young at 3–4 inches for baby greens or at full size at 35–50 days. More heat-tolerant than most mustard types.
directions: Direct sow thinly in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Maruba Santoh is a Japanese mustard green distinct from other Asian brassicas in having smooth, round, paddle-shaped leaves rather than the lobed or frilly leaves of most mustard types — the name 'maruba' means 'round leaf' in Japanese. The flavor is much milder than standard mustard greens, with a mild, slightly mustardy-sweet taste closer to bok choy or spinach, making it one of the most versatile and approachable cool-season greens for raw use in salads, stir-fries, soups, and braising. The smooth, non-frilly texture of the leaves holds dressings well without wilting and is preferred over crinkled-leaf types in delicate preparations. Maruba Santoh is faster-maturing than most brassicas and can produce a baby green harvest in 25–30 days from sowing. In zone 9 it is an excellent gap-filler for the fall and winter garden, tolerating light frosts and growing through the cool months without the bitterness that develops in other mustard greens exposed to heavy cold.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Maruba Santoh Variety Notes
University of Hawaii Extension — Asian Brassica Greens Production
Kitazawa Seed Company — Japanese Vegetable Varieties Guide

name: Marvel of Four Seasons Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow or start indoors in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop, since this French heirloom is bred for reliable heading across a range of seasons.
directions: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. A classic French heirloom whose name translates to 'Marvel of the Four Seasons,' this butterhead forms attractive heads with bronze-red outer leaves surrounding a pale, blushed-pink, buttery interior, valued for holding quality and reliable heading across spring, summer, and fall plantings better than many single-season lettuce varieties. Its rich color and sweet, tender texture have kept it popular in French market gardens and home plots for well over a century. Keep soil consistently moist and provide afternoon shade in warm weather to delay bolting.

name: Marvel Stripe Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Marvel Stripe is a large bicolor heirloom from Oaxaca, Mexico with stunning golden-yellow fruits streaked with red and orange, mild tropical flavor, low acidity, and a reputation as one of the most striking visually dramatic heirloom tomatoes for the kitchen and market table.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost and stake early as plants produce large, heavy fruit on indeterminate vines. Marvel Stripe is a large bicolor heirloom tomato of reported Mexican (Oaxacan) origin, producing very large (1–2 pound), oblate fruits with a striking golden-yellow exterior streaked and flamed with red and orange that is visually one of the most dramatic tomatoes in the garden or at a farmers market; when sliced, the interior shows a beautiful bicolor pattern of orange-gold and red. The flavor is mild, sweet, and tropical with notably low acidity — more fruity and candy-like than most large red tomatoes — making it particularly appealing to those who find red tomatoes too sharp. An outstanding choice for fresh slicing, caprese salads, and market display where visual drama matters.

name: Masai Bush Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to 60°F; Masai is a compact bush-type filet bean that stays productive over a longer window than most bush filet types before needing succession sowing.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 3-4 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest every 1-2 days once pods reach 4-5 inches and are still pencil-thin. Masai is an American Award of Merit-winning French filet bush bean, prized for combining the slender, tender, seedless-tasting pods typical of haricots verts with a compact, upright, easy-to-harvest bush habit that needs no trellising. The plants hold their pods up off the ground and above the foliage, making picking fast and keeping pods cleaner and less prone to soil-splash disease than sprawling bush types. Because filet beans mature quickly from flower to overgrown pod, harvest frequently to maintain the fine, tender texture; pods left even a day or two too long become coarser and more fibrous. Succession sow every 2-3 weeks through the season for a continuous harvest, since bush types produce a concentrated flush rather than the extended season of pole filet beans.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Filet Bean Growing Guide

name: Mascara Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November or January–February. Mascara holds dark red color remarkably well in warm fall conditions that cause most red lettuces to revert toward green. Harvest outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again harvest or pull entire plants at maturity.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Mascara is a deeply red-colored romaine-type lettuce producing upright, compact heads of dark wine-red to nearly black-red leaves with the crisp, crunchy texture and pronounced midrib of romaine — combining the structural quality of cos-type lettuces with an extreme depth of red pigmentation that rivals the darkest red looseleaf varieties. The dramatic, almost black-red color maintains well through the warm fall temperatures that cause most red lettuces to lighten; Mascara's consistent dark color regardless of temperature makes it valuable for market growers who need reliable color in variable fall conditions. The flavor is mild, slightly sweet, and crisp — very similar to standard romaine in taste despite the striking color difference. In mesclun and mixed salad plantings, the very dark Mascara leaves provide the strongest color contrast against green lettuces. The intense red-black coloring indicates very high anthocyanin content and corresponding antioxidant value.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Mascara Romaine Variety Notes
University of California Cooperative Extension — Red Romaine Lettuce Varieties
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Red Romaine Types

name: Mascotte Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed in warm soil; Mascotte is a 2014 All-America Selections winner bred as a compact bush filet bean that holds its pods well above the foliage for easy picking, making it ideal for containers.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants closely since the compact habit does not need the room a pole bean requires. Mascotte, a 2014 All-America Selections winner, was bred specifically for container growing, holding its slender, straight, tender filet-type pods well above the tidy, upright foliage where they are easy to spot and pick without stooping or digging through leaves. It matures quickly and produces a concentrated, heavy set of pods over a shorter window than many pole beans, making it well suited to succession planting in small beds or pots on a patio. Harvest pods young and slender for the best filet-bean texture, picking every day or two once production begins to keep new flowers coming.

name: Masterpiece Green Longpod Fava Bean
plantingNote: Also sowable in autumn in mild climates for an overwintered crop; direct sow as soon as soil can be worked.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep into cool, workable soil as early as late winter, spacing plants close together so they support each other without staking. This RHS Award of Garden Merit variety is prized by British allotment growers for pods near a foot long holding six or seven large, flavorful beans that freeze especially well, and pinching the growing tips once the lowest flower trusses set pods helps deter aphids and encourages even filling.

name: Matador Shallot
plantingNote: Sow true seed indoors in trays or modules 8-10 weeks before the last frost, keeping soil around 60F for best germination, then transplant hardened-off seedlings out once hard frosts have passed.
directions: Matador is a Dutch-bred F1 hybrid shallot grown from true seed rather than planted as clonal sets, a modern approach that avoids the virus buildup that can weaken old set-propagated shallot lines. Each seed-grown plant typically produces a broad, obovate pair of bulbs rather than the large multi-bulb cluster typical of open-pollinated shallots, with thick reddish-brown papery skin protecting crisp, richly flavored white flesh. Keep the bed evenly moist through spring growth and reduce watering as the foliage yellows and topples over in midsummer, then lift and cure the bulbs in a warm, airy spot for storage. Matador is widely offered by seed companies on both sides of the Atlantic and is valued for consistently heavy, uniform yields.

name: Matina Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Matina is one of the earliest-maturing indeterminate tomato varieties, producing ripe fruit as soon as 58–65 days from transplant — which in zone 9 (transplant February–March) can mean first ripe tomatoes as early as late April. This ultra-early production window before June heat arrives is Matina's primary advantage for zone 9 gardeners, where the spring tomato season is compressed. The variety is indeterminate and continues producing over a long season, but the earliest flush of fruit in late spring before heat stress is when Matina shows its greatest advantage over later-maturing types. Stake or cage plants at planting — though not as large as full-season indeterminate types, Matina reaches 3–4 feet and produces enough to require support.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Stake or cage plants. Harvest when fully red and slightly soft. Matina is a German open-pollinated heirloom tomato from the Quedlinburg region of Saxony-Anhalt — a historically important German seed-saving and plant breeding center that preserved many traditional German vegetable varieties through the 20th century. Matina is among the most respected early tomatoes in European heirloom tomato tradition: a variety that consistently delivers ripe, flavorful tomatoes earlier in the season than almost any other indeterminate heirloom, making it a first-pick benchmark for season extension and early production. The fruits are small to medium (2–3 oz), round, smooth, and deep red at full ripeness — the classic small salad tomato form used throughout Germany and much of northern Europe for sliced tomatoes, salads, and fresh eating where the relatively small size provides good proportionality for whole slices. The flavor is exceptional for an ultra-early variety: sweet with a good acid balance and genuine tomato complexity that many early-maturing hybrid tomatoes lack. Early-ripening tomato varieties often sacrifice flavor to achieve early maturity; Matina demonstrates that early harvest and excellent flavor are compatible. In zone 9 gardens, Matina's ultra-early ripening makes it particularly practical: the variety delivers its best production before the June-July heat that suppresses fruit set in most tomato varieties, allowing harvest of the critical first tomatoes of the season before summer limits production.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Matina tomato heirloom German variety documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Matina tomato variety notes and history
Tatiana's TomatoBase — Matina tomato detailed variety review and trial data

name: Matt's Wild Cherry Tomato
scientificName: Solanum lycopersicum var. cerasiforme 'Matt's Wild Cherry'
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Matt's Wild Cherry is a variety collected from a wild or semi-wild population in the Hidalgo region of Mexico by Matt Liebman and introduced to the seed-saving community — it produces extremely small (pea-sized, 3/8–1/2 inch), intensely flavored red fruits with a bold, complex, acidic-sweet tomato flavor that recalls the taste of truly wild tomatoes and is unlike any commercial cherry tomato.
directions: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Matt's Wild Cherry is an extremely vigorous grower requiring sturdy staking; the pea-sized fruits are prone to cracking when ripe and should be harvested frequently; self-sows readily in mild climates — may reappear without replanting. Matt's Wild Cherry is a tomato variety with an interesting origin: it was collected by Matt Liebman from a wild or semi-wild population (possibly a naturalized escape) in the Hidalgo state of Mexico — an area near the center of origin of the domestic tomato — and introduced to North American seed-saving networks through the Seed Savers Exchange and similar organizations.
