The variety is classified as Solanum lycopersicum var. cerasiforme, the wild cherry tomato type considered ancestral to all cultivated tomatoes, and it displays many wild-type characteristics: extremely small fruits (pea-sized, only 3/8 to 1/2 inch in diameter), prolific production (literally hundreds of fruits per plant), high seed-to-flesh ratio, thin skin prone to cracking, and exceptional flavor intensity that is quite different from cultivated cherry tomatoes. The flavor is extraordinarily complex for such small fruits — intensely tomato-ish, with high acidity balanced against good sweetness, and a deep, earthy, wild tomato character that reflects the original tomato flavor before centuries of breeding selected for larger, milder, less acidic fruits. For flavor enthusiasts and tomato purists, Matt's Wild Cherry offers a connection to the ancestral tomato that no commercial variety can provide.

name: Mattu Gulla Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Mattu Gulla is traditionally grown in the sandy coastal soils of Udupi, India, and appreciates loose, well-drained beds.
directions: Mattu Gulla is a round green eggplant, grown traditionally on the sandy coastal fields of Mattu village near Udupi in Karnataka, India, where it holds a Geographical Indication tag tying it to that specific growing region; it is notably green rather than purple, distinguishing it from most other brinjal grown nearby. Start seed indoors in warm soil and transplant into loose, sandy, well-drained beds once nights are reliably warm, since this type is adapted to lean coastal soil rather than rich garden loam. The fruit is prized in Udupi's temple-associated cuisine for its mild, slightly sweet flavor and tender flesh, most famously in the regional Mattu Gulla curry. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and firm, and pick regularly to keep the compact plants productive through the season.
sources: Geographical Indications Registry of India - Mattu Gulla
general horticultural reference on Udupi regional heirloom vegetables

name: Maverick Spelt
plantingNote: Drill or broadcast in mid-fall so plants establish before winter dormancy; Maverick is a shorter-strawed, more lodging-resistant modern spelt widely grown by organic grain farmers as an alternative to tall heirloom lines.
directions: Maverick was bred to give organic and specialty grain growers a spelt option with a shorter, sturdier straw than older heirloom lines like Oberkulmer, cutting down on lodging losses in wet or windy years while still delivering the hulled kernel and nutty flavor spelt is grown for. Sow into a firm, well-worked seedbed in mid-fall, using a slightly heavier seeding rate than for common wheat since spelt tillers less. Plants overwinter low to the ground and resume vigorous growth in spring, typically heading out and ripening around the same window as other winter spelt lines. Because the tough hull remains fused to the kernel at harvest, plan on a dedicated dehuller or mill built for spelt rather than a standard combine setup used for free-threshing wheat.

name: Maxifort Rootstock Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors early alongside a favorite scion variety; graft the two together once stems are pencil-thick, heal in a humid shaded chamber, then transplant after frost into full sun.
directions: This exceptionally vigorous interspecific hybrid rootstock is grown to be grafted onto a favorite heirloom or hybrid tomato scion, not eaten itself, offering a much larger and more disease-resistant root system that in turn boosts scion vigor, fruit size, total yield, and season length compared to an ungrafted plant on its own roots. Widely used in commercial greenhouse and high tunnel tomato production, it carries broad resistance to soil-borne diseases including fusarium wilt, verticillium wilt, and corky root rot, extending productive plant life well past what many own-root tomatoes achieve in intensive production. Start rootstock and scion seed together indoors, graft when stems are pencil-thick using a tube or splice graft, keep grafted plants in a humid, shaded healing chamber for about a week, then harden off and transplant after frost into full sun with sturdy staking or trellising to support the extra vigor.

name: May Queen Lettuce
plantingNote: Sow directly as early as soil can be worked, or start under cold frame protection for an even earlier crop, since it tolerates light frost well.
directions: Sow directly as early as soil can be worked, or start under cold frame protection for an even earlier crop, since it tolerates light frost well. This German heirloom butterhead, also called Maikönig or May King, dates to before the 1880s and was bred to be the very first lettuce ready in spring, producing tender, rosy-blushed rosettes in under two months. Market gardeners historically relied on it to fill the earliest gap in the spring salad season.

name: Mayflower Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost at the base of poles or a trellis; allow the full season for pods to dry down for shelling.
directions: Mayflower, sometimes called the Amish Knuttle Bean, is a long-cultivated heirloom pole bean grown chiefly for its small, oval seeds marked with maroon-and-white or rose speckling on a white background. Pods can be picked young as snap beans, but the variety is best known and most valued as a dry shelling bean with rich, dense flavor well suited to baking, soups, and long-simmered dishes. Train the vigorous vines up 6 to 8 foot poles or a trellis and leave pods on the plant until they rattle and the pods turn tan and papery before harvesting for storage. Its long history and vigorous, reliable production make it a good choice for gardeners wanting a dual-purpose bean with strong heirloom provenance.

name: Mazuma Wasabi
plantingNote: Plant rhizome divisions or nursery starts in cool, constantly moist, richly organic, slightly acidic soil in full to partial shade, ideally beside a shaded spring or stream; like all wasabi, Mazuma collapses quickly if soil temperatures climb much above 70F for long.
directions: Mazuma is one of only a small handful of wasabi cultivars reliably available to growers outside Japan, prized alongside Daruma for its vigor and reasonably forgiving nature by wasabi-farming standards. Its distinctive purple-tinged stems and rhizome mark it out from greener cultivars, and farmers often favor it for fresh paste-making because the finished rhizome delivers a notably strong, clean pungency with a touch of underlying sweetness. Like all wasabi it is an obligate shade and cold-water plant, demanding deep shade, constant moisture, and a long one-and-a-half to two-year growing cycle before the rhizome bulks up to harvestable size, making it a patience-testing but singular crop for a cool, boggy, shaded garden corner. The broad, glossy, heart-shaped leaves are also edible and make an attractive textural groundcover above the slowly swelling rhizome.

name: McCaslan Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost danger passes; McCaslan is a vigorous, heat-loving climber that keeps producing through the hottest part of the Gulf South summer.
directions: McCaslan traces to a Georgia family garden bean grown before 1900, later refined and released commercially as 'McCaslan 42' by the Corneli Seed Company in 1962. The heavy-producing vines climb readily on a pole or trellis and set slightly flattened, meaty pods up to 8 inches long that stay stringless and fine-grained when picked young. Left longer on the vine, pods can be shelled fresh or dried for ivory-white beans, giving the variety a useful two-stage harvest. McCaslan is prized in Deep South gardens for its heat tolerance and reliable yields through summer conditions that slow down less vigorous pole beans.

name: McCormack's Green Glaze Collard
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. acephala 'McCormack's Green Glaze'
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring; frost sweetens the leaves as with other collards.
directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. This variety was preserved by the McCormack family and is one of dozens of distinct named greasy-leaf collards documented through the Heirloom Collards Project, a collaboration between Seed Savers Exchange and Southern seed keepers that has traced individual family lines of collards across the Carolinas and Gulf South back for generations. Its rounded, glossy, deeply dentate leaves carry the same waxy sheen found in other 'glaze' collards, giving natural resistance to leaf-chewing pests, and the plant is slow to bolt and holds well through cold snaps without heading. Because it survives today as a small, actively regenerated seed stock rather than a mass-market variety, gardeners who grow it out and save seed are directly helping preserve a piece of African American Southern foodways.

name: Medallion Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–February for spring. Medallion is compact and fast-maturing, making it excellent for succession planting every 2–3 weeks to maintain a continuous supply of small heads. In zone 9 the relatively quick maturity (45–55 days) allows multiple crops in the cool season window. Pull entire plants at harvest.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Medallion is a mini-romaine type lettuce producing compact, upright, 5–6 inch heads with tightly wrapped inner leaves and crisp, crunchy texture — the small-head format that has become standard in grocery produce departments and upscale food service. Mini-romaine heads like Medallion are harvested at one-quarter to one-third the size of full-sized romaine but with the same crunchy, mild, slightly sweet romaine flavor in a single-serving portion size. The compact heads also allow significantly closer spacing (6–8 inches) than full-sized romaine, making them more efficient in raised beds and small gardens. The crisp, upright inner leaves hold dressings exceptionally well for Caesar-style preparations, and the compact whole head can be split lengthwise and grilled or broiled as a dramatic presentation. Medallion has been widely adopted in restaurant supply chains precisely because the single-serving size reduces food waste compared to large head lettuces.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Medallion Mini-Romaine Variety Notes
University of California Cooperative Extension — Mini-Romaine Lettuce Production
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Compact Romaine Types

name: Megaton Leek
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile soil for an early-maturing, high-yield fall crop.
directions: Megaton is a vigorous F1 hybrid leek grown for its exceptional uniformity and speed to maturity compared with older open-pollinated types, producing long, thick, upright shanks under wide dark green leaves. Its hybrid vigor means less outer-leaf cleaning is needed at harvest to reveal a straight, market-ready stalk, which makes it popular with growers who sell bunched leeks. Give plants rich, consistently moist soil and hill soil around the base as they thicken to extend the blanched white shank. Because Megaton matures earlier than winter-hardy heirloom leeks, it suits gardeners wanting a heavy early-to-mid fall harvest rather than a leek held in the ground through deep winter.

name: Mei Qing Choi
scientificName: Brassica rapa subsp. chinensis 'Mei Qing Choi'
plantingNote: Direct sow, or start indoors and transplant, shortly before the last frost, and again in late summer for a fall crop, since Mei Qing Choi bolts quickly under long, hot days.
directions: Direct sow, or start indoors and transplant, in early spring after the last hard freeze, and again in late summer for a fall crop, since Mei Qing Choi bolts quickly in long, hot days. Mei Qing Choi is a compact, vase-shaped hybrid pac choi with thick, pale jade-green stems and glossy, rounded dark green leaves, bred for a uniform, tightly packed miniature head that is smaller and more tender than standard-sized bok choy. It combines useful heat and cold tolerance with strong bolt resistance for a bok choy of its type, giving gardeners a wider planting window than many other Asian brassica greens. Harvest whole heads at baby size for salads or at full size for stir-fries, cutting at the base just above the soil line.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension Asian Vegetables

name: Melanzana Rossa di Rotonda Scarlet Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before transplanting; this Italian heirloom DOP crop from Rotonda, Basilicata ripens to an intense red and benefits from a full, hot summer season.
directions: Melanzana Rossa di Rotonda is a scarlet eggplant (Solanum aethiopicum) grown under Italy's DOP protected-origin designation around the town of Rotonda in Basilicata, ripening to an intense red with a ribbed, rounded shape closely resembling a large tomato rather than a typical eggplant. Start seed indoors with warm soil and transplant only after the weather is reliably warm, since this type needs a long season to fully color. The dense, meaty flesh is traditionally harvested at the red stage and is prized in southern Italian cooking for stuffing, grilling, and preserving in oil. Stake plants as the fruit load builds, and pick regularly to encourage continued set through the season.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity - Melanzana Rossa di Rotonda

name: Melbourne Whiteskin Parsnip
plantingNote: Direct sow into deep, loose, stone-free soil in full sun; parsnip seed is slow and sometimes erratic to germinate, so keep the bed consistently moist until seedlings emerge.
directions: Direct sow into deep, loose, stone-free soil in full sun; Melbourne Whiteskin is an old Australian heirloom parsnip with long, smooth, tapered white roots carrying a sweet, nutty flavor that improves further after a frost. It is a vigorous grower with good tolerance of common parsnip pests and diseases, maturing in about 120 days. Leave roots in the ground through the first hard frosts of fall to maximize sweetness, then harvest as needed for roasting, steaming, or adding to soups and stews.

name: Melitopolski Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after the last frost, giving vines plenty of room to sprawl in full sun.
directions: Sow directly into warm soil once frost danger has passed, and provide consistent moisture while vines establish and fruit sizes up. This heirloom traces to the Melitopol region of southern Ukraine, a historic melon and watermelon growing district, and was bred for a relatively short, reliable season compared to many large Southern watermelon types. Fruits are round with dark green striping and crisp, sweet pink-red flesh, making it a favorite among gardeners in cooler climates who still want an authentic watermelon harvest.

name: Melody Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Melody, a 1971 All-America Selections winner, is a smooth-leaf spinach bred for good disease resistance and reliable performance.
directions: Direct sow seed a half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, thinning seedlings to final spacing. Melody, a 1971 All-America Selections winner, produces smooth to slightly savoyed, dark green leaves with good disease resistance to common spinach ailments, on plants that are somewhat more heat- and bolt-tolerant than many older spinach varieties, useful for extending the harvest a bit later into spring in the Gulf South. Its smooth leaves are easier to clean of grit than heavily crinkled savoy-type spinach. Harvest outer leaves as needed for cut-and-come-again picking, or cut the whole plant at once for a single harvest, and provide light afternoon shade as the weather warms to delay bolting.

name: Melrose Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Melrose is an Italian-American heirloom frying pepper long grown by home gardeners in central New York's Mohawk Valley, producing elongated, thin-walled, pale green fruits that ripen to red with a sweet flavor and only the faintest hint of heat.
directions: Sow seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Melrose is an Italian-American heirloom frying pepper long cultivated by home gardeners in central New York's Mohawk Valley, prized for the elongated, thin-walled, pale green fruits that mature to red and carry a sweet flavor with only the faintest whisper of heat. The tender walls cook down quickly when sautéed in olive oil with garlic, making it the traditional pepper folded into Utica-style braised greens alongside hot cherry peppers, breadcrumbs, and provolone. Pick some pods green for a milder, grassier flavor and let others ripen fully red on the vine for maximum sweetness.

name: Meraviglia di Venezia Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost and provide a trellis or poles at least 7 feet tall; pick frequently to keep this prolific climber producing.
directions: Meraviglia di Venezia, known in English as Marvel of Venice, is an Italian heirloom pole bean bearing flat, lemon-yellow Romano-type pods up to 10 inches long with a buttery texture and no stringiness. It is an early-maturing, white-seeded strain of this classic Venetian bean, ready to pick in about 55 days, notably fast for a climbing variety. The meaty pods hold their quality well even as they lengthen on the vine and are traditionally sliced and dressed simply with lemon, olive oil, and herbs. Because it has become uncommon in commercial production, it is listed on the Slow Food Foundation's Ark of Taste as a variety worth preserving.
sources: Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste

name: Mercado Amaranth
plantingNote: Wait until soil is thoroughly warm and frost risk has passed, since this is a late, long-season type that needs the full summer to fill its seed heads.
directions: Surface-sow seed in warm soil after frost danger has fully passed, pressing it in rather than burying it, since this variety is slow to finish and benefits from the longest possible season. Mercado grows into a tall, lodge-resistant plant topped with apple-green, cockscomb-shaped seed heads that mature to a tan, protein-rich grain prized for popping and milling. Thin seedlings to allow sturdy stems to develop, and let plants stand in full sun with only occasional watering once established. Harvest when seed heads feel dry and papery and seed threshes free with light rubbing.

name: Merit Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F, planting in solid blocks of at least 4 rows for adequate wind pollination; Merit is a classic early-to-midseason yellow hybrid sweet corn long grown for its reliable, heavy yields.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil in solid blocks rather than single rows to ensure thorough wind pollination of the ears. Merit is a classic standard-sugary yellow hybrid sweet corn that has been a dependable home-garden and market variety for decades, valued for consistent, heavy ear production and good, traditional sweet corn flavor on a vigorous, adaptable plant. Its early-to-midseason maturity makes it a good choice for a first planting in a succession sweet corn schedule through the Gulf South growing season. Harvest when ears are well filled and kernels exude a milky liquid when pressed, and cook or refrigerate promptly, since standard sugary sweet corn converts sugar to starch faster after picking than sugary-enhanced or supersweet types.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Sweet Corn Variety Evaluation
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sweet Corn for Florida Gardens

name: Merlin Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool soil; Merlin carries intermediate resistance to downy mildew and Cercospora leaf spot along with high resistance to bolting, a strong disease package for the Gulf South's humid, changeable spring beet season.
directions: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Merlin is a hybrid beet bred with intermediate resistance to downy mildew and Cercospora leaf spot, two fungal diseases that can blemish and weaken beet tops in humid, wet conditions, along with high resistance to bolting even through a swing of cool-to-warm spring weather. It produces smooth, uniformly round, deep red roots with sweet, tender flesh and good, dark green tops usable as cooking greens. Thin seedlings to 3-4 inches apart for well-sized roots, keep soil consistently moist, and harvest once roots reach 1.5-2.5 inches across for the best texture and flavor.

name: Merlot Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, and again in fall for a second crop; the deep burgundy color intensifies with cooler temperatures and higher light, making fall plantings especially vivid.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, thinning seedlings to six to eight inches apart. Merlot is a loose-leaf lettuce grown as much for its striking appearance as for eating, producing deeply ruffled, glossy leaves in one of the darkest, most saturated wine-red colors available in lettuce, deepening further with cool nights and bright light. The flavor is sweet and mild despite the intense color, and the ruffled texture and dramatic hue make it a standout addition to salad mixes and a popular choice for edible landscaping in ornamental beds and containers. Harvest outer leaves as needed for a cut-and-come-again crop, or cut the whole loose head once it reaches full size; like most leaf lettuces it bolts and turns bitter in sustained summer heat, so plan plantings for the cooler shoulder seasons.

name: Merlot Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors about 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after danger of frost has passed.
directions: Merlot is an early, compact F1 sweet bell hybrid grown for its unusual color sequence, shifting from green to white before purple stripes spread and merge into a deep wine-purple fruit that finishes red if left on the plant. Its short, sturdy habit and disease tolerance make it dependable in both cool springs and hot, humid summers, and the thick walls hold up well for stuffing or fresh slicing. Choose it for a striking, out-of-the-ordinary bell pepper color in mixed vegetable and ornamental edible plantings. Regular harvesting at the purple stage encourages continued fruit set through the season.

name: Merveille des Quatre Saisons Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring through early summer (succession sow every 3 weeks), or in late summer for fall harvest; Merveille des Quatre Saisons (French for 'Marvel of Four Seasons') is one of the most beautiful French butterhead heirlooms, producing bicolor heads of deep red-bronze outer leaves surrounding creamy pale-yellow inner leaves — a centerpiece of the classic French kitchen garden for more than a century.
directions: Sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 10–12 inches apart; Merveille des Quatre Saisons produces its most stunning red coloration when nights are cool (45–55°F); succession sow every 3 weeks for continuous harvest; harvest full heads by cutting at the base or harvest outer leaves as cut-and-come-again. Merveille des Quatre Saisons is a classic French butterhead heirloom lettuce with roots in the traditional potager (kitchen garden) of France, where it has been grown and selected for generations as both an ornamental and culinary variety of exceptional beauty. The heads are distinctly bicolor: the outer leaves are deep crimson to mahogany-bronze with the red intensifying dramatically in cold weather, while the inner leaves are creamy pale yellow-green — the contrast between brilliant red outer leaves and golden interior makes this one of the most photographed and admired lettuces in the garden. The 'quatre saisons' (four seasons) name reflects its traditional use throughout the growing year in French kitchen gardens. The flavor is excellent: sweet, buttery, and mild with the silky tenderness characteristic of well-grown butterhead types. The name and variety appear in French seed catalogs dating to at least the 1880s, making it among the oldest continuously cultivated lettuce varieties still widely available.

name: Mesa Queen Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Mesa Queen is an All-America Selections winner combining a more compact vine with deeply grooved, dark orange-red kabocha-type fruit.
directions: Direct sow seed in hills after the last frost in rich, well-drained soil, spacing hills to suit the shorter-running vines. Mesa Queen won an All-America Selections award for producing deeply ridged, dark orange-red kabocha-type squash on a plant noticeably more compact than typical maxima vines, making it a practical option for gardeners who want kabocha's dense, dry, sweet flesh without a sprawling vine. Fruit averages 3 to 4 pounds, a convenient size for roasting or steaming whole halves. Harvest once the deep grooves and rich color have fully developed and the rind resists a fingernail, then cure briefly before storing in a cool, dry spot.

name: Mesilla Hot Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant once nights stay reliably warm.
directions: Mesilla is a large New Mexico-style hot pepper bred to be useful at every stage of ripeness, from mild jalapeno-like heat when picked green to a sweeter, more intense flavor once fully red. Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil after danger of frost passes. The thick-walled, meaty pods hold up well to roasting, stuffing, and frying.

name: Messidor Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves in fall a few weeks before the ground freezes so roots establish before winter dormancy.
directions: Separate a bulb into individual cloves and push each one pointed-end-up about two inches into fertile, well-drained soil. This French-origin hardneck forms large bulbs under a papery white skin and sends up an edible flower scape in late spring that should be snapped off to redirect energy to the bulb. Harvest once the lower leaves brown and cure in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks before storing.

name: Metechi Hardneck Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, several weeks before the ground freezes, in loose, fertile, well-drained soil; Metechi is a Rocambole type and needs a real winter chill to size up properly, so it performs best where winters are reliably cold.
directions: Plant cloves pointed end up, 2 inches deep, in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Metechi is a Rocambole-type hardneck heirloom brought out of the Republic of Georgia, grown for its rich, robust, full-bodied garlic flavor and large, easy-to-peel cloves arranged in a single ring around a hard central stalk. Like other Rocamboles it sends up a distinctive coiling scape in early summer, which should be cut once it curls to redirect the plant's energy into bulb size, and the bulbs store only moderately well compared to porcelain or silverskin types, so plan to use this variety earlier in the storage season. It demands a genuine cold winter to break dormancy and form full-sized bulbs, making it best suited to northern and mountain gardens rather than the Deep South.

name: Metro PMR Butternut Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; Metro PMR was bred jointly by Cornell University and a commercial seed company specifically for high powdery mildew resistance, an important trait for keeping butternut vines productive through the humid second half of a Gulf South growing season.
directions: Sow seed directly in warm soil after all danger of frost, allowing the vines room to spread; Metro PMR is a butternut squash hybrid bred specifically for high resistance to powdery mildew, so foliage stays greener and more productive later into summer than standard butternut varieties, which typically succumb to mildew before the crop has fully sized and cured. It produces the classic tan, bottle-shaped butternut fruit with dense, sweet, deep orange flesh well suited to roasting, soups, and purees. Let fruit mature fully to a hard rind before harvest, then cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot for one to two weeks; properly cured squash stores for several months in a cool, dry pantry.

name: Mexican Red Oca
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep after last frost; tuber initiation occurs after the fall equinox as days shorten, with harvest following the first killing frost.
directions: Mexican Red is an oca strain grown in the mountains of Mexico, distinguished by its dark, blood-red, flattened-cylindrical tubers with a crisp, apple-like texture and a flavor ranging from mildly sweet to tangy. Plant tubers in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; the tall, sprawling plants produce tubers on intermediate-to-long stolons, so give them room to spread or mound soil around the base as they grow. Tuber initiation begins after the fall equinox and continues until frost kills the foliage, which signals it's time to dig. The reddish color holds up reasonably well in cooking, turning a muted red when boiled or roasted.

name: Mexico Midget Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably above 50°F; in zone 9, set out in March for a spring crop and again in July for a heavy fall crop that runs until frost.
directions: Transplant into warm soil after all danger of frost, staking or caging the sprawling vines since a single plant can carry hundreds of tiny fruit clusters by midsummer. Mexico Midget is a wild-type heirloom currant tomato collected in Mexico, producing an explosion of pea-sized, intensely sweet-tart red fruits in loose clusters continuously from early summer to frost. The tough little vines shrug off the heat, humidity, and disease pressure that slow down larger-fruited tomatoes, making this one of the most productive and trouble-free tomatoes for Gulf South gardens. Fruits are best picked and eaten straight off the vine or tossed whole into salads, since their small size makes stemming tedious for cooking; a light monthly feeding and consistent watering keep the sprawling plants producing all season.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomato Variety Trials

name: Mickylee Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm and all frost danger has passed; the compact icebox-type vines fit well in smaller gardens.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Mickylee was released by the University of Florida and bred for early maturity and reliable resistance to fusarium wilt, a soil-borne disease that can devastate watermelon plantings in warm, humid growing regions where the fungus persists in the soil for years. The round, medium-small icebox-type fruit has sweet, crisp, deep red flesh with a thin rind, making a single melon a manageable size for a small household without leftovers going to waste. The compact vines and early ripening window make it a good choice for shorter growing seasons or for gardeners wanting an earlier harvest than larger, later-maturing watermelon varieties provide. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit stem browns and dries, and the ground spot beneath the melon turns from white to creamy yellow.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Micro Tom Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting; Micro Tom's extremely small size (under a foot tall) suits it to 4-6 inch pots, windowsills, and classroom or laboratory growing without any staking.
directions: Sow seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into a small pot once true leaves appear, since the plants never need staking and stay compact from seed to fruit. Micro-Tom was bred at the University of Florida from a cross of 'Florida Basket' and 'Ohio 4013-3' and carries a mutation that stunts its growth to just a few inches tall with a life cycle of only a few months, making it one of the most widely used model organisms in tomato genetics research worldwide. Home gardeners grow it mainly as a novelty for windowsills and tiny containers, where it still produces a modest crop of small, edible red fruit.

name: Midnight Black Turtle Soup Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed above 60°F; an upright, self-supporting bush bean that needs no staking and dries down for harvest in early fall.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in rows 24 to 30 inches apart in warm, fertile soil; this compact, upright bush selection holds its pods well off the ground for easier hand or mechanical harvest. Midnight Black Turtle Soup traces to a small black bean brought into the United States in the early 1800s and later refined into a tidy, heavy-yielding bush strain long grown for classic black bean soup. The small, glossy black seeds cook down creamy and rich while holding their shape, making them a favorite for soups, stews, and Latin-style rice and beans. Pull entire plants once most pods have dried and rattle, then finish curing indoors before shelling.

name: Midnight Roma Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed on a heat mat 5-6 weeks before the last frost, then harden off and transplant after frost danger passes.
directions: A paste tomato developed at Oregon State University, this semi-determinate variety produces 3-4 inch deep purple-red fruit whose anthocyanin coloring intensifies with more direct sun exposure. Provide trellis or stake support and fertile, well-drained soil near pH 6.5, watering with drip irrigation to keep foliage dry and reduce disease pressure. Prune nearby foliage that shades the fruit if you want to maximize the purple color for sauces and roasting.

name: Midnight Snack Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Midnight Snack is an indeterminate cherry tomato developed through the Oregon State University anthocyanin tomato breeding program and received All-America Selections recognition for its unique color-change ripeness indicator: the fruit develops deep blue-black (anthocyanin) coloring on the sun-exposed upper portions of the cherry while the shaded underside remains red, and when fully ripe the red area spreads to cover the underside — providing a clear ripeness signal without needing to squeeze or taste individual cherries. In zone 9, transplant March–April and provide cage or stake. The dark anthocyanin coloration in the sun-exposed skin has nutritional significance — anthocyanins (the same pigments in blueberries and blackcurrants) are potent antioxidants, and Midnight Snack's production is maximized in high-light conditions like zone 9's full sun. The cherry-red underside plus dark-blue top creates a striking bicolor appearance unlike any other cherry tomato.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and cage or stake. Harvest when underside turns fully red to match upper blue-red skin. Midnight Snack Tomato is one of the most visually distinctive cherry tomato varieties available — a product of the Oregon State University tomato breeding program's work on anthocyanin accumulation in tomato fruit skin. Anthocyanins are a class of pigments responsible for blue, purple, and red colors in many plants (blueberries, purple cabbage, red grapes, black currants), and OSU researchers identified and bred for a trait that causes anthocyanins to accumulate in tomato fruit skin in response to light exposure. In Midnight Snack, the sun-exposed upper portion of each cherry develops a dramatic deep blue-black to dark indigo color while the shaded underside remains the conventional cherry-red of a ripe tomato — creating a two-toned fruit unlike any traditional tomato variety. When fully ripe, the red color from the underside gradually encompasses the fruit, providing a visual cue: as the red progresses upward to meet the darkening blue-black, the fruit is at peak ripeness. The flavor combines genuine sweetness with a fruity, complex quality that reflects the improved eating quality bred into OSU's anthocyanin lines beyond their visual novelty. Beyond appearance, the high anthocyanin content of Midnight Snack skin provides measurable antioxidant value — anthocyanins contribute to the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant capacity associated with blueberry and dark fruit consumption — with zone 9's intense sun exposure maximizing anthocyanin production in the fruit.
sources: Oregon State University Tomato Breeding Program — Anthocyanin cherry tomato development
All-America Selections — Midnight Snack tomato AAS recognition documentation
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Dark anthocyanin cherry tomato variety comparison

name: Miike Giant Mustard
plantingNote: Give plants ample room to reach full size; also excellent sown in late summer for a fall crop, as cool weather deepens the bronze-red color.
directions: Miike Giant is a Japanese heirloom mustard prized for its huge, savoyed leaves that emerge green and develop striking bronze-purple coloring and deep-cut, ruffled margins as they mature. Direct sow into fertile soil and thin generously, since mature plants form large, dramatic rosettes over two feet across. Young leaves are milder and good raw, while mature leaves carry substantial heat and are best braised, stir-fried, or used in kimchi-style ferments. The plant's size and color also make it a striking addition to ornamental vegetable plantings.

name: Millionaire Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Millionaire is an early, heavy-yielding hybrid well suited to a long, hot Gulf South growing season.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Millionaire is a widely grown Asian-type hybrid eggplant producing long, slender, glossy dark purple fruit with tender, nearly seedless flesh and thin skin that needs no peeling. It bears exceptionally early and heavily, often setting its first harvestable fruit faster than most other eggplant types, and continues producing steadily through hot, humid summer weather that can slow other varieties. The slim fruit is well suited to quick-cooking methods like stir-frying and grilling, since it cooks through fast without the bitterness or heavy seediness of larger globe eggplants. Pick fruit while the skin is still glossy and firm, about 6-9 inches long, since overripe fruit turns dull and develops tougher skin and larger seeds.

name: Millionaire Japanese Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; eggplant requires sustained warmth and benefits from bottom heat during germination. In zone 9 transplant February–March for a long growing season through October–November. Millionaire thrives in summer heat and continues setting fruit when cooler-season crops fail.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Millionaire is a Japanese-type hybrid eggplant producing long (8–10 inch), slender, deep purple-black fruits of exceptional quality and high yields — the name reflects its extraordinary productivity under good growing conditions. The thin, tender skin and nearly seedless, non-bitter flesh make it ideal for slicing, stir-frying, and grilling without peeling or salting. It is a high-yield variety developed in Japan and widely grown in zone 9 commercial and home gardens for the Southern Asian food market. The plants are vigorous and productive from summer through fall, with fruit set continuing reliably even in the peak heat of Gulf Coast summers. Harvest when skin is deep purple and glossy at 6–8 inches — fruits become seedy and bitter if allowed to grow to full size.
sources: Sakata Seed Company — Millionaire Japanese Eggplant
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Eggplant Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Asian Eggplant Production

name: Millionaire Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed; Millionaire's early maturity makes it a strong choice for gardeners in shorter-summer parts of okra's growing range.
directions: Millionaire is an F1 hybrid bred from Clemson Spineless lines to mature earlier and set pods more heavily than many open-pollinated okra varieties. Sturdy, medium-large plants hold up well to wind and heavy fruit load, producing flavorful pods best cut at three to four inches for peak tenderness. Its early start makes it well suited to regions with a shorter warm season, since it begins yielding before many heirloom types hit their stride. Frequent picking through the heat of summer keeps this vigorous hybrid setting new flowers rather than diverting energy into oversized, fibrous pods.

name: Mini Love Watermelon
plantingNote: Start indoors or transplant after soil is thoroughly warm; Mini Love is a 2017 All-America Selections winner producing personal-size, 3-6 pound melons on more compact vines than standard watermelon, a good fit for small Gulf Coast gardens and trellising.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Mini Love is a personal-size seeded watermelon bred for early maturity and crack resistance, producing round, 3-6 pound fruit with sweet, crisp, deep red flesh perfect for a single small household to finish in one sitting. Its shorter vines and lighter fruit make it a good candidate for growing up a trellis with fruit slings for support, saving ground space in a small garden. Because it matures faster than standard full-size watermelon, it also fits well into a shorter spring or fall planting window. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned.
sources: All-America Selections — Mini Love watermelon AAS winner 2017

name: Miniature White Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Miniature White is a compact, prolific old heirloom suited to small gardens or short trellising, grown mainly for its tiny ivory-white fruit.
directions: Sow directly in warm soil after frost and thin seedlings to a foot or more apart, since this older heirloom produces a mass of short vines rather than one dominant leader. Pick fruit at 1-2 inches, round to slightly oval, while the thin skin is still fully creamy white; left longer on the vine the fruit coarsens and loses the delicate texture that makes it good for whole-fruit pickles. Because the fruit stays small even at full maturity, plan on frequent picking every day or two during peak season to keep plants productive and to catch fruit before it becomes misshapen. This variety is maintained mainly through heirloom seed-saver collections rather than large-scale commercial production.

name: Minicor Carrot
plantingNote: Suits Gulf Coast fall sowing in loose beds; fast-maturing baby type also works for succession spring plantings.
directions: A Dutch Nantes-type carrot bred with an especially small core, giving straight, uniform roots with fine grain and reliable sweetness. It matures quickly enough to be pulled small as a baby carrot or left slightly longer for full-size roots without losing tenderness. Its short stature and forgiving root shape make it a good fit for heavier or shallower garden soils that stunt longer carrot types.

name: Mino Early Daikon
plantingNote: Sow from late spring through midsummer since Mino Early tolerates heat and resists bolting better than most daikon types, making it a reliable choice for a summer-to-fall crop.
directions: Mino Early is an old open-pollinated Japanese heirloom prized for producing long, slender white roots weeks faster than standard Minowase types, with late-developing pithiness that keeps texture crisp even at full size. Work soil deeply and stone-free before sowing, since the smooth cylindrical roots can reach 14-16 inches and require loose ground to grow straight. Its combination of speed, heat tolerance, and mild, tender flavor makes it a dependable choice for growers wanting daikon without the long season standard winter types demand.

name: Minowase Daikon
plantingNote: Direct sow into deep, loose soil 8-10 weeks before the first fall frost; a light frost after sizing up improves sweetness and crispness.
directions: Thin seedlings early to prevent forked roots, and keep soil evenly moist to avoid splitting as the roots elongate. Minowase is the foundational Japanese daikon type behind many named strains, producing smooth, pure-white roots 18-24 inches long that taper only slightly. It is the traditional choice for takuan pickles as well as fresh grating and simmering, valued for its mild, clean flavor and dependable uniformity.

name: Minuet Napa Cabbage
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 7-10 weeks before first fall frost for the most reliable heads, since spring sowings are prone to bolting as days lengthen.
directions: Direct sow or set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping moisture consistent for fast, uninterrupted growth. Minuet is a compact mini napa cabbage forming dense, upright heads only about 9 inches tall, with dark green outer leaves wrapping a sweet, pale yellow interior, making it a good fit for small households or closer spacing than standard-size napa types. It holds well in the field without splitting and resists tipburn and bottom rot better than many older varieties. Harvest when heads feel firm when squeezed, and store trimmed heads refrigerated for use in kimchi, stir-fries, and soups.

name: Mirai 301 Bicolor Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Wait until soil has warmed well above 65 degrees F before direct sowing, since this tender-hulled hybrid germinates poorly in cold, wet ground.
directions: Bred in Japan and marketed under the Mirai trademark, this bicolor hybrid is prized for exceptionally thin, tender pericarps and very high sugar content that many gardeners describe as fruit-like sweetness eaten raw off the cob. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil and give it consistent moisture through silking, since the thin-walled kernels are more sensitive to stress cracking than standard sh2 supersweets. Ears fill out to the tip reliably with 7 to 8 inch cobs on sturdy stalks, and the variety holds refrigerated quality in the husk for up to two weeks, longer than most sweet corn. Choose this cultivar when the priority is the sweetest possible fresh-eating experience rather than maximum yield or field storability.

name: Misato Rose Radish
plantingNote: Best as a fall crop — direct sow in late summer 10–6 weeks before first frost; Misato Rose is a Japanese winter radish with green or greenish-white exterior skin and a spectacular vivid rose to magenta-pink interior flesh — one of the most visually stunning root vegetables available, making it a centerpiece of any vegetable display and exceptionally attractive in slaws, salads, and pickles where the color impact is full.
directions: Direct sow in late summer or fall; thin to 4–6 inches for full root development; Misato Rose grows to 3–4 inches in diameter over 60–70 days — much longer than spring radishes; harvest before hard freeze; the vivid interior color intensifies in cool fall weather; slice thin to showcase the color in salads. Misato Rose is a traditional Japanese winter radish (daikon type) from the Misato region of Japan, where it has been grown for centuries as a specialty vegetable known for its extraordinary interior color. The exterior of the root is pale green to greenish-white — completely unremarkable from the outside — but when the root is cut crosswise, the interior reveals a brilliant ring of vivid rose to magenta-pink extending from the interior outward, with a paler white core and a narrow white zone just inside the green skin. The effect is striking: the pink-fleshed cross-section looks like a small decorative disc with a rose-colored center zone. The vivid pink color comes from betalain pigments similar to those in beets and watermelon radishes, and it intensifies dramatically in the cooler temperatures of fall growing. The flavor is mild, slightly sweet, and crisp — much milder than the small red spring radishes most American gardeners know, and excellent for slicing thin in Japanese-style pickles (where the pink color turns the pickling liquid a beautiful deep rose), for raw salads where the color provides visual drama, and for Korean-style seasoned vegetable preparations. Also called 'Beauty Heart Radish' in some markets.

name: Misome
plantingNote: Direct sow from early spring through fall; Misome tolerates heat better than tatsoi and can be sown in successive batches through the warmer months for a continuous supply.
directions: Misome is a relatively recent Japanese cross between komatsuna and tatsoi, combining tatsoi's glossy, savoyed, rounded leaf with a more upright, komatsuna-like growth habit that is easier to harvest cleanly. The thick, tender leaves and stems have a sweet, mild flavor raw that turns more robust and mustardy once cooked, and the plant holds up well in the field without turning tough or bitter. It matures quickly from direct sowing and shows good tolerance of both heat and cool weather, making it a flexible filler green for spring, summer, and fall plantings. Harvest whole heads or take outer leaves individually for a cut-and-come-again crop.

name: Mission Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; its early maturity helps finish a spring melon crop before peak summer disease and heat stress build up.
directions: An Asgrow-bred hybrid producing round, medium-large, sutureless melons with a small cavity, strong rind net, and firm interior, maturing roughly 5 to 6 days earlier than the industry-standard Top Mark. LSU AgCenter includes it among its Louisiana cantaloupe list. Its early maturity is an advantage for Gulf Coast gardeners trying to finish a spring melon crop before peak summer disease and heat stress build up.
sources: LSU AgCenter / Seeds to Success - Recommended Cantaloupe and Watermelon Varieties for Louisiana
NC State University - Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America

name: Mississippi Cream Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mississippi Cream peas can be planted in succession every 3–4 weeks from April through August for continuous summer production — they thrive in the summer heat that limits most other garden vegetables.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Mississippi Cream is a traditional Gulf South cream pea variety — producing small to medium-sized, cream-white seeds with the mild, sweet, nutty flavor characteristic of cream peas that distinguishes them from the earthier, bolder flavor of blackeye peas and cowpeas. Mississippi Cream is a semi-bush type with good productivity in Gulf South conditions and excellent heat tolerance — continuing to produce through the summer heat of zone 9 when most cool-season vegetables have ended. As a cream pea type, Mississippi Cream has slightly smaller seeds and a sweeter, more delicate flavor than standard crowder or blackeye types — the creamier texture and milder flavor of cream peas generally makes them preferred for certain traditional preparations including fresh summer pea succotash, cream peas and okra, and fresh peas braised with ham or fatback. Southern peas as a group are the most important summer legume vegetable of Gulf Coast traditional gardens — providing fresh protein through the hottest months when other vegetables fail. The nitrogen-fixing root system enriches garden soil for subsequent crops. Harvest pods at the green-shell stage (well-filled hulls but still green) for fresh eating or continue to dry maturity for storage.

name: Mississippi Crowder Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant March–May for spring and July–August for fall. Mississippi Crowder is a vigorous bush variety with higher tolerance for clay soils than many southern pea types — particularly valued in heavy Gulf Coast soils.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any reasonably well-drained soil; Mississippi Crowder is a bush-type crowder pea with tightly packed seeds that turn light brown at maturity. It is a traditional Mississippi variety well-adapted to the heavy clay soils common along the Gulf Coast and Mississippi Delta, where it tolerates temporary waterlogging better than many other cowpea types. The crowder seeds develop a creamy texture when cooked with excellent flavor for fresh-shell eating, and they also dry well for storage as dried beans. The vigorous vines shade out weeds effectively once established, and the roots fix substantial nitrogen, improving soil for the following season.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension — Southern Pea Production
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Southern Pea Varieties
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Crowder Pea Varieties

name: Mississippi Hot Pickle Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 55°F; this heirloom sets fruit well through Gulf Coast summer heat.
directions: This old Mississippi dooryard heirloom produces slender, tapered fruit that ripen from pale yellow-green through orange to bright red, with a medium heat similar to a cayenne. It was passed down among home gardeners specifically for pickling whole in vinegar brine, and the thin-walled pods also dry and grind well for homemade hot pepper flakes or vinegar-pepper sauce. Compact, heavily branched plants handle Deep South humidity and heat well and keep setting new pods through summer if picked regularly rather than left to fully color on the plant. Because it is open-pollinated, isolate it from other annuum peppers by distance if you intend to save true seed.

name: Mississippi Nemaheart Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; this heirloom-grade open-pollinated release carries the original N-gene root-knot nematode resistance later bred into many modern Southern pepper cultivars, making it a dependable choice for sandy Gulf Coast soils with heavy nematode pressure.
directions: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, well-drained soil once nights stay reliably above 55 degrees F. Mississippi Nemaheart was released by Mississippi State University in 1966 as an open-pollinated pimiento-type pepper bred by recurrent backcrossing into 'Truhart Perfection,' and it remains historically significant as the original source of the dominant N gene that confers resistance to southern, peanut, and tropical root-knot nematodes in modern pepper breeding. Plants are moderately vigorous with heart-shaped, thick-walled sweet fruit that ripens from green to deep red and is well suited to canning, roasting, and pimiento cheese. Because root-knot nematodes are endemic in the sandy, poorly drained soils common across the Gulf Coast, this cultivar performs far more reliably there than standard susceptible pimiento types, though its plants can be somewhat weaker-growing than modern hybrids bred from it.
sources: Mississippi State University Agricultural Experiment Station

name: Mississippi Pinkeye 2 Purplehull Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow a bit earlier in the window than most cowpeas, since this cultivar was specifically improved for stronger seedling emergence and cold tolerance in cooler early-season soil.
directions: Take advantage of this variety's improved cold tolerance by sowing it slightly earlier in spring than standard Mississippi Pinkeye Purple Hull, since breeding work focused on stronger emergence and seedling survival in cooler soil. Covered by a U.S. plant patent as an improved selection of the older Mississippi Pinkeye Purple Hull, this cultivar reaches shelling stage in roughly 60 days, a few days ahead of its parent. Pods carry the classic purple hull color over pink-eyed cream peas with excellent flavor, equally good eaten fresh or dried for winter storage. Keep plantings picked regularly through the heat of summer, since consistent harvest keeps the compact bush setting new flushes of pods.
sources: US Patent US8658859B2 — Cowpea cultivar Mississippi Pinkeye 2 Purplehull
Willhite Seed Company southern pea variety records

name: Mississippi Pinkeye Purple Hull Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably above 65°F; Mississippi Pinkeye is an upright, semi-bush type bred with multiple disease resistances, making it one of the more reliable purple hull peas for humid Deep South gardens.
directions: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep in rows 24-30 inches apart, thinning to 4-8 inches; like other cowpeas it fixes its own nitrogen and needs little to no supplemental fertilizer. Mississippi Pinkeye is a semi-crowder Southern pea bred with resistance to fusarium wilt, root-knot nematode, and several strains of blackeye cowpea mosaic virus, distinguishing it from older purple hull types that lack that disease package. Pods emerge light green with a distinct pink 'eye' blush, then color to deep purple at the green-shell stage, and the upright plant habit holds pods above the foliage for easier hand harvest. Shell at the purple-podded green-shell stage for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully on the vine for storage peas with the characteristic cream seed coat and maroon-pink eye.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension — Southern Peas variety guide
HOSS Tools — Mississippi Pinkeye Purple Hull pea variety notes
Holmes Seed Company — Mississippi Pinkeye Purple Hull BVR pea

name: Mississippi Purple Hull Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil temperature is reliably above 65°F; Southern peas are extremely heat and drought-tolerant once established and require no special soil preparation. In zone 9, plant April–August — Southern peas can be succession-sown throughout the Gulf South summer for continuous harvest. Mississippi Purple Hull is a crowder-type pea with distinctive purple pods that turn green when shelled and cooked. Harvest at the green shell stage (pods are fat and round but before they begin to dry) for fresh eating, or allow to dry fully for storage. The purple pod color makes the harvest stage visually easy to determine.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in rows 24–30 inches apart; thin to 4–6 inches. No fertilizer needed on most soils — cowpeas fix nitrogen. Harvest at the green shell stage for the best fresh flavor. Mississippi Purple Hull Pea is a Southern pea (cowpea, Vigna unguiculata) — a warm-season legume that is one of the most historically important and widely grown vegetables of the American Gulf South and Deep South, where the hot summers that challenge many other vegetables are actually the conditions Southern peas thrive in. The name 'purple hull' describes the distinctive coloration of the pods at harvest: the pods are vivid purple-red, making the harvest stage visually unmistakable in the garden and distinguishing purple hull types from the silver/green pods of cream peas and the tan pods of blackeye peas. Mississippi Purple Hull is a crowder-type pea (the seeds are crowded tightly in the pod, creating the characteristic dimpled, round shape of the shelled peas) — crowder types are considered by many Gulf South cooks to have the richest, meatiest flavor of the Southern pea types, ideal for the slow-cooked preparations that are central to Gulf South foodways. Southern peas are nitrogen-fixing legumes that improve soil fertility while producing — one of the most productive and soil-improving summer crops for zone 8–10 gardens.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Mississippi Purple Hull pea variety notes
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Southern pea variety collection
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Southern Pea Production for the Gulf South

name: Mississippi Silver Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; Mississippi Silver shows good resistance to common Southern pea diseases, making it a reliable choice for humid Gulf South gardens.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and harvest pods once they turn from green to a silvery, pale green-white color at the crowder stage. Mississippi Silver is a productive crowder-type cowpea whose closely packed, squarish peas fill the pod so tightly they are pressed ('crowded') against one another, developing a rich, hearty flavor prized in traditional Southern cooking. Its pale, silvery pod color at harvest makes ripeness easy to spot, and the variety is noted for good tolerance to common cowpea diseases and heat stress, producing reliably through the hottest part of the Gulf South summer when many other vegetables decline. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil for whatever crop follows. Harvest continuously at the silver-green stage for fresh shelling, or allow pods to dry fully for long-term storage.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension — cowpea variety notes

name: Mississippi Silver Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil warms above 65°F; Mississippi Silver is a semi-erect bush type Southern pea producing distinctive silver-tan, slightly inflated pods with a speckled cream-and-purple seed — one of the most productive and flavorful crowder-type Southern peas grown in Mississippi and the Gulf South, and a staple of traditional Southern summer gardens for many decades.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun, well-drained soil; Mississippi Silver can be succession-planted every 3–4 weeks from spring through late summer for continuous production; plants fix atmospheric nitrogen and require no supplemental fertilizer in average garden soil; harvest at the green-shell stage when pods are well-filled and slightly silvery-tan in color. Mississippi Silver is a traditional open-pollinated Southern pea variety that derives its name from the distinctive silvery-tan to pale buff color of its mature pods — a different visual marker from the purple-hull and black-eyed types more familiar to outside the South. The variety is classified as a crowder type because the seeds are tightly packed ('crowded') inside the pod, causing them to develop flat sides from pressing against each other — the classic crowder characteristic that gives the type its name. The seeds are cream-colored with purple or red-purple speckled markings that fade to a uniform tan when cooked, as with most field peas, and the flavor is the rich, earthy, savory character of Southern field peas that is quite different from garden peas or snap beans. Mississippi Silver is one of the most widely recommended varieties by Mississippi State University Extension and LSU AgCenter for home garden Southern pea production — consistently rated highly for both yield and eating quality in regional trials. Like all Southern peas (Vigna unguiculata), it thrives in the heat and humidity of the Gulf South through summer months when most other vegetables have ended, making it one of the primary summer food crops of the region.

name: Missouri Wonder Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; traditionally grown at the base of corn stalks, which the vines climb in place of a trellis, though a pole or fence works just as well in a home garden.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun, giving vines a tall pole, fence, or living corn stalk to climb since plants can reach six to eight feet. Missouri Wonder is a traditional cornfield bean from the early twentieth century, grown intercropped with corn so the climbing vine needed no separate support, a companion-planting approach once common across Southern and Midwestern subsistence farms. The thick, slightly curved pods stay stringless and tender while young, making excellent snap beans, while mature seed can be dried for use as a hearty soup bean through winter. It is notably tolerant of heat and garden stress compared with many bush varieties, and steady daily picking keeps the vigorous vines producing over a long harvest window.
sources: Sand Hill Preservation Center heirloom bean records

name: Mitoyo Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Mitoyo is an old Japanese market variety traditionally grown around the Mitoyo and Kanonji districts and benefits from a full warm season to size up its teardrop fruit.
directions: Mitoyo is an old Japanese market eggplant traced to the Mitoyo and Kanonji districts, grown for oval, teardrop-shaped fruit that ripens to a deep, near-black purple. Transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun once nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 55F, and keep the soil evenly moist to encourage the tender, sweet flesh the variety is known for. Harvest fruit at 4-6 inches long while the skin is still glossy; the flesh is mild enough to slice thin and eat raw, though it takes equally well to grilling, pickling, or classic Japanese nasu dishes. Regular picking keeps plants productive and prevents fruit from developing the bitterness and toughened skin of overripe eggplant.

name: Miz America Mizuna
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep into fertile, well-drained soil in early spring or, better, six to eight weeks before the first fall frost, since this deep-red mizuna holds its color and mild flavor best in cool weather.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep into fertile, well-drained soil in early spring or, better, six to eight weeks before the first fall frost, since this deep-red F1 mizuna holds its uniform maroon color and mild, non-bitter flavor best in cool weather. Thin seedlings to allow the deeply serrated, feathery leaves room to form their signature vase-shaped rosette, and harvest whole heads or individual leaves for cut-and-come-again picking. Its consistent color on both leaf surfaces makes it popular for baby-leaf salad mixes, garnishes, and mixed ornamental plantings as well as stir-fries.

name: Mizen Potato
plantingNote: A high-yielding variety with good foliar and tuber blight tolerance, making it forgiving in cool, damp maincrop seasons.
directions: Mizen was developed in 1978 at the Teagasc Oak Park breeding centre in County Carlow, part of the same Irish program that later produced Rooster, and was selected for its long, smooth-skinned, creamy yellow tubers and dependable yield. The white flesh carries medium dry matter, giving a texture between waxy and floury that works well for boiling and general cooking. Plant seed pieces in fertile, well-drained soil and hill the rows as shoots emerge, taking advantage of the plant's good resistance to foliar and tuber blight in wetter summers. Lift the crop once the tops die back, since Mizen was bred as a maincrop variety rather than an early one.

name: Mogette de Vendée Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; traditionally trained up chestnut stakes in the Vendée region of western France, so provide tall poles or a trellis.
directions: Mogette de Vendée is a Protected Geographical Indication white kidney bean from France's Atlantic-coast Vendée region, where it is the traditional accompaniment to local ham and is celebrated every autumn at regional mogette festivals. The plump, pure-white seeds cook to a smooth, mild-flavored, creamy finish that absorbs butter, garlic, and herbs readily, making it a staple of simple rustic French cooking. Allow pods to dry fully and turn pale tan before harvest, then shell and finish curing indoors for a week or two. Give vines full sun, steady moisture during pod fill, and a tall, sturdy support since plants can reach 8 feet.
sources: Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualité (INAO)

name: Molokai Purple Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F, in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic sandy soil in full sun; Molokai Purple is a Hawaiian-origin heirloom distributed by small specialty growers alongside other named purple types such as All Purple and Purple Passion.
directions: Molokai Purple is a Hawaiian-origin heirloom sweet potato named for the island of Molokai, producing roots with dark purple to nearly black skin over dense, vividly purple flesh that holds its color well through baking and steaming. The vines are vigorous and trailing with purple-tinged foliage, and the roots are somewhat smaller and more irregular in shape than mainstream commercial purple varieties, reflecting its heirloom, unselected background. Set slips in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping fertility moderate since rich soil favors vine growth over root development; the vine tolerates the heat and humidity of a long warm season well. Harvest once vines begin to yellow and before frost threatens, then cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for a week or two to firm the skin and develop full sweetness before storing in a cool, dry place.
sources: Sand Hill Preservation Center — Sweet Potato Variety List
University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Sweet Potato Varieties

name: Momotaro Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March for spring production and again late July–August for fall. Momotaro requires staking or caging as an indeterminate vine and benefits from consistent moisture to prevent blossom-end rot and cracking in summer heat.
directions: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil with a sturdy cage or stake; Momotaro is Japan's most celebrated fresh tomato — an indeterminate, pink-fruited hybrid with exceptionally low acidity and high sugar content that has dominated the Japanese fresh tomato market since Sakata Seed Company introduced it in 1985. The smooth, round, 6–8 ounce fruits have thin, tender skin, almost no gel around the seeds, and a dense, sweet, mild flesh that requires no sugar addition in cooked preparations and is prized for fresh eating. The plant produces steadily over a long season and shows better resistance to blossom-end rot than many large-fruited varieties. In zone 9 the flavor is best in spring and fall crops; the fruits produced through peak summer heat tend toward milder, less complex flavor.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Specialty Tomato Varieties
Sakata Seed Company — Momotaro Tomato History
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Pink Tomato Types

name: Monaco Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; Monaco needs two to three weeks longer than Covington to finish, so set slips out promptly once the soil has warmed to give roots a full season to size up.
directions: Plant certified slips in well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost; Monaco is a North Carolina State University release valued for a broad disease-resistance package — it stands up to Fusarium wilt, Streptomyces soil rot, and southern root-knot nematode, though it remains susceptible to guava root-knot nematode, an emerging pest in parts of the South. Its rose-pink skin fades somewhat in storage over dark orange flesh, and the plant grows in a dense, upright habit rather than sprawling widely, which helps it shade out weeds within the row once established. Monaco needs a longer season than standard varieties like Covington — plan on two to three extra weeks in the ground — and while its disease resistance makes it a strong option for low-spray or organic plantings, expect somewhat lower yields than top commercial varieties. Cure roots at 85-90°F and high humidity for about a week to heal the skin and develop full sweetness before storing.
sources: North Carolina State University — Potato and Sweetpotato Breeding and Genetics Program variety descriptions
North Carolina State University — NC Plant Breeding Consortium sweetpotato cultivar profiles

name: Monarch Celeriac
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, since germination is slow and erratic at cool temperatures; transplant out once nights stay reliably above freezing.
directions: Monarch is a widely grown European celeriac that holds the Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for its reliable, high-yielding globes. Start seed indoors well ahead of the last frost and transplant out into deeply worked, fertile soil once frost danger has passed, setting plants at the same depth they grew in their cells. Keep the bed evenly moist all season and strip away side shoots and surface rootlets as the crown swells to encourage a smooth, round, white-fleshed globe. Harvest once roots reach 3-5 inches across; Monarch stores well through winter in a cool root cellar or can be left in the ground under mulch in milder climates.

name: Moneta Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, 2-4 weeks before the last frost; because each seed produces a single seedling, thinning is rarely needed.
directions: Direct sow thinly in early spring or late summer, since each seed ball contains only a single embryo and germinates as one seedling rather than the tangled cluster typical of most beets. Moneta is an All-America Selections winner valued for this true monogerm trait, which eliminates the tedious thinning normally required for beets and makes precision seeding practical for both home gardeners and small-scale growers. It produces smooth, uniformly round, deep-red roots with sweet flavor and tender greens suitable for salad mixes.

name: Mongeta del Ganxet Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; this indeterminate climbing bean needs tall poles or a trellis for its vigorous vines.
directions: Mongeta del Ganxet is a flattened, glossy white bean with a distinctive hooked shape (ganxet means 'little hook' in Catalan), grown around the Valles and Maresme regions of Catalonia, Spain and protected as a DOP since 2007. Plants are tall indeterminate climbers with white flowers and need sturdy support to carry the season's vine growth. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant before shelling, then store the hooked white seeds for use in slow-cooked Catalan bean dishes prized for their smooth, buttery texture. It commands a premium price in Spain for its distinctive cooking qualities.
sources: EU eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register — Mongeta del Ganxet DOP
Generalitat de Catalunya DOP product documentation

name: Montana Gold Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is warm; this ultra-early variety was bred for high-altitude and short-season regions where standard cantaloupes cannot ripen in time.
directions: Montana Gold was originally offered as an ultra-early cantaloupe for gardeners coping with high elevation and short, cool growing seasons. Its compact vines set small fruit with notably thick, sweet flesh, ripening well ahead of the 85-90 day eastern cantaloupe standards most catalogs offer. It remains a practical choice anywhere summers run too short or too cool for full-season melons, though its fruit size and yield are modest compared with longer-season heirlooms. The variety persists today mainly through small regional seed-saving networks rather than large commercial suppliers.

name: Montauk Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 60 degrees; Montauk is a synergistic (SE-sh2) bicolor hybrid noted for good vigor in cooler soil than many supersweet types tolerate well, useful for an early Gulf South planting.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Montauk is a synergistic-type bicolor sweet corn hybrid, blending sugary-enhanced and supersweet genetics for excellent flavor and good cool-soil vigor at germination, letting Gulf Coast gardeners plant slightly earlier than standard supersweet types allow. It produces large, jumbo-sized ears packed with tender yellow and white kernels on tall, vigorous stalks. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill for well-filled ears. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed.
sources: seed catalog reference (Jung Seed, Rupp Seeds, Holmes Seed Company)

name: Monticello White Chayote
plantingNote: Bury the whole fruit on its side with the pointed stem end tilted upward and just above the soil line after the last frost; this pale-skinned cultivar, named for the North Florida research station where it was selected, benefits from a warm, sheltered planting spot to get the long vine established early.
directions: Monticello White is a cream-to-pale-skinned chayote cultivar, one of the two commercially cloned selections most commonly sold at Florida garden centers alongside Florida Green, and named for the north Florida city near the research station associated with its selection. Its smooth, ivory fruit is slightly milder and more tender-skinned than the common green types, and it is prized in home gardens both for fresh eating and for its ornamental pale coloring on the vine. Like all chayote it needs a season of six months or more of warmth to fruit heavily, so Gulf Coast growers should plant as early as safely possible after frost and provide a large, strong trellis. The vine's large starchy tuberous root, which develops after a full growing season, is also edible and can be dug and cooked like a yam once the vine dies back for winter.

name: Montreal Market Melon
plantingNote: Sow directly into warm, fertile soil after the last frost, or start indoors in short-season climates and transplant carefully to avoid root disturbance.
directions: Sow directly into warm, fertile soil after the last frost, or start indoors in short-season climates and transplant carefully to avoid root disturbance. This heavy-feeding Quebecois heirloom was cultivated by market gardeners around Montreal in the late 1800s and prized for producing enormous, heavily netted, nutmeg-type melons that could reach 10-15 pounds under generous manuring and glass-frame protection. Its green flesh is exceptionally sweet and aromatic, though the variety demands rich soil and a long, warm season to reach its famous size. Nearly lost to commercial cultivation, it survives today largely through heirloom seed-saving networks.

name: Montreal Muskmelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, deeply enriched soil; Montreal Muskmelon is a large, historic Canadian heirloom that dominated North American melon production from the 1860s through the 1920s and was once the most celebrated melon on the continent, shipped to New York and Boston in elegant straw-packed wooden crates as a luxury product.
directions: Sow in deeply enriched, well-drained hills after last frost; Montreal Muskmelon is a large, demanding variety that needs rich soil and ample space — traditional Montreal growers would excavate three-foot-deep planting holes and fill them with aged manure before planting.
