Montreal Muskmelon was the most celebrated North American melon from roughly 1850 to 1920, grown on the Island of Montreal (particularly in the Rivière-des-Prairies area) in intensively managed, manure-enriched beds and shipped to Montreal, New York, and Boston as a luxury fruit commanding premium prices; the Ferme Onésime Pépin operation shipped 11,000 melons daily at peak production. The large (10–15 lb), deeply ribbed, heavily netted fruits have orange flesh with a rich, intensely sweet, musky perfume that made it the yardstick by which all other melons were judged. It went extinct in commercial production by the 1940s but was revived from Seed Savers Exchange members; now being recultivated by slow food advocates in Montreal.

name: Montserrat Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and stake heavily once transplanted, since the deeply lobed, flattened fruit of this Catalan heirloom grows large and heavy on indeterminate vines.
directions: Named for the serrated mountain outside Barcelona, this heirloom produces deeply ribbed, flattened pink-red beefsteak fruit with a thin skin and a pronounced acidic-sweet balance that Catalan cooks favor for pa amb tomàquet and fresh salads. Provide a sturdy trellis or cage, since vigorous indeterminate vines and heavy fruit clusters need support to keep fruit off the ground. Keep watering even through fruit set to avoid blossom-end rot and catfacing in the deep lobes, and pick at full color while still slightly firm for the best texture in raw preparations.
sources: Institut de Recerca i Tecnologia Agroalimentàries (IRTA) tomato germplasm collections
Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Catalan tomato varieties

name: Monument Napa Cabbage
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 10-12 weeks before first fall frost; Monument is a mid-season type best grown as a fall crop, since its longer maturity window leaves more time for spring bolting.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, with steady moisture to support the long, narrow heads through their extended growing season. Monument is a mid-season napa cabbage forming tall, narrow, densely wrapped heads rather than the broader barrel shapes of many faster-maturing types, with crisp, mild-flavored leaves well suited to kimchi, hot pot, and long storage. Because it takes longer to mature than types like Minuet or Bilko, timing a fall sowing early enough is important so heads finish well before hard frost. Harvest when heads are firm and tight, and store trimmed heads refrigerated for several weeks to months.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Brassica rapa Pekinensis Group

name: Moody Family Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; give this tall-growing West African okra plenty of vertical space and a long Gulf Coast season to size up.
directions: Soak seed and direct sow into warm, fertile soil, allowing room for a very tall plant that can tower well over most garden okra by late summer. Moody Family is a distinct West African okra species, Abelmoschus caillei, rather than the common garden okra, stewarded for generations by an African American family carrying it forward from West African ancestors. Pink-tinged stems carry long, light green pods that blush pink at the tip and stay tender at a larger size than typical okra. Harvest regularly for frying and gumbo, and keep picking to sustain production through the hottest months.

name: Moon and Stars Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, in deeply worked, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give vines 8-10 feet of room to sprawl.
directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained, deeply worked soil in full sun once soil has warmed; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off watering as melons near ripeness. Moon and Stars is a striking American heirloom watermelon, first documented in the late 1800s and rescued from near-extinction in the 1980s after seed saver Merle Van Doren shared surviving seed with Kent Whealy of Seed Savers Exchange, reviving a variety that had all but vanished from commerce. Its dark green rind is scattered with one large yellow 'moon' spot and many smaller yellow 'star' speckles, a genetically distinctive and instantly recognizable pattern; the leaves also show smaller yellow speckling, making the plant ornamental even before fruiting. Flesh is sweet, deep red, and classic in flavor, and large fruits commonly reach 20-40 pounds. Because it is an open-pollinated heirloom, seed saves true when isolated from other watermelon varieties, making it a favorite for gardeners who want to preserve genetic and horticultural history alongside a tasty harvest.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Moon and Stars variety history

name: Morado Yacon
plantingNote: Set out rhizome crown divisions around last frost in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Morado is a darker-skinned Andean strain and is otherwise grown exactly like standard yacon, dying back at first fall frost while its roots and crowns overwinter in the ground in zones 7-9 under mulch.
directions: Morado is a traditional Andean strain of yacon distinguished from the common tan-skinned type by its deep reddish-purple tuber skin and correspondingly purple-flushed stem bases, though the crisp, juicy, pear-like flesh inside remains cream to pale yellow. Grow it exactly as standard yacon: propagate only from the knobby rhizome crowns at the base of last season's stalks (never from the large storage roots, which lack buds and will not sprout), and give it a long, frost-free season of at least five to six months to bulk up its tubers. Many growers who maintain both types report Morado yields slightly smaller but more numerous roots than pale-skinned strains, with a similar sweet, watery crunch that intensifies after a week or two of post-harvest curing in a warm, sunny spot. Because it is an old landrace rather than a registered cultivar, plant vigor and skin color can vary somewhat between sources.
sources: International Potato Center (CIP) -- Andean Roots and Tubers

name: Moranga Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow or start indoors 3 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 direct sow February–April for summer harvest or August for fall. Moranga does best with a long, warm growing season and heavy, fertile soil; in zone 9 it benefits from fall planting to avoid peak summer heat during fruit development.
directions: Sow 2–3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep in deeply amended, fertile soil and thin to the strongest plant when 3 inches tall; Moranga is a large, flat-ribbed, orange-red Brazilian pumpkin (Cucurbita maxima) with deep orange, dense, sweet flesh used throughout Brazil as the traditional vessel for stuffed shrimp dishes (camarão na moranga) and as a soup tureen. The large fruits, averaging 15–25 pounds, are oval to flat with a warty, orange skin and extraordinarily thick, starchy-sweet flesh with minimal seed cavity. The Moranga type is closely related to Hubbard squash and has been cultivated in Brazil for centuries. The flesh makes exceptional purées, soups, and savory stuffings. Store cured fruits for 3–4 months in cool conditions.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Cucurbita maxima Types
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Large Heirloom Squash

name: Morex Barley
plantingNote: Broadcast or drill as soon as the ground can be worked in spring; Morex is a six-row spring barley bred at the University of Minnesota and remains a reference variety for malting quality.
directions: Morex is a six-row spring barley developed by the University of Minnesota and has long served as the benchmark variety against which other malting barleys are measured for enzyme activity and extract yield. Drill into a firm, fertile seedbed as early in spring as the soil can be worked, since barley germinates in cooler ground than corn or sorghum and benefits from getting ahead of summer heat. The plant tillers readily and fills its heads with plump kernels well suited to malting for beer and whiskey as well as livestock feed. Harvest once the heads have dried to a uniform straw color and the kernels are hard, then store the threshed grain in a cool, dry space to preserve germination and malting quality.

name: Moriguchi Daikon
plantingNote: Direct sow into very deeply worked, stone-free sandy loam at least a season's worth of weeks before the first fall frost, since the root can grow a meter or more and needs loose soil with no obstruction to elongate fully.
directions: Traditionally grown in the soft, sandy riverbank soils near Nagoya, this extraordinary daikon produces one of the longest edible roots of any vegetable, commonly exceeding a meter with only a slender two-inch diameter. Deep, stone-free, well-irrigated soil is essential, since the root follows the path of least resistance and will fork or stunt in compacted ground. It is grown chiefly for moriguchizuke, a specialty pickle made by repeatedly aging the root in sake lees over several years, so roots are typically pulled whole with care to avoid snapping the brittle tip. Given the long growing season required, gardeners outside its native river-valley climate should expect a correspondingly later harvest window.

name: Moritz Walking Onion
plantingNote: Plant topset bulbils in early fall so they root before winter; spring planting also works but fall planting produces a larger clump sooner.
directions: Moritz is a heirloom strain of Egyptian walking onion distinguished by unusually large topset bulbils with a deeper red-purple blush than the common strain, and by occasionally producing a secondary whorl of bulbils partway up the flowering stalk in addition to the main cluster at the tip. Otherwise it is grown exactly like other walking onions: plant the topset bulbils an inch or two deep in fall, harvest green tops continuously through the season like scallions, and dig the small underground bulbs once the foliage begins to die back. As the topset clusters grow heavy, the stalk bends over and the bulbils root where they touch soil, letting the clump slowly migrate and expand the planting without any replanting needed. Divide crowded clumps every few years to keep the strain vigorous and true to type.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange heirloom onion archive

name: Morris Heading Collards
plantingNote: Direct sow or set transplants 10–12 weeks before the first fall frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; in zone 9, Morris Heading can also be sown in late winter for a spring crop, but the fall-sown crop is sweetest since frost converts starches to sugars.
directions: Set transplants or thin direct-sown seedlings to 24–30 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; wider spacing than most collards is needed because Morris Heading forms a loose, cabbage-like head rather than a simple open rosette of leaves. This old Southern heirloom collard is distinctive among collard varieties for its semi-heading habit — the inner leaves cup and fold inward to form a loose head reminiscent of a savoy cabbage, while the outer leaves remain harvestable individually as with any collard. The smooth, tender, blue-green leaves have a sweeter, milder flavor than many open-leaf collard varieties, and the heading habit helps blanch and protect the inner leaves from cold and insect damage. Long grown in home gardens across the Carolinas and Georgia, it is well suited to the mild winters of the Gulf South, where fall-planted crops can be harvested over many months. Zone 6–10.

name: Mortgage Lifter Lima Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–May and again July–August for fall. Mortgage Lifter is a pole type requiring a sturdy trellis 6 feet or taller. In zone 9 the vines produce prolifically through the long warm season and may survive mild winters as short-lived perennials, returning from the roots.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Mortgage Lifter lima bean is an Appalachian heirloom from Virginia and West Virginia — an exceptionally productive, large-seeded pole lima with big, flat seeds that can reach half an inch across and fill the pod tightly with 3–5 massive seeds per pod. The sheer yield of these large limas made the variety valuable for subsistence gardeners who could shell, cook, and preserve enormous quantities of butter beans from a small planting, historically giving the variety its name. Fresh-shelled Mortgage Lifter limas have an exceptionally creamy, buttery, starchy flavor — richer than most commercial lima beans and similar in quality to the best Virginia butter beans. Like all limas, they thrive in Gulf Coast heat and continue producing through summer when most other legumes have failed. Harvest pods when plump and the seeds inside are full but still green for fresh eating; allow to fully dry on the vine for dry beans.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Mortgage Lifter Lima Bean Heritage Variety
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Appalachian Heirloom Limas
University of Virginia Cooperative Extension — Lima Bean Production in Virginia

name: Mortgage Lifter Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; this is an indeterminate variety that benefits from robust caging or staking to support the 1–2 pound fruits; excellent disease resistance for an heirloom.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, amended soil after frost risk passes; Mortgage Lifter is a legendary American heirloom developed by M.C. Byles of Logan, West Virginia in the 1930s by crossing four large tomato varieties over six years — the resulting tomatoes sold so well at 50 cents each that he paid off his mortgage in six years, giving the variety its unforgettable name. Fruits are very large (1–2 pounds), pink-red, with meaty flesh, few seeds, and a mild sweet flavor excellent for fresh eating and slicing. One of the most reliable and high-yielding large heirloom beefsteak types, with better disease tolerance than many heirlooms.

name: Mostoller Wild Goose Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed at the base of a tall pole or sturdy trellis, since the vigorous vines can reach 8-10 feet and will swamp light supports.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep after the soil has warmed, training vines up a tall pole, corn stalk, or trellis rather than a light fence. Mostoller Wild Goose is a Pennsylvania heirloom pole bean with a famous origin story: seed was reportedly found in the crop of a wild goose shot in the 1860s and has been passed down through the Mostoller family ever since. The plump, kidney-shaped white beans with a faint pink blush cook to a smooth, creamy texture that many gardeners favor for baking and hearty winter soups. Let pods dry fully on the vine before shelling, and expect strong vigor and heavy yields from a relatively small planting.
sources: Slow Food USA - Ark of Taste
Landis Valley Museum Heirloom Seed Project

name: Mostruosa di Sicilia Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out only once nights stay reliably warm; this heirloom needs a long, hot season to size up its enormous fruit.
directions: Mostruosa di Sicilia is a traditional Sicilian eggplant grown for enormous, rounded fruit streaked white and lavender-purple that can reach several pounds apiece on a single sturdy plant. Give it fertile, well-drained soil, consistent moisture, and steady feeding to support the oversized fruit, and stake plants where wind or heavy fruit load threatens to topple them. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and the flesh firm, since oversized, dull-skinned fruit turns bitter and seedy; younger specimens are tender enough for grilling, stewing, or roasting whole in Sicilian caponata and parmigiana preparations. Because fruit size varies widely from seed, Sicilian gardeners traditionally let a few of the most impressive specimens mature fully for seed saving.

name: Moulin Rouge Beet
plantingNote: Sow as soon as soil can be worked, or in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9; succession sow through the cool season for a continuous harvest.
directions: Sow half an inch deep and thin seedlings to 3-4 inches once true leaves appear; keep soil consistently moist for smooth, evenly shaped roots. Moulin Rouge is a modern hybrid cylindrical beet, similar in form to heirloom cylindrical types like Forono but bred for more uniform root shape, smoother skin, and reliable germination and sizing, making slicing and pickling more efficient with less trimming waste. The deep red, sweet, tender flesh holds its color well when cooked, and the long, straight roots make it a favorite for home canning and pickling where consistent slice size matters. Because the roots grow mostly upright rather than wide, plants can be spaced somewhat closer than round beet varieties for the same yield. The greens are also edible and good cooked as beet greens.
sources: Renee's Garden Seeds — Moulin Rouge variety notes

name: Mountain Fresh Plus Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Mountain Fresh Plus is a determinate hybrid well-suited to Southern spring and fall growing windows. In zone 9, transplant February–March for spring harvest and August for fall harvest.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Mountain Fresh Plus is a North Carolina State University-bred determinate hybrid tomato from the Mountain series (which also includes Mountain Merit, Mountain Spring, and Mountain Pride), developed to combine excellent fruit quality with broad disease resistance for Southern and transitional-climate production. The large (8–12 oz), globe, bright red fruits have firm, crack-resistant skin, good internal color, and balanced sweet-acid flavor — a reliable all-purpose slicing tomato without the flavor complexity of heirlooms but with vastly superior disease resistance and shelf life. Disease resistance includes Fusarium wilt races 1, 2, and 3, Verticillium wilt, gray leaf spot, tomato spotted wilt virus, and root-knot nematodes (races 0, 1, 2, 3) — one of the broadest resistance packages available in a Southern-bred tomato. An excellent choice for zone 8–10 home gardens and market growers who need reliable, marketable tomatoes with broad disease protection in humid, challenging Southern conditions.
sources: North Carolina State University Mountain Horticultural Crops Research and Extension Center
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Variety Evaluation
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Vegetable Variety Evaluations

name: Mountain Magic Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Mountain Magic is a North Carolina State University-bred hybrid with exceptional resistance to late blight, early blight, and septoria leaf spot, making it one of the most disease-tolerant tomatoes available for the humid, blight-prone Gulf South growing season.
directions: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, then stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines; Mountain Magic was bred by Dr. Randy Gardner at North Carolina State University specifically to combine outstanding disease resistance with excellent flavor, standing up to late blight, early blight, and septoria leaf spot far better than most home-garden tomatoes. It produces heavy clusters of 1-2 ounce, deep red cocktail-sized fruit with rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor prized by growers who find most disease-resistant hybrids bland by comparison. Because it keeps producing healthy foliage and fruit even under the fungal disease pressure that builds in humid Gulf Coast summers, it is an especially good choice for gardeners who have struggled with blight on other varieties. Pick fruit as it ripens to bright red and keep harvesting regularly to encourage continued production through the season.
sources: North Carolina State University — Tomato Breeding Program

name: Mountain Pima Vavuli Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after frost danger passes; Vavuli is grown by Mountain Pima (O'ob) farmers at roughly 7,000 feet in the Sierra Madre Occidental of western Chihuahua, Mexico, a cooler highland setting than most Sonoran Desert native squash.
directions: Vavuli is a highland squash grown by Mountain Pima (O'ob) farmers in the Sierra Madre Occidental of western Chihuahua, Mexico, at elevations near 7,000 feet — considerably cooler and higher than most Sonoran Desert native cucurbits. Fruits ripen to a pale green-to-yellow skin surrounding cream-colored flesh. Because it comes from mountain rather than low-desert agriculture, it tolerates cooler nights better than many Southwestern native squash while still needing a full warm season to mature. Direct sow in warm soil after frost danger passes and give the vines ample room to sprawl.

name: Mountain Pride Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Mountain Pride is a compact determinate hybrid suited to staking or caging rather than a full trellis.
directions: Mountain Pride was released by North Carolina State University's vegetable breeding program in 1979 as one of the earliest entries in what became the Mountain series, bred as a determinate hybrid carrying resistance to Verticillium wilt and Fusarium wilt for more reliable production in the humid Southern Appalachians. Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun after frost danger passes, staking or caging the relatively compact plants to keep the developing fruit off the ground. It sets a concentrated main crop of firm, medium-large red globes with good old-fashioned tomato flavor over a shorter harvest window than later Mountain-series introductions bred for extended production. Though largely superseded in modern trials by Mountain Spring and its descendants, Mountain Pride is still offered by a few heirloom-minded seed companies for gardeners wanting the original Mountain-series disease package.
sources: North Carolina State University Mountain Horticultural Crops Research and Extension Center
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Variety Evaluation
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Vegetable Variety Evaluations

name: Mountain Rose Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost in well-drained, slightly acidic, loose soil; in zone 9 plant January–February for April–May harvest before summer heat sets in. Mountain Rose is a mid-season variety well-suited to zone 9's cool winter potato-growing window.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 2–3 inches deep 4–6 weeks before last frost, after curing cut surfaces for 1–2 days; Mountain Rose is a striking and delicious red-fleshed potato — the skin is red, but when cut, the flesh is also vivid rose-red to pink throughout, distinguishing it from standard red-skinned potatoes (like Red Pontiac) that have white flesh inside. The rosy-red flesh is high in anthocyanin antioxidants (the same pigments that color red cabbage, blueberries, and beets) and retains some color through cooking, making baked, mashed, and roasted Mountain Rose potatoes visually dramatic. The flavor is rich and earthy with good potato character; the texture is medium-moist and moderately waxy, excellent for baking, roasting, and boiling. Mountain Rose is a versatile all-purpose potato that performs well in both Southern cool-season production and in more northerly climates, and its beautiful color makes it outstanding for farmers' markets and gourmet home cooking. The red flesh fades somewhat during boiling or steaming but is better maintained when roasted or baked.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Specialty Potato Varieties
University of Maine Cooperative Extension — Potato Variety Guide

name: Mountain Rouge Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights are reliably mild; Mountain Rouge, a 2019 All-America Selections winner, is an indeterminate pink beefsteak bred to perform especially well in cooler climates.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into full sun with sturdy caging or staking for the vigorous indeterminate vines. Mountain Rouge yields large, 12-14 ounce pink beefsteak fruits with a balanced sweet-acid heirloom-style flavor and minimal seed, and it carries resistance to Late Blight, Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt, and root-knot nematode for improved reliability. It performs notably well in cooler growing regions where many beefsteak types struggle to size up fully. Feed and water consistently through fruit set to support the large fruit size.

name: Mountain Spring Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Mountain Spring is a sturdy determinate hybrid that benefits from staking or caging to support its heavy fruit load.
directions: Mountain Spring followed Mountain Pride out of the North Carolina State University breeding program, released in 1991 with broader disease resistance and a heavier, more concentrated fruit set that made it a standard commercial and home-garden slicer across the Southeast through the 1990s. Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun, staking the sturdy determinate plants to carry the crop of large, firm red globes. It carries resistance to Verticillium wilt and multiple races of Fusarium wilt along with useful field tolerance to early blight, a combination that kept foliage productive later into the season than older Southern-bred tomatoes of its era. Mountain Spring was eventually followed by newer Mountain-series releases such as Mountain Fresh and Mountain Merit, but it remains a dependable, widely adapted choice for home gardens across USDA zones 6-9.
sources: North Carolina State University Mountain Horticultural Crops Research and Extension Center
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Variety Evaluation
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Vegetable Variety Evaluations

name: Mountaineer Half Runner Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; half-runner types produce short runners longer than a true bush bean but shorter than a full pole bean, and benefit from light staking or a low trellis even though they can be grown unsupported.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil after last frost, providing light support such as a low trellis or twiggy brush for the heaviest yields. Mountaineer is a West Virginia Appalachian heirloom half-runner bean, a growth habit intermediate between bush and pole types that produces short climbing runners while still setting a concentrated, earlier harvest more like a bush bean. The tender, stringless, flavorful pods are a favorite for fresh eating and traditional Appalachian canning and pickling ('leather britches' style stringing and drying is also common with half-runner types), and the plants tend to keep producing over a longer window than most bush beans. Pick regularly once pods reach full size but before seeds bulge visibly inside, since frequent picking is the single most effective way to keep any snap bean, including half-runners, producing longer.

name: Mr. Big Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter to early spring, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Mr. Big is an All-America Selections winner bred for unusually large, sweet pods on vigorous vines.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked, providing a trellis or netting for the vines to climb. Mr. Big is an All-America Selections winner prized for its unusually large, plump, sweet pods, often 4-5 inches long and packed with 9-10 large peas, produced heavily on vigorous vines over a fairly long harvest window for the cool season. Its exceptional pod size makes shelling faster and more rewarding than many standard shelling peas. Harvest pods when well-filled but still bright green and firm, picking every couple of days to encourage continued production before summer heat ends the crop.

name: Mr. Snow Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Mr. Snow is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bearing pale ivory-white fruit on a compact plant.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Mr. Snow bears medium fruit in a pale, creamy ivory-white with mild, low-acid, sweet flavor typical of white tomato varieties, on a compact Dwarf Tomato Project plant that brings this unusual color to a small-space garden. Its pale fruit stands out strikingly against green foliage and in a mixed harvest basket. Harvest when fruit softens slightly and develops a faint cream-yellow tone, since it never colors red.

name: Mr. Stripey Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Mr. Stripey is not the same as the British 'Tigerella' tomato — Tigerella is a smaller red-and-yellow striped variety; Mr. Stripey is a larger American heirloom bicolor with different size and flavor characteristics.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Mr. Stripey is a large bicolor heirloom beefsteak tomato producing very large (10–20 oz), somewhat flattened, irregularly shaped fruits with a yellow-to-golden exterior prominently striped and mottled with red or pink-red in an irregular, abstract pattern across the fruit surface. The bicolor exterior reveals a matching interior when sliced — yellow and red-tinted flesh arranged in an irregular pattern that makes each fruit slightly different in cross-section. The flavor is sweet and mild with low acidity — characteristic of yellow-dominant bicolor tomatoes — and with a melon-like, fruity quality that is outstanding in fresh eating. Mr. Stripey is an indeterminate heirloom with vigorous vines requiring sturdy support throughout the season. The very large size of the fruits makes them slow to mature — zone 9 gardeners should start seeds early (8 weeks before last frost) and plant out as early as safely possible to maximize the spring growing window before summer heat arrives. As with most large bicolor heirlooms, the thin skin requires careful handling. Not to be confused with the British variety 'Tigerella' which shares a similar name but is a much smaller (4–6 oz), earlier-maturing, red-with-yellow-striped variety of completely different character.

name: Mt. Washington Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Mt. Washington was selected and released for its ability to set fruit in cold conditions similar to those at the summit area of Mt. Washington in New Hampshire — one of the coldest and windiest spots in the eastern United States — making it among the earliest-producing cherry tomato varieties available and suitable for the most challenging cold-summer and short-season climates.
directions: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Mt. Washington is a compact, determinate-type cherry tomato that does not require staking; the plants concentrate production in a relatively tight window (good for canning or preserving in quantity); harvest when fully red and slightly soft. Mt. Washington is an ultra-early cherry tomato selected specifically for cold-tolerance and short-season performance, named for Mt. Washington in New Hampshire — famous for its extreme weather (the site held the world record for the highest surface wind speed ever recorded at 231 mph in April 1934) and the notoriously harsh conditions of its summit area. The variety produces small, round, red cherry tomatoes (about 1 inch) with good, sweet-tart flavor in 52–60 days from transplant — one of the fastest-maturing cherry tomatoes available. The compact, determinate plants (24–36 inches) are appropriate for container growing and produce a compressed flush of fruit ideal for gardeners who want to can or preserve cherry tomatoes in quantity rather than harvest over an extended season. Cold tolerance allows fruit set at nighttime temperatures approaching 45°F, making this variety one of a handful suitable for truly short growing seasons with cold nights throughout the summer.
sources: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension

name: Muchamiel Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; this Alicante market tomato is traditionally grown under light greenhouse cover for an extended, humidity-buffered fruiting season.
directions: Named for the town of Mutxamel near Alicante, this smooth-shouldered, pale green-to-pink beefsteak tomato is a staple of Valencian market gardens, grown for a balanced, low-acid flesh with few seeds that holds up well in thick slices. Stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vines and keep moisture consistent through fruit development, since irregular watering tends to show up as cracking around the shoulders on this smooth-skinned type. Harvest when fruit has colored but is still firm, and expect strong production into early autumn where summers run long and hot.
sources: Generalitat Valenciana Conselleria d'Agricultura landrace documentation

name: Mucho Nacho Jalapeño Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Mucho Nacho is an All-America Selections award-winning jalapeño variety producing exceptionally large fruits (4–5 inches long versus standard jalapeño's 2–3 inches) with thick, meaty walls and heat in the 10,000–12,000 SHU range — hotter than TAM Jalapeño but similar in shape, designed for nachos and poppers where large size matters.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; Mucho Nacho is a vigorous, productive plant well-suited to Gulf Coast and Southern growing seasons. Mucho Nacho is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning jalapeño developed specifically to produce extra-large (4–5 inch long), thick-walled jalapeño fruits that are large enough for easy stuffing for jalapeño poppers and have enough surface area for maximum nacho topping use — the name directly references its intended use. The heat level (10,000–12,000 SHU) is somewhat hotter than many standard jalapeño varieties and significantly hotter than TAM Jalapeño, making it authentic jalapeño heat in a much larger package. The very thick walls (up to 1/4 inch) make Mucho Nacho excellent for grilling whole (the thick walls hold up without burning through) and for stuffing with cream cheese or other fillings. Ripens from dark green to red; can be harvested and used at the green stage (most common) or allowed to ripen red for a slightly different, sweeter flavor. High productivity and disease resistance make it one of the most reliable jalapeño varieties for home garden use.

name: Muir Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring through late spring, or in fall for a cool-season crop; Muir is notably heat- and bolt-tolerant for a loose-leaf lettuce, extending the harvest window later into warm weather than most leaf types.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; thin to 6–10 inches and harvest as cut-and-come-again or as full heads. Muir is a French heirloom oakleaf-type loose-leaf lettuce developed as a heat-tolerant selection, producing a loose, upright rosette of thick, savoyed, chartreuse-green leaves with a distinctively crisp, succulent texture and mild, sweet flavor that holds up better than most leaf lettuces once temperatures start climbing. Its unusually thick, crinkled leaf texture also makes it more forgiving of the wilting summer sun than thinner-leafed varieties, and it is slower to turn bitter as it approaches bolting. A useful bridge variety for gardeners who want fresh salad greens into the early part of a Gulf South summer before switching to heat-adapted greens, in zone 3–10.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Mulato Isleno Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March. Mulato Isleno is a dried chile variety that requires the full summer season to develop and ripen; allow fruits to turn chocolate-brown on the plant before harvesting for drying. In zone 9 the long, warm growing season is ideal for this variety's development.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Mulato Isleno is a poblano-type dried chile grown specifically for its distinctive chocolate-brown dried form rather than for fresh use — unlike the more common ancho (dried red poblano), the mulato is harvested at a later stage when fruits turn from green directly to dark brown, producing a darker, smokier, more complex dried chile with chocolate, coffee, and dried fruit undertones. It is one of the three chiles traditionally used in mole negro (with ancho and pasilla), contributing a smoky depth that neither ancho nor pasilla provides alone. Dry fully ripe, dark-brown fruits in a dehydrator or low oven for 2–4 hours until leathery and pliable. Plants are productive on fertile soil in zone 9 and tend to be tall with upright growth habit.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — Mulato Type Chile
University of California Cooperative Extension — Dried Chile Types
Slow Food USA — Mexican Dried Chiles

name: Mulato Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start January–February and transplant February–March. Mulato is a full-season pepper requiring 80–100 days to first mature fruit — start early for best zone 9 production before summer heat peaks.
directions: Start seeds at 75–80°F and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Mulato is a Mexican dried chile closely related to poblano but from a distinct gene pool (the seed color is tan, versus black for poblano/ancho) that produces heart-shaped, medium-large fruits, dark green turning dark brownish-black (rather than red) when fully ripe and dried. In dried form, mulato is one of the trio of chiles (together with ancho and pasilla) used in traditional Mexican mole negro sauce — its distinctive contribution is a dark, chocolate-tobacco, raisin-like complexity that makes mole negro deep and bittersweet. Heat level is mild to moderate (500–2,500 Scoville). Fresh mulato fruits are used in chiles rellenos and sauces; dried mulatos are rehydrated for mole and enchilada sauces. The plants are productive in zone 9's warm season and the fruits dry naturally on the plant in hot, dry conditions or can be dried in a dehydrator. An essential ingredient for serious Mexican cooking and home food preservers.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University — Mulato Pepper
Diana Kennedy: The Art of Mexican Cooking, Bantam Books 1989
National Plant Germplasm System — Capsicum annuum accessions

name: Mule Team Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; stake or cage this indeterminate vine, and expect steady production right up to frost.
directions: Mule Team belongs to a small family of Americana-named heirloom tomatoes developed by the same hobbyist breeder as Box Car Willie, and the seed nearly disappeared before being rediscovered stored in glass jars decades later and grown out by tomato collector Dr. Carolyn Male. The sturdy, drought-tolerant indeterminate vines are abundant producers of eight to twelve ounce beefsteak fruit with rich, juicy, zippy-sweet flavor, and the plants keep fruit quality consistent from the first harvest through the last frost of the season rather than tapering off in late summer heat. It is a dependable choice for gardeners who want a hearty slicing tomato without the fussiness of some other large-fruited heirlooms.

name: Multipik Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70°F; Multipik carries the 'precocious yellow' gene, which keeps fruit a clean, bright yellow even when the plant is infected with mosaic viruses that would otherwise mottle and discolor the skin of most yellow squash — a real practical advantage in aphid-prone Gulf South gardens where mosaic virus is common.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Multipik is a widely grown yellow straightneck summer squash hybrid valued for heavy, sustained production and for its 'precocious' gene, which masks the green mottling that mosaic viruses normally cause, so fruit keeps its attractive, uniform bright yellow color for market and table even under virus pressure. The compact, open bush habit produces slender, smooth-skinned fruit best picked young at 5-6 inches for the most tender texture. Because summer squash is highly attractive to aphids that spread mosaic viruses in humid Gulf Coast gardens, Multipik's cosmetic virus tolerance helps keep the harvest looking good even in a bad aphid year. Check plants daily during peak production and pick promptly, since squash left on the vine quickly grows oversized and seedy.
sources: seed catalog reference (Harris Seeds, Holmes Seed Company)

name: München Bier Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring 2–6 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for fall harvest; München Bier (Munich Beer) is a large, round, white-skinned German radish cultivated specifically for the traditional Bavarian custom of serving thick radish slices with beer — large (tennis ball to baseball-sized) round roots with pure white skin and flesh, mild-to-moderate radish bite, and a dense, juicy texture ideal for the accordion-sliced 'Radi' presentation traditional in Bavarian beer gardens.
directions: Sow 1/2 inch deep in cool weather; thin to 4–6 inches apart (important for large root development); keep consistently moist to prevent cracking; harvest when roots reach 2–3 inches in diameter for best flavor — overripe roots become pithy and hot. München Bier is a traditional Bavarian radish variety with an intimate connection to German beer garden culture: in Munich's famous outdoor beer gardens and throughout Bavaria, a 'Radi' (the Bavarian German word for radish) served alongside a Masskrug (liter) of beer is as traditional and culturally fixed as pretzels and sausages. The Bavarian Radi is always München Bier or a similar large, white, round variety — never the small red radishes of American experience — and it is served in a specific traditional way: the entire large root is scored with a spiral cut from top to bottom using a special tool (a Radihobel), accordioned apart to fan out into a long, beautiful spiral, rubbed with salt to draw out the juices, and eaten slice by slice as an accompaniment to beer. The flavor is mildly peppery and refreshing, with good crunch and juiciness, and the large size allows the elaborate spiral cutting presentation impossible with small radishes. München Bier is one of the few radish varieties specifically sized and textured for this presentation; it is also excellent sliced thick for salads, grated for German-style radish salads with vinegar and oil dressing, or pickled.
sources: German Federal Office for Plant Varieties (Bundessortenamt)

name: Munchkin Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills or rows after last frost; Munchkin pumpkin vines are shorter and more compact than full-sized pumpkin vines, making them suitable for smaller garden spaces. For fall decorative harvest, count back 100 days from desired harvest date. In zone 9, plant May–June for a September harvest. Each vine typically produces 8–15 miniature pumpkins; harvest when rind is hard and fully orange.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 2–3 plants after last frost in full sun; harvest when rind has hardened completely and is uniformly deep orange. Munchkin is a 1996 All-America Selections-winning miniature pumpkin that produces perfectly proportioned, small (4–5 inches in diameter, 3–5 oz) pumpkins with the classic Halloween pumpkin shape — deeply ridged, round, bright orange, with a proportionally large corky stem — in quantities of 8–15 per vine. The scale and perfect form of Munchkin pumpkins have made them the dominant decorative miniature pumpkin in the American market: they look like standard pumpkins shrunk to one-tenth their normal size, with all the visual appeal intact. Their most popular use is as tabletop decorations, door step arrangements, and centerpieces for autumn events; the small size and hard rind give them good postharvest longevity (4–8 weeks in cool conditions) for extended decorative use. Munchkin also has the distinction of being edible — the sweet, dense flesh makes excellent pumpkin puree, though the small size means significant work for a small yield — but most growers treat it purely as a decorative crop. Very productive and highly marketable at farm stands, farmers markets, and pumpkin patches where customers specifically seek miniature varieties. A top-selling item for autumn specialty crop producers.
sources: All-America Selections — Munchkin pumpkin AAS winner 1996
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Mini Pumpkin Variety Comparison
University of Illinois Extension — Specialty Pumpkin and Gourd Production

name: Munich Bier Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool weather; Munich Bier grows considerably larger than salad radishes and needs a bit more room and time to size up, so thin seedlings generously.
directions: Sow seed directly half an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and thin to a few inches apart, since this variety forms a substantially larger root than typical salad radishes. Munich Bier is an old German heirloom traditionally served whole, sliced, or spiraled and lightly salted as a salty, crunchy snack alongside beer in Bavarian beer gardens, a use quite different from the quick-growing salad radishes most American gardeners know. Its large white roots stay crisp and mild-flavored even at full size, resisting the pithiness and heat that ruins many radishes left in the ground too long. Harvest once roots reach 3-4 inches across, and keep soil evenly moist throughout growth for the best crisp, mild-flavored roots.

name: Murasaki Fioretto Cauliflower
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in midsummer for a fall crop; Murasaki (Japanese for 'purple') is part of the long-stemmed Fioretto series rather than a traditional single-head cauliflower.
directions: Start transplants and set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Murasaki Fioretto is an AAS-winning stick-type cauliflower that first forms a compact purple head, then elongates into loose, bunchable, tender-stemmed florets that can be harvested at 3-4 inches for bagging or left to reach 8 inches for bunching, similar in habit to broccolini. Its vivid violet-purple color is heat tolerant and stays vibrant through cooking, shifting to fuchsia when pickled and to golden brown when roasted or sautéed. The mild, sweet flavor and tender stems need no peeling, and the compact plant holds in the field well past typical cauliflower harvest windows without declining in quality.
sources: All-America Selections — Cauliflower Murasaki Fioretto 70 F1 winner announcement

name: Murasaki Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips 2–4 weeks after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Murasaki requires a full 95–110 days, so plant as early as possible in the South. It performs well in the Gulf Coast heat and produces excellent tubers with a slightly longer season than standard varieties.
directions: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose, sandy-loam soil in full sun; murasaki (purple in Japanese) sweet potato is a Japanese-origin variety producing long, slender tubers with striking dark purple skin and off-white to cream-colored flesh — a distinct and useful contrast to the Okinawan purple-flesh type, with a dry, chestnut-like sweetness and firm texture that holds up beautifully in roasting, frying, and sautéing where orange-flesh sweet potatoes would become too soft. The flavor is rich, mildly sweet, and nutty with a savory quality that makes it more versatile in non-sweet preparations than moist orange types. Widely grown in Japan and increasingly popular in the United States as interest in Asian sweet potato varieties grows; excellent for Japanese-style roasted sweet potatoes, tempura, and savory preparations that benefit from a firmer texture.

name: Murasaki-29 Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; a distinct Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station release bred from L89-72, separate from the older Japanese Murasaki cultivar already grown, and selected for root-knot nematode resistance.
directions: Murasaki-29 was bred by the Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station from an open-pollinated cross with the female parent L89-72 as a specialty white-flesh alternative to orange-fleshed dessert types like Beauregard. It has purple skin and white flesh, with shorter, elliptical, non-lobed storage roots compared to Beauregard. Unlike many other white-flesh specialty types such as O'Henry, Murasaki-29 carries useful resistance to southern root-knot nematode, comparable to Covington, Evangeline, and Jewel. Its firmer, less sweet flesh suits roasting and savory preparations rather than the moist, syrupy texture of orange-fleshed baking types.

name: Music Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Music is one of the most widely grown porcelain hardneck garlics in North America, prized for very large, easy-to-peel cloves.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Music is a Canadian-origin porcelain hardneck that has become one of the most popular garlic varieties in North America, producing large bulbs with just four to six exceptionally big, easy-to-peel cloves under bright white skin, and a rich, full, well-balanced flavor that holds up well raw or cooked. As a hardneck, it sends up a curling flower scape in late spring that should be removed once curled to redirect the plant's energy into bulb development; the scapes are edible and excellent in stir-fries or pesto. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded spot, then trim and store; Music has moderate storage life, typically five to seven months under good conditions.

name: Musica Romano Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 60°F; Musica is a Dutch-bred flat Romano-type pole bean with unusually wide, flat pods (up to 1 inch wide) reaching 8–10 inches long. It requires a trellis or pole support to 6–7 feet. Unlike round-podded pole beans that become stringy and coarse as they size up, Musica maintains remarkable tenderness and sweet flavor well past the size at which most beans become tough — pods can be harvested at full size (9–10 inches) without significant loss of texture. This characteristic makes Musica one of the most forgiving pole beans for busy gardeners who cannot harvest daily. In zone 9, direct sow March–April after last frost for spring production and again August–September for fall harvest.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 4–6 inches apart; provide a sturdy trellis or poles to 7 feet and harvest pods when flat and full-length (8–10 inches) but before seeds develop prominently inside. Musica Romano Pole Bean is a Dutch commercial variety developed specifically to combine the flat Romano-style pod shape beloved in Italian cuisine with the productivity and extended harvest window of a modern pole bean. The flat pod shape — wide (nearly 1 inch across) with a slightly rectangular cross-section rather than round — is the defining characteristic of the Romano bean type, which originated in Italy and represents a fundamentally different pod morphology from the round, pencil-thin beans of French filet types or the oval cross-section of standard American snap beans. Romano types are prized for a distinctive beany, almost meaty flavor that is more pronounced than round-podded types; this flavor intensity comes partly from the thicker pod walls and slightly higher dry matter content of the flat pod structure. Musica improves on older Romano varieties in two key ways: pods remain tender and stringless at large sizes (a significant practical advantage, since older Romano types become stringy once pods exceed 6–7 inches), and the plant produces heavily over an extended harvest window rather than the concentrated burst typical of bush bean types. The vigorous climbing plant (to 7 feet) is highly productive in warm conditions and particularly well-suited to zone 9's long warm season, where it can continue producing through fall when given a midsummer break from heat. Steam or blanch briefly for the best texture; Musica also holds up well in longer-cooked dishes like minestrone where flat Romano beans contribute body without dissolving.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Musica Romano Pole Bean variety notes and harvest timing recommendations
Territorial Seed Company — Flat Romano pole bean comparison and Italian cooking applications
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Romano-type bean variety descriptions and culinary uses

name: Musquée de Maroc Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost in warm soil; Musquée de Maroc is a Moroccan heirloom distinguished from the smoother Musquée de Provence by its heavily warted, deeply ribbed rind.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in enriched hills once soil has warmed well after the last frost, giving vines ample room to sprawl. Musquée de Maroc is a Moroccan heirloom winter squash related to the better-known Musquée de Provence but set apart by its rough, heavily warted, deeply ribbed, orange-red rind, which encloses dense, sweet, deep orange flesh prized for roasting and soup. Fruits run large, commonly 15 to 25 pounds, so give hills generous spacing and a full warm season to finish. Harvest when the rind has hardened fully and the stem has begun to dry, cure for a couple of weeks, then store in a cool, dry spot where it keeps for months.

name: Musquee de Provence Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; in zone 9 plant March–June. Musquee de Provence requires a long, warm growing season — at least 110 days of warm weather. In zone 9 planting in April gives the fruit time to cure fully on the vine. As a Cucurbita moschata, it has better heat and humidity tolerance than Cucurbita maxima types. The large fruits (12–20+ lbs) benefit from being elevated on boards or straw to prevent rot where soil stays moist.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, rich, slightly acidic soil; Musquee de Provence (Musk of Provence) is a magnificent French heirloom pumpkin from the Provence region, producing large, deeply ridged, flat-round fruits with a muted tan to bronze-brown skin that develops rich russet-copper tones when fully mature. The deep orange-yellow flesh is exceptionally sweet, dense, and aromatic — the 'musquee' (musky) name refers to the intensely sweet, rich, slightly musky fragrance and flavor of the ripe flesh, considered among the finest-flavored of any large pumpkin. Fully matured fruits from this Cucurbita moschata variety develop complex flavor notes beyond ordinary pumpkin sweetness. The large, photogenic fruits (often 12–20 pounds) are classic French market pumpkins seen in Provençal farmers' markets in fall. In zone 9 the summer heat and humidity are well tolerated by this C. moschata type, which is more disease-resistant in warm climates than C. maxima varieties.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Musquee de Provence Pumpkin
Seed Savers Exchange — French Heirloom Pumpkin Varieties
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Winter Squash and Pumpkin Production

name: Musquée de Provence Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Musquée de Provence is a large, sprawling Cucurbita moschata pumpkin requiring substantial space (15–20 feet vine length) and a long, warm growing season of 95–115 days, making it well-suited to the Gulf South's extended warm season.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills (3–4 seeds per hill, thinned to 2) after last frost in warm, rich soil; Musquée de Provence is a spectacular heirloom pumpkin from the Provence region of southern France that produces deeply ribbed, flat-lobed, heavily textured fruits that turn from dark green to a rich tan-bronze at maturity, resembling giant rounds of aged cheese (it is often sold under the marketing name 'Fairytale Pumpkin' in the US). The large fruits (10–20 pounds, sometimes to 30 pounds) are as stunning ornamentally as they are culinarily valuable — the deep orange, dense, sweet flesh is comparable to butternut squash in flavor (Musquée de Provence is Cucurbita moschata, the same species as butternut) with excellent sweetness, minimal stringiness, and superb flavor when roasted, pureed into soups, or made into pie. The thick skin and hard rind give outstanding storage life (6–12 months in a cool, dry location), and the impressive size and dramatic appearance make the fruits valuable for both Thanksgiving decorations and serious cooking. Well-adapted to the heat and humidity of Gulf South summer production and a rewarding long-season crop in zone 8–11.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cucurbit Production Guide

name: My Joanie Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70F; My Joanie is a Mississippi heirloom on compact 4-foot plants that trialed as an early producer despite its late-variety reputation, making it a good fit for the long, hot Gulf Coast growing season.
directions: Soak seed overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep once soil is reliably warm; harvest pods at 3-4 inches every couple of days to keep plants productive. My Joanie is a Mississippi heirloom okra passed along through home gardeners before being preserved by Midwest seed-saving growers, distinguished by a dusky rose blush that washes over its grass-green pods rather than the solid red found in burgundy-type okra. Plants stay a manageable 4 feet tall and hold up well in a Kerr Center trial of heirloom okra varieties, where it out-yielded many taller types despite being marketed as a late producer. The mix of ornamental color and heavy yield makes it a good double-duty choice for a Gulf Coast vegetable bed that also needs to look good.
sources: Kerr Center for Sustainable Agriculture — Heirloom Okra Variety Trial

name: Nabechan Bunching Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring, or start a fall crop in midsummer; hilling soil around the base as stems lengthen produces the long blanched shanks traditional for negi.
directions: Nabechan is a traditional Japanese negi-type bunching onion grown for its long, thick, upright white shanks that resist splitting and curling even in hot weather. Sow into a shallow furrow and gradually mound soil around the base every few weeks as the plants grow, which blanches the lower stalk into the long white shaft prized for hot pot dishes. The sweet, mild flavor and non-bulbing habit make it equally useful sliced raw as a garnish or cooked whole in soups and nabemono. It tolerates both summer heat and winter cold well, allowing extended harvest windows in most temperate gardens.

name: Nadia Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Nadia is a vigorous, heat-tolerant hybrid that sets fruit reliably even in the hottest part of a Gulf South summer, when many eggplant varieties slow production.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm. Nadia is a widely grown hybrid eggplant producing glossy, deep purple-black, oval fruit with tender, non-bitter flesh and few seeds, on a vigorous, high-yielding plant especially valued for continuing to set fruit through peak summer heat when many other eggplant varieties slow down. Harvest fruit while the skin is still glossy and firm; dull, soft skin signals overripe fruit with more seeds and tougher flesh. Regular harvesting every few days keeps the plant productive over a long season, and staking helps support the heavy fruit load on the branches.

name: Naga Morich Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, then transplant once soil has warmed thoroughly.
directions: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks ahead of the last frost, providing bottom heat to speed the naturally slow chinense germination, and pot up seedlings before setting them out in warm soil. Give plants a long, hot growing season and steady moisture for the heaviest pod set. Naga Morich is a traditional Bangladeshi and northeastern Indian pepper closely related to bhut jolokia, prized for its intense heat and slightly fruity aroma, and it is a parent of several later superhot hybrids. Pods ripen from green to a wrinkled orange-red and should be handled with gloves.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Naga Viper Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, since this hybrid superhot germinates slowly.
directions: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost with consistent bottom heat, then harden off and transplant once nights stay warm, since this hybrid resents cool, wet soil. Keep the compact plants evenly watered and staked once fruit sets heavily along the branches. Naga Viper was bred in England by crossing Bhut Jolokia, Naga Morich, and Trinidad Scorpion lines, and it briefly held recognition as the world's hottest pepper around 2011 before later superhots surpassed it. The knobby pods ripen from green to red and carry a sharp, lingering heat.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Nagasaki Long Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant once nights are reliably above 55F.
directions: A Japanese heirloom producing extra-long, slender dark purple fruit with a velvety, nutty flavor that stays sweet and never bitter even as pods size up. Tender skin allows the fruit to be eaten raw, grilled, or sauteed without peeling. Plants show good tolerance for summer heat and humidity, making this a reliable choice for warm climates. Harvest regularly to keep the glossy skin tight and encourage continued fruit set.

name: Naked Bear
plantingNote: Start indoors about three weeks before the last frost and transplant out once danger of frost has passed, since direct sowing germinates unreliably.
directions: This squat, orange F1 mini pumpkin was bred to deliver hull-less, roastable seeds alongside flesh sized for a single pie. Because direct seeding is unreliable for this type, start it indoors and transplant once the weather is settled and warm. It is a heavy nitrogen feeder, so work compost or fertilizer into the bed before setting plants out, and give vines room to ramble. At 2-4 lbs apiece with a thick stubby handle, each fruit is a tidy one-pie portion, and the seeds roast well as a snack.

name: Nancy Hall Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant rooted slips 2–4 weeks after last frost once soil is thoroughly warm, in loose, well-drained soil built into ridges in full sun; Nancy Hall is an old Deep South dooryard heirloom grown for its exceptionally moist, sweet flesh.
directions: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in well-drained, loose soil formed into ridges in full sun; Nancy Hall is a Deep South heirloom variety grown since the early 20th century for pale copper-pink skinned tubers with soft, exceptionally moist, deep-orange flesh that cooks up custardy rather than dry or mealy, a texture many older Southern gardeners still prefer to modern commercial types like Beauregard. Vines are long and vigorous and tubers form somewhat irregularly shaped, so hill soil up generously and harvest carefully to avoid bruising the tender skin. Dig once vines begin to yellow in fall, before the first frost, and cure at warm temperatures and high humidity for one to two weeks to firm the skin, heal nicks, and sweeten the flesh before storing.

name: Nankeen Cotton
plantingNote: Direct sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep once soil has thoroughly warmed well past last frost, into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Nankeen is a naturally tan-to-brown-lint heirloom selection of upland cotton requiring the same long, hot, frost-free season as any cotton.
directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the growing season is reliably warm, following the same culture as any upland cotton. Nankeen is one of the oldest documented naturally colored cotton types, its warm tan-to-brown lint historically spun and woven into the durable buff-colored cloth that gave Nanjing, China's export cotton -- and eventually the color name "nankeen" -- its fame; Thomas Jefferson is recorded growing nankeen cotton in his Monticello gardens in the early 1800s. The lint's natural color eliminates the need for dyeing and tends to darken slightly with washing and UV exposure over the life of the finished cloth. Showy pale yellow flowers fade to pink before dropping to reveal green bolls that split open at full maturity, exposing the naturally tan lint; pick promptly once open to keep it clean and free of weathering stains. Rotate the planting site yearly and watch for the same boll weevil and aphid pressures as other cotton.
sources: Thomas Jefferson's Monticello -- Historic Vegetable and Fiber Varieties

name: Nansemond Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; grown in Southside Virginia since 1850 and is one of the oldest sweet potato heirlooms still in cultivation.
directions: Nansemond is a 19th-century heirloom named for Nansemond County in Southside Virginia, where it has been a favorite home-garden variety since 1850. It produces yellow-fleshed roots on vigorous vines, with a red-skinned subvariety also historically grown in the region. Regionally it has traditionally been baked into sweet potato pies, sometimes made with toasted peanuts or peanut flour worked into the crust. Along with Southern Queen and Hayman, it remains one of the dependable pre-1900 sweet potato varieties still maintained by heirloom seed preservationists.

name: Nantes Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in loose, deep, stone-free soil; Nantes-type carrots are virtually coreless and have a nearly cylindrical shape that requires deep loose soil — break up any compaction to 12 inches before sowing.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, deep, stone-free, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches when 2 inches tall; Nantes is the most widely grown home garden carrot type, originating in Nantes, France — producing 6–7 inch, blunt-tipped, cylindrical carrots with remarkably sweet, crisp, virtually coreless flesh and thin skin that doesn't require peeling. The standard against which other home garden carrots are judged for flavor and tenderness. Requires loose, deep, stone-free soil for best shape; rocky or compacted soils produce forked, stunted roots. Excellent raw, steamed, or roasted; also one of the best for juicing.

name: Nanticoke Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed; allow ample room for vigorous vines.
directions: Nanticoke is an heirloom landrace squash grown for generations by the Nanticoke people of the Delmarva Peninsula, Delaware and the Eastern Shore of Maryland, and is one of the few surviving Native American winter squash lines from the Eastern Woodlands. Fruits have a mottled, speckled green rind that cures to a hard protective shell suited to long winter storage. The flesh is rich golden-orange, dense, fine-grained, and sweet, good for baking and roasting. It is maintained today primarily by seed-preservation and Indigenous seed-rematriation projects.
sources: The Seed Farm at Princeton University

name: Napa Cabbage Blues
plantingNote: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for fall harvest. Blues is particularly tolerant of warm fall temperatures at the start of the season, which is the most common reason napa cabbage fails in zone 9 — it sets heads even when early fall temperatures are still warm, then matures perfectly in December–February. Spring plantings in zone 9 (January–February transplant) are shorter-season and may bolt before heading fully.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Blues is a high-performing napa cabbage hybrid selected specifically for resistance to tipburn and premature bolting — the two primary failure modes for napa cabbage in warmer regions. The compact, upright heads weigh 4–6 pounds with tightly wrapped, pale yellow-green interior leaves and crisp, juicy, mildly sweet flavor that is ideal for fresh eating, kimchi, stir-fries, braises, and raw slaws. Blues develops solid heads without the loose, poorly-wrapped outer structure common in heat-stressed napa cabbage; the improved tip-burn resistance means more marketable heads per planting. In zone 9 fall is the primary season — transplant in September for harvest from November through January. Consistent soil moisture is critical for head development; water stress causes loose, poorly-filled heads and encourages premature bolting.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Blues Napa Cabbage Performance Trials
University of California Cooperative Extension — Asian Brassica Crops for California
Rutgers University — Asian Vegetables: Napa Cabbage Production

name: Napoli Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow in well-tilled, loose soil; Napoli is a fast-maturing Nantes type that can be sown earlier than most carrots in spring as it germinates reliably in cool soils. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall/winter harvest. Napoli is particularly well-suited to early spring sowing in colder climates (USDA zones 5–7) where it can be direct-sown as soon as soil can be worked, producing an early crop before summer heat arrives. Harvest when roots reach 6–7 inches for best flavor.
directions: Direct sow seeds thinly, 0.25 inch deep, in loose, well-amended soil; thin to 2–3 inch spacing when plants are 2 inches tall. Napoli is a Bejo Seeds Nantes-type hybrid that has earned a strong reputation among market gardeners and home growers as one of the most consistent early-season carrots available — reliably producing smooth, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots 6–7 inches long with rich orange color, good internal uniformity, and the clean, sweet Nantes flavor in just 58–68 days. The Nantes type is distinguished from other carrot forms by its nearly cylindrical shape (minimal taper from shoulder to tip), blunt end, almost coreless interior with minimal differentiation between phloem and xylem, and clean, crisp texture that makes it the most versatile shape for both fresh eating and cooking. Napoli's early maturity makes it especially valuable for areas where the growing season is short or where spring planting must be followed by summer crops. The roots have good storage quality and hold well in the ground after reaching maturity without significant quality loss. Napoli has been a consistent top performer in university carrot variety trials across the northeastern United States and Europe, where its combination of earliness, quality, and reliable stand establishment have made it a standard recommendation. A dependable all-purpose Nantes carrot well suited to both home garden and small-farm production.
sources: Bejo Seeds — Napoli carrot variety notes
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Spring Carrot Variety Trial Results
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Nantes Carrot Comparison Chart

name: Natacha Escarole
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant out in late summer for a fall harvest; in mild-winter climates it also works as an overwintering crop when set out in early fall for winter and early-spring cutting.
directions: Natacha is a French-bred escarole selected for large, heavy heads packed with abundant, tender leaves surrounding a creamy, well-blanched heart. It stands out for its strong resistance to bolting, tipburn, and bottom rot, which lets it hold in the garden longer than many older escarole types, especially in hot or humid weather. As with other broad-leaved endives, gathering and tying the outer leaves a week or two before harvest deepens the self-blanching of the heart and mellows the characteristic mild bitterness.

name: Navajo Cushaw Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in full sun after last frost; this cushaw was collected at the Navajo Fair in Shiprock, New Mexico, and is maintained at roughly 4,900 feet on the Colorado Plateau, a cooler high-desert setting than most Sonoran cushaws.
directions: Navajo Cushaw, also called Tail Squash for its long, curved neck, was collected at the Navajo Fair in Shiprock, New Mexico, and has since been maintained by seed-saving partner farmers at around 4,900 feet elevation on the Colorado Plateau. Its elongated fruit has green-and-white striped skin and a more dramatically curved neck than most other Southwestern cushaws, with cream-to-light-orange flesh inside. Like other Cucurbita argyrosperma cushaws it keeps well in storage, making it a useful winter staple for high-desert households. Direct sow after last frost in full sun and give the sprawling vines plenty of room to run.

name: Navan Potato
plantingNote: Grows and stores much like its parent Maris Piper; give it a full maincrop season and hill well to keep the developing tubers covered.
directions: Navan was bred in Northern Ireland in 1987 from Maris Piper stock, inheriting that parent's high dry-matter flesh while being selected specifically for frying performance. Plant seed potatoes into loose, fertile soil and hill the rows as growth progresses to prevent the tubers near the surface from greening in the light. Because Navan was bred with chip-shop use in mind, it holds its shape and crisps well when cut into chips or wedges, a step up from boiling-focused varieties. Lift the maincrop once foliage has yellowed and died down, then cure and store tubers in a dark, cool space before use.

name: Naxos Potato
plantingNote: Plant seed tubers as soon as soil can be worked in spring; growers on Naxos take advantage of the island's fertile plain and spring rains to grow the crop without irrigation until tubers bulk up.
directions: Naxos potato is grown on the fertile central plain of the Cycladic island of Naxos, the only island in the group with enough fresh water and arable soil to support a significant potato crop, and it holds European PDO status. Plant seed tubers in well-drained, moderately fertile ground as soon as the soil can be worked, and hill soil around the stems as they grow to protect developing tubers from sun greening. Harvest once foliage yellows and dies back, curing tubers briefly in a shaded, airy spot before storage. The crop is known locally for a smooth, thin skin and firm, flavorful flesh well suited to roasting and the island's traditional potato dishes.
sources: Greek Ministry of Rural Development and Food

name: Neal's Paymaster Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks after soil is reliably warm; this variety's tall stalks and double-ear habit reward deep, fertile soil and a full-length warm season.
directions: Bred by farmer William Haskell Neal of Wilson County, Tennessee, beginning his field selection in 1898 and introducing seed to neighbors by 1912, Neal's Paymaster was the first reliably two-ears-per-stalk dent corn, with white kernels on a distinctive red cob and towering 9-10-foot stalks; by 1937 it reportedly accounted for roughly a third of Tennessee's entire corn crop, prized for shrugging off heat and marginal soil that defeated other field corns of the day. Plant it in blocks for wind pollination, give it a full season of warmth and moisture, and expect genuinely heavy yields per stalk thanks to the twin ears. This is a field (not sweet) corn grown to dry for cornmeal, grits, hominy, or livestock feed, so let ears cure fully on the stalk before shelling and storing.
sources: Main Street Media of Tennessee, Cheatham County Exchange

name: Nebraska Wedding Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Nebraska Wedding grows on relatively compact plants that still benefit from a stake or cage as fruit loads increase.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed, providing support for the fruit-laden branches. This variety was carried by pioneer families from Minnesota to the Nebraska plains in the late 1800s, and tradition held that a pinch of its seed was given to Nebraska brides as a wedding gift so they could grow it in their own gardens. The plants yield deep orange, globe-shaped fruit with a rich, sweet flavor and few seeds, and the variety was later documented and preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange network.

name: Nebula Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant after frost; the determinate habit and tolerance for cool nights make it a good match for short or marine-influenced growing seasons.
directions: Nebula is a determinate Wild Garden Seed original that fills the gap between its sister varieties, with red, slightly flattened fruit a bit larger than Estate but smaller than Home Stoop. Fascinated locules give the flesh a softer, juicier slice than Estate's firmer texture. It is a heavy yielder bred to perform well under moderate warmth with cool nighttime temperatures, which suits Pacific Northwest and other marine-climate gardens. Because it is determinate, it needs less aggressive staking than the farm's taller indeterminate lines, though a cage still helps keep fruit-laden branches off the ground.

name: Neckarkönigin Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; provide a tall pole or trellis, since vines climb vigorously and crop over a long season.
directions: Sow seed directly 1 inch deep at the base of poles or a trellis once soil is warm, thinning to 4-6 inches between plants. Neckarkönigin ('Queen of the Neckar,' named for the river running through the Swabian region of southwestern Germany where it was traditionally grown) is a vigorous German heirloom pole bean producing long, flat, green pods on tall climbing vines. Pick pods young and tender at 6-8 inches for the best snap-bean texture, and harvest frequently, since regular picking keeps vines setting new pods through the warm months rather than diverting energy into maturing seed.

name: Nelson Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost; Nelson is a fast-maturing Nantes-type carrot bred to hold good sweetness even when sown or harvested in warm weather, a real advantage in the Gulf South where summer heat usually turns carrots bitter and woody.
directions: Sow seed thinly, 1/4 inch deep, in well-loosened, stone-free soil 2-4 weeks before last frost; thin to 2-3 inches between plants when seedlings are 2 inches tall. Nelson is a fast-maturing Nantes-type hybrid carrot specifically noted for retaining good, consistent sweetness even when grown through warmer weather than most carrots tolerate well, since heat typically pushes carrots toward a stronger, more bitter flavor and woody texture.
