The smooth, cylindrical, blunt-tipped roots are uniformly deep orange with a small core and crisp, juicy texture. In zone 8-9, sow in late winter for an early spring harvest and again in late summer for a fall crop, and expect Nelson to hold its sweet flavor through a wider harvest window than standard carrot varieties.

name: Nemagold Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F; Nemagold's nematode resistance makes it a good choice for older Gulf Coast garden beds with a history of root-knot nematode.
directions: Nemagold was developed in the mid-20th century as an improved, root-knot-nematode-resistant strain within the Puerto Rico type of sweet potato, released to protect Gulf South growers from nematode damage that plagued earlier orange-fleshed varieties. The moist, deep-orange flesh and coppery-orange skin closely resemble Beauregard and Puerto Rico in flavor and texture, producing smooth, blocky roots that store and cure well. Because it tolerates the sandy, nematode-prone soils common across the Gulf Coast, Nemagold remains a dependable heirloom choice for gardeners battling nematode pressure in older vegetable beds. Set slips after the soil has warmed in late spring and let the long, warm Gulf Coast season fully mature the crop before the first fall frost.

name: Neon Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F. Neon is compact and early-maturing, making it a good fit for containers as well as garden beds.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Neon produces smooth, glossy, vividly hot-pink to magenta fruit that stands out sharply against the plant's foliage, with mild, tender, nearly seedless flesh similar to standard Italian eggplants. It matures notably early for an eggplant and sets fruit heavily on a relatively compact plant, making it a productive choice for smaller gardens and containers as well as open beds. Harvest at 4-6 inches long while the skin is still glossy and firm, since fruit left too long dulls in color and toughens. Its striking coloring also makes it a popular market and specialty-produce variety.

name: Neos Frisée Endive
plantingNote: Start indoors 3-4 weeks before transplanting out; in most regions transplant in late summer for a fall harvest. Neos is a uniform hybrid frisee bred for reliable self-blanching and faster maturity than heirloom curly endives.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun once seedlings have several true leaves. Neos is a hybrid frisee endive selected for a compact, upright habit and finely cut, curled leaves that shade the heart naturally, producing a pale, tender center with little need for tying. It matures faster and more uniformly than many open-pollinated curly endives, which makes it a favorite among market growers for consistent harvests. Use the mildly bitter, delicate leaves raw in composed salads such as salade lyonnaise, or briefly wilted with warm bacon dressing.

name: Nepal Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost; transplant into warm soil after frost danger passes and stake the vigorous, potato-leaved vines.
directions: Collected from a Himalayan village garden, this heirloom is distinguished by soft, blue-green, potato-leaf foliage and heavy clusters of smooth, pink-red, medium-large globe fruits with few seeds and a rich sweet-tart flavor. The vigorous indeterminate vines are reliably productive through hot, humid conditions and have shown good foliage disease tolerance in Gulf South trial gardens compared to many other pink heirlooms. Stake or cage plants well, since the potato-leaf vines are dense and heavy once fruit sets, and pick at full color for the best flavor.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds Variety Catalog

name: Neptune Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January for March transplanting. Neptune was bred by the University of Florida specifically to keep setting fruit through the high-heat, high-humidity stretch of the Gulf South summer.
directions: Start seeds 6-8 weeks before transplanting at 70-80F; Neptune is a heat-set tomato developed by the University of Florida as part of a long-running Southeastern breeding effort to keep fruit set going once nighttime temperatures climb into the mid-70s, a point at which most standard hybrids stop setting fruit. The medium-to-large, round, red fruits have solid, well-balanced flavor and enough firmness to ship and hold well, making Neptune a dependable choice for a continuous summer harvest rather than a single early flush. Plants carry good resistance to common Southern tomato diseases, but a preventive fungicide or copper spray schedule still helps in the humid Gulf South. Stake or cage plants early, since they grow vigorously, and keep watering consistent to avoid blossom end rot in the region's heavy summer rains followed by dry spells.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Variety Trials
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomato Variety Selection
Clemson Cooperative Extension — Heat-Set Tomato Varieties

name: Nerima Daikon
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer in deeply worked soil for a long, slow fall-to-winter finish; Nerima needs more time than quick commercial daikon types to develop its signature long, tapering root.
directions: Sow directly into deeply tilled, stone-free soil since this long heirloom root forks or distorts in compacted or shallow beds. Named for the Tokyo district where it was developed generations ago, Nerima produces a slender, tapering, mostly below-ground root historically prized above all other daikon for making takuan, the crunchy yellow pickled radish served throughout Japan. Roots hold their dense, fibrous texture well through curing and fermentation, which is exactly the quality that made this variety the traditional choice for pickling rather than fresh eating. Harvest in late fall once roots reach full size and before hard freezes, and allow a few days of post-harvest withering if preparing for traditional sun-dried pickling.

name: Nero di Milano Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost; its compact bush habit suits raised beds and smaller Gulf Coast garden plots better than sprawling vine-type squash.
directions: Nero di Milano, meaning 'black of Milan,' is a traditional Italian zucchini from Lombardy prized in home gardens for its very dark, near-black-green skin and compact, open bush growth habit that makes fruit easy to spot and pick. It is among the earliest zucchini to begin bearing, and fruit is best harvested young at 6-8 inches, when the skin is tender and the flavor sweetest. The tidy, non-sprawling plant produces steadily over a long season, making it a practical choice for gardeners who want continuous zucchini without the vine sprawl of many other summer squash types. As an open-pollinated Italian heirloom, its seed can be saved true from year to year.

name: Nero di Toscana Kale
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. palmifolia 'Nero di Toscana'
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for a November–March harvest. Nero di Toscana is cold-hardy to about 10–15°F and is one of the kales with the longest productive season in zone 9, providing a continuous harvest of lower leaves from fall through late spring. The flavor improves dramatically after cold exposure — first frost converts starches to sugar and deepens the savory, mineral flavor of the dark leaves.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Nero di Toscana (also known as Lacinato kale, Dinosaur kale, or Cavolo Nero) is the traditional Italian black kale of Tuscany, producing long, strap-like leaves with a deeply blistered (savoyed) surface and an almost blue-black dark green color — the darkest of all kale types. The texture is firmer and the flavor is more savory, mineral, and complex than curly kale, with less bitterness and a sweeter, earthier depth that develops most fully after frost. Nero di Toscana is the authentic ingredient in ribollita (Tuscan bread and vegetable soup), farinata di cavolo nero, and braised Tuscan kale side dishes where curly kale cannot substitute. The long, upright growth habit exposes the lower leaves for continuous harvest while the growing tip extends upward — a productive cut-and-come-again pattern that provides months of harvest from a single planting. Remove individual outer leaves for harvest to allow continuous new growth from the center growing point.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Cavolo Nero di Toscana Presidio
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Kale Varieties for Florida
Seeds of Italy — Nero di Toscana Kale Growing Notes

name: Nero Tondo Radish
plantingNote: Sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, since roots develop their best flavor and store best when they mature in cool weather.
directions: Nero Tondo, Italian for round black, is a refined selection of the old Black Spanish type bred for rounder, more uniform roots and notably better bolt tolerance than the traditional heirloom strain. The rough, matte-black skin conceals dense, snow-white flesh with a sharp, peppery bite that mellows into an earthy sweetness when roasted or braised. Because the roots hold in the ground and in storage far longer than spring radishes, gardeners grow it as a keeper crop, pulling roots through fall and into winter for slaws, pickles, and cooked preparations.

name: Netted Gem Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed following last frost; Netted Gem, introduced around 1881, is the historic Michigan-area heirloom widely credited as the direct ancestor of the modern netted commercial cantaloupe.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following the last frost, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Introduced around 1881, Netted Gem produces small, round, densely netted fruit with sweet, salmon-orange flesh, and its heavy netting pattern and reliable sweetness made it enormously influential in American melon breeding — most of the netted cantaloupe types sold in grocery stores today trace back to selections made from this variety. The compact vines are productive and well suited to home gardens. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with gentle pressure and the netting has fully developed, indicating peak ripeness and sweetness.
sources: United States Department of Agriculture Pomological Watercolor Collection

name: Nevada Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or fall; in zone 9 sow January–February for spring or September–October for fall. Nevada is particularly tolerant of heat and is one of the best choices for extending the spring lettuce season in zone 9 — it holds without bolting 1–2 weeks longer than most lettuce varieties under warm conditions. Successive sowings every 3 weeks extend the harvest window. Shade cloth in late spring reduces bolting pressure.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Nevada is a French batavian-type lettuce selected specifically for heat tolerance and slow bolting — it holds usable quality in warm spring conditions 1–2 weeks longer than standard butterhead or looseleaf varieties before flowering, providing a meaningfully extended harvest window in warm climates like zone 9. The large, crisp, slightly frilly green leaves form a dense, semi-heading rosette similar to a looseleaf but with better structure and more crunch than floppy butterhead types. The flavor is fresh, mild, and slightly crisp — closer to iceberg in texture but without the blandness, and closer to looseleaf in flavor but with more body. Nevada is widely used by commercial producers in California and the Southwest who need a heat-tolerant green-leaf lettuce for late spring production windows. In zone 9 it is one of the most reliable lettuces for bridging the February–May spring season before summer heat ends production.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Nevada Lettuce Variety Notes
University of California Cooperative Extension — Heat-Tolerant Lettuce Varieties
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Batavian Lettuce

name: Neves Azorean Red Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Neves Azorean Red is a Portuguese-American heirloom brought to the United States by Azorean immigrant families and preserved through home seed saving, valued for its huge, meaty, low-seed fruit.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date and provide sturdy staking, since the vigorous indeterminate vines carry a heavy load of large fruit. Neves Azorean Red traces to Azorean immigrant families who brought tomato seed with them to New England and California and kept it going in home gardens for generations before it entered the wider heirloom seed trade; the deep pinkish-red beefsteak fruit is prized for its dense, meaty flesh, relatively small seed cavities, and low acidity, which makes for a tomato with almost no watery waste when sliced. Individual fruits commonly reach a pound or more on well-grown plants, and the rich, well-balanced flavor holds up in sandwiches and fresh salads as well as in sauce. As an open-pollinated heirloom it saves true from seed with basic isolation, letting gardeners keep the family line going the same way it has been passed down for decades.

name: New Big Dwarf Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the sturdy, potato-leaf dwarf habit needs only light staking and suits raised beds and large containers.
directions: New Big Dwarf was introduced by the Livingston Seed Company in 1917 as an improvement on earlier dwarf tomato lines, combining a compact, potato-leaf, non-sprawling habit with unusually large fruit for its class. Mature pink beefsteak-type tomatoes can approach a pound, with smooth shoulders and rich, well-balanced flavor on plants short enough to grow without a full cage. Its early-20th-century dwarf, rugose-leaved genetics made it a natural choice for modern hybridizers, and it stands behind later Dwarf Tomato Project crosses, including as a parent of Tasmanian Chocolate alongside Paul Robeson. Harvest as fruit fully colors and softens slightly at the blossom end for best flavor.

name: New Hampshire Midget Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, or start indoors 3 weeks early in short-season areas.
directions: Bred at the University of New Hampshire and released in 1951, this is one of the earliest true short-vine watermelons ever developed, making it a workhorse for northern gardeners and anyone with a short frost-free window. Vines stay compact enough for a large container or a small raised bed, and the round 4-6 pound fruits with pale flesh mature fast rather than for exceptional sweetness. Keep soil evenly moist through fruit set, then ease off watering as the melons near ripeness to concentrate what sugar they do develop. Its main value is reliability where longer-season Southern varieties simply run out of summer.
sources: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension

name: New Mexico No. 6 Chile
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; New Mexico No. 6 is an early New Mexico State University green chile release grown the same way as later Hatch-type selections.
directions: New Mexico No. 6 was released in 1950 by Dr. Roy Harper at New Mexico State University in Las Cruces, selected in 1947 from an unnamed local chile population growing in the Mesilla Valley. Compared with Fabian Garcia's earlier New Mexico No. 9, its pods dried roughly a fifth faster and carried only about half the pungency, qualities that suited it well to the chile processing industry as well as the fresh green chile market. It served directly as the parent stock for New Mexico No. 6-4, selected from it in 1957 to reduce pod heat even further, and that later selection went on to become the long-running commercial standard for New Mexico green chile while New Mexico No. 6 itself faded from wide cultivation. Grow it exactly as later NMSU green chile releases: start indoors, transplant after frost danger passes into full sun and well-drained soil, and harvest pods green for roasting or allow them to ripen fully red for drying and grinding.
sources: New Mexico State University — The Chile Cultivars of New Mexico State University, 1913-2022
Paul W. Bosland and David Votava, 'Peppers: Vegetable and Spice Capsicums' (CABI, 2012)

name: New Mexico No. 6-4 Green Chile
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; New Mexico No. 6-4 is the foundational Hatch-type green chile developed at New Mexico State University in the 1950s from the original New Mexico No. 6. It produces long, pendant pods (6–8 inches) with mild-to-medium heat (1,000–4,000 SHU) that are the standard for roasting green chiles. In zone 9, transplant March–April; the Hatch valley grows these chiles from June through September in a desert climate, but the variety also performs in humid Gulf Coast conditions if given well-drained soil and good airflow to minimize fungal issues. Harvest green (before color break) for roasting; allow to ripen red for dried red chile powder.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost and stake lightly. Harvest green pods at full size before any color break for roasting, or allow to ripen to deep red for drying. New Mexico No. 6-4 is the chile pepper variety that defined an entire regional food culture: the mild, thin-walled roasting pepper grown in the Hatch Valley of southern New Mexico and marketed under the 'Hatch Chile' designation that drives an enormous annual harvest festival and roasting tradition every August and September in New Mexico and throughout the American Southwest. The variety was developed by Dr. Roy Harper at New Mexico State University in Albuquerque in the 1950s through selection from the original New Mexico No. 6 variety, with the '6-4' designation referring to the parents used in the cross. The resulting variety became the commercial standard for New Mexico green chile production because it combined the mild-to-medium heat level preferred by most consumers with a pod shape and size (6–8 inches long, 1.5–2 inches wide) that roasts evenly on a flame or in a large drum roaster without burning before the flesh is fully cooked through. Thin walls and high moisture content allow steam to separate the charred skin from the flesh during roasting, enabling the characteristic step of peeling the blackened skin to reveal the moist, mildly pungent chile beneath. Home gardeners can replicate commercial roasting by placing whole pods under a broiler or directly on a gas burner flame, turning until charred on all sides, then placing in a sealed plastic bag for 10–15 minutes to steam before peeling. For red chile production, allow all pods to fully ripen to deep red on the plant or allow to ripen after harvest in a warm, dry location before drying whole or grinding to powder.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — NM 6-4 variety origin, development history, and production standards
Paul W. Bosland and David Votava, 'Peppers: Vegetable and Spice Capsicums' (CABI, 2012) — Hatch variety documentation
NMSU Extension — Home Production of New Mexico Chile Peppers

name: New Queen Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after the last frost, or transplant young seedlings for an earlier start in short-season areas.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed, or start transplants a few weeks early to get a jump on the season, and thin to strong single plants once vines begin to run. New Queen was named an All-America Selections winner in 1999 for its early, compact icebox-sized fruit and its unusual bright orange-yellow flesh, a departure from typical red-fleshed watermelons of its era. The globe-shaped fruits typically weigh 5 to 6 pounds and offer crisp, honey-sweet flavor well suited to small gardens.

name: New Red Fire Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; New Red Fire is an improved loose-leaf red lettuce bred for better heat tolerance and slower bolting than older red leaf varieties, making it one of the more reliable red lettuces for a longer Gulf South spring and fall season.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. New Red Fire is a loose-leaf lettuce bearing large, ruffled, deep red-tinged leaves over a green base, an improved selection bred for better heat tolerance and slower bolting than older red leaf lettuce varieties, which makes it noticeably more forgiving for gardeners in warm climates trying to stretch the lettuce season into early summer or start it earlier in late winter. Because it is a loose-leaf type, it never forms a tight head, and outer leaves can be harvested continuously while the center keeps producing new growth, extending the useful harvest window from a single planting. Flavor is mild and pleasant even as leaves size up, without the pronounced bitterness that develops quickly in less heat-tolerant lettuce under stress. Provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture for late-spring or early-fall plantings in zone 9 to further delay bolting as temperatures climb.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — New Red Fire Lettuce variety notes
Territorial Seed Company — Heat-Tolerant Lettuce Varieties
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Lettuce Variety Trials

name: New Red Intermediate Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow into very deep, loose, stone-free soil in full sun; New Red Intermediate needs extra-deep cultivation for its long, pointed exhibition-length roots.
directions: Direct sow into very deep, loose, stone-free soil in full sun; New Red Intermediate is a classic English show and exhibition carrot with very long, pointed roots falling between half-long and long carrot types, part of the historical lineage behind record-length show carrots. Maturing in 80-100+ days, it produces sweet, tender flesh that keeps well into winter storage. Double-dig or use a deep raised bed to give the roots the uninterrupted depth they need to grow straight and reach full exhibition length.

name: New York Improved Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and hold seedlings under warm, bright conditions until the soil has warmed thoroughly.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, keeping the soil warm since eggplant germinates poorly below 70F, then transplant out only after nights stay reliably warm. Give plants full sun, even moisture, and a stake or cage to support the heavy fruit load once pods set. This is one of the oldest American commercial eggplant selections, dating to the late 1800s, prized for its large glossy purple-black fruit and mild, tender flesh, and it stands as a direct ancestor of many modern hybrids sold today. Because it lacks the disease tolerance bred into newer types, gardeners often see best results with crop rotation and floating row cover early in the season.

name: New York White Garlic
scientificName: Allium sativum var. ophioscorodon 'New York White'
plantingNote: Plant cloves 2 inches deep in mid-fall once soil has cooled, mulching after the first hard frost.
directions: New York White is a long-preserved heirloom Porcelain hardneck strain maintained in northeastern American seed-saver collections for generations, valued for dependable bulb formation in cold Northeast winters and clean, glossy white wrappers. Bulbs typically produce 4-6 large cloves with a hot, pungent raw bite that sweetens dramatically when roasted or slow-cooked. As a true Porcelain type it needs a sustained cold period to vernalize properly, so gardeners in mild-winter climates should choose a different type. Grow it for its regional heirloom story and its reliability as an old New York homestead strain that has outlasted many modern hybrids.

name: New Zealand Yacon
plantingNote: Set out rhizome crown divisions around last frost into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give this tall-growing strain extra staking or wind shelter since it often exceeds 7 feet by season's end.
directions: New Zealand is a widely grown heirloom yacon strain, likely originally from Ecuador but long cultivated commercially in New Zealand, valued for reliable production across a range of climates. Propagate from the knobby rhizome crowns saved from the base of the previous year's stalks, not from the large storage roots, which have no buds and will not sprout. Set divisions out after the last frost in deep, fertile soil, since this is one of the tallest yacon strains and continues growing even after flowering begins. The tan tubers develop purple-red blushing with exposure and have the species' typical sweet, crisp, watery texture, best after a week or two of post-harvest curing in a warm, sunny spot.

name: Nickajack Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when the soil has warmed, providing poles or a strong trellis for this vigorous climbing heirloom.
directions: Direct sow after last frost when the soil has warmed, providing poles or a strong trellis for this vigorous climbing heirloom. Nickajack traces its name to a historic Cherokee community in the Tennessee River valley of the southern Appalachians, and it has been passed down among mountain gardeners as a reliable dual-purpose bean, with large, flat pods that can be picked young for snapping or left to mature into tan, speckled dry beans. Harvest at the snap stage for the tenderest eating, around 70 days, or let pods dry fully on the vine for a longer-season soup bean. The vines are productive and well adapted to the humid summers of the Southern Appalachians.

name: Nigerian Garden Egg
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile soil after frost danger has passed. This dual-purpose type yields leaves at 30 days and fruit at 60 days.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; Nigerian Garden Egg is a dual-purpose African eggplant known as Efo Igbo or Ganyen Gauta, grown both for its leaves, harvestable in about 30 days for garden egg leaf soup and dishes like abacha, and its fruit, ready around 60 days. Plants reach 3-5 feet, thriving in heat with no frost tolerance. Harvest leaves regularly to encourage continued production through the warm season.

name: Night Shadow Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Night Shadow is a Seminis-bred hybrid listed among Cornell's recommended disease-tolerant eggplant varieties, valued for its consistent yield and classic fruit quality.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date, once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Night Shadow is a hybrid eggplant bred for reliable, sustained production of classic glossy black-purple, oval fruit on a sturdy, vigorous plant that tolerates the heat of a Gulf South summer well. It is listed among Cornell University's recommended disease-tolerant eggplant selections, giving it an edge in the humid, disease-prone conditions common across the Southeast. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and the fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure, since dull, hard fruit signals it has gone past peak quality and developed more seeds and bitterness. Keep soil consistently moist and pick regularly to encourage the plant to keep setting new fruit through the season.
sources: seed catalog reference (Stokes Seeds, Rupp Seeds, Seedway)

name: Nigral Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 60 F; Nigral is bred to set fruit reliably even under variable early-season conditions, giving some flexibility on transplant timing.
directions: Nigral is a modern F1 hybrid bred as an earlier-maturing, more reliable improvement on classic black Italian eggplant types, reaching harvest about a week sooner than comparable standard hybrids. The spineless plants carry a green calyx and set glossy, deep purple-black fruit up to 6 inches long even when spring weather is cool or inconsistent. Its dependable fruit set and compact habit make it a good choice for growers who want classic Italian eggplant character without the lower yields of older heirloom black types. Harvest while the skin remains glossy and firm, and pick regularly to keep plants flowering and setting new fruit.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Nigral F1 Eggplant
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Eggplant Variety Database

name: Nine Star Perennial Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to its permanent position as nine star broccoli is a long-lived perennial that does not want to be moved once established. It requires a permanent, deeply dug, fertile position.
directions: Transplant to deeply dug, richly amended soil in full sun; nine star is a remarkable perennial broccoli variety that sends up multiple small white or pale yellow broccoli-like heads in early spring, year after year, for up to 4–5 years from a single planting. The key to maintaining the perennial habit is to harvest all the heads before any can flower and set seed — once a plant is allowed to flower, it may cease to perennial and become biennial. The heads are smaller than commercial broccoli (tennis ball-sized) but very numerous on established plants, and the flavor is excellent. After harvesting the heads, the plant sends up side shoots producing cut-and-come-again broccoli for weeks. Feed heavily after harvest to support the following year's growth.

name: Niranjan Bhata Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil has warmed and nights stay above 55F.
directions: An Indian heirloom-type eggplant producing strikingly long, slender fruit with marbled green-and-purple skin that can reach two feet or more under good growing conditions. Flesh is tender and mild-flavored, well suited to roasting, frying, or traditional curries and stir-fries. Plants are vigorous and productive over a long harvest season; stake tall fruiting branches to keep elongated pods off the ground. Harvest while skin is still glossy for the best texture, as overripe fruit turns dull and develops seeds.

name: Niue Taro
plantingNote: Grow as an upland taro in evenly moist, rich beds rather than flooded water; underplant beneath open tree canopy for part-day shade.
directions: Grown principally as a table taro rather than for poi, this medium, well-spreading, stocky cultivar is traditionally raised under upland rather than flooded culture. It suits a shaded border bed kept constantly damp rather than a true bog planting, and its white, yellow-fibered corm flesh cooks up firm for boiling or roasting. Expect corms to size up roughly 9 to 12 months after planting corm sections or huli. As with all taro, cook corms and greens thoroughly before eating to break down irritating calcium oxalate crystals.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR, Taro Varieties in Hawaii database (Niue-ulaula)

name: Nkruma Tenten Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is warm; this slow-starting variety rewards the Gulf Coast's long, hot frost-free season with months of continuous production on very tall plants.
directions: Known in Ghana as tall okra, this West African heirloom can tower 8 to 12 feet given a long enough hot season, making it one of the largest okras a gardener can grow. Red-tinged stems and huge, tender leaves top a slow-starting plant that, once established, produces thick-walled, deep green pods often tinged with red continuously until frost. Beyond the pods, its large leaves are traditionally cooked like a mucilaginous spinach among cooks in West Africa. In frost-free tropical climates it behaves as a short-lived woody perennial for years, but in a zone 9a garden it is best grown as a single tall-season annual with plenty of room to spread.

name: Noir des Carmes Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow an inch deep in hills or rows after soil has warmed; a fast-maturing, historic French variety well suited to succession planting for continuous harvest.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in hills or rows after the soil has warmed, and provide a trellis or ample vine room. Documented in French seed catalogs since the mid-1800s, Noir des Carmes produces short, chunky, dark-green fruit that ripens quickly and is covered in distinctive black spines when young, an old-world trait bred out of most modern cucumbers. It is one of the fastest-maturing open-pollinated cucumbers available, ready in under two months from sowing, making it a good choice for short-season succession planting through the summer. Pick fruit small and young for the sweetest, least bitter flavor, and harvest frequently to keep vines productive.

name: Noir des Carmes Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-amended soil; Noir des Carmes is a French heirloom melon dating to at least 1883, one of the earliest-maturing Charentais-type melons, with dark green to almost black skin that ripens to orange-yellow and contains brilliant, deep-orange, extraordinarily fragrant flesh — one of the finest European muskmelons.
directions: Sow in hills or rows after last frost in warm, enriched, well-drained soil; Noir des Carmes performs best with reduced watering as the fruits approach maturity — drying out slightly at the end concentrates the sugars and perfume. Noir des Carmes (Black of the Carmelites, named for the dark-robed Carmelite friars who reportedly cultivated it) is a French heirloom muskmelon first listed in catalogs in 1883 and described by Vilmorin-Andrieux in their famous 1885 The Vegetable Garden; the young fruits are dark green to nearly black (the 'noir'), ripening to orange-yellow at maturity with a pronounced perfume. Inside, the flesh is deep orange, very sweet, and extraordinarily fragrant in the way characteristic of the finest Charentais-type melons of Poitou-Charentes. One of the earliest European muskmelons (70–80 days from seed), making it suitable for shorter seasons. Somewhat rare but increasingly available from specialty seed companies.

name: Non-Tough Half Runner Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; half-runners send out short runners so a light trellis or brush support improves yield and airflow.
directions: Non-Tough Half Runner is a preserved Appalachian bean selected and maintained by Dr. Bill Best of the Sustainable Mountain Agriculture Center after decades of commercial half-runner seed losing the tenderness that once made the type popular, as seed producers had inadvertently bred in a toughening trait to extend shelf life. Its plump pods stay tender-eating even when the seeds inside swell to full size, which sets it apart from most modern half-runners that toughen quickly, and it remains a favorite for traditional leather-britches drying as well as fresh snap use, canning, and freezing. The half-runner growth habit sends out short runners beyond a bush frame, so light support or brush keeps pods off the ground and easy to pick.

name: Nootka Rose Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Nootka Rose is a rocambole-type hardneck named for Nootka Sound in the Pacific Northwest, valued for rich flavor and attractive rose-tan bulb wrappers.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Nootka Rose is a rocambole-type hardneck garlic prized for rich, full-bodied flavor and attractive bulbs wrapped in rose-tan skin over large, easy-to-peel cloves arranged in a single layer typical of rocamboles. Like other hardnecks, it sends up a dramatic double-curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to direct the plant's energy into bulb development; the scapes are excellent eaten fresh or cooked. Its rich flavor comes with the tradeoff of shorter storage life typical of rocamboles, generally four to five months, so plan to use it earlier in the storage season relative to porcelain or softneck types. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, and cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded location before trimming.

name: Nora Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Nora fruit must be left on the plant until fully red and wrinkled before harvest, since it is grown exclusively for drying rather than fresh eating, so plan for a full-length warm season.
directions: Nora is a small, round, thick-fleshed sweet pepper grown mainly in Murcia and Valencia in eastern Spain, where the deep red, fully ripe fruit is sun-dried whole rather than ground into powder, giving it a distinctively wrinkled, tomato-like appearance in the kitchen. Its heat is negligible, well under 1,000 Scoville units, so its value lies entirely in a sweet, earthy, almost raisin-like dried flavor that develops through slow drying and forms the flavor backbone of romesco sauce, arroz negro, and many Murcian and Valencian braises and rice dishes. Fruit should be harvested only after turning fully red and slightly soft, then air-dried or dehydrated over several weeks until the skin is leathery and the pepper rattles faintly with loose seeds, similar in method to the Mexican cascabel. Because Nora needs a long season to reach full red ripeness, gardeners outside mild climates should start plants early and grow them in the warmest, sunniest spot available.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Spanish dried pepper variety documentation

name: Norquay Garlic
plantingNote: Prairie-bred for extreme winter hardiness; plant cloves in fall in cold climates for a reliable overwinter crop.
directions: Plant individual cloves in fall, pointed end up, in loose fertile soil ahead of hard frost. This porcelain-type hardneck was selected for resilience in short-season, cold-winter growing regions and produces a handful of large, easy-to-peel cloves per bulb. Cut the flowering scape before it fully uncurls and cure harvested bulbs in a dry, shaded, well-ventilated space.

name: North and South Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past last frost; North and South is an Alabama heirloom passed down on Sand Mountain, prized for tender pods produced over a long season.
directions: North and South is a Southern heirloom okra preserved by gardening families on Sand Mountain in northeast Alabama, grown for slim, ridged green pods that stay tender well past the size most okra turns woody. Direct sow after the soil is reliably warm, since okra seedlings are slow to establish in cool soil, and thin plants to give them room to branch. The tall, productive plants keep setting pods over a long summer season if picked every day or two at 3-4 inches. As an open-pollinated heirloom it is easy to save seed from, helping keep a piece of Alabama foodways history in circulation.

name: North Georgia Candy Roaster
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; North Georgia Candy Roaster is a very large squash (15–30 lbs) requiring 100–120 days and substantial space (vines 12+ feet). In zone 9, plant March–April for October–November harvest. The variety is cold-sensitive as a young plant but very heat-tolerant once established, making zone 9's long warm season ideal for the extended maturation time this variety requires. Fruit is large, elongated to cylindrical with slight taper, with salmon-pink to apricot-tan skin with a distinctive bluish bloom at full maturity. The flesh is thick, bright orange-yellow, sweet, and very dry — the 'candy roaster' name references the traditional method of roasting the squash in front of a fireplace or in a slow oven until the flesh caramelizes, producing a very sweet, concentrated flavor.
directions: Direct sow in hills 5–6 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when skin turns salmon-pink and develops waxy bloom. North Georgia Candy Roaster is one of the most historically significant Appalachian heirloom vegetable varieties — a large winter squash that has been grown in the mountain regions of North Georgia, North Carolina, Tennessee, and adjacent Appalachian areas for centuries, with the variety associated with Cherokee and Scots-Irish Appalachian agricultural traditions of the southern mountain region. The 'candy roaster' name is shared by several closely related Appalachian squash varieties that differ somewhat in size, color, and shape but all share the characteristic of extraordinary sweetness when roasted — the candy-like sweetness that develops when the dense, high-starch flesh is slowly baked or roasted until caramelized. The specific 'North Georgia' designation distinguishes this variety from the similar but distinct 'Tennessee Candy Roaster,' 'Big Orange Candy Roaster,' and other regionally-named selections, with the North Georgia type typically producing cylindrical to elongated fruits with characteristic salmon-pink to apricot skin. The squash can reach enormous sizes: typical fruits are 15–20 lbs, and exceptional specimens exceed 30 lbs, making this one of the largest winter squash varieties in heirloom cultivation. The flesh — thick, dense, bright orange-yellow — is exceptional in nutritional value (very high beta-carotene) and flavor, with a sweetness and complexity that rewards the long growing season required. The variety has been maintained by Appalachian farming families and seed-saving organizations including the Seed Savers Exchange as an important cultural heritage variety of the southeastern mountain region.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — North Georgia Candy Roaster Cherokee heritage squash documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Candy Roaster squash Appalachian heirloom variety notes
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — North Georgia Candy Roaster heritage winter squash description

name: North Holland Blood Red Onion
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil is workable; this long-day Dutch heirloom needs a full season to size up its large flattened bulbs.
directions: North Holland Blood Red is a long-day Dutch heirloom valued for its large, slightly flattened bulbs covered in shiny, deep ox-blood red skin. The pungent flesh is layered with red and white rings and mellows noticeably with storage, making mature bulbs milder than fresh-pulled ones. This variety has a long history of supplying Dutch markets through winter, reflecting its exceptional keeping quality compared to most red onions. Harvest once tops fall over and cure thoroughly in a dry, airy spot before storing in a cool location for extended use.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange international variety records

name: North Pole Lettuce
plantingNote: Sow in late summer to fall for winter harvest under row cover or in a cold frame; also suitable for early spring sowing.
directions: Sow in late summer for a fall crop, or in early spring for a quick spring harvest; North Pole thrives in cold, short-day conditions and largely stops growing once winter cold sets in, then resumes as days lengthen. Small, unprotected plants can survive temperatures well below freezing, and with the light protection of a cold frame or row cover it reliably carries a crop of compact, buttery, lime-green heads through winter in cold climates. It resents summer heat and bolts quickly if grown in warm conditions, so it is best reserved for the coldest part of the lettuce calendar. Harvest whole heads once they feel dense, or pick individual leaves through the winter for a slower, extended harvest.

name: Northeaster Pole Bean
plantingNote: Sow in warm soil at the base of tall fencing; make a second sowing in midsummer for a fall crop before frost.
directions: Also sold under the name Kwintus, this pole bean ripens nearly two weeks ahead of Kentucky Wonder, making it useful where the growing season runs short. Its flattened 7-8 inch pods stay tender and resist getting stringy even when left to grow large, with flavor that actually improves after a quick blanch. Pick thoroughly and often, since leaving overgrown pods on the vine slows new production. For continuous harvest through frost, sow a second round in July or pair it with a later-maturing variety.

name: Northern Star Artichoke
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into a sunny, well-drained bed after frost danger passes. In cold-winter regions apply a thick winter mulch over the dormant crown to help the root system survive freezing temperatures and resprout the following spring.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into a sunny, well-drained bed after frost danger passes. In cold-winter regions apply a thick winter mulch over the dormant crown to help the root system survive freezing temperatures and resprout the following spring. Northern Star was selected specifically for the ability to survive winters far colder than traditional Mediterranean-bred artichoke varieties can tolerate, extending true perennial artichoke growing into regions that previously had to treat the crop strictly as an annual. It produces medium-sized green buds with good flavor, and growers in cold climates report it returning from the crown for multiple seasons when given adequate mulch protection.

name: Nothstine Dent Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Nothstine Dent is a Wisconsin farm-family heirloom yellow dent corn preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting in blocks rather than single rows to ensure good pollination. Nothstine Dent is a Wisconsin heirloom yellow dent corn passed down within a single farm family for generations before being preserved and distributed through the Seed Savers Exchange, valued for reliable yields of good-quality meal and feed corn adapted to short-season Upper Midwest growing conditions. Its relatively short season to maturity makes it a practical choice for regions with a shorter frost-free window than the Gulf South typically has. Harvest and dry ears fully before shelling and storing kernels for grinding or seed.

name: Novella Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; the tangled, tendril-heavy growth is largely self-supporting and needs only minimal staking.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in cool, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, sowing a bit thicker than usual so plants can lean on and support one another. Novella is a semi-leafless ('afila') type pea in which most of the normal flat leaflets are replaced by curling tendrils, causing plants to knit themselves together into a dense, self-supporting tangle that stands mostly upright with little or no staking, a real convenience compared to conventional pea vines that flop without support. The reduced foliage also means better airflow and light penetration through the planting, which can reduce fungal disease pressure, while still producing a solid crop of sweet, tender shelling peas in well-filled pods. Pick regularly once pods fill out for the best flavor, and enjoy the relatively low-maintenance, self-supporting habit that sets this type apart from standard pea varieties.

name: Nubia Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Nubia matures somewhat later than many Italian hybrids, so give it the full length of a warm Gulf Coast season to size up properly.
directions: Nubia produces oval fruit boldly variegated in purple and white, growing 6-7 inches long and 3-4 inches across, with dense, cream-colored flesh and a mild, semi-sweet flavor. Because it fills out its fruit over a slightly longer window than many hybrids, keep plants evenly watered and well fed through the back half of summer rather than expecting an early flush. Slicing the flesh and salting it briefly before cooking helps draw out moisture and firms the texture for roasting, grilling, or caponata. Pick fruit while the variegated skin is still glossy, since it dulls noticeably once past peak ripeness.

name: Numane Pickling Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after soil has warmed well past last frost; Numane is a heat-loving traditional Japanese pickling melon and will sulk or rot in cold, wet soil.
directions: Give vines a trellis or ample ground space, since Numane produces long, vigorous runners that can sprawl 8-10 feet if left unsupported. This oshiro uri type bears pale green, smooth-skinned fruit up to a foot long that resembles an overgrown cucumber but has crisp, nearly white flesh with almost no sweetness, the traditional starting point for Japanese narazuke and shiozuke pickles. Harvest fruit while still firm and immature for pickling, or let a few size up and use the mature flesh in stir-fries, since overripe melons turn soft and seedy. Pick regularly to keep the vine productive through the heat of summer.

name: NuMex Big Jim Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; NuMex Big Jim was released in 1975 by New Mexico State University (NMSU) plant breeder Dr. Roy Nakayama and holds the Guinness World Record for the longest chile pepper — individual fruits can reach 12–13 inches — it is the standard New Mexico/Hatch green chile for roasting, stuffing, and making authentic red and green New Mexico chile sauces.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, well-drained soil with consistent moisture for maximum fruit size; NuMex Big Jim is most famous when roasted over open flame or under a broiler in the New Mexico tradition. NuMex Big Jim was developed at New Mexico State University's Chile Pepper Institute by Dr. Roy Nakayama and released in 1975 as a breakthrough in Hatch/New Mexico green chile breeding; it holds the Guinness World Record for the world's longest chile pepper, with individual fruits measured up to 13 inches in length and 2–2.5 inches in diameter — fruit of this size are capable of being stuffed whole (for chile rellenos) without cutting, which drove the commercial appeal. The heat level is moderate (500–2,500 SHU — from virtually nil to mild-moderate depending on growing conditions, with hotter summers producing hotter fruit), characteristic of New Mexico green chiles rather than the sharp heat of jalapeños or serranos. The flavor when roasted is rich, smoky, earthy, and complex with characteristic New Mexico chile character — the basis of authentic Hatch green chile sauce, the iconic topping of New Mexico cuisine from green chile cheeseburgers to burritos and sopapillas. One of the most important American regional chile varieties.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute

name: NuMex Easter Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay above 55F; NuMex Easter is a compact, early-maturing ornamental well suited to patio containers and hanging baskets as well as garden beds.
directions: NuMex Easter was released by the New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute and named a 2014 All-America Selections winner for its striking clusters of small, upright, teardrop-shaped fruit that shift through pastel lavender, cream, and yellow before finishing bright orange, often showing several colors on the same compact plant at once. The dense, fasciculate fruiting habit and dwarf stature, typically under a foot tall and about as wide, make it one of the most reliable ornamental peppers for small containers, window boxes, or mixed spring bedding displays. The fruit carries real heat, roughly in the cayenne-to-habanero range, and is technically edible, but it is grown almost exclusively for its ever-changing color display rather than culinary use. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture and light monthly feeding to keep fruit set continuous through the season.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute
New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension

name: NuMex Joe E. Parker Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; NuMex Joe E. Parker is the dominant commercial green chile variety for the New Mexico Hatch Valley and performs comparably well throughout the Gulf South where its heat tolerance and thick-walled flesh suit the long, warm growing season. Harvest at the mature green stage (full size, firm, bright green) for fresh roasted green chile use; leave remaining fruits to mature to red for dried red chile or ristras.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 75–85°F; transplant to full sun, deeply watered soil after last frost. NuMex Joe E. Parker is one of the most commercially important New Mexico chile varieties — a New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute release named in honor of Joe E. Parker, a former NMSU Board of Regents member. The variety occupies the essential middle ground of New Mexico chile heat: mild to medium-hot, approximately 500–2,500 Scoville Heat Units, hot enough to have authentic New Mexico chile character but mild enough for broad consumer acceptance. Joe E. Parker is the standard commercial variety for Hatch-brand green chile operations, grown across thousands of acres in the Rio Grande Valley and producing the long (7–9 inch), flat, meaty-walled green fruits used for fresh-roasted whole chiles, canned green chile, green chile stew, and freezing. The fruits roast exceptionally well: thick walls hold up under direct flame, the skin blisters and chars cleanly, and the interior steams to the silky texture essential for authentic New Mexico green chile preparations. When left to mature to red and dried, NuMex Joe E. Parker produces the bright, papery-red pods used in New Mexico ristras and traditional dried red chile. For gardeners who want to grow the authentic Hatch valley chile experience, NuMex Joe E. Parker is the single most representative variety — it defines the flavor and character that New Mexico green chile has meant to American Southwestern cuisine for generations.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — NuMex Joe E. Parker variety description
NMSU College of Agricultural, Consumer and Environmental Sciences
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Chile Pepper Production

name: NuMex Joe Parker Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once all frost danger has passed and give plants consistent moisture through fruiting.
directions: NuMex Joe E. Parker was released in 1990 by New Mexico State University's chile breeding program and named for a longtime agricultural evaluator who helped select it; it is one of the standard named cultivars behind commercial Hatch green chile alongside NuMex Big Jim. Pods run six to eight inches, thick-walled and mild to medium in heat, and are traditionally picked green for roasting and stuffing or left to ripen red for drying and sauces. The plants are productive and relatively compact for a New Mexico-type chile, making them a manageable choice for home gardeners who want authentic Hatch flavor without the largest-fruited varieties.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: NuMex Suave Orange Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost on a heat mat, since chinense seed is slow and erratic to germinate; transplant once nights are reliably warm.
directions: NuMex Suave Orange was bred at the New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute as a companion to NuMex Suave Red, combining the classic wrinkled, lantern-shaped habanero pod and citrusy, apricot-toned chinense aroma with almost none of the heat, typically measuring under a thousand Scoville units. The plump pods ripen from green to a rich orange over a long, warm growing season, so give plants the full run of summer and avoid letting nighttime temperatures dip into the 50s while fruit is setting. Because so little capsaicin is present, cooks can use whole or pureed pods generously in salsas, marinades, and fruit-forward hot sauces to capture authentic habanero flavor without overwhelming heat. Rich, well-drained soil and consistent watering through fruit set keep yields high on the compact, bushy plants.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute
New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension

name: NuMex Suave Red Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, providing bottom heat for slow-to-germinate chinense seed, and transplant once nights stay warm.
directions: NuMex Suave Red was released by the Chile Pepper Institute at New Mexico State University as a nearly heatless habanero, measuring only a few hundred Scoville units yet retaining the same fruity, tropical aroma prized in hot habaneros. Plump, wrinkled fruit ripens from green to a deep red on productive plants that need a long, warm season to reach full size. Because the pepper carries little to no burn, it lets cooks use habanero flavor generously in salsas and sauces without overwhelming heat. Give it the same rich soil, consistent watering, and full sun that other chinense peppers require to perform well.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute
New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension

name: NuMex Twilight Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; NuMex Twilight was developed at New Mexico State University's Chile Pepper Institute as a compact ornamental-edible pepper producing upright, small fruits that ripen through an extraordinary sequence of colors — purple, yellow, orange, and red — all simultaneously visible on a single plant, resembling a fiesta of colors inspired by the Southwestern twilight sky.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; NuMex Twilight is compact enough for containers (8–12 inches) and makes an outstanding patio plant both for ornamental color and edible use. NuMex Twilight was developed at New Mexico State University's internationally renowned Chile Pepper Institute as part of their ornamental-edible pepper breeding program; the variety takes its name from the brilliant multicolor sky of a New Mexico twilight that it is said to evoke — each plant produces upright clusters of small (1–2 inch), conical fruits that transition through the colors purple (immature) → yellow → orange → red (fully ripe), with all four colors simultaneously visible on a mature, productive plant. The heat level is approximately 50,000–75,000 SHU — significant but not extreme, in the range of cayenne peppers — and the small fruits are fully edible at any color stage; purple fruits are mildest, red fruits are hottest. As an ornamental plant, NuMex Twilight is among the most stunning of all edible plants, combining constant visual interest through the growing season with genuine culinary utility for dried chile flakes, hot sauces, and fresh use. Outstanding in containers, as a border plant, or as an annual focal point in vegetable and ornamental beds.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute

name: Nya Nya Chungu African Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger has passed.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Nya Nya Chungu is a Congolese African eggplant maturing in about 60 days from transplant, its fruit traditionally peeled and halved for cooking with meat, fish, and greens, or salted and eaten raw. It is a heat-loving warm-season annual with no frost tolerance, needing full sun and a long growing season for best production. This cultivar carries a folk reputation among growers for traditional blood-sugar-management use, though that claim is anecdotal rather than clinically established.

name: O'Henry Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F; O'Henry is a white-skinned, white-fleshed sport of Beauregard with a milder, less sweet flavor than orange-fleshed types.
directions: O'Henry arose as a natural sport of Beauregard, sharing its parent's vigor and productivity but with cream-white skin and white flesh in place of Beauregard's copper skin and orange flesh, giving a milder, less sweet, drier-textured potato favored by cooks who want a sweet potato that behaves more like a baking potato. Vines are vigorous and trailing, producing heavy yields of smooth, uniform, blocky roots under the same growing conditions Beauregard thrives in. Cure freshly dug roots at warm temperature and high humidity for about a week before storage to heal skin cuts and convert starches to sugars, improving both flavor and keeping quality. Roots can develop pronounced lenticels if soil stays wet close to harvest, so time digging for a dry stretch.
sources: Louisiana State University sweet potato variety trials

name: Oak Leaf Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; oak leaf lettuce is distinguished by its distinctive deeply lobed, oak leaf-shaped leaves that make it one of the most heat-tolerant looseleaf lettuces and among the slowest to bolt in warm conditions — an excellent choice for spring and fall production in zones 8–11.
directions: Scatter seed thinly on the soil surface and firm in; keep consistently moist until germination at 50–70°F. Oak Leaf lettuce is one of the most recognizable and popular looseleaf lettuces in American home gardens, with deeply lobed, ruffled leaves that resemble the silhouette of an oak leaf — a form distinct from the curled frill of Lollo Rosa types or the smooth curves of Butterhead. The bright green (or burgundy, in the 'Red Oak Leaf' variety) deeply cut leaves form loose, open rosettes that can be cut-and-come-again repeatedly; the leaf texture is tender and buttery, and the flavor is mild with excellent heat tolerance compared to most lettuces. It was one of Thomas Jefferson's preferred salad plants at Monticello and has been grown in American gardens continuously since the colonial era. Outstanding for cut-and-come-again salad production in spring and fall.
sources: Monticello Heritage Harvest Festival Seed List

name: Oaxacan Green Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for wind pollination after the danger of frost has passed; Oaxacan Green is a traditional Mexican heirloom dent-flour corn grown for tortillas, tamales, and pozole.
directions: Sow in blocks of at least four rows for reliable wind pollination, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Oaxacan Green is a tall, traditional Zapotec heirloom corn from the Oaxaca region of Mexico, grown for large ears of pale green kernels that dry to a soft cream-green color and grind into a flour prized for tortillas, tamales, and masa-based dishes with a distinctive sweet, complex corn flavor. It grows notably tall, often exceeding 8 feet, reflecting its origins in traditional milpa polyculture systems where it was often interplanted with beans and squash in a Three Sisters-style planting. Allow ears to dry fully on the stalk before harvesting, then cure further indoors before grinding or storing whole. Isolate from other corn varieties by distance or planting-date offset to keep the strain true from seed saved for replanting.

name: Oaxacan Green Dent Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of 4+ rows; isolate from other corn by 300 feet to preserve the distinctive green-blue kernel color — cross-pollination with yellow or white corn will dilute the color. In zone 9, plant March–May. Harvest as dried corn when ears are fully mature and husks are completely dry; the blue-green color may fade slightly in storage but remains distinctive. Oaxacan Green was traditionally grown in the short-day conditions of southern Mexico and may require some adaptation in longer-day northern locations.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in blocks of 4 rows; harvest when husks are completely dry and papery. Oaxacan Green Dent is a traditional flour and dent corn from the valley of Oaxaca, Mexico — a staple landrace corn of the indigenous Zapotec and Mixtec agricultural traditions maintained over centuries in the high-altitude valley environment of southern Mexico. The most visually striking characteristic is the kernel color: at maturity, the kernels are an unusual blue-green to aqua-blue, sometimes with silvery-white highlights — a color found in few other corn varieties and quite distinct from the blue-black of Hopi Blue or the rainbow of Glass Gem. The color comes from the same anthocyanin pigments that color other colored corns, but in a combination that expresses specifically in the blue-green range. In traditional Oaxacan cuisine, Oaxacan Green corn is used as masa for the deep green, smoky-flavored specialty tamales and tlayudas, where the colored masa produces a visually distinctive product unlike standard yellow or white corn preparations. The ears are medium to large, somewhat irregular in kernel arrangement as expected of a landrace variety, and the plants are tall. Oaxacan Green is maintained and distributed by Native Seeds/SEARCH and the Seed Savers Exchange as part of preserving Mesoamerican corn diversity.
sources: Native Seeds/SEARCH — Oaxacan Green corn documentation
Seed Savers Exchange — Mexican heirloom corn collection
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Oaxacan Green corn notes

name: Oberkulmer Rotkorn Spelt
plantingNote: Broadcast or drill in mid-fall into lean, unamended ground; unlike most modern grains, Oberkulmer spelt actually lodges and underperforms on rich, heavily fertilized soil.
directions: Oberkulmer Rotkorn is a Swiss landrace spelt prized for its genetic purity, having never been crossed back into common bread wheat the way many modern spelt lines have. It grows quite tall, easily reaching five to six feet, and is deliberately grown lean: skip added compost or fertilizer, since excess nitrogen and rich soil cause this old variety to lodge before harvest. Sow into weed-free ground in mid-fall so plants overwinter as a low rosette, then resume growth in spring and ripen for a late-summer harvest. The red-husked grain threshes with more effort than free-threshing wheat because the tough hull clings to the kernel, but it rewards the work with flour that heritage bakers describe as unusually flavorful and easy to digest.

name: Obsession Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees; keep isolated from standard or sugary-enhanced corn to protect kernel sweetness. Obsession is a vigorous supersweet (sh2) bicolor hybrid bred for strong stalk vigor and high-quality ears for Southern home gardens.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Obsession is a supersweet bicolor sweet corn hybrid bred for vigorous stalk growth and consistent ear quality under warm Southern growing conditions. It produces well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels that stay sweet in storage longer than standard sugary-type corn thanks to its supersweet genetics. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill, since drought stress at this stage leads to poorly filled ears. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed.
sources: seed catalog reference (HOSS Tools, University of Florida Seed Program)

name: Ochsenherz Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes; stake or cage, since fruit grows large and heavy on indeterminate vines.
directions: Transplant into well-amended soil after hardening off, staking tall to support the heavy, pointed fruit. Ochsenherz, literally 'ox heart' in German, is a traditional German heirloom of the oxheart tomato type, bearing large, deeply lobed, heart-shaped fruit with dense, meaty flesh and a notably small seed cavity compared to round slicing tomatoes. That low-moisture, low-seed character makes it especially well suited to thick sauces and pastes that need little reduction, as well as hearty slicing for sandwiches. Water consistently through fruit set to avoid blossom end rot, since the large fruit size makes this variety more sensitive to irregular watering than smaller-fruited tomatoes.

name: October Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is consistently warm; in zone 9 plant March–May and again August–September. October Bean is a climbing pole bean requiring a trellis, fence, or pole support 5–8 feet tall. The primary fresh-shelled eating stage (the classic Southern 'shellout') is when pods are plump and seeds are fully developed but still moist — at this stage they cook quickly and have a rich, creamy flavor. Pods allowed to dry fully can be stored and used as dry beans through winter.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic soil and provide sturdy pole or trellis support; October Bean is an Appalachian mountain heirloom shellout bean (also called 'fall bean', 'shelly bean', or 'October shellout') that has been grown in Southern Appalachian kitchen gardens continuously for generations — the bean is named for its traditional harvest period in September and October when the seeds have filled the pods but before autumn frosts dry the plants down. The large, tan to cream-colored, maroon-streaked seeds inside swollen pods are shelled and cooked fresh like a combination between fresh lima beans and dry beans — with a rich, meaty, potato-like texture and earthy, slightly sweet flavor quite different from green snap beans or fully dried beans. The freshly shelled October bean is a cornerstone of traditional Appalachian cooking, served with cornbread, potatoes, and green onions. The climbing vines produce abundantly over a long season, and any mature pods that escape the fresh-shelled harvest can be allowed to dry for a dried soup bean with excellent winter storage.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — October Bean Appalachian Heirloom
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — October Shellout Bean
University of Kentucky Cooperative Extension — Heirloom Beans of Appalachia

name: October Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost; October bean is a pole or half-runner type requiring 4–6 foot support; in zone 9 plant in May–June to mature in September–October when cooler temperatures improve the flavor of the shelled beans.
directions: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing 4–6 feet of vertical support; October bean is a traditional Appalachian heirloom pole or half-runner bean whose primary value is as a shelling bean — harvested when pods are fully filled but still green to slightly dried ('fall colored'), when the speckled tan-and-maroon seeds shell out easily and cook quickly with a rich, creamy, almost peanut-buttery flavor. Named for October when they traditionally matured in the mountain regions of the southern Appalachians, the plants produce best when planted in late spring to mature into cooler fall temperatures. In zone 9 a June planting produces a September–October shell bean harvest with ideal timing. The shelled beans cook in 45–60 minutes without soaking, absorbing seasoning beautifully, and are outstanding cooked with ham hocks and served over cornbread.

name: Ogle Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed; a bushy, short-runnered purple hull type that holds pods upright for easier hand harvest.
directions: Ogle was bred by longtime Clemson horticulturist Roy (W.L.) Ogle, the same breeder behind the classic Colossus and Hercules southern peas, and was released commercially by Clemson University decades after he first developed the line. It is a purple hull type selected for a large eating seed, strong yield, and resistance to blackeye cowpea mosaic virus, a disease that has historically limited purple hull production in humid climates. Like other purple hull peas it can be picked green for fresh shelling or left to dry fully for storage peas.

name: Ohno Scarlet Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer or fall for fall harvest; Ohno Scarlet is the older, once-rare Japanese turnip variety from which seed savers selected the modern Scarlet Ohno Revival.
directions: Ohno Scarlet is the older, once-rare Japanese heirloom turnip that seed savers selected from to create the modern Scarlet Ohno Revival, which takes its name directly from this parent variety and was bred to bring back a type that had become scarce in seed collections. Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in late summer or fall and thin seedlings to 4-6 inches apart for best root development. As with its better-known descendant, both the root and leaves are traditionally used in the kitchen rather than the root alone.

name: Oka Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is warm; Oka was bred for Quebec's short, cool season and performs best in a warm microclimate at more northern latitudes.
directions: Oka was bred in the early twentieth century at the Trappist monastery of Oka, Quebec, as a deliberate cross of the Montreal Melon and the Banana Melon, aimed at combining rich flavor with a shorter season than the giant Montreal type required. It produces small, flattened, roughly ten-ribbed fruit with aromatic, sweet orange flesh well suited to Quebec's cool summers. It fell out of wide commercial circulation by mid-century as industrial melon varieties took over, only to be rediscovered decades later from seed preserved near Montreal. It is grown today largely through Quebec heirloom seed farms working to keep the revival going.

name: Okinawa Pink Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past last frost; soaking seed overnight speeds germination. Okinawa Pink is a fast, ribless okra prized for smooth pink pods that hold their color and tenderness even past typical picking size.
directions: Sow seed a half inch deep directly in the garden once soil is thoroughly warm, thinning seedlings to a foot or more apart in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Okinawa Pink is a heirloom from Okinawa, Japan valued for smooth, ribless, rosy-pink pods that resist the toughening and stringiness common in other okra as pods pass the ideal picking size, making the harvest window more forgiving for home gardeners. Pods are best cut at three to six inches long for eating fresh, pickled, or sauteed, though the pink color fades to green when cooked. Harvest every day or two once plants begin producing to keep the compact, branching plants flowering steadily through the heat of summer.

name: Okinawa Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant April–June for a fall harvest. Okinawa sweet potato requires a long season (100–120 days) and does not produce quality roots if harvested early; the full summer growing period is needed for the characteristic purple flesh to fully develop. Grow in the ground rather than containers for best root development.
directions: Plant slips 4–6 inches deep in loose, slightly sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Okinawa sweet potato is a Japanese heirloom variety with cream-colored skin and brilliantly purple flesh — the vibrant purple color comes from exceptionally high anthocyanin content, among the highest of any food crop. The slightly sweet, nutty, dry-textured flesh holds its purple color through roasting, steaming, and baking (though water boiling may leach some pigment). Okinawa sweet potato is a staple of the Okinawan diet, studied extensively as part of the traditional diet associated with unusual longevity on the island. The flavor is subtly sweet and starchy with an earthy, slightly nutty aftertaste. Cure harvested roots at 85°F and 90% humidity for 10 days before eating or storing to develop sweetness and heal any cuts.
sources: University of Hawaii Extension — Okinawa Sweet Potato
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sweet Potato Varieties
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Sweet Potato Breeding

name: Okinawan Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips in warm soil (above 65°F) after last frost; Okinawan purple sweet potato requires a longer growing season (100–130 days) than standard varieties — plant as early as possible in the season in the South.
directions: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, loose, warm soil in full sun after last frost; Okinawan sweet potato has creamy-white skin concealing spectacularly vivid purple-violet flesh — the deep purple color comes from extremely high anthocyanin content (among the highest of any sweet potato), making it a genuine superfood with powerful antioxidant properties. The flavor is mildly sweet, slightly nutty, and drier than orange-flesh types; it is prized in Hawaiian cuisine (where it's called 'Hawaiian purple sweet potato'), Japanese cuisine, and modern farm-to-table cooking for its dramatic color that holds remarkably well through most cooking methods. Excellent roasted, steamed, in ice cream, and in colorful desserts.

name: Old Brooks Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Old Brooks is a vigorous, drought-tolerant indeterminate heirloom suited to a sturdy cage or stake.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into well-drained soil after frost risk has passed, staking or caging the vigorous vines. Old Brooks is an old American heirloom slicing tomato noted among seed savers for holding up well in hot, dry conditions where many modern varieties falter, producing medium to large red fruit with a solid, meaty interior and good old-fashioned tomato flavor. The indeterminate vines are vigorous and generally need only routine staking and watering to perform well through a full season. Harvest at full color and keep plants evenly watered to reduce blossom-end rot during dry stretches.

name: Old Fashioned Ragged Edge Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow for a quick spring crop or, in the Gulf South, from late summer into fall for a winter harvest of greens.
directions: Also sold under the folk names Hen Pecked Mustard and Ragged Edged Mustard, this black-seeded, open-pollinated type is an old standby of Southern home gardens grown both for salad and cooking greens and for its own seed. The long, narrow leaves are deeply cut and ruffled along the margin, giving the variety its ragged edge name and setting it apart from the broader, less-dissected leaves of Southern Giant Curled or Florida Broadleaf. Flavor is notably sharp and aromatic, with a horseradish-like bite that mellows somewhat when cooked, and the short days-to-maturity make it a reliable fast crop for both spring and fall sowings.

name: Old German Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Old German is believed to have originated with Mennonite German immigrant communities in Virginia and been preserved by Mennonite seed-saving traditions before entering the American heirloom seed trade.
