directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Old German is an heirloom beefsteak tomato of Mennonite German ancestry — producing very large (1–2 lb), deeply flattened, lobed beefsteak fruits with a striking bicolor pattern of golden-yellow skin marked with deep-red and orange streaks, marbling, and patches distributed across the fruit surface in irregular patterns. The cut interior reveals the characteristic bicolor flesh of this German heirloom tradition: yellow and red sectors arranged in a beautiful mosaic pattern that is outstanding in sliced fresh presentations — the multicolored cross-section of Old German makes it one of the most visually beautiful tomatoes when displayed on a cutting board or serving plate. The flavor follows the pattern of the best bicolor heirlooms: very sweet, extremely low-acid, with a complex, fruity, mild quality that makes it exceptional for fresh eating. Old German is most clearly distinguished from similar bicolor heirlooms (Pineapple, Hillbilly, Big Rainbow) by the specific distribution and proportion of its red-and-yellow coloring — the exact pattern varies somewhat from fruit to fruit but consistently produces the beautiful bicolor marbled effect. An open-pollinated heirloom with saveable seed. In zone 9, grow as a spring crop for best results before summer heat.

name: Old Ivory Egg Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Old Ivory Egg is a highly productive indeterminate variety that benefits from staking or caging to manage prolific small egg-shaped fruit clusters.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil, staking to support the abundant fruit set. Old Ivory Egg produces small, egg-shaped, 2-3 ounce fruit that ripens from pale ivory to a soft creamy yellow, with a mild, sweet flavor carrying a hint of citrus, and is prized for its striking pale coloring in salads and mixed cherry-tomato plates. The variety was distributed in a mid-1980s Seed Savers Exchange yearbook by a Wisconsin member who traced the seed stock back to Australia.

name: Old Timey Blue Collard
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring for a spring crop; Old Timey Blue is an heirloom passed down within Southern families for generations and is prized for reliable cold hardiness and traditional flavor.
directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and thin or transplant to final spacing as seedlings develop true leaves. Old Timey Blue is a traditional Southern heirloom collard, one of many regional strains passed down and re-saved within families for generations before being preserved by seed-saving organizations, valued for its dependable vigor, good cold tolerance, and classic blue-green collard flavor that sweetens after a frost. Tall, productive plants yield heavily over a long harvest window when picked cut-and-come-again, taking outer leaves while the center keeps producing. Fertilize with a balanced or nitrogen-rich feed through the season for the best leaf growth, and watch for cabbage worms and aphids, managing with row cover or a targeted organic insecticide if needed.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange heirloom collard archive
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Collard Production

name: Old Timey Green Collard
plantingNote: Start indoors or direct sow 10-14 weeks before first fall frost; in zone 9, set out transplants in late summer for a fall-through-winter harvest that sweetens after frost.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously since this heirloom spreads wide and low rather than growing into a tall, upright stalk collard. Old Timey Green is a rare non-heading North Carolina family strain, saved for decades before passing into seed-bank preservation efforts, and it remains scarce in cultivation today, distinct from the separately preserved Old Timey Blue strain. Leaves are broadly elliptic with a wavy edge and only light blistering, often carrying purple tinting at the stem and leaf base, and cook up with a notably strong, earthy flavor and a bit more bitterness than milder modern collard hybrids. Harvest outer leaves continually through the cool season, and consider saving seed from vigorous plants to help keep this dwindling family heirloom in circulation.

name: Old Tokyo Komatsuna
plantingNote: Direct sow before the last frost, and again in late summer for a fall and winter crop; Old Tokyo is a traditional Tokyo-area strain of komatsuna that has been grown as a cool-season spinach substitute for generations.
directions: Direct sow into fertile soil and thin progressively, eating the thinnings as baby greens while remaining plants develop into full-sized rosettes. Old Tokyo carries the smooth, glossy, dark green leaves and mild, faintly sweet, spinach-like flavor typical of heirloom komatsuna, with a slightly milder bite than many modern hybrid strains. It grows well in the dappled light under taller crops or along the partly shaded edge of a bed, needing less direct sun than full-sized napa cabbage or mustard greens to size up properly. Harvest outer leaves continuously from about a month after sowing, or cut whole rosettes at the base once they reach full size; cold weather sweetens the flavor further.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Ole Timey Blue Collards
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. acephala 'Ole Timey Blue'
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12-14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August-September for fall and winter production. Ole Timey Blue is a tall, vigorous, open-pollinated Southern heirloom maintained by generations of home seed savers.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Ole Timey Blue is a tall, vigorous, open-pollinated Southern heirloom collard with broad, blue-green leaves, representing the traditional dooryard collard type grown throughout the Deep South long before modern compact hybrids became widely available. Plants grow quite tall over a long season, and the leaves carry the classic robust, full-bodied collard flavor that sweetens further after the first light fall frosts. Because it is a genuine open-pollinated landrace rather than a stabilized commercial variety, some plant-to-plant variation in leaf shape and color is normal and part of its heirloom character, and seed can be saved from the best plants to maintain the strain. Harvest outer and lower leaves as needed, leaving the central growing point intact so the plant continues producing fresh leaves from the top through a long cool-season harvest.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Collard Production in the Southeast

name: Olena Ukrainian Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Olena Ukrainian sets large, heart-shaped orange fruit on vigorous indeterminate vines.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed, staking plants to support the large oxheart fruit. Olena Ukrainian is an orange-fruited heirloom from Ukraine that forms distinctly pointed, heart-shaped fruit often exceeding a pound, with dense, meaty, low-acid flesh and relatively few seeds. The mild, sweet flavor and smooth texture make it popular for slicing and sauce alike, and the indeterminate vines crop steadily through a long warm season. Water evenly during fruit development to limit cracking on the large, heavy fruit.

name: Oliver Brussels Sprout
plantingNote: Start indoors 12–16 weeks before first fall frost; Oliver is a very early-maturing F1 Brussels sprout that initiates sprout development earlier in the season than most varieties, making it one of the best choices for short-season northern gardens (zones 3–5) where the growing window is compressed, and for Gulf Coast gardeners who need sprout harvest to complete before heat arrives in spring.
directions: Start seeds indoors 12–16 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into firm, rich, consistently moist soil; stake tall plants against wind; remove the growing tip when bottom sprouts reach marble size to encourage rapid maturing of the rest; harvest from the bottom upward when sprouts are 1–1.5 inches across. Oliver is an F1 hybrid Brussels sprout bred for early sprout initiation — one of the earliest-maturing Brussels sprout varieties commercially available — that produces uniform, round, high-quality sprouts beginning earlier in the fall season than standard types. The relatively compact plants (24–30 inches) with short internodes produce sprouts packed closely on the stem in tight, uniform clusters that are excellent for harvest. The early initiation of sprout development makes Oliver particularly valuable in two challenging situations: in zones 3–5 where the growing season is short and standard Brussels sprouts often don't finish before hard freeze, and in zones 7–9 where the goal is to get sprout harvest completed before the arrival of hot spring weather. Oliver's flavor is mild and sweet, comparable to other modern hybrid Brussels sprouts, with the characteristic improvement in flavor and sweetness after frost exposure. A practical, reliable choice for gardeners who want Brussels sprouts without the 100–120 day wait of heirloom types.

name: Olympia Spinach
plantingNote: In zone 8-9 gardens sow in fall for a winter and early spring harvest; elsewhere sow 4-6 weeks before the last spring frost.
directions: Direct sow a half inch deep into cool, moist soil and thin seedlings once true leaves appear, harvesting outer leaves or whole plants as needed. This hybrid produces smooth to lightly crinkled, dark green leaves on a slow-to-bolt plant, making it a reliable choice for stretching the spring harvest window a bit longer than older heirloom types. It performs well as both a baby-leaf and full-size crop and holds quality in cool, short-day conditions common to winter gardening in the Gulf South.

name: Omaha Squash
plantingNote: Sow directly once the danger of frost has passed, as this fast-maturing heirloom was selected for a short continental summer and rewards early planting.
directions: A rare Native American heirloom preserved from the Omaha people of the Missouri Valley, bearing small cylindrical fruit typically three to five pounds with smooth tan-orange rind. It matures notably faster than most winter squash, making it well suited to gardeners with cool or short-season climates. The dense, sweet flesh is good for baking and keeps in storage for several months after curing. Because the vines are relatively modest in reach compared to many maxima types, it also suits smaller garden plots.

name: Omar Arab Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Omar Arab is a Middle Eastern heirloom with elongated, pleated, deep red fruits that are outstanding for stuffing whole in the traditional Levantine style; well-adapted to hot, dry summer conditions and therefore an excellent choice for zone 8–11.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed. Omar Arab is a Syrian heirloom tomato with elongated, ribbed or lobed, deep red to crimson fruits 8–12 ounces in weight with a distinctive beaked tip and meaty, near-seedless flesh with very few gel pockets that makes it outstanding for traditional Levantine-style stuffed tomatoes (mahashi), where the tomato is cored, filled, and cooked whole; the balanced, savory-sweet flavor is excellent fresh as well. Adapted to hot, dry Mediterranean-type climates, it performs reliably in zone 8–11 high-summer conditions where other heirlooms drop flowers or crack. Seed was collected and introduced more widely through the work of heritage seed savers in the Arab world.

name: Omar's Lebanese Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil in full sun; the huge, heavy fruit clusters need sturdy caging or staking from an early age.
directions: Set out transplants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes, spacing plants generously to allow air movement around the sprawling vine. Omar's Lebanese is a Middle Eastern heirloom brought into wider American circulation through the Seed Savers Exchange network, grown for enormous, smooth, pale to deep pink beefsteak fruit that regularly reaches one to two pounds with a mild, low-acid, juicy sweetness. The indeterminate vines are notably productive for such a large-fruited variety, setting fruit steadily through summer heat where many other big pink slicers slow down. Provide even moisture and consistent feeding, since fruit of this size draws heavily on the plant, and support the heaviest clusters to prevent limb breakage.

name: Omny F1 Daikon
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep and thin generously, since this hybrid produces unusually large, heavy roots that need more room than typical spring radishes.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep and thin generously, since this Sakata-bred hybrid produces unusually large, heavy roots that need more room than typical spring radishes to size up properly. Omny is grown through spring and summer for a dependable harvest of smooth white daikon suited to grilling, baking, stir-frying, or simmering as well as fresh salads. Keep soil consistently moist as roots swell to prevent splitting, and harvest before roots become oversized and woody.

name: On Deck Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed to at least 65F; because plants stay short, block-plant even a small number of stalks in a large container or short row for reliable wind pollination.
directions: Direct sow in blocks of at least four rows, even in a large container, once the soil has warmed to ensure adequate cross-pollination between the short stalks. On Deck is an All-America Selections winner bred specifically for small-space and container gardening, reaching only about 4-5 feet tall while still producing two 7-8 inch bicolor ears per stalk with classic sweet corn flavor. Its shrunken stature makes it one of the few sweet corn varieties genuinely practical for a patio or deck planter.

name: Onaway Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost, or January-February in zone 9; Onaway's very early maturity lets Gulf Coast gardeners harvest new potatoes well before summer heat sets in.
directions: Onaway was released by Michigan State University in the 1950s and remains prized among home growers as one of the earliest potatoes available, often ready for new potatoes within about ten weeks of planting. The round, white-skinned tubers have shallow eyes and white flesh with good flavor, best used fresh rather than for long-term storage. Its rapid maturity makes Onaway a strong choice for a quick Gulf Coast spring crop planted in late winter, allowing harvest well before the region's summer heat sets in. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge to protect the shallow-set tubers from sunlight and pests.

name: One Ball Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed; compact size suits succession planting through a long warm season.
directions: One Ball is the bright yellow counterpart to the dark green Eight Ball and pale Cue Ball round squash, bred by Hollar Seeds to round out a trio of billiard-themed globe-shaped summer squash. The vigorous, disease-resistant bush plant sets shiny yellow fruit best picked at 2-3 inches across for the crispest texture and nuttiest flavor, well before the rind toughens. Its resistance to watermelon mosaic virus and zucchini yellow mosaic virus is valuable in warm, humid Gulf Coast gardens where these aphid-vectored viruses are common late-season problems. The compact habit and small mature fruit size make it a good choice for succession planting in raised beds through a long Texas growing season.

name: Onyx Red Ornamental Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant after all danger of frost into full sun; Onyx Red is grown chiefly as an ornamental bedding and container pepper, prized for foliage and fruit color over culinary use.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after all danger of frost; Onyx Red is an AAS-winning ornamental pepper bred for striking near-black, glossy purple foliage that provides season-long color contrast even before fruiting begins. Small, upright, conical fruits emerge dark purple-black and ripen through red-orange to bright red, often showing several colors on the plant at once against the dark leaves, creating a dramatic, jewel-toned display in beds, borders, and mixed containers. The compact, uniform mounded habit and heat tolerance make it a reliable performer through the full Gulf South growing season, needing only light, regular feeding to keep the color intense. Fruits are technically edible and quite hot, but the variety is bred and marketed primarily as an ornamental rather than a culinary pepper.
sources: PanAmerican Seed — Onyx ornamental pepper series notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bedding Plant Trials

name: Opal Artichoke
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost; Opal flowers readily in its first year without a demanding cold-treatment schedule, so a simple cool spell of a couple of weeks after transplanting is generally enough to bring on good bud set.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Opal is an F1 hybrid bred for fast, dependable first-year bud production and stands out for the striking violet-purple color of its rounded, tender buds, which hold their color well even after light cooking. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining strong ornamental appeal with genuine first-year productivity from seed, making it a popular dual-purpose choice for gardeners who want both a harvest and a bold accent plant among vegetables or in a mixed border. Plants are moderately compact for an artichoke and produce a good number of secondary buds after the central bud is harvested. Keep soil evenly moist and harvest buds while still tightly closed, since the purple color and tender texture are both best before scales begin to loosen.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Artichoke Production Guide

name: Opalka Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Opalka is a Polish heirloom paste tomato renowned for producing extraordinarily long, pointed, banana-pepper-shaped fruits 4–8 inches in length with extremely thick, meaty walls, minimal seeds, concentrated flavor, and very low moisture content — considered by many tomato growers the finest heirloom paste variety for sauce and preserving.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; provide staking or caging as plants grow 5–7 feet tall. Opalka is a Polish heirloom paste tomato (named for the Opalka family who brought it to America) producing distinctively long, tapering, banana-pepper to Italian horn-shaped fruits of 4–8 inches with a pointed blossom end and the distinctive characteristic of exceedingly thick, dense walls surrounding very small seed cavities — the result is a paste tomato with more dry matter per pound than virtually any other variety, producing sauce with exceptional body and concentrated tomato flavor without hours of reduction time. The flavor fresh is rich and complex, with more sweetness and less tartness than most red paste types; the thick walls and dry flesh make Opalka exceptionally well-suited to drying (dried Opalka are comparable to sun-dried tomatoes in Italy). An indeterminate plant that bears a large late-season crop; very productive in Southern and Gulf Coast gardens in spring and fall seasons.

name: Opo Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, or start indoors 3-4 weeks early in short-season regions; provide a trellis or arbor so the club-shaped fruit hangs straight and stays clean.
directions: Opo, also called upo in the Philippines and known across Southeast and East Asian cuisines as a mild, absorbent summer vegetable, is a shorter, plumper, club-shaped bottle gourd cultivar harvested young and tender rather than left to mature and dry like ornamental or dipper-type gourds. Train the sprawling vine onto a trellis or overhead arbor so fruit hangs straight instead of curling on the ground, and hand-pollinate at dusk with a soft brush where moth activity is low, since the large white flowers open only in the evening. Harvest fruit at 10 to 14 inches long while the skin is still glossy and easily pierced with a fingernail; overmature fruit develops a tough rind and spongy, seedy flesh unsuitable for cooking. Peeled and sliced, the mild flesh readily takes on the flavor of broths, stir-fries, and sautés, making it a staple in Filipino sinigang and ginisang upo as well as Vietnamese and Chinese home cooking.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

name: Opopeo Amaranth
plantingNote: Direct sow on the soil surface after the last frost, since seed needs warmth and light to germinate quickly.
directions: Scatter seed thinly over warm, prepared soil and press it in without burying it deeply, as germination is fast once temperatures climb. Opopeo is a traditional Mexican landrace named for a town in Michoacan, grown both for its tender young leaves, which can be harvested repeatedly through the season, and for its abundant cream-colored grain borne on deep magenta seed heads. Allow top growth to slow and seed heads to dry and bronze before harvesting for grain, threshing and winnowing by hand. It tolerates poor soil and drought well once rooted in, making it a reliable dual-purpose crop for hot gardens.

name: Orange Banana Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Orange Banana is a tall indeterminate heirloom that needs a sturdy stake or cage for the full season.
directions: Orange Banana is an open-pollinated heirloom paste tomato from Elberta, Alabama, grown for its elongated, curved, banana-shaped fruit in a bright tangerine orange rather than the usual red or yellow of most paste types. The dense, meaty, low-moisture flesh with few seeds makes it excellent for sauces, salsas, and drying, and the striking color adds visual interest to canned goods and mixed-color tomato dishes. Stake the vigorous indeterminate vine well, and pick fruit as it colors fully to avoid the splitting that heavy paste-type fruit can suffer after a sudden rain.

name: Orange Blaze Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Orange Blaze is a compact, upright sweet bell pepper variety that produces medium-sized (3–4 inch) blocky orange fruits on a plant shorter and more manageable than standard bell pepper varieties. In zone 9, start seeds January–February and transplant March–April. Orange Blaze was an AAS winner recognized for its earlier production timeline compared to standard orange bell peppers — orange bells typically require very long maturity periods because they must reach full green bell size and then ripen fully to orange, a process that can take 75–90+ days from transplant. Orange Blaze achieves mature orange color faster without sacrificing fruit quality. The compact plant habit (18–24 inches vs. 30–36 inches for standard bells) makes Orange Blaze practical for containers and smaller garden spaces. Fruits are blocky, firm, and uniformly orange with sweet, crisp flesh.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost. Harvest at full orange for maximum sweetness; can harvest at green stage but flavor improves considerably at full ripeness. Orange Blaze Pepper won the All-America Selections award in 2010 for its compact plant habit, early production of fully mature (orange-colored) fruit, and excellent flavor quality in a category (orange sweet bell peppers) where most available varieties required exceptionally long growing seasons that limited their usefulness in many North American climates. Standard orange bell peppers are derived from bell pepper varieties with the genetic trait for orange ripening (rather than red or yellow), and this trait is typically associated with an extended maturation period: the fruits must first reach full green bell size before beginning the color transition, and the transition from green to full orange requires additional time beyond what red peppers need for their color change. The result is that many orange bells require 80–95 days from transplant to reach edible orange maturity — too long for gardens with short warm seasons, and even in zone 9 limiting the productive harvest period. Orange Blaze's AAS recognition reflected its ability to achieve full orange maturity 10–15 days earlier than other orange bell varieties while maintaining good fruit size and quality, expanding the practical use of orange bell peppers in home gardens. For zone 9 spring gardens where April–May transplanting targets a June–July harvest before extreme summer heat, Orange Blaze's earlier maturity maximizes the productive harvest window within zone 9's optimal pepper-growing period.
sources: All-America Selections — Orange Blaze pepper 2010 AAS winner documentation
PanAmerican Seed — Orange Blaze compact bell pepper variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sweet Bell Pepper Variety Selection for the Gulf South

name: Orange Fantasia Swiss Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow around the last frost date; sow again in mid to late summer for a fall and winter crop in mild climates.
directions: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil and thin seedlings to 8-10 inches apart. Orange Fantasia stands out among chards for its vivid, saturated carrot-orange stalks, midribs, and veining, a deeper and more solidly orange tone than the paler gold seen in yellow-stemmed chards, set against dark, glossy, savoyed green leaves. It is slow to bolt and holds its color well when cooked, making it a favorite for both the ornamental vegetable garden and the kitchen. Harvest baby leaves at about a month for salads, or let plants mature for six to eight weeks and harvest outer stalks continually, since the plant regrows from the center through a long season.

name: Orange Habanero Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost in warm soil and transplant out after all frost danger has passed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; habanero needs consistent heat and a long growing season to fully ripen and develop maximum heat and fruitiness.
directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost in warm soil and transplant out after all frost danger has passed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; habanero needs consistent heat and a long growing season to fully ripen and develop maximum heat and fruitiness. This classic habanero selection produces small, lantern-shaped fruit that ripens from green through yellow to a vivid bright orange, carrying an intense, fruity, floral heat in the 100,000-350,000 Scoville range that has made habanero peppers a staple of Caribbean, Yucatecan, and hot sauce cuisine. The compact, bushy plants are heavy producers over a long season and thrive in the same hot, humid conditions favored by many tropical Capsicum species, continuing to set fruit through the hottest part of summer when some other peppers slow down. Harvest fruit at full orange color for maximum heat and flavor, wear gloves when handling, and avoid touching your face or eyes after working with the fruit.

name: Orange Pop Sweet Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; move transplants outside once the weather has warmed.
directions: Orange Pop is a compact snacking pepper bred for container growing, producing a heavy set of small, bright orange fruit that ripens sweet with almost no seed cavity. Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and move transplants out once the weather has warmed. The tidy, well-branched plant stays productive on a patio or balcony through the season, and ripe fruit can be eaten straight off the plant.

name: Orange Smoothie Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, rich soil, giving vines room to run; Orange Smoothie is an AAS-winning small pumpkin bred for an unusually smooth, rib-free rind, unlike the deep ridges typical of most jack-o-lantern and pie pumpkins.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vines room to spread. Orange Smoothie is an AAS-winning small-to-medium pumpkin distinguished by an unusually smooth, nearly rib-free rind — most pumpkins have pronounced vertical ridges, but Orange Smoothie's clean, rounded surface gives it a distinctive look for decoration and makes it especially easy to carve or paint without ridges interrupting the design. The fruit is a good size for both decorative use and cooking, with reasonably good flesh quality for pies and purees. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and color deepens to solid orange, cutting the stem with a few inches attached, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before use or fall display.
sources: All-America Selections — Orange Smoothie Pumpkin winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Orange Strawberry Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March. The elongated, oxheart shape makes the large fruits (1–2 pounds) less likely to crack than large round beefsteak types. In zone 9 the fall planting in August produces particularly sweet, rich-flavored fruits as cooler October-November temperatures concentrate the sugars and reduce water content in the flesh.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with cage or stake support; Orange Strawberry (also known as Strawberry Oxheart Orange) is an oxheart-type heirloom tomato producing large, elongated, pointed fruits with a distinctive heart or strawberry silhouette in vivid, deep orange — the 'strawberry' in the name refers to the fruit shape, not the flavor. The thick, meaty, deep orange flesh is extraordinarily dense and nearly seedless, with a small hollow interior cavity common to oxheart types — the low water content and minimal seed-gel gives Orange Strawberry one of the meatiest, most substantial textures of any tomato type, with a concentrated, rich, fruity-sweet tomato flavor that becomes even more intense when the dense flesh is sliced for sandwiches or diced for salads. Orange tomatoes are distinguished by their lycopene profile — beta-carotene and tetra-cis-lycopene rather than the all-trans lycopene of red tomatoes — which is more bioavailable than the red form and contributes to the characteristic rich, fruity sweetness of orange-fleshed varieties.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Orange Strawberry Oxheart Tomato
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Oxheart Tomato Varieties
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Orange and Yellow Heirloom Tomatoes

name: Orange Sun Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Orange Sun is a fully orange-ripening bell pepper that reaches mature orange color rather than the halfway-ripened red-orange of some varieties that are harvested early. In zone 9, transplant March–April for spring production; a fall crop started from seed in July can extend production into October–November. The full orange color develops several weeks after the green harvest stage — allow peppers to reach full orange before picking for the sweetest, most nutritious fruit. Orange bell peppers are higher in certain carotenoids (beta-cryptoxanthin) than red or green bells, and the flavor at full orange ripeness is sweet and mild with none of the grassy notes of green-stage peppers. Plant in full sun with good drainage; consistent watering during fruit development prevents blossom end rot and promotes even development.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Allow to fully color orange before harvesting for best flavor. Orange Sun is an F1 hybrid bell pepper variety selected for fully orange fruit at maturity — the distinctive bright orange color of an orange-ripe bell pepper rather than the mixed red-orange of incompletely ripened red varieties harvested early. Orange bell peppers as a category occupy an intermediate position in the bell pepper maturity and flavor spectrum: green peppers are harvested immature, red peppers are harvested fully ripe (or harvested orange-yellow then gassed), yellow and orange peppers represent distinct genetic selections that color differently from red-maturing types. True orange varieties like Orange Sun have the genetics to produce stable, uniform orange coloring at maturity — different from red varieties picked early, which produce a mottled, inconsistent orange appearance and inferior flavor. The walls of Orange Sun are thick and firm, excellent for fresh eating, roasting, and stuffing. The flavor at full orange ripeness is notably sweeter and more complex than green bells from the same plant, as the conversion of chlorophyll to carotenoids during ripening is accompanied by conversion of starches to sugars and development of aromatic compounds. Orange Sun is early-maturing for a bell pepper, reaching the green harvest stage approximately 70 days from transplanting and full orange ripeness a few weeks later — making it practical for the Gulf South's spring production window before summer heat limits continued setting.
sources: Harris Seeds — Orange Sun bell pepper variety description and performance notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Orange bell pepper variety comparison
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sweet Pepper Variety Selection for Florida and the Gulf South

name: OrangeGlo Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil thoroughly warmed; in zone 9 plant March–May. OrangeGlo produces large (20–30 lbs) oblong fruits — space rows widely. The orange flesh can be difficult to judge for ripeness by internal color alone; use the standard external cues: yellow ground spot, dried tendril nearest the fruit, and hollow thump. In zone 9 the long, hot summer is ideal for this variety's full flavor development.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy to loamy, fertile, slightly acidic soil; OrangeGlo is an heirloom watermelon producing large, oblong fruits with striped yellow-green skin and vivid deep orange flesh — the orange color results from high beta-carotene content rather than the lycopene responsible for red watermelon flesh, giving OrangeGlo significantly higher vitamin A precursor content than conventional red varieties. The flavor is sweet and mild with a distinctive tropical, honey-melon note that many tasters describe as sweeter and less watery than red watermelons — the orange flesh has a slightly different sugar profile and flavor that creates a tropical-fruity sweetness. OrangeGlo has been selected from an heirloom lineage for consistent large size (typically 20–30 pounds), high sugar content, and the distinctive orange flesh color that makes it immediately striking when cut open at the table. The unusual orange interior creates a dramatic visual contrast in fruit arrangements and makes OrangeGlo watermelon a reliable conversation piece at summer gatherings.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — OrangeGlo Watermelon Heirloom
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — OrangeGlo History and Production
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Watermelon Variety Trials

name: Orangetti Spaghetti Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Orangetti is a compact, early-maturing spaghetti squash that matures to a vivid deep orange exterior (rather than the cream-white of standard spaghetti squash) with higher beta-carotene content and the same characteristic stranded flesh texture — it is earlier, more flavorful, and more nutritious than standard spaghetti squash.
directions: Direct sow after last frost; Orangetti is semi-compact with shorter vines than standard spaghetti squash; harvest when the outer skin is a uniform deep orange and the rind is firm; bake halved at 375°F for 40–50 minutes and scrape the interior with a fork to produce the characteristic pasta-like strands that give spaghetti squash its name. Orangetti is a distinctive type of spaghetti squash developed in Israel through breeding work at the Negev branch of the Agricultural Research Organization, selected for its vivid orange skin color (versus the pale cream-yellow of standard spaghetti squash), higher beta-carotene content in both the skin and the stranded flesh, and slightly earlier maturity than most spaghetti squash varieties. The vegetable has the same characteristic feature that makes all spaghetti squash unique — the interior flesh separates into long, pasta-like strands when cooked — but the Orangetti variant produces strands that are slightly yellower-orange than the pale yellow of standard varieties, reflecting the higher pigment content. The flavor of Orangetti is considered by many cooks to be sweeter and more complex than standard white spaghetti squash, though still with the mild, somewhat neutral quality that makes spaghetti squash a versatile pasta substitute for low-carbohydrate diets. The compact, semi-bush vine habit is more manageable than standard spaghetti squash in small gardens. Orangetti typically yields 3–5 fruits per vine weighing 2–4 lbs each.

name: Orazio Fennel
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in spring, or again in mid- to late summer for a fall crop, since Orazio matures quickly enough to fit both windows.
directions: Orazio is a fast-maturing F1 hybrid Florence fennel bred for uniform, thick, rounded bulbs that size up notably sooner than older open-pollinated strains. Direct sow into rich, well-drained soil and thin seedlings early, since fennel's taproot makes it a poor candidate for transplanting. Harvest tender baby bulbs at around 50 days or let plants continue to full size; mounding soil around the swelling base as it develops helps keep the bulb pale and sweet rather than fibrous.

name: Orca Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Orca is a bush dry bean type that matures in 75–90 days to full dry-shell stage; the beans are famous for their striking two-tone coloring — exactly half black, half white on each bean — that resembles the coloring of orca (killer) whales and makes them one of the most visually distinctive dry beans available.
directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in full sun; harvest for dry beans when pods are fully dry and papery on the vine; in humid climates pull whole plants before complete drying and hang in a sheltered, airy space to finish drying to prevent mold on pods. Orca beans are a relatively modern open-pollinated dry bean variety that quickly gained wide popularity among seed savers and heirloom gardeners for their extraordinary visual appearance: each bean is precisely two-toned, with exactly one half black and one half white in a pattern that closely resembles the distinctive black-and-white coloring of the orca whale — hence the common names 'Orca Bean' and 'Killer Whale Bean.' The coloring is remarkably consistent across all seeds from a plant, though the exact position of the color boundary and the ratio of black to white can vary slightly between individual seeds. The seeds are medium-sized, slightly plump, and oval. When cooked, the dramatic two-tone coloring fades and the beans become a more uniform dark brown to black, as with most vividly colored beans — the show is in the seed, not the cooked dish. The flavor is mild and creamy, similar to black beans, with a pleasantly earthy character. Orca beans are excellent in soups, stews, rice dishes, and any preparation where black beans are used. They are often added to seed displays and mixed bean soups specifically for visual interest, and the raw seeds make a striking addition to craft projects, seed collages, and botanical displays.

name: Orchard Baby Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after frost danger passes; its short stalks and quick maturity suit close spacing, raised beds, and large containers.
directions: Bred in Canada and introduced commercially in the 1940s by a North Dakota seed house, this extra-dwarf sweet corn nearly disappeared after the original seed house closed before being rescued and preserved by heirloom growers. Stalks stand a compact 3 to 5 feet yet still carry two ears each, with small five- to six-inch ears bearing eight to ten rows of tender yellow kernels and old-fashioned, mildly sweet flavor rather than the intense sweetness of modern hybrids. Its short stature and fast finish make it one of the better sweet corns for small gardens, raised beds, or large patio containers. Because it is open-pollinated, isolate it from other corn varieties if you intend to save true seed.

name: Oregon Spring Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before transplanting; Oregon Spring can be set out slightly earlier than most tomatoes since it sets fruit at cooler temperatures than typical varieties.
directions: Start seed indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into the garden with minimal staking needed, since the compact determinate plants stay under three feet. Oregon Spring was bred by Dr. James Baggett at Oregon State University from a cross involving the cold-adapted Russian variety Severianin, and it was released in 1984 specifically for short, cool growing seasons in the Pacific Northwest and similar climates. The nearly seedless, medium-sized fruit sets even when nights stay chilly, giving gardeners in short-season regions a dependable early, low-acid harvest.

name: Oregon Sugar Pod Snow Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–8 weeks before last frost; Oregon Sugar Pod is a 1971 All-America Selections winner snow pea with large, flat, edible pods and resistance to pea enation mosaic virus — one of the most popular and disease-resistant snow peas available, excellent for both Pacific Northwest and Southern gardens.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep in rows 18–24 inches apart; provide a 2–3 foot trellis or fence for support. Oregon Sugar Pod pea won the All-America Selections award in 1971 and remains one of the most widely grown and most reliable snow peas, selected for both outstanding pod quality and resistance to pea enation mosaic virus (PEMV), a significant disease problem in humid growing regions. The semi-dwarf plants produce large (4–4.5 inch), flat, very sweet pods harvested when the pod wall is still translucent and peas inside are just barely beginning to swell — the 'snow pea' harvest window when the entire flat, stringless pod is eaten. Used in stir-frying, sautéing, and raw in salads, where the flat pods retain their crisp texture and bright color well when cooked quickly over high heat.

name: Orient Express Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Orient Express is an All-America Selections award-winning Japanese-type eggplant producing long (8–10 inch), slender, dark purple fruits in 58–68 days from transplant — one of the earliest-maturing eggplants available — making it the top choice for northern gardeners with short seasons and for Gulf Coast gardeners who want eggplant harvest to begin before peak summer heat reduces fruit set.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 80°F; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil; Orient Express benefits from staking in windy locations; harvest fruits when 6–10 inches long and the skin is glossy dark purple — do not allow to over-ripen; continuous picking encourages continued fruit production. Orient Express is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning F1 hybrid Japanese-type eggplant that combines the long, slender fruit shape, thin skin, and tender flesh of Asian eggplant varieties with very early maturity (58–68 days from transplant) — a combination that makes it highly productive across a wide range of climates. The long (8–10 inch), slender (1.5–2 inch diameter) fruits have glossy, near-black purple skin and white, very tender flesh with minimal seeds and virtually no bitterness — the thin skin makes Orient Express excellent for eating with skin on in stir-fries, Japanese-style preparations (nasu dengaku — miso-glazed grilled eggplant), grilling, and dishes where the skin texture would be noticeable in a thick-skinned globe eggplant. The early maturity is particularly valuable for Gulf Coast and Southern gardeners who want to get the eggplant harvest in before peak summer heat reduces fruit set, and for northern gardeners who need production in 60–70 days rather than 80–90 days. Highly productive — a well-grown plant can produce 6–10 fruits at once — and the early season timing allows for multiple successive harvests.

name: Orion Florence Fennel
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost, or start a fall crop in mid to late summer since Orion resists bolting better in longer days than older Florence types.
directions: Orion is a hybrid Florence fennel selected for improved bolt resistance and uniform, rounded bulb formation, making it more reliable than open-pollinated types for both spring and fall sowings. Bulbs develop a tight, flattened-round shape with tender, sweetly anise-flavored flesh and stay in good condition in the field longer than older cultivars before splitting or flowering. Give it consistent moisture and full sun to encourage smooth, well-formed bulbs, and harvest promptly once bulbs reach baseball to tennis-ball size. Gardeners who have struggled with fennel bolting in variable spring weather choose Orion for its dependability across a wider sowing window.

name: Orleans Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65F in well-drained, loamy soil in full sun; Orleans is an LSU AgCenter release bred as a higher-yielding, more disease-resistant alternative to Beauregard for Gulf South growers.
directions: Plant certified sweet potato slips after the last frost in well-drained, loamy to sandy loam, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Orleans is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release developed as a modernized alternative to the industry-standard Beauregard, bred for higher yields, improved resistance to soil-borne diseases, and a slightly longer storage life after curing. Skin and flesh are both a rich orange, with smooth, uniformly shaped roots that store and cure well. Like all sweet potatoes, newly dug roots are starchy rather than sweet; cure at 85-90F and 85-90% humidity for 5-7 days to heal skin wounds and convert starches into the sugars that give sweet potatoes their characteristic flavor. Plant certified, virus-indexed slips rather than home-grown slips from grocery-store roots to avoid introducing sweet potato virus disease, which reduces yield over successive seasons. Well suited to Louisiana's long, humid growing season and heavy summer rainfall.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Potato Variety Releases
North Carolina State Extension — Sweet Potato Production
Mississippi State University Extension — Sweet Potato Variety Guide

name: Ormskirk Late Cabbage
plantingNote: Start seed in late summer for transplanting out for a winter harvest, or start in early spring for fall harvest; Ormskirk Late is a very cold-hardy Savoy-type winter cabbage from Lancashire, England.
directions: Start seed in a nursery bed or trays and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, timing planting so heads mature through the cool season. Ormskirk Late is a traditional Savoy-type winter cabbage bred in the town of Ormskirk in Lancashire, England, valued for its deeply crinkled, dark blue-green leaves and dense, sweet-flavored heads that improve in flavor after exposure to frost, and for standing in the garden through hard winter weather without splitting. It is well suited to a long, cool fall-to-winter growing season in mild climates like the Gulf South. Harvest heads once firm, cutting at the base and leaving the outer wrapper leaves in the garden.

name: Oro de Valle Quinoa
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun; Oro de Valle is a heat-adapted quinoa selection developed for the American Southwest, more tolerant of warm growing conditions than most quinoa varieties.
directions: Direct sow in early spring into average, well-drained soil in full sun. Oro de Valle, meaning 'gold of the valley,' was developed in Arizona specifically to adapt quinoa to hot, arid, low-elevation growing conditions unlike the cool highland climate quinoa traditionally requires, making it one of the more heat-tolerant quinoa selections available for warmer American gardens. It produces bright golden seed heads on tall, upright stems, valued for both grain production and its striking garden presence. Harvest seed heads once they dry and the seeds rattle loosely, then thresh and winnow before rinsing to remove the bitter saponin coating and cooking or storing.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

name: Osage Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost once soil is warm; Osage is an early-1900s American heirloom muskmelon, also sold historically as Miller's Cream, valued for its smooth rind and richly flavored salmon flesh.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained hills after danger of frost has passed, thinning to the strongest seedlings and training vines with room to spread. Osage is an early twentieth-century American heirloom muskmelon, also offered under the name Miller's Cream, distinguished from netted-rind types like Hearts of Gold by its comparatively smooth, faintly ribbed skin and its exceptionally sweet, deep salmon-orange flesh. Water consistently while vines establish and fruit sizes up, then reduce moisture as the melons approach ripeness to intensify flavor. Harvest at full slip, when the stem releases from the fruit with gentle pressure and the blossom end gives slightly and smells sweetly fragrant.

name: Osaka Purple Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer or fall (zones 7–11) or early spring (zones 3–7); Osaka Purple is a distinctive Japanese mustard green with round, semi-blistered, bright purple-red leaves — the color intensifies in cool weather, making it one of the most visually striking cool-season greens; the flavor is milder than large-leaved Southern mustard types when young, making it excellent for fresh salads and Asian-style applications.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in cool weather; thin to 6–12 inches for mature plants or sow thickly for baby leaf harvest at 3–4 inches; the rich purple color intensifies dramatically as temperatures cool (40–55°F); harvest outer leaves for cut-and-come-again production or harvest whole plants at the baby leaf stage. Osaka Purple is a Japanese mustard green variety with notably different characteristics from the large-leaved American mustard green types — rather than elongated, flat leaves, Osaka Purple produces compact, round, slightly blistered leaves (mildly puckered like a miniature Savoy cabbage) with an intense purple-red color on the upper surface that deepens in cold weather, making it among the most visually attractive winter vegetables for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens. The 'Osaka' name references Japan's second-largest city and its long vegetable-growing tradition. The flavor is milder and more delicate than large-leaved mustard greens — a gentle mustard note and pleasant sweetness that make it excellent raw in salads and fresh spring rolls, as a substitute for radicchio in salad mixes, or lightly stir-fried in Japanese and Korean cooking. Osaka Purple is one of the most visually useful plants for fall and winter salad mixes, providing intense purple-red color that contrasts beautifully with pale green lettuces and white mizuna; it pairs particularly well with arugula, watercress, and baby spinach for color and flavor contrast in mesclun-style mixes.

name: Oscar Blanco Amaranth
plantingNote: Direct sow lightly and keep soil evenly moist until seedlings establish, giving this towering variety the longest possible warm season.
directions: Sow seed shallowly once soil has warmed and thin seedlings at the two-to-four-leaf stage to give this exceptionally tall heirloom room to develop its sturdy stalks. Oscar Blanco, an old Bolivian grain type, produces long, drooping, beige-to-pink tasseled seed heads reminiscent of foxtail amaranths, reaching well over ten feet in good conditions. Support plants against wind if grown in an exposed site, since the heavy, pendant seed heads can be top-heavy on tall stems. Harvest the panicles once they feel dry and papery, then thresh by rubbing or beating the heads over a cloth to collect the grain.

name: Ostrich Plume Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall for the mildest, most tender leaves; this old curled heirloom bolts and turns sharply pungent quickly once heat arrives, so it is best treated strictly as a cool-season crop in zone 8-10 gardens.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Ostrich Plume is a long-grown American heirloom curled mustard named for its finely cut, deeply frilled, feather-like leaf margins that resemble ostrich plumage more than the coarser curling seen in many mustard types. The tightly ruffled bright green leaves make an attractive garnish planting as well as a cooking green, and young leaves are mild enough for fresh salad use before the plant matures into fuller mustard heat. Like other curled mustards, it is fast to bolt once day length and temperature increase, so successive small sowings through the cool season give a steadier harvest than one large planting. Older, larger leaves develop a stronger peppery bite and are best suited to cooked greens rather than raw eating.

name: Otto File Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in blocks of at least 4 rows; Otto File is a Tuscan yellow flint corn named for its defining characteristic — exactly eight rows of kernels on each ear (otto = eight, file = rows in Italian) — and the traditional grain for authentic Tuscan polenta, where its deep yellow color and nutty flavor produce a superior porridge distinct from the pale commercial product.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in well-prepared, fertile soil; Otto File is an eight-row flint corn that produces compact ears with exactly 8 rows of golden-yellow kernels; allow ears to dry fully on the stalk; stone-grind for the authentic coarse-textured, deeply flavored polenta that is standard in Tuscany and distinguishes Italian-style polenta from American cornmeal mush. Otto File (Italian: otto fila = eight rows) is the traditional polenta corn of Tuscany, the Italian region where polenta — while less dominant than in the Venice region of northeastern Italy — has been made from this specific eight-row flint corn for generations. The variety name precisely describes the defining characteristic of the ear: each cob bears exactly eight rows of kernels, a consistent genetic trait that is visible at harvest and that Italian farmers used for centuries as a way to identify and maintain the variety. The yellow flint kernels are deeply golden to amber-yellow at maturity, and when stone-ground they produce a meal with a rich, nutty, complex flavor and a pleasantly coarse, somewhat granular texture that gives polenta its characteristic hearty body. Otto File is shorter-season than the Floriani Red Flint (90–110 days versus 100–120) and adapts well to a wide range of climates including the humid Southeast and Gulf South. The compact plant height (5–7 feet) makes it somewhat easier to manage in wind-prone garden situations than taller heritage corns. Otto File is prized by Italian-American home cooks and professional chefs who seek the authentic grain for traditional polenta preparations.

name: Outredgeous Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Outredgeous is a deep burgundy-red romaine lettuce famous as the first crop grown and eaten by astronauts aboard the International Space Station, and a reliable, richly colored performer in the home garden.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Outredgeous is an open-pollinated romaine lettuce selected for intensely dark red-burgundy outer leaves that shade to green toward the crisp, upright heart, giving each head striking two-tone color as well as classic romaine crunch and mild, sweet flavor. It gained widespread recognition in 2015 as the first food crop grown, harvested, and eaten by astronauts aboard the International Space Station as part of NASA's Veggie experiment, chosen partly for its rich anthocyanin pigmentation and reliable performance. In the home garden it is simply a vigorous, dependable, good-flavored red romaine, harvested either as whole heads once firm or as individual outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again approach. It bolts and turns bitter in sustained summer heat, so plant in early spring and again in fall for the best quality in zone 9, providing afternoon shade for plantings that overlap with warm weather.
sources: NASA — Veggie Experiment and Outredgeous Lettuce on the ISS
Seed Savers Exchange — Outredgeous Lettuce variety notes
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Red Romaine Varieties

name: Oxheart Carrot
plantingNote: Sow direct and thin early, since crowded roots distort quickly given their broad, blunt shape.
directions: A French heirloom, known in its homeland around Guérande in Brittany, bred specifically for heavy clay and stony soils that defeat long, tapered carrot types. The blunt, conical roots grow only 4-5 inches long but swell wide at the shoulder, so they size up reliably without forking where deep, loose ground is unavailable. Sow direct and thin early, since crowded roots distort quickly given their broad shape; the dense orange flesh is sweet and stores well through fall.

name: Ozark Giant Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant outdoors once the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed.
directions: Ozark Giant is an old regional heirloom prized for producing some of the largest bell peppers a home gardener can grow, with fruit commonly reaching six inches or more in length on sturdy, heavy-bearing plants. The thick, crisp flesh ripens from green to red and is noted for a flavor considered sweeter and more robust than many modern bell hybrids. Because the plants carry an unusually heavy fruit load for their size, staking helps prevent branches from snapping once peppers begin to size up. It performs especially well through hot, humid Southern summers, making it a strong choice for gardeners in the region where it originated.

name: Ozark Razorback Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed past 65°F and frost danger has passed; this vigorous climbing type does best with a trellis or fence to keep vines and pods up off the ground.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide a trellis, fence, or tall stakes since Ozark Razorback is a true climbing cowpea rather than the semi-bush habit of most Southern pea varieties. It is an Ozark Mountain heirloom prized for outstanding drought tolerance and the ability to produce reliably on thin, poor soils where richer garden peas struggle. Each dried seed carries a distinctive calico pattern, with mottled color covering roughly half the seed coat, making saved seed easy to identify from season to season. The fresh-shelled peas cook up creamy and richly flavored, similar to a black-eyed pea, and the vigorous vines also work well as a nitrogen-fixing summer cover crop when a section of the garden is resting between plantings.

name: Ozette Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces after the soil has warmed slightly; this late fingerling needs a long full season to fill out its knobby tubers.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Ozette is descended from fingerling potatoes brought to the Pacific Northwest coast by Spanish explorers in the late 1700s and preserved for generations by the Makah Tribe near Neah Bay, Washington. The tubers are long, narrow, and knobby with tan skin and dense, waxy, slightly nutty yellow flesh that holds together well when steamed or roasted whole. It is listed on the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste as a culturally significant heirloom variety worth preserving in home gardens. Grow it for its genuine Indigenous heritage and distinctive narrow fingerling shape rather than for high yield, since production is modest compared to modern cultivars.
sources: Slow Food USA - Ark of Taste

name: Pablo Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest, or in late summer for a fall crop; Pablo is a dark red romaine hybrid grown for its uniform, upright heads and slower bolting than many older red romaine varieties.
directions: Sow seed shallowly and keep the bed consistently moist for even germination, then thin seedlings to their final spacing once true leaves appear. Pablo is a dark burgundy-red romaine hybrid that holds its rich color and upright, well-filled head shape more reliably than many open-pollinated red romaines, with a crisp texture and mild flavor typical of romaine types. It tolerates a bit more heat before bolting than many red lettuces, giving it a somewhat longer productive window into late spring, though it still performs best in the cool shoulder seasons in a Gulf Coast garden. Harvest whole heads once fully formed, or pull individual outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again harvest over several weeks, and provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture to further delay bolting as temperatures rise.

name: Pachino Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed; Pachino types thrive in lean, sandy, slightly saline soil and intense heat, so avoid overwatering or overly rich ground.
directions: Pachino takes its name from the town at Sicily's southeastern tip, where volcanic, sandy, mineral-rich soil and near-constant sun and sea breeze concentrate sugars in small, intensely flavored cherry and plum-shaped fruit, earning the tomato PGI (IGP) status in Italy. Grow on a trellis or stake and let the soil run drier than typical tomato culture, since mild water stress is part of what produces the variety's concentrated sweetness and thin, glossy skin. Fruit is traditionally harvested still on the vine in small clusters and sold or stored that way, since the cluster habit extends shelf life for weeks at room temperature. Use fresh in salads, on bruschetta, or simply halved and dressed with olive oil, where the tomato's natural sweetness needs little embellishment.
sources: Consorzio di Tutela Pomodoro di Pachino IGP

name: Pacific Purple Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant dormant crowns in early spring in a trench 6-8 inches deep, spreading roots over a mound of loose soil and backfilling gradually as spears emerge over the season. Withhold harvest for the first two years to let the extensive purple-tinged root system establish fully.
directions: Plant dormant crowns in early spring in a trench 6-8 inches deep, spreading roots over a mound of loose soil and backfilling gradually as spears emerge over the season. Withhold harvest for the first two years to let the extensive root system establish fully. Pacific Purple was bred in New Zealand from purple-skinned asparagus germplasm and is notable for spears with a naturally higher sugar content and lower fiber than most green cultivars, giving it a mild, sweet flavor that many gardeners enjoy raw as well as cooked. The purple pigment fades to green when spears are cooked, but the tenderness and sweetness carry through, and the thick spears also tend to be less fibrous and easier to trim than many green varieties.

name: Packman Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 transplant February–March for spring harvest or August–September for fall. Packman is an early variety well-adapted to the shorter cool seasons available in zone 9's spring and fall broccoli windows.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 60–75°F; Packman broccoli is a 1982 All-America Selections-winning hybrid that remains one of the most widely grown garden broccoli varieties — an early-maturing variety (65–75 days from transplant) producing large, blue-green central heads with a domed, attractive appearance and good flavor. After the central head is harvested, Packman produces generous side shoots that continue through the season, extending harvest considerably beyond what determinate, single-head broccoli types provide. The early maturation is particularly valuable for zone 9 gardeners who need a broccoli that produces before summer heat terminates the season, and for northern gardeners who want to beat early fall frosts. Packman is dependable, widely available, and well-adapted to a range of growing conditions — making it an excellent beginner's broccoli and a reliable backbone variety for any broccoli production.
sources: All-America Selections — Packman broccoli AAS winner 1982
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Broccoli Production Guide
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Vegetable Variety Trials

name: Padrón Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes into warm, well-drained soil in full sun. Harvest small and green, at 2–3 inches, for the classic blistered tapas dish — heat varies unpredictably fruit to fruit, part of the traditional appeal.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after frost danger passes into warm, well-drained soil in full sun. A traditional pepper from the Galicia region of Spain, Padrón is grown almost exclusively for the classic tapas dish 'pimientos de Padrón' — small peppers quickly blistered whole in hot olive oil and finished with coarse salt — and is famous for its unpredictable heat, where most fruit stay mild but roughly one in ten packs a surprising, sharp bite, a trait tied to growing conditions and picking size. Harvest fruit small and green, at 2–3 inches, well before they mature to red, since flavor and the traditional use are built around the small, immature stage. The compact, productive plants set fruit heavily over a long season, rewarding frequent picking.

name: Painted Lady Runner Bean
plantingNote: Sow around or just after last frost at the base of a tall, sturdy trellis; like other runner beans, Painted Lady prefers cooler summers and drops flowers in intense heat.
directions: Sow seeds 2 inches deep at the base of a robust trellis or obelisk at least 6 feet tall; this vigorous climber needs a sturdy support and will overwhelm light structures. A 19th-century English heirloom, Painted Lady is grown as much for its striking bicolor red-and-white flowers as for its edible pods, the two-toned blossoms making it a favorite for cottage gardens and pollinator plantings as well as the vegetable patch. Hummingbirds and bumblebees visit the flowers heavily, and the tender young pods can be picked at 6–8 inches for fresh eating, while pods left to mature yield large, attractively mottled purple-and-cream dry beans. Pick pods frequently to keep the vigorous vines flowering and producing over a long season.

name: Painted Mountain Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow at last frost — Painted Mountain tolerates light frost and can be planted earlier than most corns; it was developed in Montana by Dave Christensen specifically for cold, short-season mountain growing conditions, maturing in 65–85 days from seed at altitudes over 5,000 feet.
directions: Sow in blocks of at least 4 rows after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Painted Mountain is shorter than most corns and somewhat drought-tolerant once established. Painted Mountain corn was developed over 30 years by Dave Christensen of Montana through selection from hundreds of traditional Native American and pioneer corn varieties, specifically to produce an open-pollinated flour corn that matures in 65–85 days in the short growing seasons of Montana mountain communities; the resulting variety is extremely early-maturing, cold-tolerant, and drought-resistant compared to most corns. The ears are 6–8 inches long with strikingly beautiful, multi-colored kernels in a palette of crimson, blue, gold, yellow, orange, and white that can produce rainbow-like color gradients even on a single ear. The flour ground from Painted Mountain has sweet, complex flavor; the variety is also grown as a ornamental corn and for whole-grain cooking.

name: Painted Pony Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Painted Pony is a determinate bush dry bean that sets pods over a 2–3 week window. Allow pods to dry on the vine until the pods are tan, papery, and the beans rattle inside, then harvest and finish drying indoors before shelling. In zone 9, a short spring sowing (March–April) before summer heat sets in is ideal.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 60°F; allow pods to fully mature and dry on the vine before harvesting. Painted Pony is a visually spectacular heirloom dry bean producing medium-sized beans with a beautiful swirled pattern of deep maroon-red, tan, and cream — each bean unique in its markings, resembling the coat of an Appaloosa or pinto horse, which gives the variety its evocative name. The ornamental markings unfortunately fade significantly when cooked (as with most colorfully marked dry beans), but the flavor is excellent — rich, slightly earthy, and starchy with the substantial body that makes it outstanding in soups, chilis, stews, and baked bean preparations. Painted Pony beans hold their shape reasonably well when cooked, making them suitable for preparations where bean integrity matters. A productive bush-type bean (no staking required) that fits well into small gardens and is an outstanding choice for seed saving due to its distinctive and reliably reproduced markings. An excellent heirloom variety for bean enthusiasts who value genetic and visual diversity in their garden and pantry.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Painted Pony bean variety notes
Native Seeds/SEARCH — Heirloom bean germplasm collection

name: Painted Serpent Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained, moist, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Painted Serpent is a striped heirloom Armenian cucumber (botanically a muskmelon) with alternating light and dark green ribbing along its long, curved fruit.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, moderately fertile, moist soil in full sun; provide a trellis for the straightest fruit shape and harvest at 12-18 inches for the best texture. Painted Serpent bears the same extraordinarily long, curling fruit typical of Armenian cucumber, but distinguished by striking alternating stripes of light and dark green running the length of the fruit, an eye-catching heirloom pattern that sets it apart in the garden and at market. Like other Armenian cucumbers it is botanically a muskmelon rather than a true cucumber, giving it notably better heat tolerance through Gulf Coast summers than standard cucumbers, with thin, edible skin and mild, non-bitter, faintly melon-scented flesh. Harvest regularly to keep vines productive, since old, oversized fruit develops tougher skin and more prominent seeds.

name: Paladin Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Paladin was among the first bell peppers bred with good resistance to Phytophthora blight, a devastating soil-borne disease that thrives in the wet, poorly drained conditions common after heavy Gulf South rain.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Paladin was one of the first commercially significant bell pepper hybrids bred with meaningful resistance to Phytophthora blight, a fast-moving soil-borne disease that can wilt and kill an entire pepper planting within days after heavy rain leaves soil saturated, as commonly happens in Gulf Coast summer storms. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good flavor and sweetness if left on the plant. Because good drainage alone cannot fully protect against Phytophthora in a wet season, Paladin's genetic resistance gives it a real advantage in low-lying or poorly drained garden beds. Harvest at the green stage for milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red, and keep picking regularly to encourage continued production.
sources: seed catalog reference (Johnny's Selected Seeds, Stokes Seeds)
Rutgers University — Pepper Disease Resistance Trials

name: Panache Parsnip
plantingNote: Direct sow fresh seed as soon as soil is workable in spring, in deep, loose, stone-free ground; parsnip seed loses viability quickly, so use current-year seed.
directions: Panache is a vigorous modern F1 parsnip that produces long, wedge-shaped roots with notably smooth white skin and sweet, creamy flesh, developed as a rival to show-quality types while remaining practical for ordinary garden use. It combines good field resistance to canker with strong storage quality, holding well in the ground or in cool storage after harvest. Sow shallowly into loosened, stone-free soil and keep the seedbed consistently moist, since parsnip germinates slowly and unevenly and dry spells reduce stands further. As with all parsnips, delay harvest until after one or more hard frosts, which convert root starches to sugars for noticeably sweeter roots.

name: Pantano Romanesco Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Pantano Romanesco is a traditional deeply ribbed Roman heirloom tomato named for the Pantano d'Ardea area near Rome.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Pantano Romanesco bears medium-to-large, deeply ribbed red-pink fruit with a flattened shape and rich, complex flavor prized in Roman home cooking for both fresh eating and sauce, the pronounced ribbing and slightly irregular form typical of many traditional Italian heirloom slicers. Its productive vines and well-adapted heat tolerance suit warm growing regions. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

name: Papaya Pear Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis if space is limited, since vines can sprawl widely.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vine plenty of room or a sturdy trellis to climb. Papaya Pear is a small, distinctively pear-shaped squash with pale, mottled skin, harvested young at three to four inches as a tender, mild summer squash for cooking, or left to mature into a firmer, longer-keeping fruit valued as a novelty ornamental for fall displays alongside gourds and pumpkins. This dual-purpose flexibility — usable young in the kitchen or later as an attractive harvest decoration — makes it a fun addition to a vegetable garden looking for something beyond standard zucchini and yellow squash. Pick young fruit every few days for the best culinary texture, or leave select fruit to fully mature and harden for fall display and longer storage.

name: Par-Cel Celery
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Par-Cel is grown for its leaves rather than a blanched stalk and is much easier and faster to raise than standard stalk celery.
directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Par-Cel is grown for its leaves rather than a blanched stalk and is much easier and faster to raise than standard stalk celery. This cutting-type celery produces a bushy clump of thin, dark green, flat-leaf-parsley-like stems and foliage with full, concentrated celery flavor, cut and used as a seasoning herb rather than eaten as a crunchy stalk vegetable. It resists bolting and disease better than conventional celery, tolerates the light shade and humidity of a Gulf South summer far better than blanched celery, and regrows readily after cutting for a season-long harvest. Snip outer stems as needed for soups, stocks, and stuffing, always leaving the center growing point intact to keep the plant productive.

name: Parade Bunching Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for winter harvest or January–February for spring. Parade is a non-bulbing type that produces a single upright stem rather than multiple small bulbs, giving cleaner, more uniform appearance. Successive sowings every 4 weeks provide continuous harvest of young green onions. Plants can also be harvested at baby green stage (25–30 days) or at full size at 60–70 days.
directions: Direct sow thinly in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Parade is a bunching onion (Japanese-type scallion or green onion) producing straight, uniform, single-stemmed plants with bright white bases, upright green tops, and a clean, mild, sweet flavor — the ideal scallion for fresh eating, garnishing, and all uses where an attractive, uniform appearance matters. Unlike multiplying types that form clusters of small bulbs, Parade produces a single straight stem that is easier to harvest, wash, and present. The non-bulbing, perennial-type Allium fistulosum species tolerates more cold, heat, and wet soil than common bulbing onions, making it well-suited to zone 9 year-round production. Parade is widely used in commercial food service and restaurant settings precisely because the straight, single-stem habit provides uniform portions without the cleaning and sorting of cluster types. In zone 9 plant Parade in fall for the cleanest, sweetest harvest through winter and spring.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Parade Bunching Onion Variety Notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Scallion and Green Onion Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bunching Onions for Texas Gardens

name: Parbhani Kranti Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil; valued where whitefly-transmitted yellow vein mosaic virus is a regional problem for okra.
directions: Parbhani Kranti is a widely grown Indian okra release bred from a backcross of the wild relative Abelmoschus manihot into the cultivar Pusa Sawani, giving it strong resistance to yellow vein mosaic virus, a serious whitefly-transmitted disease that can devastate susceptible okra crops.
