Plants are tall and single-stemmed with dark-green foliage, flowering around 45-50 days and ready for first harvest near 55 days. Pods are slender and dark green, best picked young for the most tender texture; this variety outyielded older standard cultivars in multi-site Indian field trials.
sources: peer-reviewed okra yellow vein mosaic virus resistance trials

name: Pardina Lentil
plantingNote: Direct sow in late winter to early spring into well-drained soil in full sun; Pardina is a Spanish regional lentil type from the Tierra de Campos area.
directions: Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun; Pardina is a small, brownish-grey Spanish lentil from the Tierra de Campos DOP region, grown on a thin-stalked, branching plant typical of lentils. It holds its shape well when cooked, unlike some softer lentil types, making it well suited to the classic Spanish lentejas stew and other slow-cooked dishes. Like other lentils it is drought-tolerant once established and fixes its own nitrogen, making it a low-input addition to a home vegetable garden.

name: Paris White Cos Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring in loose, fertile soil; Paris White Cos naturally folds its own leaves to self-blanch the heart without the tying older romaine culture once required.
directions: Paris White Cos is a classic upright romaine heirloom grown in French and American kitchen gardens since at least the 19th century, prized for its self-folding habit that naturally blanches the inner leaves without tying. Direct sow in early spring in loose, fertile soil, thinning seedlings to about 8 to 10 inches so the tall, narrow heads can stand upright without crowding each other. The slightly savoyed outer leaves are pale green, wrapping a crisp, sweet, almost-white heart milder than most modern romaines. Succession sow through the cool season and harvest whole heads once the center feels firm.

name: Parisian Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or late summer into loosened, stone-free soil; the round, golf-ball-sized roots size up fast and are well suited to shallow or heavy clay soils that stunt long-rooted carrots.
directions: Sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fine, well-worked soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently moist until seedlings establish, since carrot seed germinates slowly and unevenly. Parisian, also sold as Tonda di Parigi, is a 19th-century French heirloom grown for round, roughly golf-ball-sized roots rather than the long tapered shape of most carrots, which makes it a reliable performer in the shallow, rocky, or heavy clay soils that deform standard long carrots. The sweet, tender orange flesh and small size also make it an excellent choice for container growing on patios and small raised beds. Thin seedlings to two to three inches apart for well-rounded roots, and harvest as soon as they reach full size, since the round shape can turn woody if left too long in warm soil.

name: Parisian Gherkin Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed to at least 70 degrees F after the last frost; Parisian Gherkin, a 2015 All-America Selections winner, is a semi-vining mini cucumber bred specifically for midget pickles.
directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large patio container, since the semi-vining habit stays compact. Parisian Gherkin produces numerous small, black-spined cucumbers best harvested at the midget or small-pickle stage for crisp, sweet flavor, though it can also be enjoyed fresh in salads. The variety carries resistance to scab and cucumber mosaic virus with tolerance to powdery mildew, giving it good vigor through a long picking season. Water deeply and infrequently rather than with frequent light sprinklings to encourage strong root development and reduce disease pressure.
sources: university extension AAS trial garden reports

name: Parisian Pickling Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Parisian Pickling is a classic French cornichon-type cucumber grown for tiny, crisp fruit harvested daily at just an inch or two for traditional French pickles.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile soil, and provide a low trellis or ample ground space for the compact vines. Parisian Pickling is a traditional French cornichon cucumber grown for centuries around Paris and other French market gardens, producing an abundance of small, bumpy, dark green fruit that must be picked daily, often at under two inches long, to catch them at the ideal size for classic French cornichon pickles served alongside pâté and charcuterie. The vines are prolific once picking begins in earnest, since frequent harvest of the smallest fruit encourages continuous new fruit set through the season. Flavor is crisp and mild even at the smallest sizes, distinguishing true cornichon types from cucumbers merely picked young.

name: Paro Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm; like other Peruvian highland maize races, Paro tolerates the cool nights of mid-elevation Andean valleys better than lowland tropical corn types.
directions: Grow as a standard dry field corn, direct sown in full sun and left to mature fully on the stalk before harvest. Paro is one of the soft, starchy flour-type maize races documented among Peru's highland corn landraces, with kernels that grind easily once dried, traditionally parched or ground into meal for soups and breads rather than eaten fresh. Dry ears thoroughly on the stalk or under cover before shelling, and store cleaned kernels in a sealed, rodent-proof container. Because it is an open-pollinated highland landrace rather than a modern hybrid, expect more variability in ear size and kernel color between individual plants than with commercial corn.
sources: National Research Council — Races of Maize in Peru (Grobman et al.)

name: Parris Island Cos Romaine
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Parris Island Cos is the standard tall romaine lettuce of American commercial production and home gardens — a variety so widely planted that it defines the romaine category for most American growers. In zone 9, transplant September–November for fall and winter production, or February–March for spring. Romaine lettuces tolerate light frost (28–30°F) but are damaged by hard freezes. In zone 9, romaine's best quality window is November–April when temperatures keep heads tight and prevent bolting. Direct sowing works well for romaine: scatter seeds 0.25 inch deep and thin to 8–10 inches for full-sized heads, or 4–6 inches for harvesting as cut-and-come-again.
directions: Transplant or direct sow; thin to 8–10 inches for full heads. Harvest whole head or pull outer leaves. Parris Island Cos is a tall romaine (cos) lettuce — named for Parris Island, South Carolina, from the coastal region where the variety was developed and popularized — that became the dominant commercial romaine type in the United States during the mid-20th century and has remained the standard against which other romaine varieties are measured. Romaine (cos) lettuce differs from butterhead and loose-leaf types in its characteristic tall, upright, tightly folded form — the outer leaves are held upright and pressed together, creating a tall, narrow head with a pale, creamy, slightly blanched interior of great crispness and sweetness that is unavailable in the more loosely arranged butterhead types. The inner heart leaves of Parris Island Cos are the hallmark of a proper Caesar salad — the firm-textured, slightly bitter, crisp interior ribs and pale yellow-green heart that define the authentic Caesar experience. Parris Island Cos has good bolt resistance for a romaine (better than some other varieties) and thrives in the cool fall-through-spring window of Gulf South gardens in zone 8–9, where it produces high-quality heads with the sweetness and crispness that makes this variety so widely planted.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Parris Island Cos romaine variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Romaine lettuce variety history
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lettuce Production in the Gulf South

name: Partenon Zucchini
plantingNote: Because fruit sets without pollination, seed can go in slightly earlier than standard zucchini and grow well under row cover or in a high tunnel.
directions: Because Partenon sets fruit without pollination, it can be sown a bit earlier than standard zucchini and grown successfully under row cover or in a high tunnel where pollinator activity is limited. Direct sow or transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun, spacing plants about 30 inches apart. The dark-green, cylindrical fruit is exceptionally uniform, making Partenon a favorite among market growers who need consistent size and shape for bunching. Harvest young at 6-8 inches, since parthenocarpic zucchini can size up quickly once fruit set begins.

name: Pasilla Bajio Chile
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; the chilaca/pasilla is used fresh when dark green and dried (as pasilla) for authentic Mexican sauces and moles — most gardeners grow it specifically for drying.
directions: Start seeds at 80°F 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil after all frost danger has passed. Pasilla Bajio — meaning 'little raisin from the lowlands' — is the dried form of the fresh chilaca chile, producing narrow, 6–9 inch, wrinkled dark green to near-black fruits that dry to a very dark reddish-black with a distinctive fruity, dried-fruit, earthy flavor and medium heat (1,000–2,500 SHU). Pasilla is one of the three essential dried chiles used together in authentic Mexican mole negro (along with mulato and ancho) and is used extensively in Oaxacan and central Mexican cooking. The tall, upright plants produce cascading clusters of long, drooping fruits; harvest green for fresh use or allow to ripen fully dark and dry on the plant.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Pasilla de Oaxaca Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Pasilla de Oaxaca is traditionally wood-smoked and dried, distinct from the standard pasilla (chile negro) pepper used elsewhere in Mexico.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into rich, well-drained soil in full sun. Pasilla de Oaxaca produces elongated, dark green pods that ripen to deep red-brown and are traditionally cured over wood smoke before drying, a regional Oaxacan specialty distinct from the standard pasilla (chile negro) grown elsewhere in Mexico and prized in stews and moles for its smoky, fruity heat. The plants bear well over a long warm season in a climate similar to their native highland Oaxacan growing region. Harvest pods once fully colored for drying and smoking, or use fresh while still green.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

name: Pasilla Mixe Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost in a warm spot and transplant out only after soil and night air are reliably warm.
directions: Give plants full sun, warm nights, and moderate consistent water; the tall bushy plants benefit from staking once fruit-heavy. This landrace is grown in the highlands of the Mixe region of Oaxaca and traditionally left to ripen to a deep brownish-black before being slow smoke-dried over wood fires, producing a chile with intense smoky, fruity, tobacco-like depth and considerable heat. Use dried pods rehydrated into moles, adobos, and salsas where a smokier alternative to chipotle is wanted.

name: Pasilla Negro Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Pasilla Negro is typically harvested at the dark chocolate-brown to very dark green stage (not fully red — though the fruits do ripen through dark brown to red). In zone 9, transplant March–April. Allow some fruits to dry completely on the plant or harvested and air-dry for storage as the dried pasilla chile used in mole negro, enchilada sauces, and other traditional Mexican preparations. Fresh pasilla is used as a stuffed pepper (chile relleno) and in sauces.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 78–85°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Pasilla Negro (also called Chile Pasilla, Chile Negro, or Pasilla Bajío) is a long, narrow, dark-fruited Mexican chile pepper that, when dried, becomes one of the essential dried chiles of Mexican cuisine alongside ancho and mulato. The fresh pepper is 6–9 inches long, narrow (1–1.5 inches diameter), and deep dark green to near-black at the harvest stage — the name 'Pasilla' (little raisin) refers to the wrinkled, dark, raisin-like appearance of the dried pepper. The heat level is mild to medium (1,000–2,500 Scoville units) — substantially milder than serrano or jalapeño — making the peppers appropriate for use in larger quantities in sauces and moles. The flavor is rich, earthy, and slightly fruity with a complex character that makes pasilla one of the most important 'flavor' peppers in Mexican cooking rather than primarily a heat source. Mole negro, the complex black mole of Oaxaca and southern Mexico, typically uses pasilla negro (along with mulato and ancho) as its primary chile base, and the dried, toasted pasilla contributes the dark color and deep, earthy flavor that defines the sauce.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Pasilla Negro chile variety notes
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Mexican dried chile collection
University of New Mexico — Chile Pepper Institute: Pasilla Negro documentation

name: Passport Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow or set out transplants after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed well into the 70s; Passport ripens earlier than most French Charentais types, making it a good option where the season is too short for classic imported Charentais melons.
directions: Passport is a compact-vined hybrid bred to bring true French Charentais eating quality within reach of gardeners with shorter or cooler summers than the Charentais region of France. Fruit is small and round, about 2-3 pounds, with smooth gray-green skin faintly ribbed at the blossom end and deep orange, intensely aromatic flesh with a very high sugar content. Because Charentais types slip cleanly from the vine only when fully ripe, check daily near the expected harvest window and cut fruit that shows a slight crack or softening at the stem rather than waiting for it to detach on its own. Its shorter vines and earlier maturity make it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting restaurant-quality melon flavor without a long, hot growing season.

name: Patio Baby Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Patio Baby stays under two feet tall, making it well suited to containers, patios, and small raised beds where full-sized eggplants would not fit.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or a large container with good drainage; Patio Baby is an All-America Selections winner bred specifically for compact, spineless, well-behaved growth that fits easily on a patio or in a small raised bed while still producing a heavy crop of glossy, deep-purple, egg-sized fruit. It bears notably early and continues producing over a long season, with tender, mild, nearly seedless flesh typical of good eating quality eggplant. Harvest fruit at 2-3 inches long while glossy and firm, and its small stature and prolific habit make it a favorite for container vegetable gardens with limited space.

name: Patio Snacker Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Patio Snacker is specifically bred for container and small-space growing — the compact vines require minimal support and grow well in large containers (5-gallon minimum) where standard vining cucumbers would be impractical.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Patio Snacker is a compact, semi-vining cucumber variety selected for container and patio growing — producing shorter, more manageable vines (18–30 inches) than standard cucumber varieties while maintaining prolific fruit production of small (3–4 inch) snacking-size cucumbers. The small fruit size and compact plant habit are ideally matched for patio container growing: the cucumbers are sized for fresh snacking without slicing, and the plant fits in a large container (5-gallon minimum, 10-gallon ideal) with a simple stake or small trellis. Patio Snacker produces crisp, thin-skinned, nearly seedless cucumbers with mild, sweet flavor and no bitterness — characteristic of the modern small-cucumber/snacking types bred for fresh eating without the preparation steps (peeling, seed removal) required for large slicing varieties. In zone 9, cucumbers are most productive in the spring shoulder season (February–April) and the fall shoulder season (August–September) — summer heat reduces fruiting and increases disease pressure. The compact size and container suitability make Patio Snacker particularly useful for zone 9 gardeners who can move containers to optimize microclimate conditions during the challenging summer transition period.

name: Patio Star Summer Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after frost danger passes; the extremely compact habit makes this one of the few summer squash well suited to a large container on a patio.
directions: Patio Star is an All-America Selections winner bred for its dwarf, tidy bush habit, making it one of the only pattypan-type squash that performs well in a large pot or half-barrel rather than a garden bed. Plants stay compact and open, setting pale green to creamy-white, flying-saucer-shaped fruit that hold their tender texture and mild, buttery flavor even when a few are missed at the ideal 2-3 inch picking size. Harvest every day or two once fruiting begins, since the small plant size means missed fruit can slow overall production more noticeably than on a sprawling vine type. Feed container-grown plants regularly, since frequent watering in a pot leaches nutrients faster than in garden soil.

name: Patio Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into a large pot or garden bed after frost danger passes; a very short, stocky plant that thrives in patio containers as small as 12 inches across.
directions: Sow indoors and transplant into a sunny patio container or garden bed once frost danger has passed, keeping the compact plant evenly watered since small pots dry out quickly. Patio, an early All-America Selections winner, was one of the original dwarf tomato hybrids bred specifically for container growing, staying under 24 inches tall while still bearing clusters of 3-4 ounce round red fruit with reliable, old-fashioned tomato flavor. It remains a benchmark heirloom-era patio variety that predates the many modern compact hybrids it inspired.

name: Patisson Panache Jaune et Vert
scientificName: Cucurbita pepo 'Patisson Panache Jaune et Vert'
plantingNote: Direct sow once the soil is reliably warm after the last frost; scallop-type squash resents cold, soggy soil at germination.
directions: Patisson Panache Jaune et Vert is a traditional French scallop squash, its saucer-shaped fruit mottled in yellow and green rather than solid white, gold, or green like more common pattypans. Harvest small, at 2-3 inches across, when the rind is still soft enough to pierce with a fingernail, for a sweet, delicate squash best simply sauteed or steamed. Left on the vine, the fruit develops a harder rind and coarser flesh more suited to drying or ornamental use than fresh eating. Like other scallop types, it benefits from frequent picking to keep the compact bush setting new fruit through the season.

name: Patterson Onion
plantingNote: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; Patterson is a long-day (14–16 hour) hybrid yellow storage onion widely recognized as one of the most reliable and highest-yielding yellow onions for northern gardens — it produces large, globe-shaped, golden-yellow-skinned bulbs that store exceptionally well for 8–12 months in ideal conditions, making it the premier variety for northern gardeners who want a full year's supply from a single planting.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; space 4–6 inches apart in rows 12–18 inches apart; Patterson is a long-day variety requiring 14+ hours of daylight to form bulbs — performs in zones 3–8 north of the 35th parallel; harvest when 80% of tops fall naturally and cure 3–4 weeks in a warm, dry location with good airflow. Patterson is a long-day hybrid yellow storage onion widely considered one of the gold standards for reliable, high-yielding yellow onion production in northern gardens (zones 3–8); it has been a staple recommendation of Johnny's Selected Seeds — the primary commercial source — and university extension services throughout the Northeast and Midwest for its combination of high yield, consistent bulb quality, and exceptional storage performance. The large, globe-shaped bulbs have smooth, dark golden-amber skins that cure tightly and resist breakdown in storage; the flesh is white, firm, moderately pungent, and full-flavored in the traditional yellow onion style — excellent for all cooking purposes: caramelizing, soups, stews, roasting, and pickling. The standout characteristic that makes Patterson the choice of serious northern vegetable gardeners is storage life: under ideal conditions (33–40°F, low humidity, good airflow), Patterson onions store 8–12 months — essentially the full year from one harvest to the next — with far less deterioration, sprouting, or softening than most other onion varieties. This durability in storage is the result of tight, multiple layers of dry outer scales that seal the bulb against moisture and pathogens.

name: Paul Robeson Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Paul Robeson is named in honor of the American singer, actor, and civil rights activist Paul Robeson — a Russian heirloom commemorating a figure celebrated in the Soviet Union for his commitment to racial justice.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Paul Robeson is a celebrated Russian heirloom tomato that is consistently rated by connoisseurs as one of the finest-flavored dark tomatoes available — producing medium-large (7–10 oz), round to oblate fruits in a distinctive deep brick-red to mahogany-brownish-purple color with dark-green shoulders that is the hallmark of the 'black' Russian tomato aesthetic. The flavor is remarkable: deeply complex, rich, smoky, and earthy with a balanced sweetness and moderate acidity that creates a dimensional, wine-like flavor profile that many experienced tomato tasters consider superior to any other tomato type. The flavor intensity — often described as the most complex and layered of all dark heirloom tomatoes — makes Paul Robeson outstanding for fresh eating (particularly with nothing more than salt and olive oil), in Caprese-style presentations, and in cooking where the rich, smoky character concentrates further. Paul Robeson was introduced to American seed savers from a Russian collection by Marina Danilenko in the 1990s and has become one of the most respected and sought-after heirlooms in the American seed-saving community. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds save true to type. In zone 9, Paul Robeson produces best in the spring growing window (February–June) and requires the long spring season to develop its finest fruit quality.

name: Payroll Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70°F; Payroll is a commercial hybrid zucchini bred for tolerance to common squash mosaic viruses and powdery mildew, holding production longer into a humid Gulf South summer than older open-pollinated zucchini varieties.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Payroll is an early, high-yielding hybrid zucchini bred with tolerance to several common squash viruses and powdery mildew, letting it hold healthy foliage and keep setting fruit later into the season than many older varieties once disease pressure builds. It produces uniform, dark green, cylindrical fruit on a compact, open bush habit that makes spotting and harvesting fruit easy even as the plant fills out. Pick at 6-8 inches for the best eating quality, checking daily during peak summer production since zucchini left on the plant even a day or two too long quickly grows oversized and seedy.
sources: seed catalog reference (Holmes Seed Company, Harris Seeds)

name: Peacevine Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Peacevine is a vigorous, early-bearing indeterminate cherry tomato suited to a sturdy cage or trellis.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger passes, providing a tall cage or trellis for support. Peacevine is an open-pollinated red cherry tomato bred for home and market gardeners, setting heavy clusters of small, sweet, well-flavored fruit over a long harvest season on vigorous indeterminate vines. It tends to begin bearing earlier than many other cherry types and continues steadily through summer with regular picking. Harvest fruit at full color for the best sweetness, and pick frequently to keep the vines setting new clusters.

name: Peach Bhut Jolokia Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; germination is slow and uneven below 80F soil temperature.
directions: Peach Bhut Jolokia ripens to a warm apricot-peach hue instead of the classic red, on the same wrinkled, thin-fleshed pods and blistering heat associated with ghost peppers. Growers often note a subtly sweeter, fruitier aroma compared to red strains, though the Scoville load remains firmly in superhot territory. Give plants full sun, rich well-drained soil, and consistent watering to avoid blossom drop during fruit set. Use gloves when harvesting and processing pods, since capsaicin oils are persistent on skin.

name: Peach Ghost Scorpion Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this superhot is slow to germinate and needs the longest warm season possible.
directions: Peach Ghost Scorpion (also called Jay's Peach Ghost Scorpion) is a naturally occurring open-pollinated cross between ghost pepper (bhut jolokia) and Trinidad Scorpion lines, discovered by grower Jay Weaver in a Pennsylvania ghost-pepper field and later stabilized from saved seed, selected for pale peach-orange, gnarled, scorpion-tailed pods instead of the red or chocolate tones typical of similar hybrids. Start seed early and keep soil consistently warm, since chinense superhots stall in cool conditions and this slow-ripening type needs every extra week of a long growing season to color up fully. Stake plants once the heavy fruit clusters develop, and keep moisture even, since inconsistent watering triggers blossom drop. Handle ripe pods with gloves and eye protection, as the heat is well into superhot territory with persistent oleoresin transfer.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Peach Habanero Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; Peach Habanero, like all Capsicum chinense, requires very warm germination temperatures (80–95°F) and is slow to germinate compared to Capsicum annuum — allow 14–21 days and use a heat mat. In zone 9, transplant March–April; Capsicum chinense thrives in Gulf Coast heat and can produce abundantly through summer and fall. Peach Habanero plants may behave as short-lived perennials in zone 9b if protected from frost, potentially living 2–3 years and producing heavier crops in subsequent seasons. The pale peach color of ripe fruits is the defining characteristic — do not harvest until the green fruits have fully transitioned to the cream-peach color.
directions: Start seeds on heat mat at 85–90°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. Harvest when fully peach-colored. Peach Habanero is a color variant of the habanero pepper group (Capsicum chinense) producing fruits that ripen to a distinctive peach to pale apricot-cream color rather than the familiar orange of standard habanero. The heat level is comparable to orange habanero (100,000–350,000 Scoville units) — full habanero-class heat that demands careful handling and measured use — but the flavor character is perceived by many tasters as slightly different: more floral, sweeter, and with a pronounced fruity quality that some describe as reminiscent of apricot or tropical fruit. The habanero group includes color variants ranging from white through yellow, orange, peach, red, chocolate, and nearly black, with all variants sharing the distinctive fruity-floral habanero aroma that distinguishes Capsicum chinense from the more neutral Capsicum annuum species. Peach Habanero is valued by hot sauce makers, hot pepper enthusiasts, and gardeners interested in the visual diversity of the habanero color spectrum — the pale peach fruits are visually striking against the deep green foliage and make an attractive presentation in fresh pepper mixes and hot sauce. In zone 9, Peach Habanero is one of the most productive hot peppers available: the combination of the species' heat and humidity tolerance with the long Gulf Coast growing season produces prolific crops of fruits through summer and into fall.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Peach Habanero pepper variety notes
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University — Capsicum chinense color variants and heat levels
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Habanero Pepper Production in Florida

name: Peach Scotch Bonnet Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; vigorous 3-4 foot bushes handle Gulf Coast humidity well, consistent with other chinense Scotch Bonnets already thriving there.
directions: Lantern-shaped pods ripen from green to a distinctive peach or apricot color, carrying 100,000 to 350,000 Scoville units with a mango-apricot fruitiness favored in Caribbean and West African cooking, a natural color-range companion to the chocolate and red Scotch Bonnets already in cultivation. Vigorous bushes handle Gulf humidity well, matching the performance of other chinense Scotch Bonnet types. Harvest fully colored pods for the best balance of fruitiness and heat.
sources: Pepper Joe's - Peach Scotch Bonnet Pepper Seeds
Caribbean Garden Seed - Peach Scotch Bonnet

name: Peaches and Cream Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep, 8–12 inches apart in blocks of at least 4 rows (not single long rows) for adequate pollination; in zone 9, plant in February–March for spring harvest or late July for fall harvest; sweet corn requires a large block planting for wind pollination — isolated rows produce poorly filled ears.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows for adequate cross-pollination; Peaches and Cream is the most popular bicolor sweet corn cultivar in American home gardens — producing medium-large ears with yellow and white kernels in a random bicolor mosaic pattern that gives the variety its name and provides both sweet varieties in a single ear. The flavor is typically described as rich, sweet, and complex — the combination of white (typically sweeter) and yellow (typically more 'corny' in flavor) kernels in each bite creates a distinctive eating experience that many gardeners prefer to all-yellow or all-white varieties. Peaches and Cream is an 'SE' (sugar-enhanced) sweet corn type — sweeter than standard su sweet corn but not as sweet or tender-skinned as sh2 (supersweet) types. The SE type is more forgiving of growing conditions and holds its sweetness longer after harvest than standard sweet corn. In zone 9, sweet corn is a spring and fall crop — plant in late February for June harvest and in late July for October harvest. The hot summer is too demanding for quality corn. Corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder — side-dress with nitrogen fertilizer when plants are 12 inches tall and again when tasseling. Corn earworms are the primary pest and must be managed with Bt applications at silk emergence.

name: Pearl Goya Bitter Melon
plantingNote: Direct-sow after soil has warmed above 70°F, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early; train vines onto a tall trellis from planting time.
directions: Pearl Goya is an Okinawan selection that produces round, pearl-white fruit closer in shape to a golf ball than the typical elongated bitter melon, with a milder, almost umami flavor that suits simple soups. Grow it on a tall trellis in full sun with consistently moist, compost-rich soil, training vines vertically and pruning lateral shoots to keep air moving through the foliage. Harvest fruit while still pale and firm, picking early and often to extend the fruiting season.

name: Peking Black Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Peking Black is a vigorous climbing type that benefits from a trellis at least 4 feet tall to keep its long vines and pods off the ground.
directions: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep and provide a trellis at least 4 feet tall, since Peking Black is a vigorous climbing Southern pea rather than a compact bush type. Vines reach about 5 feet and bear abundant 8-9 inch pods that mature to fully black, glossy seed, giving high shelled yields for drying and storage. Like other cowpeas it fixes atmospheric nitrogen and tolerates heat and drought well once established, thriving through the hottest weeks of the Southern summer that slow down snap beans and other legumes. Trellising keeps pods clean and off the soil, and also makes the long harvest season easier to manage than letting the vines sprawl.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Peking Black Southern Pea (Cowpea) variety notes
Hawaii Seed Growers Network — Peking Black Southern Pea variety notes
university extension Southern pea production guides

name: Pele's Smoke Sugarcane
plantingNote: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. Pele's Smoke is grown as an ornamental sugarcane for its very dark, smoky purple-black stalks rather than for sugar or syrup production.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. Pele's Smoke is grown primarily as a dramatic ornamental grass for its deep, smoky purple-black stalk coloration, which darkens further with sun exposure and cool weather, creating a striking vertical accent in borders and large containers. Like other sugarcanes it can also be chewed fresh or pressed for juice, but it is chiefly valued in Gulf South gardens for foliage color rather than sweetness or yield. The tall, clumping perennial grass typically freezes back to the rhizome in hard winters in zone 8-9 and regrows from the root each spring.

name: Pelican Processor Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost; Pelican Processor was bred in Louisiana for the canning and processing industry, with cream skin and light cream flesh that holds its color and shape after cooking.
directions: Set rooted slips into ridged, well-drained soil two to four weeks after the last frost. Pelican Processor was developed by Louisiana sweet potato breeders specifically for the canning and processing trade, producing cream-skinned roots with light cream flesh that stays firm and holds its shape well after cooking rather than breaking down into the soft, custardy texture typical of deep-orange baking types. Home gardeners who want sweet potatoes for frying, dicing, or canning rather than for traditional baked orange-flesh dishes may find it a useful change of pace from standard Beauregard-type roots. Harvest before frost, cure for about a week in warm, humid conditions, and store cool and dry.
sources: NC State University Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America

name: Pencil Cob Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil in blocks of 4+ rows; Pencil Cob is a distinctive North American heritage corn with narrow, pencil-thin cobs densely packed with small, cream-to-yellow kernels — used primarily as a flour corn for fine-grained, delicate-flavored cornmeal and grits prized in the Appalachian and mid-Atlantic tradition.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in blocks of 4+ rows for good pollination; thin to 9–12 inches within the row. Pencil Cob corn (sometimes called Cob Corn or Ashworth type) is a distinctive Appalachian and Midwestern heritage flour corn named for the distinctive narrow, slender cob (roughly pencil-diameter, compared to the fist-thick cobs of modern hybrids) that is densely covered in small, tightly packed kernels; the cobs are long for their diameter (8–12 inches) and produce flour corn with a fine-grained texture and delicate, sweet corn flavor that is different from the coarser, more assertive flavor of modern hybrid cornmeal. Ground into a fine, cream-colored meal that makes exceptionally tender and flavorful cornbread; many Southern cornbread enthusiasts claim it produces the finest cornbread of any heritage variety. Also used for hominy, grits, and polenta.

name: Pencil Pod Black Wax Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Pencil Pod Black Wax is an 1880s heirloom yellow wax (golden) bush snap bean, producing round, cylindrical (pencil-shaped), golden-yellow pods with black seeds — one of the classic American wax beans prized for its crisp texture, mild flavor, and beautiful color that holds when canned or cooked.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in rows 18–24 inches apart after last frost; succession sow every 2–3 weeks for continuous harvest through spring. Pencil Pod Black Wax is an American heirloom wax bean introduced around 1880, named for its distinctive round, cylindrical pods (resembling a pencil in shape — round rather than flat) and black seeds; the 'wax' designation refers to the golden-yellow color of the pods, which are more ornamentally attractive than standard green beans and have a somewhat different, milder flavor. The pods are harvested at 4–6 inches when crisp and tender; like all wax beans, the yellow color holds through cooking and canning better than green beans, making the finished product more visually appealing in jars. Black Wax beans were a standard American commercial canning variety in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; now maintained by heirloom seed companies. One of the most productive and reliable early wax beans for succession planting.

name: Penjar Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant after frost into lean, dry-farmed conditions; vines are grown through summer specifically to be harvested green-mature in autumn for winter storage rather than fresh summer eating.
directions: This small, thick-skinned Catalan and Valencian landrace tomato is bred specifically for storage, not fresh slicing: fruit is picked while still firm and barely turning color, then braided by the stem into ristras and hung indoors, where it slowly ripens and keeps for months into winter. Grow it lean, with minimal irrigation once established, since dry-farmed conditions concentrate the thick skin and low water content that make it such a reliable keeper. Harvest the whole vine or individual clusters just as color begins to break, and store the hanging fruit in a cool, airy, dark space, checking occasionally and removing any that spoil.
sources: Institut de Recerca i Tecnologia Agroalimentàries (IRTA) tomato germplasm collections
Generalitat de Catalunya Departament d'Agricultura landrace registers

name: Pennsylvania Dutch Crookneck Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost in warm soil; this colonial-era Mid-Atlantic heirloom, also called Neck Pumpkin, produces a long curved neck with buff skin and deep orange flesh.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in hills after danger of frost has passed, once the soil has warmed thoroughly. Pennsylvania Dutch Crookneck, also known regionally as Neck Pumpkin, is one of the oldest named moschata squashes still grown in North America, dating to colonial-era Mid-Atlantic farms, with long curving necks, buff to tan skin, and deep orange flesh that bakes dry and sweet. Because the seed cavity sits low in the bulbous blossom end, most of the fruit is solid, usable neck, giving a high yield of flesh per squash. Allow fruit to fully harden on the vine before cutting with a few inches of stem attached, cure in a warm spot for one to two weeks, then store in a cool, dry location where it keeps well into winter.

name: Pentagreen Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil warms; Pentagreen tolerates cooler soil and air temperatures better than most okra, giving Gulf Coast gardeners a wider early-season sowing window.
directions: Direct sow into warm soil in full sun; Pentagreen stays notably compact compared to most Southern okra varieties while still producing heavily once plants begin branching early in the season. Pods are sharply five-angled and medium green, best picked at around 3 inches since they are slower to develop fiber than many varieties, giving a longer harvest window at any given size. This variety is unusually tolerant of cool conditions for an okra, making it productive even during cooler spring and fall stretches in zone 9a. Keep picking continuously through summer to keep plants flowering heavily.

name: Pentland Brig Kale
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring for a fall/winter crop, or sow in mid-summer for overwintering; Pentland Brig is exceptionally cold-hardy and is grown through winter specifically to produce tender flowering shoots the following spring.
directions: Sow directly or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously to allow the tall, semi-open habit room to develop. Pentland Brig was bred in the 1960s at the Scottish Plant Breeding Station from a cross of Thousand-Head kale and curly kale, combining loose, lightly frilled, medium-green leaves with an unusual second act: overwintered plants send up abundant tender flowering shoots in early spring that are harvested and cooked exactly like sprouting broccoli. This dual-purpose habit, cut-and-come-again leaves through autumn and winter, then a flush of sweet flower shoots in the notorious late-winter hungry gap before other vegetables are ready, is what has kept it a favorite kitchen-garden variety in Britain for decades even though it remains uncommon in American seed catalogs. The flavor is notably mild and sweet for a kale, without the toughness of older curly types, and both the leaves and the immature flower buds are good raw or lightly cooked. Choose Pentland Brig where reliable winter survival and an early-spring harvest gap-filler matter more than a single big autumn leaf crop.

name: Peperone di Senise
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; traditionally grown in the hot, dry summers of Basilicata and best suited to a long, warm season for full drying.
directions: Peperone di Senise takes its name from the town of Senise in the Basilicata region of southern Italy, where farmers have long selected this thin-fleshed sweet pepper and it now carries a protected geographical indication. Pods are elongated and tapering, hooked or twisted depending on the strain, and their unusually thin flesh dries quickly on strings hung in the sun without rotting. Once fully dried, the pods are known as peperoni cruschi, deep-fried briefly until shatteringly crisp and used as a garnish or snack throughout Basilicata, or ground into a red seasoning. Because the whole point of the variety is easy sun-drying, it performs best where summers are long, hot, and relatively dry.

name: Pepitas Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, rich soil, giving vines room to run; Pepitas is an AAS-winning pumpkin bred specifically for its naked, hull-less seeds, harvested and roasted for snacking rather than grown primarily for the flesh.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun, giving the vines room to spread. Pepitas is an AAS-winning pumpkin bred specifically as a seed crop — the medium-orange fruit is filled with abundant naked, hull-less green seeds (the same type sold commercially as pepitas), which can be scooped out, rinsed, and roasted directly with no shelling needed, unlike the tough-hulled seeds of most pumpkin varieties. It is a fun, productive choice for gardeners who want a real harvest of roastable snacking seeds without buying store pepitas, and the flesh, while secondary to the seed crop, is still usable in cooking. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and the vine begins to decline, then scoop and separate the seeds from the pulp before rinsing and roasting or drying them for storage.
sources: All-America Selections — Pepitas Pumpkin winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Peppadew Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before the last frost, since Peppadew is a long-season pepper that needs a head start to fruit before fall; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun only after the soil has warmed and night temperatures stay reliably above 55°F.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay warm; Peppadew is the trademarked name for a piquanté pepper discovered as a chance seedling in a South African garden in the 1990s and now grown commercially worldwide for pickling. The plant is a vigorous, sprawling Capsicum baccatum shrub that produces small, round, tomato-shaped fruit that ripens from green through orange to deep red, carrying a sweet-tart flavor with a mild, tingling heat far gentler than most hot peppers. Because it needs a long, warm growing season to size up and color fully, gardeners in shorter-season climates should start seed extra early and expect the first ripe fruit late in the season; in the Gulf South's long summers it has time to produce a heavy crop. Pick fruit once fully colored and pickle or roast to mellow the skin, as Peppadew is traditionally eaten cured rather than fresh off the plant.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Capsicum baccatum
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Pepper X
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last expected frost, since Capsicum chinense germinates slowly and needs a long warm season to ripen.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost using a heat mat to keep soil near 85F, since chinense types germinate unevenly and slowly compared to annuum peppers. Transplant into warm soil only after nighttime temperatures stay reliably above 60F, and stake plants as the heavy fruit load develops. Pepper X was bred by Ed Currie of PuckerButt Pepper Company and was certified by Guinness World Records in 2023 as the hottest pepper ever measured, surpassing the Carolina Reaper. Handle ripe pods with gloves, as the capsaicin level is extreme even by superhot standards.

name: Peppermint Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for a fall and winter crop in zone 9; the candy-striped stalks are most vivid when cut young for salad use.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Peppermint chard produces glossy, savoyed green leaves on stalks striped in bands of pink and white, resembling the candy for which it is named and giving it strong visual appeal both in the garden and sliced into salads. Flavor is typical of Swiss chard, with tender leaves that cook down like spinach and crisp stalks that can be prepared like celery, and the coloring holds reasonably well when lightly cooked. Harvest outer leaves regularly as needed to keep the plant productive, and expect continued cropping over a long cool-season harvest window with cut-and-come-again picking.

name: Pepperoncini
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January and transplant February–March. Pepperoncini is harvested green (2–3 inches long) for pickling, or allowed to turn red for a sweeter, riper flavor. In zone 9, the long warm season enables outstanding production through spring and fall.
directions: Start seeds at 75–80°F and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pepperoncini is the classic Italian pickling and frying pepper, widely grown throughout Tuscany and the Greek Peloponnese for centuries and the pepper that fills the olive bar jars in every American grocery store. The thin-walled, mildly hot (100–500 Scoville), wrinkled fruits are harvested at 2–3 inches when bright green for pickling in white wine vinegar — the standard preparation produces the distinctive brine-pickled pepperoncini familiar from Italian sub sandwiches and antipasto. When allowed to ripen fully red, the fruits sweeten considerably and are excellent fresh or roasted. The plants are productive and undemanding, bearing heavily over a long season in full sun with consistent moisture. In Italian cooking, fresh pepperoncini are used whole in pasta sauces (arrabbiata), braised with olives and capers, and roasted under poultry. The Greek variety (often called 'Golden Greek' or 'Greek Golden') is essentially the same pepper and is the primary type pickled for commercial sale in the US.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Pepperoncini variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Italian Pepper varieties
Italian Ministry of Agricultural Policy — Protected traditional pepper varieties
University of California Cooperative Extension — Specialty Peppers

name: Peredovik Black Oil Sunflower
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Peredovik is a multi-stemmed, multi-head oilseed sunflower producing many 3–5 inch flower heads per plant (unlike the single giant-headed ornamental sunflowers grown for show). In zone 9, plant March–May; for fall dove season, plant July–August to time seed maturity with the September–October dove hunting season. The oil sunflower habit (shorter, multi-branching, many small heads) maximizes seed yield per plant and provides more uniform ripening than single-headed types. Harvest when seed heads are thoroughly dry and birds begin eating the seeds.
directions: Direct sow 0.5–1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest when seed heads are completely dry and brown. Peredovik (also spelled 'Peredovik') is a Russian open-pollinated oilseed sunflower developed in the Soviet Union specifically for oil production — one of the most widely planted sunflower varieties in the world and the standard variety used in commercial sunflower oil production globally before the development of modern high-oleic hybrids. The Peredovik breeding emphasized oil percentage over seed size: the thin, black seeds contain 42–45% oil by weight (compared to 24–28% for striped ornamental/snack sunflower types), and this high oil content is what gives 'black oil sunflower' its distinct value. In the bird-feeding context, black oil sunflower seeds (Peredovik or similar black-seeded varieties) are universally recommended as the premier wild bird food: the thin, easy-to-crack shell is accessible to a wider range of small songbirds than the thick-shelled striped types, and the high oil content provides superior energy density for birds — particularly important for overwintering and migratory species. For wildlife food plots in the Gulf South, Peredovik-type black oil sunflower is one of the primary dove and songbird attractants planted specifically for the September-October dove season. The seeds are also excellent for human consumption (roasting, pressing for oil) though small in size.
sources: USDA National Agricultural Library — Helianthus annuus oilseed variety documentation
Cornell Lab of Ornithology — Black oil sunflower as premier bird food
Russian Institute of Plant Industry — Peredovik sunflower variety development

name: Perfection Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring; like all garden peas it needs to mature before summer heat sets in.
directions: Perfection is an early-20th-century heirloom shelling pea, one of the smooth-podded, wrinkled-seeded 'marrow' dessert types once widely offered in market and home garden seed catalogs before modern hybrid peas became dominant. Sow seed directly into cool, workable spring soil, since like all garden peas it germinates and grows best well ahead of summer heat. The vigorous vines climb readily with light brush or netting support and set pods over several weeks of cool weather, yielding sweet, full-flavored peas typical of the wrinkled-seed dessert type. Perfection is historically notable as one of the two parent varieties, alongside Laxton's Progress, crossed by USDA breeders in 1943 to create the heat-tolerant Wando pea.
sources: USDA plant introduction and pea breeding records
Seed Savers Exchange heirloom pea archives

name: Perkins Dwarf Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Perkins Dwarf is an early, compact strain of the classic Perkins okra line, reaching only 3-5 feet, so it fits small Gulf Coast beds and containers better than the tall Perkins Long Pod and Perkins Mammoth Long Pod types.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil is thoroughly warm; harvest at 3-5 inches for the most tender eating, though pods stay usable up to 8-9 inches longer than most okra. Perkins Dwarf is a compact-growing strain within the old Perkins okra family, bred down from the tall Southern heirloom standard to a manageable 3-5 foot plant while keeping the same ribbed, dark green pods and early, heavy production. The shorter stature means less staking and easier picking through the peak of a Gulf Coast summer, and the extended window of pod tenderness gives more forgiveness if a hot spell delays harvest by a day or two. It remains an excellent choice for canning, pickling, and frying, and its early start lets Gulf Coast gardeners begin harvesting well before many full-size heirloom types come into production.
sources: Victory Seed Company — Perkins Okra Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Easy Gardening: Okra

name: Perkins Long Pod Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (65°F+); Perkins Long Pod is a classic tall Southern heirloom okra and the parent line behind later spineless Perkins selections.
directions: Soak seed overnight to soften the hard seed coat, then direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures are reliably above 65°F. Perkins Long Pod is a traditional Southern heirloom okra grown for generations before the spineless Perkins strains were selected from it, producing heavy yields of long, ribbed, dark green pods on tall, vigorous plants that can reach 6 feet or more by season's end. Harvest pods every two to three days at 2-4 inches long for the most tender eating, since larger pods quickly turn woody and fibrous; regular picking keeps the plant producing continuously through the hottest part of the Gulf South summer. Stake or support plants in windy sites, and remove any overgrown pods promptly to keep new flowers and pods coming.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Okra Production

name: Perkins Mammoth Long Pod Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Perkins Mammoth Long Pod is an 1890s heirloom okra that produces very long (up to 8–10 inch), slightly ridged, green pods with outstanding flavor and a notably long harvest window before pods become tough — a longtime favorite in Southern and Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is warm; soak seeds overnight to improve germination. Perkins Mammoth Long Pod is an heirloom okra variety introduced in the 1890s that produces exceptionally long (6–10 inch) ribbed green pods with a more tender quality at larger sizes than most okra varieties — meaning the pods remain acceptable for eating somewhat longer than standard varieties, which quickly become fibrous and tough once they exceed 3–4 inches. The plants are vigorous (5–8 feet), highly productive, and heat-tolerant, performing well throughout the Gulf Coast and Deep South. Harvest pods at 4–6 inches for optimal tenderness; though the pods can be eaten somewhat larger, regular harvesting every 1–2 days in hot weather is essential to keep production high — missed pods left on the plant stop production quickly.

name: Perla Negra Chayote
plantingNote: Plant the entire fruit (not just the seed inside) sideways in a hole with the narrow tip pointed slightly upward and the stem end just below the soil surface, exactly as with common green chayote; Perla Negra is a smooth, spineless, dark green selection popular in Mexican and Central American markets.
directions: Perla Negra is a dark green, smooth-skinned, spineless chayote selection, distinguished from common pale-green mirliton by its deeper color and glossier, blemish-free skin, traits favored in Mexican and Central American fresh markets. Plant the whole fruit at an angle in well-worked soil with the narrow stem end barely covered, since chayote's single large seed cannot be separated from the flesh and the entire fruit is the planting unit. Provide a sturdy trellis, fence, or arbor, since the vigorous vine can run 20-40 feet and becomes extremely productive once established in zones 9-11, typically bearing in fall and again in early spring. Fruit, tender young shoots, and leaves are all edible, and mature plants develop large starchy edible tubers as well; harvest fruit young and firm for the mildest flavor and most tender texture.

name: Perpetual Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for a fall and winter crop in zone 9; unlike true spinach, this leaf beet resists bolting through summer heat while still tasting spinach-like.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Perpetual Spinach is an old English strain of leaf beet grown specifically as a heat- and bolt-resistant substitute for true spinach, with smaller, smoother, thinner-stalked leaves than standard Swiss chard and a milder, more spinach-like flavor when cooked. Unlike true spinach, which bolts quickly in warm weather, this leaf beet keeps producing tender new leaves through much of the growing season, giving gardeners a reliable spinach-flavored green across a far longer window. Harvest outer leaves continuously as needed, leaving the growing center intact, and expect the plant to keep cropping for months with regular cutting.

name: Persian Cress
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool weather into average, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike baby-leaf cress types, Persian cress is usually left to grow tall for its airy sprays of seed pods rather than cut young.
directions: Persian cress is a distinct, upright-growing strain of garden cress grown less for cutting as salad microgreens and more for its tall, airy sprays of tiny silvery seed pods, prized by floral designers as a delicate cut-flower filler. Left to mature past the baby-leaf stage, plants send up branched, wiry stems topped with small white flowers that quickly form the decorative seed heads for which the variety is grown. Direct sow in cool weather into average, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings a few inches apart to give the branching stems room to develop. Succession sow every few weeks in spring and fall for a continuous supply of cutting stems, since plants bolt and decline quickly once summer heat arrives.

name: Persian Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Persian melon is a large-fruited, heavily netted muskmelon type popular in California and the American West, producing large (8–15 lb), round, deeply netted, fragrant fruits with deep salmon-orange flesh of excellent sweetness — one of the standard commercial and home-garden melons for hot, dry Western climates.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Persian melon requires hot, dry conditions for best sweetness and is most successful in California, Arizona, Texas, and Gulf Coast gardens. Persian melon is a large-fruited, heavily netted muskmelon of Middle Eastern origin that became a California commercial standard in the early 20th century; the large (8–15 lb), round to slightly oval fruits have a thick layer of fine, closely woven gray-green netting over dark green skin that transitions to golden-green at maturity, with deeply aromatic, thick, deep salmon-orange flesh with a rich, spicy sweetness. Persian melon is rounder and larger than cantaloupes and has thicker, denser flesh with a more pronounced, spicy aromatic complexity than American cantaloupe types. It requires a longer season (90–100 days) and performs best in hot, dry conditions; California's Central and Imperial Valleys have historically produced most commercial Persian melons sold in Western markets. The thick rind and firm flesh give Persian melon better shipping quality than more delicate muskmelon types, and it stores 1–2 weeks refrigerated after harvest.

name: Persian Star Hardneck Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 4–6 weeks before first frost in fall; Persian Star is a Marbled Purple Stripe hardneck garlic collected in Samarkand, Uzbekistan (the historic Silk Road city) by John Swenson for the Seed Savers Exchange in 1989 — it produces strikingly beautiful bulbs with vivid violet-purple inner clove skins and a rich, earthy, complex flavor characteristic of the Marbled Purple Stripe type.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end up, 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall 4–6 weeks before hard freeze; mulch after planting; keep weed-free and consistently moist in spring; remove scapes when they curl; harvest in early to midsummer when 5–6 lower leaves have yellowed and cure in a warm, dry, airy location. Persian Star is a Marbled Purple Stripe-type hardneck garlic with a remarkable provenance: it was collected in Samarkand, Uzbekistan — the ancient Silk Road city at the crossroads of Central Asia — by John Swenson, a garlic enthusiast and Seed Savers Exchange member who traveled to the former Soviet Union in 1989 collecting traditional garlic varieties grown in the region for centuries. The provenance from Samarkand, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world and a center of Central Asian agricultural tradition, gives Persian Star historical and botanical significance as a window into the genetic diversity of garlic in its center of diversity (Central Asia is believed to be the region where cultivated garlic first developed). The bulbs are 2–3 inches across with 8–12 cloves; the outer skin is white with subtle purple striping typical of the Marbled Purple Stripe group, while the inner clove skins are often vivid violet-purple — beautiful when peeled. The flavor is rich, earthy, moderately pungent, and complex — slightly different from Rocambole types with a distinctive minerality. Storage life is better than Rocambole (5–7 months) but less than softneck types.

name: Persimmon Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed; a large, golden-orange beefsteak heirloom with very low acid and sweet, fruity flavor — an excellent choice for gardeners who want an orange type that ripens reliably in hot summer conditions.
directions: Start seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil after all frost risk has passed, burying the stem deeply and staking or caging firmly. Persimmon is a Ukrainian heirloom beefsteak tomato with fruit that resembles the color of a ripe persimmon — vivid golden-orange — with very meaty flesh, a small seed cavity, extraordinarily sweet, low-acid, fruity flavor, and fruits weighing 10–16 ounces; it is among the finest-tasting orange or golden beefsteak heirlooms and has been prized by serious tomato growers since its introduction through Seed Savers Exchange. The vigorous indeterminate vines produce steadily through the season; stake firmly and maintain consistent moisture to prevent blossom-end rot. Harvest when fruits are fully colored and yield slightly to pressure at the blossom end.

name: Perth Pride Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Perth Pride is an Australian-bred Dwarf Tomato Project release producing red beefsteak-type fruit on a compact plant.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Perth Pride, developed through the Australian arm of the international Dwarf Tomato Project, bears deep red, beefsteak-style fruit with good, rich flavor on a compact plant, combining full-size tomato quality with a footprint suited to small gardens and containers. It reflects the collaborative, worldwide nature of the Dwarf Tomato Project breeding effort. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

name: Peruano Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow once the soil has warmed well after last frost, since this bush-type dry bean, like most common beans, resents cold or waterlogged ground at germination.
directions: Direct sow once the soil has warmed well after last frost, since this bush-type dry bean, like most common beans, resents cold or waterlogged ground at germination. Also sold as Mayocoba or canary bean, Peruano is a pale golden-yellow bean central to everyday Mexican and Mexican-American cooking, valued for a creamy texture and mild flavor that holds up well in refried preparations. The compact bush habit needs no staking and produces a concentrated harvest suited to home drying. Let pods mature fully and dry on the plant before shelling, then store the beans in a cool, dry, airtight container.
sources: University of California, Davis Dry Bean Breeding Program

name: Peruvian Purple Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Peruvian Purple is a compact ornamental edible pepper (18–24 inches) with distinctive deep purple-black foliage, purple stems, and small upright fruits (1.5–2 inches) that mature from purple-black through a transitional stage to vivid red. The purple pigmentation in both foliage and immature fruits results from anthocyanin accumulation triggered by light exposure, making it one of the most visually striking ornamental peppers available. Heat level is high (estimated 50,000–80,000 SHU), reflecting the small fruit size typical of high-heat Capsicum annuum types. In zone 9, transplant March–April; the compact habit makes it excellent for containers and ornamental mixed plantings where edible and decorative plants are combined.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost to full sun and harvest fruits at any stage from purple-black (immature, high heat) to fully red (ripe). Peruvian Purple Pepper is a compact ornamental-edible hot pepper variety distinguished by its unusual anthocyanin-rich foliage — a deep purple-black that makes the plant visually dramatic from seedling stage through maturity. The purple coloration in the leaves and immature fruits results from anthocyanin pigments produced in response to high light intensity; the same plant grown in reduced light will show less purple coloration and more green foliage, making sun exposure a direct visible factor in the plant's ornamental effect. Fruits emerge deep purple-black and upright — pointing skyward rather than pendant — which is a characteristic of many small ornamental hot pepper types and adds visual interest as the small fruits are held prominently above the purple foliage. As fruits ripen to full maturity they transition through a mottled purple-and-red stage before reaching solid vivid red; many gardeners harvest throughout this color progression since the flavor and heat level remain high at all stages. The heat level is substantial for a Capsicum annuum variety — comparable to Thai or bird's eye types — and is proportional to the small fruit size, as capsaicin concentration tends to increase as fruit diameter decreases within the species. Culinary uses mirror those of other small hot peppers: used fresh in salads, salsas, and stir-fries; pickled; or dried whole for later use. As a compact container plant with dramatic foliage, Peruvian Purple also functions effectively as a purely ornamental annual in mixed containers where its purple leaves provide contrast against chartreuse, silver, or deep green companions.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Peruvian Purple Pepper variety description and ornamental characteristics
Seed Savers Exchange — Purple-leaved Capsicum annuum varieties and anthocyanin expression notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Ornamental Edible Peppers for Florida Home Gardens

name: Pescadero Red Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep, in October-November in zone 9; Pescadero Red is a Creole-type garlic that needs little winter chill to bulb properly, making it far more reliable than hardneck types in mild-winter climates.
directions: Pescadero Red, also called Fisherman's Garlic for its coastal California origins near Pescadero, is a Creole-type softneck garlic grown for its symmetrical bulbs wrapped in brilliant burgundy-streaked skins and a mild, mellow garlic flavor with far less bite than typical hardneck varieties. It is an unusually vigorous grower for a Creole, often producing bulbs larger than its relatives, with 8-12 plump cloves arranged in the tight circular pattern characteristic of the group. Because it needs minimal cold exposure to form bulbs, it thrives in the same mild Gulf South and coastal winters where northern Rocambole and Porcelain garlics routinely fail. Harvest in early summer when the lower leaves brown and 4-5 green leaves remain, then cure in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks; well-cured bulbs store from early summer through winter into mid-spring.
sources: Filaree Garlic Farm — Pescadero Red variety notes
Gourmet Garlic Gardens — Creole garlic variety descriptions

name: Petch Siam Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed and soil is warm.
directions: A Thai specialty eggplant producing small, round, pale-green fruit about 1.5 to 2 inches across with distinct dark-green striping and slight ribbing. Flesh is mild and faintly sweet, popular raw or cooked in Thai, Indian, and Vietnamese curries. Plants are well-branched and somewhat less vigorous than standard round Thai types, so give consistent water and fertility. Pick young while pale green for the mildest flavor, as pods yellow and toughen with age.

name: Peter Pan Pattypan Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Peter Pan is a bush-type pattypan suitable for smaller gardens than vining summer squash. In zone 9, plant March–May and again August for fall harvest. Harvest at 3–4 inches diameter for best flavor and texture — pattypan squash becomes seedy and watery if allowed to grow much beyond 4–5 inches. The scalloped edges that give pattypan its distinctive star or UFO shape become more pronounced and decorative as fruits approach full harvest size.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost; harvest fruits at 3–4 inches diameter for best eating quality. Peter Pan is a 1982 All-America Selections-winning pattypan (scallop) summer squash — an early-maturing, bush-habit variety producing pale green, disc-shaped fruits with the characteristic scalloped, fluted edges of the pattypan type. The distinctive flat, disc-like shape with scalloped margins distinguishes pattypan squash from all other summer squash types (zucchini, yellow crookneck, yellow straightneck) and has no equivalent in other vegetable categories — the shape makes individual fruits look like tiny flying saucers or UFOs and creates an unusually attractive presentation on the plate when halved or stuffed whole. Peter Pan's light green color is gentler and less common than the white pattypans that dominated before its introduction. The flavor is mild and slightly sweet — similar to other summer squash but with a distinctive nuttiness that develops in the scallop varieties at the ideal 3–4 inch harvest size. The bush habit (24–36 inch spread vs. the 6–8 foot spread of vining squash) makes Peter Pan practical for smaller raised beds and gardens.
sources: All-America Selections — Peter Pan pattypan squash AAS winner 1982
Burpee Seeds — Peter Pan scallop squash variety notes
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Summer Squash Production

name: Peter Pan Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Peter Pan is a scallop (pattypan) squash that produces pale sage-green to silvery-green flat, scallop-edged fruits on a compact bush plant. In zone 9, plant March–May and August–September for fall production. Harvest Peter Pan at 3–4 inches when the skin is still tender and the green color is uniform and pale — the skin toughens significantly if the squash is left to grow beyond 4–5 inches. The distinctive pale green-grey color (lighter than most green summer squash) and scalloped edge make Peter Pan one of the most immediately recognizable summer squash varieties at harvest. The flavor is mild and nutty, somewhat different from zucchini in a pleasant way — scallop types have a slightly different flesh texture and a subtly nuttier quality that distinguishes them from elongated zucchini types.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches when pale sage-green and tender. Peter Pan Squash is an All-America Selections (AAS) winner in the summer squash category, honored for its early production, compact plant habit, and the distinctive pale sage-green to silvery-blue-green color of the scallop-shaped fruits. The AAS recognition confirmed Peter Pan's performance advantage over other scallop squash varieties of its time in trials across multiple growing regions and climates. The scallop squash form — a flat, disc-shaped fruit with distinctively scalloped or fluted edges — is one of the oldest American summer squash forms, with historical precedent in both Native American cultivation and early colonial American gardens. Peter Pan's F1 hybrid vigor contributes to both its compactness (more manageable plant than many bush zucchini) and productivity (abundant fruit set throughout the season). The color is a notable characteristic: the pale, muted sage-green to silvery green of Peter Pan is unlike the darker green of standard zucchini or the yellow of Sunburst, occupying its own distinctive color space that many gardeners find attractive for mixed variety plantings and market displays where color diversity is valued. The flat scallop form also makes Peter Pan an exceptionally attractive stuffed squash: the naturally hollow interior of the scallop form (relative to the solid flesh core of zucchini) allows more filling capacity per fruit when halved for stuffing, and the shallow depth of the squash makes even cooking possible at the small sizes most suitable for stuffing preparations.
sources: All-America Selections — Peter Pan scallop squash AAS recognition documentation
Burpee Seeds — Peter Pan squash compact summer squash variety notes
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Summer Squash Variety Evaluation for Home Gardens

name: Peter Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat; transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the danger of frost has fully passed and soil has warmed.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; stake taller plants if heavily loaded with fruit. Peter Pepper is a well-known Southern heirloom hot pepper, famous for its unmistakably novelty shape, which has made it a popular curiosity and conversation piece for generations of home gardeners across Texas and Louisiana. The medium-heat fruits (roughly 10,000–25,000 Scoville units, comparable to a strong jalapeño or mild cayenne) ripen from green to red and carry a fruity, tangy flavor good in salsas, pickling, and hot sauce once the novelty value has been enjoyed. Plants are productive and reasonably compact, performing well in containers as well as garden beds, and the fruit's thick walls hold up nicely to stuffing or pickling whole. A fun, genuinely productive heirloom for gardeners who want something distinctive alongside their standard pepper lineup, in zone 4–11.

name: Petit Gris de Rennes Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Petit Gris de Rennes is a French muskmelon type that requires warmer growing conditions than some European varieties — it performs well in the Gulf South's warm summer climate but needs protection from excessive humidity that can cause Alternaria blight. In zone 9, plant March–April for June–July harvest. The 'Petit Gris' (little gray) refers to the grayish-green skin when fully ripe.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost; maintain consistent moisture during vine development and reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity. Harvest when the skin transitions from green to gray-green (the characteristic 'petit gris' color) and the stem cracks slightly at the base — this muskmelon type does not 'slip' from the vine like American cantaloupes but has a less decisive harvest cue. Petit Gris de Rennes (small gray of Rennes) is a traditional French muskmelon heirloom from Brittany, the coastal region of northwestern France, where it has been grown for centuries as the area's distinctive local melon. In France, Petit Gris de Rennes has Slow Food Ark of Taste recognition as a threatened traditional variety of significant cultural importance. The small to medium (1–2 lb) round fruits are distinguished by their unusual grayish-green to slate-green skin coloration with shallow ribs and fine, irregular netting — a very different appearance from the tan-netted American cantaloupe standard. The deeply orange, firm-textured, extremely sweet and aromatic flesh has a rich, complex character that many tasters consider superior to standard Western cantaloupe types — more complex in flavor, with floral and spicy notes beyond simple sweetness. Petit Gris de Rennes represents the French horticultural tradition of flavor breeding, where appearance is secondary to eating quality, and is a fascinating variety for gardeners interested in growing traditional European melon types beyond the standard muskmelon.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Petit Gris de Rennes melon variety notes
Slow Food Ark of Taste — Petit Gris de Rennes traditional variety documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — European heirloom melon collection

name: Petite Treat Watermelon
plantingNote: Start seed indoors and transplant after soil is thoroughly warm; as a seedless triploid, Petite Treat needs a nearby seeded watermelon variety planted for pollen to set fruit properly.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, planting a seeded watermelon variety nearby to supply pollen for this seedless triploid to set fruit.
