Petite Treat is an All-America Selections winner bred for genuinely personal-sized fruit, producing round melons small enough for one or two people to finish in a single sitting, with sweet, crisp, deep red, seedless flesh and a thin rind. The compact vine takes up less garden space than standard large-fruited watermelon varieties, and the smaller fruit size means a shorter time from pollination to harvest-ready ripeness. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit stem browns and dries and the ground spot beneath the fruit turns creamy yellow, the most reliable ripeness indicators for seedless types.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Petrowski Turnip
plantingNote: Sow direct in late summer for a fall crop, since cool weather brings out its characteristically sweet, mild flavor.
directions: A Central/Eastern European heirloom turnip grown historically in Poland and Russia for its round, golden-skinned roots with pale yellow flesh, a distinct look and flavor compared to the purple-top white types common in American gardens. It was traditionally valued for dual use as both a table vegetable and livestock forage. Sow direct in late summer for a fall crop, since cool weather brings out its characteristically sweet, mild flavor and reduces the sharper bite common in summer-grown turnips.

name: Philadelphia White Box Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow shallowly in loose, fertile soil as soon as it can be worked, succession sowing every two weeks; this compact heirloom also performs well in shallow containers and window boxes.
directions: Developed by Philadelphia seedsmen in the late nineteenth century from older European white radish stock, this heirloom forms small, round, pure-white roots with crisp, mild flesh. It was bred specifically for the shallow soil of urban window boxes and tight market-garden rows, so it tolerates closer spacing than most globe radishes without turning woody. Harvest promptly once roots size up, since white-skinned types show pithiness quickly in warm weather. A reliable choice for gardeners wanting an authentic nineteenth-century American market variety rather than a modern hybrid globe.

name: Phoenix Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably above 55°F. Phoenix continues setting fruit through the high daytime and nighttime temperatures of a Gulf South summer that cause blossom drop in most other tomato varieties.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake or cage for support; consistent watering reduces blossom end rot in humid conditions. Phoenix is a tomato variety developed by the Texas A&M AgriLife vegetable breeding program specifically to keep setting fruit through the extreme heat of a Texas and Gulf South summer, when night temperatures above 75°F cause pollen sterility and blossom drop in most standard varieties. The medium-sized, firm, deep red globe fruits also carry useful resistance to common soilborne diseases and cracking, and the vines continue producing through the hottest stretch of summer that typically causes a production gap in southern tomato gardens. It also carries a degree of protection against sunscald thanks to good foliage cover. A dependable choice for Gulf Coast gardeners who want tomatoes to keep coming through July and August rather than stalling out, in zone 4–11.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Program
Texas A&M AgriLife Research — Vegetable Breeding

name: Pick a Bushel Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Pick a Bushel is a compact, semi-bush pickling cucumber bred for container and small-space growing, needing far less room than vining pickling types.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container with a small trellis. Pick a Bushel is an AAS-winning pickling cucumber bred for a genuinely compact semi-bush habit, producing full-size yields of crisp, uniform, 3-5 inch pickling cukes on a plant small enough for patios, raised beds, and tight garden spaces where a standard vining pickler would sprawl out of bounds. It bears heavily and continuously over a relatively short, concentrated season, ideal for gardeners who want a big pickling harvest all at once for a canning batch. Pick fruit at the size wanted for the pickle style being made — small gherkins to full-size dills — and harvest every day or two once fruiting begins, since oversized cucumbers slow down further production. Keep soil evenly moist, especially as fruit is sizing, to avoid bitter or misshapen cucumbers.
sources: All-America Selections — Pick a Bushel Cucumber winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Pick-N-Pop Yellow Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably warm; Pick-N-Pop Yellow holds its compact habit well in both garden beds and containers.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, spacing plants about 18-24 inches apart to let the compact frame fill out. Pick-N-Pop Yellow is a 2025 AAS National Edible-Vegetable Winner bred by Seminis, producing a prolific crop of bright canary-yellow, pointed conical snack peppers roughly 4 inches long that are extra sweet, juicy, and crunchy. The manageable 24-inch plant carries resistance to bacterial leaf spot races 0-10 and ripens earlier with higher yield than comparison snack peppers, making it well suited to both in-ground rows and patio containers. Harvest continuously as fruit reaches full yellow color to encourage further fruit set through the season.
sources: All-America Selections -- AAS Edible National Winners for 2025

name: Pickle Bush Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pickle Bush's compact, bush-habit vines (18–24 inch spread) make it excellent for raised beds and container growing — no trellis required and the plants are self-supporting.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pickle Bush is a bush-type pickling cucumber producing compact, self-supporting vines 18–24 inches across rather than the sprawling 4–6 foot vines of standard pickling cucumbers — making it the preferred choice for raised beds, containers, and small gardens where trellises are impractical and space is limited. The short (3–4 inch), blocky, warted, pickling-type cucumbers mature very early (48–55 days) in prolific clusters that concentrate harvest in a short window ideal for batch processing and canning. Pickling cucumbers are specifically bred for thin, tender skin that absorbs brine quickly, mild-to-bland flavor that allows pickle seasonings to dominate, and firm flesh that maintains crunchiness through the pickling process — qualities that distinguish them from slicing cucumbers in important culinary ways. In zone 9, the very early maturity (48–55 days) of Pickle Bush is a practical advantage — it completes its production cycle before summer heat drives cucumbers into bitter, poor-quality fruit stage. The bush habit allows high-density planting in raised beds (18 inches apart) compared to the 3–4 foot spacing required for trellised vining types. AAS Honorable Mention recognized Pickle Bush's outstanding performance in the small-space home garden category.

name: Pico Pardal Chickpea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost into well-drained soil in full sun; Pico Pardal is a Spanish heirloom known as the 'sparrow-beak' chickpea for its distinctively pointed seed shape.
directions: Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Pico Pardal is a small-seeded chickpea from León, Spain, named 'sparrow-beak' for the pronounced pointed beak on each seed. It carries a creamy, thin-skinned texture that cooks quickly compared to larger chickpea types, and is a traditional ingredient in the regional cocido maragato stew. Like other chickpeas it tolerates heat and drought well once established and needs minimal supplemental water through a hot summer.

name: Picolino Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow or set out transplants after the last frost in warm soil, providing a trellis to keep fruit straight; Picolino is a parthenocarpic mini cucumber bred to set seedless fruit without pollination.
directions: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed, training vines onto a trellis or cage for straighter, cleaner fruit. Picolino is a parthenocarpic mini cucumber, meaning it reliably sets thin-skinned, seedless, 3-4 inch fruit without needing pollinator activity, making it dependable even in low-bee conditions or under row cover. The skin is tender enough to eat without peeling and the flavor is mild and non-bitter, making it a popular choice for lunchbox snacking and pickling whole. Because fruit sizes up quickly, plants need picking every day or two at peak season to prevent cucumbers from overgrowing and to keep the vine setting new fruit.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Picolino Cucumber variety description
Rijk Zwaan — mini cucumber breeding notes

name: Piedmont Mâche
plantingNote: Sow 4-8 weeks before first fall frost for a winter and early-spring crop, or as soon as soil can be worked in earliest spring; this large-seeded European strain germinates evenly in cold soil that would stall most other salad greens.
directions: Piedmont is a large-seeded continental European heirloom mâche valued for vigorous, slightly larger rosettes and good resistance to the mildew that often plagues this classic cool-season green through damp winters. Its dark green, rounded leaves keep the same mild, nutty flavor typical of mâche but fill out a bit faster and fuller than smaller-seeded strains, making harvest easier on a cut-and-come-again schedule. Mâche is one of the most genuinely shade-tolerant salad crops available, content with the low winter light under deciduous trees or the dappled shade of a cold frame, and it actually prefers the cooler, softer light of a partly shaded bed once days lengthen in spring. Keep soil consistently moist and harvest whole rosettes at the base once they reach full size, since mature plants bolt quickly as the weather warms.

name: Piel de Sapo Melon
scientificName: Cucumis melo var. inodorus 'Piel de Sapo'
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after the soil is thoroughly warm; Piel de Sapo needs a long, hot growing season to fully sweeten, making it a strong fit for the extended Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vines plenty of room or a sturdy trellis with slings to support the heavy fruit. Piel de Sapo, meaning 'toad skin' in Spanish, is a classic Spanish winter melon named for its distinctive mottled dark and pale green rind, an oblong fruit that hides sweet, crisp, pale green-white flesh with a mild, delicate flavor. Unlike musky cantaloupe types, this inodorus-group melon develops little to no aroma at the stem even when fully ripe, so growers judge readiness by days from planting, a slight softening at the blossom end, and a duller rind color rather than by scent, and the fruit also stores notably longer after harvest than most melons. Water deeply but infrequently once fruit begins sizing up, and reduce watering in the final week or two before harvest to concentrate sugars.

name: Piennolo del Vesuvio Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Piennolo del Vesuvio is a traditional small red cherry-type tomato grown on the volcanic slopes of Mount Vesuvius near Naples, prized for its thick skin and long storage life.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking or caging as plants grow. Piennolo del Vesuvio is a traditional small, oval red tomato grown for centuries on the mineral-rich volcanic soils of the Mount Vesuvius region near Naples, its thick skin and low water content allowing whole trusses to be hung in bunches ('piennoli') and stored through winter without refrigeration, slowly concentrating in flavor as they cure. The tangy, intensely tomato flavor makes it prized in Neapolitan cooking, especially for a quick, bright sauce. Harvest whole clusters when fully colored and hang them in a cool, airy spot to store, checking periodically and using fruit as it continues to ripen.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

name: Pikant Shallot
plantingNote: Plant sets about an inch deep and four to six inches apart as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, or in fall in mild-winter regions; Pikant is among the fastest-maturing shallot sets commonly grown.
directions: Pikant is a widely grown European set-shallot producing clusters of medium-sized, slightly elongated bulbs wrapped in rich copper-red to mahogany papery skin over red-tinged flesh. Its flavor is noticeably more pungent and assertive than the milder Dutch Yellow types, as its name suggests, which makes it a favorite where a stronger shallot bite is wanted in cooking. Plant sets shallowly in loose, well-drained soil and keep the row weed-free while bulbs size up through late spring and early summer. Pikant matures quickly for a shallot and, once cured, keeps for an unusually long stretch in cool, dry storage.
sources: Crate and Basket shallot variety guide

name: Pike Rutabaga
plantingNote: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a frost-sweetened fall and winter storage crop.
directions: Direct sow in mid to late summer so roots size up through the cooling days of fall, when frost converts starches to sugars and mellows typical rutabaga bite. Bred in Maine by Radcliffe Pike from an interspecific cross with Chinese cabbage, this variety has purple-topped white skin reminiscent of Laurentian but a notably fine-grained, sweeter yellow flesh, and it stores exceptionally well in a cold root cellar.

name: Piko Uliuli Taro
plantingNote: Best suited to a permanently flooded or continuously saturated bed rather than ordinary garden soil, mimicking a wetland lo'i.
directions: Historically one of the most important commercial poi taro varieties on Oahu, this stocky, erect selection is grown almost exclusively as a flooded wetland crop rather than in upland beds. It tolerates lowland heat and humidity with less corm rot than many other wetland types, making it a sturdy choice for a pond-edge or bog planter in a partly shaded Gulf Coast garden. Keep the roots submerged or saturated at all times and expect a long season, with corms maturing 12 to 15 months after planting. The chalky-white corm flesh must be cooked before eating.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR, Taro Varieties in Hawaii database (Piko Uliuli)

name: Pima Mottled Lima Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; lima beans germinate poorly in cool, wet ground. This pole lima is grown by Akimel O'odham (Pima) families around St. John's in the Gila River Indian Community of Arizona and is notably drought- and heat-tolerant.
directions: Pima Mottled Lima is a pole lima bean grown by Akimel O'odham (Pima) farming families around St. John's in the Gila River Indian Community of Arizona. The pale beige seeds are patterned with black mottling in stripes, spots, and solid patches, closely resembling the related Pima Beige lima. Vigorous vines need a trellis or other support and reward it with good yields in both spring and fall low-desert plantings, tolerating heat and drought far better than lima beans bred for cooler, wetter climates. Direct sow only once the soil is reliably warm, since lima beans are slow and unreliable to germinate in cool ground.

name: Pimento L Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; the compact 18-inch plants do well in containers or raised beds and need no staking.
directions: Pimento L is a compact, open-pollinated pimiento-type sweet pepper long grown in home gardens for its heart-shaped, thick-walled fruit and reliable tobacco mosaic virus resistance, a trait that made it a dependable choice before modern hybrid pimientos were widely available. Fruits run about four and a half inches long, ripening from green to a glossy bright red with very few seeds and exceptionally sweet, mild flesh (under 500 Scoville units). The short, tidy plants make this a good fit for small beds or containers, and the thick walls hold up well for stuffing, roasting, or slicing raw into salads.

name: Pimiento Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Pimiento is the traditional variety for making pimiento cheese — the classic Southern spread requiring the specific thick-walled, sweet, very mild flesh of the true pimiento variety.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Pimiento (also spelled pimento) is the traditional thick-walled sweet pepper of Spanish and Southern American tradition — producing heart-shaped to rounded, medium-sized (3–4 inches) fruits with exceptionally thick, sweet, juicy walls and very mild, sweet flavor with no heat. The thick walls and very sweet, low-acid flesh are the defining qualities that distinguish pimiento from other sweet peppers: the wall thickness (often twice that of standard bell peppers) makes pimiento ideal for roasting, stuffing, and jar-packing, while the sweetness and mildness make it the original pepper for stuffed olives and the authentic ingredient in Southern pimiento cheese. The fruits ripen from green to a deep, vivid red and are at their best flavor when fully red. Pimiento is less commonly found in grocery stores than bell peppers (most commercial pimiento production goes to food processing), making it a particularly worthwhile home garden variety for cooks who want the authentic ingredient. The plants are productive, compact, and well-adapted to Gulf South growing conditions. In zone 9, pimiento peppers have two productive seasons: spring planting (February–March transplant, harvest May–July) and fall planting (August transplant, harvest October–November). The rich red color and exceptional thick-walled quality make pimiento one of the finest peppers for roasting whole.

name: Pineapple Ground Cherry
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Pineapple ground cherry is a named selection of the cape gooseberry type with especially sweet, intensely tropical pineapple-vanilla flavor in small, papery-husked fruits that drop from the plant when ripe — an extraordinary, underused fruit for snacking, baking, and preserves.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Pineapple Ground Cherry is a named selection of the ground cherry (Physalis pruinosa) grown for its small (1/2–3/4 inch), golden-yellow fruits enclosed in dry, papery, tan husks (lantern-like husks much smaller than tomatillo husks) with an intensely sweet, tropical flavor reminiscent of pineapple, vanilla, and caramel — completely unlike tomatillos in flavor despite being related. The fruits drop from the plant when fully ripe and are gathered from the ground (hence the name); this drop-when-ripe characteristic is the easiest ripeness indicator. Extraordinarily productive in warm weather, with hundreds of fruits per plant. Delicious eaten fresh, in pies (often compared to cape gooseberry pies), in jams, and dried like raisins. A charming and unusual fruit for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens that is barely known to most gardeners.

name: Pineapple Tomatillo
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March for spring and July for fall. Tomatillos require at least two plants from different seed sources for cross-pollination and reliable fruit set; plant Pineapple Tomatillo alongside a green-fruiting type for maximum production. The papery husk turns tan and splits as fruits mature to gold-yellow.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Pineapple Tomatillo is a named selection of Physalis ixocarpa that ripens to a distinctive golden-yellow rather than the standard tomatillo green, with a noticeably sweeter, more tropical flavor that includes a pineapple-like brightness absent from green-fruiting types. The medium-sized fruits, typically 1–1.5 inches in diameter, fill and split the papery husk as they ripen to gold, at which point they are at peak sweetness. The sweeter profile makes Pineapple Tomatillo less acidic than standard green tomatillos and more suitable for fresh eating out of hand, in fruit salsas, or in preparations where a less tart tomatillo flavor is desired. Standard green tomatillos provide better classic salsa verde acidity; Pineapple works best where a milder, sweeter, more unusual tomatillo experience is the goal. Like all tomatillos, plant at least two individuals for cross-pollination.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Tomatillo Specialty Varieties
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Pineapple Tomatillo Variety Notes
New Mexico State University Extension — Tomatillo Cultivar Selection

name: Pineapple Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Pineapple produces very large fruits that take significant time to develop — start seeds early to maximize the harvest window before summer heat causes fruit quality to decline.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Pineapple is one of the most visually spectacular heirloom beefsteak tomatoes — producing enormous (1–2 lb), irregular, slightly ribbed fruits with a stunning bicolor pattern of golden-yellow base skin marked with bold red and orange streaking and marbling that creates a stained-glass appearance when sliced. The cut surface reveals a similarly bicolor red-and-yellow flesh pattern — an ornamental quality that makes Pineapple outstanding for fresh salads and sliced presentations where the visual effect can be appreciated. The flavor matches the visual quality: intensely sweet, fruity, and complex with a low-acid, tropical quality that justifies the variety's evocative name — the combination of golden-yellow color and sweet, fruity flavor genuinely suggests tropical fruit. Large, vigorous indeterminate plants require sturdy support (minimum 6-foot cage or stake). As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved from the most characteristic fruits for replanting. In zone 9, Pineapple produces best in the spring season (March–June) before summer heat arrives; the very large fruits require a relatively long, cool growing period for maximum development.

name: Ping Tung Long Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Ping Tung Long is a Taiwan heirloom adapted to hot, humid conditions, making it an excellent choice for Gulf South gardens. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer and fall harvest. Harvest fruits when 10–15 inches long and still deep lavender-purple before any brown coloration develops at the calyx. Plants benefit from staking when fruit load is heavy — the long fruits can cause branches to lean.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun in rich, well-drained soil. Harvest fruits when 10–15 inches and still vivid lavender-purple. Ping Tung Long (named for Pingtung County in southern Taiwan where it originates) is a Taiwanese heirloom eggplant representing the classic Asian long eggplant type at its finest — producing exceptionally long (12–16 inch), slender, slightly curved, vivid lavender-purple to violet fruits with thin, tender skin. The variety is among the most widely grown and highly regarded long Asian eggplants in Taiwan and throughout the Chinese-American gardening community in the United States, where it has been maintained as an open-pollinated heirloom for multiple generations. The fruits are characterized by extremely thin, tender skin (no peeling needed), virtually no seeds, and very sweet, mild flesh with no bitterness — a flavor profile considered superior for raw preparations and quick stir-fries where the tender skin softens immediately without extended cooking. The vivid lavender-purple color is particularly attractive in the garden and at the table. Ping Tung Long's heat tolerance and prolific production in hot conditions make it especially well-suited to southern gardens.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Ping Tung Long eggplant variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Taiwanese heirloom eggplant collection
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Eggplant Production in the Southeast

name: Pingtung Long Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; eggplant needs sustained warmth and benefits from bottom heat during germination. Transplant in zone 9 February–March for a long growing season; eggplant thrives in the heat and often continues producing through October–November.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Pingtung Long is a Taiwanese heirloom eggplant that produces slender, 12–18 inch fruits in a vibrant lavender-purple, among the longest eggplant fruits available. The skin is exceptionally thin and tender with minimal bitterness, making it prized for quick stir-fries and grilling without peeling. Plants are productive and heat-tolerant, continuing to set fruit through the hot zone 9 summers when other eggplant varieties may pause. Harvest fruits young when skin is glossy and before seeds develop; overripe fruits become seedy and bitter. A heavy producer that may need light staking to support the long, heavy fruits.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Pingtung Long Eggplant
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Eggplant Production in Florida
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Pingtung Long

name: Pink Accordion Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Pink Accordion sets deeply ribbed, hollow-chambered fruit and benefits from sturdy staking like other large French-type heirlooms.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after frost danger passes, staking vines to support the oddly shaped fruit. Pink Accordion bears dramatically ribbed, pleated pink fruit in the French coeur de boeuf tradition, with meaty, low-seed flesh and a mild, sweet flavor well suited to slicing and stuffing. The deep folds of the fruit give it an almost sculptural appearance that sets it apart on a market table or in a mixed heirloom display. Harvest at full color and inspect the folds for hidden moisture that can encourage rot in humid weather, since the deep ribbing can trap water after rain.

name: Pink Beauty Radish
plantingNote: Well suited to Gulf Coast fall sowing 6-8 weeks before first frost; performs best in cooler soil rather than spring heat.
directions: An All-America Selections-winning open-pollinated radish prized for round roots in a clear bright pink over crisp white flesh. Its flavor is notably gentle and mild rather than sharp, making it a favorite for market growers selling to customers who find standard radishes too peppery. Strong tops make it easy to bunch for market, and the roots resist splitting even when left in the ground a few extra days.

name: Pink Berkeley Tie Dye Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the indeterminate vine as it grows.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Pink Berkeley Tie Dye is a modern open-pollinated variety related to the original green Berkeley Tie Dye, bred by Wild Boar Farms and prized for its striking exterior of pink and green streaks and blushes, which give way when sliced to a marbled, jewel-toned interior of pink, red, and gold swirled together in a genuinely tie-dye pattern. Beyond the visual novelty, the flavor is rich, sweet, and complex, ranking among the better-tasting of the modern striped 'tie dye' tomato series that has become popular with heirloom and specialty tomato growers. The indeterminate vine is productive over a long season; water evenly through fruit development to reduce cracking, and harvest once the distinctive coloring fully develops.

name: Pink Brandywine Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Pink Brandywine is the original pink-fleshed Brandywine heirloom and the one that gave the variety its legendary reputation for flavor — the Sudduth strain and Platfoot strain are the two main true-breeding lineages, both producing large, pink, irregular fruits of extraordinary depth of flavor.
directions: Start indoors under grow lights 6–8 weeks before last frost; plant deeply after frost, burying 2/3 of the stem, and stake or cage immediately — Pink Brandywine produces tall, sprawling, potato-leaved vines that are challenging to support and slow to set fruit. Pink Brandywine (distinct from the yellow Brandywine and red Brandywine strains) is widely considered by heirloom tomato enthusiasts to be the definitive Brandywine — a large (12–24 oz), oblate to irregular, deep pink-skinned, pink-fleshed tomato with extraordinary, complex, sweet-rich flavor that lacks the sharp acidity of red tomatoes; many growers consider it the best-tasting tomato they have ever grown. The Sudduth and Platfoot strains (the two main documented lineages preserved by Seed Savers Exchange) are both potato-leaved (a genetic marker associated with the true Brandywine) and behave similarly in the garden. A notoriously slow, difficult, but rewarding grow — plants are late to mature and require long, warm seasons, but the fruit quality when conditions are right is unmatched.
sources: Weaver, William Woys. Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

name: Pink Bumble Bee Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Pink Bumble Bee is a vigorous indeterminate cherry tomato that needs a tall stake or trellis for its long fruiting season.
directions: Pink Bumble Bee is a member of Wild Boar Farms' Bumble Bee series of striped cherry tomatoes, bearing small round fruit in rosy pink overlaid with fine gold stripes that radiate from the stem end. The thin-skinned fruit has an intense, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor typical of the series, and the heavy-yielding vine produces in long clusters through most of the season. Provide a tall stake or trellis for the vigorous indeterminate growth and pick fruit promptly at full color, since ripe cherry tomatoes soften and can crack quickly in wet weather.

name: Pink Eye Purple Hull Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pink Eye Purple Hull peas are highly heat-tolerant — they thrive and produce abundantly in Gulf South summer heat that limits production of most other vegetables.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Pink Eye Purple Hull is one of the most widely grown and deeply traditional southern pea varieties of the Gulf South — a semi-bush to vining type producing distinctive purple-hulled pods that make harvest timing and identification visually clear (green hulls shade to purple as the peas approach maturity), with cream-white peas marked by a distinctive pink to rose-colored 'eye' or hilum that gives the variety its evocative name. The pink eye is the identifying mark: when a pot of fresh-shelled Pink Eye Purple Hull peas is spread on the counter, the cream peas with their small pink-rose eye marks are immediately recognizable as this specific variety. The flavor is excellent — classic southern pea quality with a rich, earthy, beany sweetness that is characteristic of the Gulf South summer pea tradition. Pink Eye Purple Hull is extremely productive in Gulf South conditions, continuing to produce through summer heat that limits most other garden vegetables. It is among the most important vegetable crops of the traditional Gulf South summer garden, providing fresh food through July, August, and September when garden production from other crops has ended. Nitrogen-fixing root system improves soil. The purple hulls are ornamentally attractive in the garden and make identifying ripe pods easy and unambiguous.

name: Pink Fir Apple Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces after soil has warmed slightly; as a late maincrop fingerling it needs the longest season of any common salad potato.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in light, well-drained soil, and be patient, since this is a true late-season variety and tubers will not fully knobble and size up until the last weeks of the growing season. Pink Fir Apple is a Victorian-era heirloom fingerling named for its long, narrow, knobbly tubers with pink-blushed skin and waxy, nutty, pale-yellow flesh that holds its shape beautifully when boiled whole. It remains a favorite of chefs and home cooks for cold potato salads because the dense waxy texture does not turn mealy or fall apart. Choose it over a modern fingerling hybrid when a genuinely old salad-potato flavor and the classic irregular fingerling shape are the goal.

name: Pink Lipstick Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow around the last frost date; in warm winter regions like the Gulf Coast also sow in fall for a winter harvest.
directions: Sow seed clusters directly into fertile soil and thin to final spacing, watering consistently to keep leaves tender through summer heat. Bred for its intensely saturated hot-pink stalks and veins, this selection stands out even among rainbow chard mixes and holds its color well after cooking. Its heavily crumpled, deep green leaves are produced over a long season, and repeated cutting encourages continued new growth from the crown.

name: Pink Passion Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost, or in late summer for a fall and winter crop in zone 9; Pink Passion holds its bright stem color well through the cool season.
directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Pink Passion is a modern chard cultivar bred for exceptionally vivid, saturated hot-pink stalks and midribs that stand out strongly against dark, glossy, savoyed green leaves, making it a favorite for ornamental edible plantings as well as the kitchen. Both leaves and stalks are edible with classic chard flavor, the leaves cooking down like spinach and the crisp, colorful stalks holding their hue reasonably well when sautéed or roasted. Harvest outer leaves continuously as needed, leaving the growing center intact, and expect strong production through the cool season with regular cutting.

name: Pink Ping Pong Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 5-6 weeks before the last frost; Pink Ping Pong is a small round pink cherry tomato that fruits early and sets heavy clusters.
directions: Sow indoors 5-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once the soil has warmed, providing a cage or trellis for the sprawling indeterminate vines. Pink Ping Pong produces round, smooth, pink cherry tomatoes about the size and shape of a table-tennis ball, borne in heavy clusters with a sweet, well-balanced flavor. The compact-fruited habit makes it a reliable early producer for fresh snacking and salads through a long summer season. Pick fruit promptly as it ripens to encourage continued flowering and set.

name: Pink Ponderosa Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant in February–March for a spring crop. Stake or cage heavily — Pink Ponderosa vines are tall (5–7 feet) and produce very large, heavy fruits that require solid support. In zone 9 a fall planting in August for October–November harvest often produces better-quality fruit with fewer cracks.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and provide sturdy staking; Pink Ponderosa (also called 'Henderson's Pink Ponderosa') is a late 19th-century American heirloom tomato introduced by the Henderson seed company around 1891, noted for producing enormous, beefsteak-type fruits of a distinctive deep rose-pink color — the 'pink' refers to the red flesh showing through the colorless (no yellow pigment in skin) skin, creating the characteristic pink-red appearance of traditional beefsteak-type heirlooms. The very large fruits (often 1–2 pounds each) are meaty, low-acid, and juicy with a mild, sweet, rich tomato flavor that made Ponderosa-type tomatoes the standard fresh-eating tomato for most of the 20th century before uniform-color commercial hybrids replaced them. The indeterminate vine produces continuously until frost and can be especially productive in zone 9's long growing season. The mild, low-acid flavor makes Pink Ponderosa particularly appealing for sliced tomatoes where the full fruit flavor is experienced without cooking.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Pink Ponderosa Heirloom Tomato
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Pink Ponderosa History
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Heirloom Tomato Production Guide

name: Pinkeye Purple Hull BVR Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep once soil has warmed past 65°F; BVR's resistance to blackeye cowpea mosaic virus makes it a safer choice where that disease has shown up in previous seasons.
directions: Direct sow in full sun after the soil has warmed, spacing plants to allow good air movement, which helps keep foliage disease in check even though BVR already carries built-in virus resistance. Selected at the University of Georgia in Athens from the classic Pinkeye Purple Hull and released in 1984, this bush-to-semi-vining type was bred specifically for resistance to blackeye cowpea mosaic virus, a problem that can stunt and discolor susceptible cowpea plantings. Pods set up above the foliage for easy picking and start out green before coloring to the familiar rosy-purple hull, with the peas themselves turning cream with a distinctive maroon pink eye. Pick pods at the green-shell stage for the mildest flavor, or let them dry fully on the vine for long-keeping dried peas.
sources: University of Georgia cowpea breeding program variety records
Victory Seed Company southern pea variety descriptions
Willhite Seed Company cowpea catalog records

name: Pinkeye Purple Hull Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep, 3–4 inches apart in rows 24–36 inches apart after soil thoroughly warms to 65°F and all frost danger passes; in zone 9, plant from late March through late July for successive harvests — Pinkeye Purple Hull is one of the most heat-tolerant crops and thrives in the peak Gulf South summer.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after soil warms to 65°F; Pinkeye Purple Hull is the most widely grown and most beloved Southern pea (cowpea) cultivar in Gulf South gardens — a semi-vining bush variety producing pods with a distinctive purple hull (pod exterior) that turns from green to vivid purple-magenta at the ideal harvest stage for fresh-shelling, making it easy to identify perfect harvest timing. The peas inside have the distinctive pink 'eye' (hilum marking) characteristic of this type, with a rich, full, starchy-creamy flavor that is the authentic taste of Southern cooking — distinctive, earthy, and satisfying in ways that fresh garden peas cannot replicate. Cowpeas are among the most heat-tolerant vegetables in cultivation and actually perform best during the hottest summer months when most other crops fail — the Gulf South summer that defeats beans, cucumbers, and squash is ideal cowpea growing weather. They fix atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule bacteria, enriching the soil for follow-on crops. For fresh eating, harvest when the majority of the pod has turned purple and feels firm and fully rounded but before the pod dries. For dried peas, allow the pods to turn tan and dry completely on the vine. The dried peas store indefinitely and are the foundation of traditional Southern New Year's black-eyed pea dishes.

name: Pinot Noir Sweet Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; a good patio or container choice for zone 9a where summer highs regularly exceed the typical bell-pepper fruit-set ceiling.
directions: An ornamental-edible F1 bell pepper bred for a wide performance window, cycling through citrus, berry, lilac, and violet tones before ripening to cherry-red, with foliage and flowering that merely pause rather than abort during the worst heat spikes. The compact habit and striking color stages make it a strong patio or container choice where conventional bells stall out in peak Gulf Coast summer heat. Harvest at any color stage for fresh eating or let fruit fully ripen to red for maximum sweetness.
sources: True Leaf Market - Pinot Noir F1 Hybrid Sweet Pepper
Burpee - Pepper, Sweet, Pinot Noir Hybrid

name: Pinto Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; in zone 9 plant March–April for spring and July–August for fall. Pinto beans are primarily a dry bean — the plant must be allowed to fully mature and dry before harvest, which takes the full season. In zone 9 the spring crop typically produces dry beans by June–July; a fall planting dried in November–December. Bush habit requires no staking.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; pinto beans are the most widely grown dry bean in the United States, accounting for nearly half of all dry bean production, and the foundation of Southwestern and Mexican cooking — the primary bean in refried beans (frijoles refritos), bean soup, and chili. The tan seeds with reddish-brown speckles (the Spanish name 'pinto' means 'painted') turn uniformly tan-brown when cooked, at which point the flavor is rich, earthy, and starchy with a creamy texture that falls apart when mashed. Bush-habit pinto plants are compact and self-supporting, producing a single concentrated harvest suitable for home-scale production and storage. The dry beans store for 2–3 years in a cool, dry location. In zone 9 the plants are susceptible to bean rust in humid conditions; provide adequate spacing for air circulation.
sources: University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Dry Bean Production
New Mexico State University Extension — Common Dry Beans
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Phaseolus vulgaris Cultivar Development

name: Piquillo Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes; piquillo is a compact, highly productive sweet Spanish pepper turning vivid red at maturity with a characteristic pointed tip (piquillo = 'little beak') — the most important preserved pepper in Spanish cuisine, roasted and packed in jars, and a staple ingredient in tapas, pintxos, and modern Spanish cooking.
directions: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant to a sunny, fertile bed after frost danger passes; piquillo plants are compact and productive, setting numerous small, triangular fruits; harvest at full vivid red maturity; roast over open flame or under a broiler until charred, steam to loosen skin, peel and seed for the classic preparation. Piquillo is the defining preserved pepper of northern Spain, particularly the Navarra region around the town of Lodosa (in the Ebro River valley) where the Denomination of Origin 'Piquillo de Lodosa' protects the traditional pepper and its preparation. The pepper is small (2–3 inch), triangular to slightly flattened-conical with a characteristic pointed 'beak' tip (piquillo = 'little beak'), vivid scarlet-red at maturity, and sweet to very mildly pungent with no significant heat. The flesh is thin but intensely sweet and slightly fruity, with a subtle bitterness that is balanced by the roasting process — fire-roasting is inseparable from the piquillo's culinary identity. The traditional preparation involves hand-roasting individual peppers over wood fires, peeling and seeding each one by hand without any water washing (to preserve flavor and sugars), and packing them in their own juices in jars or tins without any additional preservation except salt. The result is one of the most refined and flavorful preserved vegetables in world cuisine. Jarred piquillo peppers are a staple of Spanish kitchens and are used stuffed with salt cod or cheese, arranged on pintxos, layered in pasta dishes, and pureed into smooth sauces. Growing piquillo at home and roasting them yourself produces a quality that commercially jarred peppers rarely match.
sources: Consejo Regulador de la D.O. Piquillo de Lodosa

name: Piracicaba Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting to garden; in zone 9, start seeds in August–September for fall transplanting in September–October, targeting harvest December–March. Piracicaba was developed in Brazil for production in subtropical warm-winter conditions where standard heading broccoli (such as Packman or Marathon) struggles with heat-induced bolting and premature heading. Rather than forming a single large central head, Piracicaba produces an abundance of small, tender loose florets on branching side shoots over an extended harvest period — a sprouting habit similar to De Cicco broccoli but with dramatically better heat tolerance. In zone 9, Piracicaba can be harvested continuously through the mild winter rather than requiring a single-harvest timing, and it continues producing side shoots well into spring when standard broccoli bolts.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant to garden in fall for zone 9 winter harvest. Harvest loose florets continuously. Piracicaba Broccoli originated at the Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP) and agronomic research stations near Piracicaba, a city in São Paulo state, Brazil — a major center of Brazilian tropical agricultural research. The variety was developed specifically to address the fundamental incompatibility between standard broccoli breeding (which targets cool-climate heading formation) and the subtropical conditions of southern Brazil and other warm-climate growing regions. Standard broccoli varieties were bred primarily in Europe and California's cool coastal fog belt, where temperature ranges precisely suited to head development allow reliable production; in warm climates, standard broccoli heats prematurely, forms loose, open heads of poor quality, or bolts before any marketable crop develops. Piracicaba's breeding solution was to select for a sprouting growth habit that produces continuously rather than forming a single marketable head — an approach that converts the temperature sensitivity of head formation from a problem into an advantage. Since the plant never forms a central head to be ruined by heat, there is no precise temperature window to miss, and the plant produces usable florets across a much broader temperature range. The florets of Piracicaba are small and tender, with a delicate texture superior to the sometimes-coarse texture of oversized main-head broccoli, and the continuous harvest over weeks or months provides far greater total yield per plant than single-harvest heading types in favorable conditions.
sources: Universidade Estadual de Campinas (UNICAMP) — Piracicaba broccoli variety development for subtropical production
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Heat-Tolerant Broccoli Varieties for Gulf South Fall Production
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Piracicaba broccoli variety notes and trial data

name: Piri Piri Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; Capsicum frutescens peppers benefit from a longer indoor growing period than C. annuum. In zones 9–11 the plants grow as woody perennials and become increasingly productive in their second and third years.
directions: Start indoors early and transplant to warm, well-drained soil; piri piri is an African cultivar of Capsicum frutescens (the same species as tabasco pepper) producing small, erect, vivid red to orange fruits 1–2 inches long with an intense, bright heat (50,000–175,000 SHU). It is the essential ingredient in the famous Portuguese piri piri sauce, brought to Portugal from its colonies in Angola and Mozambique in the 1500s, and is now central to Portuguese, South African, and Mozambican cuisines. Nando's Peri-Peri sauce is based on this pepper. The fruits are blended with garlic, lemon, and oil to make a marinade-sauce for grilled chicken. Plants become perennial subshrubs in zones 9–11 and produce prolifically year-round.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops

name: Pizzutello di Paceco Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this rustic ecotype tolerates dry, saline soils once established.
directions: Grown for generations on the saline clay soils around Paceco in the Ericine Valleys near Trapani, Sicily, this rustic variety produces small, round red fruit with a distinctive pointed 'pizzo' tip at the blossom end, giving the variety its name. It is a Slow Food Presidium-recognized ecotype, traditionally raised without irrigation and prized for its sweetness fresh off the vine, in sauce, or hung in bunches to dry for winter use. The resilient plants show good tolerance of local pests and disease pressure.

name: Plainsman Amaranth
plantingNote: Sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Plainsman was one of the first grain amaranth selections bred specifically for reliable, comparatively early maturity in temperate US growing regions.
directions: Plainsman came out of the grain amaranth breeding work done at the Rodale Research Center in the early 1980s, part of the push to turn amaranth into a viable modern US grain crop rather than strictly a garden curiosity. It bears tan to golden upright seed heads on tall, sturdy plants and was selected in large part for maturing reliably within a single Midwestern growing season, a trait that made it a common choice in early commercial grain amaranth trial plots. Sow shallowly in warm soil once frost danger has passed, thin to a wide spacing, and let plants grow largely unattended through summer heat. Harvest once the seed heads dry and shed seed readily when rubbed between the hands, then thresh and winnow thoroughly, since amaranth seed is small and light.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

name: Planters Jumbo Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed and frost danger has passed; Planters Jumbo is a 1930s commercial-standard cantaloupe that was widely grown across the South before modern hybrid melons became dominant.
directions: Direct sow seed in hills of two to three plants in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once soil has thoroughly warmed. Planters Jumbo is an heirloom cantaloupe dating to the 1930s, once a standard commercial variety grown widely across the South before modern hybrid melons largely replaced older open-pollinated types, prized for heavily netted rind and sweet, aromatic salmon-orange flesh. The vigorous, sprawling vines need plenty of room to run and benefit from consistent moisture during fruit development, tapering off as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest when the melon slips easily from the vine at full slip, with a strong, sweet aroma at the blossom end signaling peak ripeness.

name: Plein Blanc Inerme Cardoon
plantingNote: Start indoors six to eight weeks before last frost and transplant out once frost danger has passed; this old French cultivar is prized as a nearly thornless cardoon that makes blanching the stalks far less of a chore.
directions: Plein Blanc Inerme is a traditional French cardoon selected for broad, fleshy leaf ribs that carry almost no spines, unlike most cardoon strains whose sharp-edged leaves make harvest and blanching an unpleasant task. Plants form an imposing architectural clump of long, deeply cut, silvery-gray foliage a yard or more tall and wide before the ribs are ready to bundle and blanch in autumn. Wrap the outer leaves around the stalks and cover with cardboard, straw, or black plastic for several weeks before harvest to sweeten the ribs and reduce bitterness. Give it deep, rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture through the growing season for the tenderest stalks.

name: Plum Regal Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Plum Regal is a determinate paste-type tomato that sets a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks. In zone 9, aim for spring harvest in May–June by transplanting in early March.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Plum Regal is a determinate plum-type paste tomato developed by Cornell University's tomato breeding program specifically to improve on the disease susceptibility of heirloom Roma and similar paste types while maintaining the thick walls, dense flesh, and low moisture content that make plum tomatoes superior for sauce-making and processing. Plum Regal carries resistance to late blight (Phytophthora infestans) — the disease that wiped out heirloom paste tomatoes across much of the Northeast during the late blight epidemic of 2009 — as well as Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and Verticillium wilt. The medium-large (3–5 oz), deep red, oval fruits have very thick walls, small seed cavities, and excellent sauce-making characteristics with rich, concentrated tomato flavor. An outstanding choice for humid-climate paste tomato production, for home canners who want reliable crops without the disease susceptibility of traditional paste heirlooms, and for any gardener growing tomatoes where late blight or Fusarium are recurring problems.
sources: Cornell University vegetable breeding program publications
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Plum Regal variety notes

name: PMR 45 Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; PMR 45 was released in 1937 as the first cantaloupe bred for resistance to powdery mildew race 1 after the disease devastated California's Imperial Valley melon crop in the 1920s, and it remains foundational breeding stock for mildew-resistant melons today.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after soil has warmed well past last frost, spacing hills 24-36 inches apart in rows several feet apart. PMR 45 produces medium-sized, well-netted, oval fruits with thick, sweet orange flesh, and was a landmark release in melon breeding as the first commercial cantaloupe bred specifically for resistance to powdery mildew, a disease that had caused catastrophic losses in California melon fields during the 1920s. Its resistance genes have since been used extensively by breeders to create many modern mildew-resistant melon hybrids, making it a historically significant variety as well as a solid, productive open-pollinated choice for home gardens. Water consistently through vine growth and fruit development, then taper off as melons approach maturity, and harvest at full slip when the stem separates cleanly from the fruit.
sources: UC Riverside Department of Plant Pathology
Cucurbit Breeding, North Carolina State University

name: Poblano Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost date; transplant into warm, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun at or just after the last frost date; in zone 9, transplant in mid-February for spring production and again in late July for fall production.
directions: Set out transplants in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; Poblano is the classic Mexican culinary pepper — a mildly hot (1,000–2,000 Scoville units), wide, heart-shaped to triangular pepper that is the foundational ingredient in chiles rellenos, mole negro, and dozens of traditional Mexican dishes. Harvested green (poblano) or dried red (ancho or mulato depending on variety), these peppers have a rich, complex, slightly smoky flavor with moderate heat that defines the deep, layered character of traditional Mexican cuisine. The large, thick-walled fruits reach 4–5 inches long and 2.5–3 inches wide, with deep green color maturing to red-brown. Poblano is one of the most heat-tolerant culinary peppers and performs exceptionally well in zone 9's summer temperatures — unlike many sweet bell peppers, poblano tolerates the high summer heat of the Gulf South and continues producing through the hottest months with consistent irrigation. In zone 9, the plant can become a perennial woody shrub if protected from hard freezes, producing for 2–3 years from a single planting. Dry ripe red-brown poblanos to make ancho chiles — a key ingredient in red mole — by hanging in bundles in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location for 3–4 weeks.

name: Poinsett 76 Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Poinsett 76 is a Clemson University breeding program selection from the original Poinsett variety, released in 1976 and still widely grown in the Southeast for its outstanding combination of disease resistance, heat tolerance, and production in hot, humid conditions that challenges most cucumber varieties.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; provide support or allow vines to sprawl with 3–4 feet between hills. Poinsett 76 was developed by the Clemson University vegetable breeding program in South Carolina and released in 1976 as an improved selection of the original Poinsett cucumber (released 1966) — both named for Joel R. Poinsett, the South Carolinian who brought the poinsettia plant from Mexico. Poinsett 76 is distinguished by its outstanding disease resistance package (angular leaf spot, anthracnose, downy mildew, mosaic, and powdery mildew resistance) and heat tolerance that makes it the cucumber of choice for hot, humid Southeastern gardens where most varieties decline quickly in summer; fruits are 7–8 inches long, dark green, cylindrical, and of good eating quality. An open-pollinated, seed-saveable classic that remains one of the best choices for Gulf Coast and Deep South summer cucumber production.

name: Poinsett Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Poinsett was released by the Clemson University vegetable breeding program in 1966 as one of the earliest slicing cucumbers bred with a combined resistance package to several major foliar diseases, and it became the parent line for the later, further-refined Poinsett 76.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil after all frost danger has passed, and provide a trellis or allow the vigorous vines to sprawl on 3-4 feet of row spacing. Named for Joel R. Poinsett, the South Carolinian diplomat who introduced the poinsettia to the United States, this cucumber was a genuine breeding milestone: it was among the first commercial slicers to stack resistance to angular leaf spot, anthracnose, downy mildew, and mosaic virus into one dependable open-pollinated line, which sharply reduced losses in the humid Southeast. Fruits are dark green, cylindrical, and 7-8 inches long with good flavor, though the plant is somewhat less heat-tolerant in peak midsummer than the 1976 selection later bred from it. Save seed from fully mature, yellowed fruit for a true-breeding crop the following year.

name: Polar Bear Pumpkin
subcategory: giant white pumpkin for exhibition and carving
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 3 to 4 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into rich soil with generous spacing once soil is warm; Polar Bear is a giant-type squash bred for smooth, snow-white rind rather than the orange color of most large pumpkins.
directions: Start seed indoors ahead of the last frost, then transplant into deeply worked, richly amended soil with plenty of room, since fruit can reach 50 pounds or more under good growing conditions. Polar Bear stands out among giant pumpkins for its smooth, pure white rind, a striking contrast to the orange skin of most large exhibition types, making it a favorite for painted or decorated giant-pumpkin displays as well as competitive weigh-offs. Keep soil consistently moist during vine growth and fruit set, and remove all but one or two developing fruits per vine if maximum size is the goal. Harvest before hard frost once the rind has fully hardened and the vine has begun to decline, handling the heavy fruit carefully to avoid cracking the shell.

name: Polar Bere Oca
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep after last frost; Polar Bere's mild, sweet flavor (rather than the typical oca tang) makes it a good introductory variety for cooks new to this crop.
directions: Plant tubers in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Polar Bere is an oca cultivar with pure bone-white to very pale yellow tubers carrying a mild, sweet flavor distinct from the sharper acidic tang typical of many oca lines, making it a gentle introduction to the crop for first-time growers. Tuber bulking is triggered by shortening fall daylength as with all oca, and the tubers are considerably more frost-tolerant than the foliage, which dies back at the first hard freeze. Hardy to roughly zone 7a-9a with heavy mulch over winter.

name: Pole Seychelles Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed once soil has warmed; Pole Seychelles is a 2017 All-America Selections winner from Dutch breeders Bakker Brothers, grown on a 5-6 foot trellis for repeated harvests through the season.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep at the base of a sturdy 5-6 foot trellis or support in full sun, since this is a true climbing pole type. Pole Seychelles produces long, slender, uniform, stringless 5-6 inch pods with excellent flavor on vigorous dark-green vines, yielding multiple flushes of pods across the growing season rather than one concentrated harvest. The variety carries resistance to Bean Common Mosaic Virus, improving reliability in humid climates. Trim vine growth once it reaches the top of the trellis to encourage fuller pod set lower on the plant, and pick every few days to keep production going.

name: Polish Linguisa Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; provide staking or caging, since the indeterminate vine carries a heavy load of elongated fruit.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost, staking early to support the long fruit clusters. Polish Linguisa is a Polish heirloom paste tomato named for its distinctive elongated, curved, sausage-like fruit shape, which sets it apart from the blockier Roma and San Marzano types most gardeners know. The deep red fruit is dense and meaty with very little seed cavity or juice, cooking down quickly into a thick, richly flavored sauce or paste with minimal simmering. The vigorous indeterminate vines are heavy producers over a long season; pick fruit as it colors fully and process promptly, since the thin skin is more prone to splitting after heavy rain than dedicated modern paste hybrids.

name: Polish White Softneck Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves in fall at or around first frost; Polish White is a traditional Eastern European softneck garlic (Artichoke type) with origins in Poland and surrounding countries, where garlic has been grown as a staple crop for centuries — it produces medium-large bulbs with 10–16 tightly packed cloves, clean white skins, and a reliable, full-flavored character suited to all cooking uses and excellent storage of 10–12 months.
directions: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall from 4 weeks before first frost to shortly after; Polish White performs well in both cold northern climates and mild southern winters; harvest in summer when 5–6 lower leaves have yellowed and cure thoroughly before storage; braid the flexible stems for attractive long-term storage. Polish White is an Artichoke-type softneck garlic originating in Poland and the broader Eastern European garlic-growing tradition, where garlic has been a staple culinary and medicinal crop since ancient times; it entered the North American heirloom garlic collection through the immigrant communities and seed-saver networks that preserved traditional European agricultural varieties throughout the 20th century. The bulbs are medium-large (2–3 inches across) with tightly packed multiple layers of cloves (10–16 per bulb) in the characteristic Artichoke arrangement, with clean white to ivory outer skins and a compact, rounded shape. The flavor is full, moderately pungent, and satisfying — not as complex as the finest Rocambole or Marbled Purple Stripe hardnecks, but very reliable and versatile for all cooking uses from fresh salsas and aioli to long-cooked soups, stews, and roasted garlic. The primary virtues of Polish White are reliability (excellent performance in a wide range of climates), productivity (high-yielding compared to hardneck types), and outstanding storage life of 10–12 months under proper conditions (cool, dry, dark) — making it the garlic of choice for those who want a year-round supply from a single fall planting.

name: Pomegranate Crunch Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before last frost; fast-cropping habit suits tight succession planting schedules.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil and thin to 8-10 inches; Pomegranate Crunch is a medium-size red romaine bred for a texture between crisp romaine and tender butterhead, with thick, glossy cherry-red outer leaves wrapped around a heart that often blushes pink toward the center. It grows faster and more uniformly than many older red romaines while showing good resistance to downy mildew, making it a dependable choice for gardeners who want striking color without giving up productivity. The balance of sweetness and a light bitter edge suits both whole-leaf salads and Caesar-style preparations. Harvest as a full head once dense, or take outer leaves individually for an extended harvest.

name: Pomodoro Siccagno
plantingNote: Start seed indoors and transplant once nights stay warm, then withhold supplemental irrigation once plants establish; siccagno means 'dry-farmed' and the variety is traditionally grown on stored winter soil moisture alone.
directions: Pomodoro Siccagno, most famously grown in the Belice Valley of western Sicily and recognized as a Slow Food Presidium, is a rustic, irregularly shaped tomato traditionally raised without any irrigation beyond what deep winter rains leave stored in the clay-rich soil through the dry Sicilian summer. The resulting water stress concentrates sugars and acids into a smaller, thicker-skinned, deeply ribbed fruit with a flavor local growers describe as more intense than irrigated tomatoes, and the thick skin lets whole plants be pulled and hung indoors at season's end so fruit continues ripening for months. Space plants generously in deeply worked soil to encourage roots to range widely in search of residual moisture, and avoid the temptation to water once fruit set begins. Use fresh in salads, sun-dried, or cooked down into concentrated sauces that keep well into winter.

name: Ponca Baby Butternut Squash
plantingNote: Sow seeds directly in warm soil after the last frost, spacing to allow moderate vine spread, and keep soil evenly moist to support a heavy set of small fruit.
directions: Sow seeds directly in warm soil after the last frost, spacing to allow moderate vine spread, and keep soil evenly moist to support a heavy set of small fruit. Developed by breeders at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln and named an All-America Selections winner in 2021, this butternut produces compact, single-serving fruit under a pound with tan skin and dense, nutty-sweet orange flesh, bred with organic and small-farm production in mind. Its shorter vines and high fruit count per plant make it productive even in modest garden spaces. Allow fruit to fully harden on the vine before harvest, then cure for improved storage and flavor.

name: Ponderosa Red Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the heavy, potato-leaf vine needs sturdy staking or caging from an early stage.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, and stake the heavy vine well before fruit sets. Ponderosa Red is a classic American heirloom beefsteak dating to the late 1800s, grown for very large, deep red, meaty fruit with a dense, low-moisture, few-seeded interior that made it a favorite for slicing thick, generous sandwich rounds long before modern hybrid beefsteaks existed. The potato-leaf foliage typical of Ponderosa strains sets it apart visually from regular-leaf tomatoes, and the plant carries a genuinely old-fashioned, rich tomato flavor prized by heirloom growers over the milder taste of many modern varieties. Water evenly to reduce cracking on the large fruit, and support heavily, since individual tomatoes commonly exceed a pound and can snap unsupported branches.

name: Poona Kheera Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Poona Kheera is an Indian heirloom cucumber that dramatically changes color as it matures — from white to pale yellow to apple-yellow and finally to russet-tan — and is prized for its exceptional flavor at the yellow stage and above, good heat tolerance, and thin, easily digestible skin; one of the most beloved traditional cucumber varieties in the Pune (Poona) region of Maharashtra, India.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep and provide a trellis for best production; harvest at any stage from white (mild, crisp) to apple-yellow (sweetest, most complex) to russet (mellow, slightly sweet and aromatic); the yellow-to-russet stage is the traditional eating stage in India but many American gardeners prefer the pale yellow stage for fresh salads. Poona Kheera is an heirloom cucumber from the Pune (formerly Poona) region of Maharashtra state in western India, where it has been grown for centuries as the primary cucumber of the region and is still widely available in Indian markets. The most distinctive characteristic of this variety is its remarkable color change through the maturation cycle: young fruits are white or pale ivory, then transition to pale yellow, apple-yellow, golden-yellow, and finally to a warm russet-tan at full maturity — no other commonly grown cucumber goes through such a dramatic color progression. The flavor also changes with color: white fruits are mild, crisp, and relatively bland; yellow fruits have developed characteristic cucumber fragrance, sweetness, and complexity; russet fruits have an almost apple-like sweetness and aroma distinct from young cucumber flavor. In the Indian culinary tradition, the yellow-to-russet stage is preferred for eating raw out of hand, in raitas, and for cooking; American gardeners often prefer the yellow stage for salads where the flavor is sweet and the flesh remains crisp. Poona Kheera has good heat tolerance compared to standard slicing cucumbers and adapts well to Gulf Coast and Southern growing conditions.

name: Porcelain Doll Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in rich, well-amended soil; a hybrid Cinderella-type pumpkin whose flattened fruit deepens from pale cream to soft peachy pink as it matures, prized for both display and eating quality.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing hills 6-8 feet apart to give the vigorous vines room to spread. Porcelain Doll is a hybrid Cinderella-type pumpkin producing flattened, deeply ribbed fruit in the 20-24 pound range that shifts from pale yellow to cream and finally to a distinctive soft pink as it fully ripens on the vine. Beneath the showy pink rind lies a thick wall of sweet, dense, edible flesh that holds up well for roasting and pureeing, making this variety popular with both farmstand growers and cooks. Harvest once the rind has fully hardened and colored, then cure for one to two weeks before moving to cool, dry storage.

name: Porter Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Porter is an outstanding heat and drought-tolerant tomato for Texas and the Gulf Coast — historically the most widely grown home garden tomato in Texas, it performs reliably in hot, dry conditions where other varieties wilt and fail to fruit.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set plants in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Porter tomato is a Texas heirloom introduced around 1897–1900 by the Porter & Sons seed company of San Antonio, developed or selected specifically for the demanding conditions of Texas summers — heat, drought, and alkaline soils that would destroy most Eastern varieties. The small to medium (4–6 oz), pinkish-red, slightly oval fruits grow in clusters and have rich, concentrated flavor enhanced by mild water stress. Porter is genuinely drought tolerant and produces in Texas summer heat when standard varieties quit blooming. Historically the most important garden tomato in Central and South Texas, where generations of families grew it through conditions that would kill Brandywine or Cherokee Purple. For any gardener in the hot, dry interior South or Southwest struggling with summer tomato production, Porter is the essential starting point.

name: Porto Rico Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips (rooted cuttings from sprouted storage roots) after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant April–June for a September–November harvest. Porto Rico is a full-vine variety that spreads more widely than bush types and is best grown with ample space or on a mound system to control spreading.
directions: Plant slips 4–6 inches deep in loose, well-drained, slightly sandy soil amended with organic matter in full sun; Porto Rico is one of the oldest named American sweet potato varieties, recorded since the early 1900s and widely grown in Louisiana, Mississippi, and the Gulf Coast region for generations before the introduction of Beauregard and Covington. The medium-sized, copper-skinned tubers have bright orange, moist flesh with a rich, sweet, creamy flavor — considered by many Southern gardeners to have superior taste to modern commercial varieties. The vining plants spread widely, up to 10 feet, and should be positioned in open areas or at garden edges. Cure harvested roots at 85°F with high humidity for 7–10 days before storage to maximize sweetness and shelf life.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Potato Varieties for Louisiana
Mississippi State University Extension — Sweet Potato Production
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Porto Rico Sweet Potato Slips

name: Pot-a-peno Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Pot-a-peno is an All-America Selections winner bred specifically for container growing, producing a full crop of true jalapeño-flavored peppers on a compact plant well under a foot tall.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost date and transplant into a large container or garden bed after danger of frost has passed. Pot-a-peno was bred specifically to solve a common problem with growing jalapeños on a patio or balcony — most jalapeño varieties grow too large and sprawling for small containers — by combining a genuinely dwarf, compact plant habit with full-sized, full-flavored jalapeño fruit and strong productivity. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining container-friendly size with reliable yield and classic jalapeño heat and flavor, unlike many ornamental dwarf peppers bred for looks rather than culinary use. Fruits mature from green to red if left on the plant, with red fruits noticeably sweeter and slightly hotter than green. Because the plant is so compact, it benefits from a slightly richer potting mix and more frequent watering and feeding than an in-ground pepper, since a small root zone dries out and depletes nutrients faster. Harvest fruits at the green stage for classic jalapeño flavor or let them ripen to red for a sweeter, smokier heat, useful for chipotle-style drying.
sources: All-America Selections — Pot-a-peno Pepper award notes
PanAmerican Seed — Compact Container Pepper Breeding

name: Prairie Blush Potato
plantingNote: Plant seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; this clonal Yukon Gold sport matures only about 5 days later than its parent.
directions: Discovered as a single off-type hill growing within a planting of Yukon Gold on Wood Prairie Farm in 2001, this early-season sport was selected and stabilized for its golden skin overlaid with a distinctive pink blush. Tall-medium plants with light purple flowers produce medium-large, slightly oblong tubers with the same excellent flavor as Yukon Gold but a long dormancy that extends storage life. Give plants moderate spacing and expect medium yields with moderate resistance to blight and scab.

name: Précoce d'Argenteuil Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant crowns 6–8 inches deep in a prepared trench in early spring; Précoce d'Argenteuil is an old open-pollinated heirloom rather than an all-male hybrid, so expect some female plants among the seedlings that will bear seed and require weeding out of volunteer seedlings over time.
directions: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, forgoing any harvest in the first year to build the root system. Précoce d'Argenteuil is a classic 19th-century French heirloom named for the asparagus-growing town of Argenteuil near Paris, historically prized for thick, tender spears with purple-tinged tips that emerge notably earlier in spring than most varieties, giving the earliest asparagus harvest of the season. Because it is an open-pollinated variety rather than a modern all-male hybrid, yields run lower than modern hybrids and plantings include both male and female plants, with the females producing red berries in summer that should be removed before they scatter volunteer seedlings through the bed. It remains popular with heirloom growers and in traditional French cuisine for its rich, distinctive flavor; harvest spears once they reach 6–8 inches by snapping or cutting at soil level.

name: Prelude II Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed past 65°F, or start seed indoors in biodegradable pots 3-4 weeks ahead in short-season climates to gain extra time before frost.
directions: Prelude II is a hybrid okra bred to set pods reliably in shorter, cooler growing seasons where classic Southern heirloom okra often struggles to mature a full crop before fall's first frost. Its compact, earlier-flowering plants begin producing spineless green pods notably sooner than tall heirloom types, making it a practical option for northern gardens and short-summer regions that still want a real okra harvest. Soak seed overnight before sowing to speed germination in cool spring soil, and harvest pods every one to two days at two to three inches for the most tender texture. Because the plant stays shorter and more compact than traditional Southern varieties, it tolerates closer spacing and needs less staking in exposed sites.
sources: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension
