name: Preludio Florence Fennel
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring after frost danger passes, or sow again in mid-summer for a fall bulb crop in cooler weather.
directions: Preludio is an early-maturing hybrid Florence fennel bred to size up quickly into smooth, glossy white bulbs while resisting the premature bolting that plagues fennel sown in lengthening spring days. Its speed makes it a favorite for the first fennel planting of the season, when growers want a harvestable bulb well before summer heat sets in. The flesh is crisp and mildly sweet with the characteristic anise flavor, equally good raw in salads or roasted. Choose Preludio specifically for early-season plantings where bolt resistance and a short days-to-maturity window matter most.

name: Premium Crop Broccoli
plantingNote: Start seed indoors for a spring crop, or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest; Premium Crop, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, remains a benchmark hybrid broccoli for large, uniform, dense central heads.
directions: Start seed indoors for a spring crop or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, spacing transplants 18 to 24 inches apart. Premium Crop, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, has remained a benchmark hybrid broccoli for decades, prized for exceptionally large, dense, uniform blue-green central heads and reliable heading even under variable growing conditions that can cause other broccoli to head poorly. After the main head is harvested, the plant produces a useful flush of smaller side shoots, extending the harvest for several more weeks. Cut the central head while buds are still tight and before any yellow flowers show, and keep harvesting side shoots as they develop.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Broccoli Production

name: Premium Late Flat Dutch Cabbage
scientificName: Brassica oleracea var. capitata 'Premium Late Flat Dutch'
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost for spring planting, or in early summer for a fall/winter storage crop; this improved strain of the old Flat Dutch line needs the full growing season to bulk up its heads.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil, giving plants extra room since this is one of the larger-headed cabbages. Premium Late Flat Dutch is a 19th-century American heirloom line prized for its very large, flattened, blue-green heads that can reach ten pounds or more and hold together tightly rather than splitting. Its long time to maturity and dense, thick leaves make it an excellent late-season crop for slaw, kraut, and cold storage, where whole heads keep for months in a cool root cellar. Because of its size, allow it a full, uninterrupted season of growth and avoid crowding neighboring plants.

name: Prescott Fond Blanc Melon
scientificName: Cucumis melo var. cantalupensis 'Prescott Fond Blanc'
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil is reliably warm; this heavily ribbed French heirloom needs a long, hot summer to fully sugar up, so gardeners in short-season climates should start plants indoors 3-4 weeks early.
directions: Start seed indoors in short-season regions or direct sow into warm soil after frost, spacing vines generously to allow good air circulation and reduce fungal disease pressure. Prescott Fond Blanc is a traditional French market melon named for its deep, warty ribbing and the pale, creamy patch, or fond blanc, where the fruit rests on the ground as it ripens. The orange flesh is dense, sweet, and highly perfumed, and the variety has long been prized in Provençal markets as one of the most flavorful of the old French cantaloupe types. Harvest when the stem begins to crack and separates cleanly from the fruit, the classic slip stage that signals full sweetness.

name: President Celeriac
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; this fast-growing F1 can be transplanted out slightly earlier than open-pollinated types since it matures quickly once warm weather arrives.
directions: President is a vigorous European F1 hybrid celeriac prized by market growers for forming large, clean, smooth-skinned white roots faster than many open-pollinated types. Start seed indoors in cell trays and transplant into fertile, moisture-retentive soil once frost danger has passed, setting plants slightly deeper than they grew to help anchor the developing globe. Water consistently through summer and remove lower leaves and surface rootlets periodically to keep the crown clean. Roots size up reliably even in shorter growing seasons, making President a good choice where summers are cool or compressed.

name: President Hybrid Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost into warm, fertile soil, or transplant young seedlings started 2-3 weeks earlier indoors.
directions: President was one of the first hybrid zucchinis to combine early vigor with a long, productive harvest window, and it remains a benchmark against which newer hybrid zucchinis are still compared. The upright, semi-open plant carries glossy, dark green, cylindrical fruit that stay tender even a bit past the ideal 6-8 inch harvest size, giving gardeners more forgiveness than many modern types. Its reliable, heavy set makes it a solid choice for gardeners who just want zucchini without babying a temperamental variety. Keep fruit picked regularly to prevent the plant from slowing production.

name: Presidio Rice
plantingNote: Direct-sow into saturated beds or shallow paddies once soil warms past 65F; performs reliably under both continuously flooded and consistently moist home-garden culture.
directions: A long-grain rice from a Jefferson by Maybelle by Rosemont cross, released in 2005 by USDA and Texas A&M AgriLife's Beaumont rice program and long the quality benchmark for Texas Gulf Coast rice because of its unusually low chalky-grain percentage and excellent milling yield. Harvest when panicles droop and turn golden-tan, then dry and hull. Its clean milling makes it a forgiving first rice variety for gardeners new to hulling by hand.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife - Texas Rice Production Guidelines
Rice Farming - Louisiana and Texas Release Long-Grain Varieties

name: Pride of Wisconsin Melon
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 3 to 4 weeks before the last expected frost date, then transplant out once soil has warmed and frost danger has passed.
directions: Start seeds indoors a few weeks ahead of the last frost to give this melon a head start in shorter growing seasons, then transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun. Originally sold as 'Queen of Colorado' in the early 1920s before being reintroduced under its current name in 1937, this heirloom produces oval, 4 to 8 pound melons with apricot-orange flesh that is notably sweet with little of the musky aftertaste typical of many muskmelons. It was long grown as a market melon for Milwaukee before nearly disappearing from trade, and it remains valued today for good powdery mildew tolerance.

name: Primo Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; its powdery mildew resistance is the key reason it performs through humid Gulf summers better than non-resistant heirloom cantaloupes.
directions: An early, large oval melon with heavy netting, a small seed cavity, and firm, dark-orange flesh, carrying resistance to powdery mildew races 1 and 2. LSU AgCenter lists it among its Louisiana cantaloupe recommendations; the mildew resistance is the key reason it performs through humid Gulf summers better than non-resistant heirloom cantaloupes.
sources: LSU AgCenter / Seeds to Success - Recommended Cantaloupe and Watermelon Varieties for Louisiana

name: Prince Albert Rhubarb
plantingNote: Set crown divisions into rich, deeply dug soil in early spring, positioning the growing bud level with or just below the soil surface. Mulch around, but not over, the crown to conserve moisture and suppress weeds while the plant establishes.
directions: Set crown divisions into rich, deeply dug soil in early spring, positioning the growing bud level with or just below the soil surface. Mulch around, but not over, the crown to conserve moisture and suppress weeds while the plant establishes. Prince Albert is one of the oldest named rhubarb cultivars still in cultivation, dating to the early nineteenth century in England and named for the consort of Queen Victoria, and it is notable for pushing up some of the earliest stalks of the season. Its early, tender pink-red stalks made it historically popular for the first forced rhubarb of spring, and it remains valued by heirloom growers for its long cultivation history and reliable early cropping.

name: Principe Borghese Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; this determinate variety requires only modest staking; prolific bearer best harvested in quantity for drying or canning.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant to full sun after frost risk passes; Principe Borghese is the traditional Italian tomato for sun-dried tomatoes, a compact determinate vine bearing enormous clusters of small (2–3 oz) plum to egg-shaped fruits with thick dry flesh, thin skin, few seeds, and very low moisture content — the characteristics that make it ideal for halving and drying in the sun or dehydrator. The variety's name refers to the Borghese family of Rome who historically grew them on terraced hillsides; the dried product is intensely flavored and chewy. It bears all at once in a concentrated flush, making it excellent for large-batch canning and preserving as well.

name: Prinz Celeriac
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost transplant date; Prinz has notably strong bolt resistance, so it can be set out earlier under cover than most celeriac without the risk of premature flowering that cold shock triggers in less resistant varieties.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, consistently moist, very fertile soil; Prinz is a German-bred celeriac valued for producing rounded, smooth, light-skinned globes that clean up easily compared with the rougher-skinned older varieties, with dense, firm, pure white interior flesh. Its strong resistance to premature bolting makes it more forgiving of an early start under row cover or plastic than most celeriac, while it also performs reliably as a later, unprotected planting. The flavor is a clean, nutty, concentrated celery essence, equally good raw and grated into rémoulade or cooked into soups, purees, and roasts. As with all celeriac, keep the soil evenly moist throughout the long growing season and remove small side roots from the developing globe to encourage a smooth, well-formed root.

name: Prisma Shallot
plantingNote: Plant individual bulbs about an inch deep and four to six inches apart as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, or in fall in mild-winter regions; Prisma is a Dutch-bred shallot valued for uniform, high-yielding clusters.
directions: Prisma is a modern Dutch shallot cultivar bred for uniform, copper-skinned, round-to-oval bulbs and dependably heavy yields, making it one of the more widely available shallots in the commercial seed trade. Plant sets shallowly in loose, well-drained soil, and each will multiply into a tight cluster of several bulbs by midsummer. Keep the bed evenly moist during active growth and taper off watering once the foliage begins to yellow and topple over. Cure the harvested cluster in a warm, airy, shaded spot for a couple of weeks before separating and storing, where well-cured Prisma bulbs keep respectably for a shallot, typically several months.

name: Prize Choy Pak Choi
plantingNote: Direct sow after the soil has warmed slightly in spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; give it partial shade in warm-summer regions to delay bolting.
directions: Prize Choy is an open-pollinated pac choi tracing back to Alf Christianson Seed Company breeding from an era when major companies still maintained open-pollinated Asian brassica lines. It forms vase-shaped, 15-18 inch plants with celery-like white stems and tender, glossy green leaves, and is notably uniform and slow to bolt for an open-pollinated type. Grow it as a substitute for napa cabbage in stir-fries and soups, harvesting whole heads at full size or picking outer leaves for a cut-and-come-again baby crop.

name: Prizehead Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or fall; in zone 9 sow February–March for spring or September–October for fall. Prizehead is one of the fastest-maturing looseleaf lettuces and can be harvested as baby leaves in 25–30 days or at full size in 45–55 days. The quick maturity makes it excellent for succession planting every 2 weeks through the cool season.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Prizehead is a classic American heirloom looseleaf lettuce developed by W. Atlee Burpee Company in the 1880s and still widely grown for its exceptional flavor and striking red-bronze tipped leaves. The large, frilly, bright green leaves are broadly and dramatically tipped in red-bronze to burgundy at the leaf edges, creating a distinctly two-toned effect that makes Prizehead one of the most ornamental of all heirloom lettuces and an enduring favorite in kitchen gardens. The flavor is superb — mild, tender, and buttery with a crisp texture that surpasses many newer commercial varieties in taste trials — and the quick maturity (45–55 days to full size) allows it to be harvested before summer heat arrives. The frilly, slightly ruffled leaf texture holds dressings well. In zone 9 Prizehead is equally at home in spring and fall gardens; the red tips intensify in cooler weather and provide the most dramatic color in fall plantings.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Prizehead Lettuce Heritage Variety
W. Atlee Burpee Company — Classic American Heirloom Vegetables
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Heat-Tolerant Heirloom Lettuces

name: Prizetaker Leek
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this large-growing heirloom needs a long season to bulk up before harvest.
directions: Prizetaker, also sold as Lyon Prizetaker, is an English heirloom leek dating to the 1880s that was bred for exhibition size, producing some of the thickest, tallest shanks of any leek variety while staying remarkably tender for its bulk. Give it wide spacing and rich, deeply worked soil so roots have room to support the plant's large stature, and hill soil progressively around the base through the season to blanch a long white shank. Its dark green leaves and pure white, solid base have made it a favorite for county-fair and garden-show exhibitors for over a century, but it performs equally well as a substantial main-season leek for the kitchen. Because it needs a long growing season to reach full size, start it early and expect a later harvest than quick early-season types.

name: Prizetaker Onion
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 10-8 weeks before the last frost, since Prizetaker needs a long season to reach its full exhibition size; transplant once the soil can be worked.
directions: Prizetaker is a long-day Spanish-type heirloom introduced by W. Atlee Burpee and Co. in 1888 and prized for producing some of the largest bulbs of any yellow onion, often reaching a pound or more under good conditions. The globe-shaped bulbs have thin golden-brown skin over mild, sweet, white flesh well suited to fresh eating, slicing, and frying rather than long storage. Grow in deeply worked, fertile soil with steady moisture through bulb swell, since the variety's size depends on an uninterrupted growing season. Harvest once tops fall over and cure briefly before use, as the high moisture content of this sweet type limits how long it keeps.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee and Co. historical catalog records
Mother Earth News heirloom onion variety guide

name: Prizewinner Pumpkin
subcategory: F1 hybrid giant pumpkin for exhibition growing
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 3 to 4 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into a heavily amended, sun-drenched bed with room to spare.
directions: Start seeds indoors a few weeks before the last frost to maximize the growing season, then transplant into deeply enriched soil with generous room for the vines to sprawl, thinning each plant down to a single developing fruit for maximum size. This F1 hybrid giant pumpkin was bred for exhibition growers chasing very large fruit, with mature specimens commonly reported in the 100 to 300 pound range under attentive feeding and watering. Its smooth, glossy orange rind and classic rounded pumpkin shape make it as suitable for display as it is for competition.

name: Prizm Kale
plantingNote: Start indoors or direct sow; kale is also an excellent fall crop, since cool weather and light frost sweeten the leaves' flavor.
directions: Start indoors or direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Prizm is an All-America Selections-winning kale bred for a compact, dense, more uniform habit than older kale varieties, with tender, tightly curled, blue-green leaves that hold good quality and mild flavor even as the plant matures. Its smaller stature makes it well suited to containers and smaller garden beds, and the tender texture requires less cooking time than some older, tougher kale cultivars, making it popular for salads as well as cooked greens. Harvest outer leaves regularly to encourage continued production, and like other kale, flavor sweetens after light frost in a fall crop.

name: Progress No. 9 Garden Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked; Progress No. 9 is a semi-dwarf shelling pea (18–24 inch plants) that may need light support (twiggy branches pushed in near plants works well) but is manageable without formal trellising. In zone 9, direct sow November–February for spring harvest (February–April); peas are a cool-season crop that thrives in zone 9's mild winter and will bolt and die in summer heat. Harvest pods when plump and round — shell immediately or refrigerate for up to one week. Progress No. 9 is one of the earliest shelling peas, producing usable pods at 60–68 days.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in rows 18 inches apart; thin to 2–3 inches. Support with short twiggy branches or a low string trellis. Shell pods when plump and round; do not allow to over-mature. Progress No. 9 (also called Laxton's Progress or simply Progress) is a classic English garden pea with a history in British kitchen gardens extending back to the work of Thomas Laxton, the 19th-century English plant breeder who made significant improvements to pea varieties through systematic cross-breeding. The variety produces heavy yields of large, dark green, round pods containing 6–9 large, sweet, wrinkled peas — the wrinkled seed (rugose type) is a characteristic of sweeter, higher-sugar garden peas versus the smoother seeds of field peas, and Progress No. 9 exemplifies the sweet, tender, wrinkled-pea style. The semi-dwarf habit (18–24 inches) makes Progress No. 9 more manageable in home gardens than the tall pole peas like Alderman (Telephone) that require 4–5 foot trellises, while still producing full-sized, well-filled pods of excellent quality. Progress No. 9's early maturity (60–68 days) is particularly valuable in zone 9 where the window between suitable pea-growing temperatures and summer heat is brief — earlier-maturing varieties like Progress complete their harvest before heat stress arrives.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Progress No. 9 garden pea heirloom variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — English garden pea variety notes
Royal Horticultural Society — Historical pea variety documentation (Laxton's Progress)

name: Prosper Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; bred for strong downy mildew and fusarium resistance, it holds up well in variable spring weather.
directions: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in spring, or again in late summer for a fall harvest, covering seed lightly and keeping it evenly moist until germination. Thin seedlings to 4-6 inches apart and harvest outer leaves continuously once plants reach usable size, which encourages a longer productive period before the plant eventually bolts in warm weather. Its strong disease resistance makes it a dependable choice for gardeners who have struggled with downy mildew on spinach in the past.

name: Prosperosa Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F, staking heavily loaded plants for support.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Prosperosa is a traditional Italian heirloom producing large, round to oval fruit in deep violet-purple with faint pale striping near the calyx, and dense, creamy, mild-flavored flesh well suited to grilling, roasting, and classic Italian preparations like eggplant parmesan. Plants are vigorous and productive, often needing staking to support the weight of the large fruit, and perform reliably through a long, hot growing season. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and firm and the fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure, since overripe fruit develops a bitter edge and coarser seeds.

name: Providence Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees; Providence carries resistance to bacterial mottle and downy mildew-related diseases, a useful disease package for a humid main-season Gulf South corn crop.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Providence is a bicolor sweet corn hybrid combining sugary-enhanced tenderness with supersweet-level sugar content, bred with disease resistance including tolerance to bacterial mottle, a bacterial disease that can streak and discolor kernels in warm, wet conditions. It produces large, well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels on sturdy stalks over a main-season 82-day maturity. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill for the best results. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed.
sources: seed catalog reference (Stokes Seeds, Rupp Seeds)

name: Provider Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow starting 2 weeks before last frost; Provider germinates in cooler soils (as low as 50°F) than most beans, allowing earlier planting. In zone 9, sow February–April for spring production and August–September for fall production. The cold-soil tolerance allows earlier planting and fall planting into cooling soils, extending the productive season at both ends.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep; Provider is one of the most widely grown and recommended bush snap bean varieties in the United States — a 1965 release that has remained a cornerstone home garden and commercial variety for 60 years due to its combination of reliable production, consistent quality, and unusually cold-tolerant germination. Provider's ability to germinate reliably in cooler soils (down to about 50°F, compared to the 60°F minimum for most beans) allows it to be planted 1–2 weeks earlier than standard beans in spring and later into fall, giving it a significant practical advantage for extending the bean season in both directions. The round, medium-length (4–5 inch), dark green pods are harvested when young and tender and have clean snap-bean flavor — honest, straightforward, and pleasant rather than refined. A vigorous, upright bush habit requires no staking and produces heavily over a 2–3 week period per planting; successive sowings every 2–3 weeks provide continuous harvest. Provider has been the standard reliable bush bean against which others are compared — not glamorous, but dependable, productive, and universally adaptable from the earliest spring planting to late fall production in virtually any vegetable garden climate.
sources: University of Missouri Extension — Bean Variety Evaluation
Fedco Seeds — Provider bean variety notes
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Snap Bean Variety Trials

name: Pruden's Purple Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Pruden's Purple is a large, potato-leaved, purple-pink beefsteak tomato saved by William Pruden of Roanoke Rapids, North Carolina, closely related to Brandywine in flavor and character but often producing more reliably and slightly earlier — considered by many tomato enthusiasts an excellent alternative or companion to Brandywine.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost into fertile, deeply prepared, well-drained soil. Pruden's Purple was saved by William Pruden of Roanoke Rapids, North Carolina and entered the Seed Savers Exchange network in the 1980s; it is a large, indeterminate, potato-leaved (smooth, undivided leaf form, as in Brandywine) beefsteak tomato producing very large (12–24 oz), flattened, lobed, dusky rose to purple-pink fruits with dense, meaty, sweet, complex flesh with the rich, full tomato flavor characteristic of the best pink beefsteak heirlooms. Many tomato growers consider Pruden's Purple slightly more productive and reliably earlier than Brandywine Sudduth while producing nearly identical flavor; the two make excellent companions in the garden. Days to maturity of 65–80 from transplant make it one of the earlier large beefsteak heirlooms. A consistently excellent performer in Southern and Gulf Coast gardens.

name: Pskem Garlic
plantingNote: Plant large cloves 2-3 inches deep and well spaced in fall, since this porcelain type forms big bulbs with relatively few but substantial cloves.
directions: Pskem traces to the Pskem River valley in the Tian Shan mountains of Uzbekistan and is classed as a porcelain hardneck, forming a tall woody scape and a bulb wrapped in smooth white skin over just four to six oversized cloves. The outsized cloves make it a favorite for cooks who dislike peeling many small pieces, though the plant itself demands more spacing and richer soil than smaller-clove types to reach full size. Remove the scape once curled to push growth into the bulb, and wait to harvest until the lower leaves have browned while several upper leaves stay green. Cure in a shaded, ventilated space for three to four weeks before trimming roots and tops for storage.
sources: Peaceful Valley Farm Supply growing guide

name: Puerto Rico Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is warm; give this heirloom extra spacing, since it grows much taller and leafier than most okra varieties.
directions: Puerto Rico okra is a striking tropical heirloom that towers over most garden okra, often reaching 8-12 feet in a long, warm growing season, with correspondingly large leaves and pods that need to be picked young to stay tender. Give it plenty of room and rich soil, since the plant puts substantial energy into its height and canopy before pods come on in quantity. It thrives in the long, hot, humid summers of the Deep South and Gulf Coast, where shorter-season okra varieties can start to slow down in peak heat. Choose it as a dual-purpose plant, since the tall, leafy stand also works as a temporary summer privacy screen or windbreak in the vegetable garden.

name: Puerto Rico Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips (rooted vine cuttings) 2–4 weeks after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; in zone 9 plant April–June. Puerto Rico sweet potato thrives in zone 9's long, warm season and requires no supplemental care once established. Harvest when the skin resists scratching and vine leaves begin to yellow. Cure harvested roots at 85–90°F with high humidity for 2 weeks to convert starches to sugars and develop sweetness; uncured sweet potatoes taste bland and starchy.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, loose, slightly acidic, moderately fertile sandy soil — sweet potatoes require loose soil for the roots to expand and develop properly; Puerto Rico was the dominant commercial sweet potato variety in the United States for much of the 20th century, and under various synonyms ('Southern Queen', 'Vineless Puerto Rico') it formed the backbone of American sweet potato production in the Southeast, where it became the foundation of Southern sweet potato cuisine. The moist-flesh, orange sweet potato familiar as a Thanksgiving side dish, sweet potato pie filling, and candied yam is essentially the Puerto Rico type — the moist, sweet, orange-fleshed character that most Americans think of as the defining sweet potato quality. The large, uniform, blocky-to-slightly-tapered roots have deep orange skin and vivid orange flesh with an intensely sweet, moist, smooth texture after curing and baking. Puerto Rico is well-adapted to Gulf Coast conditions and produces very large yields in zone 9's long, warm growing season with minimal care.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Potato Variety Guide
North Carolina State University Extension — Sweet Potato Cultivar Trials
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Sweet Potato Production for Texas

name: Puno Quinoa
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring around the last frost; Puno was among the first quinoa varieties successfully trialed outside the Andes in Colorado during early American efforts to adapt the crop.
directions: Puno was one of the original quinoa lines used in early Colorado field trials that first demonstrated quinoa could be grown successfully in North America outside its native Andean highlands, and it remains a useful reference variety for cool, high-altitude growing conditions. Direct sow into well-drained, average soil in full sun in early spring, since the plant tolerates light frost better than most warm-season grain crops. It grows tall with a prominent central seed head typical of Andean quinoa types, so stake or plant in blocks for mutual wind support in exposed gardens. Harvest once the seed heads dry and the grain rattles loose, then thresh and rinse well to strip away the bitter saponin coating before cooking.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

name: Puntarelle Chicory
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer 8–10 weeks before first fall frost for a fall-winter-spring harvest; in zone 8–10, sow in September for a winter harvest of the tender inner shoots that are the prized Roman 'puntarelle' salad vegetable; the plant survives light freezes and is best treated as a cool-season crop.
directions: Direct sow in late summer in rich, well-drained soil; thin to 12–18 inches once established. Puntarelle is the Italian Catalogna-type chicory grown for its distinctive hollow, asparagus-like inner shoots that emerge from the crown in fall and winter and are the centerpiece of the classic Roman winter salad — thin strips of the shoots are soaked in cold water to curl them, then tossed with a pungent anchovy, garlic, and olive oil dressing in one of Rome's most iconic dishes. The outer leaves are cooked like bitter greens or braised, while the inner shoots and their hollow stems (the puntarelle themselves) are harvested by cutting just above the root crown. In warm-climate gardens (zones 8–11), puntarelle is an outstanding cool-season crop that fills the winter vegetable gap when few other greens are available.

name: Purceddu Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost in warm soil; this long-season Sicilian winter melon needs a full hot summer to fill out fruit that will then be stored and ripen further off the vine into winter.
directions: Purceddu is a traditional Sicilian landrace winter melon, smooth-skinned and pale green to yellow, grown across the island for its unusual keeping quality: fruit is harvested still under-ripe in late summer, then hung in nets or stored in a cool, dry place where it continues to slowly ripen and sweeten for weeks, traditionally lasting through the winter and often appearing on the Christmas table. Give vines full sun, rich soil, and even moisture through fruit set, then taper watering as fruit matures to improve storage quality. The pale flesh is milder and less aromatic than summer muskmelons, with a crisp texture that holds up well to the long storage period. Select only fully intact, unblemished fruit for storage, since any bruising or cracked skin shortens keeping time dramatically.

name: Purple Beauty Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Purple Beauty is a compact, early-maturing bell pepper suited to zone 9 where the long warm season allows plenty of time for full purple maturity. In zone 9, transplant March–April. The purple color at harvest is a fully mature stage — not an intermediate green-to-red stage. If left on the plant beyond the purple stage, Purple Beauty peppers will turn red, but the ornamental and culinary purpose of this variety is the purple color, which should be harvested at full purple development. The anthocyanin pigment in Purple Beauty's skin makes the fruit mildly antioxidant-rich. Purple color fades to brown-green when cooked.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 78–85°F; transplant after last frost. Compact plants do not require staking. Harvest peppers at full purple color for best appearance. Purple Beauty is a 1990 All-America Selections-winning bell pepper — a fully blocky, 4-lobed, medium-large sweet bell pepper that matures to a deep purple-violet color rather than the standard red, yellow, or orange of typical bell pepper types. The purple coloration comes from anthocyanin pigments produced in the skin (not the flesh, which remains pale green-white), and the purple color intensifies as the pepper approaches maturity, creating one of the most striking visual effects in the summer garden among vegetables. Purple Beauty is frequently planted in ornamental-edible garden designs and kitchen garden borders where the dark purple fruits contrast dramatically with the green plant and with neighboring yellow and orange peppers. The flavor is standard sweet bell pepper — no heat, with a clean, slightly grassy-sweet taste similar to green bell peppers (purple bell peppers are harvested at the same maturity stage as green bells in terms of flavor development). Purple Beauty's compact plants (18–24 inch) set fruit heavily and are among the earlier-maturing bell peppers, making them well-suited to short-season gardens and zone 9 spring plantings before summer heat affects fruit set.
sources: All-America Selections — Purple Beauty bell pepper AAS winner 1990
Burpee Seeds — Purple Beauty pepper variety description
North Carolina State University Extension — Bell Pepper Variety Production Guide

name: Purple Beauty Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost under warm conditions, then transplant into the garden after nighttime lows stay above 55°F. In zone 9, set out transplants in March for a spring crop and again in July for a fall crop, since fruit set slows once summer temperatures exceed the mid-90s.
directions: Start seed indoors under grow lights or a warm sunny window 6–8 weeks before the last frost, and harden off before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil after all frost danger has passed. Pick fruit at the deep purple stage for a mild, crisp bell flavor, or leave on the plant to ripen fully to red for a sweeter finish. Purple Beauty is a compact, high-yielding bell pepper cultivar that produces blocky, medium-sized fruit that emerges green, matures to a glossy deep purple, and eventually ripens to bright red if left on the plant, giving gardeners three color and flavor stages from a single planting. The eye-catching purple stage retains crisp texture and holds up well raw in salads or on a crudité tray, and the plants tend to be sturdy and productive in home garden conditions across a wide range of climates. Because purple pigment can fade to green when cooked, Purple Beauty is best showcased fresh.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Purple Beauty pepper variety notes
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — pepper variety descriptions

name: Purple Calabash Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Purple Calabash is a sprawling indeterminate variety that needs sturdy staking or caging, and its heavily ruffled fruit benefits from good airflow to reduce rot in the folds.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil, staking well to support the sprawling vines. One of the oldest known tomato heirlooms, Purple Calabash produces small to medium, deeply ruffled and pleated fruit that ranges from dusky pink-burgundy to dark purple-brown, believed to closely resemble tomatoes as they looked before generations of breeding smoothed and enlarged the fruit. The flesh is complex and tangy with a distinctive rich flavor, and the variety was preserved and distributed through Seed Savers Exchange in the early 1990s.

name: Purple Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow fall through early winter (September–November in zone 9) in deeply tilled, loose, stone-free, lean to moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Cosmic Purple carrot has deep purple-skinned roots with orange and yellow interior flesh — the purple color from anthocyanin pigments intensifies in cool weather and makes this one of the most nutritionally rich carrot varieties available to home growers.
directions: Direct sow seeds thinly (1/4 inch deep) in deeply tilled, loose, stone-free, lean soil in full sun; thin to 2–3 inches; harvest at 6–8 inches for best color and flavor. Daucus carota 'Cosmic Purple' (purple carrot or anthocyanin carrot) is an open-pollinated purple-rooted carrot variety developed by the USDA Agricultural Research Service — one of the most richly pigmented and nutritionally dense carrot varieties available to home growers. The root has deep purple to nearly black outer skin from very high anthocyanin concentrations (the same antioxidant pigments found in blueberries and red cabbage) with orange interior flesh, creating a dramatic color contrast when sliced. The flavor is significantly different from standard orange carrots: 'Cosmic Purple' is notably sweeter, with a mild, distinctive flavor complexity from both sugars and secondary compounds. Anthocyanins in the skin are heat-labile and can fade during cooking — roasting at high heat preserves them better than boiling or steaming. Eating purple carrots raw in salads or quick-pickling with vinegar (which intensifies the purple to fuchsia-red) are excellent ways to enjoy both flavor and color. In zone 9, purple carrots are planted in fall for winter harvest when cool temperatures concentrate sugars; spring-planted carrots in warm areas tend to be less sweet and may bolt before fully sizing. A beautiful addition to diverse carrot sowings alongside orange, yellow, and white types.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Purple Carrot Breeding
University of Wisconsin Extension — Specialty Carrots

name: Purple de Milpa Tomatillo
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Purple de Milpa is a traditional small-fruited tomatillo of the Mexican milpa system, highly prized by Mexican cooks for its richer, more complex flavor and purple-green to deep purple color compared to the standard large-fruited green tomatillos used in commercial salsa verde production.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost and provide staking or caging as plants become sprawling. Purple de Milpa is a traditional Mexican tomatillo variety grown in the traditional milpa polyculture system; it produces small (1–1.5 inch diameter), round fruits with papery husks that burst and split when ripe, ripening to purple-green to deep purple-green rather than the standard yellow-green of commercial tomatillos. The flavor is more concentrated, fruitier, and tangier than standard green tomatillos, with a more complex background of citrus, herbs, and earthiness that many Mexican cooks and chefs consider superior for salsa verde, enchiladas verdes, and mole verde when an authentic deep flavor is desired. Plant in pairs or groups as tomatillos need cross-pollination for best fruit set; highly productive in warm weather.

name: Purple Dragon Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in loose, deep, stone-free soil; Purple Dragon develops its deepest, most vivid color when harvested in cool conditions — fall-sown roots grown into winter have significantly more intense purple pigmentation than spring-sown roots harvested in warming temperatures.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, deep, stone-free, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Purple Dragon is among the darkest-colored purple carrots available, producing 6–7 inch Chantenay-type roots with an almost purple-black exterior of extraordinary depth — the highest anthocyanin content of the major purple carrot varieties on the market, with the deep pigment extending well into the shoulder of the carrot. The interior flesh is vivid orange, creating a dramatic two-toned cross-section when sliced that makes Purple Dragon the most visually striking carrot in a rainbow mix. The flavor is earthy and subtly spicy with good sweetness, distinctly more complex than standard orange carrots. Raw eating shows the anthocyanin benefits and full visual impact; cooking at high heat fades the exterior purple toward brown, but moderate-heat roasting preserves considerable color. Outstanding raw in salads, crudités, and juicing where the deep purple color makes an impression.

name: Purple Flash Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; Purple Flash is a Texas Superstar ornamental pepper grown primarily for its striking near-black, purple-and-white variegated foliage rather than for the fruit, and thrives in heat.
directions: Start seeds indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a container. Purple Flash is a Texas Superstar-designated ornamental pepper valued mainly as a striking foliage plant — its leaves are marbled in near-black purple, deep green, and creamy white, giving it a bold variegated presence unmatched by most other heat-loving bedding plants, and it holds this dramatic coloring through the hottest part of summer when many foliage plants fade. It does produce small, round, very hot purple-to-red fruit, but flowering and fruiting are secondary to its role as a colorful accent in mixed beds and containers. It performs best in full sun, where the foliage color intensifies, and tolerates heat and drought once established better than many variegated foliage plants. Pinch growing tips occasionally to encourage a fuller, bushier shape.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

name: Purple Glazer Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, several weeks before the ground freezes, in loose, fertile, well-drained soil; Purple Glazer is a Glazed Purple Stripe type that needs a real winter chill to size up well.
directions: Plant cloves pointed end up, about two inches deep, in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Purple Glazer is a Glazed Purple Stripe heirloom out of the Republic of Georgia, prized for its striking bulb wrappers of deep violet-purple washed with a metallic gold or silver sheen, wrapping six to nine plump, easy-to-peel cloves with a rich, balanced flavor that starts sweet and finishes with a gentle, lingering warmth. Like other hardnecks it sends up a coiling scape in early summer that should be cut once curled to redirect energy into bulb growth, and the scapes are excellent chopped into pesto or stir-fries. It stores respectably for a hardneck and performs best in regions with a genuinely cold winter to break dormancy, making it best suited to northern and mountain gardens.

name: Purple Haze Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; purple color develops best in cool conditions — fall-harvested roots have deeper color than spring-harvested ones.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, deep, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Purple Haze is an All-America Selection Edible Vegetable winner with striking purple-skinned, orange-fleshed 10-inch carrots that turn purple skin orange when cooked (the purple color fades with heat), with slightly higher anthocyanin content than orange carrots. When eaten raw, the purple exterior provides both visual drama and a hint of earthiness that complements the sweet orange interior. Excellent for rainbow carrot mixes, farmers markets, and home gardens looking for an unusual and conversation-starting variety with genuinely good flavor.

name: Purple Hull Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil reaches 65°F; in zone 9 this is typically February–March for spring and again August–September for a productive fall crop. Purple hull peas thrive in high heat and humidity and are the classic summer legume of the Gulf Coast.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any well-drained soil in full sun; purple hull peas are exceptionally drought and heat tolerant once established and require no added fertilizer on moderately fertile ground since they fix atmospheric nitrogen. The distinctive purple-hull pods flush violet-pink to purple at maturity, making them easy to spot at harvest time — pick pods when the hull is fully colored but before it begins to dry and yellow. Fresh-shelled purple hull peas cook faster than dried beans and have a richer, earthier flavor than black-eyed peas; they are a staple of Southern cooking, particularly New Year's Day hoppin' john and summer side dishes. The vines sprawl moderately — plant in wide rows or support with short stakes for easier harvest.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Southern Pea Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Southern Pea
Alabama Cooperative Extension System — Growing Southern Peas

name: Purple Karma Barley
plantingNote: Sow in early spring around the last frost date; Purple Karma is a spring-planted barley, hardier than a warm-season crop but less winter-tolerant than fall-sown cereal rye or winter wheat.
directions: This six-row hulless barley traces back to a single seed sample collected in Tibet in 1924 and deposited in the USDA seed repository, where it sat unnoticed for decades before researchers rediscovered and propagated it under the name Karma. Its deep purple-black kernels carry an anthocyanin-rich bran layer, and because the hull is only loosely attached, most of it falls free during ordinary threshing rather than requiring a pearling mill. Sow in early spring into well-drained soil; the plant is notably drought-tolerant once established and performs well on modest, low-input ground. Harvest when heads are fully dry and kernels are hard, then thresh and winnow to reveal grain that cooks up chewy and nutty, similar to pearled barley but with substantially more fiber, zinc, and B vitamins than hulled white barley.

name: Purple Lady Bok Choy
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant in early spring or late summer into fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Purple Lady holds its color and resists bolting better in the shorter days of fall than in the heat and long days of spring.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in early spring or late summer into fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Purple Lady holds its color and resists bolting better in the shorter days of fall than in the heat and long days of spring. Glossy, deep purple-black leaves top pale green petioles in a compact, upright rosette, giving this bok choy strong ornamental value alongside its mild, sweet, crisp flavor, and it holds its rich color whether cooked or eaten raw in salads. Bred as a hybrid for uniform heads and improved bolt resistance compared to open-pollinated purple pak choi types, it matures quickly enough for two full crops in a single spring-to-fall season in most climates. Harvest whole heads at full size or pick outer leaves individually for a cut-and-come-again harvest, and provide light afternoon shade to extend the harvest window into warmer weather.

name: Purple Magic Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in midsummer for a fall crop; heat- and stress-tolerant, Purple Magic performs across a wider range of regions and seasons than most broccoli.
directions: Start transplants and set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or midsummer. Purple Magic is an AAS-winning broccoli notable for carrying purple color not just in the head but through the stems and leaves as well, a first among broccoli breeding, driven by a high anthocyanin content that also gives the roughly 1-pound domed heads a sweeter taste than green broccoli. The uniform, well-domed crowns hold their vivid color well after harvest and even through light cooking. Harvest the central head while buds are still tight, then keep picking side shoots as they form to extend the season; the plant tolerates heat stress better than many broccoli varieties, easing timing in warmer regions.
sources: All-America Selections — Broccoli Purple Magic F1 winner announcement

name: Purple Majesty Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.8–6.5) soil in full sun; Purple Majesty retains its vivid purple color best when steamed or microwaved rather than boiled — water-cooking leaches anthocyanins and dilutes the distinctive purple color in the finished dish.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Purple Majesty is a Colorado State University potato introduction producing tubers with dramatic deep-purple skin and equally vivid deep-purple flesh throughout — not a surface tint or partial coloring but consistently, intensely purple from skin to center in every tuber. The purple coloration comes from high concentrations of anthocyanin pigments that are the same class of antioxidants found in blueberries and acai — Purple Majesty has among the highest anthocyanin levels of any potato variety tested, providing both the extraordinary visual quality and the health-attributed benefits associated with anthocyanin-rich foods. The color partially survives light cooking — steamed or microwaved Purple Majesty retains much of its striking purple appearance, while hard-boiled or oven-roasted preparations create dramatic visual presentations unlike any other potato. The flavor is mild and pleasant — comparable to other specialty potatoes — with the skin adding a slightly earthy complexity. Purple Majesty is oblong-shaped with smooth skin and produces well under typical potato growing conditions. In zone 9, plant in January–February for spring harvest. The vivid color makes Purple Majesty outstanding in mixed potato salads where the purple tubers contrast dramatically with red, gold, and white varieties.

name: Purple Majesty Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after the last frost in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun; Purple Majesty does not tolerate wet, poorly drained ground, so avoid low or flood-prone beds where Gulf Coast summer downpours can pool.
directions: Plant certified slips in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil in full sun after the last frost; Purple Majesty is a North Carolina State University release with dark purple skin and equally dark purple flesh throughout, colored by a high concentration of anthocyanin pigments that give cooked roots a moderately dry texture and mild sweetness. It produces uniform, elliptic roots and performs especially well on sandy ground, reaching harvest in around 100 days from transplanting. The variety resists Fusarium wilt but remains susceptible to Streptomyces soil rot and both southern and guava root-knot nematodes, so rotate away from beds with a recent history of those problems. Purple Majesty ships and stores well after curing, but it does poorly in wet or flooded soil, so Gulf Coast gardeners should plant it on raised beds or well-drained ground rather than low-lying areas prone to standing water after heavy rain.
sources: North Carolina State University — NC Plant Breeding Consortium sweetpotato cultivar profiles
North Carolina State University — Potato and Sweetpotato Breeding and Genetics Program variety descriptions

name: Purple of Romagna Artichoke
scientificName: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Purple of Romagna'
plantingNote: Set out rooted offshoots or nursery transplants in spring after danger of frost, into deeply worked soil enriched with compost. In mild-winter regions plants persist for several years as a true perennial; in colder zones, mulch heavily or grow as an annual from an early indoor sowing.
directions: Set out rooted offshoots or nursery transplants in spring after danger of frost, into deeply worked soil enriched with compost. In mild-winter regions plants persist for several years as a true perennial; in colder zones, mulch heavily over winter or grow as an annual from an early indoor sowing with a cold treatment. This classic Italian heirloom from the Romagna region produces elongated, spineless purple buds that are notably tender at a small, immature size, which is why they are traditionally harvested young and eaten raw, thinly sliced, in salads such as pinzimonio rather than only cooked whole like larger green cultivars. Its purple coloring and slender bud shape distinguish it visually from rounder green types like Green Globe.

name: Purple Passion Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant 1-year crowns in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked; in zone 8–9 plant December–February for winter establishment before spring emergence. Allow plants to establish for two full seasons without harvesting before taking a full crop in the third year. In zone 9 asparagus goes dormant in summer heat and re-emerges in fall; harvest timing differs from northern gardens and is primarily a spring vegetable.
directions: Plant 1-year crowns 6–8 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil amended with compost in full sun; Purple Passion is a New Zealand-bred asparagus cultivar that produces vivid deep-purple spears with 25–40% higher sugar content and significantly lower fiber than standard green varieties — the purple color comes from anthocyanins concentrated in the outer tissues. The raw spears are noticeably sweeter and more tender than green asparagus and can be eaten raw in salads and crudités where the color is preserved; cooking turns the spears green as the anthocyanins break down under heat. Flavor is superior to most green varieties whether raw or cooked. Established beds are productive for 15–25 years. In zone 9 the plant benefits from a sandy, well-drained location and may require supplemental irrigation in the long, dry spring. Skip the first two seasons' harvest to allow crown development; thereafter harvest only the first 4–6 weeks of the spring flush.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Purple Passion Asparagus
University of California Cooperative Extension — Asparagus Variety Trials
New Zealand Asparagus Council — Purple Passion Introduction

name: Purple Passion Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F, in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic sandy soil in full sun; Purple Passion is a specialty heirloom purple sweet potato distributed by small growers alongside other named purple types such as All Purple and Molokai Purple.
directions: Purple Passion is a specialty heirloom sweet potato grown as a distinct named selection within the loose group of purple-skinned, purple-fleshed sweet potatoes maintained by small seed-saving farms, producing roots with purplish skin over moderately deep purple flesh and a drier, denser texture than orange-fleshed mainstream varieties. Flavor is mildly sweet and earthy, holding its purple color best when roasted or steamed rather than boiled in acidic water, which fades the pigment. Set slips in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun and keep fertility moderate, since excess nitrogen pushes vine growth at the expense of root formation; sprawling, purple-tinged vines tolerate a long, hot growing season well. Harvest after vines begin to yellow and before frost, then cure at warm temperature and high humidity for a week or two to heal skin wounds and develop full sweetness before moving roots to cool, dry storage.
sources: Sand Hill Preservation Center — Sweet Potato Variety List
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Sweet Potato Varieties
North Carolina State Extension — Sweet Potato Production

name: Purple Peacock Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant in early spring for a spring crop, or in mid to late summer for a fall and winter harvest; frost sweetens the deep purple foliage and improves flavor, much like ornamental kale.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Purple Peacock is an open-pollinated cross between purple broccoli and Russian kale, producing deeply lobed, ruffled, purple-veined leaves along with small, tender purple broccoli-like side shoots rather than one large central head. Both the ornamental foliage and the small flowering shoots are edible, making it a dual-purpose plant valued equally for cut-and-come-again greens and for its striking, frost-enhanced color in the fall and winter garden. Harvest outer leaves and side shoots regularly to encourage continued production, and expect the purple coloring and flavor to intensify after the plant experiences a light frost.

name: Purple Peruvian Fingerling Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; Purple Peruvian is an Andean heirloom fingerling potato originating in the Andes of Peru and Bolivia where hundreds of diverse potato varieties developed over 8,000+ years of indigenous cultivation — it produces long, slender, finger-shaped tubers with deep purple skin and deep purple flesh, representing one of the many colorful heritage potato types from the center of potato genetic diversity.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces (whole small tubers work best for fingerlings) 10–12 inches apart, 3–4 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost; fingerling potatoes produce many small, elongated tubers that benefit from slightly closer planting than large-tuber varieties. Purple Peruvian fingerling potatoes come from the Andean highlands of Peru and Bolivia, the center of origin of the domestic potato (Solanum tuberosum), where indigenous Quechua and Aymara peoples developed thousands of diverse potato cultivars over 8,000+ years — the wild ancestral diversity of potatoes in this region dwarfs the few dozen varieties commonly grown in North America. Purple Peruvian produces long (2–4 inch), slender, finger-shaped tubers with intensely dark purple to near-black skin and uniformly deep purple to violet flesh throughout; the color comes from the same anthocyanin pigments found in Adirondack Blue and All Blue but at high concentrations. The texture is waxy and the flavor is earthy, slightly nutty, and distinctly more complex than commercial potato varieties — reflecting centuries of selection in high-altitude Andean environments. The fingerling shape makes them visually dramatic on the plate and ideal for roasting whole (the skin caramelizes beautifully), potato salads, and presentations where the purple color adds visual impact. High in antioxidants.

name: Purple Pickling Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Purple Pickling is a midseason variety, so transplant promptly once soil and nights are reliably warm to give the longer fruit-set time it needs.
directions: Purple Pickling is a traditional Italian heirloom grown on distinctive purple-stemmed, thornless plants that make harvest easier than most eggplant varieties. It bears abundant pear-shaped, deep purple fruit up to 8 inches long, maturing a bit later than many standard types at around 90 days from transplant. Despite its name the fruit is equally good roasted, grilled, baked, or stewed fresh, with pickling and relish-making as its traditional specialty use. Keep plants picked regularly, since thornless stems make frequent harvest of young, glossy fruit simple and encourage continued production through the season.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Purple Pickling Organic Eggplant
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Eggplant Variety Database

name: Purple Plum Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow October–March for fall through spring harvest. Purple Plum is one of the fastest-maturing radish varieties — ready in as little as 25 days. Sow in succession every 7–10 days for continuous harvest through the cool season. In zone 9 fall sowings in October–November produce the best radish quality; spring radishes may bolt quickly as temperatures rise. Thin to 2 inches apart for proper round shape development. Harvest promptly when roots reach 1 inch diameter — oversize radishes become pithy and unpleasantly hot.
directions: Plant in full sun in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Purple Plum is a round, globe-shaped spring radish with uniformly deep violet-purple skin — a dramatic and attractive departure from the familiar red-and-white Cherry Belle type, with the rich purple skin creating an unusual ornamental effect in the radish row and on vegetable platters. When sliced, Purple Plum reveals clean white flesh with only the thin purple skin providing color — the interior is typical crisp, juicy, peppery radish with the same satisfying bite as standard spring radishes. The flavor is classic spring radish: pungent, peppery, slightly sweet when very fresh, and progressively hotter as the root ages or the weather warms. The round, smooth shape and uniform size make Purple Plum excellent for sliced vegetable platters, salads, and garnishes where the deep purple skin creates visual contrast with other vegetables. As one of the fastest-maturing vegetables available, radishes including Purple Plum are often direct-sown between slow-growing transplants (tomatoes, peppers, squash) to use the space productively while the main crop establishes.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Purple Plum Radish Description
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Spring Radish Production
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cool-Season Radishes for Florida

name: Purple Podded Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost and provide a trellis or pole support; Purple Podded Pole bean is one of the most visually dramatic vegetable plants available — producing vines covered in deep purple pods that stand out brilliantly against the green foliage, though the pods turn standard green when cooked; a beautiful edible ornamental for trellises and arbors.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost at base of a trellis, poles, or fence that will support 6–8 foot vines; thin to 4–6 inches apart in rows 24–30 inches apart. Purple Podded Pole bean is an old American heirloom snap bean with the dramatic characteristic of deep purple pods that develop against the green foliage — a striking visual contrast in the garden that makes this one of the most ornamentally interesting of all vegetable plants. The long (6–8 inch), round-sectioned pods are deep maroon-purple when raw and suitable for fresh eating or canning; however, the anthocyanin purple pigment is water-soluble and the pods turn standard green when cooked in water, a characteristic that surprises many gardeners. The flavor is excellent, similar to other pole snap beans; the raw purple pods are also edible in salads where the color can be appreciated. Very productive and continuous bearing through summer; the purple color also makes the beans somewhat easier to spot for harvesting against the green foliage.

name: Purple Splendor Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun, and space plants generously; Purple Splendor is an unusually prolific plant producer and can overcrowd the row if set too closely. Avoid heavy, flood-prone ground, since it cannot tolerate standing water.
directions: Plant certified slips in well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing plants a bit wider than usual since Purple Splendor produces slips prolifically and quickly crowds a tightly spaced row; Purple Splendor is a North Carolina State University release notable for purple flesh pigment that stays vivid through cooking rather than fading the way many purple sweet potato varieties do. Roots form uniform blocky to round-elliptic shapes and stay compact even in deep sandy soil, with a moderately dry texture and moderate sweetness once cured. It carries resistance to Fusarium wilt, Streptomyces soil rot, and southern root-knot nematode, though it remains susceptible to guava root-knot nematode. Purple Splendor stores and ships well but cannot tolerate flooded or poorly drained fields, so Gulf Coast gardeners should plant it on raised beds or well-drained soil rather than low spots that collect water after summer storms.
sources: North Carolina State University — Potato and Sweetpotato Breeding and Genetics Program variety descriptions
North Carolina State University — NC Plant Breeding Consortium sweetpotato cultivar profiles

name: Purple Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips (rooted cuttings from sprouted tubers) 2–3 weeks after last frost in full sun in loose, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in zone 8–12; Purple Sweet Potato varieties (Okinawan, Japanese, Stokes) produce deeply purple-fleshed tubers with exceptional levels of anthocyanin antioxidants — 2–3 times higher than blueberries — distinct from the orange-flesh sweet potatoes, with a slightly drier, nuttier, less sweet flavor profile valued in Asian-American cooking and superfood markets.
directions: Plant slips 2–3 weeks after last frost in loose, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic (pH 5.5–6.5) soil in full sun; Purple Sweet Potato produces better tubers in slightly poor, loose soil rather than heavily amended rich soil — excess nitrogen encourages vine growth at the expense of tuber development; harvest 90–120 days after transplanting when the vines begin to yellow. Ipomoea batatas 'Purple' (Purple Sweet Potato, Okinawan Sweet Potato, or Stokes Purple Sweet Potato) encompasses a group of purple-fleshed sweet potato varieties — including 'Okinawan,' 'Japanese Purple' (Satsumaimo), and 'Stokes Purple' — sharing the characteristic of producing tubers with deep violet-purple flesh caused by exceptionally high concentrations of anthocyanin pigments (cyanidin and peonidin glycosides). These anthocyanins give purple sweet potatoes one of the highest antioxidant levels of any commonly eaten vegetable — ORAC values 2–3 times higher than blueberries — and have generated significant interest in functional food and nutraceutical research. Purple-fleshed sweet potatoes retain their vibrant purple color when baked or boiled (better than in acidic cooking), are somewhat drier and nuttier in texture than orange sweet potatoes, and are traditional in Okinawan Japanese cuisine (where they are called 'beni imo'), Hawaiian cuisine (Okinawan sweet potato poi), Filipino cuisine, and increasingly in American superfood markets. Grow exactly like standard sweet potato: loose, sandy soil, full sun, long warm season. Slips (not tubers or seeds) are the standard planting material.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Sweet Potato Production
Okinawan Foods Research — Purple Sweet Potato Anthocyanins
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Sweet Potato Varieties

name: Purple Top Milan Turnip
scientificName: Brassica rapa subsp. rapa 'Purple Top Milan'
plantingNote: Sow very early in spring before other crops are ready, or as a quick fall catch crop; pull roots promptly at 2-3 inches across.
directions: A traditional Italian heirloom prized for being one of the fastest turnips to reach the table, producing flattened white discs capped in bright purple-red in as little as five to six weeks. Its speed makes it ideal for very early spring sowing before other crops are ready, or for a quick fall catch crop after summer vegetables finish. The flesh is notably tender and mild when harvested young and small, becoming pithier if left to size up, so pull roots promptly at 2-3 inches across.

name: Purple Top Strap Leaf Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow 6-10 weeks before the first fall frost for the sweetest roots, or in very early spring for a quicker, less reliable spring crop; the upright strap leaves stay cleaner than cut-leaf types, making them easier to harvest for greens without soil-splashed foliage.
directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in rows and thin to 4-6 inches, using thinnings as tender greens. Purple Top Strap Leaf is a nineteenth-century dual-purpose heirloom distinguished from ordinary purple-top turnips by its smooth, non-lobed 'strap' leaves, which grow upright rather than sprawling and stay cleaner in wet weather, making them a preferred choice for market growers selling bunched turnip greens alongside the roots. The flattened globe roots are white below the soil line with a purple-red crown above, mild-flavored when harvested young. This foliage trait, rather than root shape or color, is what sets it apart from other purple-top selections still common in seed catalogs.

name: Purple Top White Globe Turnip
scientificName: Brassica rapa subsp. rapa 'Purple Top White Globe'
plantingNote: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; in zone 9 sow September–February for a fall through spring harvest — fall planting produces the finest quality turnips as cool temperatures sweeten the roots and reduce bitterness. Sow thickly and thin to 4–6 inches after seedlings establish; thinnings at 3–4 inches tall are edible as turnip greens. Harvest roots at 2–3 inches diameter for the most tender, mildest flavor — oversize roots become pithy and bitter. Both roots and greens are productive throughout the zone 9 cool season.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of stones and compaction; Purple Top White Globe is the definitive American turnip variety — the standard against which all other turnip cultivars are measured, with over a century of continuous cultivation making it the most widely recognized turnip appearance in North America. The smooth, round roots develop their characteristic two-tone coloration from the soil surface: the shoulder (exposed to light above ground) develops a rich, vivid purple-violet pigmentation while the buried portion stays clean creamy white, creating the immediately recognizable bicolor that defines the visual identity of a turnip. Both the roots and the large, hairy, dark green leaves (turnip greens) are edible — the mild, slightly sweet, pleasantly peppery roots can be eaten raw at small size or cooked in soups, stews, and roasted vegetable preparations, while the greens are a classic Southern potherb simmered with smoked pork and eaten alongside collards and mustard. Fall-planted turnips develop the finest flavor in zone 9 as cool temperatures concentrate sugars and reduce any harshness in the roots.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Purple Top White Globe Turnip History
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Turnips for Gulf South Gardens
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cool-Season Root Vegetables

name: Purple Top White Globe Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall (August–October in zone 9) in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral (pH 6.0–7.0), fertile, loose soil in full sun; Purple Top White Globe is the standard fall turnip for Gulf South gardens — sow every 3 weeks from August through October for a continuous harvest from October through February.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile, loose soil in full sun; Purple Top White Globe is the classic American turnip — an old open-pollinated variety that has been the standard American garden turnip for generations and remains by far the most widely grown turnip variety in both home gardens and commercial production. The medium-large globe roots (3–4 inches diameter at ideal harvest size) have a distinctive two-tone appearance: the upper portion (exposed above the soil line) turns vivid purple to purple-red in sunlight, while the lower portion remains white. The firm, crisp, sweet-peppery flesh is mild when harvested young (under 3 inches) and becomes stronger and more pungent as roots age and enlarge — harvest promptly at desired size for best quality. The tender, nutritious greens (tops) are equally valuable: they are among the best-flavored of all Southern cooking greens, prized in traditional Gulf South cooking simmered with pork and seasonings. In zone 9, Purple Top White Globe is strictly a fall and winter crop — heat above 75°F causes the roots to become pithy, bitter, and tough. Sow from August through early October and harvest from October through February. Turnips are extremely fast-maturing and exceptionally cold-hardy — they tolerate freezes to the mid-20s°F without damage and flavor actually improves after frost exposure.

name: Purple Tree Collard
plantingNote: Propagate from stem cuttings rooted in spring once frost danger passes; Purple Tree Collard rarely sets viable seed and is grown almost entirely from vegetative cuttings of an existing plant.
directions: Purple Tree Collard is a perennial, non-flowering collard selection that grows a tall, woody, cane-like stalk topped with a rosette of broad, purple-tinged blue-green leaves, living for years in frost-free or mild-winter climates rather than completing its life cycle in one season. Root sturdy stem cuttings in moist potting mix or water, then set out in rich, well-drained soil in full sun, staking tall canes as they grow top-heavy. Harvest lower leaves continuously as the plant grows taller, leaving the top rosette intact, which encourages a steady supply of tender, mildly sweet, slightly purple-tinted greens that many gardeners find milder than annual collards. In climates with hard freezes it can be grown as a large annual or overwintered indoors as a potted cutting, since it typically does not survive temperatures much below the mid-20s Fahrenheit.
sources: UC Santa Cruz Center for Agroecology

name: Purple Vienna Kohlrabi
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for fall and January–February for spring. Purple Vienna has slightly better heat tolerance than white-stemmed types and can hold at harvest size slightly longer without becoming pithy. Harvest when stems are 2–3 inches across for the best texture — over-mature kohlrabi become fibrous and woody regardless of variety.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun; Purple Vienna Kohlrabi is the standard purple-skinned kohlrabi, identical in flavor and culture to white-stemmed types but with a striking deep purple-red skin color that makes it visually distinctive in the garden and at market. The interior flesh is white, mild, and sweet — identical to white kohlrabi in texture and taste despite the purple exterior. The purple color, from anthocyanin pigments, is present only in the skin and does not penetrate the flesh; peeled Purple Vienna looks and tastes exactly like White Vienna. The visual contrast between the purple skin and white interior makes it popular for raw preparations like kohlrabi slaws, crudités, and salads where slicing reveals the striking bicolor cross-section. In zone 9 kohlrabi is primarily a fall vegetable transplanted in September–October; it withstands light frosts and can be harvested from November through February. Remove leaves and store harvested kohlrabi in a plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to 3 weeks.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Kohlrabi Types
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Brassica Crop Production
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Kohlrabi Variety Comparison

name: Purple Viking Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January-February for harvest before summer heat sets in. Cut seed pieces to egg size with 1-2 eyes each and let cut surfaces cure a day or two before planting.
directions: Plant seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun. Purple Viking produces large, oval tubers with striking purple-splashed pink skin over dense, moist, pure white flesh that holds together well when boiled, making it a favorite for potato salad as well as roasting and mashing. The vigorous plants are heavy yielders and the thick skin gives the tubers good storage life compared to thinner-skinned varieties. Hill soil around the stems as they emerge to keep developing tubers covered and prevent greening, and harvest after the vines die back for the best storage tubers.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Potato Production for Texas Home Gardens
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Potato Production in Florida

name: Purple Zebra Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the indeterminate vine as it grows.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking the vine as it grows. Purple Zebra is a small, round striped tomato in the same family of striped varieties as the well-known Green Zebra, but ripening to a deep purple-red base color striped with contrasting gold-green, giving fruit an eye-catching jewel-toned appearance both on the vine and sliced on a plate. The flesh carries a bright, tangy-sweet flavor typical of striped 'zebra' tomatoes, with a bit more acidity than fully ripe solid-colored types, making it a favorite for salads and mixed heirloom tomato platters where visual variety matters. The indeterminate vine is productive over a long season; harvest once the stripe pattern and base color are both fully developed, and water evenly to reduce cracking on the thin skin.

name: Purple-Podded Asparagus (Yardlong) Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is thoroughly warm well after last frost; this heat-loving vine germinates poorly in cool soil.
directions: Distinct from the common Red Noodle type, this asparagus bean produces slender pods up to 18 inches long in a deep, glossy purple that holds its color well even after light cooking or stir-frying. Provide a tall, sturdy trellis, since vines climb vigorously and thrive in the same hot, humid conditions that stress common snap beans. Harvest pods young and pencil-thin, well before the seeds inside swell, checking plants every day or two during peak season since pods lengthen quickly. This variety tolerates heat, humidity, and many common bean pests and diseases better than Phaseolus beans, making it a reliable warm-season substitute where snap beans struggle in midsummer.

name: Purplette Onion
plantingNote: Fast-maturing miniature onion; can also be direct-sown for baby bunching onions once soil is workable.
