directions: This Dutch heirloom produces round, golf-ball-sized bulbs with glossy burgundy skin that fades to a soft pastel pink once cooked or pickled. Because it matures far faster than standard storage onions, it can be harvested young as a purple-tipped bunching onion or left to size up into a small mild bulb. The flavor is notably gentle, making raw slices in salads or quick pickles a popular use. Cluster plantings closely since bulbs stay small even at maturity, and harvest as soon as tops begin to fall for the sweetest flavor.

name: Pusa Makhmali Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is warm and settled; Pusa Makhmali was released by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute from selection within local West Bengal okra germplasm and later served as one of the two parents, crossed with IC-1542, used to breed the widely grown disease-resistant Pusa Sawani.
directions: Pusa Makhmali is an open-pollinated okra selected by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute for smooth, light green pods on tall, productive plants well suited to warm-season cropping. Unlike its own offspring Pusa Sawani, which was specifically bred for resistance, Pusa Makhmali is highly susceptible to yellow vein mosaic virus, a whitefly-transmitted disease that can devastate plantings in regions with heavy vector pressure, so it performs best where okra pests and this virus are not a persistent problem. Pick pods every couple of days at 4-5 inches long, before the ribs toughen, to keep plants setting new fruit through the season. Give plants wide spacing and consistent moisture during flowering and pod set for the heaviest, most tender harvest.
sources: Indian Agricultural Research Institute (IARI) — okra breeding history
National Horticulture Board (India) — Okra Varieties bulletin

name: Pusa Purple Cluster Brinjal
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 55°F, since this variety is grown for both spring and monsoon-season crops in its native India.
directions: Released by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute, Pusa Purple Cluster is an early-maturing brinjal prized for bearing its small, dark purple, medium-long fruits in dense clusters of four to nine rather than singly, giving a notably concentrated harvest per picking. Plants show good tolerance to bacterial wilt, making this a reliable choice in warm, humid growing conditions where that disease limits other brinjal varieties. Begin picking as soon as fruits reach a glossy, firm stage, since frequent cluster harvesting keeps plants setting new flushes through a long warm season. Its compact, heavy-bearing habit suits both home gardens and market growing in regions with an extended frost-free period.

name: Pusa Purple Long Brinjal
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay above 55°F; it is grown for both spring and autumn crops in its native India.
directions: Bred and released by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute, Pusa Purple Long is a widely grown Indian brinjal variety valued for its glossy, light purple, slender fruit reaching 10 to 12 inches long with smooth, tender skin and few seeds. Plants are early and heavy yielding, well suited to both spring and autumn plantings in warm climates, and the long, uniform fruit is prized for slicing into rounds for frying or grilling as well as for classic Indian preparations like baingan bharta. Give plants rich, well-drained soil, steady moisture, and support if fruit loads get heavy, and harvest while skin is still glossy, since dull skin signals over-mature, seedier fruit. Its long harvest window and reliable production make it a staple variety across Indian home gardens and market farms.

name: Pusa Sawani Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is warm and settled; this vigorous, widely adapted variety can also be sown again in midsummer for a rainy-season crop in warm climates.
directions: Released by the Indian Agricultural Research Institute as a cross between IC-1542 and Pusa Makhmali, Pusa Sawani is a vigorous, open-pollinated okra with medium-tall, short-jointed plants that adapt to a wide range of warm climates and cropping seasons, and it carries resistance to yellow vein mosaic virus, a damaging disease of the crop. Its dark green, smooth, five-ridged pods reach best eating quality at 4 to 5 inches long, well before they toughen, so frequent picking every couple of days keeps plants productive. The tall, sturdy plants benefit from wide spacing and steady moisture during pod set, and because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from year to year if plants are isolated from other okra. It remains one of the most widely grown okra varieties across South Asia for its reliability and wide climatic adaptability.

name: Quadrato d'Asti Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Quadrato d'Asti ('square from Asti') is a traditional Piedmontese Italian sweet pepper producing blocky, deeply four-lobed fruits with thick, crisp walls that ripen from green to golden yellow or red.
directions: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks ahead of the last frost, keeping soil warm for even germination, then transplant once frost danger has passed. Quadrato d'Asti ('square from Asti') is a traditional Piedmontese sweet pepper named for its home region in northern Italy, producing blocky, deeply four-lobed fruits with thick, crisp walls that ripen from green to golden yellow or red depending on the strain grown. The dense flesh holds its shape well when roasted, grilled, or stuffed, and the flavor turns notably sweeter and richer as the fruit fully colors. Give plants sturdy support in windy gardens, since the heavy fruit can weigh down brittle branches.

name: Queen Anne Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm; the bush habit and concentrated pod set make Queen Anne well suited to a single large harvest for freezing or canning rather than a long trickle crop.
directions: Queen Anne is a true bush-type blackeye pea with no runners at all, holding its pods bunched up at foliage level where they are easy to spot and pick. It sets its crop early and all at once, which suits growers who want one concentrated harvest rather than a plant that trickles peas over many weeks. The seed itself closely resembles California Blackeye 5 but runs a bit smaller, with the same creamy flavor Gulf Coast cooks expect from a classic blackeye pea. Its compact, non-sprawling frame also makes it a practical pick for raised beds or smaller garden rows where space is tight.
sources: Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (cucurbit.info)

name: Queensland Blue Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Queensland Blue is a classic 19th-century Australian heirloom pumpkin prized for its deeply ribbed, hard, blue-gray rind, dense sweet orange flesh, and outstanding storage life of six months or longer.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, allowing generous room for the vigorous vines. Queensland Blue is a classic Australian heirloom pumpkin, developed in the 19th century and still one of the most widely grown pumpkin varieties in Australia, valued for its distinctive, deeply ribbed, slate-blue-gray rind — a color that stands out dramatically against typical orange pumpkins in a fall display — and its dense, dry, sweet, deep orange flesh well suited to roasting, soups, and pies. The hard rind, while tough to cut into, is also the reason for the variety's outstanding keeping quality; well-cured fruit routinely stores for six months or longer in a cool, dry location, among the best storage life of any winter squash. Fruits typically run 8-12 pounds with a flattened, ribbed shape. Vines are vigorous and productive given full sun, fertile soil, and consistent moisture during fruit set. Harvest when the rind is fully hardened and resists a fingernail, and the stem has dried and corked, then cure in a warm, dry spot for two to three weeks before moving to cool storage, where the flavor continues to sweeten over the following months.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Queensland Blue Pumpkin heirloom notes
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Queensland Blue variety description
Digger's Club (Australia) — Queensland Blue Pumpkin history

name: Quickpick Pinkeye Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is reliably above 65F; determinate, erect habit holds pods high above the compact ~20-inch canopy, making it easy to spot and hand-pick in a home garden row.
directions: Quickpick was released by the Louisiana Agricultural Experiment Station as a compact pinkeye purple hull type bred for resistance to blackeye cowpea mosaic virus. Pods are dark purple, 7-8 inches long, and set simultaneously at the top of the plant, giving the variety its name and making a single harvest pass practical. Seeds are cream colored with a large maroon eye, larger than older purple hull standards, and cook up with classic pinkeye flavor. Matures quickly at around 60 days, making it useful for a second planting later in the Gulf Coast summer.

name: Quickstar Kohlrabi
directions: Keep soil evenly moist as the pale-green, flattened-round bulbs size up to about six inches across, since inconsistent watering is the usual cause of woody or split kohlrabi. This Sakata hybrid's dark, upright leaves and slow-to-bolt habit make it forgiving of a slightly delayed harvest, and the white interior flesh stays sweet and crisp whether eaten raw in slaws or roasted like a root vegetable.

name: Quncho Teff
plantingNote: Sow after last frost once soil is warm; Quncho is an improved white-seeded teff variety released by Ethiopian national agricultural research and now one of the most widely grown teff varieties in Ethiopia.
directions: Quncho is an improved white-seeded teff variety released through Ethiopian national agricultural research that combined the preferred light seed color of older landraces with higher yield and better lodging resistance, and it has since become one of the most widely planted teff varieties in its home country. Mix the dust-fine seed with sand or dry compost for even broadcasting onto a firm, well-prepared bed, then roll or tamp rather than burying the seed deeply. The crop forms a fine-textured, airy stand that should be cut once most seed heads have dried, since mature teff shatters easily in wind or heavy rain. Dry the cut bundles thoroughly, then thresh and winnow in a light breeze to recover the tiny, nutrient-dense grain used for injera and other foods.

name: Racer Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow in warmed soil after the last frost; the short, compact vines and rapid ripening let southern gardeners harvest well ahead of peak late-summer disease and heat stress.
directions: Sow seeds directly in hills once soil has warmed, thinning to two or three vigorous plants per hill spaced roughly three to four feet apart. Racer was developed through a University of New Hampshire and Johnny's Selected Seeds breeding collaboration for exceptionally rapid ripening, producing blocky 12-16 pound fruit with dark green handles well before most other jack-o'-lantern types color up. In Gulf Coast gardens the short vine and early finish are real advantages, letting fruit set and mature before the worst of late-summer humidity drives powdery mildew and vine borer pressure. Harvest once the rind has hardened to a deep, uniform orange and cure in a warm, airy spot for about a week before moving pumpkins to cooler storage.
sources: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension

name: Radar Onion
plantingNote: Plant sets in early autumn so roots establish before winter dormancy; Radar is a modern F1 overwintering onion bred for uniform round bulbs and reliable cold survival through a mild winter.
directions: Radar is a widely grown F1 overwintering onion bred to give gardeners a bulb harvest weeks ahead of spring-sown types by getting a head start on root growth before the ground freezes. Set out young bulbs in firmed, well-drained soil in early autumn, leaving the tip just above the surface, and keep beds weed-free through the mild winter growth period. The straw-yellow, semi-globe bulbs bulk up rapidly once spring days lengthen, typically ready weeks earlier than spring-set maincrop onions. Because overwintered bulbs are generally milder and less firm than maincrop storage onions, use the harvest within a couple of months rather than holding it long term.

name: Radicchio Rossa di Verona
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 direct sow or transplant August–September for a November–February harvest. Radicchio intensifies in color and flavor after light frosts — temperatures of 25–32°F trigger the characteristic deepening of the red-purple color and the development of the bittersweet flavor. In zone 9, the mild winters allow radicchio to head up and be harvested through February without protection.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Rossa di Verona is the classic round-headed radicchio from the Verona region of Italy and the dominant variety in world commerce — the compact, baseball-sized heads of deep red-purple leaves with white midribs are the defining image of radicchio. The bitter, slightly sweet flavor is characteristically Italian and develops most fully after light frost exposure, which converts some starches to sugars and intensifies the red-purple anthocyanin pigmentation. In zone 9 plant in August–September for a fall-through-winter crop; the heads form and mature in cool weather from October through February. For sweeter flavor, blanch heads by loosely tying outer leaves over the center 1–2 weeks before harvest, reducing bitterness 30–40%. Rossa di Verona is excellent grilled (the bitterness mellows dramatically under high heat), used in risotto bianco, or eaten raw in Gorgonzola and walnut salads where the bitter note is a feature rather than a flaw.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Chicory and Radicchio
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Radicchio
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cool-Season Vegetables for Florida

name: Ragged Jack Kale
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring for a summer crop, or in late summer for a fall and winter harvest; flavor sweetens noticeably after frost.
directions: Ragged Jack is an open-pollinated heirloom kale in the Red Russian family, with deeply serrated, oak-leaf-shaped gray-green leaves veined in purplish-red that deepens with cool fall temperatures. It is tender enough to eat raw in salads while young, becoming better suited to cooking as leaves mature and toughen slightly. Long grown and seed-saved in Southern gardens, it tolerates both summer heat and winter cold better than many curly kale types, often overwintering in milder zones to provide an extended harvest. Harvest outer leaves continuously from the base, leaving the growing crown intact for continued production over many months.

name: Rainbow Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–March for fall through spring harvest. Rainbow chard includes red, yellow, orange, white, and pink-stalked plants in each packet — plant thickly and thin, saving the thinnings for salads. Harvest outer leaves as needed starting when plants are 6–8 inches tall; this 'cut and come again' approach keeps plants productive for months. In zone 9 the cool season from fall through early spring is prime time; plants may bolt in spring heat but often resprout and produce again in fall.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Rainbow Chard is a mixture of Swiss chard varieties with stalks in multiple vivid colors — red, yellow, orange, gold, pink, white, and bicolors — creating one of the most visually striking vegetable plantings possible in a kitchen or ornamental garden. The broad, crinkled, dark green leaves and brilliantly colored stalks make Rainbow Chard simultaneously one of the most productive and most ornamental vegetables available. Nutritionally, Swiss chard is among the most nutrient-dense vegetables: extremely high in vitamins K, A, and C, iron, calcium, and magnesium. The mild, spinach-like flavor of young leaves is pleasant raw in salads; older leaves and the colorful stalks are best sautéed, stir-fried, or added to soups where the color partially fades but the substantial flavor and nutrition remain. The partial shade tolerance makes Rainbow Chard one of the best vegetables for gardens with limited full-sun exposure.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Swiss Chard Production
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Chard Varieties for Florida
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Chard for Gulf South Gardens

name: Rainbow Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost or direct sow again in late summer for fall crop; rainbow chard is biennial but grown as an annual; one of the most ornamental edible garden plants suitable for flower borders as well as vegetable beds.
directions: Direct sow seed 1/2 inch deep in fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil, thinning to 6–12 inches; rainbow chard is a mixture of white, yellow, orange, red, and vivid pink-stemmed chard varieties grown together, producing an exceptional display of color in the garden while providing the same mild, earthy leaves as single-colored chard. The stems of different colors have slightly different flavor intensities (red-stemmed are earthier, white-stemmed milder) but all are equally nutritious and versatile in cooking. Harvest outer leaves regularly to keep plants productive for months. An outstanding cut-and-come-again green for the productive ornamental garden.

name: Ramapo Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Ramapo is a vigorous indeterminate slicing tomato bred at Rutgers University in 1968 and revived by popular demand decades later specifically for old-fashioned, full-bodied tomato flavor.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking or caging the vigorous indeterminate vine. Ramapo was bred at the Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station in 1968 and quickly became beloved throughout the New Jersey area for its rich, well-balanced, old-fashioned tomato flavor, but it fell out of commercial availability for decades until gardener demand led Rutgers to bring seed back into production through its 'Rediscover the Jersey Tomato' program. It combines much of the deep, sweet-tart flavor complexity associated with heirloom tomatoes with the disease resistance and reliability of a modern hybrid, producing medium-to-large red slicing fruit over a long summer season. Prune suckers lightly on the lower part of the plant for better airflow in humid climates, and mulch to keep soil moisture consistent, which reduces cracking and blossom-end rot on the larger fruit.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station — Rediscover the Jersey Tomato Project

name: Rarámuri Ojo de Cabra Bean
plantingNote: This Rarámuri (Tarahumara) pole bean from above 6,500 feet in Mexico's Sierra Madre is day-length sensitive and performs best sown with the summer monsoon in low-desert gardens rather than on a fixed last-frost date farther north.
directions: Ojo de Cabra, or 'Goat's Eye,' is a pole bean maintained by Rarámuri (Tarahumara) farmers at high elevation, above 6,500 feet, in Mexico's Sierra Madre. Its large seeds carry a striking pattern of dark stripes over a speckled light background inside purple-streaked pods, with occasional red, pinto, or gold-seeded beans turning up in a saved-seed population. Cooked beans are prized for a sweet, mild, creamy character that holds up well in simmered dishes like burritos and bean burgers. The variety is day-length sensitive and performs best when sown with the summer monsoon in low-desert gardens rather than on a fixed last-frost schedule farther north.

name: Rarámuri Vayo Bean
plantingNote: Like other Rarámuri (Tarahumara) beans from the high Sierra Madre (this selection from nearly 7,800 feet), Vayo is day-length sensitive and grows and flowers best when timed to the summer monsoon rather than a strict last-frost date.
directions: Vayo is another Rarámuri (Tarahumara) pole bean from the high Sierra Madre of Mexico, selected independently from the similarly named Ojo de Cabra and distinguished by light tan seeds flecked with occasional pink and golden seed coats. The vines need sturdy trellising and, like other Rarámuri beans, are day-length sensitive, growing and setting pods best when timed to the summer monsoon rather than a strict last-frost planting date. Cooked seeds have a mild flavor and smooth, creamy texture typical of well-adapted Sierra Madre dry beans. Gardeners well north of the low desert may find it reluctant to flower and set pods before fall frost arrives.

name: Rattlesnake Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed in warm soil, providing a sturdy pole or trellis; Rattlesnake is a classic heirloom pole snap bean named for the distinctive purple streaking on its green pods.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a sturdy pole or trellis for the vigorous climbing vines. Rattlesnake is a classic heirloom pole snap bean named for the purple streaking that mottles its green pods, an old Southern favorite valued for good production even in hot, humid summer conditions that stress many other snap beans, along with reliable flavor and good tolerance of drought once established. The purple markings fade during cooking, leaving a green bean with excellent flavor. Harvest pods young and tender for the best snap bean texture, picking every couple of days to keep the vigorous vines setting new pods through the long growing season.

name: Raven Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Raven's compact, open plant habit improves air circulation around the crown — a practical advantage in the humid Gulf South where powdery mildew is a consistent challenge for summer squash.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Raven is an All-America Selections-winning zucchini hybrid notable for its very dark green to nearly black-green skin color, compact open plant habit, excellent flavor, and improved disease tolerance. The extremely dark skin — darker than standard dark-green zucchini — is the most visually distinctive quality: Raven zucchini are nearly black-green at harvest size, creating a visually striking contrast with yellow and light-green squash in market displays and mixed vegetable presentations. The compact, open plant habit (non-vining, upright-spreading, with good air circulation through the plant canopy) reduces powdery mildew pressure in Gulf South humid conditions where powdery mildew often devastates standard bush-type zucchini by mid-season. The earlier maturity (48–55 days) compared to many other zucchini allows faster first harvest and more production within the spring window before summer heat. In zone 9, plant in February–March for spring production and again in August–September for fall production. Harvest Raven at 6–8 inches for best flavor and texture — the dark skin makes it slightly harder to judge size at a glance, so check plants frequently during peak production. An outstanding choice for Gulf South summer gardens where disease pressure is the primary limitation of zucchini production.

name: Re Umberto Giallo Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant once soil has warmed.
directions: Re Umberto Giallo is the golden-yellow sport of the old Italian paste tomato Re Umberto, itself named for 19th-century King Umberto I of Savoy. It sets clusters of four to five small cylindrical-to-oval fruits, occasionally with a slight pointed nipple at the blossom end, over tall indeterminate vines. The dense, paste-like flesh carries very little juice and a mild, faintly sweet flavor, making it well suited to sauces and preserves rather than fresh slicing. Growers prize its strong keeping quality; in its native Italy, whole vines were traditionally pulled in autumn and hung indoors so immature fruit could finish ripening off the plant.

name: Re Umberto Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil has warmed.
directions: This old Italian paste tomato, named for 19th-century King Umberto I, bears small elongated-oval fruits around 2-3 inches long with glossy deep-red skin and firm, low-juice, meaty flesh. Its rich flavor and sturdy texture suit whole canning, drying, and sauce-making, and the indeterminate plants crop reliably even in less than ideal conditions. A yellow-fruited sport, Re Umberto Giallo, is also grown, and historical accounts credit this variety as a parent of the San Marzano paste tomato.

name: Really Red Deer Tongue Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow or start indoors in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; red pigmentation deepens with cooler temperatures and more sun.
directions: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. A red-leaved selection of the classic Amish Deer Tongue type, Really Red Deer Tongue forms upright rosettes of triangular, pointed leaves flushed deep burgundy-red over green, the red intensifying in cool weather and full sun, adding strong color contrast to salad mixes and garden beds alike. Like its green counterpart, it is notably heat-tolerant and slow to bolt for a loose-leaf lettuce, holding good quality longer into warm weather than most lettuce varieties. Harvest outer leaves individually as a cut-and-come-again crop for a steady, colorful supply.

name: Rebelski Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Rebelski carries a comprehensive disease-resistance package — Fusarium crown and root rot, Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, powdery mildew, several races of leaf mold, tobacco mosaic virus, and Verticillium wilt — originally bred for greenhouse and high-tunnel production but valuable for the heavy disease pressure of Gulf South gardens.
directions: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, then stake or trellis the tall, vigorous indeterminate vines; Rebelski was bred for greenhouse and high-tunnel growers and carries one of the broadest disease-resistance packages available in a beefsteak-type tomato, including Fusarium crown and root rot, Fusarium wilt, powdery mildew, multiple races of leaf mold, tobacco mosaic virus, and Verticillium wilt. It produces large, crack-resistant, deep red beefsteak fruit with excellent classic tomato flavor on a plant that continues setting fruit reliably even under heavy disease pressure. In an open Gulf South garden, this extensive resistance package helps the vines stay productive later into the humid summer than most beefsteak varieties. Pick fruit as it ripens to full red color and keep vines pruned and tied to their support for the best air circulation and fruit quality.

name: Red Ace Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in well-tilled, fertile soil; thin to 4–6 inches for best root development. Red Ace germinates reliably across a wide soil temperature range and is particularly valued for its tolerance of Cercospora leaf spot — the main disease limiting beet production in humid regions. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall/winter harvest; Red Ace holds well in the ground after reaching maturity without becoming pithy or woody.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in well-amended, fertile soil with consistent moisture; thin to 4–6 inch spacing. Red Ace is a Bejo Seeds F1 hybrid beet that has become one of the most widely recommended standard beet varieties for home gardens and commercial production alike — a globe-shaped, smooth, uniformly sized hybrid that consistently produces high-quality roots with reliable stand establishment, uniform maturity, and excellent disease tolerance (particularly for Cercospora leaf spot, the fungal disease that causes disfiguring brown leaf spots in humid regions). The roots are uniformly round to slightly oval, medium-large (2.5–3 inches diameter), with very smooth, deep red-purple skin, excellent internal uniformity and color (consistently dark red throughout with minimal zoning), and a tender, sweet, earthy-sweet flavor that compares favorably with the best heirloom types while delivering the hybrid advantages of uniformity, consistency, and disease resistance. Red Ace is an all-season variety that performs reliably in spring, fall, and winter production, holds well in cold storage, and has excellent greens quality for dual-purpose use (root plus cooking greens). One of the most practically reliable and consistently productive beet varieties available, recommended by university extension services across North America as a benchmark hybrid against which other beets are evaluated.
sources: Bejo Seeds — Red Ace beet variety notes
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Beet Variety Evaluation
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Beet variety comparison chart

name: Red Acre Cabbage
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant as soon as soil can be worked; in zone 9 start seeds in September and transplant October for fall through winter maturity. Red Acre reaches full maturity in 75–85 days from transplant — plant timing to ensure heads mature before summer heat. Heads split if left too long after maturity; harvest when heads are firm and solid. In zone 9 the fall planting is preferred, with heads maturing December–February when cool weather develops the fullest red-purple color and sweetest flavor.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Red Acre is a classic open-pollinated red cabbage variety producing firm, round, 5–7 inch heads with deep red-purple to burgundy outer leaves and a bright magenta-red interior — the characteristic vivid color that makes red cabbage one of the most ornamental vegetables and the most visually distinctive cole crop. The red-purple color comes from anthocyanin pigments that are pH-sensitive: the same compound that makes red cabbage turn blue when cooked with alkaline water is stabilized and brightened by adding acid (vinegar, apple juice) during cooking — a useful culinary fact for maintaining the vivid color in braised preparations. Red Acre's flavor is slightly stronger and more peppery than green cabbage, with a firmer texture that holds up extremely well to long braising, pickling, and fermentation. Braised red cabbage with apples, vinegar, and spices (the classic German Rotkohl) and quick-pickled red cabbage for tacos and grain bowls represent the two most common culinary applications, both of which take advantage of the vivid color and firm texture that make Red Acre specifically valuable.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Red Acre Heirloom Cabbage
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Cabbage Variety Trial
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cool-Season Cabbage for Florida

name: Red Baron Onion
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or set out transplants/sets 2-4 weeks before last frost once soil is workable.
directions: Red Baron is a compact, early-maturing intermediate-day storage onion with deep red-purple skin and firm, pink-tinged white flesh with a moderately pungent, well-balanced flavor. Its smaller bulb size and quick maturity make it a favorite for gardeners who want reliable red onions without a long growing season, and its skins hold color and firmness well in storage for several months. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil with consistent moisture, keeping beds weed-free since onions compete poorly with weeds during bulb sizing. Choose Red Baron where garden space or season length is limited but a dependable, good-keeping red onion is still wanted.

name: Red Beard Bunching Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow or start transplants in early spring; can also be sown in late summer for a fall crop in zone 9. Red Beard develops its reddish shank color best in cool weather with full sun.
directions: Sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to about an inch apart for straight, uniform stalks. Red Beard is a non-bulbing bunching onion selected for shanks that develop an attractive reddish-pink blush, especially in cool weather, adding color contrast to salads, garnishes, and stir-fries beyond standard all-green scallions. It is cold-hardy and can be sown in late summer for a fall and winter harvest in mild climates, standing in the garden through cool weather without bolting. Harvest at scallion size for the best color and tenderness, or let a portion mature further for thicker stalks; successive small sowings every few weeks keep a continuous supply through the cool season.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing Onions

name: Red Belgian Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; this fast-maturing heirloom suits short-season gardens where longer-season bells never fully ripen.
directions: Red Belgian is a compact, early heirloom sweet pepper valued by northern gardeners for its speed to harvest, with blocky conical fruit reaching edible creamy-yellow stage well before most bells and fully ripening to sweet, thick-walled red. Its naturally shorter season and productive, compact plants make it a reliable choice where summers are cool or short. Harvest some fruit at the yellow stage for a milder, crisper bite, or let fruit finish to red for full sweetness. Provide full sun and consistent moisture, and stake plants in windy sites since the compact branches can still be weighed down by heavy fruit set.
sources: Seed catalog descriptions (True Leaf Market, Tradewinds Fruit)

name: Red Burgundy Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks after last frost when soil reaches 70°F in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, loamy soil in full sun; soak seeds 12–24 hours in warm water before planting to speed germination; Red Burgundy is an AAS award-winning heirloom okra variety producing deeply colored deep-red to burgundy-purple pods that are as ornamental as they are edible — the pods maintain their color fresh but turn green when cooked.
directions: Direct sow after soil warms to 70°F+ in full sun, well-drained, moderately fertile soil; harvest pods at 3–4 inches for best tenderness; Red Burgundy produces excellent fresh pods and makes a very beautiful ornamental edible garden plant. Abelmoschus esculentus 'Red Burgundy' is an All-America Selections award-winning heirloom okra variety selected for its striking deep red-burgundy to near-black pod color — one of the most visually dramatic okra varieties available. The compact, 4–5-foot plants produce deep-red stems, leaf veins, and pods that create a stunning ornamental effect in the edible garden or mixed border. The pods are tender, flavorful, and productive at 3–4 inches; they have the same culinary properties as green okra but with the added visual appeal of the deep color. The color is caused by anthocyanin pigments, the same antioxidant compounds found in red cabbage and purple sweet potatoes; like other anthocyanin-rich vegetables, Red Burgundy okra pods lose most of their red color and turn green when cooked, though the anthocyanins are still consumed. The flavor and texture are essentially identical to high-quality green okra. Red Burgundy is productive in the long, hot Gulf Coast summer and was a 1988 AAS winner — one of the most enduringly popular colored okra varieties in American seed catalogs.
sources: All-America Selections — Red Burgundy Okra (1988 Award Winner)
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Okra
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Heirloom Okra Varieties

name: Red Catawissa Walking Onion
plantingNote: Plant topset bulbils in early fall so they root before winter; this red-skinned strain of Catawissa walking onion is otherwise grown identically to the standard heirloom.
directions: Red Catawissa is a color-selected strain of the historic Catawissa walking onion, distinguished by a reddish-bronze blush on its topset bulbils and sometimes the base of the stalks, while sharing the same loose, open bulbil clusters and occasional true flowers that set true Catawissa apart from the common Egyptian walking onion. As the aerial bulbils swell and grow heavy, the seed stalk bends toward the ground and roots the bulbils wherever they touch soil, allowing the clump to slowly migrate through the bed year after year with no replanting needed. Harvest green shoots through the season like scallions, dig underground bulbs once tops begin to yellow, and collect or replant the colorful topset bulbils to expand the planting or share with other gardeners. Divide congested clumps every few years to keep vigor and bulbil production high.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange heirloom onion archive
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange variety notes

name: Red Choi Bok Choy
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–November for harvest November–February. Red Choi can also be sown January–February for a spring crop. Successive sowings every 3 weeks provide continuous harvest. Cool temperatures intensify the red-purple color; heat causes plants to revert toward green and bolt quickly. Baby leaves are harvestable 25–30 days from sowing.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil; Red Choi is a red-leafed bok choy (pak choi) selection producing compact rosette plants with deep burgundy-red to purple-red leaves with contrasting white or pale pink midribs — visually striking in both the garden and on the plate. The flavor is identical to standard green bok choy — mild, slightly mustardy, very tender — but the anthocyanin pigments in the red leaves indicate additional antioxidant content. Red Choi performs best and shows the deepest color in cool weather; warm temperatures cause the plants to green up and bolt quickly. The compact size and partial-shade tolerance make it ideal for intercropping under taller crops, growing in containers, or filling shady corners of the fall garden where other vegetables would fail. Harvest the whole head at 45–55 days or cut outer leaves for continuous baby green harvest. Stir-fry briefly to preserve some color, or use raw in salads where the red color provides striking visual contrast.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Red Choi Bok Choy Variety Notes
University of Hawaii Extension — Asian Brassica Varieties for Hawaii
Rutgers University — Red-Leafed Asian Vegetables for the Home Garden

name: Red Creole Onion
plantingNote: In zone 9, sow seeds or set transplants in October–November for harvest in March–April; Red Creole is a short-day onion (requires about 12–13 hours of daylight to bulb) well-matched to the Gulf South's winter day length. Direct sow or set transplants 4 inches apart.
directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Red Creole C-5 is the predominant short-day red onion of the Gulf South, widely grown in Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas, and Alabama and a staple of Gulf Coast kitchen gardens for generations. Unlike the mild, low-pungency sweet onions prized in other regions, Red Creole is a distinctly pungent, storage-type red onion — strongly flavored, with a sharp, assertive onion bite that makes it preferred for Creole and Cajun cooking where onion flavor needs to stand up through long cooking in jambalayas, étouffées, and red beans. The medium-sized, somewhat flattened bulbs cure well and keep for several months in a dry, well-ventilated location. Red Creole bolts in long days, so it MUST be grown on the short-day winter schedule in zone 9 (planted October–December, harvested March–April). It is heat-tolerant once past the bulbing stage and handles the warming temperatures of spring well. A foundational vegetable of Louisiana foodways alongside celery and bell pepper in the Cajun 'holy trinity.'
sources: LSU AgCenter Publication — Short-Day Onion Varieties for Louisiana
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Onion Variety Selection for the Gulf South
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Red Creole Onion notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Onion Production for Florida

name: Red Deuce Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Red Deuce is a vigorous determinate that benefits from staking or caging to keep the heavy fruit clusters off the ground.
directions: Red Deuce is a determinate hybrid slicer bred for commercial fresh-market production in the Southeast that has become a popular choice for home gardeners wanting a tough, reliable main-crop tomato. It produces large, smooth, deep-red 10-12 ounce globes on a compact, high-yielding plant with resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, Verticillium wilt, and tomato spotted wilt virus. Stake or cage the sturdy determinate vines to keep the heavy fruit clusters clean and off the soil, and expect a concentrated main harvest typical of determinate types.

name: Red Drumhead Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost for spring planting, or start in midsummer for fall harvest 90–105 days before first frost; Red Drumhead is a traditional European heirloom red cabbage producing large, flat to slightly rounded, very densely packed deep red-purple heads of excellent quality for fresh eating, braising, pickling, and long-term storage.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 3–4 weeks before last frost (cabbage tolerates light frost); space 18–24 inches apart in rows 24–30 inches apart. Red Drumhead is a traditional European heirloom red cabbage with a distinctive flattened or slightly convex head shape — broader and flatter than the round heads of varieties like Red Acre or Mammoth Red Rock — that packs very tightly with dense, waxy, deep red-purple leaves. The name 'Drumhead' refers to this characteristically wide, flat shape reminiscent of a drum (a category designation historically used for flat-headed cabbages in both red and green forms). The flavor is bold, earthy, and slightly peppery when raw — excellent for traditional German red cabbage dishes (braised with apples and vinegar), pickling, sauerkraut, and coleslaw; the purple pigment (from anthocyanins) is water-soluble and will turn the cooking liquid blue-purple, traditionally corrected by adding vinegar or apple to keep the red color. Individual heads weigh 4–8 lbs at full maturity; the dense heads resist splitting and store well in cool conditions (35–40°F) for 3–4 months after harvest. Excellent cold hardiness — can withstand frosts to 20°F, making it suitable for overwintering in mild climates.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Heritage Variety List

name: Red Epicure Fava Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring (or fall in mild-winter climates) into fertile soil in full sun; Red Epicure grows tall and needs staking to support the heavy pod load.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, staking the tall 5-foot plants to support the pod load; Red Epicure is a rare English heirloom fava bean with distinctive chestnut-red seeds, often described as carrying a genuine chestnut-like flavor unusual among fava types. Shell beans dry to a deep burgundy color but keep their bright red hue if steamed rather than boiled. In mild-winter climates it can be fall-sown to overwinter for an earlier spring crop, since the plants tolerate frost well as seedlings.

name: Red Express Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Red Express is particularly well-suited to fall production — the cool temperatures of fall intensify the anthocyanin red-purple color and sweeten the flavor. In zone 9, transplant mid-August through September for October–December harvest. The small, compact heads (1.5–3 lbs) reach maturity in just 63–72 days from transplant and hold in the garden without splitting for several weeks after reaching maturity.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 65–75°F; transplant to full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil. Red Express is an early-maturing red cabbage that matures 2–3 weeks faster than standard red varieties like Red Acre or Ruby Ball, producing small to medium (1.5–3 lb), nicely rounded, deep purple-red heads in just 63–72 days from transplant. Red cabbages in general contain significantly more anthocyanin antioxidants than green types and have a characteristic slightly sharper, more peppery flavor profile; Red Express delivers these attributes in an early-maturing, compact form well-suited to small gardens and fall production windows where there may not be time for the standard 80–85 day maturity of most red cabbage varieties. The red-purple pigmentation intensifies with cool fall temperatures — heads started in late summer and maturing in fall have dramatically deeper, more saturated color than spring-grown heads. Red Express holds well in the garden after reaching maturity and stores very well in refrigeration (4–6 months at 32°F), making it an excellent variety for gardeners who want to put up a supply of red cabbage for winter coleslaw and braised preparations.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Red Express cabbage variety notes
High Mowing Organic Seeds — Red cabbage variety comparison
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Cabbage Production Guide

name: Red Fife Wheat
plantingNote: Sow as early as the ground can be worked in spring; needs a cool start and a short, reliable growing season.
directions: Sow as early as the ground can be worked in spring, since Red Fife is a spring wheat that needs a cool start and a short, reliable growing season to head out before the heat of summer. Ontario farmer David Fife is credited with selecting this variety from a chance seed lot in the 1840s, and its earliness and hardiness made it the dominant wheat of the Canadian prairies for decades, underpinning the growth of the wheat trade that built Winnipeg and much of western Canadian agriculture. The kernels mill into strong, flavorful bread flour with a distinctive nutty character prized by heritage-grain bakers, and the variety is enjoying a revival among small growers seeking flavorful, regionally adapted wheat.

name: Red Fuseau Sunchoke
plantingNote: Plant tuber sections 3-5 inches deep around the last frost date in any well-drained soil in full sun; Red Fuseau is an old French heirloom valued for its elongated, red-skinned tubers, which are smoother and easier to clean than many knobby sunchoke varieties.
directions: Plant tuber pieces in a dedicated, well-drained bed in full sun, since this vigorous heirloom spreads readily by underground tubers and can be difficult to eradicate once established. Red Fuseau is a long-grown French heirloom sunchoke prized for its elongated, finger-shaped, red-skinned tubers, which are smoother-skinned and easier to scrub clean than the knobby tubers of many other varieties, and its nutty, sweet-earthy flavor is well regarded among heirloom growers. The tall plants produce cheerful small yellow sunflowers in late summer before dying back with frost, which signals it is time to dig the tubers; cold exposure is said to sweeten the flavor by converting stored inulin to sugar. Harvest from fall into early spring as needed, and leave a portion of tubers in the ground each year to regenerate next season's crop while thinning the bed to keep it contained.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Jerusalem Artichoke

name: Red Giant Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; in zone 9, sow September through January for fall and winter production; the striking purple foliage makes Red Giant ornamentally valuable in cool-season beds alongside kale and Swiss chard.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade during the cool season; Red Giant is the most widely grown purple mustard green — a Japanese mustard variety with large, deeply frilled to semi-smooth leaves in a striking deep burgundy-purple to reddish-purple color that makes it simultaneously ornamental and edible. The bold purple color intensifies with cool temperatures and frost exposure, making Red Giant one of the most visually dramatic cool-season vegetables for the Gulf South garden — combining beautifully with green kale, white cauliflower, and orange-flowered pansies in the fall edible landscape. The flavor is distinctly pungent and spicy with a mustard heat that develops more fully in mature leaves; young leaves at 4–6 inches are milder and excellent for salads and slaws. In hot weather, the plant bolts and the leaves become extremely pungent and bitter — in zone 9, grow strictly as a fall/winter/spring crop. The purple color partially transfers to cooking liquid and mixed dishes, giving cooked dishes a beautiful purple-tinted sauce. The combination of culinary value and ornamental purple foliage makes Red Giant an excellent choice for edible landscape plantings where vegetables serve double duty as ornamentals.

name: Red Hubbard Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Red Hubbard requires a long season (92–105 days) and is harvested as a storage squash in fall. In zone 9, plant March–April for September–October harvest. Cure harvested fruits at 80–85°F for 2 weeks to harden the skin before moving to cool, dry storage (50–55°F) where they keep 3–5 months. The very hard shell and warty skin require a heavy, sharp knife or cleaver to cut — many cooks bake the whole squash before cutting.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 3 seeds after last frost; thin to 2 plants. Cure harvested fruits 2 weeks at warm temperature before cool storage. Red Hubbard is a classic large Cucurbita maxima winter squash — one of the largest commonly grown winter squash types, producing fruits typically weighing 10–15 lbs with distinctive warty, orange-red to brick-red-orange skin and a teardrop to large, irregular form with a knobby, pointed blossom end. The Hubbard class of squash has a long American horticultural history, dating to the mid-19th century when the Blue Hubbard type was brought to New England and became a regional storage squash staple. Red Hubbard is a warmer-colored variant with orange-red skin rather than the Blue Hubbard's steel-blue-gray. The very thick, hard shell provides exceptional storage capability (stored roots keep 4–6 months) and was important in pre-refrigeration households where squash served as an important carbohydrate source through winter. The deep orange flesh is very dense, dry, and sweet — the classic winter squash flavor in concentrated form, excellent for pies, soups, and roasted preparations where the flavor holds up to extended cooking.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Red Hubbard squash variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Hubbard squash collection
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Winter Squash Storage and Curing

name: Red Impact Sweet Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Red Impact is a Lamuyo-type sweet pepper, an elongated, blocky Mediterranean type that is notoriously fussy in other varieties but bred here for easier, more reliable garden performance.
directions: Start seed indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant into full sun once frost danger has passed. Red Impact is an AAS-winning Lamuyo-type sweet pepper bearing large, roughly 7-inch tapered fruit that ripens from green to deep red, with unusually thick, sweet walls even before the fruit fully colors. Plants grow upright and tidy with a strong disease-resistance package, setting a heavy load of uniform fruit that finishes reliably. Harvest green for a milder, crisper pepper or let fruit ripen fully to red for the sweetest flavor and best eating quality; consistent watering during fruit set helps prevent thin walls and blossom-end rot.
sources: All-America Selections — Pepper Red Impact F1 winner announcement

name: Red Japanese Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; matures in about 95 days, a relatively short season for a dry-fleshed type, and is offered as slips by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange.
directions: Red Japanese produces deep reddish-purple skin over creamy white flesh, with a drier, denser texture than common moist orange varieties and a sweet, nutty flavor suited to roasting, steaming, frying, and baking. It is a vigorous, disease-resistant vine that reaches maturity in about 95 days, a shorter season than many dry-fleshed sweet potatoes require. Its adaptability to a range of summer climates has made it a long-standing offering among heirloom seed exchanges. Cure roots at warm temperature and high humidity after digging to firm the skin and develop full flavor.

name: Red Kingdom Mizuna
plantingNote: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–March for fall through spring harvest. Red Kingdom produces baby salad leaves in as little as 21 days and reaches full size by 35–40 days — one of the fastest-growing cool-season greens available. Harvest as baby leaves for mild salad use or allow to reach full size for a more pronounced peppery flavor. In zone 9 successive sowings every 2–3 weeks maintain continuous supply through the cool season. The vibrant red-purple color makes Red Kingdom an excellent cut-and-come-again salad green that persists beautifully through zone 9 winters.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Red Kingdom is a red-leaved selection of mizuna (Brassica rapa var. japonica) that combines the deeply cut, feathery leaf shape of traditional green mizuna with vivid deep ruby-red to burgundy-purple leaf color — creating one of the most ornamental salad greens available for kitchen garden beds and mixed containers. Mizuna is a Japanese mustard green with a mild, slightly peppery, pleasantly tangy flavor that is substantially less harsh than red mustard or arugula, making Red Kingdom one of the most approachable and versatile peppery greens for fresh salads. Baby leaves harvested at 2–3 inches have a particularly mild and delicate flavor that works well in mixed salad blends; mature leaves develop more pronounced peppery notes similar to mild arugula. The vivid red-purple color is most intense in cool weather and fades somewhat as temperatures rise in spring — a cool autumn or winter planting in zone 9 produces the most visually striking, deeply colored leaves. Red Kingdom's partial shade tolerance makes it a productive salad green for kitchen gardens with limited full-sun space.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Red Kingdom Mizuna Description
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Asian Greens for Florida Gardens
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Cool-Season Salad Greens for Gulf South

name: Red Kitten Spinach
subcategory: baby-leaf hybrid spinach with red veining
plantingNote: Direct sow thickly in wide bands 2-4 weeks before the last frost for a quick baby-leaf harvest.
directions: Broadcast or row sow seed thickly and shallowly, keeping the bed consistently moist for even germination, then cut leaves with scissors once they reach salad size. This smooth, arrow-shaped hybrid is distinguished by its bright pink-red midribs and veins running through tender green leaves, adding color and a mild, slightly sweet flavor to fresh salad mixes. It resists bolting better than many baby-leaf types and regrows readily for repeat cuttings.

name: Red Knight Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Red Knight is harvested green at 65 days from transplant or left to ripen red at 80–85 days. The red-ripe stage has much higher vitamin C and sweetness than the green stage. In zone 9, transplant March–April for June–August harvest. Red Knight shows excellent resistance to Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV), which helps maintain productivity in summer stress conditions.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun, well-drained soil after last frost. Red Knight is a premium F1 hybrid bell pepper from PanAmerican Seed that has become one of the most consistently recommended thick-walled, high-quality bell peppers for both home gardens and commercial production in the eastern United States — a large (4 x 4 inch), blocky, 4-lobed bell pepper with very thick walls (0.3–0.35 inch) that set it apart from thinner-walled standard bell types. The thick walls are the key eating-quality trait: they provide a satisfying crunch, substantial texture for stuffing (the walls hold up to heat without collapsing), and a longer postharvest shelf life than thin-walled types that wilt rapidly after picking. Red Knight ripens from deep, dark green to a uniformly rich red with clean, complete color change. The fruit flavor at the red stage is noticeably sweeter and more complex than at the green stage — the extended ripening time converts starches and develops sugars, creating a pepper that many cooks use specifically in the red stage for roasted red pepper, jarred pimento-style preparations, and raw salads. Disease resistance includes Tobacco Mosaic Virus (TMV), which can devastate pepper plantings in summer heat — a practical advantage in zone 8–10 summer production.
sources: PanAmerican Seed / Ball Horticultural — Red Knight bell pepper variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Bell pepper thick-wall comparison
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pepper Production in Florida

name: Red Komatsuna
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Komatsuna develops its deepest purple-red color in cool weather and with strong light, fading toward green in hot summer conditions or deep shade.
directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and thin to final spacing for full-sized rosettes or grow tightly spaced for a cut-and-come-again baby-leaf harvest. Red Komatsuna is a purple-red-leaved selection of komatsuna, the fast-growing, cold-hardy Japanese mustard spinach, offering the same tender, mild, slightly mustardy flavor as the standard green form but in leaves flushed deep maroon-purple, especially vivid in cool fall and winter growing conditions. It is a productive, quick-maturing green well suited to a fall or early-spring planting, tolerating light frost better than true spinach while adding striking color contrast to salad mixes and stir-fries. Harvest whole young plants or pick individual outer leaves for a repeated cut-and-come-again harvest, since the plant regrows readily from the crown after cutting.
sources: Kitazawa Seed Co. — Asian vegetable seed catalog
Evergreen Seeds — Chinese and Japanese vegetable growing notes
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database

name: Red Kuri Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May for summer harvest. Red Kuri stores remarkably well — properly cured fruits (2 weeks at 85°F, then cool dry storage) keep 5–6 months, providing winter squash into late winter. The medium-size fruits (5–8 lbs) are manageable for home cooking. In zone 9 the long, warm season allows the fruit to cure fully on the vine — leave until the vine withers and the skin is hard before harvesting.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Red Kuri (also known as Red Hokkaido, Orange Hokkaido, or Uchiki Kuri) is a Japanese heirloom winter squash producing distinctive, medium-sized, pear-to-teardrop-shaped fruits with deep reddish-orange skin and bright orange, dry, starchy flesh. The flavor is described as a rich chestnut-like sweetness with buttery, nutty notes and an exceptionally dense, dry texture that distinguishes it from the moister, stringier flesh of butternut and acorn squash. The dry, starchy texture makes Red Kuri outstanding for soups and purees (where it thickens naturally), Japanese-style simmered preparations (kabocha), and stuffed squash presentations where watery flesh would dilute the flavor. The medium size (5–8 pounds) is more practical for home cooking than very large winter squash. Red Kuri has been popular in French and Japanese cuisine for decades and is now widely grown in American specialty gardens and farmers markets.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Specialty Winter Squash
Cornell University Extension — Cucurbita maxima Heirloom Varieties
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Red Kuri History and Production

name: Red LaSoda Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces January–February in zone 9 for May–June harvest; Red LaSoda is specifically adapted to the Gulf South's winter planting schedule and performs better in warm, humid climates than most northern potato varieties. It tolerates slightly warmer soil temperatures than white potatoes and handles the transition into warm spring weather better.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in well-drained, loose soil; Red LaSoda is a red-skin, white-flesh potato variety developed at Louisiana State University specifically for Gulf Coast and Southern growing conditions — it is one of the few potato varieties bred with the hot, humid Deep South in mind rather than the cool Pacific Northwest or Northeast where most commercial varieties originate. The round, attractively smooth, deep-red skinned tubers have firm, white, waxy flesh excellent for boiling, potato salads, and roasting — the waxy texture holds shape during cooking rather than falling apart. Red LaSoda shows better tolerance of warm temperatures, clay soils, and the wet winters common to the Gulf South than most commercial varieties. It is the most widely recommended red potato for Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Texas Gulf Coast gardens, and is a staple offering at Southern feed-and-seed stores each January. Harvest as new potatoes when plants bloom; for storage potatoes, harvest after vines begin yellowing and dying back.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Red LaSoda potato development
LSU AgCenter Publication — Potato Production in Louisiana
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Potato Variety Recommendations for Texas
Mississippi State University Extension — Home Garden Potato Production

name: Red Leaf Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in spring, or in late summer 6–8 weeks before first fall frost; red leaf lettuces are loose-head types harvested as cut-and-come-again crops by removing outer leaves as needed, or as whole heads — heat bolts them quickly so sow again in early fall for best flavor.
directions: Sow seed thinly on the surface and press in gently; lettuce seeds need light to germinate and should not be covered more than 1/8 inch deep; keep moist until germination. Red leaf lettuce encompasses looseleaf types with varying degrees of red-to-burgundy pigmentation in the leaves, including classics like 'Lollo Rossa,' 'New Red Fire,' 'Red Sails,' and 'Oak Red' — the anthocyanin pigmentation develops best in cool temperatures and direct sunlight, with heat causing color to fade and bitterness to increase. Red leaf lettuces are the most commonly grown looseleaf types in American home gardens, valued for their visual appeal, nutritional density (the red pigment is anthocyanins with antioxidant value), and ease of growing as cut-and-come-again salad plants. Harvest outer leaves when 4–6 inches long, leaving the center to continue growing; provide shade cloth (30%) in warm climates to extend the season. Interplant with taller vegetables for natural afternoon shade.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Vegetable Production Guide

name: Red Long of Tropea Onion
plantingNote: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start August–September and transplant October–November. Red Long of Tropea is a long-day onion adapted to the short winter days and mild temperatures of coastal Mediterranean and Gulf South climates. In zone 9 it produces a winter-to-spring crop, bulbing up in January–March as day length increases. Unlike short-day bulbing onions, Red Long of Tropea can be pulled young as a sweet salad onion before full bulb development.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Red Long of Tropea (Cipolla Rossa di Tropea) is the iconic long, elongated red onion of the Calabrian coast town of Tropea in southern Italy, with IGP protected status as a geographic-origin food product. The bulbs are strikingly elongated — cylindrical to torpedo-shaped rather than globe-shaped — with brilliant deep-magenta-red skin and white-to-light-pink flesh with exceptionally low pungency and high natural sweetness. The Tropea onion is the standard for Italian raw onion preparations — sliced thin on bruschetta, dressed with olive oil and herbs, or pickled in vinegar — where the mild, almost sweet flavor allows the onion to be eaten raw without the harsh bite of standard globe onions. The visual appeal of the deep red, elongated shape makes it a striking addition to salads and charcuterie boards. In zone 9 it bulbs up reliably through the mild winter and produces excellent results in the sandy loam soils typical of Gulf Coast gardens.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Presidia Red Onion of Tropea
University of Naples Federico II — Italian Heirloom Onion Varieties
Seeds of Italy — Cipolla Rossa di Tropea Production Notes

name: Red Marconi Frying Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Red Marconi is an open-pollinated Italian frying pepper that can be seed-saved year to year — select the best-shaped, most productive fruits from the healthiest plants. In zone 9, transplant March–April. Harvest green for frying (sweeter and more delicate) or let ripen to full deep red for roasting — the red-ripe stage has dramatically more sweetness and vitamin C than the green stage.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 78–85°F; transplant to full sun, fertile, well-drained soil. Red Marconi is the classic Italian open-pollinated sweet frying/roasting pepper — a traditional heirloom variety that produces long (6–8 inch), moderately tapered, thick-walled, slightly ridged fruits of the Italian frying type, ripening from medium green to deep, vivid red. Unlike the Giant Marconi hybrid (AAS 1997), Red Marconi is open-pollinated, allowing seed to be saved and maintained from year to year — the preservation choice for gardeners who want a self-sustaining seed supply. The traditional Italian frying pepper form is distinctive: longer and more tapered than bell peppers, with a slightly irregular, ridged exterior and relatively thick, meaty walls. At the green stage, the flavor is mild, fresh, and subtly sweet — the standard for Italian sautéed peppers (peperoni fritti) where the pepper is sliced and cooked in olive oil until tender. At the red stage, the flavor concentrates into a sweet, rich, complex character ideal for roasting, peeling, and incorporating into antipasto, stuffed preparations, or the classic Italian peperonata. Red Marconi plants are tall (30–42 inches), productive, and require staking when loaded with fruit.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Italian frying pepper collection
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Red Marconi variety notes
Franchi Sementi (Italy) — Italian heirloom pepper documentation

name: Red Noodle Yard-Long Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 70°F in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; provide a trellis or fence at least 5 feet tall — Red Noodle vines grow vigorously to 10+ feet and require substantial support for the trailing bean clusters.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Red Noodle is a striking red-podded yard-long bean (Vigna unguiculata subsp. sesquipedalis) producing deep burgundy-red to dark red pods 18–24 inches long — the dramatic red color and extraordinary length combine to make this one of the most visually spectacular edible climbing plants available for Gulf South summer gardens. Yard-long beans (also called asparagus beans or Chinese long beans) are a tropical subspecies of cowpea adapted to hot, humid conditions that make them particularly suitable for Gulf South summer production when standard snap beans decline. The pods should be harvested at 12–18 inches for best tenderness and flavor — they become tough and fibrous when allowed to develop past 20 inches. Red Noodle maintains its red color when raw and in raw preparations but turns greenish-brown when cooked — similar to the color loss in Burgundy snap beans and Red Russian kale. The cooking texture is similar to standard yard-long beans: slightly firmer and less watery than snap beans, holding texture well in stir-fries and sautés. The vines grow vigorously to 8–12 feet in Gulf South heat and require substantial trellis support (minimum 5–6 foot fence or trellis height) — the trailing red bean clusters hanging from overhead structures create a dramatic ornamental and productive display simultaneously.

name: Red Noodle Yardlong Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1–3 weeks after last frost (yardlong beans are more heat-loving than Phaseolus beans and benefit from warmer soil, 70°F+); provide a trellis 6–8 feet tall; Red Noodle is the most visually dramatic yardlong bean variety, producing 18–24 inch pods of an extraordinary deep burgundy-crimson color that fade to purple-gray when cooked — the intensely colored pods are the most striking visual feature of any long bean grown in American gardens.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after the soil reaches 70°F or more (1–3 weeks after last frost) at the base of a sturdy trellis 6–8 feet tall; Red Noodle bean is extremely heat-tolerant and actually performs best in the hottest summer conditions — it continues producing during summer heat that stops most beans from setting pods. Red Noodle is a cultivar of the yardlong bean (also called asparagus bean, long bean, or snake bean), which is the same species as the cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) but selected for long pod production — the typical yardlong bean produces green pods 18–24 inches long; Red Noodle produces pods of the same length but in a spectacular deep burgundy to crimson-red color that is unique among commonly grown beans and makes the loaded trellis a visual centerpiece of the summer garden. The flavor is similar to standard green yardlong beans — somewhat starchier and with more umami than fresh Phaseolus beans — and is excellent stir-fried in Chinese cooking (the primary culinary tradition that uses yardlong beans), in pad thai, in Southeast Asian salads and pickles, or simply sautéed with garlic and soy. The dark color fades significantly when cooked, but remains visually interesting as a dark grayish-purple. Yardlong beans including Red Noodle are far more heat-tolerant than any Phaseolus bean variety and are ideal for Gulf Coast gardeners in zones 8b–10 who want continuous summer bean production through July and August when other beans fail.

name: Red Norland Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces (each with at least one eye) 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 5.8–6.5) soil in full sun; Red Norland is one of the earliest-maturing potato varieties (70–80 days) making it well-suited to the short cool season in zone 9 before summer heat arrives.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4–6 weeks before the last frost in loose, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Red Norland is one of the finest early-maturing red potato varieties for home garden production — producing attractive, smooth, bright-red-skinned, white-fleshed tubers that mature in only 70–80 days from planting, making it the best choice for Zone 9 gardeners whose spring potato window closes when summer heat arrives. The smooth red skin (without the russeting or rough texture of some red varieties) and excellent appearance make Red Norland outstanding for presentation at harvest — new Red Norland potatoes dug fresh from the garden have bright color and clean appearance. The white flesh is excellent for boiling, steaming, and potato salad — waxy enough to hold its shape when cooked, with a moist, creamy texture and mild potato flavor that excels in salads, soups, and boiled presentations. In zone 9, plant seed potatoes in January–February for a May–June harvest before summer heat makes potato production impractical. Hill soil over the developing plants 2–3 times as they grow to ensure tubers do not green from light exposure. Red Norland has been one of the most widely grown early red potato varieties in American home gardens since its introduction in the 1950s — a reliable, consistent producer of high-quality fresh-eating potatoes.

name: Red Oak Leaf Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–February for spring. Red Oak Leaf is exceptionally heat-tolerant for a red lettuce and holds quality longer than most red types before bolting. Succession sow every 3 weeks through fall for continuous harvest. Harvest outer leaves for cut-and-come-again or pull entire plants.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Red Oak Leaf is the red-leafed counterpart to the classic green Oak Leaf lettuce — producing deeply lobed, sinuate leaves with an outline resembling the characteristic deeply-indented silhouette of an oak leaf, in deep burgundy-red to bronze-red coloring. The deeply-indented, non-frilly leaf form distinguishes Oak Leaf types immediately from the more common looseleaf lettuces with wavy or ruffled edges. The flavor is mild, tender, and slightly nutty — one of the better-flavored looseleaf lettuces with a soft, non-bitter quality. Red Oak Leaf lettuce is notably heat-tolerant and slow-to-bolt compared to most red lettuces, making it particularly valuable for extending the spring harvest season in zone 9 and for reliable color retention in warm fall conditions when other red varieties revert to green. The striking leaf form and consistent deep-red color make it one of the most popular lettuces for mesclun mixes and specialty salad blends.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Red Oak Leaf Lettuce Heritage Variety
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Oak Leaf Lettuce Types
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Looseleaf Lettuce

name: Red Pear Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Red Pear is the red-fruited counterpart to the Yellow Pear tomato, with the same diminutive, pear-shaped fruit and prolific production of sweet, bite-sized cherry tomatoes but ripening to brilliant red rather than yellow — excellent for snacking, salads, and garnishing.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; provide sturdy caging or staking as Red Pear is an indeterminate vine that reaches 5–7 feet and produces abundant clusters of small fruit through the season. Red Pear is the red-fruited version of the classic pear tomato type, producing small (1–1.5 inch), distinctively pear-shaped, bright red fruits in prolific hanging clusters from midsummer through frost; the flavor is sweet and mild, slightly less complex than larger tomatoes but ideal for snacking directly from the vine, halved in salads, and as a colorful contrast to yellow or orange cherry types. Like Yellow Pear, Red Pear is indeterminate and extremely vigorous, producing continuously until frost and sometimes overloading cages with fruit weight; the plants may need supplemental tying. Resistant to cracking even in wet conditions. Popular in children's gardens for the playful shape and snacking appeal.

name: Red Pontiac Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January–February for May harvest. Red Pontiac is a late-season potato that performs well in the South's cool winter window, producing large, round tubers that are harvested before summer heat terminates the season.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 2–3 inches deep, 4–6 weeks before last frost, after cutting to egg size with 1–2 eyes and allowing cut surfaces to cure for 1–2 days. Red Pontiac is the most widely grown red-skinned potato in the United States for over 50 years — a late-season, round, medium to large potato with smooth, dark red skin and white, waxy to slightly waxy flesh with moderate moisture content that holds its shape when boiled (making it excellent for potato salad, boiled potatoes, and roasting) while also mashing reasonably well. The bright red skin is attractive when left on for roasted preparations, and the firm texture keeps it together in soups and stews. Red Pontiac produces large, impressive tubers and is very productive in a wide range of soils, making it a reliable choice for home gardeners who want attractive, versatile red potatoes with a genuine all-purpose cooking character. In zone 9, plant in late January or early February and harvest in late April through May before summer heat causes plant decline.
sources: University of Maine Cooperative Extension — Potato Variety Guide
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Potato Production Guide

name: Red Pop Sweet Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors once danger of frost has passed.
directions: Red Pop delivers maximum crunch and refreshingly light sweetness with minimal seeds, bred for popping straight from the plant into your mouth. The compact habit is designed for easy growing in small spaces, including patios and balconies. Start indoors and move outside after frost for a steady supply of super-sweet snacking peppers.

name: Red Port Potato
plantingNote: Bred for impressive tuber set and red color retention in storage; plant seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost.
directions: Originally bred in North Dakota and further developed at the Aroostook Farm Potato Experiment Station in Maine, Red Port is an early-to-early-midseason potato with bright red skin that holds its color well in storage over white flesh. Medium plants with pink flowers set tubers moderately to heavily, giving heavy overall yields, and the variety shows moderate resistance to scab, blackspot, and shatter bruise alongside medium late blight tolerance. Its short-to-medium dormancy means stored tubers sprout relatively soon after harvest, so plan storage timing accordingly.

name: Red Potato Onion
scientificName: Allium cepa var. aggregatum 'Red Potato Onion'
plantingNote: Plant small saved bulbs in fall in mild-winter areas for the largest bulbs the following summer, or in very early spring once soil is workable where winters are severe.
directions: Red Potato Onion is a coppery-red to purple-skinned heirloom multiplier onion maintained within the same potato-onion tradition as the better-known Yellow Potato Onion, propagated vegetatively from saved bulbs rather than seed.
