Each planted bulb splits underground into a cluster of several new bulbs by midsummer, giving gardeners a perpetual, pungent storage onion without annual seed purchases. It is notably drought tolerant once established and keeps well in storage over winter. Plant divisions about two inches deep with the tip near the soil surface, and replant the largest bulbs from each harvest to maintain vigor in the strain.

name: Red Racer Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Red Racer is a 2018 All-America Selections winner bred with high resistance to Fusarium wilt, root-knot nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus, and Verticillium wilt — the nematode resistance is especially valuable in the sandy, nematode-prone soils common along the Gulf Coast.
directions: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F; Red Racer is a compact, determinate cocktail-sized tomato recognized as an All-America Selections winner for its exceptionally early maturity and broad disease resistance, including root-knot nematodes, a soil pest that stunts and weakens tomato roots and is a persistent problem in the sandy soils common across the Gulf Coast. It produces an early, concentrated crop of round, deep red, 2-3 ounce fruit with good, well-balanced flavor on plants compact enough for containers or small raised beds. Because of its resistance to nematodes as well as Fusarium wilt, tobacco mosaic virus, and Verticillium wilt, Red Racer performs reliably even in garden soil where other tomatoes have struggled. Pick fruit as it ripens to full red color for the best flavor.
sources: All-America Selections — Red Racer tomato AAS winner 2018

name: Red Ripper Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F, in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; give the vigorous vining plants a trellis, fence, or plenty of ground to sprawl, and expect a long production season lasting until frost.
directions: Direct sow in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established, thriving with minimal irrigation through the hottest, driest part of the Gulf South summer. Red Ripper is a vigorous, long-vining heirloom cowpea grown across the South since the 19th century both as a food crop and as a dependable summer cover crop and livestock forage, valued for its toughness in poor soil and drought that would fail most other legumes. The sprawling vines carry deep red-brown, kidney-shaped seeds in long pods over an extended late-summer season, continuing to set new pods until the first frost, which makes it one of the longer-producing Southern peas for a continuous late-season harvest. Beyond the table, Red Ripper is prized as a nitrogen-fixing green manure and grazing forage crop, tilled or turned under at the end of the season to build soil fertility for the following year. A dual-purpose, low-input heirloom well suited to the toughest garden conditions, zone 5–11.

name: Red Ripper Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Red Ripper is an heirloom Southern pea variety with distinctive reddish-tan to red-brown seeds with darker mottling — one of the most heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant of all Southern pea types, widely used as both a summer vegetable and a warm-season cover crop for building organic matter in hot, dry conditions where other cover crops struggle.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms; Red Ripper is semi-vining and may need minimal support or can be left to sprawl; for cover crop use broadcast at 5–10 lbs per 1000 sq ft; harvest pods at green-shell stage for fresh eating or allow to fully dry for storage as dry peas. Red Ripper is one of the most heat-tolerant and drought-tolerant Southern pea varieties available, valued for both its role as a food crop and its exceptional performance as a summer cover crop in the hot, dry conditions of the Southern Plains and Gulf Coast. The plants are semi-vining (not quite as bushy as modern varieties, not as long-vining as pole types) and produce prolifically under conditions that would reduce the yield of more refined modern varieties — poor, sandy soil, minimal rain, and sustained heat above 95°F. The seeds are distinctive: larger than many Southern peas, reddish-tan to brown with darker mottling, with a hearty, earthy cowpea flavor when cooked. As a cover crop, Red Ripper builds nitrogen at high rates (80–120 lbs N/acre under good conditions), suppresses summer weeds aggressively with its spreading canopy, and its large biomass decomposes quickly in the warm soil to build organic matter. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and LSU AgCenter recommend Red Ripper as one of the top summer cover crops for the Gulf South. For food production, Red Ripper is an old heirloom with deep roots in Southern and Texan food traditions — used as fresh shelled peas, dried peas, and as the source of pot likker in traditional Southern cooking.

name: Red Robin Micro Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Red Robin's extremely compact size (8–12 inches) makes it suitable for growing in 6–8 inch pots, hanging baskets, or window boxes — one of the few tomatoes practical for small apartment balconies and windowsills. In zone 9, transplant March–April. The determinate habit means all fruits ripen over a relatively short window (2–3 weeks); start 2–3 pots in succession for continuous harvest.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; grow in 6–8 inch containers or hanging baskets. Red Robin is a micro-dwarf determinate tomato — one of the smallest tomato plants available to gardeners, typically reaching only 8–14 inches tall and 8–12 inches wide at maturity. The extreme compact size distinguishes Red Robin from standard 'patio' tomatoes (which reach 24–36 inches) and makes it the tomato of choice for situations where space is extremely limited: kitchen windowsills, apartment balcony pots of any size, children's garden projects, hanging baskets, and window box plantings. Despite its tiny size, Red Robin produces red, round, 1-inch cherry tomatoes of acceptable sweet-tangy flavor in small but meaningful quantities — a single plant might produce 30–50 fruits over its harvest period, sufficient for salads and snacking. The determinate habit means the plant stops growing at its genetic maximum size and sets a crop over a 2–3 week window, making it ideal for succession planting (start a new plant every 3 weeks from late winter through late summer for continuous small harvests). Red Robin requires no staking, no pruning, and no trellising — it simply grows into a self-supporting mound and fruits.
sources: Burpee Seeds — Red Robin micro tomato variety notes
Stokes Seeds — Micro-dwarf tomato variety comparison
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Compact Tomato Varieties for Container Production

name: Red Rubine Brussels Sprout
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting, setting plants out 12-16 weeks ahead of the first fall frost so this long-season heirloom matures in cool weather and sweetens after frost.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting, setting plants out roughly 12-16 weeks ahead of the first fall frost so the long-season crop matures in cool weather. Red Rubine is a Dutch open-pollinated heirloom dating to the mid-20th century, prized for its striking purple-red buttons and matching purple-veined foliage, a dramatic contrast to standard green Brussels sprouts. Its sprouts are smaller and yields somewhat lighter than modern green hybrids, but the flavor is rich and nutty and intensifies with sweetness after hard frost, and the purple color often persists lightly even after cooking. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved from year to year, making Red Rubine a favorite of heirloom seed savers and gardeners seeking ornamental as well as edible value in the fall garden.

name: Red Russian Kale
plantingNote: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall through spring harvest. Red Russian is the most tender and mildest-flavored kale — young leaves harvested before 4 inches are excellent raw in salads without any massage or marinating required. In zone 9 fall planting in September–October produces beautiful leaves through the cool season; the red-purple color intensifies with cold temperatures, making fall-harvested Red Russian particularly attractive.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Red Russian Kale is widely considered the most versatile and palatable kale variety for fresh and minimally processed use — the flat, deeply indented, gray-green leaves with red-purple stems and leaf margins have a tenderness and mild sweetness that allows them to be eaten raw in salads (particularly baby leaves) without the fibrous toughness and bitterness that makes many kale varieties unpleasant uncooked. Unlike the curly kales that require extensive massage to soften for salad use, Red Russian baby leaves can be used directly in mixed green salads, smoothies, and fresh preparations. The flavor is distinctly sweeter and less bitter than curly kale, with a mild earthiness and peppery undertone that becomes even more pleasant after frost — cold temperatures convert starches to sugars, dramatically improving the sweetness of all kale but especially Red Russian. The partial shade tolerance makes Red Russian one of the better kale choices for kitchen gardens with limited full-sun space.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Kale Variety Trial
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cool-Season Kale for Florida
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Kale and Collards for Gulf South

name: Red Rustproof Oat
plantingNote: Broadcast or drill in fall across the Deep South and Gulf Coast so plants establish a rosette before winter; this old landrace is only half-hardy and needs the mild winters of USDA zones 7-9 rather than true Northern cold.
directions: Red Rustproof arrived in the Deep South around 1849, reportedly carried home from the Mexican War, and by the early 1900s it was the dominant winter oat grown from Georgia through Texas because of its strong immunity to crown rust, a disease that regularly wiped out other oat stands. Drill or broadcast in fall into worked ground; the crop overwinters as a leafy rosette on cotton-worn soils and resumes vigorous growth once days lengthen in late winter. It is markedly less cold-hardy than northern oat types, so it belongs in mild-winter regions rather than areas with hard, prolonged freezes. Cut and thresh in early summer once the panicles dry to gold, saving the light, thin-hulled grain for livestock feed or replanting the following fall.
sources: USDA Bureau of Plant Industry historical bulletins

name: Red Sails Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool weather, barely covering seeds with soil; Red Sails tolerates heat somewhat better than many lettuces and is slower to bolt, making it a good choice for extending the spring lettuce season. In zone 9, direct sow September–February for fall and winter production, or February–March for a brief spring window before summer heat.
directions: Sow seeds shallowly in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in cool weather; Red Sails is a 1985 All-America Selections winner red leaf lettuce that has remained one of the most widely grown and recommended loose-leaf lettuces for over 40 years, valued for its combination of attractive deep burgundy-red to bronze coloring, excellent flavor, and — most practically — its slow bolting characteristic that gives it several weeks longer in the garden before going to seed than most lettuces under warming spring conditions. The large, ruffled, wavy leaves are moderately to deeply red throughout, with a mild, sweet lettuce flavor that is pleasant and non-bitter even in moderate heat. As a loose-leaf type, Red Sails can be harvested by removing outer leaves continuously (cut-and-come-again), or the entire plant can be cut at once. Red Sails is excellent for mixed salad bowls and provides visual contrast when grown alongside green lettuce varieties. In zone 9, it excels in the fall-through-winter season (September–February) when temperatures are cool enough for crisp lettuce production.
sources: All-America Selections — Red Sails lettuce AAS winner 1985
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lettuce Production Guide

name: Red Samurai Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow in a deeply tilled, well-amended bed free of rocks and clods; thin seedlings to 2–3 inches apart when plants reach 2 inches tall. In zone 9, sow September through October for December–February harvest; the cool fall/winter season produces the sweetest roots. Red Samurai develops best color and sweetness when grown in cool weather — summer production produces paler, less sweet roots.
directions: Direct sow seeds thinly, 0.25 inch deep, in deeply tilled, loose, rock-free soil; thin to 2–3 inches when seedlings are 2 inches tall, keeping thinnings for salads. Red Samurai is a Japanese-bred Nantes-type carrot (developed by Takii Seeds of Kyoto) that stands apart from most modern carrot varieties through its extraordinary deep scarlet-red to crimson skin and pinkish-red interior flesh, coloration that comes from lycopene — the same red pigment in tomatoes — rather than from the beta-carotene responsible for orange carrot color. The rich red color makes Red Samurai visually striking in the garden (the feathery tops are standard-green, revealing nothing of the flamboyant root below), stunning when sliced for salads and crudités, and exceptionally nutritious from a lycopene perspective. The roots are long (7–8 inches), slender, tapered in the classic Nantes style, with excellent sweet, mild flavor that compares favorably to the best orange Nantes varieties — the red pigmentation does not negatively affect flavor. Red Samurai is one of the most ornamentally distinctive of all carrot varieties and serves as an outstanding conversation piece in CSA boxes and farmers market displays where its unusual color draws immediate attention. Grows best in cool weather when the roots develop their deepest color; summer-grown roots are paler and somewhat less flavorful. An excellent addition to rainbow carrot mixes or grown on its own for maximum visual impact.
sources: Takii Seeds — Red Samurai carrot variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Specialty Carrot Variety Trial
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Specialty Carrot Variety Evaluation

name: Red Savina Habanero Pepper
plantingNote: Start on a heat mat 8–10 weeks before last frost; Red Savina is a selected strain of habanero developed by Frank Garcia of GNS Spices that held the Guinness World Record for hottest pepper from 1994 to 2006, reaching 350,000–580,000 Scoville units — significantly hotter than standard habaneros.
directions: Germinate on a heat mat at 85°F and grow under strong grow lights until transplanting outdoors after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; Red Savina grows as a compact, bushy plant and does best with consistent moisture and fertilization in full sun. Red Savina was developed by Frank Garcia in Walnut, California as a selected sport of the standard orange habanero and registered with the US Plant Variety Protection office; from 1994 until 2006 it held the Guinness World Record for hottest pepper at 350,000–580,000 Scoville Heat Units — since surpassed by even hotter superhot varieties but still among the most intensely hot widely available peppers. The fruits are classic habanero-shaped, medium-sized, bright red at maturity, with the characteristic fruity, apricot-like habanero aroma and overwhelming heat. Often grown by heat enthusiasts who want a genuinely hot habanero with well-established provenance and consistent heat levels.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University
Dave DeWitt's The Chile Pepper Encyclopedia

name: Red Scotch Bonnet Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors on a heat mat; transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 60°F.
directions: This Scotch Bonnet selection ripens from green to a deep red instead of the more familiar yellow or orange, with the same squat, crinkled bonnet-shaped pods and a heat level in the typical Scotch Bonnet range of roughly 100,000-350,000 Scoville units, comparable to a habanero. Its fruity, slightly sweet flavor makes it a staple of Jamaican and wider Caribbean jerk seasoning, pepper sauces, and stews. Start seed indoors with bottom heat, since chinense types germinate slowly, and transplant into full sun once the weather is reliably warm. Plants are compact and heavily productive, so stake or cage them once fruit load builds to keep brittle branches from snapping.
sources: True Leaf Market / Mountain Valley Seed Company - Red Scotch Bonnet Seeds
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Red Toch Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves 2 inches deep in fall; Artichoke types adapt well from cold to mild-winter zones.
directions: Collected near Tochliavri in the Republic of Georgia in the late 1980s, Red Toch is an Artichoke-type softneck valued among garlic growers for the striking red and pink streaking on its clove wrappers. Plant cloves pointed-end-up in fertile, well-drained soil in fall and mulch to protect against winter heaving. It forms the overlapping, many-layered cloves typical of Artichoke garlics, with a flavor that is well balanced rather than sharply hot, making it popular both raw and cooked. Harvest once the lower leaves have dried while four or five green leaves remain, then cure for three to four weeks before storing.

name: Red Treviso Radicchio
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for a November–February harvest. Rossa di Treviso is the elongated, pointed-head variety of Treviso radicchio — distinct from the round-head Rossa di Verona and from the forced Tardivo type. It heads naturally in cool weather without the forcing process required for Tardivo, making it the more accessible Treviso-type for home growers. In zone 9 light frosts intensify the red-purple color and reduce bitterness.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Rossa di Treviso (Red Treviso Radicchio) is the elongated, cone-to-torpedo-shaped Treviso type of radicchio, producing pointed heads of 10–14 inches long with deep wine-red to burgundy leaves with prominent white midribs — visually distinct from the round, compact Rossa di Verona radicchio. The naturally-heading (non-forced) Treviso type forms its distinctive elongated shape through the cool-weather growing process without requiring the dark forcing period of Tardivo, making it accessible to home growers who want Treviso-type radicchio without the complexity of forcing. The flavor is bittersweet and complex — similar to Rossa di Verona but with the elongated form lending itself to halving and grilling (the standard preparation for Treviso-type radicchio) where the heads can be placed directly on the grill without splitting apart. In zone 9 it is planted in fall and harvested November through February, with color and flavor improving with each frost.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Radicchio Rosso di Treviso Precoce
Seeds of Italy — Rossa di Treviso Growing Notes
University of California Cooperative Extension — Radicchio and Chicory Varieties

name: Red Velvet Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Red Velvet is an ornamental-edible okra with stunning deep burgundy-red to velvet-red pods, stems, and veins that make it one of the most visually striking plants in the summer vegetable garden while producing tender, flavorful pods identical in taste to standard green okra.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Red Velvet is well-suited to the edible landscape as both a productive vegetable and ornamental plant with dramatic color. Red Velvet okra is one of the most ornamentally striking of all vegetable plants, producing intensely pigmented deep burgundy-red to crimson-velvet pods, stems, leaf veins, and even young leaves that make it outstanding as an edible ornamental in landscape plantings and containers; the yellow hibiscus flowers with purple-red centers add additional ornamental value. The pods are edible and flavorful at 3–4 inches, with a taste and texture identical to standard green okra; when cooked they unfortunately lose much of their dramatic red coloring (it leaches into the cooking water, which turns bright pink — interesting for certain preparations like red okra pickles). Plants are more compact than many okra varieties (4–6 feet), making them practical for smaller gardens.

name: Red Welsh Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring once soil is workable, or in late summer for an overwintered clump; despite the name this is an Asian-origin perennial scallion, not a true Welsh native, and it is happy in cool weather at either end of the season.
directions: Red Welsh Onion produces hollow, grey-green to blue-green stalks rising from a red-skinned, white-centered base, with the color deepening toward the root end rather than covering the whole plant. Harvest outer stalks continuously like scallions while leaving the center of each clump to keep growing, and expect the clump to widen to about a foot across in a single good season. Left unharvested into its second year, it sends up tall flowering stems topped with off-white globe-shaped flower heads that are highly attractive to bees and other pollinators, after which the clump can be divided to renew vigor and start new plantings. It tolerates a wide range of garden soils and, once established, can often be harvested in some form in every season of the year.

name: Red Wethersfield Onion
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Red Wethersfield is one of the oldest documented American onion varieties, originating in Wethersfield, Connecticut, where it was the commercial engine of an extraordinarily productive onion trade with the West Indies and Eastern Seaboard ports that began in the late 1600s and made the town famous throughout Colonial and Federal-era America.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost when seedlings are 6–8 inches tall; direct seed outdoors can also be attempted in early spring when soil is workable. Red Wethersfield (also called 'Large Red Wethersfield') is perhaps the oldest onion variety with documented continuous American cultivation, grown commercially in Wethersfield, Connecticut since the late 17th century; colonial-era records describe the Wethersfield onion trade as one of the most profitable agricultural enterprises of early New England, with flat-bottomed boats (called 'onion sloops') carrying Wethersfield red onions to New York, Boston, and West Indies markets. The medium to large (3–4 inch), flattened-globe bulbs have deep red-purple to dark crimson skin and white-to-pinkish flesh with a moderately pungent flavor that mellows to mild sweetness when cooked. A long-day variety suited to zones 3–7 northern growing conditions where summer day length exceeds 14–16 hours; the thick skin provides excellent storage quality with bulbs keeping 4–6 months when properly cured in a warm, dry location before transferring to cool storage.

name: Red Wine Velvet Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F, in loose, well-drained soil formed into ridges in full sun; Red Wine Velvet is a mid-season vining heirloom kept alive mainly by small seed-saving growers.
directions: Plant slips 12-18 inches apart in loose, well-drained soil ridged up for good drainage, and avoid heavily nitrogen-rich amendments that favor foliage over root bulking. Red Wine Velvet is a mid-season, normal-leaf vining heirloom sweet potato prized for its deep wine-red skin wrapped around moist, richly colored orange flesh, offering a striking contrast to the paler skin of standard commercial types like Beauregard. Yields run average rather than exceptional, which is part of why the variety has stayed a small-grower specialty rather than a commercial staple, but the flavor is sweet and the deep-red roots make an eye-catching addition to a home harvest basket. Dig once vines begin to yellow in fall and cure in warm, humid conditions for one to two weeks before storing to sweeten the flesh and toughen the skin.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Sweet Potato Production

name: Red Zinger Roselle
plantingNote: Direct sow after the soil has warmed or start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting out; Red Zinger is the roselle strain long associated with the tart, ruby-red herbal tea blend of the same name.
directions: Grow Red Zinger in full sun and warm, well-drained soil, spacing plants generously since the tall, reddish-stemmed bushes branch widely by late summer. It is a short-day plant that holds off flowering until the days begin to shorten in late summer, then quickly loads its branches with the thick, tart, deep-red calyces that give the tea blend bearing its name its characteristic color and tang. Harvest calyces within a week or two after the petals drop, while they are still crisp, since they toughen and lose quality if left too long on the plant. Dry the harvested calyces thoroughly for tea, or use fresh for syrups, jams, and sauces before the first frost ends the season.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa)

name: Red-Striped Greasy Pole Bean
plantingNote: Sow directly around a sturdy pole or trellis once the soil has warmed, since this vigorous climber needs support from the seedling stage onward.
directions: Pods on this Appalachian heirloom are about five inches long, lightly striped, and smooth-skinned in classic greasy-bean fashion, maturing to mottled brown seed. It is grown both as a quick-cooking snap bean while pods are young and tender, and left to dry fully for a flavorful shelling bean. Vines are long and productive, so plan for a tall support and regular picking to keep pods coming. Flavor is considered a step above ordinary snap beans by many Appalachian growers, which is part of why the greasy-bean tradition persists in home gardens.

name: Redventure Celery
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-10 weeks before last frost; transplant into rich, evenly moist soil after frost danger passes. Redventure holds up well to cool fall weather, making it a good candidate for a second, later-season planting.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun; Redventure is a stabilized modern breeding-line celery developed by plant breeder Frank Morton in the early 1990s from a cross of the tough, strongly flavored heirloom Giant Red celery and the smoother, more tender Ventura celery. The result combines brilliant red-to-magenta stalks and luminous emerald leaves with a chewy but non-stringy texture and a more intense, concentrated celery flavor than typical green cultivars. Because the flavor and color are so pronounced, Redventure is especially well suited to soups, stocks, and braises where its stalks and leaves add both color and depth rather than being eaten raw on their own. It is notably cold-tolerant for a celery, extending the usable harvest window well into fall.

name: Redwing Onion
plantingNote: Intermediate-day F1 hybrid; late-maturing, so transplants outperform direct seeding in most climates.
directions: Bred for the market grower who needs a red onion that actually lasts through winter, Redwing forms uniform, hard globes with thick, deep-red skins that resist bruising in storage. Start seed indoors under lights and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed, spacing plants to encourage full-sized bulbs. Its late maturity means it needs a full season, but the payoff is a storage onion whose color and firmness actually improve over months in a cool, dry room. Reduce watering as tops begin to fall and cure thoroughly before bagging for storage.

name: Regal Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed; Regal matures quickly and does well even in a shorter warm season.
directions: Regal was jointly developed by the USDA and the South Carolina and Texas agricultural experiment stations as a reliable, disease-resistant sweet potato for Southern home gardens and market growers. Its light orange skin and flesh give a classic sweet, moist baked texture, and broad resistance to common soil diseases and insect pests makes it more forgiving than many older heirlooms in beds that have grown sweet potatoes before. It matures a bit faster than many standard orange cultivars, which is useful insurance in a Gulf Coast garden where an early tropical storm can end the season abruptly. Grow it the same way as Beauregard or Centennial, in loose, well-drained, ridged soil in full sun.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

name: Regiment Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; excellent cold-soil germination suits very early sowing.
directions: Direct sow thinly into cool, moist, fertile soil as early as the ground can be worked, since Regiment germinates and establishes unusually well in cold soil. It produces dark green, semi-savoyed, arrowhead-shaped leaves on a fast-bunching plant that reaches harvest size in as little as five to six weeks, one of the quickest turnarounds among savoy-type spinach. Strong resistance to multiple downy mildew races keeps quality high through humid spring weather, and the leaves stay tender even as plants size up, reducing the pressure to harvest at a small stage. Cut whole plants at the base for bunching or pick outer leaves for a longer cut-and-come-again harvest.

name: Reid's Yellow Dent Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is above 55°F, in blocks of at least four rows for reliable cross-pollination; give this tall, vigorous dent corn deep, fertile soil and consistent moisture through pollination and kernel fill.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least four rows in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and keep the crop consistently watered through tasseling, silking, and kernel fill for full ears. Reid's Yellow Dent traces to a farm in Illinois in the 1840s and became, through decades of careful ear-to-row selection in the late 1800s, one of the most influential open-pollinated corn varieties in American agricultural history, serving as foundational breeding stock behind much of the hybrid corn later developed across the Corn Belt. It produces tall, sturdy stalks with well-filled ears of smooth, deep-yellow dent kernels, valued for grinding into cornmeal, livestock feed, and general grain use, with a rich flavor typical of good open-pollinated dent corn. Allow ears to dry fully on the stalk, or pull and cure them indoors on a dry rack, before shelling and storing the grain in a cool, dry, rodent-proof container.

name: Reisetomate Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost; give plants a long, warm growing season and sturdy staking, since the fused fruit clusters are heavier and more awkward than a normal tomato truss.
directions: A German novelty heirloom grown less for yield than for its bizarre fruit form: individual tomato segments fuse together as they develop into a lobed, rose- or brain-like cluster that can be broken apart by hand into bite-sized pieces, each with its own thin skin. The red-orange fruit is thin-walled and only moderately flavorful, so Reisetomate is best treated as a conversation-piece crop for gardeners with room for a vigorous, heavy-vining indeterminate plant rather than a primary sauce or slicing tomato. It needs a full, warm season to size up and is most reliable where summers are long and hot, making it a good fit for a Gulf South vegetable garden with space to spare.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds Variety Catalog

name: Rendidora Tomatillo
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes, spacing plants somewhat closer than sprawling types since Rendidora holds an upright habit; plant at least two for cross-pollination.
directions: Rendidora is a Mexican-improved tomatillo selection bred for a notably upright, self-supporting growth habit rather than the sprawling vines typical of most tomatillo varieties, making it easier to manage and harvest in a small garden bed without extensive staking. Its name, roughly translating to high-yielding, reflects its reputation for heavy, dependable fruit set: round, slightly flattened, pale yellow-green fruit that fills its papery husk fully at maturity with the classic tart, citrusy tomatillo flavor. The more compact, upright plants can be spaced closer together than standard sprawling tomatillo types, making Rendidora a good choice for raised beds and smaller Gulf Coast vegetable gardens where space for wide-spreading vines is limited. As with all tomatillos, plant at least two individuals to ensure cross-pollination and fruit set.
sources: Utah State University Extension — Tomatillos in the Garden

name: Renegade Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall for cool-season production, or in late winter for an early spring crop; Renegade carries resistance to numerous downy mildew races plus cucumber mosaic virus, and shows good bolt and cold tolerance suited to high-tunnel or open-garden winter production in the mild Gulf Coast climate.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; thin to 2-4 inch spacing and use thinnings in salads. Renegade is a spinach hybrid bred with resistance to numerous races of downy mildew along with tolerance to cucumber mosaic virus, giving it a broader disease package than most spinach varieties and helping it stay productive through the damp, changeable weather of a Gulf South winter. It also shows good bolt tolerance, holding a harvestable rosette longer into warming spring weather than many varieties. The upright, dark green leaves are well suited to both fresh eating and cooking. Harvest by cutting outer leaves for continued production or cutting the whole plant at the base once it has filled out.

name: Resisto Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips into warm, well-drained ridges after all frost danger passes; Resisto's broad disease resistance makes it forgiving of garden beds with a history of soil-borne sweet potato problems.
directions: Choose Resisto for a bed where previous sweet potato crops have struggled with soil insects or disease, since it was bred specifically for a broad combination of resistances rather than for any single standout trait. Developed jointly by the USDA and the South Carolina and Texas Agricultural Experiment Stations as a seedling selection from the older W-56 line, Resisto produces reddish-copper skin over dark orange flesh with notably high beta-carotene content and roots that store and can well. Vines are vigorous and open-pollinated, performing reliably across a wide range of Southern soils and summers. Cure roots in a warm, humid spot for about a week after digging to heal skin nicks and concentrate sweetness before moving them to long-term storage.
sources: Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (cucurbit.info sweetpotato records)
Clemson University / South Carolina Foundation Seed Association variety records
CIP and international sweetpotato breeding program parentage records

name: Revolution Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Revolution carries resistance to multiple races of bacterial leaf spot, cucumber mosaic virus, and Phytophthora root rot — a broad disease package well matched to the wet, humid disease pressure of Gulf South summers.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Revolution is a bell pepper hybrid bred for an unusually broad disease package, combining resistance to several races of bacterial leaf spot with tolerance to cucumber mosaic virus and Phytophthora root rot, a soil-borne disease that thrives in the heavy rain and poorly drained spots common in Gulf Coast gardens. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good sweetness if left on the plant. Because it resists both a major foliar disease and a major root disease, Revolution tends to hold up better than many varieties through a wet, humid growing season. Harvest at the green stage for milder flavor or allow fruit to fully ripen to red, and keep picking regularly to encourage continued production.
sources: seed catalog reference (Tomato Growers Supply Company, Holmes Seed Company)
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pepper Production

name: Rezista Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring or fall; in zone 9 sow January–March for spring or September–October for fall. Rezista's primary value is extreme heat tolerance that allows it to produce harvestable lettuce through zone 9 warm springs when standard varieties have bolted. Provide shade cloth (30%) in late spring to extend the season further.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Rezista is a heat-tolerant, slow-bolting European butterhead lettuce selected specifically for warm-climate production — it remains productive 2–3 weeks longer than standard butterhead varieties under heat stress before bolting, providing a meaningfully extended spring harvest window in zone 9 and making it one of the most useful warm-season lettuces for Gulf Coast gardeners. The medium-sized butterhead heads have soft, mild, tender leaves typical of the butterhead type, with a flavor and texture that are difficult to distinguish from standard butterhead when grown in cool weather. Rezista's key value is in the warm-spring transition period (March–May in zone 9) when most lettuces have given up but cool-season crops are still preferred over summer alternatives. Partial shade from established transplants or shade cloth reduces heat stress further during this critical period. Successive sowings every 3 weeks through winter maximize the productive season.
sources: Territorial Seed Company — Rezista Butterhead Lettuce
University of California Cooperative Extension — Heat-Tolerant Lettuce Varieties
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Warm-Season Lettuce Performance

name: Rhode Island Whitecap Flint Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks after soil has warmed; allow the full season to maturity since this is a long-season flint grown for dry cornmeal rather than fresh eating.
directions: This is the flint corn traditionally used to make Rhode Island jonnycakes, a cornmeal flatbread with a legal pedigree: Rhode Island law has at times specified that cornmeal sold for jonnycakes must be ground from whitecap flint grown in the state. Grow it in blocks for wind pollination and expect a single ear per stalk on tall, sturdy plants. Leave ears on the stalk until the husks dry and kernels are rock-hard, then finish curing indoors before shelling and grinding; the kernels have a hard, glassy texture that mills into the coarse, slightly sweet meal classic jonnycake recipes call for.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

name: Rhodos Escarole
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer for a fall crop, or in early spring for a quicker early-season harvest; Rhodos matures faster than heirloom Batavian types and tolerates a wider sowing window.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to allow heads room to fill out. Rhodos is a modern Batavian-type escarole bred for a fast, uniform habit with semi-savoyed, dark green outer leaves surrounding a naturally pale, self-blanching heart, sparing gardeners the need to tie leaves for blanching. It resists bolting and tipburn better than many older escarole strains, making it reliable for both spring and fall plantings. Harvest whole heads or strip outer leaves for a milder, less bitter flavor than curly frisee types.

name: Rhubarb Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep in fertile, well-amended soil; chard seeds are multi-germ clusters (1–4 seedlings emerge per seed), so thin after germination to 6–9 inches for full-sized leaves. Harvest outer leaves from about 30 days for baby greens, or wait for full-size at 55–65 days. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall and winter harvest; spring sowing in February–March provides excellent spring production.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in fertile, moist, well-amended soil; thin to 6–9 inches. Harvest outer leaves regularly to encourage continued growth — leaving some inner leaves promotes sustained production. Rhubarb Chard (also called Ruby Red Swiss Chard or simply Red Chard) is the classic red-stemmed form of Swiss chard, grown for centuries for both its striking ornamental appearance and excellent culinary value. The deep, vivid crimson-red to ruby-red stems and ribs contrast dramatically against the dark green, deeply crinkled leaves, creating one of the most visually attractive vegetables in the edible garden and making Rhubarb Chard a staple in ornamental kitchen gardens and edible landscape plantings. The name references the stems' resemblance in color (but not flavor) to rhubarb. The red pigmentation comes from betalain pigments — the same compounds in red beets — which are vibrant raw but bleed into cooking water, giving a pinkish tint to any cooking liquid and fading the stems somewhat when cooked. The leaves are excellent cooked like spinach or kale (sauté with garlic and olive oil is the classic preparation), and young leaves are delicious raw in salads. Rhubarb Chard is more heat-tolerant than spinach and more cold-tolerant than basil, occupying a useful niche as a year-round leaf vegetable in zone 8–9 gardens where it often grows through the winter as an important fresh green when other vegetables are unavailable.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Rhubarb chard variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Swiss chard variety comparison
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Swiss Chard Production

name: Richmond Green Apple Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and August for fall. Richmond Green Apple is harvested when the skin has turned from green to pale ivory-green with a slight yellowish tint — at this stage the flavor is at its sweetest and most apple-like. Do not allow fruits to turn fully yellow, which indicates over-maturity. The vines are vigorous and productive; provide a trellis for best air circulation.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; Richmond Green Apple is an Australian heirloom cucumber producing small, round, apple-shaped fruits of 2–3 inches diameter with smooth, pale green to ivory-green skin and crisp, exceptionally sweet, very mild, lightly perfumed white flesh with minimal seeds. The round shape and pale coloration are genuinely apple-like, and the name is descriptive — the flesh has a fresh, delicate sweetness with a faint floral note unlike the somewhat vegetal flavor of standard slicing cucumbers. The skin is thin and does not require peeling; the whole fruit can be eaten like an apple or sliced into salads where its elegant shape makes for attractive presentation. Richmond Green Apple has a reputation for very low bitterness and is considered by some cucumber enthusiasts the sweetest and most refined of the heirloom cucumber types. In zone 9 it performs well in the spring and fall cucumber seasons; the small fruit size and productive vines make it excellent for container growing on a small trellis.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Australian Cucumber Varieties
Seed Savers Exchange — Apple Cucumber Types
University of Queensland Extension — Australian Heirloom Vegetable Varieties

name: Riesentraube Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Riesentraube (German for 'giant bunch of grapes') is a 19th-century German heirloom cherry tomato that produces the most spectacular, enormous hanging clusters of small red fruits of any heirloom variety — clusters of 20–40 or more fruits per stem that cascade down the vine in a grape-like arrangement of extraordinary visual impact.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; provide substantial staking, caging, or trellis support as plants grow vigorously to 6–8 feet; Riesentraube benefits from pruning to 1–2 leaders for best cluster development and air circulation. Riesentraube is a German heirloom cherry tomato documented in American seed catalogs by the 1850s and one of the oldest cherry tomato varieties maintained in continuous cultivation; the name 'Riesentraube' translates as 'giant bunch of grapes,' which perfectly describes the plant's most distinctive characteristic — enormous, pendulous clusters of 20, 30, or even 40+ small (1–1.5 oz) round, red fruits hanging in tight, cascade-like grape formations from the indeterminate vines. Each individual fruit has a pointed blossom end, which together with the cluster arrangement gives the plant an unmistakable profile compared to modern cherry tomatoes. The flavor is rich, tangy, and well-balanced with classic cherry tomato sweetness; the pointed fruits with thicker skin crack less than many cherry types and hold on the cluster longer after ripening. Riesentraube is both ornamentally spectacular in the garden (the cascading clusters are genuinely striking) and extremely productive, with harvests continuing from midsummer through first frost.

name: Rijnsburger Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring; as a long-day type it needs the longer summer daylengths of northern latitudes to bulb well.
directions: Rijnsburger is a classic Dutch maincrop storage onion named for the bulb-growing region around Rijnsburg in the Netherlands, and it serves as the foundation strain behind many modern Dutch yellow storage onion selections still sold today. It forms large, uniform, globe-shaped bulbs with thin necks and a firm straw-to-bronze skin over crisp white flesh. Harvested bulbs cure well and are known for holding in storage from late summer harvest through the following winter and into early spring. Grow in fertile, well-drained soil with even moisture, and allow tops to fall over naturally before curing bulbs in a dry, airy spot.

name: Ring of Fire Cayenne Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Ring of Fire is an All-America Selections award-winning cayenne pepper developed by Park Seed — earlier-maturing and more compact than standard Long Red Cayenne, with upward-pointing fruits that ripen earlier (60–75 days) and can be dried in clusters on the compact plant for ornamental as well as culinary use; heat is typical cayenne range (70,000–85,000 SHU).
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 75–85°F; transplant after last frost into warm, well-drained soil; Ring of Fire is compact enough for containers (5-gallon minimum) and makes an excellent patio pepper both for culinary use and as an ornamental with upright clusters of ripening red fruits. Ring of Fire is an All-America Selections (AAS) award-winning cayenne pepper introduced by Park Seed that distinguished itself in AAS trials for its early maturity and compact plant habit compared to standard Long Red Cayenne types. Where standard Long Red Cayenne reaches 24–36 inches and takes 70–80 days from transplant, Ring of Fire is more compact (18–24 inches) and earlier (60–75 days), making it better suited for containers, shorter growing seasons, and gardeners who want cayenne peppers without managing large, sprawling plants. The fruits are classic cayenne in form — pencil-thin, 4–5 inches long, tapering to a point — and ripen from green through yellow to red in an attractive cluster that gives the variety its name; fruits remain attached to the plant well through ripening, making the loaded plant highly ornamental. Heat level is typical cayenne range (70,000–85,000 SHU) — significantly hotter than jalapeños and suitable for use in all traditional cayenne applications: fresh salsa, hot sauce, cayenne powder, drying into ristras, and as a heat element in cooking. Ring of Fire is particularly well-suited to Gulf Coast home gardeners who want a reliable cayenne producer through the long warm season.

name: Rio Verde Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 Gulf Coast gardens, sow in June-July for late-summer transplanting and a December-January harvest. Rio Verde is one of the longest-standing Texas A&M AgriLife-recommended cabbages precisely because it holds up through the lingering heat of a Gulf Coast September and October before sizing up in cooler weather.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 15-18 inches apart in rows 24-36 inches apart, and keep moisture even as heads begin to fill out. Rio Verde is a main-season hybrid cabbage bred for exceptional tolerance of heat and humidity, producing large, slightly flattened, dense blue-green heads that commonly reach 4-6 pounds without splitting even when harvest is delayed. It has been a long-running recommendation from Texas A&M AgriLife Extension and LSU AgCenter for southern fall gardens because it germinates and establishes reliably in late-summer heat that stalls many other cabbages, then finishes with good size and quality through the cooler months. Choose Rio Verde where a proven, widely adapted variety with a long track record in hot, humid climates matters more than novelty.

name: Rio Zape Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; a pole bean requiring 5–6 feet of support; drought-adapted from its desert Southwest origins, requiring less water than many beans once established.
directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost at the base of sturdy poles or trellises in full sun; Rio Zape is an ancient bean of Aztec and Hopi origin with distinctive dark purple-brown seeds streaked and spotted with maroon or lavender markings that fade to a deep chocolate color on cooking. It has an exceptional rich, chocolatey-earthy flavor with complex undertones — often called the best-tasting dry bean by chefs who discover it — and a creamy texture excellent in tacos, soups, and refried beans. Drought-adapted from its desert Southwest heritage; it performs well in hot, dry conditions where other beans struggle. A prized heirloom for serious bean enthusiasts.

name: Ripbor Kale
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 4-6 weeks before the last frost, or sow in summer for a fall and winter harvest.
directions: Direct sow or start indoors and transplant, giving plants ample room to reach their full upright height, and harvest lower leaves first as the plant continues growing from the top. This hybrid was bred as a red-purple counterpart to the popular green curly hybrids, with tightly ruffled maroon-purple leaves on tall, sturdy stems. Cold exposure deepens its color and sweetens its flavor, and its height makes it a striking option for both the vegetable garden and cut-foliage use.

name: Riverside Giant Rhubarb
plantingNote: Plant crown divisions in early spring, allowing extra spacing beyond typical rhubarb cultivars since Riverside Giant produces unusually large leaves and stalks. Work generous compost into the planting hole and keep young plants well watered until established.
directions: Plant crown divisions in early spring, allowing extra spacing beyond typical rhubarb cultivars since Riverside Giant produces unusually large leaves and stalks. Work generous compost into the planting hole and keep young plants well watered until established. This traditional English allotment variety is grown chiefly for its exceptional vigor and heavy yields, throwing thick green-to-pink stalks large enough to have made it a favorite for exhibition growers as well as home cooks wanting a high volume of stalks for freezing and preserving. Its productivity comes with a mild, less intensely tart flavor than some red-skinned cultivars, so it is often paired with strawberries or extra sugar in desserts.

name: Rivoli Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or again in late summer for a fall crop; Rivoli is an AAS-winning radish bred to grow large without becoming pithy, holding dense, crisp white flesh even at an oversized root diameter.
directions: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep into fertile, well-drained, loose soil in full sun as soon as the soil can be worked. Rivoli is an AAS-winning radish notable for growing to a substantially larger round size than most globe radishes — up to 2 inches or more across — while keeping its white flesh dense and crisp rather than turning pithy or hollow the way an oversized radish typically does, giving gardeners a bigger harvest window and more flexibility about exact pick timing. Its bright red skin and clean round shape make it visually appealing for slicing and garnishing as well as eating whole. Keep soil consistently moist for the best size and texture, and it was, at the time of its award, the first radish AAS winner in several decades — reflecting a genuinely useful improvement over standard varieties rather than just a color or shape novelty.
sources: All-America Selections — Rivoli Radish winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Robust Barley
plantingNote: Broadcast or drill in early spring as soon as soil is workable; Robust is a six-row spring malting barley bred at North Dakota State University for the Upper Midwest.
directions: Robust is a six-row spring barley bred at North Dakota State University that became a widely grown malting standard across the Upper Midwest for its combination of yield and acceptable malting quality. Sow into a firm seedbed as soon as the ground can be worked in spring, since the crop needs a long cool stretch to fill its heads before summer heat sets in. It carries moderate straw strength and performs reliably under the dry, continental growing conditions of the northern Great Plains. Swath or straight-combine once the kernels are hard and the straw has turned from green to gold, then dry and store the grain to protect its malting value.

name: Rocambole Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves 2–3 inches deep in October–November; Rocambole requires 6–8 weeks of vernalization below 40°F for proper bulb formation, making it best suited to zone 4–7. In zone 9, pre-chill cloves in the refrigerator for 6–8 weeks before planting to compensate for mild winters — or choose Creole garlic instead, which requires no pre-chilling.
directions: Plant pre-chilled cloves 2–3 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Rocambole is considered by most garlic connoisseurs to be the finest-flavored garlic group — rich, complex, deeply savory, and mellow with a characteristic lingering warmth and almost chocolate-like earthiness that no other garlic group fully matches. Named varieties include 'Spanish Roja,' 'German Red,' 'Killarney Red,' and 'Music.' The medium-sized, brownish-purple skinned bulbs contain 8–12 cloves per head arranged in a single layer. The paper wrapping is loose, almost shaggy, and the inner skins of individual cloves are characteristically streaked with purple-brown. Rocambole is a hardneck garlic producing a central flower stalk (scape) that should be removed in June to direct energy into bulb formation; scapes are edible and delicious in stir-fries and pestos. In zone 9, Rocambole requires refrigerator pre-chilling of cloves for 6–8 weeks before October planting, or better yet, substitute Creole garlic, which is naturally adapted to mild winters without chilling. Rocambole stores only 3–5 months.
sources: Ron Engeland: Growing Great Garlic, Filaree Farm Press 1991
Seed Savers Exchange — Rocambole garlic documentation
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Hardneck Garlic notes
Keene Organics — Rocambole garlic variety descriptions

name: Rocky Ford Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; Rocky Ford reaches peak flavor in dry, hot summer conditions and performs best in climates with hot days, warm nights, and low humidity — it is excellent in the arid Southwest and Mountain West but somewhat prone to fungal diseases in humid Gulf Coast conditions.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; harvest when stem slips easily from the vine ('slip' stage) and the blossom end is slightly soft. Rocky Ford is the historic heirloom cantaloupe variety that made the Arkansas River Valley around Rocky Ford, Colorado famous for melon production in the late 19th century — producing medium-sized, netted, round to slightly oval fruits with bright green skin under tan netting and pale green to orange flesh with exceptional sweetness and classic old-fashioned cantaloupe flavor. The variety was so famous that 'Rocky Ford' became synonymous with high-quality cantaloupe across America in the early 20th century, and special rail cars shipped Rocky Ford melons to Chicago, New York, and other major cities during the peak season. Rocky Ford performs best in dry climates with hot days and cool nights (like the high-altitude semi-arid conditions of Colorado) where low humidity reduces fungal disease and water-stressed plants concentrate sugars at maturity. In humid Gulf Coast conditions it requires careful disease management, but dedicated heirloom melon enthusiasts appreciate its distinctive flavor, which has a more complex, old-fashioned character than modern hybrids.
sources: Colorado State University Extension — Melon Production
Seed Savers Exchange — Rocky Ford cantaloupe variety history

name: Rocotillo Pepper
plantingNote: Start on a heat mat 6–8 weeks before last frost; Rocotillo is a traditional Caribbean seasoning pepper related to the habanero but with minimal heat (1,500–2,500 SHU), prized entirely for its intensely tropical, fruity habanero aroma and flavor with none of the fire — a favorite seasoning pepper in Cuban, Puerto Rican, and Dominican cooking.
directions: Germinate on a heat mat at 80°F; transplant outdoors after frost when soil is warm and nights are above 60°F. Rocotillo is a Capsicum chinense seasoning pepper of Caribbean origin that looks remarkably like a miniature, squashed habanero with its distinctive ribbed, round, flattened form — but carries minimal heat (1,500–2,500 SHU) while retaining the intensely fruity, tropical, citrusy habanero aroma that makes this species unique; it is used in Cuban, Puerto Rican, Dominican, and Venezuelan cooking wherever the habanero flavor without the fire is desired. The small, round, ribbed fruits ripen from green through yellow to orange or red and are used fresh in sofrito, salsas, sauces, and seasoning blends. Related to and sometimes confused with the aji dulce (sweet habanero) and cachucha peppers of the Caribbean. Highly productive in hot weather; perennial in zone 9b–12.
sources: Dave DeWitt's The Chile Pepper Encyclopedia
University of the West Indies Agricultural Research

name: Rocoto Canario Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 12-14 weeks before the last frost, as this pubescens type is notoriously slow to germinate and needs a long season to mature.
directions: Start seed indoors 12-14 weeks before the last frost, as this pubescens type is notoriously slow to germinate and needs a long season to mature its blocky, irregularly shaped fruit. Pods hold black seeds and thick, juicy flesh typical of rocoto, ripening to a bright yellow with heat ranging from moderate to fiercely hot (roughly 10,000-60,000 Scoville units). Plants form a more compact bush than typical rocoto and, like other pubescens types, set fruit best where summer nights stay relatively cool.

name: Rocoto Chocolate Pepper
plantingNote: Sow indoors 12-14 weeks ahead of the last frost; performs best with some afternoon relief from peak summer heat, since pubescens sets fruit poorly above roughly 90°F.
directions: Sow indoors 12-14 weeks ahead of the last frost, giving this rare rocoto selection the long, patient start every pubescens variety demands. Medium-sized fruits mature to a distinctive chocolate-brown, with the thick, crunchy walls and fruity, apple-like heat characteristic of the species. Because pubescens sets fruit poorly above roughly 90°F, plants perform best with some afternoon relief from peak summer heat in hot-summer regions.

name: Rocoto Perón Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 12-14 weeks before the last frost, well ahead of standard peppers, since pubescens seed is slow and erratic to germinate.
directions: Start indoors 12-14 weeks before the last frost, well ahead of standard peppers, since pubescens seed is slow and erratic to germinate. Unlike the round, apple-shaped manzano rocoto, the Perón type produces elongated, pear-shaped pods with thick, juicy walls that hold up especially well to stuffing and roasting. Deep purple flowers and fuzzy, hairy foliage distinguish the plant from every other cultivated pepper species, and it tolerates cooler nights better than typical warm-season chiles.

name: Rodelika Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow into deep, loose, fertile soil in full sun; Rodelika was bred for high sugar content, making it a favorite for home juicing.
directions: Direct sow into deep, loose, fertile soil in full sun; Rodelika is a German biodynamic carrot bred at Dottenfelderhof and registered in 1998, producing long, blunt, deep orange-red roots prized for their unusually high sugar content. It matures in about 75-80 days and is a favorite among home growers for fresh juicing as well as general kitchen use, and it stores well through winter. Thin seedlings early to give roots room to reach full length and sweetness.

name: Roderique Shallot
plantingNote: Plant divisions in fall in mild-winter regions for a late-spring harvest, as is traditional in south Louisiana, or in very early spring where winters are severe.
directions: Roderique is a French banana-type shallot that French settlers brought to south Louisiana in the 1700s, where it became a Creole kitchen-garden staple still grown from saved bulb divisions rather than seed. Its tall, narrow, uniformly copper-skinned bulbs are white-fleshed and quick to peel with a single slice up the side, and each planted bulb is a highly productive multiplier, typically dividing into six to twelve new shallots in a season. Reduce watering once the foliage yellows and falls over, then lift, cure in a warm airy spot, and store; properly cured bulbs keep for nine to twelve months, among the longest storage life of any shallot type. Save a portion of the best bulbs each year to replant and keep the heirloom line going.

name: Rodina Beet
plantingNote: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep in loose, stone-free soil 2-4 weeks before last frost; the smooth cylindrical roots slice into uniform rounds.
directions: Direct sow in loose, fertile soil in full sun as soon as the ground can be worked in spring. Rodina produces long, smooth, tubular roots with a dark red color and blunt end, a shape that yields uniform slices from end to end and makes it a favorite for pickling and processing. Its dark green tops are notably slow to bolt and show good tolerance to common leaf diseases, so plantings stay productive longer into summer heat than many round beet types. Because the roots size up evenly along their length, successive sowings give a steady, predictable harvest for fresh eating or canning.

name: Romance Nantes Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow thinly; carrot seed is tiny and needs consistent moisture for the 10–21 day germination period. In zone 9, sow August–November for fall and winter harvest when carrots are at their best; spring planting (February–March) is possible but quality diminishes as temperatures rise. Romance is a Nantes-type hybrid: 7–8 inch, blunt-tipped, cylindrical, uniform roots. Thin to 2–3 inches after seedlings establish (3 weeks after germination); crowded roots become forked and deformed. Romance is noted for excellent crack resistance — roots hold in the ground without splitting even when mature, which extends the harvest window.
directions: Sow seeds 0.25 inch deep in loose, deep, well-worked soil free of rocks and clods; thin to 2–3 inches. Keep soil consistently moist until germination. Romance is a Nantes-type hybrid carrot from Bejo Seeds, a Dutch vegetable breeding company with a long history of Nantes-type carrot refinement. The Nantes type — originating in the Nantes region of western France — defines a carrot form that differs fundamentally from the long Imperator types common in grocery stores: Nantes carrots are shorter (6–8 inches vs. 9–11 inches), blunt-tipped rather than tapering to a point, rounder in cross-section, and notably sweeter with more tender, less fibrous flesh. Romance carries Nantes-type characteristics to a high standard: the roots are uniformly 7–8 inches long with a clean, blunt Nantes tip, bright orange interior color throughout (no pale core), very high sugar content, and notably fine-textured, tender flesh that makes Romance excellent for eating raw as well as cooked. The crack resistance that gives Romance particular value means that unlike some other sweet, high-sugar varieties that develop radial cracks if left in ground too long, Romance holds well after reaching maturity — a practical advantage for home gardeners harvesting over weeks rather than in a single commercial harvest. Fall-grown carrots in zone 9 achieve maximum sweetness as cold nights concentrate sugars in the roots.
sources: Bejo Seeds — Romance carrot F1 hybrid variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Nantes carrot variety comparison
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Carrot Variety Evaluation Guide

name: Romanesco
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10–14 weeks before desired transplant date (July–August in zone 9 for a fall transplant); plant out in September–October in moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Romanesco produces its characteristic spiraling, lime-green fractal heads (a naturally occurring example of a logarithmic spiral and Fibonacci sequence) and has a milder, nuttier flavor than either standard broccoli or cauliflower.
directions: Start seeds indoors 10–14 weeks before transplanting; plant in moderately fertile, well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; cover heads as they develop to maintain lime-green color if desired. Brassica oleracea var. botrytis 'Romanesco' (Romanesco or Roman broccoli) is a variety of Italian origin — known since the 16th century in Rome — that produces one of the most visually spectacular vegetables in existence: a tightly packed head of lime-green, spiraling conical florets arranged in a precise logarithmic spiral following the Fibonacci sequence, creating a fractal pattern of remarkable mathematical beauty. Each floret replicates the overall head shape at a smaller scale, in a perfect example of self-similar fractal geometry visible to the naked eye. The flavor is equally noteworthy: milder, sweeter, and nuttier than both standard broccoli and cauliflower, with a crisp-firm texture that holds up well when roasted or steamed. Romanesco requires similar growing conditions to cauliflower — it is the most temperature-sensitive of the three major brassica heading types, requiring consistent temperatures during head formation for proper development; heat causes premature bolting or loose, irregular heads. In zone 9, grow as a fall crop, planted September–October for December–February harvest. The stunning heads make excellent centerpiece dishes and are highly popular at farmers markets.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Brassica Production
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Romanesco Cultural Information
Slow Food Foundation — Romanesco di Verona Ark of Taste

name: Romanesco Artichoke
plantingNote: Transplant rooted divisions or seedlings after last frost into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Romanesco is the traditional round-headed heirloom type long grown around Rome and typically needs a full season or overwintered crown before it flowers heavily.
directions: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil worked with compost, siting plants in full sun with room to form a large clump. Romanesco is a classic Italian heirloom type from the countryside around Rome, producing broad, rounded, purple-flushed green buds with fleshy, nearly spineless scales and a tender heart, the type traditionally used for carciofi alla romana. As a true perennial type it is slower to reach full production than seed-grown annual hybrids, generally needing an established second-year crown for its heaviest harvest, though in mild coastal climates it can be grown as a long-season annual from an early transplant. Cut buds while the scales are still tightly closed and before they begin to spread open for the best flavor and texture.
sources: Slow Food Foundation -- Ark of Taste
University of California Cooperative Extension -- Artichoke Production Guide

name: Romano Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil near a support structure; Romano is the Italian flat-podded snap bean standard in Italian and Mediterranean cooking, prized for its wider, flatter pods, tender texture when cooked, and rich, nutty flavor that is distinctly superior to standard round snap beans for braising and sautéing.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in warm soil after last frost; provide a 5–6 foot trellis or teepee for the vines and begin harvesting when pods are flat and 4–5 inches long, before they string. Romano is the classic Italian flat-podded or 'Italian flat bean,' a pole type with wide, flat, 5–7 inch pods that have a different texture and flavor profile from standard round snap beans when cooked — more tender, less fibrous, with a rich, earthy, slightly nutty flavor that makes them the preferred snap bean for Italian sautés (fagioli in padella), long-braised dishes with olive oil and garlic, and agrodolce preparations. The flat pods become stringy if left to mature too long; harvest when pods are still flat and not yet showing bean bulges. A bush Romano type is also available. Highly productive in warm climates; excellent for Gulf Coast spring and fall bean production.

name: Ronde de Nice Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-amended soil; Ronde de Nice is a classic French Provençal heirloom round zucchini, the traditional squash for stuffing in the Niçoise manner — the small, round fruits are hollowed out, filled with herbed meat or rice, and baked or braised in tomato sauce in what is arguably the definitive French stuffed squash preparation.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in well-amended, well-drained soil after last frost in full sun; Ronde de Nice is a bush-type that needs 2–3 feet of space and no support. Ronde de Nice is a French heirloom round summer squash of Provençal origin, the classic stuffing squash of Niçoise cuisine (courgettes rondes farcies à la niçoise) and one of the oldest and most culinarily significant French kitchen garden varieties still in regular cultivation. The fruits are perfectly spherical, 2–4 inches in diameter, with smooth, thin, pale to medium green skin and tender, mild, cream-colored flesh that has a somewhat denser texture than elongated zucchini — well-suited to stuffing as it holds its shape better during cooking. Harvest at 2–3 inches for fresh eating and 3–4 inches for stuffing; slightly larger fruits (4–5 inches) can still be stuffed but become seedy. Highly productive and heat-tolerant; excellent for Gulf Coast spring and fall production.

name: Ronde de Valence Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant only once nights stay reliably warm; Ronde de Valence is an early, rustic French variety that sets fruit well even on the shorter side of the eggplant season.
directions: Ronde de Valence is a traditional French market eggplant named for the city of Valence on the Rhône, long grown in home gardens of southern France for its smooth, glossy, deep purple-black fruit that fades to pale greenish-white at the stem end. The medium-sized rounded fruits form on compact, rustic, heavily productive plants that tolerate variable conditions better than many finicky heirloom types. Grow it in full sun on fertile, well-drained soil with even moisture, and harvest while the skin is still glossy and taut for the sweetest, least bitter flesh. Its round shape and creamy, non-bitter interior make it a good all-purpose eggplant for stuffing, grilling, or classic ratatouille.
sources: Kokopelli Seed Foundation — Ronde de Valence Heirloom Eggplant
Ferme de Sainte Marthe — Aubergine Ronde de Valence
Exotic Seeds — Ronde de Valence Eggplant Seeds

name: Rongai Lablab
plantingNote: Direct sow 1-1.5 inches deep after soil has warmed above 65°F and frost danger has passed; Rongai is a late-flowering, photoperiod-sensitive lablab selection bred to stay vegetative and keep producing heavy biomass well into fall rather than setting seed early.
directions: Direct sow into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after all danger of frost has passed, inoculating seed with a cowpea-type Rhizobium inoculant for best nitrogen fixation in fields with no prior lablab history. Rongai is a vigorous, twining lablab selection valued as a summer cover crop for its late, photoperiod-triggered flowering, which keeps the plant putting energy into leafy vine growth and root nodulation for months rather than shifting early to seed production, producing an unusually heavy mat of biomass that smothers weeds and builds organic matter. It climbs readily on trellis, fence, or companion crop and can also be grown as forage or green manure, mowed or rolled and left as mulch, or turned under ahead of a fall planting. As a legume, it fixes substantial atmospheric nitrogen through root nodule symbiosis and tolerates heat and drought once established, making it a reliable warm-season soil builder for the Gulf South growing season.

name: Rooster Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces once soil has warmed past frost risk; this red-skinned, yellow-fleshed variety needs a full season to bulk up its round, shallow-eyed tubers.
directions: Rooster was bred in 1990 at the Teagasc Oak Park research centre in Carlow, Ireland, by potato breeder Harry Kehoe, and went on to dominate Irish potato growing, accounting for roughly a third of national production by the mid-2000s. Plant seed pieces into well-worked, well-drained soil and hill the rows as shoots emerge to keep the dull red skins from greening. The floury yellow flesh holds its shape just enough to make Rooster a true all-rounder in the kitchen, equally good boiled, mashed, roasted, or chipped. Lift maincrop tubers once the foliage dies back in autumn and cure them briefly before storing in a cool, dark, frost-free space.

name: Roquette Arugula
plantingNote: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost as soon as soil can be worked; in zone 9 sow October–March for fall through spring harvest. Roquette bolts quickly in warm weather — sow in succession every 2–3 weeks for continuous harvest through the cool season. In zone 9 the fall sowing in October–November produces the best quality, most flavorful crop before the plant bolts in warm spring weather. The small white flowers that appear when the plant bolts are edible with the same peppery flavor as the leaves.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil; Roquette is the Italian heirloom arugula variety — the specific selection used for millennia in Italian cuisine that gave arugula its character and reputation as the quintessential Italian salad green. The deeply lobed, dark green leaves have the intense peppery, nutty, slightly bitter flavor that defines the arugula experience — more pronounced than milder modern selections. The flavor becomes sharper and more assertive as the weather warms (approaching bolting), while young winter-grown leaves are milder and more delicate. Roquette's use in Italian cooking spans from the simple classic of arugula, shaved Parmesan, and lemon in a pizza topping, to fresh salads with olive oil, to pasta dishes and antipasto plates across Italy. The small, lobed leaf shape and strong flavor make Roquette the most authentic form for Italian culinary preparations. The partial shade tolerance allows it to be grown under taller plants in a kitchen garden, extending the season slightly.
sources: Slow Food Presidia — Italian Heritage Arugula Varieties
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Arugula Production Guide
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cool-Season Salad Greens

name: Rosa Bianca Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm. In zone 9 start in January and transplant in March–April. Rosa Bianca eggplants reach eating quality when the skin shows the characteristic white-lavender blush and the fruits feel firm — overripe fruits turn yellow and develop bitterness. In zone 9 eggplant thrives in the heat and can be grown as a perennial, overwintering with light frost protection and returning to produce in spring.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil in the warmest available position; Rosa Bianca is an Italian heirloom eggplant producing large, round to slightly oval fruits with a beautiful rosy-lavender and creamy-white skin that lightens to nearly white at eating maturity — the name means 'pink and white' in Italian and accurately describes the distinctive pastel bicolor appearance that makes Rosa Bianca the most visually elegant of heirloom eggplant varieties. The white to very pale cream flesh has the mildest, least bitter flavor of any eggplant variety — traditional eggplant bitterness is largely absent in Rosa Bianca, which has a delicate, sweet, slightly creamy taste that has made it the preferred eggplant of Italian chefs for generations. The flesh does not need salting before cooking as most other eggplant varieties require. The large, bulbous fruits (6–8 inches across) have a spongy, moist texture that absorbs olive oil and seasonings beautifully in roasted, grilled, and baked preparations — particularly in traditional Italian dishes like caponata, parmigiana, and grilled vegetable preparations.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Rosa Bianca Italian Heirloom Eggplant
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Italian Eggplant Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Specialty Eggplant for Florida

name: Rosa di Gorizia Radicchio
plantingNote: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a late-fall and winter harvest; the rosette only forms its namesake shape and loses bitterness after repeated hard frosts, so growers in the variety's native Friuli-Venezia Giulia traditionally dig and trim roots after freezing weather, then force new pale growth in cellars or covered beds through winter.
