directions: Rosa di Gorizia is a prized open, loose-rosette radicchio from the countryside around Gorizia in Friuli-Venezia Giulia, forming elongated pink-and-cream leaves with white ribs that fan outward into a shape resembling a rose once cold weather arrives. Unlike closed-head radicchio types, plants are often lifted after the first hard frosts, trimmed of outer leaves and roots, and set in sand in a cool cellar or cold frame to blanch and sweeten further before the final winter harvest. Give plants a long, cool growing season and avoid rushing summer sowings, since heat keeps the rosette green and bitter. Harvest after repeated freezes for the sweetest flavor and most vivid rose coloring.

name: Rosalie Roselle
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed; Rosalie is a bushier, more compact roselle selection bred to set a heavier crop of thick red calyces on a smaller frame than older tall roselle strains.
directions: Sow Rosalie in warm, fertile soil after the soil has warmed well past 70°F, since roselle seedlings are frost-tender and slow to establish in cool conditions. This selection branches low and fills out into a dense, rounded bush that carries a heavier concentration of plump, deep red calyces per plant than taller heirloom roselle types, making it a good fit for smaller vegetable beds or large containers. Like other roselle, it is day-length sensitive and begins setting flowers and calyces as days shorten in late summer, so harvest continues from late summer until frost. Pick the fleshy calyces about a week after the petals fall, while still tender, for fresh use, drying, or syrup.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa)

name: Rose de Berne Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; a vigorous 6-8 foot indeterminate vine that needs firm staking and shows good resistance to cracking.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil after frost risk passes. Rose de Berne is a classic heirloom from the Bern region of Switzerland, often described as the European counterpart to Brandywine for its reputation as one of the best-tasting pink tomatoes grown in France, Germany, and Switzerland. The smooth, deep-rose fruit has thin but durable skin and creamy, richly sweet-tart flesh. The vigorous 6-8 foot vines need firm staking and reward a long warm season with heavy, reliable yields.

name: Rose de Lautrec Garlic
plantingNote: Separate cloves and plant pointed end up, about 2 inches deep, in fall around the time of first frost; Rose de Lautrec holds Protected Geographical Indication status in France for garlic grown around the town of Lautrec in the Tarn region.
directions: Rose de Lautrec is a celebrated French softneck garlic named for the town of Lautrec, where it has earned Protected Geographical Indication status for its rose-pink-blushed skin and distinctive, refined flavor. Plant cloves pointed end up in loose, well-drained soil in fall, mulching lightly in colder regions to buffer winter temperature swings. Keep beds weed-free through spring and reduce watering as the lower leaves begin to brown ahead of harvest. Because it is a softneck type, the flexible stems can be braided for storage, and well-cured bulbs are prized in French markets for their long shelf life and delicate, slightly sweet garlic flavor.

name: Rose Finn Apple Potato
plantingNote: Plant seed potato pieces with 2-3 eyes per piece in cool soil; Rose Finn Apple is a late-season Scandinavian heirloom fingerling. In zone 9, plant January-February for a spring harvest before summer heat arrives.
directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil, hilling as vines grow; harvest when vines begin to die back. Rose Finn Apple is a Scandinavian heirloom fingerling potato with rose-pink to tan skin and creamy yellow flesh, valued for its smooth, dense, waxy texture and sweet, rich flavor that holds up especially well in roasting and potato salads. The elongated, knobby tubers form in loose clusters and the plant is a dependable, moderately productive grower. Being a later-maturing variety, it benefits from a full growing season; dig for tender new potatoes once flowering finishes, or let the vines die back naturally for mature tubers with better storage qualities. Like other fingerlings, its low-starch flesh keeps its shape well through cooking rather than turning mealy.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Rose Finn Apple variety notes
Wood Prairie Family Farm — Fingerling Potato Descriptions
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Fingerling Potato Comparison

name: Rose Gold Potato
plantingNote: One of the farm's best-selling varieties; plant seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost in hilled rows.
directions: Rose Gold is a mid-season potato with light red skin over golden flesh, grown on medium plants with dark pink flowers that set tubers moderately to heavily. It is marketed by its Maine grower as among the best of the red-skinned, golden-fleshed potatoes for its attractive round tubers and excellent, creamy mid-dry eating quality. High scab resistance pairs with only medium blight tolerance, so good air circulation and crop rotation help it reach its medium yield potential.

name: Rosella Purple Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Rosella Purple is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bred to bring rich, dusky purple-pink 'black' tomato flavor to a compact plant.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Rosella Purple bears medium fruit in a rich, dusky purple-pink, the deep, complex flavor typical of dark-fleshed 'black' tomato varieties, on a compact plant from the Dwarf Tomato Project bred to bring heirloom-quality flavor to gardens without room for a full-size indeterminate vine. Its manageable size suits raised beds and large containers. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

name: Rosita Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant once nights stay warm. Rosita was bred at Rutgers specifically for growers serving Puerto Rican and Caribbean markets.
directions: Rosita produces blocky, egg-shaped fruit with pale lavender-pink skin and creamy white flesh that stays mild and tender even as fruit sizes up, a trait bred in by Rutgers to suit fresh-market growers serving Caribbean and Latino communities. The vigorous, heat-loving plants set fruit reliably through hot, humid summers and hold up well without staking in most home gardens. Pick fruit while still glossy at 4-6 inches long for the best texture, since the thin skin means it bruises more easily than thicker-skinned purple types. Its milder flavor and lower seed count make it a good choice for cooks who find standard purple-black eggplant too bitter or seedy.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

name: Rossa di Chioggia Radicchio
plantingNote: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop, since plants grown in warm weather stay green and only redden as temperatures drop.
directions: Sow in mid-to-late summer for a fall crop, since plants grown in warm weather stay green and only redden and firm up as temperatures drop, with a light frost sweetening the flavor. Named for the lagoon town of Chioggia near Venice, this classic Italian radicchio forms tight, round, cabbage-like heads of deep wine-red leaves once cool autumn nights trigger the pigment. It is one of the most widely grown radicchio types in Italy and forms the template most people picture when they hear the word radicchio.

name: Rossa di Milano Onion
plantingNote: Intermediate-to-long-day heirloom; needs roughly 12-16 hours of daylight to bulb properly.
directions: A centuries-old open-pollinated onion from the countryside around Milan, prized for its teardrop-shaped bulbs with deep garnet skin and pink-streaked white flesh. Give plants rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture through bulb swell, then withhold water once tops begin to yellow and topple. Cure bulbs in a warm, airy location for two to three weeks before storage; this variety is noted for holding firm and flavorful well into winter. The rich, slightly sharp flavor mellows nicely when roasted or grilled.

name: Rostov Sunflower
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep and space closely, 8-12 inches apart, to encourage a single unbranched stalk; Rostov is a Russian open-pollinated oilseed cultivar, named for the Rostov-on-Don region, grown for small, high-oil, black-hulled seed rather than the large striped seed of confection sunflowers.
directions: Rostov is a traditional Russian oilseed sunflower bred for a single sturdy stalk topped by one large head up to 10 inches across, densely packed with small black seeds carrying an unusually high oil content compared to snacking types. It matures faster than many oilseed cultivars, typically finishing within about ten to thirteen weeks, which suits it to shorter growing seasons or a late-summer succession planting. Harvest once the back of the head turns from green to yellow-brown and the seeds rattle loosely, then cut the head and hang it to finish curing in a dry, airy, rodent-proof space before threshing. Whole seed can be cold-pressed for oil, roasted for snacking, or offered whole to backyard poultry and wild birds.
sources: Association Kokopelli — Rostov heirloom sunflower seed

name: Rotonda Bianca Sfumata di Rosa Eggplant
scientificName: Solanum melongena 'Rotonda Bianca Sfumata di Rosa'
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before transplanting; this heirloom has a medium-late cycle, so give it the full length of a hot Gulf Coast summer to size up its large, egg-shaped fruit fully.
directions: Rotonda Bianca Sfumata di Rosa is an Italian heirloom producing large, rounded, egg-to-pear-shaped fruit 5-6 inches across, with creamy white skin that gradually takes on a soft lavender-pink blush as it ripens. The firm, creamy white flesh is sweet and free of the bitterness found in many older eggplant types, so it needs no pre-salting before cooking. Its classic rounded shape and thick flesh walls make it especially well suited to stuffing and baking whole, in addition to standard slicing preparations. Harvest as soon as the rosy blush develops fully across the skin, since fruit left on the vine longer turns fully rose-colored and the texture coarsens.

name: Rouge d'Hiver Lettuce
plantingNote: Sow in late summer 8–10 weeks before first fall frost for a fall-into-winter harvest; Rouge d'Hiver is a French heirloom romaine lettuce bred specifically for cold weather production, surviving temperatures well below freezing and producing elongated, bronzy-red to burgundy heads through winter and early spring in zones 6–10.
directions: Sow in late summer in rich, moist, well-drained soil and thin to 9–12 inches; Rouge d'Hiver tolerates hard frost and is best grown as a fall-to-winter crop in mild climates, or with cold frame protection in colder zones. Rouge d'Hiver (Red Winter) is a French heirloom romaine-type lettuce bred for extreme cold tolerance — a critical trait in French kitchen garden tradition where gardeners have long maintained winter salad production under cloches and frames. The upright, elongated, semi-cos heads develop deep bronzy-red to burgundy coloring that intensifies in cold weather, with firm, crunchy texture and rich, slightly nutty flavor that is superior to most warm-season lettuces. In zones 8–10 it can be grown outdoors through winter without protection; in zones 6–7 it thrives in cold frames or low tunnels. One of the most valuable and underused lettuces for Gulf Coast and Southeastern winter salad gardens where it will produce from October through March.

name: Rouge et Noir Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Rouge et Noir is a sprawling bush-type Southern pea that sends out long runners, so give it room or light support even though it does not require a full trellis.
directions: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep after the soil has warmed; Rouge et Noir ('red and black') is a Louisiana heirloom Southern pea traditionally grown in Washington Parish, named for its seed color change from vivid red when freshly shelled to glossy black once fully dried. Long, slender pods up to about 10 inches hold as many as 18 seeds and can be picked young and cooked whole like a snap bean, or left to fill out for shelling and drying. The vigorous, drought-tolerant bush habit produces long running vines that sprawl well beyond the main crown, so allow generous row width or provide a low support. In Louisiana foodways this variety is traditionally simmered together with lima beans and fresh green peanuts, and the dried seed has also been roasted as a coffee substitute.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Rouge et Noir (Red and Black) Southern Pea variety notes
Truelove Seeds — African Diaspora Collection, Rouge et Noir field pea
Sistah Seeds — Rouge et Noir pea variety notes

name: Rouge Grenobloise Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–November for harvest November–February. Rouge Grenobloise is exceptionally cold-hardy for a butterhead type, surviving temperatures to 15–20°F, which makes it the standard butterhead for fall-through-winter production in zone 9. A spring planting in January–February provides a second harvest before heat causes bolting. The deep red color intensifies in cold weather — fall and winter heads are the most deeply colored.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Rouge Grenobloise is a French heirloom butterhead lettuce from the Grenoble region of southeastern France, selected for exceptional cold-hardiness in the alpine climate of the French Alps — its ability to withstand temperatures to 15–20°F makes it one of the most cold-tolerant butterhead lettuces available. The large, loose heads have deeply red-bronzed outer leaves with green-to-yellow-green interior leaves, creating a bicolor head that is visually striking at harvest. The flavor is the classic buttery, tender, mild butterhead type with a slight sweetness that intensifies with cold exposure — the deep burgundy-red outer leaves have a richer, slightly more complex flavor than the green interior. In zone 9 Rouge Grenobloise provides the most reliable fall-to-winter butterhead harvest of any lettuce variety, forming substantial heads from October plantings that are ready from November through February. Harvest whole heads or strip outer leaves for a continuing harvest.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Rouge Grenobloise Lettuce Variety Notes
Seeds of Italy — French Heirloom Lettuce Varieties
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Cold-Hardy Lettuce Types

name: Rouge Vif d'Etampes Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in deeply amended soil; the 'Cinderella pumpkin' of legend — deeply ribbed, brilliant red-orange, and flat like a coach wheel — sold at Parisian markets since the 1880s and still considered one of the finest pumpkins for French cuisine.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in enriched, well-drained soil, hills spaced 6–8 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill once true leaves appear. Rouge Vif d'Etampes — 'vivid red of Etampes,' the French market town where it was sold — is a century-old French heirloom pumpkin famous for its dramatically flattened, deeply ribbed, vivid red-orange form that resembles the coach from the Cinderella fairy tale; fruits weigh 15–35 pounds and have brilliant orange, fine-grained, dry, sweet flesh of outstanding quality for soups, gratins, and tarts in the French culinary tradition. Cure for 2 weeks at warm temperatures after harvest and store in a cool, dry place for up to 4 months; the unusual shape makes it a dramatic autumn centerpiece as well as an excellent culinary pumpkin.

name: Roulette Habanero Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; habanero types are slow to germinate and benefit from consistently warm soil.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun well after the last frost. Roulette delivers the fruity, citrusy flavor of a classic habanero pepper in thick-walled, dark red fruit, but with almost none of the characteristic heat, making it an AAS-winning option for cooks who want habanero flavor without the burn. Its productive, well-branched plants hold fruit upright for easy harvest and good air circulation. Because it has so little capsaicin, this variety is also a reasonable choice for gardeners who want to introduce kids or heat-sensitive cooks to habanero flavor.

name: Round Green African Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile soil after frost danger has passed. This heat-loving African eggplant has no frost tolerance.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed; Round Green African Eggplant produces round, green-and-white striped fruit about 4 inches across, maturing in roughly 90 days. The fruit is eaten boiled, fried, or simmered into sauces, often as a meat substitute in West African cooking. Like other Solanum aethiopicum types it thrives in heat and needs a full warm season to produce a good crop, performing especially well in hot Gulf Coast summers.

name: Round Winter Melon
plantingNote: Start indoors 3-4 weeks before the last frost and transplant into hot, fertile soil once nights stay above 60°F, giving vines a large trellis or ample ground space.
directions: A round-fruited strain of winter melon that develops large, globe-shaped fruit up to 14-22 pounds, in contrast to the more common oblong wax gourd types. As fruit matures it develops the characteristic waxy white bloom on pale green skin that gives the vegetable its storage-friendly reputation; whole melons can keep for months in a cool, dry spot after harvest. Its round shape and generous size make it the traditional choice for the banquet presentation known as dong gua zhong, where the entire hollowed melon is steamed and served as a soup tureen. Give the sprawling vines plenty of room or a very sturdy trellis with fruit slings, since ripe melons are heavy.

name: Roxanne Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or again in late summer for a fall crop; Roxanne is an AAS-winning early radish bred for strong resistance to pithiness and heat stress, holding good quality longer than most globe radishes.
directions: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep into fertile, well-drained, loose soil in full sun as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring; Roxanne is an AAS-winning globe radish producing uniform, bright-red, smooth roots with crisp, mild white flesh, bred for unusually strong resistance to the pithiness and hollow centers that often develop in radishes that sit in the ground a few extra days past ideal harvest size or face a warm spell. This forgiveness makes it a good choice for gardeners who cannot harvest on the exact first day of readiness. It matures quickly, in as little as 24 days, allowing several successive plantings through a spring or fall cool season. Keep soil consistently moist for smooth, fast-sizing roots, and harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch across for the crispest texture.
sources: All-America Selections — Roxanne Radish winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Roy's Calais Flint Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as danger of frost passes; among the most cold-adapted flint corns available.
directions: Direct sow as soon as danger of frost passes; this is among the most cold-adapted flint corns available and reliably dries down even in short, cool Vermont-style growing seasons. Roy's Calais Flint traces to Abenaki agriculture in the Calais, Vermont area and was preserved through the twentieth century by farmer Roy Fair before seed steward Sylvia Davatz continued growing and distributing it, making it one of the best-documented survival stories among Northeastern landrace corns. Ears show a striking mix of yellow, red, and burgundy kernels on the same cob, and the corn is prized both for cornmeal and for polenta with a distinctively rich, sweet flint-corn flavor.

name: Royal Burgundy Bush Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 60°F in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; the purple pod color disappears when Royal Burgundy is blanched or cooked — pods turn standard green, which some gardeners find surprising.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1–2 inches deep after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun, thinning to 4–6 inches apart; Royal Burgundy is a bush snap bean producing vivid deep-purple pods that are immediately striking in the garden and make harvesting easy — the bright-purple color stands out against green foliage so ripe pods are much easier to spot than the green pods of standard snap beans. The purple color comes from anthocyanin pigments that disappear completely when the beans are cooked — pods turn a standard snap-bean green when blanched or boiled, which is useful to know so the color loss is not mistaken for poor quality. The flavor is excellent: full, classic snap bean flavor with slightly more robust character than some modern hybrids. Royal Burgundy is notably cold-soil tolerant for a snap bean — germinating reliably in soil temperatures down to 60°F (versus the 65°F+ preferred by most snap beans), making it a good choice for early spring and fall plantings in zone 9 where soil temperatures can be borderline for bean germination. The bush habit (18–24 inches, no staking required) and reliable early productivity (50–60 days) make Royal Burgundy one of the more practical ornamental-vegetables for Gulf South kitchen gardens, combining harvest efficiency with decorative garden impact.

name: Royal Corona Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed, and set tall poles or a trellis at planting time; like other runner beans, flower and pod set slow down in extreme summer heat, so cooler-summer regions or a fall planting often perform best.
directions: Royal Corona was developed and popularized by California heirloom seed company Rancho Gordo as a domestically grown alternative to Italy's prized gigante beans, selecting a large-seeded white runner bean strain grown in Mexico's highlands for exceptional size and a dense, creamy texture. The oversized white seeds swell further when cooked, becoming meltingly tender while holding their shape, a texture prized for simple olive-oil-and-herb preparations that let the bean's quality shine. As with other runner beans, give plants tall, sturdy supports and consistent moisture, since shallow roots make the vines quick to stop setting pods in hot, dry conditions. Let pods dry fully on the vine before harvest, then shell and cure before storage.

name: Royal Crown Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, and again in late summer for a fall crop; roots mature quickly and hold quality well at either end of the cool season.
directions: Royal Crown is a fast-maturing F1 hybrid turnip grown for both its roots and its abundant dark green tops, making it a genuine dual-purpose crop rather than a greens-only or roots-only type. The slightly flattened, globe-shaped roots are smooth and creamy white with a bright purple-blotched crown, and stay sweet and mild if pulled small rather than left to size up. Because the leafy top is unusually productive relative to the root, it is a good choice for gardeners who want a steady cutting of turnip greens alongside a modest root harvest. Direct sow shallowly into loose soil and thin early, since crowded roots become misshapen.

name: Royal Roja Oca
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep after last frost in loose, well-drained soil; like other oca, tuber formation is triggered by shortening autumn day length.
directions: Royal Roja is a productive oca variety named for its striking bright magenta tuber skin, which holds its color well after cooking. Plant tubers in full sun to partial shade in loose, well-drained soil of nearly any pH, and grow exactly as other oca: the sprawling, clover-like foliage needs a long frost-free season to bulk up tubers, which form only after days shorten in autumn. Harvest after the first frost kills the foliage, typically in the November-to-January window. As with other oca, let freshly dug tubers sit in a sunny spot for several days to convert starch to sugar and mellow the tartness before eating.

name: Royalty Purple Pod Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Royalty Purple Pod germinates well in cooler soil than most snap beans (down to 55°F) — an advantage for early planting in zones 5–7 where it is often planted 2 weeks before the safe date for other beans. In zone 9, plant March–May or August–September. The purple pod color allows easy pod detection during harvest — the purple pods stand out visually against the dark green foliage, making picking faster and more complete than with green-podded varieties.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost; harvest pods when 5–6 inches long, while still tender and before the purple color begins to fade. Royalty Purple Pod is a 1976 All-America Selections-winning bush bean known for its striking deep purple pods — an unusual color in the snap bean world and a practical advantage because the vivid pods are easy to see against green foliage during harvest. The purple color results from anthocyanin pigments that disappear completely when cooked, leaving behind the standard green of cooked snap beans — a fact that surprises first-time growers who expect to retain the purple color. The flavor of Royalty is notably good — richer and slightly more complex than many modern bush bean hybrids — and the plants show slightly better cool-soil germination tolerance than green-podded snap beans. Royalty Purple Pod has maintained its status as a respected open-pollinated variety for nearly 50 years since its AAS award, used both as a practical garden bean and as a visual accent in edible landscapes where the purple-podded plants contrast attractively with green foliage.
sources: All-America Selections — Royalty Purple Pod bean AAS winner 1976
Seed Savers Exchange — Purple pod bean collection
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Snap bean variety comparison

name: RST-04-106 Rootstock Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors early alongside a favorite scion variety; graft the two together once stems are pencil-thick, heal in a humid shaded chamber, then transplant after frost into full sun.
directions: This widely used interspecific hybrid rootstock is grown to be grafted onto a favorite tomato scion variety rather than eaten itself, valued by home and market growers for moderate, manageable vigor along with broad resistance to fusarium and verticillium wilts, root-knot nematodes, and corky root rot that substantially extends productive plant life in soils with a history of these problems. Its more restrained growth compared to the most aggressive rootstock cultivars makes it a favorite for home high tunnel and small-scale market growers who want the disease resistance and yield benefits of grafting without an overly rampant root system demanding constant pruning. Start rootstock and scion seed together indoors, graft when stems are pencil-thick, heal grafted plants in a humid, shaded chamber for about a week, then harden off and transplant after frost into full sun with sturdy support.

name: Rubicon Napa Cabbage
plantingNote: Start seed indoors and transplant 8-10 weeks before the first fall frost for the classic autumn crop; Rubicon's bolt tolerance also allows a riskier late-summer direct sowing in cooler climates.
directions: Transplant into rich, consistently moist soil, keeping plants well watered to prevent tipburn and premature bolting. Rubicon forms dense, barrel-shaped heads with good resistance to fusarium yellows, making it a reliable choice where soilborne disease has hurt other napa types. Harvest when heads feel firm and heavy; the tight wrap holds well in the field and in cold storage. Its balanced sweet-mild flavor suits both fresh kimchi and quick stir-fries.

name: Ruby Ball Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9, set out transplants in late summer for a fall crop or in very early spring for a quick spring harvest before summer heat arrives. The compact, uniformly round heads mature quickly and hold in the garden for a week or two past maturity without splitting.
directions: Start seeds indoors six to eight weeks before the planned transplant date, then set hardened-off seedlings into full sun in fertile, well-drained soil. Ruby Ball is an F1 hybrid red cabbage that won an All-America Selections award in 1960 for its ability to form small, dense, perfectly round purple-red heads earlier and more uniformly than the open-pollinated red cabbages that were standard at the time. The compact three- to four-pound heads are notably crack-resistant and hold in the garden for a week or two past maturity, giving some flexibility in harvest timing. Like other red cabbages, Ruby Ball carries a sharper, slightly peppery flavor and higher anthocyanin content than green types, and it is well suited to coleslaw, quick braises, and short-term cold storage.
sources: All-America Selections — historical AAS vegetable winners list
Burpee — Ruby Ball Hybrid Cabbage variety description
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Cabbage Variety Guide

name: Ruby Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–March. Ruby chard is more ornamental than standard white-stalked chard — the deep crimson stems and dark green leaves are striking in kitchen and ornamental gardens. Harvest outer leaves continuously to extend production. In zone 9 Ruby Chard is productive from fall through early spring; it tolerates light frost and continues growing through mild zone 9 winters, providing fresh greens when little else is producing.
directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Ruby Chard is the classic red-stemmed Swiss chard variety with deep crimson-red midribs and stems against dark, slightly crinkled green leaves — one of the most ornamental of all vegetables and a perennial favorite in both kitchen gardens and edible ornamental designs. The striking color contrast of red stem against dark green makes Ruby Chard effective as a garden border plant, in containers, and in ornamental beds where most vegetables would look out of place. The same mild, slightly earthy, spinach-like flavor of all Swiss chard makes Ruby excellent for sautéing with garlic, adding to soups, and wilting into pasta dishes where the vibrant red stems retain some color even after cooking. As a dual-use ornamental and culinary vegetable, Ruby Chard demonstrates that the most productive kitchen garden plants need not sacrifice ornamental appeal. The partial shade tolerance makes it one of the better vegetables for partially shaded kitchen garden spaces.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Swiss Chard Production Guide
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Chard for Florida Gardens
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Leafy Greens for Gulf South

name: Ruby Crush Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Ruby Crush is a Texas Superstar determinate grape tomato bred with a broad disease resistance package, previously honored as a San Antonio Stock Show and Rodeo tomato before its Superstar designation.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Ruby Crush is a Texas Superstar-designated determinate grape tomato, compact enough for smaller garden beds and large containers, bred with a broad package of disease resistance that helps it hold up through the humid, disease-prone conditions of a Texas and Gulf South growing season. It produces heavy clusters of sweet, crack-resistant red grape tomatoes over a concentrated harvest window typical of determinate varieties, making it a good choice for gardeners who want a big, manageable crop for fresh eating or canning without the sprawling growth of an indeterminate vine. A light stake or cage helps keep the fruit-laden branches off the ground. Harvest regularly as fruit ripens to keep the plant productive through its season.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

name: Ruby King Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant outdoors once nights stay reliably above 55°F.
directions: Ruby King is an American heirloom sweet bell pepper documented since at least 1902 and preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange network after a 1977 donation. It sets heavy clusters of blocky, thick-walled fruit that ripen from green to a deep glossy red, with a mild, sweet flavor that holds up well fresh or cooked. Give plants full sun and consistent moisture, and stake or cage heavily loaded branches since the large fruit can weigh down stems. Its earlier maturity than many modern giant bells makes it a reliable choice for gardeners in shorter-season regions.

name: Ruby Perfection Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant out for a spring crop, or start in mid to late summer for a fall and winter harvest; Ruby Perfection is an All-America Selections winner bred for uniform, dense red heads and reliable performance.
directions: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before setting out sturdy transplants, or direct sow in late summer for a fall crop. Ruby Perfection, an All-America Selections winner, forms dense, round, deep reddish-purple heads that hold their color and quality well, both in the garden and in storage, on a compact plant bred for uniform heading and dependable performance across varying growing conditions. Its rich color makes it a striking addition to salads, slaws, and pickled preparations in addition to standard cooked use. Keep soil evenly moist through head formation to prevent splitting, and harvest when heads feel firm and dense to the touch.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Cabbage Production

name: Ruby Queen Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks after danger of frost has passed; plant alongside another sugary-enhanced variety to improve pollination and kernel fill.
directions: Ruby Queen is a sugary-enhanced hybrid grown as much for its deep ruby-red kernels as for its old-fashioned corn flavor, with 8 inch ears carrying 16 to 18 rows on 7-foot stalks. Harvest at the blush stage for the sweetest eating, or let ears ripen further to full red for a richer, more traditional corn taste; steam, grill, or microwave rather than boil to keep the color from fading into the cooking water. The red tassels and husks make the standing plants attractive in the garden and useful for fall decorating even before the ears are picked. Choose it when a gardener wants a novelty-colored sweet corn that still delivers genuinely good fresh eating rather than an ornamental-only variety.

name: Ruby Red Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow fall through early winter (September–November in zone 9) in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, moisture-retentive soil in full sun; Ruby Red chard is one of the most ornamental edibles for the vegetable garden — the brilliant crimson stems and red-veined, glossy dark-green leaves are as decorative as they are nutritious.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1/2 inch deep in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; thin to 6–9 inches; harvest outer leaves continuously. Beta vulgaris 'Ruby Red' (Ruby Red chard or Rhubarb chard) is a variety of Swiss chard selected for its dramatic, brilliant red stems (petioles) and red-veined dark-green to red-flushed leaves — making it simultaneously one of the most ornamental and one of the most nutritious crops in the vegetable garden. The vivid crimson stems get their color from betalain pigments (the same pigment group responsible for red beet color) which have antioxidant properties. The flavor is mild and slightly earthy, similar to spinach with a slightly stronger taste; the stems are firmer and need slightly longer cooking than the leaves. In zone 9, Ruby Red chard is a superb fall-through-spring crop, sown from September through November for harvest from November through May — it tolerates light frost and performs through the cool season until summer heat bolts it. The ornamental value is substantial: planted in rows or mixed borders, the glowing red stems create strong visual impact, making this one of the few vegetables that earns a place in ornamental beds. As with all chard, cut-and-come-again harvest extends production for months.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Swiss Chard
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Cool-Season Vegetables
North Carolina State Extension — Chard Production

name: Ruby Red Swiss Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow or start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9, sow September–November for fall and winter harvest, or February–March for spring. Ruby Red is one of the most cold-tolerant chard varieties, surviving light freezes and tolerating temperatures into the mid-20s°F in established plantings. The intense red stem color develops most vividly in cool fall and winter growing conditions — heat reduces the pigmentation intensity. Begin harvesting outer leaves once plants are 6–8 inches tall; regular harvest encourages continued production from the growing center.
directions: Direct sow 0.5 inch deep; thin to 9–12 inches. Harvest outer leaves regularly, leaving the growing center intact. Ruby Red Swiss Chard (also called Rhubarb Chard for the resemblance of the brilliant crimson stems to culinary rhubarb stalks) is the original and defining red-stemmed chard — the variety from which all colored-stem selections and rainbow chard blends derive. Ruby Red produces large, dark green, heavily crinkled and savoyed leaves on vivid crimson to ruby-red stems and midribs — a color combination that makes the plant one of the most ornamentally striking vegetables in the cool-season garden, visually dramatic against the dark green leaf tissue. The crimson pigment in Ruby Red's stems is betacyanin — the same class of pigment found in red beets (Beta vulgaris, the same genus) — a natural antioxidant with deep red to violet-red coloration. Ruby Red has longer American cultivation history than most colored chard types, appearing in American seed catalogs under 'Rhubarb Chard' nomenclature for well over a century. The flavor is classic chard — mild and slightly earthy-sweet when young, more substantial and beet-adjacent in mature leaves. The red stem color is retained reasonably well through steaming but bleeds in boiling water; roasting or sautéing in fat preserves the best color.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Ruby Red chard / Rhubarb chard variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Rhubarb chard variety notes
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Swiss Chard Variety Evaluation

name: Ruby Rhubarb
plantingNote: Set dormant crowns or divisions in early spring while still leafless, burying the crown bud just at or slightly below soil level in rich, well-drained ground.
directions: Ruby is an older English-raised rhubarb selection valued for stalks that stay a rich wine-red well up their length rather than fading to green partway, giving a more visually striking harvest than many all-purpose varieties. Flavor is bright and tart with the moderate acidity typical of good culinary rhubarb, making it well suited to pies, sauces, and preserves where color matters as much as taste. Divide crowns every four to six years once the center of the clump begins to thin, replanting divisions with at least one strong bud each. Skip harvest the first year after planting and take only a light cutting the second spring to let the crown build reserves for a long productive life.

name: Ruby Streaks Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer or fall (zones 7–11) or early spring (zones 3–7); Ruby Streaks is a deeply serrated, feathery, ruby-red to dark burgundy mustard green whose finely cut leaves resemble flat-leaf parsley in form but are dramatically larger, more colorful, and with the characteristic sharp mustard bite — it is the standard 'red frills' mustard in mesclun and salad mix production and one of the most visually striking cool-season greens available.
directions: Broadcast seed thinly or sow in rows 1/4 inch deep; for baby leaf harvest sow thickly and cut at 3–4 inches (2–3 weeks); for mature plants thin to 6–8 inches; harvest outer leaves or cut the whole plant at 4–6 inches above the crown for cut-and-come-again; the pungent flavor mellows with cooking. Ruby Streaks is a deeply serrated, feathery-leaved mustard green with deeply incised, almost pinnately cut leaves that create a lacey, frilly appearance dramatically different from the broad flat or ruffled leaves of traditional Southern mustard varieties — the leaf form is sometimes compared to flat-leaf parsley or baby arugula but scaled up and colored an intense burgundy-red to dark purple-red throughout. The name describes the appearance perfectly: the stems and veins are ruby-red while the deeply cut leaf tissue is a rich burgundy-maroon that becomes most intense in cold weather, making Ruby Streaks one of the most visually dramatic cool-season greens available for garden beds and mesclun mixes. The flavor is strongly mustardy with a sharp, spicy edge that makes it an excellent salad mix component providing flavor contrast to milder greens (lettuce, spinach, mild arugula) and visual color interest; young leaves (3–4 weeks) are mild enough for raw eating while mature leaves (5–6 weeks) have significant heat that benefits from brief cooking or a vinegar-dressed wilted salad. Ruby Streaks is one of the standard components of the premium mesclun salad mix sold under names like 'Braising Mix' and 'Asian Salad Mix' in American specialty markets.

name: Rubybor Kale
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; kale is also a strong candidate for fall planting since cool weather and light frost sweeten the leaves.
directions: Direct sow or start transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Rubybor is an AAS-winning curly kale that scored a Gold Medal in both ornamental and vegetable trials, an unusual double distinction, thanks to finely frilled leaves with deep purple stems and veining that hold their color even through summer heat. The leaves stay tender and mild enough for raw salads while remaining sturdy enough for cooking, and the compact, bushy plant produces roughly twice the yield of older red kale varieties. Harvest outer leaves from the bottom up as needed, and expect improved sweetness in leaves picked after a light frost.
sources: All-America Selections — Kale Rubybor F1 winner announcement

name: Ruddy Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil is warm above 65°F; Ruddy grows vigorously through a full Gulf Coast summer and rewards a long season with heavy yields.
directions: Ruddy is a fresh-market sweet potato released by North Carolina State University's breeding program, selected for its notably darker, deeper rose-red skin than Jewel or Beauregard, which makes it stand out visually at market and in home harvests. The flesh is moist, deep orange, and sweet, with smooth, uniform roots and good resistance to several common sweetpotato diseases. It grows vigorously in the long, hot Gulf Coast season and produces heavily from a modest planting of slips. Harvest before soil temperatures drop in fall and cure promptly to bring out its full sweetness and deepen the skin color further.

name: Rudolf Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in spring or 4-6 weeks before first fall frost; Rudolf is one of the fastest-maturing spring radishes available, producing smooth, bright red, round roots in as little as three weeks.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart. Rudolf is bred for extremely fast maturity, often ready to harvest in as little as three weeks from sowing, among the quickest radishes available, making it an excellent choice for gardeners wanting the fastest possible turnaround or squeezing in an extra succession planting before summer heat arrives. Roots are smooth, round, and bright cherry-red with crisp white flesh and a clean, mild flavor typical of quick-maturing spring radishes. Because it matures so fast, timing the harvest promptly is especially important, since even quick radishes turn pithy and hollow if left in the ground too long after reaching full size. Like all spring radishes, it bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather; in zone 9, fall and very early spring are the practical growing windows.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Rudolf Radish variety notes
Territorial Seed Company — Fast-Maturing Radish Varieties
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Radish Variety Trials

name: Rugosa Friulana Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills once soil is reliably warm; give the long, vigorous vines generous room to sprawl or train them up a sturdy support.
directions: Rugosa Friulana is a traditional Italian heirloom from the Friuli region prized for its warty, tan-beige rind and remarkably dense, sweet, deep-orange flesh, long favored in northern Italy for filling tortelli di zucca and other stuffed pastas. The pear-to-oblong fruit develops a rough, bumpy skin as it matures, a trait that distinguishes it visually from the smoother Marina di Chioggia despite both being Cucurbita moschata types from neighboring regions. Vines are vigorous and productive, so provide rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture through fruit development, then reduce watering as the rind hardens to concentrate sugars. Cure fruit in a warm spot for a couple of weeks after harvest before storing to further develop its characteristic sweetness.

name: Ruhm von Braunschweig Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant one- or two-year crowns in trenches enriched with well-rotted manure as soon as the soil can be worked; this older open-pollinated strain is dioecious, so expect both male and female plants in the bed.
directions: Ruhm von Braunschweig ('Glory of Brunswick') is a nineteenth-century German open-pollinated asparagus that became one of the standard garden and market strains across Central Europe for generations before modern all-male hybrids took over commercial production. It produces thick, well-flavored green spears on a vigorous, dioecious planting, with female plants setting red berries that can self-sow into a weedy stand if left uncollected each fall. Because every seedling varies slightly, older beds grown from this strain show more variation in spear thickness and timing than named hybrid crowns, which breeders prized as useful raw material for more uniform supermale lines. It remains historically important as a direct ancestor of modern Dutch all-male hybrids such as Franklim, bred from a supermale line developed through self-pollination of this very cultivar.

name: Running Conch Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil has warmed past 65°F and frost danger has passed; give plants a trellis, fence, or tall companion crop to climb, since Running Conch retains the rangy vining habit of its 19th-century Florida ancestors rather than growing as a compact bush.
directions: Sow directly in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun, and let the long vines climb a trellis or scramble over corn or sorghum stalks in the old co-cropping style. Running Conch belongs to the Conch group of cream-seeded southern peas, first documented along the St. Johns River in north Florida in the late 1800s and likely introduced from the West Indies. The narrow, slender pods hold medium-sized cream-colored peas prized for a delicate flavor and notably fast, easy cooking compared with other dried peas. Harvest pods green for fresh shelling once they fill out, or leave them on the vine to dry fully for storage peas; like other cowpeas it fixes nitrogen and tolerates heat and drought well once established.
sources: Sandhill Preservation Center — cowpea variety list
Utopian Seed Project — Conch southern pea seeds
Afroculinaria — history of the Florida field/conch pea

name: Runway Arugula
plantingNote: Direct sow every 2-3 weeks from early spring through fall; Runway was bred for a slower bolt response, extending the harvest window in warm weather compared to older arugula strains.
directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed shallowly into cool, moisture-retentive soil for fast, even germination. Runway produces smooth, rounded, dark green leaves with a clean, moderately spicy flavor and was selected by seed breeders for a notably slower bolt response, letting growers hold plantings longer into warm weather before they turn bitter and go to seed. It performs well both as a quick baby-leaf crop for salad mixes and, with wider spacing, as a full-size bunching arugula. Succession sow every couple of weeks for continuous cutting through the cool season.

name: Russet Burbank Potato
plantingNote: Plant seed potato pieces (each with 2–3 eyes) in cool soil; Russet Burbank is a late-season variety requiring 80–100 days and a long cool season to develop its characteristic large, well-formed tubers. In zone 9, plant January–February for a spring harvest (April–June), before summer heat forces the plant into dormancy. Russet Burbank performs better in cool climates (zones 3–7) than in zone 9, where the brief cool window and tendency for early spring heat can limit tuber size and number; varieties such as Red Norland or Kennebec may perform more consistently in zone 9. However, the Russet Burbank can produce good crops in zone 9 with January planting in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil. Harvest when vine tops die back and skins have set. Cure in a cool, dark location for 10–14 days before storage.
directions: Plant certified seed potato pieces in trenches 4 inches deep; hill soil around plants as they grow. Harvest when tops die back. Russet Burbank is the most economically important potato variety in the United States — the potato that defined American french fry culture and continues to be the dominant variety grown commercially in Idaho, Washington, and Oregon. The variety's history traces to Luther Burbank, the famous plant breeder of Lunenburg, Massachusetts, who developed the 'Burbank' potato in 1875 — a white-skinned, prolific variety. A natural bud sport of the Burbank with netted russet skin emerged in the late 19th century and was selected for its superior baking qualities: the russet skin variety produced the floury, high-starch, dry flesh that makes for the ideal baked potato — a fluffy interior with a crisp, well-cured skin that holds its shape. The high starch content of Russet Burbank also makes it the preferred variety for making french fries: when fried, the high starch content produces the crispy exterior and fluffy interior texture that defines the classic fast-food french fry. McDonald's adopted Russet Burbank (specifically the 'Russet Burbank' and later selected clones) as the basis for their standardized french fry program, and this relationship made the variety synonymous with American potato processing. The tubers are very large (often 8–16 oz), oblong, with rough russet-brown skin and bright white flesh — the visual standard for 'Idaho potato' that most Americans associate with baked potatoes.
sources: University of Idaho Extension — Russet Burbank variety history and commercial potato production
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Potato variety database and commercial statistics
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Cool-Season Potato Production in the Gulf South

name: Russet Norkotah Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost, or January-February in zone 9, well ahead of the longer maturity window; hill regularly to prevent sunburned, green shoulders before summer heat arrives.
directions: Russet Norkotah was released by North Dakota State University in 1987 and quickly became one of the most widely grown russet potatoes in North America, prized for its uniform, oblong tubers, attractive netted brown skin, and consistent yields. The dry, fluffy white flesh is a classic baking and frying russet that holds up well in storage after curing. Though bred for the northern Plains, it can adapt to a Gulf Coast winter-planted crop if seed pieces go in early enough to mature before summer heat arrives. Hill the plants as they grow to prevent sunburned, green-shouldered tubers and harvest once the vines die back.

name: Russian Banana Fingerling Potato
plantingNote: Plant whole small tubers or cut large ones with 1–2 eyes in January–February in zone 9; Russian Banana fingerlings are typically planted whole (they are small enough) rather than cut. They mature in 70–90 days and should be harvested before summer heat in zone 9 — target April–May harvest.
directions: Plant whole small tubers or cut pieces 3–4 inches deep in loose, rich soil; Russian Banana is the most widely grown fingerling potato in the United States, an heirloom variety brought from Eastern Europe (likely Latvia or Russia) by immigrants in the early 20th century. The distinctive, curved, 3–4 inch tubers with smooth, pale yellow skin and deep golden-yellow flesh look remarkably like small bananas when harvested and rinsed — hence the name. Flavor is exceptional: buttery, nutty, and intensely potato-tasting with the creamy texture of a waxy potato that holds its shape beautifully when roasted, boiled, or pan-fried with herbs. Russian Banana fingerlings have become the premium specialty potato at farmers' markets and upscale restaurants because of their appearance, flavor, and versatility. Harvest when plants begin to die back; fingerlings store well in a cool, dark location after curing. In zone 9, plant January–February for April–May harvest. The small size makes them quick to cook — roasted whole with olive oil and rosemary, they are outstanding.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Russian Banana Fingerling documentation
Wood Prairie Family Farm — Fingerling potato varieties
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Fingerling Potato variety notes

name: Russian Giant Scorzonera
plantingNote: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep as early as 2-4 weeks before last frost into deeply worked, stone-free soil; roots fork badly in compacted or rocky ground.
directions: Russian Giant is a high-yielding European scorzonera selection grown for its long, sweet, black-skinned roots with creamy white flesh. Sow thinly and directly in the garden, since scorzonera resents transplanting, and thin seedlings to 4-6 inches apart once established. Keep the deeply dug bed evenly moist through the long growing season to encourage straight, unforked roots. Roots can be harvested in the first autumn but develop their best flavor after overwintering in the ground and being dug the following spring; peel freshly dug roots under water, since the cut ends ooze a bitter milky latex.

name: Russian Red Garlic
plantingNote: Separate bulbs into cloves and plant pointed-end-up 2 inches deep about a month before the ground freezes so roots form before winter dormancy.
directions: Russian Red is a cold-hardy hardneck long grown in the Pacific Northwest from stock originally brought over from Russia, producing a tall central scape and a moderate number of large, easy-to-peel cloves wrapped in reddish-brown-streaked skins. It wants a genuine winter chill to divide properly into cloves, so it performs best where soil freezes at some point each year. Cut or snap off the curling scape once it makes a loop or two to redirect energy into bulb size, and harvest when the lower several leaves have browned while a few green ones remain. Cure in a shaded, airy spot for several weeks before trimming and storing.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange growing guide

name: Rutgers Beacon Asparagus
plantingNote: Set crowns into a 6-8 inch deep trench as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, backfilling progressively through the season.
directions: Rutgers Beacon is an early dioecious asparagus hybrid developed at the Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station, part of the university's long-running asparagus breeding program that later produced the all-male Jersey series. Unlike the all-male supermale hybrids bred afterward, Rutgers Beacon includes both male and female plants, so some volunteer seedlings can appear in an established bed over time. It was grown across the Midwest and East Coast for its solid field performance before being largely superseded by higher-yielding all-male hybrids, and its male lines were themselves used as breeding stock for later Rutgers supermale releases such as Eros, Atlas, and Apollo. Give crowns two full seasons to establish before harvesting, then cut spears daily during the spring flush to keep the plant signaling new growth.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station
New Zealand Journal of Experimental Agriculture

name: Rutgers Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Rutgers is an indeterminate variety that performs well with staking or caging and produces reliably in a wide range of climates from spring through early fall.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Rutgers tomato is a historically significant American heirloom, developed in 1934 as a joint project between Rutgers University and the Campbell Soup Company, that became the dominant processing and fresh-market tomato in America from the 1940s through the 1970s — the reference standard for what a traditional American garden tomato should taste like. The medium-large (6–8 oz), slightly flattened, deep red, globe-shaped fruits have a firm but yielding texture with balanced sweet-acid traditional tomato flavor that is widely praised as a benchmark for real tomato taste in contrast to modern flavorless commercial varieties. Rutgers is neither the most disease-resistant nor the highest yielding tomato today, but it remains a beloved open-pollinated heirloom for gardeners who want authentic vintage tomato flavor, the ability to save seeds, and a piece of American agricultural history. The indeterminate plants reach 4–5 feet and benefit from staking; Rutgers is well-suited to the Northeast and mid-Atlantic where it was developed but grows well in most climates including the Gulf South in spring and fall seasons.
sources: Rutgers University New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station historical variety records
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Heirloom Tomato Varieties

name: Sadandy Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep once soil has warmed past 65°F and frost danger has passed; Sadandy is a fast, heat-tolerant Louisiana heirloom that can be succession sown every few weeks through midsummer for a continuous Gulf South harvest.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing seeds a few inches apart in rows and thinning if needed. Sadandy is a Louisiana heirloom purple hull-type southern pea prized for its unusually early maturity and heavy, concentrated fruit set on compact, bushy plants, letting gardeners get a full picking in one or two passes rather than the extended trickle typical of many purple hulls. Pods mature to a deep purple that shows clearly against the green foliage, signaling when the cream-colored peas inside are ready to shell, and the pods hold well without shattering even in Gulf Coast heat and humidity. Like other cowpeas its roots fix nitrogen, so it also serves well as a quick-turnaround soil-building crop between spring and fall vegetables. Harvest at the purple-pod stage for fresh shelling or let dry fully on the vine for storage peas.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Southern Pea Variety Trials
Mississippi State University Extension — Southern Pea Production Guide

name: Safari Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; in zone 9, spring-sow February–March and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Safari is a modern hybrid zucchini bred for a strong disease-resistance package, including tolerance to several common squash viruses and powdery mildew, which helps the compact, open bush stay productive and healthy later into the season than many older open-pollinated varieties manage in humid climates. The smooth, dark green, cylindrical fruit has tender, mild flesh typical of good zucchini, and the plant's heavy, sustained yield makes it a solid choice for gardeners who have struggled with squash bugs, vine borers, or mildew shortening the productive life of past plantings. Pick at six to eight inches long for the best texture, and harvest every day or two once fruit begins setting to keep the vigorous plant in steady production.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Saint Valery Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall (August–September in zone 9) in deep, loose, sandy loam or well-prepared raised beds; Saint Valery produces long roots (8–10 inches) requiring very deep, stone-free, loosened soil — amend heavy clay with raised beds or deep double-digging for good root development.
directions: Direct sow in deep, loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Saint Valery is one of the oldest and most prestigious heritage carrot varieties — a 19th-century French heirloom from the Normandy coast town of Saint-Valery-en-Caux, producing long (8–10 inches), tapered, vivid deep-orange roots with a smooth skin, blunt tip, and sweet, richly flavored orange flesh that is considered among the finest-flavored of all heirloom carrot varieties. The deep, saturated orange color (more vivid than many modern varieties) comes from very high beta-carotene content, giving Saint Valery both excellent flavor and outstanding nutritional quality. The long, tapering root form requires deep, loose, stone-free soil for straight, well-formed roots — in shallow or compacted soil, the roots fork and twist around obstacles. Raised beds filled with deep, friable, sandy loam produce the best specimens. In zone 9, Saint Valery is a fall and winter crop: sow in August or September for harvest from November through February when the cool temperatures bring out the characteristic sweetness that makes heritage carrots like Saint Valery memorable. Carrots actually improve in flavor after light frost exposure — the cold converts starches to sugars, intensifying sweetness. Leave in the ground and harvest as needed through winter rather than pulling the entire crop at once.

name: Sakata's Sweet Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-drained soil, or set 2-3 plants per hill; Sakata's Sweet has shown good tolerance of powdery mildew and fusarium wilt relative to many older open-pollinated melon types.
directions: Sakata's Sweet is an East Asian heirloom melon grown for centuries across the region before Sakata Seed Company in Japan rebranded and introduced it more widely; it has since been picked up by a handful of North American heirloom seed sellers. Fruit are small, oval to round, about the size of a baseball at ten to twelve ounces, with pale white-green skin that ripens to yellow-green and soft, barely green flesh that is smooth and notably sweet rather than strongly musky. The compact vines still sprawl in typical melon fashion but the modest fruit size makes it a good fit for smaller trellised plantings or raised beds. Grow on well-draining, fertile loam with consistent moisture at the soil line, and harvest as the skin fully yellows and develops a sweet fragrance at the blossom end.
sources: True Leaf Market — Sakata's Sweet Melon Seeds
Specialty Produce — Sakata Melons Information and Facts

name: Sakura Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Sakura is a vigorous indeterminate cherry tomato that needs a tall stake or trellis for its long fruiting season.
directions: Sakura is a widely grown F1 red cherry tomato prized by market growers and home gardeners alike for its combination of very heavy, early yields and fruit that resists splitting after rain far better than most cherry types. The small, round, bright red fruit hangs in long trusses with good classic cherry-tomato sweetness and holds well on the vine without over-softening. Provide a tall stake or trellis for the vigorous indeterminate vine, prune to a few main leaders for easier harvest, and pick regularly to keep the heavy-bearing trusses coming.

name: Sakura Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after the last frost in well-drained, loose soil in full sun; Sakura finishes well ahead of most Louisiana sweet potato releases, so it tolerates a later transplant date and still matures before fall weather turns.
directions: Plant certified slips in well-drained, loose garden soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing plants to allow vines room to run; Sakura is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release named for its deep purple skin wrapped around an unusual light purple flesh, giving cooked roots a soft lavender color rather than the deep violet of typical purple sweet potatoes. Its standout trait for Gulf Coast growers is speed — Sakura roots reach harvestable size in roughly 90 days from transplanting, well ahead of the 110-120 days most varieties need, which lets gardeners get a crop in even from a late-set planting or squeeze in an earlier harvest before hurricane season disruptions. Like other LSU AgCenter releases bred for the region, it carries resistance to southern root-knot nematode, a persistent problem in sandy Gulf Coast garden soil. Cure harvested roots at 85-90°F and high humidity for about a week to heal the skin and sweeten the flesh before storage.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Potato Research Station variety descriptions
LSU AgCenter — Seeds of Success sweet potato licensing program notes

name: Sakurajima Daikon
plantingNote: Direct sow in deeply worked, stone-free soil 12-16 weeks before the first fall frost; this landrace needs a long, cool finishing period to bulk up its enormous root.
directions: Sow directly since the massive taproot resents transplanting, and thin aggressively to give each plant a full 2-3 foot circle of loose, deeply tilled soil. Named for the volcanic island near Kagoshima where it originated, this cultivar can swell to 40-100 pounds while staying surprisingly dense and low-fiber compared to other giant radishes. Harvest before hard freezes and store in a cool root cellar; despite its size the flesh stays sweet and is prized locally for simmered dishes and pickling.

name: Salad Bush Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Salad Bush is a compact bush-type cucumber with vines spreading only 24–30 inches — approximately half the spread of standard vining types — making it well suited to raised beds, container gardens, and small gardens where standard cucumbers would take too much space. No trellis is required, though light support improves air circulation. Plant 2 per 15-gallon container for patio production.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; no trellis required for bush types, though light support improves air circulation and fruit quality. Salad Bush is a 1988 All-America Selections-winning slicing cucumber selected specifically for compact, bush-type growth that makes cucumber growing accessible in small gardens, raised beds, and large containers. Standard cucumber vines sprawl 5–8 feet in diameter and require significant trellis support; Salad Bush was bred to produce a compact plant (vines spreading only 24–30 inches) that fits in a large container or small raised bed section without consuming excessive space. The compact habit comes without sacrificing fruit quality: the 8-inch, dark green fruits have the same smooth, mild, sweet flavor and tender skin of the best standard slicing cucumbers, with good disease resistance including cucumber mosaic virus, scab, angular leaf spot, and powdery mildew. Fruit production is concentrated over a shorter window than vining types but can be extended with succession sowings 2–3 weeks apart. Salad Bush remains one of the most practical cucumber choices for balcony, patio, and small-space gardeners who want fresh cucumbers without a large garden footprint.
sources: All-America Selections — Salad Bush cucumber AAS winner 1988
Burpee Seeds — Container cucumber growing guide
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Cucumber Variety Trials

name: Saladmore Bush Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Saladmore Bush is a compact, semi-bush slicing cucumber (about 24 inches of spread) bred for strong disease resistance and small-space growing.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container. Saladmore Bush is an AAS-winning slicing cucumber bred for a genuinely compact semi-bush habit that still delivers a full-size harvest of straight, dark-green, 8-inch slicing cucumbers with crisp texture and mild, sweet flavor, on a plant that fits easily into small beds and large pots where a standard vining slicer would sprawl. It also carries strong resistance to several common cucumber diseases, giving it good vigor through a long summer season in humid climates. Keep soil evenly moist, especially as fruit is sizing, to avoid bitterness and misshapen cucumbers, and harvest regularly once fruiting begins to keep the plant productive.
sources: All-America Selections — Saladmore Bush Cucumber winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Salamander Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow shallowly in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; keep soil consistently moist while the head forms.
directions: Salamander was among the most widely grown lettuces of the nineteenth century, a black-seeded cabbaging type that forms a dense head of thick, heavily savoyed, deep green leaves. Its crinkled leaf texture and firm heart gave it good heat tolerance for its era, letting nineteenth-century gardeners hold it in the garden longer than many delicate butterheads of the time. The mature heads have a satisfying crunch and mild flavor typical of old cabbage-type lettuces, distinct from the smoother butterheads more common today. It is a worthwhile variety for gardeners wanting to taste a lettuce type that has largely fallen out of modern seed catalogs.
sources: William Woys Weaver - Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

name: Salanova Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Salanova is a breeding breakthrough lettuce series designed so that a single head, cut once at the base, falls apart into dozens of perfectly bite-sized, ready-to-eat baby leaves, dramatically speeding harvest compared to picking individual leaves by hand.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Salanova is a lettuce series bred specifically to solve the labor problem of harvesting baby salad greens leaf by leaf: each Salanova head grows as a tight rosette of dozens of small, uniform, bite-sized leaves attached at a single central core, so cutting the plant once at the base instantly yields a full bowl of ready-to-eat, pre-washed-looking salad leaves rather than a single lettuce head that needs chopping. It comes in multiple types — butterhead, oakleaf, and incised (frilly) forms in both green and red — allowing gardeners to plant a mix for varied color and texture in a single cutting. Because the leaves are already small, individual heads can be spaced fairly closely for high-density production, and successive sowings every two to three weeks keep a steady supply coming through the cool season. It bolts readily in summer heat, so plant in early spring and again in fall for the best results in zone 9, and provide afternoon shade for any late-spring or early-fall plantings that overlap with warm weather.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Salanova Lettuce Series notes
Territorial Seed Company — Salanova variety descriptions
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Baby Leaf Lettuce Production

name: Salt and Pepper Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Salt and Pepper is a parthenocarpic (sets fruit without pollination) compact vining cucumber that can be grown in tunnels or outdoors. In zone 9, plant March–May for spring production and August for fall. The parthenocarpic character means the plant produces fruit without bees visiting — an advantage in early spring or in protected tunnel growing environments where pollinator access is limited. Harvest at 3–4 inches before the characteristic speckled pattern begins to fade to solid cream — once the speckles disappear the cucumber has become slightly overripe and may develop a slightly bitter note. The compact vine (4–5 feet) does not require extensive trellising but benefits from support for cleaner, straighter fruit.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 12 inches. Harvest at 3–4 inches when speckles are visible. Salt and Pepper is an F1 hybrid cucumber that received All-America Selections recognition for its distinctive appearance and exceptional eating quality. The fruit skin is white to pale cream with characteristic dark green to near-black speckles distributed across the surface — the 'salt and pepper' pattern that gives the variety its name and makes it immediately visually recognizable. Unlike heirloom types with similar light-colored skin (such as Boothby's Blonde), Salt and Pepper is an F1 hybrid bred for the parthenocarpic (seedless) character that allows fruit set without pollination — the interior is nearly seed-free and extremely tender, with no tough seed cavity. The resulting texture is among the finest of any outdoor cucumber: exceptionally crisp, with virtually no bitterness, tender skin that requires no peeling, and very high water content producing a refreshing fresh-eating quality. Salt and Pepper produces abundantly and early — with the first ripe fruit typically appearing 57 days from direct sowing, making it one of the earliest-producing cucumbers available. For zone 9 gardeners, the early maturity and heat-set ability allow the variety to produce heavily in spring before summer heat becomes limiting, and the fall planting typically produces prolifically through October or November. The seedless character and very thin skin make Salt and Pepper one of the few cucumbers that market gardeners can sell without refrigeration for brief periods, as the intact skin and low seed cavity reduce the moisture loss that causes conventional cucumbers to shrivel.
sources: All-America Selections — Salt and Pepper cucumber AAS winner recognition
Harris Seeds — Salt and Pepper cucumber commercial production notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Parthenocarpic cucumber variety comparison

name: San Joaquin Jalapeño Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; San Joaquin forms a compact, upright bush around 30 inches tall that suits a large container as easily as an open bed.
directions: Start seed indoors at warm soil temperature and transplant after all frost danger has passed into full sun. San Joaquin is an AAS-winning jalapeño bred for a tidy, determinate bush habit that concentrates its heavy fruit set into a shorter window, often producing dozens of thick-walled, crack-resistant, roughly 4-inch pods per plant. Peppers hold mild jalapeño heat and can be picked green for classic use or left to ripen to red for a sweeter, still-mild flavor. The sturdy, compact plant needs little staking and performs well in containers, making it a good choice for smaller gardens wanting a big jalapeño harvest for pickling and stuffing.
sources: All-America Selections — Pepper jalapeno San Joaquin F1 winner announcement

name: San Marzano Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights stay above 55°F. In zone 9 transplant February–March for a spring crop and again in August–September for a fall crop, as the extreme summer heat causes blossom drop. San Marzano is an indeterminate vine requiring sturdy caging or staking.
directions: Plant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil with a sturdy cage or stake as San Marzano is a vigorous indeterminate vine reaching 5–6 feet or more. The elongated, plum-shaped fruits with pointed blossom ends are the gold standard for pasta sauce and canned tomatoes — they are low in moisture, dense in flesh, mildly acidic, and have few seeds, making them ideal for reduction into rich sauces. Prune to 2–3 main stems for the largest individual fruits; unpruned plants produce more fruits but smaller. This Italian heirloom from the Campania region near Naples has DOP status in Italy, though the variety sold in the U.S. performs very differently from its Italian counterpart under different soil and climate conditions.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Heirloom Tomato Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Production in Florida
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — San Marzano

name: Sandia Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Sandia is a medium-hot New Mexico-style green chile excellent for roasting at both the immature green stage and the fully ripe red stage. Harvest green peppers when they are full-sized (6–8 inches) for fresh roasted green chile use; allow remaining fruits to mature to red for dried red chile production.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 75–85°F; Sandia is a New Mexico State University-developed chile variety named after the Sandia Mountains near Albuquerque, bred to fill a flavor and heat niche between the mild Anaheim-type peppers and the hotter NuMex Big Jim — producing long (6–8 inch), meaty, thick-walled green chiles with a medium heat level (approximately 1,000–2,500 Scoville units) that provides a pleasant warmth without overwhelming heat and excellent roasted green chile flavor. The thick walls and dense flesh roast beautifully — the skin blisters and chars evenly while the interior steams to a silky, rich texture — making Sandia an excellent choice for all traditional New Mexico green chile preparations including green chile stew, chile rellenos, and roasted chiles packed in the freezer for winter use. As the fruits mature to red and dry, Sandia provides good red chile powder with medium heat and authentic New Mexico chile flavor. Sandia performs well in a wide range of climates including the humid Gulf South, where its thick-walled flesh resists decay better than thinner-walled varieties. One of the most important green chile varieties in the New Mexico tradition alongside NuMex Big Jim, Hatch, and Numex Joe E. Parker.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — Variety descriptions
