University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Chile Pepper Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Green Chile Production

name: Sandul Moldovan Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Sandul Moldovan is an Eastern European pink beefsteak heirloom that fruits reliably even in shorter, cooler summers.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil after frost danger passes, staking or caging the vigorous indeterminate vines. Sandul Moldovan is a pink beefsteak heirloom from Moldova valued for setting a heavy crop of smooth, meaty, 8-12 ounce fruit even where summers run shorter or cooler than the Deep South. The flavor is mild, sweet, and well balanced, with dense flesh and relatively few seeds that make it a good choice for slicing and canning alike. Maintain even soil moisture during fruit development to minimize cracking on the smooth-skinned fruit.

name: Sandy Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 2-4 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, and again in late summer for fall harvest; Sandy is a compact oakleaf lettuce, the first AAS lettuce winner since 1985, bred for slow bolting and strong powdery mildew resistance.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or late summer, thinning to about 8-10 inches apart since Sandy forms a compact, uniformly mounded loose head rather than a large sprawling plant. Named an All-America Selections winner as the first lettuce to earn the award since 1985, Sandy is an oakleaf type with a multitude of sweet, frilly, dark green lobed leaves, notable disease resistance (especially to powdery mildew), and a strong tolerance for heat and heat-stress bitterness that lets it hold quality well past when older lettuces would bolt. Its compact 10-12 inch mounded habit fits neatly into a flowerpot, raised bed, or tight garden row. Harvest by cutting whole loose heads at maturity, or pick outer leaves cut-and-come-again style for baby leaf salads in as little as 30 days.
sources: All-America Selections — Sandy Lettuce winner announcement
Park Seed — Sandy Lettuce variety description

name: Sangre Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces once soil is workable; this early-to-mid season red potato sizes up quickly for a June or early-summer harvest.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun; Sangre is a Colorado-bred round red potato developed for the western US fresh-market trade, prized for its smooth, bright red skin and shallow eyes that make for clean, attractive market tubers. The white flesh is moderately moist and holds its shape well when boiled, making it a solid choice for potato salads, roasting, and general table use. It bulks up earlier than many maincrop reds, making it a good option where an early harvest of good-looking red new potatoes is wanted. Grow it alongside a russet or yellow variety for a mixed-color early harvest.

name: Sangria Watermelon
plantingNote: Start indoors or transplant after soil is thoroughly warm; Sangria carries resistance to anthracnose and Fusarium wilt and produces the classic large, oblong shipping-type melon long grown across Southern watermelon country.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm; Sangria is a widely grown seeded watermelon hybrid bred with resistance to anthracnose and Fusarium wilt, giving it reliable performance in the hot, humid disease pressure typical of a Gulf South summer. It produces large, oblong, dark green-striped fruit in the classic 20-24 pound shipping-melon range, with firm, deep red, sweet flesh that holds up well to handling and short-term storage. The vigorous vines set fruit dependably over a long harvest window. Harvest when the ground spot beneath the fruit turns from white to creamy yellow and the nearest tendril has dried and browned.
sources: seed catalog reference (Harris Seeds, Rupp Seeds, Territorial Seed)

name: Santa Claus Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Santa Claus melon (Piel de Sapo = 'Toad's Skin' in Spanish) is a late-season Spanish heirloom with extraordinary keeping quality — mature fruits store for 3–6 months at room temperature, traditionally used to provide fresh melon for the Christmas holiday season, which gives it both its nicknames.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Santa Claus melon requires 90–110 days to maturity, so start early or choose a long-season location; it is well-suited to Gulf Coast and California gardens. Piel de Sapo (literally 'Toad's Skin') is a Spanish winter melon variety widely grown throughout the Iberian Peninsula and used as the Christmas melon (melon de invierno) because its extraordinary keeping quality — 3–6 months at room temperature without refrigeration — allows harvest in October to be enjoyed fresh through December and January. The large (8–15 lb), elongated-oval fruits have mottled green and yellow skin with irregular markings resembling a toad's skin (the Spanish common name); the flesh is pale green to white-cream with a sweet, mild, refreshing flavor different from the aromatic intensity of muskmelon types. Sold in American markets as 'Santa Claus melon' and widely available in Hispanic grocery stores year-round due to its storage ability. Requires full sun and a long, warm season; sets fruit reliably in Gulf Coast and Western gardens.
sources: Spanish Ministry of Agriculture Heirloom Variety Registry

name: Santa Fe Grande Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March. Santa Fe Grande is an outstanding heat-tolerant pepper that produces prolifically through the Gulf Coast summer and is highly resistant to tobacco mosaic virus.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Santa Fe Grande is a versatile wax-type pepper that ripens through yellow, orange, and finally red, with heat levels ranging from very mild at the yellow stage to moderately hot at full red maturity (500–1,000 SHU). This variety is particularly valued by Southern gardeners for its exceptional summer productivity — the plants set fruit even in high heat and humidity and continue producing well past the point where most pepper varieties slow down. The thick, waxy, cone-shaped fruits are 3–4 inches long with a crisp texture excellent for pickled peppers, fresh eating, and stuffing. Excellent disease resistance including tobacco mosaic virus.
sources: New Mexico State University Extension — Pepper Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pepper Production
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Hot Pepper Varieties

name: Santana Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil once nights stay reliably above 55F. Santana's tolerance of verticillium wilt makes it a dependable choice for gardens with a history of eggplant or tomato soil-borne disease.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil has warmed. Santana is a Dutch-bred hybrid eggplant selected for verticillium wilt tolerance and a heavy, extended set of glossy, deep-black, oval fruit on a vigorous, productive plant, making it a favorite of market growers who need consistent yields through a long season. The dense white flesh has few seeds and holds up well to roasting, grilling, and frying without becoming watery. Keep soil evenly moist and side-dress with compost or balanced fertilizer as fruiting begins to sustain production over the full harvest window.

name: Santé Onion
plantingNote: Plant sets or transplants in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Santé is a Dutch-bred long-day storage onion selected for uniform, semi-globe bulbs and strong disease resistance in the field.
directions: Santé is a widely grown European storage onion producing firm, semi-globe bulbs with tight straw-yellow skin and pungent, long-keeping flesh. Plant sets or young transplants in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing them to allow full bulb development, and keep the row weeded since onions are shallow-rooted and slow to establish. It has good field tolerance to downy mildew and onion white rot compared with many older cultivars, making it a dependable choice in humid climates. Harvest once most tops have fallen over, cure thoroughly in a warm, airy location, and expect several months of firm storage from well-cured bulbs.

name: Santorini Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into lean, fast-draining ground; this landrace is traditionally grown dry-farmed without irrigation, so established plants should be watered sparingly to concentrate flavor.
directions: Santorini's small, ribbed cherry tomato carries European PDO status and is traditionally dry-farmed in the island's porous volcanic ash, where roots chase moisture deep underground and fruit ripens intensely sweet, concentrated, and low in water content. Give it lean, extremely well-drained soil and withhold supplemental water once plants are established, since irrigation dilutes the characteristic flavor that makes this tomato prized for the fried tomato fritters (tomatokeftedes) of Cycladic cooking. Harvest in small clusters as fruit turns deep red, and expect a sprawling, somewhat untidy plant habit typical of island landraces grown for flavor rather than uniformity.
sources: Greek Ministry of Rural Development and Food

name: Santorini Fava
plantingNote: Direct sow in autumn once summer heat breaks, so the crop develops through the mild, rain-fed Cycladic winter and dries down before summer; this legume is not the broad bean (Vicia faba) despite the shared culinary name.
directions: Santorini fava is a small-seeded legume landrace, distinct from the broad bean despite sharing its common Greek name, grown on the island's volcanic soil without irrigation and holding European PDO protection. Sow thickly in well-drained ground in autumn and let the crop grow through winter rains with no supplemental water, since the plant's deep taproot is adapted to the island's dry farming tradition. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant before threshing, then simmer the small yellow-brown seeds into the creamy pureed dish, also called fava, that gives the crop its name. The lean volcanic soil and minimal irrigation are credited with the seed's fast-cooking texture and mild, slightly sweet flavor compared to related legumes grown in richer ground.
sources: Greek Ministry of Rural Development and Food

name: Sarah's Choice Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow 1-2 weeks after last frost once soil reaches 65F, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early; Sarah's Choice was bred by Dr. Brent Loy at the University of New Hampshire for unusually high sugar content and resistance to powdery mildew and Fusarium wilt.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, fertile hills after all frost danger has passed, planting 4-5 seeds per hill and thinning to 2. Sarah's Choice is a widely respected muskmelon bred by Dr. Brent Loy's public breeding program at the University of New Hampshire, selected for unusually high sugar content — commonly 14-15% Brix, well above many commercial cantaloupe varieties — along with resistance to powdery mildew and Fusarium wilt, two of the most common disease problems that shorten the productive life of melon vines. The medium-sized, heavily netted fruit has firm, deep-orange, aromatic flesh with excellent flavor. Reduce watering as fruits near maturity to concentrate sugars further. Ripe melons develop a sweet fragrance at the blossom end and slip easily from the vine with gentle pressure — the classic 'full slip' sign of peak ripeness. Avoid overwatering late in the season, which dilutes flavor and can cause fruit to split.
sources: University of New Hampshire — Brent Loy Cucurbit Breeding Program

name: Sardinian Spiny Artichoke
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant, or set out rooted suckers in spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Sardinia's mild, dry-summer climate suits long-lived perennial stools that are increased by division rather than annual reseeding.
directions: Spinoso di Sardegna is Sardinia's DOP-protected spiny artichoke, grown mainly on the island's southern plains where mild winters and sandy coastal soils support heavy perennial production of elongated, sharply spined, violet-green heads. The spines mark the outer bracts but not the tender heart and inner bract bases, which Sardinian cooks favor raw and thinly sliced with olive oil and pecorino, or stewed whole with fava beans in the classic spring dish carciofi e fave. Plants are long-lived perennials traditionally increased from rooted suckers rather than seed, forming dense clumps that remain productive for many years with periodic division. Full sun and deep, well-drained soil with a dry summer rest between crops suit this variety best.
sources: Regione Sardegna — Carciofo Spinoso di Sardegna DOP Disciplinare
European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register
Slow Food Presidia — Italian Heritage Artichoke Varieties

name: Sarpo Una Potato
plantingNote: The earliest-maturing variety in the Sarpo blight-resistant lineup; plant 4-6 weeks before last frost.
directions: Sarpo Una, imported from Hungary's Sarvari Research Trust, is the earliest-maturing member of the Sarpo family of potatoes bred specifically for outstanding late blight resistance. Medium plants with lavender flowers produce long, red-skinned, white-fleshed tubers with moderate-to-heavy tuber set and heavy overall yields. The waxy-moist texture suits soups, stews, and salads, and it also bakes and roasts well, combining strong disease resistance with very good eating quality.

name: Saticoy Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm and all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Saticoy is a California commercial cantaloupe variety bred with good resistance to powdery mildew and fusarium wilt, two diseases that shorten productive vine life in warm growing regions, helping the vine stay healthy and productive through a full summer season. The uniform, well-netted, orange-fleshed fruit has good sweet flavor and consistent size, traits that made it a reliable choice for commercial growers and equally useful for home gardeners wanting dependable production. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with a gentle tug and the rind's netting has turned from green to tan, and hold off on extra watering in the final week before harvest for the sweetest flavor.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Savanna Hybrid Mustard
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or late summer; Savanna tolerates more heat than most mustard without bolting, extending the harvest window on both ends of the season.
directions: Savanna is a fast-growing F1 hybrid mustard bred for exceptionally tender, smooth leaves and stems that stay mild and non-fibrous even as plants size up, letting the whole leaf and stem be harvested without trimming. It grows quickly enough to cut for baby salad greens within three weeks or left longer for a traditional cooked green, and its slow-bolting habit keeps it productive across a wider temperature range than older open-pollinated Southern mustards. Home gardeners and market growers choose it for cut-and-come-again harvesting, since new leaves regrow readily after cutting through the cool season.

name: Savannah Komatsuna
plantingNote: Direct sow from early spring through fall; Savannah tolerates more heat than many komatsuna types without bolting, extending the harvest window into warmer weather.
directions: Savannah is a komatsuna selection bred for improved heat and bolt tolerance compared to older Japanese mustard spinach varieties, letting it be sown over a longer part of the season. Leaves are smooth, glossy, and dark green on slender white stalks, with a mild flavor closer to spinach than to sharper mustard greens. Harvest whole young plants for salad mix or cut individual outer leaves from more mature plants, which regrow readily for repeat picking. It performs equally well raw in salads or lightly cooked in stir-fries and soups, wilting quickly like true spinach.

name: Savor Charentais Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into warm soil; Savor has good resistance to Fusarium wilt and intermediate resistance to powdery mildew, helping fruit finish well in humid climates.
directions: Savor is a mid-to-late French Charentais hybrid prized by market growers for combining classic Charentais eating quality with a notably long shelf life of up to two weeks after harvest. The small, slightly flattened, 1.5-2 pound fruit has faintly ribbed, smooth gray-green skin enclosing deep orange, intensely aromatic flesh. Because Charentais types only slip cleanly from the vine when fully ripe, inspect plants daily near the expected harvest window and look for a slight crack or softening at the stem end. Its disease resistance and extended keeping quality make it a reliable choice for roadside stands and farmers markets as well as home gardens.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Savor (F1) Melon Seed
Osborne Seed Company — Savor F1 Melon Seeds

name: Savoy Ace Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant out for a spring crop, or start in mid to late summer for a fall and winter harvest; Savoy Ace is an All-America Selections winner bred for reliable heading and the tender, crinkled leaves characteristic of savoy-type cabbage.
directions: Start seeds indoors about six weeks before setting out sturdy transplants, or direct sow in late summer for a fall crop, spacing plants to allow full head development. Savoy Ace, an All-America Selections winner, forms attractive, deeply crinkled, blue-green leaves wrapped into a dense, tender head, with the savoy type's characteristically milder flavor and more tender texture compared with smooth-leaf cabbage, making it excellent for salads as well as cooked dishes. It heads reliably even in less-than-ideal conditions that can cause other savoy cabbages to form loose or split heads. Keep soil evenly moist through head formation to prevent splitting, and harvest when heads feel firm when squeezed.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Cabbage Production

name: Savoy Express Cabbage
plantingNote: Start transplants 4-6 weeks before setting out; set out 8-12 weeks before first fall frost for the classic autumn crop, or 3-4 weeks before last spring frost for an earlier spring crop, since Savoy Express matures notably faster than most savoy cultivars.
directions: Savoy Express is a fast-maturing, compact savoy cabbage bred to bring the deeply crinkled, tender-leaved character of savoy types to gardeners in far less time than standard savoy cultivars, forming smallish, round, moderately dense heads in about two months from transplant. Its early maturity and small footprint make it a good fit for succession planting, small raised beds, and gardeners in short-season climates who still want the delicate, sweet flavor and tender texture savoy cabbage is prized for. Like other savoy types it tolerates hard frost well and improves in sweetness after cold exposure, though its quick maturity also lets it beat summer heat in a spring planting where standard cabbages would bolt or turn bitter. Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and rotate with non-brassica crops on a three-year cycle to prevent clubroot buildup.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Savoy Express cabbage variety notes
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Cabbage Variety Trials

name: Savoy King Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9, start in July and transplant late August–September for November–January harvest. Savoy King's crinkled leaves make it the most cold-hardy of common cabbage types — the loose, blistered structure allows the cells to flex during freezing rather than rupturing. Use savoy cabbage raw in salads (the tender leaves are softer than standard cabbage), cooked in soups where the crinkled leaves add texture, or wrapped around meat for stuffed cabbage rolls.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to full sun, fertile soil. Savoy King is a 1965 All-America Selections-winning savoy (crinkle-leaved) cabbage — a type that differs fundamentally from standard smooth-headed cabbages in leaf texture, flavor, and culinary applications. Savoy cabbage produces the characteristic deeply blistered, puckered, crinkled leaves that make the head appear almost frilly compared to the smooth-skinned heads of standard green or red types. The crinkled texture comes from the faster growth rate of the leaf blade relative to the midrib — the excess blade tissue buckles and folds into the distinctive savoy pattern. Flavor-wise, savoy cabbage is notably sweeter, more tender, and less sulfurous than standard round cabbages — the crinkled leaves have a more delicate character that makes savoy preferred for raw salads (the soft, tender leaves wilt pleasantly rather than staying tough) and for elegant stuffed cabbage preparations where the flexible leaves wrap easily around fillings. Savoy King produces large (4–6 lb), well-domed, attractive heads with deep blue-green coloring and the decorative crinkled surface that makes it one of the most ornamental cabbages in the winter garden.
sources: All-America Selections — Savoy King cabbage AAS winner 1965
Burpee Seeds — Savoy King variety notes
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Savoy Cabbage Production and Variety Comparison

name: Sayamusume Edamame Soybean
plantingNote: Direct-sow once soil has warmed well past last frost, since seedlings are sensitive to cold, wet ground; a floating row cover can help hold heat for an earlier start.
directions: Sow seed about an inch deep in full sun, inoculating with soybean-specific rhizobium if soybeans haven't grown in the bed before. Sayamusume is a Japanese edamame heirloom valued for its large, elongated, light-green beans and reliably sweet, tender flavor, carried on upright plants with pods clustered two to four per cluster. Pick pods while still bright green and fully plump for fresh edamame, or leave plants to dry down further for shelling as dry soybeans. Steam or boil harvested pods briefly in well-salted water, then pop the beans free to eat as a snack or use in salads and stir-fries.

name: Scallopini Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil, thinning seedlings to give each compact bush adequate airflow to reduce powdery mildew risk.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil, thinning seedlings to give each compact bush adequate airflow to reduce powdery mildew risk. Introduced in the mid-1970s as an All-America Selections winner, this cross between zucchini and pattypan types yields small, dark-green scalloped fruit with a mild, nutty flavor and tender skin that needs no peeling. Harvest young at 3-4 inches across for the best texture, picking every day or two once plants begin producing heavily. Its compact, non-vining habit made it a popular choice for small-space and container vegetable gardens when it was introduced.

name: Scarlet Frills Mustard
plantingNote: Sow in early spring or late summer; cooler temperatures deepen the maroon color and mellow the mustard's heat.
directions: This ornamental-edible mustard produces deeply fringed, almost lacy leaves in a rich burgundy-maroon that intensifies in cool weather and full sun. Direct sow into loose, fertile soil and thin to final spacing, using thinnings as spicy microgreens. Leaves can be harvested young for salad mix, where the color and frilled texture stand out, or left to mature for a peppery cooked green. Plants are attractive enough for mixed ornamental beds as well as the vegetable garden, but bolt quickly once summer heat arrives.

name: Scarlet Ohno Revival Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer or fall for fall harvest; Scarlet Ohno Revival is a visually stunning Japanese turnip with dramatic red-scarlet to magenta skin and flesh — one of the most beautiful root vegetables available — with mild, sweet turnip flavor at the small 2–3 inch stage; both the root and the brilliant red-tinged leaves are edible, making it a dual-purpose vegetable.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in cool weather; thin to 4–6 inches apart for best root development; harvest at 2–3 inches diameter for the sweetest, mildest eating quality; the red coloration intensifies in cool weather; the leaves can be harvested as greens throughout the season. Scarlet Ohno Revival (sometimes marketed as 'Scarlet Queen Turnip') is a Japanese turnip variety with striking visual characteristics: the round roots have vivid scarlet to magenta-red skin with pink-red flesh throughout — much more deeply and uniformly colored than the more common 'Tokyo' types — and the broad basal leaves have dramatic red-tinged stems and midribs that make the plant ornamental in the garden as well as functional. The turnip was selected from an older Japanese variety ('Ohno Scarlet') by seed savers and represents a revival of an older type that had become rare. At harvest size (2–3 inches), the roots have a mild, slightly sweet turnip flavor quite different from the sharp, peppery bite of older turnip types — the Japanese breeding tradition favors mild, salad-turnip types that can be eaten raw, and Scarlet Ohno follows this tradition. The roots are excellent sliced thin into salads (the red color is dramatic against green lettuce), quick-pickled in the Japanese style (the red pigment turns the pickling brine a beautiful deep pink), roasted with the skin on (which deepens the color), or used in any turnip recipe where visual impact is valued.

name: Scarlet Queen Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow two to four weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer for a fall harvest when cooler nights sweeten the roots.
directions: Sow seed shallowly into loose, stone-free soil and thin seedlings to a few inches apart so the globes can size up without forking. Scarlet Queen produces smooth, uniform roots with brilliant scarlet-red skin, crisp white flesh, and a reddish blush that runs up into the petioles, making it as ornamental as it is edible. Harvest while roots are still small to medium for the mildest, sweetest flavor, since the variety is bred for salad-turnip use rather than long storage. The colorful skin and tender texture make it popular sliced raw into salads or lightly pickled.

name: Scarlet Red Tatsoi
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for fall harvest; a red-pigmented sport of traditional tatsoi grown both for baby greens and mature rosettes.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or again in late summer, thinning to 6-10 inches apart for full rosettes or growing tighter for a cut-and-come-again baby-green harvest. The deep red-purple leaves intensify in cooler weather and hold their color well in salads or quick saute. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut the whole rosette at the base once it reaches full size, and expect the plant to bolt once daytime temperatures climb in late spring.

name: Scarlet Turnip White-Tipped Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow from 4 weeks before the last frost into late spring, and again in late summer for fall harvest; being a fast, small-rooted type it is well suited to tight succession sowing every 10-14 days.
directions: Sow 1/2 inch deep and thin to about 1-2 inches apart; harvest promptly once roots reach 1 inch across, as the globe shape turns pithy faster than elongated types if left in the ground. Scarlet Turnip White Tipped is an old French and American market-garden heirloom distinguished by its round, turnip-like shape rather than the oblong 'half-long' form of French Breakfast, with bright scarlet skin fading to white at the root tip. It was cultivated as a distinct forcing and early-market variety well before French Breakfast rose to prominence, and the two were listed as separate cultivars in nineteenth-century French seed catalogs. Its crisp texture and mild bite make it a good choice for growers wanting a quick round radish with more color contrast than solid-red types.

name: Scarlette Chinese Cabbage
plantingNote: Sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest; the longer maturity window needs an earlier start than standard green napa cabbage.
directions: Scarlette is a napa-type Chinese cabbage whose outer leaves develop a deep magenta-purple blush over crisp white midribs, giving whole or sliced heads a striking two-tone look that most green napa varieties can't match. Direct-sow shallowly in mid to late summer, allowing the full 70-plus days to maturity, and thin to 10 to 12 inches so heads can fill out properly. The color holds up well in slaws and quick pickles, where the contrast between purple leaf and white vein stays vivid even after dressing. Harvest when heads feel firm and dense, since the color intensifies as the head matures.

name: Schimmeig Striped Hollow Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; this German heirloom forms hollow, air-pocketed fruit prized for stuffing rather than dense slicing flesh.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil once nights warm, caging the indeterminate vines for support. Schimmeig Striped Hollow is a German heirloom whose red-and-orange striped fruit develops distinctive hollow chambers around the seed cavities instead of dense slicing flesh, a trait that makes it a novelty choice for stuffing with rice, meat, or grain fillings. Flavor is mild and the texture is notably different from typical slicing tomatoes, so it is grown more for its unusual form and culinary use than for fresh eating. Harvest when fully striped and firm, since overripe fruit can collapse at the hollow centers.

name: Schoon's Hard Shell Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; Schoon's Hard Shell is a heirloom muskmelon long prized for its exceptionally tough, durable rind that let it stand up to shipping and field handling far better than most old melon varieties, while still ripening to richly flavored salmon flesh.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after soil has warmed well past last frost, allowing ample room for the vigorous vines to sprawl. Schoon's Hard Shell is a long-season heirloom muskmelon producing large, oval, heavily netted fruits, 7-8 inches long and 5-8 lbs, encased in an unusually thick, tough rind that made it an outstanding shipper and field-stander in an era before refrigerated transport, while the thick red-salmon flesh ripens to an intensely sweet, richly aromatic flavor. Because it is slow to mature relative to modern hybrids, gardeners in shorter-season regions may want to start it a bit earlier or choose a warm, sheltered planting site. Keep soil consistently moist through vine growth and fruit development, then reduce watering as melons approach maturity, and harvest at full slip when the stem separates cleanly from the fruit.

name: Scotch Bonnet Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 10 weeks before last frost; Capsicum chinense is slow to germinate and requires warm soil (80°F+) and a long growing season. In zone 9 start in January for a March transplant date. The plants thrive in the Gulf Coast's summer heat and produce prolifically through the fall; they may overwinter in protected zone 9b–10 locations.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil and nights have thoroughly warmed; the Scotch bonnet is the defining pepper of Caribbean cuisine, particularly Jamaican jerk and Trinidadian cooking, with a distinctive fruity-floral heat (100,000–350,000 SHU) and a unique, tropical, almost fruity aroma that separates it from habanero despite the close botanical relationship. The small, flattened, wrinkled fruits ripen from green through yellow, orange, and red, and can be used at any ripe stage — the green stage has the most vegetal flavor while red fruits are sweetest and hottest. Unlike habaneros, genuine scotch bonnets have a more complex, sweeter aroma profile with notes of cherry and apple. The plants are tall and bushy, very productive in warm conditions, and benefit from staking as fruit clusters become heavy.
sources: University of the West Indies — Capsicum chinense in the Caribbean
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Specialty Pepper Production

name: Sea Island Red Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is warm and frost danger has passed; this okra traces to Gullah Geechee seed-keeping on Sapelo Island, Georgia, associated with matriarch Cornelia Bailey and later maintained through University of Georgia's research and education program at Wormsloe.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in full sun in warm, fertile soil; Sea Island Red is a moderately branching okra with striking dark red stems and velvety, lightly ridged red pods that run 6 to 8 inches at full size. It carries deep cultural significance as a Gullah Geechee coastal heirloom and remains rare in commercial seed trade, so growing it out and saving seed helps keep the line going. Harvest regularly at 3-4 inches for the most tender pods, and expect the ornamental dark coloring of stems and pods to make this a standout plant in the summer vegetable bed.
sources: Sow True Seed — Sea Island Red Okra
University of Georgia Center for Research and Education at Wormsloe

name: Sea Island Red Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; in zone 9 plant March–May for spring harvest and July–August for fall. Sea Island Red Pea is a deeply historic Gullah/Geechee heirloom preserved for generations on the sea islands of Georgia and South Carolina, recently revived as part of Southern food heritage preservation.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in any well-drained soil in full sun; the Sea Island Red Pea is a semi-vining, dark-red-to-brown speckled cowpea that was the foundation of Gullah/Geechee cuisine on the sea islands of Georgia and South Carolina from the colonial period through the early 20th century. The variety served as the original ingredient in hoppin' john and purloo dishes before black-eyed peas replaced it in most recipes. It is an exceptional-flavored cowpea with earthy, rich, deeply savory notes and a dense, creamy texture when fresh-shelled that surpasses commercial black-eyed peas in the estimation of many who have tasted both. The vine habit is moderate — plants sprawl 2–3 feet and may benefit from short supports. Revived through efforts by the Anson Mills and Slow Food USA Ark of Taste programs.
sources: Anson Mills — Sea Island Red Pea Heritage Grain
Slow Food USA Ark of Taste — Sea Island Red Pea
University of Georgia Extension — Georgia Heirloom Seeds

name: Sea of Red Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 2-4 weeks before last frost for spring harvest; Sea of Red is a deeply colored, frilly-leaved oakleaf lettuce that holds its intense burgundy-red color and resists bolting and bitterness longer than many other red lettuce varieties, making it a reliable performer through a wider harvest window.
directions: Sow on the soil surface and press in gently; germinate at 50-70F. Sea of Red is an oakleaf-type lettuce prized for deeply lobed, ruffled, deep burgundy-red leaves that stay glossy and appetizing-looking even as outer leaves are repeatedly harvested, making it a favorite for cut-and-come-again baby leaf production as well as full-head harvest. It holds its rich color and resists premature bolting and the bitterness that develops in many red lettuces once temperatures climb, giving it a somewhat longer productive window than more heat-sensitive varieties, though it still performs best in the cooler shoulder seasons in zone 9. Harvest outer leaves as needed for continuous production, or cut the whole loose head at once for a single larger harvest. Provide afternoon shade and consistent moisture for late-spring or early-fall plantings to further delay bolting as the weather warms.
sources: Botanical Interests — Sea of Red Lettuce variety notes
Territorial Seed Company — Oakleaf Lettuce Varieties
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Lettuce Variety Trials

name: Seaside Spinach
plantingNote: Sow in early fall while soil is still warm for a long fall-through-winter harvest window in mild-winter climates.
directions: Direct sow into well-drained beds and thin to stand a few inches apart, keeping soil consistently moist to support quick establishment in warm soil. This hybrid was bred with above-average heat tolerance and downy mildew resistance, allowing it to be sown earlier in fall or later into spring than many spinach types without bolting prematurely. Its dark green, savoyed leaves hold good texture and flavor even as temperatures rise, making it a strong pick for extending the cool-season window along the Gulf Coast.

name: Self Blanche Cauliflower
plantingNote: Start seed indoors for a spring crop, or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest; Self Blanche is a classic cauliflower whose leaves naturally curl inward over the developing head, largely eliminating the need to manually tie leaves for blanching.
directions: Start seed indoors for a spring crop or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, spacing transplants 18 to 24 inches apart. Self Blanche is a classic cauliflower variety whose outer leaves naturally curl inward to cover the developing head as it forms, largely eliminating the tedious task of hand-tying leaves over the curd to keep it white, a labor-saving trait especially appreciated by home gardeners growing more than a plant or two. It produces solid, well-formed white heads of good size and quality with this convenient self-blanching habit doing most of the work automatically. Check occasionally to make sure leaves are covering the head adequately, tying loosely if needed, and harvest promptly once heads reach full size before curds begin to separate or yellow.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Cauliflower Production

name: Selma Fino Fennel
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in mid- to late summer for a fall crop; Selma Fino is bred for reliable bulbing without premature bolting.
directions: Selma Fino is an Italian Florence fennel cultivar selected for large, heavy, uniform white bulbs and strong resistance to bolting when sown in cool spring conditions. Sow directly and thin seedlings so bulbs have room to swell, then hill soil around the base as the bulb develops to keep it blanched, tender, and mild. Its sweet, pronounced anise flavor makes it popular for both raw and cooked preparations, and it holds in the garden longer than many older bulbing strains before splitting or flowering. A fall sowing timed to mature in cool autumn weather often produces the largest, most tender bulbs.

name: Selma Zebra Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost at the base of a trellis or pole; matures earlier than many pole beans, making it useful where the growing season is shorter.
directions: Selma Zebra is a distinctively marked pole snap bean, its green pods streaked with purple zigzag patterning that fades somewhat when cooked but makes for an eye-catching harvest basket. It matures notably early for a climbing bean, and the tender, fleshy pods are best picked young for fresh snap use. Like other regionally maintained heirlooms, it is kept alive mainly through small seed companies and seed-saver networks rather than large commercial catalogs. Give it a sturdy trellis and pick often to encourage continued pod set through the growing season.

name: Selma Zesta Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost at the base of a trellis or pole; a lesser-known heirloom kept in circulation mainly through regional seed savers and small seed houses.
directions: Selma Zesta, also circulated under the spelling Zelma Zesta, is a Southern heirloom pole snap bean maintained in small-scale seed exchange circles rather than mass commercial production. Vigorous climbing vines produce rounded, fleshy pods with good snap-bean flavor and texture, harvested young for fresh eating in the tradition of Appalachian and Southern cornfield-style pole beans. It is a good candidate for gardeners looking to grow out and help preserve a regionally distinct heirloom that has not been widely commercialized. Provide a tall, sturdy support and pick regularly to keep vines productive through the season.

name: Seminole Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained soil; in zone 9–10 an excellent late summer/fall planting (August–September) allows the long vines to run through fall when powdery mildew pressure is lower. The Seminole pumpkin is the most heat-tolerant, disease-resistant winter squash for Gulf Coast and Florida gardens and should be a standard in zone 8–10 gardens where other pumpkins and squash struggle in summer humidity.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in any well-drained soil in full sun; Seminole pumpkin is a historic Native American heirloom cultivated by the Seminole people of Florida for generations and is exceptionally well-adapted to the hot, humid Gulf Coast climate where most pumpkins and butternut squash struggle with vine borers, powdery mildew, and heat collapse. It produces tan-buff, round to pear-shaped fruits weighing 5–10 pounds on very vigorous vines that can reach 15–20 feet — the vines are traditionally trained up trees or fences in Florida to keep the fruits off the moist ground. The buff-orange flesh has excellent butternut-like flavor, keeping quality of months, and outstanding resistance to diseases and insects that devastate other squash. Once established, vines are genuinely drought-tolerant. One of the most important heirloom vegetables for sustainable subtropical gardening.
sources: Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services

name: Seneca White Corn
plantingNote: Sow in blocks of several short rows in fertile soil, hilling stalks slightly as they grow; let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvest and shelling.
directions: Sow in blocks of several short rows in fertile soil, hilling stalks slightly as they grow for stability, and let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvest and shelling. Seneca White is a traditional white flour/flint corn central to Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) agriculture in what is now upstate New York, grown for generations alongside beans and squash in the Three Sisters planting system. The soft, starchy white kernels are traditionally parched, ground, or simmered into corn soup, and community-led seed-saving efforts such as the Iroquois White Corn Project have kept this culturally vital variety in cultivation after it nearly disappeared from wider circulation in the twentieth century.

name: Senposai
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer to early fall for fall/winter/spring production in zones 7–11; Senposai is a Japanese hybrid leafy green that is significantly more heat-tolerant than standard cabbages and brassicas, making it one of the better cool-season leafy greens for the Gulf South where the heat ends conventional brassica production early — it continues producing into warmer temperatures than kale, collards, or Chinese cabbage.
directions: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 8–14 inches apart; harvest outer leaves continuously as cut-and-come-again from about 30 days; Senposai is mild enough to eat raw as well as cooked; spring plantings should go in very early since it bolts in sustained heat. Senposai is a hybrid leafy green developed in Japan by crossing common cabbage (Brassica oleracea) with komatsuna or Japanese mustard spinach (Brassica rapa var. perviridis), producing a vigorous, fast-growing green that combines characteristics of both parents — the large, smooth, broadly oval leaves of cabbage with the faster maturity, milder flavor, and somewhat greater heat tolerance of komatsuna. The resulting hybrid fills a useful niche in both Japanese home gardens and warm-climate gardens worldwide: it is ready for harvest significantly faster than heading cabbages (40–60 days versus 80–120), produces continuously as a cut-and-come-again crop rather than requiring a single heading harvest, and tolerates heat better than most brassicas while retaining the mild, slightly sweet, cabbage-family flavor without the sharpness of mustard greens. Senposai is versatile in the kitchen — the large, smooth leaves are excellent raw in salads, quickly stir-fried or sautéed, braised in Japanese-style dashimono or miso soup, or used like savoy cabbage leaves for wrapping. In zone 9a and the Gulf South, Senposai is most valuable as a fall-through-spring cool-season green, sown from September through February for harvest from October through April. Available from Kitazawa Seed Company and other Asian vegetable seed specialists.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

name: Serendipity Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees; Serendipity was the original TripleSweet-type bicolor hybrid, blending sugary-enhanced tenderness with supersweet-level sugar content for excellent flavor and good holding quality.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Serendipity is a widely grown bicolor sweet corn hybrid combining sugary-enhanced tenderness with the high sugar content and slower sugar-to-starch conversion typical of supersweet types, giving it both excellent eating quality and good holding time after picking. It produces large, well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels on tall, vigorous stalks. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill for the best-filled ears. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed.
sources: seed catalog reference (Rupp Seeds, Elk Mound Seed, Andrews Seed Company)

name: Sessantina Grossa Broccoli Raab
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in late summer for a fall crop; broccoli raab bolts quickly once days lengthen and warm, so time plantings for cool weather.
directions: Sessantina Grossa is a classic Italian landrace broccoli raab whose name translates roughly to 'big sixty-day,' describing its larger leaves and buds compared to faster, smaller rapini types. Direct sow thickly in cool weather and thin as needed, harvesting whole young plants or cutting the central shoot with its small flower buds once they appear but before petals open. The deeply lobed, dark green leaves and slightly nutty, pleasantly bitter buds are traditionally sauteed with garlic and olive oil or added to soups and pasta dishes. Keep soil consistently moist and harvest promptly, since heat brings on rapid bolting and increased bitterness.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Seven Top Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall (August–October in zone 9) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Seven Top can be sown thickly and harvested by cutting young, regrowing from the base for multiple cuttings over the cool season.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Seven Top is a turnip variety grown exclusively for its prolific, tender, flavorful greens (tops) rather than its roots — the roots of Seven Top are small, tough, and not typically eaten, but the plant produces an extremely vigorous canopy of large, lush, tender, deeply flavored greens that are among the most productive and flavorful of all Southern cooking greens. The variety's name describes its characteristic of producing an exceptionally dense canopy of seven or more vigorous shoots per plant — creating a tall, productive leafy mass that yields far more greens per plant than Purple Top or other root-type turnips when grown for tops. Seven Top is a staple of traditional Gulf South fall and winter gardening — it's the turnip greens variety most commonly grown for pot greens in Mississippi, Louisiana, Alabama, and Georgia gardens where a large quantity of flavorful cooking greens from a small space is the primary objective. The greens are best harvested young and tender (6–10 inches tall) and become progressively more robust in flavor as they mature — a quality that appeals to those who prefer the traditional strong, minerally flavor of Southern cooking greens. Seven Top tolerates temperatures well into the teens once established. Cut-and-come-again harvesting (cutting to 4 inches, allowing regrowth) produces multiple flushes through the cool season.

name: Seven Year Love Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is thoroughly warm, giving the vigorous vines plenty of room to ramble; cure harvested fruit in a warm, dry spot for a couple of weeks before moving to cool, dry long-term storage.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep once soil has thoroughly warmed after the last frost, spacing hills to give the sprawling vines room to run, and water deeply but infrequently to encourage a strong root system. Seven Year Love is a Japanese heirloom moschata squash, named and prized above nearly all other winter squash for its exceptional keeping ability — properly cured fruit stored in a cool, dry spot can remain sound and good to eat for many months, and the name reflects a reputation for storage life that far outlasts typical winter squash. The tan to buff, hard-shelled fruit has dense, sweet, deep orange flesh that, like other moschata types, holds its quality and flavor well even after long storage rather than turning stringy or bland. Cure fruit in a warm, dry location for one to two weeks after harvest to harden the rind and improve storage life, then keep in a cool, dry, well-ventilated space out of direct sun.

name: Shaman's Blue Popcorn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks well after last frost and isolate from other corn by distance or staggered timing to protect popping quality and kernel color.
directions: Shaman's Blue was the first widely offered dark-blue hybrid popcorn, bred for large, tender kernels that pop bright white despite their deep bluish-purple hull color, unlike the small, chewy kernels typical of older open-pollinated blue popcorns. Leave 8 inch ears on the stalk until husks are fully dry and kernels are hard, then cure indoors before shelling and storing in a sealed container to preserve popping moisture. The anthocyanin-rich hull gives raw kernels a deeper color than yellow popcorns, which growers selling at farmers markets often use as a selling point alongside its reliably fluffy pop. Choose this variety when a gardener wants the visual novelty of blue corn without sacrificing tender, large-kernel popping performance.

name: Shanghai Green Pak Choi
plantingNote: Direct sow from early spring through late summer for successive crops; Shanghai Green was selected in the 1970s by the Shanghai Municipal Agricultural Science Research Institute for disease resistance and quick, uniform growth, and it bolts fast once days lengthen and warm, so time spring sowings to finish before the heat sets in.
directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed thinly and thin to final spacing once seedlings have two true leaves, since crowding pushes this compact type to bolt prematurely. Shanghai Green forms a tight, vase-shaped rosette of dark jade, spoon-shaped leaves on pale green, celery-like petioles, and its dwarf habit makes it one of the most reliable baby bok choy types for close spacing and container growing. Keep soil evenly moist and feed lightly, since even brief drought or a nutrient check can trigger bolting in warm weather. Harvest whole heads at 5-6 inches tall for the classic baby size, or let plants grow on another week or two for slightly larger heads with the same tender, mild flavor.

name: Shanghai Pak Choi
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before the last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer/early fall for a fall crop; Shanghai pak choi bolts quickly in long, hot days, so in zone 8–9 it performs best as a fast fall-through-winter and very early spring green rather than a summer crop.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade; keep evenly watered, since any dry stress speeds bolting. Shanghai pak choi is a compact, fast-maturing bok choy type with pale jade-green, spoon-shaped petioles and glossy dark green leaves that form a tidy, vase-shaped rosette — smaller and quicker to mature than standard white-stemmed bok choy varieties, and prized for its exceptionally tender, mild, sweet stems that need no peeling or trimming before cooking. Its speed and compact size make it ideal for succession sowing every couple of weeks through the cool season, providing a steady supply of baby greens for stir-fries, soups, and quick braises. In warm-winter climates like the Gulf South it can be grown nearly through the whole cool season, from fall through early spring, before rising temperatures push it to bolt. Zone 2–10.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Shantung Purple Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves 2 inches deep in fall, well before the ground freezes, in loose fertile soil to let this productive porcelain type size up fully.
directions: Shantung Purple traces to Shandong province in China and is grown as a porcelain-type hardneck, forming smooth white-skinned bulbs sometimes blushed with purple streaking around five to seven plump cloves. Growers favor it for consistent bulb size and good yields compared to some finickier heirloom porcelains. Snap off the scape once it curls to direct energy into the bulb, and harvest when the lowest few leaves have browned while upper leaves remain green. Cure for several weeks in a shaded, well-ventilated spot before trimming and storing in a cool, dry place.
sources: Washington State University Extension garlic production guide

name: Sharlyn Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil in hills or rows; Sharlyn is a hybrid type combining honeydew and cantaloupe parentage and needs a long, warm growing season to fully sweeten.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in hills 4 feet apart or in rows 6 feet apart, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Sharlyn is a hybrid melon combining traits of honeydew and cantaloupe, with smooth, pale ribbed skin like a honeydew but sweet, aromatic, pale orange flesh with the rich flavor of a cantaloupe, giving it an unusual combination of exterior and interior appearance that often surprises gardeners who haven't grown it before. Unlike true cantaloupe, ripe fruit does not slip easily from the vine, so judge ripeness by a color shift toward pale cream-yellow and a sweet fragrance at the blossom end rather than by fruit separation. It stores somewhat better after harvest than standard cantaloupe, making it a good choice for gardeners wanting a melon that holds a bit longer at peak quality.

name: Sheepnose Pimento Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant after danger of frost has passed; an Ohio Amish heirloom pimento pepper grown for its thick, sweet flesh.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, then transplant into the garden after soil has warmed and space plants 18-24 inches apart. Sheepnose Pimento is a cherished Ohio Amish heirloom named for its squat, heart-shaped fruit, which ripens from green to a glossy deep red and is prized for exceptionally thick, meaty walls and an intensely sweet, almost sugary flavor. Sturdy, bushy plants are highly productive over a long season, yielding abundant fruit well suited to roasting, stuffing, canning, and fresh eating. Keep soil evenly moist and fertile through fruit set, and harvest at full red ripeness for the best flavor and thickest flesh.

name: Sherwood Red Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm; this fast-growing Tennessee heirloom tolerates the long, humid summers of the Gulf Coast well.
directions: Donated to Southern Exposure Seed Exchange by a Tennessee grower in the late 1970s, this fast-growing, non-prickly okra bears fat, four-inch red-and-green pods on plants with striking red stems and leaf veins. Its low mucilage keeps pods tender even when allowed to grow larger than most varieties, which forgives a missed picking day or two during peak summer harvest. The colorful pods are excellent fried and add both color and mild flavor when sliced raw and young into salads. As with most heirloom okras, its color fades toward green once cooked, but the ornamental red-tinged plants remain a garden standout all season.

name: Shimonita Negi Bunching Onion
plantingNote: Sow in a nursery bed in spring, then transplant seedlings into a trench in early-to-mid summer, gradually backfilling and hilling soil around the stems through fall to blanch the thick white shank; a long cold period after the first hard frosts concentrates the sugars that make this variety famous.
directions: Shimonita Negi comes from Shimonita Town in Japan's Gunma Prefecture and, unlike most bunching onions, grows as a single thick, unbranched stalk rather than dividing into a clump of thin shoots. Transplant seedlings into a trench and progressively mound soil up the stem over the growing season, a technique called hilling that blanches the shank to a diameter rivaling a small leek. It needs a long season, typically six to twelve months from sowing, and is traditionally harvested in late fall or early winter after frost has sweetened the stalk and softened its raw pungency into a mellow, umami-rich flavor. Use the thick blanched shanks whole in sukiyaki, nabe hot pots, and grilling, where the interior turns tender and almost custardy when cooked.

name: Shintokiwa Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun; train the vigorous vines onto a trellis to encourage long, straight fruit.
directions: Shintokiwa is a Japanese heirloom cucumber brought into American cultivation through biodynamic seed growers and producing long, slender, smooth-skinned fruit 9-12 inches long. The thin, tender skin and dense, nearly seedless flesh give it a crisp, sweet flavor with virtually no bitterness, making peeling unnecessary. Plants are vigorous and productive, with good resistance to bacterial wilt. Excellent for fresh eating and light pickling, and well suited to trellising for long, straight fruit.

name: Shirofumi Edamame Soybean
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep once soil has warmed well past last frost, since this open-pollinated Japanese heirloom edamame needs consistent summer warmth to fill its pods.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep once soil has warmed well past last frost, since this open-pollinated Japanese heirloom edamame needs consistent summer warmth to fill its pods. Plants set heavy clusters of two- to three-bean pods on compact, well-branched bushes and are valued in trials for their reliably smooth, sweet, nutty-flavored beans. Harvest whole pods when plump but still green, then steam or boil briefly in salted water for a classic edamame snack; being non-hybrid, seed can be saved from healthy plants for replanting.

name: Shishigatani Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is thoroughly warm; as a Cucurbita moschata type it tolerates heat and humidity well.
directions: Shishigatani is a traditional Kyoto heirloom squash and one of the certified Kyo-yasai heritage vegetables, developed in the 19th century from chrysanthemum-type pumpkins brought south from Tsugaru in northern Japan. Fruits develop a distinctive bumpy, waisted, gourd-like snowman shape rather than the rounded form of typical kabocha. The squash carries deep cultural significance in Kyoto, where Anraku-ji Temple holds an annual squash-blessing ceremony each summer, and it is traditionally simmered in shojin ryori Buddhist vegetarian cooking. It remains a rare specialty variety outside Japan.

name: Shishito Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant after nights stay consistently above 55°F. In zone 9 transplant in February–March and expect harvests from May through October. The plants tolerate heat well and remain productive through the Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; shishito peppers are a slender, thin-walled Japanese variety harvested green at 3–4 inches long, when they are mild and sweet with an occasional — roughly 1 in 10 — surprisingly hot fruit that keeps diners guessing. Plants produce prolifically once they begin fruiting and require consistent moisture and monthly fertilization with a balanced vegetable fertilizer to maintain production. Harvest frequently to keep plants productive; once fruits redden they become hotter and the plant redirects energy away from new fruit. The standard preparation is to blister whole fruits in a dry or lightly oiled cast-iron skillet over high heat until charred and softened, then finish with sea salt and a squeeze of lemon.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pepper Production
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners Database — Shishito

name: Shogoin Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall (August–October in zone 9) in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Shogoin is an excellent dual-purpose turnip — the mild, sweet roots are outstanding for fresh eating and the tender tops are milder-flavored than most American turnip greens.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; Shogoin is a Japanese heirloom turnip cultivar that is outstanding in two distinct ways: it produces unusually mild, sweet, tender-fleshed white roots appropriate for fresh eating and light cooking, and simultaneously produces exceptionally mild, tender, palatable greens that are significantly less pungent than the traditional American turnip greens grown for Southern cooking. This dual mildness — both roots and tops — makes Shogoin the turnip of choice for those who find standard American turnips too strongly flavored but want to grow a dual-purpose root vegetable for fall and winter. The pure-white, globe-shaped roots reach 2–3 inches in diameter at ideal harvest size — smaller and more tender than Purple Top White Globe when harvested young. The roots are outstanding raw in salads and slaws, steamed or roasted with light seasoning, and pickled (Shogoin is commonly used for Japanese-style pickled turnips). The tender greens can be used raw in salads when young, stir-fried, or lightly sautéed. In zone 9, Shogoin is a fall and winter crop — sow from August through October for harvest from October through February. The mild flavor makes Shogoin an outstanding variety for introducing turnips to gardeners and cooks unfamiliar with or averse to the pungency of traditional varieties.

name: Shoya Long Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Shoya Long is an early, upright hybrid that suits both open-field summer plantings and season-extending tunnel culture in cooler climates.
directions: Shoya Long is a Japanese-type hybrid bred for exceptionally long, slender fruit with glossy deep-purple skin and a matching dark calyx, often reaching 14-16 inches with tender, nearly seedless flesh. The upright, vigorous plant habit keeps the long fruit off the ground and makes picking easier than with sprawling heirloom types. It matures early and yields heavily over a long harvest window, staying productive through the hottest stretch of a Gulf Coast summer. Harvest while the skin still has a bright sheen, since fruit left too long on the plant dulls and toughens.

name: Shunkyo Semi-Long Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow in loose, fertile soil in early fall or late winter, thinning seedlings so roots have room to size up without crowding.
directions: Direct sow in loose, fertile soil in early fall or late winter, thinning seedlings so roots have room to size up without crowding. This Japanese heirloom produces rose-pink, tapered roots four to five inches long with crisp, notably sweet and mild flesh that holds its quality and stays crisp longer than typical round spring radishes as temperatures fluctuate. Its extended harvest window and resistance to turning pithy or overly hot in warm soil make it a reliable choice for Gulf Coast gardeners working with a short, mild winter rather than a true hard freeze. Both the roots and the peppery young leaves are edible.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

name: Shvelisi Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves pointed end up in fall, several weeks before the ground freezes, so roots develop ahead of winter.
directions: Set cloves 2 inches deep in loose, fertile soil and mulch well for the winter, uncovering gradually as spring shoots appear. Cut the curling scape in early summer to focus growth into the bulb, then cure harvested heads in a dry, shaded, airy location for a few weeks. Shvelisi is a Republic of Georgia heirloom porcelain hardneck brought to the United States by garlic researcher Ron Engeland, known for its tall stature, large white bulbs, and rich, warm flavor that reflects its Caucasus mountain origins.

name: Siamese Bitter Melon
plantingNote: Direct-sow after soil has warmed above 70°F, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early; provide a tall trellis for this vigorous Thai type.
directions: This slender Thai type produces small, deeply ridged fruit with a notably assertive bitterness prized in Southeast Asian cooking. Provide a tall trellis in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and harvest young and often, since frequent picking of immature fruit keeps the vigorous vine flowering and setting new fruit. Left unpicked, fruit ripens to orange and splits open to reveal red-coated seeds, which can be saved after a short drying period.

name: Siberian Hardneck Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 4–6 weeks before first frost; Siberian is a Marbled Purple Stripe hardneck garlic of Russian origin, known for exceptional cold hardiness that makes it one of the most reliable varieties in zones 3–4 — it produces large, 5–9 clove bulbs with a rich, full-bodied flavor and an attractive purple-striped outer wrapper typical of its garlic group.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end up, 2 inches deep and 4–6 inches apart in fall 4–6 weeks before hard freeze; mulch heavily after the ground cools (especially important in zones 3–4); keep consistently moist in spring; remove scapes when they curl and straighten; harvest in early to midsummer when lower leaves yellow. Siberian is a Marbled Purple Stripe hardneck garlic originating in Russia and introduced to North American garlic culture through seed-saver networks and specialist garlic growers in the 20th century; it is particularly valued for its exceptional cold hardiness, with reliable performance in zones 3–4 where many garlic varieties struggle with winterkill or produce reduced bulb size. The bulbs are medium-large (2–3 inches across) and typically contain just 5–9 large, easy-to-peel cloves — fewer than most garlic types but each clove is substantial in size, making them easy to use in cooking. The outer skins are cream-colored with distinctive purple-violet streaking and spotting characteristic of the Marbled Purple Stripe group; the flavor is rich, moderately pungent, and earthy with good complexity — similar in character to Persian Star and other Marbled Purple Stripe types. Siberian is an excellent choice for northern gardeners in zones 3–5 who struggle with hardneck variety performance, and for seed-saving gardens that want geographic diversity in their garlic collection. Storage life of 5–7 months under good conditions.

name: Siberian Kale
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer for a fall and winter harvest, or in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked; a hard frost sweetens the flavor considerably.
directions: Siberian kale is an old, extremely cold-hardy strain of Brassica napus grown across northern Russia and Siberia long before it reached North American seed catalogs, and it stands behind many of the popular 'Russian' type kales, including the purple-stemmed Red Russian selections bred from it. Unlike the tightly curled Scots kales of Brassica oleracea, Siberian kale has flat, deeply lobed, blue-green leaves with a milder, sweeter flavor that improves further after frost. Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to about a foot apart, and harvest outer leaves continually as the plant regrows from the center. It tolerates hard freezes better than almost any other garden brassica, often surviving under snow cover well into winter.
sources: Seed Ambassadors Project — Russian & Siberian Kale
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Brassica napus Pabularia Group

name: Sibley Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Sibley, also known as Pike's Peak squash, is an 1880s heirloom prized for its distinctive teardrop shape, thin blue-gray rind, and exceptionally sweet, dry, fine-grained orange flesh that many heirloom growers consider among the best-flavored of all winter squash.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills, allowing generous room for the long, vigorous vines. Sibley squash, introduced in the 1880s and also sold as Pike's Peak squash, is an American heirloom valued by generations of gardeners for its unusual teardrop or pear shape, thin, smooth, blue-gray rind, and exceptionally sweet, dry, fine-textured deep orange flesh with almost no fiber, a texture and flavor that many long-time growers rank above modern hybrid winter squash. Fruits typically run 6-10 pounds, large enough to serve a crowd, and the thin rind, while making the squash slightly more vulnerable to handling damage than thick-shelled types, also makes it easier to peel and cook than harder-shelled Hubbard-type squash. Vines are long and productive given full sun and consistent moisture during fruit set. Harvest when the rind has hardened and resists a fingernail and the stem has begun to dry, then cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry location before storing in a cool, dry spot, where well-cured fruit keeps for several months while its sweetness continues to improve.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Sibley Squash heirloom documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Sibley (Pike's Peak) Squash variety notes
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Heritage Winter Squash Comparison

name: Sieglinde Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; Sieglinde is an early-to-second-early German variety that bulks up quickly in cool soil.
directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep and 10-12 inches apart in rows 24-30 inches apart, hilling soil over the base of the stems as plants grow. Sieglinde is a long-established German heirloom producing smooth, elongated-oval tubers with pale yellow skin and pale yellow, waxy flesh that holds its shape well when boiled, making it a classic choice for potato salad across Central Europe. It bulks early relative to many other European heirloom potatoes, so plan to begin harvesting new potatoes once plants flower if a tender early crop is wanted, or leave tubers to mature fully for storage.

name: Sierra Blanca Onion
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter zones; Sierra Blanca is an intermediate/short-day white hybrid onion widely recommended across Texas, New Mexico, and the Gulf South as one of the most reliable large sweet onions for home gardens.
directions: Start seeds indoors or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter regions, since this intermediate/short-day hybrid needs a southern winter's shorter daylight to bulb well. Sierra Blanca is an All-America Selections-winning white onion widely grown across the Southwest and Gulf South for its large, globe-shaped bulbs, crisp white flesh, and consistently mild, sweet flavor, making it a favorite for fresh eating as well as cooking. It bulbs reliably and stores somewhat better than the thinnest-skinned sweet onions, though it is still best used within a few months for peak quality. Keep soil evenly moist through bulb development and ease off watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall over ahead of harvest.
sources: New Mexico State University Cooperative Extension

name: Sierra Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; Sierra's exceptional heat and bolt resistance makes it valuable for extending the lettuce season into early summer; an excellent choice for warm-climate gardeners.
directions: Sow seed on or just below the soil surface in fertile, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sierra is a batavian-type lettuce combining the crisp texture of a crisphead with the loose, outer-leaf harvest convenience of a loose-leaf type — producing green, ruffled, tender-crisp heads with outstanding bolt and heat resistance that extends the spring lettuce season significantly later than butterhead or loose-leaf types. An excellent choice for zone 8–10 gardeners where spring heat arrives quickly, giving a several-week extension window before quality declines. Harvest heads when firm but before any heat stress causes bitterness.

name: Sikkim Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following last frost; Sikkim is a vigorous vining heirloom best grown on a trellis or sturdy fence to support its large fruit.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile soil after frost danger has passed, and train the vigorous vines up a trellis to keep the large fruit clean and well-shaped. This Himalayan heirloom from the Sikkim region of India is unlike most garden cucumbers in that it is prized for its mature stage, when the oval fruit develops a thick, netted, rust-brown to reddish skin and sweeter, firmer flesh well suited to cooking or pickling rather than fresh eating. Keep plants evenly watered through fruit set, since the long maturation period makes this variety more drought-sensitive than quick-maturing slicers. Harvest some fruit young and green for a milder, more traditional cucumber use, but allow others to color fully on the vine to see the variety's distinctive russet skin develop.

name: Siletz Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Siletz is an Oregon State University development bred specifically for cool, short-season growing in the Pacific Northwest, setting fruit at temperatures below 55°F when standard varieties fail, and producing large red beefsteak-style fruits in as few as 52 days from transplant — ideal for cloudy coastal gardens where summers are cool and brief.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Siletz can be transplanted 1–2 weeks before last frost in mild climates due to its cold tolerance for a tomato; it is determinate and does not require staking, though a cage helps manage the heavy fruit load. Siletz was developed by Dr. Jim Baggett at Oregon State University as part of the Pacific Northwest vegetable breeding program, named for the Siletz River in Oregon's Coast Range; it was released specifically to address the challenge of growing tomatoes in the cool, overcast summers of the Pacific Coast where nighttime temperatures regularly fall below the fruit-set threshold of standard varieties. The large (8–12 oz), round to slightly flattened, bright red fruits have good meaty texture and pleasant, balanced sweet-acid flavor — not the most complex among heirloom varieties, but reliably excellent given its exceptional earliness and cold tolerance. In Gulf Coast gardens, Siletz makes an outstanding early-season variety when planted in February–March, producing ripe fruit well before the onset of summer heat that terminates most tomato production. Its determinate growth habit allows clean harvest before the hot season, with plants ripening a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks.

name: Siling Labuyo Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; harvest frequently to keep the compact, heavily branching bush setting new fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this Filipino landrace grows into a shrubby perennial in frost-free climates but performs well as a warm-season annual elsewhere. The tiny, tapering pods — among the smallest of any cultivated chile — pack intense heat around 80,000-100,000 Scoville units and are used both fresh and dried in staples like sinigang, bicol express, and vinegar-based dipping sauces; young leaves are also edible and used in some regional dishes. Harvest frequently to keep the compact, heavily branching bush setting new fruit.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

name: Silver Queen Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow an inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65 degrees F; soak seeds overnight in warm water before planting to improve germination.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Silver Queen is an heirloom okra valued for its pale, silvery ivory-green pods and foliage, a striking, almost ghostly color that sets it apart from the deep green of most okra varieties and makes it as much an ornamental curiosity as a productive vegetable. The tender pods have the classic okra flavor and texture, well suited to frying, gumbo, and pickling, and the plant produces reliably through the heat of a Gulf South summer. Harvest young, at three to four inches, for the best tenderness, and pick regularly to keep the plant producing over a long season.

name: Silver Queen Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks (at least 4 rows wide) for adequate wind pollination; Silver Queen is a late-season variety at 88–94 days, making it the last corn of the season for most gardeners. In zone 9, plant March–April for a June–July harvest, or plant again in August for a fall harvest. Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil amended with balanced fertilizer; side-dress with nitrogen fertilizer when plants reach knee height.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks at least 4 rows wide for adequate wind pollination; fertilize at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Silver Queen is perhaps the most historically influential and recognizable white sweet corn variety in American horticulture — an su (standard sugar) white hybrid introduced around 1955 that rapidly became the benchmark white sweet corn against which all others were measured for decades. The large, 8–9 inch ears carry 14–16 rows of pure white, tender, milky kernels with the classic, unmistakable sweet corn flavor that made Silver Queen famous across the mid-Atlantic and southeastern states, where roadside stands and home gardens grew Silver Queen as the late-summer corn of choice for multiple generations of cooks who planned their summer around it. At 88–94 days, Silver Queen is a late-season variety that reaches peak quality in the hottest part of summer, a timing that traditionally marked the height of summer corn season in the South and Midwest.
