The flavor at peak maturity — kernels plump, skins tender, sugar at maximum before starch conversion begins — is the standard by which many older gardeners still evaluate all corn. Silver Queen must be harvested and consumed or preserved within a narrow window (1–3 days after peak) as the su type converts sugar to starch more rapidly than modern se or sh2 types. In the Gulf South, Silver Queen is a classic late-spring-to-early-summer variety with a dedicated following among gardeners who grew up eating it.
sources: Burpee Seeds — Silver Queen sweet corn history and variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sweet Corn Production
North Carolina State University Extension — Sweet Corn Variety Recommendations

name: Silver Rose Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 1-2 inches deep in fall; Silver Rose is a fast-maturing silverskin softneck with a low chilling requirement, tolerating mild Gulf Coast winters better than hardneck types that need sustained cold to divide properly.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 1-2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in loose, well-drained soil in fall; Silver Rose is a silverskin softneck garlic prized for maturing earlier than many other varieties and for exceptional storage life, often keeping 9 months or longer in a cool, dry pantry when properly cured. Bulbs form tight, papery white to rose-blushed wrappers around a good number of small to medium cloves with a strong, well-rounded flavor that mellows considerably when cooked. Like other silverskins, it tolerates mild winters far better than hardneck types, making it one of the more dependable garlics for zone 8-10 gardens. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have yellowed, cure in a warm, dry, shaded, well-ventilated spot for 3-4 weeks, then trim and store.
sources: Filaree Garlic Farm — Silverskin variety descriptions
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Garlic Variety Selection for Texas
University of California Cooperative Extension — Garlic Production in California

name: Silvery Fir Tree Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Silvery Fir Tree is determinate and compact (24–30 inches), making it well-suited for containers and small gardens. In zone 9, transplant February–March for the earliest spring tomato harvest (May–June); as a determinate variety, the plant ripens most of its fruit within a concentrated 3–4 week window. A second planting in late July or August can produce a fall crop. The variety's very early maturity (58–65 days from transplant) is a significant advantage in zone 9 where the spring tomato window is narrow before summer heat limits production — Silvery Fir Tree can begin producing in late April to May when planted on schedule, before most standard varieties set their first ripe fruits.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. No staking needed for compact plants. Harvest when fruits are uniformly red and slightly soft. Silvery Fir Tree is a Russian heirloom tomato of exceptional visual distinction — the variety is immediately recognizable in the garden by its foliage, which is finely dissected and ferny in appearance, closely resembling carrot leaves or fir tree needles rather than the broad, palmately lobed leaves of standard tomato types. The silvery-green color of the leaves (more gray-green than the typical bright green of most tomato foliage) reinforces the fir tree visual impression and gives the variety its English common name. Botanically, the finely cut leaf form is a recessive mutation in leaf architecture that has been maintained in this Russian variety through traditional seed saving — the same mutation appears occasionally in other tomato varieties but rarely becomes the defining characteristic of a named variety. The plants are determinate and compact (24–30 inches), producing clusters of small-medium red round fruits (2–3 oz each) that ripen in a concentrated season-appropriate window. The flavor is excellent for an early determinate — sweet, well-balanced, genuine tomato character without the flatness that sometimes characterizes early-season determinate types. Silvery Fir Tree has become popular in North American heirloom tomato cultivation not only for its early production and good flavor but also as an ornamental garden plant: the unusual ferny foliage makes it visually striking in container plantings, edible landscapes, and kitchen gardens where visual diversity among plants adds character.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Silvery Fir Tree tomato Russian heirloom variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Silvery Fir Tree tomato variety description
Adaptive Seeds — Early and compact tomato variety comparison for short seasons

name: Simpson Elite Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Simpson Elite is an All-America Selections winner bred as an improved version of the classic Black Seeded Simpson, with better bolt resistance.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, thinning seedlings to final spacing. Simpson Elite, an All-America Selections winner, improves on the classic heirloom Black Seeded Simpson looseleaf lettuce with notably better resistance to bolting in warm weather, extending the harvest window later into spring and giving Gulf South gardeners more usable growing time before summer heat sets in. It forms loose, tender, light green frilled leaves ready for cut-and-come-again harvest within weeks of sowing. Harvest outer leaves as needed while the center continues to produce, and provide light afternoon shade in the warmest weeks of the season to further delay bolting.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lettuce Production

name: Simpson Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed past 70°F; soaking seed overnight speeds germination in Simpson's slightly slower-sprouting seed coat.
directions: Keep pods picked every day or two once they reach 3 inches, since Simpson's smooth, straight pods pass from tender to woody faster than many longer-podded types. The family lineage traces to the Simpson household in Rogersville, Tennessee, where it was grown and passed down at least since the 1940s, giving it a straight, light-green pod very similar in appearance to Clemson Spineless. Plants tolerate the heat and dry spells of a Gulf Coast August with little complaint, continuing to set pods as long as harvest stays current. Because it is open-pollinated, gardeners can save seed from dried pods left on the plant at season's end for replanting the following year.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange heirloom variety records

name: Sioux Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Sioux is one of the most heat-tolerant tomatoes available, originally developed by the University of Nebraska in the 1940s specifically for hot, humid Midwestern conditions and still treasured by Gulf Coast and Southern gardeners for its ability to set fruit through summer heat that defeats most other varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost and stake or cage early — Sioux is an indeterminate variety that sets fruit continuously through the season. Sioux was introduced by the University of Nebraska Agricultural Experiment Station in 1944, bred specifically for heat tolerance and disease resistance in hot, humid, continental climates; it remains one of the most reliably productive tomatoes for hot Southern summers and Gulf Coast conditions where other varieties drop blossoms during heat waves — Sioux continues setting medium-sized (6–8 oz), round, bright red fruits even when nighttime temperatures stay above 75°F. The flavor is classic, balanced, and mildly acidic — a dependable slicer with good disease resistance and continuous production from early summer until frost. Highly recommended for gardeners in zones 8–11 who struggle to keep tomatoes producing through midsummer.
sources: University of Nebraska Agricultural Experiment Station

name: Sivan Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm, or start indoors 3 weeks early in short-season climates; Sivan is an Israeli-bred Galia-type hybrid prized for its intensely sweet, aromatic pale green flesh and reliably early, heavy fruit set.
directions: Sow 3-4 seeds per hill after soil has warmed and danger of frost has passed, thinning to two vigorous plants per hill, or transplant tender young seedlings if a short growing season demands a head start. Sivan is a Galia-type F1 hybrid melon bred in Israel, popular there and across the Mediterranean and Middle East for its round, heavily netted rind that shifts from green to golden yellow at ripeness and its highly aromatic, pale green, sugary flesh that develops flavor unusually fast for a muskmelon, typically ready 75-85 days from sowing. Grow it like other Galia types on black plastic mulch to warm the root zone and suppress weeds, keep watering consistent through fruit set, then taper off as fruits near maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip, when the fruit separates cleanly from the vine with gentle pressure and the blossom end gives off a strong sweet fragrance.

name: Six Weeks Purple Hull Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F, in average, well-drained soil in full sun; the very short 6-week maturity makes this an excellent choice for succession planting through the whole Gulf South growing season, from spring through a final late-summer sowing.
directions: Direct sow in average, well-drained soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and one of the fastest-maturing Southern peas available, ready to pick as fresh shell peas in as little as six weeks. Six Weeks Purple Hull is a classic, widely grown heirloom cowpea prized above all for its speed — the compact, semi-bush plants set pods and fill out quickly, making it the go-to variety for gardeners who want an early first picking or need to squeeze in extra succession plantings between other summer crops. The pods mature to a deep purple that makes ripe pods easy to spot against the green foliage, and the cream-colored peas inside have the classic mild, earthy purple hull flavor, excellent fresh-shelled and cooked down Southern-style with a bit of pork or simmered as a simple pot of field peas. Reliable, heat-tolerant, and fast, it is a Gulf South garden staple for a quick, dependable pea crop, zone 5–11.

name: Skyphos Lettuce
plantingNote: Start indoors 3-4 weeks before transplanting out around last frost; transplanting gives more uniform heading than direct seeding.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant out once seedlings have several true leaves, spacing 8-10 inches apart in fertile, moisture-retentive soil. Skyphos is a European-bred red butterhead prized for forming reliably dense, well-rounded heads even in variable weather, unlike many red butterheads that head loosely or split. Its deep burgundy-red outer leaves wrap around a contrasting lime-green heart, with color intensifying in cool weather and softening to more green in heat, and the buttery texture holds a mild, sweet flavor. It is a good choice for gardeners who want the visual drama of a red lettuce without sacrificing the reliable heading habit of a classic Boston type.

name: Skytree Broccoli
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant out while nights are still cool; this 2024 AAS Regional Winner also suits a late-summer sowing for a fall crop in most regions.
directions: Skytree grows noticeably taller and more upright than typical broccoli, carrying its 4- to 8-inch central crown well above the foliage on a sturdy stalk that stays easy to harvest without bending or kneeling. The compact 10- to 12-inch footprint lets it fit into containers and tight raised beds despite its height, and judges noted the tender, sweet-flavored florets and stems held up well under heat stress. Keep soil evenly moist and feed at transplanting for the fastest, most uniform crown development, and harvest the central head promptly to encourage a flush of side shoots afterward.

name: Sleeping Lady Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Sleeping Lady is a Dwarf Tomato Project release named for an Alaskan mountain, bearing pink fruit on a compact plant.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Sleeping Lady bears medium pink fruit with sweet, well-rounded flavor on a compact Dwarf Tomato Project plant, named for the Sleeping Lady mountain near Anchorage, Alaska, home to one of the breeding program's participating gardeners. Its manageable size and reliable production suit raised beds and containers. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

name: Slim Jim Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant into containers or garden beds once the weather is reliably warm.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into a sunny spot or a large container after the last frost, keeping the compact plants consistently watered since their smaller root systems dry out faster than standard eggplant. Deadheading spent fruit encourages continued production through the season. Slim Jim produces slender, finger-sized purple fruit on a small, bushy plant, making it a popular choice for patio containers and small gardens where space is limited. Its petite size and attractive purple flowers also make it a common pick for ornamental-edible plantings.

name: Slo-Bolt Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Slo-Bolt is a classic looseleaf lettuce bred specifically to resist bolting and bitterness longer than most lettuce as weather warms.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, thinning seedlings to final spacing. Slo-Bolt lives up to its name as one of the most heat-resistant looseleaf lettuces available, holding good flavor and resisting the bitterness and premature flowering that end the harvest of most lettuce varieties once temperatures climb, making it a favorite for extending the spring lettuce season deeper into the Gulf South's warm months. It produces medium green, slightly frilled leaves in a loose, open rosette well suited to cut-and-come-again harvest. Pick outer leaves as needed while the center continues producing, and provide light afternoon shade during the hottest stretches to push the harvest window even further.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Lettuce Production

name: Small Wonder Spaghetti Squash
plantingNote: Direct-sow or transplant after frost danger has passed; the compact vine takes noticeably less space than standard spaghetti squash.
directions: Small Wonder is a hybrid spaghetti squash bred for a compact, space-saving vine that still delivers high yields of personal-sized fruit, each weighing roughly 1.5 to 2 pounds, about half the size of standard spaghetti squash. The oval fruit yield the same pale-yellow, stringy flesh that separates into spaghetti-like strands when cooked, making it well suited to single servings without the leftovers a full-sized fruit produces. Because the vines take up notably less garden space than traditional spaghetti squash, it is a practical choice for smaller vegetable beds or intensive plantings. It also matures somewhat earlier than many full-sized spaghetti squash varieties, giving a head start in shorter growing seasons.

name: Smooth Boy Luffa
plantingNote: Direct sow or set out transplants after soil is thoroughly warm; Smooth Boy is a reliable smooth-skinned selection recommended by University of Florida extension programs, harvested young for cooking or left to mature and dry for sponges.
directions: Smooth Boy is a widely available named cultivar of smooth luffa, recommended by University of Florida gardening programs for home dual-purpose growing: young fruit picked at 6-8 inches has mild, zucchini-like flesh good for stir-fries and soups, while fruit left on the vine to mature and turn brown yields the classic fibrous bath and cleaning sponge once peeled and cured. It produces cylindrical, smooth to faintly ribbed fruit on a fast-climbing vine that thrives in Gulf Coast summer heat and humidity, and it flowers with showy bright-yellow blossoms that attract pollinators. Give it a tall, strong trellis or arbor, since vines readily reach 15-20 feet, and keep soil evenly moist through fruit set for the straightest, best-formed sponges.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gardening Solutions

name: Snack Jack Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after the last frost once soil is warm; Snack Jack needs a full season for both the fruit and the hull-less seed inside it to mature fully.
directions: Direct sow seed in hills after frost danger passes, giving the sprawling vines ample room to spread. Snack Jack is grown chiefly for its naked, hull-less seeds, which lack the tough outer shell of standard pumpkin seeds and can be roasted straight from the fruit without hulling, while the medium orange fruit itself is sound enough for carving or cooking. Allow fruit to fully mature and the rind to harden before harvest, since immature fruit yields underdeveloped, less flavorful seed. Scoop seeds out promptly after harvest, rinse away the clinging pulp, and dry thoroughly before roasting or storing to prevent mold.

name: Snow Crown Cauliflower
plantingNote: Start seed indoors for a spring crop, or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest; Snow Crown, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, is one of the earliest-maturing cauliflower varieties, forming smooth white heads reliably.
directions: Start seed indoors for a spring crop or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, spacing transplants 18 to 24 inches apart. Snow Crown, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, is one of the fastest-maturing cauliflower varieties available, reliably forming smooth, dense, pure white heads well ahead of many other cultivars, an important advantage in the Gulf South where cauliflower's narrow cool-season window can cut short slower-maturing varieties. Its early maturity also makes it more forgiving of the unpredictable spring warm-ups that can stall cauliflower head formation. Tie or fold outer leaves over the developing head once it is a couple of inches across to blanch it and keep the curds bright white, and harvest promptly once heads reach full size before they begin to separate or discolor.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Cauliflower Production

name: Snow White Bok Choy
plantingNote: Direct sow shortly before the last frost, and again in late summer for a fall crop; Snow White was collected as a traditional cool-season green near Nanjing, China, and its stems sweeten noticeably after exposure to light frost.
directions: Direct sow thinly in fertile, moisture-retentive soil, thinning seedlings once true leaves appear; Snow White is a tall heirloom bok choy type distinguished by unusually broad, glistening white petioles topped with crisp, dark green leaves. Unlike many bok choy types that need full sun to size up quickly, Snow White holds its quality and resists premature bolting when given afternoon shade during the warmer edges of the growing season, making it a useful pick for beds that only get partial light. Harvest whole heads once the thick white stems have filled out, or take outer stalks individually for a longer cut-and-come-again season; the crunchy stems are good raw, and both stems and leaves hold up well in stir-fries and soups.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Snow White Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6 weeks before the last frost; transplant after frost danger passes and stake or cage the vines, watering consistently once fruit sets to reduce cracking of the thin, pale skin.
directions: A pale ivory-yellow cherry tomato with such low acidity and high sugar that it is regularly ranked among the sweetest cherry tomatoes grown, with a near-translucent skin over blushing golden flesh. The heavy-yielding indeterminate vines set long clusters of one-inch round fruit continuously through the season and benefit from steady, even watering, since the thin skin cracks readily after a dry spell followed by heavy rain. Its mild, sugary flavor and pastel color make it a favorite for fresh eating and mixed cherry-tomato salads rather than cooking.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds Variety Catalog

name: Snowball Y Cauliflower
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplant date; in zone 9 start in August–September and transplant September–October for fall through winter harvest. Blanching is required for white curds: when the central head begins to form, gather the outer leaves over the developing curd and secure with a rubber band or clothespin to exclude sunlight — cauliflower exposed to sun develops yellow color and may lose some quality. Self-blanching varieties with overlapping leaves reduce this labor requirement. Harvest before heads loosen or develop a rice-like granular texture.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, very fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — cauliflower requires more nitrogen and consistent moisture than any other Brassica; Snowball Y is one of the classic open-pollinated white cauliflower varieties — an improved selection from the Snowball strain that has defined the white-headed cauliflower in American horticulture for a century. The compact, round, pure white heads (when properly blanched) represent the culmination of cauliflower development — the plant's edible curd is composed of densely packed, malformed (fasciated) flower buds arrested before they develop, creating the characteristic curded texture of cauliflower. Unlike broccoli, where the flower buds are visible and intact, cauliflower's curd represents a complete developmental halt before budding — a botanical curiosity that produces one of the most unusual vegetable textures available, simultaneously firm and mealy, dense and delicate. Cauliflower's reputation for difficulty is warranted — it requires the most specific temperature range (50–70°F) of any commonly grown vegetable, failing in heat or extreme cold. In zone 9 this restricts successful cauliflower to a narrow fall window of September–December planting.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Cauliflower Production Guide
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Cauliflower for Gulf South
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cool-Season Cauliflower

name: Snowbird Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Snowbird is an early, dwarf shelling pea bred to mature quickly before hot weather ends the pea season in Southern gardens.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked. Snowbird is a short, self-supporting dwarf shelling pea bred to mature very quickly, an important trait in the Gulf South where the cool-season pea window is narrow before summer heat arrives and stops pod production. Its compact vines need little to no staking, and the concentrated, early harvest lets gardeners get a pea crop in before spring warms up too much. Harvest pods when well-filled but still bright green and firm, picking regularly to encourage the plant to keep flowering during its short productive window.

name: Snowcap Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Snowcap is a compact bush bean with strikingly beautiful seeds — white with maroon-red markings concentrated around the hilum — and outstanding flavor as both a shell bean and dried bean, with a creamy texture and rich taste that earned it wide popularity among heirloom bean enthusiasts.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Snowcap is a bush-type bean that needs no support and can be direct-seeded in rows 18 inches apart. Snowcap is an heirloom bush dry bean producing attractive, round-to-oval seeds that are white with a distinctive cap of maroon-red coloring concentrated around the seed scar (hilum) — the 'snowcap' pattern from which it takes its name. The flavor is rich, buttery, and creamy when cooked, with a thin skin that doesn't need pre-soaking for most applications; it is outstanding in soups, chilis, and bean salads where its firm-yet-creamy texture holds up well. An attractive plant for the vegetable garden with modest height and compact habit; the ornamental seeds are a bonus when drying for seed saving. One of the most beautiful and best-flavored heirloom dry beans in the Seed Savers Exchange collection.

name: Snowman Mix Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow outdoors once soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; pumpkins resent root disturbance from transplanting.
directions: Snowman Mix produces white pumpkins in three different sizes that all mature around the same time, making them easy to stack into creative fall displays. The sprawling vines need ample garden room but reward growers with a coordinated harvest of small, medium, and large ghostly-white fruit. Direct sow after the soil has warmed for best results.

name: Socrates Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost into warm soil in full sun; provide a trellis for straight fruit and good air circulation; works well in high tunnels or protected culture as well as the open garden.
directions: Socrates is an organic, gynoecious, parthenocarpic Beit Alpha-type cucumber that sets seedless fruit without pollination, making it reliably productive even where pollinator activity is inconsistent. The dark green, thin-skinned fruits grow 7-8 inches long with tender, sweet, non-bitter flesh that needs no peeling. Bred for cooler growing conditions and protected culture, it also performs well in open garden plantings during the warm season. Harvest regularly at 7-8 inches for the best texture and flavor.

name: Soissons Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following last frost, and set poles or a trellis at planting time, since this semi-climbing French heirloom benefits from support.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following last frost, and set poles or a trellis at planting time, since this semi-climbing French heirloom benefits from support to keep its long pods off the ground. Named for the town of Soissons north of Paris, this large, flat, ivory-white bean has been the traditional centerpiece of French cassoulet for generations, valued for its creamy texture and its ability to hold shape after long, slow cooking. Let pods dry fully on the vine before shelling, then store the beans in a cool, dry place. A single planting yields a substantial harvest of beans well suited to soups, stews, and braises.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste

name: Solar Eclipse Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Solar Eclipse is an All-America Selections winner producing miniature pumpkins with a dark, near-black cap over an orange base, resembling a partially eclipsed sun.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in full sun, spacing hills to allow the productive vines to spread. Solar Eclipse produces palm-sized pumpkins whose deep, near-black coloring on the upper half of the fruit fades into bright orange toward the base, a striking pattern that gave the variety its name and earned it an All-America Selections award for novelty color. Plants set a heavy number of the small fruits over a long harvest window, making it useful for gardeners assembling mixed miniature pumpkin displays rather than growing for eating. Pick once the color pattern has fully developed and the rind has hardened, and the small fruits need no curing before use in fall arrangements.

name: Solar Fire Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Solar Fire's All-America Selections recognition reflects outstanding performance across multiple growing regions, including the hot, humid Gulf South.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Solar Fire is an All-America Selections-recognized tomato hybrid developed at the University of Florida for superior performance in hot climates — combining good heat tolerance for extended fruit set with excellent fresh-eating flavor, disease resistance, and attractive fruit appearance. The medium-large (8–10 oz), round, firm, bright-red fruits are well-suited to Gulf South conditions — they hold well on the vine and in post-harvest storage better than some softer hybrid types. Solar Fire carries resistance to the major tomato diseases of the humid Gulf South including Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt (races 1 and 2), Alternaria stem canker, Gray leaf spot, and Nematodes — a disease package that significantly reduces the fungicide and nematicide inputs required for production. The determinate to semi-determinate growth habit reaches 4–6 feet with moderate staking requirements. Solar Fire typically performs well for zone 9 gardeners in both spring (February–June) and fall (August–November) planting windows. The spring crop produces the largest volume of fruit before summer heat; the fall crop frequently produces the best-quality fruit as temperatures cool. An excellent choice for Gulf South gardeners seeking a reliable, productive, disease-resistant red tomato with better heat tolerance than standard commercial varieties.

name: Solar Set Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 transplant February–March for spring harvest and August for fall. Solar Set was specifically developed to set fruit at higher temperatures than standard varieties — the key trait for Gulf South spring production where nighttime temperatures frequently exceed 75°F before the crop is finished. Unlike most tomatoes, which fail to pollinate when nights stay above 70–75°F, Solar Set continues fruit set during warm spells.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Solar Set is a determinate hybrid tomato developed by the University of Florida specifically to address the most critical failure point in Gulf Coast tomato production — the inability of most varieties to set fruit when nighttime temperatures exceed 70–75°F. In standard tomatoes, high night temperatures destroy pollen viability and prevent fruit set even when flowering is abundant, causing the characteristic 'drop-out' where plants flower profusely but set no fruit as spring transitions to summer. Solar Set was bred to maintain viable pollen and fruit set at higher temperatures than standard varieties, extending the productive window by 2–4 weeks in warm spring conditions — a significant advantage in zone 8–11 where the spring growing window is narrow. The medium-large (6–10 oz), round, firm, bright red fruits have good flavor and adequate disease resistance including Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt, and gray leaf spot. Solar Set is not as widely known as Solar Fire or Heatmaster but performs a similar heat-set function and has been a reliable variety in UF variety trials for Gulf Coast spring production. Best suited to spring and fall production in zone 8b–11 where heat-setting capacity provides measurable yield advantages.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Gulf Coast Research and Education Center — Tomato Breeding Program
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Commercial Tomato Production Guide
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Vegetable Variety Evaluations

name: Solar Yellow Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost; yellow carrots retain their color both raw and cooked, making them visually distinctive in soups, roasted vegetable dishes, and salads.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in loose, deep, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning to 2–3 inches; Solar Yellow is a bright lemon-yellow carrot with Nantes-type cylindrical shape and excellent flavor — somewhat milder and less earthy than orange carrots with a clean, slightly sweet taste and better carotene stability (it holds its yellow color both raw and when cooked, unlike purple carrots that fade to orange). Rich in xanthophylls rather than beta-carotene, with distinct nutritional benefits associated with yellow pigments. An excellent variety for multicolored carrot mixes alongside orange, purple, red, and white types for maximum visual and nutritional diversity.

name: Solaris Fennel
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or succession-sow through summer for a fall crop, since Solaris is bred to bulb quickly across multiple seasonal slots.
directions: Solaris is an early F1 Florence fennel selected for stout, heavy bulbs that size up faster than most other bulbing types, making it a dependable choice for growers wanting an early harvest window. Sow directly into evenly moist, fertile soil and avoid root disturbance, since fennel seedlings transplant poorly once the taproot is established. The bulbs stay juicy and crisp rather than woody even as they reach 3 to 4 inches across, and the plant's dense feathery top can be harvested separately as a mild anise-flavored herb. Mound soil around the base as bulbs swell to keep them blanched and tender.

name: Soldacki Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Soldacki is a tall, potato-leaf indeterminate that needs sturdy staking or caging to support its heavy pink beefsteak fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil once the weather has warmed, staking or caging plants early. Soldacki is a Polish heirloom beefsteak with distinctive potato-leaf foliage and smooth, rosy-pink fruit often exceeding a pound, carrying a rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor typical of the best pink heirlooms. The vigorous indeterminate vines keep producing over a long season and tend to hold up reasonably well under variable summer weather. Pick fruit when fully colored but still firm at the shoulders, and watch for cracking after heavy rain on a dry spell.

name: Soldier Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil; Soldier bean is a New England heirloom dry bean with large, white seeds marked with a distinctive red figure near the hilum that resembles a standing soldier or musketeer — one of the most visually striking and historically significant New England heirloom beans.
directions: Direct sow 1.5 inches deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil; soldier bean is a bush type that performs best in cool to moderate summer climates (zones 3–7) but is grown across a wide range. Soldier bean is a New England heirloom dry bean with a long history in Maine and New England, documented in American seed catalogs for well over a century; the seeds are large, kidney-shaped, and pure white with a striking red figure near the hilum that — with some imagination — resembles a soldier or musketeer with a distinctive hat and cloak, making it one of the most visually interesting of all heirloom beans. The cooked flavor is mild, creamy, and rich, similar to navy beans but larger; soldier beans are the traditional bean of New England baked beans, Boston baked beans, and bean soups and make excellent succotash. An outstanding heirloom for seed saving, showing true and breeding reliably from year to year.

name: Solent Wight Garlic
plantingNote: Separate cloves and plant pointed end up, about 2 inches deep, in fall; Solent Wight is an English hardneck bred on the Isle of Wight and requires a genuine cold winter to vernalize and divide into full-sized bulbs.
directions: Solent Wight is a British hardneck garlic developed on the Isle of Wight and grown for its large, purple-streaked bulbs and strong, well-rounded flavor suited to the cooler, damper UK climate. Plant cloves pointed end up in fall in loose, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and mulch after the ground cools to guard against frost heaving. As with other hardnecks, cut off the curling scape in early summer to redirect the plant's energy into bulb size. Harvest once the lower leaves have browned, then cure the bulbs in a dry, airy, shaded spot for a few weeks before trimming and storing.

name: Soler Calabaza
plantingNote: Give this large-fruited vine ample hill spacing and a long warm season, since fruit can take the full growing season to size up fully.
directions: Selected in Puerto Rico, this open-pollinated calabaza is prized throughout the Caribbean and Gulf South for its flattened, deeply lobed, dark-green fruit that regularly reaches well over 15 pounds. The dense yellow-orange flesh holds up to long cooking and stores for weeks after a hard-rind harvest. Its vigorous long vines reward generous spacing and thrive in the same heat and humidity that limits many temperate squash varieties.
sources: University of Puerto Rico Agricultural Experiment Station

name: Sonora Wheat
plantingNote: Sow in fall in the low desert Southwest, where it grows through the mild winter; in cooler regions can also be sown as an early spring wheat.
directions: Sow in fall in the low desert Southwest, where it grows through the mild winter and matures before the onset of intense spring heat; in cooler regions it can also be sown as an early spring wheat. Sonora wheat was brought to the Sonoran Desert missions by Spanish colonists in the 1700s and became the dominant wheat of California and the Southwest well into the 1800s, prized for thriving with minimal water on desert soils. Its soft, low-protein white kernels mill into a fine, tender flour especially suited to tortillas and pastries rather than yeasted bread, and the variety has been actively revived by Southwestern seed-saving organizations after nearly vanishing from cultivation in the twentieth century.

name: Sora Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool to moderately warm weather; succession sow every one to two weeks for continuous harvest. Sora is notably heat tolerant, holding round roots without becoming pithy or hollow even as soil warms toward summer, extending the Gulf South radish season past the point where most varieties fail.
directions: Sow seed directly half an inch deep and thin to about an inch apart for well-formed roots; Sora is a round red radish notable for holding good quality in warmer soil than most radish varieties tolerate well, resisting the pithy, hollow centers that quickly ruin radishes grown too far into rising spring heat. This heat tolerance makes it a useful choice for extending the Gulf South radish season later into spring or for an earlier-than-usual fall planting while soil is still warm. Keep soil evenly moist for the crispest texture, and harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch across, since even heat-tolerant radishes eventually turn woody if left too long.

name: Sorcerer Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, rich soil; Sorcerer is an AAS-winning semi-bush pumpkin producing uniform 10-12 pound classic jack-o-lantern fruit on a much more compact vine than traditional sprawling pumpkin varieties.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil in full sun. Sorcerer is an AAS-winning jack-o-lantern pumpkin bred with a semi-bush habit, taking noticeably less garden space than traditional sprawling pumpkin vines while still producing a full-size crop of classic round, deep-orange, 10-12 pound carving pumpkins with the strong, smooth handle and even shape prized for jack-o-lanterns. Its more compact vine makes it a practical choice for smaller vegetable gardens that still want to grow real carving-size pumpkins rather than miniatures. Harvest when the rind hardens fully and the color deepens to solid orange, cutting the stem with a few inches attached rather than pulling it, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two to improve storage life before Halloween display.
sources: All-America Selections — Sorcerer Pumpkin winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Sorrento Broccoli Raab
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for a fall crop into fertile, well-drained soil; Sorrento matures very fast and bolts quickly in heat, so avoid summer sowings.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sorrento is a fast-maturing Italian broccoli raab producing uniform, dark green florets about 2 inches across on blue-green plants, ready in just 40 days from seed. Sow in late summer for a fall harvest or very early spring for a spring crop, since hot weather pushes it to bolt quickly. Harvest the whole flowering shoot while buds are still tight and sauté with garlic and olive oil, the classic preparation for this slightly bitter, mineral-rich green.

name: South Jersey Hopniss
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in spring into moist, sandy to loamy, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, with a trellis or shrub nearby for the twining vine to climb; this regional landrace is well suited to the damp, sandy wetland-edge conditions of its native range.
directions: South Jersey hopniss is a regional American groundnut landrace maintained from wild populations native to the damp, sandy soils of the New Jersey Pine Barrens and surrounding coastal plain, kept distinct by small seed-saving growers for its vigor in exactly that kind of acidic, moisture-retentive, part-shaded ground. Like all groundnut it is a twining perennial legume that fixes its own nitrogen while producing strings of starchy, protein-rich tubers, historically an important food source for the Lenape and other Indigenous peoples of the mid-Atlantic region. It is well adapted to the filtered light found along streambanks, pond margins, and the edges of pine-oak woodland, tolerating considerably more shade than most food crops in this database. Allow the vine a full season or more to bulk up its tuber chain before harvesting in fall, and replant a few tubers immediately to keep the patch going the following year.

name: Southern Comet Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors 5-6 weeks before transplanting; in zone 8-9 gardens transplant in late August-September for a crop that heads through the milder, more forgiving fall temperatures instead of spring's fast run-up to heat.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart with 3 feet between rows to give the large frame room to develop. Southern Comet is an All-America Selections-winning F1 hybrid selected specifically for its ability to hold up to heat and humidity better than most broccoli, forming dense, deep-green 8-inch domed heads that resist the loose, ricey curd broccoli often develops when temperatures spike during head formation. Its strong side-shoot production after the main head is cut extends the harvest window considerably, an advantage in southern fall gardens where the cool season is often shorter than the plant's full production potential. Keep soil evenly moist and side-dress with nitrogen after the first head is harvested to sustain shoot production into winter.

name: Southern Giant Curled Mustard Green
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for the superior fall crop. Southern Giant Curled is cold-hardy to about 20°F when established and thrives in the cool, mild winters of the Gulf Coast.
directions: Broadcast seeds and rake in lightly, or sow 1/4 inch deep and thin to 12–15 inches; Southern Giant Curled is the classic all-purpose mustard green of the American South, grown for over a century in Gulf Coast and Southeastern gardens and still the standard by which other mustard greens are judged for traditional Southern cooking. The large, heavily ruffled and curled, bright yellow-green leaves are pungent and mustardy, with a characteristic bite that is best tamed by long, slow cooking with pork (a smoked ham hock or fatback) in the traditional Southern style. The big, broad leaves are also excellent braised in olive oil with garlic for a more Mediterranean preparation, or wilted into beans and soups. Flavor improves dramatically after a frost — the cold converts starches to sugars and mellows the pungency, making fall mustard greens distinctly better than spring. In zone 9, plants sown in October are typically at their peak in December–January. Harvest outer leaves for continuous production; entire heads can also be cut at once for batch cooking. An exceptionally easy, productive, nutritious cool-season crop.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Southern Giant Curled documentation
LSU AgCenter — Mustard Greens for Louisiana Gardens
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mustard Green Production

name: Southern Queen Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips after last frost when soil has warmed above 65F; a dependable 19th-century heirloom, introduced from South America around 1870, that matures in roughly 105 days.
directions: Southern Queen is a vining 19th-century heirloom, introduced into the United States from South America around 1870, that produces long, narrow tubers with white skin and white, dry-cooking flesh. Sometimes called the White Yam, it is one of the oldest sweet potato varieties still maintained in American cultivation, alongside Nansemond and Hayman. Its dry, starchy texture and mild flavor make it well suited to traditional Southern cooking styles that favor a less-sweet, more potato-like sweet potato. It matures in roughly 100-110 days and adapts to a wide range of growing conditions.

name: Southport Red Globe Onion
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; Southport Red Globe is a classic American heirloom red storage onion from Southport, Connecticut — where it was the foundation of a thriving 19th-century commercial onion trade — producing medium to large, globe-shaped, deep red-purple bulbs with white, mildly pungent flesh and excellent long storage quality.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 4–6 weeks before last frost when seedlings are 6–8 inches tall and pencil-width. Southport Red Globe is a long-day heirloom red onion from Southport (now part of Fairfield), Connecticut, where it was the commercial foundation of one of the most important onion-growing regions of 19th-century America — the Connecticut shoreline towns of Southport, Wethersfield, and Granby exported enormous quantities of dried storage onions to markets up and down the Eastern Seaboard and into the Caribbean. The medium to large (3–4 inch diameter), globe-shaped bulbs have deep red-purple skin and white flesh lightly tinged with red at the outer rings; the flavor is moderately pungent when raw, milder when cooked, with a typical red onion character. As a long-day type, Southport Red Globe performs best in northern gardens (zones 3–7) where the long summer days trigger good bulb development; in Gulf Coast gardens (short-day conditions), use short-day red onion varieties instead. Excellent storage quality — properly cured bulbs keep 4–6 months.

name: Southport White Globe Onion
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant as soon as the soil can be worked; this is a long-day heirloom that needs the extended summer daylength of northern latitudes to bulb well.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 4–6 inches apart, and keep beds weed-free and evenly watered through the bulbing period. Southport White Globe is a 19th-century American heirloom that became the standard of the old Southport, Connecticut onion-growing district, producing perfectly round, pure-white, mild-flavored bulbs with thin papery skin over crisp white flesh. It is a long-day type best suited to northern gardens with long summer daylength, and while its white skin makes it more prone to sunscald and bruising in storage than yellow or red types, well-cured bulbs still keep respectably for a winter storage onion. Stop watering once tops begin to yellow and fall over, then pull, cure in a warm, dry, airy spot for two to three weeks, and store the largest, firmest bulbs for later use.

name: Southport Yellow Globe Onion
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once the soil is workable; Southport Yellow Globe is a long-day heirloom best suited to northern gardens with a full summer growing season.
directions: Southport Yellow Globe is a nineteenth-century American heirloom onion from Southport, Connecticut, and the yellow-skinned counterpart to the better-known Southport White Globe and Southport Red Globe. It forms well-rounded, medium-large globes of tan-gold skin over firm, pungent, long-storing flesh. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and keep the bed weeded, since this open-pollinated heirloom is slower to establish than modern hybrids. Harvest once most of the tops have fallen and dried, cure fully in a warm, airy spot, and expect good keeping quality typical of the classic Southport globe strains.

name: Space Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow October–February for fall through early spring harvest. Space is an F1 hybrid with outstanding downy mildew resistance — particularly important in zone 9 where the warm, humid fall climate creates conditions favorable for mildew. The smooth, upright leaves are easy to harvest and clean, with less dirt trapping than savoy-type spinach. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks for continuous harvest; even heat-tolerant spinach will bolt in zone 9's rising spring temperatures. Partial shade extends the season slightly.
directions: Plant in partial shade to full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — spinach benefits from afternoon shade protection in warmer climates to delay bolting; Space is an F1 hybrid spinach developed specifically for exceptional downy mildew (Peronospora spinaciae) resistance — the most significant disease of fresh-market spinach. The smooth, slightly cupped, dark green, upright leaves are the commercial fresh spinach leaf type: uniformly sized, easy to wash without the texture trapping of savoy (crinkled) types, and attractive in fresh salads and smoothies. Unlike savoy-type spinach that requires multiple washings to remove soil from the heavily crinkled leaves, Space's smooth, upright leaves release dirt easily and drain well in salad spinners. The F1 hybrid vigor produces noticeably more uniform and productive plants than open-pollinated varieties. Space's disease resistance makes it the practical choice for zone 9 fall spinach where warm, humid conditions can destroy less resistant varieties; the resistance ratings cover multiple races of downy mildew, providing durable protection across multiple seasons.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Space Spinach F1 Description
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Spinach Production for Florida
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Cool-Season Greens for Gulf South

name: Spadona Chicory
plantingNote: Sow directly in spring for a quick cutting crop or in late summer for a fall and early-winter harvest, cutting leaves at the base to encourage regrowth.
directions: Sow directly in spring for a quick cutting crop or in late summer for a fall and early-winter harvest, cutting leaves at the base to encourage regrowth. An Italian dandelion-leaf chicory of the Catalogna group, with long, smooth, sword-shaped serrated leaves and a mildly bitter, herbaceous flavor best known cooked but also usable young in salads. It has long been a staple green in southern Italian cooking, traditionally sautéed with garlic and olive oil.

name: Spaghetti Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. The cream-colored, football-shaped fruits should be left on the vine until the skin is hard and turns from yellow-green to deep golden-yellow. Cure harvested fruit at room temperature for 2 weeks, then store in a cool, dry place for up to 3 months. In zone 9 the long warm season allows fruits to cure fully on the vine before harvest.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Spaghetti Squash (also called Vegetable Spaghetti) is a unique winter squash whose cooked flesh separates naturally into long, thin strands closely resembling spaghetti pasta — when halved and baked cut-side down, the flesh is scraped out with a fork to produce a pile of mildly sweet, slightly crunchy, pasta-like strands. The mild, neutral flavor serves as an effective low-carbohydrate substitute for pasta under tomato sauces, pesto, or any pasta topping, and has become one of the most popular low-carb vegetables for health-conscious cooks since the 1970s. The oblong, cream-to-golden fruits (4–8 pounds) are a Cucurbita pepo type with the same excellent disease resistance and productivity as other C. pepo squash. In zone 9 the long warm season is ideal for spaghetti squash, which requires the full warm season to develop and cure properly on the vine.
sources: Cornell University Extension — Cucurbita pepo Winter Squash Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Winter Squash Production
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Pumpkin and Winter Squash Production

name: Spanish Roja Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 2 inches deep in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; Spanish Roja is a rocambole-type hardneck with a strong cold requirement for good bulb formation, best suited to zone 3-7 with a real winter chill.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in well-drained, fertile soil enriched with compost. Spanish Roja is a classic rocambole-type hardneck garlic, brought to the Pacific Northwest by Spanish settlers generations ago, and widely considered by garlic growers and chefs to have some of the finest, most complex flavor of any garlic variety — rich, hot, and full without being harsh. Bulbs have a distinctive rich reddish-brown skin over 8-12 large, very easy-to-peel cloves arranged in a single layer typical of rocamboles. Like other hardnecks, it produces a dramatic double-curling flower scape in late spring that should be cut once curled to focus the plant's energy on bulb development; the scapes are excellent eaten fresh or cooked. The main tradeoff for its superior flavor is shorter storage life than porcelain or softneck types, typically only 4-5 months, so plan to use Spanish Roja earlier in the storage season. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have browned, and cure for 2-3 weeks in a warm, dry, airy, shaded location before trimming.
sources: Chester Aaron: The Great Garlic Book, Ten Speed Press 1997

name: Sparkler Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in spring or 4–6 weeks before first fall frost; Sparkler is a fast-maturing spring radish with a distinctive two-toned coloring — vivid red on the upper two-thirds of the root and bright white on the lower third — that makes it one of the most visually attractive spring radishes for fresh eating, relish trays, and kitchen display.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep as early as soil can be worked; thin to 2 inches apart; Sparkler matures very quickly (22–30 days) and becomes pithy and hollow if left too long in the ground — harvest promptly when roots reach 3/4 to 1 inch in diameter; succession-plant every 2–3 weeks for continuous supply. Sparkler is a classic American heirloom spring radish that dates to the late 19th century and remains a popular choice in home gardens for its distinctive bicolor appearance: the round, smooth roots are vivid scarlet-red on the upper portion and a clean, bright white on the lower third to half — a sharp, clean color transition that gives the radish a visually appealing two-toned look unlike the solid red of Cherry Belle or the pure white of White Icicle. The name 'Sparkler' is apt — the red-and-white coloring is eye-catching and festive in a salad bowl or on a relish tray. The flavor is crisp and mildly peppery, slightly milder than some all-red varieties, and the texture at perfect maturity is ideal — firm, juicy, and snap-crisp. Like all spring radishes, Sparkler bolts rapidly in summer heat and should be grown only in cool weather (spring and fall); in zone 9a, the fall season (September through November) and very early spring (January through March in coastal areas) are the practical growing windows. Sparkler is valued by gardeners who want visual variety in their radish plantings beyond the standard all-red types.

name: Sparx Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring, summer, or fall; Sparx holds its upright heart shape and resists bolting and bitterness in warm conditions better than standard romaine, making it a useful choice for extending the Gulf Coast lettuce season into late spring.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil, thinning to 8-12 inches, and harvest whole hearts once the upright heads have filled out. Sparx is a modern romaine bred for the fresh-market 'hearts' trade, producing dense, uniform, upright heads of crisp, sweet leaves on a plant noted for holding quality through hot spells that cause many other romaine types to turn bitter or bolt prematurely. Its dependable performance across spring, summer, and fall plantings makes it a practical choice for Gulf Coast gardeners looking to stretch romaine production beyond the short cool-season window most lettuce requires. Provide light afternoon shade during the hottest stretches to further slow bolting and preserve leaf quality.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database

name: Speckled Butter Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil exceeds 70°F; in zone 9 plant April for spring and late July for fall. Speckled Butter Bean is a pole type requiring a trellis, fence, or teepee of stakes at least 5–6 feet tall; it is a vigorous climber that performs well in the Gulf South's long warm season.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep at the base of a fence, trellis, or pole teepee in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Speckled Butter Bean (also called Sieva or Carolina Sieva) is a small-seeded, pole-type lima bean of a different genetic character from the large-seeded butter bean types — it traces ancestry to indigenous lima varieties of the American South and Caribbean and has been cultivated in the Gulf South for centuries. The flat, cream-colored seeds are distinctively speckled with purple-maroon markings that fade during cooking. Flavor is extremely buttery, nutty, and rich — many Southern gardeners consider the Speckled Butter Bean to have a more complex, 'butter' flavor than large Fordhook-type limas. The vining plants are highly heat-tolerant and thrive through Gulf Coast summers that stop most shell beans cold, continuing to set pods at temperatures that wilt other legumes. Harvest fresh for the traditional Southern preparation: shell and cook with a piece of fatback or smoked sausage and season with salt and pepper. Dried seeds also cook into excellent soups and stews. A true Southern heirloom with deep historical roots in Gulf Coast foodways.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Speckled Butter Bean documentation
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Heritage Southern beans
William Woys Weaver: Heirloom Vegetable Gardening
Mississippi State University Extension — Butter Bean Production

name: Speckled Cutshort Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm (65°F+), at the base of a sturdy 6–8 foot pole or trellis, since Speckled Cutshort is a vigorous heirloom climber.
directions: Sow at the base of poles or a trellis in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest pods young and tender for snap use, or let mature for a flavorful dry soup bean. Speckled Cutshort is a member of the Appalachian 'cutshort' family of heirloom pole beans, so named for the short, blunt, somewhat flattened pod tip characteristic of the type, and passed down for generations among mountain families in Kentucky, Tennessee, Virginia, and the Carolinas, with many named strains maintained within individual families and communities. The pods are speckled with purple-brown markings while developing, turning fully green as they mature, and the tender, meaty texture makes them excellent as a snap bean; left to dry, the attractively speckled seeds cook into a rich, traditional Appalachian soup bean. Vigorous and productive on a sturdy support, it is a genuine piece of living Appalachian food heritage for gardeners who want an authentic regional heirloom, zone 4–10.

name: Speckled Graham Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow with a trellis or ample room to sprawl; this type is strongly daylength-sensitive and won't bulk up its main pod flush until day length shrinks back toward 13 hours in late summer, so don't expect an early harvest.
directions: A pre-1940 South Carolina heirloom collected in 1992 and now maintained by USDA-ARS in Charleston, about as regionally Gulf and Southeast-pedigreed as a cowpea gets. Vigorous 10-15 foot sprawling or climbing vines need a trellis or plenty of room, producing a big flush of 9-inch pods in late summer into fall rather than early in the season. The gray-and-tan speckled seed carries good resistance to root-knot nematode, and seed coats are selected to be permeable enough that volunteers don't survive winter, a useful 'won't become a weed' trait.
sources: USDA-ARS Plant Germplasm System (Charleston, SC maintenance records)

name: Speckled Hound Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow into warm soil after frost danger has passed; Speckled Hound is a moschata-type heirloom pumpkin with distinctive dark green speckling over an orange rind and dense, sweet, moist flesh good for pies and roasting.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in hills of warm, fertile soil and give the vigorous vines room to sprawl, since Speckled Hound belongs to Cucurbita moschata, the same heat- and pest-tolerant species as butternut squash and generally outperforms Cucurbita pepo pumpkins in hot, humid Southern gardens. The medium-sized, slightly flattened fruit has a striking dark green speckled pattern over deep orange skin, and the moist, dense, sweet flesh is well suited to pies, soups, and roasting, holding its flavor and texture through long storage better than most jack-o'-lantern types. Moschata squash also tends to shrug off vine borers better than pepo types, a real advantage in the Gulf South where borers are a persistent problem. Harvest once the rind resists a fingernail scratch and the stem has begun to dry, and cure fruit in a warm, airy spot for a week or two before moving to cool winter storage.

name: Speckled Hound Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Speckled Hound is a modern chef-bred delicata-type squash selected for sweetness and a longer-storing, tougher rind than standard delicata.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving the sprawling vine plenty of room to spread. Speckled Hound was bred by Row 7 Seed Company in collaboration with chefs specifically for improved flavor over standard delicata squash, producing oblong, cream-colored fruit speckled and streaked with green, with notably sweet, dense, richly flavored orange flesh and a somewhat tougher rind that stores longer than typical delicata types. Harvest when the rind hardens and speckled coloring fully develops, usually as the vine begins to decline in late summer or fall, and cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two before storing to improve flavor and shelf life. Like other Cucurbita pepo squash, watch for squash vine borer and squash bugs in Gulf South gardens.

name: Speckled Purple Hull Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65F and all frost danger has passed; Speckled Purple Hull, sometimes called Old Timer, is a semi-crowder pea with curved purple pods and cream peas mottled with tan-brown speckles.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun. Speckled Purple Hull, an old Southern heirloom also known as Old Timer, bears curved, rich purple pods about seven inches long, shelling out to reveal cream-colored peas mottled with distinctive tan-brown speckles, a semi-crowder texture prized for the classic flavor it brings to a pot of Hoppin' John. Its purple pods turn a deeper shade as they mature, making picking time easy to judge, and like other cowpeas it thrives through the hottest, most humid stretch of the Gulf South summer when many other vegetables falter. As with other cowpeas, its roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil for whatever crop follows. Harvest continuously at the green-shell stage for fresh eating, or let pods dry fully for long-term storage.

name: Speckled Roman Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Speckled Roman is a distinctive paste-type heirloom with dramatically striped red-and-orange fruits and equally striped leaves, producing meaty, flavorful paste tomatoes with more complex flavor and better fresh-eating quality than standard smooth-skinned paste varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; provide substantial staking or caging as plants grow 5–7 feet tall. Speckled Roman tomato was discovered by Doreen Howard in Illinois and is distinguished from virtually all other paste tomatoes by its dramatically striped appearance — the fruits have alternating red and orange stripes (or speckles when young) that persist to full ripeness, making them visually striking among the usually uniformly red paste types. The foliage is similarly striped, with green and yellow banding on the leaves. Beyond the ornamental appeal, Speckled Roman produces exceptionally flavorful paste tomatoes with more complexity and better texture for fresh eating than standard San Marzano or Roma types while retaining the meaty, low-moisture flesh needed for sauce and paste production. Medium-large (4–8 oz), cylindrical to elongated-oval fruits. Outstanding for both fresh use and preserving, and a beautiful conversation piece in the garden.

name: Speckles Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall-winter harvest or January–February for spring. Speckles is an Austrian heirloom butterhead type with excellent cold hardiness and some heat tolerance. In zone 9 it is most productive from October through March; the red-speckled pattern on the leaves intensifies in cool weather. Successive sowings every 3 weeks extend the harvest season.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Speckles is an Austrian heirloom butterhead lettuce distinguished by large, soft, pale-green leaves heavily spotted and speckled with red-maroon freckles — a distinctive appearance unlike any other lettuce. The speckle pattern varies from plant to plant, and no two heads are identically spotted, making it one of the most visually interesting lettuces for mixed salads and fresh presentations. The flavor is classic butterhead — tender, buttery, mild, and slightly sweet — without the bitterness of some red-pigmented lettuces. Speckles is a slow-to-bolt Austrian type that holds quality in the garden longer than many butterhead varieties before heat causes it to flower. The unique spotted appearance makes it highly marketable at farmers' markets and popular in mesclun mixes where the speckled leaves stand out visually. In zone 9 it produces excellent fall-through-winter heads with the speckle pattern intensifying in cool temperatures.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Speckles Lettuce Heritage Variety
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Austrian Heirloom Lettuce Types
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Butterhead Lettuce

name: Spineless Beauty Hybrid Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost, or start indoors 3-4 weeks early; use drip irrigation to help manage mildew in humid climates.
directions: Spineless Beauty is a widely grown commercial-grade hybrid zucchini bred with smooth, nearly spine-free petioles, sparing gardeners the itchy rash that comes from brushing bristly zucchini foliage during harvest. The open, mounding plant sets glossy, speckled medium-green fruit that hold quality even when picked slightly larger than typical zucchini, at 6-8 inches. Because powdery and downy mildew can move fast through humid Gulf Coast gardens, growers should keep foliage dry with drip irrigation and watch closely during rainy spells since this variety carries no built-in mildew resistance. Regular harvest every two to three days keeps the vigorous, heavy-yielding plant productive through the season.

name: Spinoso di Palermo Artichoke
scientificName: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Spinoso di Palermo'
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or plant rooted offshoots in early spring; established clumps bloom through fall and winter in Sicily's mild Mediterranean climate.
directions: Grown in market gardens around Palermo and now protected as an IGP product, Spinoso di Palermo produces large, elongated, violet-green globes armed with long, sharp spines on the bracts, a trait many Sicilian cooks associate with superior flavor and tenderness in the heart compared to spineless modern hybrids. Handle harvested heads with gloves and a sharp knife, cutting the main terminal bud first to encourage a long season of smaller side buds through late winter. Rich, deep, well-drained soil and consistent moisture produce the best size, while mild Mediterranean-style winters without hard freezes let plants bloom nearly year-round. In the kitchen the tender hearts and bracts star in carciofi alla palermitana (stuffed and braised) and are prized sliced raw into salads while still young.
sources: Consorzio di Tutela Carciofo Spinoso di Palermo IGP

name: Spirit Pumpkin
subcategory: AAS-winning semi-bush jack-o-lantern and baking pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost; the semi-bush habit takes noticeably less garden space than sprawling heirloom pumpkins, a real benefit in smaller Gulf Coast vegetable beds.
directions: Sow seeds directly in hills once the soil has warmed, thinning to two or three plants per hill; the compact, semi-bush vine allows closer spacing than traditional long-vined field pumpkins. Spirit was named an All-America Selections winner in 1977 for producing bright orange, deeply oval fruit averaging 10-15 pounds on a plant that stays far more contained than open-pollinated heirlooms. The thick, meaty flesh makes it genuinely dual-purpose, equally suited to a classic jack-o'-lantern face and to being baked down for pumpkin puree. Harvest once the rind has hardened and colored fully, cure briefly in a warm spot, and store in a cool, dry location out of direct sun.

name: Spring Raab Broccoli Raab
plantingNote: Direct sow in earliest workable spring soil; this variety was selected specifically for spring planting without the premature bolting that affects many raab types sown before long days arrive.
directions: Spring Raab was bred by Oregon plant breeder Frank Morton specifically to solve broccoli raab's biggest flaw: most varieties were selected for fall planting and bolt to seed almost immediately if sown in spring's lengthening days. This selection holds its vegetative, leafy-budded stage longer under spring conditions, giving a reliable harvest window instead of an instant bolt. Cut the central flowering shoot once small buds form but before yellow petals show, then continue picking side shoots for several weeks. Flavor is milder and less bitter than many older raab landraces, making it a good entry point for gardeners new to the crop.

name: Sputnik Upland Rice
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant into moist, fertile soil once the weather has warmed; stake or support in exposed sites since tall stands can lodge after heavy rain.
directions: Sputnik is a modern awnless upland rice bred in Primorsky Krai in the Russian Far East, a region with a climate cool enough that it has proven workable for temperate North American gardens. It produces a short-grain brown rice and tillers vigorously, giving good yields per plant, though its taller stature makes it somewhat prone to lodging in wind and heavy rain. Start seed indoors and transplant it out once the soil has warmed, since like most upland rices it is slow to establish from seed and needs a head start against weeds. It is best suited to gardeners already growing other upland rice types who want a taller, higher-tillering variety to diversify their planting.

name: Stampede Jerusalem Artichoke
plantingNote: Plant tuber sections with one or more eyes 4 inches deep in early spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Stampede is the earliest-maturing Jerusalem artichoke variety — tubers are ready approximately 90–110 days from planting vs. 130+ days for unnamed varieties. In zone 9 this makes a spring planting viable for summer-fall harvest before the worst heat. Jerusalem artichokes spread aggressively — plant where containment is possible or in isolated beds. Harvesting all visible tubers at the end of the season prevents uncontrolled spread.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, loose, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — Jerusalem artichoke is forgiving of poor soil and minimal care; Stampede is an early-maturing selection of Jerusalem artichoke (Helianthus tuberosus) that was developed for northern short-season gardens where standard varieties may not mature tubers before killing frost. The smooth, relatively uniform, white-to-tan tubers are significantly easier to clean and prepare than the knobby irregular tubers of wild-type plants, and the early maturity reduces the waiting period before harvest. Jerusalem artichoke (sunchoke) tubers have a crunchy, slightly sweet, nutty flavor reminiscent of water chestnuts when eaten raw, and a creamy, buttery quality when roasted or pureed — they are used in soups, stir-fries, gratins, and roasted as a potato substitute. The tubers store inulin (a prebiotic fiber) rather than starch, making them lower-glycemic than potatoes but causing digestive discomfort in some people — the nickname 'fartichoke' reflects this effect, which diminishes with acclimation.
sources: University of Vermont Extension — Jerusalem Artichoke Varieties
Rodale Institute — Stampede Sunchoke Variety Notes
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Jerusalem Artichoke Production

name: Stampede Sunchoke
plantingNote: Plant tuber sections 3-5 inches deep around the last frost date in any well-drained soil in full sun; Stampede matures noticeably earlier than most sunchokes, forming large tubers before other varieties have finished bulking up, which suits areas with a shorter frost-free window.
directions: Plant tuber pieces in well-drained soil in a dedicated bed, since sunchokes spread aggressively from any tuber left in the ground and are difficult to fully remove once established. Stampede is prized among Jerusalem artichoke growers for maturing its large, smooth-skinned tubers earlier than most other varieties, allowing an earlier fall harvest and giving northern growers a reliable crop even where the growing season is on the short side. Foliage grows tall and topped with small yellow sunflowers in late summer before dying back after frost, at which point the tubers are ready to dig; a light frost is said to improve their sweet, nutty flavor by converting stored inulin into simple sugars. Harvest tubers from fall through early spring as needed, leaving a few in the ground to resprout the following year, and rotate or contain the bed to keep the planting from spreading into unwanted areas.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Jerusalem Artichoke

name: Star of David Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Star of David is an Israeli heirloom okra producing fat, round, six-ridged pods that look like a Star of David in cross-section, with a distinctive flavor and substantially larger pod diameter than standard American okra varieties — excellent for stuffing whole.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm; soak seeds 12–24 hours for faster, more uniform germination. Star of David okra (also called Israeli okra or Giant Israeli okra) is a Middle Eastern heirloom producing fat, broadly triangular, six-ridged pods that create a hexagonal or Star-of-David shape in cross-section; the pods are substantially wider in diameter (1.5–2 inches) than the slender American varieties, making them excellent for stuffing whole (halved lengthwise and filled with seasoned meat and rice in the Middle Eastern manner, or stuffed and baked with tomato sauce). The flavor is mild and tender at 3–4 inch harvest size; the large pod diameter keeps them from becoming stringy at slightly larger sizes than standard okra. Plants are very tall (6–9 feet), vigorous, and ornamental with large yellow hibiscus flowers.

name: Starbor Kale
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 4-6 weeks before the last frost; also sow in mid to late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow seed a half inch deep and thin or transplant to final spacing, side-dressing with compost as plants size up. This compact, uniform hybrid produces tightly curled, dark blue-green leaves on short stems, making it well suited to close spacing and mechanical or hand bunch harvesting. Its short, dense habit and slow bolting have made it a standard choice for market growers wanting a tidy, consistent curly kale.

name: Starbrite Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm and all frost danger has passed.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Starbrite is a widely grown hybrid watermelon producing large, oblong fruit with the classic dark and light green striped rind most gardeners picture when they think of watermelon, and sweet, crisp, deep red flesh with a small, manageable seed cavity. The vigorous vine carries good resistance to fusarium wilt and anthracnose, two diseases that shorten productive vine life in warm, humid growing regions, helping the plant stay healthy and productive through a long summer season. As a dependable, well-proven hybrid with a long track record, it remains a solid standard choice for gardeners wanting a classic, reliable watermelon without the added complexity of seedless triploid pollination requirements. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit browns and the ground spot turns creamy yellow.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Starship Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; in zone 9, spring-sow February–March and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun.
