Starship is a distinctive pale, cream-white zucchini that stands out visually from the far more common dark green types, with smooth, cylindrical fruit and tender, mild flesh good for all standard zucchini preparations, from grilling to sautéing to baking into bread. Beyond its novelty color, the compact, productive bush is a reliable, disease-tolerant performer well suited to home gardens wanting to diversify a summer squash planting beyond the usual green varieties. Pick fruit at six to eight inches for the best eating quality, and harvest frequently once production ramps up, since oversized fruit turns seedy and tough quickly, a trait shared by all zucchini types regardless of skin color.

name: Statissa Mangetout Fava Bean
directions: Plant this short, sturdy, wind-tolerant broad bean in a sunny bed, raised bed, or even a large container, since compact plants rarely need staking. Marketed by Suttons as the first broad bean created especially for eating in the pod, Statissa carries thin, short pods with small, delicate beans that can be steamed whole like mangetout, and it earned the RHS Award of Garden Merit for reliable, heavy early-summer cropping.

name: Steirische Käferbohne
plantingNote: Direct sow after frost danger passes and provide sturdy poles; pods are left on the vine to dry fully rather than picked green.
directions: Sow seed directly at the base of tall poles once soil is warm, and let pods mature and dry fully on the vine rather than harvesting them green. Steirische Käferbohne is an Austrian heirloom runner bean from Styria, recognized under the European Union's Protected Geographical Indication scheme since 2011, named for the dark maroon-brown mottling on its large beige seeds that resembles a beetle's shell ('Käfer' means beetle). Grown specifically as a dry bean rather than a snap bean, it is traditionally boiled, cooled, and dressed with vinegar, onion, and Styrian pumpkin seed oil to make the classic regional dish Käferbohnensalat. Harvest whole dried pods once they rattle, then shell and finish drying the beans indoors before storage.
sources: European Commission Protected Geographical Indication register

name: Stereo Mangetout Fava Bean
directions: Sow this compact, container-friendly broad bean close together in rich soil and start picking pods early while they are still flat and only a few inches long. Bred specifically for a thin, tender pod wall rather than for the beans inside, Stereo can be snapped and eaten whole like a mangetout pea, though left longer it also yields a conventional crop of sweet, nutty-flavored shelled beans.

name: Stewart's Zeebest Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm (65°F+); soak seed overnight to speed germination. Stewart's Zeebest is a tall, vigorous Louisiana heirloom that continues producing tender pods over a long, hot Gulf South summer.
directions: Sow directly into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest pods every 1–2 days at 3–4 inches, since this tall, heavy-yielding variety puts on pods quickly in summer heat and older pods turn woody fast. Stewart's Zeebest is a Louisiana heirloom okra, grown for generations by home gardeners in the Gulf South for its tall, vigorous plants and heavy, extended production of smooth, tender, dark green pods with excellent flavor and relatively low fiber even at a slightly larger picking size than typical spineless varieties. The tall habit (commonly 6–8 feet by late summer) makes it useful as a seasonal privacy screen or windbreak in the vegetable garden in addition to its culinary value, and the plants shrug off the heat and humidity that stress many garden crops in July and August. A reliable, long-producing regional heirloom for Gulf South okra lovers, zone 5–11.

name: Stickless Wonder Yardlong Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is reliably above 70 degrees F, 1-3 weeks after last frost; no trellis is needed, which makes this the easiest yardlong bean to fit into a small bed or container planting.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm soil; unlike nearly every other yardlong bean, Stickless Wonder grows as a compact, self-supporting bush rather than a climbing vine, so it needs no trellis and matures noticeably faster than pole-type long beans. Pods still reach an impressive 12-15 inches even without the extra growing time a vine gets, and they hold a good tender texture if picked young. Because the plants stay low and open, watch more closely for pods hiding under the foliage so none are missed and left to toughen. A light stake can still help keep top-heavy plants upright in windy Gulf Coast summer storms, even though the vines themselves need no support to climb.

name: Stockbridge Arrow Rhubarb
plantingNote: Plant dormant crowns in autumn or early spring in a sunny, well-drained bed enriched with aged manure or compost.
directions: Stockbridge Arrow is a modern British-bred maincrop rhubarb selected for long, straight, uniformly deep-red stalks and strong disease resistance, and it has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. It holds its color and firm texture well into midsummer rather than fading to green like many older varieties, which makes it popular with market growers as well as home gardeners. Vigorous, disease-resistant crowns establish quickly and produce heavy yields once mature. Divide congested clumps every four to six years in dormancy to keep stalk quality high.

name: Stockton Red Onion
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once the soil is workable; Stockton Red is an intermediate-day type adaptable to a fairly broad range of latitudes, including much of the mid-South.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing 4–6 inches apart, and water evenly through the growing season. Stockton Red is an old California heirloom onion, named for the San Joaquin Valley growing district around Stockton, producing flattened, deep-red-skinned bulbs with pink-tinged white flesh and a flavor milder than many storage reds, making it good for both fresh eating and cooking. It is an intermediate-day type with somewhat more latitude flexibility than strict long-day heirlooms, and it stores respectably for a red onion when properly cured. Taper off watering once the tops begin to yellow and topple, then pull the bulbs, cure in a warm, dry, airy location for two to three weeks, and store in a cool, dry spot out of direct light to preserve color and firmness.

name: Stocky Golden Roaster Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out only once soil and nights are reliably warm, since fruit wall thickness and smooth skin develop best with steady heat.
directions: Stocky Golden Roaster is a Wild Garden Seed farm original bred for a broad, smooth, thick-walled golden fruit that holds up well over coals or a flame, since its unwrinkled skin slips off cleanly once charred. Early fruits typically reach about 6 inches before later sets taper to a smaller size as the plant keeps flowering through the season. Give it full sun, warm soil, and even moisture; stake or cage plants once they begin loading up with fruit.

name: Stokes Purple Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips after last frost when soil warms above 65°F; Stokes Purple needs a full 110–125 days and benefits from the long season of Gulf Coast and warm Southern gardens; developed by Stokes Tropicals nursery in Lafayette, Louisiana, selected for extraordinarily high anthocyanin content — higher per serving than blueberries — making it one of the most antioxidant-rich foods commercially available.
directions: Plant slips 12–18 inches apart in loose, well-drained soil after soil warms above 65°F; Stokes Purple needs its full 110–125 days to develop; harvest after first frost threat in cooler climates. Stokes Purple was developed by Stokes Tropicals nursery in Lafayette, Louisiana from crosses involving Asian purple-flesh sweet potato types and selected specifically for American growing conditions and maximum anthocyanin content; the resulting variety has skin ranging from deep purple to nearly black and flesh that is uniformly rich purple-violet throughout — the highest level of anthocyanin pigments of any readily available sweet potato cultivar, higher per serving than blueberries or Concord grapes. The flavor is less sweet and more starchy than orange-flesh types, with an earthy, wine-like complexity and dense texture suited to roasting, savory preparations, smoothies, and applications where the dramatic color matters most. The vivid purple holds reasonably well through cooking, making dishes visually spectacular. Now grown commercially in California and Hawaii; available in health food stores and some major grocery chains.

name: Stone Mountain Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; give vines 8–10 feet of room to sprawl.
directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; keep evenly watered through fruit set and ease off as melons near ripeness to concentrate sugars. Stone Mountain is a classic early 20th-century Southern heirloom watermelon, grown for generations across the South for its large, oblong, dark green fruit and exceptionally sweet, deep red, fine-grained flesh with relatively small seed count for an old-time variety. The vigorous vines are productive and well adapted to the long, hot growing season of the Gulf South, and the tough rind travels and stores reasonably well for a heritage variety, a trait that made it a popular market melon in the era before modern shipping cultivars took over. Its rich, old-fashioned flavor and reliable performance in southern heat and humidity have kept it a favorite among heirloom gardeners who want the taste of a bygone-era watermelon, zone 4–11.

name: Stone Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Stone is a vigorous indeterminate regular-leaf variety with above-average foliage disease tolerance for an heirloom, but still benefits from staking.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile soil, staking the vigorous vines. Introduced by Livingston Seed Company in 1889 from a market grower's field near Grandville, Ohio, Stone produces dense, heavy, 6-8 ounce red fruit with an old-fashioned tangy acidity that made it a favorite for canning, juice, catsup, and chili sauce in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Its name references the notable density and weight of its fruit compared to other varieties of the period, and the plants show better foliage disease resistance than many contemporaries.

name: Stonehead Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9, transplant late August through September for November–January harvest. Stonehead is also excellent for spring production: start indoors January–February and transplant when temperatures allow. The compact size makes Stonehead ideal for small gardens where a full-sized cabbage would take too much space; plant at 12–15 inch spacing for full-sized heads or 10 inch spacing for smaller, tennis-ball-size heads.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 65–75°F; harden off before transplanting to full sun in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil. Stonehead is a 1969 All-America Selections-winning hybrid cabbage that earned recognition for combining early maturity with compact plant size — producing well-formed, 3–5 lb solid round heads on plants that occupy roughly half the space of standard cabbage types. The 'stone' in the name refers to the rock-solid firmness of the tightly packed, dense heads — when thumped, a properly matured Stonehead sounds and feels like a stone ball. The compact habit (spread of 12–15 inches vs. the 18–24 inches of standard types) at 12-inch spacing allows 25–30% more plants per row, making Stonehead one of the most space-efficient cabbage varieties for home gardens. The heads are round, attractively formed, medium blue-green with smooth skin (not savoy-type), and crack-resistant — holding in the garden for an extended period after reaching maturity without splitting. The mild, tender cabbage flavor is excellent raw in coleslaw, fermented as sauerkraut, or cooked; the dense texture holds up well in both applications. Stonehead remains one of the most widely recommended cabbage varieties in the United States more than 55 years after its AAS recognition.
sources: All-America Selections — Stonehead cabbage AAS winner 1969
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Cabbage variety comparison
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Cabbage Production Guide

name: Stoplight Red Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks ahead of the last frost; this is one of the earlier-ripening bells in the Stoplight series, useful for shorter growing seasons.
directions: Stoplight Red is part of Wild Garden Seed's Stoplight bell series, selected for large, deep red fruit with thick flesh, prominent lobes, and sweet flavor that is also good eaten green before it fully colors. All the Stoplight bells were bred for earlier ripening than typical bell peppers, which is especially useful in the cool, short summers of the Willamette Valley. Give plants full sun and consistent watering, and expect a flush of green fruit early that gradually ripens to deep red through the season.

name: Storage No. 4 Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, or in early summer for a fall harvest destined for winter storage; this Danish-type cabbage is bred specifically for keeping quality rather than early eating.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, timing the crop to mature in the cooler days of fall. Storage No. 4 is a Danish-type cabbage bred above all for keeping quality, forming dense, hard, pale green heads that resist splitting in the field and hold their crispness for months in cold, humid storage such as a root cellar. Its heads are somewhat smaller and firmer than fresh-market types, a trait that directly supports its long shelf life. Harvest before hard freezes settle in and store whole heads with roots trimmed for the longest keeping.

name: Stowell's Evergreen Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for wind pollination; Stowell's Evergreen is a large, late-maturing corn (90–100 days) suited to long-season climates. In zone 9, plant February–March for a May–June harvest, or plant mid-August for a fall crop. The 'Evergreen' name refers to the variety's long window for harvesting in the roasting ear stage — the kernels remain tender and at peak quality for a longer period than most corn before starch sets in, a trait that made this variety especially valued in the 19th and early 20th centuries before home refrigeration.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in full sun in blocks at least 4 rows wide for adequate wind pollination; fertilize well at planting and side-dress with nitrogen when plants reach knee height. Stowell's Evergreen is one of the oldest and most important heirloom sweet corn varieties in American gardening tradition — a white su (standard sugary) corn introduced before 1848 by Nathan N. Stowell of Burlington, New Jersey, who reportedly sold the variety for $4 (a substantial sum) before it was propagated and spread widely by seed companies. The variety dominated American sweet corn production and home gardens throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries, remaining one of the most popular sweet corn varieties in America for over 100 years before hybrid varieties began displacing open-pollinated types in the mid-20th century. The 'Evergreen' in the name refers to the variety's characteristic long harvest window in the milk stage — the kernels remain tender and edible for longer than most corn before converting sugar to starch, a property especially valuable before refrigeration when fresh corn had to be consumed quickly. Stowell's Evergreen produces large (8–9 inch) ears with 14–20 rows of pure white kernels that are tender, sweet (for an su type), and deeply flavored with the rich, starchy-sweet character of traditional open-pollinated corn that many old-timers consider superior to modern hybrids for preserving, canning, and creamed corn preparations. An irreplaceable heirloom variety with a direct connection to the entire American sweet corn tradition.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Stowell's Evergreen corn variety history
Iowa State University Extension — Heirloom Vegetable Varieties

name: Stowell's Evergreen Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost when soil is warm; in zone 9 plant March–April for a late spring/summer crop. Stowell's Evergreen has a long harvest window (the 'Evergreen' name refers to the fact that the milky stage stays edible for an extended period, unlike earlier varieties that must be harvested within hours).
directions: Sow 1–2 inches deep in blocks of at least 3–4 rows in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Stowell's Evergreen was introduced in 1848 by Nathan Newman Stowell, originally a hybrid between a white field corn and an early sweet type. It was the dominant home garden sweet corn throughout the latter half of the 19th century and remained popular well into the 20th. The tall (7–8 feet) plants produce 8–9 inch ears with white kernels in 16–20 rows, each kernel deep and richly flavored with classic sweet corn taste. The name refers to an actual characteristic: unlike many older sweet corns where the milky eating stage lasts only a few days, Stowell's Evergreen holds at milk stage for 1–2 weeks — a valuable trait before refrigeration and the dominant reason for its century-long popularity. The tall stalks require some wind protection in exposed sites. An important heirloom for corn breeding and a satisfying producer for gardeners who prioritize old-fashioned flavor and the ability to harvest over an extended window.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Stowell's Evergreen historical documentation
William Woys Weaver: Heirloom Vegetable Gardening, Henry Holt 1997
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds variety notes

name: Straight Eight Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Straight Eight is the All-America Selections-winning classic American slicing cucumber of the mid-twentieth century, the standard by which all slicers were measured from its 1935 AAS Gold Medal through the 1980s — still an excellent garden variety with reliable production and the classic cucumber form.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills or rows after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; train vines up a trellis for cleaner fruits or let sprawl in ample space. Straight Eight won the All-America Selections Gold Medal in 1935 and for decades became the definitive American garden cucumber — named for its uniform, straight, exactly 8-inch, dark green fruits with rounded tips, blunt blossom ends, thin skin, crisp flesh, and reliable productivity. It remained the standard garden slicing cucumber through the mid-twentieth century and was the one cucumber every American seed company carried. While modern hybrids have surpassed it in disease resistance and uniformity, Straight Eight remains a beloved heirloom for gardeners who want a reliable, seed-saveable, classic slicer. Produces well in warm conditions; good for Gulf Coast spring and fall production.

name: Stratagem Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool soil ahead of the last frost; this dwarf, large-podded Victorian pea stays shorter than many main-crop types but still benefits from light brush support.
directions: Sow directly in cool, well-drained soil in early spring; Stratagem stays relatively compact for an heirloom marrowfat pea, but its unusually large, dark blue-green pods still benefit from a low brush or netting support to keep them off the ground. First described in English horticultural literature around 1880 as a dwarf wrinkled marrow selected from the old Telegraph pea strain, it was prized in its day both as a late-season table pea and as an exhibition variety for its outsized pods. Pick pods while they remain plump and glossy for the best flavor and texture, since this older type sweetens less in storage than modern varieties.

name: Strawberry Popcorn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm (60°F+); in zone 9 plant March–May. Strawberry Popcorn is harvested for dry kernels rather than fresh eating — leave ears on the stalks until the husks are fully dried and brown, then harvest and continue drying in a warm, well-ventilated location for 3–4 weeks. When the kernels are completely dry, rub ears together to shell the kernels off the cob. The dried ears are ornamental for months before shelling and can be used as fall decorations. Plant in blocks of at least 4 rows (not single long rows) for good wind pollination.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil — corn is a heavy feeder requiring nitrogen-rich soil and consistent moisture during ear development; Strawberry Popcorn is an heirloom ornamental and edible popcorn variety producing tiny, round, deep burgundy-crimson ears that are remarkably realistic miniature strawberry look-alikes — the round, plump shape and rich dark red color create an almost uncanny resemblance to a strawberry when the ear is viewed with fresh eyes. The small ears (2–3 inches long) are produced one to two per stalk on compact (4–5 foot) plants, making Strawberry Popcorn both a space-efficient popcorn crop and one of the most attractive ornamental corn varieties for fall decoration. The dark red kernels pop into white popcorn — the kernel color disappears in the heat of popping — producing popcorn with the same light, airy, slightly sweet flavor as standard popcorn. The ornamental appeal (dried ears make excellent fall table decorations, wreaths, and displays) combined with the culinary value (genuinely edible popcorn) makes Strawberry Popcorn one of the best dual-purpose plants for the home garden, particularly appealing to children who delight in both the process of growing them and the surprise of popping the dramatic red kernels into white popcorn.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Strawberry Popcorn Heirloom Corn
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Strawberry Popcorn Description
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Specialty Popcorn Varieties

name: Strawberry Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after soil has warmed well past last frost; bred from Florida stock, it is naturally well suited to the long, humid growing season of Gulf Coast gardens.
directions: Strawberry Watermelon was selected from an older Florida heirloom by grower Walt Childs and introduced by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange in 1989, making it a relatively recent release built on genetics already adapted to hot, humid Southern conditions. The long, dark green striped fruits reach 15-25 pounds when well fed and watered, with vivid strawberry-red flesh, white seeds, and very good disease resistance for an heirloom watermelon. It shows good tolerance of common Southern disease pressure compared to many older watermelon heirlooms, making it a practical choice for humid Gulf Coast summers. Give vines ample room to run and consistent moisture while fruit is sizing for the best flavor and texture.

name: Striato d'Italia Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed well past the last frost date, giving the semi-trailing vines ample room to spread.
directions: Striato d'Italia is a long-grown Italian market variety, its medium green skin broken by pale longitudinal stripes that run the length of the fruit, distinguishing it at a glance from the deeply ribbed Costata Romanesco. Harvest at 6-8 inches, before the stripes fade and the rind thickens, for the finest-textured flesh and the mildest flavor. The vines are more rangy than modern bush hybrids and benefit from occasional redirection so fruit doesn't hide and oversize under the leaves. It holds up well in classic Italian preparations such as frying in rounds or grilling, where its firm, less watery flesh is an advantage over standard green zucchini.

name: Strike Bush Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed; Strike is an early-maturing bush bean noted for disease resistance and a long harvest window, with good heat tolerance suited to a long, warm Gulf South growing season.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm, fertile soil after all frost risk has passed; Strike is an early, disease-resistant bush snap bean prized for a long, sustained harvest window rather than a short, concentrated flush of pods like many bush varieties. It holds up well to summer heat, continuing to set new pods over an extended period when many other bush beans slow down. Pods are straight, tender, and best picked young before seeds bulge visibly through the pod wall. Harvest every couple of days to encourage continued flowering, and succession sow every 2-3 weeks through the warm season for an even longer supply of fresh beans.
sources: seed catalog reference (High Mowing Organic Seeds, True Leaf Market, Victory Seeds)

name: Striped Garden Egg
scientificName: Solanum aethiopicum var. gilo 'Striped Garden Egg'
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger has passed.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Striped Garden Egg is a Gilo-type African eggplant producing 3-inch, lightly bitter striped fruit on tall 4-5 foot plants, traditionally harvested green-and-white and eaten raw, boiled, sautéed, or added to soup. The young leaves are also cooked into stews, giving the plant dual culinary use. Give it the full warm season it needs to mature, performing especially well in long, hot Gulf Coast summers.

name: Striped German Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Striped German produces very large fruits on vigorous indeterminate vines — provide sturdy support to 6+ feet and prune to one or two main stems for largest fruit development.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Striped German is a classic bicolor beefsteak heirloom — a large (10–16 oz), irregularly shaped, old-fashioned beefsteak type with golden-yellow skin striped and mottled with red, creating a vibrant, contrasting bicolor appearance on the exterior. The cut interior reveals the characteristic bicolor flesh of this variety: red and yellow sectors arranged in alternating patterns that create an artistic cross-section pattern — a visually striking effect that makes Striped German outstanding for fresh sliced presentations. The flavor is exceptional — sweet, rich, low-acid, and complex in the tradition of old German beefsteak heirlooms. Striped German is believed to have originated in Appalachia from German immigrant seed stock and has been maintained by Appalachian seed savers for generations before entering the commercial heirloom seed trade. As with most large bicolor heirlooms, Striped German produces best in the spring season in zone 9 (March–June) and can be challenging to grow in the high summer heat that damages large fruit quality. The combination of visual beauty, excellent flavor, and historical significance makes Striped German one of the most rewarding heirlooms for zone 9 spring production.

name: Stripetti Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Stripetti crosses spaghetti squash with delicata, producing cream-and-green striped fruit with sweeter, less watery flesh than standard spaghetti squash.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost in full sun and well-drained soil, giving vines moderate room to spread. Stripetti combines the stringy, noodle-like flesh texture of spaghetti squash with the sweeter, richer flavor of delicata, and the cream skin striped in dark green makes it easy to identify at harvest or on a market table. The strands separate cleanly when the cooked flesh is scraped with a fork, but taste noticeably sweeter and less bland than standard spaghetti squash, appealing to cooks who want the low-carbohydrate pasta substitute without sacrificing flavor. Pick once stripes darken and the rind resists denting, and use within a couple of months since it does not store as long as full-season winter squash.

name: Stubby Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow into warm soil after frost danger has passed; Stubby's shorter stature makes it a good fit for tighter garden rows or raised beds.
directions: Stubby is a shorter heirloom okra, staying noticeably more compact than rangy Southern types while still producing steadily through summer heat. Its blunt, stumpy pods should be picked young, around two to three inches, since the thick shape can turn fibrous quickly once past prime size. The lower profile makes this variety easier to manage in smaller plots or where wind exposure would otherwise call for staking taller okra. Keep pods picked frequently to prevent the compact plant from shutting down seed-pod production early.

name: Student Parsnip
plantingNote: Sow fresh seed shallowly as early as the soil can be worked, and leave roots in the ground through the first hard frosts to sweeten.
directions: Bred in England in the mid-1800s through deliberate selection from wild parsnip stock, Student was one of the first named parsnip cultivars developed with a scientific breeding approach rather than simple farm selection. It produces smooth-skinned, creamy white roots with strong vigor and reliable germination for a crop notorious for erratic sprouting. Sow fresh seed shallowly as early as the soil can be worked, and leave roots in the ground through the first hard frosts, which convert stored starches to sugar and sweeten the harvest considerably.

name: Stump of the World Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 start January–February and transplant March. Stump of the World is an indeterminate variety that continues producing through the season; in zone 9 the heavy spring flush continues until peak summer heat slows setting, then resumes in fall. Prolific production means fruit load can be heavy — provide sturdy caging or staking.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Stump of the World is a Russian heirloom tomato preserved by Seed Savers Exchange, producing abundant clusters of small to medium (2–3 ounce) round to slightly oval red fruits with a rich, sweet-tart old-fashioned tomato flavor. The prolific, indeterminate vines are particularly valued for their consistent production even during hot, humid periods when many larger-fruited heirlooms stop setting — a significant advantage in zone 9 where the growing season is compressed and productivity through heat stress is paramount. The firm-skinned fruits hold well on the vine and in storage longer than thin-skinned heirlooms, and their medium size makes them versatile for fresh eating, salads, and saucing where small cherry tomatoes are too small and large beefsteaks are too large for single-use. The Russian origin suggests cold-climate breeding priorities — early maturity and prolific production — that translate to better zone 9 heat performance than many European heirloom varieties.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Stump of the World Tomato
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Russian Heirloom Tomatoes
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Heat-Tolerant Heirloom Tomatoes

name: Stupice Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Stupice is a Czech heirloom from Stupice in the former Czechoslovakia, one of the earliest-ripening tomatoes available for cool-climate and short-season gardens — producing ripe fruit in 52–65 days from transplant with exceptional cold tolerance that allows fruit set at temperatures too low for most varieties.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors after danger of frost passes; Stupice is unusually tolerant of cold nighttime temperatures and can be transplanted somewhat earlier than standard heat-loving varieties. Stupice (pronounced 'STOO-peet-seh') originates from the village of Stupice in what is now the Czech Republic and was brought to the Seed Savers Exchange network by gardener Dr. Carolyn Male in the early 1990s, where it rapidly became one of the most popular heirloom tomatoes in cold-climate gardens of the Pacific Northwest, Canada, and Northern states. It is a potato-leaved, indeterminate variety producing clusters of small to medium (2–4 oz), round, uniformly deep red fruits — not large by beefsteak standards, but remarkable for their combination of earliness (ripening weeks before most other varieties) and rich, full-flavored, sweet-tart tomato character that is often absent in other very-early varieties. The ability to set fruit in cool temperatures makes Stupice the first choice for short-season gardeners in coastal climates and high altitudes; it also makes an excellent spring variety for Gulf Coast and Southern gardens planted early in the season.

name: Sturon Onion
plantingNote: Plant onion sets as soon as the soil is workable in early spring, pushing each bulb in root-side down until just the tip shows; Sturon is a Dutch-bred long-day maincrop onion widely sold as sets for spring planting in temperate climates.
directions: Sturon is one of the most widely planted Dutch maincrop onion cultivars, grown from sets for its round, golden-brown-skinned bulbs and dependably heavy yields. Plant sets shallowly in fertile, well-drained soil and firm the soil around them so birds cannot pull the sets loose, then keep the row weed-free while bulbs size up over summer. It is valued as a strong keeper, with well-cured bulbs commonly holding firm in storage for several months past harvest. Bend or wait for tops to fall over naturally before lifting, then dry the bulbs thoroughly in a warm, airy spot before trimming and storing.

name: Stuttgarter Giant Onion
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost or plant onion sets directly 4–6 weeks before last frost; Stuttgarter Riesen ('Stuttgart Giant') is a traditional German heirloom short-to-medium-day onion prized throughout Europe for its distinctive flat-globe shape, pale yellow-brown skin, mild-sweet flavor, and exceptional keeping quality — the standard European storage onion for much of the 20th century.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost, or plant sets directly in early spring 4–6 weeks before last frost at 2–4 inches apart; for seed-grown bulbs, thin to 4–6 inches in rows 12–18 inches apart. Stuttgarter Riesen (literally 'Stuttgart Giant') is a traditional German heirloom onion named for Stuttgart in Baden-Württemberg and widely grown throughout Central Europe as the standard yellow storage onion; it is recognized by its distinctive flattened or slightly disc-shaped globe form (wider than tall), straw-yellow to golden-brown thin papery skin, and crisp white flesh with a mild-sweet flavor that is less pungent than many other yellow storage types. The relatively flat shape and thin skin were historically valued because the flatter bulbs cured and dried quickly without molding, and the thin skin peeled easily — practical advantages that made Stuttgarter both the preferred home-garden and commercial variety. Now widely grown from sets (small bulblets sold by the bag) as well as from seed; set-planted Stuttgarter is often the earliest onion to mature in northern gardens. Exceptional storage quality — properly cured bulbs keep 6–9 months in cool, dry conditions.

name: Success PM Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70°F; Success PM was bred specifically for resistance to powdery mildew, the fungal disease that typically ends a Gulf South summer squash planting by midsummer once the white, dusty coating spreads across the foliage.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; Success PM is a yellow summer squash bred to carry meaningful resistance to powdery mildew, the fungal disease that coats squash leaves in a white, dusty film and typically shuts down production in a Gulf South garden by midsummer, well before the season would otherwise end. Because the foliage stays healthier and photosynthesizing longer, plants tend to keep setting good-quality fruit later into the summer than mildew-susceptible varieties. Harvest fruit young, at 5-6 inches, for the most tender texture and mildest flavor, checking plants daily during peak production since summer squash quickly grows oversized if missed for even a couple of days.
sources: seed catalog reference (Fruition Seeds, Turtle Tree Seed)

name: Sucrine du Berry Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm, spacing hills generously since vines spread widely, and reduce watering as fruit matures to concentrate sugars.
directions: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm, spacing hills generously since vines spread widely, and reduce watering as fruit matures to concentrate sugars. Originating in the Berry region of central France, this squash produces flattened, deep-orange, lightly ribbed fruit with notably dense, dry, sweet flesh reminiscent of chestnuts, making it a favorite for soups and roasting. It shares ancestry with Musquée de Provence but stays smaller and matures faster, fitting gardens with shorter seasons. Cure fruit in the sun for a week or two after harvest to harden the rind and intensify flavor before storing.

name: Sucrine Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November or January–February. Sucrine is a small-heading type that produces compact, single-serving heads of 4–5 inches — plant more densely at 6–8 inch spacing. Succession sow every 2–3 weeks for a continuous harvest. The sweet, crisp flavor and compact size make Sucrine a favorite for container growing and raised beds.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Sucrine is a French mini-romaine lettuce producing compact, upright, 4–5 inch heads with thick, crunchy, deeply green leaves and an exceptional sweetness that is apparent even in the name — 'sucrine' derives from the French 'sucre' (sugar). It is considered by many French market gardeners to have the best flavor of any small lettuce, combining the crunch and structure of romaine with a delicate sweetness entirely absent from full-sized romaine varieties. The small, compact heads are the right size for a single salad portion, and the thick leaves hold up to dressings without wilting — ideal for individual Caesar salads and composed appetizer plates. Sucrine is the standard small romaine type in French markets and has become highly popular in North American specialty food markets and upscale restaurants. The tight, compact head formation and small size allow close spacing (6–8 inches) that maximizes production from small garden spaces.
sources: Territorial Seed Company — Sucrine Lettuce Variety Notes
Seeds of Italy — French Mini-Romaine Varieties
University of California Cooperative Extension — Specialty Lettuce Production

name: Sugar Ann Snap Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost as soon as soil can be worked; in zone 9 sow November–February for a winter-spring harvest. Sugar Ann is a compact, bush-type snap pea requiring no staking — plants reach only 18–24 inches and are self-supporting. In zone 9 the fall-through-spring season is ideal; pods are ready to harvest in 52 days (faster than most snap peas) before spring heat causes the plants to decline. Pick pods when the peas have just begun to swell in the pod.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly acidic soil; Sugar Ann is the first snap pea cultivar to achieve a compact, self-supporting, bush habit — it was awarded the All-America Selections award in 1984 for this breakthrough characteristic, which made snap pea growing practical for small gardens and container growing where the typical 4–6 foot Sugar Snap vines require substantial trellis infrastructure. The pods are genuine snap peas (edible pod, no strings in the eating-ripe stage) with sweet, crunchy, crisp pod walls and rounded, sweet peas inside — the classic snap pea flavor that has made snap peas one of the most popular garden vegetables since their introduction in the late 1970s. At only 52–56 days to maturity, Sugar Ann is also the fastest-maturing of the main snap pea varieties, providing an early crop before hot weather ends the pea season. In zone 9 the bush habit and fast maturity make Sugar Ann particularly valuable for the short cool-season window available.
sources: All-America Selections — Sugar Ann Snap Pea 1984 Award
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Snap Pea Varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — English and Snap Peas for Florida

name: Sugar Baby Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm (70°F+); in zone 9 plant March–May. Sugar Baby produces 7–10 lb icebox-sized fruits — small enough to fit in a refrigerator whole. Judge ripeness by the tendril nearest the fruit turning brown and dry, the ground spot (where it rests on soil) turning yellow, and a dull hollow sound when thumped. In zone 9 watermelons perform excellently in summer heat; provide consistent moisture during fruit development but reduce watering as fruits approach maturity to concentrate sweetness. Allow 6–8 feet between hills for the sprawling vines.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral sandy or loamy soil — watermelons require deep, loose, well-drained soil and abundant heat to develop properly; Sugar Baby is the classic icebox watermelon variety — the small, round, dark-green fruits (7–10 pounds) that fit neatly into a home refrigerator, in contrast to the large oblong types (20–30+ pounds) traditional in Southern watermelon culture. The small fruit size makes Sugar Baby the most practical watermelon for small family gardens where a single large watermelon represents more than could be consumed before spoiling. The bright red, crisp, very sweet flesh with few seeds has made Sugar Baby one of the most popular home garden watermelons for decades — reliable, productive, and delivering the classic watermelon experience in a manageable size. As a true tropical fruit, watermelon is perfectly suited to zone 9's long, hot summers — in fact, the consistent 90°F+ temperatures of June through August produce the sweetest, most flavorful watermelons possible, as the combination of intense sun and heat maximizes sugar development in the fruit.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Sugar Baby Watermelon Description
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Watermelon Production for Gulf South
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Watermelon Growing Guide

name: Sugar Bon Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Sugar Bon is an All-America Selections winner bred as a dwarf snap pea that needs little to no staking while still producing sweet, crisp pods.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in cool, well-drained soil in full sun as early as the ground can be worked. Sugar Bon, an All-America Selections winner, combines the sweet, crisp, whole-pod-edible quality of snap peas with an unusually compact, dwarf vine that needs little to no staking, making it a convenient choice for small gardens, containers, or gardeners who want to skip trellising. It sets pods heavily and matures quickly, an advantage in the Gulf South's relatively short cool-season pea window before summer heat arrives. Harvest pods once they fill out but are still tender and glossy, picking every couple of days to encourage the vine to keep producing through its productive window.

name: Sugar Buns Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches at least 60 degrees; Sugar Buns germinates more reliably in cooler soil than many sugary-enhanced corn varieties, allowing an earlier first planting in the Gulf South's spring corn window.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil, planting in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination; Sugar Buns is an early, sugary-enhanced (se) yellow sweet corn valued for reliable germination in cooler soil than many other sweet corn types tolerate well, letting Gulf Coast gardeners get a jump on the spring planting window. It produces 7-inch ears with tender, sweet, deep yellow kernels that hold their eating quality well for several days after picking. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill, since drought stress at this stage causes poorly filled ears. Harvest when silks have browned and kernels are plump and release a milky juice when pressed.

name: Sugar Cube Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills of 3 seeds after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Sugar Cube can be trellised on a sturdy fence or arbor, with individual fruits supported in cloth slings — the small fruit size (2 lbs) makes vertical growing practical. In zone 9, plant March–April for June–July harvest. The personal-sized fruits are ideal for harvesting 2–3 at a time as they ripen sequentially, providing a more extended harvest than single large-fruited types.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after last frost; reduce irrigation as fruits approach maturity to maximize sugar concentration. Harvest at full slip or when the stem end yields to gentle pressure and the typical musky cantaloupe aroma is detectable. Sugar Cube is a 2000 All-America Selections-winning personal-size cantaloupe from Burpee that produces small (1.5–2.5 lb), round, heavily netted fruits — perfectly sized for a single serving, an individual lunch, or a couple's dinner without leftover melon. The personal melon size (compared to the 4–8 lb fruits of standard cantaloupe varieties) addresses the practical issue of melon waste in smaller households: a 6-lb cantaloupe purchased for one or two people must be stored cut for multiple days, losing quality rapidly, while a 2-lb Sugar Cube is consumed in one sitting at peak freshness. Beyond the practical size advantage, Sugar Cube produces exceptional flavor — dense, aromatic, intensely sweet orange flesh with the classic cantaloupe character that earned it AAS recognition. Each plant typically produces 4–6 fruits per vine, ripening over 2–3 weeks rather than all at once, providing a longer harvest window than some single-headed varieties. Sugar Cube also has the advantage of being growable on a trellis (the small fruits can be supported in fabric slings), making it one of the few viable trellis-grown melons for gardens where horizontal space is limited.
sources: All-America Selections — Sugar Cube melon AAS winner 2000
Burpee Seeds — Sugar Cube cantaloupe variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Personal-size melon variety comparison

name: Sugar Drip Sorghum
plantingNote: Direct sow into warm soil once all frost danger has passed; Sugar Drip is a tall, long-season sweet sorghum that benefits from the Gulf Coast's long, hot growing season to fully load the stalks with sugar before harvest.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in rows in fertile, well-drained soil once the soil has warmed, thinning seedlings to their final spacing. Sugar Drip is a classic Southern heirloom sweet sorghum, grown not for grain but for its tall, juicy canes, which are cut, crushed, and boiled down into sorghum syrup — a traditional sweetener across the rural South before cane sugar became widely available and still prized today for its distinctive, robust, molasses-like flavor. Plants grow into tall, cane-like stalks resembling corn, topped with a grain head that can be left for birds or harvested for feed once the syrup-bearing stalks are cut. Harvest when seed heads reach the hard-dough stage and stalks are packed with sweet juice, typically signaled by the lower leaves beginning to dry; press stalks promptly after cutting, since sugar content declines quickly once cut canes sit.

name: Sugar Dumpling Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Sugar Dumpling is a miniature winter squash producing 1–2 pound individual fruits about 4 inches in diameter — the personal serving size of the squash is one of its primary practical advantages, as each fruit is exactly right for halving and stuffing or baking as a single portion without the waste of cutting a large squash. The striped cream-and-green skin pattern closely resembles the Delicata/Sweet Dumpling type but Sugar Dumpling produces distinctly smaller, rounder, slightly more compact fruits. In zone 9, plant March–May for summer production and again in late July–August for fall harvest. The flesh is deep orange-yellow, very sweet (high in natural sugars), and dry-textured with excellent baking quality. Sugar Dumpling's compact vining habit (4–5 foot vines) is more manageable than large winter squash varieties.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 36–48 inches. Harvest when skin shows orange or cream color without green and stem begins to dry. Sugar Dumpling Squash is a miniature winter squash variety in the Cucurbita pepo species that combines the sweet, dry, chestnut-flavored flesh of the best small winter squash types with an individual serving size (1–2 lbs, 4 inches diameter) that makes it supremely practical for home cooking. Unlike large winter squash varieties that require days of eating to finish once cut, Sugar Dumpling's small fruits provide a single meal's worth of squash for 2–4 people when halved and baked — eliminating the challenge of storing cut large squash and the quality loss that comes with refrigerating cut raw winter squash. The skin is a distinctive cream-white with thin green stripes that transition as the squash matures, eventually showing more orange-cream at full maturity (a ripeness indicator). The flesh is deep orange-yellow, very sweet, with the dense, dry texture that characterizes the best winter squash for baking and stuffing rather than the watery texture of summer squash types. Sugar Dumpling's vines are shorter (4–5 feet) than large pumpkin or Hubbard varieties, making the variety more practical for smaller garden spaces. For zone 9 fall production, plants started in late July can produce ripe squash by October–November, well-timed for the fall harvest and holiday table.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Sugar Dumpling mini winter squash variety notes
Burpee Seeds — Sugar Dumpling compact winter squash growing guide
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Winter Squash Variety Selection for Gulf South Production

name: Sugar Hubbard Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed after last frost; give vines a long, frost-free season to reach full size.
directions: Developed in the late 1940s as a cross between Blue Hubbard and Sweet Meat squash, this heirloom keeps the rich, sweet flesh of its parents in a more manageable, thinner-shelled fruit. Sow directly in well-amended hills spaced widely apart, since vines are vigorous and long-running. Fruits have blue-gray, lightly warted skin and grow to fifteen pounds or more. Harvest before the first hard freeze once the rind is fully hardened, cure for a week in a warm room, and store in a cool, dry location, where it will keep for months longer than standard Blue Hubbard.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

name: Sugar Kiss Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed well into the 70s; Sugar Kiss sets fruit reliably over a compact vine, making it a good fit for smaller vegetable gardens.
directions: Sugar Kiss is a modern hybrid cantaloupe bred by Sakata Seed and recognized with an All-America Selections award for combining exceptionally high sugar content with a compact, manageable vine that suits smaller home gardens better than traditional sprawling cantaloupe types. Fruits are heavily netted, medium-sized, and ripen with a strong sweet aroma at the blossom end, developing flesh that consistently tests sweeter on the brix scale than many older open-pollinated cantaloupe varieties. Sow into warm, fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost and keep moisture consistent through flowering and fruit set, then ease back on watering as fruit nears maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip, when the fruit separates cleanly from the vine with gentle pressure and the netted rind has taken on a golden cast beneath the netting.
sources: All-America Selections — Sugar Kiss melon variety notes
Sakata Seed America — Sugar Kiss cantaloupe

name: Sugar Lace II Snap Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked, 4-6 weeks before the last frost; the compact, mostly self-supporting vines need little or no trellising compared to standard snap peas.
directions: Sugar Lace II is a semi-leafless snap pea, meaning many of its leaflets are replaced by extra curling tendrils that let neighboring plants hook together into a self-supporting mass, reducing or eliminating the need for a trellis. It was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for combining good disease tolerance, including resistance to powdery mildew, with heavy sets of sweet, crisp, stringless pods that are eaten whole. Direct sow early in cool soil and keep evenly moist through flowering and pod fill for the best flavor and texture. Harvest when pods are plump and glossy but before they lose their bright green color.

name: Sugar Loaf Chicory
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for a November–February harvest. Sugar Loaf chicory is considerably milder and less bitter than radicchio or Belgian endive — the name 'Pain de Sucre' (bread of sugar) reflects its unusual sweetness for a chicory. In zone 9 it produces consistently through winter without protection and is harvested before spring warmth causes the plant to bolt.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sugar Loaf Chicory (Pain de Sucre) is a French chicory producing tall, upright, cylindrical heads similar in shape to a Belgian endive or small romaine — but green throughout rather than blanched white. The name reflects the characteristic sweetness of this chicory type: the tightly-wrapped leaves are significantly milder and less bitter than radicchio or loose-leaf chicories, making Sugar Loaf accessible to people who find standard chicory too bitter for raw salad use. The crisp, substantial leaves with a mild, slightly bitter, refreshing flavor are excellent raw in salads, braised, or used as a sturdy wrap for composed appetizers. Sugar Loaf tolerates storage better than most lettuces — wrapped heads keep 2–3 weeks in the refrigerator, providing fresh salad greens long after harvest. In zone 9 the fall-through-winter growing season produces excellent Sugar Loaf chicory from October plantings harvested through February, when mild winters allow unprotected outdoor overwintering.
sources: Seeds of Italy — Pain de Sucre Sugar Loaf Chicory Growing Notes
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Chicory and Radicchio
University of California Cooperative Extension — Chicory Production Guide

name: Sugar Nut Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed well into the 70s.
directions: Sugar Nut is a personal-size muskmelon bred for small households and small gardens, producing heavily netted, orange-fleshed fruit that average just under 2 pounds so a single melon serves one or two people without waste. Its compact vines and shorter internodes let it perform well in raised beds and large containers compared with sprawling standard cantaloupe types. High sugar content and a small seed cavity give a favorable flesh-to-seed ratio for its size, and its early maturity suits gardeners in shorter-season regions who struggle to ripen full-size cantaloupe. Vine to a trellis or let it sprawl, keeping fruit off wet soil to prevent rot.

name: Sugar Rush Peach Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; stake or cage the tall, rangy plants and provide consistent moisture through fruit set.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this modern baccatum selection, first found as a natural mutation of a South American aji type, needs the long, warm season typical of the species to size up. The glossy, peach-colored pods bring a habanero-adjacent heat wrapped in intense sweetness, with tropical and citrus notes that make them popular fresh in salads and ceviche or fermented into hot sauce. Plants grow tall and rangy, so stake or cage them and provide consistent moisture through fruit set.

name: Sugar Rush Red Sunrise Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; provide staking for the tall, productive plants and harvest regularly to prolong the season.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost. This variety arose as an off-type selection within Sugar Rush Stripey plantings and ripens to a solid, glossy red rather than the parent's stripe pattern, with a milder heat range of about 5,000-45,000 Scoville units. It shares the same sweet, tropical-fruit flavor profile as its siblings and works well fresh, fermented, or dried. Provide staking for the tall, productive plants and harvest regularly to prolong the season.

name: Sugar Rush Stripey Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, and give this vigorous baccatum plenty of vertical support since it can top 5 feet in a single season.
directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, and give this vigorous baccatum plenty of vertical support — it can top 5 feet in a single season. Fruits begin lime green and ripen through a striking peach-and-red striped pattern that stays fairly stable from seed, with a Scoville range of roughly 25,000-100,000 that leans hotter than most other aji types. The flavor combines sweet, fruity, citrus, and stone-fruit notes, making it a favorite for colorful hot sauces and fresh garnishes.

name: Sugar Snap Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked; in zone 9 sow January–February. Sugar Snap pea requires a trellis at 4–6 feet tall for the original tall strain; dwarf bush strains are available but the original tall type produces more heavily over a longer period. In zone 9 the pea season closes in April–May when heat arrives; maximizing yield requires early planting and heavy harvesting every 2–3 days. Powdery mildew can be a problem in humid zone 9 springs; plant early to harvest before disease pressure peaks.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in loose, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a trellis or fence for the tall vines; Sugar Snap Pea was bred by Calvin Lamborn and introduced in 1979, winning the All-America Selections award and transforming the edible-pod pea category — it combined the thick, succulent, fleshy pod of snow peas with the full, plump, sweet peas inside, creating a pod that is outstanding eaten raw, pod-and-all, with no tough strings to remove at the right harvest stage. The crisp snap when a mature pod is broken — and the burst of sweetness from the swollen peas inside — made Sugar Snap immediately distinctive from flat snow peas. Harvest when pods are round and full but still bright green before the pod skin begins to wrinkle; at this stage the natural sugars are at their peak. Overmature pods develop a tough string along the suture and the peas inside become starchy. In zone 9 Sugar Snap pea is primarily a January–April crop that provides the most rewarding fresh vegetable of the cool season.
sources: All-America Selections — Sugar Snap Pea 1979 Award Record
University of California Cooperative Extension — Edible-Pod Pea Production
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Snap Peas

name: Sugar Sprint Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring, since this pea thrives in cool weather and finishes before summer heat arrives.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in double rows along a low trellis or netting, since the compact vines benefit from light support even though they stay shorter than many climbing snap peas. This variety was bred for extra earliness and a concentrated harvest window, producing thick, crisp, stringless pods that are sweet enough to eat whole straight off the vine. Its shorter, sturdier vines make it a good choice for windy sites or gardeners who want snap peas without tall trellising, and it shows good tolerance to powdery mildew compared to older snap pea varieties. Pick pods promptly once they fill out to keep plants productive and pods tender.

name: Sugaretti Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Sugaretti is a compact, bush-habit spaghetti squash bred for sweeter flavor than standard spaghetti squash on a vine that takes much less space to grow.
directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, or grow in a large container. Sugaretti is an AAS-winning spaghetti squash bred for a genuinely compact, bush-type habit that fits into much smaller garden spaces than traditional sprawling spaghetti squash vines, while also improving on the flavor of standard spaghetti squash with noticeably sweeter, less bland flesh once the strands are separated after cooking. The fruit is a good single-family size, with pale-yellow, oval, ridged rind. Fruit is ready to harvest when the rind hardens fully and turns a deep golden-yellow; cure in a warm, dry spot for a week or two after harvest before storing or cooking. Roast, bake, or boil the whole squash, then scrape the cooked flesh with a fork to separate it into spaghetti-like strands.
sources: All-America Selections — Sugaretti Squash winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Sugarloaf Chicory
plantingNote: Sow in midsummer (July to early August) in most climates for fall harvest; in zone 9, sow in August–September for harvest from November through January. Sugarloaf is harvested in fall after cool nights sweeten the heads.
directions: Sow seeds 1/4 inch deep in rows 18 inches apart, thinning to 12 inches when seedlings are established; Sugarloaf or Pan di Zucchero is a distinctive Italian chicory that forms an upright, elongated pale green head resembling a light-green romaine lettuce — quite different in form from the compact red Chioggia or the torpedo-shaped Treviso radicchios. The flavor is characteristically chicory-bitter when young, but sweetens considerably after several frosts or cold nights, becoming almost endive-like in the inner white heart. The heads can be stored after harvest for several weeks in a cool, humid location; the outer leaves are removed and the inner pale heart is eaten fresh in salads or braised. Self-blanching as the tight leaves exclude light from the interior; no additional blanching is required.

name: Sugarsnax 54 Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow in deep, very loose, stone-free soil — Sugarsnax develops long roots (8–9 inches) and requires at least 10–12 inches of deep, unobstructed, well-amended soil for straight root development. Thin to 2–3 inches apart when seedlings reach 2 inches tall. In zone 9, sow September through November for harvest December through February. The cooler temperatures of fall and winter enhance sweetness significantly over summer-grown crops.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.25 inch deep in very deeply tilled, loose, stone-free soil enriched with compost; water consistently through germination (10–14 days) and thin to 2–3 inches when plants are 2 inches tall. Sugarsnax 54 (developed by Harris Moran Seed Company) is an Imperator-type hybrid carrot bred specifically for maximum sweetness at minimum days-to-maturity — its name reflects the two core attributes, 'sugar' for sweetness and '54' for the early maturity date that brings exceptionally sweet carrots to harvest in just 54–60 days. The roots are long and slender (8–9 inches) with a tapered Imperator shape, smooth bright-orange skin, and orange flesh that is noticeably sweeter than most other carrot varieties when grown under ideal cool conditions — the elevated sugar content is a breeding trait rather than solely a growing-condition effect, though cool weather amplifies it further. Sugarsnax is one of the most popular carrots for direct fresh-eating, CSA bunching, and farmers market premium carrot sales because customers can taste the difference: the sugar content is high enough to be perceptibly sweeter than standard storage carrots when eaten raw. The slender shape and smooth skin make Sugarsnax particularly attractive in bunched presentation with the green tops attached. Requires loose, deep soil to develop full-length roots without forking; heavier soils produce shorter, sometimes misshaped roots.
sources: Harris Moran Seed Company — Sugarsnax 54 carrot variety description
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Imperator-type carrot trial results
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Carrot Variety Evaluation for New York

name: Sugg Peanut
plantingNote: Direct sow shelled seed into loose, sandy soil once it has warmed well past the last frost; give this Virginia-type peanut the full length of a Gulf Coast summer to finish its large pods.
directions: Plant shelled, raw seed about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, mounding soil lightly around the base at flowering to give the pegs an easy path into the ground. Sugg was released in 2009 by North Carolina State University's multi-disease-resistance breeding program and stacks resistance to tomato spotted wilt virus, Cylindrocladium black rot, Sclerotinia blight, and early leaf spot into one Virginia-type line, a combination useful under the hot, humid disease pressure typical of Southern growing seasons. It carries a distinctive pink seed coat and produces a high share of the large fancy and jumbo pods valued for in-shell roasting and boiling. Keep soil evenly moist through flowering and pod fill, then dig the whole plant once foliage yellows and cure pods in a warm, airy spot before shelling.
sources: North Carolina Crop Improvement Association — Peanut Variety Information

name: Summer Cross No. 3 Daikon
scientificName: Raphanus sativus var. longipinnatus 'Summer Cross No. 3'
plantingNote: Sow from late spring into midsummer; this hybrid was specifically bred to resist bolting and disease under the heat and humidity that cause most daikon to fail in summer plantings.
directions: Bred by Takii as a Minowase-type hybrid for the summer sowing window, Summer Cross No. 3 combines a distinctive white-shouldered, cylindrical root with strong tolerance to heat, virus, and Fusarium wilt that ordinarily plague daikon planted before cool fall weather sets in. Direct sow into deeply worked soil and thin to a wide final spacing so roots can size up straight and unforked. Growers who want daikon in mid-to-late summer, rather than waiting for a fall-only crop, choose this hybrid specifically for its ability to hold quality and resist bolting through hot conditions that would ruin open-pollinated types.

name: Summer Fest Komatsuna
plantingNote: Bred specifically for heat tolerance, this F1 komatsuna can be sown from spring through the hottest part of summer; give it afternoon shade in July and August to slow bolting and keep leaves tender.
directions: Summer Fest is a Japanese F1 hybrid mustard spinach bred to resist bolting through the heat of summer, when most other Asian greens fail. Sow seed directly and thin as needed; leaves can be cut at baby-salad size in about three weeks or left to size up into full bunching plants within five to six weeks. Its glossy, rounded leaves have the mild mustard-spinach flavor typical of komatsuna, and afternoon shade during peak summer heat further extends the harvest window before the plants eventually bolt.

name: Summerfest Komatsuna
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in rich, moisture-retentive soil; repeat-sow every two to three weeks through summer and into fall for a steady supply.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/4 inch deep in rich, moisture-retentive soil and thin young plants for baby-leaf harvest or wider spacing for bunching-size heads; Summerfest is an upright hybrid komatsuna bred specifically for heat and disease tolerance, so it can be sown through the warmer months when standard mustard spinach types would bolt. The smooth, spinach-like dark-green leaves and pale stems have a mild flavor that holds up well in stir-fries, soups, and quick braises. Successive small sowings every two to three weeks keep a steady supply of tender greens.

name: Summertime Green Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Summertime Green is a Dwarf Tomato Project release bearing sweet, green-fleshed-when-ripe fruit on a compact plant.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Summertime Green bears medium fruit that ripens to a translucent amber-green, the flesh staying green even at full ripeness, with a sweet, mild flavor typical of green-when-ripe tomato types, on a compact Dwarf Tomato Project plant bred to bring specialty tomato flavor to small-space gardens. Its manageable size suits raised beds and large containers where indeterminate vines would be impractical. Harvest when fruit softens slightly and develops a faint amber blush, since color alone won't signal ripeness.

name: Summertime Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow from early spring through early summer; bred specifically to resist bolting in warm weather better than most crisphead lettuce, extending the harvest window into the early Gulf Coast summer.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to ten to twelve inches apart. Summertime is a crisphead lettuce bred specifically to resist bolting under the lengthening days and rising heat of late spring and early summer, holding its tight, crisp head and mild flavor for a longer harvest window than most iceberg-type lettuces manage before turning bitter and sending up a seed stalk. The dependable heat tolerance makes it a useful choice for stretching the fresh lettuce season further into warm weather on the Gulf Coast than most crisphead varieties allow. Harvest once heads feel firm and solid, and monitor closely as temperatures climb, since even heat-tolerant lettuce will eventually bolt once conditions become too warm.

name: Sumor Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost in warm soil; Sumor needs a full, long warm season to size up its roots properly.
directions: Sumor stands apart from most named sweet potato cultivars by being dry and mild rather than sweet and moist, with tan-to-yellow skin and firm white to pale yellow flesh that holds its shape when cooked. It behaves in the kitchen more like a russet potato than a typical Southern sweet potato, making it a useful choice for cooks who want a starchy, low-sugar substitute for regular potatoes in a Gulf Coast garden too hot for real potatoes in summer. The vines are vigorous and the roots show good field resistance to fusarium wilt and root-knot nematode, both common headaches in Southern sweet potato beds. Because it is slower to mature than orange types, get slips in the ground as early as the last frost date allows.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

name: Sun Gold Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Sun Gold is an indeterminate cherry tomato that produces continuously from June through frost in zone 9 when kept well-staked and fertilized.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Sun Gold is widely considered the finest-tasting cherry tomato ever developed and consistently ranks as the top-rated cherry tomato in taste trials — a Japanese hybrid producing small (3/4-inch), round to slightly elongated, deep orange fruits with exceptional sweetness, complex fruity-tropical flavor notes, and almost no acidity. The fruity, candy-sweet flavor of Sun Gold is distinctly different from other cherry tomatoes — a tropical, almost perfumed sweetness that makes it irresistible eaten directly from the vine. In zone 9, Sun Gold can be expected to produce continuously from transplanting in February through June and again from September through frost in the fall — the summer heat above 95°F temporarily stops fruit set but the plant remains and produces heavily once temperatures moderate. The vigorous, indeterminate vine requires a sturdy cage or staking to 5–8 feet and sets fruit in prolific clusters (trusses) of 10–20 tomatoes simultaneously. Sun Gold is a patented F1 hybrid — seed cannot be saved true-to-type. The attractive orange fruit color and extraordinary flavor make it one of the most popular and most widely recommended garden tomatoes.

name: Sun Gold Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile seed mix; transplant after all frost danger passes in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Sun Gold is consistently rated among the sweetest, most intensely flavored cherry tomatoes in existence — an F1 hybrid producing small, tangerine-orange, bite-sized fruits with extraordinarily high sugar content and a complex, tropical-sweet, apricot-citrus flavor.
directions: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; plant in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun with strong support; harvest clusters of cherry tomatoes when bright tangerine-orange. Solanum lycopersicum 'Sun Gold' (Sun Gold cherry tomato) is arguably the most beloved cherry tomato in home gardening — a Japanese F1 hybrid that consistently receives top ratings for flavor in nearly every comparative tasting. The fruits are small (3/4 to 1 inch), round to slightly oblong, brilliant tangerine-orange when ripe, and remarkably sweet — consistently the highest sugar content among widely grown cherry tomato varieties — with a complex, aromatic flavor combining intense sweetness with tropical-fruit and apricot notes and just enough acid to balance. The flavor is so intense that eating a ripe Sun Gold warm from the vine is often cited by gardeners as a transformative experience — the difference from a grocery store tomato is dramatic. 'Sun Gold' is an indeterminate vine that grows vigorously (staking required), produces prolifically throughout the season, and sets fruit reliably in a wide range of conditions. The thin skin causes occasional cracking near harvest in wet conditions — harvest promptly when ripe. In Gulf Coast zone 9, grow in spring (March–June harvest) and again in fall (September–November harvest), skipping the hottest summer months when fruiting stalls. A must-grow for anyone who wants to understand what a truly great tomato tastes like.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Variety Trials

name: Sun Leaper Tomato
plantingNote: Transplant after all frost danger has passed and nights stay reliably above 60°F; Sun Leaper keeps setting fruit through warm summer nights that stall most other slicing tomatoes.
directions: Sun Leaper was bred at North Carolina State University from the heat-tolerant breeding line NC HS-1 specifically to keep setting fruit when nighttime temperatures stay warm — a common failure point for standard slicing tomatoes across the Deep South. The determinate vines carry thin foliage that sheds heat well, so give plants a stake or cage and moderate afternoon shade in the hottest zone 9 gardens to reduce sunscald on the shoulders. Fruit are large, firm, deep red with a small blossom scar, and hold up better against cracking and rough-scar disorders than comparable heat-set hybrids like Solar Set. Because it is determinate, plan a second late-summer transplanting for a fall crop rather than relying on a single planting to carry through the whole season.

name: Sun Sugar Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Sun Sugar is an indeterminate cherry tomato that benefits from caging or staking and grows throughout the season. In zone 9, transplant March–April for summer production. Sun Sugar's exceptional crack resistance — unusual in cherry tomatoes, which commonly split at the stem end when they absorb excess water rapidly after dry periods — makes it more practical in zone 9's irregular summer rainfall than crack-prone cherry types. The fruits are orange to golden-orange (slightly deeper than the orange of Sungold under some growing conditions — though Sun Sugar and Sungold are sometimes confused in the US market, they are distinct varieties), and the sweetness consistently registers among the highest of any commercial cherry tomato variety. The flavor profile combines intense sweetness with mild acidity and a complex, fruity tomato character. Harvest clusters when uniformly orange.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F; transplant after last frost and stake or cage. Harvest clusters when uniformly orange. Sun Sugar is an F1 hybrid cherry tomato developed by Tokita Seeds of Japan — one of the premier vegetable seed breeding companies in the world — and became widely popular in North America through distribution by companies including Park Seed and Renee's Garden Seeds, where it is sometimes sold under the Park Seed exclusive name 'Sun Sugar.' Sun Sugar consistently ranks among the highest-rated cherry tomato varieties for sweetness and flavor in home garden and market garden trials — its Brix (sugar content) measurements frequently exceed 10 (compared to 6–8 for standard slicing tomatoes), and the flavor combines this exceptional sweetness with mild acidity and what tasters frequently describe as a complex, almost citrus-tropical fruitiness distinct from standard red cherry types. The color — orange to golden-orange, slightly more orange than Sungold (which is from Takii Seeds, a different Japanese company) — is part of the flavor differentiation: orange cherry tomatoes in this category contain different proportions of carotenoids than red types, often with higher beta-carotene content and lower lycopene, contributing to their distinctively fruity, mild-acid flavor. Sun Sugar's crack resistance in the field is a practical advantage that Sungold (its main competitor) has been criticized for lacking — the characteristic of splitting when water uptake increases rapidly after drought periods plagues many cherry tomato varieties, and Sun Sugar's better resistance reduces the frustration of finding split fruit after rain events.
sources: Tokita Seeds Japan — Sun Sugar cherry tomato F1 hybrid development
Park Seed — Sun Sugar cherry tomato performance and sweetness documentation
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Orange cherry tomato variety comparison and Brix data
