name: Sunburst Pattypan Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; an All-America Selections winner with brilliant yellow, scallop-edged pattypan fruits and bushy, compact habit that produces prolifically over a long season in hot climates — well-suited to Gulf Coast spring and fall gardening.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile soil; Sunburst is a bush-type pattypan that requires no support and takes up significantly less space than vining squash. Sunburst is an All-America Selections award-winning summer squash producing vivid golden-yellow, flying-saucer-shaped pattypan fruits with slightly scalloped edges and tender, mild, buttery white flesh that is best harvested at 3–4 inches when the skin is still soft and the seeds are immature; left to grow larger the skin toughens and flavor diminishes. The compact bush plants are highly productive in hot weather and are excellent for Gulf Coast gardens where the fast harvest window allows planting in both spring and early fall. Sunburst is virtually identical to Bennings Green Tint but with consistent bright yellow rather than pale green coloring.

name: Sunburst Scallop Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Sunburst is an AAS-winning hybrid patty pan squash producing bright golden-yellow, scalloped, saucer-shaped fruit best picked small and tender.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Sunburst is a widely grown hybrid patty pan (scallop) squash producing cheerful, bright golden-yellow, saucer-shaped fruit with the classic scalloped edge, best harvested small, at two to three inches across, when the skin is tender and the flavor is sweetest. Picking regularly, every day or two during peak season, keeps the compact, bushy plants productive over a long summer harvest and prevents fruit from becoming tough and seedy. Like other summer squash it is a heavy producer and benefits from consistent moisture and monitoring for squash vine borer and squash bugs, common pests in Gulf South gardens.

name: Sunburst Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Sunburst is a bush-type pattypan/scallop squash with a compact growth habit that is significantly more manageable in small gardens than the sprawling zucchini types. In zone 9, plant March–May and August–September for fall production. The distinctive golden-yellow color at harvest maturity is an important cue: harvest Sunburst when the fruits are 2–3 inches across and uniformly golden-yellow. At this small size the skin is tender and edible, the flesh is firm and slightly sweet, and the distinctive scalloped edge with pale yellow skin is at its most attractive for presentation. Larger fruits (5+ inches) become tough-skinned and starchy. Sunburst's compact plant habit and prolific production make it one of the best summer squash varieties for containers and raised beds in zone 9.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest at 2–3 inches when golden-yellow and edges still tender. Sunburst Squash is an All-America Selections (AAS) winning summer squash recognized for its distinctive golden-yellow color, compact plant habit, and excellent productivity in home garden conditions. The pattypan or scallop squash form (a flattened disc with scalloped edges, sometimes called 'flying saucer' for its distinctive shape) represents an older squash form that predates the elongated zucchini in American kitchen garden history; pattypan varieties were among the first summer squash grown widely in early American gardens, and the distinctive scalloped shape remains one of the most visually attractive squash forms. Sunburst's breakthrough was producing the pattypan form in a vivid, uniform golden-yellow rather than the pale yellow, white, or green of earlier pattypan varieties — the bright color made it immediately eye-catching at farmers markets and in garden displays, and its AAS recognition reflected consistent performance across trial locations. The flavor of small Sunburst squash is mild and slightly sweet, with a firmer texture than zucchini at comparable sizes — the denser flesh of scallop types holds up better in sauté, roasting, and stuffed preparations than the waterier flesh of standard zucchini. For zone 9 gardeners, the compact plant size and abundant production of Sunburst make it one of the more practical summer squash choices for space-limited raised beds and containers, where a standard zucchini plant's 3–4 foot spread would be excessive.
sources: All-America Selections — Sunburst squash AAS recognition and trial performance documentation
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Sunburst pattypan squash variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Summer Squash Variety Selection for the Gulf South

name: Sunchaser Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; plan a second planting 3-4 weeks later for continuous summer harvest rather than relying on one big flush.
directions: Listed by LSU AgCenter as heat-tolerant with Alternaria and Fusarium race 1/2 resistance, this variety was originally popularized as a heat-set performer for the arid Southwest, but the same ability to set fruit when days top 90F and nights stay above 75F makes it valuable for the Gulf South's humid-heat fruit-set problem, not just dry heat. It's a determinate, medium-fruited red slicer around 7 ounces that produces a concentrated harvest window. Stake it at transplant and keep irrigation steady through fruit set.

name: SunGold Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; SunGold is an F1 hybrid cherry tomato from Takii Seed (Japan) widely considered the sweetest and most popular cherry tomato in American home gardens — the small, golden-orange fruits ripen early and continuously, offering exceptional sweetness with tropical-fruity overtones unlike any other cherry tomato.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun after last frost; SunGold is an indeterminate vine that benefits from strong staking or a tomato cage at least 5–6 feet tall; remove suckers for concentrated fruiting or allow to develop for maximum production; harvest when golden-orange and slightly soft. SunGold is an F1 hybrid cherry tomato developed by Takii Seed of Japan and first introduced to American gardeners in the early 1990s; it has since become the most widely grown and most frequently praised cherry tomato in American home gardens, consistently ranked first or near-first in taste comparisons by extension services, seed companies, and tomato enthusiasts for its exceptional sweetness and complex flavor. The small (3/4 to 1 inch), round to slightly oval fruits ripen from green through yellow to a distinctive rich golden-orange color; the flavor at peak ripeness is extraordinary — intensely sweet, with brix values of 9–10 or higher (far above standard tomato sweetness), and distinct tropical-fruity notes (mango, passion fruit, tangerine) that are unique among tomatoes and make SunGold recognizable in a blind taste test. The indeterminate vines are extremely productive, bearing prolific clusters of 15–30 fruits from early summer until frost; the fruits are crack-resistant for a cherry type. Not an open-pollinated heirloom (seed saved from SunGold will not come true), but the exceptional flavor makes it a standard in virtually every serious home garden.

name: Sunmaster Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March for spring production. Sunmaster is specifically bred to set fruit at temperatures above 90°F when most varieties drop blossoms, making it one of the best heat-set tomatoes for the Gulf Coast.
directions: Transplant into deeply amended, well-drained soil with a sturdy cage or stake; Sunmaster is an indeterminate heat-set tomato developed by the University of Florida specifically for production in hot, humid climates where daytime temperatures regularly exceed 90°F. Unlike many tomato varieties that drop blossoms at high temperatures, Sunmaster sets fruit reliably even when nights stay above 75°F, giving zone 9 gardeners a productive window from early May through June and again in September–November from fall plantings. The large, smooth, red globe fruits average 8–10 ounces with good flavor and crack resistance. Consistent watering is essential — irregular moisture leads to blossom-end rot and fruit cracking in the summer heat.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Production for Florida
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Heat-Tolerant Tomatoes
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Tomato Varieties for Louisiana

name: Sunrise Rhubarb
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant seedlings into a permanent, well-drained bed once soil is workable in spring. Because Sunrise is a seed strain rather than a division-propagated clone, expect some natural variation in stalk color and vigor among seedlings.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, then transplant seedlings into a permanent, well-drained bed once soil is workable in spring. Because Sunrise is a seed strain rather than a division-propagated clone, expect some natural variation in stalk color and vigor among seedlings, though most produce attractive red-tinged stalks in their first full season. Sunrise was selected to reach usable harvest size faster than older seed-grown rhubarb strains, giving gardeners who cannot source crown divisions a practical way to start a rhubarb patch from seed. Its flavor is bright and tart, typical of the species, and plants continue to improve in yield for several years after establishment.

name: Sunset Oca
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep after last frost; Sunset begins tuberizing roughly two weeks earlier than most oca varieties, which helps it finish bulking in shorter-summer climates.
directions: Sunset is among the highest-yielding oca varieties available in North America, reported to produce over two pounds of tubers per plant under good conditions. Plant seed tubers in loose, fertile soil in full sun after the last frost; Sunset is a vigorous early sprouter with green stems and foliage, and it initiates tuber formation about two weeks earlier than most other oca strains once day length shortens in late summer. Tubers emerge yellowish-orange with red eyes and develop a carrot-like, slightly sweet flavor after a period of post-harvest sun exposure. Harvest after the first frost kills back the foliage.

name: Sunset Torch Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Sunset Torch is a vigorous indeterminate grape tomato that needs a full-length warm season and sturdy staking or caging to support the long fruiting vine.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, then stake or cage the vine well since it is a tall, vigorous indeterminate grower. Sunset Torch is an AAS National Winner prized for fruit that ripens through a striking flame-like progression — green fruit color up in streaks of gold, orange, and finally red as they mature, so a single cluster shows several colors at once and individual fruits look hand-painted. The oblong grape-type fruits are sweet and crack-resistant, produced in long, heavy clusters over a long harvest window. Pick fruit as it fully colors for the sweetest flavor; because color develops gradually, clusters can be harvested a few fruits at a time as each one finishes ripening. Prune suckers lightly to keep air moving through the dense foliage in humid climates.
sources: All-America Selections — Sunset Torch Tomato winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Sunshine Kabocha Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Sunshine is an All-America Selections award-winning (2004) kabocha-type winter squash producing compact 3–4 lb fruits with brilliant orange skin and intensely sweet, rich, dry orange flesh — the classic kabocha-style eating quality in a smaller, more manageable fruit size than traditional green Japanese kabocha varieties.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in a warm, well-prepared bed; Sunshine squash vines are moderately vigorous and less sprawling than giant winter squash types; harvest when the stem corks and the skin is uniformly bright orange and resists fingernail denting; flavor improves significantly with 2–4 weeks of curing after harvest. Sunshine is a kabocha-type F1 hybrid winter squash that won the All-America Selections award in 2004 for outstanding garden performance — its combination of attractive appearance, reliable productivity, and outstanding eating quality made it an immediate success with home gardeners across the country. The squash belongs to the kabocha type (Cucurbita maxima), an East Asian tradition of winter squash with dry, dense, intensely sweet flesh that is considered the finest eating quality among all winter squash types. While traditional Japanese kabocha cultivars have dark green or grey skin with pale stripes, Sunshine was selected for brilliant orange skin that is instantly attractive and visually distinctive in the garden and at market. The flesh is the characteristic kabocha type: intensely deep orange, very dry, sweet, and starchy — so dense and sweet that it bakes without becoming watery, purées into thick soups without thickening, and can be used in dessert preparations. The compact 3–4 pound fruit size is practical for household use (one squash makes 2–4 servings without left-over waste) and the moderate vine size makes it manageable in home gardens with less space than butternut or hubbard types. Excellent storage for 3–4 months under cool conditions.

name: Sunshine Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Sunshine is a kabocha-type Cucurbita maxima producing small to medium fruits (3–5 lbs) with a distinctive bright orange skin — virtually identical in form to red kuri / Uchiki Kuri except with orange skin rather than red-orange. In zone 9, plant March–April for a fall harvest (October–November) as the squash approaches maturity in cooler fall weather that improves sweetness. The skin of fully ripe Sunshine changes from mottled orange-tan at immature stages to a uniform, vivid orange at harvest. The small size (3–5 lbs) makes Sunshine practical for single-household use without the waste of cutting into a very large squash. Sunshine received All-America Selections (AAS) recognition for consistent performance across North American trial locations, including warm climates where some kabocha types underperform.
directions: Direct sow in hills 3–4 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when fully vivid orange and stem begins to dry. Sunshine Squash is an F1 hybrid kabocha-type winter squash that received All-America Selections recognition for its exceptional productivity, vibrant visual appearance, and excellent eating quality in the kabocha class — a category of Cucurbita maxima squash that includes some of the highest-rated winter squash varieties for flavor intensity, flesh texture, and sweetness. Kabocha squash (from the Japanese name for pumpkin, itself derived from 'Cambodia' in Portuguese, reflecting the trade route by which the squash reached Japan) have been developed in Japan into a distinctive style — typically flattened globe form, dense, dry, sweet orange to yellow-orange flesh, and rich, complex chestnut-like flavor — that differs substantially from the North American traditions of summer squash (Cucurbita pepo) and large pumpkin (C. maxima). Sunshine's orange skin sets it visually apart from the dark green and grey-green Japanese kabocha types that inspired it — the vivid orange exterior makes it immediately recognizable at harvest and provides a decorative harvest-season display function alongside its culinary utility. The flesh is dense, dry (low water content), very sweet at full maturity, and with the characteristic kabocha texture that some cooks describe as between sweet potato and chestnut — a distinctive dry, starchy sweetness that makes kabocha the preferred squash for soups, tempura, and Japanese-inspired preparations where excess moisture would dilute the flavors.
sources: All-America Selections — Sunshine squash AAS winner recognition and trial documentation
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Sunshine kabocha squash F1 variety notes
Harris Seeds — Sunshine squash commercial performance comparison

name: Super Chili Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed. Super Chili is an All-America Selections award-winning hybrid bred for a compact habit and heavy, early fruit set, making it a long-standing favorite for containers.
directions: Transplant into well-drained soil in full sun or grow in a large container, spacing plants to let the compact, bushy habit fill in. Super Chili sets large numbers of small, slender, upward-facing fruit that ripen quickly from green to bright red, carrying sharp, well above cayenne-level heat in a two to three inch pod. The dense fruit set against dark green foliage also makes this an attractive dual-purpose ornamental and culinary pepper for patios and small beds. Harvest continuously through the season to encourage further flowering and fruit set, or let a flush ripen fully red for drying.
sources: Burpee Seeds — Super Chili Hybrid Pepper

name: Super Fantastic Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Super Fantastic is indeterminate and requires staking or caging — the plant produces heavy crops of large fruits over a long season that weigh down unsupported canes. In zone 9, transplant February–March for spring production. Super Fantastic is noted for producing fruits later into the warm Gulf Coast spring than some other beefsteak varieties — its heat tolerance gives it slightly extended production in zone 9 before summer heat stops fruit set. The disease resistance (VF — Verticillium and Fusarium wilt resistance) is particularly valuable in the Gulf South's humid soil conditions.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 75–80°F; transplant after last frost. Stake or cage immediately. Super Fantastic is a Burpee F1 hybrid tomato released in 1978 — one of the most successful and widely sold hybrid tomatoes of the latter 20th century, bred at the W. Atlee Burpee Company by Dr. Elwyn Meader's breeding program. Super Fantastic hit the market at a time when home gardeners were increasingly adopting the first generation of disease-resistant hybrid tomatoes, and the combination of large fruit size (fruits commonly 12–16 oz), vigorous plant growth, early maturity (70–80 days), and dual disease resistance (VF designation) made it extremely popular in the American home garden market through the 1980s and 1990s. The fruits are classic large red beefsteak form — round to slightly oblate, firm, meaty, with relatively few seeds and good thick walls — the standard large slicing tomato character for sandwiches, burgers, and fresh eating. Super Fantastic remains in production and widely sold despite the explosion of alternative hybrid and heirloom beefsteak types since its introduction, maintained in home garden seed racks and catalogs by its reputation for reliable, heavy production and disease resistance across a wide range of conditions. For zone 9 gardeners, the VF disease resistance tag is particularly relevant in humid soils where Fusarium and Verticillium wilt are common causes of premature plant death.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee Company — Super Fantastic tomato F1 hybrid release notes 1978
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Large hybrid beefsteak tomato variety comparison
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Disease-Resistant Tomato Variety Recommendations

name: Super Sioux Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6 weeks before the last frost; Super Sioux was bred to keep setting fruit and resist cracking through extreme heat, making it well suited to a Gulf South spring crop.
directions: Super Sioux is a semi-determinate heirloom tomato bred in 1944 at South Dakota State University specifically to withstand extreme heat and resist fruit cracking, qualities that made it a favorite far beyond its Great Plains origin in hot, humid regions such as the Gulf South. The compact plants set medium-sized, 6-8 ounce red fruit with good flavor even when summer nights stay warm enough to shut down fruit set in less heat-tolerant varieties. Stake or cage plants for support and maintain even soil moisture to minimize blossom end rot and cracking during heavy summer rains.

name: Super Sugar Snap Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked and set a sturdy 5-6 foot trellis at planting time, since vines are tall and vigorous and set pods quickly once warm days arrive.
directions: Super Sugar Snap is an improved selection bred from the original Sugar Snap pea to offer stronger vigor, better tolerance of powdery mildew, and a few days' earlier, heavier first flush of pods. The tall vines still need a sturdy trellis or fence but reward the extra support with thick-walled, sweet, fully edible pods over a longer harvest window than the older strain. Pick every two to three days once pods are round and glossy to keep plants producing and to catch pods before the pod wall starts to toughen. Because it holds up well to warm spring weather, it is a good choice for gardeners in regions where the cool pea season is short.

name: Super Sweet 100 Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Super Sweet 100 is a vigorous indeterminate that needs very sturdy staking or caging to at least 6 feet.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Super Sweet 100 is one of the most prolific and most frequently recommended cherry tomato varieties in American home gardening — a hybrid producing massive, long clusters (trusses) of 20–30 small (1-inch), round, brilliant red cherry tomatoes with exceptional sweetness and high sugar content that makes each fruit taste like concentrated tomato candy. The 'Sweet 100' line was introduced in the 1970s and immediately became one of the best-selling tomato varieties; 'Super Sweet 100' is an improved hybrid with better disease resistance. In zone 9, Super Sweet 100 produces from February or March transplanting through June, and again from September through November transplanting for a fall crop — two productive growing windows that can yield hundreds of fruits per plant. The enormous, arching clusters of brilliant red tomatoes draping from a well-established vine are a spectacular sight. The high Brix (sugar content) makes Super Sweet 100 outstanding for snacking, caprese salads, and any use where raw tomato sweetness is the primary quality desired. Vigorous growth requires staking or caging — an established Super Sweet 100 vine can reach 8 feet or more and must be supported to prevent collapsing under the weight of developing fruit clusters.

name: Superschmelz Kohlrabi
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors and transplant carefully; give this giant type much more room than standard kohlrabi so the stem can bulk up over a long season.
directions: Sow into fertile, well-drained soil with wide spacing, since Superschmelz — German for super melter — is bred to swell to eight or ten pounds while staying crisp and tender rather than turning woody like most oversized kohlrabi. Keep watering consistent through the growing season to avoid splitting the enlarging stem, and side-dress with compost as the bulb sizes up. Harvest young for a milder, thinner-skinned bite, or let it grow to full giant size for slicing, roasting, or long winter storage.

name: Supersett Crookneck Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Supersett is a disease-resistant hybrid yellow crookneck bred to hold foliage and production longer into the season under powdery mildew pressure than open-pollinated crookneck types.
directions: Supersett is a hybrid yellow crookneck squash bred for improved tolerance to powdery mildew, a disease that shuts down foliage and yield on older open-pollinated crookneck varieties by midsummer in humid climates. Its compact bush habit and heavy, sustained fruit set make it a productive choice for gardeners who have struggled with mildew collapse on standard crookneck squash, particularly in the humid Southeast and Gulf South where warm, humid nights favor the disease. Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger passes; harvest young at 5-6 inches long for the best tenderness, picking every day or two during peak production since crookneck squash left on the plant quickly becomes tough and seedy and signals the plant to slow production. Scout regularly for squash vine borer and squash bugs, which affect Supersett the same as other Cucurbita pepo crooknecks despite its improved mildew tolerance.
sources: Willhite Seed Co. — Supersett Hybrid Crookneck

name: Supersonic Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Supersonic's outstanding crack resistance is particularly valuable in Gulf South gardens subject to alternating wet and dry periods — irregular watering that causes cracking in thin-skinned varieties has less impact on Supersonic.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Supersonic is a classic large-fruited beefsteak-type hybrid tomato developed for outstanding crack resistance — one of the most crack-resistant large-fruited tomato varieties available, a quality of significant practical importance in Gulf South gardens where irregular rainfall and alternating wet-dry conditions cause cracking in thin-skinned large varieties. The large (8–12 oz), round to slightly flattened, deep-red, firm-fleshed fruits have classic fresh-eating and slicing quality — Supersonic produces the large-scale, meaty beefsteak tomato slices valued for sandwiches and fresh presentations. Supersonic is an indeterminate variety reaching 5–7 feet that requires sturdy staking or caging throughout the season. The crack resistance advantage comes from a thicker skin and firmer flesh than many large-fruited varieties — the practical benefit is significantly less fruit loss during wet periods that would crack softer-skinned types. Supersonic carries V and F disease resistance. In zone 9, Supersonic is best grown as a spring crop (February–May) to maximize the early harvest before summer heat affects fruit set on large-fruited types. The variety has been in continuous production since its introduction in the 1970s — maintained by home gardeners who value the reliable production of large, crack-resistant, good-quality red slicing tomatoes.

name: Supersteak Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once frost danger has passed; Supersteak is a Burpee hybrid bred for exceptionally large beefsteak fruit, some of the biggest slicing tomatoes available, on a vigorous indeterminate vine.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, providing sturdy staking or caging since this vigorous vine bears exceptionally heavy fruit. Supersteak is a Burpee hybrid beefsteak tomato bred for some of the largest fruit of any tomato variety, often exceeding a pound per tomato, with meaty, flavorful flesh well suited to thick slices for sandwiches. Its designation as VFN indicates built-in resistance to verticillium wilt, fusarium wilt, and nematodes, helping it stay productive through a long, humid Gulf South growing season. Water deeply and consistently to prevent blossom-end rot and cracking on the large fruit, and feed generously to support the heavy crop load.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Production

name: Supersweet 100 Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Supersweet 100 is an indeterminate vine that produces prolifically throughout the season when grown with strong support (cage or stake 6+ feet tall). In zone 9, transplant late February through early March for harvest May through July, with a second planting in August–September for fall production. The long clusters (20–30+ tomatoes) must be harvested regularly; overripe fruits split easily.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; transplant to full sun with strong support and consistent, even watering to prevent blossom end rot. Supersweet 100 is one of the most important cherry tomato varieties ever developed — a Petoseed hybrid released in the 1980s that set the standard for sweet cherry tomatoes and has remained one of the top-selling cherry tomatoes in America for over 40 years based solely on its exceptional eating quality. The name states the performance promise: 'super sweet' flavor from fruits with approximately twice the sugar content of beefsteak types, and '100' (now sold as 'Supersweet 100 F1') referencing a very early working name for the variety's productivity. The red, round, 1-inch fruits are produced in long, abundant clusters of 20–50+ tomatoes per cluster on indeterminate vines that require staking or caging and continue producing until frost. The flavor is memorably sweet, bright, and richly tomato-forward — thin-skinned enough to burst slightly on the palate, sweet enough to eat like candy, and balanced with just enough acidity to be complex rather than cloying. Supersweet 100 has also demonstrated excellent virus resistance for a variety of its era, which contributes to its continued commercial success. Every tomato gardener who grows cherry tomatoes should try Supersweet 100 as the benchmark against which other cherry varieties are compared.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Variety Evaluation
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Cherry Tomato Variety Comparison

name: Surati Ravaiya Brinjal
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil once nights stay reliably above 55°F.
directions: Surati Ravaiya is a traditional landrace brinjal from the Surat area of south Gujarat, grown for its round, glossy purple fruits that typically reach a substantial 150 to 200 grams each. Its tender, mild flesh and sturdy round shape make it the classic choice for bharela ravaiya, the popular Gujarati dish of baby eggplants stuffed with a spiced peanut-and-coconut masala and simmered in sauce. Plants show useful field tolerance to shoot and fruit borer as well as little leaf disease, both common regional pests, but fruit set can be uneven during heavy monsoon rains, so good drainage helps steady production. Harvest fruits while still firm and glossy for the best texture in stuffed preparations.

name: Sure Pick Summer Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost in warm, fertile soil.
directions: Sure Pick is a dark-green zucchini bred for reliability, continuing to set fruit through heat spells and periods of light pollinator activity when other squash plantings stall. Direct sow after the last frost and keep plants picked every couple of days to encourage continued production. Its weather and disease tolerance make it a dependable main-season squash for gardeners in variable climates.

name: Surefire Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Surefire is a determinate tomato bred by Texas A&M AgriLife specifically to keep setting fruit through the high nighttime temperatures that shut down bloom-to-fruit set in most tomato varieties across the Gulf South and Deep South summer.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Surefire is a Texas A&M AgriLife release and Texas Superstar-designated tomato bred specifically to hold fruit set through the punishing high nighttime heat of a Central and South Texas summer, when most tomato varieties stop setting fruit almost entirely — a trait directly useful across the wider Gulf South wherever midsummer heat causes the familiar tomato slump between the spring and fall crops. The compact, determinate plant produces a concentrated, heavy crop of medium-size, firm, flavorful red fruit over a shorter, more manageable staking and pruning window than a sprawling indeterminate vine. Because it is bred to keep fruiting through heat rather than avoid it, it is a good choice to extend the harvest into the hottest stretch of a zone 9 summer where other varieties stall.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas Superstar Plant Program

name: Susanville Garlic
plantingNote: Plant individual cloves 1-2 inches deep in fall; Susanville is a California-origin artichoke-type softneck bred from California Early stock and noted for reliable low-chill performance, adapting well to both warm and cold-winter climates alike.
directions: Plant individual cloves pointed-end-up, 1-2 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart, in loose, well-drained soil in fall; Susanville is an artichoke-type softneck improved from California Early stock, valued for a wide climate range and dependable bulbing even where winters are too mild to satisfy hardneck garlic's chilling needs. Bulbs form in a layered, artichoke-like pattern with a good number of easy-to-peel cloves in white to lightly purple-streaked wrappers, carrying a robust flavor that mellows nicely when roasted or cooked. As a softneck it braids easily and cures into long-storing bulbs. Harvest when the lower third to half of the leaves have yellowed, cure in a warm, dry, shaded, well-ventilated spot for 3-4 weeks, then trim and store for use through much of the year.
sources: Filaree Garlic Farm — Artichoke variety descriptions
University of California Cooperative Extension — Garlic Production in California
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Garlic Variety Selection for Texas

name: Sutton's Seedless Rhubarb
plantingNote: Plant dormant crowns in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, setting the crown bud 1-2 inches below the soil surface.
directions: This classic English heirloom was selected specifically for its reluctance to bolt, so it channels far less energy into flower stalks than older rhubarb strains and instead keeps producing thick, tender leafstalks through most of the season. Divide and replant crowns every four to six years once the clump becomes congested, discarding the woody center and replanting vigorous outer sections. Top-dress heavily with compost or well-rotted manure each spring since rhubarb is a hungry, long-lived perennial, and remove any flower stalks promptly to redirect energy into stalk production. Stop harvesting by mid-summer to let the plant rebuild root reserves for the following year, and always discard the toxic leaf blades, using only the petioles.

name: Suyo Long Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Suyo Long is a traditional Chinese burpless cucumber with exceptionally long (12–18 inch), ribbed, slightly curved fruits, tender thin skin, seedless-to-few-seed interior, and mild, sweet, non-bitter flavor — one of the finest cucumbers for fresh eating and extraordinarily productive in hot weather.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; train vines up a trellis to keep the long fruits straight and prevent rot — trellising is particularly important for Suyo Long to develop straight fruits. Suyo Long is a traditional Chinese slicing cucumber producing very long (12–18 inch), slightly ribbed, tapered fruits with a distinctive light green, slightly warted skin and an interior that is almost entirely flesh with very few seeds; the flavor is exceptionally mild, sweet, and refreshing with none of the bitterness common in cucumbers grown in heat stress. It is the burpless cucumber par excellence — the thin skin and low cucurbitacin content make it highly digestible and virtually non-gassy even when eaten in large quantities. Extremely productive in hot weather and much more heat-tolerant than European greenhouse cucumbers; outstanding for Gulf Coast and Southern summer production. Best trellised vertically for straight fruits and improved air circulation.
sources: Kitazawa Seed Company Asian Vegetable Guide

name: Suzhou Baby Bok Choy
plantingNote: Direct sow around the last frost, and again from late summer into fall; Suzhou Baby is a market-garden staple around Suzhou, China, valued for holding tender texture even as heads size up and for tolerating only a few hours of direct sun per day.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, evenly moist soil and thin to allow heads room to fill out into their characteristic tight, rounded form. Suzhou Baby forms a dense, compact rosette of pale green petioles and rounded, glossy leaves that stays tender and mild-flavored well past the size where many baby bok choy types turn fibrous, and it shrugs off both a warm spell and a light cold snap better than most spring-planted greens. Because it needs only a partial day of direct sun to size up properly, it performs well tucked into beds that get shade from taller neighboring crops for part of the day. Harvest whole heads at the base once they feel firm, or pick outer leaves progressively for a steady kitchen supply.

name: Swedish Brown Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; a Scandinavian heirloom bush bean documented since the 1890s and traditionally grown on the island of Öland.
directions: Sow seeds directly 1 inch deep after the last frost date, spacing compact bush plants 4-6 inches apart; the low, sturdy habit needs no support. Swedish Brown, also sold as Öland Swedish Brown, is a Scandinavian heirloom dating to at least the 1890s that produces short pods holding five to seven glossy tan-brown seeds marked with a small white eye. Leave pods on the plant until they dry and rattle, then shell and store the beans, which cook to a nutty, dense texture well suited to baked bean dishes and hearty soups. The short, stocky plants tolerate cooler summers better than many bean varieties, reflecting their northern European origin.

name: Sweet 100 Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Sweet 100 is a vigorous indeterminate plant that grows very tall (6–8+ feet) and produces enormous clusters of cherry tomatoes throughout the season — staking is essential, with minimum 6-foot stakes or a sturdy cage recommended. In zone 9, transplant March–April for early summer production that continues until fall or first frost. The '100' in the name references the extremely large number of tomatoes per cluster — a single cluster can hold 50–100 or more cherry tomatoes, and a well-established plant in zone 9's long season produces continuously from June through November with minimal stopping. Sweet 100 is somewhat susceptible to cracking in irregular watering conditions (a common complaint), but the sheer productivity and classic sweet-acid cherry tomato flavor have maintained its popularity for decades.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and provide minimum 6-foot stake. Harvest clusters when uniformly red. Sweet 100 is one of the most famous and historically significant cherry tomato varieties in American home gardening — an F1 hybrid first introduced in the early 1980s that set a new standard for cherry tomato productivity and established the category of 'sweet cherry tomato' as distinct from larger slicing tomato types. Before Sweet 100, cherry tomatoes were typically valued for novelty and ease of snacking rather than for the combination of extremely high productivity and genuinely sweet, complex flavor that Sweet 100 provided. The variety produces long, branching clusters with an extraordinary number of fruits per cluster — sometimes 50–100 per cluster, as the name implies — with uniformly round, 1-inch red fruits and a flavor that combines sweetness with the right amount of acidity to create what many gardeners consider the definitive cherry tomato flavor. The flavor balance of Sweet 100 — sweet but not cloying, with genuine tomato acid and complexity — made it the reference standard against which subsequent cherry varieties were judged for a generation. Sweet 100's high vitamin C content (documented to be substantially higher than larger slicing tomatoes) and prolific production made it popular both as a garden plant and as a crop for farmers markets where volume production of cherry tomatoes was economically important. Several improved varieties building on Sweet 100's genetics followed, including Sweet Million (improved crack resistance), Supersweet 100 (same name but improved disease package), and others — but the original Sweet 100 remains widely grown and available.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee — Sweet 100 cherry tomato historical introduction documentation
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Sweet cherry tomato variety comparison and productivity data
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cherry Tomato Variety Selection for the Gulf South

name: Sweet 100 Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–80°F and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; Sweet 100 is an exceptionally vigorous indeterminate hybrid and needs a tall, sturdy cage or trellis to support its long, heavily fruiting vines.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, providing a tall, sturdy cage or trellis for the vigorous, sprawling vines. Sweet 100 is a classic F1 hybrid cherry tomato introduced in the 1980s, prized for producing extraordinarily long clusters of small, intensely sweet, bright red fruit in such abundance that a single healthy plant can yield hundreds of tomatoes over the season, giving the variety its name. Its exceptional sweetness, disease tolerance, and reliable heavy production made it one of the most widely grown cherry tomatoes for home gardens and remains a benchmark variety against which many newer cherry tomato hybrids are compared. Harvest continuously as fruit ripens to encourage ongoing production, since the plant sets new clusters rapidly throughout a long summer season.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database

name: Sweet Adelaide Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the compact, tree-like 2-4 ft dwarf-indeterminate habit suits raised beds and large containers.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking the sturdy, tree-like stems lightly for support. Sweet Adelaide bears meaty pink fruit ranging from round to boat-shaped with somewhat ruffled shoulders, prized for its excellent, well-balanced sweetness on a compact plant. It descends from a New Big Dwarf x Paul Robeson cross and was named by Patrina Nuske Small, one of many collaborative releases from the Dwarf Tomato Project bred to bring heirloom flavor to small-space gardens. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

name: Sweet Baby Cos Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant in cool weather at 6-8 inch spacing; the compact habit suits close succession plantings or containers.
directions: Sweet Baby Cos is a Wild Garden Seed farm original developed by crossing 'Concept' with 'Flashy Butter Oak,' resulting in short, dense, compact medium-green heads sized for single servings. A high proportion of the leaves are bite-sized straight off a mature head, with thick blades and crunchy midribs that make good hand-held 'half shell' salad servings. In bright light the leaf tips pick up a slight color tint, a typical sun-stress response in many lettuces. Space plants 6-8 inches apart and keep soil evenly moist, since cos types can turn bitter or bolt quickly if they dry out or hit a late-season heat spike.

name: Sweet Banana Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Sweet Banana peppers are excellent for pickling — harvest at the pale yellow to light orange stage for maximum crispness in pickled applications.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Sweet Banana is one of the most popular sweet pepper varieties in American home gardens — a long (6–8 inch), tapering, banana-shaped pepper with thin to medium walls and very mild, sweet flavor with absolutely no heat at any stage of maturity. The fruits ripen from pale creamy-yellow through orange to red, with the best flavor for fresh eating at the orange to red stage and the best texture for pickling at the pale yellow stage. Sweet banana peppers are the standard pepper for the famous deli-style pickled banana peppers — the crunchy, mildly tangy, bright-yellow pickled pepper slices ubiquitous on Italian subs, pizza, and in Greek salads. Home-pickled banana peppers from fresh-harvested yellow fruits are far superior in flavor and crunch to commercially processed versions. For fresh use, allow to ripen fully red — the red stage develops sweeter, richer flavor approaching the sweetness of roasted red pepper. The productive, upright, sturdy plants are easily distinguished by the numerous hanging yellow peppers at varying stages, creating a colorful harvest display. In zone 9, sweet banana peppers are among the most productive warm-season vegetables — the long growing season allows multiple picks per plant from spring through late fall.

name: Sweet Beauty Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed, or start indoors 3 weeks ahead for an earlier harvest; this variety was recognized by All-America Selections judges specifically for its eating quality.
directions: Sweet Beauty is a small-space, single-serving icebox watermelon that won an All-America Selections award for consistently outscoring other compact varieties in sugar content during trials, with recorded Brix readings above 11. Fruits are oblong, 5-7 pounds, with dark green rind and medium green stripes and dense, sweet red flesh, and the vines stay manageable at roughly 8-10 feet, making the variety a good fit for smaller vegetable gardens. Grow it with full sun and even moisture through fruit development, then cut back watering as fruits ripen to keep the sugar concentration high. Its combination of compact vine habit and top-tier flavor makes it an easy choice for gardeners who don't have room for sprawling full-size Southern types but still want genuinely sweet, crisp melon.

name: Sweet Daisy Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the compact, well-branched plant benefits from a cage or stake for support.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, providing a cage or stake for support. Sweet Daisy is a modern grape tomato bred for exceptionally heavy, early, and sustained production of small, sweet, crack-resistant fruit on a compact, well-branched plant that fits well into smaller garden beds and large containers. The reliable disease tolerance and continuous fruit set through summer heat have made it a popular choice for gardeners wanting a low-maintenance, high-yield snacking tomato without the sprawling size of full-scale indeterminate vines. Harvest fruit as clusters fully color, picking regularly to keep the productive plant setting new fruit throughout a long summer season.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Sweet Dumpling Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow 1–2 weeks after last frost once soil is thoroughly warm above 65°F; Sweet Dumpling is a moderately vining variety that fits well in smaller gardens compared to full-size winter squash types — it can be grown on a sturdy trellis with the developing fruits supported in mesh slings.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in compost-enriched hills 2–3 weeks after last frost, thinning to 2 plants per hill; Sweet Dumpling is one of the most popular small winter squash varieties, producing cream-colored, deeply ribbed, round to slightly flattened fruits weighing 1–2 pounds with distinctive dark green stripes and flecks that turn orange at full maturity. The single-serving-size fruits are among the sweetest of all winter squash — the pale yellow-orange flesh is dry, fine-textured, and sweet enough to eat simply baked with butter and a touch of salt, making it an outstanding small family vegetable garden variety for households that do not need the large quantity of a full butternut or Hubbard. Harvest when the rind is fully hard and the green striping has faded to cream or begun turning orange; cure for 1–2 weeks at room temperature before storing.

name: Sweet Favorite Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills after soil warms to 70F and all frost danger passes; Sweet Favorite is a long-standing AAS-winning watermelon prized for exceptional sweetness on a large, classic oblong striped fruit good for feeding a crowd.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after soil warms. Sweet Favorite is a long-established AAS-winning watermelon, producing large, oblong, classically striped fruit in the traditional picnic-watermelon style, prized above all for exceptional sweetness that has kept it a favorite for decades since its introduction. Fruit commonly reaches 15-25 pounds with crisp, bright-red flesh and a good, thin-but-sturdy rind for handling and short-term storage. Its large size makes it well suited to feeding a crowd at a summer gathering, in keeping with its classic picnic-watermelon role. Watermelons need deep, well-drained soil, ample space, and consistent irrigation through fruit development, since drought stress during fruit fill causes smaller fruit and hollow heart. Judge ripeness by the ground spot yellowing, the tendril nearest the fruit drying and curling, and a dull, hollow thump when tapped.
sources: All-America Selections — Sweet Favorite Watermelon winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Sweet Garleek
plantingNote: Start seed in plug trays indoors about 6 weeks ahead, then transplant 3-4 plants per plug at 6-inch spacing to keep shafts straight rather than curved.
directions: Ten years in the breeding of Hans Bongers, this allium merges leek sweetness with a mild hint of garlic in one mild-flavored shaft. Seedlings do best in cooler 60-70F conditions since warmer temperatures reduce germination, and crowding more than four seedlings per plug cell causes shafts to bend instead of growing straight. Harvest while shafts are still about half an inch across for the most tender texture, and watch for allium leaf miner, using exclusion netting if it is a problem in your area.

name: Sweet Granite Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed; Sweet Granite was bred specifically for far-northern, coastal, and mountain gardens with short cantaloupe seasons.
directions: Sweet Granite was released by a University of New Hampshire plant breeding program as one of the earliest-ripening eastern-type cantaloupes available at the time, developed specifically for gardeners in short-season northern, coastal, and mountain climates. The oblong fruit carries light netting over sweet, orange flesh and averages about three pounds, smaller than many long-season commercial cantaloupes but far more reliable where summers run cool or short. It remains a dependable option today for gardeners north of the traditional cantaloupe belt who still want genuine muskmelon flavor. Give it full sun and consistent moisture through fruit set, tapering off as melons approach full slip.
sources: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension

name: Sweet Hungarian Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 start November–December and transplant February–March. Sweet Hungarian is a prolific, dependable frying pepper well-suited to zone 9 heat; the compact plants continue setting fruit through the summer heat when bell peppers often pause. A second planting in July provides fall production. Plants benefit from light afternoon shade in peak summer to prevent blossom drop.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Sweet Hungarian is a classic frying and pickling pepper producing long, tapered, light yellow-green to red fruits of 5–8 inches with thin, tender walls, very mild heat (500–1,000 SHU), and a sweet, slightly tangy flavor that makes them the preferred pepper for Hungarian paprika production, pickled peppers, stuffed peppers, and traditional frying preparations. The thin-walled, tapered fruits cook quickly without the wateriness of thick-walled bell peppers, making them excellent for sautéing whole in olive oil, frying until blistered, stuffing with rice and ground meat, or pickling in brine. The fruit color progression from yellow-green through orange to brilliant red allows harvest at multiple stages — yellow-green for crisp, mild frying, red for maximum sweetness and paprika production. In zone 9 the compact, productive plants withstand summer heat far better than bell peppers and continue producing through the warmest months.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Sweet Pepper Varieties
Seed Savers Exchange — Sweet Hungarian Pepper Heritage Variety
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Frying Pepper Production for Texas

name: Sweet Hungarian Wax Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March after nights stay above 55°F. Sweet Hungarian Wax is productive through Gulf Coast summers and handles high humidity well, producing heavily from June through October with regular fertilization.
directions: Transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Sweet Hungarian Wax is the mild counterpart to the hot banana pepper — a waxy, thick-walled, banana-shaped variety that ripens from pale yellow through orange to red and carries virtually no heat (0–500 SHU). The sweet, crisp, 5–7 inch fruits are outstanding for pickling, fresh eating, roasting, and stuffing, and their attractive color progression makes them ornamental on the plant. Harvest at yellow to orange stage for the sweetest, mildest flavor; the fully red fruits are slightly sweeter but softer. This variety is particularly valued for pickling operations as the thick walls hold their crunch through the canning process. Plants are compact and tidy, ideal for raised beds and container growing.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pepper Varieties for Florida
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Hungarian Wax
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Wax Pepper Types

name: Sweet Jade Kabocha Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, or start indoors a couple weeks early; Sweet Jade grows on a more restrained vine than standard kabocha types and rewards a bit less garden space.
directions: Direct sow in warm, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, giving the semi-compact vine room to ramble. Sweet Jade is an AAS-winning kabocha bred by Johnny's Selected Seeds for a personal-serving size, yielding round, 1 to 2 pound fruit with a jade-green, lightly speckled rind that encloses deep orange, richly sweet flesh often compared to a blend of pumpkin, sweet potato, and roasted chestnut. Let fruit fully harden on the vine before cutting, then cure in a warm spot for a week or two to concentrate sugars before moving to cool storage. Its smaller fruit size makes it easy to portion a whole squash per person for roasting or stuffing.
sources: All-America Selections — Sweet Jade Kabocha winner announcement

name: Sweet Mama Kabocha Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for a May–June harvest and August for fall. Kabocha-type squashes including Sweet Mama are more heat-tolerant than most maxima types, making them better suited to zone 9 than Blue Hubbard or Buttercup. The compact vine is more manageable than sprawling maxima types, but still needs 5–8 feet of space per plant.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Sweet Mama is an All-America Selections-winning kabocha-type squash selected for exceptional sweetness and a compact vine habit. The small, flattened, dark green fruits (3–4 pounds) have brilliant deep-orange flesh with an almost impossibly sweet, nutty, dry flavor — more concentrated and dessert-like than butternut or acorn squash. When cut open the flesh is so dense and dry that it steams and bakes with a chestnut-like texture, and the sugar content is high enough to caramelize beautifully on cut surfaces. The thin edible skin softens when cooked, eliminating the need for peeling. Sweet Mama's superior flavor comes from its Japanese kabocha parentage, which Japanese breeders developed over decades specifically for sugar content and dry, flavorful flesh. In zone 9 harvest when the stem has dried and corked over and the skin has hardened — squeezing should produce no give in the flesh. Cure 2–4 weeks at room temperature before eating for best flavor development.
sources: All-America Selections — Sweet Mama Squash Award Record
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Kabocha Squash Types
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Winter Squash Varieties for Florida

name: Sweet Meat Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Sweet Meat is a large (8–15 lb) slate-blue to gray-green winter squash of the Cucurbita maxima species, historically important in the Pacific Northwest as a premier eating and storing squash; it is the variety that defined the 'gray Hubbard' category of dry, sweet, long-storing winter squash in American home gardens.
directions: Direct sow in hills after last frost in rich, well-drained soil; Sweet Meat requires a long vine (8–12 feet) and ample space; harvest when the skin is fully gray-blue and rock-hard; it stores exceptionally well (6–8 months in cool, dry conditions) and the flavor improves with several months of storage as starches convert to sugars. Sweet Meat squash is a prized heirloom of the Pacific Northwest, where it has been grown in Oregon and Washington for generations as the gold standard of winter keeping squash — valued above all other varieties for the combination of very long storage life, exceptional flavor, and high-quality flesh. The fruits are large (8–15 lbs), somewhat flattened round to oval, with a smooth, dry, slate-blue to gray-green skin that turns distinctly grayish-blue at full maturity — a color that is characteristic of the very best long-storing Cucurbita maxima varieties. The flesh is uniformly deep orange, very dry, dense, and extremely sweet — with a characteristic thick, starchy quality that makes it ideal for baking, puréeing, and any preparation where flavor concentration and dry texture are paramount. The famous Oregon home economist and food writer Carol Deppe championed Sweet Meat squash extensively in her book 'The Resilient Gardener' as the ideal squash for serious food gardeners seeking long storage life and superior flavor; her advocacy brought Sweet Meat to wider national attention. Unlike most winter squash that peak at harvest and slowly decline in storage, Sweet Meat actually improves for the first 2–3 months in storage as the chemistry continues to develop, making it the ideal squash for a Thanksgiving centerpiece planted in late spring.

name: Sweet Million Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant after last frost into full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Sweet Million is a widely grown F1 red cherry tomato bearing prolific clusters of crack-resistant, uniformly sized 1-inch red fruits with excellent sweet flavor — an improvement on the classic Sweet 100 type with better crack resistance, disease resistance, and fruit quality for both home gardens and market growers.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after last frost; stake or cage early as Sweet Million produces vigorous indeterminate vines; the fruits ripen in large clusters of 15–30 and can be harvested cluster by cluster. Sweet Million is an F1 hybrid red cherry tomato developed as an improved successor to the classic Sweet 100 cherry tomato — retaining Sweet 100's exceptional productivity and sweet flavor while adding meaningfully better crack resistance, improved disease resistance (including resistance to fusarium and verticillium wilts), and more uniform fruit sizing than the original Sweet 100. The fruits are small, round, and uniformly 3/4 to 1 inch, ripening a brilliant red; the flavor is classic cherry tomato — sweet, high in sugar relative to acids, bright and fruity with good tomato character. The vines are indeterminate and extremely productive, bearing what appears to be a literally endless succession of clusters from midsummer through frost — the name 'Sweet Million' suggests the volume of fruit a well-grown plant produces. Sweet Million is an outstanding choice for home gardeners who want maximum production of reliable, sweet red cherry tomatoes for fresh eating, salads, and snacking; it is particularly recommended for humid climates (including the Gulf Coast) where crack-prone cherry varieties fail in summer rains. Disease-resistant foliage is an advantage in humid zone 8–10 conditions.

name: Sweet Olive Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Sweet Olive's thick skin and oval shape give it significantly better shelf life and handling durability than round cherry tomatoes — the firmer skin resists cracking and damage during harvest.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Sweet Olive is a grape-type cherry tomato — small (1–1.5 inch), oval to elongated, bright-red fruits with thick skin and meaty, low-moisture flesh that gives this type better handling durability, shelf life, and crack resistance than round cherry tomatoes. The grape-type classification refers to the oval, elongated shape resembling table grapes rather than the classic round cherry tomato form. The flavor is very sweet and concentrated — the firm, meaty flesh with lower water content intensifies the sweetness-per-bite relative to juicier round types. Sweet Olive produces large trusses of fruit on vigorous indeterminate vines. The thick skin and oval shape make grape-type tomatoes like Sweet Olive particularly practical for container growing, patio harvesting, and fresh snacking — the fruits don't burst when squeezed gently and hold their quality well at room temperature for several days after harvest. In zone 9, grape-type cherry tomatoes are among the most reliable summer producers because the thick skin provides some protection against cracking from uneven moisture that affects large-fruited and thin-skinned types. An excellent choice for continuous production through the warm season in zone 9 gardens.

name: Sweet Paprika Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; sweet paprika pepper is a Hungarian/Central European cultivar group bred specifically for drying and grinding into paprika powder, with extraordinarily high carotenoid content giving both the brilliant red color and the sweet, distinctive paprika flavor — grown domestically to produce fresh, vivid paprika far superior in flavor to commercial dried paprika.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; sweet paprika peppers are harvested when fully red and then dried whole (traditionally strung on twine and air-dried) or split and dehydrated before grinding. Sweet (édes) paprika peppers are a cultivar group of Capsicum annuum developed in Hungary for the production of paprika spice, the defining seasoning of Hungarian cuisine and a cornerstone of Central and Eastern European cooking; the peppers themselves are characterized by exceptionally high carotenoid content (primarily capsanthin and capsorubin) that produces both the brilliant deep red color of dried paprika and its characteristic sweet, slightly fruity, mildly smoky flavor with zero heat. Fresh sweet paprika peppers can be eaten like any sweet bell pepper — they have a somewhat thicker, crunchier texture and a distinctive paprika aroma even when raw. For making paprika powder, dry the fully ripe red fruits at 140–160°F until brittle, then grind; freshly ground home paprika is dramatically more vivid in color and flavor than commercial imported paprika.

name: Sweet REBA Acorn Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; the compact bush habit suits smaller gardens and tighter row spacing than vining acorn types.
directions: Sweet REBA (Resistant Early Bush Acorn) is a Cornell University release bred for a truly compact, non-vining bush habit combined with earliness and improved powdery mildew tolerance, making it well suited to short-season and small-space gardens. Despite its small footprint, plants set heavy yields of dark green, ribbed, one-to-one-and-a-half-pound fruit with notably sweet, dry, deep-orange flesh. Its bush form allows closer in-row spacing than sprawling acorn varieties, so it fits well in raised beds or intensive plantings. Choose Sweet REBA when garden space is limited but you still want reliably sweet, early-maturing acorn squash for fall roasting.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

name: Sweet Sandwich Onion
subcategory: storage onion, hybrid long-day sweet type
plantingNote: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant seedlings outside about 4-6 weeks before the last expected frost.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant seedlings into fertile, well-drained soil once frost risk has passed, spacing them to allow bulbs room to size up. Maintain even moisture through the growing season and let foliage fall over naturally before curing bulbs in a dry, ventilated space. Sweet Sandwich is a long-day hybrid bred for a rare combination of mild, sweet flavor and genuinely good storage life, addressing the usual tradeoff where sweeter onions typically spoil faster than pungent storage types.

name: Sweet Siberian Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Sweet Siberian is one of the shortest-season watermelons available, maturing in 65–75 days, with more cold-tolerant germination than most varieties — making it the top choice for zone 3–5 gardens with short summers where most watermelons cannot ripen, while still producing sweet, flavorful fruit.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in full sun; Sweet Siberian can germinate in soils as cool as 60°F (compared to 70°F+ needed by most watermelons), making early establishment easier in northern gardens. Sweet Siberian is a Russian heirloom watermelon developed for the short, cool growing seasons of Siberia and Central Russia, where conventional watermelon varieties fail to ripen before fall frost; it is one of the most cold-tolerant watermelons for germination and early growth while maturing in 65–75 days from seed — roughly 15–25 days earlier than most mainstream varieties. The small to medium fruits (8–15 lbs) have pale green, lightly striped skin and unusual salmon-orange to pale yellow flesh that is surprisingly sweet and fragrant with a distinctive aroma different from standard red-fleshed varieties. Compact vines suit smaller gardens. An outstanding variety for northern zone 3–5 gardeners who have given up on watermelons, and produces a fast summer crop in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens as well.

name: Sweet Slice Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, or start indoors for an earlier crop; Sweet Slice was an AAS award winner bred for long, thin-skinned fruit with little to no bitterness.
directions: Sweet Slice is a burpless-type slicing cucumber that grows long, slender, mild fruit with thin, tender skin that rarely needs peeling. Its low cucurbitacin content keeps the flesh sweet and free of the bitterness and burping aftertaste that can come with standard slicers, making it popular for fresh eating and salads. The vigorous vines benefit from trellising, which keeps fruit straighter and easier to pick while improving air circulation in humid Gulf Coast summers. Pick fruit regularly once it reaches full length to keep vines producing over a long harvest season.

name: Sweet Success Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65°F; Sweet Success is parthenocarpic (self-fruitful without pollination), making it valuable in greenhouses, low-pollinator areas, and early in the season when bee activity is low. Train vines vertically for best fruit quality — fruits grown suspended tend to be longer and straighter than those touching the ground. Harvest fruits at 9–12 inches for best quality; overripe fruits develop seeds.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost when soil is above 65°F; train vines to a vertical support for best fruit quality and air circulation. Sweet Success is a 1983 All-America Selections-winning burpless cucumber from Burpee that was among the first parthenocarpic (sets fruit without pollination) cucumbers released for home garden use — a trait that allows fruit production in greenhouses, screen porches, or early in the season when pollinators are scarce, without any compromise in fruit quality. The long (10–14 inch), thin, dark green fruits have tender, smooth skin that doesn't require peeling, virtually no seeds when harvested at the right size, and the characteristically mild, sweet, non-bitter flavor of 'burpless' cucumber types — the term referring to reduced cucurbitacin content that causes the bitterness and digestive upset some people experience with older cucumber types. Sweet Success carries resistance to cucumber scab, cucumber mosaic virus, and angular leaf spot. The thin, tender skin and virtually seedless flesh make Sweet Success excellent for fresh eating and sandwich slicing, with a crisp, sweet quality that compares favorably to expensive English greenhouse cucumbers. A landmark variety in the development of the American burpless-seedless cucumber category and still a strong performer nearly 40 years after its introduction.
sources: Burpee Seeds — Sweet Success cucumber AAS winner 1983
All-America Selections — Sweet Success variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Cucumber Production in Florida

name: Sweet Superior Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed. A thin-skinned slicing type bred for low bitterness, it benefits from a trellis to keep fruit straight and clean.
directions: Direct sow once soil temperature is reliably above 70F, planting several seeds per hill and thinning to the strongest vine, or start indoors 2-3 weeks early for a jump on the season. Train vines up a trellis to save space and produce straighter fruit, and keep soil evenly moist to prevent bitterness and misshapen cucumbers. Harvest regularly while fruit are still slender since the thin, tender skin needs no peeling but turns tougher if left to oversize.

name: Sweet Zellow Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; stake or cage the vigorous indeterminate vine, which produces heavy clusters of small yellow fruit all season.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes, staking or caging the vine as it grows. Sweet Zellow was recognized as an All-America Selections winner for its exceptionally sweet, crack-resistant small yellow fruit borne in long, heavy clusters on a vigorous indeterminate vine, producing snacking tomatoes over a long season with far less splitting than many older yellow cherry types. The mild, low-acid, sugary flavor makes it a favorite for eating straight off the vine, and the tough but tender skin holds up well to handling and short-term storage. Pick fruit as it fully colors to golden-yellow for the sweetest flavor, and keep the vine well supported, since clusters can get heavy as they fill in. Even watering helps prevent the fruit cracking that plagues less crack-resistant yellow cherry tomatoes in wet weather.
sources: university extension tomato variety trial reports

name: Sweetie Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; Sweetie is an indeterminate vine that produces prolifically on a long, cascading vine — provide a 5–6 foot cage or strong staking. In zone 9, transplant March–April for May–October production. Like most cherry tomatoes, Sweetie can crack if irrigation is inconsistent (wet-dry-wet cycles cause rapid fruit expansion); consistent moisture management reduces cracking.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; cage or stake before growth gets away from support. Sweetie is an open-pollinated small cherry tomato that has been grown in American gardens since at least the 1970s — one of the classic heirloom small cherry tomatoes alongside Sweet 100 and Gardener's Delight. The round, 0.75–1 inch fruits are produced in large clusters of 15–25 or more on long, indeterminate vines, and have a flavor profile that lives up to the name: very sweet, with high sugar content relative to acid, and the concentrated pure tomato essence that has made small cherry tomatoes universally popular. Sweetie is open-pollinated, meaning seed can be saved from year to year to maintain a self-sustaining garden supply — an advantage over Sweet 100, which is a hybrid. The plants produce heavily from midsummer through frost, providing abundant cherry tomatoes for snacking, salads, roasting, and pasta for the entire season. Sweetie is particularly well-suited to gardeners who want to maintain their own seed from a reliable, high-quality cherry tomato variety.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Sweetie cherry tomato variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Small cherry tomato collection
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Open-pollinated cherry tomato comparison

name: Sweetie Pie Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 55 degrees F; Sweetie Pie is a 2017 All-America Selections winner bred as a true miniature bell pepper small enough for little hands and container gardens.
directions: Transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all danger of frost has passed, and stake the heavily-laden plants to keep fruit off the ground. Sweetie Pie produces abundant 2.5-3 inch, thick-walled miniature bell peppers that can be picked green or left to sweeten to red, on compact plants that excel in hot, humid conditions where standard bells often struggle. Its small fruit size and sweet flavor make it a favorite for introducing children to growing and eating vegetables. Harvest regularly to keep plants productive through the full warm season.

name: Sylvesta Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or fall; Sylvesta is a French Batavian-type lettuce prized for holding its crisp texture and mild flavor and resisting bolting longer than many lettuce varieties as the weather warms.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Sylvesta is a French Batavian-type lettuce forming loose, semi-crisp heads with a texture between soft butterhead and crunchy iceberg, valued for holding good quality and resisting premature bolting longer than many lettuce varieties as spring temperatures rise, extending the harvest window into warmer weather. The pale green leaves have a mild, sweet flavor and good crispness that holds up well in salads. Harvest as a loose head or pick outer leaves individually for a cut-and-come-again approach, and provide light afternoon shade in the warmest part of the season to further extend its quality.

name: Sylvetta Wild Arugula
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or late summer; Sylvetta is a refined, more compact selection of wild arugula bred specifically for salad-mix growers and tolerates heat better than standard arugula.
directions: Scatter seed thinly over cool, fertile soil and cover lightly, since Sylvetta germinates best when kept consistently moist. This named selection of wild arugula produces smaller, more deeply lobed leaves than the species and a denser, more compact rosette that regrows readily after cutting. Its flavor is intensely nutty and peppery, sharper than salad arugula, and it holds up in heat and resists bolting far longer than Eruca types, making it a mainstay of Italian-style mesclun mixes. In mild-winter regions it behaves as a short-lived perennial and can be harvested for several seasons from the same planting.

name: Tabasco Greenleaf Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once soil has warmed. Bred at Auburn University in the 1970s to replace tobacco-mosaic-susceptible stock, this cultivar produces the same slender, upward-facing, fiery fruit as classic tabasco but on virus-resistant plants, making it a more dependable choice for home growers and small producers. Pods ripen from pale yellow through orange to red, and are traditionally mashed and aged into vinegar-based hot sauce, though they work equally well fresh or dried.

name: Table Ace Acorn Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost; in zone 9 direct sow February–March for spring and August–September for fall. Table Ace's semi-bush habit is more compact than most acorn squash, making it suitable for smaller garden plots where standard spreading vines would overwhelm the space.
directions: Direct sow 2–3 seeds per hill 1 inch deep in rich, well-drained soil and thin to the strongest plant; Table Ace is an All-America Selections award-winning hybrid acorn squash with a compact, semi-bush habit that takes up considerably less garden space than standard vine-type acorn squash. The dark green, 1–2 pound fruits have the classic acorn shape with ridged skin and deep orange, dry, sweet flesh that pairs well with butter and brown sugar. Harvest when the skin resists fingernail pressure and the underside rind in contact with the soil turns orange; fruits left on the vine too long become fibrous. Store cured fruits in a cool, dry location for up to 3 months. The semi-bush habit makes Table Ace the preferred choice for gardeners who want acorn squash flavor in a space-efficient plant.
sources: All-America Selections — Table Ace Award Record
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Acorn Squash
University of Illinois Extension — Winter Squash Varieties

name: Table Dainty Marrow
plantingNote: Direct sow after frost danger passes; its smaller bush habit suits allotments and raised beds better than the big trailing marrows.
