directions: Table Dainty is a classic English bush marrow bred to stay smaller and more manageable than old-fashioned trailing marrows, producing pale green, lightly striped fruit on compact plants. Cut fruit young, around 6-8 inches, to eat it like a zucchini, or let it grow toward a modest 10-12 inches for a true marrow to halve, stuff, and bake. Its restrained size and bush habit make it a practical choice for smaller UK allotment plots where a full-sized trailing marrow would sprawl out of bounds. Pick regularly once fruiting starts, since even this compact variety will stop setting new fruit if a few are left to grow oversized.

name: Table Gold Acorn Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost once soil has warmed, allowing room for the bushy, semi-compact vines.
directions: Sow directly in warm soil after frost danger has passed, and keep plants evenly watered through fruit set for the best flavor. Table Gold was bred by horticulturist Dr. Oved Shifriss, known for his work developing compact bush-type squash, and produces bright golden-yellow acorn-shaped fruit on space-saving vines. The tender flesh has a notably nutty, sweet flavor that distinguishes it from the more common dark-green acorn types.

name: Table Queen Acorn Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer (July–August in zone 9) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for a fall harvest; acorn squash can also be direct sown in March–April for a spring crop in zone 9, harvested before summer heat.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Table Queen is the classic American acorn squash — an heirloom variety that has defined the acorn squash category since its introduction in the 1890s and remains one of the most widely recognized winter squash forms in American cooking. The deeply ribbed, dark-green to nearly black fruits (1.5–2 lb, 4–6 inches long) have dense, golden-yellow, sweet flesh with a nutty, slightly dry texture that is outstanding for baking: cut in half, brush with butter, season with brown sugar and cinnamon, and bake until caramelized — the classic American acorn squash preparation. The deep ribs and dark color are distinctive enough that 'acorn squash' has become synonymous with Table Queen's specific shape. As an open-pollinated heirloom, seeds can be saved from season to season. Table Queen stores well for 1–2 months at cool room temperature after proper curing (10 days at 80°F). In zone 9, acorn squash is most reliable as a fall crop (August planting, October–November harvest) — the spring planting often struggles in early summer heat. The fall crop benefits from the cooling temperatures of fall that improve the sweetness and flavor of the flesh. Space plants generously as the vines spread 6–8 feet in all directions.

name: Table Star Acorn Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Table Star is an All-America Selections winner producing full-size acorn squash on a semi-bush plant that yields earlier and more heavily than older open-pollinated acorn strains.
directions: Direct sow in hills after the last frost in fertile, well-drained soil, spacing plants for the semi-bush habit rather than a full sprawling vine. Table Star won an All-America Selections award for combining a compact plant with an unusually high yield of dark green, deeply ribbed acorn squash, often setting more fruit per plant than older acorn varieties while reaching harvest earlier in the season. The sweet, fine-grained orange flesh is well suited to roasting halves or stuffing, and the smaller plant footprint makes it a good fit for raised beds. Harvest once the rind has darkened fully and the underside patch has turned from white to yellow-orange, then use within a couple of months since acorn types are not long-term keepers.

name: Table Top Ground Cherry
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Table Top is a compact, upright ground cherry selection bred for a tidier, less sprawling habit than typical Physalis pruinosa, making it well suited to raised beds, small plots, and large containers.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, well-drained soil after danger of frost has passed. Table Top was selected for a low, mounding, self-supporting habit that stays far more contained than the wide-sprawling growth typical of ground cherries, so it fits neatly into small raised beds or a large patio pot without staking. Plants still bear the same small, sweet-tart, husk-wrapped golden fruits and drop them naturally when ripe, so spread a light mulch or row cover beneath plants to make gathering the fallen fruit easier and cleaner. Productive over a long summer season; pinch off any wayward stems if an especially neat, dwarf profile is wanted for container growing.

name: Table Treat Acorn Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after the last frost once soil has warmed; Table Treat vines are productive and benefit from full-season warmth to set multiple fruit per plant.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in hills after the last frost, thinning to the strongest two seedlings per hill. Table Treat is a vining acorn squash that sets a generous number of dark green, deeply ribbed fruit per plant, each with dry, sweet, pale orange flesh typical of the acorn type and a convenient single-serving size. The productive habit makes it a reliable choice for gardeners who want multiple small squash rather than fewer large ones. Harvest once the rind has dulled from glossy to matte green and resists a fingernail, then cure briefly in a warm spot before moving to cool storage; acorn types keep for a shorter period than hubbard or butternut squash, so plan to use them within a couple of months.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Tadorna Leek
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or start in summer for a fall/winter main crop; Tadorna is a reliable open-pollinated leek noted for strong cold tolerance and good disease resistance, making it well suited to the Gulf South's cool-season leek window.
directions: Start Tadorna leeks indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting, or start seed in summer for a main fall and winter crop, then set pencil-thick seedlings 4-6 inches apart into fertile, well-drained soil. Tadorna is a dependable open-pollinated leek that produces long, thick, blue-green stalks with excellent cold tolerance, standing well in the garden through cool weather without becoming tough or bitter, and shows good resistance to common leek diseases. Hill or trench soil around the stems as they grow to blanch and lengthen the tender white portion. In the Gulf South's mild winters, Tadorna can often be left in the ground and harvested as needed through the cool season rather than lifted all at once, giving a long, flexible harvest window.

name: Tahitian Melon Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed, giving the long rampant vines plenty of room or a sturdy trellis to climb.
directions: Tahitian Melon Squash grows a huge, pale blue-green, club-shaped fruit that can reach 2 feet long and 20-plus pounds, with dense, deep orange flesh notably lower in fiber and sweeter than most butternut types, closer in eating quality to a sweet potato. The extremely long, vigorous vines need generous space or a strong trellis to support the developing fruit off the ground. Despite its huge size, a single fruit stores well for months and yields a lot of smooth, easily pureed flesh for soups and baking. A conversation-piece squash for gardeners with room to let vines ramble and a taste for very sweet, low-fiber winter squash.
sources: University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources

name: Tai Guo Bitter Melon
plantingNote: Direct-sow after soil is thoroughly warm, or transplant seedlings started 3-4 weeks earlier; this vigorous hybrid Chinese type climbs quickly and begins bearing large fruit in as little as 50-55 days from transplant.
directions: A widely grown Chinese-type hybrid bitter melon producing large, cylindrical, glossy dark-green fruit with thick, crisp flesh, typically 9-11 inches long and up to 3 inches across, with individual fruits often weighing a pound or more. Its size and thick walls make it especially well suited to stuffing and to the stir-fries and braises common in Cantonese and other Chinese preparations, where the mild-to-moderate bitterness pairs with garlic, black bean sauce, or egg. The vigorous vine grows quickly in hot weather and benefits from a tall, sturdy trellis to support both its rampant growth and the weight of the large fruit. Harvest while the skin is still firm, glossy, and fully dark green, before any yellowing begins, for the best texture and flavor.
sources: Urban Farmer — Tai Guo Gourd Seeds
True Leaf Market — Bitter Gourd Tai Guo Hybrid

name: Taiwanese Flat Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost and transplant as young seedlings; in zone 9, the primary growing season is October–March for spring harvest, as summer heat causes bolting and poor head formation.
directions: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost or direct sow in fall for cool-season production; Taiwanese flat cabbage is a classic East Asian cabbage variety producing distinctly flat, wide, loosely-structured heads (12–16 inches in diameter but only 4–6 inches tall) with extremely tender, delicate leaves — a completely different texture and flavor experience from the dense, hard European round-head cabbages. The tender leaves are less pungent and more delicate than round cabbage, with a slightly sweet, mild flavor that holds up beautifully in quick-cooked preparations like stir-fries, hot pots, and braised dishes, while also working well in fresh preparations like slaws and salads. The flat shape and loose construction mean the heads do not store as long as round types but they are extraordinarily tender and pleasant to eat. Very popular in Taiwanese and Chinese fresh markets, restaurant kitchens, and among Asian-American home gardeners; the quick maturation (60–80 days from transplant) and cool-season preference make it an excellent fall-to-spring crop in the Gulf South.
sources: Kitazawa Seed Company Asian Vegetable Guide
Taiwan Agricultural Research Institute vegetable publications
University of Hawaii Cooperative Extension — Asian Vegetables

name: Takanotsume Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors with bottom heat 8 weeks before last frost and transplant only once nights stay reliably warm; the compact upright plants do well in containers.
directions: Named for its resemblance to a hawk's talon, Takanotsume is a small, slender Japanese chile that sets fruit pointing upward in dense clusters rather than hanging, distinguishing it from similar Japanese types like Santaka. Fruits ripen from green to bright red and carry moderate heat with a clean, fruity flavor, historically dried for storage and ground into shichimi togarashi and other spice blends. Grow it like other hot peppers in full sun with even moisture, and harvest red for maximum heat and the best drying results; whole dried pods keep well for months. Its compact habit and heavy, ornamental fruit set make it a good choice for containers and small gardens.

name: Takinogawa Burdock
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost into deep, loose, stone-free soil; Takinogawa needs at least 18-24 inches of unobstructed depth for its long taproot to develop straight.
directions: Direct sow into deep, loose, stone-free soil in full sun; Takinogawa is the standard Japanese market variety of burdock, grown as an annual for its long, slender, aromatic taproot that can reach 2-3 feet if the soil allows. Loosen the bed a full spade's depth or more before sowing, since any obstruction causes the root to fork or twist. Harvest in fall once roots reach full size, and use the earthy, mildly sweet root in classic preparations like kinpira gobo and other simmered dishes.

name: Talladega Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March for spring production. Talladega is a heat-set determinate hybrid with excellent blemish resistance in humid conditions — it is among the most reliable heavy-cropping varieties for the hot, humid Gulf Coast and Deep South.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil with a cage or stake; Talladega is a determinate, heat-tolerant hybrid tomato that produces large harvests of smooth, firm, 8–10 ounce red globe tomatoes with excellent shelf life and crack resistance. It was bred specifically for commercial and home production in the hot, humid South, where disease pressure from early blight, grey leaf spot, and bacterial spot is severe — Talladega carries broad disease resistance that keeps foliage healthy through the summer months when other varieties defoliate. The concentrated fruiting habit of this determinate variety makes it easy to time a large harvest for canning or preserving. Fall plantings in late July–early August often produce the heaviest yields as the fruits ripen into the cooler October–November weather.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Varieties for Florida
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomato Variety Trials
North Carolina State Extension — Tomato Variety Recommendations

name: Talpiot Artichoke
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and give seedlings 10-14 days near 50F once several true leaves have formed to promote earlier, more uniform bud set; in mild zone 9 winters, a late-summer sowing for fall transplant is also common in commercial production.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, rich, well-drained soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Talpiot is an Israeli-bred F1 hybrid developed alongside Tavor for seed-propagated, first-year annual production, forming a large, vigorous, spineless plant that sets medium green buds over a long harvest window. It shares the strong heat tolerance of other Israeli annual artichoke selections, making it a dependable choice for hot-summer growing regions, and continues to push side buds after the central bud is harvested. Keep soil consistently moist and fertile through the season and cut buds while the scales are still tight, before they begin to loosen and spread.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension -- Artichoke Production Guide
American Society for Horticultural Science -- artichoke cultivar trial literature

name: TAM Dew Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after soil has warmed well past 70°F; bred for the long, hot summers of the southern Great Plains and Gulf Coast, so it needs a full warm season to size up and sweeten properly.
directions: TAM Dew was released by Texas A&M's melon breeding program to give southern growers a honeydew with better resistance to downy mildew than older honeydew varieties, which historically struggled in humid southern conditions. Vines carry smooth, creamy-white rinds around thick, sweet, light green flesh on fruit that typically run 4-6 pounds at harvest. Like other honeydew types it does not slip from the vine, so watch for the rind to shift from a hard green-white to a softer creamy yellow-white and the blossom end to yield slightly to gentle pressure. Give it the full length of a hot summer and consistent moisture through fruit sizing for the best sugar content at harvest.

name: TAM Jalapeño Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; TAM Jalapeño was developed by Texas A&M University in 1992 in partnership with USDA to produce a jalapeño pepper with dramatically reduced heat (400–1,500 SHU versus the standard jalapeño's 2,500–8,000 SHU) while retaining the characteristic jalapeño flavor, size, and appearance — important for the food industry and gardeners who want jalapeño flavor without significant heat.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost into warm, well-drained soil in full sun. TAM Jalapeño-1 was developed by Texas A&M University's pepper breeding program in cooperation with the USDA and released in 1992 specifically for the commercial food processing industry, which required a jalapeño with the characteristic jalapeño flavor, uniform size (3–4 inches), and appearance for use in products like jalapeño poppers, nachos, and salsas — but without enough heat to cause consumer complaints when consumed in quantity. The resulting variety has the same thick, meaty walls, dark green color, and characteristic jalapeño aroma as standard jalapeños but only 400–1,500 SHU (compared to 2,500–8,000 SHU in standard varieties), making it easily tolerable for most heat-sensitive individuals. TAM Jalapeño is an outstanding choice for Gulf Coast home gardeners who want to grow their own jalapeños for cooking without excessive heat, and for making fresh salsa, pico de gallo, and pickled jalapeños accessible to children and heat-sensitive family members.

name: TAM Jalapeño Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; TAM Jalapeño performs best in full sun with consistent moisture and modest fertilization. In zone 9, transplant March–April for a June–August harvest. The plants are productive and compact, well-suited to container growing, and perform reliably in the Gulf South warm season.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; TAM Jalapeño is compact, productive, and easy to grow as a warm-season annual in any vegetable garden. TAM Mild Jalapeño I is a Texas A&M University release (developed in 1992 by the university's vegetable breeding program) that addressed a specific and widely held preference: many cooks and eaters want the distinctive fresh, grassy jalapeño flavor that defines Tex-Mex and Southwestern cooking without the significant heat of a standard jalapeño. Standard jalapeños test at 2,500–8,000 Scoville Heat Units — enough to be noticeably and persistently hot for heat-sensitive eaters; TAM Jalapeño measures approximately 1,000–3,500 SHU, a 70–80% reduction in heat while retaining the characteristic jalapeño aroma and flavor profile. The fruits are indistinguishable from standard jalapeños in size and appearance — medium-large (3–4 inches), dark green to red, thick-walled, and blocky — making them ideal for all jalapeño applications where the full flavor is wanted without the burning heat: nachos, salsa, pickled jalapeños (called escabeche), jalapeño poppers, and fresh eating. TAM Jalapeño is widely grown in Texas for processing and fresh market and has developed a devoted following among home gardeners who cook frequently with jalapeños and want to moderate the heat for family members of different heat tolerances. Very productive plants with a long harvest window from green through red ripeness.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Research — TAM Mild Jalapeño I variety release
New Mexico Chile Pepper Institute — Jalapeño variety comparison
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Chile Pepper Production

name: TAM Mild Habanero Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant into fertile soil in full sun after frost danger passes.
directions: Released by Texas A&M's South Texas breeding program from a cross of a Yucatan habanero and a heatless Bolivian habanero, bred specifically for the region's heat. It matures about 10 days earlier and out-yields standard orange habanero by roughly 25 percent, carrying full habanero aroma and flavor with only a fraction of the capsaicin, good for cooks who want fruitiness without the burn. It was field-trialed in and performs well under South Texas and Gulf Coast humidity.
sources: ResearchGate - TAM Mild Habanero, a Low-Pungency Habanero Pepper

name: TAM Mild Jalapeno Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; TAM Mild was bred at Texas A&M to keep the classic jalapeno shape and flavor while cutting the heat to a fraction of a standard jalapeno's, making it a good choice for gardeners who want jalapeno flavor without much bite.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date, and harvest fruit at any stage from glossy dark green through fully ripe red. TAM Mild Jalapeno was developed by the Texas A&M AgriLife breeding program specifically to lower the capsaicin content of a standard jalapeno to a mild 500-2,500 Scoville units, roughly a tenth the heat of a typical jalapeno, while keeping the same thick-walled, classic jalapeno shape, size, and flavor that makes it useful for salsas, poppers, and pickling. The compact, productive plants set fruit heavily over a long season and tolerate Southern heat well, though heat and moisture stress can occasionally nudge individual peppers hotter than the variety's baseline. It's a good choice for gardeners, and especially families with children, who want the jalapeno's flavor and crunch without much of its punch.

name: TAM Uvalde Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; TAM Uvalde is an open-pollinated cantaloupe developed by Texas A&M for better tolerance of powdery mildew in hot, humid growing regions.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained hills once frost danger has passed, thinning to the strongest plants. TAM Uvalde is an open-pollinated cantaloupe bred at Texas A&M for improved resistance to powdery mildew, a common problem for melons grown through hot, humid summers. It produces medium-sized, heavily netted fruit with sweet, salmon-orange flesh typical of Western cantaloupe types. Keep soil evenly moist during vine growth and fruit sizing, then ease off watering as melons near ripeness, harvesting at full slip when the fruit separates cleanly from the vine.

name: Tampiqueno Serrano Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. Tampiqueno is a classic serrano cultivar producing small, thin-walled, very hot pods used fresh in salsas and Mexican cooking.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Tampiqueno is a widely grown, classic serrano pepper cultivar producing small, slender, thin-walled pods that ripen from green to red, packing more heat than jalapeno in a smaller package, and used extensively fresh in salsas, pico de gallo, and other Mexican dishes where a bright, grassy heat is wanted. The compact, productive plants set fruit heavily over a long season and tolerate heat well, making serrano peppers one of the more reliable hot pepper choices for Gulf South gardens. Harvest pods at any stage of ripeness, though full red pods have somewhat more sweetness alongside the heat.
sources: New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute

name: Tan Cheese Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, since moschata types are slow to establish in cool ground.
directions: One of the oldest documented American pumpkin varieties, dating to before 1824, this heirloom produces a flattened, wheel-of-cheese shaped fruit with smooth tan skin and moderate ribbing. Sow directly in hills after the soil warms, allowing plenty of room for the sprawling vines. Fruit is ready when the rind hardens and takes on a uniform tan color; harvest with several inches of stem attached. The deep orange flesh is dense, sweet, and stores exceptionally well through winter, making it a reliable keeper for pies and baking.

name: Tango Celery
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost, since celery seed is slow to germinate and seedlings grow slowly at first; transplant out after danger of hard frost has passed, keeping soil consistently moist through the season.
directions: Start seed indoors well ahead of transplanting, since celery germinates slowly and seedlings need a long head start before warm weather arrives. Tango is a modern celery cultivar bred for compact size, crisp, stringless stalks, and good resistance to common celery diseases that plague older cultivars in humid climates, producing dark green, flavorful stalks over a somewhat shorter growing season than heirloom types. Consistent, even soil moisture is essential throughout the growing season, since celery stalks turn stringy and bitter under moisture stress. In hot-summer regions it does best as a fall or early spring crop rather than attempting to carry it through peak summer heat, since celery bolts and becomes bitter in prolonged high temperatures.

name: Tango Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or fall; in zone 9 sow January-February for spring or September-October for fall. Tango produces deeply frilled, ruffled, bright green leaves and is a popular cut-and-come-again variety for baby leaf and mesclun mix production.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Tango produces densely frilled, deeply cut, curly bright green leaves that hold up well as a cut-and-come-again crop, regrowing quickly after repeated light harvests for baby leaf salads and mesclun mixes. Its crisp, mild flavor and attractive ruffled texture make it a popular addition to mixed salad greens, and it tolerates cool weather well, making it a strong choice for both an early spring and a fall crop in zone 8-9 gardens. Harvest outer leaves as needed or cut the whole head an inch above the crown to allow regrowth for a second and sometimes third harvest.

name: Tappy's Heritage Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Tappy's Heritage is a pink beefsteak heirloom preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange network.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply prepared, fertile soil after all danger of frost has passed, supporting vines with a sturdy cage or stake from the start. Tappy's Heritage is a pink beefsteak heirloom that produces large, meaty, slightly flattened fruit with a classic sweet-tart old-fashioned flavor on vigorous indeterminate vines. It rewards consistent watering and feeding through the season with a long harvest window rather than one concentrated flush. Pick fruit when fully colored but still firm for the best balance of flavor and shelf life.

name: Tar Heel Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after frost danger has passed at the base of a sturdy 6-8 foot trellis; vigorous vines need real climbing support and will keep producing if kept picked.
directions: Tar Heel is an old pole bean reportedly carried west by North Carolina natives from the Jackson/Haywood county area who migrated to Washington state for timber work around the turn of the twentieth century, taking on the Tar Heel name in honor of that origin. The vigorous climbing vines are heavy yielders of five to six inch, flattened pods that bulge as the seeds inside develop, with a hearty, old-fashioned flavor reminiscent of a greasy bean even though the pod surface itself is not shiny. It is a good pick for gardeners who want a traditional pole snap bean with real heirloom character rather than a modern high-production hybrid.

name: Tarbais Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost near a trellis or tall support in full sun; Tarbais is a semi-vining pole-type bean traditionally grown up corn stalks in southwestern France and is best harvested dry for the classic cassoulet preparation, though it can be eaten as a fresh shell bean earlier in the season.
directions: Sow after last frost near a trellis, fence, or tall pole in full sun; Tarbais is the classic French heirloom bean of Gascon cuisine, historically grown climbing up corn stalks in the countryside around Tarbes in southwestern France, and it is the traditional bean specified in authentic cassoulet, the slow-cooked white bean and meat casserole of the region. The dry beans are creamy white, thin-skinned, and known for cooking up exceptionally tender and creamy while holding their shape, absorbing the rich flavors of the pork, duck, and sausage traditionally simmered with them in cassoulet. While best known dried, pods can also be picked earlier at the plump green shell-bean stage for a more delicate fresh bean dish. Let pods mature and dry fully on the vine for the classic dry-bean harvest, picking before fall rains can cause mold, and finish drying indoors in a well-ventilated spot before shelling and storing.

name: Tardivo Radicchio
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before fall transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October for a December–February harvest. Tardivo requires a forcing technique: in late fall, cut the tops of the plants to 1 inch, dig the roots, pack them tightly in boxes of moist sand or sawdust, and force in darkness at 50–60°F for 3–5 weeks. This forcing step is essential — without it, Tardivo produces standard chicory leaves rather than the distinctive elongated, curled Tardivo form. In zone 9 the mild winter allows some growers to force plants in place with dark covers.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Tardivo is the most prized and most expensive radicchio in Italy — a Treviso-type radicchio that requires a traditional forcing process in which the plants are dug after fall frosts, packed in darkness, and allowed to produce elongated, curved white-and-red leaf chicons resembling a firework spray or an open hand. The resulting forced Tardivo heads have long, narrow, spoon-shaped, curling red-and-white leaves with a dramatic, sculptural appearance that makes them a luxury vegetable in Italian restaurants and specialty markets — they are served raw in salads, grilled whole, braised, or used as striking garnishes. The bittersweet flavor is the most refined of all radicchio types, with the forcing process reducing bitterness while concentrating sweetness. Tardivo commands the highest price of any radicchio in Italian markets; in home gardens the complex forcing requirement is rewarded with a genuinely special vegetable unlike any other readily available.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Presidia Radicchio di Treviso Tardivo
University of California Cooperative Extension — Radicchio and Chicory Forcing
Seeds of Italy — Tardivo Radicchio Growing and Forcing Notes

name: Tasmanian Chocolate Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the compact 2-4 ft dwarf-indeterminate habit, taller than most dwarfs, still benefits from container or raised-bed growing with light staking.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking to support the plant as it can grow taller than most dwarf-indeterminate releases. Tasmanian Chocolate bears oblate, beefsteak-style fruit in a deep purple-black hue with well-balanced, rich flavor typical of dark-fleshed 'black' tomatoes. It resulted from a 2006 cross of New Big Dwarf and Paul Robeson made by Patrina Nuske Small in Australia, selected and named by Linda Reid of Tasmania, and released through the Dwarf Tomato Project. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine for the best flavor.

name: Tasti-Lee Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Tasti-Lee is an indeterminate tomato released by the University of Florida IFAS program with both disease resistance appropriate for Gulf South conditions and substantially higher lycopene content than standard red tomato varieties. In zone 9, transplant March–April. The elevated lycopene content produces a slightly more orange-red skin color than typical red tomatoes — the skin appears almost orange-red rather than crimson red. Tasti-Lee's disease resistance package (Fusarium, Verticillium, root-knot nematodes) addresses the primary limitations of home tomato production in zone 9. The variety was released with the specific goal of delivering both health value (high lycopene) and genuine flavor — a combination not typical of the commercial tomato market, which has historically prioritized yield, appearance, and shelf life over flavor and nutrition.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant after last frost and stake or cage. Harvest when uniformly red-orange and gives to slight pressure. Tasti-Lee Tomato was released by the University of Florida Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences (UF/IFAS) around 2010, developed through a breeding program that specifically targeted the combination of high lycopene content, improved flavor, and Gulf South disease resistance in a single red slicing tomato variety. The UF/IFAS vegetable breeding program, one of the most active in the southeastern United States, has produced multiple important commercial tomato varieties for Florida's significant commercial tomato industry; Tasti-Lee represents a branch of that program targeting quality attributes (flavor, nutrition) rather than the shipping durability and uniformity that commercial Florida tomato breeding has primarily emphasized. The variety's elevated lycopene content — documented by UF/IFAS researchers as substantially higher than industry-standard slicing tomatoes — combined with higher-than-typical sugar content and genuine tomato flavor creates a profile closer to the flavor of a well-grown heirloom tomato than most disease-resistant hybrid varieties provide. The variety has been noted by home gardeners and researchers for producing genuinely good-flavored tomatoes in zone 9's challenging summer heat, a combination difficult to achieve with either heirloom varieties (which lack disease resistance) or standard commercial varieties (which sacrifice flavor for durability). Tasti-Lee is sold through specialty seed companies and has been grown for research comparisons confirming its superior flavor and nutritional profile relative to commercial standards.
sources: University of Florida IFAS — Tasti-Lee tomato release and high-lycopene breeding documentation
UF/IFAS Extension — Flavor and Nutrition-Focused Tomato Variety Development
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Tomato Variety Evaluation for Gulf South Home Gardens

name: Tasty Jade Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 70°F; in zone 9 plant March–May for main crop and again in August–September for fall production. Tasty Jade is a long, thin burpless-type cucumber that produces abundantly on vigorous vines; provide a trellis or cage. In zone 9 the fall crop often produces higher-quality fruits as temperatures moderate after September.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Tasty Jade is an AAS Award-winning Asian burpless cucumber hybrid producing very long (10–12 inch), slender, uniformly dark green fruits with thin, tender, virtually seedless flesh and an exceptionally mild, non-bitter flavor. Unlike slicing cucumbers that can be bitter and require peeling, the thin skin and low cucurbitacin content of Tasty Jade makes it excellent for eating without peeling — just wash and slice. The crisp, sweet, mild-flavored fruits are ideal for fresh eating, salads, sushi accompaniments, and quick pickling. Tasty Jade's All-America Selections award recognized its superior flavor, production, and disease resistance compared to competing Asian cucumber types. In zone 9 the vigorous vines produce abundantly in spring and again in fall; summer production may slow during the hottest weeks of July–August but resumes as temperatures moderate in September.
sources: All-America Selections — Tasty Jade Cucumber Award
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Asian Cucumber Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Burpless Cucumber Production

name: Tatume Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; tatume is one of the most heat-tolerant summer squash for Gulf Coast and Texas gardens, producing well through summer heat where zucchini collapses. In zone 9 it can be grown as a first planting in spring and a second planting in late August for fall harvest.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after last frost; tatume is a traditional Mexican summer squash producing round to slightly oval, smooth, dark green fruits 3–5 inches in diameter that are harvested young (before the rind hardens) for use as a summer squash, or left to mature fully into a yellow-tan winter squash. Young fruits have mild, tender flesh similar to zucchini but firmer and slightly sweeter; mature fruits have dry, pale orange flesh similar to a butternut squash. This dual-use quality, combined with exceptional heat tolerance that keeps plants productive through Texas and Gulf Coast summers when standard zucchini quits, makes tatume one of the most practically useful squash for hot-climate gardeners. Extremely popular in Mexican American communities in Texas, where it is used in caldos, guisados, and stuffed as chiles rellenos de calabaza. The vining plants produce abundantly over a long season.
sources: University of Texas at Austin Native Plant Collection

name: Taunton Deane Perennial Kale
plantingNote: Root stem cuttings in spring and set rooted plants into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Taunton Deane rarely flowers and is propagated almost entirely from cuttings, so a single sourced plant can supply an entire perennial kale patch within a season or two.
directions: Set rooted stem cuttings into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and stake young plants in windy sites; Taunton Deane is a centuries-old English heirloom perennial kale from Somerset, traditionally called cottager's kale for its long history in small kitchen gardens. It develops into a sprawling, thick-stemmed woody shrub that can eventually reach 6-7 feet tall and as wide, distinguishing it from the smaller, more upright Daubenton's kale, yet its leaves stay remarkably tender for such a large plant and are harvested continuously as a cut-and-come-again green. Because it flowers and sets viable seed only rarely, propagation is done almost exclusively by rooting stem cuttings taken any time during the growing season. Prune hard every couple of years to rejuvenate leggy stems and keep the plant productive; in favorable sites a single specimen can supply greens for a decade or more, making it a cornerstone perennial for food forest and permaculture kitchen gardens.
sources: Incredible Vegetables (Mandy Barber, UK) — Taunton Deane Perennial Kale

name: Tavor Artichoke
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and give seedlings 10–14 days near 50°F once they have several true leaves to encourage earlier, heavier bud set; in zone 9, an August–September sowing for a fall transplant also performs well and often yields the largest buds.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into deep, rich, well-drained soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Tavor is a vigorous Israeli-bred F1 hybrid selected for heavy, reliable production of medium, tightly closed green buds on a large, upright, spineless plant, and it is widely favored by growers in hot, dry-summer climates for its strong heat tolerance and steady yield of multiple side buds after the central bud is cut. Like other seed-grown annual types it flowers and produces a usable first-year harvest without needing the extended cold vernalization that older perennial varieties require, though a short cool spell after transplanting still improves bud set and uniformity. Keep soil consistently moist and fertile through the growing season, and cut buds while still tight and firm, well before the scales begin to loosen and spread.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Artichoke Production Guide

name: Taxi Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Taxi is a determinate tomato that sets its crop over a concentrated 3–4 week window before slowing. In zone 9, transplant late February through early March for a May harvest; the early to mid-season maturity makes Taxi practical for both spring and fall Gulf Coast production windows.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Taxi is a determinate yellow tomato that produces a concentrated crop of uniformly bright taxi-yellow, medium (6–8 oz), round to slightly flattened fruits with a smooth, attractive appearance and mild, sweet, low-acid tomato flavor — the distinctive mellow sweetness typical of most yellow tomatoes, which have lower levels of the malic and citric acids that give red tomatoes their sharpness. The low-acid character makes Taxi an excellent choice for gardeners and eaters who find standard red tomatoes too acidic, for children who prefer milder flavors, and for fresh applications where the visual contrast of bright yellow adds interest to a salad or platter. The meaty flesh has a good firm texture that holds up in sliced presentations without becoming watery. Taxi is practical, productive, and early enough to complete its crop before the worst Gulf South summer heat; its concentrated set makes it useful for batch processing or sharing. A reliable, attractive yellow option for home gardens where some visual and flavor variety beyond standard red tomatoes is desired.
sources: Fedco Seeds — Taxi tomato variety notes
University of Minnesota Extension — Tomato Variety Guide

name: Taylor Dwarf Horticultural Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Taylor Dwarf Horticultural is grown primarily as a shell bean — harvested when pods have begun to turn from green-streaked to fully tan/buff and the beans inside are plump and fully developed but not yet dry. This 'shelling' window lasts about 2 weeks per planting; successive sowings extend the season.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; harvest as shell beans when pods have mottled tan-and-red coloring and beans are plump. Taylor Dwarf Horticultural is a classic New England and Mid-Atlantic heirloom horticultural (shell) bean — one of the oldest and most storied varieties in American seed saving tradition, producing beautiful red-streaked, cream-and-crimson pods and plump, cranberry-red-speckled beans that are used primarily at the fresh-shelled stage, when they have a rich, creamy, potato-like flavor and a velvety texture that is quite different from the firmer, drier character of the same beans when fully dried. Fresh-shelled horticultural beans are a seasonal delicacy that was once far more common in American cooking — they require no soaking, cook in 20–30 minutes, and have a rich, substantial flavor and a dense, satisfying texture that is superior to the canned or dried equivalents. Taylor Dwarf is compact (14–20 inches), making it well-suited to small gardens, and produces abundantly over a 2–3 week harvest window. As a dry bean it is also excellent (the same as a cranberry or borlotti bean), providing versatility across the whole season. A foundational heirloom with genuine culinary value and beautiful pod markings.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Horticultural bean variety collection
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Snap Bean and Shell Bean Varieties

name: Telegraph Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost, or start indoors for an earlier crop; provide a sturdy trellis so the long fruit hangs straight, since fruit that rests on the ground tends to curl.
directions: Sow seed an inch deep in warm, fertile, well-drained soil, then train vines up a trellis for the straightest fruit and easiest picking. Telegraph is a Victorian-era English heirloom, originally bred for greenhouse culture, that produces long, slender, dark green fruit twelve to eighteen inches at full size, with thin, tender, nearly seedless flesh and a mild, sweet, non-bitter flavor prized for slicing. It performs well outdoors in warm climates given a trellis and consistent moisture, though fruit is best picked at eight to twelve inches for the crispest texture, since fully mature fruit can turn coarse. Keep watering even throughout fruit development, since irregular moisture is the most common cause of bitterness and misshapen fruit in this and most cucumber varieties.

name: Telegraph Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter to early spring. Telegraph was bred by William Culverwell, gardener to Sir Frederick Milburn of Thorpe Perrow in Yorkshire, England, prior to 1878, and needs a sturdy 6-8 foot trellis for its tall climbing vines.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and provide tall trellising for the vigorous climbing vines. Telegraph produces abundant large pods holding 8-9 sweet peas each over a long harvest window. In 1878, James Carter & Co. introduced 'Telephone' as a selection from Culverwell's stock after buying out virtually his entire supply; Culverwell publicly objected in the January 1879 Gardeners' Chronicle to Carters marketing a selection of his own Telegraph under a new name, a dispute that makes Telegraph the documented ancestor of the whole Telephone/Alderman group of tall marrowfat peas still grown today. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, since peas fix their own.
sources: The Garden History Blog — 'War and Peas' (Telegraph/Telephone pea history)
The Seed Detective — Heritage Pea Varieties

name: Telephone Pea
plantingNote: Sow 4–6 weeks before last frost date; Telephone is a tall climber reaching 5–6 feet and requires sturdy support — grow on strong netting or trellis strung between tall posts.
directions: Sow seed 1–2 inches deep and 2–3 inches apart in cool, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, 4–6 weeks before last frost; Telephone pea (sold in Britain as Alderman) is the classic tall heirloom main-crop shell pea, a vigorous climber to 5–6 feet that produces large, curved dark-green pods with 8–10 sweet, tender peas per pod — significantly more productive per plant than bush varieties and the pod size that made it famous in Victorian kitchen gardens. Requires strong netting or pea sticks for support. Harvest when pods are well-filled and peas are young and sweet; productivity drops rapidly if pods are left to mature fully on the vine.

name: Tellus Celeriac
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant into fertile, moisture-retentive soil once frost danger has passed. Tellus is an old English heirloom valued for genuine, strong celeriac flavor.
directions: Transplant into fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun; Tellus is an old English heirloom celeriac sourced from the UK's Heritage Seed Library, producing vigorous roots slightly darker than modern hybrid types with distinctive reddish leaf stalks. It matures in roughly 110 days and is cold-hardy to around 25°F, allowing late-season harvest after light frost. Growers favor it for its genuinely strong, old-fashioned celeriac flavor, which many modern bred-for-smoothness cultivars have lost; keep soil evenly moist throughout the season to avoid hollow or cracked roots.

name: Teltow Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow 8-10 weeks before the first fall frost in lean, sandy soil; unlike most turnips, Teltow develops its characteristic concentrated flavor best when grown lean rather than in rich, heavily amended beds.
directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep in rows and thin to 2-3 inches apart, since this variety forms small, slender, finger-sized roots rather than a large globe. Teltow Turnip is a German heirloom from the sandy soils around Teltow near Berlin, historically prized enough that it was reportedly shipped to Weimar for Goethe's table, and it remains catalogued in European heirloom seed-saving collections today. The roots are pale yellowish-white with a dense, waxy texture and an intense, nutty flavor unlike the milder taste of larger globe turnips, traditionally used in slow-simmered stews rather than eaten raw. Growing it in poor, sandy ground rather than rich garden soil is essential to concentrating its distinctive flavor.
sources: Slow Food International, Ark of Taste catalog
Kokopelli Seed Foundation heirloom vegetable collection

name: Temuco Quinoa
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring while the soil is still cool, barely covering the tiny seed; Temuco tolerates light frost as a seedling but grows best where summers are mild.
directions: Temuco is a lowland coastal quinoa selected from an isolated population near Temuco in Chile's Araucania region, and it has proven to be one of the easier quinoas for cool, maritime climates because it sets seed reliably at low elevation and short day length. Its small, pale, cream-colored seed carries unusually little bitter saponin coating compared to many other quinoas, which cuts down on the rinsing needed before cooking. Grow it like other quinoas in average, well-drained soil, thinning seedlings to give plants room to branch, and watch for birds as the heavy seed heads ripen and dry in late summer. Cut whole panicles once the leaves have dropped and seed rubs free easily, then dry further indoors before threshing.

name: Tender and True Parsnip
plantingNote: Direct sow fresh seed as soon as soil can be worked in spring; parsnip seed loses viability fast, so buy new seed each year.
directions: Sow seed shallowly into deeply worked, stone-free soil, since forked or stunted roots result from compacted ground; keep the seedbed evenly moist through slow germination and thin seedlings to a few inches apart. This long-standing English heirloom is prized for roots that are smooth-skinned, nearly coreless, and unusually tender for a full-season parsnip, with good field tolerance to canker. Leave roots in the ground through the first hard frosts, which convert starch to sugar and give the roots their signature sweet, nutty flavor.

name: Tender Sprout Sprouting Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors for a spring crop, or sow in midsummer for a fall harvest in cooler regions.
directions: Tender Sprout is a sprouting-type broccoli grown for its long, slender side shoots rather than one central head, producing repeated harvests of foot-long stems over many weeks. Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost, or sow a second planting in midsummer for a fall crop. Cut stems regularly once the first shoots appear to keep the plant sending up fresh growth.

name: Tenderette Bush Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed after the last frost, sowing in succession for continuous pods through summer.
directions: Plant seeds an inch deep directly in warm garden soil, thinning to a few inches apart so bushy plants have room to fill out without crowding. This long-popular bush bean produces slender, rounded, curved pods that are notably tender and stay stringless even at a fairly large size, giving gardeners a wider harvest window than many snap beans. Plants are heat tolerant and continue setting pods reliably through summer warmth, making this a dependable choice for extending the fresh bean harvest. Pick regularly to encourage continued flowering and pod set throughout the season.

name: Tenderglow Summer Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed after the last frost date.
directions: This Lebanese-type zucchini produces slightly wider, nutty-flavored fruit on an open, easy-to-pick bush habit. Direct sow after the soil has warmed following the last frost, spacing hills generously since the plant spreads nearly a yard across. Harvest young for the sweetest flavor when roasting, stuffing, or frying; the open habit makes spotting ripe fruit under the leaves easier than with older bush types.

name: Tendergreen Bush Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed well past last frost; this 1922 AAS-winning bush snap bean tolerates heat better than many modern bush types, so successive sowings through midsummer keep pods coming.
directions: Sow seed directly into warm soil after frost danger passes, spacing plants to allow good air movement around the dense bushy canopy. Pods set heavily even in hot, humid weather, carrying slight purple flecking on a medium-dark green round pod. Pick every two to three days once pods reach five to six inches to keep them snapping tender and to encourage continued flowering. Avoid working around wet plants to reduce the spread of bacterial and fungal leaf diseases common to bush beans.

name: Tendral Verde Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-drained soil in full sun; Tendral is a long-season Spanish winter melon that needs an extended hot summer to ripen and is valued for its exceptional storage life.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep after the last frost once soil has thoroughly warmed, and reduce watering as fruit nears maturity to concentrate sweetness. Tendral Verde is a traditional Spanish winter melon with smooth, dark green rind and firm, pale green flesh that is mildly sweet rather than intensely aromatic, similar in style to Piel de Sapo but prized above all for its remarkable keeping quality. Properly cured fruit can be stored for weeks to a few months in a cool, dry place, which historically made it a valued melon for eating well past the end of the growing season. Harvest when the rind dulls and the blossom end yields slightly to gentle pressure.

name: Tennessee Britches Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out once frost danger has passed; this is a very tall, late-maturing indeterminate vine that needs a sturdy cage or stake set in place at transplanting.
directions: Tennessee Britches is a family heirloom beefsteak tomato traced to a gardener named Buckley of Dresden, Tennessee, whose seed was passed down to Joe Atnip, who named the variety after his young daughter. The indeterminate vines grow unusually tall, often reported to reach 8-10 feet, and need robust staking or caging to support the heavy fruit load through a long, late season. Fruits are large (1-2 pounds), ruffled, dark pink beefsteaks with a wide, corky depression at the stem end, prized for a sweet, full-bodied flavor well suited to slicing for sandwiches and salads. As a rare heirloom with a documented single-family lineage, it has been preserved mainly through heirloom seed specialists rather than large commercial catalogs.

name: Tennessee Candy Roaster
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills 5-6 feet apart after last frost; Tennessee Candy Roaster is a regionally distinct Appalachian candy roaster strain, similar to but selected separately from the North Georgia and Big Orange candy roaster types.
directions: Tennessee Candy Roaster is one of several closely related, regionally maintained Appalachian candy roaster strains, distinguished from the salmon-pink North Georgia type by generally more elongated, tapered fruit with tan to golden-bronze skin and less pronounced blue bloom at maturity. Like other candy roasters it carries dense, deep orange-yellow flesh with exceptionally high sugar content that concentrates further with roasting, the trait that gives the whole candy roaster group its name and its devoted following among Appalachian home gardeners and seed savers. Give the long, vigorous vines ample room to sprawl in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, and provide consistent moisture during flowering and fruit set to size the large fruit properly. Harvest once the rind has hardened fully and resists a fingernail and the stem has begun to dry and cork, then cure for two to three weeks in a warm, dry spot before moving to cool storage, where the flavor continues to improve for months.
sources: Sow True Seed — Tennessee Candy Roaster
Seed Savers Exchange — Candy Roaster squash heritage documentation
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Appalachian heirloom squash notes

name: Tennessee Cutshort Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil has warmed above 60°F, next to a tall pole or trellis for this vigorous Appalachian climbing heirloom.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep at the base of poles or a trellis once soil has warmed, allowing the vigorous vines room to climb 6 to 8 feet. Tennessee Cutshort is one of the classic Appalachian "greasy" and cutshort pole beans kept alive by mountain seed savers, named for the way its pods pack so tightly with brown seeds that the bean ends square off against one another inside the pod. Pods can be snapped and cooked fresh while still tender, or left to dry fully on the vine for a flavorful soup bean later in the season. Pick frequently during the fresh-eating stage to keep plants productive through a long harvest window.

name: Tennessee Red Cob Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile soil; Tennessee Red Cob is an Appalachian heirloom dent corn grown for cornmeal and grits, easily identified in the field by its distinctive dark red cob under white kernels.
directions: Sow directly in well-drained soil in blocks for reliable pollination, and let ears dry fully on the stalk before harvest since this is a grinding corn rather than a fresh-eating sweet corn. Tennessee Red Cob is a long-grown Appalachian and upland Southern heirloom prized by home millers for producing a notably white, fine-textured meal, with the vivid red cob making it easy to sort visually from other corn at harvest. Plants tolerate the hot, humid conditions and periodic dry spells typical of Southern summers reasonably well once established, and the variety has a long history of on-farm seed saving. Store dried ears in a mouse-proof container with good airflow, and shell only what you need for milling at a time to keep meal fresh.
sources: Sustain Southern Appalachian Highlands Conservancy Seed Program

name: Tennessee Sweet Potato Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil, giving vines ample room to run; this Southern heirloom is well adapted to hot, humid summers and performs reliably across the Gulf South.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in hills in full sun, allowing generous room for the sprawling vines. Tennessee Sweet Potato is an old Southern heirloom squash bearing pear- to bell-shaped, buff-tan fruit with a smooth rind and dense, sweet, fine-textured orange flesh reminiscent of sweet potato, a resemblance that gives the variety its name. As a moschata-type squash it shows good resistance to squash vine borer and performs reliably through hot, humid Southern summers, making it a dependable choice for Gulf South gardens where other winter squash struggle. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists a fingernail scratch, then cure for a couple of weeks in a warm, airy spot to concentrate sweetness before moving to cool, dry storage.

name: Tennis Ball Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow or start indoors in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop; sow shallowly, since lettuce needs light to germinate.
directions: Sow seed just 1/8 inch deep and barely cover, since lettuce needs light to germinate and prefers cool soil. Tennis Ball is a small, dense, dark-green butterhead lettuce documented in Thomas Jefferson's Monticello garden records from the early 1800s, forming tight, tennis-ball-sized heads with a sweet, buttery, mild flavor and crisp inner leaves. Its small, quick-maturing heads make it well suited to close spacing, containers, and succession planting for a steady supply of tender lettuce through the cool season. Keep soil consistently moist and provide afternoon shade as temperatures rise in late spring to delay bolting.
sources: Monticello Thomas Jefferson Center for Historic Plants

name: Terenzo Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Terenzo is a compact, self-branching trailing cherry tomato bred specifically for hanging baskets and containers, needing no staking or pruning.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into a hanging basket, window box, or large container filled with fertile, well-drained potting mix in full sun. Terenzo is an AAS-winning cherry tomato bred as a true tumbler type — a compact, mounding, self-branching plant that spills gracefully over the edge of a container rather than climbing, producing a heavy, non-stop crop of small, sweet red cherry tomatoes without any staking, caging, or pruning. Its small scale and container-ready habit make it one of the easiest tomatoes for a patio, balcony, or small-space garden with no in-ground bed at all. Water container plantings regularly, since pots dry out faster than garden soil, and feed every couple of weeks through the season to sustain the heavy, continuous fruit set.
sources: All-America Selections — Terenzo Tomato winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Tetsukabuto Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; this interspecific kabocha-butternut cross needs a long, vigorous vine run and rewards gardeners with unusually heavy yields even in stressed conditions.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills after all danger of frost has passed, spacing hills 6-8 feet apart to accommodate the exceptionally vigorous vines. Tetsukabuto is a hybrid cross between a kabocha-type Cucurbita maxima and a moschata parent, prized by growers for hybrid vigor that shrugs off vine borers and powdery mildew far better than either parent species alone. Fruits are near-round, 4-6 pounds, with dark, mottled black-green skin and deep orange-yellow flesh that is dry, dense, and nutty-sweet, closer in eating quality to a fine kabocha than a butternut. Cure in a warm spot for a week after harvest before moving to cool storage, where the fruit keeps remarkably well, often into the following spring.

name: Texas 1015 Sweet Onion
plantingNote: In zone 8–10, set transplants in October through December for spring harvest; Texas 1015 is a short-day onion requiring less than 12 hours of daylight to bulb up — it is specifically adapted to the Gulf Coast climate and should be planted in fall for harvest in April–May. Named '1015' for its ideal planting date of October 15 in South Texas.
directions: Set transplants 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun in October–December for Gulf Coast and South Texas; Texas 1015 (Texas Super Sweet) is the premier commercial and home garden short-day sweet onion of Texas and the Gulf Coast, developed by Texas A&M AgriLife Research and named for its recommended planting date of October 15 in the Rio Grande Valley. The large, globe-shaped, golden-yellow onions have exceptionally mild, sweet, low-pyruvate flesh with virtually no sharpness — one of the mildest onions grown anywhere in the world, comparable to Vidalia and Walla Walla in sweetness and suitable for eating raw in salads, sandwiches, and fresh salsas without the bite of storage onions. It has the distinctive pale yellow, thin skin and high moisture content of sweet onions. Harvest when tops fall over naturally; cure in a warm, airy location for 2 weeks before storing in a cool, dry spot (sweet onions have shorter storage life than sharp onions due to high moisture and sugar content).
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension

name: Texas 1015Y Supersweet Onion
plantingNote: Start transplants indoors in September–October; the traditional planting date is October 15 in South Texas (the '1015' in the name), and transplants should go into the ground mid-October through November in zone 9. 1015Y is a short-day onion that requires day lengths under 12 hours to initiate bulbing — it cannot be grown in northern zones where short-day conditions don't align with warm enough temperatures for bulb development. Harvest in late March–May when tops begin to fall over naturally. Cure bulbs in a warm, airy location before storage.
directions: Start transplants indoors in September–October at 60–70°F; set out in the garden mid-October in zone 9. Apply nitrogen fertilizer every 2–3 weeks through winter and spring. Texas 1015Y Supersweet (the name means: Texas, October 15 planting date, Yellow skinned) is the signature short-day sweet onion of the Gulf Coast and South Texas — a variety developed at Texas A&M University by Dr. Leonard Pike and released in 1983 that became the defining onion of Gulf Coast commercial and home production. The '1015' refers to the optimal planting date of October 15 in the Rio Grande Valley, where the variety's potential is most fully realized — planted on that date, the onions experience the precise seasonal day-length and temperature progression that produces the largest, sweetest bulbs. Texas 1015Y is the Vidalia of the Gulf Coast: producing enormous (3–5 inch diameter), slightly flattened, sweet, mild bulbs with very low pungency and high water content — a mild enough onion to eat like an apple. The sweetness comes from low pyruvic acid content (the compound responsible for onion bite and tear-inducing character); 1015Y has some of the lowest pyruvic acid levels measured in onion varieties. It stores only moderately (2–3 months) due to the high moisture content that gives the sweet flavor, distinguishing it from pungent storage types.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Texas 1015Y Supersweet onion development by Dr. Leonard Pike
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Short-Day Onion Production in the Gulf South
Texas Department of Agriculture — Texas Sweet Onion documentation

name: Texas Cream 12 Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed past 65°F; Texas Cream 12's wilt and nematode resistance make it a dependable repeat crop in beds that have grown southern peas for several seasons.
directions: Direct sow in full sun in warm soil of moderate fertility, and expect a tidy, upright bush habit that stays easy to pick through the season. Released by the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station in 1953, Texas Cream 12 was bred for resistance to both fusarium wilt and root-knot nematode, two of the most persistent soil-borne threats to repeated southern pea plantings. Pods are greatly curved with slight constrictions between the attractive cream-colored peas, turning from green at fresh-shell stage to dark straw at the dry stage. The variety performs reliably through Gulf Coast summer heat and makes an excellent fresh shelling pea for market growers and home gardeners alike.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension southern pea (cowpea) publication
Victory Seed Company southern pea variety records
Stoner Seed Company / Stokes Seeds cowpea catalog descriptions

name: Texas Cream 40 Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; the compact, bush habit and short 55–65 day maturity make Texas Cream 40 well suited to successive plantings for an extended harvest through summer.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and harvest pods when they lighten from green to a pale cream color. Texas Cream 40 is a compact, bush-type cowpea bred for a short, roughly 55–65 day maturity and a concentrated pod set well suited to gardeners who want an early, efficient harvest without the sprawling vines of older heirloom cowpea types. The smooth, cream-colored peas have a mild, sweet flavor and tender texture prized for fresh shelling, and the plant's compact size makes it a good fit for smaller garden beds or closer spacing than rangier Southern pea varieties. Its short season also allows two or more successive plantings through the Gulf South summer for an extended harvest window. As with other cowpeas, the roots fix nitrogen, leaving the soil enriched for the next crop.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — cowpea variety trials
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners database

name: Texas Cream 40 Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Texas Cream 40 is a semi-vining selection from the Texas A&M cream pea breeding series, bred to hold a longer, later harvest window than the more compact Texas Cream 8.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Texas Cream 40 is part of the Texas A&M cream-type southern pea breeding series, selected for a longer, more extended pod set than the earlier-released Texas Cream 8, giving home gardeners a steadier trickle of pods for fresh picking rather than one concentrated flush. Seeds are creamy-white with the mild, delicate, slightly sweet flavor typical of cream peas, prized for fresh shelling and quick cooking. Plants are semi-vining and slightly more sprawling than Texas Cream 8, so allow a bit more row width or provide light support for easier picking. Pick pods while still slightly immature and the seeds are plump but not hardened for the best fresh-shell texture; pods left to fully dry make good storage peas as well. Consistent moisture during flowering and pod fill improves yield in the Gulf Coast heat of midsummer.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Southern Pea Variety Trials

name: Texas Cream 8 Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Texas Cream 8 is a semi-determinate, compact bush type that can be grown without staking — the self-supporting, upright plants concentrate pod set for a defined harvest window.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Texas Cream 8 is a compact, high-yielding cream southern pea selected through the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station breeding program — producing uniform, cream-colored seeds in short, upright plants that are self-supporting and well-suited to intensive raised-bed production. The 'Cream 8' number designation indicates its classification in the cream-type southern pea category, where seeds are creamy-white to tan without the eye coloring of black-eyed peas or the mottled colors of crowder types. Cream peas have a mild, sweet, delicate flavor considered more refined than the earthier crowder types — they are prized for their tender texture when fresh-shelled and their clean, creamy appearance in finished dishes. Texas Cream 8 has performed consistently well in Gulf Coast trials for productivity, uniformity, and disease resistance. The compact, semi-determinate bush habit allows closer spacing (3–4 inches in rows) than standard sprawling cream peas, increasing productivity per garden square foot. The concentrated pod set makes Texas Cream 8 practical for batch shelling and freezing — the defined harvest window means a larger quantity of pods reaches maturity simultaneously, enabling more efficient processing than the trickle harvest of indeterminate types.

name: Texas Gourdseed Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows for reliable wind pollination, in fertile soil in full sun, after all frost danger has passed; allow ears to fully dry down on the stalk before harvest for grinding into meal.
directions: Sow in blocks at least 4 rows wide in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; drought-tolerant once established and well adapted to the heat of a long Texas or Gulf South growing season. Texas Gourdseed is an old Southern dent corn named for the distinctive deep, thin, wedge-shaped indentation at the crown of each dried kernel, resembling the shape of a small gourd seed — a hallmark trait of the historic 'Gourdseed' corn family that was among the most widely grown field corns across the antebellum and postbellum South before hybrid corn displaced open-pollinated varieties in the 20th century. The tall, vigorous stalks are well adapted to hot, humid Southern summers and produce a reliable grain crop even under the drought stress that limits many other corns, grinding into a flavorful, traditional cornmeal and grits. A genuine piece of Southern agricultural history for gardeners interested in growing and preserving heritage field corn, zone 6–10.

name: Texas Grano Onion
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter zones; Texas Grano is a short-day onion requiring only 10-12 hours of daylight to bulb, making it well suited to fall planting and spring harvest in zone 8-9 Gulf Coast gardens rather than a spring-planted crop as in the North.
directions: Start seeds indoors or direct-seed in the fall in mild-winter areas, since Texas Grano is a short-day type that needs the shorter daylight of southern winters to trigger bulbing rather than the long summer days farther north. Developed in Texas in the early 20th century, it became one of the foundational sweet onion cultivars of the Gulf South and is a direct ancestor of many modern short-day sweet onions, including some of the parent lines behind Vidalia-type onions. The large, globe-shaped bulbs have straw-yellow skin and mild, sweet flesh with low pungency, best used fresh rather than stored long term since sweet onions generally keep less well than pungent storage onions. Keep soil consistently moist through bulb formation and reduce water as tops begin to fall over before harvest.

name: Texas Legend Onion
plantingNote: Set transplants or seedlings in fall to early winter in the Gulf South so the short-day bulbs size up before spring heat arrives; Texas Legend was released by Texas A&M specifically for Rio Grande Valley and Gulf Coast production.
directions: Texas Legend is a Texas A&M AgriLife release bred as a sturdier, longer-storing alternative to older Grano-type short-day onions like Texas 1015Y. It forms globe-shaped, straw-colored bulbs with a somewhat firmer texture and more pungency than the sweetest Texas onions, which helps it hold up in storage for weeks after curing rather than needing quick use. The variety also carries improved field tolerance to Fusarium basal rot and pink root, both persistent problems in warm, humid Gulf Coast onion beds. Set out transplants in fall through early winter so the short-day bulbs have time to size up before lengthening spring days trigger bulbing.

name: Texas Pinkeye Purple Hull Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is reliably above 65°F; this tall, upright bush type was bred for mechanical harvest but shells easily by hand in the home garden too.
directions: Developed by the Texas Agricultural Experiment Station as a canning-industry selection, Texas Pinkeye Purple Hull is a tall, erect bush-type southern pea bred for once-over mechanical harvest, but it performs just as well picked by hand through a long Gulf Coast summer. Pods are green-and-purple when immature and deepen to full purple at maturity, shelling out cream-colored peas with the classic bright pink eye in as little as 55 days. Direct sow 1 inch deep in warm soil; like other cowpeas it fixes its own nitrogen, so skip heavy fertilizing and keep watering light once plants are established. Succession sow every 2-3 weeks through midsummer for a steady supply of fresh shelling peas ahead of fall frost.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture (FSA-6102)

name: Texas Supersweet Onion
plantingNote: Start seed or set transplants in fall for a spring harvest in the Gulf South; Texas Supersweet is a short-day onion bred specifically for the mild winters and short-day length of the Texas Gulf Coast and similar regions.
directions: Start seed or set transplants in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; as a short-day onion, Texas Supersweet needs the shorter day lengths of a Southern fall-to-spring growing season to bulb properly. Texas Supersweet produces large, globe-shaped, pale yellow bulbs with mild, sweet flavor and low pungency, bred as a regional alternative to Georgia's Vidalia-type onions for growers in Texas and across the Gulf South. Its short-day requirement and heat tolerance make it well matched to zone 9 growing conditions, where long-day storage onion types typically fail to bulb at all. Harvest when tops fall over and yellow, and cure in a warm, dry, well-ventilated location; like other sweet onions it has a shorter storage life than pungent long-day types and is best used within a few months of harvest.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Vidalia Onion Production

name: Thai Bird Chili
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; Thai bird chili requires high soil temperature (80–95°F) for germination — use a heat mat and be patient, as germination can be slow (14–21 days). In zone 9, transplant March–April; Capsicum frutescens is actually a short-lived tropical perennial that may overwinter in zone 9b–10 in protected locations, potentially producing for 2–3 seasons. Plants become highly productive in Gulf Coast summers, setting hundreds of small peppers per plant. Harvest green for a fresher, slightly less hot flavor or allow to ripen red for maximum heat and a fruitier note. One plant produces more peppers than most households can use.
directions: Start seeds on heat mat at 85–90°F; transplant to full sun after last frost. A single plant produces abundantly — dry excess peppers for storage. Thai Bird Chili (Bird's Eye Chile, Phrik Khi Nu in Thai) is the foundational hot pepper of Thai, Vietnamese, and Southeast Asian cuisines — small (0.5–1 inch), thin, pointed, upright peppers that measure 50,000–100,000 Scoville heat units, making them significantly hotter than jalapeños (8,000 SHU) and approaching the lower range of habaneros. The name 'Bird's Eye' or 'Bird Chile' refers to the upright-pointing, small fruit that resembles a bird's eye, and also to the belief that birds (which lack capsaicin receptors) eat the peppers and spread seeds — a genuine ecological relationship that explains why the plant produces small, highly visible peppers. Thai Bird Chili is not a single variety but a group of similar Capsicum frutescens and Capsicum annuum types grown across Southeast Asia under various local names. The peppers are used in Thai cooking in virtually every form of heat addition — fresh sliced in curries and soups, dried and ground in chili pastes, pickled, or dried whole for fish sauce preparations. For Gulf South gardeners, Thai Bird Chili is one of the most productive and low-maintenance hot peppers in the summer garden: the plant thrives in heat and humidity that challenges most other pepper types, setting fruit prolifically even in July-August conditions that cause many pepper varieties to drop flowers.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Thai Bird Chili variety notes
Kitazawa Seed Company — Southeast Asian hot pepper varieties
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Hot Pepper Production for Florida and Gulf South

name: Thai Bird's Eye Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting after last frost; in zone 9 Thai bird peppers are effectively perennial — established plants survive mild winters, producing prolifically for 2–3 years before eventually declining. To overwinter, mulch heavily at the base; plants resprout from roots in spring if temperatures don't drop below about 28°F.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–90°F; Thai bird's eye pepper (called 'phrik khi nu' — literally 'mouse dropping pepper' — in Thai, or simply 'bird's eye chile' across Southeast Asia) is the small, intensely hot pepper that provides the backbone of heat in Thai, Vietnamese, Lao, and Cambodian cuisines. The tiny fruits (1/2 to 3/4 inch long, narrow, conical) start green and ripen to vivid red, with heat levels measuring 50,000–100,000 Scoville units — substantially hotter than jalapeños but less scorching than habaneros — and a clean, bright, fruity heat without the floral overtones of chinense-type peppers.
