The small size means many peppers are sliced directly into dishes or pounded whole in mortars; Thai bird's eye peppers carry their heat through both flesh and seeds with essentially no mild portion, making them one of the most reliably fiery culinary peppers. Capsicum frutescens produces smaller, more compact plants than C. annuum with multiple upright-pointing fruits on each branch — the characteristic upright fruit habit distinguishes it from most common peppers. In zone 9+, plants become woody perennial shrubs (2–3 feet tall and wide) producing enormous numbers of peppers continuously from summer through fall and into winter during warm years. Production per plant is staggering once established — a mature zone 9 plant produces thousands of peppers per season, far more than most families can use fresh.
sources: Kitazawa Seed Company — Asian Vegetable Pepper Guide
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Hot Pepper Production
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Capsicum germplasm database

name: Thai Dragon Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost at warm soil temperature; transplant once nights stay reliably above 55-60F. Thai Dragon is a hybrid cayenne-type chile bred for a more upright, compact habit than traditional Thai bird peppers, making it easier to manage in beds and containers.
directions: Transplant into warm, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, spacing plants to allow good air circulation in humid climates. Thai Dragon produces narrow, 2-3 inch fruit held upright above the foliage in heavy clusters, ripening from green to glossy red with intense, lingering heat well above standard cayenne types. The compact, well-branched plants are productive over a long season and tolerate container culture better than many Southeast Asian chile types. Harvest fruit at any stage for fresh use, or let clusters ripen fully red and string them for drying and grinding into chile flakes.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Thai Dragon Hot Pepper
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Thai Extra Long Sponge Luffa
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost in most regions; this extra-long selection needs a full 120-130 day warm season to mature fruit for sponges.
directions: Selected in Thailand for exceptional length, this smooth luffa can produce fruit exceeding four feet if left to mature, though it is best picked at 12-18 inches for cooking, when the flesh is still tender and mild like zucchini. Because it needs a long 120-130 day warm season and vines that can reach 15-25 feet, give it the tallest trellis or arbor available and start seed indoors where summers are short. Allow a portion of the crop to fully ripen and dry on the vine for use as natural bath and cleaning sponges, peeling and rinsing the skin away once it turns brown and papery.

name: Thai Green Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; set out into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55F. Thai Green thrives in Gulf South heat and humidity, continuing to produce through the hottest part of summer.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; harvest young at golf-ball to small-egg size for the crisp, mild, low-seed texture prized in Thai cooking. Thai Green is a small, round eggplant with pale to medium green skin lightly streaked with cream, borne in heavy clusters on compact, productive plants that thrive in hot, humid conditions. The firm, dense flesh holds its shape well when simmered whole or halved directly into Thai green curry, a traditional use where the small green fruit is added along with pea eggplants and other aromatics. Its heat tolerance and continuous production over a long summer season make it an excellent, prolific choice for Gulf South vegetable gardens.

name: Thai Hot Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed and soil is warm. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant in March–April. Thai Hot plants become large and very productive in zone 9's long warm season and often overwinter as woody perennials, returning to bear even heavier crops in subsequent seasons. Plants are ornamentally attractive when laden with clusters of upright red and green fruits in different stages of ripeness.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil; Thai Hot (also called Thai Bird Pepper or 'prik kee noo' in Thai, meaning 'mouse droppings pepper') is the standard small, intensely hot pepper used in authentic Thai, Vietnamese, Lao, and broader Southeast Asian cuisines. The thin, pointed, upright fruits (1–2 inches long, pencil-thin) ripen from bright green through red, with clusters of fruits in different ripening stages creating an ornamental display. The heat level of 50,000–100,000 Scoville Heat Units produces the sharp, penetrating, instant heat characteristic of Thai cuisine — different in character from the deeper, slower-building heat of dried Mexican chiles. Both green (unripe) and red (ripe) fruits are used in Thai cooking — green fruits appear in green curry paste, papaya salad, and stir-fries; red fruits are used in red curry paste and dried for chile flakes. The highly prolific plants bear continuously through warm weather, producing far more peppers than most home cooks can use fresh.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Hot Pepper Production for Florida
New Mexico State University Chile Pepper Institute — Asian Hot Pepper Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Specialty and Ethnic Peppers

name: Thai Kang Kob Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost; vines show strong tolerance to squash bugs and common cucurbit diseases.
directions: Thai Kang Kob was brought from Thailand to the United States by Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds' Andrew Kaiser in 2006 and has since become popular for its productivity and disease resistance. The heavily ribbed, warted fruits are sea-green at harvest and age to chestnut brown in storage, weighing about 6-8 lbs. The deep orange flesh is sweet and fragrant, traditionally used in Thai coconut curries, soups, and stir-fries, as well as the custard-filled dessert sangkaya. Vines tolerate squash bugs and common cucurbit pests and diseases better than many winter squash.

name: Thai Long Green Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger passes and soil is warm. This slender Southeast Asian type sets fruit reliably through Gulf South summer heat and humidity.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once nights stay reliably warm. Thai Long Green produces slender, curved, pale jade-green fruit up to a foot long with a mild flavor and few seeds, a traditional Southeast Asian type widely used in stir-fries, curries, and grilling, where the thin skin and tender flesh cook quickly without needing to be peeled. The productive, heat-loving plants continue setting fruit through the hottest, most humid stretch of summer, when many Western eggplant varieties slow down. Harvest fruit young and glossy for the best texture — overripe fruit turns dull and develops tougher flesh and larger seeds — and pick every few days to keep plants producing.

name: Thai Red Roselle
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 plant March–May. Thai Red is a short-day plant that begins flowering as days shorten in August–September; calyces are harvested through October until frost. Plant early enough to establish before the heat of summer.
directions: Sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Thai Red is a deeply pigmented roselle cultivar from Southeast Asia, selected for extraordinarily high anthocyanin content that produces calyces (the fleshy red structures around the seed pod) of an intense ruby-red that yields a dramatic magenta-crimson juice when steeped. Harvest calyces when they are plump, firm, and fully red — typically 5–7 days after the flower petals drop — by snapping them off the branch. Thai Red calyces produce a more intensely flavored, darker red hibiscus tea (agua de Jamaica) than standard roselle varieties, and are prized for naturally colored beverages, syrups, jellies, and dried flower teas. The tall, bushy plants are as ornamental as they are productive, with attractive red-veined leaves and showy flowers.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Roselle for Florida
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Anthocyanins in Hibiscus sabdariffa
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Roselle Production

name: The Sutton Fava Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter or earliest spring, or in autumn in mild-winter regions; its compact habit also suits large containers and exposed, windy plots.
directions: Bred by Suttons Seeds in England in the 1920s and still carrying a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit, this is the classic dwarf broad bean, reaching only about a foot to eighteen inches tall while still setting a full crop of well-filled pods holding three to five beans apiece. The short, sturdy stems rarely need staking even in exposed or windy gardens, and the compact footprint makes it a favorite for raised beds, containers, and small-space plots where standard tall favas would sprawl. Sow directly into cool soil as early as it can be worked, spacing plants closely so they lean on one another for support, and pinch the growing tips once the lowest pods have set to discourage aphids. Harvest pods young for tender fresh shelling or let some dry fully on the plant for winter storage.

name: Theis Sorghum
plantingNote: Direct sow into warm soil well after last frost; Theis is a tall, late-maturing Mid-South syrup sorghum that ripens two to three weeks behind mid-season varieties like Dale, so it rewards gardeners with a long, hot growing season such as the Gulf Coast provides.
directions: Sow seed about an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil once frost danger has fully passed, thinning seedlings to allow thick, sturdy canes to develop. Theis is a Mid-South heirloom syrup sorghum distributed through Mississippi's foundation seed program, growing noticeably taller and maturing later than standard varieties like Dale, and it holds up well to some of the organophosphate insecticides sometimes used on nearby cotton fields. Let the canes stand until the seed heads reach hard-dough stage before cutting and pressing, since Theis is valued for producing a notably mild, high-quality syrup once the juice is boiled down. Because of its long season, it performs best where summers run hot and frost-free well into fall.

name: Thelma Sanders Sweet Potato Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Thelma Sanders Sweet Potato Squash produces medium-sized fruits (2–3 lbs) with a form similar to acorn squash but with cream to tan skin rather than acorn squash's dark green, and the characteristic lightly ridged, oval to oblong shape. In zone 9, plant March–April for summer production or July–August for a fall crop that matures in October–November when cooler weather improves flavor and texture. The cream skin color deepens to tan as the squash fully cures, providing a visual harvest maturity cue. Thelma Sanders is an open-pollinated heirloom available through Seed Savers Exchange — it originated with Thelma Sanders of Missouri who maintained the seed before the Seed Savers Exchange helped distribute it more broadly, a typical pattern for regional heirloom vegetable varieties preserved by individual gardeners.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills; thin to 2 plants per hill. Harvest when skin is tan-cream and stem has dried. Thelma Sanders Sweet Potato Squash is a Missouri heirloom winter squash with an unusually devoted following among winter squash enthusiasts — one of the open-pollinated acorn-type squashes most frequently cited for superior eating quality among the many heirloom varieties preserved through the Seed Savers Exchange network. The variety produces oval to oblong fruits, 6–8 inches long, with smooth to lightly ridged cream to tan skin that turns uniformly tan at full maturity. The name 'sweet potato squash' references the flesh character: the texture is drier and denser than standard acorn squash, with a sweet, slightly dry, nutty quality reminiscent in some ways of baked sweet potato — particularly the way the flesh separates into fibrous, sweet sections when baked. This dry, dense texture is highly valued by cooks who find standard acorn squash flesh too watery: Thelma Sanders bakes to a fluffy, dry interior that absorbs butter and seasonings distinctly better than wet-fleshed varieties, and the sweetness at full maturity is exceptional. The flavor is genuinely complex — sweet, nutty, slightly starchy — in a way that distinguishes it from hybrid acorn types selected for uniformity and yield rather than flavor depth. Thelma Sanders' origin traces to an individual Missouri gardener of the same name who maintained the seed through her personal gardening before sharing it through the Seed Savers Exchange community.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Thelma Sanders sweet potato squash Missouri heirloom documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Thelma Sanders squash variety notes and flavor description
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Heritage winter squash variety comparison

name: Thermidrome Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves in fall about 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes so roots establish before winter; in mild-winter regions it can also go in as a late-winter planting for an earlier, smaller harvest.
directions: Thermidrome is a softneck garlic that traces to the Drome valley of southeastern France, long favored there for its earliness and reliability in a maritime climate. Plant individual cloves pointed end up about 2 inches deep, mulch over winter, and keep beds weeded through spring since garlic competes poorly with weeds. Because it matures earlier and stores well into the following year, it is a dependable choice for gardeners in milder, wetter winter regions where hardneck types can rot. The flavor is notably milder than most hardnecks, making it popular for raw use.

name: Thessaloniki Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Thessaloniki is a Greek pink beefsteak heirloom valued for good crack resistance and heavy yields.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil after frost risk has passed, caging or staking the indeterminate vines early. Thessaloniki is a Greek heirloom named for the region around its namesake city, producing abundant clusters of medium-to-large pink fruit with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor and notably good resistance to cracking in humid weather. The vines are productive over a long season and tend to hold up well under heat stress typical of Mediterranean-climate summers. Harvest regularly once fruit colors fully to keep plants setting new flushes.

name: Thomas Laxton Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as the soil can be worked in early spring; the medium-height vines benefit from light staking or pea netting to keep pods off the ground and easy to pick.
directions: Thomas Laxton was introduced in England in 1898 by the Laxton Brothers breeding firm as an improved early-to-main-season shelling pea and has remained popular with seed savers ever since for its reliable yields and classic sweet English pea flavor. Vines are shorter and easier to manage than tall telephone-type peas but still produce well-filled pods over a solid harvest window. Sow early for the sweetest peas, and pick pods promptly once they fill out, since flavor declines quickly as peas mature and starch content rises. Its heirloom status and open-pollinated seed make it a good choice for gardeners who want to save their own seed year to year.

name: Thorogreen Lima Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm, above 65°F; a compact bush type needing no trellis.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in warm, fertile soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F. Thorogreen is a bush-type baby lima bean prized for seeds that stay a pale green color even after cooking, rather than the more common cream or white of most lima beans, giving finished dishes an appealingly fresh, vibrant appearance. The compact plant sets pods over a relatively short, concentrated window typical of bush lima types, making it convenient for a single main harvest for canning or freezing, and the small, tender seeds cook quickly with a mild, sweet flavor. Harvest pods at the green shell stage once well filled, and pick promptly once pods mature, since lima pods left too long on the plant can toughen.

name: Thumbelina Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or late summer for fall harvest; Thumbelina, an All-America Selections winner, forms small, round, golf-ball-sized roots that mature quickly and grow well even in shallow or heavy, rocky soil unsuited to long-rooted carrot varieties.
directions: Direct sow seed a quarter inch deep in loose, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings so roots have room to size up. Thumbelina, an All-America Selections winner, produces small, round, sweet roots about the size of a golf ball rather than the long tapered shape of standard carrots, making it uniquely well suited to shallow, rocky, or heavy clay soils where long-rooted carrots often grow forked or stunted, as well as to container growing. Its quick maturity and compact size also make it a fun, kid-friendly carrot for small gardens. Harvest as soon as roots reach full size, since round carrots can become woody if left in the ground too long, and keep soil consistently moist for the sweetest, most tender roots.

name: Thunder Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 65F; trellis the vigorous vines to support extra-long fruit.
directions: A gynoecious hybrid producing extra-long, smooth, dark green slicers on vigorous vines, with resistance to scab, downy and powdery mildew, anthracnose, and several mosaic viruses. LSU AgCenter recommends it as an early, heavy producer well suited to Louisiana's humid growing season; its broad mildew resistance is the main reason it holds up through Gulf Coast summer humidity better than older slicers.
sources: LSU AgCenter / Seeds to Success - Recommended Cucumber Varieties for Louisiana

name: Tiara Cabbage
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in late summer for a fall crop; Tiara is a fast-maturing, small-headed cabbage bred for close spacing and high-density planting, giving a much larger yield per bed than standard full-size cabbage.
directions: Start transplants and set out in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants closely since Tiara is bred specifically for high-density planting. It forms small, dense, round green heads of about 1-2 pounds in a notably short season, one of the fastest-maturing cabbages commonly grown, which lets gardeners fit in an extra planting or squeeze a crop into a narrow spring or fall window between other vegetables. The compact head size also suits smaller households better than a large storage cabbage does. Harvest as soon as heads feel firm and solid, since fast-maturing types can split if left in the ground too long after reaching full size. Watch for cabbage worms and aphids, common pests on all brassicas in the Gulf South.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Tiara Cabbage variety notes

name: Tifgrain 102 Pearl Millet
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed well past the last frost; Tifgrain 102 is a grain-type pearl millet hybrid bred at the University of Georgia for bird seed and feed-grain production.
directions: Tifgrain 102 is a grain-type pearl millet hybrid developed at the University of Georgia and selected specifically for seed production rather than forage, producing dense, well-filled heads popular for wild bird seed mixes and poultry feed. It tolerates heat and drought far better than corn and can be grown successfully on sandier, less fertile ground where other grain crops struggle. Sow into warm soil after all danger of frost has passed, since pearl millet germinates poorly in cool conditions. Cut whole heads once the grain has dried and hardened, then thresh and screen to separate the small round seed from the chaff.

name: Tifguard Peanut
plantingNote: Direct sow shelled seed into loose, sandy soil once it has warmed well past the last frost date; this variety is the strongest choice for Gulf Coast gardens on sandy, root-knot-nematode-prone ground where other peanuts struggle.
directions: Plant shelled, raw seed about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun, mounding soil gently at the base as flowering begins to give the pegs an easy route downward. Tifguard was released in 2007 by the USDA Agricultural Research Service and the University of Georgia Coastal Plain Experiment Station, bred from a cross of the nematode-resistant line 'C-99R' with the spotted-wilt-resistant 'COAN', making it the first peanut cultivar combining strong resistance to both peanut root-knot nematode and tomato spotted wilt virus. That dual resistance is especially valuable on the light, sandy Gulf Coast soils where root-knot nematode pressure often limits other peanut varieties. Keep soil evenly moist through flowering and pod fill, then dig the whole plant once foliage yellows and cure pods in a warm, airy location before shelling.
sources: University of Georgia Coastal Plain Experiment Station

name: Tifleaf Pearl Millet
plantingNote: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep after the last frost when soil is consistently warm (65°F+); Tifleaf 3 can be broadcast-seeded or drilled at 15–25 lbs/acre for cover crop use; for garden plots, 1 oz per 100 square feet provides dense stand coverage; plant after spring crops are removed for a summer-to-fall cover crop terminated before fall vegetable plantings.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained to moderately moist, average to fertile soil in full sun; Tifleaf Pearl Millet is the premier summer cover crop and wildlife food plot annual grass for Gulf South gardens and farms — a rapidly growing warm-season grass developed by the University of Georgia that establishes extremely quickly in warm conditions, producing dense, tall (5–8 foot) stands within 6–8 weeks of planting. The rapid establishment makes pearl millet exceptionally effective as a summer cover crop in Gulf South gardens that experience the challenging June–August gap between spring vegetable harvest and fall planting — a period when bare soil erodes, weeds proliferate, and soil organic matter degrades under summer sun. Tifleaf 3 is one of the most productive of all cover crop grasses for total biomass per acre in summer conditions, providing substantial green manure when terminated by mowing or incorporation before fall planting. The tall, dense stand also creates an effective summer screen, privacy hedge, or windbreak for garden areas. For wildlife gardeners, pearl millet provides outstanding deer forage and dove attractant — the seed heads produced in late summer are among the most palatable of all wildlife food plot plantings for mourning doves. Drought-tolerant once established. Terminated easily by mowing at the soil surface — the shallow root system decomposes quickly, improving soil organic matter. Grows as a warm-season annual, killed by first frost.

name: Tiger Baby Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills 1-2 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed, or transplant 3-week-old seedlings to avoid disturbing the taproot.
directions: Tiger Baby gets its name from the dark gray-green rind striped with bold tiger-like markings, wrapped around a compact 7-8 pound icebox-size fruit with sweet, crisp red flesh. Its shorter maturity window compared to full-size Southern heirlooms makes it a good pick for gardeners north of the traditional watermelon belt who still want a full-flavored melon. Fertilize modestly since excess nitrogen favors vine growth over fruiting, and thump or check the ground spot for creamy yellowing to judge ripeness. The single-serving size makes it easy to chill whole and slice fresh without leftovers going to waste.

name: Tiger Collard
plantingNote: Sow in late summer for a fall-through-winter Gulf South crop, or in early spring; a light frost sweetens the leaves.
directions: Tiger Collard is an African American heritage collard distinguished by its dramatically frilled, deeply serrated leaf margins that give the plant its striped, tiger-like appearance. It was preserved within Southern seed-keeping networks and has more recently been distributed by seed companies working to document and conserve distinct family collard lines, including through the Heirloom Collards Project. The plant is vigorous and productive, tolerating both summer heat and winter cold well enough to provide greens across much of the year in zone 8-10 gardens, and its ruffled texture holds up well when cooked low and slow in traditional Southern style.

name: Tiger Eye Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; a bush bean needing no support; pick pods frequently if harvesting as a snap bean.
directions: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; Tiger Eye is a stunning heirloom bush bean with large seeds in a rich golden-yellow to tan background covered with auburn to deep brown streaking and marbling — the pattern resembles a tiger's eye gemstone and retains some color on cooking. The flavor is particularly rich and buttery for a dry bean, often described as creamy with a hint of chestnut, making it excellent in soups and stews or as a simple side dish. A productive and reliable bush bean that dries beautifully on the plant and stores well.

name: Tigerella Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost risk has passed; an indeterminate variety that needs staking or caging despite its compact clusters of small-medium fruit.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before last frost in a warm, moist seed-starting mix kept at 70–85°F; transplant deeply after frost danger has passed, burying the stem up to the lowest leaves to encourage a strong root system. Tigerella is a British heirloom also sold under the name Mr. Stripey in the UK, producing heavy clusters of 2–3 ounce fruits with vivid red skin and irregular gold-yellow stripes and a tangy, balanced flavor that is excellent fresh or in sauces. Stake or cage plants early and begin harvesting when the fruit is firm but fully colored at the blossom end; unlike many striped types it ripens evenly and does not crack easily. Regular irrigation helps maintain even soil moisture and reduces blossom-end rot.

name: TigerPaw-NR Habanero Pepper
plantingNote: Start on a heat mat 8-10 weeks before last frost; released by USDA-ARS in 2006 as the first commercial habanero with root-knot nematode resistance, it is well suited to the sandy, nematode-prone soils common along the Gulf Coast.
directions: Germinate on a heat mat at 80-90 degrees F and transplant outdoors only after nights stay reliably warm. TigerPaw-NR was released by USDA-ARS in 2006 after a recurrent backcross program moved a dominant root-knot nematode resistance gene from a Scotch Bonnet accession into a habanero-type line, producing the first commercially available habanero cultivar resistant to southern, peanut, and tropical root-knot nematodes. Plants are compact and productive, bearing attractive lantern-shaped orange fruit that is extremely pungent, in the same fiery range as standard habaneros. The resistance package makes it a strong choice for home gardeners and small-scale growers along the Gulf Coast, where nematode pressure in light, sandy soils often stunts unprotected habanero plantings.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science (HortScience, Vol. 42)

name: Tigger Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, well-amended soil; Tigger melon is a striking ornamental-edible Middle Eastern/Central Asian heirloom with bright yellow skin dramatically striped and splashed with crimson and orange, producing small to medium fruits with cream to pale orange flesh and a sweet, spicy, slightly fruity flavor.
directions: Sow in hills after last frost in warm, well-amended, well-drained soil; thin to 2 plants per hill and allow vines to sprawl or train on a sturdy trellis with sling support for fruits. Tigger is a Central Asian or Middle Eastern heirloom melon with one of the most striking exteriors in the melon world — the smooth, round to oval, medium-sized (1–2 lb) fruits are a brilliant golden-yellow with dramatic crimson-to-orange zigzag stripes, spots, and splashes that make them resemble the fictional tiger character they are named for. The flesh is cream-colored to pale orange with a sweet, spicy, slightly fruity aroma that is pleasant rather than intensely musky; more of an ornamental conversation-piece melon than a flavor standout, but still delicious and perfectly edible. Extremely heat-tolerant and productive in hot climates; outstanding as a farmers market novelty and ornamental edible.

name: Timperley Early Rhubarb
plantingNote: Plant crowns or divisions in early spring while dormant in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Timperley Early is the classic English cultivar bred specifically for forcing an extra-early harvest, and like other rhubarb it needs a period of winter chilling for vigorous spring growth.
directions: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Timperley Early is a long-established English rhubarb cultivar bred and selected specifically for forcing — covering the crown in late winter with an upturned pot or forcing jar to exclude light produces exceptionally early, pale pink, sweet, tender stalks weeks ahead of an uncovered planting, a traditional practice in British kitchen gardens. Left unforced, it is simply an early-cropping, reliable garden rhubarb with slender, bright red-pink stalks and good flavor. As with all rhubarb, it performs best where winters provide real cold to satisfy its chilling requirement, so it is more reliable in temperate and upper Southern gardens than in the mild winters of the Deep South. Harvest by pulling individual stalks from the outside of the crown rather than cutting, always leaving several stalks per plant to sustain it, and never eat the leaves, which contain toxic levels of oxalic acid.

name: Tiny Temptations F1 Orange Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into containers or baskets after frost danger has passed; this trailing type is bred for pots rather than staked garden rows.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into a hanging basket or large container in full sun once frost danger has passed, since Tiny Temptations grows as a petite trailing bush rather than an upright, staked vine. It produces an exceptionally heavy set of small, intensely sweet bright-orange cherry fruits over its small, sturdy green leaves, and the Fleuroselect jury singled it out for combining strong flavor with a tidy, self-contained habit that needs no pinching or staking. Its foliage shows good tolerance of common tomato diseases, keeping plants productive from early summer right through to frost. Harvest the fruit regularly, since they hold well on the plant without splitting or dropping.

name: Titicaca Quinoa
plantingNote: Direct sow a couple of weeks before to a couple of weeks after the last frost; Titicaca was bred in Denmark for day-length neutrality and reaches maturity far faster than most quinoa lines, making it one of the more reliable choices for short, cool growing seasons.
directions: Titicaca was developed through a Danish university breeding program aimed at bringing quinoa into higher-latitude, shorter-summer climates where standard Andean lines fail to ripen before fall frost. It grows notably shorter and more compact than most heirloom quinoa strains, an advantage for reducing lodging in windy gardens, and its day-neutral flowering habit lets it set seed reliably regardless of daylength. Direct sow into well-drained soil in full sun and thin to a wide enough spacing for the plants to bulk up their seed heads. Cut whole plants once the seed heads dry and rattle, then thresh and rinse the harvested seed thoroughly to strip the bitter saponin coating before cooking or storing.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

name: Tivoli Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Tivoli is a compact bush-habit spaghetti squash that produces the familiar cream-colored oval fruits (4–5 lbs) on a plant only 3–4 feet wide — dramatically smaller than standard spaghetti squash vines that can trail 6–10 feet. In zone 9, plant March–May for summer harvest and again August for fall production. Tivoli won an All-America Selections award for this characteristic compact bush habit combined with full-sized, excellent-quality spaghetti squash fruits; standard spaghetti squash requires far too much space for most home gardens, where a single plant's sprawling vines can take over a 6×8 foot area. Tivoli's bush habit limits spread to approximately 3×3–4 feet, making it practical for raised beds and small gardens. The flesh, when cooked, separates into the characteristic spaghetti-like strands that give the squash type its name — mild, slightly sweet, and excellent as a low-carbohydrate pasta substitute.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; thin to 24–36 inches. Harvest when skin is cream-yellow and thumps with a hollow sound. Tivoli Squash was developed by W. Atlee Burpee and received All-America Selections recognition in 1991 specifically for solving one of the primary practical limitations of spaghetti squash production in home gardens: the sprawling, space-consuming vine habit of standard spaghetti squash varieties makes them impractical for most garden spaces. While standard vining spaghetti squash can trail 6–10 feet in multiple directions from a single plant, requiring 40–80 square feet per plant for uncrowded production, Tivoli's compact bush habit limits the footprint to approximately 3–4 feet in diameter — manageable within a raised bed or small garden plot. The fruits produced by Tivoli are standard-sized spaghetti squash (4–5 lbs, 8–10 inches long, cream-colored skin), with the same characteristic flesh that separates into noodle-like strands when cooked — a texture that makes spaghetti squash one of the most popular vegetable substitutes for pasta. For zone 9 gardeners, spaghetti squash performs well in spring (transplanted or direct sown in March–May for a June–August harvest) and in fall (planted in late August for October–November harvest), with the compact bush habit of Tivoli making both planting windows practical in average-sized raised bed gardens.
sources: W. Atlee Burpee Seeds — Tivoli compact bush spaghetti squash AAS recognition
All-America Selections — Tivoli squash 1991 AAS winner documentation
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Winter Squash Production and Variety Selection

name: Tohono O'odham 60-Day Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is reliably warm; Tohono O'odham 60-Day Corn was bred by the Tohono O'odham people of the Sonoran Desert to mature quickly, ahead of the end of the summer monsoon season.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained soil in full sun, planting in blocks rather than single rows to ensure good pollination. Tohono O'odham 60-Day Corn is a remarkably fast-maturing flour corn developed by the Tohono O'odham people of the Sonoran Desert of Arizona and Sonora, bred to reach maturity in about two months so a crop could be planted and harvested within the brief window of the summer monsoon rains. Its speed and drought adaptation make it valuable for short-season gardens or a fast succession planting anywhere. Harvest and dry ears fully before grinding the kernels into flour for traditional dishes like pinole and tortillas.

name: Tohono O'odham Ha:l Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost; Ha:l is a rapidly maturing, exceptionally heat-tolerant squash grown by the Tohono O'odham Nation in the low Sonoran Desert near 1,900 feet elevation, prized for both its flesh and its roasted seeds.
directions: Ha:l is a Cucurbita argyrosperma squash grown for generations by the Tohono O'odham Nation in the low Sonoran Desert near 1,900 feet elevation, valued as much for its roasted seeds as for its flesh. Mature fruit has light orange, mildly flavored, starchy flesh that stores well and can be sun-dried and resoftened by boiling later in the season; immature fruits, called ha:al mamat, are picked and cooked like zucchini. Vigorous, rapidly maturing vines are exceptionally heat tolerant and set a large fruit load even through intense desert summer heat. The blossoms are traditionally used as well, stirred into wheat flour to make a simple porridge.

name: Tokinashi Daikon
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep into loose, deeply cultivated soil free of stones so the long, tapering roots can grow straight; also sown in late summer for fall harvest.
directions: Direct-sow seed 1/2 inch deep into loose, deeply cultivated soil free of stones so the long, tapering white roots can grow straight and unforked. Tokinashi is a traditional Japanese heirloom valued for its unusual all-season adaptability and its resistance to becoming pithy, allowing roots to be left in the ground to reach 15-18 inches without losing quality. The firm, crisp, assertively pungent flesh is a staple for grating, pickling, and simmering, and the variety is a reliable open-pollinated choice for gardeners who want to save their own seed.

name: Tokyo Cross Turnip
plantingNote: Sow directly as soon as soil can be worked, and again in late summer for fall roots; thin early since this hybrid grows fast and can crowd itself.
directions: Tokyo Cross is a fast-maturing F1 hybrid turnip, an All-America Selections winner bred from the open-pollinated Tokyo Market type, valued for producing smooth, pure-white globes that stay tender, mild, and crack-free even if left in the ground past ideal size. Direct sow shallowly into loose soil and thin to a few inches apart, keeping the bed consistently moist for the fastest, sweetest roots. Both the crisp roots and the tender young tops are edible, making it a dual-purpose crop for salads, quick pickles, or braising greens. Its speed and heat tolerance for a turnip make it well suited to succession planting through much of the season.

name: Tokyo Market Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer for fall harvest or in early spring; Tokyo Market is a very fast-maturing Japanese salad turnip (30–40 days) producing small, round, smooth, pure white roots with very mild, sweet flavor — harvested at golf-ball to tennis-ball size for the finest eating quality; similar in type to Hakurei but a slightly larger, more market-focused variety.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in cool weather; thin to 3–4 inches apart; harvest at 2–3 inch diameter for finest quality (overripe roots become pithy and strongly flavored); both roots and tender greens are edible. Tokyo Market is a Japanese-type salad turnip closely related to (but distinct from) Hakurei — both belong to the mild, sweet, fast-maturing Japanese turnip tradition that is quite different from the traditional European turnip types grown for cooking. Tokyo Market matures in just 30–40 days from direct seeding, producing smooth, round, pure white roots with a mild, slightly sweet, and almost fruity flavor that is excellent raw — sliced thin into salads, served with dipping sauces, or eaten out of hand like an apple in the garden. Unlike European cooking turnips (which are generally too sharp and starchy to eat raw), Japanese salad turnip types like Tokyo Market and Hakurei have been bred for low pungency and high sugar content, making them the most accessible and enjoyable turnips for most modern palates. The tender, mild young greens are equally edible — excellent in salads, stir-fries, and anywhere turnip greens are used with a preference for milder flavor. Tokyo Market is preferred in farmers market growing for its consistent, uniform appearance and rapid turnover; for home gardeners it provides the fastest-maturing turnip option for succession planting every 3–4 weeks.

name: Tokyo Silky Sweet Turnip
plantingNote: Sow in early spring or, for the best flavor, in late summer for a fall harvest; roots are best pulled small rather than left to size up.
directions: Tokyo Silky Sweet is a Japanese-type salad turnip bred to be eaten raw, with a smooth, glassy-white root that is crisp, juicy, and notably sweet rather than peppery. Direct-sow shallowly and thin to 3 to 4 inches apart, harvesting roots at about 2 inches across for the best texture before they start to toughen. The tender greens are mild enough to eat raw as well, making the whole plant useful rather than just the root. Like other fast salad turnips, it's best grown in a quick-succession planting schedule rather than left in the ground for long-term storage.

name: Tom Thumb Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow thinly with barely 0.125 inch of soil coverage; Tom Thumb forms very small heads (3–4 inches in diameter) that can be planted at much closer spacing than standard lettuce — 6 inches apart rather than the 10–12 inches standard butterheads require. The small head size allows one head per person per serving, making it practical for restaurant-style presentation. In zone 9, sow September–November for fall and winter harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds on the surface of moist, fertile soil with barely 0.125 inch coverage; keep consistently moist through germination. Tom Thumb is an English heirloom butterhead lettuce that produces perfectly proportioned miniature heads — fully formed, well-blanched butterhead-type lettuce compressed into a head 3–4 inches in diameter and 4–6 inches tall at maturity, roughly one-quarter the size of a standard butterhead like Buttercrunch or Boston. The miniature scale is not a compromised or immature form of standard lettuce; Tom Thumb is a true miniature variety that completes its growth cycle and forms a proper, compact head with the characteristic blanched, cream-colored inner leaves and tender, buttery texture of butterhead types. The small head size makes Tom Thumb exceptionally practical in multiple ways: it can be spaced 6 inches apart rather than 10–12 inches, fitting significantly more plants in a given area; it produces one serving per head, eliminating the common problem of leftover half-heads wilting in the refrigerator; and it is particularly suited to container growing, window boxes, and very small raised beds where a full-sized lettuce would be overwhelming. Tom Thumb has been grown in English kitchen gardens since at least the 19th century and represents the miniaturization approach to vegetable breeding that has recently become popular again in urban and space-limited gardening.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Tom Thumb lettuce variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Heirloom lettuce collection
Royal Horticultural Society — Lettuce variety guide

name: Tom Thumb Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow thickly in cool early spring soil; this dwarf Victorian-era heirloom needs no staking and matures quickly.
directions: Direct sow thickly in cool early spring soil; this dwarf Victorian-era heirloom needs no staking and matures quickly, making it one of the earliest garden peas to harvest. Bred in England in the mid-1800s as a compact alternative to the era's towering pea vines, Tom Thumb tops out under a foot tall, which has made it a longtime favorite for small beds, cold frames, and containers. Because the plants are so short, keep them weed-free, as taller neighbors will shade them out quickly. Harvest pods as soon as they plump for the sweetest flavor, since this small-statured variety produces a modest but concentrated crop over a short window.

name: Tom Thumb Popcorn
plantingNote: Sow in blocks in average garden soil or containers; its dwarf habit lets it thrive in small spaces.
directions: Sow in blocks in average garden soil or containers; its dwarf habit lets it thrive in small spaces where a full-size popcorn would be impractical. Tom Thumb is a diminutive heirloom popcorn reaching only three to four feet tall, producing small, deep-red ears reminiscent of miniature Strawberry Popcorn but on an even more compact plant. Left to dry fully on the stalk, the small hard kernels pop up light and tender, and the short ears and petite plants also make this variety popular for autumn ornamental displays as well as a genuinely productive novelty popcorn for the home popper.

name: Tom Watson Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm (70°F minimum); Tom Watson is a very large variety requiring substantial space — vines spread 10–15 feet and individual fruits can weigh 30–50 pounds, requiring ample room and warm nights for full sugar development. In zone 9, plant April–May. The oblong, mottled-green striped fruits (12–18 inches long) develop over 85–95 days of warm weather. Tom Watson needs a long, hot summer to reach full size and sweetness — the Gulf South's reliable summer heat is ideal. Harvested before full ripeness, Tom Watson can be bland and watery; the full flavor requires the heat accumulation that makes zone 9 an excellent watermelon climate. Detect ripeness by dried tendril adjacent to fruit, creamy yellow ground spot, and hollow thud when thumped firmly.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms; space hills 6–8 feet apart. Harvest when tendril dries and ground spot turns creamy yellow. Tom Watson is one of the most historically important American watermelon varieties — a large, oblong, Southern heirloom that was the dominant commercial watermelon in the southeastern United States from approximately 1906 through the mid-20th century, and that is named (with slight uncertainty as to whether intentionally or as a coincidence of personal name similarity) after one of Georgia's most prominent politicians of the era. Tom Watson melons are large to very large (typically 25–50 lbs), oblong with mottled medium-dark green skin and faint lighter stripes, with red to deep red flesh and moderate seed content. The flavor at full maturity is excellent — sweet, richly flavored, and typifying the character of old-style Southern watermelons grown in sandy, hot-summer soil. Tom Watson was particularly prized for its performance in the sandy, well-drained soils of the Georgia and Carolina coastal plain, where the warm nights, deep sandy loam, and long growing season produced melons with exceptional sweetness and the size that made watermelons the centerpiece of summer picnics, church suppers, and community celebrations throughout the South. The variety's historical significance extends beyond flavor: Tom Watson represents a type of community and agricultural identity in the South where the production of very large, high-quality melons was a point of regional pride and a staple of summer social life in farming communities.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Tom Watson watermelon Georgia heirloom documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Tom Watson watermelon historical variety notes
Georgia Agricultural Experiment Station — Historical watermelon variety production in Georgia

name: Tomhannock Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow shallowly in early spring, and again in late summer for a fall crop.
directions: Documented as far back as an 1837 English gardening magazine, Tomhannock traces to French seed distributed through the London Horticultural Society but became far more popular in American gardens than in England. Nineteenth-century American seedsmen sold the same lettuce under other names as well. It forms a butterhead-type, somewhat savoyed and blistered head of medium green leaves with distinctive reddish-brown speckling, giving it a decorative look beyond its eating quality. This old dual-purpose butterhead is a good option for gardeners wanting a lettuce with genuine nineteenth-century American roots.
sources: William Woys Weaver - Heirloom Vegetable Gardening

name: Tommy Toe Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost at 70–80°F and transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed; stake or cage firmly, since Tommy Toe is a vigorous, heavy-yielding indeterminate variety.
directions: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, deeply prepared, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger has passed, staking or caging plants firmly to support the vigorous vines. Tommy Toe is a beloved Australian heirloom producing an abundance of round, golf-ball-sized fruit larger than a typical cherry tomato but smaller than a standard slicer, with rich, well-balanced, classic tomato flavor that many gardeners rate above modern cherry hybrids for taste. Its heavy, sustained production over a long season and good disease tolerance have made it a favorite for fresh eating, salads, and snacking straight off the vine, occupying a useful middle ground in size between cherry and full-sized tomatoes. Harvest regularly as fruit ripens to keep the prolific vines setting new fruit throughout the summer.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — heirloom tomato variety notes

name: Tonatico Cherry Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Tonatico is a tall, upright indeterminate cherry tomato that benefits from staking or caging to support its long fruit trusses.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun after the last frost, staking or caging the tall indeterminate vine well before it needs the support. Tonatico is an AAS regional winner producing round, bright red, roughly 1.5-inch cherry fruit with a notably high sugar content and juicy, sweet flavor, carried on long, easy-to-harvest trusses that can number up to 200 fruits per plant over the season. Fruit resists cracking and the plant shows good disease resistance, so the uniform clusters hold up well through variable watering and weather. Pick trusses as fruit fully colors for the sweetest eating, and maintain consistent moisture to keep the high yields coming.
sources: All-America Selections — Tomato Tonatico F1 winner announcement

name: Tondo di Paestum Artichoke
scientificName: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Tondo di Paestum'
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant, or set out rooted offshoots in spring; in zone 9 plant February–March. Established stools flower over a long season in mild coastal climates, so harvest the central bud first and keep cutting side buds as they tighten.
directions: Tondo di Paestum is the traditional round-headed artichoke landrace grown on the coastal plain around Paestum and Battipaglia in Campania, Italy, where it carries IGP protected status for its tender, compact, violet-tinged green heads harvested from late winter into spring. The mild coastal Mediterranean winters of its home region allow continuous bud production over several months, with the earliest central buds valued for their uniform roundness and the smaller side buds suited to braising or preserving in oil. Plants are traditionally kept as perennial stools and increased by dividing rooted offshoots rather than grown fresh from seed each year, which preserves the landrace's characteristic head shape and timing. Give it deep, well-drained coastal soil and full sun, and mulch crowns if a rare hard frost threatens.
sources: Consorzio di Tutela del Carciofo di Paestum IGP
European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register
Slow Food Presidia — Italian Heritage Artichoke Varieties

name: Tongues of Fire Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Tongues of Fire (Lingua di Fuoco in Italian) is a traditional Italian borlotto bean variety famous for its spectacular appearance — the pods are cream-colored with dramatic scarlet-red flame streaks (the 'tongues of fire') and the shelled beans within are cream-white with vivid red speckles that fade to a uniform brown when cooked; harvested as a shell bean or allowed to dry completely for a dry borlotto bean.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost, 4–6 inches apart in rows 18–24 inches apart; Tongues of Fire is a bush bean that can also be harvested as a snap bean at 5–6 inches (though the pods are somewhat coarse) — harvest as a shell bean when pods are plump and fully developed (60–70 days) or allow to dry completely for a dry borlotto bean (75–85 days). Tongues of Fire (Lingua di Fuoco) is a traditional Italian borlotto bean with some of the most dramatically beautiful pods in the vegetable garden — the medium-length pods are a creamy or pale yellow background completely covered with irregular streaks, splashes, and flames of scarlet-red that give the variety its evocative Italian name. The raw pods are so visually striking that harvesting them from the plant is genuinely exciting; unfortunately (from a visual standpoint), both the red pod markings and the speckled cream-and-red seed coloring fade completely when the beans are cooked, resulting in uniform tan to brownish seeds. The flavor of shell-stage Tongues of Fire beans is excellent — rich, earthy, and starchy in the characteristic Italian borlotto style that makes them the preferred bean for ribollita soup, pasta e fagioli, and other classic bean dishes of central and northern Italian cooking. Borlotti are used across Italy as the fresh shell bean equivalent of cranberry beans in New England cooking — they are always shelled before cooking, never eaten as whole pods. Tongues of Fire is reliable and productive in summer gardens throughout the US.

name: Top Crop Bush Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is at least 60°F; beans rot in cold, wet soil. Top Crop is a classic early bush snap bean that can also tolerate warm conditions — it was originally selected and trialed specifically for heat resistance and productivity under the warm, humid conditions of the southeastern United States and received an All-America Selections award in 1951 for its superior performance over existing bush bean varieties. In zone 9, direct sow March–May for spring production and August–September for fall production; bean plants decline quickly when summer temperatures consistently exceed 95°F but spring and fall crops can be very productive. The plants are compact and upright (18–24 inches), producing straight, round, stringless or nearly stringless pods 5–6 inches long in abundance at 49–54 days.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; space 4–6 inches in rows 18 inches apart. Harvest at 5–6 inches before seeds bulge. Top Crop is one of the historically significant All-America Selections winners in the vegetable category, recognized in 1951 for performance and quality that exceeded the bush bean standard of the era. At the time of its AAS recognition, Top Crop represented a meaningful improvement over other widely grown bush bean varieties in terms of pod quality (straight, stringless, and uniform), plant habit (upright and compact, making harvest easier), and importantly for southeastern gardens — its tolerance for warm, humid growing conditions that cause many bean varieties to set pods poorly or produce stringy, misshapen pods. The variety became one of the most widely grown bush snap bean varieties in American home and market gardens through the 1950s, 1960s, and 1970s, establishing itself as a regional standard especially in the South where the heat tolerance advantage mattered most. Top Crop produces round, stringless pods (the 'Top Crop' designation reflects the goal of beans that crop densely at the top of the plant, making harvest efficient) that are firm, tender at optimal harvest size (5–6 inches), and of classic, straightforward snap bean flavor. The variety is open-pollinated and remains available through seed companies as a historical heirloom standard. For zone 9 spring and fall gardens, Top Crop's heat tolerance and early maturity (49–54 days) make it practical for getting a bean crop harvested before summer heat peaks or after it subsides in fall.
sources: All-America Selections — Top Crop bush bean 1951 AAS recognition documentation
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Top Crop heirloom bush bean variety notes
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Bush Bean Variety Recommendations for Gulf South Home Gardens

name: Top Mark Cantaloupe
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; Top Mark was bred by the Dessert Seed Company of El Centro, California as a firm-fleshed Western shipping cantaloupe and remains popular with home gardeners for its reliable disease tolerance and classic flavor.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of two to three plants in full sun once soil has warmed well past last frost, thinning to the strongest seedling per hill. Top Mark produces slightly oblong, well-netted, 3-4 lb fruits with thick, firm, sweet salmon-colored flesh, and was long grown as a standard commercial shipping melon in California's Imperial Valley thanks to good tolerance of powdery and downy mildew. Keep soil evenly moist through vine growth and fruit set, then reduce watering as melons approach maturity to concentrate sweetness. Harvest at full slip, when the stem separates cleanly from the fruit with light pressure and the blossom end yields slightly to thumb pressure.

name: Top Pick Brown Crowder Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after soil is thoroughly warm; like its sibling Top Pick Pinkeye, this crowder type was bred to set pods concentrated near the top of the plant for faster, cleaner once-over picking during peak Gulf South summer harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil is thoroughly warm. Top Pick Brown Crowder is an improved brown crowder-type Southern pea bred, like the related Top Pick Pinkeye, so pods set concentrated near the top of the plant instead of scattered through the foliage, letting a picker fill a basket quickly during the heaviest part of the summer flush instead of hunting for hidden pods. The tightly packed, squarish brown seeds develop the rich, hearty flavor traditional to crowder-type field peas, and plants hold up well through the hottest, most humid stretch of the season when many other vegetables falter. As with other cowpeas, the roots fix atmospheric nitrogen and improve soil fertility as the crop grows. Harvest pods at the green-shell stage for fresh shelling, or let them dry fully on the plant for long-term storage.
sources: seed catalog reference (Sow True Seed, Rupp Seeds)

name: Top Pick Pinkeye Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun after soil is thoroughly warm; Top Pick Pinkeye is an improved open-pollinated pinkeye purple hull type bred to concentrate its pods at the top of the plant for faster, cleaner picking — a real time-saver during the peak of a Gulf South summer harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in lean to moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the soil is thoroughly warm; Top Pick Pinkeye is an improved pinkeye purple hull southern pea bred so that pods set concentrated near the top of the plant rather than scattered throughout, letting a picker harvest a full basket quickly without hunting through foliage — a meaningful advantage during the heavy summer flush when Southern peas are at their most productive. The cream-colored peas with a distinctive pink eye have the classic mild, slightly sweet flavor prized in Southern cooking. Harvest pods when they've turned the characteristic purple-pink color and the peas inside have filled out but are still tender for fresh shelling, or let pods dry fully for storage. Like other Southern peas, the plant fixes nitrogen and improves soil fertility as it grows, and thrives in the long, hot Gulf South summer.
sources: seed catalog reference (Stokes Seeds, Rupp Seeds, Holmes Seed Company)

name: Topper Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow thickly for a cut-and-come-again greens crop from late summer through fall in zone 8-10; a spring sowing before hot weather sets in is also workable since this type resists bolting better than root-focused turnips.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, loose soil in full sun and thin lightly, since this variety is grown for its leaves rather than a marketable root and tolerates closer spacing than globe-type turnips. The smooth, broad, dark green leaves grow rapidly and regrow readily after cutting, making Topper well suited to a repeated cut-and-come-again harvest schedule rather than a single whole-plant pull. It resists the bitterness and rapid bolting that hot weather causes in many greens turnips, giving Southern gardeners a wider planting window than strictly cool-season varieties allow. The small, often forked roots are edible but are not the point of growing this variety, so gardeners aiming for a good turnip root should choose a globe type instead.

name: Torasan Komatsuna
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or, for the sweetest leaves, in late summer for an autumn crop; light frost improves flavor by reducing the mustard-like bite.
directions: Torasan is a Japanese F1 komatsuna prized for dark, glossy, spoon-shaped leaves and a sturdy, upright habit that holds up well to cutting. It grows quickly from direct-sown seed and tolerates both cool spring conditions and light autumn frost, which sweetens the leaves and mellows their mustard-spinach bite. Because it bolts readily once days lengthen and warm, gardeners in hotter regions do best sowing it in a partly shaded bed or as a fall crop rather than pushing it through summer.

name: Toro Rice
plantingNote: Direct sow in flooded or consistently moist ground after last frost when soil temperature reaches 65°F; Toro was developed at the LSU AgCenter Rice Research Station near Crowley, Louisiana, as a specialty long-grain with the clingy cooked texture normally associated with short- and medium-grain rice.
directions: Sow seed 0.5–1 inch deep in rich, heavy, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, keeping the bed consistently saturated or flooded through the growing season. Toro is a specialty long-grain rice released by the LSU AgCenter Rice Research Station near Crowley, bred with low amylose content and a low gelatinization temperature that give the cooked grain a soft, clingy, jasmine-like texture despite its long-grain shape — unlike the fluffy, separate-grain texture of standard American long-grain rice. Unlike aromatic Louisiana specialty rices such as Della and Jazzman, Toro carries no distinctive fragrance; its value is purely in cooking texture, making it popular for dishes and cuisines that call for a stickier grain. The tall plants perform well through the hot, humid Gulf Coast growing season. Harvest when seed heads droop and grain turns golden-brown, then thresh and dry thoroughly before storage or milling.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — H. Rouse Caffey Rice Research Station Released Varieties
Louisiana Rice Promotion Board — Varieties & Nutrition
Camellia Brand — Rice Right (Louisiana specialty rice types)

name: Torvum Vigor Rootstock Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors well ahead of the scion variety, since seed germinates slowly and unevenly, then graft a favorite eggplant scion onto it once stems are pencil-thick, heal in a humid shaded chamber, and transplant after frost into full sun.
directions: This wild, thorny relative of eggplant is grown as a grafting rootstock rather than for its own small, bitter fruit, valued for an exceptionally vigorous, deep root system that confers strong resistance to bacterial wilt, fusarium wilt, verticillium wilt, and root-knot nematodes, all serious soil-borne problems that shorten the productive life of own-root eggplant in warm, humid climates. Grafting a favorite eggplant scion onto this rootstock is a traditional practice in parts of Asia and is gaining adoption among home and market growers in the humid Gulf South seeking longer-lived, more disease-resistant eggplant plants without resorting to soil fumigation or long rotations. Start rootstock seed well ahead of the scion, since germination is slower and less even than standard eggplant, graft when stems are pencil-thick, heal grafted plants in a humid, shaded chamber for about a week, then harden off and transplant after frost into full sun with sturdy support.

name: Totem Witloof Chicory
plantingNote: Direct sow in late spring; this later-maturing forcing hybrid is best suited to growers who want a longer field season and roots that hold well in cold storage for staggered forcing batches deep into winter.
directions: 'Totem' is a later-maturing F1 witloof chicory bred for growers who want to stagger their Belgian endive harvest well into winter, since its roots hold in cold storage and continue to force well after several months. Direct sow in late spring and grow through summer to develop a thick, straight taproot; in fall, trim the foliage to an inch above the crown, lift the roots before hard freezes, and store them cold and dark until needed. Force a batch every few weeks by replanting roots upright in moist sand or soil in complete darkness at 50-60F, and expect compact, ivory-white chicons in three to four weeks. Compared to earlier-maturing forcing hybrids, its slightly longer field season produces larger roots that can support a second, smaller flush of growth if the first chicon is cut and the root is forced again.

name: Touchon Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow in loose, stone-free soil as soon as it can be worked, keeping the bed evenly moist until seedlings emerge since carrot seed germinates slowly.
directions: Touchon is a classic French heirloom carrot of the Nantes type, prized for smooth, nearly coreless, cylindrical roots with a blunt tip and exceptionally sweet, crisp flesh. Direct sow seed thinly and shallowly in deeply worked, stone-free soil, then thin seedlings to about 2 inches apart once true leaves appear to give roots room to size up straight and uniform. It tolerates light frost well and holds good eating quality in the ground longer than many thin-skinned Nantes types, making it useful for a succession of plantings from early spring into fall. Harvest at finger size for the sweetest, most tender roots, or let them reach full size for storage.

name: Trafalgar Brussels Sprout
plantingNote: Start indoors 14-18 weeks before first fall frost; Trafalgar is a late mid-season hybrid that fills the harvest window from mid-November into January, sweetening further with each hard frost.
directions: Start seeds indoors 14-18 weeks before first fall frost; transplant into firm, fertile, well-drained soil and stake the medium-tall stems against wind; top the plants once lower sprouts reach marble size to even out ripening, and harvest from the bottom up as sprouts firm up. Trafalgar is a British-bred F1 hybrid valued for producing abundant, uniformly round, tightly wrapped sprouts with a sweet, low-bitterness flavor that holds up well through a long late-season harvest window running from mid-autumn into the new year. Its intermediate resistance to powdery mildew and reliable, heavy-yielding habit have made it a standard late mid-season choice in UK trial and market gardens, and the sprouts stand well on the stalk without splitting, giving flexibility about exactly when to pick. Choose Trafalgar when the goal is a long stretch of classic, mild-flavored sprouts spanning Thanksgiving through the winter holidays rather than a single early flush.

name: Traveler 76 Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant once frost danger passes; in zone 9 it also performs well as a second, late-summer planting for a fall crop, since it keeps setting fruit through high heat that stalls many other tomatoes.
directions: Start seed indoors in warm starting mix and transplant into full sun after frost risk passes; Traveler 76 was released by the University of Arkansas in 1976 as an improved successor to the original 1930s-era Traveler variety, bred specifically to correct that older tomato's tendency to crack in Southern humidity. The determinate plants set uniform, medium-sized, deep-pink globes with a well-balanced, low-acid flavor and skin that resists splitting after summer rains far better than most heirlooms. It shares the same heat-set reliability that makes Arkansas Traveler famous in Gulf Coast gardens, continuing to produce through the punishing midsummer stretch that causes many varieties to drop blossoms, but its firmer, more uniform fruit and improved crack resistance made it a favored market grower's choice across the mid-South.
sources: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service

name: Traveler Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant once frost danger passes; Traveler was released by the University of Arkansas in the 1930s and was the direct parent of the later, crack-resistant Traveler 76 selection.
directions: Start seed indoors in warm starting mix and transplant into full sun once frost risk has passed, spacing plants generously for good air movement in humid climates. Traveler was bred to keep setting fruit through the same brutal midsummer heat that stops many tomatoes from pollinating, a trait that made it a dependable choice for Arkansas and mid-South gardeners decades before modern heat-set hybrids existed. Its medium-sized, pink, globe-shaped fruits have good old-fashioned flavor, but the skin is noticeably more prone to splitting after summer rain than later selections bred from this line. Because it predates the disease and cracking improvements added in 1976, it is now grown mainly by heirloom seed savers rather than commercial producers.
sources: University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service

name: Traviata Eggplant
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Traviata is an early, disease-resilient Italian-type eggplant bred by Vitalis Organic Seeds and listed among Cornell's recommended disease-tolerant eggplant varieties, a useful trait for humid Gulf South gardens.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date, once nights stay reliably above 60°F; Traviata is an early-maturing, high-yielding Italian-type eggplant hybrid bred for vigor and improved disease resilience, producing a heavy, sustained crop of glossy, deep purple-black, oval fruit with few seeds and tender, mild flesh. Its early maturity lets Gulf Coast gardeners get a jump on the harvest before summer disease pressure builds, and the sturdy, well-branched plant continues setting fruit steadily through the season. Harvest while the skin is still glossy and the fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure, since dull skin signals overripe fruit with more seeds and a bitter edge. Keep soil consistently moist, since eggplant grown under drought stress develops tougher skin and a more bitter flavor.
sources: seed catalog reference (Osborne Seed Company, High Mowing Organic Seeds)

name: Travis Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Set slips 2-4 weeks after last frost; Travis is an early-maturing white-fleshed sweet potato released for local fresh-market and garden use through North Carolina Foundation Seed Producers.
directions: Plant slips into loose, ridged soil two to four weeks after the last frost, in full sun. Travis is a rose-skinned sweet potato noted in university cultivar trial descriptions as both an orange-fleshed early type and, in white-fleshed seed strains, a high-yielding market and garden variety distributed through North Carolina Foundation Seed Producers; either way it is valued for its earlier maturity relative to standard-season types like Beauregard. The vines are productive and the roots size up quickly enough to allow an earlier first harvest window in short-season gardens. Dig as soon as roots reach usable size to beat frost, then cure in warm, humid conditions for roughly a week before moving to cool storage.
sources: NC State University Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America

name: Trebi Barley
plantingNote: Broadcast or drill in early spring as soon as the ground can be worked; Trebi was developed for irrigated Western valleys and also performs well as a rain-fed spring barley on the Northern Plains.
directions: Trebi was collected by USDA plant explorer Mark Carleton in Russia in the early 1900s and released after testing by the USDA Office of Cereal Investigations, quickly becoming a benchmark six-row spring barley across irrigated valleys of the Western United States for its high yield and strong straw. Sow into a firm, fertile seedbed in early spring; it responds especially well to irrigation but also holds up under rain-fed Northern Plains conditions. The stiff-strawed plant resists lodging better than many barleys of its era, letting it carry a heavy head of grain without falling over before harvest. Cut and thresh once the heads dry to straw-gold, and use the plump kernels for livestock feed, malting trials, or seed increase.
sources: USDA Office of Cereal Investigations historical records
University of California Sustainable Agriculture Research and Education Program

name: Trero Kohlrabi
directions: Sow thickly and thin to final spacing; this open-pollinated Swiss kohlrabi, listed by the heirloom seed house Sativa Rheinau and the ProSpecieRara conservation network, forms smooth, pale-green globes with notably thin, tender skin that rarely needs peeling even at full size. Because it's open-pollinated rather than a hybrid, seed can be saved from year to year, and succession sowing every two to three weeks keeps a steady supply of crisp, juicy bulbs for slaws through a long cool season.

name: Tres Fine Endive
plantingNote: Start indoors 3–4 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 transplant September–October. Tres Fine is the most finely cut of the frisee endive types, with leaf cutting so delicate it resembles ornamental moss — making it the premium choice for restaurant-quality frisee presentations. In zone 9 fall planting from September transplants produces full heads by November.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Tres Fine (Very Fine) is the most elegantly cut of all frisee endive varieties, producing an open, flat rosette of very finely divided, thread-like, deeply lacinated leaves with a delicate, airy, almost moss-like texture — more finely cut than standard frisee types and considered the premium grade for restaurant use. The characteristic pale yellow to cream heart forms naturally as the outer leaves shade the center; for maximum blanching, loosely tie the outer leaves 10 days before harvest. The very fine leaf cutting makes Tres Fine endive the lightest, most delicate-textured of the endive family in the salad bowl, where it provides a feathery contrast to dense leaves and holds vinaigrette dressings in the finest leaf surfaces. The flavor is gently bitter with a clean, slightly nutty edge. Tres Fine is widely used in French and Italian fine dining as the benchmark frisee for composed salads and the traditional salade lyonnaise.
sources: Seeds of Italy — Tres Fine Endive Growing Notes
Territorial Seed Company — Fine-Cut Frisee Varieties
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Curly Endive and Frisee

name: Tres Fine Maraichere Frisee Endive
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring once the soil has warmed a little, or again in late summer for a fall crop; this quick, petite frisee type resists bolting better than larger endive types, so it tolerates a bit of afternoon shade well.
directions: Tres Fine Maraichere, sometimes sold as the Olesh strain, is an old French heirloom frisee endive valued for its petite size and quick growth compared to standard curly endives. Its narrow, deeply cut outer leaves curl into a naturally self-blanching rosette around a tender, creamy heart, and tying the outer leaves closed about a week before harvest whitens the center further. It can be cut young as a frilly, mildly bitter baby green for salad mixes or allowed to fill out into a full head, and it attracts relatively few pests along the way.

name: Treviso Radicchio
plantingNote: Sow in mid-summer for a fall harvest; in warm climates like zone 9, sow in August–September for harvest from October through December. The variety requires exposure to cool temperatures (below 50°F at night) to trigger the formation of tight, red-veined heads.
directions: Sow seeds in summer for fall harvest, thinning to 10–12 in apart when seedlings are established; Treviso radicchio forms elongated, torpedo-shaped heads with deep red leaves and contrasting white veins, quite different in form from the round Chioggia-type radicchio. Flavor is intensely bitter before cold exposure, then sweetens significantly after several frosts. Some gardeners cut the plant back to 1 inch above the crown after initial growth, then allow it to resprout for tighter, sweeter heads — a technique called 'forcing.' In zone 9, the best crops are grown from September sowing, harvested November through January. The grilled heads, split lengthwise and drizzled with olive oil, are a classic Italian preparation.

name: Triamble Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; a rare 19th-century Australian heirloom valued for its unmistakable three-lobed shape and exceptionally long storage life.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in enriched, well-drained soil, giving the sprawling vines 6-8 feet of room. Triamble is an Australian heirloom dating to at least the 1820s, named for its distinctive tri-lobed, clover-like shape formed by three fused lobes curving back toward the stem; the tough, slate-blue-grey rind gave rise to its nickname 'Ironbark pumpkin.' Fruits average around 8 pounds and hold sweet, dry, deep-orange flesh similar in quality to Queensland Blue. The hard rind makes Triamble notably difficult to cut but also gives it outstanding keeping quality, with properly cured fruit reported to store for a year or more in a cool, dry space.

name: Tribeca Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; cage or stake at transplant since determinate plants still need support once loaded with fruit, and irrigate consistently to avoid blossom-end rot.
directions: Listed by LSU AgCenter among determinate, heat-tolerant tomatoes carrying tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV) resistance, the thrips-vectored virus that is one of the biggest headaches for Gulf Coast tomato growers. As a determinate, bush-habit hybrid it suits a compressed, cage-supported spring crop timed to set fruit before peak July-August heat, with a second planting possible for fall. TSWV resistance reduces but doesn't eliminate thrips-management needs, so reflective mulch is still worthwhile in zone 9 gardens.

name: Tribute Tomato
