plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; stake or cage at transplant and irrigate consistently to avoid blossom-end rot in uneven Gulf Coast summer soil moisture.
directions: Appears alongside Tribeca on the same LSU AgCenter recommended list, determinate, heat-tolerant, and TSWV-resistant, making it one of the extension service's standard picks for a Louisiana or Gulf South spring tomato crop that needs to keep setting fruit as nights stay warm. Treat it as a direct substitute or companion planting for other heat-set determinate slicers if you want to compare performance side by side in your own yard. Consistent irrigation through fruit set matters more than fertility for avoiding cracking and blossom-end rot in this type.

name: Trinidad Moruga Scorpion Pepper
plantingNote: Start on a heat mat 10–12 weeks before last frost; Trinidad Moruga Scorpion is one of the hottest naturally occurring chiles in the world, measured at 1.2–2.0 million Scoville units — handle with gloves and avoid touching eyes or face; it was certified by the Chile Pepper Institute as the world's hottest pepper in 2012.
directions: Germinate at 85–90°F on a heat mat — germination can take 3–4 weeks for superhot varieties; grow under bright lights and transplant only when nighttime temperatures are consistently above 60°F. Trinidad Moruga Scorpion originated in the Moruga district of Trinidad and was certified by the Chile Pepper Institute at New Mexico State University as the world's hottest pepper in 2012, with an average heat of 1.2 million SHU and individual samples reaching 2 million SHU — making it one of the hottest naturally occurring chile varieties ever measured. The fruits are round to elongated with a characteristic tail or 'stinger,' ripening to red (sometimes yellow or chocolate depending on the phenotype), with intense fruity tropical flavor beneath the extraordinary heat. Widely grown by superhot enthusiasts for hot sauce and extreme culinary use; handle seeds and fruits with nitrile gloves and eye protection.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Trinidad Perfume Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Trinidad Perfume is a heatless habanero-type pepper prized for the intense fruity, floral, apricot-like aroma and flavor typical of Capsicum chinense peppers, without any of the heat.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors 2 weeks after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil. Trinidad Perfume is a heatless selection within the Capsicum chinense species, the same species as habaneros and Scotch bonnets, bred to capture the intensely fruity, floral, almost apricot-and-citrus aroma and flavor characteristic of that species without any of the fiery heat, making it usable in far larger quantities than a true habanero for salsas, sauces, and dishes where habanero flavor is wanted but the heat is not. The wrinkled, lantern-shaped fruits look nearly identical to a habanero, ripening from green to orange or red, and can be used fresh, dried, or blended into sauces for a burst of tropical fruit flavor. Plants are productive and grow similarly to other Capsicum chinense peppers, benefiting from a long, warm growing season. Harvest regularly to encourage continued fruit set through the season.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Trinidad Perfume Pepper variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Heatless Habanero-Type Peppers
Chile Pepper Institute — Capsicum chinense Culinary Types

name: Trinidad Scorpion Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost using bottom heat, as chinense superhots germinate slowly and need a long season.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, since germination can be slow and irregular, then transplant into warm, well-drained soil after all frost danger passes. Stake plants and prune early flowers to build a stronger frame before letting the heavy fruit set develop. This is the original Trinidad Scorpion strain from which the later 'Butch T' selection was bred, named for the narrow curled tail at the pod's tip and known for ferocious, lingering heat. Wear gloves when harvesting and processing the ripe red pods.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Trinidad Seasoning Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10–12 weeks before the last frost with bottom heat, since Capsicum chinense germinates slowly; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after nights stay reliably above 55°F.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the plants are productive and reasonably compact, doing well in raised beds or large containers. Trinidad Seasoning Pepper is a habanero-relative (Capsicum chinense) grown not for heat but for its intense, distinctively fruity, floral habanero-type aroma without the accompanying pungency — a genetic quirk that produces essentially all of the characteristic C. chinense flavor with almost none of the capsaicin heat. It is a foundational ingredient in Trinidadian and broader Caribbean cooking, where it is blended into 'green seasoning' marinades, curries, and sauces to deliver deep habanero-family flavor that can be used generously without overwhelming heat. The wrinkled, lantern-shaped fruits ripen from green through yellow, orange, or red depending on the specific strain. An essential, distinctive pepper for gardeners interested in Caribbean cuisine who want the flavor of a habanero without the fire, zone 8–11.
sources: Trinidad and Tobago Ministry of Agriculture
Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Trinity Rice
plantingNote: Direct-sow into flooded or consistently moist beds after last frost; after cutting the main crop, leave stubble in place and keep the bed flooded or moist for a ratoon second harvest.
directions: A 2021-2022 Texas A&M AgriLife release from a Saber by Cocodrie by Presidio cross, bred specifically to outperform Presidio with notably higher main-crop and ratoon-crop yields at comparable grain quality. The ratoon advantage is the most garden-relevant trait: after the main crop is cut, keep the bed flooded or moist and let regrowth from the cut stems produce a second, smaller harvest within the same Gulf Coast season. A logical companion to the Cocodrie and Presidio-type rice releases already in the collection.
sources: Samonte et al., Journal of Plant Registrations, 2022 - Registration of Trinity Long-Grain Rice Cultivar
Rice Farming - Honoring the Trinity River

name: Trinity Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed, in blocks of at least four short rows for reliable pollination. Trinity's cool-soil vigor and early maturity make it a good choice for a first succession planting in short-season gardens.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the ground has warmed. Trinity is a synergistic (SY) bicolor hybrid that combines sugary-enhanced and supersweet genetics on the same ear, giving tender, creamy kernels with good sweetness retention without the tough pericarp of straight sh2 types. It is among the earliest-maturing bicolor hybrids available, germinating well in cooler soil than most supersweet corn and making it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting the first fresh corn of the season. Water consistently from tasseling through ear fill to ensure full, well-formed ears.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds variety trial notes

name: Triomphe de Farcy Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in full sun; Triomphe de Farcy is one of the most important French heirloom haricot vert varieties — a fine-podded bush bean with elegant, slender pods featuring distinctive red-violet streaks and speckles on a green background (the markings fade when cooked), harvested at pencil-thin stage for the finest haricot vert quality.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost, 4–6 inches apart in rows 18 inches apart; harvest when pods are 4–5 inches long and pencil-thin for the finest haricot vert quality; pick every 2–3 days to maintain production; the red-violet streaking on raw pods fades to a uniform green when cooked. Triomphe de Farcy is a French heirloom bush bean dating to the 1880s, when it was listed in Vilmorin's famous seed catalog as one of the finest haricots verts — the slender, pencil-thin snap beans of French cuisine that differ fundamentally from the round, plump beans favored in American cooking. The variety is named for its triumphal quality (triomphe = triumph in French) and the Farcy region of Brittany where a similar bean type was cultivated. The pods are distinctive: slender (3/8 inch diameter at most), long (5–7 inches), and marked with beautiful irregular red-violet streaks and flecks on a pale green background — the coloration is reminiscent of a speckled trout and makes raw pods strikingly beautiful in the kitchen; the markings fade completely to solid green when cooked. The flavor is characteristically French haricot vert — tender, fine-grained, buttery, and subtly sweet — quite different from the starchier, coarser texture of standard American snap beans harvested at the same age. Triomphe de Farcy is the bean for gardeners who want authentic French-style haricots verts; harvest young and often, steam or blanch briefly, and serve with good butter.

name: Trionfo Violetto Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed and set a trellis or poles at planting time, since this vigorous Italian climbing bean quickly reaches six to eight feet.
directions: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed and set a trellis or poles at planting time, since this vigorous Italian climbing bean quickly reaches six to eight feet. Long grown in Italian kitchen gardens, Trionfo Violetto is prized for its double ornamental value — deep violet flowers followed by glossy purple pods — as much as for the table, and the pods turn a deep green when cooked, losing their color but keeping excellent flavor and tenderness. Pick pods young and often, around five to six inches, to encourage continued production and to catch them before they toughen. The striking purple pods also make the plants easy to spot for harvest against their green foliage.

name: Triple Treat Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after all danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed; Triple Treat earns its name by combining a decorative round orange fruit, pie-quality flesh, and hull-less seeds that can be roasted without shelling.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil after the last frost, thinning to two or three vigorous plants per hill. Triple Treat produces a 6 to 8 pound jack-o-lantern-shaped pumpkin whose flesh is sweeter and less watery than typical carving pumpkins, but the real distinction is its naked, hull-less seeds, which can be scooped out, rinsed, and roasted directly without the tough seed coat found in most pumpkin varieties. Harvest once the rind has hardened fully and resists a fingernail scratch, then cure in a warm, airy spot for a week before moving to cool storage. Because it excels at carving, baking, and snacking all from one fruit, it rewards gardeners who want maximum use from a single vine.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Trocadero Lettuce
plantingNote: Sow directly in early spring and again in late summer, since it resists bolting better than most soft-leaf lettuces.
directions: Sow directly in early spring and again in late summer, since it resists bolting better than most soft-leaf lettuces and holds quality through warm spells. A French Batavian heirloom dating to the 1880s, Trocadero forms loose, crunchy pale-green heads with a crisp, sweet, faintly nutty flavor reminiscent of iceberg but grown far more easily. It was long grown in French market gardens as a reliable source of crisp texture without the fuss of true crisphead types.

name: Trombetta di Albenga Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil is thoroughly warm and frost risk has passed; train the vigorous climbing vines onto a sturdy trellis to keep the long fruit straight and off the ground.
directions: Trombetta di Albenga is a climbing zucchetta-type summer squash from the Ligurian coast of Italy, related to the more widely known Tromboncino but grown and selected as its own distinct regional strain around the town of Albenga. The curved, trumpet-shaped fruit reaches twelve to fifteen inches and is prized for its firm, nearly seedless flesh concentrated in the long neck (seeds sit only in the small bulbous end), with a mild, artichoke-like flavor that holds up better than typical zucchini when sliced and sauteed. Because it is a true climber, giving it a trellis rather than letting it sprawl saves garden space and produces straighter, easier-to-harvest fruit; left on the vine past the summer-squash stage it also matures into a nutty-flavored winter squash.

name: Tromboncino Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost and provide a trellis or sturdy fence immediately; tromboncino climbs vigorously and produces better-formed, straighter fruits when grown vertically than when sprawling on the ground.
directions: Sow seeds and train the vine up a strong trellis or chain-link fence; tromboncino is an Italian heirloom climbing zucchini with long, curved fruits shaped like a trombone — reaching 20–30 inches when mature — harvested young at 10–15 inches as a summer squash substitute with a nutty, buttery flavor. Being Cucurbita moschata rather than C. pepo, tromboncino has excellent resistance to squash vine borer — the borer does not prefer this species, making it the best choice for gardeners who have lost zucchini crops to this destructive pest. It also tolerates heat and humidity better than most summer squash. Fruits left to mature fully develop into golden winter squash with superb flavor; the seeds are also edible roasted.

name: Tropic Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9–11 this is an outstanding tomato for both spring and fall production — developed specifically for tropical and subtropical climates where standard varieties fail to set fruit in summer heat. In South Florida and the Gulf Coast, Tropic outlasts other varieties well into summer.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set plants in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil; Tropic tomato was developed at the University of Florida IFAS and released in 1963 specifically for tropical and subtropical climates — the most durable, disease-resistant open-pollinated tomato for zone 8b–12. It continues setting fruit at temperatures where most tomatoes stop, has resistance to fusarium wilt, verticillium wilt, and gray leaf spot (the diseases that devastate most tomatoes in South Florida's humid heat), and produces good-sized (6–8 oz), red, globe-shaped fruits with solid, meaty flesh and good flavor from spring well into summer. For Gulf Coast and Florida gardeners who struggle with tomato diseases and summer heat, Tropic remains the benchmark open-pollinated variety after 60 years because no other variety has combined its disease resistance and tropical performance as consistently.

name: Trucker's Favorite Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; in zone 9 plant March–May. Plant in blocks of at least 4 rows for good wind pollination — long single rows pollinate poorly, resulting in incomplete ear fill. In zone 9 plant in spring and again in August for a fall crop. Trucker's Favorite has a broader window between roasting-ear and field-corn stages than modern sweet corn — if roasting-ear harvest is missed, the larger, dough-stage ears can be used for grits and dried cornmeal.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil with good air circulation; Trucker's Favorite is an open-pollinated Southern heirloom corn variety that was the standard large-eared roasting corn sold at Southern roadside stands, farmers markets, and farm stands for much of the 20th century — the 'trucker' in the name refers to produce truck farmers who grew it as their preferred selling variety because the large ears (8–10 inches, white to yellow-white kernels) made an impressive and reliably satisfying roasting ear crop. At the roasting-ear stage (about 20 days after silk), the white to cream-colored ears are tender, starchy-sweet, and deeply flavored with the old-fashioned, rich, full corn character that modern hybrid sweet corns bred for extreme sugar content often lack — a more complex, substantial corn flavor similar to mid-century American corn. As a dual-purpose variety, Trucker's Favorite dried to an excellent yellow cornmeal with full corn flavor prized for Southern cornbread, grits, and polenta.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Trucker's Favorite Heirloom Corn
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Southern Heirloom Corn Varieties
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Heirloom Sweet and Field Corn

name: Trucker's Favorite Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Trucker's Favorite is a vigorous indeterminate variety with good foliage disease tolerance that still benefits from staking to keep fruit clusters off the ground.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil, staking to support the vigorous vines. Trucker's Favorite is a pre-1900 heirloom traced to Burlington County, New Jersey and offered commercially by W. Atlee Burpee before 1899; it was named for its popularity among market gardeners hauling produce to city markets. The plants set clusters of 3-4 crack-resistant, 6-12 ounce pink beefsteak-type fruit with a rich, sweet, old-fashioned flavor and notably good foliage disease resistance for an heirloom of its era.

name: Truckers Favorite White Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil reaches 60°F; Truckers Favorite White is one of the most historically significant Southern market garden corns — grown for over 150 years by market farmers (the 'truckers' who hauled produce to market) for its excellent fresh-eating quality at the roasting ear stage, large white kernels, tall productive plants, and reliable performance in the hot, humid summer conditions of the South.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least 4 rows for good pollination; thin to 8–12 inches; Truckers Favorite is tall and produces 1–2 ears per stalk; harvest at the milk stage (when kernels exude a milky liquid when punctured) for best fresh-eating quality; allow to dry on the stalk for grinding into grits or cornmeal. Truckers Favorite White Corn is a classic Southern open-pollinated white dent corn that has been grown in the American South since before the Civil War and takes its name from the small-scale produce farmers ('truckers') who grew and hauled vegetables to regional markets throughout the 19th and early 20th centuries — the same context that gave rise to terms like 'truck farming' and 'market gardening.' The variety was selected over generations specifically for the combination of early-maturing roasting ear quality (harvested at the milk stage for fresh eating) and excellent flour/grits quality when allowed to dry fully. The white kernels are large and doughy at the roasting ear stage, sweet enough for fresh eating but not as sugary as modern sweet corn varieties — the characteristic semi-sweet, starchy quality that old-fashioned cornbread and grits recipes were designed around. In the Gulf South, Truckers Favorite White is particularly valued as a heritage Southern cornbread corn — ground into coarse grits or fine meal, it produces the authentic white stone-ground cornmeal preferred in traditional Southern cooking. Plants are tall (7–9 feet), productive, and heat tolerant, maturing in the relatively modest time of 85–95 days that suits the Gulf Coast growing season.

name: True Red Cranberry Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after frost danger passes and soil has warmed; pole plants need a sturdy trellis. Pick at the shell stage around 65 days or let pods dry fully for storage beans around 90–100 days.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep directly in warm soil at the base of a sturdy pole or trellis, since this is a vigorous climbing variety. True Red Cranberry is a New England heirloom dating to the 1700s, producing plump, cream-colored pods streaked in deep red-maroon that shell out to reveal beans mottled in burgundy and cream, cooking up to a rich, nutty flavor and creamy texture prized for baked beans and soups. Pick pods at the shell-bean stage for the best flavor and texture, or leave them to dry fully on the vine for long-term storage as a dry bean. Because it is open-pollinated, seed can be saved season to season to continue the variety.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

name: Truhart Perfection Pimiento Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; Truhart Perfection was released by the Georgia Experiment Station in 1943 through pedigree selection out of the older Perfection pimiento for a higher percentage of uniform, heart-shaped, thick-walled fruit, and it became the standard variety of the American pimiento canning industry for decades.
directions: Truhart Perfection traces to a single outstanding plant selected from the original 1913 Perfection pimiento introduction, and the Georgia Experiment Station's pedigree breeding program refined it into the thick-walled, carmine-red, heart-shaped fruit that defined jarred pimientos and pimiento cheese for most of the twentieth century. Unlike its later nematode-resistant derivative Truhart-NR, the straight Truhart Perfection line carries no built-in resistance to root-knot nematode, so gardeners on sandy, nematode-prone soils should rotate plantings or solarize beds between crops. The blocky, three-lobed fruit ripens from green to deep red with sweet, dense flesh well suited to roasting, canning, and stuffing. Stake or cage plants once fruit loads heavily, and pick at full red color for the richest flavor and color in preserved pimientos.
sources: University of Georgia College of Agriculture Experiment Stations — Truhart Perfection Pimiento
ResearchGate — Truhart-NR, a Root-Knot Nematode Resistant Pimento-Type Pepper Cultivar

name: Truhart-NR Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; released by USDA-ARS in 2009, it combines the classic 'Truhart Perfection' pimiento type with the nematode resistance of Mississippi Nemaheart, giving Gulf South gardeners a higher-yielding nematode-resistant pimiento than older resistant lines.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once the soil has warmed. Truhart-NR was developed by USDA-ARS through a backcross program that introduced the dominant root-knot nematode resistance gene from Mississippi Nemaheart into the 'Truhart Perfection' pimiento background, and it was released in 2009 after field trials showed it outyielding its susceptible parent with heavier, longer, thicker-walled fruit. The blocky, three-lobed pimiento fruit ripens to deep red with sweet, thick flesh suited to fresh eating, roasting, and pimiento cheese. It is particularly valuable for organic and specialty growers along the Gulf Coast who lack easy access to chemical nematicides and garden in nematode-infested sandy soils.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service, U.S. Vegetable Laboratory (Charleston, SC)

name: Tsakoniki Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm, well-drained soil once nights stay reliably above 55°F.
directions: Tsakoniki is a slender heirloom eggplant traditionally grown around Leonidio in the Tsakonia region of the Greek Peloponnese, where it holds European Protected Designation of Origin status. Fruits are thin and elongated with a pointed end, their purple skin softened by pale white streaks, and the flesh is notably sweet and tender with little of the bitterness common to larger eggplant types. Local growers traditionally raise it on sandy, terraced plots near the coast, but it adapts well to any warm, well-drained garden bed with full sun. Harvest fruits while still slender and glossy for the mildest flavor, and pick regularly to keep plants setting new fruit through the season.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity (Ark of Taste)

name: Tudela Artichoke
plantingNote: Establish from rooted offshoots or crowns in autumn along the irrigated Ebro riverbanks of Navarra, where mild winters let plants push the small, tender buds prized for canning.
directions: Grown along the fertile Ebro floodplain around Tudela in Navarra, this artichoke is harvested young and small, often as whole baby buds or hearts, and is the classic ingredient behind Spain's prized jarred corazones de alcachofa. Give it deep, rich, constantly moist soil, since the region's river-fed irrigation is what produces the characteristically tender, nearly spineless bud that needs little trimming. Harvest buds while still tight and only a few inches across for the best canning quality, cutting continuously through the cool growing season to encourage further lateral budding.

name: Tumbling Tom Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Tumbling Tom is specifically bred for hanging baskets, window boxes, and tumbling over the edges of large containers — the cascading, pendulous stems trail 18–24 inches and look spectacular draped over pot edges. Plant one per 12-inch hanging basket or 2–3 per large container. In zone 9, transplant in March–April for a May–June cherry tomato harvest from the patio or balcony.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into a hanging basket, window box, or large container with rich, well-draining potting mix. Water consistently (containers dry out faster than in-ground plantings) and fertilize every 2 weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer for best production. Tumbling Tom is a compact, pendulous-stemmed cherry tomato developed specifically for container and hanging basket growing — the first cherry tomato variety widely distributed with 'tumbling' in the name to describe its characteristic cascading habit, where the naturally trailing stems drape over pot edges and hang 18–24 inches below the rim, making it one of the most dramatic edible container plants available. Unlike most cherry tomatoes, which require staking and training on indeterminate vines that climb 5–8 feet, Tumbling Tom is a bushy, pendent type that requires no staking, no caging, and no training — just water, light, and fertilizer. The plants produce abundant clusters of small (1–1.5 inch), round, bright red cherry tomatoes with good sweet tomato flavor on the pendulous stems; a large hanging basket with a well-established Tumbling Tom plant loaded with red fruits is a genuinely beautiful and productive edible ornamental display. Available in both red and yellow strains ('Tumbling Tom Red' and 'Tumbling Tom Yellow'). Ideal for balconies, patios, decks, and any space where in-ground gardening is not possible.
sources: Thompson & Morgan — Tumbling Tom cherry tomato variety notes
Suttons Seeds — Container tomato growing guide
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato for Home Landscapes

name: Tumbling Tom Yellow Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Tumbling Tom Yellow is the golden-fruited counterpart to the standard red Tumbling Tom, bred for the same hanging basket and container use. Plant one per 12-inch hanging basket or 2-3 per large container.
directions: Tumbling Tom Yellow is the yellow-fruited strain sold alongside standard red Tumbling Tom, sharing the same compact, naturally trailing, pendent growth habit bred specifically for hanging baskets, window boxes, and large containers rather than staking or caging. Plants stay small, under a foot wide, but the cascading stems drape 12 to 18 inches over the basket rim, loaded with abundant small, sweet, fruity golden-yellow cherry tomatoes that ripen a few days later than the red strain. Because containers dry out faster than garden soil, water consistently and feed every 1-2 weeks with a balanced liquid fertilizer to sustain the heavy, continuous fruit set. No staking, caging, or pruning is needed; simply keep picking to encourage continued flowering, and pair it with the red strain in matched baskets for a two-tone display.

name: Turban Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost; Turban squash is both an ornamental and edible winter squash producing the most architecturally dramatic fruits in the cucurbit family — a protruding 'cap' or acorn-like secondary lobe emerges from the top of the main squash creating the distinctive turban shape in brilliant orange and cream and green swirling patterns.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost in rich, well-amended soil in full sun; provide 6–8 feet of space for sprawling vines. Turban squash (also called Turk's Cap, Turk's Turban, or French Turban) is one of the most visually distinctive of all winter squash, producing medium to large (5–10 lb) fruits with a dramatic secondary lobe or 'cap' protruding from the blossom end in a shape resembling a Turkish turban or Ottoman fez — this unusual morphology is a Cucurbita maxima trait that occasionally appears in several varieties but is most pronounced and reliable in this dedicated 'Turban' selection. The skin is spectacularly patterned in orange, cream, and green with mottled, swirling patterns that vary between fruits; the ornamental quality makes Turban squash one of the most popular fall decorative squashes alongside regular pumpkins. The flesh is edible with a mild, somewhat dry, floury texture and pleasant squash flavor well-suited to stuffing — the cap portion is often removed and used as a natural serving bowl for soups or stuffings.

name: Turga Parsnip
plantingNote: Direct sow fresh seed as soon as the soil can be worked in spring; Turga is a long-season Hungarian heirloom that tolerates heavier soils better than many parsnip types.
directions: Sow seed thinly and shallowly in deeply worked, stone-free soil, keeping the bed evenly moist through the slow, erratic germination and thinning seedlings to a few inches apart once established. Turga is a Hungarian heirloom valued for producing stout, smoothly tapered roots that size up reliably even in soils too heavy or shallow for some other parsnip types, with a dense, creamy-white interior and a rich, distinctly sweet flavor. Leave roots in the ground through the first hard frosts before digging, since the cold converts starches to sugar and gives Turga its full sweet, almost nutty character. Because parsnip seed loses viability quickly, always start with fresh seed for the season.

name: Turk's Turban Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm; Turk's Turban is grown as much for ornament as for eating — the extraordinary multi-colored fruits with their protruding turban-shaped secondary lobe are among the most visually dramatic of any squash, making them a centerpiece of autumn decorations and farmers' market displays as well as a rich-flavored eating squash.
directions: Direct sow in hills of 3 seeds (thin to 2) after last frost in a fertile, well-drained bed; Turk's Turban produces medium-length vines of 6–8 feet; harvest when the skin is fully hard and the color has developed to its mature orange-red with green and white swirling markings; cure at room temperature for 2–3 weeks to harden the rind and improve flavor. Turk's Turban is one of the most visually spectacular squashes in cultivation — an heirloom Cucurbita maxima variety that has been grown in American and European gardens since the 19th century, renowned for the extraordinary shape of its fruits: a squat, flattened orange-red primary body topped by a rounded, turban-like secondary lobe that protrudes from the blossom end, often striped or mottled in contrasting shades of green, cream, and orange. The distinctive shape comes from an unusual growth pattern in which the secondary floral section of the fruit expands outward from the blossom end, creating the appearance of a hat or turban imposed on top of the primary fruit body. No two Turk's Turban fruits are exactly alike in their color patterning — each shows a unique arrangement of orange, green, cream, and white in swirls and stripes that makes them natural art objects. The flesh beneath is the dense, sweet, orange type characteristic of the best Cucurbita maxima varieties; at full maturity after curing, the flavor is rich and sweet with a dry, starchy texture excellent for baking, soups, and puréeing. While widely grown as a purely ornamental squash for autumn display, Turk's Turban is fully edible and good-flavored — it deserves to be eaten rather than simply displayed.

name: Turkey Craw Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in well-drained soil; Turkey Craw is a half-runner or semi-vining type requiring 2–3 feet of support. It is heat-tolerant once established and produces prolifically through Gulf Coast summer conditions that discourage northern bean varieties.
directions: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing low supports of 2–3 feet for the semi-vining plants; Turkey Craw is an Appalachian heirloom snap bean dating back at least to the 19th century, named for seeds reportedly found in the crop (craw) of a wild turkey shot by a hunter — the story illustrating how food plants spread naturally through the American South via birds and early farmers. It is a cutshort type, meaning the seeds are crowded together in the pod and shortened in length to accommodate more seeds — the characteristic shape that identifies many traditional Southern snap beans. The pods are tender and flavorful when harvested young as snap beans, or the plants can be allowed to mature for dry bean use. Excellent heat tolerance and prolific production make it a dependable Southern garden bean; the seeds' tan and brown mottling is distinctive and appealing.

name: Turkey Red Wheat
plantingNote: Drill or broadcast in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, so seedlings establish a strong root system and low rosette before winter dormancy.
directions: Drill or broadcast in fall, 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes, so seedlings establish a strong root system and low rosette before winter dormancy, then resume growth and head out in late spring. Turkey Red was carried to Kansas by Mennonite immigrants from the Crimea and southern Russia in the 1870s, and its exceptional cold hardiness and drought tolerance helped transform the Great Plains into the wheat-growing heartland of the United States, effectively founding the American hard red winter wheat industry. The bran-red kernels mill into strong, high-protein bread flour with a robust, slightly sweet flavor, and the variety remains popular today among heritage-grain bakers and small growers for its resilience on marginal, low-input land.

name: Turkish Orange Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Turkish Orange can be harvested at two stages — green (immature, mildest) or orange (ripe, slightly sweeter and more complex). Harvest at the orange stage for the full Turkish Orange experience; at this stage the skin may show some streaking or mottling. In zone 9, transplant March–April. The plants are ornamental as well as edible — the clusters of round, orange, tomato-like fruits are visually striking in the garden.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 80–85°F; transplant to full sun. Harvest at the orange stage when fruits are 2–3 inches in diameter for full flavor development. Turkish Orange is an heirloom eggplant from Turkey that produces compact, round fruits 2–3 inches in diameter that ripen from green to a deep, vibrant orange-red — a color completely unlike any other common eggplant and more reminiscent of a small tomato or tomatillo than a traditional eggplant. This color difference signals a different flavor profile: Turkish Orange eggplants are slightly sweeter than standard purple types, with less bitterness and a slightly more complex, slightly acidic note at the ripe orange stage. The plants are productive and ornamental — clusters of round, orange fruits hanging from attractive, somewhat spiny plants create a striking garden display that frequently prompts questions from visitors unfamiliar with the variety. The flesh is firm, white to cream-colored, and suitable for all standard eggplant preparations; the round shape makes them particularly interesting for stuffing whole, hollowing and filling with rice-and-meat preparations in the Turkish culinary tradition from which the variety originates.
sources: Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Turkish Orange eggplant variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — Heirloom eggplant collection
Seeds of Change — Unusual eggplant variety descriptions

name: Turnpike Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Turnpike carries resistance to an unusually wide range of bacterial leaf spot races plus Phytophthora blight and tobacco mosaic virus, one of the broadest disease packages available in a bell pepper for humid, disease-heavy climates like the Gulf South.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Turnpike is a bell pepper hybrid bred with resistance to a wide range of bacterial leaf spot races along with Phytophthora blight and tobacco mosaic virus, giving it one of the broadest disease packages available in a commercial bell pepper and making it especially well suited to the combination of heat, humidity, and rainfall pressure found across the Gulf South. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good eating quality if left on the plant. Because it resists so many distinct disease pathogens at once, Turnpike tends to hold healthy foliage and continue setting fruit through conditions that would knock back less resistant varieties. Harvest at the green stage for milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red for maximum sweetness.
sources: seed catalog reference (Rupp Seeds, Harris Seeds, Seedway)
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pepper Production

name: Tuscarora White Corn
plantingNote: Sow in blocks in fertile, hilled soil; this soft flour corn needs the full warm season to fill out its large, starchy kernels and should dry fully on the stalk before harvest.
directions: Plant in blocks of several rows, hilling soil slightly around the base of the stalks as they grow for stability. Tuscarora White is a traditional soft flour corn grown by the Tuscarora Nation, one of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy centered historically in present-day New York, and documented in American agricultural writing since the colonial period for its large, chalky-white kernels. The soft starch content makes the kernels especially suited to hominy and parching, as well as fine grinding into flour. Let ears cure fully on the stalk through fall before harvesting and shelling.

name: Tuxana Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil after frost; plant in blocks for pollination and give the full-season plants room to reach their mature height.
directions: Tuxana is a modern, open-pollinated white sweet corn developed in southern Oregon by stabilizing a cross between an Anasazi flour corn landrace and a sugary-enhanced hybrid, now maintained and distributed as an Open Source Seed Initiative-pledged variety. Seven-foot stalks generally produce two eight-inch ears with twelve to sixteen rows of large, deep kernels that cook up rich, creamy, and sweet without the cloying intensity of supersweet hybrids. Because it breeds true, gardeners can save seed year to year, making it a good option for anyone wanting hybrid-level ear quality in a variety they can maintain themselves. Isolate from other corn types at pollination time to keep seed pure.

name: Tuxedo Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow in blocks of at least 4 rows wide for wind pollination; Tuxedo is a supersweet (sh2) type that requires isolation of at least 250 feet from su, se, or other sh2 varieties with different genetics to prevent starchy cross-pollination. Sh2 varieties also require warmer soil temperatures for reliable germination (65°F minimum, ideally 70°F) and should not be planted as early as su or se types. In zone 9, plant March–April when soils have warmed adequately.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil (65°F minimum) in full sun in blocks of at least 4 rows; fertilize at planting and side-dress with nitrogen at knee height. Isolate from other corn varieties (including other sh2 types) by 250+ feet or stagger planting dates by 2+ weeks. Tuxedo is a bicolor (white and yellow kernel) supersweet (sh2) hybrid that has become one of the most popular bicolor fresh-market and roadside stand corns in the eastern United States — a Syngenta/Rogers Brothers variety that delivers the maximum sweetness possible from the sh2 gene type combined with a visually appealing bicolor kernel appearance that many consumers associate with premium sweet corn. The sh2 (shrunken-2) mutation creates corn with up to 4 times the sugar content of standard su types at harvest, and unlike se types, sh2 varieties retain their sweetness for 5–7 days after picking under refrigeration — a major commercial advantage that has made sh2 types dominant in the fresh sweet corn market. Tuxedo produces large (7.5–9 inch), well-filled ears with 16–18 rows of alternating white and yellow kernels; the kernels are very tender with thin skins and intensely sweet flavor when harvested at peak. The bicolor appearance in uniform, well-filled ears of Tuxedo is particularly attractive for roadside stand and farmers market sales where visual appeal drives purchasing decisions. One of the most commercially successful bicolor sh2 varieties of the past two decades.
sources: Syngenta Vegetables / Rogers Brothers — Tuxedo sweet corn
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Supersweet Bicolor Corn Variety Comparison
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Sweet Corn Cultivar Evaluation

name: Two Star Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or fall; Two Star is a dark green Waldmann's-type leaf lettuce bred to bolt roughly a week later than standard Waldmann's Green while holding good flavor into warm weather, useful for stretching the Gulf Coast spring lettuce season.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil; Two Star is a dark green, savoyed leaf lettuce bred as a slower-bolting improvement on the classic Waldmann's Green type, holding its mild, sweet flavor and tender texture longer into warm weather before turning bitter and running to seed. The loose, upright rosette of ruffled leaves is well suited to cut-and-come-again harvesting, letting a single planting supply salads over several weeks. Provide afternoon shade during hot spells to further slow bolting, and keep soil evenly moist, since drought stress speeds up flowering in any leaf lettuce. Sow successively every 2-3 weeks through the cool season for a steady, continuous harvest.
sources: seed catalog reference (Harris Seeds, Territorial Seed Company, Stokes Seeds)

name: Tycoon Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost; transplant in zone 9 February–March for spring production and again in early August for a fall crop. Tycoon is a heat-tolerant determinate hybrid bred specifically for the Southern United States with strong resistance to Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt races 1–2, and nematodes.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil with a cage or stake; Tycoon is a determinate, heat-tolerant hybrid tomato that produces concentrated harvests of large, smooth, firm red globe tomatoes averaging 10–12 ounces. Its compact determinate habit keeps the plant manageable in the garden while still delivering excellent yields suited to canning, slicing, and fresh eating. Bred for Southern growing conditions, Tycoon sets fruit reliably when temperatures climb into the upper 80s and maintains production longer than many other large-fruited varieties. Strong disease resistance package including resistance to Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt (races 1 and 2), and root-knot nematodes makes it especially valuable in zone 9 soils where these pathogens are widespread.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Florida Tomato Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomato Varieties for Texas
North Carolina State Extension — Determinate Tomato Variety Trials

name: Tyee Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall for cool-season production; Tyee is particularly valued for fall and overwinter production where its disease resistance and cold tolerance are most advantageous. In zone 9, sow September–November for harvest November–February. For spring production, sow February–March as soon as soil can be worked. Germination occurs in very cool soils (35°F) but is slowest below 45°F; optimal germination is at 50–65°F.
directions: Direct sow seeds 0.5 inch deep in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil; thin to 2–4 inch spacing as seedlings develop and use thinnings in salads. Tyee is a 1987 All-America Selections-winning spinach that has maintained its status as one of the most recommended disease-resistant spinach varieties for over 35 years — a semi-savoy (slightly crinkled leaf) hybrid that combines excellent productivity with broad disease resistance. The 'semi-savoy' designation means the leaves have moderate crinkle — more texture and surface area than flat leaf types but less crinkle than fully savoy varieties, striking a balance between the ornamental quality of savoy and the easy washing of flat types. Tyee's most important attributes are its comprehensive disease resistance: it carries resistance to five races of downy mildew (Peronospora farinosa), the primary fungal disease that terminates spinach crops early in humid and wet conditions. This resistance profile extends the productive season dramatically compared to susceptible varieties that collapse when mildew strikes. The dark green, upright, medium-large leaves are tender and mild-flavored with the classic, clean spinach taste. Tyee remains the benchmark spinach variety against which others are evaluated in university trials, consistently placing at or near the top for yield, disease resistance, and leaf quality.
sources: All-America Selections — Tyee spinach AAS winner 1987
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Spinach variety disease resistance comparison
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Spinach Variety Evaluation

name: Tygress Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 start in January for March transplanting. Tygress was an AAS Vegetable Award winner selected in part for resistance to tomato spotted wilt virus, a serious thrips-spread disease in warm climates.
directions: Start seeds 6-8 weeks before transplanting at 70-80F; Tygress is a beefsteak-type hybrid tomato and All-America Selections vegetable winner bred with strong resistance to tomato spotted wilt virus (TSWV), a thrips-vectored disease that can devastate warm-climate tomato plantings with little warning. Fruits are large, meaty, and red with the classic beefsteak texture prized for slicing and sandwiches, produced on vigorous indeterminate vines that need sturdy staking or caging. Because TSWV pressure is worst where thrips populations build up in hot weather, Tygress is a particularly useful choice for Gulf South gardens that have struggled with sudden wilting and bronzed, ring-spotted fruit in past seasons. Keep watering even to avoid cracking and blossom end rot, and scout for thrips on new growth even though the plant tolerates the virus they carry.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Variety Trials
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomato Variety Selection

name: Uber Arugula
plantingNote: Direct sow every 2 weeks from early spring through fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Uber combines the fast, uniform growth of standard salad arugula with the deeply lobed, wild-arugula-style leaf shape favored by chefs.
directions: Broadcast or row-sow seed shallowly (about 1/8 inch deep) into cool, moist soil for quick, even germination. Uber produces fast-growing, deeply lobed leaves that give it the refined look of wild arugula while keeping the speed and uniformity of a standard salad-type strain, with a mild, nutty, peppery flavor. It performs especially well as a winter crop in high tunnels or cool greenhouses and tolerates cold better than many salad arugulas. Cut leaves about an inch above the soil line for quick regrowth, and cover new plantings with floating row cover to keep flea beetles off young seedlings.

name: UC 157 Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant one-year-old crowns in early spring in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; UC 157 is a classic hybrid asparagus bred at the University of California, valued for concentrated, uniform spear emergence that suits both machine and hand harvesting.
directions: Plant crowns 6-8 inches deep in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, backfilling gradually as shoots emerge. UC 157 is a long-standing, widely planted hybrid asparagus developed by the University of California, prized for producing spears in a more concentrated, uniform flush than many older varieties, along with good heat tolerance that suits warmer growing regions better than some Northeastern-bred cultivars. It has been a mainstay of commercial asparagus production for decades and performs well in home gardens too, given deep, well-drained soil and full sun. As with other asparagus, avoid harvesting the first year and harvest lightly the second year to let the crown establish a strong root system for many years of future spring harvests.

name: Udumalapet Eggplant
subcategory: large green-striped South Indian heirloom eggplant
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost date and transplant into warm soil once nighttime temperatures stay above 55F.
directions: Sow indoors and transplant into full sun once the weather is reliably warm, giving plants sturdy stakes since the fruit can grow quite large and heavy. Regular, deep watering helps produce tender, sweet flesh. Udumalapet takes its name from a town in Tamil Nadu, India, and is grown for its large, rounded fruit with pale green skin marked by faint white striping. Home cooks favor it for curries and roasting because of its mild flavor and relatively few seeds.

name: Ukrainian Purple Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into full sun once frost danger has passed, giving the long vines a tall support from the start.
directions: Ukrainian Purple, also sold as Purple Russian, is an indeterminate heirloom valued for its elongated plum-shaped fruit that ripens to a deep, dusky purple-brown often tinged with green near the shoulders. The rich, sweet-tart flesh is meaty and relatively low in juice, so the fruit holds together well in sauces and salsas while still tasting good eaten fresh. It stays productive later into cool fall weather than many heirlooms, tolerating temperatures that would stop lighter-fruited varieties. Stake or cage the vigorous vine early and keep watering consistent to limit cracking on the thin-skinned fruit as it ripens.

name: Ulster Emblem Potato
plantingNote: A reliable grower on damp ground; its foliage carries above-average late blight resistance, so it can be left standing a little longer in a wet autumn.
directions: Ulster Emblem was bred in 1966 by J. Clarke of Ballymoney, County Antrim, part of a wave of Northern Irish varieties selected specifically for standing up to late blight. The plants carry red-violet flowers and pink sprouts, useful markers for identifying seed stock, before setting long oval tubers with white skin and a semi-waxy white flesh. That semi-waxy texture keeps slices intact through boiling, so it suits potato salads and gratins better than heavy mashing. Harvest once the vines have largely died back, since the variety's main strength is a dependable, disease-resistant yield rather than exceptional earliness.

name: Ultra Violet Corn
plantingNote: Direct seed once soil has reached at least 55-60F (treated seed) or 65F (untreated); plant in blocks of at least 4 rows for pollination.
directions: Ultra Violet is a new-for-2026 sh2 super-sweet corn from Johnny's Selected Seeds, prized for 8-inch ears with 14-20 rows of multicolored pink, purple, and white kernels that hold their vivid color through boiling, blanching, or grilling. Plants grow tall, 6-12 feet, with deep purple stalk coloration, strong husk protection, and excellent row fill even late in the sh2 maturity window of about 80 days. Direct seed 3/4-1 inch deep and 6-9 inches apart in rows 30-36 inches apart, thinning as needed, and plant in blocks rather than single rows to ensure full pollination. Give it full sun and consistent moisture through tasseling and ear fill.

name: Uluru Ochre Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; the compact 2-4 ft dwarf-indeterminate habit suits raised beds and containers, and it is an early, prolific producer among dwarfs.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost into fertile, well-drained soil, staking lightly since the sturdy stems need less support than sprawling indeterminate types. Uluru Ochre bears ruffled, oblate fruit with orange flesh tinged in green, giving each tomato an amber, earthy appearance that inspired its name after the Australian landmark; the flavor is rich and complex when the plant is at its best. It began as a cross between an orange heirloom and Rosella Purple made by Patrina Nuske Small, stabilized by a team of Dwarf Tomato Project volunteers, and released as an OSSI-pledged variety. Harvest as fruit ripens fully on the vine.

name: Umpqua Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors 5-6 weeks before transplanting; for zone 8-9 fall crops, transplant in late August-September so the long harvest window carries production through the cooler months without bolting.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 14-20 inches apart in rows 24-36 inches apart. Umpqua is an open-pollinated variety developed at Territorial Seed Company in Oregon and named for the Umpqua River; it is prized for producing large, uniform, dark-green 5-8 inch heads with big beads that size up quickly, then continuing to yield heavily from side shoots over an unusually long harvest window. Because it is open-pollinated rather than a hybrid, home gardeners can save true-to-type seed from year to year, making it a good choice for growers who want to build a self-sufficient seed-saving rotation into their fall brassica planting. Its long production season rewards steady feeding and consistent moisture, since plants left to dry out or run short on nitrogen will cut the side-shoot harvest short.

name: Uncle David's Dakota Dessert
plantingNote: Direct seed after soil is warm, or save up to 20 days by transplanting started seedlings out after frost.
directions: David Podoll's family has grown and reselected this buttercup for about 70 years, crossing it with Hubbard-type maximas along the way to boost sweetness, vigor, and cold hardiness, which is why he calls it 'the original buttercup.' The green-skinned fruits have thick flesh and small seed cavities, and the family bakes them into pies with no added sweetener needed. Give the sprawling vines plenty of room and a full season of warmth, and expect somewhat bumpy, button-ended fruit typical of the type. It stores well into winter as a dense, all-purpose squash for both savory and dessert uses.

name: Unity Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-7 weeks before transplanting; supplemental lighting recommended for greenhouse/tunnel production.
directions: Unity is a new-for-2026 organic F1 beefsteak tomato bred by Dr. Kevin Cook at Johnny's Selected Seeds in collaboration with NCSU, built for high-performing early production in field and tunnel. Fruit is attractive with a light green shoulder, weighing 8-12 ounces with few defects and a mild, pleasing flavor typical of the beefsteak class. The compact, generative indeterminate plants are easier to train than average and come into production early, backed by a disease resistance package covering Fusarium wilt, late blight, nematodes, leaf molds, and verticillium wilt. Allow 4-6 square feet of growing area per leader when trellising and pruning for tunnel or greenhouse culture.

name: Unrivalled Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow thinly in early spring in moist, fertile soil; Unrivalled is a Victorian-era English kitchen garden heirloom grown for dependable heading under cool, short-season conditions.
directions: Unrivalled is an English butterhead heirloom from Victorian-era kitchen garden seed catalogs, grown for dependable, well-formed heads under the cooler, shorter-season conditions typical of British gardens. Direct sow thinly in early spring in moist, fertile soil, thinning seedlings to about 8 to 10 inches apart so each plant can round out into a compact, soft-leaved head. The pale green outer leaves wrap a creamy, tender heart with the mild, buttery flavor typical of older European butterhead types. Succession sow every few weeks through the cool season for a steady supply, since like most butterheads it bolts quickly once hot weather arrives.

name: Up to Date Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow once frost danger has passed and soil is warm; this late-Victorian English heirloom was bred for cool-summer frame and ridge culture and appreciates a trellis for straight, clean fruit.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil after last frost, or start under glass and transplant carefully where summers run cool, since this old English variety was originally developed for outdoor ridge culture and cold-frame growing in Britain. Train vines up a trellis or string support to produce long, smooth, dark green fruit with fewer kinks than unsupported sprawling vines typically produce. Harvest at 10-12 inches while the skin is still glossy and firm, picking regularly to prevent any one fruit from maturing fully and slowing further production. Up to Date remains one of the old English slicing cucumbers still occasionally offered by British heritage seed houses alongside better-known Victorian types.

name: Upper Ground Sweet Potato Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in well-drained soil; this moschata heirloom shrugs off Gulf South heat and resists squash vine borer far better than maxima or pepo types, making it a reliable choice where summer squash borer pressure is severe.
directions: A rugged Appalachian heirloom with vigorous vines and large, dark green metallic-striped leaves, producing abundant round-to-bell-shaped fruit with tan skin and moist, deep-orange flesh that bakes with a texture and sweetness reminiscent of baked sweet potato. Fruits typically run from a few pounds up to 20 pounds at full maturity, and the plant's tolerance for hot, dry conditions and resistance to vine borers make it notably well suited to Southern gardens where many winter squash struggle. Thomas Jefferson grew and documented a squash matching this description at Monticello in the 1790s, and it is still cultivated there today. Give the long vines plenty of room to run and cure harvested fruit for a few weeks before eating to let the sweetness fully develop.

name: Urfa Biber Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Urfa Biber is grown primarily as a drying and spice pepper, traditionally harvested fully ripe, sun-dried by day and sweated under cover by night, a slow process that gives the finished flakes their deep purple-black color and raisiny, smoky flavor.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, then let fruit ripen fully to deep red before harvesting for drying. Urfa Biber takes its name from the city of Sanliurfa in southeastern Turkey, where the pepper is traditionally processed by day-drying the ripe fruit in the sun and wrapping or covering it at night so it sweats and partially reabsorbs moisture, a cycle repeated over several days that develops its signature near-black color, raisin-like sweetness, and mild, smoky, wine-like heat around 30,000-50,000 Scoville units. The moist, oily flakes it produces are a staple spice in Turkish and increasingly in Western kitchens, used to finish roasted vegetables, meats, and eggs where a coarser, sweeter, less sharply hot flavor than crushed red pepper is wanted. A single well-grown plant can produce enough fruit for a good supply of home-dried flakes, and the peppers can also be strung and air-dried in a covered, well-ventilated spot if a controlled sweating setup isn't practical.

name: Ustica Lentil
plantingNote: Direct sow in late winter to early spring while soil is still cool; this small volcanic-island lentil is traditionally dry-farmed and grows best through a cool, rain-fed stretch before summer heat sets in.
directions: Grown on the small volcanic island of Ustica off Sicily's northern coast and recognized as a Slow Food Presidium, this lentil has been cultivated in tiny plots on mineral-rich volcanic soil for generations, surviving almost entirely on winter and spring rainfall with no irrigation. Plants are low, wiry, and bushy with small, pale, quick-cooking seeds that need no pre-soaking and hold a tender bite in soups and simple preparations dressed with local olive oil. Sow in lean soil without added nitrogen, since rich ground pushes foliage instead of pods, and hand-harvest or pull whole plants once most pods have dried and begun to rattle. The crop's isolation on a small island with no large-scale commercial lentil production has helped preserve a distinct, long-standing local landrace.

name: Utah Celery
plantingNote: Start indoors 10–12 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start July–August and transplant September–October for a December–March harvest. Celery germination is slow and requires light — sow on the surface and keep evenly moist at 60–65°F. In zone 9 celery is a winter crop; the Gulf Coast's mild winters allow consistent production from November through March without protection. Consistent irrigation is critical — celery is among the most water-demanding vegetables.
directions: Start indoors and transplant into very fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Utah 52-70 is the standard commercial and home garden celery in North America — an improved Utah-type celery producing tall, upright stalks of thick, crisp, rounded (not hollow) pale-green to cream-colored ribs with a classic, full celery flavor. The '52-70' designation refers to the original development period. Utah-type celery has largely replaced older Pascal types in commercial production because of superior rib thickness, crunchiness, and reduced stringiness compared to older varieties. Celery is among the most demanding vegetables in terms of water and fertility requirements; it grows naturally in moist, fertile wetland soils and demands consistent irrigation and rich soil throughout its long growing period. Blanch by earthing up or wrapping paper around the stalks 2 weeks before harvest to lighten the color and reduce bitterness. In zone 9 celery is exclusively a cool-season vegetable, transplanted in fall and harvested through winter.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Celery
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Celery Production for Florida
University of California Cooperative Extension — Celery Production Guide

name: Uzbek Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves in fall; Turban types like Uzbek sprout and mature earliest of all garlic groups, so they can also be planted a bit later than other hardnecks in mild climates.
directions: Uzbek is a Turban-group hardneck garlic traced to Uzbekistan and brought into North American seed stock decades ago; Turban types are named for the way their bulb wrappers twist and swirl like fabric wound around the cloves. It is among the earliest garlics to mature, with shiny purple-streaked skins over big, earthy-flavored cloves that carry a surprising spicy kick. Because Turban types generally store more briefly than Porcelain or Silverskin garlic, plan to use Uzbek bulbs within a few months of curing rather than holding them for a full year. Give it the same fall planting, spring scape removal, and full-sun culture as other hardnecks.

name: Valencia Peanut
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed well after the last frost, as this variety needs a long, warm growing season to mature its pods underground.
directions: Plant shelled, unroasted seeds about 1.5 inches deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil, since heavy clay makes it hard for pegs to penetrate and form pods. After yellow flowers fade, the plant sends down slender pegs that bury themselves and swell into pods, so hilling loose soil around the base at flowering time helps maximize pod set. Valencia is distinguished from other peanut types by clusters of three or four seeds per pod covered in a thin, bright reddish skin, and its notably sweet flavor makes it the classic choice for boiled peanuts across the South. Plants grow as an upright bunch rather than sprawling, so they fit well in raised beds and smaller garden rows.

name: Valencia Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Valencia is an open-pollinated heirloom — seeds can be saved from the best fruits for successive seasons to maintain a low-acid orange tomato supply.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Valencia is one of the finest and most widely grown orange-fruited heirloom tomatoes — an open-pollinated variety producing medium-large (6–8 oz), round to slightly oblate, smooth, vivid orange fruits with meaty, dense flesh in an orange-gold color and characteristically low acid content combined with fruity sweetness that creates a very clean, mild, sweet flavor quite different from the sharper acid quality of standard red tomatoes. The vivid orange exterior color is striking in the garden and at market — Valencia's clear, bright-orange skin lacks the russet or reddish tones of some orange varieties and produces a consistent, pure-orange appearance across the crop. The low-acid quality makes Valencia particularly appealing to people sensitive to tomato acidity, and the sweet, fruity flavor is excellent in fresh eating, mixed tomato salads (where the orange color provides contrast to red and yellow types), and in light cooking where the low-acid character is preserved. As an open-pollinated heirloom, Valencia produces reliable seed that comes true to type, allowing gardeners to maintain a permanent seed supply. Valencia is an indeterminate variety requiring staking and producing consistently through the season rather than in a single concentrated flush. In zone 9, Valencia performs best in spring (February–May) before summer heat reduces fruit quality.

name: Valentine Rhubarb
plantingNote: Plant crowns or divisions in early spring while still dormant, in deep, fertile soil in full sun; Valentine needs a real winter chill to break dormancy vigorously each year and struggles in mild-winter climates like the Gulf South.
directions: Plant crowns in deep, fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, in full sun. Valentine is a widely grown American rhubarb variety valued for producing thick, deep-red stalks with good color even in the first year or two after planting, when many other rhubarb varieties are still mostly green, and for a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that holds up well in pies, sauces, and preserves. It is a heavy, dependable producer of large stalks on vigorous plants, and the color intensifies further with consistent cold winters and full sun exposure. Harvest by pulling individual outer stalks with a firm twist rather than cutting, leave at least a third of the stalks on the plant at all times to keep it vigorous, and always discard the leaves, which contain oxalic acid and are not safe to eat.

name: Valentine Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; Valentine is a vigorous indeterminate grape tomato bred for very early, heavy, and sustained fruit set, and needs sturdy staking or caging for the long fruiting vine.
directions: Start seeds indoors and transplant after the last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, then stake or cage the vigorous vine well before it needs support. Valentine is an AAS National Winner producing deep red, oblong grape tomatoes with an exceptionally sweet, well-balanced flavor and a notably early, heavy first flush of fruit compared to most grape tomatoes, extending the harvest window at both ends of the season. The disease-resistant vine is highly productive over a long season and holds up well to the heat and humidity of a full Gulf South summer. Harvest fruit as it fully colors for the best sweetness, and pick regularly to keep new clusters setting; the crack-resistant skin makes fruit more forgiving of uneven watering than many cherry and grape types.
sources: All-America Selections — Valentine Tomato winner announcement
university extension AAS trial garden notes

name: Valgros Mâche
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer through early fall for a fall-to-spring harvest in milder climates, or as early as soil can be worked in spring; large seed size makes Valgros easy to space precisely by hand compared to smaller-seeded mâche strains.
directions: Valgros is a named large-seeded mâche strain grown for its bigger, rounder, dark green leaves and the easier, more uniform germination that bigger seed tends to deliver in cold soil. It forms dense, substantial rosettes with the same mild, nutty character common to all corn salad, standing up well to hard frost and light snow once established. As one of the few salad crops that genuinely thrives in the low light of winter, Valgros is a good choice for the shaded side of a cold frame, under the leafless canopy of deciduous trees, or tucked into a partly shaded bed that would otherwise sit empty through the cool months. Keep the soil evenly moist through germination and harvest whole heads once rosettes fill out, well before any hint of a flowering stalk appears as the days lengthen.

name: Valley Girl Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Valley Girl carries resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and Verticillium wilt, and is especially noted for continuing to set fruit under heat stress that causes many other tomatoes to drop blossoms — a strong match for Gulf South summers.
directions: Start seeds at 70-80°F, transplant after soil warms and nights stay above 50°F, then stake or cage the vigorous semi-determinate vines; Valley Girl combines resistance to Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2 and Verticillium wilt with an unusually reliable ability to set fruit under heat stress, when high nighttime temperatures cause many tomato varieties to drop their blossoms without setting fruit. It produces medium-sized (6-8 oz), round, deep red fruit with well-balanced, classic tomato flavor over a long harvest season. Because it keeps fruiting through the hottest stretch of a Gulf South summer that stalls many other varieties, Valley Girl helps bridge the gap between the spring and fall tomato crops. Pick fruit as it ripens to full red color and keep the vines picked regularly to encourage continued production.
sources: seed catalog reference (commercial hybrid seed listings)
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomato Variety Selection for Texas

name: Valmaine Cos Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool soil in early spring and keep moisture even through heading; Valmaine was selected from older cos lines specifically to resist the rib tipburn that even watering was found to prevent.
directions: Valmaine is a tipburn-resistant cos lettuce selected for more dependable heading than older romaine lines prone to rib scorch under heat or irregular watering. Direct sow in cool soil in early spring, thinning to roughly 8 to 10 inches, and keep moisture consistent through head formation since uneven watering is what triggers the tipburn this variety was bred to resist. It forms upright, medium-green heads with crisp ribs and the mild flavor typical of classic cos types, standing a bit longer in the field before bolting than many older selections. Harvest whole heads at firm maturity or pull outer leaves as a cut-and-come-again crop.

name: Vanguard Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date. Vanguard carries resistance to multiple races of bacterial leaf spot, cucumber mosaic virus, and Phytophthora root rot, documented in university trial reports as a strong performer under heavy disease pressure.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost date; Vanguard is a bell pepper hybrid bred with resistance to multiple races of bacterial leaf spot along with tolerance to cucumber mosaic virus and Phytophthora root rot, a combination that has made it a strong performer in university disease-pressure variety trials across the humid Southeast. It produces large, thick-walled, blocky green bells that ripen to red with good sweetness if left on the plant. Because it resists both a major foliar bacterial disease and a major soil-borne root disease, Vanguard tends to hold up better than many varieties through a wet, humid Gulf South growing season. Harvest at the green stage for milder flavor or let fruit fully ripen to red, and keep picking regularly to encourage continued production.
sources: Rutgers University — Pepper Disease Resistance Trials

name: Vaquero Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow into warm soil after last frost; a distinctive black-and-white patterned dry bean popularized by Rancho Gordo and related to the Anasazi bean.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 60F, spacing plants 4-6 inches apart on a bush habit that needs no staking. Vaquero produces striking black-and-white speckled dry seeds reminiscent of an Appaloosa horse's coat, with a light, faintly earthy flavor and a texture often described as potato-like when cooked. Let pods mature and dry fully on the plant before harvesting, then shell and cure the beans in a warm, airy spot for another week or two before storing. This variety cooks into a rich, dark broth and holds its shape well through long, slow simmering, making it a favorite for chilis and pot beans.

name: Vardaman Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips in warm soil after last frost; Vardaman is an exceptionally compact sweet potato whose naturally short vines (24–30 inches) make it the best choice for small beds, containers, and home gardens with limited space.
directions: Plant rooted slips in well-drained, sandy-loam soil in full sun after last frost when soil reaches 65°F; Vardaman is a compact, short-vined sweet potato (24–30 inch vines versus 6–10 feet for standard varieties) developed at Mississippi State University specifically for the home garden, where its restrained spread and ornamental purple foliage make it an attractive edible landscape plant. The orange-flesh tubers are typically smaller than commercial varieties but have excellent rich, sweet flavor and moist texture. An outstanding choice for container growing, raised beds, and small garden spaces where standard sweet potatoes would overwhelm their neighbors. Keeps well in storage and is the most popular sweet potato for the home garden in the southeastern United States.

name: Variegated Daubenton's Kale
plantingNote: Root 4-6 inch stem cuttings in spring or late summer in free-draining potting mix, then plant out into fertile, moisture-retentive soil once well rooted; this sport almost never flowers or sets seed, so cuttings are the only reliable way to propagate true plants.
directions: This is a naturally occurring variegated sport of Daubenton's kale, the centuries-old French perennial brassica that never bolts to seed and is propagated entirely from cuttings. Its thick, slightly crinkled leaves are edged in cream to white, making it as much an ornamental foliage plant for a shaded border as a steady, low-effort source of mild, tender kale leaves year-round in frost-free or lightly frosted climates. Like its all-green parent it tolerates a surprising amount of shade for a brassica and can keep producing usable growth with just a few hours of direct sun a day, though some light helps maintain strong variegation and compact growth. Harvest young side leaves regularly to encourage branching, and bring potted specimens under cover where winters drop much below the mid-teens Fahrenheit, since this selection is somewhat less cold-hardy than common kale.

name: Variegato di Lusia Radicchio
plantingNote: Sow in mid-to-late summer for an autumn and early-winter crop, since cool nights are needed to trigger the characteristic red-and-cream variegation and to firm up the loosely folded heads.
directions: Variegato di Lusia carries Protected Geographical Indication (IGP) status for the Rovigo-province town of Lusia in the Veneto, where it is grown in the sandy alluvial soils of the Adige river valley. Heads are loosely folded rather than tightly closed, with crisp cream-colored leaves marbled and streaked in deep wine-red, a pattern that intensifies as autumn nights cool. The flavor is milder and less bitter than many red radicchio types, making it popular both raw in salads and lightly grilled. Sow in summer for fall harvest and avoid waterlogged soil, which the variety's sandy native ground does not replicate well.

name: Varna Leek
plantingNote: Start indoors in late winter and transplant seedlings out around the last frost, or make a second sowing in early summer for a fall crop of baby leeks.
directions: Named for the Bulgarian city where the type originated, Varna is a quick-cycling summer leek prized for reaching usable size well ahead of longer-season winter storage leeks. Because it matures so fast, gardeners can crowd seedlings three or four inches apart and pull the whole planting young as slender, sweet salad leeks, or space them wider and let a portion size up into full stalks for cooking. The blue-green foliage tops slim, mild-flavored white shanks that blanch readily with light hilling. It handles a light frost but is best harvested through summer and early fall rather than overwintered, since it lacks the cold hardiness bred into dedicated winter leek types.

name: Vates Collard
plantingNote: For fall planting in zone 9, start transplants in late August–September and set out October–November; in the Gulf South, collards are primarily a fall through spring vegetable — the mild winters allow nearly year-round harvests. In zone 9 summer heat, plants often go to seed; replant fresh transplants each fall for the best quality greens.
