directions: Set transplants 18–24 inches apart in fertile, well-drained soil; in zone 9 plant fall transplants October–November for harvest December through March; Vates is the classic Southern collard variety developed at the Virginia Truck Experiment Station in the 1950s and for decades was the standard garden collard of the South — compact, slow to bolt, very cold hardy (surviving temperatures well below 20°F with frost actually improving the flavor by converting starches to sugars), and producing thick, blue-green leaves of the authentic Southern collard flavor. The name 'Vates' (meaning 'prophet' in Latin) was chosen by the Virginia researchers. Harvest outer leaves regularly from the bottom of the plant upward, leaving the growing tip to continue producing; plants that are allowed to keep their lower leaves become leggy and produce smaller, tougher leaves. The slow-bolt characteristic makes Vates substantially more useful in cool-season gardens than older varieties that rush to flower.

name: Vates Collards
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Vates is a compact collard (18–24 inch plants) appropriate for small gardens where the 3–4 foot Georgia types would be too large. In zone 9, transplant August–September for fall and winter harvest. Vates shows excellent cold hardiness and slow bolting in spring, which extends the harvest into early spring when other types bolt prematurely.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Vates is an open-pollinated collard developed at the Virginia Agricultural and Experiment Station (the acronym 'VATES' gives the variety its name) specifically for compact size, dark color, and improved cold tolerance compared to the taller, more open Georgia types. Vates produces distinctly compact plants (18–24 inches tall vs. the 36–48 inches of Georgia Southern), with upright, heavy, dark blue-green leaves that are more tightly held on the stem than the open habit of older types. The compact habit makes Vates practical for smaller garden spaces and easier to manage in the fall garden without the sprawling character of the traditional large types. The dark blue-green color is visually attractive and indicates high chlorophyll content. Vates shows better cold hardiness than Georgia types — surviving temperatures to 15–18°F rather than the 20–23°F limit of less cold-hardy types — and is notably slow to bolt in spring. This slow-bolting character extends the productive leaf harvest into late spring, 2–4 weeks beyond when other varieties have bolted and become bitter. Vates is consistently recommended by eastern U.S. extension services as one of the most reliable all-purpose collard varieties.
sources: Virginia Cooperative Extension — Vates collard development and notes
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Vates collard variety description
North Carolina State University Extension — Collard Variety Recommendations

name: Vates Kale
plantingNote: Direct sow or start indoors; also an excellent fall crop, since Vates is especially cold-hardy and its flavor sweetens noticeably after frost.
directions: Direct sow or transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart. Vates is a classic dwarf selection of curly Scotch kale, bred at Virginia's Truck Experiment Station for a compact, low, uniform habit that resists bolting and lodging better than taller curly kales, with tightly ruffled blue-green leaves. It is exceptionally cold-hardy, tolerating hard freezes and actually improving in flavor as cool weather converts starches to sugars, making it a mainstay of fall and winter kale plantings across a wide range of climates. Harvest outer leaves regularly as needed, leaving the growing center intact for continued production over a long harvest season.

name: Vedrantais Melon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant once soil is reliably warm; Vedrantais rewards a hot, dry finish that concentrates its intensely perfumed flesh.
directions: Vedrantais is a classic, open-pollinated French Charentais heirloom that many chefs and growers regard as the truest expression of the Charentais type, distinct from generic Charentais seed blends sold under that name alone. Fruit is small and round with a smooth, gray-green rind lightly ribbed toward the blossom end, enclosing deep-orange flesh with an intensely honeyed, floral aroma prized in French markets. Because Charentais types slip cleanly from the vine only at full ripeness, check plants daily as harvest approaches and watch for a faint crack or softening at the stem end rather than waiting for the fruit to fall free on its own. A hot, relatively dry growing season brings out the fullest sugar and fragrance this variety is known for.

name: Ventura Celery
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once soil has warmed, keeping the bed evenly moist throughout the season.
directions: Ventura is a vigorous, disease-resistant green stalk celery bred for reliable performance in home gardens and market rows alike, producing thick, crisp, well-filled ribs without the fussiness of older heirloom types. Its heat tolerance and slow-to-bolt habit make it more forgiving than many stalk celeries during warm spells, and it needs no blanching to stay pale and mild. Feed heavily and keep the root zone consistently moist, since any drought stress produces stringy, hollow stalks. Gardeners choose Ventura when they want a dependable, all-purpose green celery that performs well from spring through fall without special handling.

name: Verde Puebla Tomatillo
plantingNote: Start indoors 6 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes; Verde Puebla is a traditional Mexican landrace type that continues producing into cool fall weather better than many modern tomatillo selections, and can tolerate a light frost without immediately declining. Plant at least two for cross-pollination.
directions: A traditional Mexican tomatillo landrace from the state of Puebla, producing large, round, golden-green fruit that fills and splits its papery husk with a firmer texture and a sweeter, more lemony tang than many standard green tomatillo selections. The vigorous, sprawling plants bear over a long season and hold up better than most tomatillos to cool weather at the end of the season, continuing to set fruit as temperatures drop and tolerating a light frost without a sharp decline in production. Use the ripe golden-green fruit for a milder, less acidic salsa verde, or harvest slightly underripe for the sharper tartness preferred in some traditional recipes. Like all tomatillos, plant at least two for reliable cross-pollination and stake or cage the sprawling vines to keep fruit off the ground.
sources: Hudson Valley Seed Company — Puebla Verde Tomatillo
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Tomatillo for Texas

name: Vermillion Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified slips after the last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, loamy to sandy soil in full sun; Vermillion was bred at the LSU AgCenter Sweet Potato Research Station and matures noticeably faster than older Louisiana releases like Covington, so slips can go in slightly later and still finish before fall's first cool nights.
directions: Plant certified virus-indexed slips in well-drained, loose loamy to sandy soil after the danger of frost has passed and the ground has warmed; Vermillion is a Louisiana State University AgCenter release (formerly trial line LA13-81) bred to combine the deep orange flesh of established Gulf South varieties with a distinctive red-purple skin that stands out on the market table and holds its color well through months of storage. It was developed to mature roughly ten days faster than Covington, giving Gulf Coast gardeners a shorter window between transplanting and harvest and a bit more flexibility for late plantings or short-season sites. Roots size up reliably in both sandy and heavier garden soils, though as with any sweet potato, deep, loose ground produces the straightest, most uniform tubers. Cure freshly dug roots at 85-90°F and high humidity for about a week before storing to heal skin wounds and convert starches to the sugars that give sweet potatoes their flavor.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sweet Potato Research Station variety descriptions
LSU AgCenter — Sweet Potato Research Station field day and new variety updates

name: Vermont Cranberry Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Vermont Cranberry is an heirloom bush shell bean from New England with a centuries-long tradition of cultivation in Vermont and New Hampshire — the round, red-and-cream speckled beans were the traditional baked bean of New England cooking and remain one of the finest-flavored shell beans for baking, soups, and traditional New England bean dishes.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost; can be harvested as a shell bean at 55–65 days (when pods are plump and mottled red-cream) or allowed to dry fully for 75–90 days for a dry-bean crop; succession sow every 2–3 weeks for continuous shell bean harvest. Vermont Cranberry is a heirloom bush bean with deep New England roots — the speckled red-and-cream oval seeds are the traditional 'cranberry bean' of Vermont and New Hampshire, where they have been grown for baked beans since at least the 1700s. The name 'cranberry bean' (also applied to other speckled beans throughout New England) refers to the red cranberry-like speckled coloration of the pods and seeds at the shell bean stage, not to any relationship with cranberries. The shell beans have a rich, creamy, full flavor that is considered by many cooks superior to navy beans or Great Northern beans for traditional New England baked beans — the beans hold their shape well under long, slow baking while developing a creamy, dense interior texture that absorbs the sweet-savory baked bean flavors. At the dry bean stage the seeds turn darker and lose their red mottling; still excellent for winter cooking. Adapted to short New England growing seasons; performs equally well in Gulf Coast fall gardens.
sources: Vermont Institute of Natural Science Heritage Seed Library

name: Veronica Romanesco
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or in mid to late summer for a fall crop; Romanesco needs a longer, cooler season to head well than standard broccoli.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants generously to give the large outer leaves room to develop. Veronica is an early-maturing, reliable Romanesco selection known for its striking, spiraling, fractal-patterned chartreuse-green heads made up of pointed, pyramidal spirals, a strikingly geometric vegetable with a mild, nutty flavor closer to cauliflower than broccoli. It matures notably faster and more dependably than older Romanesco varieties, an important advantage in regions with a shorter cool season for heading brassicas to develop properly. Harvest the central head while the spirals are still tight before it begins to loosen and flower; in the Gulf South, a fall planting timed to head in cool weather generally outperforms a spring crop, which can bolt as temperatures rise.

name: Vert de Massy Cornichon
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Vert de Massy is the classic French cornichon pickling cucumber used to produce the tiny, intensely flavored gherkins traditional in French charcuterie and cuisine, harvested at just 1–2 inches long for the smallest and finest quality, or at 2–3 inches for a slightly larger cornichon.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile, well-drained soil; harvest every 2–3 days to keep plants productive, picking at 1–3 inches long. Vert de Massy (Green of Massy) is the traditional French cornichon gherkin, a small, bumpy-skinned pickling cucumber prized in France for the production of cornichons — the tiny, intensely flavored pickles that accompany pâté, charcuterie, and raclette throughout French cuisine. The fruits are small, cylindrical to slightly tapered, dark green with small warts and spines, and have firm, crisp flesh with excellent flavor even when very small (1–2 inches). Harvest every 2–3 days to keep plants productive — if fruits are allowed to mature they divert energy from new production. Pickled in white wine vinegar with tarragon, chervil, and pearl onions in the traditional French method; also excellent as fresh gherkins. The vines are compact and productive.

name: Verte Non Coureuse des Maraichers
scientificName: Cucurbita pepo 'Verte Non Coureuse des Maraichers'
plantingNote: Direct sow once soil has warmed after the last frost; its compact bush habit suits smaller garden beds better than trailing marrow types.
directions: Verte Non Coureuse des Maraichers -- literally the market gardeners' 'green, non-running' squash -- was selected as a tidy bush zucchini for growers who needed productive plants without the sprawl of older trailing French varieties. Pick the dark green fruit young, around 6-7 inches, when the skin is still glossy and the seeds are barely formed, for the best texture in classic French preparations like ratatouille. Its compact habit makes it a good choice for raised beds or smaller kitchen gardens where trailing marrows would take over. Keep picking regularly, since like most bush zucchini it will quickly funnel energy into a few oversized fruit if left unharvested.

name: Victor Roselle
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 4 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 plant March-June. Like other roselle, Victor is a short-day plant that sets flowers as late-summer days shorten, with calyx harvest running from late summer until frost.
directions: Victor is one of the oldest named roselle selections grown in the United States, introduced in Florida in the early twentieth century and still favored by south Florida home gardeners for large, bright-red, exceptionally plump calyces. The tall, vigorous plants yield a heavier calyx crop per bush than many seed-strain roselles sold today, and the reddish stems and lobed foliage make an attractive hedge-like screen through the season. Grow it in full sun, fertile well-drained soil, and generous spacing, harvesting calyces about a week after the petals drop while still firm and before the inner seed pod toughens. Use the tart calyces fresh or dried for tea, syrup, and jelly.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Roselle (Hibiscus sabdariffa)

name: Victoria Rhubarb
plantingNote: Plant crowns or divisions in early spring; in zone 7–8 plant January–February while dormant. Rhubarb requires 500+ hours below 40°F to break dormancy and produce vigorously — it performs best in zones 3–7 where cold winters are reliable. In zone 8 rhubarb is possible with adequate winter cooling but may decline after a few years. In zone 9 rhubarb is very challenging as insufficient chilling produces poor growth; gardeners in zone 9 should consider growing rhubarb in containers that can be refrigerated in winter. Do not harvest stalks in the first year — allow the plant to establish.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil with high organic matter content; Victoria is the oldest and most widely grown named rhubarb variety, introduced in the 1830s in Britain and remaining the standard variety against which others are compared — it has an exceptionally long cultivation record of nearly 200 years as a garden and commercial vegetable. The thick, large, greenish-pink to light red stalks are produced in large quantities and have the classic, sharp, tart-sour rhubarb flavor used in pies, crumbles, jams, and sauces — the pairing of rhubarb's tartness with strawberry sweetness in strawberry-rhubarb pie is one of the iconic spring desserts of North American and British cooking. Victoria produces primarily green to light pink stalks rather than the deep red of ornamental varieties like Crimson Red; the color is purely cosmetic with no effect on flavor. As a cool-climate perennial, Victoria thrives best where winters are cold and long (zones 3–6) but performs adequately through zone 8 with attention to soil improvement and consistent watering.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Rhubarb Variety Selection
University of Illinois Extension — Rhubarb for the Home Garden
Pennsylvania State University Extension — Victoria Rhubarb Production

name: Victorio Fennel
plantingNote: Sow in mid-to-late summer heat for fall-into-winter bulbing; unlike most Florence fennel types it holds vegetative without bolting through summer warmth and bulbs size up as days shorten.
directions: Bred by Bejo Seeds specifically as a short-day Florence fennel for Southern states, this is one of the few bulbing fennel selections actually suited to Gulf Coast heat rather than fighting it. Sow in the heat of mid-to-late summer rather than spring, and let the bulb size up as days shorten into fall and winter. Harvest once the bulb reaches a good hand-sized diameter, before hard freezes set in.
sources: Osborne Seed - Victorio F1 Organic Fennel

name: Vidora Onion
plantingNote: Sow indoors mid-September through mid-October, 6-8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into the garden in late fall to overwinter for an early bulb harvest.
directions: Vidora is a new-for-2026 short-day F1 onion from Johnny's Selected Seeds bred for early, highly bolt-resistant bulbing, producing uniform globe-shaped bulbs with a classic sweet Granex flavor. It carries intermediate resistance to pink root and stores up to about three months under good conditions, reaching maturity roughly 130 days from fall planting. Start seed indoors in trays in mid-September through mid-October and transplant into fertile, well-drained soil with a pH of 6.0-7.0. Space plants 1.5-2 inches apart for maximum yield of smaller bulbs, or 3-4 inches apart for larger onions.

name: Vietnamese Red Garlic
plantingNote: Plant cloves in fall 4-6 weeks before the ground freezes; a mid-season hardneck that does well across a broad range of climates including the Midwest.
directions: Vietnamese Red is a purple-striped hardneck garlic prized for a creamy, buttery texture and a sweetness that intensifies with roasting, distinguishing it from sharper rocambole types. Bulbs typically hold 9 to 12 large cloves wrapped in skins streaked with rose and purple. Grow it as a standard hardneck: plant cloves pointed end up in fall, cut the scape once it curls to push more energy into the bulb, and cure the harvested bulbs in a shaded, airy spot for a few weeks before storage. It has become a favorite among cooks who want sweetness without excessive heat.

name: Viking KB3 Asparagus
plantingNote: Plant one-year crowns in a trench in early spring in the northern half of its range, timing planting to local frost so young spears are not caught by a hard late freeze.
directions: Viking KB3 is an open-pollinated strain developed in Canada and long favored in short-season, cold-winter growing regions for its exceptional hardiness and reliable rust tolerance. Unlike the all-male Rutgers hybrids, Viking KB3 produces both male and female plants, so expect some volunteer seedlings to appear around the bed over time and thin them out to avoid overcrowding. Its spears are medium-thick with tight, purple-tinged tips and hold up well to the freeze-thaw cycles of prairie and northern climates. Because it is open-pollinated, saved seed from a healthy stand will grow true enough for home use, making it a practical choice for gardeners wanting a self-sustaining asparagus patch.
sources: Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs

name: Vinson Watts Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; an Appalachian family heirloom from West Virginia producing extraordinarily large and meaty orange beefsteak fruits — a lesser-known gem introduced through Seed Savers Exchange that rivals better-known orange types in flavor and productivity.
directions: Sow seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant into deeply prepared, fertile, well-drained soil after all frost danger has passed and stake or cage firmly from the start. Vinson Watts is a West Virginia Appalachian family heirloom that arrived at Seed Savers Exchange through Vinson Watts, who grew it for many years before contributing it to the seed exchange; it produces very large, 1–2 pound orange beefsteak fruits with deep, meaty, mostly seedless flesh and a mild, sweet, low-acid flavor that rivals the better-known Kellogg's Breakfast and Dr. Wyche's Orange. The vigorous indeterminate vines are productive and the fruits have a pleasing globe shape and smooth skin that resists cracking better than some large heirlooms. An excellent choice for anyone building a collection of orange heirloom beefsteak tomatoes.

name: Violet de Gournay Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow from 4 weeks before the last frost through late spring, then resume in late summer for a fall crop; roots hold in the ground and keep their texture longer than fast round red radishes, making this a useful bridge variety between spring and autumn plantings.
directions: Sow seed 1/2 inch deep directly in the garden and thin seedlings to 2-3 inches apart once true leaves appear. Violet de Gournay is a French market-garden heirloom named for the Normandy town of Gournay, producing round to slightly oval roots with smooth deep violet-black skin surrounding crisp white flesh. It matures faster than the larger Black Spanish winter radishes it is sometimes confused with, and its flavor is notably milder, making it suited to fresh eating rather than storage. Keep soil evenly moist during root sizing to prevent the skin from cracking or turning woody.
sources: Kokopelli Seed Foundation heirloom radish collection

name: Violet de Provence Artichoke
scientificName: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Violet de Provence'
plantingNote: Transplant after last frost into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this nineteenth-century Provençal heirloom is grown for small, tender buds traditionally eaten whole, raw or braised, while young.
directions: Violet de Provence is a classic French heirloom prized for its slender, pointed buds flushed deep violet-purple over green bracts, picked small and young before any fibrous choke develops so the whole bud can be trimmed and eaten. It produces earlier and more heavily than many of the large-headed globe types, throwing numerous side shoots that extend the harvest over several weeks. Cutting the entire plant back hard after the first flush encourages a second smaller crop of buds within a couple of months. It is a true perennial in mild-winter climates but needs a thick mulch or overwinter protection anywhere winter temperatures drop much below the mid-teens Fahrenheit.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

name: Violet Queen Cauliflower
plantingNote: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting; in zone 8-9 gardens transplant in July-August so curds finish sizing and coloring during the shorter, cooler days of fall, which deepens the purple pigment.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, spacing plants 18-24 inches apart, and keep soil evenly moist since curds can lose color and flavor if plants are stressed by drought as they mature. Violet Queen is an open-pollinated cauliflower whose deep purple curds come from anthocyanin pigments, the same antioxidant compounds found in red cabbage and purple carrots, and the color contrasts strikingly with its dark green wrapper leaves in the garden. Because it is not a hybrid, seed can be saved from year to year, and the curds hold their purple color raw but fade to green when cooked, so it is best featured in salads, slaws, or briefly steamed dishes where the color matters. Harvest promptly once curds are full-sized, since heads left too long in warm or bright conditions can dull from vivid violet toward a duller, greener tone.

name: Violet's Multicolored Butterbeans
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm, above 65°F; a vigorous semi-bush to pole type that readily tops a 7-foot pole and benefits from sturdy trellising.
directions: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F, providing a sturdy trellis or pole for the vigorous semi-bush vines, which will readily top a 7-foot support and can reach 10 feet. This Georgia family heirloom, preserved for four generations by Violet Brady Westbrook's family in Banks County, produces 3-5 inch pods filled with small, richly flavored seeds displaying a striking rainbow of colors — cream, beige, red-brown, and violet-purple, swirled and speckled so that no two beans look quite alike. Plants show good disease and drought resistance, useful traits for humid Gulf Coast summers. Pick pods at the green shell stage for fresh butterbeans or let them dry fully on the vine for long-term storage; the colorful seed coats fade somewhat with cooking but the flavor remains excellent fresh or dried.

name: Violetta Artichoke
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before transplanting; Violetta requires vernalization, a period of cool temperatures around 50 degrees F for about 10 days, once seedlings have several true leaves, to trigger flower bud formation in the first year.
directions: Transplant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after vernalization. Violetta is a classic Italian heirloom artichoke producing smaller, tender, purple-tinged buds traditionally harvested young and eaten whole, including the tender inner leaves and heart, either braised, fried, or grilled in traditional Italian preparations like carciofi alla romana. The striking violet-purple coloring on the bud scales, especially pronounced in cooler weather, makes it as ornamental as it is productive. Like other seed-grown artichokes it can flower and produce a harvest the first year if properly vernalized as a young seedling, and in mild-winter zones it may persist as a short-lived perennial for a second season of harvest.

name: Violetta di Firenze Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost; transplant after soil warms to at least 70°F and nights are reliably above 55°F; Violetta di Firenze is an Italian heirloom eggplant from the Florence area of Tuscany, producing large, round to slightly oval, deeply ribbed fruits with dramatic lavender-purple and white vertical striping — one of the most visually stunning and historically important eggplant varieties in Italian kitchen garden tradition.
directions: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before last frost at 80°F; transplant into warm, fertile, well-drained soil with consistent moisture; Violetta di Firenze produces fewer, larger fruits than Asian types — typically 2–4 fruits per plant at a time — harvest when fruits reach 4–6 inches across and the skin is still glossy; do not allow to over-ripen (seeds enlarge and flesh becomes bitter). Violetta di Firenze (Florentine Violet) is a traditional Italian heirloom eggplant from the Florence area of Tuscany, where it has been grown for generations as the quintessential garden eggplant of the region — so important locally that it appears in Florentine recipe traditions and Renaissance-era botanical descriptions of the kitchen garden. The variety is immediately recognized by its dramatic appearance: very large (6–10 inches across), round to pear-shaped, deeply ribbed fruits with beautiful vertical striping in shades of lavender-violet and white; no other commonly grown eggplant has the same combination of large round shape, deep ribbing, and purple-white striping. The flesh is creamy-white with a mild, sweet, slightly nutty flavor with less bitterness than many eggplant varieties — the large cavity and abundant flesh make it particularly suited for stuffing (ripieno), slicing and grilling, or layering in the classic Italian Parmigiana di Melanzane. The plant is robust and tall (30–48 inches) and requires staking; it is adapted to long, warm Mediterranean summers and performs well in Gulf Coast zone 8b–10 conditions with the hot summers they provide.

name: Violetta Lunga di Napoli Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out only once nights stay reliably above 55°F in rich, well-drained soil.
directions: A traditional heirloom from the Naples region of southern Italy, Violetta Lunga di Napoli produces smooth, cylindrical, deep purple fruits reaching roughly 8 inches long on early-bearing, prolific plants. The flesh is notably mild and nearly seedless, with a sweet, nutty flavor that distinguishes it from larger, seedier eggplant types, making it a favorite sliced into rounds for grilling, baking, or sautéing. Stake plants once fruit begins to set heavily, since the slender fruiting habit can bend stems under a full crop. Pick fruit while the skin is still taut and glossy for the best texture and to encourage continued flowering.

name: Violetta Pak Choi
plantingNote: Sow after soil has warmed in spring, or again in late summer for a fall crop; purple pigmentation intensifies in cooler weather.
directions: Violetta is a small, fast-maturing pak choi whose leaf tops darken to a deep violet-purple while the stems and undersides stay bright green, giving it strong visual interest in salad mixes as well as in the garden row. Direct-sow shallowly and thin to 6 to 8 inches for baby heads, harvesting whole plants once they reach a compact, crisp rosette. Flavor is sweet and mild with none of the toughness that can show up in larger pak choi types left too long in the field. Because its purple coloring deepens with cooler temperatures, a fall sowing generally produces the most striking color along with the sweetest flavor.

name: Violette di Firenze Eggplant
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before transplant; in zone 9 start December–January and transplant February–March. Violette di Firenze is an Italian market type that performs well in zone 9 heat. A second planting in July extends production into fall. The plants are larger and more vigorous than most eggplants; provide generous spacing and heavy staking to support the large fruits.
directions: Transplant into rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Violette di Firenze (Violet of Florence) is a striking Italian heirloom eggplant from the Tuscany region, producing large, squat, round to pear-shaped fruits with distinctive lavender-to-violet skin streaked with white — a bicolor pattern that is dramatically different from the solid-purple standard eggplant. The large fruits (6–8 inches across, up to 2 pounds) have flesh that is notably sweeter, milder, and less bitter than standard globe eggplant types, with fewer seeds and a creamier texture when cooked. The Italian tradition of grilling, broiling, or pan-frying Violette di Firenze without salting (a technique used to reduce bitterness in standard eggplant) reflects the naturally mild, sweet character of this variety. The striking bicolor appearance makes it a showstopper in the garden and at market. Cut fruits at their most beautiful stage — when lavender-violet with white streaks and still firm — rather than allowing them to develop the dull, fully-mature purple that indicates over-ripeness.
sources: Seeds of Italy — Violette di Firenze Eggplant Growing Notes
Slow Food Foundation — Tuscan Heirloom Vegetables
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Italian Eggplant Varieties

name: Violetto Artichoke
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant; in zone 9 plant February–March. Violetto produces smaller, more numerous buds than Green Globe — harvest the central bud first when tightly closed, which stimulates production of side-shoot buds for a longer season of smaller edible heads. In Italian and French cuisine, these smaller side buds (carciofini) are the prized preparation stage for pickling in olive oil, braising whole, and raw artichoke salads where tender, non-fibrous bracts are required.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, deep, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Violetto is an Italian artichoke type producing elongated, conical to teardrop-shaped heads with striking purple-green bracts that deepen to rich violet as the buds develop — the ornamental purple coloration makes Violetto one of the most attractive artichokes for kitchen garden displays and edible landscape design. The heads are smaller than American Green Globe types (typically 2–3 inches across) but considerably more tender in the bract meat and heart, with a milder, slightly more nutty flavor that is less assertive than the large green varieties. Smaller Violetto heads can be eaten raw when very young and tender — an important distinction from large artichokes that require cooking. In Italian cooking, Violetto di Romagna and similar purple artichoke types are specifically selected for preparations requiring tenderness: carciofi alla giudea (deep-fried), carciofi sott'olio (preserved in olive oil), and raw shaved artichoke salads. The purple color is heat-sensitive and fades during cooking, but the ornamental value in the growing plant is substantial.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Italian Artichoke Varieties
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Specialty Artichoke Production
Slow Food Presidia — Italian Heritage Artichoke Varieties

name: Violetto di Sant'Erasmo Artichoke
scientificName: Cynara cardunculus var. scolymus 'Violetto di Sant'Erasmo'
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost and transplant, or set out rooted offshoots in spring; in zone 8 plant March–April. The prized castraura, the plant's small first central bud, is removed early to redirect vigor into later side buds.
directions: Violetto di Sant'Erasmo is grown on Sant'Erasmo, an island in the Venice lagoon, where the sandy, lightly saline soil and lagoon microclimate are credited with the exceptional tenderness of this violet-tinged artichoke, recognized as a Slow Food Presidium product. The most prized harvest is the castraura, the plant's small, tender first central bud removed in spring to redirect vigor into the larger side buds that follow, and it is traditionally eaten raw, thinly sliced. Plants are maintained as perennial stools and increased by dividing rooted offshoots, consistent with lagoon market-garden tradition rather than seed propagation. Grow in full sun in loose, well-drained, sandy soil, and where lagoon salt-air conditions do not apply, provide winter mulch for crown protection.
sources: Slow Food Presidia — Carciofo Violetto di Sant'Erasmo
European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register
University of California Cooperative Extension — Italian Artichoke Varieties

name: Violina Butternut Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed following last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Violina needs a full warm season and ample vine space to mature its large fruit.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Violina is a Southern Italian heirloom butternut squash, its elongated, violin-shaped fruit (3-4 kg) covered in wrinkled, creamy-tan skin over dense, deep-orange, sweet flesh. It stores exceptionally well into winter, and its intense flavor and texture make it especially prized for risotto, gnocchi, and roasting in Italian cooking. Give the vigorous vines ample room to spread, and harvest once the rind hardens fully and resists thumbnail pressure, curing fruit in a warm, dry spot for a week before storage.

name: Virginia Jumbo Peanut
plantingNote: Direct sow shelled, raw (untreated) seed into warm soil once nights stay above 60°F; peanuts need a long, warm, frost-free season, which makes the extended Gulf Coast growing season an excellent fit.
directions: Plant shelled seed about an inch and a half deep in loose, sandy, well-drained soil, since peanuts push their flower stalks ('pegs') down into the soil to form pods underground and need friable soil for those pegs to penetrate easily. Virginia Jumbo is the classic large-seeded Virginia-type peanut behind most of the boiled and roasted-in-shell peanuts sold across the South, prized for producing the biggest pods and kernels of any common peanut type, typically two large seeds per pod. Hill soil slightly around the base of plants as they grow to give pegs an easier path into the ground, and keep soil evenly moist through flowering and peg development, since drought stress at that stage sharply reduces yield. Dig the whole plant once leaves begin yellowing in fall, and cure pods in a warm, airy spot for one to two weeks before shelling or storing.

name: Virginia Sweet Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; a large bicolor beefsteak that needs staking; the striking yellow and red coloring of the flesh and exterior make it a showstopper at market and on the table.
directions: Sow seed at 70–80°F 6–8 weeks before last frost; transplant to rich, deeply prepared soil after all frost risk has passed, burying the stem and staking firmly to support the large fruits. Virginia Sweet is a stunning American heirloom bicolor beefsteak tomato with large, 1–2 pound fruits that are golden-yellow with dramatic red streaking on the skin and brilliant pink-red and golden-yellow marbled flesh that is as beautiful to look at as it is flavorful — sweet, rich, and low-acid. It is related to other bicolor heirlooms like Big Rainbow and striped varieties that are prized both for taste and visual appeal; the swirling interior color pattern is most pronounced in cool weather. Harvest when the fruit softens slightly and the yellow shoulder transitions fully from green.

name: Vit Mâche
plantingNote: Sow 4-6 weeks before first frost for a fall and winter harvest, or as soon as soil can be worked in earliest spring; Vit is a classic large-leaved mâche selection favored for its vigorous, uniform rosettes.
directions: Sow seed thinly at a shallow depth in cool soil, since mâche germinates poorly once temperatures climb into summer range. Vit is a widely grown European strain prized for producing larger, rounder, more upright rosettes than generic corn salad, giving a better yield of tender leaves per plant. The mild, faintly nutty flavor and buttery texture make it a classic addition to winter salads, often paired with beets or walnuts in French cuisine. Rosettes tolerate hard frost and light snow cover, so plantings can be harvested through much of the winter with minimal protection.

name: Vitamin Green
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–March for spring. Vitamin Green is one of the fastest-maturing Asian brassicas — baby leaves are harvestable in 20–25 days for baby green mixes. It is more heat-tolerant than most Asian brassicas and can extend into early summer in zone 9 before bolting. Successive sowings every 2 weeks provide a continuous harvest of tender young greens.
directions: Direct sow thinly in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Vitamin Green is a non-heading Asian brassica green selected for extremely rapid growth, mild flavor, and excellent nutritional value — the name reflects its high vitamin content (particularly vitamins A, C, and K) relative to other leafy greens. The smooth, round to slightly oval, bright medium-green leaves are strikingly mild in flavor — among the mildest of all Asian brassica types, with a clean, grassy-vegetable taste more like spinach or mild bok choy than the mustardy pungency of standard Asian mustard greens. This mildness makes Vitamin Green accessible to people who find other Asian greens too strongly flavored. In the kitchen it is interchangeable with bok choy or baby spinach in virtually any preparation — stir-fries, soups, braising, steaming, and raw use in salads and baby green mixes. The combination of very rapid growth (30–45 days to full size, 20–25 days to baby green stage), mild flavor, and excellent nutritional content makes it one of the most practical cool-season greens for zone 9.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Vitamin Green Asian Brassica
Kitazawa Seed Company — Mild Asian Greens
University of Hawaii Extension — Asian Vegetable Production Guide

name: Vitaverde Cauliflower
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant after last frost; also does well as a late-summer planting timed to mature in cool fall weather.
directions: Vitaverde produces a pale apple-green curd with the domed, tightly beaded texture of a classic cauliflower rather than the looser florets of broccoli, giving it a hybrid appearance often marketed as broccoflower. The lime-green color comes from chlorophyll in the curd tissue and carries a milder, slightly sweeter flavor than white cauliflower with no need for blanching or leaf-tying. It holds its curd quality in the field longer than many white types before the curd begins to open or discolor, giving a wider harvest window. Grow Vitaverde for a striking, easy-care alternative to white cauliflower that performs reliably without extra fussing.

name: Vitelotte Noire Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces after soil has warmed slightly; Vitelotte Noire is a French heirloom fingerling with deep purple skin and flesh, also called 'Truffe de Chine.'
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 3-4 inches deep in light, well-drained soil; as a late-maturing fingerling it needs a full season to size up its knobby tubers. Vitelotte Noire is a classic French heirloom potato with deep purple skin and equally deep purple flesh throughout, nicknamed 'Truffe de Chine' (Chinese truffle) for its dark, irregular tuber shape, and prized by chefs for the striking color it brings to gratins, chips, and purées without losing much pigment when cooked. Its dense, nutty flavor and firm texture hold up well in roasted and sautéed preparations. Harvest once foliage yellows and dies back, and cure tubers in a cool, dark spot before storage.

name: Viva Italia Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; Viva Italia is a determinate paste tomato that ripens a concentrated crop over 3–4 weeks, ideal for sauce-making; in zone 9 aim for spring harvest in May–June before summer heat.
directions: Start seeds 6–8 weeks before transplanting at 70–80°F; Viva Italia is an improved hybrid roma-type paste tomato that addresses the main weakness of heirloom Roma — its susceptibility to disease. An AAS (All-America Selections) winner, Viva Italia combines the thick-walled, low-moisture flesh and rich, concentrated paste-tomato flavor of traditional Roma with VFFNTA disease resistance (Verticillium wilt, Fusarium wilt races 1 and 2, root-knot nematodes, tobacco mosaic virus, and Alternaria), making it far more reliable in humid climates and typical garden soils than open-pollinated Roma varieties. The determinate, compact (3–3.5 foot) plants produce large, concentrated sets of uniform, thick-skinned, 2–4 oz, elongated-oval, bright red fruits with very low moisture content and dense, meaty flesh — exactly what's needed for sauce, paste, sun-dried tomatoes, and canning. Because of the dense flesh and concentrated flavor, Viva Italia produces much higher yields of usable sauce per pound of fruit than wet, beefsteak-type tomatoes. An outstanding choice for serious sauce-makers who want disease resistance and reliability.
sources: All-America Selections — Viva Italia AAS winner
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Production Guide

name: Vorlon Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after all frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March. The deep purple-blue exterior color of Vorlon develops most intensely with sun exposure on the skin — fruits shaded by foliage will be less colorful. In zone 9 fall planting in August for October–November harvest often produces the best fruit quality. Support with cages or stakes as the large, indeterminate vines require substantial support.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and provide sturdy cage or stake support; Vorlon is a large beefsteak tomato bred by Tom Wagner, the Washington State plant breeder also responsible for Green Zebra, known for developing novel tomato colors and flavors. Vorlon produces large (often 12–20 ounce) fruits with a distinctive deep purple-to-near-black exterior that develops from sun exposure on the skin — the dark color comes from anthocyanin pigments (the same blue-purple compounds in blueberries and purple cabbage) that accumulate in the skin when exposed to sunlight. When sliced, Vorlon reveals a complex interior with dark-streaked red flesh and a rich, full-bodied, complex tomato flavor with earthy, wine-like undertones that distinguish dark tomato varieties from standard red types. The anthocyanin content in dark tomatoes like Vorlon represents significantly higher antioxidant levels than red-only tomatoes — a characteristic that has made dark-skinned tomatoes of interest in nutritional research. The dramatic appearance of the purple-black exterior with rich red interior when sliced makes Vorlon outstanding in salads and fresh presentations.
sources: Tom Wagner's Tater-Mater Seed Company — Vorlon Tomato Introduction
Seed Savers Exchange — Dark-Skinned Tomato Varieties
Oregon State University Extension — Anthocyanin Tomato Varieties

name: Vulcan Swiss Chard
plantingNote: Direct sow around the last frost date and thin seedlings once established; plants tolerate light frost in fall.
directions: Direct sow into loose, fertile soil and thin seedlings to their final spacing, watering consistently to keep stalks tender and prevent bitterness. This French heirloom is grown chiefly for its glossy, deep crimson stalks and veins that hold their vivid color even after cooking, contrasting with dark green, slightly savoyed leaves. It is a dependable cut-and-come-again green that keeps producing new leaves from the crown for months.

name: Wa Wa Tsai
scientificName: Brassica rapa subsp. pekinensis 'Wa Wa Tsai'
plantingNote: Best as a late-summer sowing for fall harvest to avoid bolting; can also be sown in very early spring where the season is long enough.
directions: Wa Wa Tsai is a miniature napa cabbage that forms a tight, barrel-shaped head only about 9 inches tall, making it a practical choice for small beds or succession plantings where a full-sized Chinese cabbage would be too much plant. Direct-sow shallowly in late summer and thin to 8 to 10 inches, since crowded plants fail to form a dense head. The interior is pale, crisp, and sweet with none of the bitterness that can develop in larger, slower-maturing napa types. Its small stature and relatively quick maturity make it one of the earliest mini napa cabbages to harvest in a fall garden.

name: Waido Mizuna
plantingNote: Give plants more room than standard mizuna since Waido forms noticeably larger, more upright rosettes; also suited to a late-summer sowing for fall harvest.
directions: Waido, meaning wide leaf in Japanese, is a larger-statured mizuna selection bred for bunching markets, with broader, less deeply cut leaves than standard mizuna and thicker, crisp petioles. Direct sow into fertile soil and keep evenly moist to encourage tender, mild-flavored growth. Whole heads can be cut for bunching or leaves picked individually for stir-fries and hot pot greens. Cold-hardy and slow to bolt compared to smaller mizuna types, making it a good choice for extended fall harvest.

name: Waldspindel Jerusalem Artichoke
plantingNote: Plant whole or cut seed tubers with at least one or two eyes 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil once soil can be worked in spring; choose a permanent bed, since any tuber left behind will resprout.
directions: Waldspindel (German for 'forest spindle') is an Austrian heirloom Jerusalem artichoke prized for its small, elongated, deep red-skinned fingerling tubers, which are easier to clean than the knobby tubers of unnamed sunchoke stock. Plant seed tubers in spring in loose, fertile soil in full sun; stems grow thick and lush, somewhat shorter and stockier than tall field types such as Fuseau. Tall late-summer sunflower-like blooms are followed by a fall tuber harvest that can continue through winter and into early spring wherever the ground is workable, with flavor and sweetness improving after exposure to cold.

name: Walking Stick Collard
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9, start seeds in August for September transplanting ahead of fall. Walking Stick Collard is a truly perennial (or at minimum biennial) collard that develops an upright, thick stem over multiple years of growth — eventually reaching 4–8 feet in height with a distinctive woody stem that in the South was historically harvested for use as a walking stick, giving the variety its name. Unlike annual collard varieties grown as single-season crops, Walking Stick Collard can remain productive for 2–5 years in zone 9's mild winters, producing new growth from the upper portion of the plant as it elongates. Individual leaves are harvested from the lower portion of the stem as new growth continues from the top. In zone 9, the plants perform well through winter (tolerating multiple frosts and brief freezes) and may slow in summer heat but rarely die entirely, giving them a distinctly perennial character that sets them apart from annual collard varieties. Space widely (24–36 inches) to allow each plant to develop its multi-year structure.
directions: Start seeds indoors; transplant to permanent location and allow to develop over multiple seasons. Harvest outer lower leaves as needed year-round. Walking Stick Collard is one of the most historically distinctive vegetables of the American South — a tall, perennial collard type that was maintained for generations in family gardens across the Carolinas, Georgia, and the Gulf South as a semi-permanent garden plant rather than an annual crop. The 'walking stick' in the name refers to the thick, woody stems that develop as the plant grows upward over multiple years: historical accounts describe Southern farmers and homesteaders harvesting old Walking Stick Collard stems, drying them, and using them as walking sticks, canes, and tool handles — a practical byproduct of a plant grown primarily for its edible leaves. The leaves are classic collard — large, blue-green, thick, and of the rich, mild-bitter flavor that defines Southern greens cuisine — harvested continuously from the lower stem as the plant elongates upward. A well-established Walking Stick Collard plant can produce leaves continuously for 3–5 years in zone 9's mild climate, making it a true perennial food plant for gardens where winter rarely kills brassicas completely. The variety is maintained by seed savers and small heirloom seed companies as a Southern heritage vegetable; it is not available in commercial mass-market seed catalogs but has been preserved through the living tradition of Southern kitchen gardens and organizations like Seed Savers Exchange and Southern Exposure Seed Exchange. Walking Stick Collard's extraordinary height (sometimes reaching 6–8 feet) and its multi-year productive life make it one of the most distinctive and visually arresting vegetables possible in zone 9 gardens, forming a structural element with year-round productivity that no annual collard variety can match.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Walking Stick Collard Southern heirloom perennial collard documentation
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Walking Stick Collard heritage vegetable variety notes
North Carolina State University Extension — Heirloom Collard Varieties of the Carolinas and Gulf South

name: Walter Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; in zone 9 Walter is an outstanding spring and fall tomato with excellent disease resistance for humid Gulf Coast conditions. Determinate habit means a concentrated, predictable harvest good for canning large batches.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; set determinate plants 2–3 feet apart in full sun, fertile, well-drained soil; Walter tomato was released by the University of Florida in 1963, the same year as Tropic, and quickly became a commercial and home garden staple in the Southeast for its reliable production, disease resistance, and compact determinate growth habit. It produces medium-large (6–8 oz), red, round fruits with smooth skin, firm flesh, and good canning and fresh-eating quality, with resistance to fusarium wilt and gray leaf spot. Walter's determinate habit (which concentrates flowering and ripening into a defined period rather than producing continuously like indeterminate types) makes it efficient for gardeners who want a single large harvest for preserving and canning. Once the standard commercial processing tomato in Florida, it remains an important heirloom for Gulf Coast gardeners who need a reliably productive, disease-resistant, compact-season tomato.

name: Waltham 29 Broccoli
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost for spring planting, or sow in midsummer for a fall crop; Waltham 29 is a classic American open-pollinated broccoli developed by the Massachusetts Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1954 — long the standard garden broccoli before modern hybrids and still prized for heat tolerance, blue-green color, and reliable production.
directions: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after hardening off when temperatures are consistently below 80°F during the day. Waltham 29 broccoli was developed by the Waltham Field Station of the Massachusetts Agricultural Experiment Station and released in 1954 as an improvement over earlier open-pollinated varieties; for decades before hybrid broccoli varieties became dominant in the 1970s and 80s, Waltham 29 was the standard home garden and market broccoli. It produces a large, domed, blue-green to grey-green central head of excellent flavor and tight bead formation, followed by adequate sideshot production; it is notably more tolerant of fall frost than many varieties and holds well in the field without yellowing. Still widely grown for its reliable open-pollinated nature (seed-saveable), cold tolerance, and classic blue-green broccoli flavor. Excellent for fall production in zones 5–11.
sources: University of Massachusetts Extension Vegetable Notes

name: Waltham Butternut Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in late summer (July in zone 9) in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun for a fall harvest; Waltham Butternut is a Cucurbita moschata variety with better heat and humidity tolerance than pepo-type winter squash — an important practical advantage for Gulf South production.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; Waltham Butternut is the standard commercial and home garden butternut squash — developed by Robert Young at the Waltham Experiment Station in Massachusetts and recognized with an All-America Selections award for its exceptional production, uniformity, and storage quality. The classic cylindrical fruits with tan skin, small seed cavity, and large neck of deep-orange flesh represent the butternut ideal: consistent shape, excellent flavor, and long storage life (3–6 months at cool room temperature). The Cucurbita moschata species provides better heat and humidity tolerance than C. pepo winter squash types — allowing Waltham Butternut to succeed in Gulf South conditions where pepo types (acorn, Delicata) often struggle with disease and heat in late-season production. In zone 9, the most reliable production method is a late-summer planting (July–August direct sow) for a fall harvest (October–November) — the fall planting avoids peak summer heat during vulnerable early growth and produces during the cooler fall weather that improves storage quality. Cure harvested fruits for 10 days at 80–85°F to harden the skin and develop the characteristic butterscotch sweetness that distinguishes fully cured butternut from freshly harvested green fruit. Waltham Butternut vines spread extensively (6–10 feet) and require substantial garden space.

name: Waltham Washington Asparagus
plantingNote: Set crowns 6-8 inches deep in a prepared trench in early spring, backfilling as spears grow; direct seeding indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost is also an option for this open-pollinated strain.
directions: Waltham Washington was selected at the University of Massachusetts's Waltham Field Station from Mary Washington lines for improved cold hardiness and stronger resistance to asparagus rust, making it a reliable choice for shorter, colder growing seasons than the original Mary Washington tolerates well. Spears emerge thick and green with a light purple blush at the tightly closed tip, in the classic heirloom shape home gardeners expect. As an open-pollinated strain it produces both sexes, so female plants will drop red berries in late summer that can self-sow into the row if not managed. Allow two full seasons of unharvested fern growth before cutting begins, then harvest for six to eight weeks each spring once the bed is mature.

name: Wando Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–6 weeks before last frost in spring or in fall 8–10 weeks before first frost; Wando is the most heat-tolerant commonly available shelling pea, developed by USDA for Southern gardens — it sets pods in warmer conditions that cause bloom drop in all other pea varieties, making it the recommended choice for Gulf Coast and Southern spring pea planting.
directions: Sow 1–1.5 inches deep 2–6 weeks before last frost; Wando tolerates both cool and moderately warm conditions and is particularly valuable for later-season spring planting in Southern zones. Wando pea was developed by USDA and named for the Wando River in the Charleston, South Carolina area, reflecting its adaptation to warm Southern conditions. Unlike most shelling peas that drop flowers and fail to set pods when temperatures rise above 75°F, Wando continues producing pods at temperatures 5–10°F warmer than other varieties, extending the harvest window in Gulf Coast and Southern gardens. The 24–30 inch plants produce smooth-seeded peas (less sweet than wrinkled but better adapted to warm-soil planting) in pods with 6–8 peas; the flavor is good. Exceptionally valuable for fall pea production in zones 7–10 when planted in late August–September.
sources: Virginia Cooperative Extension Vegetable Production Guide

name: Wapsie Valley Corn
plantingNote: Sow in blocks of at least four rows in average garden soil; forgiving for gardeners outside the traditional Corn Belt.
directions: Sow in blocks of at least four rows in average garden soil; its relatively short season and dent-flint hybrid vigor make it forgiving for gardeners outside the traditional Corn Belt. Wapsie Valley is an Iowa heirloom named for the Wapsipinicon River valley and preserved by Sand Hill Preservation Farm, combining dent and flint characteristics in the same ears along with striking orange, red, and multicolor kernels. It is valued both for its ornamental appeal on the stalk and for producing flavorful cornmeal, and it has become a favorite among small-scale growers seeking a productive, easy-to-grow open-pollinated corn with real regional history.

name: Wapsipinicon Peach Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 4–6 weeks before transplanting; Wapsipinicon Peach is an indeterminate open-pollinated cherry tomato producing 1–1.5-inch round fruits with a distinctive pale peach-yellow color and a slightly fuzzy-looking surface texture that inspired the 'peach' descriptor. Named for the Wapsipinicon River in northeastern Iowa where it originated, this variety has been maintained by seed-savers as an example of mid-American heirloom tomato diversity. In zone 9, transplant March–April and stake or cage to 6 feet; indeterminate growth continues until frost. The pale coloration indicates low lycopene (the pigment responsible for red color) and high carotenoid content of a different type, contributing to the notably sweet, low-acid flavor profile that has made this variety a favorite among cherry tomato enthusiasts seeking flavor over color.
directions: Start seeds indoors at 70–85°F; transplant after last frost and stake or cage to 6 feet. Harvest when fruits yield gently to pressure and separate easily from the calyx. Wapsipinicon Peach Tomato is an Iowa heritage cherry tomato distinguished by its pale peach-yellow coloration and the exceptionally sweet, low-acid flavor that develops as fruits ripen fully. The name refers to both the peach-like appearance of the ripe fruit (the pale skin with a subtle blushed tinge on the sunny side closely resembles a small yellow peach) and the Wapsipinicon River region of northeastern Iowa where the variety was grown and saved by farm families through the twentieth century. The variety reached national seed-saver networks through the Seed Savers Exchange network and has been grown in trial gardens across the country where it consistently earns high marks for flavor complexity — a balance of sweetness with sufficient acid to provide depth, rather than the flat sweetness of some low-acid cherry types. As an indeterminate variety, Wapsipinicon Peach continues to grow and produce throughout a long warm season, which is particularly advantageous in zone 9 where the long frost-free period extends production well into fall. Fruits cluster in modest-sized trusses and are best harvested when fully colored and just soft; they have a thinner skin than many modern cherry types, which is prized for fresh eating but means they are more susceptible to cracking after rain or irrigation following dry periods. Cage or stake firmly and prune suckers selectively to manage plant size and improve air circulation in humid conditions.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Wapsipinicon Peach Tomato heirloom variety history and regional origin notes
Carolyn Male, '100 Heirloom Tomatoes for the American Garden' (Storey Publishing, 1999) — Iowa heritage tomato documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Wapsipinicon Peach variety trials and flavor notes

name: Warba Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost, or January-February in zone 9; Warba's very short season lets Gulf Coast gardeners dig new potatoes well ahead of summer heat and humidity.
directions: Warba was developed at the University of Minnesota and released in the 1930s, valued ever since as an exceptionally early, reliable red-skinned potato for gardeners who want new potatoes as soon as possible after planting. The round tubers have light red skin and white flesh with good flavor, best eaten fresh since Warba does not store as well as later-season varieties. Its very short season makes it a practical option for a Gulf Coast spring potato crop planted in late winter, since it can be dug well before summer heat and humidity set in. Hill soil around the base of the plants as they grow to protect the shallow tubers and increase yield.

name: Warren Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after last frost; this Maine-bred buttercup-type squash matures reliably within a shorter northern season than many maxima types.
directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in hills after frost danger passes, thinning to two or three vigorous plants per hill. Warren is a buttercup-type winter squash selected in Maine and long distributed through regional New England seed sources as a reliable short-season keeper. The blue-green skinned fruits hold dense, deep-orange flesh that is notably sweet and dry-textured, excellent for baking, mashing, and pies, and the fruits store well into winter when cured properly. Harvest when the rind has hardened fully and the stem begins to dry, then cure for a week or two in a warm spot before moving to cool storage.

name: Warsaw Pasta Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after danger of frost; compact bush habit suits smaller gardens.
directions: Warsaw Pasta is a spaghetti-type squash from Poland, offered in the United States by Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds. Compact, disease-resistant bush plants bear pale yellow, elongated-oval fruits weighing about 2-5 lbs. When cooked, the fine-grained flesh separates into tender, mild-flavored strands like traditional spaghetti squash, and the bush habit makes it a good choice for gardeners with limited vine space.
sources: ECHO Book and Gift Store and Nursery

name: Warted Hubbard Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in fertile, deeply amended soil; needs a long season of 100–115 days; this is the classic 'True Hubbard' type with heavily warted, dark blue-green skin and exceptional 6-month storage life.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, in hills enriched with compost, spacing 5–7 feet apart; thin to 2 plants per hill and provide consistent moisture through the long growing season. True Hubbard is the heavily warted, dark blue-green Hubbard squash that was a staple of 19th-century New England kitchens; fruits weigh 10–20 pounds and have extremely hard, deeply ribbed and warted blue-green skin and dense, dry, bright orange flesh with outstanding sweet, nutty flavor. The exceptional storage quality — fruits in good condition can last 6 months or more at cool temperatures — made it the premier cellar squash before canning became widespread. Harvest only after the vine has fully died back and the rind cannot be dented with a thumbnail; cure for 2 weeks in a warm, airy spot before moving to cold storage.

name: Warty Goblin Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm, fertile soil; a novelty hybrid grown for its heavily warted rind rather than eating quality, popular for spooky fall displays.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in fertile, well-drained soil, giving vines 6 feet of room to sprawl. Warty Goblin is a novelty hybrid pumpkin bred purely for eerie ornamental appeal, producing 8-20 pound fruit with a hard orange rind studded in dense, gnarled green warts that persist for weeks after harvest before slowly fading. The plants show useful intermediate resistance to powdery mildew, helping the vines stay productive later into the season than many older open-pollinated types. Because the flesh is stringy and thin compared to culinary pumpkins, Warty Goblin is grown strictly for Halloween decorating rather than cooking; harvest once the rind has fully hardened and cure briefly before display.

name: Wasabi Arugula
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wasabi arugula bolts and turns fiery hot quickly in summer heat, so plan for cool-season harvest and succession sow every two to three weeks.
directions: Direct sow in early spring or late summer into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Wasabi arugula bolts and turns fiery hot quickly in summer heat, so plan for cool-season harvest and succession sow every two to three weeks. This selection of salad arugula is bred for an intense, sinus-clearing heat reminiscent of true wasabi, with deeply lobed, dark green leaves that pack noticeably more pungency than standard arugula, especially as plants mature or experience heat or drought stress. Harvest young leaves for a milder bite in mixed salads, or let plants grow larger for a bold, spicy addition to sandwiches and cooked greens where its heat mellows somewhat with cooking. Partial shade in warm climates helps delay bolting and keeps the intense flavor from becoming overwhelming; keep soil consistently moist to slow premature flowering.

name: Wasabina
plantingNote: Best harvested young as a baby-leaf salad green; the horseradish-like bite intensifies as leaves mature and in warmer weather.
directions: Wasabina is a mizuna-type mustard green selected for a sharp, wasabi-like bite that adds punch to salad mixes without needing actual wasabi root. Direct sow shallowly into rich soil and grow as a cut-and-come-again crop, snipping the glossy, deeply serrated leaves at baby size for the mildest, most versatile flavor. It thrives in cool spring and fall conditions and tends to bolt in summer heat, so succession sow every few weeks for continuous harvest. Use sparingly as a spicy accent in mesclun mixes, sandwiches, or sushi-style garnishes.

name: Washday Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed; half-runner vines benefit from a bit of extra spacing or light support.
directions: Washday is an old-time Tennessee heirloom southern pea, so named because its small cream-colored seeds with dark hilums cooked up quickly enough to fit into a busy laundry day. Half-runner vines set clusters of 3-4 pods, each 5-6 inches long, for relatively easy picking despite the vining habit. It is now a rare, at-risk heirloom, listed among threatened Place-Based Foods of Appalachia varieties, making it a good conservation choice for gardeners wanting to keep an old regional pea in circulation.

name: Watermelon Beefsteak Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Watermelon Beefsteak is a large-fruited indeterminate variety that needs sturdy staking or caging to support fruit that can reach 1-2 pounds.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil, staking firmly to support the very heavy fruit. Watermelon Beefsteak is a West Virginia heirloom dating to the 1800s, later listed in a 1958 seed catalog, that produces huge, pink-skinned beefsteak fruit with purplish-red flesh reminiscent of watermelon coloring, weighing up to 1-2 pounds at maturity. The flavor is mild, juicy, and sweet, and the large flattened fruit is prized for slicing into broad rounds for sandwiches and salads.

name: Watermelon Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall through spring harvest. Watermelon radish performs best in cool fall weather — the pink interior color is more vivid and the flavor milder in fall-grown roots than spring plantings. In zone 9 the fall planting (September–November) produces the finest quality. The large roots (2–4 inches diameter) require 60–70 days — significantly longer than small spring radishes — and develop best in cool soil with consistent moisture. Thin to 4–5 inches apart.
directions: Plant in full sun in deep, loose, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil free of rocks and compaction; Watermelon Radish is a Chinese heirloom daikon-type radish producing large (golf ball to small apple sized), round roots with an unremarkable white-green exterior that opens to reveal a dramatically vivid magenta-pink interior — when sliced crosswise the cross-section closely resembles a miniature watermelon, with the pale green rind and pink-red interior creating the watermelon pattern that gives this radish its common name. The visual reveal of slicing a Watermelon Radish is one of the most surprising in the vegetable garden — the dramatic interior color makes it the most visually striking vegetable for salads, garnishes, and decorative vegetable presentations. The flavor is milder, sweeter, and less pungent than small red radishes, with only moderate spiciness and a crisp, juicy texture. The large size provides substantial raw radish slices for salads, vegetable platters, and pickled preparations. Fall-grown roots develop the most vivid pink color.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Watermelon Radish Description
University of Wisconsin Extension — Specialty Radish Production
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Asian Radish Varieties

name: Webbs Wonderful Lettuce
plantingNote: Sow directly and thin to full spacing so heads can size up over a long, cool growing season.
directions: Sow directly and thin to full spacing so heads can size up over a long, cool growing season, since it matures more slowly than modern hybrid icebergs. Introduced by the Webbs seed company of Stourbridge, England, in the early twentieth century, this crisphead forms large, dense, frilly-edged pale green heads with a satisfying crunch and is long considered one of England's finest garden icebergs. It remains a staple of British allotments, valued for standing in the garden without premature bolting.

name: Wee-B-Little Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; a 1999 All-America Selections winner with true bush habit and short vines, making it one of the most space-efficient pumpkins for containers or small beds.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile soil; Wee-B-Little's compact bush habit and short 6-8 foot vines mean it needs far less garden space than standard pumpkins and grows well in large containers. This 1999 All-America Selections winner produces three to four miniature, deep-orange pumpkins per plant, each weighing only 8 ounces to a pound, with smooth skin that takes paint and carving detail beautifully. The uniform bush habit and heavy fruit set make it a favorite for classroom gardens and children's plots where kids can grow and claim their own small pumpkin. Harvest once the rind hardens and resists a fingernail scratch, leaving 3-4 inches of stem attached to extend shelf life.

name: Wehani Rice
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant into flooded paddy beds after all danger of frost, in a long, warm growing season; Wehani needs more heat and time than short-season rice types like Duborskian.
directions: Wehani was developed over roughly a decade by a California rice-growing family, working from basmati-type parent stock, and its name is drawn from the initials of five family members. It is grown as a whole-grain (brown) rice with a reddish-brown bran layer left intact, and it is one of the longer-season aromatic rices, needing a generous warm summer to fill and ripen its large, basmati-shaped grains. Grow it flooded in a paddy bed or lined stock tank, keeping standing water over the root zone through most of the season and drawing it down as the heads dry and color darkens toward harvest. When cooked it releases a toasty, peanut-like aroma that has made it a favorite in home rice blends and pilafs.

name: Wenk's Yellow Hot Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; transplant into warm soil after frost danger has passed. Wenk's Yellow Hot is an Iowa heirloom maintained and distributed through Seed Savers Exchange, prized for dependable production of tapering yellow hot peppers.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost, spacing plants to accommodate the tall, productive habit. Wenk's Yellow Hot bears tapering, 3-4 inch fruit that ripens from pale yellow-green to a bright golden yellow, with a brisk, moderate-to-hot heat well suited to pickling and hot sauce. The vigorous, upright plants set fruit heavily over a long season and hold up well in home garden conditions without special care. This Midwestern family heirloom has been passed down and preserved through seed-saving networks rather than commercial breeding.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Wenk's Yellow Hot Pepper

name: Wes Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Wes is a potato-leaf indeterminate heirloom that needs a sturdy cage or stake to carry its large pink fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into deeply worked, fertile soil after frost risk passes, staking plants early to support the heavy fruit. Wes is a potato-leaf heirloom out of West Virginia producing large, smooth, rosy-pink beefsteak fruit with the rich, well-rounded flavor characteristic of the best Appalachian pink tomatoes. The vigorous indeterminate vines crop steadily through a long season with routine staking and watering. Harvest when fully colored but still firm, and water evenly during fruit development to limit cracking and blossom-end rot.

name: Westland Winter Kale
plantingNote: Start indoors or direct sow; kale is also an excellent fall crop, since cool weather and light frost sweeten the leaves' flavor.
directions: Start indoors or direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Westland Winter is a classic, cold-hardy curly kale long grown in Britain for reliable winter harvests, producing dense, tightly ruffled, blue-green leaves on sturdy, productive plants that stand up well to cold, wind, and less-than-ideal soil. Its exceptional cold hardiness makes it a strong choice for extending the harvest deep into winter in colder climates, and like other kale it becomes noticeably sweeter and more tender after exposure to frost. Harvest outer leaves regularly from the bottom of the plant upward, leaving the central rosette to continue producing new growth over the season.

name: Whale Spinach
plantingNote: Sow in late summer to early fall for continued production into the warm shoulder season; can also be sown in early spring before heat sets in.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil and thin to final spacing, watering deeply to sustain the plant's large leaf size through warm weather. Named for its oversized, smooth blue-green leaves, this hybrid was selected specifically to resist bolting under longer days and warmer temperatures than most spinach can tolerate. It gives Gulf Coast growers a wider sowing window on either end of the cool season, holding productive quality later into spring and earlier into fall.

name: Whaley's Favorite Cabbage Collard
plantingNote: Sow for a fall harvest; leaves sweeten and become more tender after light frost, and the plant can also be timed for spring crops in cooler zones.
directions: Kept for generations by a South Carolina family as a home-garden seed-saving tradition, this variety is part of the same cabbage-collard lineage as White Mountain and Yellow Cabbage Collard. Its broad, smooth, light-to-medium green leaves have slightly crinkled edges and gather into a loose, rounded, cabbage-like head rather than growing fully open like a typical collard. The texture is markedly more tender than standard collards, and the flavor is milder and sweeter, especially after a frost, which suits it to quick sautes as well as the long, slow-simmered pots traditional to Southern cooking.

name: Wheatland Heirloom Grain Sorghum
plantingNote: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep after danger of frost has passed and soil has warmed, then thin to final spacing; sorghum germinates poorly in cold soil so waiting an extra week or two past last frost pays off.
directions: Wheatland is an open-pollinated heirloom grain sorghum, sometimes marketed as milo, that produces large, well-filled heads of round, off-white seed on stalks 6 to 7 feet tall. It is drought-tolerant once established and thrives in the same hot, dry conditions that stress corn, making it a reliable backup grain crop in areas prone to summer dry spells. The dried grain can be ground into a gluten-free flour or cracked for cereal, and the mature stalks and leftover heads make useful livestock and poultry feed. Harvest whole heads once the seed has hardened and the plant has begun to dry down, then thresh and winnow before storage.

name: Whidby White Okra
