plantingNote: Direct sow once frost danger has fully passed and soil has warmed; Whidby White was donated to Seed Savers Exchange in the mid-1980s by a Georgia family that had kept it since the mid-1800s, then nearly vanished before the Utopian Seed Project and regional seed growers revived it around 2018.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep in full sun in warm, well-drained soil; Whidby White is a rare Southern heirloom grown for its short, pale, deeply ridged pods that are naturally spineless and easy to handle at harvest. The pale coloring sets it visibly apart from the standard green okra most Gulf South gardeners are used to, and the short pod length means it needs closer watching to catch pods at their most tender. This variety was nearly lost entirely before community seed-saving efforts restored it, so it is a genuine rescue heirloom rather than a long-available commercial strain.
sources: Sow True Seed — Whidby White Okra

name: Whippoorwill Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; Whippoorwill is a rangier, semi-vining heirloom that benefits from a bit more spacing than compact modern cowpea cultivars.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean soil in full sun, and avoid rich, heavily fertilized ground, which pushes vine growth at the expense of pod production in this vigorous heirloom. Whippoorwill is one of the oldest documented Southern cowpea varieties, grown since before the Civil War and named for its speckled brown-and-tan seed coat, which resembles the mottled plumage of the whippoorwill bird. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant, it was historically valued as a dual-purpose crop, grown both for its rich, earthy-flavored dried and fresh peas and as a soil-building, nitrogen-fixing cover crop plowed under to enrich depleted fields, a role it still serves well in a home garden rotation. Its tough constitution and long history make it a genuine piece of Southern agricultural heritage as well as a reliable, low-input summer crop. Harvest pods green for fresh shelling or let them dry fully on the vine for long-term storage.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Whippoorwill cowpea heritage notes
USDA National Genetic Resources Program — cowpea germplasm records

name: Whippoorwill Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant March–May for spring harvest and August–September for fall. Whippoorwill is a sprawling, vigorous heirloom that does best with room to spread; allow 36–48 inches between rows.
directions: Direct sow 1–1.5 inches deep in well-drained soil and allow vines to sprawl freely; Whippoorwill is a pre-Civil War Southern heirloom with a sprawling, semi-vining habit that naturalizes well in field conditions. The speckled brown-and-cream seeds are distinctive and historically used both as a fresh shell pea and a dry bean, with a rich, slightly nutty flavor preferred by many Southern gardeners over modern varieties. It is particularly favored for field cultivation as a dual-purpose food and cover crop in the South, where it fixes substantial nitrogen and suppresses summer weeds. Seeds are saved easily — allow selected pods to dry fully on the vine.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Whippoorwill Pea
Seed Savers Exchange — Heirloom Southern Peas
Alabama Cooperative Extension System — Southern Pea Varieties

name: White Acre Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after the last frost when soil has warmed above 65°F in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun; White Acre pea is heat-tolerant and thrives in Gulf South summer heat — plant succession crops through summer for continuous fresh production from May through September in zone 9.
directions: Direct sow after the last frost when soil is warm in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; White Acre pea is one of the most distinctive and prized southern pea varieties of the Texas and Gulf Coast tradition — a small-seeded cream pea producing petite, white to cream-white seeds with exceptionally sweet, buttery, delicate flavor that differs meaningfully from the larger-seeded, more robust flavor of standard cream peas and blackeye peas. The small seed size of White Acre is characteristic — the peas are notably smaller than regular cream peas, more compact in the shelled bowl, and cook to a sweeter, creamier texture with a refined flavor profile that has made White Acre the preference of many Gulf South cooks for fresh summer pea dishes. In zone 9, White Acre produces abundantly from its first harvest through summer and into fall — planting succession crops every 3–4 weeks from April through August provides continuous fresh pea production throughout the longest part of the growing season. White Acre is a semi-bush to vining type reaching 18–24 inches and performs well without staking in most garden conditions. The vines fix atmospheric nitrogen, improving soil fertility for subsequent crops. Harvest when hulls are well-filled but still green for fresh-shelled use; allow to dry completely for storage. White Acre is particularly important in Gulf Coast cuisine and is a foundational variety of the traditional summer pea dishes of Louisiana, Texas, and Mississippi.

name: White Bermuda Onion
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter zones; White Bermuda is a short-day type well suited to fall planting in the Gulf South, producing flattened bulbs with thin, papery white skin and very mild flesh.
directions: Start seeds indoors or direct-seed in fall in mild-winter regions, since this classic short-day onion needs the shorter daylight of a southern winter to bulb properly. Long grown in Texas, Louisiana, and other Gulf Coast states before more modern hybrid sweet onions became common, White Bermuda produces flattened, disc-shaped bulbs with thin, pure white skin and mild, tender flesh with relatively low pungency. Because the papery skin is thin, cured bulbs do not store as long as pungent storage onions and are best used within a few months of harvest. Keep soil evenly moist through bulb development and reduce watering as the tops begin to yellow and fall over ahead of harvest.

name: White Chia
plantingNote: Sow after last frost; chia is a short-day plant that flowers in fall, so it is best suited to climates with a long frost-free autumn. White Chia produces pale cream-to-white seed rather than the typical dark brown-black.
directions: Surface-sow seed on a firm, moist seedbed and barely press in, as chia seed is mucilaginous and will stick to the surface when wet; thin plants to 18-24 inches once seedlings emerge. White Chia produces pale cream-to-white seed rather than the typical dark brown-to-black coloring of standard chia, an attractive variant for gardeners wanting visual variety in a home-grown chia harvest, with the same nutritional profile and whorled purple flower spikes appearing in autumn as day length shortens. Chia does not respond well to transplanting and should be direct-sown where it will grow. Harvest stalks when the calyces begin to dry and before birds consume the seed, placing harvested stalks head-first into paper bags to finish drying, then shake out seed and screen away debris.

name: White Egg Turnip
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall (late August–October in zone 9) or very early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; White Egg is one of the fastest-maturing turnips and quickly turns pithy if left in the ground past size, so sow in succession and pull promptly.
directions: Direct sow in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and thin young seedlings to a few inches apart; White Egg is a classic 19th-century American heirloom prized for its smooth, pure-white, egg-shaped roots that sit mostly above the soil line, making them easy to spot and pull. Flesh is exceptionally fine-grained, crisp, and mild for a turnip, holding its quality raw in slaws as well as cooked, and the roots reach usable size faster than almost any other turnip variety. Because it matures so quickly it is an excellent choice for a fast catch crop between other plantings or for gardeners who want an early fall harvest well before frost; roots left in the ground too long lose their fine texture and become woody, so check size regularly and harvest promptly once roots reach 2–3 inches across.

name: White Emergo Runner Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost against a tall, sturdy trellis or pole structure; this vigorous climbing runner bean performs best where summer nights stay cool.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep at the base of a tall trellis, teepee, or fence once the soil has warmed, since vines can climb 8 to 10 feet and need sturdy support. White Emergo is a long-grown heirloom runner bean valued for its cream-white blossoms, smooth stringless green pods 8 to 12 inches long, and creamy white seeds that can be eaten as a fresh snap bean, shelled green as a butterbean, or dried for winter storage. It has earned recognition from the Royal Horticultural Society for its reliable, heavy yields and fine flavor. Keep pods picked regularly to extend the harvest and prevent the plant from slowing production.

name: White Gem Parsnip
plantingNote: Direct sow fresh seed once soil can be worked in spring, into deep, loose, well-prepared ground free of stones and clods for straight, unforked roots.
directions: White Gem is an English garden parsnip selected for very pale, smooth skin, a bluntly wedge-shaped root, and good field tolerance to canker, making it a reliable choice where older heirloom types tend to scar and rot at the shoulder. Keep the bed consistently moist through slow, patchy germination and thin seedlings early to prevent crowding, which encourages forked roots. Its clean, uniform appearance and sweet, fine-grained flesh have made it a popular choice for both kitchen use and vegetable show competitions in the UK. Leave roots in the ground until after several hard frosts, since the cold converts starches to sugar and produces the variety's characteristic sweetness.

name: White Greasy Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, setting up a sturdy pole or trellis at planting time since vines climb tall and keep producing over a long season.
directions: This Appalachian heirloom produces smooth, stringless, shiny pods typical of the greasy bean group, with no fuzz on the pod surface. Seeds are notably large and white, and the vines are vigorous, heavy-bearing climbers that benefit from a tall trellis or pole. Pick pods young for snap use or let them mature for shelling and drying. Save seed from fully dry pods for the truest flavor and productivity in following years.

name: White Half Runner Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost in any fertile, well-drained soil; white half runner needs only 2–3 feet of support — short stakes or a low fence is sufficient for the semi-vining habit. Successive plantings every 2–3 weeks extend the harvest through the season.
directions: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, providing 2–3 feet of support for the semi-vining plants; white half runner is the most popular snap bean in the home gardens and farmers markets of the Appalachian mountains and Southern uplands, occupying the productive middle ground between bush beans (no support needed, shorter production) and full pole beans (requires tall trellis, longer season). The semi-vining plants produce abundantly over a concentrated 2–3 week period, making them excellent for canning and freezing in large batches as well as fresh table use. The pods are round, stringless when young, and have excellent fresh-eating flavor. White seeds make it useful as a dry bean after pods mature fully. The Mountaineer White Half Runner was bred at the West Virginia Extension station specifically for the cool-summer Appalachian region but is equally productive in the Gulf South when planted in spring or fall.

name: White Icicle Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall 4–6 weeks before first frost; White Icicle is an elongated, all-white heirloom radish producing 4–6 inch cylindrical roots that remain crisp, mild, and tender at larger sizes than typical round red varieties — making it a preferred choice for fresh eating and cooking when the texture and flavor of a larger, milder radish are desired.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep and thin to 2–3 inches apart; White Icicle is faster-maturing than daikon (25–35 days vs. 60+ days) and milder than Chinese black radish, fitting into the cool-season rotation between spring planting and summer heat; harvest before roots reach maximum size for finest quality. White Icicle is a classic heirloom radish that has been grown in American gardens since the 19th century and appears in Victorian-era seed catalogs as one of the standard garden radish varieties. Unlike the small, round, red radishes (Cherry Belle, Champion, Sparkler) that dominate modern radish offerings, White Icicle produces elongated, cylindrical, all-white roots 4–6 inches long with a gentle taper — resembling a large, smooth, pale daikon in miniature. The flavor is milder and less pungent than round red varieties at the same stage of maturity, and the texture is firm and crisp without the slight woodiness that can develop in large round varieties. White Icicle is excellent for fresh eating in salads (the white color is elegant against greens), for cutting into sticks for crudités platters, for Japanese-style pickles, for cooking in stir-fries (where it holds its shape better than rounder types), and for the traditional French preparation of radishes served with butter and salt. The elongated shape also makes White Icicle more practical for slicing in certain applications where round radishes are inconvenient.

name: White Jersey Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant slips after last frost when soil warms above 65°F; White Jersey is an old American heirloom sweet potato grown in New Jersey since at least the mid-1800s, producing tan to buff-white-skinned, cream-to-white-fleshed roots of the 'dry' (starchy) type preferred in traditional American cooking before moist orange-fleshed types became dominant in the late 19th century.
directions: Plant slips 12–18 inches apart in well-prepared, loose, well-drained, sandy loam soil after soil warms above 65°F; White Jersey produces best in sandy or light soils. White Jersey is an American heirloom sweet potato representing the 'dry' type that was dominant in American cooking before the mid-20th century when moist orange-fleshed varieties became the standard; grown in New Jersey's sweet potato tradition since at least the 1850s, it produces pale buff to tan-skinned roots with cream-white flesh that cooks to a dry, fluffy, mealy texture resembling an Irish potato more than a modern sweet potato. The flavor is mild, subtle, and lightly sweet without the intense caramel sweetness of orange varieties. This dry, starchy texture was highly prized in traditional American cooking for sweet potato pie (which sets firmer), sweet potato biscuits, and baked goods where a drier texture improved the final product. Now maintained by seed savers as a historical artifact of early American sweet potato culture; an excellent educational variety for understanding the dramatic change in American sweet potato preferences over 150 years.

name: White Malabar Spinach
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant March–May. Soak seeds 24 hours in warm water before sowing to speed germination. White Malabar Spinach grows best in the hottest part of summer when all other spinach has bolted — it thrives from June through September in zone 9 and is one of the most productive summer leafy greens available. Provide a trellis or fence for the vigorous vines, which can reach 10 feet or more.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained, consistently moist soil in full sun to partial shade; White Malabar Spinach (Basella alba 'Alba') is the green-stemmed, white-flowered form of Malabar spinach — distinct from the red-stemmed Basella rubra (Ceylon Spinach) in having entirely green stems, greener foliage, and smaller white berries. The large, thick, glossy, heart-shaped to oval leaves have the same mild, slightly mucilaginous spinach substitute quality as the red form, used raw in salads when young and tender or cooked in the same manner as spinach — sautéed, in soups, curries, and braised dishes throughout Southeast Asian, Indian, and West African cooking. The white form is favored in some cuisines where the red pigment of the red form is undesirable in finished dishes; the green stems and white berries also make it slightly more attractive as an ornamental vine for trellises and fences. In zone 9 White Malabar Spinach is the premier summer leafy green — a vigorous, heat-loving vining plant that fills the summer gap when all cool-season greens have finished and heat prevents new sowings.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Malabar Spinach Production
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Summer Leafy Greens for the Gulf South
University of Hawaii Extension — Basella alba Growing Notes

name: White Mountain Cabbage Collard
plantingNote: Sow in spring for a loose cabbage-like head by fall, following the traditional South Carolina cultivation timing for this family line.
directions: This South Carolina family heirloom was donated to Seed Savers Exchange along with a family memory of the leaves being used for homemade sauerkraut. Unlike open-leaf collards, White Mountain is compact with short stems, and when spring-sown it draws its yellow-green-blue leaves into a fairly tight cabbage-like head by fall rather than staying loose and upright. It represents the cabbage-collard branch of Southern collard breeding, alongside Yellow Cabbage Collard and Whaley's Favorite, where growers selected for a heading habit combined with collard-style leaf texture.

name: White Pearl Bitter Melon
plantingNote: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep after soil has thoroughly warmed and all frost danger has passed, providing a sturdy trellis for the vigorous climbing vines.
directions: This Taiwanese-type bitter melon produces oblong fruit that opens pale green and ripens to a smooth, ivory-white skin, a milder-tasting and visually striking alternative to the typical dark green Chinese and Indian types. Fruits run 6-9 inches long and about 3 inches across, with noticeably less bitterness than most bitter melon selections, making it a good introduction to the crop for first-time growers. Grow it on a sturdy trellis in full sun with consistent moisture, and harvest while the skin is still firm and pale rather than letting it soften and yellow. It has become popular in West Coast Asian markets, commanding a premium price over standard green types.

name: White Portugal Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow as early as soil can be worked in late winter for fall harvest, or set out transplants 4–6 weeks before last frost; White Portugal is intermediate-day type performing well in zone 6–8 spring plantings where day length increases properly for bulb initiation. In zone 9, fall planting (October–November) as a short-day-adapted spring harvested variety is also possible. White Portugal is excellent harvested young as a scallion (bunching onion) before bulbs develop, making it dual-purpose.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in early spring; pull at any size from scallion stage through full bulb maturity. White Portugal (also called White Silver Queen, Italian White, or White Silverskin in some seed catalogs) is a traditional open-pollinated white-skinned onion with a long history in American and European kitchen gardens — one of the primary heirloom white onions before the development of modern F1 hybrid white types. The bulbs are medium-large, somewhat flattened to globe-shaped, with silvery-white papery skin and white flesh. The flavor is notably milder than yellow storage onions — White Portugal has lower pungency than standard yellow types, making it well-suited for fresh eating, pickling, and preparations where mild onion character is preferred. White Portugal is the traditional pickling onion for pearl onion preparations and for cocktail onions; the white color remains clean through pickling without the discoloration that sometimes occurs with yellow-skinned types. The variety is also excellent harvested young as a green/bunching onion (scallion), where the white sheath and mild flavor make it among the most attractive bunching onions. Being open-pollinated, seed can be saved year to year from the best-formed bulbs.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — White Portugal onion variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — White onion collection
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Onion Variety Comparison

name: White Proso Millet
plantingNote: Sow after last frost once soil is warm; white proso is the pale, food-grade seed class preferred for birdseed blends and home milling over the red or golden proso types.
directions: Drill or broadcast seed about 1/2 inch deep into warm, weed-free soil and thin stands to 4-6 inches apart; white proso is the pale-hulled market class grown for birdseed and human food rather than wildlife plots, and buyers pay a premium for clean, unmixed white seed lots. The plant tillers moderately and produces a loose, drooping panicle that ripens unevenly from the top down, so watch for shattering once the lower seeds harden. Cut whole stalks when most of the panicle has turned from green to straw color, then finish drying the bundles under cover for 10-14 days before threshing and winnowing. Because proso millet is one of the shortest-season grains available, a second planting is often possible in zones with a long enough frost-free window.

name: White Spear Bunching Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow from early spring through midsummer; White Spear was selected to resist bulbing, splitting, and leaf-curl through hot summer weather better than most bunching types.
directions: White Spear produces tall, straight, blue-green tops over long, cylindrical white shanks that stay uniform and resist the splitting and curling that plague many bunching onions during peak summer heat. It is less winter-hardy than overwintering types such as Evergreen Hardy White, so it performs best sown for a spring-through-fall harvest window rather than left to stand through hard freezes. Its clean, uniform stalks and heat tolerance make it a dependable choice for a continuous summer scallion supply. Harvest at pencil thickness for the mildest flavor and most tender texture, or let shanks thicken slightly for a stronger bite.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange catalog description

name: White Sprouting Broccoli
plantingNote: Start seed in mid- to late summer and transplant in early fall so plants are well established but not yet flowering before winter; the plants overwinter as compact rosettes and send up their edible flowering shoots in late winter to early spring, well ahead of purple sprouting types.
directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in late summer or early fall, spacing plants wide to accommodate a full season of growth before the harvest of edible flower shoots the following late winter. White Sprouting is a classic English heirloom broccoli grown as a hardy biennial: plants spend fall and winter building a large rosette of foliage, then in late winter to early spring send up a profusion of small, tender, cream-white flowering shoots that are harvested continually over several weeks, much like purple sprouting broccoli but ivory-headed and typically a touch earlier. Regular picking of the central and side shoots before flowers open encourages continued production, and the long harvest window makes it valuable for filling the late-winter garden gap when little else is producing. It needs a long, cool growing season to perform well and is best suited to mild-winter climates like the Gulf South where it can overwinter in the open ground without protection.

name: White Sweet Spanish Onion
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 10-12 weeks before last frost and transplant after danger of hard frost has passed; White Sweet Spanish is a long-day type needing 14+ hours of summer daylight to bulb, making it best suited to northern and mid-latitude gardens rather than the short-day Gulf South.
directions: Start seeds indoors in late winter and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after the last hard frost. This long-established long-day onion produces large, globe-shaped bulbs with clean white skin and mild, juicy, sweet flesh with a milder bite than most storage onions, making it a popular choice for fresh eating, salads, and onion rings. Because long-day onions need the extended summer daylight of higher latitudes to bulb properly, it performs best north of about zone 7 and tends to produce poorly or bolt in the short-day Deep South. Keep soil consistently moist through bulb development and cure bulbs in a warm, airy spot after the tops fall over, though sweet types like this one store for a shorter time than pungent storage onions.

name: White Transparent Sugarcane
plantingNote: Plant stalk sections (billets) with 2-3 nodes horizontally in a shallow furrow after last frost; in zone 9 plant February-April. White Transparent is a pale-stalked heirloom chewing cane preserved in the small dooryard-cane collections maintained in Florida and Louisiana.
directions: Plant billets of two or three nodes in loose, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, keeping soil consistently moist through the growing season. White Transparent is an old chewing-cane heirloom with pale, whitish-yellow-green stalks, distinct from the purple, red, and striped canes traditionally grown alongside it in the same dooryard patch. Like other chewing types it has a soft rind and high juice content, with fibers that cling together in a wad rather than shredding when gnawed, making it a favorite for fresh peeling and eating rather than crushing for syrup, though the juice can be pressed like any cane. It is maintained today mainly through small heirloom cane collections and informal seed-saver networks in Florida and Louisiana rather than commercial nurseries. Propagate from stalk sets saved over winter: cut healthy, disease-free stalks before the first hard freeze, bed them horizontally in a shaded, well-drained trench, and cover heavily with soil, pine straw, or plastic to keep them dormant without freezing until replanting the following spring once soil has warmed. Harvest for fresh chewing from October through December after cool nights have sweetened the stalks.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Backyard Sugarcane (SS-AGR-253/SC052)
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Sugarcane Production and Heirloom Varieties
Southern Foodways Alliance — Cane Syrup Traditions

name: White Triumph Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed above 65F, in loose, well-drained soil formed into ridges in full sun; White Triumph is one of the older dry-fleshed sweet potato types still kept in circulation by heirloom growers.
directions: Set slips 12-18 inches apart in loose, sandy-loam soil hilled into ridges, and hold off on nitrogen-rich fertilizer since it pushes vine growth at the expense of root formation. White Triumph is a vintage dry-type sweet potato with tan to yellowish-white skin and snow-white flesh that cooks up firm and mealy rather than moist, closer in texture to a baking potato than to a modern orange-fleshed variety, with a mild, only lightly sweet flavor. Vines are vigorous and the roots are known to resist soil rot and scurf better than many old white-fleshed types, giving reliable mid-season yields around 90-105 days. Dig before the first frost once vines start to yellow, then cure in a warm, humid spot for a week or two to firm the skin and improve keeping quality.
sources: North Carolina State Extension - Sweet Potato Production

name: White Velvet Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is thoroughly warm (70°F minimum); White Velvet okra produces round, pale green to cream-white pods rather than the elongated, ridged form of standard okra. In zone 9, plant April through July for summer production. Soak seeds overnight before planting to improve germination. The pods are smooth and rounded in cross-section (unlike the distinctly ribbed, angular pods of most standard okra) — the 'round' pod character reduces toughness at larger sizes, allowing harvest at 3–4 inches without the fibrous, over-mature texture that makes standard okra unpalatable when left too long. White Velvet has an old, well-documented history in American seed saving and is available through heirloom seed companies. The slightly different pod form and smooth surface give the cooked pods a different texture than standard okra — less 'slimy' than some types, which some cooks prefer.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after soil warms to 70°F; thin to 12–18 inches. Harvest pods at 2–3 inches for most tender pods. White Velvet Okra is an heirloom okra variety distinguished from the standard elongated ridged types by its round, smooth pods — the 'velvet' texture of the surface, which lacks the prominent longitudinal ridges of varieties like Clemson Spineless, and the pale green to cream-white color at harvest maturity (before fully ripening to cream-white and drying). The round-pod okra group, of which White Velvet is one of the best-known American heirloom examples, represents a different selection from the standard commercial okra breeding that prioritized uniformly ridged, elongated pods for mechanical harvesting and packing. Round-pod types have thinner, more tender pod walls and a slightly different texture and mucilage content than ridged types — attributes that some cooks prefer, particularly for preparations where the 'sliminess' of okra is considered a negative quality. White Velvet's pods harvested at 2–3 inches have a tender, delicate texture and mild flavor appropriate for sautéing, grilling, pickling, and use in gumbo where the mucilaginous properties of okra serve as a natural thickener. The plant is vigorous and heat-tolerant — essential qualities for zone 9 summer production — and produces prolifically throughout the summer if harvested regularly. The cream-white color at harvest maturity (before pods fully dry and tan) makes White Velvet visually distinctive from the dark green and burgundy okra varieties and attractive for fresh-market presentation.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — White Velvet round-pod heirloom okra documentation
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — White Velvet okra historical variety notes
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Heritage okra variety descriptions for the South

name: White Wing Onion
subcategory: fresh-eating onion, hybrid white sweet type
plantingNote: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant seedlings outside about 4-6 weeks before the last expected frost.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights and transplant hardened seedlings into rich, well-drained soil once frost danger has passed, spacing plants to let bulbs expand freely. Keep soil consistently moist through bulb development, since this fast-maturing type sizes up quickly and does not tolerate drought well during that stage. White Wing is a widely grown hybrid valued for its early maturity, glossy white globe-shaped bulbs, and mild sweet flavor best used fresh, as short-season sweet onions like this one are not bred for long winter storage.

name: White Wonder Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; in zone 9 plant February–March for spring and August for fall. White Wonder matures ivory-white and should be harvested when fully colored but before any yellowing begins — at this stage the flesh is at its most crisp, cool, and mild. Remove overripe fruits promptly to keep the vine producing. Provide a trellis for more vertical growth and cleaner fruit.
directions: Direct sow in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with consistent moisture; White Wonder is an heirloom slicing cucumber producing large, 7–8 inch fruits with ivory-to-cream-white skin, crisp white flesh, and an exceptionally mild, cool, lightly sweet flavor with virtually no bitterness — the mildest of all cucumber types. The white color results from the absence of chlorophyll in the skin rather than from immaturity; properly ripe White Wonder fruits are uniformly ivory-white and are never green. The skin is thin and does not require peeling, and the flesh is juicier and more tender than standard green cucumbers with the same thin-skinned type. White Wonder cucumbers are a curiosity and conversation piece in the garden and at farmers' markets, attracting attention precisely because the white color is unexpected. The heat tolerance is comparable to standard cucumber types, and the vigorous vines produce well through zone 9 spring and fall seasons. Pick every 2–3 days to maintain production.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — White Wonder Cucumber Heritage Variety
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — White Cucumber Varieties
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — White Cucumber Types

name: Whopper Improved Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once frost danger has passed; Whopper Improved is a Park Seed hybrid beefsteak bred for large fruit size and broad disease resistance on a vigorous indeterminate vine.
directions: Start seed indoors under lights, then transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after all frost danger has passed, staking or caging the vigorous vine to support the heavy fruit. Whopper Improved is a Park Seed hybrid beefsteak tomato bred for large, meaty, flavorful fruit and broad resistance to common tomato diseases, making it a reliable choice for gardeners wanting big slicing tomatoes without the disease susceptibility of many open-pollinated beefsteak heirlooms. It produces well over a long season in the Gulf South's extended warm months. Water consistently to prevent blossom-end rot and fruit cracking, and feed regularly to sustain the large fruit size through the harvest season.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Tomato Production

name: Wildcat Cayenne Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Wildcat is a compact, even-growing cayenne plant that carries an unusually heavy load of long, straight fruit.
directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun after frost danger has passed. Wildcat is an AAS regional winner selected for extra-large cayenne pods, roughly 8 inches long and straighter than typical cayenne fruit, with thicker, fleshier walls than older varieties. Heat is notably mild for a cayenne, in the 500-1500 Scoville range, giving a smoky, peppery sweetness that works well fresh, dried, or ground. The strong, compact, evenly branching plant sets fruit heavily and holds up well through the growing season with routine picking to encourage continued production.
sources: All-America Selections — Pepper cayenne Wildcat F1 winner announcement

name: Wilhelmsburger Rutabaga
plantingNote: Direct sow in mid- to late summer, roughly three months before the first fall frost, for a sweet, storable fall and winter crop.
directions: Sow seed directly and thin to a final spacing of six to eight inches, since this Central European heirloom needs room for its globe-shaped root to bulk up. Wilhelmsburger produces a purple-topped, pale yellow-fleshed root known for dense texture and a mild, almost nutty sweetness that intensifies after a light frost. Leave roots in the ground into cool fall weather before harvesting for the best flavor and longest storage life, and use the tender young tops as cooked greens if thinning early plantings.

name: William Alexander Heading Collards
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost for a spring crop, or direct sow in late summer for a fall/winter crop; a late-fall or winter harvest after frost gives the sweetest flavor.
directions: Sow seed 1/4-1/2 inch deep in fertile soil and thin or transplant to final spacing; this rare North Carolina heirloom was kept for generations by farmer William Alexander of Columbia, NC and selected specifically for its slight heading habit, giving broad, wavy, deep-green leaves that curl inward to form a loose, cabbage-like center while outer leaves stay loose. The flavor is rich and distinctly mustardy with a touch of sweetness, more assertive than milder collard types. Harvest outer leaves as needed through the season, or cut the compact center head once it firms; like other collards it is more cold-hardy than cabbage and improves in flavor after frost.

name: Willow Leaf Lima Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past frost danger, since lima beans are especially sensitive to cold, wet soil; Willow Leaf is an old heirloom pole lima named for its narrow, willow-shaped leaves and valued for continuing to set pods through summer heat that stalls many other beans.
directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun once the soil has thoroughly warmed, providing a sturdy trellis or pole for the vigorous climbing vines. Willow Leaf lima bean is a Southern heirloom named for its distinctively narrow, willow-shaped leaflets, quite different from the broader foliage of most lima beans, and is prized for continuing to flower and set pods through the intense heat of a Gulf South summer that causes many other lima varieties to drop blossoms and stall production. Harvest pods once well-filled but still bright green for fresh shelling, or let them dry fully on the vine for storage beans. Regular picking of mature pods encourages the vine to keep flowering and setting new pods through the long growing season.

name: Wilson's Sweet Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills after soil has warmed well past last frost, giving vines plenty of room to ramble.
directions: Wilson's Sweet is an American heirloom watermelon offered commercially by several seed companies by the mid-20th century before falling out of wide circulation and being kept going mainly through preservation seed banks and dedicated growers. Fruit is round to oval with a distinctive mottled, spotted green rind and crisp, deep red flesh known for unusually high sweetness. Give vines generous spacing to sprawl in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and keep watering even through fruit set, tapering off as melons approach ripeness to help sugars concentrate. Because it is open-pollinated, isolated plantings allow home gardeners to save true seed from year to year.

name: Win-Win Choi
plantingNote: Direct sow shortly before the last frost, and again in late summer for a fall crop; Win-Win Choi's improved heat tolerance allows a somewhat longer planting window than many pac choi types.
directions: Direct sow in early spring after danger of hard frost has passed, or in late summer for a fall harvest, spacing seedlings close together for the miniature form Win-Win Choi is bred to produce. Win-Win Choi is a compact, white-stemmed hybrid pac choi that forms a bulky, uniform, vase-shaped head only about a foot tall at full size, making it well suited to close spacing, containers, and gardeners who prefer a smaller-format bok choy to the larger green-stemmed types. Its improved heat tolerance compared to many pac choi varieties allows for a longer planting window into warmer weather before bolting becomes a concern. Harvest whole plants at the baby stage for tender salad use or let them fill out for a heartier stir-fry green.

name: Window Box Roma Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors about 6 weeks before the last frost and transplant into a window box, patio pot, or small bed after frost danger has passed.
directions: Transplant into a sunny window box or small container after the last frost; the plant stays extremely compact, so it needs no staking or cage even when loaded with fruit. Window Box Roma is an All-America Selections winner bred to bring true plum-shaped paste tomatoes to the smallest growing spaces, producing 1.5-2 ounce oblong red fruit with meaty, low-moisture flesh well suited to sauces despite the plant's diminutive 12-18 inch stature. It offers one of the few genuinely dwarf paste-tomato options for balconies and windowsills.

name: Winner Kohlrabi
directions: Thin seedlings early so bulbs have room to swell into their characteristic semi-globe shape, which at nearly a pound still holds tender, non-fibrous flesh if harvested promptly. This pale-green hybrid is a dependable market-garden standard for bulk production because the whole planting matures within a tight window, simplifying one-pass harvest.

name: Winnigstadt Cabbage
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once seedlings have several true leaves, hardening them off against light frost first.
directions: Winnigstadt is a nineteenth-century German heirloom cabbage prized for its dense, hard, cone-shaped heads that taper to a point rather than forming the rounded or flattened heads typical of most cabbage types. The tight wrapper leaves and firm interior give it good natural resistance to splitting in wet weather and reasonable tolerance of heat, making it a flexible choice for both an early spring crop and a second planting for fall harvest. Its small core and dense texture have long made it a favorite for sauerkraut and slaw, and the compact plants can be set closer together than many large-framed cabbages. Harvest when heads feel solid and firm to the squeeze, cutting before hot weather causes the points to loosen and split.

name: Winter Bloomsdale Spinach
plantingNote: Sow 4-6 weeks before the first hard fall frost so plants are established but not overly mature going into winter.
directions: Sow directly in late summer or early fall so seedlings size up before short days and cold arrive, then protect with a low tunnel or thick mulch through the coldest months for an early spring harvest. This vigorous savoy-leaf hybrid was bred specifically for exceptional cold tolerance and holds its dark, crinkled foliage through hard freezes better than standard Bloomsdale types. Many growers value it as one of the most reliable spinach selections for season extension in cold climates.

name: Winter Density Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow 4–6 weeks before last frost in spring or in late summer for fall harvest; Winter Density is the quintessential British cold-season lettuce — a Romaine/Butterhead cross with tight, upright heads, exceptionally cold-hardy (tolerating temperatures to 22°F), and slow-bolting even in warming spring conditions; outstanding for year-round production in mild climates and cold frames in zones 5–9.
directions: Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in cool weather; Winter Density tolerates more cold than most lettuces and can be direct-sown in early spring (4–6 weeks before last frost) or late summer for fall harvest; thin to 8–10 inches apart; harvest as baby lettuce at 3–4 weeks or allow heads to mature fully; the heads hold in the garden well without bolting even in warm spring weather. Winter Density is a British heirloom lettuce representing a distinct type: a cross between the upright, crisp Romaine (Cos) type and the loose, buttery Butterhead type, producing compact, upright heads with the outer leaf structure and dark green color of Romaine but the soft, buttery, pale interior leaves and gentle flavor of Butterhead. The flavor is excellent — sweet, slightly nutty, and mild — while the cold tolerance (to around 22°F without protection) and slow-bolting behavior make it one of the most productive lettuces for extended spring seasons and for winter harvests in mild climates (zones 7–10). It is notably more shade-tolerant than most lettuces, performing well under tall vegetables in summer where direct-sun types would bolt. Winter Density was widely grown in English kitchen gardens throughout the 19th and 20th centuries as a reliable, all-conditions lettuce, and has been preserved through seed-saving networks and specialty seed companies.

name: Winter Honeybaby Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow (or transplant) after the last frost once soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; Winter Honeybaby, a 2017 All-America Selections winner bred with Cornell University, is a semi-bush butternut-type winter squash sized for small gardens and containers.
directions: Direct sow into warm, fertile soil in full sun, or grow in a large container with support for the vines. Winter Honeybaby stays compact with semi-bush vines only 2-3 feet long, yet is remarkably productive, bearing numerous personal-size, light-bulb-shaped fruits with sweet, nutty orange flesh meatier than comparable mini squash. The variety shows good powdery mildew tolerance and resists cracking, making it reliable through a long storage-squash season. Allow fruit to fully mature and cure in the sun for a few days before storing for winter use.

name: Winter King and Queen Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed past 70°F; this long-season keeper needs the full summer to mature before cool weather arrives, since its value comes from storing rather than early eating quality.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep in hills spaced 6–8 feet apart. Winter King and Queen is a rare American keeper melon, offered as early as 1923 by the Aggeler and Musser Seed Company and later documented by Amy Goldman in Melons for the Passionate Grower; it produces smaller, tough-rinded fruit (roughly 9 pounds on average) with a nearly white, exceptionally hard rind striped in dark green and firm, crunchy red flesh. Unlike most watermelons it is picked and set aside to store for weeks after harvest, continuing to ripen in a cool, dry spot into the winter months, which earned it the nickname Christmas watermelon in some regions. Midwestern Mennonite communities kept the variety alive largely for its pickled rind, and the resulting vinegar pickle is now listed on the Slow Food USA Ark of Taste; fresh flavor is good but secondary to its unmatched keeping ability among heirloom watermelons.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste — Winter King and Queen watermelon pickle
Amy Goldman — Melons for the Passionate Grower (2002)
Burrell Seed Growers, LLC — Winter King & Queen watermelon variety notes
Washington State University Extension — watermelon variety trial data

name: Winter Luxury Pie Pumpkin
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills of 2–3 plants after last frost; Winter Luxury requires 95–105 days to reach harvest maturity. For fall baking pumpkins, count back 105 days from first frost date; in zone 9, plant May–June for a September–October harvest. Harvest when the skin has turned orange and the distinctive netted surface is clearly visible; the unusual lacy skin is the signature characteristic of this variety.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of 2–3 plants after last frost in full sun in well-drained, rich, well-amended soil; harvest when rind is fully orange and the characteristic netting pattern covers the surface. Winter Luxury is a heirloom pie pumpkin dating to before 1893 that is distinguished from all other pumpkins by its striking surface appearance: the orange rind is covered with a delicate pattern of raised, interlacing cream-colored corky netting that gives each fruit a lacy, elaborately textured surface unlike any other pumpkin variety. Beyond the striking visual character, Winter Luxury is widely regarded as one of the finest pie pumpkins ever developed — the smooth-grained, dense, deep-orange flesh is finely textured, very sweet, and has a silky quality when cooked that produces exceptionally smooth pumpkin puree without the stringiness or wateriness of field-type pumpkins. The 5–9 lb fruits are the ideal size for fresh pie production, yielding enough puree for two large pies per fruit while remaining manageable to handle. Seed Savers Exchange and heirloom seed preservationists have long championed Winter Luxury as an example of what specialty breeding for cooking quality can achieve, and it consistently wins pie pumpkin taste tests among gardeners who grow multiple varieties side by side. A beautiful and genuinely outstanding baking pumpkin with over 130 years of cultivation history.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Winter Luxury pie pumpkin variety history
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Cucurbit variety collection
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Specialty Pumpkin Production

name: Winter Red Kale
plantingNote: Sow in late summer for a fall-through-spring harvest window, or in early spring; plants sweeten noticeably after frost and send up early 'napini' shoots a month ahead of the main leaf harvest.
directions: Winter Red was developed by Pacific Northwest breeder Tim Peters as a more uniformly colored, more cold-hardy improvement on the old Red Russian salad kale, carrying a trace of wild mustard pungency in its sap. It is grown as a tender salad kale rather than a cooking green, with reddish-purple leaves mild enough to eat raw. Fall sowings give a continuous harvest from early autumn through spring, and darker-red 'napini' flower shoots appear about a month before the main leaf crop is ready. Direct sow and thin rather than transplant for best establishment.

name: Winter Sun Oca
plantingNote: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep after last frost in loose, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade.
directions: Winter Sun produces plump, brilliant orange tubers with contrasting pink eyes, among the more visually striking oca varieties grown in North America. Plant tubers in loose, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the sprawling, succulent-stemmed foliage grows through summer and only begins forming tubers once autumn days shorten. Harvest after frost kills back the top growth, typically from November into January depending on climate. Spread freshly dug tubers in a sunny spot outdoors for several days after harvest, which both deepens their orange color and sweetens the otherwise tart, oxalic-acid-rich flesh.

name: Winter Sweet Kabocha Squash
plantingNote: Direct-sow once soil is warm; allow full vine spacing for best yields.
directions: Winter Sweet is a kabocha squash notable for its unusual light gray rind mottled with charcoal, a departure from the typical deep green or orange kabocha skins. Fruit average 4-5 pounds and are prized for exceptional eating quality, with a flaky texture and deep, sweet flavor that continues to improve in storage. Peak eating quality develops two to five months after harvest, making it an excellent long-season keeper. Cure in a warm spot for one to two weeks before moving to cool, dry storage.

name: Winterbor Kale
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant 3–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 sow September–February for fall through spring harvest. Winterbor is an F1 hybrid with exceptional cold hardiness — repeated hard freezes convert the leaf starches to sugars, making late-winter harvested Winterbor noticeably sweeter than fall-harvested leaves. In zone 9 fall planting in September–October produces excellent quality through spring; the plants are one of the most productive over-wintering vegetables for zone 9 kitchen gardens. Harvest outer leaves from the bottom up to keep plants producing.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; Winterbor is an F1 hybrid curly kale developed for exceptional vigor, uniformity, and extraordinary cold hardiness — the 'Winter' in the name reflects its ability to withstand severe freezes that damage most other kale varieties, making it the standard commercial and home garden curly kale in northern climates. The very densely curled, heavily blistered, blue-green leaves are the archetypal kale-chip and sautéed-kale leaf — the extreme surface area created by tight curling traps oil and seasonings, making Winterbor the variety most frequently used in kale chip recipes where maximum crispiness requires maximum surface contact with the baking sheet. Unlike flat-leaf or lacinato kale varieties, the heavy curl structure of Winterbor makes the raw leaves quite firm and fibrous — they benefit from massage with oil and salt to soften before use in salads, making it primarily a cooking kale rather than a fresh salad variety. Repeated hard freezes dramatically improve the flavor of all kale, but particularly Winterbor: cold temperatures convert accumulated starches to sugars, making late-winter harvested Winterbor among the sweetest and most palatable versions of this species.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Winterbor Kale F1 Trials
Cornell University Cooperative Extension — Kale Variety Trial
University of Wisconsin Extension — Kale Production in Cold Climates

name: Winterbor Kale
plantingNote: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before first fall frost and transplant in late summer/early fall; in zone 9 direct sow or transplant September–October for fall and winter harvest. Winterbor kale tolerates temperatures to 15°F and improves significantly in flavor after frost.
directions: Start indoors 8–10 weeks before fall transplanting or direct sow in late summer for fall production; Winterbor is a Dutch hybrid kale developed by Royal Sluis that became one of the most popular commercial and home garden kale varieties worldwide, valued for its combination of highly productive, tight, attractive blue-green curly leaves, exceptional cold hardiness, and distinctively superior flavor after frost. The tightly ruffled, heavily curled leaves are more tender and less tough than some older kale varieties, making Winterbor more pleasant to eat both raw in salads and cooked. The blue-green color is attractive and the upright habit (plants grow upward rather than sprawling) makes garden management easy. Winterbor is exceptionally cold-hardy — tolerating temperatures to 15°F without damage — and the cold-sweetening effect that makes kale improve after frost is particularly pronounced in Winterbor, making late-season harvested plants dramatically sweeter and more tender than those harvested before cold weather. In zone 9, Winterbor is primarily grown as a fall-through-winter crop (September–February) when temperatures allow proper kale production; it tolerates Gulf Coast mild winters better than more tender greens.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Winterbor kale variety notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Kale Production Guide

name: Wiri Wiri Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this slow-germinating Guyanese landrace rewards patience and steady bottom heat.
directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since germination is slower and less even than most peppers; transplant only after nights stay warm. This heirloom from Guyana produces marble-sized, perfectly round fruit that dangle upright like tiny berries, ripening from pale green through orange to bright red on a compact, heavily branched bush. Heat runs fierce and fruity, typically well into habanero territory, and the little pods are the signature ingredient in Guyanese pepper sauce as well as a favorite for pickling whole. In frost-free gardens the plant persists as a short-lived shrubby perennial; elsewhere grow it as a warm-season annual and pick continuously to keep new flowers setting.
sources: Slow Food Foundation — Ark of Taste

name: Wisconsin 55 Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Wisconsin 55 is an indeterminate variety that benefits from staking to keep the disease-resistant foliage well aired.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into warm soil, staking or caging the vines for support. Wisconsin 55 was developed by plant pathologist J.C. Walker at the University of Wisconsin in the 1940s to resist early blight and leaf spot, and it went on to become one of the most popular home garden tomatoes in the upper Midwest through the mid-20th century. The round, deep red, six- to eight-ounce fruit is notably resistant to cracking and holds firm texture for slicing, canning, and cooking.

name: Wisconsin SMR 18 Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; this earlier, shorter-vined release in the Wisconsin SMR breeding line matures a bit faster than its better-known successor, Wisconsin SMR 58.
directions: Wisconsin SMR 18 (Smooth/Spot Mosaic Resistant) came out of the University of Wisconsin cucumber breeding program that also produced the longer-running Wisconsin SMR 58, bred to resist scab and mosaic virus in a period when those diseases devastated Midwest pickling cucumber crops. It is an open-pollinated, gynoecious-leaning vining type that sets fruit a touch earlier than SMR 58, producing straight, blocky, medium-green fruit best picked small for dills or gherkins. Because it is open-pollinated, isolate plantings from other cucumber varieties if saving seed. Keep fruit picked every day or two at peak production to prevent oversized cucumbers from signaling the vine to stop setting new ones.

name: Wisconsin SMR 58 Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Wisconsin SMR 58 was bred at the University of Wisconsin for scab and mosaic resistance and remains a widely grown standard open-pollinated pickling cucumber.
directions: Direct sow an inch deep after the soil has warmed, in fertile, well-drained soil with room for vines to spread or climb a trellis. Wisconsin SMR 58, standing for Smooth or Spot Mosaic Resistant, descends from a University of Wisconsin breeding program that improved disease resistance in the older Wisconsin SMR line, becoming a standard pickling cucumber for home gardeners and small-scale growers because of its reliable yields, disease tolerance, and dependable performance across varied soils. Fruit is straight, blocky, and medium green with light spines, best picked young at 2-4 inches for pickles or left a bit larger for fresh slicing. Because it remains true from seed, it can be maintained by home seed savers who isolate it from other cucumber varieties.

name: Witkiem Manita Fava Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow in late winter to early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Witkiem Manita is bred specifically to be the earliest spring-sown broad bean available.
directions: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in late winter to early spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Witkiem Manita is a Dutch-bred fava bean known as the earliest spring-sowing broad bean on the market, reaching maturity in just 75-85 days on compact 18-inch plants. Short, well-filled pods hold about five white, high-tannin seeds with a notably strong, flavorful character prized over milder modern fava types. Harvest young for fresh eating or let pods fill out fully for freezing; its compact habit means less staking than taller fava cultivars.

name: WonderStar Pink Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant once soil has warmed; this compact determinate variety suits small-space and container growing.
directions: A compact, early-maturing determinate tomato bred to produce large, oblate beefsteak-style fruit with an heirloom-style bright pink skin and ribbed shoulders, despite the plant's small container-friendly footprint. Transplant into full sun after soil has warmed, and support the upright 18-24 inch plants with a stake or small cage as fruit sets. Fruit average 8-10 ounces and roughly 2.5 by 3.5 inches, with good resistance to fusarium wilt, late blight, Septoria leaf spot, and verticillium wilt. Harvest at full color for the best sweet-tart flavor on sandwiches, in salads, or cooked.

name: World Beater Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and set transplants out once the soil has warmed and frost danger has passed.
directions: World Beater, also sold as Ruby Giant, is a pre-1912 heirloom sweet pepper bred from a cross of Chinese Giant and Ruby King, combining the size of one parent with the productivity of the other. Fruits are exceptionally large and blocky with thick, sweet flesh that ripens from green to red, making it a favorite for stuffing or roasting whole. The sturdy, three-foot plants carry a heavy fruit load, so working in compost at planting and providing steady, even moisture helps size the peppers properly. Choose this variety when garden space allows for a true old-fashioned giant bell rather than a modern hybrid.

name: Worthmore Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed well past last frost; Worthmore's upright, non-vining habit and early set make it a good choice for a quick first planting with a follow-up sowing a month later.
directions: Worthmore is a University of Georgia pinkeye-type release bred from Mississippi Silver and Pinkeye Purple Hull stock, combining the parent varieties' flavor with sturdier disease tolerance. Plants grow upright with little vining, setting pods that mature to a deep purple at the green-shell stage, each holding around sixteen light tan peas with a greenish-tan eye. It shows useful field resistance to several common mosaic viruses that trouble southern peas in humid climates, making it a reliable choice where virus pressure has been a problem. Harvest at the green-shell stage for the classic fresh Southern pea pot, or let pods dry fully for storage peas.
sources: Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (cucurbit.info)

name: Wren's Egg Pole Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost at the base of sturdy support 6–8 feet tall; Wren's Egg is one of the oldest documented American bean varieties, known since the early 19th century, producing speckled cream and red or buff and maroon pods and seeds that strongly resemble a wren's speckled egg — grown as both a snap bean and a dry bean for its excellent flavor and historical significance.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep after last frost; provide trellis or poles 5–7 feet tall for support; vines twine naturally. Wren's Egg (also called 'Bird Egg', 'Speckled Bird Egg', or 'Speckled Cranberry Pole') is one of the oldest heirloom pole beans in continuous American cultivation, documented in seed catalogs and garden records since at least the early 1800s and traditionally maintained in New England and mid-Atlantic home gardens; it is named for the distinctive speckled coloring of both the pods and the dried seeds, which closely resemble the delicate speckled pattern of a wren's egg — a mix of cream or buff background with irregular red-brown, maroon, or rose speckles. The flat pods can be harvested young (45–60 days) as a snap bean or left to mature fully (75–90 days) for dry bean use. As a dry bean, Wren's Egg produces plump, oval seeds with excellent, rich flavor for baked beans and soups. The pods become increasingly stringy as they mature; harvest snap pods at 4–6 inches for best eating quality.

name: Wrinkled Crinkled Crumpled Cress
plantingNote: Direct sow every couple of weeks from early spring through fall for a continuous supply; a bit of afternoon shade in summer keeps the leaves from turning fibrous and bitter before bolting.
directions: This cress was bred by Oregon seedsman Frank Morton as a cross between 'Persian' and 'Curly' garden cress, combining the deeply savoyed, ruffled leaf texture of curly types with a sturdier, more upright habit that lifts leaves clear of soil splash for cleaner cutting. It germinates and grows fast enough to be treated almost like a microgreen, ready for its first cutting in under three weeks, and is notably slower to bolt than most other cress selections, giving several extra cuttings per sowing. Use it as a peppery, tangy addition to salad mixes, sandwiches, and garnishes wherever a sharper bite than lettuce is wanted.

name: Xtra-Tender 277A Sweet Corn
plantingNote: Direct sow only after soil has warmed thoroughly, since supersweet (sh2) types germinate poorly in cool soil; Xtra-Tender 277A is a popular commercial and home-garden bicolor supersweet hybrid widely grown across the South for its tender, high-sugar kernels.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep only once soil has warmed thoroughly, since supersweet corn germinates poorly in cool, wet soil; plant in blocks of several short rows rather than one long row to ensure good pollination, and keep isolated from standard or sugary-enhanced corn to protect kernel sweetness. Xtra-Tender 277A is a popular bicolor supersweet hybrid known for exceptionally tender, high-sugar kernels that hold their sweetness well after picking, and it is widely grown by both market farmers and home gardeners across warm Southern regions. It produces large, well-filled ears with a mix of yellow and white kernels on vigorous stalks. Feed with nitrogen and water deeply during tasseling and ear fill, and harvest when silks have browned and kernels release a milky juice when pressed.
sources: seed catalog reference (Harris Seeds, 2B Seeds, Demeter Seeds)

name: Y-Star Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; harvest small for the sweetest flavor, or let a few fruit mature fully for seed saving.
directions: Direct sow after last frost in full sun, spacing plants about 3 feet apart in fertile, well-drained soil. Y-Star is an heirloom pattypan type distinguished by its pointed, star-like scalloped edges and rich golden-yellow color, giving it a more angular silhouette than the rounded scallop shape of other pattypan squash. Harvest small, at about 2-3 inches across, for the sweetest flavor and most tender skin; larger fruit can be left to mature for seed saving or ornamental use.

name: Yankee Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Yankee Bell was selected for reliable performance and earlier maturity in cool northern growing regions.
directions: Yankee Bell is an open-pollinated blocky bell pepper selected specifically for the shorter, cooler growing seasons of northern gardens, producing uniform three- to four-lobed fruit on sturdy, well-branched plants. Fruit can be picked green at around 60 days from transplant or left to ripen fully red for sweeter flavor at roughly 80 days. Its stronger branching habit helps support fruit load without staking in most gardens. Grow in full sun with even moisture and side-dress with compost at first fruit set to sustain production through the season.

name: Yaya Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow in deep, loose, well-amended soil; Yaya is an early maturing Nantes type that reaches harvest size in as few as 56 days — ideal for successive sowing every 2–3 weeks for continuous bunching-carrot harvest. Thin to 2 inches for bunching-size roots; allow 3 inches for larger storage roots. Harvest when roots are finger-thick and 6–7 inches long for best quality and sweetness.
directions: Direct sow 0.25 inch deep in loose, deeply tilled, stone-free soil; keep consistently moist through germination (7–14 days) and thin to 2–3 inches apart. Yaya is a Bejo Seeds hybrid Nantes-type carrot that has become one of the most popular fresh-market and home garden bunching carrots in North America — selected specifically for its early maturity, exceptional sweetness, and consistent cylindrical uniformity that makes bunches visually attractive and professionally presentable. The roots are the classic Nantes shape: blunt-tipped, 6–7 inches long, uniform diameter, with smooth, bright orange skin and minimal core differentiation from the phloem to the xylem — the internal uniformity of color contributing to the sweet, mild, candy-sweet flavor that Yaya is known for. Yaya matures 10–14 days earlier than most mid-season Nantes types, allowing early-season bunching carrot production or an additional succession planting late in the season. It holds well in the ground after reaching maturity without rapid overgrowth or cracking, giving a flexible harvest window. Market gardeners consistently rate Yaya among the highest for customer satisfaction — the exceptional sweetness and uniformity of color and shape are immediately apparent to buyers. One of the best-performing bunching carrots for both farm market sales and home garden fresh eating.
sources: Bejo Seeds — Yaya carrot variety notes
Johnny's Selected Seeds — Nantes Carrot Variety Comparison
High Mowing Organic Seeds — Carrot variety evaluation

name: Yella Bella Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes; thin walls mature faster than thick-walled roasting peppers, so fruit can be picked relatively early.
directions: Yella Bella is the yellow counterpart to Wild Garden Seed's 'Bella Red,' producing crumpled, twisted, thin-walled yellow Italian-type fruit. Because the walls are thinner than a roasting pepper, it suits raw salads or a quick saute better than fire-roasting. The irregular, folded shape makes cross-cut slices especially decorative on a plate. Grow it like other warm-season Capsicum annuum peppers: full sun, consistent water, and staking if the plant becomes top-heavy with fruit.

name: Yellow Baby Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant after last frost once soil is reliably warm; this fast-maturing hybrid rewards an early start under black plastic mulch in cooler regions.
directions: An All-America Selections winner from the 1970s, Yellow Baby was one of the first widely available yellow-fleshed watermelons bred for home gardens, packing bright lemon-yellow flesh and thin, tender rind into a round 7-pound icebox-size fruit. The novel flesh color and honeyed flavor make it a conversation piece at the table, and its fast maturity suits shorter growing seasons better than full-size Southern types. Grow it exactly as you would any bush-type icebox watermelon: full sun, consistent moisture until fruit begins to ripen, then reduced watering to concentrate sugars. Because the pale flesh makes the usual red-ripeness cues useless, rely on the drying tendril and yellowing ground spot to judge harvest timing.

name: Yellow Bell Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Yellow Bell is a heavy-yielding indeterminate paste tomato that tolerates cool, wet conditions better than many sauce varieties and benefits from staking or caging.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile soil, staking or caging to support heavy clusters of fruit. Yellow Bell is a Roma-shaped yellow paste tomato that is a family heirloom from Tennessee, introduced commercially in 1986 by Southern Exposure Seed Exchange; the vigorous plants set 5-12 fruits per cluster and bear heavily until frost, ripening from green through creamy yellow to a rich golden-yellow with a sweet, full flavor well suited to yellow sauces, salsas, preserves, and catsup.

name: Yellow Bhut Jolokia Pepper
plantingNote: Sow indoors on a heat mat 8-10 weeks ahead of the last frost date; bhut jolokia types are slow to germinate and sulk in cool soil.
directions: Yellow Bhut Jolokia is a bright lemon-to-gold-podded phenotype of the classic Northeast Indian ghost pepper, with the same characteristically wrinkled, thin-walled fruit and searing heat as the red strain. Some growers report a slightly fruitier, less smoky flavor than red bhut jolokia, making it popular for hot sauces where a lighter color is desired. Provide full sun, rich well-drained soil, and even watering, since chinense superhots are prone to blossom drop under moisture stress. Wear gloves when handling ripe pods, as the oils cling stubbornly to skin.

name: Yellow Brandywine Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost; Yellow Brandywine is a yellow-fruited strain of the famous Brandywine heirloom with the same potato-leaf foliage and large, meaty fruit but ripening to golden-yellow with exceptionally sweet, mild, low-acid flavor that many prefer to the standard pink or red strains.
directions: Start indoors under grow lights 6–8 weeks before last frost; plant deeply after frost in rich soil, staking or caging immediately. Yellow Brandywine is a yellow-fruited version of the legendary Brandywine heirloom (or a closely related strain), producing the same large, potato-leaved plants and big, meaty, irregular fruits but ripening to a beautiful golden-yellow with a noticeably sweeter, milder, lower-acid flavor than either the pink or red Brandywine strains — many tomato connoisseurs actually prefer it for its tropical sweetness and lack of sharpness. Fruits reach 12–24 oz and are outstanding for slicing, caprese preparations, and tomato salads where the golden color provides visual contrast; the low acid level means less canning stability so use for fresh eating. Shares the Brandywine family's potato-leaved foliage (a dominant genetic marker that distinguishes true Brandywines from impostors) and late, slow maturity that rewards patient gardeners with exceptional fruit.

name: Yellow Cabbage Collard
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant in late summer for a fall-through-winter crop in zone 9, or sow in early spring; unlike open, loose-leaf collards, Yellow Cabbage Collard forms a loose head, so give it slightly more room and a longer season to fully develop.
directions: Sow seed a quarter to half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, giving plants ample room to form their characteristic loose head. Yellow Cabbage Collard is a distinctive Virginia heirloom, unusual among collards for forming a semi-blanched, cabbage-like heart of pale yellow-green leaves at the plant's center rather than staying fully open-leaved, giving it a milder, sweeter flavor and more tender texture than typical collards, especially in the blanched inner leaves. Outer leaves can still be harvested cut-and-come-again style through the season, while the forming head is left to mature for a more tender harvest later. Cold exposure sweetens the flavor further, and the plant tolerates hard freezes well. Feed with a balanced or nitrogen-rich fertilizer through the growing season for the best head development.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange heirloom collard archive
Virginia Cooperative Extension — Heirloom Vegetable Notes

name: Yellow Cabbage Collards
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting or direct sow 12-14 weeks before first frost; in zone 9, transplant August-September for fall and winter production. Yellow Cabbage Collards form an unusually loose, pale yellow-green head rather than the open rosette typical of most collards.
directions: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Yellow Cabbage Collards are a distinctive Southern heirloom type that blurs the line between collards and cabbage, forming a loose, blanched, pale yellow-green head at the center of the plant rather than the fully open rosette of leaves typical of most collard varieties. The blanched inner leaves are notably tender and mild, sweeter and less assertively cabbage-flavored than standard collards, making this variety popular for gardeners who find ordinary collards too strong. Like other collards it tolerates considerable cold and its flavor improves after light fall frosts. Because the plant's value lies partly in the self-blanched head, avoid stripping too many outer leaves early in the season and let the center fill in before beginning regular harvest, then continue picking outer leaves as the plant keeps producing from the growing point.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Collard Production in the Southeast

name: Yellow Crookneck Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; the quintessential Southern summer squash, ubiquitous at roadside stands and farmers' markets across the Gulf Coast; highly heat-tolerant and productive even in zone 9–11 summer conditions.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep after last frost in warm, rich, well-drained soil; Yellow Crookneck is one of the fastest-producing and most heat-tolerant summer squashes, making it particularly well-suited to warm and humid Gulf Coast gardens where it produces heavily in spring and again in fall. Yellow Crookneck squash has been grown in American gardens since at least the 1700s — it was listed in American seed catalogs before the Civil War — producing curved, club-shaped yellow fruits with bumpy skin and mild, buttery, slightly nutty flesh that is the quintessential taste of Southern summer gardens; harvest at 4–6 inches when the skin is still tender and seeds are small. In hot climates, a fall planting (direct sow in late summer) often outperforms spring; the plants are relatively short-lived under heat stress but can be succession-planted.

name: Yellow Doll Watermelon
plantingNote: Direct sow in hills of 3 seeds after last frost when soil is above 70°F; thin to 2 plants per hill. Yellow Doll's early maturity (65–75 days) makes it one of the fastest watermelons to ripen, suitable for shorter growing seasons where standard large varieties may not mature. The small fruit size (5–8 lbs) makes individual fruits manageable for families and the compact vine habit allows closer planting than large-fruited types. In zone 9, plant March–April for June harvest.
directions: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills after last frost when soil is above 70°F; fertilize at planting and again when vines begin to run. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit turns brown and dry and the underside spot (where the melon touches the ground) turns from white to cream-yellow. Yellow Doll is an early-maturing, icebox-sized watermelon notable for its yellow flesh — a less common flesh color that surprises many people used to only red-fleshed watermelons. The small (5–8 lb), round to oval fruits have light green skin with subtle darker green stripes and the distinctive bright yellow to golden-yellow interior flesh that gives the variety its name. The yellow flesh is very sweet and mild, with a slightly different flavor character than red-fleshed types — some tasters describe it as cleaner, less assertive, and honey-sweet rather than the more complex sweetness of red watermelon flesh. This mild quality makes Yellow Doll particularly popular with children and those who find standard watermelon's flavor too strong. Yellow Doll's early maturity (65–75 days vs. the 80–95 days of standard large varieties) is a practical advantage for short-season gardeners, as is the small fruit size — a single 6-lb fruit is the right amount for 2–4 people without waste, compared to the 25+ lb fruits of standard varieties that require multiple meals to consume.
sources: Park Seed — Yellow Doll watermelon variety notes
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Yellow-fleshed watermelon comparison
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Watermelon Production Guide

name: Yellow Eye Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost when soil is above 60°F; Yellow Eye is a dry bush bean — allow pods to fully mature and begin to dry on the vine before harvesting. In zone 9, sow in March–April for a May–June dry bean harvest before summer heat peaks.
directions: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost; allow pods to dry fully on the vine before harvesting, then shell and continue drying beans before storage. Yellow Eye bean (also called Maine Yellow Eye, Steuben Yellow Eye, or Molasses Face bean) is one of the defining heirloom dry beans of New England — a white bean with a distinctive yellow-to-orange eye mark on one end (the hilum area) that resembles a yellow eye, giving the variety its evocative name.
