The bean has an extraordinarily long history in New England agriculture, where it has been the traditional baked bean variety for generations in Maine — the characteristic bean in the famous Maine Saturday Night bean suppers and baked bean tradition that stretches back centuries to Native American cooking and early colonial adaptation. The large, creamy-white beans cook to a silky, tender texture without becoming mushy, holding their shape while absorbing surrounding flavors; they have a mild, rich, nutty flavor that makes them outstanding for slow-baked preparations, bean soups, and any dish where bean quality is the focus. Yellow Eye is considered by many New England cooks to be the finest baked bean, superior in flavor and texture to navy beans or pinto beans for this application. An outstanding heirloom that connects culinary tradition, regional identity, and genuine eating quality.
sources: Fedco Seeds — Yellow Eye bean variety notes
Seed Savers Exchange — New England heirloom bean collection
University of Maine Cooperative Extension — Bean Production Guide

name: Yellow Finn Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4-6 weeks before the last frost; this mid-season heirloom performs well in cooler northern climates as well as short winter-growing regions.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun; Yellow Finn is a Finnish heirloom predating the modern yellow-flesh varieties it helped inspire, producing round to oval tubers with tan skin and dense, buttery-yellow flesh. The flavor is rich and naturally buttery even without added fat, and the moderately waxy texture holds together well for potato salad while still mashing smoothly. It stores well for a fingerling-adjacent heirloom and tends to be more drought-tolerant than many modern hybrids once established. Choose it over Yukon Gold when a true heirloom lineage and slightly denser, more old-fashioned texture are preferred.

name: Yellow Globe Danvers Onion
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into the garden as soon as the soil can be worked; Yellow Globe Danvers is a long-day heirloom bred for the summer day length of northern latitudes.
directions: Yellow Globe Danvers is a classic American heirloom onion developed near Danvers, Massachusetts, in the 1850s and grown for generations as a reliable, well-storing globe onion. The medium-sized bulbs form tight round globes with papery yellow-brown skin over firm, pungent flesh well suited to cooking rather than fresh eating. Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil and thin or space plants so bulbs can round out fully without crowding. Lift once the tops have fallen over and dried, cure in a warm, airy location for a couple of weeks, and expect this variety to store as well as any classic long-day storage onion.

name: Yellow Granex Onion
plantingNote: Start seed or set transplants in fall for a spring harvest in the Gulf South; Yellow Granex is a short-day onion requiring only about 10-12 hours of daylight to bulb, and it is the original variety behind the famous Vidalia sweet onion of Georgia.
directions: Start seed or set transplants in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; as a short-day onion, Yellow Granex needs the shorter day lengths of a Southern fall-to-spring growing season to bulb properly and will not perform well planted in spring in most of the country. Yellow Granex is the classic variety behind Georgia's famous Vidalia sweet onion, prized for large, flattened, golden-skinned bulbs with exceptionally mild, sweet, low-pungency flesh that develops from the low-sulfur soils and mild winters of the Deep South. It is one of the best-suited onion types for Gulf Coast gardens specifically because the region's short winter day length and mild temperatures match its bulbing requirements closely. Harvest when tops fall over and yellow, then cure carefully in a warm, dry, well-ventilated spot, since sweet onions like Yellow Granex have thinner skins and shorter storage life than pungent long-day storage onions.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Vidalia Onion Production

name: Yellow Indian Woman Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; a fast-maturing Montana heirloom bush bean well suited to short growing seasons.
directions: Sow seeds directly 1 inch deep after danger of frost has passed, spacing bush plants 4-6 inches apart in rows. Also known as Buckskin or Buckskin Girl, Yellow Indian Woman is a Montana heirloom that reached Native American communities through European settlers and is prized for producing heavy yields of small, milky-yellow seeds in under 75 days, among the fastest-maturing dry beans available. The mild, creamy flavor resembles a pinto bean and the seeds hold their shape well in slow-cooked soups and stews, while also cooking noticeably faster than most other dry beans. Water regularly through bloom and pod fill, then let pods dry completely on the plant before shelling and storing.

name: Yellow Jersey Sweet Potato
plantingNote: Plant rooted slips 2-4 weeks after last frost once soil is thoroughly warm, in loose, well-drained soil built into ridges in full sun; Yellow Jersey is an old Southern heirloom grown for its pale yellow skin and dry, mealy flesh, a different texture than modern moist orange types like Beauregard.
directions: Plant rooted slips 4-6 inches deep in loose, well-drained soil formed into ridges in full sun. Yellow Jersey is an old-fashioned Southern heirloom with pale yellow-tan skin and light yellow, dry, mealy flesh, a texture closer to a baking potato than the moist, syrupy sweetness of modern orange-fleshed varieties, and it was once among the most widely grown sweet potatoes in the South before moister types like Beauregard became dominant. Vines are moderately vigorous and productive, and the drier flesh makes the roots well suited to baking and frying rather than the candied dishes moist types are typically used for. Dig once vines begin to yellow in fall and before the first frost, and cure the roots at warm temperatures and high humidity for a week or two to heal cuts, firm the skin, and develop full sweetness before storing.

name: Yellow Moruga Scorpion Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost on a heat mat, since Moruga Scorpion strains germinate erratically without warmth.
directions: This is a yellow-fruited selection of the Trinidad Moruga Scorpion, sharing the same bumpy, tailed pod shape and ferocious heat as the original red strain but ripening to a bright golden-yellow instead. Growers often note the yellow form carries a slightly more citrusy, less smoky flavor than red Moruga types, making it popular for hot sauces where color as well as heat matters. Give plants the same long, warm growing season and rich soil that other Trinidad superhots require, and expect a later, more compact fruit set than milder chinense varieties. Because pod color can be the only visible way to distinguish it from other Moruga strains, keep seed-saved plants isolated from red-fruited relatives to preserve the true-to-type yellow trait.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute, New Mexico State University

name: Yellow of Parma Onion
plantingNote: Start seed indoors in late winter and transplant young onion sets outdoors about 4-6 weeks before the last expected frost.
directions: Sow seed indoors under lights in late winter, then transplant seedlings into fertile, well-drained soil once the danger of hard frost has passed, spacing plants a few inches apart to allow bulbs to swell. Keep soil evenly moist through bulbing, then stop watering and let tops fall over naturally before harvest to cure for storage. Yellow of Parma is a classic Italian heirloom valued for its large, globe-shaped, straw-colored bulbs, mild sweet flavor, and notably good keeping quality compared to other sweet onion types, making it a long-standing favorite in northern Italian kitchen gardens.

name: Yellow Oxheart Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before transplanting; Yellow Oxheart is a tall indeterminate heirloom that needs a sturdy stake or cage for its large, heavy fruit.
directions: Yellow Oxheart is a heirloom slicing tomato that produces large, pointed, heart-shaped fruit in golden yellow, with the dense, meaty, low-seed flesh typical of oxheart-type tomatoes and a mild, sweet flavor with less acidity than most red varieties. The heavy 8-16 ounce fruit and sprawling indeterminate vine both need substantial support, so use a heavy-duty cage or stake set at transplanting. Because oxheart types can be prone to blossom end rot on their first large fruit, keep watering consistent and avoid letting the soil dry out and then rewetting heavily.

name: Yellow Pear Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6–8 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Yellow Pear is an heirloom cultivar with true-to-type seed that can be saved from year to year.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun after the last frost date; Yellow Pear is an heirloom cherry tomato with a history extending back to at least the 1800s — producing clusters of small, bright-yellow, pear-shaped fruits with a distinctive teardrop shape and mild, low-acid, sweet flavor. The fruit shape and bright yellow color make Yellow Pear one of the most visually distinctive tomatoes in the garden, and it is a consistent favorite at farmers markets and in mixed salads where its cheerful yellow color and unusual shape create visual interest. The low-acid flavor profile makes it approachable for children and adults who find standard tomatoes too acidic. The indeterminate vine grows vigorously to 5–8 feet and sets fruit prolifically throughout the growing season — an established Yellow Pear plant produces hundreds of fruits over the course of the season. Seed can be saved from non-hybrid heirloom Yellow Pear true-to-type for future seasons — select fruit from the most vigorous and productive plants. In zone 9, Yellow Pear performs well in the spring window (February–June) and fall window (September–frost) but stalls during the peak summer heat above 95°F. The low-acid taste makes it excellent for children's snacking, fresh salads, and pasta dishes where a mild tomato flavor is preferred.

name: Yellow Pop Sweet Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; transplant outdoors once danger of frost has passed.
directions: Yellow Pop is a bright-yellow snacking pepper bred for eating fresh off the plant, with very few seeds and maximum sweetness. Plants are compact and container-friendly, producing handfuls of crunchy, bite-sized fruit through the season. Start seed indoors and transplant after frost danger has passed for a long, productive harvest.

name: Yellow Potato Onion
scientificName: Allium cepa var. aggregatum 'Yellow Potato Onion'
plantingNote: Plant small bulbs in fall for the largest harvest the following summer in mild-winter regions, or in very early spring as soon as soil is workable where winters are severe.
directions: Yellow Potato Onion is a true heirloom multiplier onion documented in American gardens since before 1790, grown from small saved bulbs rather than seed. Each planted bulb divides underground into a cluster of new bulbs ranging from an inch to several inches across, so a gardener can keep a perpetual supply going year after year without buying sets or seed again. It tolerates drought better than seed-grown onions and is widely adapted across the country, with fall planting generally producing larger bulbs than spring planting. Set bulbs about 2 inches deep with the tip just at the soil surface, and harvest once the tops die back, saving the largest bulbs to replant and the rest for the kitchen.

name: Yellow Stuffer Pepper
plantingNote: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Yellow Stuffer is an heirloom named for its squat, tomato-like shape that holds stuffing well without collapsing when baked.
directions: Sow seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant once nights stay reliably above 55F. Yellow Stuffer bears thick-walled, tomato-shaped fruit that ripens from green to golden yellow, bred and selected for sturdy, compact proportions that make it a favorite for whole-pepper stuffing and baking. The dense flesh holds its shape well under heat and has a mild, sweet flavor. Harvest at the yellow stage for the sweetest flavor, or use slightly earlier for a firmer texture.

name: Yellowfin Zucchini
plantingNote: Direct sow after frost danger passes, in warm, fertile soil in full sun; harvest young for the mildest flavor and most tender skin.
directions: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed, in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, spacing plants about 30 inches apart. Yellowfin produces glossy, bright golden-yellow, straight cylindrical fruit on a compact, open bush plant, offering a color and shape alternative to more common golden zucchini types. Pick regularly at 6-7 inches long, since yellow-skinned summer squash can develop a tougher skin if left to oversize. The bright color makes Yellowfin easy to spot at harvest time and an attractive addition to mixed squash displays.

name: Yellowstone Carrot
plantingNote: Direct sow 2–4 weeks before last frost in loose, well-prepared soil; Yellowstone is one of the best yellow carrots, with a bright, true yellow exterior and interior and a distinctly sweet, mild, fruity flavor that stands out from standard orange carrots.
directions: Sow seed thinly 1/4 inch deep in deeply loosened, friable, stone-free soil 2–4 weeks before last frost; thin to 2–3 inches when seedlings reach 2 inches tall. Yellowstone is one of the top-performing yellow carrots for home gardens, producing uniform, 7–9 inch, Nantes-type cylindrical roots with vivid yellow skin and flesh throughout and a notably mild, sweet, slightly fruity flavor that some tasters prefer to standard orange carrots; it lacks the beta-carotene of orange types but is rich in lutein, a carotenoid beneficial to eye health. Excellent for fresh eating, roasting (where it holds its color beautifully), and for adding visual variety to rainbow carrot mixes. The flavor improves after mild frost. Direct sow works best as the taproot does not transplant well.

name: Yeolmu
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring or late summer into fertile, loose soil; Yeolmu is harvested fast, within three to six weeks, for both its tender greens and slim root together.
directions: Direct sow into fertile, loose soil in full sun; Yeolmu is a fast-growing Korean radish type harvested young, in just three to six weeks, prized for its tender peppery greens eaten together with the slim immature root rather than a mature root alone. It is the namesake ingredient of summer yeolmu-kimchi, a quick-fermented dish traditionally served with cold noodles in hot weather. Sow successively through spring and late summer for a continuous supply, since the whole point of this cultivar is harvesting it young and fast rather than letting it mature into a full-size radish.

name: Yokohama Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after the soil warms and let the vigorous vine ramble across a wide bed or up a strong trellis, since a single plant can cover a large area over the long Gulf Coast growing season.
directions: Direct sow after the soil warms and let the vigorous vine ramble across a wide bed or up a strong trellis, since a single plant can cover a large area over the long Gulf Coast growing season. This dark-green, deeply ribbed Japanese heirloom shares Cucurbita moschata's excellent resistance to vine borers and squash bugs with better-known Gulf-adapted moschata types, making it a strong performer where humidity and pests knock out C. maxima and C. pepo squash. The dense, sweet orange flesh stores for months after curing in a warm, dry spot. Its heat tolerance and disease resistance make it a good companion or alternative to Seminole pumpkin for zone 8-10 gardeners wanting variety in their moschata winter squash.

name: Yolo Wonder Bell Pepper
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 8–10 weeks before transplanting; transplant into fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic (pH 6.0–6.8) soil in full sun; Yolo Wonder's virus resistance is a practical advantage in zone 9 where tobacco mosaic virus and pepper mosaic virus persist in soil and infect peppers through insect vectors.
directions: Set out transplants in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun at or just before the last frost date; Yolo Wonder is one of the most important open-pollinated bell pepper varieties in American horticulture — developed at the University of California, Davis, from California Wonder breeding stock specifically to incorporate resistance to tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), a common disease that devastates susceptible bell pepper varieties throughout warm-season gardens. Yolo Wonder produces large, four-lobed, blocky, thick-walled fruits in the classic California Wonder mold — essentially identical in fruit character to California Wonder but with the added practical advantage of TMV resistance that makes it significantly more reliable in gardens where the virus is endemic in the soil. The fruits ripen from green to red and have full, sweet bell pepper flavor at both stages. Yolo Wonder is the virus-resistant standard for open-pollinated bell pepper production that replaced California Wonder in many commercial plantings when TMV was recognized as a major production challenge. As an open-pollinated variety, seeds can be saved reliably from season to season. The practical combination of virus resistance, large fruit size, thick walls, and excellent flavor has kept Yolo Wonder among the most commonly recommended open-pollinated bell peppers for home gardeners in disease-prone environments throughout the Gulf South.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

name: Yorkshire Hero Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool soil a few weeks before the last frost; the tall vines of this 1860s English heirloom need sturdy netting or brush support from an early stage.
directions: Sow directly in cool, fertile soil and install support early, as Yorkshire Hero climbs tall and tangles badly without it. First grown in England around the 1860s and widely listed in British and North American seed catalogs through the late nineteenth century, it produces creamy white, deeply wrinkled seeds prized in their green stage for a delicate, sweet flavor. The variety fell out of commercial favor as newer dwarf and disease-resistant peas took over the market, and it now survives mainly through heritage seed-saving networks. Pick regularly once pods fill out, since this older type holds its quality less long on the vine than modern hybrids.

name: Yugoslavian Red Butter Lettuce
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall or early spring; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall harvest or January–February for spring. Yugoslavian Red is notable for maintaining red coloration even in warm fall conditions when many red lettuces revert to green, making it the most reliably red butterhead for zone 9 fall planting. Successive sowings every 3 weeks through fall extend the harvest window. Harvest whole heads or strip outer leaves for continuous production.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in partial shade to full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; Yugoslavian Red Butter Lettuce is a large-headed butterhead type from the former Yugoslavia, producing open, loose heads of deeply wine-red outer leaves that contrast dramatically with the pale green-to-yellow interior heart — one of the most visually striking red butterhead lettuce varieties. The large heads weigh 8–12 ounces at maturity with a buttery, tender, mild flavor characteristic of the butterhead type. Yugoslavian Red maintains its deep red color even during the warmer stretches of fall in zone 9, when most red lettuces revert to green with heat — this color stability is a primary reason it is favored for warm-climate fall gardens. The loose, open head structure forms quickly and is ready for harvest at 50–60 days. The deep red outer leaves are high in anthocyanin antioxidants; the green interior provides visual contrast when the head is split or leaves are separated in a salad.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Yugoslavian Red Butter Lettuce Heritage Variety
Baker Creek Heirloom Seeds — Eastern European Heirloom Lettuce
Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners — Red Butterhead Types

name: Yukina Savoy
plantingNote: Direct sow in fall; in zone 9 sow September–November for fall-winter harvest. Can also be sown January–February for a spring crop before heat causes bolting. Yukina Savoy is more heat-tolerant than most brassica greens and can extend into early summer in zone 9 before bolting. Successive sowings every 3 weeks extend the harvest season through the cool months.
directions: Direct sow or transplant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Yukina Savoy is a distinctive Asian brassica with dark green, heavily blistered (savoy-textured), crinkled leaves on upright rosette plants — a texture entirely unlike the smooth leaves of tatsoi, pak choi, or komatsuna. The savoy-type leaf surface catches dressings and sauces in cooking and stands up to heat and wilting better than smooth-leaved types. The flavor is mild and slightly mustardy, similar to komatsuna but with a hint of sweetness, making it suitable for stir-fries, soups, steaming, and raw use as a baby green. Yukina Savoy is notably cold-hardy (tolerating temperatures below 20°F with light mulch) and heat-tolerant for a brassica, making it one of the most adaptable fall-through-spring greens for zone 9 gardens. Cut outer leaves for continuous harvest or cut the whole head at once for cooking.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Yukina Savoy Variety Notes
University of Hawaii Extension — Asian Brassica Greens
Rutgers University — Asian Vegetables for the Home Garden

name: Yukina Savoy Brassica
plantingNote: Direct sow or transplant in fall; Yukina Savoy is a vigorous, cold-tolerant brassica green that produces abundantly in zone 9's fall and winter gardens. In zone 9, sow August–November for harvest beginning October and continuing through February or March. The deeply puckered, savoyed leaves are distinctive among Asian brassica greens — the surface texture creates an unusual visual character and traps seasonings in the leaf folds when cooking. Very cold-hardy: survives temperatures into the low 20s°F once established. Harvest outer leaves and the plant will continue producing from the center for an extended season.
directions: Direct sow 0.25 inch deep in rows 12 inches apart; thin to 9–12 inches. Harvest outer leaves from 40 days or cut whole plant. Yukina Savoy (Brassica rapa var. narinosa 'Yukina Savoy') is a Japanese brassica green that occupies an unusual position in the Asian brassica spectrum: it is not clearly tatsoi (which is also var. narinosa but with very different flat-rosette form), not bok choy, not komatsuna, and not napa cabbage, but shares characteristics with all of these while maintaining its own distinctive identity primarily defined by the heavily savoyed (puckered, crinkled, blistered) texture of the leaves. The savoy texture in Yukina produces a leaf that is visually striking — deep green, heavily textured, with bold surface relief — and practically advantageous in cooking because the crinkled surface texture holds oils, sauces, and seasonings in a way that smooth-leaved brassicas cannot. The flavor is mild and versatile, somewhat between spinach and bok choy — appealing to gardeners who find other Asian brassicas too strongly flavored but want more character than spinach. Yukina Savoy is extremely productive in cool weather, producing large rosettes of leaves over an extended harvest season. It is widely used in restaurant and specialty market salad mixes in the American Northeast and Mid-Atlantic, where its striking appearance makes it a valuable visual element in mixed greens.
sources: Johnny's Selected Seeds — Yukina Savoy brassica variety notes
Kitazawa Seed Company — Japanese brassica green varieties
Cornell Cooperative Extension — Asian Brassica Greens Production Guide

name: Yukon Gold Potato
plantingNote: Plant certified seed pieces 4–6 weeks before last frost; in zone 9 plant January–February for May harvest before summer heat. Yukon Gold is a mid-season variety (70–90 days) well-suited to the Gulf Coast's cool winter growing window. Cut seed pieces to egg size, each with 1–2 eyes; allow cut surfaces to cure 1–2 days before planting.
directions: Plant certified seed pieces 4 inches deep in loose, well-amended soil in full sun; Yukon Gold is a Canadian-bred variety introduced in 1980 that transformed the North American potato market by demonstrating that consumers would pay a premium for a potato with inherently golden flesh and superior flavor. The medium-large, round to oval tubers have smooth, thin, slightly golden skin and deep butter-yellow flesh with a naturally buttery, slightly sweet flavor that requires no added butter to taste rich and satisfying. Yukon Gold is equally excellent baked, mashed, roasted, and sautéed — its lower starch content than russets makes it a smooth masher that doesn't become gluey. It is now the most widely planted 'specialty' potato in North America and has spawned an entire category of yellow-flesh varieties. In zone 9, plant January–February in loose, well-drained soil; hill soil around stems as they emerge. Harvest new potatoes when plants flower (60–70 days); for cured storage, harvest after vines die back. Cure at 60–70°F for one week before storing in a cool, dark location.
sources: Agriculture Canada Research Station, Guelph — Yukon Gold potato release notes 1980
Seed Savers Exchange — Yukon Gold documentation
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Potato Production for Texas Home Gardens
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Potato Production in Florida

name: Zamboni Broccoli Raab
plantingNote: Direct sow from early spring through late summer for successive cool-season harvests; this hybrid holds quality a bit longer into warm weather than older open-pollinated raab types.
directions: Zamboni is a modern hybrid broccoli raab bred for a longer harvest window and better bolt tolerance than traditional Italian landrace rapini. Direct sow in rows and begin cutting the tender central shoots with their small unopened flower buds about six to seven weeks after sowing, which encourages side-shoot production for repeat harvests. Leaves, stems, and buds are all edible with the same assertive, mustardy-bitter flavor typical of broccoli raab, best tamed by a quick saute with garlic and chili flakes. Because it tolerates a slightly wider temperature range than older varieties, it is a useful choice for extending the rapini harvest into early summer or starting it earlier in fall.

name: Zapallito Squash
plantingNote: Sow seeds directly in warm soil after frost danger passes, since this compact bush type needs less room than typical maxima squash and tolerates close spacing well.
directions: Sow seeds directly in warm soil after frost danger passes, since this compact bush type needs less room than typical maxima squash and tolerates close spacing well. A traditional South American variety popular in Argentina and Uruguay, it produces small, pale-green, round to slightly ribbed fruit best picked young and tender at 3-4 inches for use in stuffed-squash dishes and stews. Frequent picking every couple of days encourages continued production through the season, much like a zucchini. Its compact habit and rapid maturity make it well suited to smaller garden beds and container growing.
sources: Instituto Nacional de Tecnología Agropecuaria (INTA) Argentina

name: Zapotec Pleated Tomato
plantingNote: Start seeds indoors 4–6 weeks before last frost; transplant after frost danger has passed. In zone 9 start in January–February and transplant February–March for an early spring crop before peak summer heat. In zone 9 a fall planting in August for harvest in October–November often produces higher-quality fruits than the spring crop.
directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic soil and stake or cage the indeterminate vines; Zapotec Pleated is a Mexican heirloom tomato from the Zapotec people of Oaxaca, producing large (8–16 ounce), deeply ridged and pleated, hollow, orange-red fruits unlike any standard tomato — the characteristic heavy ribbing creates a natural cavity in the hollow center that makes Zapotec Pleated the ideal stuffing tomato for chiles-rellenos-style preparations, baked stuffed tomatoes, and presentations where the natural hollow serves as an edible container. The thick, meaty, sweet-acidic flesh has excellent flavor and the hollow structure minimizes the gel and seeds that make most large tomatoes watery when sliced. The unusual appearance — rustic, ridged, and slightly irregular — reflects the traditional Mesoamerican approach to tomato selection where utility (hollow stuffing structure, thick walls) was prioritized alongside flavor. In zone 9 the fall planting often produces the most attractive, well-colored fruits as cooler October temperatures enhance both color development and flavor concentration.
sources: Seed Savers Exchange — Zapotec Pleated Heirloom Tomato
Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Mexican Heirloom Tomatoes
University of Arizona Cooperative Extension — Heirloom Tomato Varieties

name: Zapotec Ridged Cucumber
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; give vines a trellis or ample ground space, as this is a sprawling heirloom type maintained by Zapotec growing communities in Oaxaca, Mexico.
directions: Direct sow in warm soil after frost risk has passed, spacing plants to allow the sprawling vines room to run or climb a trellis. This Oaxacan heirloom is immediately recognizable by its deep lengthwise ridges and pleated, almost sculpted surface, which set it apart visually from the smooth or lightly warted skins of most commercial cucumbers. Pick fruit at 5-7 inches for crisp, mild flesh, since the pronounced ridging can make overripe fruit tougher to peel and eat fresh. This is one of the regional Mexican cucumber landraces maintained through community seed-saving networks rather than commercial breeding programs, so expect some natural variation in fruit size and ridge depth between plants.

name: Zavory Pepper
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, since chinense types germinate slowly and need sustained bottom heat; transplant only after the soil is thoroughly warm.
directions: Zavory was bred to deliver the full fruity, floral aroma of a habanero with almost none of the heat, registering only around 100 Scoville units compared to 30,000 or more for a standard habanero. Glossy, bullet-shaped fruit ripens through green, yellow, orange, and finally red on prolific, heat-loving plants, and any single stage can be harvested for eating. Because it needs a long, warm season to size up and ripen fully, start seed early indoors and grow it in the hottest, sunniest spot available. It suits cooks who want habanero flavor in salsas, chutneys, or fresh salads without the burn.

name: Zefa Fino Fennel
plantingNote: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring, or in mid- to late summer for a fall crop; Zefa Fino was bred at a Swiss federal research station specifically to resist the premature bolting that plagues most open-pollinated Florence fennel.
directions: Direct sow into rich, evenly moist soil since fennel forms a taproot and transplants poorly; Zefa Fino is the Swiss-bred workhorse behind much of the modern Florence fennel seed trade, prized for holding in the ground and resisting bolting far longer than older open-pollinated types even under fluctuating spring temperatures. Plants form large, dense, rounded white bulbs with a sweet, mild anise flavor and crisp texture that stays tender rather than turning pithy as the season progresses. Mound soil around the swelling base as the bulb develops to keep it pale and tender, and harvest once bulbs reach the size of a tennis ball to a fist before the plant sends up a flowering stalk.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

name: Zenzei Tomato
plantingNote: Start seed indoors 6 to 8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out once nights stay reliably warm; this 2023 AAS National Winner is an indeterminate plum type that needs staking or caging for its full season.
directions: Zenzei is a vigorous indeterminate Roma-type plum tomato bred for canning and freezing, setting heavy clusters of 4- to 5-inch, 3- to 8-ounce oblong fruits with dense, meaty flesh and little internal cavity. Its naturally tidy growth habit resists sprawl better than many indeterminate plum types, and judges praised its early, high yield along with resistance to blossom end rot and leaf spotting. Stake or cage plants at transplanting since the heavy fruit clusters need support, and keep watering consistent through fruit set to avoid cracking; no pruning is required to keep the plant productive.

name: Zephyr Summer Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; an All-America Selections winner with striking bicolor fruits — yellow with a green tip — and exceptional flavor; bush habit suits small gardens and container growing.
directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after last frost; Zephyr is a bush-type summer squash that requires no staking and produces heavily from a compact plant. Zephyr is an All-America Selections award-winning hybrid summer squash with a visually striking bicolor pattern — straight, yellow upper portion with a distinctive lime-green tip — and very nutty, firm flesh with a noticeably drier texture than standard yellow squash that holds up well to sautéing, grilling, and roasting without becoming waterlogged. Harvest at 4–6 inches for peak tenderness and flavor; the compact bush plants are excellent for small gardens where the large rambling vines of traditional squash would be impractical. Powdery mildew tolerance and prolific production make it a reliable summer standby.

name: Zeppelin Delicata Squash
plantingNote: Direct sow in warm soil once frost danger has passed; needs a long, warm growing season, so in short-season areas start indoors 3 weeks early, though Gulf Coast gardeners can generally direct sow with time to spare.
directions: Zeppelin is a modern open-pollinated delicata bred by organic seed growers to improve on older delicata strains, selected specifically for better disease tolerance and more uniform, elongated cream-and-green striped fruit. Like other delicata types the thin, edible skin means the whole squash can be roasted without peeling, and the dense, sweet, corn-and-chestnut-like flesh has made delicata squash increasingly popular at farmers markets. Vines run further than bush delicata types, so give them room to sprawl or train them up a sturdy trellis to save garden space. Because it is a stable open-pollinated variety rather than a hybrid, seed can be saved from isolated plantings for a true-breeding crop.

name: Zermatt Leek
plantingNote: Start seed indoors in late winter, about 8-10 weeks before the last frost, and transplant into the garden in spring for an early-maturing crop.
directions: Zermatt, also sold as Swiss Giant Zermatt, is an early European leek that reaches harvest size faster than most fall or winter types, making it a good lead-in variety ahead of longer-season leeks like Tadorna in a succession planting. It grows tall with a sweeter, more delicate flavor than onion, well suited to creamy soups and light braises. Grow in well-drained soil with consistent moisture and harvest before hard freezes arrive, since it lacks the deep winter hardiness of true storage leeks.

name: Zipper Cream Cowpea
plantingNote: Direct sow seeds 1 inch deep after soil has warmed to at least 65°F and all frost danger has passed; in zone 9, plant from late spring through midsummer, since Zipper Cream performs best in hot weather.
directions: Direct sow in warm, well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun, and harvest pods when they turn from green to a pale cream-tan color and feel plump. Zipper Cream is a beloved Southern heirloom cowpea named for its distinctive, easy-shelling pods — the seam splits open with a simple pinch or tug, quickly releasing rows of smooth, cream-white peas without the tedious shelling required by many other cowpea types. The mild, sweet, creamy flavor and tender texture of the peas make Zipper Cream one of the most popular fresh-shelling Southern peas for the table, while its productive, heat-loving vines perform reliably through the hottest stretch of summer when many other vegetables falter. As with all cowpeas, the roots fix atmospheric nitrogen, leaving the soil enriched for a following crop. Pick pods regularly at the cream stage for the best fresh-eating quality, or allow pods to dry fully on the vine for shelf-stable dried peas.
sources: Southern Exposure Seed Exchange — Zipper Cream cowpea variety notes

name: Zipper Cream Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow 1–2 inches deep after last frost when soil is warm; Zipper Cream is adapted to Gulf Coast and Deep South conditions and performs well in the summer heat. Multiple plantings 3–4 weeks apart extend the harvest season; in zone 9 plant from April through August for successive harvests into fall.
directions: Sow seeds 1–2 inches deep in any well-drained soil in full sun; Zipper Cream is one of the most popular Southern peas in home gardens and small farms of the Gulf Coast for its exceptionally easy shelling — the pods split along a natural 'zipper' seam that allows the cream-colored peas to fall out with almost no effort, a practical advantage that makes large harvests much faster to process. The peas themselves are plump, cream-white, and have a mild, sweet, buttery flavor prized in Southern pea dishes, boiled fresh with ham or bacon, or frozen for winter use. A bush-type plant that produces heavily over a long season; heat and drought tolerant once established. One of the most recommended varieties for first-time Southern pea growers because of the easy harvest and reliable production.

name: ZipperCream-GC Southern Pea
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed; because this type holds its green color through full dry maturity, pods can be left on the plant longer before shelling without sacrificing appearance.
directions: ZipperCream-GC was bred at the USDA Vegetable Laboratory in Charleston, South Carolina by crossing the green-cotyledon trait into a Zipper Cream genetic background, producing a large-seeded cream pea that keeps its fresh green color even when harvested fully dry. It was developed for growers using axial-flow combines, which require dry-stage harvest, so that the finished peas would not suffer the dulled color that dry-harvested cream peas usually show. Home gardeners benefit from the same trait by having more flexibility in harvest timing without the peas turning tan on the vine. Flavor and easy-shelling pod habit follow the familiar Zipper Cream type, making this a practical upgrade for anyone who already grows that classic variety.
sources: Vegetable Cultivar Descriptions for North America (cucurbit.info)

name: Zittauer Gelbe Onion
plantingNote: Direct sow in spring as soon as the soil can be worked; this late-maturing type needs a full season to size up before fall harvest and curing.
directions: Zittauer Gelbe is a German heirloom onion dating to the nineteenth century, named for the town of Zittau and long popular in Central and Northern Europe as a reliable keeper. It forms firm, semi-globe bulbs with golden-brown skin and a notably strong, assertive onion flavor well suited to cooking rather than fresh eating. As a late-season type it needs a full growing season to reach full size, with harvest typically in late summer once tops begin to fall over. Cure bulbs thoroughly in a warm, airy location before moving them to cold storage, where they are reported to keep for many months.

name: Zlata Radish
plantingNote: Direct sow in cool weather and succession sow every one to two weeks for continuous harvest; Zlata's golden-yellow skin makes it stand out easily from red radishes in a mixed planting.
directions: Sow seed directly half an inch deep in cool, moist soil and thin to about an inch apart for well-formed roots. Zlata is a round, golden-yellow-skinned radish with crisp white flesh and a mild flavor, notably slower to turn pithy or overly hot than many red radishes when the weather warms, which extends its harvest window into the edge of the cool season. The bright yellow skin adds welcome color contrast to salads, radish plates, and pickles alongside standard red and white types. Harvest promptly once roots reach about an inch across, and keep soil consistently moist through growth, since inconsistent watering causes cracked or overly pungent roots.

name: Zogola Tomato
plantingNote: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost; Zogola is an indeterminate pink slicer that benefits from staking or caging like other mid-season heirloom tomatoes.
directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into rich, well-drained soil once the weather has settled, staking vines as they grow. Zogola is a Polish heirloom producing smooth, round, rosy-pink fruit of a practical slicing size with a sweet, mild flavor typical of Eastern European pink tomatoes. The indeterminate vines are productive over a long season and tend to set fruit reliably in a range of summer conditions. Pick at full color and use promptly, since pink-fruited heirlooms generally have thinner skin and softer flesh than modern red hybrids.

name: Zolfino Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow after last frost; Zolfino is an Italian heirloom bean from the Pratomagno area of Arezzo province in Tuscany, recognized and protected as a Slow Food Presidium — it produces small, round, pale yellow beans with exceptionally thin skin and a uniquely dense, creamy, buttery texture when cooked, considered by many Italian food experts the finest cooking bean in Italy.
directions: Sow 1 inch deep in rows 18–24 inches apart after last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Zolfino beans are bush type and do not require staking; harvest when pods are dry and papery. Zolfino is an Italian heirloom bean from the Pratomagno hills of Arezzo province in Tuscany, where it has been grown for centuries at elevations between 1,300 and 2,600 feet on the slopes of the Pratomagno massif — the specific local environment (poor, well-drained, slightly acidic volcanic soil with cool nights) contributes to the bean's exceptional quality. Zolfino (the name likely derives from 'zolfo,' Italian for sulfur, referring to the pale yellow color) is a Slow Food Presidium product, meaning it is recognized as an endangered, culturally important food requiring preservation support; only farmers in the Pratomagno area using traditional methods are technically authorized to use the Zolfino denomination. The small (thumbnail-sized), round, pale yellow beans have extraordinarily thin skins — almost imperceptible when eaten — and cook to a dense, creamy, buttery texture entirely different from the grainy or mealy texture of common dried beans; the flavor is rich, earthy, and complex with sweet undertones. Outstanding in simple Italian preparations: olio e fagioli (beans with olive oil), in ribollita soup, or simply simmered with sage, garlic, and good olive oil.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity (Slow Food Presidium)
Italian Ministry of Agriculture Heirloom Variety Registry

name: Zoom Witloof Chicory
plantingNote: Direct sow in late spring to early summer so roots can bulk up over the summer before fall harvest and forcing. As an F1 hybrid, 'Zoom' produces more uniform, evenly sized roots than many open-pollinated witloof strains, which improves the percentage of well-shaped chicons from a given planting.
directions: 'Zoom' is a widely grown F1 witloof chicory selected for producing homegrown Belgian endive, valued for uniform, blemish-free, torpedo-shaped roots that size up reliably even without the deep, stone-free soil older open-pollinated witloof strains prefer. Sow directly in late spring to early summer and grow through the season to develop a taproot roughly 1.5 to 2 inches across; in fall, cut the foliage back to an inch above the crown, lift the roots, and hold them cold until ready to force. To produce chicons, replant the trimmed roots upright and closely spaced in a deep container of moist sand or soil, cover completely to exclude all light, and hold at 50-60F; pale, tightly furled chicons are ready to cut in three to four weeks. Because the roots bulk up more evenly than many older varieties, this hybrid tends to give a higher yield of usable chicons per planting.

name: Zucchini Elite
plantingNote: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed to at least 70°F; a compact, semi-bush habit suits smaller beds better than sprawling vine-type squash.
directions: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed, spacing plants about 30 inches apart in full sun. Elite is an All-America Selections-winning hybrid valued for uniform, glossy dark-green fruit, strong yields, and improved tolerance to common summer squash viruses. Its tidy, semi-compact bush habit performs well in raised beds and smaller gardens where sprawling squash would be impractical. Harvest fruit at 6-7 inches for the sweetest flavor and most tender skin, checking plants every day or two during peak production.

name: Zuni Gold Bean
plantingNote: Direct sow 1 inch deep after last frost once soil warms above 65°F; Zuni Gold is a Native American heirloom dry bean from Zuni Pueblo in New Mexico.
directions: Sow seed 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing 4-6 inches apart in rows. Zuni Gold is a Native American heirloom bush dry bean traditionally grown at Zuni Pueblo in the arid high desert of New Mexico, its smooth, golden-yellow seeds cooking up creamy with a mild, buttery flavor prized in traditional Zuni and Southwestern cooking. Adapted over generations to the low rainfall and short growing season of the Southwest, it tolerates dry conditions better than many bean varieties bred for wetter climates. Allow pods to dry fully on the plant before harvesting for storage as a dry bean.

name: Zwolle Seedling Rhubarb
plantingNote: Plant crowns in early spring while dormant into deep, fertile, well-drained soil; this classic Dutch cultivar is a heavy, reliable early producer widely grown for forcing and general garden use across Europe.
directions: Zwolle Seedling is a long-established Dutch rhubarb valued for its heavy early flush of thick, bright red-pink stalks and its tolerance of forcing under a pot or dark cover for an extra-early crop. Compared with slower-establishing cultivars it comes into full production quickly, making it a favorite where growers want an early, dependable harvest without a long wait after planting. Flavor is well balanced between tart and sweet, with tender flesh that cooks down smoothly. As with all rhubarb, satisfy its winter chilling requirement for strong spring growth, harvest by pulling rather than cutting, and never eat the leaves, which are toxic.

name: Zydeco Twist Okra
plantingNote: Direct sow after soil has warmed following the last frost, since okra seed germinates slowly and unevenly in cold soil; soaking seed overnight speeds emergence.
directions: Zydeco Twist was an All-America Selections regional winner recognized for pods that spiral and twist rather than growing straight, a shape that lets the pods stay tender and stringless a few days longer than most straight-podded types before they turn woody. The plant is compact and spineless, with no itchy prickles on the pods or foliage, making harvest far more comfortable than on older bristly okra varieties. Sow directly in warm soil after the last frost in full sun, and pick pods every day or two once production starts, since okra quickly overshoots the tender stage in hot weather. Its shorter, well-branched habit fits into smaller garden beds better than tall heirloom okra varieties while still producing heavily through the heat of summer.
